PROGRAM IN LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE Landscape architecture is dedicated to conserving and improving the quality of man's environment. It is concerned with the quality of water, the quality of air, the quality of land - how they affect man's relationship to man as well as to nature. The landscape architect approaches this task with the realization that he cannot succeed alone, but must work with the allied professions such as architecture, planning, engineering, sociology, and economics. It is toward this goal of working with others for the improvement of the human environment that this program is directed; never before have the challenges been so great. In order to achieve his goals, the landscape architect must be aware of human needs. To meet these needs he must be concerned with the natural sciences so he can speak for nature in a world that is constantly being altered by man. The understanding of nature's processes and the ability to design in terms of earth, water, and plants enable the landscape architect not just to organize but to greatly enrich man's environment. The program stresses the need for variety in the education of a landscape architect. The general studies program (humanities, natural sciences, social and behavioral studies) is a vital part of the intellectual and cultural preparation of young men and women for professional practice. The core program in design provides further contact with the general studies program as well as developing capabilities in solving small to large scale problems. The program stresses the collective approach to solving problems yet recognizes the individual and his contribution. Specialized courses provide for technical competency. It is the aim of the fiveyear program to encourage creativity and to develop sound procedures for creating an environment which is beneficial to man and nature. Landscape architecture is a departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The total of hours required on the Professional Arts Curriculum with landscape architecture as the major is 255. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula, Undergraduate) and by the area requirements given below. Verbal communication elements 4 hrs. Professional electives 8 hrs. Economics electives 8 hrs. Social sciences electives 2 hrs. Three 10-week periods of experience are required for graduation. At least one 10-week period must be spent working in a landscape architect's office - two additional periods may be spent in documented travel or in planning, architecture, or construction. Bell The College of Business has as its ultimate objective the education of men and women for professional pursuits in business, industry, and education. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the University. The College of Business recognizes the need for both breadth and depth in the total academic pattern. The curricula are designed to provide (1) a broad background in the general education areas, (2) mastery of the basic tools and an understanding of the fundamentals of business organization and procedures, and (3) specialization in a selected field of business. All curricula are designed to provide opportunity for the student to develop the ability to define and analyze problems, make value judgments, and express conclusions in a cogent and concise manner. The preparation of teachers of business subjects for secondary schools, colleges, and universities is a major responsibility of the College of Business. A twoyear secretarial program leading to the Associate in Arts degree is offered for students who wish to prepare for office positions but who prefer an intensive shortterm concentration rather than a baccalaureate degree program. Short courses on a noncredit basis are organized in cooperation with interested business and industrial groups for the specific needs recognized. The departmental majors of the four departments of instruction within the college have a common core of requirements, which is followed by requirements specialized for each field. The core provides for essentials of learning which are basic in the broad area of business administration. The College of Business offers programs for degrees at the baccalaureate and master's levels. The programs of the college are administered through its four departments: Accounting, Business Education and Office Administration, General Business Administration and Marketing. The graduate offerings of the departments in the College of Business are described in the Graduate School section. The undergraduate student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula, Undergraduate) and by the area requirements given below. DEPARTMENT OF ACCOUNTING Herring, Head; Burdeau, Cirtin, Cloyd, Flesher, Jackson, Lawrence, Neal, Ounapu, Parkison, Pfeffenberger, Shade, Walker Accounting is often described as "the language of business." To make intelligent decisions in the effective planning and controlling of the operations of a business, management must know the effect of transactions on its financial position and its earning power. Accounting, the art by which financial results are summarized and interpreted, furnishes that necessary data. The accountant as a student of management problems endeavors to meet reporting requirements and to present his data in terms of management's needs. The study of accounting is a vital part in the educational preparation of any executive and is useful in all types of business careers. Contact with all aspects and levels of business enables the accountant to acquire excellent training for executive leadership. Many and varied careers are available to the accountant both in the types of organizations and in the areas of specialization he may select. The future for men and women trained in accounting is almost unlimited as the continued growth in the uses of accounting is assured by further expansion and complex development of business activity. The increase of government influence in business affairs and industry's search for increased productivity through its emphasis on cost controls and efficiency cause the potential need for the services of accountants to increase more rapidly than the number of persons properly qualified to fill the need. A major in accounting provides a foundation for a career as a controller, financial officer, internal auditor, cost accountant, professional C.P.A., public administration officer, and teacher of accounting. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula, Undergraduate) and by the area requirements given below. The student who wishes to prepare for the teaching of accounting in the secondary school will complete the Teacher Education Curriculum with the teaching area major in business education, the teaching major in business education, option B, or the teaching minor in business education. These teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. The departmental major in accounting, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for an interesting and rewarding career in the broad fields of accounting. DEPARTMENT OF GENERAL BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION Wagoner, Head; Bowman, Casey, Engber, Hashmi, Hill, Johns, Jones, McCullough, Myers, Riggin, Ruff, Swart, Turner, Van Mele, Wagner, Wells The program of the Department of General Business Administration provides the opportunity for a student to obtain a broad business background. This background provides for an understanding of the interrelationships of the functions in business and a means of preparing the graduate of the program to fit into the general administration of a business. In addition, a student is expected to select areas of concentration in which he can obtain a proficiency beyond that acquired in an introductory or principles course. Four areas in which depth may be had are finance, law, insurance, and management. Particularly there is an opportunity to specialize in the fields of finance and of management. The management program is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them as future business executives and specialists to deal with the diversity of problems which arise in the course of daytoday business activity. The finance program is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activity. The insurance program is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. The law courses are quite broad and include the fundamentals of many essential law disciplines. These law courses are highly recommended to students in prelaw preparation. In addition to these specialized purposes, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students on other areas in the College of Business. Any student in the university may take the course in personal finance, which is offered especially to provide the general business information everyone should know. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula, Undergraduate) and by the area requirements listed below. General business administration, finance, and management courses are included in the concentration areas for the teaching of business education. The teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. The departmental major in general business administration, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for a career in the general administration of a business. DEPARTMENT OF AEROSPACE STUDIES Fraser, Head; Steen The Department of Aerospace Studies provides courses designed to prepare selected male students for commissions in the United States Air Force. Since the minimum of an undergraduate degree is required to become an Air Force Officer, the integration of formal officer training into the University curriculum provides an excellent opportunity for young men to satisfy their military obligation and broaden their educational experience. Students will develop an appreciation and knowledge of the past, present, and projected national aerospace operations; an awareness and skill in executive managerial ability needed in USAF supervisory and managerial career fields; and the ability to participate in group discussion, staff conference planning, briefings, and problem solving staff studies. The Professor of Aerospace Studies and his assistant are officers currently serving on active duty with the Air Force. Advanced teaching techniques emphasize selfgenerated study. Courses are both theoretical and practical and are fully accreditable towards degree requirements. The departmental minor is useful to students who enter professions other than the United States Air Force and selected students may register for Aerospace Studies without enrolling in the Air Force ROTC program. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula, Undergraduate) and by the area requirements listed below: Departmental minor in aerospace studies, 24 hours AER 310, 311, 312, 410, 411, 412 24 hrs. The Air Force ROTC program is open to all male students fully enrolled at Ball State University. Basic requirements are: 1. Have two academic years remaining at either undergraduate or graduate level or a combination of the two; 2. Complete the program before age 26 1/2 years for enrollment in the flying program; age 28 years for nonflying training; age 30 years for nonflying training, if student has prior active military service; 3. Pass a written qualification examination; 4. Pass a medical examination; 5. Be selected by an interview board; 6. After selection, complete a sixweek, field training course at an Air Force base. The student receives $120 pay plus travel allowance for attending field training. Upon return to campus, the student is enrolled as a Cadet in the Air Force ROTC program. Here academic concentration is on professional preparation for the future Air Force officer. Cadets are eligible for: a. Subsistence allowance of $50 a month, up to a maximum of $1,000; b. AFROTC text books on a loan basis; c. An officer's tailored uniform; d. 35 hours of flight training in light aircraft (if in prospective pilot category). Cadets completing the aerospace studies courses in a satisfactory manner and receiving at least an undergraduate degree will be eligible for a commission as a Second Lieutenant in the United States Air Force Reserve. Selected students may be designated as Distinguished Graduates and have an opportunity for a commission in the Regular Air Force, and to apply for further graduate education while on active duty at Air Force expense. Formal flying training, pilot or navigator, is taken on active duty as an officer, drawing full pay and allowances.

DEPARTMENT OF HOME ECONOMICS Moore, Head; Adams, Bruner, Caylor, Finn, Lacey, Nixon, Quesenberry, Schermer, Simpson Home economics is the field of knowledge and service that is fundamentally concerned with strengthening home and family life through educating the individuals for family living; improving the services and goods used by families; conducting research to discover the changing needs of individuals and families and to determine means of satisfying these needs; and furthering community, national, and world conditions favorable to family living. The profession of home economics synthesizes knowledge drawn from its own research from the physical, biological, and social sciences and the arts and applies this knowledge to improving the lives of families and individuals. The breadth of the field of home economics emphasizes its importance. The eleven separate, but interrelated, fields of foods, nutrition, clothing, textiles, applied art, housing, household equipment, home management, family economics, child development, and family relations provide the foundations for the good health, satisfying and successful living, psychological balance, and good management which are essential for the development of the whole personality. Needs of individuals and families in the social environment of their time are of primary concern in determining the emphases given to the various aspects of home economics. Home economics aids in helping individuals and families to make intelligent decisions concerning all aspects of family life, including the social, economic, aesthetic, managerial, health, and ethical aspects of relations, child development, foods, clothing, and housing. Home economics prepares professional personnel to carry out its objectives through education, research, social welfare and public health, dietetics, and institutional administration and business. It shares with other fields the responsibility for developing perceptive, wellinformed citizens with the ability and the initiative to further conditions favorable to effective living. The curricula for industrial education teachers are arranged in patterns which qualify persons as teachers of industrial arts at the elementary, junior high, and senior high school levels, vocationalindustrial education at the secondary and posthigh school levels, and technical education at the college level. To this end, curricula leading to the bachelor's degree, the master's degree, the specialist in education degree, and the joint doctor's degree are available. The offerings in graphic arts are used in preparation for positions in industry. The Two-Year Printing Technology Curriculum (see Curricula, Undergraduate) provides for the development of technical skills essential in qualifying for supervisory positions. Upon successful completion of the twoyear curriculum, each student receives the Associate in Science degree. Preparation for management positions in the graphic arts industry is provided in the fiveyear cooperative graphic arts management program leading to a baccalaureate degree (see the departmental major in cooperative graphic arts management following). A wide variety of industryrelated courses offers students many opportunities to explore occupational choices in the following industries: building construction, communications, manufacturing, power, and transportation. As part of a student's general studies program, the Department of Industrial Education and Technology offers courses which develop insight, understanding, and practical experience in regard to the production of goods and services, working conditions, industrial research and experimentation, and typical plant or factory organization. DEPARTMENT OF LIBRARY SCIENCE Axeen, Chairman; Coil, Hart, Kirby, Magrill, Wetmore, Yeamans Library Science is concerned with the selection, acquisition, processing, organization, utilization, and maintenance of materials in library collections. Knowledge of bibliographic aids, skill in their use, and the ability to work effectively with associates and library patrons are characteristics of the successful librarian. Thorough familiarity with materials suitable for various types of library users must be acquired by the student of Library Science, in addition to the mastery of technical routines necessary for efficient organization. Emphasis on different kinds of specialization in librarianship is reflected in the training of librarians. The purpose of the undergraduate program in Library Science at Ball State University is the preparation of school librarians. Students are qualified to meet Indiana state certification requirements. Continuing reassessment of elementary and secondary education has resulted in a renewed appreciation of the school library as an instructional materials center where educational materials in a variety of media are available to students, teachers, and administrators. School media centers at all levels have increased in number with the growth of school systems. Progress is being made in the establishment of elementary school libraries since it has been demonstrated that younger children benefit greatly from a variety of learning materials. The school librarian is educated as a teacher and must meet state requirements for a teaching certificate. The school librarian must understand fundamental learning processes, teaching methods, and child psychology. In addition, a basic knowledge of school curricula and special training in the analysis, evaluation, selection, organization, dissemination, and use of instructional materials for young people are essential. Library Science courses are designed to help the student acquire this special training. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula, Undergraduate) and by the area requirements given below. Minor and endorsement in school library and audiovisual services, 36 hours LIB 333, 342, 422, 460, 461, 462, 480 27 hrs. Directed electives in audiovisual communications and in cognate areas. Selections to be made in consultation with the Chairman of the Department of Library Science 9 hrs. The minor and the endorsement patterns in school library and audiovisual services are the same, except for electives that are chosen for their pertinence to the students' objectives. The minor on the Teacher Education Curriculum prepares for the provisional certificate in school library and audiovisual services on the secondary level. When elementary education is the major on the Teacher Education Curriculum, the endorsement prepares for such services at the elementary school level. The school library and audiovisual services minor may be used also as an area on other curricula, but, in this instance, it does not prepare for public school certification. The four prerequisites for the Ball State University Graduate Library Science Program (LIB 333, 342, 460, 480) may be secured at the undergraduate level. (See Library Science, Graduate Program.) A basic understanding of library methods, procedures, and materials is especially important to the teacher who may not be interested in qualifying for certification as a school librarian. Courses in reference materials and materials in subject areas enable the teacher to add breadth and depth to lesson plans and to cooperate with the school librarian in making the school library an integral part of the educative process. Library Science courses may be selected as electives on a program of teacher preparation. The courses in Library Science prepare students for service in accordance with the concept of school libraries as media centers rather than as collection limited to books and printed matter. DEPARTMENT OF MUSIC EDUCATION Dunham, Head; Burkart, Carr, Eberle, Nichols, Phillips, Wakeland, Wolfe The preparation of teachers of music for all scholastic levels from kindergarten through college is of primary concern within the Music Division. The task of becoming an effective music teacher not only involves developing a high degree of musicianship and scholarship, but requires of the teachermusician a sincere interest and skill in assisting others to develop musical responsiveness. Students wishing to enter the curricula leading to teacher certification are expected to have completed a piano proficiency examination at the beginning of the junior year. A student may take the examination at any time during the freshman or sophomore year upon recommendation of his piano instructor. Should a student not succeed in passing the proficiency examination at the close of the sophomore year, he may have three more quarters in which to qualify; however, after having earned six credit hours in piano, he is required to study piano on a special applied basis without credit until proficiency has been acquired. Failure to meet the proficiency requirement by the end of nine quarters will mean that the student is no longer regarded as being on a music teaching curriculum. However, some of the music credits earned may be counted toward a departmental minor in music. If the student subsequently passes the proficiency examination, he may return to a music teaching curriculum. In the event that a student has special problems, a faculty committee consisting of his piano teacher, his major area teacher, and three other faculty members will review his case and make recommendations to the faculty. Students wishing to specialize in the instrumental field as school band or orchestra directors should enroll on the teaching major in instrumental music or on the teaching area major in music. It is assumed that such students will possess or develop major performance skills in instrumental fields. Similarly, those desiring to specialize in choral activities in the public schools are expected to possess or develop major performance skills in the vocal field and should enroll on the teaching major in choralgen - eral music or on the teaching area major in music. Students wishing to take positions of greater respon - sibility in music and music education should enroll on the teaching area major in music.

DEPARTMENT OF MUSIC HISTORY AND LITERATURE Michael, Head; Boe, Elliott, Fischer, Hodgson, Nelson, Pence The music history and literature area of the Music Division serves the entire University through its program of general education: the teacher in training through courses designed to broaden his understanding of the art he interprets to his students; the student of liberal arts through enhanced cultural and historical orientation; and tht prospective graduate scholar or researcher through specialized courses exploring the great body of literature which has been accumulating in and about music for many centuries.

title: Music History 1
description: Progress in music is traced from about 1500 to about 1825. Attention is given to the music of the late Renaissance and the later developments of opera, sonata, symphony, and the related forms. Prerequisite: MUSLI 100 or 200.

title: Instrumental Music from the Time of Bach

title: Choral and Vocal Solo Literature from Haydn to the Present
description: The development of the cantata, oratorio, mass, motet, anthem, and the lied; great masterworks in these forms. Prerequisite: MUSLI 100 or 200.

title: Ballet History
description: A history of ballet, tracing its beginnings, romantic heights, and contemporary trends.

title: Music History 2
description: Developments in music from the time of Beethoven to the present. Transition from the classical to romantic periods, the various reactions to Romanticism, and trends of the twentieth century. Prerequisite: MUSLI 100 or 200.

title: Opera from the Time of Mozart
description: Following a brief survey of the early development of opera, there will be a more detailed consideration of examples of this genre from the middle of the eighteenth century to the present time. Prerequisite: MUSLI 100 or 200.

title: Dance Notation 1
description: The beginnings of dance notation and an introduction to the main systems used today (Labonotation, Benesh, etc.). Prerequisite: some previous dance experience.

title: Honors Colloquium in Music
description: Readings, reports, and discussions of various aspects of music. Restricted to students on the Honors Program.

Technical proficiency in music is not required.

title: Music History 3
description: The growth of music is traced from its beginnings through the fifteenth century. Attention is given to the origins of music, the development of notation, and the growth of early polyphonic forms. Prerequisite: MUSLI 100 or 200; restricted to music majors and minors except with permission of the division head.

title: Church Choir Repertoire

Naturally allied with musical composition, the study of music theory can do much to illuminate the forces which control the organization of musical sounds and can provide the real foundation of musicianship essential in any outlet of the musical profession. Ball State has assumed a leadership role in the field of innovations relating to teaching techniques in music theory and composition. title: Form and Analysis
description: A survey of musical forms involving successively such units of structure as: the figure, motive, phrase, cadence, period. Song forms, singlemovement forms, contrapuntal forms, multimovement and multisectional forms are studied and performed in class. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

description: Exercises in melody writing using the ecclesiastical modes and the rhythmic organization of the sixteenth century liturgical style. description: Study of the overall shaping of composition and of the variety of forces that can contribute to it such as: melodic structure, tonal organization, color, texture, thermatic development, and serialism. Special attention is paid to changing musical concepts and to newer techniques of analysis. Prerequisite: MUSTH 320.

title: Instrumentation
description: A study of the various instruments used in the orchestra and band with special attention to range, tone quality, dynamic range, methods of articulation, and the many unique characteristics requiring idiomatic treatment in notation and scoring.

title: Orchestration
description: Scoring for large and small orchestral ensembles. Particular attention is given to voice positioning, doubling, and textural deployment as regards harmonic weight and color. Prerequisite: MUSTH 441 or permission of the department head.

title: Band Arranging
description: Scoring for symphonic band and wind ensemble. Particular attention is given to voicing, sectional and crosssectional doubling, soloistic treatment of instruments, and other elements of contemporary treatment in scoring. Prerequisite: MUSTH 442.

title: Arranging for the Dance Band
description: The study and analysis of arranging techniques as employed by current leading dance band and jazz arrangers, and the practice of writing and performing scores by members of the class. Prerequisite: MUSTH 442.

title: Styles of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: Investigation of stylistic devices of selected composers in the period between 1840 and the present. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213. 471, 472, 473. Composition. (2 hours each quarter) Experience in writing more complex and extended instrumental and vocal compositions with continued emphasis on the development of style. Prerequisite: MUSTH 373.

Investigation of teaching aids including programmed material and electronic laboratory equipment. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213. DEPARTMENT OF NURSING Berry, Head; Brown, Cannell, Cheatham, Denney, Exley, Fitzpatrick, Greene, Hakes, Houghton, Ingold, Johnson, Mahoney, McConnell, Nelson, O'Connor, Spall, Titus Professional Nursing The fouryear collegiate program in nursing has been designed to prepare the graduate to function upon completion of the curriculum as a professional nurse practitioner in beginning positions of bedside nursing, team leadership, and public health nursing and to articulate into graduate study. Classroom and laboratory instruction for the curriculum is provided by the University and utilizes the facilities of Ball Memorial Hospital, adjacent to the University campus, as well as other nearby health agency facilities. The curriculum has been planned to provide general and professional educational experiences for the beginning student in nursing and the registered nurse who seeks a baccalaureate education in nursing. The registered nurse may request permission to be granted credit by examination for the courses NUR 310, 311, 316, 317, and 410 if she has the transcripts to verify her previous educational experiences. Thirty quarter hours are the maximum of college credits to be earned in nursing courses by examination. A student indicating an intent for a major in nursing begins his or her study in areas of English, social sciences, physical and biological sciences, and the fine arts. Approximately two years of academic work in the areas of humanities, social and behavioral sciences, and biological sciences are required. The major in nursing has been concentrated in the student's junior and senior years. The curriculum for students preparing for professional nursing is the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in nursing and a minor in biological science. The Bachelor of Science degree may be earned within the minimum requirements of the curriculum (186 hours), and the student may use toward a selected minor the 28 to 32 hours of electives on the curriculum. The student shall meet the general requirements of the University with respect to the professional nursing major and minor in biological science and with respect to graduation (minimum of 2.0 scholas - tic ratio in major, required minor, and overall grade point average); in addition the student will present a minimum grade of C in each clinical nursing course. The student is responsible for making appli - cation for admission to the major in nursing after he has completed 60 quarter hours of work. title: Professional Relations in Nursing
description: Introduces the concepts of professionalism, communications, interviewing techniques, and interpersonal relations. Selected learning experiences are provided. Prerequisites: ENG 205, 207, or 209; EDPSY 250; PHYSL 210. Parallel: SPCH 210.

title: Historical Factors and Trends in Nursing
description: Study of the historical development of nursing and the interrelationships and coexistence of culture, society, and nursing of various eras. Emphasis is given to the anthropological significances and developments of nursing. Prerequisite: NUR 200.

title: Maternal-Child Nursing 1
description: Fundamental concepts and skills of nursing will be introduced within the context of nursing the mother and child. Includes basic concepts of maternalchild health and selected learning experiences in the clinical setting. Prerequisites: NUR 200, HFN 340, BIO 213. Parallel: EDPSY 350.

title: Maternal-Child Nursing 2
description: Continuation of the study of mother, child, family, and related social and health problems. Progressive learning experiences provided. Prerequisite: NUR 310, ANAT 320. Parallel: EDPSY 351.

title: Medical-Surgical Nursing 1
description: Study of medicalsurgical nursing concepts and supporting principles applied in the care of adult medicalsurgical patients. Continues the study of drug therapy as well as pathological phenomena related to the field. Prerequisite: NUR 311. Parallel: GXPSY 316.

title: Medical-Surgical Nursing 2
description: Continuation of the study of medicalsurgical nursing concepts and principles. Emphasizes the importance of analyzing the patient's and family's needs relating to illness for a plan of action in the care of patients. Includes progressive learning experiences in clinical setting. Prerequisite: NUR 316.

title: Seminar on Legal Aspects of Nursing
description: Discussion of the legal aspects of nursing such as permissive law and mandatory law which regulate and govern nursing practice and the implications they have for the nurse practitioner. Prerequisites: NUR 300 and 317. Parallel: NUR 418.

title: Physiological Factors in Pharmacotherapeutics
description: Utilizes knowledge from previous science and nursing courses to form integrated whole; concept includes normal body systems function in health, altered physiology of disease, and rational approach to drug therapy. Prerequisite: NUR 317.

title: Psychiatric Nursing
description: Introduces fundamental concepts and supporting principles of nursing mentally ill patients. Continues the study of psychodynamics in nursing and emphasizes the nurse's role in the mental health team and in rehabilitating the mentally ill person. Prerequisite: NUR

title: Comprehensive Nursing
description: Guided experiences and concurrent theory to advance earlier learned skills and knowledge of nursing into beginning competency for providing professional nursing service; includes teaching health measures and certain aspects of illness to patients and their families. Prerequisite: NUR 317.

title: Management in Nursing
description: Study of team concept in nursing and health. Emphasizes role of the nurse as a leader in providing service to patients and their families; includes guided experiences of supervising the organization and personnel of a unit in nursing. Prerequisite: NUR 317. Parallel: NUR 418.

title: Seminar in Nursing
description: Group discussion of problems related to professional nursing practice and responsibilities of the nurse as a professional practitioner and a citizen in the community. Prerequisite: NUR 317.

title: Concepts of Public Health Nursing
description: Beginner's level workshop on concepts of public health nursing for registered nurses. Emphasizes family approach in public health nursing and use of communications and interviewing skills in development of case records and histories of families. Selected clinical learning experiences planned.

title: Public Health Nursing in the Family and Community
description: Workshop on public health nursing for registered nurses. Emphasis on the various roles of the public health nurse, community diagnosis, the health team, and work with other health and welfare agencies.

title: Introduction to Supervision in Public Health Nursing
description: Workshop to prepare registered nurses to assume increased responsibility in providing service to the community through an understanding of the philosophy, principles, and techniques of supervision in public health nursing. Prerequisite: NUR 491, 492, or two years of experience.

title: Leadership in Nursing
description: An introductory workshop for the professional nurse practitioner focused on nursing leadership requirements, responsibilities, and methods. Natural Resources Our affluent society and its implications for increased resource use and abuse have contributed to the deterioration of man's natural environment. This environmental crisis has accelerated the need for a more intensive and integrated approach in the area of natural resources conservation. The purpose of the natural resources program is to provide students with an opportunity to gain a better understanding of our environment and to educate them to work more effectively in establishing or reestablishing a state of harmony between people and their environment. The program in natural resources is designed to help meet the increasing demands for personnel educated in this area. Employment opportunities include working with local, state, regional, and federal units of government, industry and private organizations. Both the minor and major are multidisciplinary because the conservation of natural resources is an area of total University concern, requiring new ideas, diverse skills and integrated approaches. The student may include courses from many disciplines in meeting the curricular requirements. Students enrolled in many departments of the University are encouraged to elect a minor in natural resources; however, it should be especially useful to accompany certain majors including biology, earth science, geography, geology, journalism, landscape architecture, physical education, radio and television, regional and urban planning, speech, and in certain areas of the social sciences. Other students may elect this program as a "cultural" or "general education" type of minor. The student will enroll in the Professional Arts Curriculum with a departmental major in natural resources. Regional and Urban Planning The sharp need for regional and urban planning is a recent phenomenon that has made planning a distinctprofessional field with a course of training requiring undergraduate and graduate study. Such Interdepartmental 97 extended study is required because the planner must understand the modern region and city, exceedingly complex institutions; he must do research in its various aspects and evaluate his findings; he must make recommendations on diverse policies related to regional and urban development and be capable of presenting to official agencies and unofficial citizen organizations his conclusions with conviction, substantiation, and enthusiasm. He must be able to guide and interpret in the administration of regional and urban plans. After considerable experience and research in many of the areas of planning, he should then be equipped to move into an executive capacity where an overall grasp of the interrelationships of all functions must be coordinated. Such a coordinating position calls for close cooperation with all governmental agencies and with private and civic organizations in the determination of broad, related planning policies. The departmental major in regional and urban planning on an undergraduate curriculum leading to a bachelor's degree, with related areas of study, is the initial step in the preparation of such a professional person. This study is designed to develop beginning professional knowledge and competence in the area of urban planning, and to enable the student to acquire the skills needed to perform the advanced professional duties of the planner through further study at the graduate level, and to enter the planning field at the subprofessional level. In order to achieve these goals the student is expected to have a broad general education in the political, physical, economic, and social structure of regions and urban areas as described in the major courses. The student will take the Professional Arts Curriculum with a departmental major in regional and urban planning. Diedrich The College of Sciences and Humanities provides courses and programs for either a liberal education or for specialized and professional curricula. The liberal arts programs permit the student to elect more freely and to explore the "idea" subject matter. "Liberal" stems from the Latin liber, to free. By definition, a liberal arts education should free man from ignorance by providing him an intelligent grasp of the experiences of the past and an understanding of the interrelationship of branches of knowledge. The individual is educated to think objectively, critically, and creatively. The liberal arts include the study of foreign languages, the physical and social environment, the evolution of Western civilization, the foundations of modern science, and the classical works of man. The wide range of courses offered by the College of Sciences and Humanities provides the basis for specialized and professional curricula — offered both within the college and in the other colleges requiring service courses. Within the college preprofessional programs are specified — for medicine, dentistry, engineering, and law. A variety of specialist programs is offered, including medical technology, regional and urban planning, social work, international area studies, and natural resources. Also, the departments within the college have programs designed for those planning graduate study in the field of their choice. The college includes the following: Biology; Chemistry; Economics; English; Foreign Languages (French, German, Greek, Latin, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish); Geography and Geology; History; Center for Journalism; Mathematics; Physics; Physiology and Health Science; Political Science and Philosophy; Center for Radio and Television; Social Sciences; Sociology and Anthropology; Speech. Common background is provided for majors through a "core program in biology." The required courses of the core are organized with three levels of emphasis. The first level is designed to develop understanding of basic principles and biological processes which are common to living organisms. The second level focuses on organisms and is concerned with problems of structure, function, and classification in specific groups of plants and animals. The third level is concerned with developing understanding of interactions and adaptations of organisms in contexts ranging from world biome organization through molecular organization. In addition to the basic background work provided by courses in the core program, the department offers specialized course work in biology, botany, zoology, and science to meet the needs of particular individuals and groups. Opportunities for research participation are available at both the advanced undergraduate and graduate levels. The student who plans a career in teaching secondary school biology should take the teaching major in biology or the teaching minor in biology. The student enrolled as a biology teaching major is encouraged to take a second major in general science or a minor in chemistry. These combinations not only greatly increase employment possibilities, but contribute significantly to the understanding of biology. Students who plan careers in college biology teaching and/or research may follow either the teaching major in biology or the departmental major in biology. Such students should anticipate the requirements for graduate work in biology in addition to the major in biology. In general these recommendations are: 1. Proficiency in at least one foreign language. French, German, or Russian are almost universally recommended; some institutions also accept Spanish. 2. Chemistry through the organic sequence and preferably a course in biochemistry. 3. A year of college physics. 4. Mathematics through the calculus sequence. The student who wishes to specialize in either botany or zoology may do so by following the departmental minor in botany or the departmental minor in zoology. These minors are designed to provide professional work for the student who has completed basic course work in biology and chemistry. The liberal arts student who elects to include a concentration area in biology in his curriculum will follow either the departmental major in biology or the departmental minor in biology. All nursing majors take the departmental minor in biological science for nurses. To prepare to do laboratory work in bacteriology, pathology, chemistry, and other scientific fields necessary in the diagnosis and treatment of disease, the student will take the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in medical technology. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in premedical preparation. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry at the close of three years of predental preparation but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in predental preparation. title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth and arthropod parasites of animals. Emphasis on identification, life cycles, and hostparasite relationships. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213, or permission of the department chairman.

description: Theory and practice in the methods of quantitative analysis including gravimetric, volumetric, colorimetric, and radioactive methods. Two lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 342 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 221.

title: Qualitative Organic Analysis
description: Theory and practice in separating and identifying organic compounds. Four twohour laboratories weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232.

title: Physical-Organic Chemistry
description: An advanced course devoted to the theoretical aspects of structure, resonance, stereochemistry, acidity, basicity, and reaction rates in organic chemistry. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 232.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: The structure of matter and its relationship to properties, including considerations of modern atomic structure, bonding crystal structure, radioactivity, periodicity, oxidationreduction, and acid base relationships. Prerequisite: CHEM 342 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Inorganic Preparations
description: The preparation and study of inorganic compounds. Stress is on the preparation, purification, and identification of these compounds. Sufficient instrumental studies of compounds will be included to acquaint the student with methods of identification used in inorganic chemistry. Four threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 340 or the equivalent.

title: Principles of Biochemistry
description: Chemistry of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. Stress is on the techniques of isolation, purification, and identification of these substances. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Recommended for students seeking a major or minor in chemistry and for students in premedical and predental areas. Prerequisite: one year of organic chemistry.

title: Principles of Biochemistry
description: Continuation of CHEM

title: Special Studies in Chemistry
description: Designed to give undergraduate chemistry students an opportunity to pursue specific lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. This course may be taken for a total of 4 hours of credit.

title: Electrochemistry
description: Fundamental theory of electrochemistry and its industrial applications. Laboratory work emphasizes the application of electrochemistry to analysis, to electroplating, and to electrochemical preparations. Two lectures and two twohour laboratories weekly. Prerequisites: 20 quarter hours of chemistry.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light, with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. DEPARTMENT OF ECONOMICS Hannaford, Chairman; Gilbert, Girgis, Jost, Lawson, Patterson, Rocha, Shive, Sorathia Economics is a study of human wants and of man's efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative — relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. Among the standard categories of scarce resources in the study of economics is, first of all, labor; and courses in labormanagement relations, labor law, collective bargaining, wage theory, social security, and workmen's compensation are standard parts of university curricula in economics. Besides the study of all aspects of labor as a scarce resource, economics is concerned with the manmade resource of production called capital. For example, the accumulation of capital is a central aspect of the growth of underdeveloped countries. Economics courses called developmental economics have appeared in most universities, with separate courses being established for different backward countries or areas. The concept of interest as a physical product of physical capital equipment gives rise to courses in money and banking. A study of the valuation of the scarce resources created by nature is included in the curriculum of most universities as "land economics. While the fact of the scarcity of resources is the taproot of economics, the branches of the discipline are composed of specialized studies of the selecnon Economics 107 of alternative uses for resources. The rationale for the selection of the use pattern which will leave the least gross total of human wants unfilled varies from society to society, but normally some variant of voluntary exchange is institutionally developed. The vast complexity of the institutional exchange arrangements developed in modern society requires a set of theoretical explanations that must be equally complex. Certain classifications of exchange have unique theoretical characteristics such as an atypical number of sellers and/or buyers or supply and demand of unusual behavior, and special economics courses are devised to explore their theoretical peculiarities and significances. An example is agricultural economics. The exchange medium (money) again requires an examination of the theoretical aspects of money and of the banking arrangements which generate and control the supply of the medium of exchange. The use of scarce resources by a society involves the society's decision on the fraction of total resources that will be consumed by the community as a unit. Social consumption of resources in a discipline concerned with the scarcity of them necessarily involves economics in the total theoretical aspects of taxation and government expenditure. The exchange arrangements developed in this society and in other societies are of exhausting variations at any one point in time and have changed over time. This change is a central part of economic history which is taught as several separate courses on some university campuses. The heterogeneity of exchange dynamics, even when reduced to simplified theoretical classifications, is so remarkable that several courses in market theory are necessary if the university student's grasp of the economic aspects of even his own society is to be carried beyond the elementary level. To understand the production, exchange, and consumption arrangements in other societies requires courses in comparative economic systems. Certainly the exchanging of goods and resources through the use of a medium of exchange has one of its most sophisticated (and important) aspects when the exchange occurs across national boundaries. lierefore, international trade is an old and established part of economics offerings in all universities. title: The Economics of the Ghetto
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interests of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. The theory of wages, rent, interest, and profits. The principles of international trade and comparative economic organization. Prerequisite: ECON 200. s. s. 25-26 hrs.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Policies and Problems of Agriculture
description: Examination of the special economic conditions of demand and supply pertaining to agriculture and of problems created by changing national and international situations. Analysis of agricultural policy programs and implications of farm policy for consumers. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 200 or 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how man has looked at his economic life surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 273.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wageearner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 431.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economic Development in Latin America
description: The evaluation of theories of economic development. Sources and consequences of the economic growth and development process in Latin America analyzed in the context 'of economic theory. Attention to Common Market possibilities, monetaryfiscal factors, and trade and exchange. Examination of current national and international programs as promoters of develop - ment.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of coals and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goal s of the comunity. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

To help students gain this perspective, the English Department offers a wide variety of courses in American, British, and world literature. There are at least two good reasons for becoming better acquainted with how one's own language works. One is that a knowledge of the various patterns of language should contribute to a facility in writing and speaking. Equally important, however, is the fact that the history and structure of our language are important parts of our cultural heritage. Realizing the increasing necessity for successful college graduates to express themselves clearly in writing, the English Department requires all students to develop skill in expository writing. title: English as a Foreign Language
description: Stress on sounds, structure, and vocabulary of the English language in order to increase the student's facility in use of the English language. Cannot be counted toward general education requirements in English.

title: Literature and Composition for Foreign Students
description: Written and oral composition through reading, discussion, and interpretation of selected pieces of literature. Continued attention to the problems of syntax, pronunciation, and vocabulary which are difficult for foreign students. (This course is the equivalent of ENG 103 for foreign students.) Prerequisite: ENG 100 or satisfactory score on proficiency test in English as a foreign language.

title: Literature and Composition for Foreign Students
description: Guided exploration in the various forms of literature. Oral and written interpretation and analysis. Continued attention . to the problems of English which are difficult for foreign students. (This course is the equivalent of ENG 104 for foreign students.) Prerequisite: ENG 101 or satisfactory score on proficiency test in English as a foreign language.

title: Literature and Composition
description: English composition stressing the sentence, the paragraph, and the organization of the various types of expression through reading, discussion, and interpretation of selected pieces of literature.

title: Literature and Composition
description: Guided exploration in the various forms of literature. Also, oral and written interpretation and analysis by individuals and groups. Prerequisite: ENG 103 (106).

title: Humanities 1: Western Thought from Homer to Dante
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and general thought of the Greek, Roman, and Christian civilizations through the Middle Ages.

title: Humanities 2: Western Thought from Montaigne to Rousseau
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and science during the Renaissance and through the eighteenth century.

title: Humanities 3: Western Thought from Dostoyevsky to Sartre
description: Some major writing in literature, philosophy, and science from 1800 until the present.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of world literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 206.

title: Literature and Composition
description: Literature and composition for English majors and minors. A survey of the literature of Western civilization, exclusive of English and American literature. Prerequisite: ENG 103. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 205.

title: American Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: British Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of British literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: Grammar for Secondary School Teachers
description: asic course in traditional English grammar and usage. Close B d to those who have passed the Qualifying Test in English Grammar and not to be counted as part of the total hours in a major or minor program. Required of all English majors and minors who do not pass the Qualifying Test in English Grammar.

title: American Literature, 1607-1860
description: A survey of American literature from its beginning through the middle nineteenth century. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Literature of the Middle Ages and Renaissance
description: British literature of the Middle Ages and Renaissance emphasizing major works of a number of the literary figures in their historical and philosophical contexts. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Literature of the Seventeenth and Eignteenth Centuries
description: An extensive study of English literature of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, or from 1600 to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds of the periods. A close reading of the works of major writers is emphasized, but not to the exclusion of the works of minor writers. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Literature of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: British literature of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries emphasizing major works of a number of the literary figures in their historical and philosophical contexts. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Advanced Composition and Literature
description: An intensive study of contemporary exposition, problems of English usage, techniques of composition for advanced college and professional work, and prose fiction as a type of world literature. Required of exemptees from ENG 103 who are not English majors or minors.

title: Advanced Composition
description: Instruction in writing techniques beyond that provided for the general student. Introduction to literary research and criticism. Open only to English majors and minors. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern viewpoints and approaches in teaching language attitudes, habits, and skills. Consideration of written and oral expression, language usage, spelling, writing, and reading.

title: The English Language
description: The study of modern English with emphasis upon the application of the methods of descriptive linguistics to an understanding of modern vocabulary, usage, grammar, and phonology. Prerequisite: ENG 221 or a satisfactory grade on the Qualifying Test in English Grammar. Prerequisite waived for majors in elementary education.

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and unds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departm in ental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors English.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of the field of children's literature and an intensive study of types at various levels. The classics are emphasized.

title: American Literature, 1860-1960
description: A survey of selected writers and the various literary movements in America during the last hundred years. Prerequisite: ENG 240.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of Tw t.n. period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, ai and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: The themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Literature of Black America
description: An investigation of the literature written by black authors in the United States. Those authors to be studied will be determined by the instructor on the basis of literary merit.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to 1642
description: English drama from medieval times to the closing of the theatres in 1642, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Drama of the Restoration and Eighteenth Century
description: English drama from 1660 to 1780, including plays of Dryden, Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve, Steele, Goldsmith, and Sheridan.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenth century novels including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the Brontes, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Drama of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: A wide range of British drama, from Shelley's The Cencie, to Tennyson's Becket, to the plays of the Angry Young Men, with special attention given to the works of Shaw, Synge, Barrie, and O'Casey.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Creative Writing
description: The fundamentals of the short story, such as the use of language, image, and structure. Emphasis is put on the student's ability to write clearly and dramatically. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Fiction Writing
description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis will be placed on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Teaching of English in the Secondary School
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in the teaching of composition, language, and literature in the secondary school.

title: The Teaching of English as a Foreign Language
description: Background in modern linguistic science as applied to the teaching of English to nonnative speakers of English. Survey of methods and materials. Practice in development of teaching materials. Observation of classes in English for foreign students. Prerequisite: ENG 321, 420 or 520.

title: Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of transcendentalism. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Poe, Hawthorne, Melville
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of romanticism. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Twain, James, Adams, Crane
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of the varieties of realism. Prerequisite: ENG 340.

title: Renaissance and Seventeenth-Century Studies
description: The nondramatic literature of the Tudor, Stuart, and Puritan periods (1485-1660), exclusive of Shakespeare and Milton. Major writers such as Spenser, Donne, and Jonson will be considered in terms of their influence and of their political and philosophical backgrounds.

title: Chaucer
description: A study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several of the minor poems. Emphasis upon the structure, the sources, and the significance of the works included. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare (to 1600)
description: The earlier plays and poems, providing insights into the development of Shakespeare. Some plays such as Hamlet will be studied closely.

title: Shakespeare (from 1600)
description: The later plays, with close study of Othello, Macbeth, and King Lear.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Restoration and Eighteenth Century
description: An extensive study of the nondramatic works of Dryden, Swift, and Pope, with possible supplementary readings from other British authors of the period 1660-1745. Attention will be given to philosophical, aesthetic, and political currents in the works studied and to the distinctive character of Neo-Classicism. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Milton
description: A study of Milton's family background, political service, and poetic apprenticeship, culminating in close analytical investigation of Paradise Lost and Samson Agonistes. Attention is given also to Milton's aesthetic propositions and to his social and political prose works.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Age of Johnson
description: An intensive survey of the nondramatic works of Samuel Johnson and other British authors of the later eighteenth century, 1744-1800. Prerequisites: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Romantic Studies
description: The poetry and prose of Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Keats, and Shelley.

title: Victorian Studies
description: An intensive study of the works of Carlyle, Tennyson, Browning, Ruskin, and Arnold.

title: Twentieth-Century British Studies
description: A study in depth of several significant twentiethcentury authors (such as Shaw, Conrad, Lawrence, Joyce, Woolf, Waugh, Durrell, Beckett, and Auden) and the intellectual and literary movements closely associated with them.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Introduction to Historical Linguistics
description: An introduction to the scientific study of language for students in foreign language. An elementary survey of the methods used in historical and comparative linguistic analysis with application to language usually taught in college. Gives the language student some basic insights into the linguistic principles that underline change in language.

title: The Teaching of Foreign Language in the Secondary School
description: Methods current in foreign language teaching in the junior and senior high schools. Directed observation of classes, specific problems of presentation, choice of texts, and organization of the teaching materials and supplementary aids are worked out in detail. Attention is given to the Report of the Foreign Language Study and to the courses of study recommended by the State Department of Education. Prerequisites: two years of college credit in French, German, Latin, or Spanish, or the equivalent.

title: The Teaching of Foreign Language in the Elementary School
description: Development of foreign language instruction in the elementary school. Curricula, training of teachers, and teaching methods; also phonemics, pronunciation, and a review of other basic language elements.

title: Beginning Latin
description: The first course in the Latin language. Elements of Latin pronunciation, alphabet, rules of accent, syllabification, basic Latin grammar with oral and written exercises, reading of easy short selections from Latin authors, exercises in English derivatives, and consideration of the close connection of Latin and English vocabularies. Credit toward graduation can be given only when this course is followed by LAT 102 and 103.

title: Beginning Latin (continued)
description: Continued emphasis on pronunciation, accent, and syllabification. Oral and written exercises of greater difficulty, reading of short selections from various Latin authors, exercises in dictation, practice in comprehension, with exercises requiring comprehension of speech patterns rather than memorization of single words, and presentation of more grammatical principles. Credit toward graduation can be given only when this course is followed by LAT 103. Prerequisite: LAT 101.

title: Beginning Latin (continued)
description: Completion of presentation of the mechanics of Latin grammar. 'Stress on Latin syntax; logical structure in thought patterns. Rapid short readings illustrating grammatical principles. Emphasis on mastery of grammar through usage; oral and written exercises. Reading of relatively long essays, orations, and letters of Cicero, Pliny's letters, short poems of Horace, Catullus, and Vergil, longer reading selections chosen for importance in history of civilization rather than for illustration of grammatical principles. Prerequisite: LAT 102 or one year of . secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin
description: Rapid review of Latin grammar with oral and written exercises. Reading of selections from Caesar, Cicero, Pliny, Livy, Seneca, Vitruvius, and others, dealing with such topics as poetry, science, agriculture, medicine, religion, business, politics, history, private life, cooking, philosophy, education, and law. The aim is to interest Latin students in literary ideas drawn from representative works. Emphasis on vocabulary, increased knowledge of Latin idiom, and practice in writing Latin. Prerequisite: one year of college Latin or two years of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin (continued)
description: Emphasis on rapid reading for comprehension. Selected passages dealing with various aspects of man's life, together with comparisons taken from later periods. Celsus, De Medicina; Horace, Ars Poetica; Vitruvius, De Aqueductis; Pliny's Natural History; Cicero's De Officiis, De Republica, Epistulae, De Finibus, or Pro Archia; Juvenal, Satires; Pliny's letters (concerning the Christians), Terence's and Plautus' plays; and others. Prerequisites: 16 hours of college Latin or two and onehalf years of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin (continued)
description: Extensive reading of Roman comedies in class. Stress on rapid reading of Latin, particularly of the dramatists, Plautus and Terence. Introduction to colloquial Latin and everyday idiomatic language. Development of plot, characterization, and artistic unity of Roman comedies. Background and originality of Roman comedy; contarninatio. Play production in Rome. Comparison of Greek and Roman comedy. Aristophanes' comedies; selected plays of Terence and Plautus. Prerequisites: 20 hours of college Latin or two and onehalf years of secondary school Latin.
