DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY Beatty, Chairman; Carmin, Cass, Davis, Dillon, Grimes, Kane, Lyon, Martinson, Orr, Pal, Peterson, Roepke, Rothhaas, Samuelson, Showalter, Stevenson, Van Meter Geography explains the earth as the home of man by viewing the world in terms of the interrelationship of the natural and cultural processes in his environment. It deals with the influence of these processes on the behavioral patterns of man and how man has altered his earth home. The geography curricula reflect the nature of geography, offering general and specialized studies in cultural, physical, regional, and systematic topics. The objectives of these curricula are to (1) educate and train professional geographers for positions in colleges and universities, business and industry, governmental agencies, and elsewhere; (2) provide professional training for teachers of geography in elementary and secondary schools; and (3) contribute to the liberal education of Ball State University students. Geology is designed to train professional geologists as well as to provide professional and cultural education to students other than majors in the discipline. Geologists study the earth — its history, minerals, rocks, fossils, landforms, and structure. Today, geology is also concerned with the study of the physical aspects of the moon and other planets of our solar system. Professional geologists are employed in government, industry, and college and university teaching. Earth science incorporates much of geology and the physical aspects of geography, as well as meteorology and astronomy. It provides a broad understanding of the physical environment to the student who does not expect to specialize in any one particular area of geology or geography. Earth science graduates are in increasing demand throughout the United States, particularly in secondary schools and in lower division undergraduate teaching in colleges and universities. The geography and geology faculty specializes within the cultural, physical, and systematic topics of geography, the subareas of geology, such as geomorphology, mineralogy, petrography, paleontology, oceanography, and earth science. Students with areas in the Department of Geography and Geology may contact the departmental office for the names of faculty advisers who can offer specialized information complementary to the University curricular advising program. T. S. Eliot, Four Quartets, "Burnt Norton" By definition, history is the record of past actions of mankind based upon surviving evidence. Thus, mankind's accumulated experience, the memory of the human race, is called history. Its study, which should lead to understanding and wisdom, indicates that all problems and patterns are the result of complex processes of growth. By shedding light on these processes, history provides a vehicle for profiting from human experience. Without a knowledge of his past, man would have no landmarks,. no points of reference, and no foundations on which to build a modern world. History may be studied vicariously. Man's unique ability to utilize not only his own past experiences but also the experiences of other men and women of this and other generations sets him above the lower animals and enables him to better understand the present in order to prepare himself for the future. By studying the problems that have confronted men in the past and their attempted solutions, man also gains in tolerance, appreciation, and understanding of other people's ideas and institutions. Man's system of government, the frontiers of his country and its economy, and many other factors of direct concern to his entire existence are meaningful because of history. In the age of the hydrogen bomb, atomic propulsion, and global interdependence, to neglect history would be more than folly — it could be pure suicide. The philosopher Santayana noted that "When experience is not retained, as among savages, infancy is perpetual. Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." And Woodrow Wilson wisely noted: "The worst possible enemy to society is the man who . . . is cut loose in his standards from the past, and universities which train men to use their minds without carefully establishing the connection of their thought with that of the past, are instruments of social destruction." As we appreciate that history is a story of constant change, we live more intelligently in a world that is constantly changing. History may also be studied as literature. For over two thousand years, written history has stood as a major literary form. This vast and complex story is built upon the hopes and aspirations, the struggles, the triumphs, and also the failures of man. Effectively presented, history ranks with great novels and epic poetry. Perhaps "the supreme purpose of history is a better world." The history major may be undertaken to attain professional, academic, or cultural objectives, including preparation for graduate study and advanced degrees, teaching licenses, and proficiency for appointments as specialists in business, government, and in cultural institutions, or as a hobby. Courses in history are designed to meet the needs of students in several fields of study. The department offers a broad selection of courses in the general studies program. It offers introductory and advanced courses for students majoring in education or in liberal arts in other departments of the University. It also presents courses designed to give a broad and thorough training in the various history programs. The graduate programs are built on the foundation of undergraduate preparation. Students intending to do graduate work in history are urged to take the Bachelor of Arts degree. The master's and doctoral degrees require intensive directed study in history aimed at depth of understanding. description: A survey of the negro in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis will be placed upon the impact of the negro on American culture and vice versa.

title: The History of Canada
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of Canada from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis will be placed on the events leading to the establishment of Canada and on United States- Canadian relations and problems.

title: History of Mexico
description: Mexico from the pre-Columbian era to the present with emphasis on cultural development.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The area of cultural contact in North America among the Spanish, Anglo-American, and French empires from 1550 to 1850.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1900
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period through the Spanish American War. Prerequisites: 8 hours of United States history. 432, United States Diplomatic History since 1900. (4) Survey of the foreign relations of the United States during the twentieth century. Prerequisites: 8 hours of United States history.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1607- 1865
description: Survey of history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of the history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: The History of American Culture
description: The history of pictorial art, architecture, music, literature, and science, and the impact of these areas on the social, economic, and political history of the country.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201 or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 410.

title: Historical Method and Bibliography
description: Techniques of research and documentation.

title: History and Historians
description: Historians whose writings are basic in major fields of history.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open only to seniors of special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate investigation. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with special competence within the area involved.

title: History of World Civilization
description: A survey of the principle historical and cultural developments of ancient and medieval times to 1350, with emphasis on those institutions and events of western civilization which furnish our own cultural heritage.

title: History of World Civilization
description: From 1350 to 1870, including such major topics as the Renaissance, Reformation, rise of modern nations, discovery and exploration, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, nationalism, and the industrial revolution and resulting ideologies. Prerequisite recommended: HIST 151.

title: The World in the Twentieth Century
description: Major world events and issues of the twentieth century; the causes and results of the two world wars; the rise and decline of the colonial empires with emerging nationalism; the impact of democratic, facist, and communistic doctrines; twentiethcentury thought; the effect of science on our age; arts; attempts at international organization and cooperation; and the revolution in expectations in the oneworld of today.

title: The Rise of Modern Europe, 1500-1815
description: Political, social, and economic history of Europe from the Age of Discovery to the Congress of Vienna. Emphasis on political and economic events, the rise of national states, absolutism, religious developments, and the expansion of Europe overseas.

title: The Rise of Modern Europe, 1815 to the Present
description: Political, economic, social, and cultural history of Europe from the Congress of Vienna to the contemporary scene. Emphasis on political and economic events, the liberal and nationalist movements, industrialism, imperialism, World Wars I and II, and the conflict of national interests.

title: Cultural and Intellectual History of Modern Europe
description: Discovery, analysis, and discussion of major cultural and intellectual trends in the western world since 1815. Development of concepts and ideas that have shaped modern European history. Particular attention will be given to origins of contemporary problems and situations in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic philosophies, science, and social reform.

title: Diplomatic History of Europe, 1870-1918
description: Background, immediate causes, and the course of World War I. Prerequisites: 8 hours of European history or permission of the department chairman.

title: European Diplomatic History from 1918 to the Present
description: Ideological, economic, social, and political factors which explain the current world situation. Prerequisites: 8 hours of European history. These prerequisites may be waived for students who convince the department chairman that they are in other ways qualified to take the course.

title: The Development of Ancient Greece
description: Greek political, social, and intellectual development in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the rise and fall of Greek democracy. Prerequisite: one year of history.

title: The Development of Ancient Rome
description: Political, social, and intellectual developments of Rome from the beginning of the Republic to approximately 500 A.D. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the Republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination. Prerequisite: one year of history.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Medieval Ideas and Institutions
description: Indepth studies of selected problems concerning the social and cultural bases of medieval civilization. Emphasis on six major themes: feudalism, chivalry, manorialism, the medieval city, the Church; and the medieval university.

title: Colloquium on Problems in Medieval History
description: Discussion of major problems connected with medieval history and historiography, and current trends in medieval scholarship.

title: The Renaissance, 1400-1600
description: More specialized study of the cultural and intellectual achievement in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, often called the Renaissance.

title: History of France
description: A survey of the political, economic, and diplomatic history of France from Roman times to the present.

title: The French Revolution
description: Cultural implications of the French Revolution for modern times as well as the rise of the bourgeoisie.

title: The Rise of Modern Britain, 1485-1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor, Stuart, and early Hanoverian periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: History of England since 1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic development of England since the end of the Seven Years War. Emphasis on the modernization of the administrative machinery following the American Revolution, the development of the limited monarchy, the welfare state, and England's part in the two world wars of the twentieth century.

title: Constitutional History of England
description: A tracing of the development of the British constitutional system to the present time: development of the kingship, the common law, parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: The Modern British Commonwealth and Empire
description: British imperial and Commonwealth development, 1815 to the present. The post-Napoleonic empire, the development of dominion status, the special problem of India, the Common - wealth, the world wars, the shrinking empire, the growing Commonwealth, and the situation today. Prerequisite: HIST 153 or the equivalent.

title: Modern Germany
description: Germany from 1890 to the present. The Reign of William II, the Weimar Republic, the Third Reich, and the period since World War II. Specific attention is given to social, intellectual, and cultural developments.

title: History of Tzarist Russia
description: The Russian state and her people from her earliest beginnings to the Revolution of 1917; basic chronology of political development; other phases of Russian culture, ethnology, religion, social changes, economic structure, education, literature, and diplomacy. Journalism 125

title: History of the Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, with emphasis on Soviet political and economic institutions and the role of the U.S.S.R. in world affairs. Prerequisite: HIST 486.

title: Modern History of East-Central Europe
description: Modern history of peoples who constitute present Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and the Baltic Republics. Stress is on their struggle for and preservation of national independence and the influence of the great powers on East-Central Europe. Topics are projected against the background of the most dominant European trends and problems. Prerequisite: HIST 153.

title: Near East in Modern Times
description: The Turkish, Persian, and Arab world with particular emphasis on the period since 1800: the decay of traditional Near-Eastern institutions, the expansion of European influence, modernization, and the rise of national states in the Near East. Prerequisite: 8 hours of history or permission of the department chairman.

title: History of the Balkans since 1453
description: The development of the Balkans from the time of the Ottoman Conquest to the present with emphasis on the diversity of cultural and national development during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: The Far East
description: Survey of India, China, and Japan, and contiguous areas. Historical development of these countries, with an emphasis on their relations with Europe and America.

title: Introduction to Non-Western Civilizations
description: A broad survey of the Soviet Union and of the principal areas of the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America, with particular emphasis on contemporary political, economic, and social developments. title: Mathematical Concepts 1
description: A general education course for students who wish to know more about the contributions of mathematics to human culture. The minimal manipulative skills necessary to understand the various concepts and topics will be developed. Such topics as the number system, simple logic, the interrelations between mathematics and history, and some interesting geometries, will be covered. Prerequisites: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry.

title: Mathematical Concepts 2
description: Continuation of MATH

title: College Algebra 1
description: Fundamental operations of algebra through quadratics. Students who have credit for three semesters of secondary school algebra will not receive credit for this course. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra.

title: College Algebra 2
description: A brief introduction to sets and the logic of algebra, a discussion of inequalities, absolute values, functions and relations, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and mathematical induction. Prerequisites: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary school algebra, and one year of plane geometry, or their equivalents as determined by the Department of Mathematics.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities, and equations; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers, and De Moivre's Theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or its equivalent as determined by the Department of Mathematics.

title: Analytic Geometry
description: Use of Cartesian and polar coordinates in two and three dimensions, conic sections, transcendental curves, curve sketching, parametric equations, lines and surfaces in solid analytic geometry. Prerequisite: The equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level, or MATH 111 and MATH 112.

title: Calculus 1
description: Inequalities, limits, continuity, differentials and derivatives, introduction to the definite integral. Prerequisite: MATH 113.

title: Calculus 2
description: Continuation of the definite integral, differentiation and integration of elementary transcendental functions, derivatives in polar coordinates, integration by special methods, application of integration. Prerequisite: MATH 170.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Arithmetic 1
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Arithmetic 2
description: Extension of the number concept through unsigned rational numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 205. 28 hrs. 8 hrs.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Arithmetic 3
description: Extension of number concepts through the real numbers; elements of algebra; intuitive geometry. Prerequisite: MATH 206.

title: The Structure of the Real Number System
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and number systems. A systematic development of the real number system is emphasized. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 270.

title: Elements of Linear Algebra
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties, determinants, matrix inverses, rank and equivalence of matrices, and a matrix approach to the theory of systems of linear equations. Prerequisite: MATH 171.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 207 and 270.

title: Calculus 3
description: Continuation of the application of the integral elements of infinite series (convergent and divergent series), Taylor's series and theorem, partial differentiation, and multiple integration. Prerequisite: MATH 171.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for finite sample spaces is developed from a settheoretic basis. Probability functions, means and variances of random variables. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Statistics
description: Common distribution functions, sampling theory, correlation and regression, tests of hypotheses, and estimation techniques. Prerequisite: MATH 320.

title: Statistics 2
description: Tests of hypotheses, the chisquare, Student's t and F distributions, design of experiments, nonparametric methods, sequential sampling, Bayesian statistics. Prerequisite: MATH 321.

title: Computer Programming and Systems 1
description: Operational organization of a stored program digital computer, representation of numbers, computer arithmetic, address modification, indirect addressing, indexing, machine and assembly language. Programming of representative nonnumeric problems will be assigned. Prerequisites: ID 200 and MATH 270 or permission of the department head.

title: Computer Programming and Systems 2
description: (Continuation of MATH 330) Structure of programs, use of input/output and peripheral storage devices, common techniques. Prerequisite: MATH 330.

title: Computer Programming and Systems 3
description: (Continuation of MATH 331) The use of monitor or executive systems for computer selfoperation. Discussion of multiprogramming and multiprocessing. Description of timesharing and multiaccess systems. Prerequisite: MATH 331.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in synthetic geometry, closely related to the field of Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of compound interest, annuities, sinking funds, amortization and valuation of bonds, depreciation, and elementary life insurance topics. Prerequisite: MATH 270.

title: Differential Equations
description: Emphasis on the solution of ordinary linear differential equations. Attention to methods of numerical analysis of nonlinear equations. Applications to science and engineering stressed. Prerequisite: MATH 270 or permission of thedepartment head.

title: Computer Science and Programming 1
description: Description of a computer installation, computer logic, and general programming languages; elementary problem sessions on the University computer. Prerequisite: MATH 270 or permission of the department head.

title: Arithmetic in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching arithmetic at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Prerequisite: MATH 207.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Secondary School
description: Materials and methods used in the teaching of junior and senior high school mathematics. Survey of texts, organization of materials, testing procedures, and visual aids materials. Prerequisites: MATH 211 and 340; prerequisite or parallel: EDSEC 360.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. Restricted to honors students. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 1
description: The study of rings, integral domains, and fields, with emphasis on the development of integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, and polynomials. Prerequisites: MATH 212 and 213, or permission of the department head.

title: Linear Algebra
description: The study of some topics in linear algebra: matrix algebra and linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, inner product spaces, etc. Prerequisites: MATH 212 and 411.

title: Theory of Numbers
description: Elementary properties of integers, theory of congruences, quadratic residues, Diophantine equations, introduction to theory of groups, introduction to theory of algebraic numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Computer Logic and Algorithms 1
description: Boolean algebras and functions, normal forms, minimization, switching circuit representation, design of computer logical components. Prerequisite: MATH 332.

title: Computer Logic and Algorithms 2
description: (Continuation of MATH 433) Mechanical formulation of algorithms, Turing machines, normal algorithms, universal machines, algorithmically unsolvable problems. Prerequisite: MATH 433.

title: Introduction to Computer Languages
description: Problemoriented languages, the syntax of ALGOL and similar languages, compiler design, analysis of arithmetic and logical expressions, listprocessing languages. Prerequisite: MATH 434.

title: Advanced Analytic Geometry
description: An advanced treatment of analytic Euclidean geometry using topics from analysis and algebra as tools where helpful. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or permission of the department head.

title: Projective Geometry
description: Properties of geometric configurations which are invariant under projection. Synthetic methods emphasized, and some use is made of analytic methods. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or permission of the department head.

title: Topology 1
description: Review of basic set theory; topological spaces, metric spaces, mappings and homeomorphisms, product spaces and function spaces, and applications to the real line and to the plane. Prerequisites: MATH 211, 212, and 470 or 570.

title: History of Mathematics
description: A survey of the development of mathematics from prehistoric times to the present. The emphasis is on such topics as numbers and numerals, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, and the calculus. Prerequisites: MATH 211, and 340 or 441.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include: finite differences, interpolation of functions; approximation of functions, derivatives, and integrals; iterative and direct methods for solving linear systems. Prerequisites: ID 200 or permission of the department head; MATH 212 and 374.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics covered include: approximate solution of nonlinear equations; numerical solution of ordinary differential equations; error analysis; difference equation; matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Prerequisite : MATH 462.

title: Vector Analysis
description: An introduction to the theory and applications of vectors including the algebra, calculus, and geometry of vectors; classical theorems; applications. Prerequisite: MATH 374. Physics 129

title: Elements of Analysis
description: The real number system is developed through Dedekind cuts, Cauchy sequences, and complete ordered field postulation. Topology of the real line, sequences and series of real numbers, and limits and continuity. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 207 and 270.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Topics covered include partial differentiation and its applications, Riemann and Stieltjes integration theory, and multiple integration and its applications. Prerequisite: MATH 470.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics covered include line and surface integrals, limits and indeterminate forms, infinite series, and improper integrals. Prerequisite: MATH 471.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Arithmetic
description: For teachers in service who do not hold a degree. Prerequisite: teaching experience in the elementary school. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the Mathematics Department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 level. Its scope is broad, covering such areas as the nature of disease, the complexity of nutrition, effects of radiation, behavioral aspects of accident prevention, an understanding of health and medical care programs, significance of international health problems, selection of health products and services, environmental hazards of air and water, community health services, foundations of mental health, and family life education. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a major or minor for students who are interested in one of a variety of occupations in the health science field. Health Science is known differently in some institutions; some commonly used names are: health education, health and safety education, and school and college health education. Health Science teachers, coordinators, and directors are being sought by elementary and secondary schools, junior colleges, as well as universities. The department also offers a professional arts minor in the field of public health. It provides basic information on public health programs, problems, and practices in the United States. Opportunities include employment with official governmental and voluntary health agencies, business, industry, and professional health associations, such as the American Medical Association. Of equal importance in the department are the subject areas of anatomy and physiology. These are vital to the health sciences and biological sciences in the broad sense and, in anticipation of future development, provide a point of departure for specialization in the specific, respective disciplines of anatomy and physiology. The department also offers an undergraduate liberal arts minor in physiology. One combination that is often elected by the students is the physiology minor earned in conjunction with a biology, chemistry, or psychology major. At the present time, the department contributes required and elective courses to several academic programs at Ball State, such as regional and urban planning, preprofessional programs in allied health science areas, courses for professional nurse preparation, and general education. The preprofessional, programs in the allied health science area include premedical, predental, and prepharmacy programs; professional nurse preparation; and medical technology. The department provides guidance in enabling students to select a career in teaching, service, or research. Membership in Eta Sigma Gamma, the national honorary for men and women in health science, and Sigma Zeta, the national honorary in science, is offered to qualified students. DEPARTMENT OF POLITICAL SCIENCE AND PHILOSOPHY Gruenewald, Chairman; Andry, Annis, Baker, Chang, Davis, Dyer, Galantai, Hamilton, Hamori, Kelly, Menez, Morgan, Mueller, Reed, Robertson, Rudoni, Sargent, Sharp, Varenhorst Political Science as an Academic Discipline Political science is the study of legal governments and man's relation thereto. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Protagoras, Gorgias, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamentalquestions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (pohs or state) that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differ from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. These observations led them to ask: What is the nature of man (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between man and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of speculative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. Since comprehension of available knowledge is fundamental to intelligent valuation, emphasis must be given to the teaching and learning and to the continued accumulation and teaching of knowledge. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civic, and vocational. The first two, hopefully, are universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed populace. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz., political theory; American government; public law; public administration; parties, politics, and the political process; foreign and comparative government; and international law and diplomacy. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher certification programs, urban and regional planning, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate level for students in other departments. Philosophy as an Academic Discipline One of the earliest definitions of philosophy encountered by the beginning student is one that says it is the "love of wisdom." The philosopher, accordingly, is known as a "lover of wisdom." And it should be noted that this love of wisdom is not confined to any one field; indeed, most anything is grist for the philosopher's mill! Historically speaking, the above definition has resulted ever since the time of Plato in the general agreement that the traditional role of philosophy is one of synthesis and system building. To put the matter another way, the philosopher was seen to be one who knew something about each area of man's experience as a result of either native genius or exhaustive investigation after which he was supposed to sit down with all his knowledge and, by weaving such knowledge into a consistent and coherent whole, give to mankind a unified picture of his universe and himself. This general agreement about the role of philosophy both within and without the university produced about twenty or more centuries of some of the most magnificent albeit meaningless cogitations ever produced by the mind of man. This is not to say that these vast systems were or are without some value. As purely intellectual exercises they have their place. But surely the student has a right to note that on the assumption that synthesis is the main business of philosophy, here we are many centuries after Plato still bemused by his problems and showing very little evidence that we are any closer to solving them. Is it possible that they are not "problems" at all? In the past thirty years the role of philosophy has been changing, although not without some dire warnings as to its future if the present trend continues. Analysis has now replaced synthesis as the main job of the philosopher in his role as a member of a university faculty. This is not to say that analysis has not always been with us, philosophically speaking, but in the past it has always been subordinated to the activity known as synthesis. It is generally agreed now that the scope of man's knowledge is too large in our own century for any philosopher to pretend that he can carry on the timehonored function of philosophy described above. Perhaps this was possible in the small world in which Plato lived; it is not possible now. Given this change, then, just what is the role of philosophy and the philosopher in a modern university now? It is twofold, one relative to the other academic disciplines, and one relative to the students who pass through his classroom. Relative to the other academic disciplines on the campus, the philosopher can function in his role of critical analyst as a sort of catalytic agent by insisting that his colleagues constantly look to the meaningfulness of their ideas. Indeed, perhaps his greatest service is that of helping others make their ideas clear regardless of the nature of their academic discipline. Relative to the students exposed to him in the university, the philosopher and philosophy can serve in several ways. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all facets of life need examination if we are to get ahead with this business of living. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all of his values and beliefs would never have come to be except that men in the past were not afraid to question those that were then held, and that in all probability the same fate awaits values and beliefs held now. And lastly, philosophy can serve by showing the student that this succession is indeed a good thing. The alternative is stagnation. These two roles for philosophy have given rise on most university campuses to certain basic courses in philosophy designed to be of help to groups of students. The usual Introduction to Philosophy course is one of general interest which serves to do what its title implies. In this course the student becomes aware of the basic problems philosophers deal with as well as some of their answers. Logic, the study of deductive and inductive reasoning and the rule thereto, can be invaluable for prelaw students, math majors, and any other persons who must reason correctly. Ethics is a course of particular interest to anyone concerned in any way with man's relationship to man. For those occupied with the history of ideas, the three courses in the history of ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy are most valuable. These are the core courses in philosophy and form the necessary foundation for the more specialized courses which usually follow. DEPARTMENT OF SOCIOLOGY AND ANTHROPOLOGY Hewitt, Chairman; Brodt, Glenn, Gordon, Moore, Murphy, Neiman, Rehfeld, Schlechty, Scruton, Smith, Swartz, Tucker, Whitehead Sociology as an Academic Discipline Sociology is among the youngest of the social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades; and especially in the period since World War II, its widened inclusion in patterns of general education has resulted in exceptionally rapid growth of undergraduate enrollments. Simultaneously, rapidly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge; and the concepts of the discipline are rapidly becoming a part of "everyman's vocabulary." Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. In the early years of this century, a number of persons interested in the field of sociology saw it primarily as a tool for ameliorating the various ills and problems of the society, and especially for helping groups and individuals with special needs in "ad: justing" to the surrounding social order. Gradua.11, this emphasis has come to be more identified w!t_b e. with the special field of social work (see below), sociology as an academic discipline being perceived more as a "pure" rather than an "applied" sc ienc to Even so, the findings of sociology per se continir, .1 terms of their applicability to the range of problem s be asesed by the general public, at least, large } Sociology and Anthropology 141 relating to "group problems" and the stability of the social order. As one of the related group of social sciences, sociology focuses upon, and seeks to develop dependable generalizations about, the social life of man as an interacting participant in groups. This involves identifying, classifying, and interpreting observable regularities in human interaction and resultant patterns of social organization. An understanding of the bases for and influences of such regularities in the forms of human association is fundamental to a student's knowledge about himself and others as participants in structured group life, and about the societies in which such participation occurs. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to the student's broadened perspective of the sociocultural environment which surrounds him and his own relationship to it, thus liberating him from provincialism and the limitations of untested folk mythology. Attention to observed regularities in social structures, as well as in the processes of social change, facilitates an appreciation of the nature, functions, and limits of the social order. As a science, sociology employs the canons of empiricism, objectivity, and ethical neutrality in its search for predictive relationships. The findings derived from such investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. The methods and concerns of sociology are functionally related to those of the other social sciences as well as to a wide range of arts (teaching, medical, expressive, correctional, etc.) which involve interactions among persons performing varied roles. The discipline of sociology thus has a significant contribution to make in the area of general (liberal) education and in professional education of widely diverse emphases, along with the preparation of scholars, to expand and transmit the body of sociological knowledge itself. Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex gsroocwitahl problems, has contributed to the dramatic of the profession in recent decades. Social Work is both an art and a science. Its art is the develoeipthmere nt of special skills used in working with people, i ndividually, in groups, or through com- Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare agencies; in courts as probation officers for juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics; in schools; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as well as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Funds, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University provides for the needs of three groups of students: those who wish to qualify for firstlevel social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; and those who wish to prepare themselves for roles in community leadership as organization board members, in labor union leadership, in industrial social welfare relationships. After the basic twoyear general studies program at Ball State, students begin their specialization in social work within the sociology major. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, and methods of social work. Field trips in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. Seniors with proper qualifications who have definitely chosen social work as a career enroll in a course in basic social work methods. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of casework, group work, and community organization; practical experience is gained in field observation. Each student is assigned to a social agency for a half day each week where he works with individuals or groups under expert supervision. Although the anthropologist, as a practicing scholar, develops a limited specialty, the field itself remains convinced that man is a sociobiological whole and must finally be studied as such. This belief places a certain burden on the anthropologist and the student by requiring, for professional competence, a very wide range of content areas. In physical anthropology, for example, attention is commonly focused on such topics as the nature of the evolutionary process which is responsible, through the action of natural selection, hybridization, genetic drift and artificial selection, for the development of the largetailless, terrestrial, bipedal, orthograde primate which man is. Course work is commonly devoted to the fossil evidence of man's recent evolution, especially during the Pleistocene period. Without doubt, that aspect of physical anthropology which has the greatest potential contribution to make to man's selfunderstanding, and the aspect likeliest to be of practical application, is the study of contemporary varieties, or races, of man. There is no subject about which men seem to have the most fundamental convictions, and commonly there is none in which the unfortunate effects of total ignorance are more clearly seen. The anthropologist is deeply involved in all phases of this study, from the determination of the nature of the phenomenon itself, through the eventual genetic classification of races, to the delicate and vexing questions having to do with the significance of race differences. The pursuit of truth is the goal of the scientist. But the application of knowledge which has been secured through the scientific method is hardly avoidable. Much of cultural anthropology is closely related to history and no branch illustrates this fact more clearly than archaeology. Courses in this area provide the student of man's past with techniques which enable many of the limitations of conventional historiography to be overcome, with the result that we now possess knowledge of human behavior during times antedating writing by sometimes hundreds of thousands of years. Of course, this knowledge is rarely of the detailed and specific sort sought by the historian. But although he is commonly deprived of historical personalities, the archaeologist has the compensation of seeing the great sweep of human affairs with perhaps greater clarity. The archaeologist reminds the student that it was during prehistoric times that most of the great steps in human progress were made: the development of technology, the creation of forms of government, kinship, religion, philosophy, and art. The archaeologist also reminds the student through appropriate courses of the long and fruitful cooperation between the historian and the prehistorian, which has been responsible for the bulk of our knowledge of the ancient world of classical times, including Egypt, the Near East, Greece, Crete, and early Rome. Preparation in anthropology customarily involves some work in the field of linguistics. This is a most highly specialized area, and thorough preparation through detailed courses is less common than in the other areas. But introduction to the broad subdivisions of descriptive and historical linguistics helps to acquaint the student with more than a mere modicum of knowledge about the techniques and history of human communication, which is the most distinctive characteristic of the human animal, setting him apart, as no other single fact does, from infrahumans. It is linguistics which, in recent years, has begun to make students aware the talking is more than simply a method of communicating ideas between speakers of the same language; it is the vehicle of thought itself, and it provides the speaker not only with categories of expression, but also with the means at once of perceiving and of ordering his universe. At this point linguistics is very close to cultural anthropology. Modern cultural anthropology has grown out of the nineteenth century's interest in the accounts by travelers, explorers, missionaries, merchants, and soldiers of the frequently astonishing and sometimes hostile people whom they had met. Much of the work of the cultural anthropologist, or ethnologist, has been the gathering of accurate information about the world's nonliterate peoples. Modern ethnology, it should be noted, places little stress on the word "primitive," having been driven by the data to the conclusion that it does not separate categories of men very efficiently. But from this early interest in different societies has developed anthropology's increasingly sophisticated analysis of culture, that amorphous yet systematic mass of learned behavior patterns which provides human societies with the means to survival. Much comparative work has been done, and courses in anthropology departments reflect this, in crosscultural studies of religion, kinship and family systems, governments, technologies, value and belief systems, literatures, modes of aesthetic expression in song, dance, and the graphic and plastic arts, among other institutions. Anthropology' wrestles with countless unsolved problems in the area of relations between personalities and the social milieu in which they occur and in the area of cultural dynamics. The possibilities of practical application are numerous, and are, increasingly, being exploited. description: An introductory view of the general field of sociology including basic concepts as used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, social processes, and social institutions.

title: Contemporary Social Issues
description: An analysis of current issues of public concern stemming from economic, political, and social changes. Attention is focused on the positions of conflicting interest groups and their implications for societal integration.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors effecting the establishment and utilization of treatment programs.

title: History of Social Work
description: The history of private philanthropy and public welfare programs in Europe and America, including the Elizabethan poor law, the growth of public responsibility, the English background of American welfare programs and reform movements, and twentiethcentury developments.

title: The Field of Social Work
description: An introductory survey of the field of social work with emphasis on twentiethcentury developments. Course content will emphasize contemporary agencies and services, both public and private. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 350.

title: Public Social Welfare
description: An introduction to public welfare including policy, services and administration. Tax supported income maintenance programs are examined with special emphasis on the philosophy, methods, issues, and problems of public assistance programs.

title: Child Welfare
description: An introduction to the field of child welfare, including programs, policies, problems, and services. The principles and practices of casework for children are examined with emphasis upon state and local community resources. Prerequisites: SOC 350 and 351 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Social Work Methods
description: An introduction to the basic concepts and methods of the three areas of social work practice: casework, group work, and community organization. Examination of the basic methodology will be supplemented with field experience by the student in a social agency. Prerequisites: SOC 350, 351, 352, 353, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Development of Social Thought
description: A critical survey of influential views regarding the nature of society and human relations from the Greek period to the early twentieth century. Views of earlier social theorists are interpreted as products of the prevailing social climate, and are evaluated for the contribution to modern sociological theory.

title: Modern Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of modern sociological theories and theorists with a view toward relating theoretical positions to contemporary social and historical dynamics; an examination of the intellectual and cultural climate surrounding the individual theorists. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100.

title: Mass Society and Culture
description: Conditions giving rise to the spreading phenomena of mass culture, current expressions of these phenomena in American society and elsewhere, and an appraisal of their implications for oganizational functioning and interpersonal relationhips. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: A survey of the literature, issues, and events which focus upon the nature and types of complex social organizations with particular attention to societal consequences. Prerequisite: 8 hours of sociology or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 and POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 476.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community 'and national programs for meeting them.

title: Juvenile Delinquency
description: The nature, extent, causes, and methods of control of juvenile delinquency. Emphasis is given to the role of community agencies in prevention and treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Criminology
description: The nature and extent of individual and organized crime in modern society, contributing causes, and methods used in its control. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Introduction to Corrections
description: A beginning course in penology with emphasis on the three major components: police, courts, and correctional institutions. The history, philosophy and current programs, policies, and problems. Prerequisite: SOC 450 or 451. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 552.

title: Practicum in Corrections
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in correctional settings on the state and local level. Prerequisites: SOC 452 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Small Groups
description: Analysis of data on experimental laboratory research on small groups and field research on small group dynamics. Attention is given to the relationship between group productivity, group cohesion, size, interaction patterns, and related areas. Prerequisite: SOC 260 or GXPSY 316.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: The Community
description: Major differentiating characteristics, with special emphasis on the urban community, basic patterns of social and ecological organization, and factors contributing to community integration and disorganization. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Practicum in the Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis and evaluation of problems evolving from the changing social and demographic characteristics of urban core areas, with special emphasis given to their effects on family units and the needs of children and youth. A field work course requiring supervised participation in a designated urban neighborhood. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Sociological Research
description: Principles and techniques of organizing, conducting, and interpreting sociological research; the appropriateness of particular methodologies for different kinds of research problems. Prerequisite: SOC 482 or equivalent course in basic statistics.

title: Community Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of community surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating and utilizing sources of data; and the application of survey findings to programs of community action. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 472 or 480.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in the social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 582.

title: Independent Study in Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man as a biological unit of the animal kingdom. The human fossil record, living primates, and criteria of race and the races of man, elementary anthropometry, adaptive mechanisms, principles of biological evolution, and human genetics.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family, kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Bio-Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological and cultural evolution.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: Man's cultural achievements from their beginnings into historic times. Man's cultural development will be traced through the paleolithic hunting, mesolithic fishing, neolithic village farming, and urban living stages.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man as a unit in the animal kingdom. The principles of biological evolution and the human fossil record are stressed.

title: The American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North and South America. Each culture is described in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: World Ethnography
description: A systematic survey of the important culture areas of the world, describing and comparing major social institutions: e.g., economics and technology, family and kinship organization, political structure, religion, and art.

title: Material Culture
description: The material manifestations of culture, stressing primitive technology. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 220.

title: Human Osteology
description: The human skeleton. Bone identification, osteometry, aging, sexing, and racing a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 100.

title: Races of Man
description: Introduction to the present scientific status of the phenomenon of human subspecies, including a survey of historic concepts of race and race sorting criteria, with emphasis on recent advances in physical anthropology . Prerequisite: ANTH 10,160, or 20.

title: Race and Racism
description: Investigation in detail of the nature of race as a biological phenomenon, which will acquaint the student with the history of racism in the Western world. Stress on the necessity of employing the scientific method in studying race beliefs.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, kith particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in thei f natural setings. Prerequisite: ANTH 10 or permision o the department chairman.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old_ World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 220.

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs.

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Summer Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation: sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Field observation and interpretation are stressed. Requires full time in the field.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Utilization of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Classical Archaeology

title: Peoples of Oceania

DEPARTMENT OF SPEECH Huckleberry, Head; Artes, Benson, Bloom, Closser, Diedrich, English, Harmon, Heady, Hoops, Irving, Kramer, Lightfoot, Mannies, Robbins, Shepard, Strother General Speech The field of general speech encompasses several areas such as public address, interpretation, theatre, and speech sciences. It is a general program for undergraduate use, while persons specialize as they move toward graduate degrees. In the area of general speech, the University offers both graduate and undergraduate programs. A large proportion of those students electing a speech major plan to become teachers in the public schools. This teacher is expected to direct debating, produce theatre, and promote and direct radio and television programs. He is also asked to be in charge of special convocations. His class work is the development of the skills of public address and participation in a democratic society. Also he must develop an appreciation and skill for interpretation and theatre as performed in school theatres or through the facilities of mass media. Another responsibility is to develop an appreciation of the artistic, an understanding of the basic issues of mankind, and a respect for his cultural heritage. The profession of general speech assists liberal arts graduates to develop these same skills and attitudes. In addition, the speech major and minor are especially useful to support students who enter other professions such as law, the ministry, politics, public relations, and professional radio, television, and theatre. The University offers many student activities in the areas of intercollegiate debating, individual speech events, radio, television, and theatre. It is assumed that general speech majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office, and from the appropriate area chairman, and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Speech Pathology and Audiology The graduate with a bachelor's degree and a teaching major in speech pathology and audiology (sometimes known as speech and hearing therapy) usually works in a public school corporation. An individual with a master's degree may work in a public school, hospital speech and hearing clinic, college or university center, or communitysponsored speech and hearing agency. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers three undergraduate programs in speech pathology and audiology: a teaching major, for persons who plan to work in the public schools; a departmental major, for persons who plan to work eventually in a hospital, community or college clinic; and a departmental minor, for those students who want as much information and knowledge as they can secure regarding this discipline but who do not plan to enter the profession. Ball State also offers a program for the master's degree, necessary for those individuals who desire professional teaching certification or for those who wish to join the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs: (1) public school therapy programs, (2) hospital and physical therapy environment, (3) preschool nursery programs, and (4) the University Speech and Hearing Clinic. In the latter, children and adults come to the Ball State campus for therapy work for both speech and hearing problems. Theatre Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a most modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher education for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work is available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist man to understand himself. It also assists the student to understand his dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and arts of design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office, and from the theatre area chairman, and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Contributions of departments in other Colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by Directors of Elementary and Secondary Education, who are responsible to the Dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by a Teacher Education Committee, which represents the total University. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers for all levels of the elementary school with degree programs at the baccalaureate, master's, specialist in education, and doctoral levels. The Department of Secondary, Adult, and Higher Education, in addition to coordinating the total program for preparation of teachers for secondary schools, provides graduate level study in the field of curriculum and in preparation of teachers for adults and posthigh school levels. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate and graduate programs for teachers of the deaf, the mentally retarded, the orthopedically and physically handicapped, and the emotionally disturbed. Three departments of the Teachers College serve students in the areas of psychology. The Department of General Experimental Psychology offers majors and minors in the field at baccalaureate and master's degree levels. The Department of Educational Psychology specializes in applications of psychology, measurement, and research to areas particularly pertinent to teacher education and related fields in both undergraduate and graduate programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services concentrates on graduate level programs extending through the doctorate in its areas of specialization. The departments of the Teachers College, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public education and psychology; for production and dissemination of research; for innovation in instructional practices; and for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education. DEPARTMENT OF GENERAL AND EXPERIMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY Hill, Chairman; Deckers, Ganzhorn, Gates, Goldstone, Hewitt, Humm, James, McConnell, Myers, Palacios, Renke, Smith, Wittig Psychology is the science which studies the behavior of man as he interacts with his environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. Although housed within Teachers College, the Department of General and Experimental Psychology is primarily concerned with psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of man's behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The Department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all areas — teaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, business — increase their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a teaching minor, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for instructing in psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students choosing a teaching minor in psychology should choose a teaching major for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. In addition to a teaching minor, the Department offers a departmental major and minor in the disciplinary area of psychology. These programs provide a basic background for graduate work in any one of the many fields of psychology — clinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psychology, psychometry — and an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other areas such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of General and Experimental Psychology offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline, and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas on various advanced degree programs. Additionally, teachers of psychology may combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in the discipline of psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment, and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. DEPARTMENT OF SPECIAL EDUCATION Spencer, E., Head; Graves, Hoops, John, Laughlin, Richardson, Scott, Seitz, Twining, VanEvery, Wallace The philosophy of special education is that each child has the right to an education that will develop his capabilities to their fullest extent. The acceptance of and the application of this philosophy in America have led to an ever increasing demand for trained personnel in the various areas of special education. In recognition of this interest and of the need for university preparation for teachers and administrators, Ball State University has established the Department of Special Education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to certification to teach in the areas of Deaf Education, Mental Retardation, and Orthopedic and Special Health Problems. These programs are designed in accordance with teacher certification requirements of Indiana. Elective courses in special education that are open to future teachers, psychologists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, a course on the education of gifted children, and a course on the education of slow learners. Special Education for the Deaf Special education for deaf children was established at Ball State Special Education 159 University to assist at the national, state, and local levels in meeting the critical shortage of teachers for deaf children. The lack of academic instructors and professionals in related areas in residential and day schools, as well as in civic and medical centers, provides incentive enough for development of a collegiate program. The teaching minor in special education with deaf children is designed to prepare teachers for classroom instruction of the deaf. Courses include methodology in language, speech, lipreading, and basic school subjects and are designed with particular cognizance of the expressive and receptive communication barrier created by deafness. Observation of a demonstration class of preschool deaf children provides a laboratory experience early in the program. Student teaching is done at the state residential School for the Deaf in Indianapolis and/or in dayschool programs in Indiana and in neighboring states. Guidance and social counseling of deaf children are included in the program. The Ball State University program in deaf education meets approval of (1) The Indiana Teacher Training and Licensing Commission (providing certification coverage for teaching deaf children in all grades in Indiana), (2) The Conference of Executives of American Schools for the Deaf (making the qualified student eligible, upon application, to teach in the Residential Schools for the Deaf in the United States), and (3) The U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (providing the student with the opportunity to apply for federal scholarships made available to Ball State through this agency). Special Education for the Mentally Retarded Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to nationwide recognition of the special needs of mentally retarded children. To develop to the optimum of their ability, these children need a specially designed curriculum and specially prepared teachers who understand the learning process of mentally retarded children. To help alleviate the continued nationwide and statewide shortage of qualified teachers in this area of exceptionality, Ball State University prepares students to become professionally trained special class teachers. Both a teaching area major and a teaching minor are available to interested students. The teaching minor is also an endorsement for special education: teaching the mentally retarded. Special Education for Children with Orthopedic and Special Health Problems Within the group of children who have special educational needs are those who are orthopedically handicapped or who have other health conditions which make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for crippled or other healthimpaired children confronts the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a special classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The program is designed to offer comprehensive, professional preparation to future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children, so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers.
