Koenker HISTORICAL STATEMENT The Indiana State Legislature of 1923, in revising the legal status of teachers' certificates for Indiana, prescribed a year of graduate study for the issuance of firstgrade administrative and supervisory certificates. Shortly thereafter, the State Board of Education passed a resolution authorizing the two Indiana teachers colleges to offer a year of graduate work leading to the recommendation of students for the foregoing certificates and, on August 23, 1927, authorized the two Indiana teachers colleges to prepare students to secure firstgrade certificates in the administrative and supervisory fields. The legislative act of 1923 authorized the granting of administrative and supervisory certificates of three grades: first, second, and third. On June 5, 1931, and by interpretation on July 31 of the same year, the State Board of Education abandoned the issuance of all but firstgrade administrative and supervisory certificates, thus making it advisable for the University, then Ball State Teachers College, to offer work on the graduate level leading to such firstgrade certificates. In the spring of 1932 the College began the presentation of courses on the graduate level. The first master's degrees (Master of Arts in Education) were conferred in June, 1934. In response to public need and demand, the graduate program was expanded in 1937 to accommodate qualified candidates for the master's degree with specialization in certain teaching fields. The curriculum requirement for the superintendent certificate was advanced to an additional year of graduate study beyond a master's degree, effective June 1, 1947; and the curriculum requirement for the secondary school principal certificate, first grade, was advanced to an additional year of graduate study beyond a master's degree, effective, March 24, 1948. In July, 1948, the Doctor of Education degree, conferred jointly by either of the two Indiana state teachers colleges (now state universities) and Indiana University, was approved. For those master's candidates not preparing for teaching positions, the granting of the Master of Arts degree was approved in April, 1952, and the program for this degree was offered for the first time in the Autumn Quarter of 1952. The creative research project (four or eight hours) as an alternate for the research paper or thesis, and the graduate course paper plan or option leading to a master's degree, became effective March 15, 1954. In June, 1957, the Doctor of Philosophy degree to be conferred jointly by Ball State Teachers College and Purdue University was approved by the State Teachers College Board and the Trustees of Purdue University. This program was offered for the first time in the summer of 1957. The program for the Specialist in Education degree, approved in April, 1958, was offered first in the summer of 1959. In June, 1961, Ball State Teachers College was granted preliminary accreditation by the North Central Association of Colleges and Secondary Schools to offer the following doctorate level programs: the Doctor of Philosophy degree in the fields of elementary education and social science education, and the Doctor of Education degree in elementary education and social science education. These programs were offered for the first time in the autumn of 1961. In accordance with a ruling of the Teacher Training and Licensing Commission of the Indiana State Board of Education, all programs based on Bulletins 94 and 192 were closed out by the date September 1, 1967; Bulletin 400 is the basis for current programs. In April, 1966, Ball State University was granted full accreditation by the North Central Association of Colleges and Secondary Schools for the Doctor of Education degree in the fields of elementary education and social science education and continuing preliminary accreditation for the Doctor of Philosophy degree in these two fields; in addition, preliminary accreditation was given to the following five new fields leading to the Doctor of Education degree: art education, English education, science education, educational administration, and guidance and counseling. In July, 1968, Ball State University was granted preliminary accreditation by the North Central Association of Colleges and Secondary Schools for the Doctor of Education in the fields of English, science, and social science. FUNCTIONS AND OBJECTIVES OF GRADUATE WORK The primary function of the graduate program of Ball State University is to prepare master teachers, supervisors, administrators, and other personnel for public schools, colleges, and universities. Another function of the graduate program is to meet the needs of those preparing for nonteaching positions. The specific objectives of the graduate program are — 1. To enable the student, on the basis of his past experiences to extend, reinforce, and reorganize his knowledge, techniques, and skills in the field of his educational or professional interests; 2. To help the student comprehend the interrelations between his field and related fields; 3. To acquaint the student with those problems in his field which are under active attack in current and recent research, and with those problems that are now emerging and which will be subjected to significant investigation; 4. To acquaint the student with research techniques and the reported research so as to make him an effective user of standard and current educational studies; 5. To enable the student to draw practical implications from the result of research in his field; and 6. To give the student as severe an intellectual challenge as his abilities and maturity will tolerate so that he must really extend himself. SPECIALIST IN EDUCATION DEGREE (Ed.S.) The program for the Specialist in Education degree was offered for the first time in the summer of 1959. The major function of the program is to provide a plan of advanced study for those educators who need an additional year of study beyond the master's degree. The curricular program provides for a greater depth of specialization than is possible at the master's level, and each candidate's plan of study will be tailored to meet his specific needs. The Specialist in Education degree program is selfcontained and terminal in nature; however, in some cases certain courses may be applied to a doctorate program. Specific Functions The specific functions of the Specialist in Education degree program are: 1. To prepare more effective and competent elementary and secondary classroom teachers. 2. To prepare junior college and lower division college teachers. 3. To provide the candidate with the additional preparation needed for a specialized school position such as superintendent, principal, supervisor, counselor, subject specialist, subject consultant, and other specialized school personnel. Entrance Requirements In order to be eligible to be a candidate for the Specialist in Education degree, the candidate must meet the following entrance requirements: 1. The applicant must hold a master's degree from a regionally accredited institution. 2. The applicant ordinarily will be required to have had two years of successful teaching experience. 3. The applicant must be of good moral character, physically fit, and emotionally stable. Advancement to the Degree In the program of the candidate for the Specialist in Education degree there are three steps of advancement: (1) admission to graduate study, (2) admission to candidacy for the degree, and (3) completion of degree requirements. The student must apply for admission at each of these three levels. The graduate student is expected to know the requirements for the degree. While the personnel of the Graduate School will aid in every way possible, the responsibility for an error in the interpretation of the rules rests with the student. Admission to Graduate Study The candidate may apply for admission to graduate study leading to the Specialist in Education degree when he has met the entrance requirements and the following additional requirements: 1. He has submitted an application for admission. 2. He has submitted at least three satisfactory recommendations regarding character and professional qualifications. These recommendations must be sent directly to the Graduate School. 3. He has had previous institutions attended send official transcripts of all previous college work. 4. He has taken the required admission examinations. The student will arrange with the Counseling and Psychological Services Center for the taking of these examinations. The student will not be permitted to enroll a second time unless he has taken these examinations. 5. He has been approved by the Specialist in Education degree screening committee as a candidate for the degree. Admission to Candidacy for the Degree The student must apply for admission to candidacy for the Specialist in Education degree during the second week of the quarter or term in which he will complete all requirements for the degree. Completion of Degree Requirements The student will be awarded the Specialist in Education degree when he has met the following requirements: 1. He has satisfactorily completed all course requirements with at least a B average. 2. He has satisfactorily passed the final written and oral examinations. 3. He has submitted an acceptable thesis which has been approved by his committee. Committee The student's committee usually will be appointed during the first quarter of graduate work beyond the master's degree. Until the student's committee is appointed, the head of the department concerned or his delegated representative will act as the student's program adviser. The head of the department, in consultation with the candidate, will select a committee of three, including the student's adviser. The committee, in consultation with the student, will develop the student's plan of study and will guide the student's thesis. The committee, in cooperation with the Graduate School, will determine if and when the student is qualified to be admitted to graduate status, to candidacy for the degree, and finally, to the awarding of the degree. Area of Specialization Each candidate must have an area of specialization which is tailored to meet individual needs. In planning a student's program of studies the committee will take into consideration also the general education and professional education needs of the candidate. The student's plan of study will be filed in the Graduate School Office. Areas of specialization currently available are as follows: social science, industrial education, elementary education, reading specialist, elementary supervision, elementary administration, secondary administration, guidance and counseling, curriculum and instruction, school superintendency, music, health science, and psychometry. Course Requirements The student must complete, including the thesis, not fewer than 45 quarter hours of graduate work beyond the master's degree. At least threefourths of the course work must be in courses numbered at the 500- and 600-levels. The candidate will not be permitted to carry more than 17 quarter hours of graduate credit during a quarter, or 9 quarter hours of graduate credit during a summer term. If the student is employed, his course load will be reduced proportionately. At least 38 of the 45 quarter hours required for the Specialist in Education degree must be taken in residence on the Ball State University campus. All requirements for the degree must be met within a sixyear time limit from date of admission to the Specialist in Education degree program. A candidate must have a practicum experience (ID 558) when the committee is of the opinion that such an experience would be of definite value to the candidate's educational objective. A candidate for the Specialist in Education degree may on recommendation of his committee apply up to 12 quarter hours of graduate work taken beyond the master's degree toward the Specialist in Education degree if such course work does not violate other degree requirements. Residence Requirements A candidate officially admitted to the specialist program after September 1, 1962, must enroll as a fulltime resident student for one quarter during the academic year or for a summer quarter (two consecutive summer terms). Transfer and Extension Work The candidate may take up to 7 quarter hours of graduate credit in extension or residence graduate courses in other approved institutions of higher learning with prior consent of his committee. Selective Retention Admission to graduate study, graduate status, candidacy for the degree, and final awarding of the degree may be denied for unsatisfactory scholarship or on grounds of unsatisfactory physical, mental, moral, or emotional attributes. Thesis The thesis (8 quarter hours of credit, ID 598) must embody the results of a study on some subject directly related to the candidate's area of specialization. Three copies of the approved unbound thesis and four copies of an abstract of 1,200 or 1,500 words, suitable for publication, must be presented to the Graduate School in final approved form at least 10 class days before the close of the quarter or term in which the student is to be certified for graduation. However, during the Spring Quarter and Second Summer Term the approved thesis will be submitted 20 class days before the close of the quarter or term. While the concerned department has the responsibility for determining the manual or form to be followed in writing the thesis, such matters as weight of paper, typeface, spacing, and professional typing standards will be in accordance with How to Write a Term Paper, Graduate Course Paper, Research Paper, Thesis or Creative Project, available in the Ball State Bookstore. The general supervision of the thesis will be under the direction of the student's committee. The student's thesis topic must be approved in advance by his committee and the department head. After the topic has been approved, the student will enroll for ID 598, Thesis, 8 hours of credit. The student and committee chairman should check with the Graduate School for further instructions. Final Examinations All candidates will be required to pass final written and oral examinations, administered by the candidate's committee. The student must have his thesis approved by his committee and the department head before taking the final oral and written examinations. The final oral and written examinations must be taken at least 10 class days before the close of the quarter or term in which the student is to be certified. When the student satisfactorily passes the final oral and written examinations, his committee will file the signed approval form in the Graduate School Office. This final approval form is available in the Graduate School Office. Special Cases Special cases will be submitted to the Graduate Council for consideration and action. In general, the committee has jurisdiction but the Graduate Council is the board of appeal. DOCTORAL PROGRAMS Ball State University offers programs leading to the Doctor of Philosophy degree and the Doctor of Education degree in the fields listed below. In addition, Ball State University offers a joint program for the Doctor of Education degree with Indiana University in several fields of education and a joint program for the Doctor of Philosophy degree with Purdue University in several fields of education. BALL STATE DOCTORAL PROGRAMS Ball State University offers programs for two degrees at the doctoral level, as follows: Doctor of Education degree — specialization in art education, educational administration, elementary education, English education, guidance and counseling, science education, social science education, English, science, and social science. Doctor of Philosophy degree — specialization in elementary education or social science education. General Purposes and Functions The main purpose and function of the doctoral programs are to prepare college level instructors and supervisors. and supervisors and consultants for the public schools. The candidate for the Doctor of Education degree normally will pursue a program of study designed to give breadth of preparation, and the candidate for the Doctor of Philosophy degree will pursue a program designed to give a greater depth of preparation. Candidates for both degrees will be required to demonstrate competency with the necessary research tools and techniques commensurate with the degree, and with teaching skills and the fundamentals of education. Entrance Requirements Prior to admission to graduate study at the doctoral level, the following requirements must be met: 1. A person having received a baccalaureate degree and/or a master's degree not considered the equivalent of that of Ball State University may be admitted to the doctoral program under conditions to be determined in each case by the joint action of the department head and the Graduate School. 2. The applicant for the Doctor of Education degree or the Doctor of Philosophy degree, when the major is art education, education administration, elementary education, English education, guidance and counseling, science education, and social science education, must hold a valid teaching certificate and must have had at least two years of successful teaching experience or equivalent professional experience. Exceptions to the admission requirement of two years of experience must be approved by the Graduate Council. 3. The applicant must have made an outstanding scholastic record in his previous college work. 4. The applicant must be of good moral character, physically fit, and emotionally stable. Admission to Candidacy for the Doctor's Degree The student should apply for admission to candidacy for the doctor's degree when — 1. He has completed 45 quarter hours of graduate work beyond the master's degree with an outstanding scholastic record; 2. He has passed satisfactorily his preliminary written and oral examinations; 3. He has submitted a satisfactory plan for his proposed dissertation; 4. His committee is of the opinion that he is qualified to continue work leading to the doctor's degree; 5. If a student fails to meet adequately the foregoing requirements, he may be admitted to candidacy for the doctor's degree on a probationary basis, or he may be denied the privilege of further study leading to the doctor's degree. Completion of Requirements for the Doctor's Degree The student will be awarded the doctor's degree when — 1. He has completed satisfactorily all course work leading to the degree with an outstanding graduate scholastic record; 2. He has submitted two copies of a satisfactory dissertation and three copies of an abstract of the dissertation; 3. He has passed the final oral examination; 4. His committee is of the opinion that he is qualified in all respects for the degree; 5. He has completed one year of study in residence. Committee The student's committee usually will be appointed during his first or second quarter of graduate work beyond the master's degree. Until the student's committee is appointed, the head of the department concerned, or his delegated representative, will act as the student's program adviser. In conference with the student and his adviser, the Dean of the Graduate School will select the student's committee. The committee will consist of five members as follows: two from the student's area of specialization, one from each of the two cognate fields, and one from a field outside of the area of specialization and cognate fields. The committee chairman will represent the student's area of specialization. The committee for students pursuing Doctor of Education degree programs in art education, English education, science education, and social science education will consist of five members as follows: two representing the subject area, two from Teachers College, and a member at large appointed by the Dean of the Graduate School. The committee, on consultation with the student, will determine the student's plan of study and will guide the student's dissertation. The student's plan of study will be filed in the Graduate School. The committee, in cooperation with the Graduate School, will determine when the student is qualified to continue further study at each of the three stages leading to the doctor's degree: (1) admission to advanced graduate status, (2) admission to candidacy for the degree, and (3) the awarding of the degree. Area of Specialization Each candidate will have an area of specialization. The minimum requirement for the area of specialization will be 60 hours of graduate work beyond the bachelor's degree, including a basic core of required courses. A maximum of 15 hours of credit will be allowed for the dissertation. When the area of specialization on the Doctor of Education degree is art education, English education, science education, or social science education, the area of specialization will be 80 quarter hours as follows: 40 quarter hours in subject field including teaching skills, e.g., SS 690; 40 quarter hours in education including a course in history and philosophy of education, educational psychology, tests and measurements, research techniques, and EDHI 610. Credit for HIST 611, ID 699 (Doctor's Dissertation, 15 quarter hours), and ID 605 are required, however, credit will not apply toward the area of specialization, but will be utilized as electives. The student will also take one or more graduate courses in each of four different fields within art, English, science, or social science. These courses must be related to the area of specialization. Such courses are not to be counted in the area of specialization. All candidates for the Doctor of Education degree and the Doctor of Philosophy degree will take at least one course at the graduate level in each of the following five areas: history and philosophy of education, educational psychology, tests and measurements, research techniques, and teaching skills. All doctoral candidates will take ID 605, Research Colloquium, each of the three quarters while in residence; EDHI 610, Introduction to the Problems of Higher Education; and HIST 611, Seminar in Social and Intellectual History of the United States. In addition, doctoral candidates in elementary education will take EDEL 698, Advanced Seminar in Elementary Education, each of the three quarters while in residence; and doctoral candidates in social science teacher education will take SS 690, Teaching of Social Science in Higher Education, each of the three quarters while in residence. Cognate Fields The candidate will have two cognate fields of study which are related to, or in support of, the area of specialization. When the area of specialization on the Doctor of Education degree is art education, English education, science education, or social science education, the student has only one cognate area. The minimum course requirements for a cognate field will be 26 quarter hours of graduate work beyond the bachelor's degree, 11 quarter hours of which must be taken at Ball State University. Cognates are available in all major fields of study offered on the master's degree, specialist degree, and cooperative doctor's degrees. In addition, cognates are offered in: teacher education in higher education, adult and community education, the teaching of English when the major is English. Course Requirements The student must complete, including the dissertation, not fewer than a total of 135 quarter hours of graduate work beyond the bachelor's degree. Courses taken beyond the master's degree will be taken at the 500 and 600 levels. The candidate will not be permitted to carry more than 17 quarter hours of graduate work during a quarter, or 9 quarter hours of graduate work during any summer term. If the student is employed, the amount of graduate work he will be permitted to carry will be reduced proportionately. Residence, Transfer, and Extension Work At least three consecutive quarters of graduate work beyond the master's degree must be taken in residence at Ball State University. During the year of residence the student will complete a minimum of 36 quarter hours of credit. The candidate ordinarily will complete a minimum of 70 of the required 135 quarter hours of graduate work on the Ball State University campus. Not more than 19 of the 135 quarter hours of graduate work may be taken In extension classes. If the candidate holds a masters degree from Ball State University, up to 65 of the 135 quarter hours of graduate work may be taken in other approved institutions of higher learning with permission of the student's committee and the Grad - uate School. Selective Retention Admission to advanced graduate study, advanced graduate status, and can didacy for the degree, and the final awarding of the degree may be denied for unsatisfactory scholarsh ip' or onphysical, mental, moral a, nd emotional grounds. These examinations will be administered near the time of completion of the course work. The written examinations will be taken during a period of one week. Under extenuating circumstances these examinations may be spread over a period of two weeks. On the satisfactory completion of these preliminary examinations, as well as the two foreign language examinations for the Doctor of Philosophy degree, the student will be approved as a candidate for the doctor's degree. During the first two weeks of the final quarter or term of the student's work, he must make application for graduation. The candidate will take a final oral examination covering his course work and dissertation. The student may be required, also, to take such other written examinations as the committee sees fit. These examinations will be administered by the student's committee. When the student has passed these examinations successfully, he will be recommended formally to receive the degree. The candidate must complete all degree requirements at least 10 class days before the end of the quarter or term in which he intends to graduate. Dissertation The general supervision of the dissertation will be under the direction of the student's committee chairman. All members of his committee will advise the candidate on his dissertation whenever their assistance may be needed. The student will not enroll for dissertation (ID 699) until he has passed his preliminary written and oral examinations and has had his dissertation topic approved by his committee. The dissertation for the Doctor of Education degree candidate normally will be a study that will contribute to the solution of some important educational problem. The dissertation for the Doctor of Philosophy degree candidate will be a research problem that will contribute new knowledge or a new technique. Following the final oral examination, two typed and unbound copies of the completed dissertation, bearing the committee's approval, must be filed in the Graduate School, and in addition, three copies of an abstract of the dissertation, 500 to 600 words in length ; suitable forpublication. Dissertations will be microfilmed University Microfilms, Ann Arbor, Michigan, for which the student will pay a fee of $25 or more, depending on the length of the dissertation. Special Requirements for Research Competency The doctoral candidate will be expected to demonstrate competency with those research tools needed for his area of specialization. Such tools include foreign languages, statistical methods, and research techniques. All candidates will not be required necessarily to demonstrate competency in all or the same tools of research; however, it is expected that all Doctor of Philosophy degree candidates will have a functional reading knowledge of two foreign languages. The student's committee in consultation with the student will select the foreign language or languages required. The examining committee will consist of the head of the Foreign Language Department, the foreign language specialist, and the student's committee chairman or a member of the appropriate department appointed by the department head. The examination will consist of translating appropriate materials in his subject field selected by the student's committee. The student will be permitted the use of the appropriate foreign language dictionary at the time of the examination. The foreign language examination(s) must be passed before the student takes his preliminary oral and written examinations. Time Allowed After the student has been admitted to graduate status at the doctoral level, all requirements for the degree are to be met within a sixyear period. DOCTOR'S DEGREE — IN COOPERATION (INDIANA UNIVERSITY) Since July 26, 1948, the two Indiana state teachers colleges (now state universities) and Indiana University have collaborated in granting jointly a Doctor of Education degree. The first year of graduate work beyond the master's degree can be completed at either Ball State University or Indiana State University, and the second year of graduate work beyond the master's degree must be completed in residence at Indiana University. Upon completion of all requirements for the Doctor of Education degree, the candidate will be awarded the degree with an indication that the degree is granted by Indiana University in cooperation with the state university with which the recipient has been associated.* Advancement to the Degree The steps toward meeting the requirements for the Doctor of Education degree are (1) admission to graduate status; (2) approval of candidacy for the Doctor of Education degree; (3) passing the preliminary examination; (4) completion of required course work and thesis; and (5) passing the final oral examination. Admission to Graduate Status The student may make application for admission to graduate status leading to the Doctor of Education degree after he has met the following requirements: 1. He has submitted transcripts of record of all previous college work, showing graduation from an accredited college or university with a master's degree and not fewer than 28 quarter hours in education in accepted and proper sequence. 2. He has maintained an average grade of 3.6 (A=4, B= 3, C = 2, D=1) or better in all graduate work taken. 3. He has satisfactorily passed a physical examination at the University Health Service. Joint Approval Any person desiring to become a candidate for the Doctor of Education degree must be approved by the Dean of the Graduate School, Ball State University, and the Dean of the School of Education, Indiana University. Admission may be denied because of unsatisfactory scholarship or unfitness to engage in the profession of education on physical, mental, moral, or emotional grounds. When the applicant is deficient in undergraduate requirements in education, admission may be denied until such deficiencies are removed. Any student who has been admitted to graduate status leading to the Doctor of Education degree but who fails to meet scholastic and other requirements may be denied the privilege of further study on this curriculum. Joint Committee After approval, a committee shall be appointed by the Dean of the Graduate School, Ball State University, and the Dean of the School of Education, Indiana University. This committee will consist of five members. At least two members of the committee will be selected from the faculty of Ball State University. The fifth member of the committee will represent the candidate's minor area of study and will be selected from the institution where the candidate completes the outside minor. Therefore, if the candidate completes the course requirements for the outside minor at Ball State University, three members of the candidate's committee will be selected from the Ball State faculty. The committee will guide the candidate's subsequent work for the completion of the requirements for the degree. When the student is doing work at Ball State University, his official adviser will be a member of his committee from the Ball State faculty. During the last year of work the candidate's official adviser will be a member of his committee from the Indiana University School of Education faculty. The thesis adviser will be a member of the student's committee from the staff of the School of Education at Indiana University. Preliminary Examinations When the candidate has completed approximately 80 of the required minimum 144 quarter hours of graduate work, he shall take the preliminary written examination and preliminary oral examination. These examinations may be taken at either Ball State University or Indiana University. If the candidate passes the written examination and the oral examination and in the opinion of his committee is qualified to continue work on the Doctor of Education degree, he is then so certified by the joint committee as a qualified candidate for the degree. The written examination is designed to test the proficiency of the candidate in the required basic courses in education, in courses in his major field in education, and also in his minor field if a minor is taken in education. The oral examination is designed to test the candidate in the fields of education represented by the required basic courses and to test his ability to react in a creditable manner in dealing orally with professional subjects. Educational philosophy: 501, Philosophy of Education (ED-FON 530, Philosophy of Education). 3. Educational psychology: 511, Advanced Educational Psychology (EDEL or EDSEC 576, Recent Research on the Teaching of School Subjects). 517B, Psychology of Individual Differences (EDPSY 500, Advanced Educational Psychology: Learning). 4. Curriculum: 535, Supervision of the Elementary Curriculum (EDCUR 500, Principles and Procedures of Curriculum Development). 537, High School Curriculum (EDCUR 500, Principles and Procedures of Curriculum Development). 5. Measurements: 517, Theory and Application of Mental Measurements (EDPSY 546, Tests and Measurements) or 532, Educational Measurements (EDPSY 546, Tests and Measurements). DOCTOR'S DEGREE — IN COOPERATION (PURDUE UNIVERSITY) Since June, 1957, Ball State University and Purdue University have collaborated in granting jointly a Doctor of Philosophy degree (in guidance). The first year of graduate work beyond the master's degree ordinarily will be completed at Ball State University; the second year of graduate work beyond the master's degree will be completed in residence at Purdue University. Upon completion of all requirements for the Doctor of Philosophy degree, the candidate will be awarded the degree with the understanding that the degree is granted jointly by Ball State University and Purdue University. Admission of Students to the Program The steps listed below will be followed by students desiring admission to the cooperative Doctor of Philosophy degree program: 1. The graduate student ordinarily will complete the master's degree at Ball State University. 2. On completion of the master's degree, the student will make application to the Dean of the Graduate School of Purdue University for admission as a regular graduate student at Purdue University. 3. The candidate will be expected to pass satisfactorily the standardized examinations required of all applicants for admission as regular graduate students. Major Professor and Advisory Committee A student accepted to work on the cooperative degree program will follow the procedures outlined below: 1. The student will select a major professor at Purdue University in conference with the graduate student counselor of the Graduate Committee of the Division of Education. 2. In conference with the major professor the student will select, and request the appointment of, an advisory committee of five members, to include the major professor, two additional faculty members from Purdue University, and two faculty members from Ball State University. The appointment of this committee will be made by the Dean of the Graduate School of Purdue University and approved by the Dean of the Graduate School of Ball State University. 3. The advisory committee and the graduate student will develop the student's tentative plan of study. This tentative plan will be submitted for approval to both the Dean of the Graduate School of Purdue University and the Dean of the Graduate School of Ball State University. The Plan of Study The plan of study must be developed according to the following general provisions, including such courses from the master's degree program as are appropriate to the purpose of the Doctor of Philosophy degree program: 1. One year of course work beyond the master's degree ordinarily should be completed at Ball State University, provided the courses are available. While the student is at Ball State University, one of the Ball State faculty members of the advisory committee will serve as the student's adviser. The entire advisory committee may be called upon to consider matters relative to the student's progress. 2. At least two consecutive semesters of graduate work must be done in residence at Purdue University. A thesis and a minimum of 15 semester hours of course credit beyond the master's degree will be completed in residence at Purdue University unless permission is granted to work on the thesis in part in absentia. Such permission may be granted provided the following requirements have been met satisfactorily: (1) the foreign language requirement, (2) the preliminary examinations, (3) appropriate facilities for research, (4) adequate time for research, and (5) adequate supervision by a member of the faculty of Purdue University. 3. The student will be required (1) to pass two foreign language examinations, or (2) to pass one foreign language examination and earn six semester hours of advanced statistics or other approved research techniques in addition to the regular course work included in the plan of study. Preliminary Examinations Preliminary written examinations covering all course work will be conducted by the members of the advisory committee. Each member will read and evaluate the completed paper covering the areas for which he has responsibility. The examinations will be administered near the time of the completion of the course work, at least one academic year in advance of the time of awarding the degree. Following the written examinations, a preliminary oral examination will be administered by the entire advisory committee. On the satisfactory completion of the preliminary written and oral examinations as well as the two language examinations or one language examination and the six semester hours of advanced statistics or other approved research techniques, the student will be recommended as a candidate for the doctoral degree. Dissertation Research The general supervision of the dissertation research will be under the direction of the major professor. All of the members of the advisory committee will advise the candidate on his research project and on the writing of the thesis whenever their assistance may be needed. Publication of a Thesis The requirement as to publication of a thesis will be met by its microfilming. The availability of the dissertation in film form will be announced by a printing of the graduate's own abstract in Dissertation Abstracts. A microfilm copy will be deposited in the library at Ball State University and one in the library of Purdue University, and these copies will be available on interlibrary loan. Publication by microfilm will not preclude a printing of the dissertation, in whole or in part, in a journal or as a monograph. Final Examinations In addition to the usual current examination administered in major or minor course work, the student will be required to take such final examinations over his major subject and thesis as the examining committee may require. The final examinations will be conducted by a committee appointed by the Dean of the Graduate School at Purdue University, and approved by the Dean of the Graduate School at Ball State University. The major professor will serve as chairman of this committee. When the candidate has successfully passed these examinations, he will be recommended formally to receive the degree. CURRICULA: BACCALAUREATE DEGREES General Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The General Arts Curriculum is a program in general studies and selected concentration areas. It leads to either the Bachelor of Arts or Bachelor of Science degree. This curriculum is recommended for degree candidates who are undecided about specific educational goals in respect to graduate work, professional schools, and intensive specialization. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 48 hours approved by the department or (2) two departmental minors, 24-36 hours, approved by the departments. Physical education: General courses 6 hrs. Electives: As many hours of credit in electives as are needed to increase the total of hours to 186. Liberal Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The Liberal Arts Curriculum provides opportunity for a search for general knowledge and for specialization primarily for development of intellectual capacities. In general studies the range is extensive; in areas of specialization the goal is depth of a sufficiency to demonstrate a degree of mastery in the selected areas. It is also possible in many cases for a student to fulfill the requirements of both the liberal arts curriculum and for teacher certification. To do so, the student must be enrolled in and meet the requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum as approved by the Teacher Education Committee of Ball State University. Such a decision will require careful choice of courses and the student should plan his program with the help of his adviser. The degree to which the curriculum leads is the Bachelor of Arts. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Foreign language: One foreign language 24 hrs.' Concentration areas: (1) One departmental major of 45-60 hours and at least one departmental minor of 24-48 hours in another discipline, or (2) two departmental majors of 45-60 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statements of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Professional Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1-6 of Curricular Information.) The Professional Arts Curriculum provides for specialization to qualify for appointments in specific professional areas or for admission to professional schools which provide more intensive preparation for the desired professional or vocational competency. The degree is the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science, and if the major is architecture, the degree is the Bachelor of Architecture. Teacher Education Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees; Certificates for Teaching; and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The Teacher Education Curriculum is designed to prepare students for teaching in the elementary or secondary areas of the public schools of Indiana. It meets the requirements of the Teacher Training and Licensing Division of the State Board of Education of Indiana. UNDERGRADUATE PROGRAMS Description of Course Identification System Each prefix has its own numbering system, with a potential of numbers from 100 through 699. Courses numbered from 100 to 199 are primarily freshman courses. Courses numbered from 200 to 299 are primarily sophomore courses. Courses numbered from 300 to 399 are primarily junior courses. Courses numbered from 400 to 499 are primarily senior courses. Courses numbered from 500 up are for graduate students. Courses numbered from 600 to 699 are for graduate students with masters' degrees. In course descriptions the course number is given immediately following the prefix. If a number in parentheses follows, it is the immediately preceding number of the course. The student who has credit in a course under the parenthetical number, or any former number, may not earn credit in the course under its current number except under the terms of Course Repetition (see Credit and Grades). In the course description the number in parentheses following the descriptive title of the course is the credithour value of the course. It denotes the specific total of credit hours which may be earned in the course unless elsewhere in the description is a statement which permits the earning of a larger total of credit hours. Prerequisite refers to a course or courses which must precede the course described. Parallel indicates a course or courses which must be taken simultaneously with the described course. Two fiveyear programs of study are offered: the departmental major in architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Architecture degree; and the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree. The first two years of both programs are concurrent and include a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. The Ball State general studies program is an integral part of these first two years. The last three years provide specialization in the fields of architectural or landscape design as well as providing for specialized study in areas of the student's own choosing. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning represent a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophy. By exposure to the variety of philosophical and technical backgrounds of creative professionals, the student is encouraged to seek his own personal philosophy within a professional teamwork situation. The curricula stress character, devotion, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility. The total program is concerned with the development of a physical environment serving the best of man's aspirations. The architect must develop social awareness, creative ability, technical understanding, administrative ability, and business acuity. The program in architecture at Ball State University stresses the variety necessary in the educational background of an architect. Intellectual and cultural preparation should be as thorough as possible; therefore, the general studies courses are from the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. An area of study in depth and certain courses within the major provide further breadth and depth in general studies. The specialized courses provide for technical competence. Courses in architectural design provide experience in the integrative process of design. Thus the total program, which calls for five years of preparation, provides not only for comprehension of acceptable procedures and methods but also for stimulation of the creative process in environmental problem solving. Architecture and Planning 79 323, 324, 325, 342, 351, 402, 403, 413, 427, 431, PROGRAM IN LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE Landscape architecture is dedicated to conserving and improving the quality of man's environment. It is concerned with the quality of water, the quality of air, the quality of land --how they affect man's relationship to man as well as to nature. The landscape architect approaches this task with the realization that he cannot succeed alone, but must work with the allied professions such as architecture, planning, engineering, sociology, and economics. It is toward this goal of working with others for the improvement of the human environment that this program is directed; never before have the challenges been so great. In order to achieve his goals, the landscape architect must be aware of human needs. To meet these needs he must be concerned with the natural sciences so he can speak for nature in a world that is constantly being altered by man. The understanding of nature's processes and the ability to design in terms of earth, water, and plants enable the landscape architect not just to organize but to greatly enrich man's environment. The program stresses the need for variety in the education of a landscape architect. The general studies program (humanities, natural sciences, social and behavioral studies) is a vital part of the intellectual and cultural preparation of young men and women for professional practice. The core program in design provides further contact with the general studies program as well as developing capabilities in solving small to large scale problems. The program stresses the collective approach to solving problems yet recognizes the individual and his contribution. Specialized courses provide for technical competency. It is the aim of the fiveyear program to encourage creativity and to develop sound procedures for creating an environment which is beneficial to man and nature. To make intelligent decisions in the effective planning and controlling of the operations of a business, management must know the effect of transactions on its financial position and its earning power. The accountant as a student of management problems endeavors to meet reporting requirements and to present his data in terms of management's needs. The study of accounting is a vital part in the educational preparation of any executive and is useful in all types of business careers. Contact with all aspects and levels of business enables the accountant to acquire excellent training for executive leadership. Many and varied careers are available to the accountant both in the types of organizations and in the areas of specialization he may select. title: Beginning Typewriting
description: Principles of touch typewriting with emphasis upon technique and fluency. Only students with no secondary school credit in typewriting or with less than one semester of typewriting are eligible to receive credit in this course unless special permission is granted by the department head.

title: Intermediate Typewriting
description: Review of typewriting principles with emphasis on the development of speed and accuracy. Problems included on the application of typewriting skill to simple business situations. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one semester of secondary school typewriting.

title: Advanced Typewriting
description: Advanced, problems in typewriting including preparation of school papers and manuscripts, tabulations, rough drafts, legal documents, and business forms; continuation of speed and accuracy development. title: Office Typewriting
description: Office typing problems with emphasis on preparation of materials by various typewritten media; composition of reports, memoranda, and letters; handwritten and typewritten draft copy. title: Business Correspondence
description: Principles and techniques of effective letter writing; letter mechanics; writing of personal business letters including application letters, 38 hrs. 18-21 hrs. 12-25 hrs. fundamentals of English grammar and usage needed in business writing.

description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 2
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirements for BEOA 285. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisite: BEOA 285 or equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 3
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirement for BEOA 286. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisites: BEOA 285 and 286 or the equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Beginning Shorthand 1
description: Special emphasis upon basic theory and speed in reading from plate notes. Introduction to dictation with stress on brief forms. A student whose secondary school transcript shows two or more credits in shorthand is not eligible to receive credit in this course. Prerequisite or parallel: BEOA 111 or equivalent.

title: Beginning Shorthand 2
description: Completion of basic theory and increased emphasis upon development of skill in taking dictation. A student whose secondary school transcript shows credit for more than one semester of shorthand is not eligible to receive credit in this course. Prerequisite: BEOA 321.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Contin_ ued review of fundamentals; continued ern._ phasis on skill in taking dictation with some emphasis on transcription. Open to those students who have had BEOA 322 and stu_ dents whose secondary school transcript shows one year of shorthand. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent.

title: Advanced Shorthand 1
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, transcription, and production of mailable copy. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and at least two years of secondary school shorthand or BEOA 323.

title: Advanced Shorthand 2
description: Special emphasis upon production of mailable copy, and continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and BEOA 324.

title: Calculating Machines
description: Developing skill in using electronic calculators and other common office calculating machines as tools; emphasis is placed on developing the manipulative skills and programming abilities used to solve problems involving business data.

title: Duplicating, Machine Transcribing, and Filing
description: Preparation of ink stencils and carbon masters; operation of ink and liquid duplicators; training in machine dictation and machine transcription; indexing, coding, and filing of business correspondence; and survey of filing equipment and supplies. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems: the nature, function, and use of business papers; knowledges, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining of records of a business office, and study of records administration in business and industry.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects A
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, general business, typing, and related office skills. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250; student will have completed his requirements in typewriting and accounting. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option A.

title: Methods of Teaching Distributive Subjects
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson and unit planning; overview of cooperative education and project plan programs. The various distributive subjects are included. Prerequisite: EDPSY

title: Methodology of Relevant Work Experiences in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledges needed by persons who will be supervising and directing a cooperative education or a project plan program in distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Distributive Education
description: The principles upon which vocational distributive education is organized, administered, and supervised; the kinds of programs; federal and state regulations; relationships to programs in other vocational areas. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a teaching license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Business Communications
description: Composition and study of effective written business Economics 87 communications including business letters and simple reports; solutions to communications problems. Particularly designed for business students.

title: Business Report Writing
description: Principles and mechanics of formal and informal report writing; collecting, organizing, interpreting and summarizing data; principles of tabular and graphic presentation of information; mechanics of report style. Prerequisite: ability to type and MGT 380.

title: Secretarial Administration
description: Administrative aspects of toplevel, professional secretarial work. Emphasis on how to perform such specialized duties as the evaluation of equipment and communications media and how to assist an executive in his various tasks relating to travel, meetings, reporting, and maintaining his records. Prerequisite: BEOA 325.

title: Principles of Business and Distributive Education
description: Historical development of the field of business education. Possible future trends and their effect on the entire business education program. Open only to students who have been approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Evaluative Instruments in Business and Distributive Education
description: The importance of measurements, techniques of administering and scoring tests, methods of analyzing and recording test results, uses of tests, construction of tests for classroom use in all areas of business education. Department of Economics Hannaford, Chairman; Cheng, Ellingson, Girgis, Jost, Lawson, Pickerill, Rocha, Sorathia Economics is a study of human wants and of man's efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative— relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. Among the standard categories of scarce resources in the study of economics is, first of all, labor; and courses in labormanagement relations, labor law, collective bargaining, wage theory, social security, and workmen's compensation are standard parts of university curricula in economics. Besides the study of all aspects of labor as a scarce resource, economics is concerned with the manmade resource of production called capital. For example, the accumulation of capital is *a central aspect of the growth of underdeveloped countries. Economics courses called developmental economics have appeared in most universities, with separate courses being established for different backward countries or areas. The concept of interest as a physical product of physical capital equipment gives rise to courses in money and banking. A study of the valuation of the scarce resources created by nature is included in the curriculum of most universities as "land economics." While the fact of the scarcity of resources is the taproot of economics, the branches of the discipline are composed of specialized studies of the selection of alternative uses for resources. The rationale for the selection of the use pattern which will leave the least gross total of human wants unfilled varies from society to society, but normally some variant of voluntary exchange is institutionally developed. The vast complexity of the institutional exchange arrangements developed in modern society requires a set of theoretical explanations that must be equally complex. Certain classifications of exchange have unique theoretical characteristics such as an atypical number of sellers and/or buyers or supply and demand of unusual behavior, and special economics courses are devised to explore their theoretical peculiarities and significances. An example is agricultural economics. The exchange medium (money) again requires an examination of the theoretical aspects of money and of the banking arrangements which generate and control the supply of the medium of exchange. The use of scarce resources by a society involves the society's decision on the fraction of total resources that will be consumed by the community as a unit. Social consumption of resources in a discipline concerned with the scarcity of them necessarily involves economics in the total theoretical aspects of taxation and government expenditure. The exchange arrangements developed in this society and in other societies are of exhausting variations at any one point in time and have changed over time. This change is a central part of economic history which is taught as several separate courses on some university campuses. The heterogeneity of exchange dynamics, even when reduced to simplified theoretical classifications, is so remarkable that several courses in market theory are necessary if the university student's grasp of the economic aspects of even his own society is to be carried beyond the elementary level. To understand the production, exchange, and consumption arrangements in other societies requires courses in comparative economic systems. Certainly the exchanging of goods and resources through the use of a medium of exchange has one of its most sophisticated (and important) aspects when the exchange occurs across national boundaries. Therefore, international trade is an old and established part of economics offerings in all universities. The interrelations among exchange decisions produce economywide effects that result in a greater or lesser intensity with which resources are used and in specific resources growing or declining at explainable rates. The explanations of the intensity with which total resources are used and of changes in the total of each are studied under the general rubric of macroeconomics. The legal framework for exchange decisions gives the study of economics a sharp concern with the governmental agencies that set the limits of legal exchange activity. title: The Economics of the Ghetto
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. The theory of wages, rent, interest, and profits. The principles of international trade and comparative economic organization. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite:

title: Economic Policies and Problems of Agriculture
description: Examination of the special economic conditions of demand and supply pertaining to agriculture and of problems created by changing national and international situations. Analysis of agricultural policy programs and implications of farm policy for consumers. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 200 or 201.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how man has looked at his economic life surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 270.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 431.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry: concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Development in Latin America
description: The evaluation of theories of economic development. Sources and consequences of the economic growth and development process in Latin America analyzed in the context of economic theory. Attention to Common Market possibilities, monetaryfiscal factors, and trade and exchange. Examination of current national and international programs as promoters of development.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Each student will pursue his interest in a specialized economics subject under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in economics. This background provides for an understanding of the interrelationships of the functions in business and a means of preparing the graduate of the program to fit into the general administration of a business. In addition, a student is expected to select areas of concentration in which he can obtain a proficiency beyond that acquired in an introductory or principles course. Four areas in which depth may be had are finance, law, insurance, and management. Particularly there is an opportunity to specialize in the fields of finance and of management. The management program is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them as future business executives and specialists to deal with the diversity of problems which arise in the course of daytoday business activity. The finance program is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activity. The insurance program is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. The law courses are quite broad and include the fundamentals of many essential law disciplines. These law courses are highly recommended to students in prelaw preparation. In addition to these specialized purposes, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students on other areas in the College of Business. Any student in the university may take the course in personal finance, which is offered especially to provide the general business information everyone should know.
