Classroom and laboratory instruction for the curriculum is provided by the University and utilizes the facilities of Ball Memorial Hospital, adjacent to the University campus, as well as other nearby health agency facilities. The curriculum has been planned to provide general and professional educational experiences for the beginning student in nursing and the registered nurse who seeks a baccalaureate education in nursing. The registered nurse may request permission to be granted credit by examination for the courses NUR 310, 311, 316, 317, and 410 if she has the transcripts to verify her previous educational experiences. Thirty quarter hours are the maximum of college credits to be earned in nursing courses by examination. A student indicating an intent for a major in nursing begins his or her study in areas of English, social sciences, physical and biological sciences, and the fine arts. Approximately two years of academic work in the areas of humanities, social and behavioral sciences, and biological sciences are required. The major in nursing has been concentrated in the student's junior and senior years. Cooperative programs in nursing have been arranged between Ball State University and Anderson College, Eastern Indiana Center of Earlham College, Huntington College, Marion College, and Taylor University. A student interested in the cooperative program may enroll at one of these institutions for the freshman and sophomore years and transfer these credits to Ball State University for the remaining two years. The curriculum for students preparing for professional nursing is the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in nursing and a minor in biological science. The Bachelor of Science degree may be earned within the minimum requirements of the curriculum (186 hours), and the student may use toward a selected minor the 28 to 32 hours of electives on the curriculum. The student shall meet the general requirements of the University with respect to the professional nursing major and minor in biological science and with respect to graduation (minimum of 2.0 scholastic ratio in major, required minor, and overall grade point average); in addition the student will present a minimum grade of C in each clinical nursing course. The student is responsible for making application for admission to the major in nursing after he has completed 60 quarter hours of work. Evaluation of achievement in the first seven courses in the minor in biological science (CHEM 110, 111, 130; BIO 111, 112; ANAT 201; and PHYSL 210) is necessary before admission to the major. The guiding philosophy of the Department of Nursing has been predicated upon the belief that the aims of the University should be realized in the educational preparation of the professional nurse. It has been accepted that the professional nurse is characterized by the ability (1) to provide intelligent and skillful nursing to patients and their families in all of the basic nursing fields, (2) to guide and direct others in the performance of nursing care, (3) to utilize the democratic process for the improvement of the health services through cooperative endeavor with members of other disciplines, and (4) to maintain a personal identity and to attain individual satisfaction in daily life as the family, the community, and the profession are served. The Department of Nursing accepts the responsibility for fostering a maximal development of the student in nursing which should resolve in an optimal contribution to the profession of nursing and to society. It is believed .that the basic preparation of an individual should provide for the total development of the person. The faculty is dedicated to this realization through a synthesis of the strands of a broad cultural experience in general education with an educational experience in the professional content of nursing. The departmental objectives for students in nursing are: 1. To acquire knowledge, skills, and attitudes which will provide the foundation for the administering of comprehensive nursing to the patient and his family; 2. To develop a concept of nursing which encompasses the prevention of illness, the promotion of health for the individual, the family, and the community, as well as the care of the sick; 3. To develop an understanding of s elf and an appreciation for each nurse's contri. bution to the profession and to society . 4. To develop skill in effective hum an; relations and communications with patient s family, and coleagues; , 5. To acquire an understanding and r ec, ognition of the nurse's responsibility as a contributing member of the health team; 6. To develop an ability for critical thi nk. ing, value judgments, and selfdirectio n which wil enable the studento become a contributing member in the nursing profession and in society; 7. To develop an understanding of th e ned for continuous profesional and personal growth which includes participation and leadership in the social, cultural, and educational world. The nursing course sequence begins with NUR 200. Clinical nursing in the five basic areas is begun by the student in his junior year. It is recommended that all students enrolled in nursing report their names and current addresses to the Department of Nursing each quarter. The liberal arts programs permit the student to elect more freely and to explore the "idea" subject matter. "Liberal" stems from the Latin liber, to free. By definition, a liberal arts education should free man from ignorance by providing him an intelligent grasp of the experiences of the past and an understanding of the interrelationship of branches of knowledge. The individual is educated to think objectively, critically, and creatively. The liberal arts include the study of foreign languages, the physical and social environment, the evolution of Western civilization, the foundations of modern science, and the classical works of man. Also, the departments within the College have programs designed for those planning graduate study in the field of their choice. Department of Anthropology Scruton, Chairman; Flores-Meiser, Glenn, Swartz, Wallace, Whitehead Anthropology is scarcely a hundred years old as a formal academic discipline. Its origins are in the nineteenth century's growing awareness of non-European societies, the revelation that man's social past is of great antiquity, and the discovery by Charles Darwin of the biological mechanisms which have produced the human species. From these several awakenings has emerged a field which, as developed in this country, is neither a biological nor a social science, but is uniquely both. It is, in fact, the singular amalgamation of the two areas which is responsible for the name of the field, the Study of Man. Although the anthropologist, as a practicing scholar, develops a limited specialty, the field itself remains convinced that man is a sociobiological whole and must finally be studied as such. This belief places a certain burden on the anthropologist and the student by requiring, for professional competence, a very wide range of content areas. In physical anthropology, for example, attention is commonly focused on such topics as the nature of the evolutionary process which is responsible, through the action of natural selection, hybridization, genetic drift and artificial selection, for the development of the largetailless, terrestrial, bipedal, orthograde primate which man is. Course work is commonly devoted to the fossil evidence of man's recent evolution, especially during the Pleistocene period. Without doubt, that aspect of physical anthropology which has the greatest potential contribution to make to man's selfunderstanding, and the aspect likeliest to be of practical application, is the study of contemporary varieties, or races, of man. There is no subject about which men seem to have the most fundamental convictions, and commonly there is none in which the unfortunate effects of total ignorance are more clearly seen. The anthropologist is deeply involved in all phases of this study, from the determination of the nature of the phenomenon itself, through the eventual genetic classification of races, to the delicate and vexing questions having to do with the significance of race differences. The pursuit of truth is the goal of the scientist. But the application of knowledge which has been secured through the scientific method is hardly avoidable. Much of cultural anthropology is closely related to history and no branch illustrate s this fact more clearly than archaeology. Courses in this area provide the student of man's past with techniques which enable many of the limitations of conventional historiography to be overcome, with the result that we now possess knowledge of human b e_ havior during times antedating writing by sometimes hundreds of thousands of years. Of course, this knowledge is rarely of the detailed and specific sort sought by the historian. But although he is commonly deprived of historical personalities, the archaeologist has the compensation of seeing the great sweep of human affairs with perhaps greater clarity. The archaeologist reminds the student that it was during prehistoric times that most of the great steps in human progress were made: the development of technology, the creation of forms of government, kinship, religion, philosophy, and art. The archaeologist also reminds the student through appropriate courses of the long and fruitful cooperation between the historian and the prehistorian, which has been responsible for the bulk of our knowledge of the ancient world of classical times, including Egypt, the Near East, Greece, Crete, and early Rome. Preparation in anthropology customarily involves some work in the field of linguistics. This is a most highly specialized area, and thorough preparation through detailed courses is less common than in the other areas. But introduction to the broad subdivisions of descriptive and historical linguistics helps to acquaint the student with more than a mere modicum of knowledge about the techniques and history of human communication, which is the most distinctive characteristic of the human animal, setting him apart, as no other single fact does, from infrahumans. It is linguistics which, in recent years, has begun to make students aware that talking is more than simply a method of communicating ideas between speakers of the same language; it is the vehicle of thought itself, and it provides the speaker not only with categories of expression, but also with the means at once of perceiving and of ordering his universe. At this point linguistics is very close to cultural anthropology. Modern cultural anthropology has grown out of the nineteenth century's interest in the accounts by travelers, explorers, mission- Anthropology 151 cries, and soldiers of the frea uently astonishing and sometimes hostile people whom they had met. Much of the work of the cultural anthropologist, or ethnologist, has been the gathering of accurate information about the world's nonliterate peoples. Modern ethnology, it should be noted, places little stress on the word "primitive," having been driven by the data to the conclusion that it does not separate categories of men very efficiently. But from this early interest in different societies has developed anthropology's increasingly sophisticated analysis of culture, that amorphous yet systematic mass of learned behavior patterns which provides human societies with the means to survival. Much comparative work has been done, and courses in anthropology departments reflect this, in crosscultural studies of religion, kinship and family systems, governments, technologies, value and belief systems, literatures, modes of aesthetic expression in song, dance, and the graphic and plastic arts, among other institutions. Anthropology wrestles with countless unsolved problems in the area of relations between personalities and the social milieu in which they occur and in the area of cultural dynamics. The possibilities of practical application are numerous, and are, increasingly, being exploited. These several areas, and others which may develop, are all related through anthropology's constant emphasis on the "wholeness" of man. title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man as a biological unit of the animal kingdom. The human fossil record, living primates, and criteria of race and the races of man, elementary anthropometry, adaptive mechanisms, principles of biological evolution, and human genetics.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: Man's cultural achievements from their beginnings into historic times. Man's cultural development will be traced through the paleolithic hunting, mesolithic fishing, neolithic village farming, and urban living stages.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family, kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Bio-Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological and cultural evolution.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man as a unit in the animal kingdom. The principles of biological evolution and the human fossil record are stressed.

title: The American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North and South America. Each culture is described in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: World Ethnography
description: A systematic survey of the important culture areas of the world, describing and comparing major social institutions: e.g., economics and technology, family and kinship organization, political structure, religion, and art.

title: Material Culture
description: The material manifestations of culture, stressing primitive technology. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to honor students only or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Osteology
description: The human skeleton. Bone identification, osteometry, aging, sexing, and racing a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 100.

title: Races of Man
description: Introduction to the present scientific status of the phenomenon of human subspecies, including a survey of historic concepts of race and race sorting criteria, with emphasis on recent advances in physical anthropology. Prerequisite: ANTH 100, 160, or 120.

title: Race and Racism
description: Investigation in detail of the nature of race as a biological phenomenon, which will acquaint the student with the history of racism in the Western world. Stress on the necessity of employing the scientific method in studying race beliefs.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs.

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Summer Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation: sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Field observation and interpretation are stressed. Requires full time in the field.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Utilization of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Advanced Archaeological Field Methods
description: Advanced methods of excavation and field recording studied at the excavation site. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Midwest is traced through the Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: Traces and describes the archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic to the Historic Period.

title: Personality and Culture
description: Introduction to a major area of anthropological interest and investigation during the past three decades. This field of anthropology has grown out of recent efforts to unite studies of individual behavior and group, or cultural, behavior. The course will involve discussions on the nature of human personality and its origins, both in the individual and the species. Particular stress will be laid on the phenomenon of the model personality type.

title: Peoples and Problems of Modern Africa
description: The course is intended to acquaint the student with the vast, complex, and still comparatively littleknown continent of Africa. More particularly it will enable students to acqui re a systematic body of knowledge concerning the increasingly significant role which Africa plays in the modem world.

title: Religion, Culture, and Society
description: An investigation of theories of the possible o ni_ gins of religious behavior and experience; various types of religious practitioners; and aspects of institutionalization and function of religion in selected societies.

title: Social Organization
description: Opportunity for a_ depth study of man'social systems. Emph sis on the function of these systems and important grouping principles. The crosscultural method is employed extensively.

title: Anthropological Theory
description: Historical development of concept and theory in anthropology. Various theoretical viewpoints and schools of thought will be examined intensively. Prerequisites: ANTH 100, 160, and

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the impact of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents with European civilization.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Peoples of Oceania
description: A general survey of the ethnography of the peoples of Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia. Selected field studies will be examined in terms of the functional method and acculturation theories for which oceanic cultures and societies provide a most suitable and viable laboratory.

title: Field School in Ethnography and Ethnology
description: Methods of carrying out field research in cultural anthropology; techniques of establishing contact and rapport; interview and observation methods; problem formulation, data recording, and data preparation. Requires full time in the field. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Culture Change
description: Culture change is examined through major anthropological theories and data. Emphasis on change in nonwestern societies; implications of these studies for the western world are considered.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in Department of Biology Nisbet, Chairman; Adalis, Bennett, Bernhardt, Crankshaw, Eiser, Engstrom, Hardman, Hendrickson, Hibbs, Kirkpatrick, List, McComish, McElhinney, Mertens, Metcalf, Miller, Oliver, Olsen, Smith, Stevenson, Welker, Wise, Zimmack The programs of the Department of Biology are designed to develop appropriate levels of competence in biology for three groups of students: (1) students who wish to prepare for positions in teaching, biological research, or particular fields of biological specialization; (2) students who are interested in obtaining a liberal education; and (3) students who need basic preparation in biology for the parabiological fields of medicine, pharmacy, veterinary medicine, dentistry, medical technology, cytotechnology, and nursing. Common background is provided for majors through a "core program in biology." The required courses of the core are organized with three levels of emphasis. The first level is designed to develop understanding of basic principles and biological processes which are common to living organisms. The second level focuses on organisms and is concerned with problems of structure, function, and classification in specific groups of plants and animals. The third level is concerned with developing understanding of interactions and adaptations of organisms in contexts ranging from world biome organization through molecular organization. In addition to the basic background work provided by courses in the core program, the department offers specialized course work in biology, botany, zoology, and science to meet the needs of particular individuals and groups. Opportunities for research participation are available at both the advanced undergraduate and graduate levels. The student who plans a career in teaching secondary school biology should take the teaching major in biology or the teaching minor in biology. The student enrolled as a biology teaching major is encouraged to take a second major in general science or a minor in chemistry. These combinations not only greatly increase employment possibilities, but contribute significantly to the understanding of biology. Students who plan careers in college biology teaching and/or research may follow either the teaching major in biology or the departmental major in biology. Such students should anticipate the requirements for graduate work in biology in addition to the major in biology. In general these recommendations are: 1. Proficiency in at least one foreign language. French, German, or Russian are almost universally recommended; some institutions also accept Spanish. 2. Chemistry through the organic sequence and preferably a course in biochemistry. 3. A year of college physics. 4. Mathematics through the calculus sequence. The student who wishes to specialize in either botany or zoology may do so by following the departmental minor in botany or the departmental minor in zoology. These minors are designed to provide professional work for the student who has completed basic course work in biology and chemistry. The liberal arts student who elects to include a concentration area in biology in his curriculum will follow either the departmental major in biology or the departmental minor in biology. All nursing majors take the departmental minor in biological science for nurses. To prepare to do laboratory work in bacteriology, pathology, chemistry, and other scientific fields necessary in the diagnosis and treatment of disease, the student will take the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in medical technology. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in premedical preparation. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry at the close of three years of predental preparation but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in predental preparation. MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY The senior year (45 hours) of the major will consist of twelve months of hospital technical medical laboratory training in an ASCP approved school of medical technology. The following courses are recommended for elective credit on the major: ANAT 320, 430; BIO 311; LAT 213; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; and ZOOL 330. During the three years in Ball State University, the student pays the usual University fees and is subject to general regulations of the University. In his senior year, at the Ball Memorial Hospital School of Medical Technology, the Agnes Howe Jones Scholarship fund provides a tuition scholarship for each student. This full senior year scholarship pays the tuition fee at Ball Memorial Hospital and the student services fee at Ball State University. The hospital has a limited number of rooms for students. These are available to student technologists for a nominal fee if space permits. Meals are served at cost in the hospital cafeteria. The student must provide his own books and uniforms. The course is fifty weeks of integrated lecture and laboratory work. The University also has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with the St. John's Hickey Memorial Hospital, Anderson, Indiana; the Methodist Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana; the St. Joseph Memorial Hospital, Kokomo, Indiana; the St. Francis Hospital, Beech Grove, Indiana; and the St. Vincent's Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana. To qualify for certification as a medical technologist, the student must submit satisfactory credits to the Registry of Medical .See the professional education requirements for secondary teaching on the Teacher Education Curriculum for the requirement of an additional course in biology: BIO 391, the methods of teaching biology. Technologists of the American Society of Clinical Pathologists, which is located in Chicago, Illinois, and must pass the examination of that Registry. He must apply for certification as a medical technologist on completion of his twelvemonth senior year technical training in laboratory work in the hospital. The medical technology student is prepared to do laboratory work in bacteriology, pathology, chemistry, and other scientific fields necessary in the diagnosis and treatment of disease. There are positions calling for this preparation in hospital laboratories, physicians' and surgeons' clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories. Also, there are opportunities for work in research laboratories and in commercial companies making biological products. PREMEDICAL PREPARATION The student who wishes to qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine at the close of three years of premedical preparation will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 142 hours of liberal arts credit in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credit he earns in his first year in the Indiana University School of Medicine (45 hours) to meet his senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit in the first three years: SPCH 210, foreign language (12 hours in one language), BIO 311, 411, LAT 213, and ZOOL 447. The student who prefers to obtain a baccalaureate degree before entering Indiana University School of Medicine will do so by completing all of the work on the Professional Arts Curriculum. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in premedical preparation, it is highly recommended that the premedical student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry because the number of applicants to a school of medicine far exceeds the capacity of the school. In following this recommendation, the student will be better prepared for graduate work in these areas in the event he does not gain entrance into medical school. The student contemplating a career in medicine should bear in mind the stiff competition in the field, and if he has not exhibited keen interest and aptitude in high school courses, especially in science, it will be very difficult for him successfully to meet the high standards required for premedical work and admission to medical school. The student who wishes to obtain a degree and prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will follow the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum, will elect a teaching area major or teaching major, and will combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. Thus he prepares for teaching in the field of his elected teaching concentration. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: SPCH 210, foreign language (12 hours in one language), BIO 311, 411, LAT 213, and ZOOL 447. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many medical schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other medical schools as their objectives. Some modifications will be made to enable students to meet as closely as possible the specific requirements of the medical schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of firstyear medical school credits on the Ball State University major is Indiana University. One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory score in the aptitude test given by the American Dental Association. All applicants to dental school are eligible to take the test. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the aptitude test. PREPHARMACY PROGRAM The Prepharmacy Program is for those students who wish to apply for admission to the School of Pharmacy of Butler University or the School of Pharmacy of Purdue University. The courses designated, when completed satisfactorily, will meet the preprofessional curricular requirements of either of these institutions at the end of the first year or at the end of the second year. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to a school of pharmacy usually exceeds the capacity of the school and that a selection of students is therefore necessary, taking into consideration such factors as scholastic standing, character, and professional aptitude. The student's attention is directed to the admission and residence requirements set forth in the Bulletins of the Butler and Purdue Schools of Pharmacy. This Prepharmacy Program does not lead to graduation from Ball State University. It merely provides a student with an approved sequence of courses for the first or the first two years of the complete fiveyear pharmacy program of either of the two universities. Furthermore, physical education is not a part of this program, but a student who drops out of the prepharmacy program and elects to follow a degree program of Ball State University Will be expected to meet physical education g en_ eral course requirements and all other requirements of the elected University curricu_ lum. A careful arrangement of the program for each year is essential in order that courses may be completed in sequence and in the allotted time. Copies of the program arranged by quarters may be obtained from the Chairman of the Biology Department or the mem_ ber of the Biology Department appointed by the chairman to serve as preprofessional adviser for students on this program. The program is subject to minor differences between the School of Pharmacy of Purdue University and the School of Pharmacy of Butler University as to admission requirements. General requirements in the first year at Ball State University are a minimum of 46 quarter hours of course credits, including two courses in English and one course in general psychology. Specific courses in science in_ clude two courses in biology, three courses in human anatomy, and two courses in mathematics. General requirements for the second year are a minimum of 52 hours of course credits, including one course in business education, three courses in history, and one course in economics. Specific requirements in science include five courses in chemistry and three courses in physics.

title: Man and the Life Sciences
description: Basic biological ideas and knowledge aimed at an understanding of the life processes held in common by all organisms. The physical basis of life, development, heredity, and evolution, and consideration of current biological problems confronting man. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 102 or 111.

title: Introduction to Biological Sciences
description: Fundamentals of major areas of biology. The nature of the cell and protoplasm, reproduction, development, genetics, and evolution. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Field Biology and Conservation
description: Principles of ecology and conservation and survey of the plant and animal kingdoms. Field and laboratory work dealing with trees, other plants, insects, birds, ecological processes, and conservation practices. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Principles of biology including the physical basis of life, cell structure and function, genetics, reproduction, development, evolution, ecology, and systematics. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 100 or 102.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Continuation of BIO 111. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairman. 211. Animal Biology. (4) Major animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Biology
description: Major plant groups with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative protozoa, bacteria, viruses, fungi, and algae. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation with emphasis on meiosis, the mechanisms of heredity, Mendelian principles, linkage and crossingover, mutation, and the nature of the hereditary material. Some attention to human and applied genetics. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Normal development in plant and animal systems. Synthesis of current knowledge of the factors contributing to the development of a single cell into a differentiated organism in addition to the related phenomena of metamorphosis, regeneration, and growth. Prerequisites: BIO 211; BIO 212 (or permission of the department chairman); and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ecology
description: The relation of organisms to their physicalchemical environment and to each other. Plant and animal societies. Some attention to human and applied ecology. One weekend field trip required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisites: RIO 211 and 212, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 325 or NR 325.

title: Bacteriology
description: Bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques in culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisites: BIO 213, and CHEM 130 or 230, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Microtechniques 1
description: A laboratory course designed to give the student experience in the methods and preparation of biological materials for teaching and research. Activities include work in the areas of hematology, vital staining, and tissue culturing and the preparation of smears, squashes, and whole mounts. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212, 213, and 12 hours of chemistry.

title: Microtechniques 2
description: A laboratory course designed to give the student experience in the preparation of sectioned tissues, and histochemical treatment of materials. Activities include work in histochemistry and the preparation of paraffin and frozen sections. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212, 213, and two quarters of chemistry.

title: The Teaching of Biology in the Secondary School
description: Philosophy and methods in biology teaching. Emphasis on laboratory investigations. Concepts and conceptual schemes in biology. Levels of organization in secondary school biology courses. Evaluation of learning in biology. Supplies, equipment, and facilities. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212, and 213. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Designed to integrate and enhance understanding of basic principles of biology. Recent discoveries in biology and their implications in the biological sciences are stressed. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course with permission of the department chairman.

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including the nature of the organization of the cell, cell environment, plasma membrane and transport, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course, Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Radiobiology
description: The use of radiation equipment and radioactive isotopes in the biological sciences. Experiments and projects involving living plants and animals. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212, CHEM 130 or 230, and PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Biophysics
description: Physics of motion and locomotion in organisms, concept of wave motion, principles of sound and hearing, atomic structure, electrochemical phenomena in biological systems, electromagnetic spectrum and ramifications in biology and medicine, artificial and natural radioactivity, tracer techniques, atomic fallout, and biological problems of space flight. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212, CHEM 130 or 230, and PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Evolution
description: The principles of evolution. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Cytology
description: Structural organization of the basic unit of living organisms in both plants and animals. The cell, cytoplasmic organelles, the nucleus, mitosis, and meiosis. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 212.

title: Molecular Biology 1
description: The mechanisms which coordinate and control the activities of microorganisms. Emphasis on recent research in bacterial genetics, the nature and origin of DNA and RNA, protein synthesis, enzyme mechanisms and controls, and permease systems. Prerequisite: BIO 411 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Molecular Biology 2
description: The interrelationships of metabolic pathways, with particular emphasis on bacteria. Emphasis on the use of energy, activation processes, and biosynthetic mechanisms. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Museum Techniques
description: Techniques of preparing plant and animal specimens for display. Maintenance of museum records. Use of museum materials for educational and research functions.

title: Limnology
description: The dimensions of the physical, chemical, and biological factors of lakes, streams, and estuaries. One twohour laboratory or one halfday field trip each week will be devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of various limnological parameters. Prerequisite: BIO 313 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Anatomy
description: Origin and structure of cells, tissues, and organs of higher plants. Prerequisite: BIO 212.

title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
description: The identification of native flowering plants. Emphasis on the distinguishing features of the major plant groups and use of manuals., Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Forestry
description: Study and identification of native trees. Problems of general forestry and forest conservation. Field work in addi_ tion to regular laboratory periods may be r e . quired. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102 or 111.

title: Paleobotany
description: Morphology and anatomy of fossil plants. Correlation of exti nct and living plants with emphasis on evolution ary trends. Prerequisite: BIO 212 and B0-'- 330 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Morphology
description: Forms, life cycles, and evolution of the major plant groups. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ornamental Plants
description: Identification and uses of ornamental trees, shrubs, and vines. Selection, special characteristics, adaptability, and maintenance of ornamentals.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants as related to plant structures and environmental influences. Prerequisites : BIO 212, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Intermediate Plant Physiology
description: A continuation of BOT 451. A treatment of selected physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BOT 451 or 551.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary School
description: Recent elementary science texts, courses of study, and supplementary books are examined. Development and use of science teaching units. The use of experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and other special methods.

title: History and Philosophy of Science
description: The history of natural science. Emphasis is given to the influence of science on general philosophy.

title: Comparative Vertebrate Anatomy
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and relationships of vertebrates. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Invertebrate groups. Phylogeny, comparative morphology, and life histories. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisites: BIO 211, and CHEM 130 or 230. Ornithology. (4) Birds. Field identificaion, classification, behavior, and economic relationships. Field work in addition to regula r laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisites: BIO 100, 102, or 111. 341. Entomology. (4) Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 211.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The behavior of individuals and of populations. The economic relationships of Chemistry 159 mammals. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth and arthropod parasites of animals. Emphasis on identification, life cycles, and hostparasite relationships. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Protozoology
description: An introduction to aspects of the morphology, physiology, ecology, and development of protozoa. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on the terrestrial vertebrates of the United States. The management and harvest of wildlife. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required. title: Man and Chemistry
description: Nonmathematical treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as: organization of chemistry, language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature of matter, classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these to everyday living. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: General Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, and the nature of matter stressed. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory per week.

title: General Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 110, including properties of solutions, colloids, chemical kinetics, chemical equilibrium, and electrochemistry. Prerequisite: MATH 110 and CHEM 110 or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemistry of metals and nonmetals, chemistry of carbon compounds, nuclear structure, and radioactivity. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Prerequisite: CHEM 111 or the equivalent.

title: Chemical Principles 1
description: A comprehensive treatment of the fundamentals of chemistry, with emphasis on periodic relationships and stoichiometry. Recommended for preprofessional and science majors who plan to take more than one year of college chemistry. Three lectures, two threehour laboratories weekly. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry or CHEM 110. Prerequisite or pa r_ allel: MATH 111 or the equivalent.

title: Chemical Principles 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 113, with emphasis on solutions, chemical kinetics, energetics, and equilibria. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Three lectures, two threehour laboratories weekly. Prerequisite : CHEM 1 or 13.

title: A Brief Course in Organic Chemistry
description: Especially for nurses, biology and general science majors. Three lectures, one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: 4 hours of collegelevel general chemistry.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements. Includes gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations (neutralization, complexation, precipitation, and redox), ionexchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, polarography, and emission and absorption spectrophotometry. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: The aliphatic hydrocarbons and their derivatives, including nomenclature, chemical and physical properties, and their practical application. Three lectures, one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 230, including optical activity and the chemistry of carbohydrates and proteins. Prerequisite: CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of aromatic hydrocarbons, heterocyclic compounds, natural products, dyes, medicinals, and plastics. Prerequisite: CHEM 231.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for chemistry majors. Lecture material deals with covalent bonding, molecular structure, and the chemistry of elementary organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 225 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of

title: Chemical Calculations

title: Physical Chemistry

title: Physical Chemistry

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions, and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics, presented at a level which does not require use of calculus. Especially for premedical, biology, and general science majors. Three lectures and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 340.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry

description: Theory and practice in the use of instruments as applied to chemical analysis. Two lectures and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite or parallel: CHEM 342 or permission of the department head.

title: Physical-Organic Chemistry

description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 450. Application of basic principles to study of specific inorganic materials. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 450.

title: Principles of Biochemistry
description: Continuation of CHEM 462. Biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolic patterns of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids; metabolic interrelationships. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 462.

description: Designed to give undergraduate chemistry students an opportunity to pursue specific lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

Economics is a study of human wants and of man's efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative— relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. Among the standard categories of scarce resources in the study of economics is, first of all, labor; and courses in labormanagement relations, labor law, collective bargaining, wage theory, social security, and workmen's compensation are standard parts of university curricula in economics. Besides the study of all aspects of labor as a scarce resource, economics is concerned with the manmade resource of production called capital. For example, the accumulation of capital is a central aspect of the growth pf underdeveloped countries. Economics courses called developmental economics have appeared in most universities, with separate courses being established for different backward countries or areas. The concept of interest as a physical product of physical capital equipment gives rise to courses in money and banking. A study of the valuation of the scarce resources created by nature is included in the curriculum of most universities as "land economics." While the fact of the scarcity of resources is the taproot of economics, the branches of the discipline are composed of specialized studies of the selection of alternative uses for resources. The rationale for the selection of the use pattern which will leave the least gross total of human wants unfilled varies from society to society, but normally some variant of voluntary exchange is institutionally developed. The vast complexity of the institutional exchange arrangements developed in modern society requires a set of theoretical explanations that must be equally complex. Certain classifications of exchange have unique theoretical characteristics such as an atypical number of sellers and/or buyers or supply and demand of unusual behavior, and special economics courses are devised to explore their theoretical peculiarities and significances. An example is agricultural economics. The exchange medium (money) again requires an examination of the theoretical aspects of money and of the banking arrangements which generate and control the supply of the medium of exchange. The use of scarce resources by a society involves the society's decision on the fraction of total resources that will be consumed by the community as a unit. Social consumption of resources in a discipline concerned with the scarcity of them necessarily involves economics in the total theoretical aspects of taxation and government expenditure. Economics 163 The exchange arrangements developed in this society and in other societies are of exhausting variations at any one point in time and have changed over time. This change is a central part of economic history which is taught as several separate courses on some university campuses. The heterogeneity of exchange dynamics, even when reduced to simplified theoretical classifications, is so remarkable that several courses in market theory are necessary if the university student's grasp of i the economic aspects of even his own society is to be carried beyond the elementary level. To understand the production, exchange, and consumption arrangements in other societies requires courses in comparative economic systems. Certainly the exchanging of goods and resources through the use of a medium of exchange has one of its most sophisticated (and important) aspects when the exchange occurs across national boundaries. Therefore, international trade is an old and established part of economics offerings in all universities. The interrelations among exchange decisions produce economywide effects that result in a greater or lesser intensity with which resources are used and in specific resources growing or declining at explainable rates. The explanations of the intensity with which total resources are used and of changes in the total of each are studied under the general rubric of macroeconomics. The legal framework for exchange decisions gives the study of economics a sharp concern with the governmental agencies that set the limits of legal exchange activity. title: The Economics of the Ghetto
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interests of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics

Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. The theory of wages, rent, interest, and profits. The principles of international trade and comparative economic organization. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 270.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wageearner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 431.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting

Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

description: An overview of the field of children's literature and an intensive study of types at various levels. The classics are emphasized.

title: American Literature, 1860-1960
description: A survey of selected writers and the various literary movements in America during the last hundred years. Prerequisite: ENG 240. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: The themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Literature of Black America
description: An investigation of the literature written by black authors in the United States. Those authors to be studied will be determined by the instructor on the basis of literary merit.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to 1642
description: English drama from medieval times to the closing of the theatres in 1642, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to the plays of Marlowe, Joiison, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Drama of the Restoration and Eighteenth Century
description: English drama from 1780, including plays of Dryden, E th 160 to erege, Wycherley, Congreve, Steele, Gold_ smith, and Sheridan.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenth century novels including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot the Brontes, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequi: site: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: English Drama of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: A wide range of British drama, from Shelley's The Cencie, to Tennyson's Becket, to the plays of the Angry Young Men, with special attention given to the works of Shaw, Synge, Barrie, and O'Casey.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Creative Writing
description: The fundamentals of the short story, such as the use of language, image, and structure. Emphasis is put on the student's ability to write clearly and dramatically. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Fiction Writing
description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis will be placed on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Teaching of English in the Secondary School
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in the teaching of composition, language, and literature in the secondary school.

title: The Teaching of English as a Foreign Language
description: Background in modern linguistic science as applied to the teaching of English to nonnative speakers of English. Survey of methods and materials. Practice in development of teaching materials. Observation of classes in English for foreign students. Prerequisite: ENG 321, 420, or 520.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical aspects.

title: Short Story
description: The short story as a type of world literature. Not open to English majors and minors.

title: The Essay
description: Representative essays by English and American authors. Not open to English majors and minors.

title: American Folklore
description: Materials and English 169 techniques for presenting the American heritage of folklore and folk literature at the public school level. Books, films, filmstrips, recordings, and pictorial collections are among the materials studied.

title: Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of transcendentalism. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Poe, Hawthorne, Melville
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of romanticism. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209. 443.Twain, James, Adams, Crane. (3) An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of the varieties of realism. Prerequisite: ENG 340.

title: Renaissance and Seventeenth-Century Studies
description: The nondramatic literature of the Tudor, Stuart, and Puritan periods (1485- 1660), exclusive of Shakespeare and Milton. Major writers such as Spenser, Donne, and Jonson will be considered in terms of their influence and of their political and philosophical backgrounds.

title: Chaucer
description: A study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several of the minor poems. Emphasis upon the structure, the sources, and the significance of the works included. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare (to 1600)
description: The earlier plays and poems, providing insights into the development of Shakespeare. Some plays such as Hamlet will be studied closely.

title: Shakespeare (from 1600)
description: The later plays, with close study of Othello, Macbeth, and King Lear.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Restoration and Augustan Periods
description: An extensive study of the nondramatic works of Dryden, Swift, and Pope, with possible supplementary readings from other British authors of the period 1660-1745. Attention will be given to philosophical, aesthetic, and political currents in the works studied and to the distinctive character of Neo-Classicism. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Milton
description: A study of Milton's family background, political service, and poetic apprenticeship, culminating in close analytical investigation of Paradise Lost and Samson Agonistes. Attention is given also to Milton's aesthetic propositions and to his social and political prose works.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Age of Johnson
description: An intensive survey of the nondramatic works of Samuel Johnson and other British authors of the later eighteenth century, 1744-1800. Prerequisites: ENG 205, 206, 207, or 209.

title: Romantic Studies
description: The poetry and prose of Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Keats, and Shelley.

title: Victorian Studies
description: An intensive study of the works of Carlyle, Tennyson, Browning, Ruskin, and Arnold.

title: Twentieth-Century British Studies
description: A study in depth of several significant twentiethcentury authors (such as Shaw, Conrad, Lawrence, Joyce, Woolf, Waugh, Durrell, Beckett, and Auden) and the intellectual and literary movements closely associated with them.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War I to the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others.
