Department of Philosophy Robertson, Chairman; Andry, Annis, Foster, Miracchi Philosophy as an Academic Discipline One of the earliest definitions of philosophy encountered by the beginning student is one that says it is the "love of wisdom." The philosopher, accordingly, is known as a " lover of wisdom." And it should be noted that this love of wisdom is not confined to a ny one field; indeed, most anything is grist for the philosopher's mill! Philosophy 199 Historically speaking, the above definition has resulted ever since the time of Plato in the general agreement that the traditional role of philosophy is one of synthesis and system building. To put the matter another way, the philosopher was seen to be one who knew something about each area of man's experience as a result of either native genius or exhaustive investigation after which he was supposed to sit down with all his knowledge and, by weaving such knowledge into a consistent and coherent whole, give to mankind a unified picture of his universe and himself. This general agreement about the role of philosophy both within and without the university produced about twenty or more centuries of some of the most magnificent albeit meaningless cogitations ever produced by the mind of man. This is not to say that these vast systems were or are without some value. As purely intellectual exercises they have their place. But surely the student has a right to note that on the assumption that synthesis is the main business of philosophy, here we are many centuries after Plato still bemused by his problems and showing very little evidence that we are any closer to solving them. Is it possible that they are not "problems" at all? In the past thirty years the role of philosophy has been changing, although not without some dire warnings as to its future if the present trend continues. Analysis has now replaced synthesis as the main job of the philosopher in his role as a member of a university faculty. This is not to say that analysis has not always been with us, philosophically speaking, but in the past it has always been subordinated to the activity known as synthesis. It is generally agreed now that the scope of man's knowledge is too large in our own century for any philosopher to pretend that he can carry on the timehonored function of philosophy described above. Perhaps this was possible in the small world in which Plato lived; it is not possible now. Given this change, then, just what is the role of philosophy and the philosopher in a modern university now? It is twofold, one relative to the other academic disciplines, and one relative to the students who pass through his classroom. Relative to the other academic disciplines on the campus, the philosopher can function in his role of critical analyst as a sort of catalytic agent by insisting that his colleagues constantly look to the meaningfulness of their ideas. Indeed, perhaps his greatest service is that of helping others make their ideas clear regardless of the nature of their academic discipline. Relative to the students exposed to him in the university, the philosopher and philosophy can serve in several ways. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all facets of life need examination if we are to get ahead with this business of living. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all of his values and beliefs would never have come to be except that men in the past were not afraid to question those that were then held, and that in all probability the same fate awaits values and beliefs held now. And lastly, philosophy can serve by showing the student that this succession is indeed a good thing. The alternative is stagnation. These two roles for philosophy have given rise on most university campuses to certain basic courses in philosophy designed to be of help to groups of students. The usual Introduction to Philosophy course is one of general interest which serves to do what its title implies. In this course the student becomes aware of the basic problems philosophers deal with as well as some of their answers. Logic, the study of deductive and inductive reasoning and the rule thereto, can be invaluable for prelaw students, math majors, and any other persons who must reason correctly. Ethics is a course of particular interest to anyone concerned in any way with man's relationship to man. For those occupied with the history of ideas, the three courses in the history of ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy are most valuable. These are the core courses in philosophy and form the necessary foundation for the more specialized courses which usually follow. Department of Political Science Gruenewald, Chairman; Baker, Chang, Hamilton, Hamori, Hollands, Kelly, Mast, McGee, Menez, Perry, Rudoni, Sargent, Sharp Political science is the study of legal governments and man's relation thereto. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Protagoras, Gorgias, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polis or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differ from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask: What is the nature of man (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between man and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. Since comprehension of available knowledge is fundamental to intelligent valuation, emphasis must be given to teaching and learning and to continued accumulation, analysis, and organization of knowledge. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civic, and vocational. The first two, hopefully, are universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed populace. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and th e gradual pasing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 130) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into tjie subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz., political theory; American government; public law; public administration; parties, politics, and the political process; foreign and comparative government; and international law and diplomacy. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher certification programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate level for students in other departments. title: Problems and Prospects of American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: Honors Colloquium in Political Science
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in political science, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open to honors students. Outstanding political science majors may enroll with permission of the department chairman.

title: Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of the leading political theories evolved by mankind pertaining to the state. Emphasis on the views of such thinkers as Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Grotius, Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, and Bentham.

title: Communist Political Thought: from Marx to Present
description: A critical analysis and evaluation of Marxism, Leninism, Stalinism, Khrushchevism, post-Khrushchev Communist ideology and Maoism as a system of theoretical propositions and as an action program of an international movement. 48 hrs.

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes, and needs. Prerequisite: POLS 130 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships between government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities and finance. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda.

title: Public Interest Groups and Government
description: An examination of the internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Special attention will be given to the implications of pressure group activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and to the effects of pressure groups upon political parties and the political process.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural area, to the government and political structures of the three major powers in Western Europe— Great Britain, France, and Germany—and to the current state of the Western European integration movement. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: The United Nations
description: Concentrated study of organization and functions of the United Nations and of foreign policy of selected members of the United Nations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: International Relations of the USSR and the Soviet Bloc
description: The foreign policy of the USSR and her satellites and a survey of the Communist Party in international action.

title: Internship in American Governments and Politics
description: The student will work part time or full time (depending . on the assignment) for one quarter in the office of a public official in national, state, or local government, a candidate for public office, or a political party. Assignments will depend upon the interests of students and the convenience of sponsors. Prerequisite: 16 hours in political science including the following or their equivalents: POLS 130, 237 and 431, or 450, or 473, and permision of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate semiindependent study. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the department chairman and a professor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: basic courses in the area selected for special study, upper division standing, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Readings in Planning
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the instructor. Open only to seniors with departmental majors or minors in urban and regional planning, and other seniors of special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate investigation.

title: American Political Thought
description: American political thought from the colonial period to the present. Puritanism, nature of rights, constitutionalism and federalism, nature of the Union, democracy, liberalism, conservatism, individualism and collectivism, welfare state, isolation and internationalism, and national security and freedom.

title: Research Methods in Political Science
description: A critical examination of methodological problems and practices in the formulation, execution, evaluation, and reporting of political science research, including a comparison of data gathering techniques, their respective limitations, and appropriate application.

title: Quantitative Political Analysis
description: Introduction to data analysis computer applications in political science: minimum level of technical competence will be attained during the first two weeks; aggregate data analysis using departmental data library; formal modeling employing empirical research; intensive substantive reading. Prerequisite: POLS 425 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, Political Science 211 and centralization will be considered. Prerequisite: POLS 130, or 237.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government. Prerequisites recommended: POLS 130 and 237.

title: Metropolitan Problems
description: An analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related aspects; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation to the entire community. Prerequisites: POLS 237 and 238, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Trade Regulation
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or the equivalent; POLS 342 recommended.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and his government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content will include cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 544.

title: The Organization and Administration of American Foreign Policy
description: Deals with the process of foreign policy formulation. The course is analytic and interpretative and presents divergent views. The conception of the foreign policy process embodies the roles of the executive branch, Congress, press, public opinion, and various nongovernmental groups.

title: Planning 5: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration—national, state, and local. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Administrative organizations as going concerns composed of people taking action under conditions of conflict and cooperation: examination of nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisites: POLS 450 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes and activities of civil service agencies; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans; efficiency measurements, and rewards; training programs; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement, and other personnel processes. Prerequisite: POLS 450 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Survey of the principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances: administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, accounting of revenues, expenditures, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, management of publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 450 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services. Prerequisites: POLS 160.

title: Planning 6: Problems in Planning
description: Involves field study of selected problems in planning to emphasize the interdisciplinary character of planning and to provide an opportunity to apply political, social, economic, and a real analysis; and implementation techniques. Prerequisite: senior standing and four courses in planning.

title: American Political Parties
description: Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisites: POLS 130 and SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 426.

title: Latin-American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin-American nations.

title: Government and Politics of Africa
description: Tribal political systems, European colonial policies, nationalist movements, multiracial conflict, and accommodation; politics of independent states in Africa south of the Sahara. Secondary emphasis on United Nations control and the role of Africa in world politics. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in the field of comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of Soviet Russia
description: Structure and functions of modern Russian government, including central, regional, and local units, relationships between party and government, and such functions as law enforcement, economic planning and administration, and foreign policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 315.

title: Government and Politics of China
description: A comprehensive survey of the government and politics of modern China, both of the Republic of China and Communist China.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the law of the international community as it developed from international customs and usage and has been developed and recognized by modern states, with special reference to the position of the Western Democracies.

title: International Organizations
description: Organizations, processes, and methods devised by the nationstate system for the preservation of international peace and security and for dealing with problems of international concern.

title: International Politics
description: Analysis of general intercourse between states; normal relations, disputes and peaceful and forceful settlements; international obligations, agreements, and problems; power relationships and dominance and balance. Particular attention will be given to contemporary problems and situations.

title: Far East in World Politics
description: A comprehensive survey of contemporary international relations in the Far East mainly from post World War II to the present.

title: Communist China in World Affairs
description: A comprehensive survey of Communist China's role in international politics, with special emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Students working in these areas are given many opportunities to work with diversified audio and visual equipment. Training and experience, coupled with inclass discussions, analysis and studies of the broadcasting and motion picture industry enables the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. Department of Sociology Hewitt, Chairman: Blakely, Brodt, Dolon, Gordon, Hightower, Johnson, Kiefer, Moore, Morris, Neiman, Rehfeld, Royer, Scott, Smith, Tamney, Tucker Sociology as an Academic Discipline Sociology is among the youngest of the social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades; and especially in the period since World War II, its widened inclusion in patterns of general education has resulted in exceptionally rapid growth of undergraduate enrollments. Simultaneously, rapidly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge; and the concepts of the discipline are rapidly becoming a part of "everyman's vocabulary." Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. In the early years of this century, a number of persons interested in the field of sociology saw it primarily as a tool for ameliorating the various ills and problems of the society, and especially for helping groups and individuals with special needs in "adjusting" to the surrounding social order. Gradually this emphasis has come to be more identified with the special field of social work (see below), with sociology as an academic discipline being perceived more as a "pure" rather than an "applied" science. Even so, the findings of sociology per se continue to be assessed by the general public, at least, largely in terms of their applicability to the range of problems relating to "group problems" and the stability of the social order. As one of the related group of social sciences, sociology focuses upon, and seeks to develop dependable generalizations about, the social life of man as an interacting participant in groups. This involves identifying, classifying, and interpreting observable regularities in human interaction and resultant patterns of social organization. An understanding of the bases for and influences of such regularities in the forms of human association is fundamental to a student's knowledge about himself and others as participants in structured group life, and about the societies in which such participation occurs. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to the student's broadened perspective of the sociocultural environment which surrounds him and his own relationship to it, thus liberating him from provincialism and the limitations of untested folk mythology. Attention to observed regularities in social structures, as well as in the processes of social change, facilitates an appreciation of the nature, functions, and limits of the social order. As a science, sociology employs the canons of empiricism, objectivity, and ethical neutrality in its search for predictive relationships. The findings derived from such investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. The methods and concerns of sociology are functionally related to those of the other social sciences as well as to a wide range of arts (teaching, medical, expressive, correctional, etc.) which involve interactions among persons performing varied roles. The discipline of sociology thus has a significant contribution to make in the area of general (liberal) education and in professional education of widely diverse emphases, along with the preparation of scholars, to expand and transmit the body of sociological knowledge itself. Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or Sociology 217 undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex soc ia l problems, has contributed to the dra- -rnatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both an art and a science. Its art is the development of special skills used in working with people, either individually, in groups, or through community programs. Its science is the body of knowledge— derived from sociology, psychology, and psychiatry— about people and communities. Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare agencies; in courts as probation officers for juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics; in schools; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as welt as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Funds, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University provides for the needs of three groups of students: those who wish to qualify for firstlevel social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; and those who wish to prepare themselves for roles in community leadership as organization board members, in labor union leadership, in industrial social welfare relationships. After the basic twoyear general studies program at Ball State, students begin their specialization in social work within the sociology major. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, and methods of social work. Field trips in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. In the senior year students majoring in social work enroll in a course in basic social work practice. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of casework, group work, and community organization; practical experience is gained in field placement in a social agency for one quarter where the student works with individuals or groups under expert supervision. The Field of Criminal Justice and Corrections Only since the decade of the sixties have people in our society begun to take a greater interest in all facets of our system of criminal justice. A number of events in that decade have stimulated not only public interest, concern, and continuing dialogue, but also research, change in law and interpretation, publication and dissemination of information, and the growing awareness of the need for trained and qualified personnel in our criminal justice system. The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and possible employment: law enforcement, probation services in both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. In most instances, agencies, programs, and facilities operate on three levels of government: local, state, and federal. The departmental major in criminal justice and corrections has the following objectives: to provide students with the growing body of knowledge about the structure and functions of the basic elements comprising our society; to relate such problematic areas as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, to our system of criminal justice; to provide the student with a combination of theory and practical experience in the five areas listed above; and to enable the student to qualify for firstlevel employment positions in the criminal justice system or to qualify for future graduate study in this or related areas. Employment opportunities for trained men and women are increasing in our society. The general requirements include age 21, minimum physical requirements, and a thorough investigation into the candidates' background, integrity, maturity, and emotional stability. Civil service tests are frequently required for entrance into most positions on the state and federal levels. title: Principles of Sociology
description: An introductory view of the general field of sociology including basic concepts as used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, social processes, and social institutions.

title: The Black Community in America
description: An examination of the major social forces influencing the structure of the contemporary black American subcommunity. Emphasis also on an exploration into the strengths and weaknesses of this structure and its relations with the large community, as bases of chang e in the acomodative paterns of blackwhite relations.

title: Social Problems
description: A survey of the nature and range of social problems, the conditions which give rise to them, and the methods by which our society attempts to cope with them. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100.

title: Sociology of Law Enforcement
description: Survey of the historical development and contemporary application of law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes and needs. Prerequisites: SOC 100, 242, and permission of the department chairman.

title: History of Social Work
description: The history of private philanthropy and public welfare programs in Europe and America, including the Elizabethan poor law, the growth of public responsibility, the English background of American welfare programs and reform movements, and twentiethcentury developments.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisites: SOC 100 and GXPSY 100.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors effecting the establishment and utilization of treatment programs.

title: Police-Community Relations
description: Analysis of interrelationship between police and public in the study and control of crime. Consideration is given to problems of policecommunity relations and to ways of establishing cooperation between police and various social, economic, and ethnic groups. Prerequisite: SOC 100 and 242.

title: The Field of Social Work
description: An introductory survey of the field of social work with emphasis on twentiethcentury developments. Course content will emphasize contemporary agencies and services, both public and private. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 250.

title: Public Social Welfare
description: An introduction to public welfare including policy, services and administration. Tax supported income maintenance programs are examined with special emphasis on the philosophy, methods, issues, and problems of public assistance programs. Sociology 219

title: Child Welfare
description: An introduction to the field of child welfare, including programs, policies, problems, and services. The principles and practices of casework for children are examined with emphasis upon state and local community resources. Prerequisites: SOC 250 and 351 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Social Work Methods
description: An introduction to the basic concepts and methods of the three areas of social work practice: casework, group work, and community organization. Examination of the basic methodology will be supplemented with field experience by the student in a social agency. Prerequisites: SOC 250, 351, 352, 353, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective on life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in honors program or permission of the department chairman.

title: Development of Social Thought
description: A critical survey of influential views regarding the nature of society and human relations from the Greek period to the early twentieth century. Views of earlier social theorists are interpreted as products of the prevailing social climate, and are evaluated for the contribution to modern sociological theory.

title: Modern Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of modern sociological theories and theorists with a view toward relating theoretical positions to contemporary social and historical dynamics; an examination of the intellectual and cultural climate surrounding the individual theorists. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100.

title: Mass Society and Culture
description: Conditions giving rise to the spreading phenomena of mass culture, current expressions of these phenomena in American society and elsewhere, and an appraisal of their implications for organizational functioning and interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: A survey of the literature, issues, and events which focus upon the nature and types of complex social organizations with particular attention to societal consequences. Prerequisite: 8 hours of sociology or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 and POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 476.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Juvenile Delinquency
description: The nature, extent, causes, and methods of control of juvenile delinquency. Emphasis is given to the role of community agencies in prevention and treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Criminology
description: The nature and extent of individual and organized crime in modern society, contributing causes, and methods used in its control. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Introduction to Corrections
description: A beginning course in penology with emphasis on the three major components: police, courts, and correctional institutions. The history, philosophy and current programs, policies, and problems. Prerequisite: SOC 450 or 451. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 552.

title: Practicum in Corrections
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in correctional settings on the state and local level. Prerequisites: SOC 452 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Law Enforcement
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in police settings on the local and state levels. Prerequisite: SOC 245, 452, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Internship in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: A summer internship involving full time individual assignments under field supervision in a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: SOC 450, 451, or 452; and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Small Groups
description: Analysis of data on experimental laboratory research on small groups and field research on small group dynamics. Attention is given to the relationship between group productivity, group cohesion, size, interaction patterns, and related areas. Prerequisite: SOC 260 or GXPSY 316.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: The Community
description: Major differentiating characteristics, with special emphasis on the urban community, basic patterns of social and ecological organization, and factors contributing to community integration and disorganization. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Practicum in the Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis and evaluation of problems evolving from the changing social and demographic characteristics of urban core areas, with special emphasis given to their effects on family units and the needs of children and youth. A field work course requiring supervised participation in a designated urban neighborhood. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Sociological Research
description: Principles and techniques of organizing, conducting, and interpreting sociological research; the appropriateness of particular methodologies for different kinds of research problems. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Community Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of community surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating and utilizing sources of data; and the application of survey findings to programs of community action. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 472 or 480.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in the social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 582.

title: Independent Study in Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Senior Seminar in Sociology
description: An openended course offering for fourth year sociology majors. Both the focus of study and the format of the course will be determined by the students in conjunction with the instructor. Prerequisite: 24 hours in sociology and permission of the department chairman. Department of Speech Huckleberry, Head; Artes, Benson, Bloom, Diedrich, Dorris, English, Harmon, Heady, Hemeyer, Hoops, Hudgins, Irving, Kramer, Lindell, Maitlen, Mannies, Palkovic, Robbins, Shepard, Strother General Speech The field of general speech encompasses several areas such as public address, interpersonal communication, interpretation, theatre, and speech sciences. It is a general program for undergraduate use, while persons specialize as they move toward graduate degrees. In the area of general speech, the University offers both graduate and undergraduate programs. A large proportion of those students electing a speech major plan to become teachers in the public schools. This teacher is expected to direct debating and individual events, produce theatre, and promote and direct radio and television programs. He is also asked to be in charge of special convocations. His class work is the development of the skills of public address and participation in a democratic society. Also he must develop an appreciation and skill for interpretation and theatre as performed in school theatres or through the facilities of mass media. Another responsibility is to develop an appreciation of the artistic, an understanding of the basic issues of mankind, and a respect for his cultural heritage. The profession of general speech assists liberal arts graduates to develop these same skills and attitudes. In addition, the speech major and minor are especially useful to support students who enter other professions such as law, the ministry, politics, public relations, and professional radio, television, and theatre. The University offers many student activities in the areas of intercollegiate debating, individual speech events, conferences, pantomime troupe, and theatre. It is assumed that general speech majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office and from the appropriate area chairman and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Speech Pathology and Audiology The graduate with a bachelor's degree and a teaching major in speech pathology and audiology (sometimes known as speech and hearing therapy) usually works in a public school corporation. An individual with a master's degree may work in a public school, hospital speech and hearing clinic, college or university center, or communitysponsored speech and hearing agency. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers three undergraduate programs in speech pathology and audiology: a teaching major, for persons who plan to work in the public schools; a departmental major, for persons who plan to work eventually in a hospital, community or college clinic; and a departmental minor, for those students who want as much information and knowledge as they can secure regarding this discipline but who do not plan to enter the profession. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology, in audiology, and in speech and hearing therapy. These are necessary for those individuals who desire professional teaching certification and for those who wish to join the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs: public school therapy programs, hospital and physical therapy environment, preschool nursery programs, and the University Speech and Hearing Clinic. In the latter, children and adults come to the Ball State campus for clinical work for both speech and hearing problems. Theatre Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a most modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher education for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work is available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist man to understand himself. It also assists the student to understand his dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office, and from the theatre area chairman, and should be requested early in the student's academic career. title: Fundamentals of Public Speaking
description: Fundamentals and techniques of organizing material and presenting that material in individual speeches. Emphasis on personal speaking improvement in the classroom and in public performances.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasis is on techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Beginning Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Development and composition of the debate case and consideration of factual argumentation. Prerequisite: high school speech.

title: Intermediate Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Stress on direct clash and crossquestion debate. This course involves tournament debating. Prerequisite: SPCH 213.

title: Phonetics of Speech Science
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic voice and speech science.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Personal speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation problems.

title: Speech Practicum
description: The student works upon extemporaneous speaking, discussion, debate, oratory, or interpretive reading for intercollegiate competition, or works in theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned in this course; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: The development of principles of rhetorical criticism and the application of the principles to an intensified study of prominent platform, radio, and television speakers. title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Parliamentary Procedure
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Teaching of Speech in the Secondary School
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisites: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher.

title: Intercollegiate Forensics
description: Practical experience in speech, intercollegiate debate, discussion, oratory, extemporaneous speaking, and interpretive reading. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Advanced Public Speaking
description: An intensified study and application of the principles of effective public speaking; the ideational formulation and delivery of longer speeches; the rhetorical analysis of significant speeches. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department head.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: An examination through exposure to theory, actual practice, and criticism, of the process of communication. Will include communication models of message encoding, transmission, decoding and feedback; the complexity of language, including abstracting and determination of meaning; problems in facetoface, small group, platform speaking, and mass media communication; and communication breakdowns.

title: Internship in Speech
description: The student is assigned to onthejob experience in such places as a radio station, a television station, a community clinic, summer camp, or summer theatre. The student will be permitted to earn some payment for his work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the amount of college credit to be earned. Prerequisites: major or minor in some aspect of speech and mass communications, and permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in this course, but not more than 8 hours may be earned at one time. SPEECH PATHOLOGY AND AUDIOLOGY (SPAA)

title: Speech Science
description: An introductory study of the physical elements of sound, particularly as they apply to the communication process. Prerequisite: SPCH 216.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 261 (460).

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course for the clinic student. Designed to assist the beginning clinician to develop clinical competency, selfevaluation, improve phonetic testing, gain general knowledge of articulation problems, develop ability to use diagnostic skills and learning theory, and evaluate therapy. Prerequisite: SPCH 216.

title: Language Development
description: Development of the phonology, grammar, content and function of language in children together with a review of the environmental and individual factors acting to influence that development.

title: Survey of Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to the profession of speech pathology and audiology and the professional endeavors of speech pathologists and audiologists. Not open to majors in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Articulation Disorders
description: Designed to prepare students to diagnose and treat articulatory speech disorders, particularly in younger children. Part of the course will consist of a laboratory of observation in the treatment of defective speech. Prerequisite: SPCH 216, SPAA 260, 261. Open only to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Clinical Practice with Articulatory Disorders
description: Actual diagnosis and therapy for children with speech difficulties of an articulatory nature. Prerequisite: SPAA 300 and 410 or permission of the department head.

title: Stuttering Disorders
description: Particular attention to and study of the problem of stuttering. Prerequisite: SPAA 410.

title: Clinical Practice with Stuttering Disorders
description: The student works with persons with stuttering problems. Prerequisite: SPAA 370, 412, 414.

title: Organic Speech Disorders
description: An introductive study of neurology and anatomy of the brain and the speech disorders resulting from brain damage such as cerebral palsy and aphasia. Other physical problems such as cleft palate and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 261, 410.

title: Clinical Practice with Organic Speech Disorders
description: The student works with persons having speech defects produced by more complicated organic problems, such as aphasia, cerebral palsy, and cleft palate. Prerequisite: SPAA 412, 418.

title: Introduction to Hearing Disorders
description: Nature and causes of hearing disabilities. Techniques in the conservation of hearing and in the use of residual hearing. Problems, history, and guidance of deaf children and adults. Prerequisite: SPAA 260, 261, or permission of the department head.

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in the use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for the purpose of reeducation and the necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 442.

title: Lipreading, Auditory Training, and Hearing Aids
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for the teaching of lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite:

title: Clinical Practice with Lipreading, Auditory Training, and Use of Hearing Aids
description: Emphasis is placed upon the actual rehabilitation or habilitation of persons who have hearing deficiencies. The techniques of lipreading and auditory training will be employed, as well as the use of hearing aids. Prerequisite: SPAA 444.

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: An overview of the field of theatre with special reference to the origins of drama.

title: Stagecraft
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of the crafts involved in theatre production at the school, college, and community theatre levels. Three hours of lecture and three arranged hours of laboratory a week.

title: Theatre Production
description: Intermediate training in nonperforming theatre activities with major emphasis on front house management, ticket operation, and publicity. Secondary emphasis is on further technical training and experience. Prerequisite: TI-TEAT 220.

title: Principles of Stage Makeup
description: An in_ vestigation of the principles, techniques, and materials of stage makeup and practical experience in their application.

title: Interpretive Reading
description: Fundamentals of English speech applied to the interpretive reading of prose and poetry.

title: Acting
description: Development of physical and vocal expression in the interpretation of dramatic literature. Stress on character analysis, stage composition, movement, balance, and timing employed by the actor. One lecturedemonstration and three laboratory periods weekly.

title: Advanced Acting
description: Further investigation into the principles of acting. Laboratory work in connection with the class will culminate in public performance. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Modern Drama
description: Analysis of selected dramas from the time of Ibsen to the present day and of the conditions under which they originally were produced.

title: Directing
description: Investigation of the role of the theatre director with principal reference to conducting rehearsals. Laboratory work will include the production of studio plays. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Children's Theatre
description: The principles of theatre devoted to creative dramatics. Twothirds of the course is devoted to formal dramatics. A public performance will be arranged.

title: Advanced Theatre Practice
description: In this course the student designs and executes a theatre project in such areas as scenery designs, lighting, properties, acting, directing, oral interpretation, and house management. Prerequisites: sixteen hours of credit in theatre courses. A total of six hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: History of Theatre 1
description: The early history of theatre from its Egyptian and Grecian origins through the medieval period.

title: History of Theatre 2
description: The theatre from the Renaissance through the eighteenth century.

title: History of Theatre 3
description: The modern theatre commencing with its origins in the nineteenth century.

title: Studies in American Theatre
description: An investigation of significant movements in the American professional theatre and its drama.

title: Studies in Continental Theatre
description: An intensive study of selected continental theatre movements from the turn of the century to the present day. Prerequisite: THEAT 411 or 412.

title: Theatrical Design and Lighting
description: Advanced training and experience in the problems of set design and lighting for theatrical productions in many forms and styles. Some aspects of television design will be covered. Prerequisite: THEAT 220.

title: Theatre Costume Design
description: Practice in the research, design, and building techniques involved in the preparation of period costumes for use in theatre productions. Special consideration is given to the costume problems facing the elementary or secondary school teacher involved in drama.

title: Stage Lighting
description: The design, media, instrumentation, control, and operation of stage lighting. Practical laboratory work in stage lighting on university productions. Prerequisite: THEAT 220.

title: Problems of Play Production
description: For prospective or actual directors of secondary school plays. Choice of plays, community values, casting, secondary school stages, advanced makeup, lighting, and stagecraft. TEACHERS COLLEGE Dean of the College, John Dunworth Associate Dean, Leslie J. Mauth Assistant Dean, Charles D. Shipman The Teachers College has major responsibility for teacher education in the University. Contributions of departments in other Colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by Directors of Elementary and Secondary Education, who are responsible to the Dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by a Teacher Preparation Council which represents the total University. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers for all levels of the elementary school with degree programs at the baccalaureate, master's, specialist in education, and doctoral levels. The Department of Secondary, Adult, and Higher Education, in addition to coordinating the total program for preparation of teachers for secondary schools, provides graduate level study in the field of curriculum and in preparation of teachers for adults and posthigh school levels. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate and graduate programs for teachers of the deaf, the mentally retarded, the orthopedically and physically handicapped, and the emotionally disturbed. The Burris Laboratory School is a center for demonstration, participation, and research in elementary and secondary education and functions as a resource for the total program of teacher education in the University. The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers graduate programs at master's, specialist in education, and doctoral levels for students preparing for public school and collegiate positions in these areas of study. Three departments of the Teachers College serve students in the areas of psychology. The Department of General and Experimental Psychology offers majors and minors in the field at baccalaureate and master's degree levels. The Department of Educational Psychology specializes in applications of psychology, measurement, and research to areas particularly pertinent to teacher education and related fields in both undergraduate and graduate programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services concentrates on graduate level programs extending through the doctorate in its areas of specialization. The departments of the Teachers Col_ lege, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public education and psychology; for production and dissemination of research; for innovation in instructional practices; and for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education. Educational foundations, general field of education, and social psychology areas of study are placed administratively under the Associate Dean of the Teachers College. Faculty hold rank in departments of the College but have instructional assignments to courses in these areas. The area of educational foundations includes history of education, philosophy of education, sociology of education, and comparative education. Although study in these fields is concentrated at the graduate level, some undergraduate work is incorporated into courses constituting the professional sequence for preparing elementary and secondary school teachers. Courses included in the general field of education serve students on a wide variety of programs and are not appropriately assignable to a single department. The departmental major in crossnational study of American education is offered for foreign educators. Social psychology is offered as a major program on a Master of Arts degree and as a cognate area on doctoral degrees. CROSS-NATIONAL STUDY OF AMERICAN EDUCATION The departmental major in crossnational study of American education is for foreign educators. It applies on the General Arts Curriculum (fouryear) leading to the Bachelor of Science degree. Features of this major are (a) comprehensive crossnational studies of American educa- Teachers College 227 don, including correlation of objectives and practices observed in American schools; (b) a concentration in social sciences basic to an understanding of American education; (c) a concentration in a planned area of studies chosen by the student; and (d) instruction in English as a foreign language for the student who needs such instruction. The General Arts Curriculum on which the major applies provides the general studies program basic for all programs of Ball State University leading to a baccalaureate degree. For the visiting educator there is a 15- hour sequence of courses in the study of English as a foreign language: ENG 100, 101, and 102. The student will be examined for proficiency in the English language and given all of this sequence if it is needed. If only part of the sequence is needed, substitution of general electives may be made for the English course or courses not needed. ENG 101 and 102 are applicable to the general studies program; ENG 100 is not applicable. title: School in the American Culture
description: An introduction to the theory, scope, organization, and functions of the public school in the United States. The student will examine the role of public education at all levels at which it operates and the responsibilities carried out by the professional teachers in their educational work.

title: International Dialogue on American Education and Life
description: Perspectives on American education and its cultural setting developed through interaction among international and American students and comparative study of educational and other social institutions as they relate to education. EDUCATION: GENERAL (EDGEN)

title: Cross-National Studies in American Education 1
description: An overview of American educational institutions with visits to comprehensive elementary and high schools, trade schools, military academies, parochial institutions, and specialized institutes of art and technology. Careful studies of these programs will be made during this course.

title: Cross-National Studies in American Education 2
description: A comprehensive study of innovations in American education, including instructional television, team teaching, programmed learning, new emphasis in language, science, mathematics and social science programs, and a variety of administrative schemes within and among school systems.

title: Cross-National Studies in American Education 3
description: Emphasizes a variety of approaches to teaching, including an analysis of lecture and discussion techniques, demonstrations, experiments, project activities, audiovisual aids, and counseling and guidance of students.

title: Cross-National Studies in American Education 4

Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. Although housed within Teachers College, the Department of General and Experimental Psychology is primarily concerned with psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of man's behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The Department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all areasteaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, businessincrease their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. Wilhelmi The philosophy of special education is that each child has the right to an education that will develop his capabilities to their fullest extent. The acceptance of and the application of this philosophy in America have led to an ever increasing demand for trained personnel in the various areas of special education. In recognition of this interest and of the need for university preparation for teachers and administrators, Ball State University has established the Department of Special Education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to certification to teach in the areas of Deaf Education, Mental Retardation, and Orthopedic and Special Health Problems. These programs are designed in accordance with teacher certification requirements of Indiana. Elective courses in special education that are open to future teachers, psychologists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, a course on the education of gifted children, a course on the education of slow learners, and a course on the education of children with learning disabilities. Special Education for the Deaf Special education for deaf children was established at Ball State University to assist at the national, state, and local levels in meeting the critical shortage of teachers for deaf children. The lack of academic instructors and professionals in related areas in residential and day schools, as well as in civic and medical centers, provides incentive enough for development of a collegiate program. The teaching minor in special education with deaf children is designed to prepare teachers for classroom instruction of the deaf. Courses include methodology in language, speech, lipreading, and basic school subjects and are designed with particular cognizance of the expressive and receptive communication barrier created by deafness. Observation of a demonstration class of preschool deaf children provides a laboratory experience early in the program. Student teaching is done at the state residential School for the Deaf in Indianapolis and/or in dayschool programs in Indiana and in neighboring states. Guidance and social counseling of deaf children are included in the program. The Ball State University program in deaf education meets approval of (1) The Indiana Teacher 'Training and Licensing Commission (providing certification coverage for teaching deaf children in all grades in Indiana), (2) The Conference of Executives of American Schools for the Deaf (making the qualified student eligible, upon application, to teach in the Residential Schools for the Deaf in the United States), and (3) The U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (providing the student with the opportunity to apply for federal scholarships made available to Ball State through this agency). Special Education for the Mentally Retarded Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to nationwide recognition of the special needs of mentally retarded children. To develop to the optimum of their ability, these children need a specially designed curriculum and specially prepared teachers who understand the learning process of mentally retarded children. To help alleviate the continued nationwide and statewide shortage of qualified teachers in this area of exceptionality, Ball State University prepares students to become professionally trained special class teachers. Both a teaching area major and a teaching minor are available to interested students. The teaching minor is also an endorsement for special education: teaching the mentally retarded. Special Education for Children with Orthopedic and Special Health Problems Within the group of children who have special educational needs are those who are orthopedically handicapped or who have other health conditions which make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for crippled or other healthimpaired children confronts the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a special classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The program is designed to offer comprehensive, professional preparation to future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired Special Education 241 children, so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers. title: Introduction to Exceptional Children
description: A survey of the educational needs of children who deviate from the normal mental, physical, and social characteristics. Designed as an introduction to the field of special education.

title: Education of Preschool Deaf Children
description: The development of oral communication in preschool deaf children. Directed observations of both hearing and hearingimpaired classes, home visitations, and the parenttraining program. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 261 (460).

description: Observation and assistance of teachers in special classes for exceptional children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or may be taken parallel with

description: Major topics include identification, characteristics, and practices and procedures for meeting the needs of the slow learning child. Emphasis is placed on techniques and methods of instruction as well as research findings concerned with the slow learner and the culturally disadvantaged.

description: Deals with history of education of the deaf from ancient times to the present with primary emphasis on early teachers and schools in the United States.

title: Psychosocial Aspects of Deafness
description: Personal, social, vocational, and learning adjustment problems of hearingimpaired persons and how assistance can be given in solving these problems. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for reeducation and necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440, or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 442.

title: Lipreading, Auditory Training, and Hearing Aids
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for teaching lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite: SPAA 442 or SPCED 442.

title: Speech Development for the Deaf
description: The International Phonetic Alphabet, Northhampton Charts, diacritical markings, and other methods and techniques used to teach speech to the deaf.

title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of and individual work with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: An introductory course comparing language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Levels of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight L an_ guage for the Deaf, Barry Five-Slate, Wi n,. Symbols, and the Natural Method. Langu age age outlines from different schools are used as sup_ plementary aids.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching subjects such as arithmetic and science.

title: Psychology of Mental Retardation
description: Various types and degrees of retardation. The psychological, environmental, and cultural factors which contribute toward retardation. Emphasis on etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate retarded children. Prerequisites: EDPSY 300 and SPCED 201.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 1
description: Special class organization, curriculum practices and procedures, and the methods and techniques used in the instruction of the mentally retarded. Prerequisite: SPCED 472.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 2
description: Continuation of SPCED 474, with emphasis on the curriculum. Prerequisite: SPCED 474.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: This course is designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children. Topics include etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate children with physical disabilities. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 300.

title: Educational Methods with Physically Handicapped Children
description: Special class organization, curriculum, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of orthopedically handicapped children. Prerequisite: SPCED 482; prerequisite or parallel: EDEL 380 and MATH 391.

title: Education of Children with Learning Disability
description: Intensive study of the psychosocial and educational research findings pertaining to the education of children with learning disabilities.
