CURRICULA: BACCALAUREATE DEGREES General Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The General Arts Curriculum is a program in general studies and selected concentration areas. It leads to either the Bachelor of Arts or Bachelor of Science degree. This curriculum is recommended for degree candidates who are undecided about specific educational goals in respect to graduate work, professional schools, and intensive specialization. General Studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 48 hours approved by the department or (2) two departmental minors, 24-36 hours, approved by the departments. Physical education: General courses 6 hrs. Electives: As many hours of credit in electives as are needed to increase the total of hours to 186. Liberal Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The Liberal Arts Curriculum provides opportunity for a search for general knowledge and for specialization primarily for development of intellectual capacities. In general studies the range is extensive; in areas of specialization the goal is depth of a sufficiency to demonstrate a degree of mastery in the selected areas. It is also possible in many cases for a student to fulfill the requirements of both the liberal arts curriculum and for teacher certification. To do so, the student must be enrolled in and meet the requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum as approved by the Teacher Education Committee of Ball State University. Such a decision will require careful choice of courses and planning by the student and the curricular adviser. The degree to which the curriculum leads is the Bachelor of Arts. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Foreign language: One foreign language 24 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) One departmental major of 45-60 hours and at least one departmental minor of 24-48 hours in another discipline, or (2) two departmental majors of 45-60 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statements of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Professional Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1-6 of Curricular Information.) The Professional Arts Curriculum provides for specialization to qualify for appointments in specific professional areas or for admission to professional schools which provide more intensive preparation for the desired professional or vocational competency. The degree is the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science, and if the major is architecture, the degree is the Bachelor of Architecture. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 78 hours or more, or (2) a departmental major of 48-96 hours with a departmental minor of 24-36 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statements of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Teacher Education Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees; Certificates for Teaching; and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The Teacher Education Curriculum is designed to prepare students for teaching in the elementary or secondary areas of the public schools of Indiana. It meets the requirements of the Teacher Training and Licensing Division of the State Board of E ducation of Indiana. The objectives of teacher education at Ball State University, for which preparation is made on this curriculum are — To help students acquire (a) knowledge and understandings expected of welleducated persons in our culture, (b) respect for learning and people, (c) familiarity with the value systems influencing behavior, and (d) aesthetic appreciations; To assist students in the acquisition of teaching competence in both knowledge and skills related to their areas of specialization; To enable students to understand the way learning takes place and human beings develop; To enable students to acquire a basic knowledge of the relationship between the school and its historical and contemporary settings; To help students demonstrate in their relations with others that they value highly the freedoms and responsibilities of democratic living; To promote in students the willingness and ability to experiment with effective methods of applying their intellectual, moral, aesthetic, and professional learning in practice. The degree on this curriculum is the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science. General studies: All general education requirements are met within the teaching major for elementary education. The College of Architecture and Planning, established by the 1965 Indiana legislature, is dedicated to the development of professional competency in the functional, aesthetic, and humane design of the physical environment. Two fiveyear programs of study are offered: the departmental major in architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Architecture degree; and the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree. The first two years of both programs are concurrent and include a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. The Ball State general studies program is an integral part of these first two years. The last three years provide specialization in the fields of architectural or landscape design as well as providing for specialized study in areas of the student's own choosing. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning represent a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophy. By exposure to the variety of philosophical and technical backgrounds of creative professionals, the students are encouraged to seek their own personal philosophy within a professional teamwork situation. The curricula stress character, devotion, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility. The total program is concerned with the development of a physical environment serving the best of one's aspirations. PROGRAM IN ARCHITECTURE Architecture is the art and the science of planning one's environment. The architect must develop social awareness, creative ability, technical understanding, administrative ability, and business acuity. The program in architecture at Ball State University stresses the variety necessary in the educational background of an architect. Intellectual and cultural preparation should be as thorough as possible; therefore, the general studies courses are from the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. An area of study in depth and certain courses within the major provide further breadth and depth in general studies. The specialized courses provide for technical competence. Courses in architectural design provide experience in the integ '-'e process of design. Thus the total program, which calls for five years of preparation, provides not only for comprehension of acceptable procedures and methods but also for stimulation of the creative process in environmental problem solving. Architecture is a departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The degree is Bachelor of Architecture. PROGRAM IN LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE Landscape architecture is dedicated to conserving and improving the quality of our environment. It is concerned with the quality of water, air, land, and how they influence our human relationships as well as affect our responses to nature. The landscape architect approaches this task with the assistance of allied professions such as architecture, planning, natural resources, engineering, sociology, economics. Working with others for the improvement of the human environment is the purpose of this program; never before have the challenges been so great. The landscape architect must be aware of human needs, and to meet these needs requires a knowledge of the natural sciences. The understanding of nature's processes and the ability to design in terms of earth, water, and plants enable the landscape architect not just to organize but to enrich greatly the human environment. The program stresses the need for variety in the education of a landscape architect. The general studies program (humanities, natural sciences, social and behavioral studies) is a vital part of the intellectual and cultural preparation of young men and women for professional practice. The core program in design provides further contact with the general studies program as well as developing capabilities in solving smallto largescale problems. The program stresses the collective approach to solving problems yet recognizes individuals and their contributions. Specialized courses provide for technical competency. It is the aim of the fiveyear program to encourage creativity and to develop sound procedures for establishing an environment which benefits humanity and nature. title: Beginning Typewriting
description: Principles of touch typewriting with emphasis upon technique and fluency. Only students with no secondary school credit in typewriting or with less than one semester of typewriting are eligible to receive credit in this course unless special permission is granted by the department head.

title: Intermediate Typewriting
description: Review of typewriting principles with emphasis on the development of speed and accuracy. Problems included on the application of typewriting skill to simple business situations. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one semester of secondary school typewriting.

title: Advanced Typewriting
description: Advanced problems in typewriting including preparation of school papers and manuscripts, tabulations, rough drafts, legal documents, and business forms; continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or one year of secondary school typewriting. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 116 or 117.

title: Office Typewriting
description: Office typing problems with emphasis on preparation of materials by various typewritten media; composition of reports, memoranda, and letters; handwritten and typewritten draft copy. Opportunities for original and creative typing. Continuation of speed and accuraoy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or

title: Business Correspondence
description: Principles and techniques of effective letter writing; letter mechanics; writing of personal business letters including application letters, fundamentals of English grammar and usage needed in business writing.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 1
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teacher -coordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 2
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirements for BEOA 285. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisite: BEOA 285 or equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a dis - tributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 3
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirement for BEOA 286. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisites: BEOA 285 and 286 or the equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Beginning Shorthand 1
description: Special emphasis upon basic theory with stress on brief forms. Introduction to the skills of writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or the equivalent.

title: Beginning Shorthand 2
description: Completion of basic theory and increased emphasis upon development of skill in taking dictation. A student whose secondary school transcript shows credit for more than one semester of shorthand is not eligible to receive credit in this course. Prerequisite: BEOA 321.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on skill in taking dictation with some emphasis on transcription. Open to those students who have had BEOA 322 and students whose secondary school transcript shows one year of shorthand. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent.

title: Advanced Shorthand 1
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, transcription, and production of mailable copy. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and at least two years of secondary school shorthand or BEOA 323.

title: Advanced Shorthand 2
description: Special emphasis upon production of mailable copy, and continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and BEOA 324.

title: Calculating Machines
description: Developing skill in using electronic calculators and other common office calculating machines as tools; emphasis is placed on developing the manipulative skills and programming abilities used to solve problems involving business data.

title: Duplicating, Machine Transcribing, and Filing
description: Preparation of ink stencils and carbon masters; operation of ink and liquid duplicators; training in machine dictation and machine transcription; indexing, coding, and filing of business correspondence; and survey of filing equipment and supplies. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems: the nature, function, and use of business papers; knowledges, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining of records of a business office, and study of records administration in business and industry.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects A
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, typing, general business, and shorthand. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250; student will have completed his requirements in typewriting and shorthand. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option B.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects B
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, general business, typing, and related office skills. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250; student will have completed his requirements in typewriting and accounting. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option A.

title: Methods of Teaching Distributive Subjects
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson and unit planning; overview of cooperative education and project plan programs. The various distributive subjects are included. Prerequisite:

title: Methodology of Relevant Work Experiences in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledges needed by persons who will be super - vising and directing a cooperative education or a project plan program in distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Distributive Education
description: The principles upon which vocational distributive education is organized, administered, and supervised; the kinds of programs; federal and state regulations; relationships to programs in other vocational areas. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a teaching license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Business Communications
description: Composition and study of effective written business communications including business letters and simple reports; solutions to communications problems. Particularly designed for business students.

title: Business Report Writing
description: Principles and mechanics of formal and informal report writing; collecting, organizing, interpreting and summarizing data; principles of tabular and graphic presentation of information; mechanics of report style. Prerequisite: ability to type and MGT 380.

title: Secretarial Administration
description: Administrative aspects of toplevel, professional secretarial work. Emphasis on how to perform such specialized duties as the evaluation of equipment and communications media and how to assist an executive in various tasks relating to travel, meetings, reporting, and maintaining records. Prerequisite: BEOA 325.

title: Principles of Business and Distributive Education
description: Historical development of the field of business education. Possible future trends and their effect on the entire business education program. Open only to students who have been approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Evaluative Instruments in Business and Distributive Education
description: The importance of measurements, techniques of administering and scoring tests, methods of analyzing and recording test results, uses of tests, construction of tests for classroom use in all areas of business education. Department of Economics Jost, Chairman; Caron, Cheng, Girgis, Hannaford, Lawson, Pickerill, Rocha, Scheer Economics is the scientific study of economic institutions and systems. It is a study of human wants and of efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative — relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. It is a useful study in an intellectual sense because it trains students to think carefully and logically about complex social phenomena. By such knowledge it is possible to understand the impact on economic systems and institutions of broad social and economic developments or of new economic policies and the responses of these units to them. Given the complicated economic and social problems of the modern world, an understanding of this subject is important for intelligent citizenship and for practical application in industry, government, research, and the professions. To achieve a basic comprehension of how our economy operates, the department offers a core of courses aimed at providing (1) a sound grasp of the tools of analysis and measurement, (2) an understanding of institutional development and the interrelations of economic and social factors, and (3) an ability to apply systematic analysis and understanding to problems of public policy. title: The Economics of the Ghetto
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: The Economic Development of Communist China
description: Systematic survey of the institutions, policies, and performances of the Chinese economy since 1949. Emphasis on the strategies and institutional innovations the Chinese Communists have adopted to overcome familiar problems encountered by all developing economies.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. The theory of wages, rent, interest, and profits. The principles of international trade and comparative economic organization. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the less -developed nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the neces - sary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Policies and Problems of Agriculture
description: Examination of the special economic conditions of demand and supply pertaining to agriculture and of problems created by changing national and international situations. Analysis of agricultural policy programs and implications of farm policy for consumers. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 200 or 201.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how man has looked at his economic life surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive refor - mulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 172.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 431.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Development in Latin America
description: The evaluation of theories of economic development. Sources and consequences of the economic growth and development process in Latin America analyzed in the context of economic theory. Attention to Common Market possibilities, monetaryfiscal factors, and trade and exchange. Examination of current national and international programs as promoters of development.

title: Economic Development of China, Japan, and India
description: Comparative analysis of the economic systems and strategies of development in three major economies in Asia — China, a centralplanning economy; Japan, a freemarket economy; and India, a mixed economy.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201,and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Interest in a specialized economics subject will be pursued under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. General Business Administration 95 Department of General Business Administration Hashmi, Head; Black, Bowman, Casey, Engber, Harms, Harris, Hill, Husain, Johns, Jones, LaFollette, Lauck, Ma, McCullough, Mottola, Nelson, Riggin, Ruff, Swart, Terry, Wagoner, Wallin, Wells, Williams The program of the Department of General Business Administration provides the opportunity for a student to obtain a broad business background. This background provides for an understanding of the interrelationships of the functions in business and a means of preparing the graduate of the program to fit into the general administration of a business. In addition, a student is expected to select areas of concentration in which a proficiency beyond that acquired in an introductory or principles course can be obtained. Four areas in which depth may be had are finance, law, insurance, and management. Particularly there is an opportunity to specialize in the fields of finance and of management. The management program is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them as future business executives and specialists to deal with the diversity of problems which arise in the course of daytoday business activity. The finance program is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activity. The insurance program is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. The law courses are quite broad and include the fundamentals of many essential law disciplines.These law courses are highly recommended to students in prelaw preparation. In addition to these specialized purposes, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students on other areas in the College of Business. Any student in the university may take the course in personal finance, which is offered especially to provide the general business information everyone should know. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements listed below. General business administration, finance, and management courses are included in the concentration areas for the teaching of business education and distributive education. The teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. The departmental major in general business administration, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for a career in the general administration of a business; the finance function; or the management process. title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the viewpoint of the consumer. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation.

title: Business Applications of Electronic Data Processing
description: An introductory course in electronic data processing with special emphasis on business applications. Effects of computers on business, systems analysis, FORTRAN machine language, comparison of data processing systems, and effect of computer on management decisionmaking. Special business problems are analyzed, programmed, and run on computers, and final reports are prepared from the information accumulated.

title: Interpretation of Business Data
description: An introductory course dealing with the collection, analysis, presentation, and interpretation of statistical data. Topics include frequency distributions, sampling, basic probability, decisionmaking, regression and correlation, and time series analysis. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law, and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law, and the effect of the law in the areas of consumer credit and economic relationships.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to corporations, partnerships and agencies, in addition to the law of bankruptcy. Prerequisite: GBA 360.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principle articles of the Code including sales, commercial paper and security interests, in addition to the areas of creditor's rights and property law. Prerequisite: GBA 360.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: GBA 370.

title: Property Insurance
description: Study of fire and allied lines insurance, inland marine floaters, transportation, theft, and liability insurance, and employers' liability and workmen's compensation. Emphasis is placed on management of risks in business and on the use of insurance as a tool for handling these risks. Prerequisite: GBA 370.

title: Automobile Insurance
description: Analysis and evaluation of automobile insurance: the automobile hazard, principles underlying auto insurance, types of insurance, selection of risk, pricing, underwriting, marketing and claim administration and practices. The problem of the uninsured motorist. Crisis in auto insurance and reform proposals. Prerequisite: GBA 370.

title: Honors Colloquium in Business
description: Exploration of selected issues in business, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students or others with permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Advanced Business Statistics
description: The more commonly used advanced statistical methods, with broad coverage of estimation and tests of hypotheses, and including chisquare tests, analysis of variance, and advanced correlation and regression analysis. Prerequisite: GBA 320.

title: Real Estate
description: A survey of real estate with emphasis on the economic aspects of the development, marketing, and financing of real estate, valuation of resources, location and market analysis, and institutional influences on real estate activities. Attention is given to the growth and structure of urban areas and to emerging trends in all areas.

title: Business Administration
description: Integration at the senior level of fundamentals of operation or profitoriented firms producing goods in the private enterprise system. Emphasis is placed upon the case method in solving problems pertaining to decision making. Prerequisites recommended: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Independent Study in General Business Administration
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Money and Banking
description: The role of money, historically and in our present economic system; history of the dual system of U.S. banking, and contrasting foreign banking systems; the Federal Reserve System, including its checkcollection facilities General Business Administration 97 and its management of bank reserves; economic significance of the volume of bank credit; interrelation of banking and government.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Principles underlying managerial decisions influenced by capital markets and type of ownership; problems relating to the sources of financing; the study of financial analysis and financial management; and interrelating economic and accounting theory with other areas of business.

title: Consumer, Business, and Public Finance
description: The great importance in our national life of business credit, personal and consumer credit (including installment sales credit), bank credit, and public credit (federal, state, and municipal). Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: Managerial Finance
description: Emphasis on principles and tools for analysis and decision making in the finance function.

title: Financial Institutions
description: The structure of financial institutions in the American economy. Financial institutions as recipients and as suppliers of funds in financial markets. The identification and analysis of many kinds of financial institutions and the administration of their loan and investment portfolios. Particular emphasis on the asset, liability, and capital management with the goal of profitability.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance, import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some are emphasized. Prerequisite: FIN 250. Prerequisite recommended: senior standing.

title: Business Finance
description: Principles underlying the financial practices of business from the institutional and business manager points of view. Prerequisites: GBA 360 and ACC 203.

title: Investment Management
description: Problems of investment policy, including the study of types of investment risks, an introduction to security analysis, the analysis of investment requirements, and the kinds of investment policies.

title: Principles of Management
description: This course is founded on the four major managerial functions: planning, organizing, motivating, and controlling, which are applied to the process of management and the organic functions of a business enterprise primarily. Other significant concepts stressed are the importance of leadership, problem solving techniques applied to managerial situations, and the aspects of coordination, communication, and human relations necessary for an individual to be successful as a manager.

title: Management Information Systems
description: Systems theory and practice as they are applied to satisfying information needs for management decision makers through the analysis and design of manual and computerbased systems. The influence of information systems upon management and organization as well as upon managerial decision making. Prerequisite: MGT 380, GBA 220, or permission of the department head.

title: Business and Society
description: An interdisciplinary approach toward developing a philosophy concerning the role of business in society. Emphasis on contemporary issues requiring business people to reexamine their role and the role of the corporation in community and national life. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Organizational Behavior
description: Focuses on the management of organizational behavior. Emphasis is on the behavior of groups and individuals within organizations, and the practical interpretation of behavioral science materials so that students of management can comprehend behavioral phenomena as affected by actions of adminis - trators. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Personnel Administration

Department of Marketing Lowry, Head; Allen, Baird, Battle, Brown, Kelly, Moser, Rink, Vanderleest, Venkatakrishna The marketing process is the making of all managerial decisions in the light of consumer needs and the directing of all marketing activities toward the consumer. The reason for marketing in our economy is to provide an efficient way in which producers may meet the needs of consumers. Consumerism is actually applied marketing and, in turn, marketing is applied consumerism. Marketing management and the consumer activist both seek the same goal although from different vantage points. The marketing process involves several activities which a firm must provide to service properly the needs of consumers. These activities include the right product (style, color, package, size); the right price (costdemand relationships); the right place and time (inventory planning, transportation, channels of distribution); and the right promotional channels (personal selling, sales promotion, advertising). Marketing courses at Ball State University are designed to develop the ability to recognize and define problems, creativity in providing solutions, and the ability to make managerial decisions. Since the majority of Ball State marketing graduates go directly into business after graduation, the marketing program is career oriented. Within the program are four options, including courses which develop the important principles, concepts, and policies needed for particular fields. The four options allow for a variety of career possibilities. The sales and advertising management option prepares for careers in sales and sales management and advertising management and includes consumer product selling, industrial selling, sales training, product management, physical distribution management, purchasing management, consumer product advertising, industrial advertising, retail advertising, advertising agency management, media selection, and public relations. The retail management option emphasizes the instruction necessary for a career in retail store operation and management and prepares for jobs in merchandising and buying, fashion coordination, small business management, retail franchising, chain store operations, and wholesaling management. The marketing, planning and research option leads to careers in marketing planning and research and includes the areas of sales analysis, marketing analysis, marketing research management, sales forecasting, advertising research, product research, and product planning. The general marketing option is for students who want a foundation for a career in the marketing field. After obtaining a foundation in marketing, students are qualified to pursue many different phases of the marketing process. A marketing intern program allows juniors or seniors to relate classroom theory to practical marketing experience by working for a quarter in a variety of meaningful marketing assignments. Selected firms participate in this program in cooperation with the Department of Marketing. Students in the intern program receive eight hours of credit, and the firm pays interns for their work experience. The Marketing Club is a student organization which provides opportunity for both discussion and participation in marketing programs and for development of friendships among students with similar interests. In the past, the club has organized a project team which researched the student market for compact cars. The Marketing Club has also Marketing 99 conducted a series of minicourses on career planning and has brought to the campus selected speakers to discuss job qualifications and career opportunities in various marketing fields such as advertising, retailing, and industrial selling. The United States Department of Labor indicates that there will be many opportunities for marketing employees during the 1970s. The sales and marketing fields will continue to grow. For the past several years, starting salaries for marketing graduates have been increasing at a rate between three to five percent annually. For the student interested in preparing for teaching marketing and/or distributive education, it is possible to earn a departmental major in marketing along with the teaching area major in distributive education. Also, for the student preparing for teaching business education, marketing is a part of the major and minor areas. Teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. The departmental major in marketing on the Professional Arts Curriculum is for students who want a knowledge of marketing for an exciting and challenging business career. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements listed below. title: Credit Management

title: Advertising Management

title: Retail Management

title: Survey of Transportation

title: Marketing Research
description: A basic course in marketing research. Prerequisite: GBA 320.

title: Marketing Management

description: The development of modern architecture, sculpture, and painting from circa 1840 to the present, with emphasis on the development of twentiethcentury concepts. Open to all students. Prerequisite recommended: AHS 212.

title: Recent Trends in Contemporary Art
description: An examination of recent developments and philosophies expressed in painting, sculpture, printmaking, drawing, and crafts; concentrates on the development of the students' expressed philosophy of art as it relates to their own studio production.

title: Honors Colloquium in Art
description: A planned reading and discussion program dealing with the aesthetic problems of contemporary art. Open only to students on the Honors Program.

title: The Visual Arts
description: Survey of the means of approaching and evaluating the visual arts (architecture, sculpture, and painting). Designed for the general education program and especially for nonmajors in art.

title: Art in America
description: A lecture course designed to develop a better understanding of our American cultural traditions through an examination of three hundred years of architecture, painting, sculpture, folk arts, and related forms. Open to all students.

title: Independent Study in Art History
description: Permits the professionally oriented art student to select and explore more intensively an area of art history. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. Open only to art majors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. 431g. Aesthetics in the Visual Arts. (3) Principles underlying twentieth century art products. title: Introduction to Gallery Technics
description: Basic technics involved in such gallery work as administration, collecting, exhibitions, temporary shows, public relations, and restoration of paintings. For art majors only.

title: Art in Living 1
description: A field course in which the student will have the opportunity of studying at first hand the handicrafts, industrial arts, and the fine arts of particular areas. Open to all students. With permission of the department head can be substituted for prescribed courses. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Art in Living 2
description: This field course is similar in objectives to AHS 490, but more time is spent in the field and on the campus. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Open to all students. With permission of the department head it can be substituted for prescribed courses. Department of Home Economics Lutz, Chairman; Adams, Bruner, Caylor, Finn, Hollar, Johnston, Lacey, Nixon, Quesenberry, Roepke, Simpson, Smith, Steele, Wittig Home economics is the field of knowledge and service that is fundamentally concerned with strengthening home and family life through educating the individuals for family living; improving the services and goods used by families; conducting research to discover the changing needs of individuals and families and to determine means of satisfying these needs; and furthering community, national, and world conditions favorable to family living. The profession of home economics synthesizes knowledge drawn from its own research from the physical, biological, and social sciences and the arts and applies this knowledge to improving the lives of families and individuals. The breadth of the field of home economics emphasizes its importance. The eleven separate, but interrelated, fields of foods, nutrition, clothing, textiles, applied art, housing, household equipment, home management, family economics, child development, and family relations provide the foundations for the good health, satisfying and successful living, psychological balance, and good management which are essential for the development of the whole personality. Needs of individuals and families in the social environment of their time are of primary concern in determining the emphases given to the various aspects of home economics. Home economics aids in helping individuals and families to make intelligent decisions concerning all aspects of family life, including the social, economic, aesthetic, managerial, health, and ethical aspects of relations, child development, foods, clothing, and housing. Home economics prepares professional personnel to carry out its objectives through education, research, social welfare and public health, dietetics, and institutional administration and business. It shares with other fields the responsibility for developing perceptive, wellinformed citizens with the ability and the initiative to further conditions favorable to effective living. title: Family Life and Nutrition in Early Childhood Guidance
description: Helps leaders and workers in kindergarten or preschool community groups understand the sequential growth and development of young children and the interrelationship of family meal patterns to their physical, mental, emotional, social, and motor growth.

title: Teaching of Home Economics in the Secondary School
description: Analysis of pupil needs and the development of a home economics program to meet these needs. Organi- .See the professional education requirements for secondary teaching on the Teacher Education Curriculum for the requirement of an additional course in home economics: HED 390, the methods of teaching home economics. Home Economics 109 zation of teaching units, selection and use of teaching methods, and development and use of devices for evaluating pupil growth.

title: Problems in Teaching Home Economics
description: Organization and administration of the total home economics program, including vocational homemaking program, city junior and senior high school programs, plans and equipment for the homemaking department. Prerequisite: HED 390.

title: Food Preparation
description: Fundamental principles underlying the preparation of food. Correct techniques and methods of preparation stressed. Open to men and women.

title: Meal Planning and Table Service
description: Principles and fundamentals in planning, preparing, and serving nutritionally adequate meals which are appetizing and appealing from the aesthetics standpoint. Economic factors considered. Attention is given to foods and types of table service for various occasions. Problems in food buying stressed. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Nutrition
description: Emphasis on fundamental principles in nutrition and application to diets for children and normal adults.

title: Menu Planning for Quantity Food Service
description: Principles of nutrition applied to feeding of individuals and groups. Major emphasis placed on menu planning for institutions with consideration given to meeting nutritional needs. Limitations or problems relating to personnel, facilities, and type of patronage also stressed.

title: Practicum in Institutional Administration and Accounting
description: Stressed are the organization structure, application of principles of scientific management, and personnel administration. Experiences in actual laboratory situation in quantity food production kitchens on campus under supervision of home economics and food production personnel.

title: Practicum in Food Service Planning — Layout and Equipment
description: Designing and equipping of food facilities for schools, colleges, hospitals, industries and commercial operations. Experiences in actual laboratory situation in quantity food production kitchens on campus under supervision of home economics and food production personnel.

title: Practicum in Quantity Food Production and Purchasing
description: Offers opportunity for insight into factors related to quantity production and purchasing of foods. Experiences in actual laboratory situation in quantity food production kitchens on campus under supervision of home economics and food production personnel.

title: Meal Planning and Food Preparation
description: Designed for the nonhome economics major. Basic principles of food buying, food preparation, meal planning and preparation, and table service, along with the study of nutritive value of food. Foods and service for different social occasions.

title: Nutrition and Dietetics. 1
description: Nutritional requirements of the individual from infancy through old age; energy value of foods in the light of chemistry and physiology of digestion; nutritive properties of foodstuffs. Dietaries are planned.

title: Quantity Food Production
description: Problems involved in quantity food production, distribution, and storage. Laboratory experience in university food service units. Prerequisites: HFN 220 and 340.

title: Institutional Administration and Accounting
description: Problems pertaining to school lunchrooms, hospitals, and cafeterias as to personnel, management and organization, cost control, and apportionment of labor. Field trips to institutional kitchens.

title: Institutional Equipment, Buying, and Layout
description: Stationary and small food equipment considered. Layouts of institutional kitchens planned. Field trips to institutional kitchens and equipment companies.

title: Experimental Foods
description: Experimental studies of the different foodstuffs so that their composition and physical and chemical properties can be understood. Recipes are investigated and methods of combining foods are developed and evaluated. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Nutrition and Dietetics 2
description: Food values with emphasg on mineral and vitamin content, recent literature in the field of nutrition. Prerequisites: HFN 340 and CHEM 231.

title: Diet in Disease
description: Pathological conditions resulting from various nutritional diseases, with emphasis upon causes and effects of malnutrition and its treatment. Planning and preparation of diets for abnormal conditions. Hospital laboratory experience provided. Prerequisite: HFN 340.

title: Quantity Food Purchasing
description: Information needed by quantity food buyers; important considerations in purchasing foods and corresponding factors that determine them. Emphasis on ethics in buying.

title: Home Care of the Sick
description: Fundamentals of home nursing in relation to family living, including laboratory experience in nursing techniques. A Red Cross home nursing certificate may be earned by each student.

title: Principles of Home Art
description: Design and color principles, with practical application to home situations. Open to all students except those who have credit in ADS 104.

title: Family Housing
description: Selection of housing to meet family needs. Evaluation of house plans for convenience, art qualities, and satisfying family life. Legal and financial aspects of home ownership. Open to all students.

title: Interior Design and Home Furnishing
description: Selection and arrangement of home furnishings to create attractive, functional interiors that are in harmony with the exterior of the home and adapted to family needs. Open to all students.

title: Home Management 1
description: Management of family and community resources to achieve desired goals in the family. Emphasis on the management problems encountered by newly married couples in establishing a home. Open to all students.

title: Household Equipment
description: Selection, use, and care of household equipment. Students will have an opportunity to plan, organize, and present demonstrations on household equipment.

title: Child Development
description: Understanding of the normal growth and development of preschool children. Emphasis on the child as a member of a family group. Principles of child guidance based on the physical, intellectual, emotional, and social needs of the child. Students observe children in daycare centers, kindergarten, or play school. Open to all students.

title: Infant Development
description: Processes of growth and development during the first two years with various physical, social, and emotional aspects being emphasized. Open to all students.

title: Home Management 2
description: Residence in the home management house offers opportunity to make practical application of the principles of homemaking. Prerequi site: HFN 220.

title: Problems in Consumer Buying
description: The economic aspects of purchasing for the consumer, including marketing conditions, consumer credit, agencies that protect the consumer, and factors to consider when buying consumer goods and services. Open to all students.

title: Family Relations
description: Interpersonal relationships of family members, the forces impinging upon them today, and the changes that result in home and family living, courtship, and mate selection; preparation for marriage, marital adjustment, and parentchild relations. Open to all students.

title: Clothing Selection and Construction
description: Clothing selection and wardrobe planning. Fundamental principles of construction and their application to simple garments.

title: Advanced Clothing Construction
description: Selection and construction of tailored garments and advanced clothing problems. Prerequisite: HTC 104.

title: Apparel Design by the Flat Pattern Method
description: Adaptation of standard patterns to individual proportions, designing of garments and creating an original garment by the flat pattern method. Prerequisite: HTC 104 and 203.

title: Textiles
description: Textiles and their components as they relate to care, performance, and consumer satisfaction. Open to all students.

title: Clothing and Design
description: Special problems to meet students' needs in the clothing field. Unit on preparation of illustrative material for the teaching of clothing. title: Industry in Contemporary Society
description: An introduction to and an understanding of our complex industrial and technological society with emphasis on modern industrial organization, materials, processes, and related socioeconomic factors, including the development of manufacturing processes from crafts to automation. Laboratory experiences of a groupproblem type developed around typical industrial processes. Open to all students except those with teaching areas in industrial education.

title: Industrial Arts for Elementary Grades
description: Industrial arts emphasizing the use of tools, materials, and industrial processes which provide an enrichment of the elementary program. Methods of planning and developing individual and group activity units are examined and evaluated.

title: Practicum in Elementary School Industrial Arts
description: A classroom involvement experience for industrial arts majors in the elementary school. To familiarize the student with the philosophy, history, and principles of industrial arts in the elementary school. Affords the student the opportunity to teach a short unit of instruction in cooperation with an elementary teacher to elementary age children in the local community. Prerequisite: industrial arts major or permission of the department head.

title: Advanced Industrial Arts for Elementary Teachers
description: Industrial arts emphasizing the use of a wide variety of tools, materials, and industrial processes through the planning and organization of group activity units. Prerequisite: IED 364 or permission of the department head. GRAPHICS

title: Introduction to Graphics
description: Introductory experiences in the graphical representation of one-, two-, and threedimensional media. Theory of thirdangle projection, threedimensional coordinate notation, geometric constructions, orthographic projection, auxiliary projection, revolutions, and sections.

title: Advanced Graphics
description: A continuation of experiences gained in IED 103. Work in axonometric projection, oblique projection, perspective, intersections of planes and solids, lateral developments of geometric solids, and elements of graphical mathematics. Prerequisite: IED 103.

title: Architectural Drafting
description: Emphasis primarily on residential architecture. Basic principles of residential construction and planning, distinguishing features of different architectural styles, elementary load calculation, heat loss, and basic principles in use of transit.

title: Descriptive Geometry
description: Experiences in the graphical solution of coplaner and noncoplaner force systems, architectural graphics, bearing and slope notation of lines, geology, mining, and topology problems, and elementary problems in nomography.

title: Problems in Graphics
description: Detailed and extensive study in any of the following areas: structural design, gear design, graphic statics and dynamics, and architectural graphics. Prerequisite: IED 203.

title: Industrial Arts Design
description: Basic design principles are stressed, using both twoand threedimensional media; work with air brush, styrofoam, line drawings, and other types of materials. WOODS

title: Introduction to Woods
description: The nature and properties of wood and the manufacturing processes used to convert it from an extracted raw material to a wood product which fulfills a consumer need in American society. Some development of tool skills.

title: Woods 2
description: The conversion of primary and secondary wood materials into a consumer product. Application and understanding of basic wood product design, machining, fabrication, assembly, finishing, equipment maintenance, and safety. Prerequisite: IED 213.

title: Advanced Woods
description: Extension of knowledge and skill in processing modified wood materials. Additional emphasis upon mechanical and chemical conversion, particle and fiber processes, adhesives, treatments and coatings, drying, and wood production management. Prerequisite: IED 316.

title: Building Construction
description: Manufacture and use of building construction materials and products. Emphasis on problems of fabrication and materials in residence construction.

title: Interior Environmental Products
description: For students with areas in interior design, architecture, and home economics. Interior furnishings, furniture, and lighting are examined as elements of function. Exploratory laboratory activities include construction and evaluation of selected components commonly found in interior environments, and the materials from which they are made.

title: Problems in Woods
description: Extensive study and experimentation in one or more of the following: wood lamination, wood treatment and coating, and production management of secondary wood processing. Prerequisite: IED 316.

title: The World of Construction, Part 1
description: Class activities involve experiencing the units included in the first semester of the IACP "World of Construction" course. The course centers on planning, organizing, and controlling people and resources to produce constructed products.

title: The World of Construction, Part 2
description: Class activities involve experiencing the units included in the second semester of the IACP course. The course centers on planning, organizing, and controlling people and resources to produce constructed products. Prerequisite: IED 415. INDUSTRIAL CERAMICS

title: Introduction to Industrial Ceramics
description: Production and consumption of ceramic materials such as clay, glass, stone, plaster, abrasives, and cement in contemporary industrial technology. Experiences in casting, jiggering, throwing, extrusion, compression molding, glazing and firing, and lapidary processes.

title: Industrial Ceramics: Product Design and Mold Making
description: Individual and group problemsolving approach. Production forming processes, clay and glazing compounding, glazing and kiln operations. Prerequisite: IED 127.

title: Advanced Industrial Ceramics Technology
description: Advanced industrial techniques in ceramic processing and production with emphasis on compression, injection and extrusion molding, and glazing. Prerequisite: IED 127.

title: Research and Development in Industrial Ceramics
description: Extensive independent and group study and experimentation in the area of industrial ceramics. Prerequisite: IED 327. INDUSTRIAL PLASTICS

title: Introduction to Industrial Plastics
description: History, growth, organization, and future of the plastics industry. Thermoplastic and thermosetting materials and processes. Injection, extrusion, compression, blow and rotational molding, thermoforming and other processes. Common industrial plastics used.

title: Industrial Plastics: Design and Mold Making
description: Introduction to plastics design and mold making. Individual problemsolving approach. Injections thermoforming, rotational blow molding and/or extrusion molds, and die construction. Fiberglass and foam molds may also be made. Appropriate moldmaking techniques and equipment are demonstrated. Prerequisites: IED 125.

title: Advanced Industrial Plastics Technology
description: Advanced techniques in plastics processing. Use of automatic molding equipment, molds, and engineering plastics. Mass production techniques will be employed. Prerequisite: IED 225.

title: Research and Development in Plastics
description: Extensive study and experimentation in industrial plastics. Mold making, materials testing and/or equipment design possible. Prerequisite: IED 325. METALS

title: Introduction to Metals
description: Introduction to metals with concentration in foundry, sheet metal, bench metal, art metal, forging, and spinning. Emphasis will also be placed on safety, maintenance, and industrial procedures.

title: Metals Machining
description: Work with the lathe, shaper, milling machines, surface grinder, metal cutting saws, and electrical discharge machine to develop a basic understanding of metal removal. Work will also involve the fundamentals of metallurgy and heat treating of carbon steels. Safety, maintenance, and industrial procedures will also be emphasized. Prerequisite: IED 231.

title: Foundry and Welding
description: Includes theory and techniques in welding a variety of welds in the flat position with electric and oxyacetylene welding equipment. Limited work is done with TIG and MIG welding equipment. An introduction to the fundamentals of pattern design, permanent mold design, core design, and foundry techniques which provides a basic understanding of foundry practices. Emphasis will be placed on safety and maintenance. Prerequisite: IED 2:31.

title: Advanced Metals Machining
description: Work includes cylindrical grinding, advanced milling machine work, electrical discharge machining, tool design and grinding, metallurgy and materials testing. Emphasis is directed toward mathematics and science as it relates to machine setups and tool design. Setups relating to industrial production are discussed. Prerequisite: IED 333.

title: Problems in Sheet Metal and Machine Shop
description: Specialization in the theory and practice of sheet metal work, machine work, precision measurement, metal testing and inspection, and metallurgy. Prerequisite: IED 333 or 433.

title: Problems in Hot Metals
description: Specialization in advanced casting theory and techniques. Advanced welding will include horizontal, vertical, and overhead welding techniques with electric and oxyacetylene welding equipment. Inert gas welding theory and techniques will be studied in depth. Will also include the fundamentals of forging practices. Prerequisite: IED 334. POWER

title: Introduction to Power and Transportation
description: Concentration on the internal combustion engine. A study of power sources, basic mechanisms, component systems, efficiencies and power measurement, and the utilization and application to transportation and industry, and direct energy converters.

title: Application of Power to Land Transportation
description: To acquire fundamental skills and teaching knowledge through experience related to power development for uses applicable to land transportation. Emphasis on internal combustion engines; power development and transmission; thermal, volumetric, and mechanical efficiency; and operation and maintenance. Bicycle maintenance and repair. Factors involved in setting up a transportation unit in the industrial education program. Prerequisite: IED 140.

title: Application of Power to Air Transportation
description: Airframe and aircraft engine systems involving limited maintenance experience in engine systems; instrumentation, principles of aerodynamics and flight control; internal reaction engines, and atmospheric effects on power output and avigation. Prerequisite: IED 240.

title: Application of Power to Water Transportation
description: Small boats, outboard engines, principles of operation, components systems, with particular attention to charging circuits, maintenance, boating laws and safety, inland waterways navigation, propeller theory, boat hulls, performance, and sailing. Prerequisite: IED 240.

title: Private Pilot Ground Training
description: Designed to qualify the student for the Federal Aviation Agency written examination for the Private Pilot Certificate.

title: Special Problems in Hydraulics
description: An introduction to the fundamental principles of hydraulic circuitry. Characteristics of hydraulics, the functioning of component parts of hydraulic systems, and the application to power transmission and control. Prerequisite: IED 240.

title: Special Problems in Pneumatics
description: Introduction to the fundamental principles of pneumatic circuitry. Included is a study of the characteristics of fluids, the functioning of components, and the development of pneumatic circuits and pneumatic logic control. ELECTRICITY-ELECTRONICS

title: Introduction to Electricity
description: Introductory experiences and exploration in the broad field of electricity with special emphasis upon means of producing and transmitting electron flow. Instruction in appropriate electrical projects and familiarization with electrical measuring instruments are important experiences.

title: Applications of Electricity
description: Fundamental electrical theory, with special reference to applications in heating, lighting, electrolysis, electrical communication, and mechanical power. Individual and group experiences through the use of experiments and construction of appropriate projects. Prerequisite: IED 171.

title: Computer Fundamentals
description: Theory and basic circuits of computers. Laboratory activity will consist of group construction of basic computer circuits.

title: Advanced Applications of Electricity
description: Advanced experiences in electrical appliance design and repair, motor design and repair, and various types of interior wiring. Appropriate projects, teaching aids, and factors concerning the teaching of these areas. Prerequisite: IED 270.

title: Industrial Education Electronics
description: Theory of the vacuum tube and semiconductors, with special reference to their application in radio, television, and electronic circuits in industry. Individual and group experiences in project activity of the experi, mental, maintenance, and creative types. Prerequisite: IED 270.

title: Advanced Industrial Education Electronics
description: Special individual and group problems in advanced electrical circuitry involving most of the components of electrical circuits, with special emphasis upon thermionic emission tubes and photo emission devices. Complex problems assigned to groups of students will characterize the project activity. Prerequisite: IED 471. GRAPHIC ARTS

title: Introduction to Graphic Arts
description: Introductory experiences in the various methods used by the graphic arts industry. These include letterpress and offset printing, drypoint and block etchings, silkscreen printing, embossing and gold leaf printing, marking devices, and bookbinding.

title: Letterpress Printing and Bookbinding
description: Fundamental letterpress theory is stressed, with experiences in layout, composition, imposition, presswork and bookbinding; single and twocolor platen presswork; and looseleaf and saddlestitch binding operations.

title: Photography
description: Fundamentals of photography, including camera work, black and white film processing, enlarging, composition, and basic color photography.

title: Techniques of Color Photography
description: Fundamental theory, exposure techniques, film processing, printmaking, and composition considerations in color photography. Prerequisite: IED 386.

title: Photo-Offset Lithography
description: Principles and experiences involved in lithography as a printing process. Cold type composition, camera work, stripping, plate processing, and press work; line shots and halftones. Prerequisite: IED 281.

title: Problems in Graphic Arts
description: Problems in letterpress and photooffset lithography as applied to conventional form in contrast with design. Composition by linotype and color separation as applied to photooffset lithography. Prerequisites: IED 385 and 386 except for students on the Printing Technology Curriculum. PROFESSIONAL

title: Manufacturing Materials and Processes
description: Manufacturing processes used by industries to convert raw materials into consumer products.

title: Characteristics of Industrial Materials
description: Experimental analysis of the mechanical properties of industrial materials. Laboratory experiences involve research and experimentation.

title: Introduction to American Industry
description: The American industrial complex. Emphasis on its organization, materials, processes, products, jigs and fixtures, and socioeconomic factors. For industrial education majors only. Prerequisites: 30 quarter hours of industrial education courses. Not open to the student who has credit in IED 161.

title: Instrumentation and Control
description: The basic principles of process instruments and control systems. Content includes measuring principles, electrical/electronic circuits, calibration and standards and fluidics.

title: Teaching Contemporary Industrial Education
description: Problems of organization and management related to industrial education learning activities. Objectives, terminology, evaluation methods, teaching devices, lesson plans, textbooks, equipment, and supplies are examined. Industrial education classes in public schools are observed. Prerequisites: A minimum of 12 quarter hours from the following courses: IED 103, 125, 127, 140, 171, 213, 231, or 281.

title: Vocational Guidance
description: Principles, purposes, and practices of guidance by the teacher. Educational and occupational information, testing programs, school records, occupational trends, and jobtraining programs are examined and evaluated.

description: Criteria used in determining nature and content of learning experiences in industrial education classes. Teacherpupil planning, group activities, and problemsolving methods.
