title: Curriculum Laboratory in Industrial Education
description: Practice in various contemporary approaches to industrial education drawn from methods and curriculum problems courses. Students will plan and execute a teaching unit in one or more of the contemporary approaches to industrial education, preferably a public school. Prerequisite: IED 391 and 394. Not open to the student who has credit in IED 498.

title: American Industry Practicum
description: Advanced study of the American industrial complex with emphasis on designing and developing teaching materials and activities appropriate to class goals. Activities will be predominately studentidentified problems or research. Prerequisite: IED 361.

title: Industrial Seminar
description: A discussioncentered course in which individuals evaluate their internship experiences. Through these dialogues, individuals will become aware of a greater variety of situations. Prerequisite: a minimum of 4 hours in industrial internship courses. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to cooperative industrial technology majors.

title: The World of Manufacturing, Part 1
description: Class activities are centered around actual teaching of the units included in the first semester of the IACP "World of Manufacturing" course.

title: The World of Manufacturing, Part 2
description: Class activities are centered around actual teaching of the units included in the second semester of the IACP "World of Manufacturing" course. Prerequisite: IED 465.

title: Independent Studies in Industrial Education
description: Special investigation in industrial education on an independent basis. Experimental work, wide reading and development of research techniques and skills are emphasized. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Workshop in Industrial Education
description: Advanced study of new technological developments in related industries. Laboratory activities involve research and experimentation. Credit may be earned in the following areas: electricityelectronics, metals, graphics, power, building trades, graphic arts, and service occupations. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Industrial Education
description: Individual and group studies of one or more major problems in the industrial education field, application of research techniques to the problems for solution, and reporting of findings.

title: Advanced Practicum in Industrial Education
description: Advanced study of problemsolving techniques in industrial education. Individual and group activities involving research and experimentation.

title: Industrial Internship 1 (Quality Control)
description: Designed to give the trainee actual experience in quality control while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Industrial Internship 1 (Sales, Promotion, and Advertising)
description: Designed to provide the trainee actual experience in the sales, promotion and advertising of a product while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Theory and Practice in Letterpress Printing
description: Fundamentals of typography, handand powerfed presswork, basic bookbinding, and press maintenance and safety, while maintaining a production printing schedule.

title: Theory and Practice in Photo-Offset Lithography
description: Offset photolithographic experience covering the practice of camera operation, stripping, plate making, and offset press operation, while maintaining a production printing schedule. Prerequisite: ITE 181.

title: Theory and Practice in Commercial Printing
description: Use of the Franklin Price Catalog for letterpress and offset printing, paper schedules, postal rates, study of the Government Printing Office style book, and standard printing forms and correct terminology, while maintaining a production printing schedule. Prerequisite: ITE 182.

title: Quality Control in the Printing Industry
description: The ability to use the tools of quality control in the printing industry. Emphasis is given to the use of densitometry, correct register, proofreading, ink coverage, proper binding, cropping, paper and ink. Various other topics are considered.

title: Printing Estimating
description: Application of the Point System of Measurement; figuring the amount and cost of composition; basic size, thickness, and weight of paper stock; figuring and cutting paper stock; spoilage allowances; and figuring the cost of paper stock.

title: Internship in Printing Technology
description: A fiveweek internship in a printing industry, working under industrial standards and regulations in the type of printing industry preferred by the student, as much as possible. Prerequisite: ITE 183.

title: Industrial Internship 2 (Work Measurement)
description: Designed to provide the trainee actual experience in work measurement while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Industrial Internship 2 (Market Research)
description: Designed to provide the trainee actual experience in market research while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Theory and Practice in Publications
description: Various publication formats that are commonly used by institutions and industries. Both offset and letterpress forms of makeup will be employed in maintaining publication schedules. Prerequisite: ITE 183.

title: Theory and Practice in Estimating and Copyfitting
description: Participants will estimate costs, order appropriate stock, learn schedules, make layouts, compose forms, cut the stock, estimate waste, and other details in completely planning and executing a printing order on a previously made schedule. Prerequisite: ITE 281.

title: Theory and Practice in Color Printing and Process Work
description: Printing of letterpress and offset color work, involving technical procedures in color separation and the use of densitometer and the use of various kinds of printing plates for letterpress color work. The completion of the secondyear creative project is a requirement. Prerequisite: ITE 282.

title: Color Process Printing
description: The photographic steps in making plates for photomechanical printing of color pictures. Both color reflection and color transparency copy are considered. Prerequisite: ITE 186.

title: Type Design and Copyfitting
description: The determination of the amount of area necessary for composition according to size and family of type by use of a slide rule. The study of modern type design and usage, as well as outstanding typographers and their contributions. The place of the advertising agency in modern display composition and its contributions. Prerequisite: ITE 187.

title: Printing Mechanics and Press Design

Prerequisite: ITE 187.

title: Production Control in the Printing Industry
description: Organized and orderly methods of planning production to gain more profit, sales, production, and work. Prerequisite ITE 284.

title: Industrial Internship 3 (Plant Supervision)
description: Designed to provide the trainee actual experience in plant supervision while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Industrial Internship 3 (Traffic and Distribution)
description: Designed to provide the trainee actual experience in the techniques of traffic and distribution while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Industrial Internship 4 (Production Control)
description: Designed to give the trainee actual experience in the control of production while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Industrial Internship 4 (Sales Management)
description: Designed to provide the trainee actual experience in managing sales operations while on a work assignment in industry. The trainee is supervised by the University Coordinator and Plant Manager.

title: Printing Management

description: The student will work full time for one quarter in a position involving the supervision of production employees in a printing industry under supervision of the Department of Industrial Education and Technology. Prerequisite:

School of Music Hargreaves, Director; Albright, Baker, Dunn, Niccum, Wolfe, Woodrum The School of Music embraces four departments: Music Education, Music History and Literature, Music Theory and Composition, and Musical Performance. Administrative efficiency and scholarly pursuits are enhanced by further subgroupings within these major areas, particularly in the case of Musical Performance with its several applied music committees. A full range of large and small performing ensembles — from the professional Musical Arts Woodwind Quintet, Da Camera Brass Quintet, and the Ars Musica String Quartet to thea Concert Choir, the Wind Ensemble, and the Symphony Orchestra — provides supe rb opportunities for listening or for active participation. Less usual groups such as the Harp Ensemble, the Collegium Musicum, the String Sinfonietta, the University Sin gers, and the Ball State Ballet accent the diversity of performing outlets on the Ball State campus. Any student on the campus, regardless of major, may audition for membership in the University concert organizations. In advance of selecting the field of music for concentration, the student will consult the Director of the School of Music. In addition to the regular entrance requirements of the University, a student with a concentration area in music must have proficiency in piano, voice, or some symphonic instrument, and a working knowledge of the rudiments of music. Examinations in theory and applied music will be given at times to be announced. If a student cannot meet requirements when entering the University, arrangements may be made to meet them later. If lacking in the applied music requirement, the individual will study without credit until it can be met. All students with a concentration area in music are expected to attend the weekly recital meeting and to perform there with a frequency advised by the individual teacher of applied music. Additional information will be found in the Music Student Handbook. In advance of completing registration procedure each quarter, the student will clear through the office of th e Department of Musical Performance the names of the applied music teachers to whose classes assignment will be made. Students wishing to qualify for certification as teachers of music in the public schools should refer to the appropriate curricular information listed under the Department of Music Education as well as in the area requirements which follow. Students wishing to prepare for careers in professional performance, in composition and arranging, or in scholarly activity and research, are encouraged to enroll in the appropriate departmental major. The departmental minors also may serve some of these goals, but the total number of hours required for their completion is kept at a level which will serve the student in a liberal arts orientation who seeks broad cultural development rather than specialized proficiency. A student whose work load permits may register for additional lessons in the selected minor field or in other minor fields, provided the approval of the Director of the School of Music has been secured. Practice rooms should be reserved in the office of the School of Music at the beginning of each quarter and term. Each student with a concentration area in music is advised to have a piano available for use at a certain time daily, either at the University or elsewhere. All students with concentration areas in music will participate actively in ensembles according to their curricular requirements. Those planning to become directors of instrumental ensembles or supervisors of instrumental music ordinarily will earn ensemble credits in the University bands and University orchestras, and vocalists preparing to become directors of choral activities ordinarily will earn ensemble credits in the appropriate University choral groups. In addition, students are expected to take advantage of the opportunities for musical broadening provided by membership in the ensembles outside their special field. Unless the foregoing conditions with respect to recital attendance and performance and with respect to the earning of ensemble credits are met, credit will not be given for major or minor study of instrument or voice. Music Education 127 Department of Music Education Carr, Head; Burkart, Caldwell, Curt, Dunn, Eberle, Griner, Hiscott, Karjala, Nichols, Phillips, Wakeland The preparation of teachers of music for all scholastic levels is of primary concern within the School of Music. The task of becoming an effective music teacher not only involves developing a high degree of musicianship and scholarship, but requires of the teachermusician a sincere interest and skill in assisting others to develop musical responsiveness. Three major fields of specialization are provided for the student seeking to be certified as a music teacher. These include the teaching area major in music which prepares the student to teach instrumental, choral, and general music in grades kindergarten through twelve, the teaching major in choralgeneral music which prepares the student to teach choral and general music in grades kindergarten through twelve, and the teaching major in instrumental music which is preparation for teaching instrumental music in grades kindergarten through twelve. In addition to these three major fields of specialization, several minor concentration areas in music are available to those who wish to attain a higher level of music competency by adding a minor concentration to a music teaching major, or for those who wish to combine the study of music with that of another subject. In order to graduate from Ball State University with a major or minor in any of the music teacher preparation fields, a student must present evidence of an ability to execute certain musical and educational tasks. This evidence, in addition to the successful completion of the curriculum, is shown through the demonstration of a firm commitment to teaching and a high level of competency on both primary and secondary performance media — symphonic instruments and/or voice, and piano. *

title: The Development and Administration of School Choral Activities
description: Analysis of the choral literature available for use in the secondary school as to its technical difficulty and suitability to choral groups of various sizes and musical backgrounds. The administration and supervision of choral activities, including the general chorus, the selected groups, and the voice classes. Techniques of choral arranging.

title: Brass Techniques 1
description: A study of the brass instruments with emphasis on skill development and pedagogical understanding. Acoustical principles, basic maintenance, teaching methods and materials. Meets two hours weekly.

title: Brass Techniques 2
description: A continued study of the brass instruments with emphasis on skill development and pedagogical understanding. Acoustical principles, basic maintenance, teaching methods and materials. Meets two hours weekly. Prerequisite: MUSED 221.

title: Woodwind Techniques 1
description: A study of the woodwind instruments with emphasis on skill development and pedagogical understanding. Acoustical principles, basic maintenance, teaching methods and materials. Meets two hours weekly.

title: Woodwind Techniques 2
description: A continued study of the woodwind instruments with emphasis on skill development and pedagogical understanding. Acoustical principles, basic maintenance, teaching methods and materials. Meets two hours weekly. Prerequisite: MUSED 223.

title: Piano Technology Workshop 1
description: Basic principle and application of piano tuning and the nomenclature and repair of the piano. An elective intended for students preparing for the field of music and others who may be interested in piano technology. Open to all students.

title: Piano Technology Workshop 2
description: Advanced techniques of piano tuning, enabling the student to tune a piano independently. Principles of complete action adjustment and common minor repairs. Prerequisite: MUSED 240. 'Students are required to have completed a proficiency examination on piano and attained junior standing on their major medium of musical expression prior to enrolling in student teaching.

title: Piano Technology Workshop 3
description: Complete repair and rebuilding of the piano. Prerequisite: MUSED 241. Open to all students.

title: Basic Musical Experiences for Early Childhood Education
description: Designed to develop creative musical responsiveness in students enrolled in the 2-year early elementary education program, and to demonstrate through laboratory experiences the application of creativity to the developmental characteristics of three-, four-, and fiveyear old children.

title: Children's Music: Lower Elementary Grades
description: Methods of teaching music to children in kindergarten and grades one through three. Basic theory of music, including notation; class participation in musical activities and in the use of simple musical instruments, song books, recordings, and audiovisual aids. Parallel: MUSED 265. Not open to the student who is majoring or specializing in music.

title: Keyboard Skills for Elementary Classroom Teachers
description: Preparation of students of varying musical backgrounds and abilities in the use of the piano for teaching music in the elementary schools. Parallel: MUSED 264. Not open to the student who is majoring or specializing in music. 300. reaching and Administration of Instrumental Music. (4) Using the skills developed in instrumental minor studies as a point of departure, the student in survey classes covers the techniques of related families of instruments. Proper care of equipment, organization of physical factors, teaching of instrumental classes, and developing instrumental ensembles are made the basis for lectures and class discussions. Piano and voice majors are advised to reserve this course for the senior year. Prerequisite: minor skills in brass, woodwind, and string instruments.

title: The Teaching of Music in the Elementary School
description: The problems of teaching and supervising music in the elementary school for music supervisors and special teachers of music. Lesson planning and teaching are done in the class, and contact is made with teaching situations through directed observation. Leading music series are studied. Prerequisite: MUSTH 113 or the equivalent.

title: Methods of Teaching and Supervising Music in the Primary Grades
description: A methods course for vocal music education majors. Intensive study of materials, methods, and skills for teaching music in the first three grades; singing, rhythms, listening, creative activities, and instruments. Directed observation gives contact with actual teaching situations.

title: Methods of Teaching and Supervising Music in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: A methods course for vocal music education majors, which is a continuation of 351. Intensive study of materials, methods, and skills for teaching music in grades four, five, and six: singing, rhythms, listening, creative activities, and instruments. Directed observation gives contact with actual teaching situations. Prerequisite: MUSED 351.

title: General Music in the Junior and Senior High School
description: An exploration of the scope and character of musical activities designed to supplement membership in the established performing groups of the public schools and to provide an outlet for the many students not concerned with public performance. Acquaintance with materials and techniques appropriate to the study of music literature and music theory.

title: Introduction to Orff Schulwerk
description: The principles of the childcentered approach to music developed by Carl Orff. Classroom activities will be explored in movement, rhythm, and speech on basic and pre-Orff levels, along with creative utilization of simple percussion instruments.

title: Children's Music: Upper Elementary Grades
description: Music suitable for children in grades four, five, and six, and methods of teaching this music. Part singing and creative projects are given emphasis. New elements of musical theory are introduced and fundamentals are reviewed. Student participation in musical activities. Parallel: MUSED

title: Music Appreciation, Materials, and Methods
description: Designed to enrich the musical background of the student in the common heritage of musical literature and to suggest methods for presenting these materials to children. Parallel: MUSED 361.

title: Administration and Planning of the Church Music Program
description: Formation and training of adult and children's choirs in churches. Congregational singing. Service planning. The clergy, the congregation, and the church musician.

title: Recent Trends in Teaching Piano 1
description: Designed to improve the work of the teacher of piano in his handling of class and private instruction. Areas of interest include the child beginner, the adult beginner, class procedures in public school, educational publications, a graded curriculum, basic musicianship through keyboard study, and the analysis and development of specific pianistic skills. Music Education 129

title: Recent Trends in Teaching Piano 2
description: Designed to improve the work of the teacher of piano in his handling of class and private instruction. Areas of interest include the child beginner, the adult beginner, class procedures in public school, educational publications, a graded curriculum, basic musicianship through keyboard study, and the analysis and development of specific pianistic skills.

title: Practicum in Music Education: Elementary
description: A concentrated, shortterm course that provides practical experience in all phases of music education for the elementary schools through participation in varied musical activities, including singing, listening, playing instruments, and dancing. Contact with new materials and methods will be insured in part by the inclusion of two or more distinguished visiting instructors on the staff.

title: Practicum in Music Education: Secondary
description: Provides experiences with the materials and activities of general music classes in secondary schools. The chief concern is with possibilities of instruction in music for students who are not active in the performing groups of their schools. Prerequisite: MUSED 440.

title: The Orff Workshop — Beginning
description: Opportunities for concentrated study, by means of participation, observation, and discussion, in some of the beginning phases of the fresh and stimulating approach to children's musical education created by Dr. Carl Orff. An emphasis is placed on the basic approaches to the Orff method of teaching music to children in grades one through six. Considerable time will be devoted to the techniques of organized recorder playing and study of recorder literature.

title: The Orff Workshop — Intermediate
description: Opportunities for concentrated study, by means of participation, observation, and discussion, in some of the more advanced phases of the fresh and stimulating approach to children's musical education created by Dr. Carl Orff. An emphasis is placed on creative projects in orchestrating materials to be used with children in grades one through six. Considerable time will be devoted to the techniques of organized recorder ensemble playing and study of recorder literature. Prerequisite: MUSED 443 or permission of the department head.

title: Music in Early Childhood Education: A Practicum
description: Views the music program of early childhood education as a logical basis for creativity and as an effective and educationally sound means of eliminating inhibition from the responsiveness of three-, four-, and fiveyear old children.

title: Maintenance and Repair of Stringed Instruments 1
description: Provides a fundamental working knowledge of skills required in maintaining stringed instruments at the elementary and secondary school levels. Study and application of school repair problems in regard to the violin, viola, cello, and doublebass. General techniques in making adjustments, gluing, and using tools properly. Analyses of the various woods used in instruments and bows.

title: Maintenance and Repair of Stringed Instruments 2
description: Advanced study and experience in more specialized repairs on stringed instruments. Discussions and laboratory work including splicing, grafting, varnishing, carving and bow rehairing. Historical resume of stringed instruments and makers from the seventeenth to the twentieth century.

title: Psychology of Music
description: Presentation of materials as an aid to the understanding of the nature and extent of individual differences in musical talent. Specific preparation in the psychology of audition, motor control, and in the analysis of the musical mind leading to a natural application in the psychology of musical training.

title: Tests, Measurements, and Guidance in Music
description: Acquaints the teacher with tests of sensory capacities, appreciation, and achievement. Briefly reviews such statistical and other data as make for an enlightened evaluation of the various tests and of their results.

title: Music in Therapy and Special Education
description: The theoretical aspects of music therapy and their appropriate application to special education in the public schools. Emphasizes the power of music to elicit normal interaction with peers from the child with a learning difficulty.

title: Music in Society
description: The relationship between humanity and music from primitive culture through the present time. Emphasis on those specific contributions made by ethnic groups to the literature of music. The implications for music teachers regarding aesthetic experience.

title: Independent Study in Music Education
description: Provides the superior student with an opportunity for intensive study and research in a particular aspect of music education. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. title: Introduction to the Literature of Music
description: An overview of the many forms of musical composition and of the media for their performance to be used as a basis for subsequent musical experiences.

title: Music for the Listener: An Introduction
description: Introduction to the elements of music, followed b y a study of musical styles through a survey of the literature of music. Lectures , films, classroom discussion, and recorded music supplemented by attendance at concerts and recitals. No previous knowledge of music required. Not open to students with areas in music.

title: Collegium Musicum
description: The study, realization, and performance of Medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque music. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. 211. (410). Music History 1. Open only to students with areas in music except by permission of the department head.

title: Music History 2
description: Changes in music from the late sixteenth century through the Baroque, the Rococo, and the Classical periods. The transition from the Renaissance to the Baroque, and the developments of opera, sonata, symphony, and the related forms. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101, 211, or permission of the department head.

title: Music History 3
description: Developments in music from the time of Beethoven to the p resent. Transition from the classical to romantic periods, the various reactions to Romanticism, and trends of the twentieth century. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101, 212, or permission of the department head.

title: Collegium Musicum
description: The study, realization, and performance of Medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque music. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Instrumental Music from the Time of Bach
description: The growth and development of musical forms and styles as they apply to music for orchestra and solo instruments from the late Baroque period to our time. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101 or 213.

title: Opera from the Time of Mozart
description: Following a brief survey of the early development of opera, there will be a more detailed consideration of examples of this genre from the middle of the eighteenth century to the present time. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101 or 213.

title: Clitoral and Vocal Solo Literature from, Haydn to the Present
description: The development of the cantata, oratorio, mass, motet, anthem, and the lied; great masterworks in these forms. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101 or 213.

title: Ballet History
description: A history of ballet, tracing its beginnings, romantic heights, and contemporary trends.

title: Collegium Musicum
description: The study, realization, and performance of Medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque music. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Music in the Baroque Era
description: Vocal and instrumental music during the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, including the function of figured bass, significant contrapuntal developments, the evolution of opera, oratorio, and cantata, and the growth of various instrumental genres such as the concerto grosso, sonata, suite, and types of keyboard music. Prerequisite: MUSLI 213 or permission of the department head.

title: Music in Preclassic and Classic Eras
description: Vocal and instrumental music of the eighteenth century, including the various styles which marked the transition from Baroque to Classic music, the rise of comic opera, and the development of the sym- Music Theory and Composition 131 phony, concerto, sonata, chamber music, and keyboard literature. Prerequisite: MUSLI 213 or permission of the department head.

title: Music in the Romantic Era
description: Vocal and instrumental music of the nineteenth century and its relationship to the Romantic movement, the growth of chromatic harmony, the changes in traditional types such as the symphony and opera, the growth of the art song, the tone poem, and the character piece. Prerequisite: MUSLI 213 or permission of the department head.

title: Dance Notation 1
description: The beginnings of dance notation and an introduction to the main systems used today (Labonotation, Benesh, etc.). Prerequisite: some previous dance experience.

title: Honors Colloquium in Music
description: Readings, reports, and discussions of various aspects of music. Restricted to students on the Honors Program.

title: Hymnody in Worship
description: Hymns in early Jewish and Western Christian tradition: their historical and liturgical context and contemporary use. A summary of Western religious thought as exposed in liturgical poetry. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101, 211, 212, or 213.

title: Choral Music of the Church
description: Anthems, motets, cantatas, and oratorios from the sixteenth century to the present suitable for the church service. Prerequisite: MUSLI 101, 211, 212, or 213.

title: Collegium Musicum
description: The study, realization, and performance of Medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque music. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Independent Study in Music History
description: Provides the superior students with an opportunity for guided reading and intensive study in an area of music history of particular interest to them and for which provision is not made by the regular course offerings of the department. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Organ Literature and Design
description: The organ and its music from the Renaissance. Emphasis on baroque, romantic, and contemporary instruments and literature. Field trips to nearby instruments. Prerequisites: MUSLI 101, 211, 212, or 213.

title: Standard Repertoire of the Piano 1
description: A survey of the standard masterworks for piano from Bach through Liszt. It is not necessary for the student to be a pianist to take this course. Prerequisites: Some music literature background and an ability to read music will be expected of the student.

title: Standard Repertoire of the Piano 2
description: A survey of the standard masterworks for piano from Chopin through Samuel Barber. It is not necessary for the student to be a pianist to take this course. Prerequisites: Some music literature background and an ability to read music will be expected of the student.

title: Field Sources of American Musical Culture
description: Field study in major musical capitals, including the best known festival centers. Seminars scheduled in connection with planned travel are concerned with the orientation of members to the historic significance of composers native to the region, to the influence of nationalistic schools, and to the interaction of architectural and other physical matters with the musical output. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students on all curricula. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Music Theory and Composition Sherman, Head; Foley, Hoffmann, Knight, Pellegrini, Scott The Department of Music Theory and Composition has gained prominence for its leadership role in the development of innovative practices relating to teaching and learning in music theory and composition. The department has developed the nation's first contemporized basic music theory curriculum. The Electronic Music Theory Laboratory provides individualized instruction in the aural and visual perception of music through "Aural Comprehension in Music," a unique program of instruction developed in the lab and used nationally. The Electronic Music Studio is another facility which is rapidly growing and assuming an important role in the evolving curricula of the School of Music. The studio is fully equipped for the production and processing of electronic and concrete sounds. The ARP synthesizer is interfaced with a digital computer for full digitalanalog control. The facility is used for undergraduate and graduate research as well as electronic composition.

title: Music Fundamentals
description: Recommended for those entering freshmen whose background of experience in the fundamentals of music theory is thought to be too limited for the successful completion of MUSTH 111 or MUSED 264 and MUSED 265. The course deals with such fundamentals as music reading, spelling (intervals, scales, triads, meter signatures, key signatures), terminology, and notation. 111, 112, 113. Music Theory. (3 hours each quarter) Review of terminology and fundamentals precedes an extensive study of the tonal, rhythmic, motivic, and formal structure of melody through composition and analysis. The basic elements of music are studied through the analysis and writing of music in two, three, and four parts. Elementary work in transposition, scoring, and harmonic alterations. Music reading, aural discernment, and rhythmic training provided in class and electronic laboratory drill. These courses must be taken in course number sequence. 211, 212, 213. Music Theory. (3 hours each quarter) More complex elements of nineteenth and twentieth century music studied through composition and analysis. title: Acoustics: Natural
description: The natural acoustical phenomena related to the sound production, amplification, and characteristics of conventional instruments in the natural environment of the studio and concert hall. Prerequisites: PHYCS 184.

title: Acoustics: Electronic
description: The electronic production, reproduction, and alteration of sound as it is related to the production and reproduction of music. Prerequisite: PHYCS 184.

title: Music Calligraphy
description: Practical experience in calligraphic skills and layout procedures pertinent to the preparation of music scores and parts. Prerequisite: MUSTH 113.

title: Compositional Practices: The Baroque
description: The theoretical principles, stylistic forces, and aesthetics that characterize the compositional practices of the Baroque period. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Compositional Practices: Eighteenth-Century Classicism
description: The theoretical principles, stylistic forces, and aesthetics that characterize the compositional practices of eighteenthcentury classicism. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Compositional Practices in Electronic Music
description: A workshop in current practices of producing music by electronic means. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213. 371, 372, 373. Composition. (2 hours each quarter) Experience in writing short instrumental and vocal compositions with emphasis on developing the student's technical capacity to achieve freedom of style. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Analytical Technique
description: The development of techniques for the identification and analysis of significant compositional elements as determined by the musical context. Analysis will be applied to a broad representation of musical masterworks from various periods with examination of the macroand microstructure and construction of selected works. Special attention is given to musical practices before and after the period of tertian harmony. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Counterpoint
description: Exercises in contrapuntal writing designed to develop sensitivity to sixteenthcentury polyphonic practice. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Orchestration
description: Scoring for large and small orchestral ensembles. Particular attention given to voice positioning, doubling, and textural deployment as regards harmonic weight and color. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Band Arranging
description: Scoring for symphonic band and wind ensemble. Particular attention is given to voicing, sectional and crosssectional doubling, soloistic treatment of instruments, and other elements of contemporary treatment in scoring. Prerequisite: MUSTH 442.

title: Arranging for the Dance Band
description: The study and analysis of arranging techniques as employed by current leading dance band and jazz arrangers, and the practice of writing and performing scores by members of the class. Prerequisite: MUSTH 442.

title: Theory of Nineteenth-Century Music
description: Vocabulary, devices, tonal organization, and shaping forces that characterize the compositional practices of nineteenth -century Romanticism. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Theory of Twentieth-Century Music
description: Vocabulary, devices, tonal organization, notation, and other elements that characterize the compositional practices of twentiethcentury music. Prerequisites: MUSTH 213.

title: Theory of Medieval and Renaissance Music
description: Vocabulary, devices, and shaping forces that characterize the compositional practices of Medieval and Renaissance music. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Electronic Music Studio 1
description: An introductory course in the fundamentals of sound, its physical and perceptual dimensions, as a basis for the electronic synthesis and analysis of musical sounds. Studio laboratory time required. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Electronic Music Studio 2
description: Structured to allow the student an individualized approach in the application of electronic sound synthesis compositionally or in educational research. Studio laboratory time required. Prerequisite: MUSTH 461. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. 471, 472, 473. Composition. (2 hours each quarter) Experience in writing more complex and extended instrumental and vocal compositions with continued emphasis on the development of style. Prerequisite: MUSTH 373.

title: Music Theory in the Secondary School
description: An investigation of pedagogical precepts and problems relating to music theory in the secondary school. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213.

title: Independent Study
description: Independent study in any area of music theory via readings, analysis, and/or research. Prerequisite: MUSTH 213 and permission of the department head. Denny, Exley, Fitzpatrick, Gerhart, Gibas, Houghton, Ingold, Johnson, Mahoney, McConnell, Sargent, Scearse PROFESSIONAL NURSING The fouryear collegiate program in nursing has been designed to prepare the graduate to function upon completion of the curriculum as a professional nurse practitioner in beginning positions of bedside nursing, team leadership, and public health nursing and to articulate into graduate study. Classroom and laboratory instruction for the curriculum is provided by the University and utilizes the facilities of Ball Memorial Hospital, adjacent to the University campus, as well as other nearby health agency facilities. The curriculum has been planned to provide general and professional educational experiences for the beginning student, the registered nurse, licensed practical nurses, medical corpsmen, aides, or orderlies who seek a baccalaureate education in nursing. A student who can document educational experiences and/or work experiences in selected areas of nursing may earn credit by examination in Ball State University courses NUR 310, 311, 316, 317, and 410. Other nursing courses may be challenged with special permission. Thirtyfive quarter hours of college credits may be earned in nursing courses by examination. A student indicating an intent for a major in nursing begins study in areas of English, social sciences, physical and biological sciences, and the fine arts. Approximately two years of academic work in the areas of humanities, social and behavioral sciences, and biological sciences are required. The major in nursing has been concentrated in the student's junior and senior years. Cooperative programs in nursing have been arranged between Ball State University and Anderson College, Grace College, Huntington College, Manchester College, St. Francis College, Taylor University, and Tri-State College. A student interested in the cooperative program may enroll at one of these institutions for the freshman and sophomore years and transfer these credits to Ball State University for the remaining two years. The curriculum for students preparing for professional nursing is the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in nursing and a minor in biological science. The Bachelor of Science degree may be earned within the minimum requirements of the curriculum (186 hours), and the student may use toward a selected minor the 28 to 32 hours of electives on the curriculum. The student shall meet the general requirements of the University with respect to the professional nursing major and minor in biological science and with respect to graduation (minimum of 2.0 scholastic ratio in major, required minor, and overall grade point average); in addition the student will present a minimum grade of C in each clinical nursing course. The student is responsible for making application for admission to the major in nursing after completing 60 quarter hours of work. Completion of the first seven courses in the minor in biological sciences (CHEM 110, 130; BIO 111, 112, 213; ANAT 201; and PHYSL 210) is necessary before admission to the major. The guiding philosophy of the Department of Nursing has been predicated upon the belief that the aims of the University should be realized in the educational preparation of the professional nurse. It has been accepted that the professional nurse is characterized by the ability (1) to provide intelligent and skillful nursing to patients and their families in all of the basic nursing fields, (2) to guide and direct others in the performance of nursing care, (3) to utilize the democratic process for the improvement of the health services through cooperative endeavor with members of other disciplines, and (4) to maintain a personal identity and to attain individual satisfaction in daily life as the family, the community, and the profession are served. The Department of Nursing accepts the responsibility for fostering a maximal development of the student in nursing which should resolve in an optimal contribution to the profession of nursing and to society. It is believed that the basic preparation of an individual should provide for the total development of the person. The faculty is dedicated to this realization through a synthesis of the strands of a broad cultural experience in general education with an educational experience in the professional content of nursing. The departmental objectives for students in nursing are: 1. To acquire knowledge, skills, and attitudes which will provide the foundation for the administering of comprehensive nursing to the patient and his family; 2. To develop a concept of nursing which encompasses the prevention of illness, the promotion of health for the individual, the family, and the community, as well as the care of the sick; 3. To develop an understanding of self and an appreciation for each nurse's contribution to the profession and to society; 4. To develop skill in effective human relations and communications with patients, family, and colleagues; 5. To acquire an understanding and recognition of the nurse's responsibility as a contributing member of the health team; 6. To develop an ability for critical thinking, value judgments, and selfdirection which will enable the student to become a contributing member in the nursing profession and in society; 7. To develop an understanding of the need for continuous professional and personal growth which includes participation and leadership in the social, cultural, and educational world. The nursing course sequence begins with NUR 200. Clinical nursing in the five basic areas is begun by the student in the junior year. It is recommended that all students enrolled in nursing report their names and current addresses to the Department of Nursing each quarter. Diedrich The College of Sciences and Humanities provides courses and programs for either a liberal education or for specialized and professional curricula. The liberal arts programs permit the student to elect more freely and to explore the "idea" subject matter. "Liberal" stems from the Latin liber, to free. By definition, a liberal arts education should free people from ignorance by providing them an intelligent grasp of the experiences of the past and an understanding of the interrelationship of branches of knowledge. The individual is educated to think objectively, critically, and creatively. The liberal arts include the study of foreign languages, the physical and social environment, the evolution of Western civilization, the foundations of modern science, and the classical works. The wide range of courses offered by the College of Sciences and Humanities provides the basis for specialized and professional curricula — offered both within the college and in the other colleges requiring service courses. Within the College, preprofessional programs are specified — for medicine, dentistry, engineering, and law. A variety of specialist programs is offered, including medical technology and social work. Also, the departments within the College have programs designed for those planning graduate study in the field of their choice. The College includes the following departments: Anthropology, Biology, Chemistry, Economics, English, Foreign Languages (French, German, Greek, Latin, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish), General and Experimental Psychology, Geography and Geology, History, Journalism, Mathematical Sciences, Natural Resources, Philosophy, Physics, Physiology and Health Science, Political Science, Center for Radio and Television, Sociology, and Speech. In addition, the College offers programs in the Social Sciences and in three Institutes — Environmental Studies, International Studies, and Urban and Regional Studies. The graduate offerings of the departments in the College of Sciences and Humanities are described in the Graduate Catalog. The roster is maintained and its use supervised by an interdisciplinary advisory committee chaired by the director. At the present time, the Institute does not offer academic courses or programs. Today's college student, to be an effective individual, must be aware of the varying and constantly changing cultural conditions of other societies. This premise is the attraction and the challenge of international studies. The international studies program at Ball State University is designed for students who desire an interdisciplinary approach to contemporary world problems. Institute for Urban and Regional Studies Mitchell, Acting Director Nearly threequarters of all Americans live and work in highly concentrated urbanized areas; this proportion will most likely continue to grow. Highly intensive social and economic activity in these areas have created a host of largescale and complex problems. Meaningful analysis of these problems can only be accomplished through a spirit of collaboration among experts with different backgrounds. At Ball State, this orientation translates into an interdisciplinary undergraduate program in Urban and Regional Studies. This program draws on the strengths of various disciplines such as sociology, economics, geography, and political science. The scope of inquiry includes the nature of an urban economy, the organization of local government, city politics, public finance, the community, the problem of housing, and poverty. One goal of the program is to give students a firm understanding of urban characteristics and problems which they can employ in preprofessional work such as urban administration, the poverty field, and urban development and planning, or in pursuing graduate training in law, planning, social work, or public administration. Another goal of this program is to encourage student involvement in community problems and educational growth through internships. Students might gain work experience with a public or private social service agency, an organization involved in developing lowincome housing, a planning commission, a consulting firm, an urban redevelopment authority, or a mayor's office. A third goal is to encourage student inquiry. Much of this normally is related to internship experience. Student research is a most effective learning experience and can reinforce classroom and internship experience. An example of a student research topic might be a needs study for lowincome housing or a feasibility study for mass transit. The experiences in this program are designed primarily to educate rather than train the student. Regular training in urban affairsrelated professions is normally at the graduate level. Urban and regional studies is a departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. A departmental minor in urban and regional studies is also offered as a useful alternative for students having a more casual interest in urban affairs. This general background gives students, many if not most of whom will settle in large metropolitan areas, a degree of understanding about their urban environment which should be reflected in their future civic and professional activities. Department of Anthropology Izmirlian, Chairman; Flores-Meiser, Genz, Glenn, Scruton, Swartz, Wallace, Whitehead Anthropology is scarcely a hundred years old as a formal academic discipline. Its origins are in the nineteenth century's growing awareness of non-European societies, the revelation that man's social past is of great antiquity, and the discovery by Charles Darwin of the biological mechanisms which have produced the human species. From these several awakenings has emerged a field which, as developed in this country, is neither a biological nor a social science, but is uniquely both. It is, in fact, the singular amalgamation of the two areas which is responsible for the name of the field, the Study of Man. Although the anthropologist, as a practicing scholar, develops a limited specialty, the field itself remains convinced that the human phenomenon is a sociobiological whole and must finally be studied as such. This belief places a certain burden on the anthropologist and the student by requiring, for professional competence, a very wide range of content areas. In physical anthropology, for example, attention is commonly focused on such topics as the nature of the evolutionary process which is responsible, through the action of natural selection, hybridization, genetic drift and artificial selection, for the development of the largetailless, terrestrial, bipedal, orthograde primate which man is. Course work is commonly devoted to the fossil evidence of recent human evolution, especially during the Pleistocene period. Without doubt, that aspect of physical anthropology which has the greatest potential contribution to make to human selfunderstanding, and the aspect likeliest to be of practical application, is the study of contemporary varieties, or races of humanity. There is no subject about which people seem to have the most fundamental convictions, and commonly there is none in which the unfortunate effects of total ignorance are more clearly seen. The anthropologist is deeply involved in all phases of this study, from the determination of the nature of the phenomenon itself, through the eventual genetic classification of races, to the delicate and vexing questions having to do with the significance of race differences. The pursuit of truth is the goal of the scientist. But the application of knowledge which has been secured through the scientific method is hardly avoidable. Anthropology 163 Much of cultural anthropology is closely related to history and no branch illustrates this fact more clearly than archaeology. Courses in this area provide the student of the human past with techniques which enable many of the limitations of conventional historiography to be overcome, with the result that we now possess knowledge of human behavior during times antedating writing by sometimes hundreds of thousands of years. Of course, this knowledge is rarely of the detailed and specific sort sought by the historian. But although archaeologists are commonly deprived of historical personalities, they have the compensation of seeing the great sweep of human affairs with perhaps greater clarity. The archaeologist reminds the student that it was during prehistoric times that most of the great steps in human progress were made: the development of technology, the creation of forms of government, kinship, religion, philosophy, and art. The archaeologist also reminds the student through appropriate courses of the long and fruitful cooperation between the historian and the prehistorian, which has been responsible for the bulk of our knowledge of the ancient world of classical times, including Egypt, the Near East, Greece, Crete, and early Rome. Preparation in anthropology customarily involves some work in the field of linguistics. This is a most highly specialized area, and thorough preparation through detailed courses is less common than in the other areas. But introduction to the broad subdivisions of descriptive and historical linguistics helps to acquaint the student with more than a mere modicum of knowledge about the techniques and history of human communication, which is the most distinctive characteristic of the human animal, setting races of humanity apart, as no other single fact does, from infrahumans. It is linguistics which, in recent years, has begun to make students aware that talking is more than simply a method of communicating ideas between speakers of the same language; it is the vehicle of thought itself, and it provides the speaker not only with categories of expression, but also with the means at once of perceiving and of ordering his universe. At this point linguistics is very close to cultural anthropology. Modern cultural anthropology has grown out of the nineteenth century's interest in the accounts by travelers, explorers, missionaries, merchants, and soldiers of the frequently astonishing and sometimes hostile people whom they had met. Much of the work of the cultural anthropologist, or ethnologist, has been the gathering of accurate information about the world's nonliterate peoples. Modern ethnology, it should be noted, places little stress on the word "primitive," having been driven by the data to the conclusion that it does not separate categories of people very efficiently. But from this early interest in different societies has developed anthropology's increasingly sophis - ticated analysis of culture, that amorphous yet systematic mass of learned behavior patterns which provides human societies with the means to survival. Much comparative work has been done, and courses in anthropology departments reflect this, in crosscultural studies of religion, kinship and family systems, governments, technologies, value and belief systems, literatures, modes of aesthetic expression in song, dance, and the graphic and plastic arts, among other institutions. Anthropology wrestles with countless unsolved problems in the area of relations between personalities and the social milieu in which they occur and in the area of cultural dynamics. The possibilities of practical application are numerous, and are, increasingly, being exploited. These several areas, and others which may develop, are all related through anthropology's constant emphasis on the "wholeness" of man. title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man as a biological unit of the animal kingdom. The human fossil record, living primates, and criteria of race and the races of man, elementary anthropometry, adaptive mechanisms, principles of biological evolution, and human genetics.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: Man's cultural achievements from their beginnings into historic times. Man's cultural development will be traced through the paleolithic hunting, mesolithic fishing, neolithic village farming, and urban living stages.

title: Introduction to Language and Linguistics
description: The nature of human language as an object of scientific study, focusing on both the biological and sociocultural bases of language and its structure. Emphasis on language and thought, linguistic analysis of language structure, social and geographical dialects, and language families of the world.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family, kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Bio-Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological and cultural evolution.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man as a unit in the animal kingdom. The principles of biological evolution and the human fossil record are stressed.

title: North American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North America. Each culture is described in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: World Ethnography
description: A systematic survey of the important culture areas of the world, describing and comparing major social institutions: e.g., economics and technology, family and kinship organization, political structure, religion, and art.

title: Material Culture
description: The material manifestations of culture, stressing primitive technology. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Afro-American Anthropology
description: Afro-American cultures and their relationships to the larger societies in which they are integrated. Specific problems relevant to wider questions of theory and methodology in anthropology.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Latin America
description: A general ethnographic survey of Middle and South America. Specific emphasis on the rise of food production in the Americas, environmental and cultural diversity at the time of the Conquest, the post- Conquest situation and the rise of "peasant" society, contemporary cultures, ethnic relations, and industrial development. Prerequisite: ANTH 100, 160, SOC 100, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to honor students only or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Osteology
description: The human skeleton. Bone identification, osteometry, aging, sexing, and racing a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 100.

title: Races of Man
description: Introduction to the present scientific status of the phenomenon of human subspecies, including a survey of historic concepts of race and race sorting criteria, with emphasis on recent advances in physical anthropology. Prerequisite: ANTH 100, 160, or 120.

title: Race and Racism
description: Investigation in detail of the nature of race as a biological phenomenon, which will acquaint the student with the history of racism in the Western world. Stress on the necessity of employing the scientific method in studying race beliefs.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs.

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Summer Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation: sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Field observation and interpretation are stressed. Requires full time in the field.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Utilization of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite: ANTH 421. Anthropology 165

title: Advanced Archaeological Field Methods
description: Advanced methods of excavation and field recording studied at the excavation site. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Midwest is traced through the Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: Traces and describes the archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic to the Historic Period.

title: Personality and Culture
description: Introduction to a major area of anthropological interest and investigation during the past three decades. This field of anthropology has grown out of recent efforts to unite studies of individual behavior and group, or cultural, behavior. The course will involve discussions on the nature of human personality and its origins, both in the individual and the species. Particular stress will be laid on the phenomenon of the model personality type.

title: Peoples and Problems of Modern Africa
description: The course is intended to acquaint the student with the vast, complex, and still comparatively littleknown continent of Africa. More particularly it will enable students to acquire a systematic body of knowledge concerning the increasingly significant role which Africa plays in the modern world.

title: Religion, Culture, and Society
description: An investigation of theories of the possible origins of religious behavior and experience; various types of religious practitioners; and aspects of institutionalization and function of religion in selected societies.

title: Social Organization
description: Opportunity for depth study of man's social systems. Emphasis on the function of these systems and important grouping principles. The crosscultural method is employed extensively.

title: Anthropological Theory
description: Historical development of concept and theory in anthropology. Various theoretical viewpoints and schools of thought will be examined intensively. Prerequisites: ANTH 100, 160, and 120.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the impact of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents with European civilization.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Peoples of Oceania
description: A general survey of the ethnography of the peoples of Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia. Selected field studies will be examined in terms of the functional method and acculturation theories for which oceanic cultures and societies provide a most suitable and viable laboratory.

title: Field School in Ethnography and Ethnology
description: Methods of carrying out field research in cultural anthropology; techniques of establishing contact and rapport; interview and observation methods; problem formulation, data recording, and data preparation. The student may spend fullor halftime in the field. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Culture Change
description: Culture change is examined through major anthropological theories and data. Emphasis on change in nonwestern societies; implications of these studies for the western world are considered.

title: The Development of Near-Eastern Cultures
description: Traces the development of cultures in the Near East as revealed by archaeology and explores the presentday cultural variability.

title: The Peoples and Culture of India
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the anthropology (social organization, cultural system) of South Asia with special stress on India.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairman. Common background is provided for majors through a "core program in biology." The required courses of the core are organized with three levels of emphasis. The first level is designed to develop understanding of basic principles and biological processes which are common to living organisms. The second level focuses on organisms and is concerned with problems of structure, function, and classification in specific groups of plants and animals. The third level is concerned with developing understanding of interactions and adaptations of organisms in contexts ranging from world biome organization through molecular organization. In addition to the basic background work provided by courses in the core program, the department offers specialized course work in biology, botany, zoology, and science to meet the needs of particular individuals and groups. Opportunities for research participation are available at both the advanced undergraduate and graduate levels. The student who plans a career in teaching secondary school biology should take the teaching major in biology or the teaching minor in biology. The student enrolled as a biology teaching major is encouraged to take a second major in general science or a minor in chemistry. These combinations not only greatly increase employment possibilities, but contribute significantly to the understanding of biology. Students who plan careers in college biology teaching and/or research may follow either the teaching major in biology or the departmental major in biology. Such students should anticipate the requirements for graduate work in biology in addition to the major in biology. In general these recommendations are: 1. Proficiency in at least one foreign language. French, German, or Russian are almost universally recommended; some institutions also accept Spanish. 2. Chemistry through the organic sequence and preferably a course in biochemistry. 3. A year of college physics. 4. Mathematics through the calculus sequence. The student who wishes to specialize in either botany or zoology may do so by following the departmental minor in botany or the departmental minor in zoology. These minors are designed to provide professional work for the student who has completed basic course work in biology and chemistry. Liberal arts students who elect to include a concentration area in biology in their curriculum will follow either the departmental major in biology or the departmental minor in biology. All nursing majors take the departmental minor in biological science for nurses. MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY The senior year (45 hours) of the major will consist of twelve months of hospital technical medical laboratory training in an ASCP approved school of medical technology. The following courses are recommended for elective credit on the major: ANAT 320, 430; BIO 311; LAT 213; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; and ZOOL 330. *See the professional education requirements for secondary teaching on the Teacher Education Curriculum for the requirement of an additional course in biology: BIO 391, the methods of teaching biology. During the three years in Ball State University, the student pays the usual University fees and is subject to general regulations of the University. In the senior year, at the Ball Memorial Hospital School of Medical Technology, the Agnes Howe Jones Scholarship fund provides a tuition scholarship for each student. This full senior year scholarship pays the tuition fee at Ball Memorial Hospital and the student services fee at Ball State University. The hospital has a limited number of rooms for students. These are available to student technologists for a nominal fee if space permits. Meals are served at cost in the hospital cafeteria. The student must provide books and uniforms. The course is fifty weeks of integrated lecture and laboratory work. The University also has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with the St. John's Hickey Memorial Hospital, Anderson, Indiana; the Methodist Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana; the St. Joseph Memorial Hospital, Kokomo, Indiana; the St. Francis Hospital, Beech Grove, Indiana; and the St. Vincent's Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana. To qualify for certification as a medical technologist, the student must submit satisfactory credits to the Registry of Medical Technologists of the American Society of Clinical Pathologists, which is located in Chicago, Illinois, and must pass the examination of that Registry. The student must apply for certification as a medical technologist on completion of the twelvemonth senior year technical training in laboratory work in the hospital. The medical technology student is prepared to do laboratory work in bacteriology, pathology, chemistry, and other scientific fields necessary in the diagnosis and treatment of disease. There are positions calling for this preparation in hospital laboratories, physicians' and surgeons' clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories. Also, there are opportunities for work in research laboratories and in commercial companies making biological products. PREMEDICAL PREPARATION The student who wishes to qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine at the close of three years of premedical preparation will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 142 hours of liberal arts credit in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credits earned in his first year in the Indiana University School of Medicine (45 hours) to meet senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit in the first three years: SPCH 210, foreign language (12 hours in one language), BIO 311, 411, LAT 213, and ZOOL 447. The student who prefers to obtain a baccalaureate degree before entering Indiana University School of Medicine will do so by completing all of the work on the Professional Arts Curriculum. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in premedical preparation, it is highly recommended that the premedical student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry because the number of applicants to a school of medicine far exceeds the capacity of the school. In following this recommendation, the student will be better prepared for graduate work in these areas in the event entrance into medical school is denied. Students contemplating a career in medicine should bear in mind the stiff competition in the field, and if they have not exhibited keen interest and aptitude in high school courses, especially in science, it will be very difficult for them successfully to meet the high standards required for premedical work and admission to medical school. The student who wishes to obtain a degree and prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will follow the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum, will elect a teaching area major or teaching major, and will combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. Thus the student prepares for teaching in the field of the elected teaching concentration. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: SPCH 210, foreign language (12 hours in one language), BIO 311, 411, LAT 213, and ZOOL 447. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many medical schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other medical schools as their objectives. Some modifications will be made to enable students to meet as closely as possible the specific requirements of the medical schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of firstyear medical school credits on the Ball State University major is Indiana University. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: BOT 340, 433, 451; CHEM 232, 360; and GEOG 120. Some modifications will be made to enable students to meet as closely as possible the specific requirements of the dental schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of firstyear dental school credits on the Ball State University major is Indiana University. One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory score in the aptitude test given by the American Dental Association. All applicants to dental school are eligible to take the test. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the aptitude test.
