A total of 12 hours of credit may be General and Experimental Psychology 197 Department of General and Experimental Psychology Hill, Chairman; Clark, Deckers, Ganzhorn, Goldstone, Gordon, Hewitt, Humm, James, McConnell, Meeker, Meunier, Myers, Palacios, Renke, Wittig Psychology is the science which studies the behavior of humans as they interact with their environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. As a part of the College of Sciences and Humanities, the Department of General and Experimental Psychology is primarily concerned with psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of human behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The Department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all areas — teaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, business — increase their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a teaching minor, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for instructing in psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students choosing a teaching minor in psychology should choose a teaching major for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. In addition to a teaching minor, the Department offers a departmental major and minor in the disciplinary area of psychology. These programs provide a basic background for graduate work in any one of the many fields of psychology — clinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psychology, psychometry — and an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other areas such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of General and Experimental Psychology offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline, and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas on various advanced degree programs. Additionally, teachers of psychology may combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in the discipline of psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment, and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. Geography, geology, and the earth sciences are concerned with the study of the earth and its resources. Geography focuses attention on the earth as the home of mankind, especially the spatial interrelationships between cultural and physical environments that have developed on the earth. The geography programs reflect these aspects of the discipline, offering general and specialized studies in methodological as well as cultural, physical, and regional fields. Curricular objectives are to educate and train geographers professionally for positions in elementary and secondary schools, colleges and universities, business and industry, and governmental agencies, and to contribute to the liberal education of students. Geologists study the earth, with primary attention to its history, materials, processes, and structure. Today geologists are concerned also with the study of the moon, with the study of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, and with the discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits. The departmental major in geology on the Professional Arts Curriculum is designed to prepare geologists for immediate employment in industry and government agencies, and for graduate studies leading to research and teaching positions in industry, government, and universities. The departmental major in geology on the Liberal Arts Curriculum is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who do not wish to enter the profession. Earth science incorporates much of geology and the physical aspects of geography, meteorology, and astronomy. It provides a broad understanding of the physical environment for the student who does not expect to specialize in any one particular area of geology or geography. Earth science graduates are in increasing demand as teachers in secondary schools and colleges and universities throughout the United States. The geography and geology faculty specializes in various aspects within the dis - cipline, including the cultural, physical, and methodological topics in geography, geomorphology, geophysics, mineralogy, petrography, paleontology, and oceanography in geology and in earth science. The department also provides students with training enabling them to complete undergraduate degree programs at other universities in fields related to geography, geology, and earth science. Such fields include meteorology, oceanography, geophysics, engineering geology, environmental studies, urban and regional studies, cartography, map librarianship, industrial location, and photogrammetry. Students preparing to enter such programs at other universities should receive counseling and curriculum planning advice from department faculty members. They should understand also that they will be expected to show competence in calculus and physics and/or chemistry, and that the specific curriculum that will prepare them for their chosen field can be designed most efficiently with assistance from the appropriate departmental faculty member. Students should contact their departmental area advisers each quarter before completing their registration with the university curricular advisers. Departmental advisers help the students in developing curricular options, in selection of elective courses, and in other aspects of their major or minor program. The Department of Geography and Geology prepares students for entrance to colleges or universities which offer degrees in meteorologic and oceanographic studies. A student who desires to pursue either of these fields towards an undergraduate degree should seek the advice of the departmental adviser as soon as possible after entering Ball State University. Students wishing to complete an undergraduate degree at Ball State University, but continue meteorology or oceanography at the graduate level elsewhere, should seek this advice no later than the first quarter of the sophomore year. Basic minimum requirements to be included in first two years of undergraduate study at Ball State in preparation for study towards an undergraduate degree in meteorology elsewhere are generally 8 hours of geology, 8 hours of meteorology, 20 hours of mathematics, 12 hours of chemistry, 12 hours of physics, and 12 hours of foreign language. In addition to these 72 hours, the student who wishes to prepare for a graduate degree in meteorology elsehwere should include climatology and statistics. If the student plans to pursue a degree in agricultural meteorology at least 12 hours in biology will need to be included. Approximately 20 to 24 hours of advanced meteorology and climatology, not available at Ball State, is usually required for entrance to graduate work, and will be made up at the graduate level by assignment without credit. Acceptance into graduate work in oceanography will require a bachelor's degree in one of the sciences or mathematics, and generally including 4 hours of introductory oceanography, 23 hours of mathematics, inclusive of analytical geometry and calculus, 12 to 14 hours of general physics, and 15 to 16 hours of general chemistry. Students interested in oceanography should seek the advice of the departmental adviser. The adviser for physical and geological oceanography is located in the Department of Geography and Geology; the adviser for biological oceanography, in the Department of Biology.

title: Earth Science Field Problems
description: A series of meteorological, geological, pedological, and geodetic problems designed for beginning students in geography, earth sciences, and geology, as an introduction to physical processes in the atmosphere and near the surface of the earth and to the procedures by which the processes may be identified from their products. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110 or GEOL 101. Not open to the student who has credit in GEGE 383.

title: Seminar in Field Problems Design and Techniques
description: Discussion and identification of field problems in geography, geology, and earth science and the techniques and methods of solving these problems. Students are given the major responsibility of class plan development. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments in and near the campus and visits to places of pertinent course value within the state. Normal scheduling is Saturday mornings. Prerequisite: major or minor in geography, geology, or earth science, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geography and Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to geographic and geologic problems in a specific area. Assignments include mapping projects, including a final written report and compilation of a map either on land use or general geology. Normal scheduling is first summer term (five weeks) in a selected area of western United States. Prerequisite: GEGE 382 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching of Geography and Earth Science
description: Methods of teaching geography and earth science in secondary schools. Includes a review of appropriate textbooks, materials and equipment used in these disciplines, and problems of organization. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in geography or earth science, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Methods
description: Application of quantitative techniques to geographical problems, with emphasis on the use of models in current geographic literature. Special emphasis will be given to the interpretation of recent findings in physical, urban, economic, and regional geography, and the preparation of the student to be able to apply these techniques to his research. Prerequisite: an elementary course in statistics, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Fundamentals of Physical Geography and Earth Science
description: Activities of man and his relationship to the physical environment. Selected topics from astronomy, geography, geology, meteorology, and climatology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Elements of Physical Geography
description: The earth and its position in the universe, natural resources of climate, land forms, soils, vegetation, rocks and minerals, and animal life, with attention paid to the use and conservation of these resources.

title: World Economic Geography
description: World patterns of man's principal occupations and analysis of their distributional features. Emphasis on world interdependence on raw materials and finished products.

title: Cultural Geography
description: A spatial analysis of the interactions among selected elements of the physical and cultural environment in relation to man. Special emphasis is placed on variations in these environmental relationships and their geographic significance.

title: Introductory Meteorology
description: Introduction to meteorology, dealing with the general planetary circulation of the atmosphere, characteristics of the weather, and an examination of weather instruments. Includes a minimum of 4 hours assignment in the university weather station.

title: World Regional Geography
description: Geography of the world by regions, with selected regions given detailed analysis. Basic principles in the meaning of regions and geographic relationships within are given much emphasis.

title: Elements of Regional Geography
description: An introduction to the regional concept and regional method as related to elementary teaching. A geographic survey of the world, with selected topics and regions given detailed analysis. Prerequisite: major in elementary education or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geography of Exploration
description: Travels and discoveries of explorers who have made significant contributions to knowledge of the world and its geography, supplemented by selected readings from their works.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: The reading and interpretation of maps, charts, and diagrams, how they are used as a major tool in geography, and how their use may be applied to other areas of study; also proper care and handling of maps.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: A comprehensive survey of the geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Europe
description: The physical and cultural environment of Europe with emphasis on the economic and political factors involved.

title: Geography of Soils and Vegetation
description: World patterns of soils and vegetation, with emphasis on regional differences and relationships to climate and physiography; their significance in man's use of the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, GEOL 101, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Land Utilization
description: The varied uses of the land, with emphasis on the major categories of rural use, but with attention given to urban and industrial uses. Water use in respect to the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Structure and Functions of Cities
description: A critical examination of the major structural and institutional parts of the city and of how topographic and climatic forces have influenced their development. An understanding of the city as a functionally interdependent structure and as a physical monument to its contemporary culture is fostered.

title: The Urban and Regional Form
description: A survey of the origins of the urban and regional form and its relation to economic, social, and functional factors with special emphasis upon the modern American metropolis and its region. Prerequisite: GEOG 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Agricultural and Rural Geography
description: Agricultural development and the pattern of agriculture, particularly in respect to rural areas of the world. Attention is given the conflict of rural and agricultural development with urbanization and industrialization. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, 120, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources include minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Regularly scheduled laboratory and field work. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, NR 101, or 325.

title: Synoptic Meteorology
description: Application of the principles of meteorology to the development and analysis of weather maps and charts and the making of weather forecasts. Includes a minimum of 6 hours assignment in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Climatology
description: Introduction to the analysis and classification of climate, with emphasis on regional distribution. Basic techniques in handling climatic data. Prerequisite: GEOG 130, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Cartography and Graphics
description: Projections and other map elements, and the construction of maps, charts, and diagrams, with emphasis on the placement of distributional data.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques. Specific projects are selected within the students' field of specialization or area of interest. Emphasis on data collection, compilation, and final drafting of projects suitable for reproduction and publication. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Geography of Caribbean America
description: Physical and cultural landscape regions of Mexico, Central America, northern South America, and the islands of the Caribbean.

title: Geography of Australia and Oceania
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of Australia, New Zealand, and the southeast Pacific area.

title: Geography of East Asia
description: A geographic survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of China, Japan, Korea, Mongolia, and coastal Asia.

title: Geography of South Asia
description: A geographic survey and analysis of the physical, economic, and human elements of the Indian subcontinent and adjacent countries to the east and west.

title: Geography of South America
description: Diverse natural and human environment of South America with special focus on the Amazon Basin, arid northeastern and industrial southern Brazil, the Argentine Pampa, and the ancient Indian cultures of Peru and Ecuador.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world as these factors contribute to domestic and foreign relations and problems.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world, and of transportation patterns.

title: Urban Geography
description: The distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention is given to the geographic factors affecting urban development and growth.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration and growth, as well as the causes and consequences of these aspects on cultural landscape.

title: Geography of Regional Development
description: Geographical factors in the identity and development of specific regions of the world, both historical and modern. Special attention given to resource and river valley development. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, 120, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Meteorology
description: Air mass and storm analysis, with attention given to the physical characteristics of the air layers. Detailed forecasting techniques. Prerequisites: GEOG 330, one year of college physics, and mathematics through calculus, or permission of the department chairman. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Applied Climatology
description: The practical relationships of climate to the activities of man, especially in his adjustment to the physical and cultural environment. Included are the relationships pertinent to industrial development, and to local and regional planning, and the microrelationships of climate and architecture. Prerequisite: GEOG 110, 130, 331, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Aerial Photo Interpretation
description: Introduction to the interpretation of aerial photos as applied to studies in geography, geology, and related fields, including the physical and social sciences.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union, and the economic development of the country.

title: Geography of Africa
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of Africa, with special emphasis on recent political divisions.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: Topography, soils, climate, industries, commerce, and population of Indiana, with emphasis on physiography and economy.

title: Geography of Northwest Europe
description: Survey of the geography of the countries of northwestern Europe. Analysis of land use, physical landscape, and the economic and political development relationships.

title: Advanced Regional Geography
description: Advanced study of the geography of a selected region or regions of the world, with emphasis on the interrelationships of the physical, cultural, and human phenomena. Individual assignments. Prerequisite: introductory regional geography course or permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Advanced Cultural Geography
description: Influences of geographic environment on the development of man in major cultural regions of the world.

title: Distant Areas Field Studies
description: Study of physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Includes seminars arranged during travel. Prerequisite: major or minor in earth science, geography, or geology, or permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned, with repeated enrollment only by permission of the department chairman.

title: Seminar in Selected Studies in Geography
description: Small group discussion of geographic studies selected by instructional staff. Studies vary according to staff assignment. Prerequisite: an area in geography or earth science or permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings and Special Studies in Geography and Earth Science
description: Assigned special studies in geography and earth science, including readings, research projects, teaching problems, and assignment to an undergraduate class. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time.

title: Library Research in Geography
description: Basic research and teaching materials of geography. Designed to stimulate competence in understanding the availability and use of these materials.

title: History and Philosophy of Geography
description: The development of geographic knowledge and the status of the profession as expressed in the writings of the past and present by geographers and other individuals in related fields.

title: Physical Geology
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth and the processes responsible for their development. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: An introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Emphasis on North America. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Geomorphology
description: Landforms and the geologic processes responsible for their development. Local area field trips.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEO 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology 1
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by the invertebrate animal fossils of the earth. Fossils, fossilization, evolution, morphology, and invertebrate life associations of all the phyla from the Protozoa through the Brachiopoda throughout the various periods of earth history. Collection and identification of fossils in the field. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology 2
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by the invertebrate animal fossils of the earth. An extension of GEOL 308 to include all the phyla from the Mollusca through the Protochordata as they have occurred throughout the various periods of earth history. Collection and identification of fossils in the field. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 308 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geomorphology of North America
description: Emphasis on the occurrence, description, and geological and geomorphological problems of the geomorphic regions of North America. Nearby area field trips. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans, and related problems. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Geophysics
description: Physics of the earth; origin, age, gravity, magnetism, radioactivity, seismology, dynamics and internal structure; relation to processes active on or near the earth's surface. Prerequisites: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geotectonics
description: Worldwide activity of the earth's interior, paleomagnetism, lower crust and upper mantle relations, sea floor spreading (continental drift), and theories of mountain building. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Petrography-Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for constructing and evaluating thermodynamic theories of rock origins. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks for the purpose of determining their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: The structure, rocks, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Emphasis upon physical processes involved, especially Pleistocene glaciation. Designed for nonmajor students in the earth sciences, particularly teachers.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, MATH 111, NR 211, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Eliot, Four Quartets, "Burnt Norton" By definition, history is the record of past actions of mankind based upon surviving evidence. Thus, mankind's accumulated experience, the memory of the human race, is called history. Its study, which should lead to understanding and wisdom, indicates that all problems and patterns are the result of complex processes of growth. By shedding light on these processes, history provides a vehicle for profiting from human experience. Without a knowledge of our past, we would have no landmarks, no points of reference, and no foundations on which to build a modern world. The history major may be undertaken to attain professional, academic, or cultural objectives, including preparation for graduate study and advanced degrees, teaching licenses, prelaw or premedical preparation, qualification for appointment as specialists in business, civil service, libraries, museums, art galleries, archives, and other cultural institutions. Courses in history are designed to meet the needs of students in several fields of study. The department offers a broad selection of courses in the general studies program. It offers introductory and advanced courses for students majoring in education or in liberal arts in other departments of the University. It also presents courses designed to give a broad and thorough training in the various history programs. The graduate programs are built on the foundation of undergraduate preparation. Students intending to do graduate work in history are urged to take the Bachelor of Arts degree. title: Introduction to Civilization of Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 324.

title: Roots of the Western Tradition
description: A survey of the principal historical and cultural developments of ancient and medieval times to 1300, with emphasis on those institutions and events of western civilization which furnish our own cultural heritage.

title: Birth of the Modern World
description: From 1300 to 1815, including such major topics as the Renaissance, Reformation, rise of modern nations, discovery and exploration, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, nationalism, and the industrial revolution.

title: The World in Recent Times
description: Major world events and issues since 1815; industrialization and resulting ideologies; background, causes, and results of the two world wars; the rise and decline of the colonial empires with emerging nationalism; the impact of democratic, fascist, and communistic doctrines; nineteenth and twentieth century trends in thought; the effect of science on our age; arts; attempts at international organization and cooperation; and the revolution in expectations in the oneworld today.

title: Twentieth-Century World Leaders
description: Biographical studies of key twentiethcentury western and nonwestern men and women placed in historical perspective. Examines the leaders' characteristics, philosophy, leadership capabilities, and their resultant contributions in the field of politics, religion, military, business, and the arts.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East — the Arab world, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems; imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South Asia
description: South Asia (Afghanistan to Indonesia) since 1800: a brief description of factors influential in past history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, and eventual independence. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 498.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Foundations of the United States, 1492-1829
description: Survey of American history to 1829.

title: Development of the United States, 1829-1900
description: Survey of the history of the United States from the era of Andrew Jackson to 1900.

title: The Recent Past in the United States, 1900 to the Present
description: Political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have composed the history of the United States since 1900.

title: Black History — The United States
description: A survey of the negro in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Designed to use documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. A complete departure from the regular lecture and textbook method. The students through their own research learn how the historian defines areas of research, selects sources, both primary and secondary, evaluates materials, and describes the findings. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Latin America, 1825 to Present
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis upon contemporary civilization of Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.

title: American Leaders
description: A biographical approach to American history. An evaluation of some of the leading Americans and their contributions in the fields of politics, business, letters, the arts, pure and applied science, and education.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American/Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Provides students with an historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues in history, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students.

title: Colonial History of the United States, 1492-1754
description: The ideas and institutions developed in British North America which in the course of colonial development formed a basis for American culture. Prerequisite: HIST 201.

title: The United States from Colony to Nation, 1754-1789
description: The political, constitutional, and economic issues that developed in the thirteen British colonies of North America and culminated in revolution, independence, and the founding of a new nation in the latter part of the eighteenth century. Prerequisite: HIST 201.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis upon the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period. Prerequisite: HIST 201.

title: Nationalism versus Sectionalism in the United States 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis upon the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860. Prerequisite: HIST 202.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: From New Freedom through the New Deal
description: United States history from 1912 to 1940. The impact on the American people of the problems created by continuing industrialization at home and continued involvement in a chaotic world. Prerequisite: HIST 203.

title: Recent United States History: World War II and Afterward
description: The role of the United States in World War II and the reaction of the American people to political, economic, cultural, and social issues confronting the nation since that war. Prerequisite: HIST 203.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the State from the earliest time to the present. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: History of the Ante-Bellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum south. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: The Colonial and Trans-Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers and the events which influenced their migration. and on the impact these events and the frontier had upon national development.

title: The History of Canada
description: A survey of the political, social, and economichistory on th.e. of Canada from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis will be placed tion: events leading to the establishment of Canada and on United States-Canadian rela and problems. History 209

title: History of Mexico
description: Mexico from the pre-Columbian era to the present with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Revolution of 1910.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I. Prerequisite: 8 hours of United States history.

title: United States Diplomatic History since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War States history. I. Prerequisite: 8 hours of United

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1607-1865
description: Survey of history ,of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of the history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: The History of American Culture
description: The history of pictorial art, architecture, music, literature, and science, and the impact of these areas on the social, economic, and political history of the country.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201 or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 410.

title: Historical Method and Bibliography
description: Techniques of research and documentation.

title: History and Historians
description: Historians whose writings are basic in major fields of history.

title: American Culture Field Studies
description: A study of American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students will travel through designated areas in North America. Prior to the trip, considerable reading in various fields relative to the nature of the course will be required. At the conclusion, papers will be required.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open only to seniors of special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate investigation. Topics to be chosen and inves - tigated in consultation with the individual instructor with special competence within the area involved.

title: The Rise of Modern Europe, 1500-1815
description: Political, social, and economic his tory of Europe from the Age of Discovery to the Congress of Vienna. Emphasis on polit- - ical and economic events, the rise of national states, absolutism, religious developments, and the expansion of Europe overseas.

title: The Rise of Modern Europe, 1815 to the Present
description: Political, economic, social, and cultural history of Europe from the Congress of Vienna to the contemporary scene. Emphasis on political and economic events, the liberal and nationalist movements, industrialism, imperialism, World Wars I and II, and the conflict of national interests. 453. Cultural and Intellectual History of Modern Europe. (4) Discovery, analysis, and discussion of major cultural and intellectual trends in the western world since 1815. Development of concepts and ideas that have shaped modern European history. Particular attention will be given to origins of contemporary problems and situations in the rfeinfoer mar. ts, literature, scholarship, political and economic philosophies, science, and social

title: The Development of Ancient Greece
description: Greek political, social, and intellectual development in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the rise and fall of Greek democracy. Prerequisite: one year of history.

title: The Development of Ancient Rome
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the Republic to approximately 500 A.D. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the Republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination. Prerequisite: one year of history.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: The Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Byzantine Empire from its origins to A.D. 1453. The history, social, economic, political, religious, and cultural development; cultural contribution and relations with western Europe, the Slavic peoples and the Moslem world.

title: The Age of Renaissance, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Particular attention will be given to such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: European Culture — Field Studies
description: A study of European culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society. Students will travel through Europe. Prior to the trip, considerable reading in the various fields of European cultures will be required. At the conclusion, papers will be required.

title: Studies in European Culture
description: This offering is designed to take advantage of exchange professors who are on the Ball State University campus. Under their leadership students have a unique opportunity to learn about selected aspects of European life. Since the content of this course will vary from year to year with the background and training of the exchange professor, this course may be repeated by special arrangement with the curricular adviser and the Vice President for Instructional Affairs and Dean of Faculties.

title: History of France
description: A survey of the political, economic, and diplomatic history of France from Roman times to the present.

title: France in the Classical Age: The History of France from 1461 to the Death of Louis XIV in 1715
description: Origins and process of development of French politics, classic culture, society, and the State of France as a governed unit. Foundations of famous institutions such as monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, and Gallican Catholicism. The classic character, society, and culture of the modern Frenchman is described as it develops and influences the European character as a whole.

title: The French Revolution
description: Cultural implications of the French Revolution for modern times as well as the rise of the bourgeoisie.

title: The Rise of Modern Britain, 1485-1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor, Stuart, and early Hanoverian periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: History of England since 1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic development of England since the end of the Seven Years War. Emphasis on the modernization of the administrative machinery following the American Revolution, the development of the limited monarchy, the welfare state, and England's part in the two world wars of the twentieth century.

title: Constitutional History of England
description: A tracing of the development of the British constitutional system to the present time: development of the kingship, the common law, parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: The Modern British Commonwealth and Empire
description: British imperial and Cony monwealth development, 1815 to the present. The post-Napoleonic empire, the dev re_l . opment of dominion status, the special problem of India, Comonwealth, the w do Id wars, the shrinking empire, the growing Commonwealth, and the situation to aY. Prerequisite: HIST 153 or the equivalent.

title: Modern Germany
description: Germany from 1890 to the present. The Reign of II, the Weimar Republic, the Third Reich, and the period since World War II. SPec'n attention is given to social, intellectual, and cultural developments. Journalism 2.11

title: History of Tzarist Russia
description: The Russian state and people from earliest beginnings to the Revolution of 1917; basic chronology of political development; other phases of Russian culture; ethnology, religion, social changes, economic structure, education, literature, and diplomacy.

title: History of the Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, with emphasis on Soviet political and economic institutions and the role of the U.S.S.R. in world affairs. Prerequisite: HIST 486.

title: Modern History of East-Central Europe
description: Modern history of peoples who constitute present Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and the Baltic Republics. Stress is on their struggle for and preservation of national independence and the influence of the great powers on East-Central Europe. Topics are projected against the background of the most dominant European trends and problems. Prerequisite: HIST 153.

title: The Development of Post-Byzantine Civilization
description: Surveys the Post-Byzantine period from A.D. 1453 to 1821. Emphasis on the role of the Church in preserving the cultural, religious, and national identity and traditions of the Christian subjects in the Ottoman Empire. Prerequisite: HIST 151 or 464.

title: The Near East in Modern Times
description: The Turkish, Persian, and Arab world with particular emphasis on the period since 1800: the decay of traditional Near-Eastern institutions, the expansion of European influence, modernization, and the rise of national states in the Near East. Mainly an analytical study of the Eastern Question from 1774 to 1923. Deals with the causes (geographic, ethnic, religious, rise of nationalism) of the fall of the Ottoman Empire and its effects on all phases of European history in the period covered. Prerequisite: 8 hours of history or permission of the department chairman.

title: History of the Balkans since 1453
description: The development of the Balkans from the time of the Ottoman Conquest to the present with emphasis on the diversity of cultural and national development during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: Modern Chinese History, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japanese History, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on factors contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Introduction to Non-Western Civilizations
description: A broad survey of the Soviet Union and of the principal areas of the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with particular emphasis on contemporary political, economic, and social developments.

title: Selected Studies in History
description: Investigation of a selected topic or topics in history. Assigned readings, group discussion, lectures, and conferences. Prerequisite: senior standing. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Mathematics was defined by Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777-1855) as "the queen of the sciences. - This statement reflects the interdependency of mathematics and the sciences. While still true, this observation must now be extended to cover all areas of human endeavor in the second half of the twentieth century. The student considering mathematics as a career should realize that emphasis in mathematics courses will change as progress is made through undergraduate and graduate school. The early emphasis on solving problems is later subordinated to the more important tasks of formulating and dealing effectively with mathematical structures and abstract ideas. Every prospective mathematician should plan to pursue undergraduate and graduate training to the highest level of capability. To meet the need for mathematically competent graduates, four programs of study are available at the undergraduate level for both majors and minors. The teaching major and minor are designed to prepare classroom teachers of mathematics for the secondary school. The teaching major meets the requirements of the Committee on Undergraduate Programs in Mathematics of the Mathematical Association of America. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government as well as for further specialized study at the graduate level. In today's world, problems cut across traditionally defined areas of discipline and a departmental major offers to a student the opportunity to combine mathematics with work in other areas. The departmental major and minor on the liberal arts curriculum are programs in the liberal arts tradition. With this liberal education, the student is well prepared for additional graduate study or positions requiring education in breadth. An actuary can gain professional recognition by passing a series of examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries, and the courses in this major will aid the student toward this goal. title: Mathematical Concepts 1
description: A general education course for students who wish to know more about the contributions of mathematics to human culture. The minimal manipulative skills necessary to understand the various concepts and topics will be developed. Such topics as the number system, simple logic, the interrelations between mathematics and history, and some interesting geometries, will be covered. Prerequisites: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry. Not open to the student with collegiate credit in mathematics except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Mathematical Concepts 2
description: Continuation of MATH 100. Topics covered in-. clude simple formulas and their applications, the concept of limit, the basic ideas of differential and integral calculus, some concepts and applications of probability, and an introduction to the computer. Prerequisite: MATH 100.

title: College Algebra 1
description: Fundamental operations of algebra through quadratics. Students who have credit for three semesters of secondary school algebra will not receive credit for this course. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra.

title: College Algebra 2
description: A brief introduction to sets and the logic of algebra, a discussion of inequalities, absolute values, functions and relations, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and mathematical induction. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary school algebra, and one year of plane geometry, or their equivalents as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied in this course if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities and equations; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers, and DeMoivre's Theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or its equivalent as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Analytic Geometry
description: Use of Cartesian and polar coordinates in two and three dimensions, conic sections, transcendental curves, curve sketching, parametric equations, lines and surfaces in solid analytic geometry. Prerequisite: The equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level, or MATH 111 and 112.

title: Mathematics for Architects 1
description: Topics in analytic geometry particularly suited to the needs of the architecture major. Prerequisite: MATH 112. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 113.

title: Mathematics for Architects 2
description: Topics in calculus particularly suited to the needs of the architecture major: limits, differentiation, integration, applications of calculus such as area, volume, and center of gravity. Prerequisites: MATH 113 or 123. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 170.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 1
description: Topics in algebra particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary algebra. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 111.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics which are particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 131.

title: Calculus 1
description: Inequalities, limits, continuity, differentials and derivatives, introduction to the definite integral. Prerequisite: MATH 113.

title: Calculus 2
description: Continuation of the definite integral, differentiation and integration of elementary transcendental functions, derivatives in polar coordinates, integration by special methods, applications of integration. Prerequisite: MATH 170.

title: Calculus 3
description: Continuation of the application of the integral, elements of infinite series (convergent and divergent series), Taylor's series and theorem, partial differentiation, and multiple integration. Prerequisite: MATH 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 270.

title: Calculus 4
description: Infinite series and elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Cardinal Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: successful completion of 25 credit hours of college courses. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 205.

title: Rational Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the concept of unsigned rational numbers for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 201 or

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the real number system for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 202 or 206. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 207.

title: Geometry in the Elementary School
description: A development of geometric concepts for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 203. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 207.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Arithmetic 1
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Arithmetic 2
description: Extension of the number concept through unsigned rational numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 205.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Arithmetic 3
description: Extension of number concepts through the real numbers; elements of algebra; intuitive geometry. Prerequisite: MATH 206.

title: Elementary School Enrichment Topics
description: An examination of mathematics concepts included as enrichment topics in elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 204 or 206. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman.

title: The Structure of the Real Number System
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and number systems. A systematic development of the real number system is emphasized. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 172.

title: Elements of Linear Algebra
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties, determinants, matrix inverses, rank and equivalence of matrices, and a matrix approach to the theory of systems of linear equations. Prerequisite: MATH 171.

title: Topics from Linear Algebra
description: Determinants, matrices, and bilinear maps, polynomials and matrices, triangulation of matrices and linear maps, spectral theorems, multilinear products. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 412.

title: Topics from Modern Algebra
description: Basic topics from polynomial and integral domain theory, group theory, ring theory. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 313 or 411.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 207 and 172.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for finite sample spaces is developed from a settheoretic basis. Probability functions, means and variances of random variables. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Statistics 1
description: Common distribution functions, sampling theory, correlation and regression, tests of hypotheses, and estimation techniques. Prerequisite: MATH 320.

title: Statistics 2
description: Tests of hypotheses, the chisquare, student's t and F distributions, design of experiments, nonparametric methods, sequential sampling, Bayesian statistics. Prerequisite: MATH 321.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Problems will be considered dealing with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, t, and F distributions. Some problems with moment generating functions, tests of hypotheses, and estimation will be done. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 322 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in synthetic geometry, closely related to the field of Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Differential Equations
description: Emphasis on the solution of ordinary linear differential equations. Attention to methods of numerical analysis of nonlinear equations. Applications to science and engineering stressed. Prerequisite: MATH 172 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Arithmetic in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching arithmetic at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Prerequisite: MATH 204 or 207. Prerequisite or parallel for elementary majors: MATH 209.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Secondary School
description: Materials and methods used in the teaching of junior and senior high school mathematics. Survey of texts, organization of materials, testing procedures, and visual aids materials. Prerequisites: MATH 211 and 340; prerequisite or parallel: EDSEC 360.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. Restricted to honors students. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra
description: The study of rings, integral domains, and fields, with emphasis on the development of integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, and polynomials. Prerequisite: MATH 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Linear Algebra
description: The study of some topics in linear algebra: matrix algebra and linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, inner product spaces, etc. Prerequisites: MATH 212 and 411.

title: Theory of Numbers
description: Elementary properties of integers, theory of congruences, quadratic residues, Diophantine equations, introduction to theory of groups, introduction to theory of algebraic numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Advanced Analytic Geometry
description: An advanced treatment of analytic Euclidean geometry using topics from analysis and algebra as tools where helpful. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Projective Geometry
description: Properties of geometric configurations which are invariant under projection. Synthetic methods emphasized, and some use is made of analytic methods. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities certain, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, and capitalized cost. Both the discrete and the continuous approach to compound interest and annuities certain will be treated. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Mathematics of Life Insurance
description: An introduction to the mathematics of life insurance; mortality tables; life annuities, premiums, and reserves for basic life insurance policies; modern reserve systems. The discrete approach to contingencies of a single life will be emphasized but the continuous approach will also be introduced. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 451.

title: Topology 1
description: Review of basic set theory; topological spaces, metric spaces, mappings and homeomorphisms, product spaces and function spaces, and applications to the real line and to the plane. Prerequisites: MATH 211, 212, and 470 or 570.

title: History of Mathematics
description: A survey of the development of mathematics from prehistoric times to the present. The emphasis is on such topics as numbers and numerals, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, and the calculus. Prerequisites: MATH 211, and 340 or 441.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include: finite differences, interpolation of functions; approximation of functions, derivatives, and integrals; iterative and direct methods for solving linear systems. Prerequisites: CS 220 or permission of the department chairman; MATH 212.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics covered include: approximate solution of non.- linear equations; numerical solution of ordinary differential equations; error analysis; difference equation; matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Prerequisite: MATH 374 and 462.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, mathematical formula. Prerequisite: MATH 462 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Vector Analysis
description: An introduction to the theory and applications of vectors including the algebra, calculus, and geometry of vectors; classical theorems; applications. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Elements of Analysis
description: The real number system is developed through Dedekind cuts, Cauchy sequences, and complete ordered field postulation. Topology of the real line, sequences and series of real numbers, and limits and continuity. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 207 and 172.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Advanced calculus including real numbers, metric spaces, topology of WI and Cn, continuity of functions, uniform continuity, Stone- Weierstrass theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATH 173 or 470.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics covered include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansion. Prerequisite: MATH 471.

title: Advanced Calculus 3
description: Advanced calculus of several variables. Calculus of differential forms in three dimensions. Examples from physics. Prerequisite: MATH. 472.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Arithmetic
description: For teachers in service who do not hold a degree. Prerequisite: teaching experience in the elementary school. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the Mathematical Sciences Department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines. Timesharing computer techniques with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. An understanding of the role of the computer in the modern world. Not open to the student with areas in mathematical or computer sciences, or with credit in ID 200, CS 210, 220, or GBA 220.

title: Commercial Data Processing
description: Basic COBOL and RPG programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: ID 200 or GBA 220 or CS 200 or 220.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Basic computer programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or equivalent or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in ID 200.

title: Computer Programming and Systems 1
description: Operational organization of a stored program digital computer, representation of numbers, computer arithmetic, address modification, indirect addressing, indexing, machine and assembly -language. Programming of representative nonnumeric problems will be assigned. Prerequisite: CS 220 or equivalent or permission of the department chairman.

title: Computer Programming and Systems 2
description: Structure of programs, use of input/output and peripheral storage devices, common techniques. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Computer Programming and Systems 3
description: The use of monitor or executive systems for computer selfoperation. Discussion of multiprogramming and multiprocessing. Description of timesharing and multiaccess systems. Prerequisite or parallel: CS 330.

title: Computer Logic and Algorithms 1
description: Boolean algebras and functions, normal forms, minimization, switching circuit representation, design of computer logical components. Prerequisite or parallel: CS 332 and MATH 212.

title: Computer Logic and Algorithms 2
description: Mechanical formulation of algorithms, Turing machines, normal algorithms, universal machines, algorithmically unsolvable problems. Prerequisite: CS 332 and 433.

title: Computer Languages
description: Problemoriented languages, the syntax of ALGOL and similar languages, compiler design, analysis of arithmetic and logical expressions, listprocessing languages. Prerequisite: CS 332. Prerequisite recommended: CS 434.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Problems typical to DP centers such as file maintenance, report writing, sorting and merging are treated using COBOL. Tape oriented and direct access processing techniques. Prerequisite: CS 332. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 210.

Department of Natural Resources Hibbs, Chairman; Fisher, Judy, Mortensen, Van Meter The Department of Natural Resources is oriented toward the mission of enhancing the quality of the human experience through environmental improvement. The area of natural resources is interdisciplinary because the conservation of natural resources is an area of total University concern, requiring new ideas, diverse skills, and integrated approaches. Therefore, students may include work from many disciplines in meeting the curricular requirements. A number of courses have also been developed specifically for the natural resources areas. The environmental crisis has resulted from our rapidly expanding population and technology in combination with our affluent society and its implications for an accelerated resource use and abuse. There is an increasing need for both men and women who are educated in the area of natural resources. These areas are designed to provide students with a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of the ecosystem and to educate them to strive toward a state of harmony between people and their environment. Students considering a professional career in natural resources should plan their high school programs to include a strong background in both the sciences and the humanities. An ability to work with people is also an important prerequisite. Students may elect a general major or specialize in such areas as resource geography, fishery resources, communications, and water quality. The core requirement which all students complete includes Introduction to Natural Resources, Physical Geology, Water Resources, Soil Resources, Mineral Resources, Air Resources, Ecology, and Integrated Resources Management. Other courses which may be elected by students will be determined by the option selected, the students' background, and their professional employment interests. In addition to the traditional science courses, others which may be included are political science, sociology, communications, environmental health, physical education, statistics, computer techniques, urban and regional studies, and landscape architecture. Students with areas in other departments of the University are encouraged to elect a minor in natural resources; however, it should be especially useful to accompany certain majors including biology, earth science, geography, geology, journalism, landscape architecture, physical education, radio and television, speech, urban and regional studies, and in certain areas of the social sciences. Completion of an area in natural resources fulfills the general studies requirements in sciences and mathematics. Students with areas in natural resources should arrange to enroll in NR 101 as their first course. The student will enroll in the Professional Arts Curriculum with a departmental major in natural resources.
