title: Introduction to Natural Resources
description: The role of natural resources and their relationship to man's social and economic welfare; population growth and its impact upon resource use. The nature and interrelationships of resources with emphasis on the multipleuse concept of resource management. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to man. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as a natural resource. Hydrology, water quality, water treatment, and planning as they apply to the understanding of the resource. Prerequisite: BIO 112, CHEM 112 or 114, MATH 111, or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 211.

title: Soil Resources 1
description: The basic properties of the soil portion of the ecosystem. Prime emphasis on the genesis and resulting chemical and physical characteristics of soils. Prerequisite: BIO 112, CHEM 112 or 114, or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 221.

title: Soil Resources 2
description: Fundamental properties of soils. The classification, management, and fertility of soils will be studied in depth to develop the ability of the student to work effectively with this important resource. Prerequisite: NR 321 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources, including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325 or GEOG 325.

title: Mineral Resources
description: The relationship of minerals to renewable resources including the role of mineral fuels as a source of energy for the human ecosystem; a descriptive and interpretive treatment of the distribution, production, and use of world mineral resources with emphasis on conservation principles, practices, and techniques. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Air Resources
description: The significance of the atmosphere as a resource; the important meteorological parameters in air resources, management; the economic, sociological, technical, political and biological aspects of air pollution; with special emphasis on basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. The interrelationships of various natural resources with emphasis directed toward multipleuse concepts of management to meet existing and projected outdoor recreation demands. Administration, management, research, survey planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a particular area (not to be smaller than a county) with special emphasis on the locations of these natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence these natural resources have on the environmental quality. Each time this course is conducted a specific geographic area will be specified. Laboratory and field experiences included. Prerequisite: NR 101 and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Integrated Resources Management
description: Integrated management of resources with emphasis on combinations of principles prerequisite to the formulation and implementation of natural resources policies and programs. Attention to the economic, social, and political implications of resource development. Prerequisites: NR 101, 211, 221, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Issues
description: An opportunity to identify and gain an understanding of selected environmental issues relevant to the local geographic area. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Environmental Quality
description: Designed to give students from the various disciplines an opportunity to relate their area of competence to current environmental problems in a meaningful way. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland. waters for fish production. Prerequisite: NR 211, BIO 480, and ZOOL 444, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Natural Resources Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis on field work and creative presentation of concepts. Prerequisite: NR 101, 221, 311, 331, 341; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Organization and Management of Interpretive Programs
description: Develops skills and techniques relative to the sound organization and management of interpretive programs, including sites and facilities. Emphasis on planning procedures and field study Philosophy 225 of existing programs. Prerequisite: NR 101, 221, 311, 331, 341; BIO 313; GEOL 101. Prerequisite or parallel: NR 491.

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the curriculum, and the contribution teachers can make in developing a conservationconscious public. Sources of help in teaching conservation, including the use of resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instmctional resources that are uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 101, 325, BIO 325, GEOG 325, or BIO 103.

title: Practicum in Natural Resources
description: Supervised practical professional experience relating theory and practice by combining instruction and work activities in natural resources, including conservation education, outdoor education, or environmental education. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; 12 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources
description: An opportunity to pursue special interests in the area of environmental quality. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Department of Philosophy Robertson, Chairman; Andry, Annis, Foster, Miracchi Philosophy as an Academic Discipline One of the earliest definitions of philosophy encountered by the beginning student is one that says it is the "love of wisdom." The philosopher, accordingly, is known as a "lover of wisdom." And it should be noted that this love of wisdom is not confined to any one field; indeed, most anything is grist for the philosopher's mill! Historically speaking, the above definition has resulted ever since the time of Plato in the general agreement that the traditional role of philosophy is one of synthesis and system building. To put the matter another way, the philosopher was seen to be one who knew something about each area of human experience as a result of either native genius or exhaustive investigation after which, by weaving such knowledge into a consistent and coherent whole, gives to the human race a unified picture of the universe and the individual. This general agreement about the role of philosophy both within and without the university produced about twenty or more centuries of some of the most magnificent albeit meaningless cogitations ever produced. This is not to say that these vast systems were or are without some value. As purely intellectual exercises they have their place. But surely the student has a right to note that on the assumption that synthesis is the main business of philosophy, here we are many centuries after Plato still bemused by his problems and showing very little evidence that we are any closer to solving them. Is it possible that they are not "problems" at all? In the past thirty years the role of philosophy has been changing, although not without some dire warnings as to its future if the present trend continues. Analysis has now replaced synthesis as the main job of the philosopher as a member of a university faculty. This is not to say that analysis has not always been with us, philosophically' speaking, but in the past it has always been subordinated to the activity known as synthesis. It is generally agreed now that the scope of the knowledge of human beings is too large in our own century for any philosopher to pretend to carry on the timehonored function of philosophy described above. Perhaps this was possible in the small world in which Plato lived, it is not possible now. Given this change, then, just what is the role of philosophy and the philosopher in a modern university now? It is twofold, one relative to the other academic disciplines, and one relative to the students who pass through the classroom. Relative to the other academic disciplines on the campus, the philosopher can function in the role of critical analyst as a sort of catalytic agent by insisting that colleagues constantly look to the meaningfulness of their ideas. Indeed, perhaps the greatest service is that of helping others make their ideas clear regardless of the nature of their academic discipline. Relative to the students in the university, the philosopher and philosophy can serve in several ways. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all facets of life need examination if we are to get ahead with this business of living. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all values and beliefs would never have come to be except that people in the past were not afraid to question those that were then held, and that in all probability the same fate awaits values and beliefs held now. And lastly, philosophy can serve by showing the student that this succession is indeed a good thing. The alternative is stagnation. These two roles for philosophy have given rise on most university campuses to certain basic courses in philosophy designed to be of help to groups of students. The usual Introduction to Philosophy course is one of general interest which serves to do what its title implies. In this course the student becomes aware of the basic problems philosophers deal with as well as some of their answers. Logic, the study of deductive and inductive reasoning and the rule thereto, can be invaluable for prelaw students, mathematics majors, and any other persons who must reason correctly. Ethics is a course of particular interest to anyone concerned in any way with the relationships of huma n beings. For those ocupied with the history of ideas, thre courses in the history of ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy are most valuable. These are the core courses in philosophy and form the necessary foundation for the more specialized courses which usually follow. Religious Studies as an Academic Discipline A knowledge of the religion of any culture is essential to the understanding of that culture. This is indeed true of our own culture, as well as of other cultures. Students preparing for teaching careers will be expected to deal with religious ideas, values, institutions, and practices in their teaching. Courses in religious subject matter are being expanded in public schools. A small but increasing number of students come to Ball State to prepare for theological studies. Others decide to pursue a life of religious service after entering Ball State. To meet the increasing demands of these situations, Ball State provides students with the opportunity, which compares favorably with similar programs provided by other educational institutions, to pursue religious studies. Any student may register in courses which are designed for all four years of university life. The courses are classified. under the general headings of cultural settings of religion, Biblical studies, church history, and religions of the world. Any course in religious studies counts for credit as a general elective in any program of studies within the University, it counts for credit as a social science elective for general studies, or a student may acquire a departmental minor in religious studies by successfully completing the requirements in this area. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: The major types and principal problems of philosophy in terms of the most significant historical and contemporary schools and movements. Brings an awareness of the problems that constitute philosophy and their importance to the search for truth on the part of each student.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of Philosophy 227 the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of human thinking as far as human thinking is concerned with deduction.

title: Inductive Logic
description: An introduction to the principles and problems of inductive reasoning.

title: Ethics
description: The nature of ethical reasoning, an inquiry into the meaning of good and bad, of right and wrong. Critical analysis of leading ethical theories and their treatment of principal ethical problems in a search for criteria for an adequate ethical system for the individual and for society. The reading consists of the works of major ethical thinkers, both classical and contemporary.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the rise of philosophy in Greece about 600 B.C. to the fall of Rome. Emphasis is upon these theories in their relation to one another, the times in which they were produced, and the thinkers by whom they were offered.

title: History of Medieval Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the fall of Rome to the Renaissance. Consideration of the inheritance of medieval Europe from the Graeco-Romanearly Christian world and of the creative role played by medieval philosophy in the formation of the western tradition especially after the rediscovery of Aristotle.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the time of the Renaissance to the present. Emphasis is upon these theories as illustrative of the changing nature of philosophic speculation in modern times from that of synthesis to that of criticism and analysis.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A comprehensive survey beginning with post-Kantian philosophy and ending with the principal movements of twentiethcentury philosophy. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Aesthetics
description: An historical presentation of the major philosophical views on the concept of beauty and the relation of these views to the various forms of human expression.

title: Philosophy of Language
description: Examines the philosophical significance of language from any of various directions. May investigate philosophical theories of how language works, philosophical assumptions and implications of such theories in linguistics, or language as a tool for the philosophical exploration of the world. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Central Issues in Philosophy
description: Covers any number of traditional philosophical problems. These may include mind and body, freewill and determinism, knowledge and reality, and value and obligation. May be approached historically or by studying the works of current philosophers. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Philosophies of Science
description: An investigation of the basic assumptions, methods, and logical structure of the various sciences. Emphasis is upon epistemological problems primarily.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: The purpose of the course is to provide superior students with an opportunity for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned if approved by the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Theories of Reality
description: A critical examination of the principal problems of metaphysics, such as the nature of reality, the problem of universals, space, time, causality, mechanism, the self, substance, and process, with particular attention to the relation of metaphysical concepts to the theory of knowledge and to the factual sciences. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Theories of Knowledge
description: Problems in the theory of knowledge: origin, nature, and validity of knowledge; critical evaluation of subjectivism and realism, dogmatism and skepticism, intuitionism, pragmatism, empiricism, rationalism, and pietism ; theories of meaning, truth, and perception as they relate to the scientific method. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Continental Rationalists
description: Critical investigation of philosophies of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman; but not more than 4 hours may be earned at one time.

title: British Empiricism
description: Philosophies of Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, their critical emphases and main arguments against rationalistic assumptions historically explored and critically examined.

title: Studies in Oriental Philosophies
description: Critical investigation in major Indian, Chinese, and Japanese philosophies and their effects.

title: Plato
description: The writings of Plato.

title: Aristotle
description: The philosophy of Aristotle based on his works in relation to his environment and life.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory
description: A variety of contemporary ethical theories.

title: Existentialism
description: Selected works of several existentialists.

title: Kant
description: The philosophy of Kant with emphasis on his Critique of Pure Reason and Prolegomena.

title: Logical Empiricism
description: Early Positivism and contemporary logical Empiricism from Auguste Comte to the present.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: An introductory survey of the major religion s in the United States with emphasis on their historical development, distinctive beliefs, institutions, and practices. Attention will be given to political consequences and the social significance of American religious pluralism.

title: Old Testament
description: The origins and developments of Hebrew-Judaic thought: its progressive expressions throughout time in personalities, theologies, and various types of Hebrew-Judaic literature.

title: New Testament
description: A basic study of the origins and developments of Christian religious thought: its Jewish environment, its early expressions, the emergence of its literature, and the various forms of its expression as found in its earliest literature.

title: Evolution of Christian Thought
description: Christian thought as it evolved in early catholicism, the orthodox creeds, the eastwest schism, the medieval age, the reformation, and the controversy between rationalism and pietism. Consideration also given to recent trends in Christian thought.

title: Comparative Religions
description: A comparative study of the great world religions. Department of Physiology and Health Science Schaller, Chairman; Bock, Boyer, Caroll, Dennison, Ganion, Gowings, Henzlik, jarial, Jones, Lesh, Paschall, Payne, Pelizza, Siverly, Slobof, Travis The health science field is multidisciplinary in nature and its content is derived largely from the biological, physical, and social sciences. The fields of medicine and public health make significant contributions to the discipline of health science. Broad in scope, health science covers such areas as the nature of disease, the complexity of nutrition, effects of radiation, behavioral aspects of accident prevention, an understanding of health and medical care programs, significance of international health problems, selection of health products and services, environmental hazards of air and water pollution, community health services, foundations of mental health, family living and education for human sexuality, and drug use and abuse. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a major or minor for students who are interested in one of a variety of occupations in the health science field. Health science is known differently in some institutions; some commonly used names are: health education, health and safety education, and school and college health education. Health science teachers, coordinators, and directors are being sought by elementary and secondary schools, junior colleges, as well as universities. The department also offers a departmental minor in the field of public health. It provides basic information on public health programs, problems, and practices in the United States. Opportunities include employment with official governmental and voluntary health agencies, business, industry, and professional health associations, such as the American Medical Association. Of equal importance in the department are the subject areas of anatomy and physiology. These are vital to the health sciences and biological sciences in the broad sense and, in anticipation of future development, provide a point of departure for specialization in the respective disciplines of anatomy and physiology. The department also offers a departmental minor in physiology. One combination that is often elected by the students is the physiology minor earned in conjunction with a biology, chemistry, or psychology major. At the present time, the department contributes required and elective courses to several academic programs at Ball State, such as regional and urban planning, preprofessional programs in allied health science areas, courses for professional nurse preparation, and general education. The preprofessional programs in the allied health science area include premedical, predental, and prepharmacy programs; professional nurse preparation; and medical technology. The department provides guidance in enabling students to select a career in teaching, service, or research. Membership in Eta Sigma Gamma, the national honorary for men and women in health science, and Sigma Zeta, the national honorary in science, is offered to qualified students. Department of Political Science Gruenewald, Chairman; Baker, Chang, Corbett, Frankland, Hamilton, Hamori, Hollands, Kelly, Mast, Menez, Meyer, Perry, Rudoni, Sargent Political science is the study of legal governments and relation of people thereto. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Protagoras, Gorgias, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polis or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differ from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask: What is the nature of people (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between people and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. Since comprehension of available knowledge is fundamental to intelligent valuation, emphasis must be given to teaching and learning and to continued accumulation, analysis, and organization of knowledge. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civic, and vocational. The first two, hopefully, are universal in that serious study ofthe discipline results in a more informed populace. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 130) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz., political theory; American government; public law; public administration; parties, politics, and the political process; foreign and comparative government; and international law and diplomacy. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher certification programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate level for students in other departments. See Social Sciences for the complete patterns of the teaching area major in social studies, the teaching major in social studies, and the teaching minor in social studies. On the teaching major in social studies, 60 hours, and the teaching minor in social studies, 36 hours, concentrations are required, which may be in political science. description: The organization and operation of national government as it relates to current issues such as civil rights, welfare, ecology, consumer protection, and international relations. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 131.

title: The Now Politics
description: The American political system and the manner in which it deals with such problems as poverty, pollution, racism, women's rights, and the threat of nuclear war. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 130.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, and centralization will be considered. Prerequisite: POLS 130, or 237.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government. Prerequisites recommended: POLS 130 and 237.

title: Intergovernmental Relations
description: Analysis of relations among national, state, and local governments. Considerations of constitutional and legal bases, and the nature of relations, such as grantsinaid, tax immunity, education, and interstate compacts. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 and 238. State and Local Government

title: Comparative State Politics
description: Major problems of states and the efforts to cope with them. Will include consideration of Indiana and its position relative to other states.

title: Urban Government in the United States
description: Structure, functions, problems, and trends in city, urban, and metropolitan governments.

title: Rural Local Government
description: Structure and functions of rural local government in the United States, including counties, townships, New England towns, and special districts. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237.

title: State Legislatures
description: Legislative systems in American state government. External influences (constituencies, political parties, interest groups), internal influences (organizational structure, staff, norms, decisionmaking), issues confronting state legislatures and reform proposals. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Metropolitan Problems
description: An analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related aspects; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation to the entire community. Prerequisites: POLS 237 and 238, or permission of the department chairman. Division IV: Public Law and Policy

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes, and needs. Prerequisite: POLS 130 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships betwen government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities and finance. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: National Defense Policy
description: An international survey of military capacity and function provides the background for analysis of the national defense policy of the United States. Special emphasis on American strategic interests and problems of weapons, technology, nuclear control, and disarmament. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
description: Significant facets of legal system's response to conflicting demands upon environmental resources. Composition of environmental problems, control issues, policy formulation, and legal remedies. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Government Protection of Consumers and Competitors
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or the equivalent. POLS 342 recommended.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and his government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content will include cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies. Division V: Public Administration

title: Introduction to Planning
description: A survey of problems inherent in planning for cities and regions which utilizes contributions of other disciplines such as history, geography, sociology, and economics. Required of majors in regional and urban planning; elective for others with permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration — national, state, and local. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Administrative organizations as going concerns composed of people taking action under conditions of conflict and cooperation: examination of nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisites: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes and activities of civil service agencies; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans; efficiency measurements, and rewards; training programs; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement, and other personnel processes. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Survey of the principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances: administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, accounting of revenues, expenditures, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, management of publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Administration of American Foreign Policy
description: Deals with the process of foreign policy formulation. The course is analytic and interpretative and presents divergent views. The conception of the foreign policy process embodies the roles of the executive branch. Congress, press, public opinion, and various nongovernmental groups.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services. Prerequisites: POLS 160.

title: Problems in Planning
description: Involves field study of selected problems in planning to emphasize the interdisciplinary character of planning and to provide an opportunity to apply political, social, economic, and a real analysis; and implementation techniques. Prerequisite: senior standing and four courses in planning.

title: Administrative Problems in State and Local Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and political interaction at the state and local level for the provision of government services. Special emphasis on the major program areas such as law enforcement, education, taxation, environmental protection, housing, recreation, and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350.

title: Problems in National Administration
description: An examination in depth of uniquely national administrative problems and activities. National administrative structures and techniques are examined in detail, including their use and application in the adminis - tration of specific national policy areas. Division VI: Politics and the Political Process

title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda.

title: Public Interest Groups and Government
description: An examination of the internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Special attention will be given to the implications of pressure group activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and to the effects of pressure groups upon political parties and the political process.

title: American Political Parties
description: Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Political Sociology
description: The political scientist's view of the social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Behavior
description: An analysis of the interrelation of political attitudes and public policy formation. Special attention to the substantive areas of voting behavior, political leadership, and the rise of mass political movements. Division VII: Foreign and Comparative Governments

title: Democratic and Totalitarian Political Systems
description: A comparison of modern political systems as represented by the principal nations of the world.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: Historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 279.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural area, to the government and political structures of the three major powers in Western Europe Great Britain, France, and Germany — and to the current state of the Western European integration movement. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: British Government and Politics
description: The political system of the United Kingdom, including a discussion of the Commonwealth and Britain's place in an expanding European community. Emphasis also on Anglo-American relations and British contributions to American political arrangements. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 382.

title: Latin-American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin-American nations.

title: Government and Politics of Africa
description: Tribal political systems, European colonial policies, nationalist movements, multiracial conflict, and accommodation; politics of independent states in Africa south of the Sahara. Secondary emphasis on United Nations control and the role of Africa in world politics. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in the field of comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of Soviet Russia
description: Structure and functions of modern Russian government, including central, regional, and local units, relationships between party and government, and such functions as law enforcement, economic planning and administration, and foreign policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 315.

title: Problems and Prospects of American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: Introduction to International Relations
description: A survey of the formal relations among sovereign states in the international system, emphasizing the operation of diplomacy, the factors in international relations and procedures for the settlement of disputes.

title: The United Nations
description: Concentrated study of organization and functions of the United Nations and of foreign policy of selected members of the United Nations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: International Relations of the USSR and the Soviet Bloc
description: The foreign policy of the USSR and her satellites and a survey of the Communist Party in international action.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the law of the international community as it developed from international customs and usage and has been developed and recognized by modern states, with special reference to the position of the Western Democracies.

title: International Organizations
description: Organizations, processes, and methods devised by the nationstate system for the preservation of international peace and security and for dealing with problems of international concern.

title: World Politics
description: Analysis of general intercourse between states; normal relations, disputes and peaceful and forceful settlements; international obligations, agreements, and problems; power relationships and dominance and balance. Particular attention will be given to contemporary problems and situations.

title: Far East in World Politics
description: A comprehensive survey of contemporary international relations in the Far East mainly from post World War II to the present.

title: Communist China in World Affairs
description: A comprehensive survey of Communist China's role in international politics, with special emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Department of Sociology Scott, Chairman; Blakely, Bode, Bogg, Brodt, Burton, Carlie, Condran, Dolon, Gordon, Hewitt, Johnson, S., Johnson, W., Moore, Morris, Neiman, Rehfeld, Royer, Tamney, Tucker Sociology as an Academic Discipline Sociology is among the youngest of the social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades; and especially in the period since World War II, its widened inclusion in patterns of general education has resulted in exceptionally rapid growth of undergraduate enrollments. Simultaneously, rapidly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge; and the concepts of the discipline are becoming more widely accepted throughout society. Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. In the early years of this century, a number of persons interested in the field of sociology saw it primarily as a tool for ameliorating the various ills and problems of the society, and especially for helping groups and individuals with special needs in "adjusting" to the surrounding social order. Gradually this emphasis has come to be more identified with the special field of social work (see below), with sociology as an academic discipline being perceived more as a "pure" rather than an "applied" science. Today, however, the findings of sociology are assessed in terms of their applicability to the range, of social problems as well as in terms of their relation to the furtherance of sociological knowledge. As one of the related group of social sciences, sociology focuses upon, and seeks to develop dependable generalizations about human social life and the interaction patterns characteristic of human collectivities. An understanding of the bases for and influences of observable regularities in the forms of human association is fundamental to a student's knowledge about self and others as participants in structured group life, and about the groups in which such participation occurs. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to broadening of the student's perspective of the sociocultural environment, and to the individual's own relationship to it, thus helping to produce an outlook less restricted by the limitations of untested folk beliefs. As a science, sociology employs the canons of empiricism, objectivity, and ethical neutrality in its search for predictive relationships. The findings derived from such investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. The methods and concerns of sociology are functionally related to those of the other social sciences as well as to a wide range of arts (teaching, medical, expressive, correctional, etc.) which involve interactions among persons performing varied roles. The discipline of sociology thus has a significant contribution to make in the area of Sociology 247 general (liberal) education and in professional education of widely diverse emphases, along with the preparation of scholars, to expand and transmit the body of sociological knowledge itself. Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex social problems, has contributed to the dramatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both an art and a science. Its art is the development of special skills used in working with people, either individually, in groups, or through community programs. Its science is the body of knowledge — derived from sociology, psychology, and psychiatry — about people and communities. Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare agencies; in courts as probation officers for - juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics; in schools; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as well as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Funds, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University provides for the needs of three groups of students: those who wish to qualify for firstlevel social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; and those who wish to prepare themselves for roles in community leadership as organization board members, in labor union leadership, in industrial social welfare relationships. After the basic twoyear general studies program at Ball State, students begin their specialization in social work within the sociology major. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, and methods of social work. Field trips in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. In the senior year students majoring in social work enroll in a course in basic social work practice. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of casework, group work, and community organization; practical experience is gained in field placement in a social agency for one quarter where the student works with individuals or groups under expert supervision. The Field of Criminal Justice and Corrections Only since the decade of the sixties have people in our society begun to take a greater interest in all facets of our system of criminal justice. A number of events in that decade have stimulated not only public interest, concern, and continuing dialogue, but also research, change in law and interpretation, publication and dissemination of information, and the growing awareness of the need for trained and qualified personnel in our criminal justice system. The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and possible employment: law enforcement, probation services in both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. In most instances, agencies, programs, and facilities operate on three levels of government: local, state, and federal. The departmental major in criminal justice and corrections has the following objectives: to provide students with the growing body of knowledge about the structure and functions of the basic elements comprising our society; to relate such problematic areas as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, to our system of criminal justice; to provide the student with a combination of theory and practical experience in the five areas listed above; and to enable the student to qualify for firstlevel employment positions in the criminal justice system or to qualify for future graduate study in this or related areas. Employment opportunities for trained men and women are increasing in our society. The general requirements include age 21, minimum physical requirements, and a thorough investigation into the candidates' background, integrity, maturity, and emotional stability. Civil service tests are frequently required for entrance into most positions on the state and federal levels. title: Principles of Sociology
description: An introductory view of the general field of sociology including basic concepts as used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, social processes, and social institutions.

title: Social Organization
description: An introduction to large scale social structures including institutions, formal organizations, communities, and society in terms of the social processes involved, such as integration, status, power, and adaptation. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: The Black Community in America
description: An examination of the major social forces influencing the structure of the contemporary black American subcommunity. Emphasis also on an exploration into the strengths and weaknesses of this structure and its relations with the large community, as bases of change in the accommodative patterns of blackwhite relations.

title: Social Problems
description: A survey of the nature and range of social problems, the conditions which give rise to them, and the methods by which our society attempts to cope with them. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100. Sociology 249

title: Sociology of Law Enforcement
description: An examination of sociological research and theory bearing on major social factors that affect municipal police organizations as important coordinating agencies in society. Emphasis on: institutional context of police activity, bureaucratization of police, police professionalization, judical decisions and the police role, police militancy, and the police and community change. Prerequisite: SOC 100, 242, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors affecting utilization of treatment programs.

title: Police-Community Relations
description: Analysis of interrelationship between police and public in the study and control of crime. Consideration is given to problems of policecommunity relations and to ways of establishing cooperation between police and various social, economic, and ethnic groups. Prerequisite: SOC 100 and 242.

title: Introduction to Sociological Research
description: Principles and techniques of organizing, conducting, and interpreting sociological research; the appropriateness of particular methodologies for different kinds of research problems. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in the social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 and 380.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective on life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in honors program or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ancient and Historic Social Thought
description: A critical survey of influential views regarding the nature of society and human relations from the Greek period through the 19th century Romanticists. Social thinkers and intellectual epochs are interpreted as products of the prevailing social conditions, and are employed for purposes of illuminating contemporary social issues and sociological theories.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of sociological theories and theorists of the 19th and early 20th centuries with a view toward relating theoretical positions to contemporary social dynamics and to contemporary theoretical work in sociology. The cultural and intellectual milieu in which the theoretical works were generated will be noted. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100.

title: Mass Society and Culture
description: Conditions giving rise to the spreading phenomena of mass culture, current expressions of these phenomena in American society and elsewhere, and an appraisal of their implications for organizational functioning and interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: A survey of the literature, issues, and events which focus upon the nature and types of complex social organizations with particular attention to societal consequences. Prerequisite: 8 hours of sociology or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sociology of Religion
description: Examines religion as a social institution with particular attention to the societal functions of religion, the influence of social factors on the development of religion, the role of religion in the amelioration of contemporary social problems, and contemporary processes affecting the future of religion.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as it is related to various sociological variables. Various sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Juvenile Delinquency
description: The nature, extent, causes, and methods of control of juvenile delinquency. Emphasis is given to the role of community agencies in prevention and treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Criminology
description: The nature and extent of individual and organized crime in modern society, contributing causes, and methods used in its control. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Introduction to Corrections
description: A beginning course in penology with emphasis on the three major components: police, courts, and correctional institutions including their history, philosophy, and current programs, policies, and problems. Prerequisite: SOC 245 and either 450 or 451; and permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Corrections
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in correctional settings on the state and local level. Prerequisites: SOC 452 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Law Enforcement
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in police settings on the local and state levels. Prerequisite: SOC 245, 452, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Internship in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: A summer internship involving fulltime individual assignments under field supervision in a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: SOC 450 or 451 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Small Groups
description: Analysis of data on experimental laboratory research on small groups and field research on small group dynamics. Attention is given to the relationship between group productivity, group cohesion, size, interaction patterns, and related areas. Prerequisite: SOC 260 or GXPSY 316.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historic functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Practicum in the Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis and evaluation of problems evolving from the changing social and demographic characteristics of urban core areas, with special emphasis given to their effects on family units and the needs of children and youth. A field work course requiring supervised participation in a designated urban neighborhood. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and utilizing sources of data; the application of survey findings to programs of community action. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 472 or 480.

title: Independent Study in Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar in Sociology
description: An openended course offering for fourth year sociology majors. Both the focus of study and the format of the course will be determined by the students in conjunction with the instructor. Prerequisite: 24 hours in sociology and permission of the department chairman.

title: Field of Social Work
description: An introductory survey of the field of social work with emphasis on twentiethcentury developments. Course content will emphasize contemporary agencies and services, both public and private. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200.

title: Public Social Welfare
description: An introduction to public welfare including policy, services, and administration. Tax supported income maintenance programs are examined with special emphasis on the philosophy, methods, issues, and problems of public assistance programs.

title: Child Welfare
description: An introduction to the field of child welfare, including programs, policies, problems, and services. The principles and practices of casework for children are examined with emphasis upon state and local community resources. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200 and 310 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Social Work Practice
description: Basic social work principles, values, and skills generic to social work practice. Presentation of basic concepts underlying human behavior relevant to social work practice. Emphasis on problemsolving process, systems analysis, communication skills, and a variety of intervention procedures. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200, 310, 311, 312 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Social Work Practicum
description: A field course providing basic training and practical experience in social work methods of casework, group work, and community organization through placement in social work settings. Prerequisite: SOCWK 440 and permission of the department chairman. Department of Speech Huckleberry, Head; Artes, Benson, Bloom, Diedrich, Dorris, English, Farling, Harmon, Heady, D., Heady, S., Hemeyer, Hoops, Irving, Kramer, Lindell, Maitlen, Mannies, Pruis, Ritz, Robbins, Schmidt, Shepard, Strother, Taylor General Speech The field of general speech encompasses several areas such as public address, interpersonal communication, interpretation, theatre, and speech sciences. It is a general program for undergraduate use, while persons specialize as they move toward graduate degrees. In the area of general speech, the University offers both graduate and undergraduate programs. A large proportion of those students electing a speech major plan to become teachers in the public schools. These teachers are expected to direct debating and individual events, produce theatre, and promote and direct radio and television programs. They are also asked to be in charge of special convocations. Their class work is the development of the skills of public address and participation in a democratic society. Also they must develop an appreciation and skill for interpretation and theatre as performed in school theatres or through the facilities of mass media. Another responsibility is to develop an appreciation of the artistic, an understanding of the basic issues of people, and a respect for their cultural heritage. The profession of general speech assists liberal arts graduates to develop these same skills and attitudes. In addition, the speech major and minor are especially useful to support students who enter other professions such as law, the ministry, politics, public relations, and professional radio, television, and theatre. The University offers many student activities in the areas of intercollegiate debating, individual speech events, conferences, pantomime troupe, and theatre. It is assumed that general speech majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office and from the appropriate area chairman and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Speech Pathology and Audiology The graduate with a bachelor's degree and a teaching major in speech pathology and audiology (sometimes known as speech and hearing therapy) usually works in a public school corporation. An individual with a master's degree may work in a public school, hospital speech and hearing clinic, college or university center, or communitysponsored speech and hearing agency. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers three undergraduate programs in speech pathology and audiology: a teaching major, for persons who plan to work in the public schools; a departmental major, for persons who plan to work eventually in a hospital, community or college clinic; and a departmental minor, for those students who want as much information and knowledge as they can secure regarding this discipline but who do not plan to enter the profession. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology, in audiology, and in speech and hearing therapy. These are necessary for those individuals who desire professional teaching certification and for those who wish to join the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs: public school therapy programs, hospital and physical therapy environment, preschool nursery programs, and the University Speech and Hearing Clinic. In the latter, children and adults come to the Ball State campus for clinical work for both speech and hearing problems. Theatre Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a most modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher education for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work is available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist people to understand themselves. It also assists students to understand their dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office, and from the theatre area chairman, and should be requested early in the student's academic career.
