title: Fundamentals of Public Speaking
description: Fundamentals and techniques of organizing material and presenting that material in individual speeches. Emphasis on personal speaking improvement in the classroom and in public performances.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasis is on techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequi site: SPCH 210.

title: Beginning Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Development and composition of the debate case and consideration of factual argumentation. Prerequisite: high school speech.

title: Intermediate Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Stress on direct clash and crossquestion debate. This course involves tournament debating. Prerequisite: SPCH 213.

title: Phonetics of Speech Science
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic voice and speech science. f See the professional education requirements in the curricular outlines for the requirement of an additional course in the methods of teaching speech pathology and audiology: SPAA 411. *Courses in statistics may be substituted for GXPSY 100 and 241 with the approval of the department head.

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Personal speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation problems.

title: Speech Practicum
description: The student works upon extemporaneous speaking, discussion, debate, oratory, or interpretive reading for intercollegiate competition, or works in theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: The development of principles of rhetorical criticism and the application of the principles to an intensified study of prominent platform, radio, and television speakers. Consideration is given also to the influence of the speaker upon our social and political life. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Parliamentary Procedure
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Teaching of Speech in the Secondary School
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisites: SPCH 210, 216, and TREAT 220 or 232.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher.

title: Intercollegiate Forensics
description: Practical experience in speech, intercollegiate debate, discussion, oratory, extemporaneous speaking, and interpretive reading. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Advanced Public Speaking
description: An intensified study and application of the principles of effective public speaking; the ideational formulation and delivery of longer speeches; the rhetorical analysis of significant speeches. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or per mission of the department head.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: An examination through exposure to theory, actual practice, and criticism, of the process of communication. Will include communication models of message encoding, transmission, decoding and feedback; the complexity of language, including abstracting and determination of meaning; problems in facetoface, small group, platform speaking, and mass media communication; and communication breakdowns.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of small group literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and. structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problemsolving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech pursues a particular area of study in depth on a consultative basis with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned and a total of 4 hours may be earned at one time.

title: Internship in Speech
description: The student is assigned to onthejob experience in such places as a college classroom, a hospital, a community clinic, summer camp, or summer theatre. Students will be permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the amount of college credit to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in some aspect of speech and communications, and permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned; but not more than 8 hours may be earned at one time.

title: Speech Science
description: An introductory study of the physical elements of sound, particularly as they apply to the communication process. Prerequisite: SPCH 216. Speech 255

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 261.

title: Language Development
description: Development of the phonology, grammar, content and function of language in children together with a review of the environmental and individual factors acting to influence that development.

title: Survey of Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to the profession of speech pathology and audiology and the professional endeavors of speech pathologists and audiologists. Not open to majors in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Articulation Disorders
description: Designed to prepare students to diagnose and treat articulatory speech disorders, particularly in younger children. Part of the course will consist of a laboratory of observation in the treatment of defective speech. Prerequisite: SPCH 216, SPAA 260, 261. Open only to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course for the clinic student. Designed to assist the beginning clinician to develop an understanding of clinical competency, permit selfevaluation, improve phonetic testing, gain general knowledge of speech problems, develop ability to understand diganostic principles and procedures and learning theory, and observe and evaluate therapy. Prerequisite: SPCH 216, SPAA 410. Must be taken prior to SPAA 412, 416, 420, 446. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 300.

title: Clinical Practice with Articulatory Disorders
description: Actual diagnosis and therapy for children with speech difficulties of an articulatory nature. Prerequisite: SPAA 410 and 411 or permission of the department head.

title: Stuttering Disorders
description: Particular attention to and study of the problem of stuttering. Prerequisite: SPAA 410.

title: Clinical Practice with Stuttering Disorders
description: The student works with persons with stuttering problems. Prerequisite: SPAA 370, 412, 414.

title: Organic Speech Disorders
description: An introductive study of neurology and anatomy of the brain and the speech disorders resulting from brain damage such as cerebral palsy and aphasia. Other physical problems such as cleft palate and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 261, 410.

title: Clinical Practice with Organic Speech Disorders
description: The student works with persons having speech defects produced by more complicated organic problems, such as aphasia, cerebral palsy, and cleft palate. Prerequisite: SPAA 412, 418.

title: Introduction to Hearing Disorders
description: Review of anatomy of the ear. Nature and causes of hearing disabilities. Techniques in the conservation of hearing and in the use of residual hearing. Interpretation of audiograms. Psychological problems of persons with hearing loss. Prerequisite: SPAA 260, 261, or permission of the department head.

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in the use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for the purpose of reeducation and the necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 442.

title: Aural Rehabilitation
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for the teaching of lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite: SPAA 442. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 444. 446, Aural Rehabilitation Practicum. (3) Emphasis is placed upon the actual rehabilitation or habilitation of persons who have hearing deficiencies. The techniques of lipreading and auditory training will be employed, as well as the use of hearing aids. Prerequisite: SPAA 411 and 444.

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: An overview of the field of theatre with special reference to the origins of drama.

title: Stagecraft
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of the crafts involved in theatre production at the school, college, and community theatre levels. Three hours of lecture and three arranged hours of laboratory a week.

title: Principles of Stage Makeup
description: An investigation of the principles, techniques, and materials of stage makeup and practical experience in their application.

title: Interpretive Reading
description: Fundamentals of English speech applied to the interpretive reading of prose and poetry.

title: Acting 1
description: A lecturelaboratory class stressing the basic principles of acting. Major emphasis on stage movement.

title: Acting 2
description: A lecturelaboratory course on the principles of acting with major emphasis on character analysis and development. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Modern Drama
description: Analysis of selected dramas from the time of Ibsen to the present day and of the conditions under which they originally were produced.

title: Directing 1
description: Theory and practice of directing for the theatre. Exercises in movement, line interpretation, creation of atmosphere, and the effective use of stage areas. Prerequisite: THEAT 232 and 233.

title: Children's Theatre
description: The principles of theatre devoted to creative dramatics. Twothirds of the course is devoted to formal dramatics. A public performance will be arranged.

title: Advanced Theatre Practice
description: Students design and execute a theatre project in such areas as scenery designs, lighting, properties, acting, directing, oral interpretation, and house management. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in theatre courses and permis - sion of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Theatre 1
description: The early history of theatre from its Egyptian and Grecian origins through the medieval period.

title: History of Theatre 2
description: The theatre from the Renaissance through the eighteenth century.

title: History of Theatre 3
description: The modern theatre commencing with its origins in the nineteenth century.

title: Studies in American Theatre
description: An investigation of significant movements in the American professional theatre and its drama.

title: Studies in Continental Theatre
description: An intensive study of selected continental theatre movements from the turn of the century to the present day. Prerequisite: THEAT 411 or 412.

title: Studies in Contemporary European Theatre
description: An intensive study of contemporary European drama and theatres involving a field trip of three weeks to European theatre centers with appropriate side excursions. Discussions with leading theatre educators and professionals will be planned plus attendance at current productions. Contributions of departments in other Colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by Directors of Elementary and Secondary Teacher Education, who are responsible to the Dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by a Teacher Preparation Council which represents the total University. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers for all levels of the elementary school with degree programs at the baccalaureate, master's, specialist in education, and doctoral levels. The Department of Secondary, Adult, and Higher Education, in addition to coordinating the total program for preparation of teachers for secondary schools, provides graduate level study in the field of curriculum and in preparation of teachers for adults and posthigh school levels. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate and graduate programs for teachers of the deaf, the mentally retarded, the orthopedically and physically handicapped, and the emotionally disturbed. The Burris Laboratory School is a center for demonstration, participation, and research in elementary and secondary education and functions as a resource for the total program of teacher education in the University. The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers graduate programs at master's, specialist in education, and doctoral levels for students preparing for public school and collegiate positions in these areas of study. Two departments of the Teachers College serve students in areas of psychology. The Department of Educational Psychology specializes in applications of psychology, measurement, and research to areas particularly pertinent to teacher education and related fields in both undergraduate and graduate programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services concentrates on graduate level programs extending through the doctorate in its areas of specialization. Departments of the Teachers College, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public educa.- tion and psychology; for production and dissemination of research; for innovation in instructional practices; and for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education. The areas of educational foundations, the general field of education, and social psychology are placed administratively under the Associate Dean of the Teachers College. Faculty teaching on these programs hold rank in departments of the College but have instructional assignments to courses in these areas. The area of educational foundations includes history of education, philosophy of education, sociology of education, and comparative education. Although study in these fields is concentrated at the graduate level, some undergraduate work is incorporated into courses constituting the professional sequence for preparing elementary and secondary school teachers. Courses included in the general field of education serve students on a wide variety of programs and are not appropriately assignable to a single department. PREPARATION OF TEACHERS FOR MULTICULTURED SECONDARY SCHOOLS (MULTICUL) The MULTICUL program at Ball State offers young people an opportunity to put words, expressions, and demonstrations into actuality which hopefully will lead toward a possible solution to one of America's most crucial problems, developing racial harmony. The program is designed not only to deal with black and white relations, but it encompasses as many ethnic groups as possible. Multiculture is a part of our society at large as well as our schools; therefore, potential teachers should prepare themselves to meet realistic situations. BOYS' CLUB PERSONNEL PREPARATION Because of the increasing need for adequately prepared directors and other personnel of the numerous branches of Boys' Clubs of America, officials of the University have worked with the officials of the national organization of Boys' Clubs of America to evolve a pattern for preparation of such personnel. Boys' Clubs of America will provide some fouryear scholarships for selected students. Those who do not receive scholarships will proceed at their own expense. Boys' Clubs, like the public schools, are civic enterprises and are actively involved in the community. Often a staff member of a Boys' Club may also be a parttime teacher in the local secondary school. Because of this likely and desirable relationship and because the preparation for teaching is good preparation for Boys' Club work, this program has been so planned that each student who completes it satisfactorily will meet requirements for recommendation for a certificate to teach in an Indiana secondary school. Department of Special Education Spencer, Head; Ahlersmeyer, Hoops, Kamback, Lawyer, Pino, Richardson, Seitz, A. Twining, J. Twining, Van Every, Van Tassel, Wagner, Wilhelmi, Young The philosophy of special education is that each child has the right to an education that will develop that child's capabilities to their fullest extent. The acceptance of and the application of this philosophy in America have led to an ever increasing demand for trained personnel in the various areas of special education. In recognition of this interest and of the need for university preparation for teachers and administrators, Ball State University has established the Department of Special Education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to certification to teach in the areas of Deaf Education, Mental Retardation, and Orthopedic and Special Health Problems. These programs are designed in accordance with teacher certification requirements of Indiana. Elective courses in special education that are open to future teachers, psychologists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, a course on the education of gifted children, a course on the education of slow learners, and a course on the education of children with learning disabilities. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE DEAF Special education for deaf children was established at Ball State University to assist at the national, state, and local levels in meeting the critical shortage of teachers for deaf children. The lack of academic instructors and professionals in related areas in residential and day schools, as well as in civic and medical centers, provides incentive enough for development of a collegiate program. The teaching minor in special education with deaf children is designed to prepare teachers for classroom instruction of the deaf Courses include methodology in language, speech, lipreading, and basic school subjects and are designed with particular cognizance of the expressive and receptive communication barrier created by deafness. Observation of a demonstration class of preschool deaf children provides a laboratory experience early in the program. Student teaching is done atA-he state residential School for the Deaf in Indianapolis and/or in dayschool programs in Indiana and in neighboring states. Guidance and social counseling of deaf children are included in the program. The Ball State University program in deaf education meets approval of (1) The Indiana Teacher Training and Licensing Commission (providing certification coverage for teaching deaf children in all grades in Indiana), (2) The Conference of Executives of American Schools for the Deaf (making the qualified student eligible, upon application, to teach in the Residential Schools for the Deaf in the United States), and (3) The U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (providing the student with the opportunity to apply for federal scholarships made available to Ball State through this agency). SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE MENTALLY RETARDED Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to nationwide recognition of the special needs of mentally retarded children. To develop to the optimum of their ability, these children need a specially designed curriculum and specially prepared teachers who understand the learning process of mentally retarded children. To help alleviate the continued nationwide and statewide shortage of qualified teachers in this area of exceptionality, Ball State University prepares students to become professionally trained special class teachers. Both a teaching area major and a teaching minor are available to interested students. The teaching minor is also an endorsement for special education: teaching the mentally retarded. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR CHILDREN WITH ORTHOPEDIC AND SPECIAL HEALTH PROBLEMS Within the group of children who have special educational needs are those who are orthopedically handicapped or who have other health conditions which make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for crippled or other healthimpaired children confronts the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a special classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The program is designed to offer comprehensive, professional preparation to future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children, so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. title: Introduction to Exceptional Children
description: A survey of the educational needs of children who deviate from the normal in mental, physical, and social characteristics. Designed as an introduction to the field of special education.

title: Education of Preschool Deaf Children
description: The development of oral communication in preschool deaf children. Directed observations of both hearing and hearingimpaired classes, home visitations, and the parenttraining program. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Ntt open to the student who has credit in SPAA 261.

title: Practicum in Special Education
description: Observation and assistance of teachers in special classes for exceptional children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or may be taken parallel with SPCED 425. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Education of Gifted Children
description: Designed to help teachers in the identification of and instruction of gifted and talented children. Major topics of study are characteristics and identification of the gifted, and curriculum developments and adaptations suitable for the education of gifted children.

title: Education of Slow Learners
description: Major topics include identification, characteristics, and practices and procedures for meeting the needs of the slow learning child. Emphasis is placed on techniques and methods of instruction as well as research findings concerned with the slow learner and the culturally disadvantaged. * Students are expected to meet the prerequisites for AED 300 (AEI5 100 and 200) and for MATH 391 (MATH 204 or 207).

title: History of the Education of the Deaf
description: Deals with history of education of the deaf from ancient times to the present with primary emphasis on early teachers and schools in the United States.

title: Psychosocial Aspects of Deafness
description: Personal, social, vocational, and learning adjustment problems of hearingimpaired persons and how assistance can be given in solving these problems. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for reeducation and necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440, or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 442.

title: Aural Rehabilitation
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for teaching lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite: SPAA .440. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 444.

title: Speech Development for the Deaf
description: The International Phonetic Alphabet, Northhampton Charts, diacritical markings, and other methods and techniques used to teach speech to the deaf.

title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of and individual work with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children.

title: Manual Communications
description: Theory and research underlying the language of signs and fingerspelling (manual alphabet) is considered. Development of receptive and expressive skills in manual communications is required. Prerequisite: SPCED 448 or permission of the department head.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: An introductory course comparing language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Levels of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight Language for the Deaf, Barry Five- Slate, Wing Symbols, and the Natural Method. Language outlines from different schools are used as supplementary aids.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching subjects such as arithmetic and science.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Special Education
description: Not open to the student who has credit in EDGEN 462.

title: Psychology of Mental Retardation
description: Various types and degrees of retardation. The psychological, environmental, and cultural factors which contribute toward retardation. Emphasis on etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate retarded children. Prerequisites: EDPSY 300 and SPCED 201.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 1
description: Special class organization, curriculum practices and procedures, and the methods and techniques used in the instruction of the mentally retarded. Prerequisite: SPCED 472.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 2
description: Continuation of SPCED 474, with emphasis on the curriculum. Prerequisite: SPCED 474.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: This course is designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children. Topics include etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate children with physical disabilities. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 300.

title: Educational Methods with Physically Handicapped Children
description: Special class organization, curriculum, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of orthopedically handicapped children. Prerequisite: SPCED 482; prerequisite or parallel: EDEL 380 and MATH 391.

title: Education of Children with Learning Disability
description: Intensive study of the psychosocial and educational research findings pertaining to the education of children with learning disabilities. Emphasis on current research, appropriate educational methods, and behavior modifications. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, EDPSY 300. Undergraduate Programs Description of Course Identification System Each prefix has its own numbering system, with a potential of numbers from 100 through 699. Courses numbered from 100 to 199 are primarily freshman courses. Courses numbered from 200 to 299 are primarily sophomore courses. Courses numbered from 300 to 399 are primarily junior courses. Courses numbered 400 to 499 are primarily senior courses. Courses numbered from 500 up are for graduate students. Courses numbered from 600 to 699 are for graduate students with masters' degrees. In course descriptions the course number is given immediately following the prefix. If a number in parentheses follows, it is the immediately preceding number of the course. The student who has credit in a course under the parenthetical number, or any former number, may not earn credit in the course under its current number except under the terms of Course Repetition (see Credit and Grades). In the course description the number in parentheses following the descriptive title of the course is the credithour value of the course. It denotes the specific total of credit hours which may be earned in the course unless elsewhere in the description is a statement which permits the earning of a larger total of credit hours. Prerequisite refers to a course or courses which must precede the course described. Parallel indicates a course or courses which must be taken simultaneously with the described course. The letter g following the number of an undergraduate course indicates that the course is approved for the earning of graduate credit by eligible students properly registered for the course. The College of Architecture and Planning, established by the 1965 Indiana legislature, is dedicated to the development of professional competency in the functional, aesthetic, and humane design of the physical environment. Two fiveyear programs of study are offered : the departmental major in architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Architecture degree; and the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree. The first two years of both programs are concurrent and include a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. The Ball State general studies program is an integral part of these first two years. The last three years provide specialization in the fields of architectural or landscape design as well as providing for specialized study in areas of the student's own choosing. An environmental design major is offered on the Professional Arts Curriculum for students who have completed the first year of either the architecture or the landscape architecture program and is designed for students who wish to end their studies after four years of university work or who wish to pursue a different program at another school of environmental design. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning represent a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophy. By exposure to the variety of philosophical and technical backgrounds of creative professionals, the students are encouraged to seek their own personal philosophy within a professional teamwork situation. The curricula stress character, devotion, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility. The total program is concerned with the development of a physical environment serving the best of one's aspirations. PROGRAM IN ARCHITECTURE Architecture is the art and the science of planning one's environment. The architect must develop social awareness, creative ability, technical understanding, administrative ability, and business acuity. The program in architecture at Ball State University stresses the variety necessary in the educational background of an architect. Intellectual and cultural preparation should be as thorough as possible; therefore, the general studies courses are from the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. An area of study in depth and certain courses within the major provide further breadth and depth in general studies. The specialized courses provide for technical competence. Courses in architectural design provide experience in the integrative process of design. Thus the total program, which calls for five years of preparation, provides not only for comprehension of acceptable procedures and methods but also for stimulation of the creative process in environmental problem solving. Architecture is a departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The degree is Bachelor of Architecture. The total number of hours required on the Professional Arts Curriculum with architecture as the major is 255. PROGRAM IN LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE Landscape architecture is dedicated to conserving and improving the quality of our environment. It is concerned with the quality of water, air, land, and how they influence our human relationships as well as affect our responses to nature. The landscape architect approaches this task with the assistance of allied professions such as architecture, planning, natural resources, engineering, sociology, economics. Working with others for the improvement of the human environment is the purpose of this program; never before have the challenges been so great. The landscape architect must be aware of human needs, and to meet these needs requires a knowledge of the natural sciences. The understanding of nature's processes and the ability to design in terms of earth, water, and plants enable the landscape architect not just to organize but to enrich greatly the human environment. The program stresses the need for variety in the education of a landscape architect. The general studies program (humanities, natural sciences, social and behavioral studies) is a vital part of the intellectual and cultural preparation of young men and women for professional practice. The core program in design provides further contact with the general studies program as well as developing capabilities in solving small - to largescale problems. The program stresses the collective approach to solving problems yet recognizes individuals and their contributions. Specialized courses provide for technical competency. It is the aim of the fiveyear program to encourage creativity and to develop sound procedures for establishing an environment which benefits humanity and nature. Landscape architecture is a departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The degree is Bachelor of Landscape Architecture. The College of Business recognizes the need for both breadth and depth in the total academic pattern. Department of Accounting Parkison, Head; Barnhart, Cirtin, Cudd, Gentis, Hanks, Jackson, Lawrence, McCabe, Nolan, Ounapu, Walker Accounting is often described as "the language of business." To make intelligent decisions in the effective planning and controlling of the operations of a business, management must know the effect of transactions on its financial position and its earning power. Accounting the art by which financial results are summarized and interpreted, furnishes that necessary data. The accountant as a student of management problems endeavors to meet reporting requirements and to present data in terms of management's needs. The study of accounting is a vital part in the educational preparation of any executive and is useful in all types of business careers. Contact with all aspects and levels of business enables the accountant to acquire excellent training for executive leadership. Many and varied careers are available to the accountant both in the types of organizations and in the areas of specialization he may select. The future for men and women trained in accounting is almost unlimited as the continued growth in the uses of accounting is assured by further expansion and complex development of business activity. The increase of government influence in business affairs and industry's search for increased productivity through its emphasis on cost controls and efficiency cause the potential need for the services of accountants to increase more rapidly than the number of persons properly qualified to fill the need. A major in accounting provides a foundation for a career as a controller, financial officer, internal auditor, cost accountant, professional CPA, public administration officer and teacher of accounting. The departmental major in accounting, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for an interesting and rewarding career in the broad fields of accounting. Opportunities for original and creative typing. Continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite : BEOA 113.

title: Principles of Business Correspondence
description: Principles and basic elements of effective letter writing with emphasis on the psychological approach, reader viewpoint, positive tone, and appropriate format for personalbusiness letters and job applications.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 1
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations., Required : a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 2
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirements for BEOA 285. Required : a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisite: BEOA 285 or equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 3
description: Fulltime summer employment in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirement for BEOA 286. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during the summer and the submitting of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisites : BEOA 285 and 286 or the equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator,

title: Beginning Shorthand 1
description: Special emphasis upon basic theory with stress on brief forms. Introduction to the skills of writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or the equivalent.

title: Beginning Shorthand 2
description: Completion of basic theory and increased emphasis upon development of skill in taking dictation. A student whose secondary school transcript shows credit for more than one semester of shorthand is not eligible to receive credit in this course. Prerequisite : BEOA 321.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on skill in taking dictation with some emphasis on transcription. Open to those students who have had BEOA 322 and students whose secondary school transcript shows one year of shorthand. Prerequisite : BEOA 113 or the equivalent.

title: Advanced Shorthand 1
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, transcription, and production of mailable copy. Prerequisite : BEOA 113 or the equivalent and at least two years of secondary school shorthand or BEOA 323.

title: Advanced Shorthand 2
description: Special emphasis upon production of mailable copy, and continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and BEOA 324.

title: Calculating Machines
description: Developing skill in using electronic calculators and other common office calculating machines as tools; emphasis is placed on developing the manipulative skills and programming abilities used to solve problems involving business data.

title: Duplicating, Machine Transcribing, and Filing
description: Preparation of ink stencils and carbon masters; operation of ink and liquid duplicators; training in machine dictation and Business Education and Office Administration 99 machine transcription; indexing, coding, and filing of business correspondence; and survey of filing equipment and supplies. Prerequisite : BEOA 113.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems; the nature, function, and use of business papers ; knowledges, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining of records of a business office, and study of records administration in business and industry.

title: Principles of Office Supervision
description: Principles of effective office supervision with emphasis on the function of the office and the role of the office supervisor. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects A
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, typing, general business, and shorthand. Prerequisite : EDPSY 250 ; student will have completed his requirements in typewriting and shorthand. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option B.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects B
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, general business, typing, and related office skills. Prerequisite : EDPSY 250 ; student will have completed his requirements in typewriting and accounting. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option A.

title: Methods of Teaching Distributive Subjects
description: History and development, objectives, methods of aproach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson and unit planning; overview of cooperative education and project plan programs. The various distributive subjects are included. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250. Restricted to students pursuing a distributive education teaching area major program of study.

title: Methodology of Relevant Work Experiences in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledges needed by persons who will be supervising and directing a cooperative education or a project plan program in distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Distributive Education
description: The principles upon which vocational distributive education is organized, administered, and supervised; the kinds of programs; federal and state regulations; relationships to programs in other vocational areas. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a teaching license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Communications for Business Organizations
description: Techniques used in managementoriented internal and external communications. Emphasis on theory, planning, oral and written presentations, audience perceptions, data organization, media selection, and preparation techniques for business letters : and an overview of reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Business Reports: Written and Oral
description: Techniques for writing managementoriented informal and formal reports; including collecting, interpreting, summarizing, and synthesizing data. Principles for selection of tabular and graphic data presentations. Includes written and oral presentations of functional and analytical reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Secretarial Procedures
description: Operational functions of toplevel professional secretarial work through integration of basic skills, knowledges, and the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 323 or equivalent or permission of the 452. department head. Secretarial Administration. (4) Administrative and supervisory aspects of toplevel professional secretarial work through planning and organizing office functions to achieve smooth and efficient work flow and with emphasis on the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 451.

title: Principles of Business and Distributive Education
description: Historical development of the field of business education. Possible future trends and their effect on the entire business education program. Open only to students who have been approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

description: The importance of rmeeasrudrements, techniques of administering and scoring tests, methods of analyzing and co mg test results, uses of tests, construction of tests for classroom use in all areas of business education. 10 a ear raduate ou 8e8 497, Independent Study in Business Education, Distributive Education, or Office Administration. title: The Economics of the Ghetto
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. The theory of wages, rent, interest, and profits. The principles of international trade and comparative economic organization.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the Advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite : ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 o30r3 p. ermission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who had credit in NR

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite : ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economic Development of China
description: Systematic analysis of the economic system and economic growth in Chinca since 1949. Emphasis on three major aspects of the Chinese economy : the transformation of the economic institution, the strategies of the economic development, and the innovations and developmental experience of the Chinese model.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite : ECON 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner ; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, thee i employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 432.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the . Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON. 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This , is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economics of the 'Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: EGON 201,

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures.' Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Development in Latin America
description: The evaluation of theories of economic development. Sources and consequences of the economic growth and development process in Latin America analyzed in the context of economic theory. Attntion to Common Market possibilities, monetaryfiscal factors, and trade and exchange. Examination of current national and international programs as promoters of development.

title: Economic Development of China, Japan, and India
description: Comparative analysis of the economic systems and strategies of development in three major economies in Asia — China, a centralplanning economy; Japan, a freemarket economy; and India, a mixed economy.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capitl formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: UrbamEconoxnics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite : 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter. At the undergraduate level, the Department of Finance and Management offers three majors leading to either the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science degree. These majors are in Finance, Management, and General Business Administration. Finance. Finance is a decisionoriented discipline concerned with the investment and management of money both in the present and in the future. The Finance major is designed to provide the student with a general program in the financial aspects of business, including financial management, investments, banking, insurance, real estate, and other related financial areas. Finance courses provide knowledge of concepts, processes, and institutions involved with the financing functions of the business enterprise; acquaint students with the financial instruments, institutions, and markets in the United States and the world; provide the tools and techniques of financial analysis and decisionmaking; and expose the students to sufficient examples of financial decisionmaking to allow them to develop expertise in applied finance. The Finance major allows the student to pursue one of three finance options within the Finance major, namely, (1) Corporate Financial Management, (2) Financial Institutions, and (3) Insurance and Real Estate. The Corporate Financial Management option prepares the student for careers in the finance division of a business firm ; such as, systems analysis, budget review analysis, financial analysis, acquisitions analysis, credit management, receivables management, and short and longterm capital management. The Financial Institutions program emphasizes employment opportunities in the areas of managing stocks and bonds as a securities broker, portfolio manager, or trust department specialist and in investment banking. The option in Financial Institutions prepares an individual to work in the field of banking, savings and loan associations, loan companies, insurance companies, credit unions, pension funds, securities brokerage, and real estate brokerage. The third option, Insurance and Real Estate, allows finance students to develop competence in fields leading to the various professional positions in insurance and real estate. Students also develop a background for making informed decisions relating to business and consumer purchasing in these areas. Management. This major offers courses in the areas of (I) Personnel Management, (2) Production Management, (3) Information Management, and (4) General Management. The first three represent areas in which the student may concentrate, whereas the General Management program is for those who do not desire an area of specialty in management. Through a grouping of cultural and business subjects, it is the aim of the management courses to afford the college student a knowledge of the cultural values and social relationships of modern society followed by training in fundamental management facts, principles, and methods. Emphasis is placed on the concept that management is of universal interest, is subject to innovation, is intimately associated with decision making, and is performed to accomplish desired results. The speciality programs have been structured for students who wish to pursue careers as personnel managers, manufacturing managers, or managers of information and management systems. The Information Management option is especially attractive to women students as it facilitates their entry into management positions. General Business Administration. This major permits students to concentrate in two of the three areas available; i.e., insurance, management, and finance. Hence, this major provides a broader diversity of vocational opportunities than the other two majors but with less depth in any one area of ePnOentration. The management sequence is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them, as future business executives and specialists, to deal with diversity of problems which arise in the Mine of dayt0-day activities, The insurance sequence is designed to provide students wi a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance, Graduates in General Business Administration are qualified to accept positions as junior executives at the management level in finance, insurance, personnel administration, office administration, production supervision, or other areas, In addition, this degr particularly attractive to those students who may wish to engage in a small business OT W 0 do not wish to commit themselves to a particular vocation at this time. title: Principles of Bank Operations
description: Fundamentals of bank operations. A survey of various bank functions including accounting, trusts, demand deposits, savings and time deposits, home mortgage lending, internal controls, international financial services, and public service.

title: Bank Management
description: Trends in philosopy and practice of bank management. The nature and objective of banking; formulation of objetives and policies; organizational planning, management controls; functions of banks related to management practices policies, and procedures.

title: Credit Administration
description: Factors influencing and determining loan policy. Bank credit policies; credit department; sources of credit; credit correspondence; secured and unsecured loans to customers; loans to business ; term loans; interbank loans; real estate loans ; influence of the Federal Reserve System ; and responsibilities of bank lending officials.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Principles underlying managerial decisions influenced by capital markets and type of ownership; problems relating to the sources of financing; the study of financial analysis and financial management; and interrelating economic and accounting theory with other areas of business. Prerequisite : ACC 203, ECON 201, MATH

title: Consumer, Business, and Public Finance
description: The great importance in our national life of business credit, personal and consumer credit (including installment sales credit), bank credit, and public credit (federal, state, and municipal). Prerequisite : FIN 250.

title: Managerial Finance
description: Emphasis on principles and tools for analysis and decision making in the finance function.

title: Financial Institutions
description: The structure of financial institutions in the American economy. Financial institutions as recipients and as suppliers of funds in financial markets. The identification and anlysis of many kinds of financial institutions and the administration of their loan and investment portfolios. Particular emphasis on the asset, liability, and caital management with the goal of profitability.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some are emphasized. Prerequisite : FIN 250. Prerequisite recommended : senior standing.

title: Investment Management
description: Problems of investment policy, including the study of types of investment risks, an introduction to security analysis, the analysis of investment requirements, and the kinds of investment policies.

title: Capital Management
description: An analysis of the management aspects relating to the inflows and outflows of permanent capital in business enterprises. Examines the management of longterm assets, intermediate and longterm credit, equity, and internal financing. Corporate expansion including mergers, acquisitions, corporate reorganization, and bankruptcies. Includes case studies. Prerequisite : FIN 350.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite : permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Business
description: Emphasizes the vital role of business in our society through a discussion of both the external environment of business and the internal environment of the business enterprise. Recognition is given to the contribution of the social and behavioral sciences in decision making. Open only to freshmen or sophomores except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the viewpoint of the consumer. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation.

title: Business Applications of Electronic Data Processing
description: An introductory course in electronic data processing with special emphasis on busines applications. Effects of computers on business, systems analysis, FORTRAN machine language, comparison of data processing systems, and effect of computer on management decisionmaking. Special business problems are analyzed, programmed, and run on computers, and final reports are prepared from the information accumulated.

title: Principles of Real Estate
description: Introduction to the basic principles, practices, and theories of real property, its economic value, legal implications, purchase agreements, escrow and title work, advertising, appraisals, sales, market trends, and relationship to the salesman and broker.

title: Real Estate Appraisal and Finance
description: Financing real estate via conventional loans and government insured loans. Lending regulations, policies, and procedures applicable to financing real estate (residential, multifamily, and commercial) via conventional and governmental loans. Emphasizes money market, source of funds, and other factors in property financing. An analytical approach to determine residential property value on a cost, market, and income basis.

title: Legal. Aspect of Real Estate
description: The elementary concepts of real estate law, and practice, particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, broker's regulations, license law, and title insurance.

title: Principles of Risk Management 1
description: Defines the nature of risk, theory of probability, principles underlying insurance, the insurance contract, and the negligence concept. Major emphasis on how insurance handles each risk.

title: Principles of Risk Management 2
description: An indepth analysis of themanagement of risks for which the organization, principles, and techniques appropriate in the area of life and property insurance management are useful. Study of life and property insurance as applied to business. Prerequisite: GBA 270.

title: Interpretation of Business Data
description: An introductory course dealing with the collection, analysis, presentation, and interpretation of statistical data. Topics include frequency distributions, sampling, basic probability, decisionmaking, regression and correlation, and time series analysis. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law, and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law, and the effect of the law in the areas of consumer credit and economic relationships.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principle articles of the Code including sales, commercial paper and security interests, in, addition to the areas of creditor's rights and property law. Prerequisite: GBA 360.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: GBA 370.

title: Property Insurance
description: Study of fire and allied lines insurance, inland marine floaters, transportation, theft, and liability insurance, and employers' liability and workmen's compensation. Emphasis is placed on management of risks in business and on the use of insurance as a tool for handling these risks. Prerequisite : GBA 370.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and/or problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include no fault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, state vs. federal regulation. Prerequisite: GBA 370, 371, and 372 or permission of; the department chairman.

title: Honors Colloquium in Business
description: Exploration of selected issues in business, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students or others with permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. 420.Data Processing Systems and Procedures. (4) Emphasizes computerbased systems and business computer applications, ranging from accounting applications to operations applications and an integration of these. Provides an awareness of the procedure in designing computer systems, characteristics, and components of business applications and interrelationships between computer applications. Prerequisite: GBA 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Business Statistics
description: The more commonly used advanced statistical methods, with broad coverage of estimation and tests of hypotheses, and including

title: Personnel Administration
description: How to administer a personnel progtarn In a business organisation so as to deal effectively with such problems as selection, compensation ; promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions miplore Marketing 109 services; and industrial relations. Prerequisites recommended: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Case Problems in Personnel Management
description: Case studies depicting complex personnel issues and problems faced by organizations. Provides the student an opportunity to apply personnel policies, theories, concepts, and techniques to actual personnel situations, Prerequisite: MGT 481.

title: Production Management
description: A basic study of methods of analysis applied in functional fields of production. Decision making and quantitative analysis of production problems arising in areas of methods analysis, work measurement, wage incentives, production planning and control, inventory control, plant layout, materials handling and quality control. Prerequisite: MGT 380 and GBA 320.

title: Work Design
description: The design of office and industrial jobs to meet the needs and preferences of the worker and the management. Included are methods improvement techniques, layout of work stations, incentive and motivation techniques, and the setting of output standards. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisites recommended: ECON 200 and MGT 380.

title: Retail Merchandising
description: An introduction to the retail industry with a concentration, on the merchandising activities of buying, selling, pricing, and inventory controlling. Prerequisite; GBA 101. Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 370.

title: Salesmanship
description: Fundamentals of retail, wholesale, outside, and service selling. Sales approaches, presentation, closings, and postsale service are emphasized. Prerequisite: GBA 101. Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 370.

title: Retail Advertising
description: Introduction to the field of advertising with emphasis 9ri the, preparation, appeal, and media selection of retail advertising. Prerequisite : GBA 101, Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 370.

title: Marketing and Consumer Issues
description: Analysis of the consumer issues which affect marketing. Includes the marketing implications of consumerism, ecology, and the disadvantaged consumers. Prerequisite: MKT 370 and junior standing.

title: Purchasing Management
description: A basic course in purchasing management. Principal topics considered are make or buy analysis, quality and quantity control, value :analysis, price determination, sources of supply, the purchasing system, and legal aspects of purchasing. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Credit Management
description: Practices of businesses in granting credit both to other business firms and to individuals. Credit limits, department operations, and collection policies are analyzed. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Buyer Behavior
description: Practical business implications of the various aspects of consumer motivation and behavior. The student is provided with information to understand how and why a buyer reacts in a purchasing situation. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Selling and Sales Management
description: Practices in recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. An analysis of the stages of a sales presentation. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Advertising Management
description: Use of advertising as a communication tool in marketing management. Analysis of media selection production and layout, measurement of effectiveness, and social and economic aspects of advertising. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Retail Management
description: An investigation of store policies, organization, location, layout, buying, stock control, pricing, and sales promotion for retail stores. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Principles of Marketing
description: A basic course which examines the roles of marketing in the fulfillment of the needs of consumers and industrial users. Marketing functions, marketing institutions, and changs in marketing brought about by economic and social forces. Prerequisite: ECON 201. Not open to graduate students.

title: Marketing Simulation Game
description: A simulation game 'where students are divided into teams or companies. Management in each company makes decisions in marketing, finance, and production. Does not invovlve writing computer programs or utilizing information from a data processing class. Prequisite: MKT 370 and junior standing.

title: Promotion Strategy
description: Use of cases and problems to provide experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKT 340.

title: Channel Strategy
description: An analysis of the alternative channels of distribution available to manufacturers and producers. Management decisions necessary for an effective channel organization are stressed with emphasis upon the use of retailing and wholesaling intermediaries. Prerequisite: MKT 350.

title: Survey of Transportation
description: The economics of transportationinternal waterways, railways, highways, and airways in the United States; economic development of various means of transportation and accompanying regulatory problems. Rate, traffic service, and coordination problems of our transportation system. Advantages and disadvantages, trends, and peculiarities of each of the various modes of transportation. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: International Marketing
description: Examines legal, economic, and cultural factors influencing marketing abroad. Commercial policies, practices, and techniques needed to locate and evaluate foreign markets, as well as the problems of pricing, promoting, and distributing products in international markets. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Marketing Research
description: A basic course in marketing research. Nature and scope of marketing research; scientific method and research design; specific marketing research procedures; techniques of sampling; and research report, followup, and evaluation of research process. Selected applications in areas of motivation, advertising, and product and sales control research. Prerequisites: MKT 370 and GBA 320.

title: Quantitative Marketing
description: Exploration of the various quantitative techniques that can be utilized in solving marketing problems. Principal topics considered are linear programming methods, game theory, Markov chains, probability theory in decision making, distribution cost analysis, and use of correlation. Prerequisite: GBA 320.

title: Marketing Management
description: Marketing by manufacturers as viewed from the marketing manager's position. Principal topics are selecting channels of distribution, determining demand, pricing policies, marketing legislation, advertising policies, and methods of selling. A case study approach. Prerequisites: MKT 340, 350, and GBA 320.

title: Internship in Marketing
description: The student works full time for a summer or a quarter as an intern on an approved program with a business firm under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to thirdquarter juniors and seniors with a major in marketing. Prerequisite: permission of the department head.

title: Independent Study in Marketing
description: For students who wish to conduct independent study in some phase of marketing. Consists of an experiment, library research, or the analysis of current marketing practices and methods.
