Denny, Douglas, Exley, Fitzpatrick, Gerhart, Gibas, Guendling, Ingold, Mahoney, McConnell, Sargent, Scheerer The fouryear collegiate program in nursing has been designed to prepare the graduate to function upon completion of the curriculum as a professional nurse practitioner in beginning positions of bedside nursing, team leadership, and public health nursing and to articulate into graduate study. Classroom and laboratory instruction for the curriculum is provided by the University and utilizes the facilities of Ball Memorial Hospital, adjacent to the University campus, as well as other nearby health agency facilities. The curriculum has been planned to provide general and professional educational experiences for the beginning student in nursing and the registered nurse who seeks a baccalaureate education in nursing. Students who have been admitted to the nursing major and who can furnish documentation of previous nursing experiences may request permission to be granted credit by examination, in sequence, for the courses NUR 200, 300, 310, 311, 316, 317, and 410. A student indicating an intent for a major in nursing begins his or her study in areas of English, social sciences, physical and biological sciences, and the fine arts. Approximately two years of academic work in the areas of humanities, social and behavioral sciences, and biological sciences are required. The major in nursing has been concentrated in the student's junior and senior years. Cooperative programs in nursing have been arranged between Ball State University and Anderson College, Grace College, Huntington College, Manchester College, St. Francis College, Taylor University, and Tri-State College. The student interested in the cooperative program may enroll at one of these institutions for the freshman and sophomore years and transfer these credits to Ball State University for the remaining two years. The curriculum for students preparing for professional nursing is classified under the Professional Arts Curriculum and consists of three options. The Bachelor of Science degree is earned and may be completed within the minimum requirements of curriculum (186 hours); free and directed elective hours range from 61-73 quarter hours. The student will meet the general requirements of the University with respect to the chosen professional nursing major and required minor and with respect to graduation (minimum of 2.0 scholastic ratio in major, required minor, and overall grade point average) ; in addition, the student will present a minimum grade of C in each clinical nursing course and in Options II and III, C grades in CHEM 130; ANAT 201; PHYSL 210 and BIO 213. The student is selected for processing for admission to the major in nursing after completing 60 quarter hours of work. All options require a minimal cumulative grade point average of 2.0. The achievement in specific required minor for the chosen option is a minimal cumulative grade point average of 2.0. Option I, minor in biological science, requires seven courses to be completed; CHEM 110, 130; BIO 111, 112, 213; ANAT 201;

School of Physical Education and Athletics Reno, Chairman Recent technical and social changes are placing an increasing responsibility on physical education, while research studies in physical education, medicine, psychology, and sociology are providing an increasing scientific basis for the discipline. title: Beginning Karate
description: Introductory skills for enjoyment of karate. Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 109.

title: Beginning Modern Jazz Dance
description: Understanding and skill in basic techniques and styles (cool, hot, blues, urban, primitive) of the jazz dance.

title: Beginning Tap Dance
description: Designed to teach the basic tap steps and combinations along with their rhythmic analysis and style to be used in compositions. Designed for the student with no experience in tap dancing.

title: Paddle Sports
description: Basic skills, rules, and strategies involved in playing racket ball, paddle tennis, and other paddle sports.

title: Archery
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 121 or PGW 121.

title: Badminton
description: Introductory skills for the playing of singles and doubles badminton. Basic strategy, rules, and courtesy will be stressed. Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 122 or PGW 124.

title: Beginning Bowling
description: Introductory skills for enjoyment of bowling. Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 123 or PGW 123.

title: Bicycling
description: Bicycling techniques involving maintenance of equipment; city, open country, and endurance riding primarily to introduce the student to family bicycling for lifetime use. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Horsemanship
description: Schooling in three gaits: walk, trot, and canter.

title: Beginning Fencing
description: Basic techniques, terminology, strategy, rules, and courtesies. Includes positions, footwork, parries, and lunges.

title: Pocket Billiards
description: Assists the student in the rudimentary skills and knowledges of the sport.

title: Snow Skiing
description: Designed to teach the beginner the mechanics of snow skiing, equipment choice, and care of equipment, plus offering a laboratory experience of several days of skiing on available slopes. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Orienteering
description: Designed to introduce the student to the activity of orienteering, a sport in which the participant utilizes the skills of land navigation using maps and compass reading skills. Circulorespiratory fitness is emphasized in distance running for time.

title: Swimming 2
description: Prerequisite: PGM 201 for men or PGW 201 for women or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 202 or PGW 202.

title: Aquatic Lifeguarding
description: Develops knowledge and ability for the protection of individuals participating in aquatic activities. Certification for Senior Red Cross Life *PPW 233 not required for physical education major. Saving is covered. Prerequisite : PGM 202, PGW 202, PGC 202, or permission of the department head.

title: Aquatic Art Techniques
description: Introduces the student to the stroke modifications, standard figures and sculling techniques, and floating patterns of aquatic art. Prerequisite: PGM 201, PGW 201, or permission of the department head.

title: Springboard Diving
description: Safe performance of aerial dives from aquatic springboards. Prerequisite : PGM 201 or PGW 201 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 205 or PGW 205.

title: Scuba
description: Selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus techniques and the laws pertaining to the activity. Prerequisite: PGM 201 or PGW 201 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in PGM 206 or PGW 206.

title: Aquatic Sports and Games
description: Low organizational games, contests, and more advanced aquatic sports, with special emphasis on application for aquatic program in schools and other organizations. Prerequisite : PGC 202 (PGM 202 or PGW 202) or current lifesaving certificate from nationally recognized certifying organization.

title: Basic Canoeing
description: Includes an introduction to the basic canoeing theory, skills, and safety rules necessary for the efficient and safe handling of a canoe. Prerequisite: PGM 201 or PGW 201 or equivalent or permission of the department head.

title: Folk Dance 2
description: Prerequisite: PGC 112.

title: Intermediate Square Dance
description: Prerequisite: PGC 113.

title: Modern Dance 2
description: Prerequisite: PGC 115 or permission of the department head.

title: Intermediate Bowling
description: Designed to give the student knowledge and experience in bowling on a team, in a league, keeping league records, team standings, and computing and figuring handicaps as well as review of basic fundamentals.

title: Bicycle Touring
description: Designed to develop touring physical fitness and camping skills associated with the touring aspects of bicycling. Prerequisite : PGC 124 or equivalent. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Golf
description: Designed to offer the golfing student an opportunity to learn and practice the finer points of the game.

title: Intermediate Horsemanship
description: Work toward perfecting form in the three gaits : walk, trot, and canter. Harness driving. Stable management.

title: Sport Scuba Driving
description: Provides opportunities for refining techniques and skills necessary for using selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus. Prerequisite: PGC 206.

title: Individualized Exercise and Figure Control
description: An exercise course including individual analysis of fitness problems, development and maintenance of a fitness level. Prerequisite : PGW 106.

title: Conditioning and Exercise
description: An exercise course designed to maintain and/or increase physical fitness and aid in weight control.

title: Jogging
description: Designed to increase cardiovascular fitness through jogging.

title: Adapted Physical Education
description: Assignment will be made after the University Health Center recommends to the Department of Women's Physical Education that the student be placed in adapted physical education. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Gymnastics
description: Instruction in the basic stunts and creative routines on the following pieces of apparatus : trampoline, balance beam, uneven parallel bars, ropes, and rings. Prerequisite: PGW 107.

title: Modern Gymnastics
description: Combines gymnastics, dance, and implement manipulation with basic movement skills aimed at body control and grace in developing individual and group routines. Implements include hoops, wands, Indian clubs, ropes, scarves, and balls.

title: Swimnastics
description: Physical conditioning through water exercise, using high potential fitness activities which can be used in a small pool or in a limited area of a crowded instructional pool. Prerequisite: ability to put face in water, float on front and/or back in shallow water, and ability to regain standing position after floating.

title: Hatha Yoga
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through yoga exercises and yoga relaxation techniques.

title: Beginning/Intermediate Tennis
description: Beginning and intermediate tennis skills, rules, knowledges, and courtesies. Not open to the student who has credit in PGW 127, 227.

title: Beginning Basketball
description: For students desiring information, practice, and experience in basic skills, strategies, and knowledge. Course includes passing, shooting, dribbling, offense, defense.

title: Flag Football
description: Introduction to fundamentals and rules of football through flag football; instruction in techniques, terminology, strategies, and rules.

title: Track and Field
description: A beginning course in track and field which includes skills, rules, and knowledes of conditioning and training associated with individual activities.

title: Judo 2
description: Prerequisite: PGW 208 or permission of the department head.

title: Beginning/Intermediate Badminton
description: Beginning and intermediate badminton skills, rules, knowledges, strategies, and courtesies. Not open to the student who has credit in PGW 124 or PGC 122.

title: Intermediate Power Volleyball
description: Instruction in intermediate techniques, terminology, strategies, rules, and competition. Includes individual and team offensive and defensive techniques, offensive and team game strategies and competition. Prerequisite : PGW 133 or PPW 183.

title: General Safety Education
description: Designed to prepare prospective teachers for the comprehensive general safety education program.

title: Driver and Traffic Safety Education 1
description: Content, methods, materials, organization, and administration of the classroom and laboratory phase of the secondary school program.

title: Practicum in Aquatics
description: Gives the student supervised experience in aquatic programs. The student will work specifically in aquatic programs in existence at Ball State or other established organizations. Prerequisite : PGC 202 and 203. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Officiating Competitive Aquatic Sports
description: Gives students an understanding of desired officiating practices, a comprehension of particular aquatic performance techniques related to decision making by officials, and laboratory experience in officiating. The student is presented the opportunity for certification in various aquatic officiating areas.

title: Dance Theatre
description: Provides the dance student with experience in performing with a company of dancers who plan, rehearse, and perform both informal and formal dance performances. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Folk Dance
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PGC 112.

title: The Teaching of Folk and Square Dance
description: Materials and techniques of teaching folk dance and square dance in the secondary schools. Prerequisite: PPC 262 and 263 or the equivalents.

title: Folk Dance Theatre
description: Provides opportunities and experiences in participating with a company of dancers who plan and perform in both informal and formal folk dance presentations. Prerequisite: PGC 112 and permission of the department head. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Advanced Modern Dance
description: For students already skilled in dance who wish to increase their performing and technical aptitude in dance either for avocational or vocational reasons. Prerequisite : PGC 215 or the equivalent.

title: Dance Composition 1
description: Principal elements of dance composition. Simple compositional forms for small groups and solo work. Prerequisite: PGC 215 or the equivalent.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 1
description: Basic concepts in anatomy and physiology for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2
description: Prerequisite: PPC 292 or permission of the department head.

title: Kinesiology
description: The mechanics of motion as applied to the human body. Development of the ability to analyze activity for the purpose of improving physical skills. Prerequisite : PPC 292.

title: First Aid
description: First aid as outlined by the American Red Cross leading to standard certification. Designed for the student pursuing a major or minor program in the School of Physical Education and Athletics. Not open to the student who has credit in PPW 299 or HSC 250.

title: Simulation in Driver and Traffic Safety Education
description: Designed to meet the needs of prospective teachers in the simulation phase of driver and traffic safety education. Prerequisite : PPC 124.

title: Aquatic Art Production
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of management and staging activities involved in an aquatic art production at the high school and college levels.

title: Red Cross Water Safety Instructor
description: Prerequisite : current Red Cross senior lifesaving certificate.

title: Instructional Techniques and Analysis of Aquatic Performance
description: Selected learning theory, teaching strategies, and physical laws which affect learning and performance in the aquatic medium. Analysis of basic safety skills and stroke and diving techniques, and approaches to planning and evaluating aquatic performance by age and skill levels.

title: Field and/or Laboratory Experience
description: Provides the student with administrative aquatic experience outside the present offerings. These experiences will place the student in a leadership role. Prerequisite : permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Dance for Children
description: Basic rhythms, exploration of movement, and creative dance for the lower level of the elementary school.

title: History of Dance
description: Basic dance forms and functions from the primitive era into the 20th century.

title: Accompaniment for Modern Dance
description: Exploration and the use of accompaniment in dance. Prerequisite : PGC 115 or the equivalent.

title: Dance Production
description: Various technical and performance aspects of dance production. Prerequisite : PGC 115 or the equivalent.

title: Modern Dance 1
description: Fundamental modern dance techniques, elements of rhythmic patterns, materials of space, design, and improvisation.

title: Modern Dance 2
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques. Emphasis on composition. Prerequisite : PPC 365.

title: Modern Dance 3
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques. Emphasis on teaching modern dance in the public schools, camps, etc. Dance composition. Prerequisite : PPC 366.

title: Aquatics for the Elementary School Child
description: Assists the student to acquire an understanding of safety factors, developmental stroke and diving sequences, and teaching strategies for aquatic instruction of the young child. Prerequisite : PPC 353 or equivalent certification.

title: Diagnostic Techniques and Athletic Injury Mechanisms
description: An introduction to predisposing anatomical, kinesiological, growth stress, and other such factors that contribute to athletic injuries. Procedures for accurate recognition and evaluation of not only these factors, but also the extent of an athletic injury are presented. Prerequisite: PPC 396.

title: Administration and Organization of Programs for the Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries
description: Problems, principles, and objectives in the designing, planning, and operation of a program for the prevention and care of athletic injuries. There will also be an examination of the code of ethics of the National Athletic Trainer's Association. Prerequisite : PPC 396.

title: Athletic Training Modalities and Therapeutic Techniques
description: An introduction to mechanical therapies, thermal therapy, cryotherapy, hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, and therapeutic exercise. Only those modalities and their clinical uses that have special implications for the athletic trainer in the treatment of injuries to the athlete will be considered. Prerequisite : PPC 396.

title: Principles of Physical Education
description: General concepts based upon the scientific facts and philosophic judgments which underlie physical education.

title: Teaching of Physical Education in the Elementary School
description: Methods and consideration for teaching physical education in the elementary school that include the factors of purpose, growth and development, motor learning, program planning, and evaluation.

title: The Teaching of Physical Education in the Secondary School
description: Teaching techniques and organization of subject matter based on student needs.

title: Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries
description: Principles; practice of athletic training principles and techniques necessary for care and prevention of athletic injuries. Not open to the student who has credit in PPM 396.

title: Remedial Exercises and Rehabilitation
description: An introduction to the objectives and principles involved in designing and planning conditioning programs for the athlete. Thereapeutic exercises essential in planning the rehabilitation program of the injured athlete are introduced and developed. Prerequisite : PPC 396.

title: Driver and Traffic Safety Education 2
description: Presentation of materials and information designed to prepare for teaching driver education in the secondary schools.

title: Problems in Aquatic Programs Development
description: Programs and problems of the physical educator working in aquatics.

title: Dance for the Secondary Schools
description: Methods and materials for teaching modern dance in the secondary schools. Prerequisite: PGC 215 or the equivalent.

title: Advanced Studio in Contemporary Dance
description: Advanced technique in contemporary dance. Designed for the student who is interested in advancing his skills in contemporary dance technique beyond those developed in the regular college classes. Choreographic forms, performance, and production, using such allied fields as costuming, lighting, and accompaniment. Prerequisite : some previous study of modern dance or ballet. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Swimming for the Handicapped
description: Adaptations of strokes for people with various limitations, swimming as a rehabilitation program, facilities and pool design adaptations. Prerequisite : Current Water Safety Instructor's Certificate.

title: Physical Education for the Mentally Retarded
description: Establishes a physical education curriculum for the mentally retarded child. Includes understanding the child's experience in physical education, teaching methods, and a teaching experience.

title: Recreation
description: Presentation of the various concepts of recreation. Arts and crafts, camping, dramatics, music, and the problems of increased leisure time are discussed. Emphasis is placed upon enabling the physical education student to conduct recreational programs.

title: Skill Analysis, Theory and Practice of Play
description: Scientific principles involved in movement as they apply to specific skills in elementary school physical education. Prerequisites : PPC 292, 293, 294.

title: Physical Education in the Elementary School
description: Fundamental play needs of children; research into the play interests of children; and evaluation of space, equipment, and supervision. Results sought are appreciation of the educational values of play, necessity of adequate provisions for it, ability to select appropriate equipment, and formation of a tentative curriculum of play forms.

title: Physiology of Exercise
description: The effect of exercise on the human organism. Prerequisites : PPC 292, 293, 294, or by permission of the department head.

title: Physical Education for the Handicapped
description: Recognition of various abnormalities and physical handicaps and the limitations of each. Physical education and recreational activities for each type.

title: Clinical Experience in Athletic Training
description: Students are assigned to onthejob experience as student athletic trainers in conjunction with their student teaching assignments in an Indiana high school that is qualified to provide students with both experiences. Prerequisite : PPC 370, 371, 372, 396, and 399.

title: Evaluation in Physical Education
description: Methods of measuring and evaluating physical education results in terms of the directing philosophy. Tests and uses of test results.

title: Laboratory and Field Experience in Athletic Training 1
description: An introduction to the practical application of athletic training methods such as bandaging, adhesive strapping, massage, and other therapeutic techniques used by the athletic trainer in the prevention and care of athletic injuries. Prerequisite : PPC 370, 371, 372, 396, and 399.

title: Laboratory and Field Experience in Athletic Training 2
description: An introduction to the practical application of athletic training methods such as bandaging, adhesive strapping, massage, and other therapeutic techniques used by the athletic trainer in the prevention and care of athletic injuries. Prerequisite: PPC 370, 371, 372, 396, and 399.

title: Gymnastics: Physical Exercise Program
description: Prerequisite: PPW 157 or permission of the department head.

title: Gymnastics Apparatus
description: Instruction in the basic stunts and creative routines on the following pieces of apparatus: trampoline, balance beam, flying rings, and uneven parallel bars. Prerequisite: PPW 157 or permission of the department head.

title: Foundations of Physical Education
description: Scope of physical education, the relationship of physical education to education, and the qualifications and educational experiences needed by physical educators.

title: Principles and Problems of Coaching Sports for Girls and Women
description: Introduces students to the following: the principles and problems of coaching girls' team and individual sports at the junior and senior high school level; the philosophies and principles which underlie the development of such a program. Prerequisite recommended: junior standing.

title: Coaching Observation
description: Guided observation of coaching techniques and practices with analyzation of teaching/coaching philosophies for competitive sports in schools. Prerequisite: PPW 231.

title: Tumbling and Apparatus
description: Prerequisite : PPW 158 or permission of the department head.

title: Intermediate Badminton
description: Prerequisite: PPW 173 or permission of the department head.

title: Intermediate Tennis
description: Prerequisite: PPW 177 or permission of the department head.

title: Strategy and Techniques in Coaching
description: Presentation and discussion of coaching techniques as they relate to women's sports. Strategies of selected sports areas are presented, discussed, and practiced. Prerequisite: four to seven skill courses from directed list.

title: Role of the Official in Women's Sports
description: Understanding and appreciation of: the responsibilities of an official; desirable characteristics of competent officials; relationships among coach, official, and players; local, state, and national organizations involved in officiating.

title: Teaching and Coaching Swimming
description: Teaches the organizational and administrative procedures and policies of a school competitive aquatic program. Special attention to competitive swimming and diving. Prerequisite: PGW 201 or permission of the department head.

title: Fall Sports
description: Organization of soccer, speedball, hockey. Prerequisites: PPW 184 and 185 or permission of the department head.

title: Winter Sports
description: Organization of volleyball, basketball, badminton. Prerequisites: PPW 182 and 183 or permission of the department head.

title: Spring Sports
description: Organization of lacrosse, track and field, softball. Prerequisites: PPW 180 and 285 or permission of the department head.

title: Officiating
description: The development of officiating techniques in basketball, volleyball, and other selected sport areas. Prerequisite: PPW 158, 159, 173, 177, 180, 182, 183, 184, 185, 285.

title: Coaching Internship
description: Assist in coaching competitive sports in schools. Includes internship in coaching and indepth classroom discussions centering on selfawareness and the teaching/coaching process. Prerequisite: PPW 231. (May not be taken during student teaching.)

title: Sports Development
description: Organizational patterns in program development and exploration of current problems in girls' and women's sports. Interdepartmental AFRO-AMERICAN STUDIES The departmental minor in Afro-American studies at Ball State University is designed to assist students in acquiring basic knowledge about various facets of Afro-American community life and to provide a necessary component of specific skills to supplement the students' background of professional training for Afro-American community service. Where necessary, emphasis is placed on "nontraditional" models for analyzing social factors affecting the Afro-American community and evaluation of various strategies for resolving Afro-American community problems. To facilitate these objectives, courses are taken from several departmental offerings rather than from a single discipline. This provides students not only a broader academic perspective but also a more flexible program of study. The student will be guided by the curricula statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. title: Colloquium in Humanities
description: Guided experiences in the arts and humanities. An investigation of the major ideas and themes of specific works of art which are available and an attempt to demonstrate the interrelationships among the arts. Entails informed attendance at concerts, plays, art exhibits, and lectures.

title: Colloquium in Social and Behavioral Sciences
description: Students participate directly in the formulation and investigation of questions about man and society so that they can better understand human affairs now and in the future. The interrogations deal with matters such as violence, dissent and rebellion, university life, the cities, race relations, environmental pollution, people and political processes, and fundamental human traits.

title: Colloquium in Science and Mathematics
description: A study of "New Perspectives in the Sciences" designed to sensitize students to the implications of scientific thought for the student who is not pursuing a special area of science. One twohour lecture and two hours arranged weekly.

title: Colloquium in Business, Technology, and Applied Fields
description: A consideration of the interrelationships between business, technology, and other applied fields, and the major forces affecting the world at the present and in the future. Discussion on ways individuals may or should influence a more effective society in the United States and the world in order to live as individuals with meaning, purpose, and identity.

title: Colloquium in the Arts
description: Guided experiences in the arts and humanities. An investigation of the major ideas and themes of specific works of art which are available and an attempt to demonstrate the interrelationships among the arts. Entails informed attendance at concerts, plays, art exhibits, and lectures. Not open to the student who has credit in GENED 200. title: Reading Development and Special Problems
description: Development of general studies skills through the study of contemporary problems. Open only to students in the directed admission category with approval of the Director of Special Programs. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Symposium in Contemporary Civilization
description: An examination of some of the critical issues which confront contemporary civilization. Open only to freshmen participating in the honors program.

title: Introduction to Sport in American Life
description: A thorough examination of the various historical, sociological, and psychological aspects of sport in our society. Not sportappreciation oriented, but rather, an examination of what occurs to both competitors and spectators as they become involved with a sport activity. Open to all undergraduate students.

title: Women's Studies
description: An analysis of the role of American women in sociology, history, literature, and an attempt to define the woman biologically and psychologically.

title: Related Field Experiences
description: Departments may use this course to grant students university credit on programs under their jurisdiction for field experiences meeting departmental crediting criteria. Students must apply formally to the department chairperson for such credit and supply supporting documentation. The department determines the amount of credit to be granted and notifies the Office of Admissions and the Registrar accordingly. title: Graphic Arts Design and Layout

Diedrich The College of Sciences and Humanities provides courses and programs for either a liberal education or for specialized and professional curricula. The liberal arts programs permit the student to elect more freely and to explore the "idea" subject matter. "Liberal" stems from the Latin liber, to free. By definition, a liberal arts education should free people from ignorance by providing them an intelligent grasp of the experiences of the past and an understanding of the interrelationship of branches of knowledge. The individual is educated to think objectively, critically, and creatively. The liberal arts include the study of foreign languages, the physical and social environment, the evolution of Western civilization, the foundations of modern science, and the classical works. The wide range of courses offered by the College of Sciences and Humanities provides the basis for specialized and professional curricula—offered both within the college and in the other colleges requiring service courses. Within the College, preprofessional programs are specified—for medicine, dentistry, enginnering, and law. A variety of specialist programs is offered, including medical technology and social work. Also, the departments within the College have programs designed for those planning graduate study in the field of their choice. The College includes the following departments : Anthropology, Biology, Chemistry, Economics, English, Foreign Languages (French, German, Greek, Latin, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish), General and Experimental Psychology, Geography and Geology, History, Journalism, Mathematical Sciences, Natural Resources, Philosophy, Physics and Astronomy, Physiology and Health Science, Political Science, Center for Radio and Television, Sociology, and Speech. In addition, the College offers programs in the Social Sciences and in three Institutes—Environmental Studies, International Studies, and Urban and Regional Studies. The graduate offerings of the departments in the College of Sciences and Humanities are described in the Graduate Catalog. Institute for Environmental Studies Nisbet, Director The Institute for Environmental Studies consists of a roster of experts representing a variety of fields whose personnel and resources may be brought to bear in the solution of environmental problems. The roster is maintained and its use supervised by an interdisciplinary advisory committee chaired by the director. Presently included on the advisory committee are representatives from Teachers College, Institute for Urban and Regional Studies, Office of Continuing Education, Landscape Architecture, and the Departments of Biology, Chemistry, Geography and Geology, Natural Resources, Physical Education, Physics, Physiology and Health Science, and Sociology. Among other things, the Institute serves as an organization through which problems or projects related to mankind's natural environment may be directed to those persons, departments, or other campus groups possessing the expertise necessary for their solution. At the present time, the Institute does not offer academic courses or programs. Institute for International Studies Yuhas, Director Life in the contemporary world requires a universal outlook and a sensitivity to other cultures not demanded by any previous age. Today's college student, to be an effective individual, must be aware of the varying and constantly changing cultural conditions of other societies. This premise is the attraction and the challenge of international studies. The international studies program at Ball State University is designed for students who desire an interdisciplinary approach to contemporary world problems. Although some students use the program to prepare for careers in the international field both at home and abroad, many are attracted by the wide range of disciplines and courses represented in the curricula and the resulting opportunity to cross disciplinary boundaries in search of a contemporary liberal education. The international studies instructional programs in Asian studies and Latin-American studies are designed to meet the needs of both potential professionals in international affairs and those who have chosen a related major field of study—perhaps history, foreign languages, geography, political science, or economics—and who wish to include the international dimension as a minor field. At present, two international studies programs are available to students. These are an undergraduate minor in Asian studies and an undergraduate and graduate major and minor in Latin-American studies. These programs are directed by committees of area specialists from a wide variety of disciplines at Ball State University. The student in these programs may expect to enroll in a broad range of courses developed by several academic departments. All students enrolled in international studies programs are expected to gain some competence in foreign languages related to their study area. The departmental major in Latin-American studies on the Liberal Arts Curriculum will also complete the language requirements for the Bachelor of Arts degree. In addition to instructional programs on the Ball State University campus, the international studies program provides students with the opportunity to study overseas. Any student may apply for the foreign study programs offered by Ball State University, other American universities, or foreign universities. Details on foreign courses and credits are available from the Director of the Institute for International Studies. The student may inquire at the office of the Institute for International Studies for special counsel and guidance. Complex social and economic activity in these areas has created a host of largescale problems. Meaningful analysis of these difficult problems requires a spirit of collaboration among experts with different backgrounds. At Ball State, this orientation translates into an interdisciplinary undergraduate program in Urban and Regional Studies. The Urban and Regional Studies program draws on the strengths of various disciplines such as economics, geography, history, political science, and sociology. The scope of inquiry includes the nature of an urban economy, the structure and function of cities, historical perspective on urban development, the organization of local government, city politics, and the dynamics of urban communities. Students receive instruction in the use of various tools for analyzing urban areas and their regions. One goal of the program is to prepare students for entry level or preprofessional positions in planning, urban administration, community development, and social programs. The experiences are designed primarily to educate rather than train students, for regular training in urban affairsrelated professions is normally at the graduate level. A second goal of this program is to provide an educational foundation for those students who desire to pursue graduate training in planning, law, social work, public administration, or other urbanrelated disciplines. Another goal is to encourage student involvement in community affairs and to provide learning experiences outside the classroom. Students participate in projects with public agencies or other urban institutions. They also gain valuable work experiences through internships with plan commissions, community development agencies, local governments, and the like. Urban and Regional Studies is a departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. A departmental minor is also offered as a useful alternative for students having a more casual interest in urban affairs. Department of Anthropology Izmirlian, Chairman; Coffin, Flores-Meiser, Genz, Glenn, Scruton, Swartz, Whitehead Anthropology is scarcely a hundred years old as a formal academic discipline. Its origins are in the nineteenth century's growing awareness of non-European societies, the revelation that man's social past is of great antiquity, and the discovery by Charles Darwin of the biological mechanisms which have produced the human species. From these several awakenings has emerged a field which, as developed in this country, is neither a biological nor a social science, but is uniquely both. It is, in fact, the singular amalgamation of the two areas which is responsible for the name of the field, the Study of Man. Although the anthropologist, as a practicing scholar, develops a limited specialty, the field itself rem ains convinced that the human phenomenon is a sociobiological whole and must finally be studied as such. This belief places a certain burden on the anthropologist and the student by requiring, for professional competence, a very wide range of content areas. In physical anthropology, for example, attention is commonly focused on such topics as the nature of the evolutionary process which is responsible, through the action of natural selection, hybridization, genetic drift and artificial selection, for the development of the largetailless, terrestrial, bipedal, orthograde primate which man is. Course work is commonly devoted to the fossil evidence of recent human evolution, especially during the Pleistocene period. Without doubt, that aspect of physical anthropology which has the greatest potential contribution to make to human selfunderstanding, and the aspect likeliest to be of practical application, is the study of contemporary varieties, or races of humanity. There is no subject about which people seem to have the most fundamental convictions, and commonly there is none in which the unfortunate effects of total ignorance are more clearly seen. The anthropologist is deeply involved in all phases of this study, from the determination of the nature of the phenomenon itself, through the eventual genetic classification of races, to the delicate and vexing questions having to do with the significance of race differences. The pursuit of truth is the goal of the scientist. But the application of knowledge which has been secured through the scientific method is hardly avoidable. Much of cultural anthropology is closely related to history and no branch illustrates this fact more clearly than archaeology. Courses in this area provide the student of the human past with techniques which enable many of the limitations of conventional historiography to be overcome, with the result that we now possess knowledge of human behavior during times antedating writing by sometimes hundreds of thousands of years. Of course, this knowledge is rarely of the detailed and specific sort sought by the historian. But although archaeologists are commonly deprived of historical personalities, they have the compensation of seeing the great sweep of human affairs with perhaps greater Anthropology 183 clarity. The archaeologist reminds the student that it was during prehistoric times that most of the great steps in human progress were made: the development of technology, the creation of for ms of government, kinship, religion, philosophy, and art. The archaeologist also reminds the student through appropriate courses of the long and fruitful cooperation between the historian and the prehistorian, which has been responsible for the bulk of our knowledge of the ancient world of classical times, including Egypt, the Near East, Greece, Crete, and early Rome. Preparation in anthropology customarily involves some work in the field of linguistics. This is a most highly specialized area, and thorough preparation through detailed courses is less common than in the other areas. But introduction to the broad subdivisions of descriptive and historical linguistics helps to acquaint the student with more than a mere modicum of knowledge about the techniques and history of human communication, which is the most distinctive characteristic of the human animal, setting races of humanity apart, as no other single fact does, from infrahumans. It is linguistics which, in recent years, has begun to make students aware that talking is more than simply a method of communicating ideas between speakers of the same language; it is the vehicle of thought itself, and it provides the speaker not only with categories of expression, but also with the means at once of perceiving and of ordering his universe. At this point linguistics is very close to cultural anthropology. Modern cultural anthropology has grown out of the nineteenth century's interest in the accounts by travelers, explorers, missionaries, merchants, and soldiers of the frequently astonishing and sometimes hostile people whom they had met. Much of the work of the cultural anthropologist, or ethnologist, has been the gathering of accurate information about the world's nonliterate peoples. Modern ethnology, it should be noted, places little stress on the word "primitive," having been driven by the data to the conclusion that it does not separate categories of people very efficiently. But from this early interest in different societies has developed anthropology's increasingly sophisticated analysis of culture, that amorphous yet systematic mass of learned behavior patterns which provides human societies with the means to survival. Much comparative work has been done, and courses in anthropology departments reflect this, in crosscultural studies of religion, kinship and family systems, governments, technologies, value and belief systems, literatures, modes of aesthetic expression in song, dance, and the graphic and plastic arts, among other institutions. Anthropology wrestles with countless unsolved problems in the area of relations between personalities and the social milieu in which they occur and in the area of cultural dynamics. The possibilities of practical application are numerous, and are, increasingly, being exploited. These several areas, and others which may develop, are all related through anthropology's constant emphasis on the "wholeness" of man. title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man as a biological unit of the animal kingdom. The human fossil record, living primates, and criteria of race and the races of man, elementary anthropometry, adaptive mechanisms, principles of biological evolution, and human genetics.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: Man's cultural achievements from their beginnings into historic times. Man's cultural development will be traced through the paleolithic hunting, mesolithic fishing, neolithic village farming, and urban living stages.

title: Introduction to Language and Linguistics
description: The nature of human language as an object of scientific study, focusing on both the biological and sociocultural bases of language and its structure. Emphasis on language and thought, linguistic analysis of language structure, social and geographical dialects, and language families of the world.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family, kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Bio-Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological and cultural evolution.

title: Anthropology—Culture and Women
description: The structure of women's role in various types of societies, from hunting and gathering to urban communities. In the light of these societies the western movement to liberate women from their traditional roles may be better understood. As industrialization reaches its peak the rigid sexual division of labor gives way to the female role being modeled after the male's.

title: North American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North America. Each culture is described in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: World Ethnography
description: A systematic survey of the important culture areas of the world, describing and comparing major social institutions: e.g., economics and technology, family and kinship organization, political structure, religion, and art.

title: Afro-American Anthropology
description: Afro-American cultures and their relationships to the larger societies in which they are integrated. Specific problems relevant to wider questions of theory and methodology in anthropology.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to honor students only or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Osteology
description: The human skeleton. Bone identification, osteometry, aging, sexing, and racing a skeleton. Prerequisite : ANTH 100.

title: Race and Racism
description: Investigation in detail of the nature of race as a biological phenomenon, which will acquaint the student with the history of racism in the Western world. Stress on the necessity of employing the scientific method in studying race beliefs.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequistie: ANTH 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man as a unit in the animal kingdom. The principles of biological evolution and the human fossil record. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or 204, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 120

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs.

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Summer Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation : sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Field observation and interpretation are stressed. Requires full time in the field.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Utilization of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite : ANTH 421.

title: Advanced Archeological Field Methods
description: Advanced methods of excavation and field recording studied at the excavation site. Prerequisite: ANTH 421. Anthropology 185

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Midwest is traced through the Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite recommended : ANTH 120.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: Traces and describes the archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic to the Historic Period.

title: Peoples and Problems of Modern Africa
description: The course is intended to acquaint the student with the vast, complex, and still comparatively littleknown continent of Africa. More particularly it will enable students to acquire a systematic body of knowledge concerning the increasingly significant role which Africa plays in the modern world.

title: Religion, Culture, and Society
description: An investigation of theories of the possible origins of religious behavior and experience; various types of religious practitioners ; and aspects of institutionalization and function of religion in selected societies.

title: Social Organization
description: Opportunity for depth study of man's social systems. Emphasis on the function of these systems and important grouping principles. The crosscultural method is employed extensively.

title: Anthropological Theory
description: Historical development of concept and theory in anthropology. Various theoretical viewpoints and schools of thought will be examined intensively. Prerequisites : ANTH 100, 160, and 120.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the impact of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents with European civilization.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Peoples of Oceania
description: A general survey of the ethnography of the peoples of Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia. Selected field studies will be examined in terms of the functional method and acculturation theories for which oceanic cultures and societies provide a most suitable and viable laboratory.

title: Field School in Ethnography and Ethnology
description: Methods of carrying out field research in cultural anthropology; techniques of establishing contact and rapport; interview and observation methods; problem formulation, data recording, and data preparation. The student may spend fullor halftime in the field. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Development of Near-Eastern Cultures
description: Traces the development of cultures in the Near East as revealed by archaeology and explores the presentday cultural variability.

title: The Peoples and Culture of India
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the anthropology (social organization, cultural system) of South Asia with special stress on India.

title: Political Anthropology
description: Focuses On that dimension of social interaction which involves the articulation and aggregation of interests within the political community. Emphasis on primitive and peasant communities (smallscale societies) drawing parallels to western society where appropriate.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to a formal) view of economic behavior. Focus on social organizational units such as lineages and clans which in primitive and peasant societies are engaged in productive and distributive activities.

title: Anthropology of the Film
description: Focuses on function and content of the ethnographic film from its inception to the present. Some contemporary documentary films will also be screened. Stress on treating the media of film both in terms of its capacity to create a visual culture in contemporary society and the direct recording of primitive and peasant lifestyles.

title: Applied Anthropology and Community Development
description: Designed for persons who might become involved in planned change situations. Offers the conceptual framework and field experience to apply anthropological concepts and field research techniques to the identification and solution of practical human problems at the local level. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 160 or SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Art and Anthropology
description: Provides a crosscultural coverage of major preliterate art traditions and introduces students to art in cultural contexts.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Acquaints the prospective teacher with basic concepts in cultural anthropology and provides the conceptual and analytical tools to understand whatever cultural setting he or she might be involved in. Examines ways in which cultural institutions, e.g., family, religion, politics, economy, might impinge on educational processes.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Field Anthropology of Distant Areas
description: Anthropological field student of distant geographical regions. Exploration and field work may be involved and travel to the staging area will probably be by airline.

title: Medical Anthropology
description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating nonwestern techniques to its western counterparts. Specific contents of this comparison involves theories of disease causation, cultural taxonomy of therapeutic techniques and cure, and analysis of the role of the medical specialists (practitioners) in selected societies. Finally, the meeting together of western and nonwestern traditional and modern medicine will be assessed in terms of cultural evolutionary theory. Department of Biology Norton, Chairman; Adalis, Allamong, Ball, Bennett, Bernhardt, Crankshaw, Eiser, Engstrom, Hardman, Hendrickson, Kirkpatrick, List, McComish, McElhinney, Mertens, Nash, Nisbet, Olsen, Resh, Smith, Stevenson, Welker, Wise, Zimmack The programs of the Department of Biology are designed to develop appropriate levels of competence in biology for three groups of students : (1) students who wish to prepare for positions in teaching, biological research, or particular fields of biological specialization; (2) students who are interested in obtaining a liberal education; and (3) students who need basic preparation in biology for the parabiological fields of medicine, pharmacy, veterinary medicine, dentistry, medical technology, cytotechnology, and nursing. Common background is provided for majors through a "core program in biology." The required courses of the core are organized with three levels of emphasis. The first level is designed to develop understanding of basic principles and biological processes which are common to living organisms. The second level focuses on organisms and is concerned with problems of structure, function, and classification in specific groups of plants and animals. The third level is concerned with developing understanding of interactions and adaptations of organisms in contexts ranging from world biome organization through molecular organization. In addition to the basic background work provided by courses in the core program, the department offers specialized course work in biology, botany, zoology, and science to meet the needs of particular individuals and groups. Opportunities for research participation are available at both the advanced undergraduate and graduate levels. The student who plans a career in teaching secondary school biology should take the teaching major in biology or the teaching minor in biology. The student enrolled as a biology teaching major is encouraged to take a second major in general science or a minor in chemistry. These combinations not only greatly increase employment possibilities, but contribute significantly to the understanding of biology. Students who plan careers in college biology teaching and/or research may follow either the teaching major in biology or the departmental major in biology. Such students should anticipate the requirements for graduate work in biology in addition to the major in biology. In general these recommendations are : 1. Proficiency in at least one foreign language. French, German, or Russian are almost universally recommended; some institutions also accept Spanish. 2. Chemistry through the organic sequence and preferably a course in biochemistry. 3. A year of college physics. 4. Mathematics through the calculus sequence. The student who wishes to specialize in either botany or zoology may do so by following the departmental minor in botany or the departmental minor in zoology. These minors are designed to provide professional work for the student who has completed basic course work in biology and chemistry. Liberal arts students who elect to include a concentration area in biology in their curriculum will follow either the departmental major in biology or the departmental minor in biology. Nursing majors on Option I take the departmental minor in biological sciences for nurses. To prepare to do laboratory work in bacteriology, pathology, chemistry, and other scientific fields necessary in the diagnosis and treatment of disease, the student will take the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in medical technology. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in premedical preparation. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry at the close of three years of predental preparation but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in predental preparation.
