The following courses are recommended for elective credit on the major : ANAT 320, 430; BIO 311, 361; CHEM 300, 325; and PHYCS 110, 112, 114, 310. During the three years at Ball State University, the student pays the usual University fees and is subject to general regulations of the University. In the senior year students are required to pay no fees to the University. They must provide books and uniforms required by the school of medical technology. The 52 weeks course is an integrated lecture and laboratory clinical experience. Two weeks of vacation are included. The University has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with Ball Memorial Hospital, Muncie, Indiana; St. John's Hickey Memorial Hospital, Anderson, Indiana; St. Joseph's Memorial Hospital, Kokomo, Indiana; St. Francis Hospital, Beech Grove, Indiana; Lutheran Hospital and St. Joseph Hospital, Ft. Wayne, Indiana; Methodist Hospital and St. Vincent's Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana; and St. Elizabeth's Hospital, Lafayette, Indiana. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to our schools exceed the capacities of the schools. Selection of students is made entirely by the schools of medical technologybased upon several factors including scholastic standing, personal interviews, and recommendations. Premedical technology students are therefore encouraged to plan a second or alternate degree choice. To qualify for certification as a medical technologist, the student must submit evidence of successful completion of the clinical year plus an official transcript from the University indicating date of conferral of degree, with a major in medical technology, to the National Registry of Medical Technologist of the American Society of Clinical Pathologists in Chicago, Illinois. The student must then pass the national registry examination. The medical technologist is prepared to do laboratory work in any area of the clinical laboratory including bacteriology, chemistry, serology, and blood bank. There are positions calling for this preparation in hospital laboratories, physician's and surgeon's clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories. Also, there are opportunities for work in research laboratories and in commercial companies making biological products. Departmental major in medical technology, 63-65 hours ANAT 201; BIO 111, 112, 211, 213, 341; CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114), CHEM 225, 230, 231, 360; PHYSL 210; ZOOL 447; and 4 hours of credit in MATH 110, 111, or 112 63-65 hrs. PREMEDICAL PREPARATION The student who wishes to qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine at the close of three years of premedical preparation will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 142 hours of liberal arts credit in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credits earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Medicine (45 hours) to meet senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit in the first three years: SPCH 210; foreign language (12 hours in one language) ; BIO 311, 411; CC 214; and ZOOL 447. Except when required to complete an undergraduate major, courses in human anatomy, human physiology, bacteriology, biochemistry, pharmacology, hygiene, or public health will not be accepted by the School of Medicine as part of the 142 hours of liberal arts credit. The student who prefers to obtain a baccalaureate degree before entering Indiana University School of Medicine will do so by completing all of the work on the Professional Arts Curriculum. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in premedical preparation, it is highly recommended that the premedical student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry, because the number of applicants to a school of medicine far exceeds the capacity of the school. In following this recommendation, the student will be better prepared for graduate work in these areas in the event entrance into medical school is denied. Students contemplating a career in medicine should bear in mind the stiff competition in the field, and if they have not exhibited keen interest and aptitude in high school courses, especially in science, it will be very difficult for them to meet successfully the high standards required for premedical work and admission to medical school. The student who wishes to obtain a degree and prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will follow the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum, will elect a teaching area major or teaching major, and will combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. Thus the student prepares for teaching in the field of the elected teaching concentration. The following courses are recommended for elective credit : SPCH 210 ; foreign language (12 hours in one language) ; BIO 311, 411; CC 214 ; and ZOOL 447. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many medical schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other medical schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet specific requirements of the medical schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of the firstyear medical school credits on the Ball State University major is Indiana University. Students should take the Medical College Admission Test in the Spring Quarter fifteen months ahead of their expected entrance into medical school. Departmental major in premedical preparation, 62 -67 hours BIO 111, 112, 211, 312; CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114), CHEM 225, (230, 231, 232) or (233, 234, 235), 300; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ZOOL 330 62-67 hrs. PREDENTAL PREPARATION The student will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the major in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credit earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Dentistry (45 hours) to meet the senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: AED 200, BIO 213, CHEM 232, CC 214, SPCH 210, and courses in business management. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in predental preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many dental schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other dental schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet the specific requirements of the dental schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of firstyear dental school credits on the Ball State University majors is Indiana University. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in predental preparation, it is highly recommended that the predental student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry because the number of applicants to a school of dentistry far exceeds the capacity of the school. In following this recommendation, the student will be better prepared for graduate work in these areas in the event entrance into dental school is denied. Further, students should be aware that preference is given to applicants with four years of undergraduate work. One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory score on the admission test given by the American Dental Association. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the admission test. The test should be taken one year in advance of the student's expected entrance into dental school, but preferably only after completing the required biology and chemistry. Departmental major in predental preparation, 57 hours ANAT 320; BIO 111, 112, 211, 311; CHEM 110, 111, 112, 230, 231; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ZOOL 330 57 hrs. PREPHARMACY PROGRAM The Prepharmacy Program is for those students who wish to apply for admission to the College of Pharmacy of Butler University or the School of Pharmacy of Purdue University. The courses designated, when completed satisfactorily, will meet the preprofessional curricular requirements of Purdue at the end of the first year or those requirements of Butler at the end of the second year. At both Purdue and Butler the prepharmacy, plus pharmacy, program is a total of five years. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to a college of pharmacy usually exceeds the capacity of the school and that a selection of students is therefore necessary, taking into consideration such factors as scholastic standing, character, and professional aptitude. The student's attention is directed to the admission and residence requirements set forth in the Bulletins of Butler and Purdue. These prepharmacy programs do not lead to graduation from Ball State University. They merely provide a student with an approved sequence of courses for the first one or two years of the complete fiveyear program. Furthermore, physical education is not a part of this program for students who plan to transfer to Purdue, but it is for those who will go to Butler. A student who drops out of the prepharmacy program and elects to follow a degree program of Ball State University will be expected to meet the physical education and general course requirements of the elected University curriculum. A careful arrangement of the program for each year is essential in order that courses may be completed in sequence and in the allotted time. It is particularly important that the general chemistry be completed in the freshman year. Copies of the programs may be obtained from the Chairman of the Biology Department or the member of the Biology Department appointed by the chairman to serve as preprofessional adviser for students on these programs. There are minor differences in requirements between the School of Pharmacy at Purdue and the College of Pharmacy at Butler. Students planning to apply to Purdue's School of Pharmacy should make arrangements early in the Autumn Quarter to take the Pharmacy College Admission Test.

title: Man and the Life Sciences
description: Basic biological ideas and knowledge aimed at an understanding of the life processes held in common by all organisms. The physical basis of life, development, heredity, and evolution, and consideration of current biological problems confronting man. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 102 or 111.

title: Introduction to Biological Sciences
description: Fundamentals of major areas of biology. The nature of the cell and protoplasm, reproduction, development, genetics, and evolution. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Field Biology and Conservation
description: Principles of ecology and conservation and survey of the plant and animal kingdoms. Field and laboratory work dealing with trees, other plants, insects, birds, ecological processes, and conservation practices. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Principles of biology including the physical basis of life, cell structure and function, genetics, reproduction, development, evolution, ecology, and systematics. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 100 or 102.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Continuation of BIO 111. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Animal Biology
description: Major animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Biology
description: Major plant groups with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite : BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative protozoa, bacteria, viruses, fungi, and algae. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation with emphasis on meiosis, the mechanisms of heredity, Mendelian principles, linkage and crossingover, mutation, and the nature of the hereditary material. Some attention to human and applied genetics. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Normal development in plant and animal systems. Synthesis of current knowledge of the factors contributing to the development of a single cell into a differentiated organism in addition to the related phenomena of metamorphosis, regeneration, and growth. Prerequisites : BIO 211; BIO 212 (or permission of the department chairman); and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ecology
description: The relation of organisms to their physicalchemical environment and to each other. Plant and animal societies. Some attention to human and applied ecology. One weekend field trip required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 212, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 325, NR 101, or 325.

title: Bacteriology
description: Bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques in culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisites : BIO 213, and CHEM 130 or 230, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Immuno-Virology
description: General immunology and general virology with emphasis on practical experience in technique in the laboratory. The interrelationship of immunology laboratory techniques and viral growth techniques. Prerequisite: one course in microbiology and one course in organic chemistry.

title: Microtechnique 1
description: Methods and preparation of biological materials for teaching and research, including work in hematology, vital staining, photomicrography, and preparation of smears, squashes, and whole mounts. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and two courses in college chemistry.

title: Microtechnique 2
description: Preparation of sectioned tissues and histochemical treatment of materials, including the preparation of paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Recommended for students in research or in medical or laboratory fields. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213, and 12 quarter hours of college chemistry.

title: The Teaching of Biology in the Secondary School
description: Philosophy and methods in biology teaching. Emphasis on laboratory investigations. Concepts and conceptual schemes in biology. Levels of organization in secondary school biology courses. Evaluation of learning in biology. Supplies, equipment, and facilities. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212, and 213. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Designed to integrate and enhance understanding of basic principles of biology. Recent discoveries in biology and their implications in the biological sciences are stressed. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including the nature of the organization of the cell, cell environment, plasma membrane and transport, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Radiobiology
description: The use of radiation equipment and radioactive isotopes in the biological sciences. Experiments and projects involving living plants and animals. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212, CHEM 130 or 230, and PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Biophysics
description: Physics of motion and locomotion in organisms, concept of wave motion, principles of sound and hearing, atomic structure, electrochemical phenomena in biological systems, electromagnetic spectrum and ramifications in biology and medicine, artificial and natural radioactivity, tracer techniques, atomic fallout, and biological problems of space flight. Prerequisites : BIO 211, 212, CHEM 130 or 230, and PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Evolution
description: The principles of evolution. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite : BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Cytology
description: Structural organization of the basic unit of living organisms in both plants and animals. The cell, cytoplasmic organelles, the nucleus, mitosis, and meiosis. Prerequisites : BIO 211 and 212.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Mankind
description: Current problems in human heredity. Chromosome aberrations and developmental abnormalities. Radiation, drugs, and human chromosomal defects. DNA, genetic coding, and sickle cell anemia. Marriage of relatives and genetic defects. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems associated with genetic engineering.

title: Molecular Biology 1
description: The mechansims which coordinate and control the activities of microorganisms. Emphasis on recent research in bacterial genetics, the nature and origin of DNA and RNA, protein synthesis, enzyme mechanisms and controls, and permease systems. Prerequisite: BIO 411 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Molecular Biology 2
description: The interrelationships of metabolic pathways, with particular emphasis on bacteria. Emphasis on the use of energy, activation processes, and biosynthetic mechanisms. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Museum Techniques
description: Methods of preparing plant and animal specimens for display. Maintenance of museum records. Use of museum materials for educational and research functions. Taxidermy not included. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Limnology
description: The dimensions of the physical, chemical, and biological factors of inland waters. One twohour laboratory per week and two or three fullday field trips will be devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 313 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Water Pollution Biology
description: Water pollution with emphasis on analysis of trophic structure in polluted and nonpolluted ecosystems. Ecological change and eutrophication as affected by pollutants from industrial, municipal, urban, and rural sources. Prerequisite: BIO 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Internship in Medical Technology
description: The fourth year of the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in medical technology consists of a fiftytwo week rotating internship, gaining theory and experience in an affiliated clinical laboratory. Approximately two thousand clock hours are spent in laboratory and classroom lectures, discussions, and demonstrations. Prerequisite : completion of the third year of the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in medical technology. A total of 45 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time. Prerequisite : permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Anatomy
description: Origin and structure of cells, tissues, and organs of higher plants. Prerequisite : BIO 212.

title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
description: The identification of native flowering plants. Emphasis on the distinguishing features of the major plant groups and use of manuals. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Forestry
description: Study and identification of native trees. Problems of general forestry and forest conservation. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Paleobotany
description: Morphology and anatomy of fossil plants. Correlation of extinct and living plants with emphasis on evolutionary trends. Prerequisite : BIO 212 and BOT 330 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Morphology
description: Forms, life cycles, and evolution of the major plant groups. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ornamental Plants
description: Identification and uses of ornamental trees, shrubs, and vines. Selection, special characteristics, adaptability, and maintenance of ornamentals.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the propagation and cultivation of plants in homes, schools, gardens, and greenhouses.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on pathogenic forms. Methods for identification of fungi will be discussed along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequisite: BIO 341 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants as related to plant structures and environmental influences. Prerequisites: BIO 212, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Intermediate Plant Physiology
description: A continuation of BOT 451. A treatment of selected physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BOT 451.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection and identification of plants from fresh water and semiaquatic habitats. The importance of the various encountered plant species in the food webs of various wildlife species. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary School
description: Recent elementary science texts, courses of study, and supplementary books are examined. Development and use of science teaching units. The use of experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and other special methods.

title: The Teaching of Science in the Junior High School
description: Recent curriculum developments in junior high school science. Science curriculum instruction related to the physical, mental, and emotional characteristics of the junior high school student. Prerequisite: 36 hours of credit in courses in the sciences.

title: History and Philosophy of Science
description: The history of natural science. Emphasis is given to the influence of science on general philosophy.

title: Comparative Vertebrate Anatomy
description: Comparative student of the anatomy, development, and relationships of vertebrates. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Invertebrate groups. Phylogeny, comparative morphology, and life histories. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisites: BIO 211, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ornithology
description: Birds. Field identification, classification, behavior, and economic relationships. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisites: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 211.

title: Ichthyology
description: The student of fish with emphasis on identification, classification, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Indiana species will be emphasized but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The behavior of individuals and of populations. The economic relationships of mammals. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth and arthropod parasites of animals. Emphasis on identification, life cycles, and hostparasite relationships. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Protozoology
description: An introduction to aspects of the morphology, physiology, ecology, and development of protozoa. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on the terrestrial vertebrates of the United States. The management and harvest of wildlife. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identification, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasis placed on aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress. Prerequisite: ZOOL 341 or permission of the department chairman. Department of Chemistry Van Atta, Head; Ault, Bock, Doeden, Joyner, Kruger, Lawrence, Ma, McGrew, Meiser, Mosbo, Storhoff, Wagner, Wiseman The Department of Chemistry offers a broad program to meet the diverse needs of students. Minor programs for prospective teachers, health scientists, and others are available, as are courses meeting the needs of students in medical technology, nursing, dietetics, natural resources, physics, predental, preengineering, prepharmacy, premedical, and other programs requiring a background in chemistry. A twoyear curriculum leading to an associate degree in chemical technology is available for those wishing to complete a less intensive program of study in preparation for industrial employment as technicians. Student research is encouraged and fostered at both undergraduate and graduate levels in six fields : analytical, biological, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry, and in chemical education. Graduate major programs are based on undergraduate preparation through Physical Chemistry 3 (CHEM 345) or its equivalant, while graduate minor programs require CHEM 343 or 346 or the equivalent. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114), 225, (230, 231) or (233, 234), 300, 346 or 343,* 396 31-35 hrs. Electives in chemistry above the 100 level 1- 5 hrs. title: Man and Chemistry
description: Nonmathematical treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as : organization of chemistry, language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature of matter, classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these to everyday living. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: General Chemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Description of elements and compounds; their structure, bonding, and stoichiometry with the main emphasis placed on the solution chemistry of electrolytes. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly.

title: Organic and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of both organic chemistry and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures, one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 105 or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 111.

title: General Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, and the nature of matter stressed. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 110, including properties of solutions, colloids, chemical kinetics, chemical equilibrium, and electrochemistry. Prerequisite : MATH 110 and CHEM 110 or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemistry of metals and nonmetals, chemistry of carbon compounds, nuclear structure, and radioactivity. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Prerequisite : CHEM 111 or the equivalent.

title: Chemical Principles 1
description: A comprehensive treatment of the fundamentals of chemistry, with emphasis on periodic relationships and stoichiometry. Recommended for preprofessional and science majors who plan to take more than one year of college chemistry. Three lectures and two threehour periods for laboratory and discussion weekly. Prerequisite : one year of high school chemistry or permission of the department head. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 111 or equivalent.

title: Chemical Principles 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 113, with emphasis on solutions, chemical kinetics, energetics, and equilibria. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Three lectures, two threehour laboratories weekly. Prerequisite : CHEM 111 or 113.

title: Survey of Organic and Biological Chemistry
description: A broad based introductory course suitable for biology and general science majors. Prerequisite: CHEM 111 or equivalent.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements. Includes gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations (neutralization, complexation, precipitation, and redox), ionexchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visibleregion spectrophotometry. Prerequisite : CHEM 112 or 114. 'MATH 172 and PHYCS 114 must be elected prior to CHEM 343.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: The aliphatic hydrocarbons and their derivatives, including nomenclature, chemical and physical properties, and their practical application. Three lectures, one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite : CHEM 112 or 114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 230, including optical activity and the chemistry of carbohydrates and proteins. Prerequisite: CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of aromatic hydrocarbons, heterocyclic compounds, natural products, dyes, medicinals, and plastics, Prerequisite: CHEM 231.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material deals with covalent bonding, molecular structure, and the chemistry of elementary organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods per week. Prerequisite : CHEM 112 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 233. Lecture material covers the chemistry of common functional groups, stereochemistry, and the carbohydrates. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite : CHEM 233 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 231.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 234. Lecture material covers the chemistry of amines and phenols. Selected advanced topics will be discussed. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite : CHEM 234 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 232.

title: Chemical Calculations
description: Provides experience in solving practical chemical problems of widely varied mathematical types, including dimensional and error analysis, graphical presentation, chemical examples of simple calculus procedures, series, and symmetry. Two class discussions per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 170 or the equivalent.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentations, i.e. electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods, to industrial and environmental situations. Two lectures and four hours of arranged laboratory weekly, including a prelaboratory discussion period. Prerequisite: CHEM 225. Applicable only to chemical or medical technology programs, or to the departmental minor for life science students.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: The thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three lectures and one fourhour laboratory weekly, including a onehour discussion period. Prerequisite: CHEM 225, MATH 172, and one year of college physics.

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 343. Prerequisite : CHEM 343.

title: Physical Chemistry 3
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 344. Prerequisite : CHEM 344.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions, and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics. Does not require prior experience with calculus. Mathematical skills equivalent to those required in CHEM 300 are recommended. Especially for chemistry minors and premedical, biology, and general science majors. Three lectures and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 340.

title: Biological Chemistry
description: Chemistry of biological compounds, their metabolism and the regulation of metabolic processes. Designed for students majoring in biology, dietetics, or medical technology. Three lectures and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or the equivalent. Not open to the student with a departmental major in chemistry.

title: Scientific Glass Working
description: Laboratory work in the fundamental techniques of glass working. Prerequisite : CHEM 230 or 233 and junior standing.

title: The Teaching of Chemistry in the Secondary School
description: A study of current chemistry curricula, laboratory safety, multimedia materials development, professional organizations, lesson planning with performance objectives and integrated sciences. Required for all teaching majors and teaching minors in chemistry. One lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: 20 hours of credit in chemistry. Prerequisite or parallel: SCI 395 or an equivalent course in another subject matter field.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for the chemical technology trainee. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of the department head. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry. Chemistry 197

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Preparation and evaluation of scientific manuscripts and their oral presentation. One twohour discussion session weekly. Prerequisite: 30 quarter hours of chemistry or permission of the department head.

title: Chemical Instrumentation
description: Theoretical principles and application of selected chromatographic, spectroscopic, and electroanalytical methods, will illustrative experiments. Two lectures and four hours of arranged laboratory weekly, including a prelaboratory discussion period. Prerequisite or parallel: CHEM 345 or permission of the department head.

title: Analytical Chemistry
description: Analytical sampling, separations, statistical treatment of experimental data; selection of experimental methods; multicomponent analysis of complex materials, i.e., rocks, minerals, alloys, industrial mixtures; organic quantitative analysis. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 420.

title: Qualitative Organic Analysis
description: Theory and practice in separating and identifying organic compounds. Four twohour laboratories weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232.

title: Physical-Organic Chemistry
description: An advanced course devoted to the theoretical aspects of structure, resonance, stereochemistry, acidity, basicity, and reaction rates in organic chemistry. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 232.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: The structure of matter and its relationship to properties, including considerations of modern atomic structure, bonding crystal structure, radioactivity, periodicity, oxidationreduction, and acid base relationships. Prerequisite: CHEM 345 or permission of the department head.

title: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 450. Application of basic principles to study of specific inorganic materials. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 450.

title: Inorganic Preparations
description: The preparation and study of inorganic compounds. Stress is on the preparation, purification, and identification of these compounds. Sufficient instrumental studies of compounds will be included to acquaint the student with methods of identification used in inorganic chemistry. Four threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 343 or the equivalent.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 1
description: Chemistry of and techniques for isolation, purification, and identification of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. Three lectures and four hours of laboratory weekly. Especially for chemistry majors and premedical students. Prerequisite: one year of organic chemistry.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 2
description: Biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolic patterns of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids; metabolic interrelationships. Three lectures and one discussion period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 463.

title: Independent Study and Research
description: Scientific investigation on an individual basis under the supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, experimental work, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. No more than 4 hours may be counted as upperdivision electives on any departmental major.

title: The Teaching of Physical Science in the Secondary School
description: Study of classroom management; testing and evaluation; questioning techniques; instructional models; performance and educational objectives; multimedia materials in instructional schemes; science education trends. Required for physics and chemistry teaching majors; recommended for general science teaching majors. Three hours of class discussion weekly. Prerequisite: 20 hours of credit in either chemistry, earth science, or physics; or by permission of the department head. Department of Economics Girgis, Chairman ; Caron, Cheng, Deitsch, Geraci, Hannaford, Jost, Keil, Lawson, Lewis, Lephardt, Lynch, Seeborg, Zeyege Economics is the scientific study of economic institutions and systems. It is a study of human wants and of efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relativerelative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. It is a useful study in an intellectual sense because it trains students to think carefully and logically about complex social phenomena. By such knowledge it is possible to understand the impact on economic systems and institutions of broad social and economic developments or of new economic policies and the responses of these units to them. Given the complicated economic and social problems of the modern world, an understanding of this subject is important for intelligent citizenship and for practical application in industry, government, research, and the professions. To achieve a basic comprehension of how our economy operates, the department offers a core of courses aimed at providing (1) a sound grasp of the tools of analysis and measurement, (2) an understanding of institutional development and the interrelations of economic and social factors, and (3) an ability to apply systematic analysis and understanding to problems of public policy. College of Business students can select the economics major option B (see curricula below). The option B major is designed for those choosing a professional career in business and requires 90 hours of course work, part of which satisfies the core requirements of the College of Business. The option A major is designed for the liberal arts student and is comprised of 48 hours, part of which may be taken in other departments. In addition, the department offers a departmental minor which students may elect as well as an interdepartmental mathematical economics major. title: The Economics of the Ghetto
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite : sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. The theory of wages, rent, interest, and profits. The principles of international trade and comparative economic organization.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite : ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite : ECON 201. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite : ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economic Development of China
description: Systematic analysis of the economic system and economic growth in China since 1949. Emphasis on three major aspects of the Chinese economy : the transformation of the economic institution, the strategies of the economic development, and the innovations and developmental experience of the Chinese model.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites : ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite : ECON 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, nogotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 432.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Development in Latin America
description: The evaluation of theories of economic development. Sources and consequences of the economic growth and development process in Latin America analyzed in the context of economic theory. Attention to Common Market possibilities, monetaryfiscal factors, and trade and exchange. Examination of current national and international programs as promoters of development.

title: Economic Development of China, Japan, and India
description: Comparative analysis of the economic systems and strategies of development in three major economies in Asia—China, a centralplanning economy; Japan, a freemarket economy; and India, a mixed economy.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite : ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite : 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter. In each of these areas the Department of English has definite responsibilities not only to its own majors and minors but also to all other Ball State University students. Literature provides a perspective gained only through intimacy with the thoughts and feelings of writers of all times and all cultures. To help students gain this perspective, the Department of English offers a wide variety of courses in American, British, and world literature. There are at least two good reasons for becoming better acquainted with how one's own language works. One is that a knowledge of the various patterns of language should contribute to a facility in writing and speaking. Equally important, however, is the fact that the history and structure of our language are important parts of our cultural heritage. Realizing the increasing necessity for successful college graduates to express themselves clearly in writing, the Department of English requires all students to develop skill in expository writing. This is a primary purpose of both the general education classes and the classes in advanced composition. For students interested in creative writing, special courses are provided on both the undergraduate and graduate levels. These students are also encouraged to contribute to the Department's literary magazine, Grub Street, and to compete for annual awards made possible through the Royalty Memorial Fund and Lambda Iota Tau, the English honorary fraternity. title: English as a Foreign Language
description: Stress on sounds, structure, and vocabulary of English in order to increase the student's facility in use of the language. In addition to class instruction, students will receive individual help in a language laboratory. Cannot be counted toward general education requirements in English. Nonnative speakers of English who wish to pursue either undergraduate or graduate studies are required to demonstrate proficiency in English by examination. Those with deficiencies will enroll in English 100 until proficiency is demonstrated. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 103 or 104.

title: Literature and Composition for Foreign Students
description: Written and oral composition through reading, discussion, and interpretation of selected pieces of literature. Continued attention to the problems of syntax, pronunciation, and vocabulary which are difficult for foreign students. (This course is the equivalent of ENG 103 for foreign students.) Prerequisite: ENG 100 or satisfactory score on proficiency test in English as a foreign language.

title: Fundamentals of English Composition
description: Special attention to the problems of grammar and mechanics. Required of all students with a score of 360 or lower on the SAT verbal examination and who ranked in the lower half of their high school class as prerequisite for ENG 103. Does not substitute for ENG 103 or 104.

title: Literature and Composition
description: English composition stressing the sentence, the paragraph, and the organization of the various types of expression through reading, discussion, and interpretation of selected pieces of literature.

title: Literature and Composition
description: Guided exploration in the various forms of literature. Also, oral and written interpretation and analysis by individuals and groups. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Humanities 1: Western Thought from Homer to Dante
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and general thought of the Greek, Roman, and Christian civilizations through the Middle Ages.

title: Humanities 2 : Western Thought from Montaigne to Rousseau
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and science during the Renaissance and through the eighteenth century.

title: Humanities 3: Western Thought from Dostoyevsky to Sartre
description: Some major writing in literature, philosophy, and science from 1800 until the present.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of world literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 206.

title: Survey of World Literature
description: A survey of the literature of western civilization, exclusive of English and American literature for students who are majors or minors in English. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 205.

title: American Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: British Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of British literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar
description: Basic course in traditional English grammar and usage. Not to be counted as part of the total hours in a major or minor program.

title: Advanced Composition
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for the general student, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation. Open only to English majors and minors, except by permission of the department chairman. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent, and sophomore standing.

title: Report Writing
description: Discussion of principles of organization, structures, and style in writing reports and papers. Intensive practice in writing different types of reports and papers. Designed primarily for students pursuing the General Arts or the Professional Arts curriculum.

title: American Literature, 1607-1860
description: A survey of American literature from the beginning through the middle nineteenth century. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature of the Middle Ages and Renaissance
description: Emphasizes major works of a number of the literary figures of the period in their historical and philosophical contexts. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature of the Seventeeth and Eighteenth Centuries
description: An extensive study of English literature of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, or from 1600 to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds of the periods. A close reading of the works of major writers is emphasized, but not to the exclusion of the works of minor writers. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: British literature of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries emphasizing major works of a number of the literary figures in their historical and philosophical contexts. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Selected Topics in Language and Linguistics
description: Selected works in relation to certain themes, issues, and problems. Emphasis on class discussion, student participation, and the use of appropriate media. Topics will vary from section to section, quarter to quarter. Designed especially for nonmajors and nonminors in English. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials in teaching language attitudes, habits, and skills. Consideration of written and oral expression, language usage, spelling, writing, and literature.

title: The English Language
description: The study of modern English with Emphasis upon the application of the methods of descriptive linguistics to an understanding of modern vocabulary, usage, grammar, and phonology. Prerequisite : A satisfactory grade on the English Qualifying Test. Prerequisite waived for students with areas in elementary education or journalism.

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of the field of children's literature and an intensive study of types at various levels. The classics are emphasized.

title: American Literature, 1860-1960
description: A survey of selected writers and the various literary movements in America during the last hundred years. Prerequisite: ENG 240. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: The themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Literature of Black America
description: An investigation of the literature written by black authors in the United States. Those authors to be studied will be determined by the instructor on the basis of literary merit.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to 1642
description: English drama from medieval times to the closing of the theatres in 1642, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Drama of the Restoration and Eighteenth Century
description: English drama from 1660 to 1780, including plays of Dryden, Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve, Steele, Goldsmith, and Sheridan.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenth century novels including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the Brontes, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Drama of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: A wide range of British drama, from Shelley's The Cenci, to Tennyson's Becket, to the plays of the Angry Young Men, with special attention given to the works of Shaw, Synge, Barrie, and O'Casey.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or 206.

title: Teaching the English Bible as Literature
description: Teaching resources and selections from the English Bible designed especially for students preparing to teach the Bible as literature in English classes in junior high, middle school, or senior high school. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Special Topics in World Literature
description: Special research topics in world literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Special Topics in English Education
description: Emphasis on current issues and problems at the elementary, middle, junior high, or senior high school level. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or equivalent.

title: Special Topics in American Literature
description: Special research topics in American literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or equivalent.

title: Special Topics in British Literature
description: Special research topics in British literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Independent Study in English
description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in English. Prerequisite : 36 hours of credit in English on the 200-level or above at Ball State University and permission of the department chairman.

title: Creative Writing Workshop
description: The fundamentals of the short story, such as the use of language, image, and structure. Emphasis on the student's ability to write clearly and dramatically. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Fiction Writing Workshop
description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop
description: Practice, analysis, and criticism of the craft of poetry, with attention to prosody, traditional form, significant idea, the life of the poetic imagination, and the state of the art. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104.

title: The Teaching of English in the Secondary School
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in the teaching of composition, language, and literature in the secondary school.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in the secondary school. Emphasis on the actual reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical aspects.

title: Short Story
description: The short story as a type of world literature. Not open to students with areas in English.

title: The Essay
description: Representative essays by English and American authors. Not open to students with areas in English.

title: American Folklore
description: Materials and techniques for presenting the American heritage of folklore and folk literature at the public school level. Books, films, filmstrips, recordings, and pictorial collections are among the materials studied.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 1: Theory
description: The psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in second language teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel : ENG 420 or 321.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 2: Materials and Practice
description: An application of theories of language learning to preparation of materials in English as a second language and their use in the classroom. Students will work with students of English as a foreign language in a tutorial or laboratory situation. Prerequisite: ENG 436.

title: Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of transcendentalism. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or 206.

title: Poe, Hawthorne, Melville
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a student of the philosophical and literary implications of romanticism. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twain, James, Adams, Crane
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of the varieties of realism. Prerequisite: ENG 340.

title: American Literature, 1945 to Present
description: A survey of the works of major writers and literary trends in America since World War II. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Renaissance and Seventeenth-Century Studies
description: The nondramatic literature of the Tudor, Stuart, and Puritan periods (1485-1660), exclusive of Shakespeare and Milton. Major writers such as Spenser, Donne, and Jonson will be considered in terms of their influence and of their political and philosophical backgrounds.

title: Chaucer
description: A study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several of the minor poems. Emphasis upon the structure, the sources, and the significance of the works included. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare (to 1600)
description: The earlier plays and poems, providing insights into the development of Shakespeare. Some plays such as Hamlet will be studied closely.

title: Shakespeare (from 1600)
description: The later plays, with close study of Othello, Macbeth, and King Lear.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Restoration and Augustan Periods
description: An extensive study of the nondramatic works of Dryden, Swift, and Pope, with possible supplementary readings from other British authors of the period 1660-1745. Attention will be given to philosophical, aesthetic, and political currents in the works studied and to the distinctive character of Neo-Classicism. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Milton
description: A study of Milton's family background, political service, and poetic apprenticeship, culminating in close analytical investigation of Paradise Lost and Samson Agonistes. Attention is given also to Milton's aesthetic propositions and to his social and political prose works.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Age of Johnson
description: An intensive survey of the nondramatic works of Samuel Johnson and other British authors of the later eighteenth century, 1744-1800. Prerequisites : ENG 205 or 206.

title: Romantic Studies
description: The poetry and prose of Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Keats, and Shelley.

title: Victorian Studies
description: An intensive study of the works of Carlyle, Tennyson, Browning, Ruskin, and Arnold.

title: Twentieth-Century British Studies
description: A study in depth of several significant twentiethcentury authors (such as Shaw, Conrad, Lawrence, Joyce, Woolf, Waugh, Durrell, Beckett, and Auden) and the intellectual and literary movements closely associated with them .

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britian from World War Ito the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. Department of Foreign Languages Kasparek, Chairman; Brown, Coen, Gardiol, Gilman, Goertz, Hicks, Jenkins, Rosell, Sears, Sotiropoulos, Warner With a program of graduate assistantships in both ancient and modern languages, with language laboratories geared to course instruction as well as to selfhelp, with exchange programs with schools of other countries, with Academic Summer in Europe Programs offering travel and study in France, Germany, and Spain, with native speakers assisting in instruction and cultural enrichment, with the use of achievement tests for awarding credit and for placement in classes as well as for evaluation of intermediate students and graduate students, the Department of Foreign Languages is equipped to offer a varied program for all prospective students : —for those desiring a broad liberal education in ancient and modern languages (both a major and a minor are available, as well as elective offerings); —for preprofessional students (law and medicine) and for such areas as library science that have specific prerequisites to fulfill: —for those master's degree candidates needing foreign language competency, a program of instruction to meet their requirements; —for doctoral candidates, a program of instruction for the qualifying language proficiency examinations (Ph.D. language examinations); —for elementary and secondary teachers, courses leading to permanent certification in Indiana; undergraduate and graduate programs through the master's degree; —for those students looking forward to study at university graduate schools with the aim of becoming college and university professors. The student who begins the study of a foreign language at Ball State University will start with the initial course in the 100-level sequence. Students with secondary school credit in foreign language or other previous noncollege credit will be placed in appropriate courses through an examination administered by the Department of Foreign Languages. Students should regularly consult with foreign language departmental advisers regarding sequence of courses in accordance with individual need. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. For a statement regarding the foreign language requirements for the Bachelor of Arts degree, see Baccalaureate Degrees. The lower division courses in foreign language are highly sequential and should be taken in order except in special cases. Credit toward graduation will be given for any beginning foreign language course successfully completed.
