title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Introduces the student to the cardinal features of the Greek and Roman civilization.

title: Word Origins and Vocabulary Development
description: Latin borrowings, Latin prefixes, roots, and suffixes in English. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin is required. Open to all students.

title: Greek and Latin in Scientific Terminology
description: Considers the composition of technical words used by the physical, biological, medical, and technical sciences.

title: Roman Private and Public Life
description: All phases of Roman customs referred to in Latin commonly read in secondary school are carefully examined and understood. No reading knowledge of Latin required. Open to all students.

title: Introduction to Mythology
description: Primarily a general education course, dealing with myths of the Greeks and Romans and their use in literature and art. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin required.

title: The Old Testament as Literature
description: Considers the Old Testament as typical of, related to, and sources of some of the major literary genres, such as: history and biography, prophetic literature, lyric poetry, dramatic literature, and short stories and tales.

title: The Classical World in Film, Fiction, and Fact
description: A broad survey of life in the classical Mediterranean world through the media of motion pictures, fiction, nonfiction (such as historical, archaeological, and anthropological studies).

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selected masterpieces of classical literature; historical development of the various types of literature as a background for further study in Latin and English. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin required. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: Introduces the student to the cultural achievements of the ancient Greeks and their contribution to the modern world.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: Provides the student with a fundamental knowledge of the social, cultural, and economic framework within which the ancient Romans lived.

title: German Literature in English Translation
description: Primarily a general education course. The aim of the course is to expose the non-German reader to great German writers and thinkers. The course may not be applied toward areas in German.

title: Hispanic Literature in Translation
description: Primarily a general education course, exposing the non-Spanish reader to the great writers of the Hispanic world. The course may not be applied toward areas in Spanish.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: A literary study of representative mythologies selected from Egyptian, Sumerian, Teutonic, Slavonic, and other mythologies of the world. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures through Motion Pictures
description: Presentations of the literary matter of many nations through the medium of films. Ten films will be shown. Selected ones will be compared to the works of literature. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Linguistics and the Language Teacher
description: The application of general linguistic theory to the teaching and learning of foreign and second languages. Gives the language student some basic insights into how linguistics can help in the mastery of languages.

title: Introduction to Historical Linguistics
description: An introduction to the scientific study of language for students in foreign language. An elementary survey of the methods used in historical and comparative linguistic analysis with application to language usually taught in college. Gives the language student some basic insights into the linguistic principles that underlie change in language.

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the honors program or permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Romance Linguistics
description: Deals with a short history of Vulgar Latin and with the phonological, morphological, and syntactical evolution of the Romance Languages. Basic knowledge of a Romance language is desirable.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite : permission of the department chairman. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Language House Living and Learning
description: Offers students the option of earning a limited amount of credit for the language learning experience provided by the foreign language houses. A total of 3 hours of credit per language may be earned in any one house, but no more than 1 credit may be earned at one time. Offered on creditnocredit basis only.

title: The Teaching of Foreign Language in the Secondary School
description: Methods current in foreign language teaching in the junior and senior high schools. Directed observation of classes, specific problems of presentation, choice of texts, and organization of teaching materials and supplementary aids are worked out in detail. Attention is given to the Report of the Foreign Language Study and to the courses of study recommended by the State Department of Education. Prerequisites : two years of college credit in French, German, Latin, or Spanish, or the equivalent.

title: The Teaching of Foreign Language in the Elementary School
description: Development of foreign language instruction in the elementary school. Curricula, training of teachers, and teaching methods; also phonemics, pronunciation, and a review of other basic language elements.

title: Problems in Teaching Foreign Languages
description: Comparative study of specific strategies and approaches used in the foreign language classroom. An indepth investigation of problems often encountered, and the alternatives and resources available to meet them. Prerequisite : FL 495 or equivalent.

title: Beginning French
description: The first course in the French language.

title: Beginning French
description: Prerequisite : FR 101.

title: Beginning French (continued)
description: Prerequisite : FR 102 or one year of secondary school French.

title: The Language and People of France
description: A beginning course designed for students who are interested in the French language and the French culture but do not plan to take a teaching major or minor. Not open to the student who has credit in French except by permission of the department chairman.

title: The Language and People of France
description: A beginning course designed for students who are interested in the French language and the French culture but do not plan to take a teaching major or minor. Prerequisite: FR 104. Not open to the student who has credit in French except by permission of the department chairman.

title: The Language and People of France
description: A beginning course designed for students who are interested in the French language and the French culture but do not plan to take a teaching major or minor. Prerequisite : FR 105. Not open to the student who has credit in French except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Intermediate French
description: Prerequsite : one year of college French or two years of secondary school French.

title: Intermediate French (continued)
description: Prerequisites : 16 hours of college French or two and onehalf years of secondary school French.

title: Intermediate French (continued)
description: Prerequisites : 20 hours of college French or two and onehalf years of secondary school French.

title: Conversation
description: Drill on pronunciation and speech patterns, dictation, and recording. The object of the course is to train in ability to speak French. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or FR 504.

title: Composition
description: Grammar and composition. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or FR 505.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the French language and the application of phonetics to the understanding and speaking of French. Use of the phonetic alphabet. Prerequisites : two years of college French or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture : Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite : two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 309 prior to September, 1973.

title: Short Story
description: A study of the short story in French literature. Prerequisites : two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Classical Drama
description: The plays of Corneille, Racine, and Moliere. Prerequisites : two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Poetry
description: A study of French poetry with emphasis on the Symbolists and on contemporary poets. Prerequisites : two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Novel
description: Extensive reading in French novel. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Drama
description: Extensive reading in French drama. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Reading
description: Contemporary prose and poetry. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. Travel may be by air. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students with areas in French or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the Classical Age to 1760. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 2
description: The classical age from 1760 and the eighteenth century. Literature of the golden age of classicism and the eighteenthcentury philosophies. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 3
description: The nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The development of romanticism, realism, naturalism, and symbolism in French literature; literature of contemporary France. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Reading Course
description: Prerequisites: three years of college French or the equivalent, or permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning German
description: The first course in the German language.

title: Beginning German
description: Prerequisite: GER 101.

title: Beginning German (continued)
description: Prerequisite: GER 102 or one year of secondary school German.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Introduction to the basic German grammar needed for the reading of German texts required for science majors.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Completion of the basic German grammar needed for the reading of German texts required for science majors and some selected readings of appropriate texts. Prerequisite: GER 104 or permission of the department chairman,

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Reading appropriate German texts to build the student's competence in reading and translating expository materials. Prerequisite: GER 105 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Basic Conversational German for Travelers
description: Beginning spoken German for travelers or those seeking employment in Germany. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The first in a threequarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Not open to the student who has credit in German except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The second in a threequarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Prerequisite: GER 108. Not open to the student who has credit in German other than GER 108 except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The third in a threequarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Prerequisite: GER 108 and 109. Not open to the student who has credit in German other than GER 108 and 109, except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Guten Tag: German Language Television Course
description: Affords the student who is unable to attend a regular language course on campus the opportunity to do independent study. Gives the student a fundamental knowledge of basic conversational German. Not open to the student who has credit in GER 101, 102, and 103 or GER 108, 109, 110.

title: Intermediate German
description: Reading of representative German authors of moderate difficulty. Vocabulary, increased knowledge of German idiom, and practice in writing German are emphasized. Prerequisite: one year of college German or two years of secondary school German.

title: Intermediate German (continued)
description: Prerequisites: 16 hours of college German or two and onehalf years of secondary school German.

title: Intermediate German (continued)
description: Extensive reading of German authors in class. Prerequisites: 20 hours of college German or two and onehalf years of secondary school German.

title: Expository German
description: Review of essential German grammar. Extensive reading of technical German material. Prerequisite: one year of college German or two years of secondary school German.

title: Expository German (continued)
description: Extensive reading of technical German material. Prerequisites: 16 hours of college German or two and onehalf years of secondary school German.

title: Expository German (continued)
description: Extensive reading of technical German material. Prerequisites: 20 hours of college German or two and onehalf years of secondary school German.

title: Conversation
description: To increase fluency in speaking and ease of comprehension through conversation. Prerequisites : two years of college German or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or GER 504.

title: Composition
description: To familiarize students with the fine points of German grammar and to train them to express themselves in the correct idiom. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or GER 505.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the German language and the application of phonetics and phonemics in the understanding and speaking of German. Prerequisites : two years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Civilization and Culture
description: Civilization and cultural development of the Germans from ancient times to the present. Taught in German. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Masterpieces
description: Classical and Romantic periods. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Drama
description: Drama and theories of the drama of Goethe, Schiller, Grillparzer, and Hebbel. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Poetry
description: Introduction to German lyric poetry and survey of historical development of this literary genre. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Modern Prose
description: Growth and significance of modern prose writing in Germany. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Modern Drama
description: Extensive reading in recent German drama. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Modern Masterpieces
description: Realism, naturalism, and recent German literary periods. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Goethe
description: Intensive study of the life and of one or more of the works of Johann Wolfgang Goethe. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: German Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced German language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where German is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. Travel may be by air. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students with areas in German or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: History of German Literature 1
description: From its beginnings to 1750. A survey of German literary trends from the earliest times to the Classical Period, with illustrative readings from selected writers. Prerequisites two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: History of German Literature 2
description: From 1750 to 1850. A survey of the classical and romantic German literature, with illustrative readings from selected writers. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: History of German Literature 3
description: From 1850 to the present. A survey of recent German literature, with illustrative readings from selected writers, such as Moerike, Keller, Storm, Stifter, Thomas Mann, Hermann Hesse, and others. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Romanticism
description: Philosophical and historical background of German romanticism, the development of romantic poetry and prose. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Poetic Realism
description: Emphasis on major works representative of Poetic Realism in German literature, including works of Adalbert Stifter, Annette von Droste-Hulshoff, Gottfried Keller, C. F. Meyer, and Theodor Storm.

title: Reading Course
description: Prerequisites : three years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

Prerequisite : one year of college Latin or two years of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin (continued)
description: Emphasis on rapid reading for comprehension. Selected passages dealing with various aspects of man's life, together with comparisons taken from later periods. Celsus, De Medicina; Horace, Ars Poetica; Vitruvius, De Aqueductis; Pliny's Natural History; Cicero's De Officiis, De Rupublica, Epistulae,,De Finibus, or Pro Archia; Juvenal, Satires; Pliny's letters (concerning the Christians), Terence's and Plautus' plays ; and others. title: Intermediate Latin (continued)

Prerequisites : 20 hours of college Latin or two and onehalf years of secondary school Latin.

Department of General and Experimental Psychology Hill, Chairman; Clark, Deckers, Ganzhorn, Goldstone, Gordon, Hewitt, Humm, James, Martin, McConnell, Meeker, Meunier, Myers, Palacios, Poland, Renke, Wittig Psychology is the science which studies the behavior of humans as they interact with their environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. As a part of the College of Sciences and Humanities, the Department of General and Experimental Psychology is primarily concerned with psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of human behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The Department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all areas—teaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, business—increase their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a teaching minor, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for instructing in psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high General and Experimental .13', chology 219 school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students choosing a teaching minor in psychology should choose a teaching major for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. In addition to a teaching minor, the Department offers a departmental major and minor in the disciplinary area of psychology. These programs provide a basic background for graduate work in any one of the many fields of psychology—clinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psychology, psychometry—and an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other areas such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of General and Experimental Psychology offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline, and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas on various advanced degree programs. Additionally, teachers of psychology may combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in the discipline of psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment, and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. Department of Geography and Geology Lyon, Chairman; Beatty, Carmin, Dillon, Grimes, Justham, Kane, Martinson, Orr, Pal, Peterson, Roepke, Samuelson, Schoen, Showalter, Stanley, Stevenson, Sullivan Geography, geology, and the earth sciences are concerned with the study of the earth and its resources. Geography focuses attention on the spatial relationships apparent in the cultural and physical environments that have developed on the earth. The geography programs reflect these aspects of the discipline, offering general and specialized studies in methodological as well as cultural, physical, and regional fields. Curricular objectives are to educate and train geographers to assume positions in elementary and secondary schools, colleges and universities, business and industry, and governmental agencies, and to contribute to the liberal education of students. Geologists study the earth, with primary attention to its history, materials, processes, and structure. Today geologists are concerned also with the study of the moon, with the study of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, and with the discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits. The departmental major in geology on the Professional Arts Curriculum is designed to prepare geologists for immediate employment in industry and government agencies, and for graduate studies leading to research and teaching positions in industry, government, and universities. The departmental major in geology on the Liberal Arts Curriculum is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who do not wish to enter the profession. Earth science incorporates much of geology and the physical aspects of geography, meteorology, and astronomy. It provides a broad understanding of the physical environment for the student who does not expect to specialize in any one particular area of geology or geography. Earth science graduates are in increasing demand as teachers in secondary schools and colleges and universities throughout the United States. The geography faculty specialize in various aspects within the disciplines of physical and cultural geography, including such methodological specialities as urban and regional geography, transportation geography, land utilization, the structure and function of cities, cartography, meteorology and climatology, research in geography, and teacher education. Geology and earth science specialties include geomorphology, geophysics, mineralogy, petrography, paleontology, geotectonics, and oceanography. The department also provides students with training enabling them to complete undergraduate degree programs at other universities in fields related to geography, geology, and earth science. Such fields include meteorology and climatology, oceanography, geophysics, engineering geology, environmental studies, and photogrammetry. Students preparing to enter such programs at other universities should receive counseling and curriculum planning advice from department faculty members. They should understand, in addition, that a number of the science programs listed above require competence in calculus and physics and/or chemistry. Students should contact their departmental area advisers each quarter before completing their registration with the university curricular advisers. Departmental advisers help the students in developing curricular options, in selection of elective courses, and in other aspects of their major or minor program. The Department of Geography and Geology prepares students for entrance to colleges or universities which offer degrees in meteorologic and oceanographic studies. A student who desires to pursue either of these fields towards an undergraduate degree should seek the advice of the departmental adviser as soon as possible after entering Ball State University. Students wishing to complete an undergraduate degree at Ball State University, but continue meteorology or oceanography at the graduate level elsewhere, should seek this advice no later than the first quarter of the sophomore year. Basic minimum requirements to be included in first two years of undergraduate study at Ball State in preparation for study towards an undergraduate degree in meteorology elsewhere are generally 8 hours of geology, 8 hours of meteorology, 20 hours of mathematics, 12 hours of chemistry, 12 hours of physics, and 12 hours of foreign language. In addition to these 72 hours, the student who wishes to prepare for a graduate degree in meteorology elsewhere should include climatology and statistics. If the student plans to pursue a degree in agricultural meteorology at least 12 hours in biology will need to be included. Approximately 20 to 24 hours of advanced meteorology and climatology, not available at Ball State, is usually required for entrance to graduate work, and will be made up at the graduate level by assignment without credit. Acceptance into graduate work in oceanography will require a bachelor's degree in one of the sciences or mathematics, and generally including 4 hours of introductory oceanography, 23 hours of mathematics, inclusive of analytical geometry and calculus, 12 to 14 hours of general physics, and 15 to 16 hours of general chemistry. Students interested in oceanography should seek the advice of the departmental adviser. The adviser for physical and geological oceanography is located in the Department of Geography and Geology; the adviser for biological oceanography, in the Department of Biology.

title: Earth Science Field Problems
description: A series of meteorological, geological, pedological, and geodetic problems designed for beginning students in geography, earth sciences, and geology, as an introduction to physical processes in the atmosphere and near the surface of the earth and to the procedures by which the processes may be identified from their products. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, or GEOL 101. Not open to the student who has credit in GEGE 383.

title: Seminar in Field Problems Design and Techniques
description: Discussion and identification of field problems in geography, geology, and earth science and the techniques and methods of solving these problems. Students are given the major responsibility of class plan development. Prerequisite : permission of the department chairman.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments in and near the campus and visits to places of pertinent course value within the state. Normal scheduling is Saturday mornings. Prerequisite: major or minor in geography, geology, or earth science, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geography and Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to geographic and geologic problems in a specific area. Assignments include mapping projects, including a final written report and compilation of a map either on land use or general geology. Normal scheduling is first summer term (five weeks) in a selected area of western United States. Prerequisite : GEGE 382 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching of Geography and Earth Science
description: Methods of teaching geography and earth science in secondary schools. Includes a review of appropriate textbooks, materials and equipment used in these disciplines, and problems of organization. Prerequisite : 24 hours of credit in geography or earth science, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Methods
description: Application of quantitative techniques to geographical problems, with emphasis on the use of models in current geographic literature. Special emphasis will be given to the interpretation of recent findings in physical, urban, economic, and regional geography, and the preparation of the student to be able to apply these techniques to research. Prerequisite : an elementary course in statistics, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Fundamentals of Physical Geography and Earth Science
description: Activities of man and his relationship to the physical environment. Selected topics from astronomy, geography, geology, meteorology, and climatology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Elements of Physical Geography
description: The earth and its position in the universe, natural resources of climate, land forms, soils, vegetation, rocks and minerals, and animal life, with attention paid to the use and conservation of these resources.

title: World Economic Geography
description: World patterns of man's principal occupations and analysis of their distributional features. Emphasis on world interdependence on raw materials and finished products.

title: Cultural Geography
description: A spatial analysis of the interactions among selected elements of the physical and cultural environment in relation to man. Special emphasis is placed on variations in these environmental relationships and their geographic significance.

title: Meteorology 1
description: Introduction to meteorology, dealing with the general planetary circulation of the atmosphere, characteristics of the weather, and an examination of weather instruments. Includes a minimum of 4 hours assignment in the university weather station.

title: World Regional Geography
description: Geography of the world by regions, with selected regions given detailed analysis. Basic principles in the meaning of regions and geographic relationships within are given much emphasis.

title: Elements of Regional Geography
description: An introduction to the regional concept and regional method as related to elementary teaching. A geographic survey of the world, with selected topics and regions given detailed analysis. Prerequisite: major in elementary education or permission of the department chairman.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: The reading and interpretation of maps, charts, and diagrams, how they are used as a major tool in geography, and how their use may be applied to other areas of study; also proper care and handling of maps.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: A comprehensive survey of the geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Europe
description: The physical and cultural environment of Europe with emphasis on the economic and political factors involved.

title: Geography of Soils and Vegetation
description: World patterns of soils and vegetation, with emphasis on regional differences and relationships to climate and physiography; their significance in man's use of the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, GEOL 101, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Land Utilization
description: The varied uses of the land, with emphasis on the major categories of rural use, but with attention given to urban and industrial uses. Water use in respect to the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Structure and Functions of Cities
description: A critical examination of the major structural and institutional parts of the city and of how topographic and climatic forces have influenced their development. An understanding of the city as a functionally interdependent structure and as a physical monument to its contemporary culture is fostered.

title: The Urban and Regional Form
description: A survey of the origins of the urban and regional form and its relation to economic, social, and functional factors with special emphasis upon the modern American metropolis and its region. Prerequisite : GEOG 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Agricultural and Rural Geography
description: Agricultural development and the pattern of agriculture, particularly in respect to rural areas of the world. Conflict of rural and agricultural development with urbanization and industrialization.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources include minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Regularly scheduled laboratory and field work. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, NR 101, or 325.

title: Meteorology 2
description: Application of the principles of meteorology to the development and analysis of weather maps and charts and the making of weather forecasts. Includes a minimum of 6 hours assignment in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Climatology
description: Introduction to the analysis and classification of climate, with emphasis on regional distribution. Basic techniques in handling climatic data. Prerequisite: GEOG 130, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. Although the emphasis is upon graphic presentation of spatially disposed quantitative and qualitative data, the techniques and methods are applicable to a wide range of subject areas.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques. Specific projects are selected within the students' field of specialization or area of interest. Emphasis on data collection, compilation, and final drafting of projects suitable for reproduction and publication. Prerequisite : GEOG 340 .

title: Geography of Caribbean America
description: Physical and cultural landscape regions of Mexico, Central America, northern South America, and the islands of the Caribbean.

title: Geography of Australia and Oceania
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of Australia, New Zealand, and the southeast Pacific area.

title: Geography of East Asia
description: A geographic survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of China, Japan, Korea, Mongolia, and coastal Asia.

title: Geography of South Asia
description: A geographic survey and analysis of the physical, economic, and human elements of the Indian subcontinent and adjacent countries to the east and west.

title: Geography of South America
description: Diverse natural and human environment of South America with special focus on te Amazon Basin, arid northeastern and industrial southern Brazil, the Argentine Pampa, and the ancient Indian cultures of Peru and Ecuador.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world as these factors contribute to domestic and foreign relations and problems.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world, and of transportation patterns.

title: Urban Geography
description: The distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention is given to the geographic factors affecting urban development and growth.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration and growth, as well as the causes and consequences of these aspects on cultural landscape.

title: Geography of Regional Development
description: Geographical factors in the identity and development of specific regions of the world, both historical and modern. Special attention given to resource and river valley development. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, 120, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Meteorology
description: Air mass and storm analysis, with attention given to the physical characteristics of the air layers. Detailed forecasting techniques. Prerequisites: GEOG 330, one year of college physics, and mathematics through calculus, or permission of the department chairman. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Applied Climatology
description: The practical relationships of climate to the activities of man, especially in his adjustment to the physical and cultural environment. Included are the relationships pertinent to industrial development, and to local and regional planning, and the microrelationships of climate and architecture. Prerequisite: GEOG 110, 130, 331, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Meteorological Instrumentation
description: A comprehensive study of meteorological instruments used in weather station operation. Students will actively participate in practical weather station operation. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Aerial Photo Interpretation
description: Introduction to the interpretation of aerial photos as applied to studies in geography, geology, and related fields, including the physical and social sciences.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union, and the economic development of the country.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: Topography, soils, climate, industries, commerce, and population of Indiana, with emphasis on physiography and economy.

title: Geography of Northwest Europe
description: Survey of the geography of the countries of northwestern Europe. Analysis of land use, physical landscape, and the economic and political development relationships.

title: Advanced Regional Geography
description: Advanced study of the geography of a selected region or regions of the world, with emphasis on the interrelationships of the physical, cultural, and human phenomena. Individual assignments. Prerequisite: introductory regional geography course or permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Advanced Cultural Geography
description: Influences of geographic environment on the development of man in major cultural regions of the world.

title: Distant Areas Field Studies
description: Study of physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Includes seminars arranged during travel. Prerequisite: major or minor in earth science, geography, or geology, or permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned, with repeated enrollment only by permission of the department chairman.

title: Seminar in Selected Studies in Geography
description: Small group discussion of geographic studies selected by instructional staff. Studies vary according to staff assignment. Prerequisite: an area in geography or earth science or permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings and Special Studies in Geography and Earth Science
description: Assigned special studies in geography and earth science, including readings, research projects, teaching problems, and assignment to an undergraduate class. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time.

title: Research in Geography
description: Basic research and teaching materials of geography. Designed to stimulate competence in understanding the availability and use of these materials.

title: History and Philosophy of Geography
description: The development of geographic knowledge and the status of the profession as expressed in the writings of the past and present by geographers and other individuals in related fields.

title: Man and the Geological Environment
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to mankind's environmental and resource problems. Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: An introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Emphasis on North America. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Environmental Geology
description: An examination of geologic materials and processes affecting the immediate human environment. Geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, geohealth, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Geomorphology
description: Landforms and the geologic processes responsible for their development. Local area field trips.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology 1
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by the invertebrate animal fossils of the earth. Fossils, fossilization, evolution, morphology, and invertebrate life associations of all the phyla from the Protozoa through the Brachiopoda throughout the various periods of earth history. Collection and identification of fossils in the field. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology 2
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by the invertebrate animal fossils of the earth. An extension of GEOL 308 to include all the phyla from the Mollusca through the Protochordata as they have occurred throughout the various periods of earth history. Collection and identification of fossils in the field. Local area field trips. Regularly schelduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 308 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite : GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Regional Geology Field Study
description: Study of the geologic history, stratigraphy, structural geology, geomorphology, and economic geology of a selected region. Students will travel through the area. Normal scheduling is second summer term in a selected area outside Indiana. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geomorphology of North America
description: Emphasis on the occurrence, description, and geological and geomorphological problems of the geomorphic regions of North America. Nearby area field trips. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and MATH 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans, and related problems. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Geophysics
description: Physics of the earth; origin, age, gravity, magnetism, radioactivity, seismology, dynamics and internal structure; relation to processes active on or near the earth's surface. Prerequisites: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geotectonics
description: Worldwide activity of the earth's interior, paleomagnetism, lower crust and upper mantle relations, sea floor spreading (continental drift), and theories of mountain building. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Petrography-Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for constructing and evaluating thermodynamic theories of rock origins. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with the exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks for the purpose of determining their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: The structure, rocks, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Emphasis upon physical processes involved, especially Pleistocene glaciation. Designed for nonmajor students in the earth sciences, particularly teachers.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, MATH 111, NR 211, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time. title: Introduction to Civilization of Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 324.

title: Roots of the Western Tradition
description: A survey of the principal historical and cultural developments of ancient and medieval times to 1300, with emphasis on those institutions and events of western civilization which furnish our own cultural heritage.

title: Birth of the Modern World
description: From 1300 to 1815, including such major topics as the Renaissance, Reformation, rise of modern nations, discovery and exploration, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, nationalism and the industrial revolution.

title: The World in Recent Times
description: Major world events and issues since 1815; industrialization and resulting ideologies; background, causes, and results of the two world wars ; the rise and decline of the colonial empires with emerging nationalism ; the impact of democratic, fascist, and communistic doctrines; nineteenth and twentieth century trends in thought; the effect of science on our age; arts; attempts at international organization and cooperation; and the revolution in expectations in the oneworld today.

title: Twentieth-Century World Leaders
description: Biographical studies of key twentiethcentury western and nonwestern men and women placed in historical perspective. Examines the leaders' characteristics, philosophy, leadership capabilities, and their resultant contributions in the field of politics, religion, military, business, and the arts.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East—the Arab world, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems; imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South Asia
description: South Asia (Afghanistan to Indonesia) since 1800: a brief description of factors influential in past history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, and eventual independence. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 498.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Foundations of the United States, 1492-1829
description: Survey of American history to 1829.

title: Development of the United States, 1829-1900
description: Survey of the history of the United States from the era of Andrew Jackson to 1900.

title: The Recent Past in the United States, 1900 to the Present
description: Political, diplomp_tic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have composed the history of the United States since 1900.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of the negro in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Designed to use documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. A complete departure from the regular lecture and textbook method. The students through their own research learn how the historian defines areas of research, selects sources, both primary and secondary, evaluates materials, and describes the findings. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Latin America, 1825 to Present
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis upon contemporary civilization of Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.

title: American Leaders
description: A biographical approach to American history. An evaluation of some of the leading Americans and their contributions in the fields of politics, business, letters, the arts, pure and applied science, and education.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American/Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Provides students with an historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues in history, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students.

title: Colonial History of the United States, 1492-1754
description: The ideas and institutions developed in British North America which in the course of colonial development formed a basis for American culture. Prerequisite: HIST 201.

title: The United States from Colony to Nation, 1754-1789
description: The political, constitutional, and economic issues that developed in the thirteen British colonies of North America and culminated in revolution, independence, and the founding of a new nation in the latter part of the eighteenth century. Prerequisite : HIST 201.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis upon the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period. Prerequisite: HIST 201.

title: Nationalism versus Sectionalism in the United States 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis upon the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860. Prerequisite: HIST 202.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism : The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: From New Freedom through the New Deal
description: United States history from 1912 to 1940. The impact on the American people of the problems created by continuing industrialization at home and continued involvement in a chaotic world. Prerequisite: HIST 203.

title: Recent United States History: World War II and Afterward
description: The role of the United States in World War II and the reaction of the American People to political, economic, cultural, and social issues confronting the nation since that war. Prerequisite: HIST 203.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the State from the earliest time to the present. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: History of the Ante-Bellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum south. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865. Prerequisites: 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: The Colonial and Trans-Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers and the events which influenced their migration, and on the impact these events and the frontier had upon national development.

title: The History of Canada
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of Canada from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis will be placed on the events leading to the establishment of Canada and on United States-Canadian relations and problems.

title: History of Mexico
description: Mexico from the pre-Columbian era to the present with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Revolution of 1910.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I. Prerequisite: 8 hours of United States history. History 231

title: United States Diplomatic History since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I. Prerequisite : 8 hours of United States history.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1607-1865
description: Survey of history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu. Prerequisites : 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of the history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu. Prerequisites : 8 hours of credit in United States history.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites : ECON 200 and 201 or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 410.

title: Historical Method and Bibliography
description: Techniques of research and documentation.

title: History and Historians
description: Historians whose writings are basic in major fields of history.

title: American Culture—Field Studies
description: A study of American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students will travel through designated areas in North America. Prior to the trip, considerable reading in various fields relative to the nature of the course will be required. At the conclusion, papers will be required.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open only to seniors of special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate investigation. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with special competence within the area involved.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1500-1815
description: Political, social, and economic history of Europe from the Age of Discovery to the Congress of Vienna. Emphasis on political and economic events, the rise of national states, absolutism, religious developments, and the expansion of Europe overseas.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1815 to the Present
description: Political, economic, social, and cultural history of Europe from the Congress of Vienna to the contemporary scene. Emphasis on political and economic events, the liberal and nationalist movements, industrialism, imperialism, World Wars I and II, and the conflict of national interests.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870-1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918-1950
description: Survey of the origins, immediate causes, and the course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and After, 1950 to Present
description: Survey of the factors—ideological, political, economic, and social—underlying recent European history with stress on the East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, imperial decline, and the changing European role in world affairs.

title: Modern Extremist Movements
description: A survey and analysis of extremist movements in Europe since 1815 with particular attention to the growth of antidemocratic thought, workingclass movements, counterrevolution, international fascism, collaboration, and youth movements.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the Republic to approximately 500 A.D. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the Republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special stress on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Moslem worlds.

title: The Age of Renaissance, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Particular attention will be given to such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: European Culture—Field Studies
description: Studies of European culture—its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society—through varied European travel. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program.

title: France since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France—The Classical Age, 1461-1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focus on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715-1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization—and revolutions in general. Stress on the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Rise of Modern Britain, 1485-1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor, Stuart, and early Hanoverian periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain since 1763
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life since the Seven Years' War—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of postwar government and society.

title: Constitutional History of England
description: A tracing of the development of the British constitutional system to the present time: development of the kingship, the common law, parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern British Empire and Commonwealth
description: British imperial and commonwealth history since 1815 with emphasis on the post-Napoleonic empire, the development of dominions, the problem of India, the World Wars, the shrinking empire, the Commonwealth experience, and the current controversies.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East. 486, Tzarist Russia. (4) Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the Revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: Modern East-Central Europe
description: Survey of the peoples of presentday Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and the Baltic States with emphasis on struggles for national independence and freedom. Developments are studied within the context of European trends and changing international conditions.

title: The Modern Middle East
description: A survey of major developments and problems in the Turkish, Persian, and Arab world in the period since 1800—the decay of traditional life, the expansion of European influence, the modernization movements, the conflicts over Palestine, and the recent national and international crises.

title: The Modern Balkans
description: The development of the Balkans from about 1400 to the present with emphasis on the effects of the Ottoman conquest, the diversity of cultural and national patterns, and the recent history of the independent nations.

title: Modern Chinese History, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japanese History, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on factors contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Studies in Non-Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: Selected Topics in History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in the field of history with emphasis on fields, specialties, and materials not covered in established courses. Department of Journalism Ingelhart, Chairman : Atwell, Conn, Heintzelman, Hook, Homey, Popovich, Smith News media have become increasingly important in the lives of the American people. Not only is a mass society interested in the competencies of its journalists, but it must also concern itself with the journalism instruments within that society. Because of this philosophy, journalism courses are of value in the general education of Ball State University students as well as in the professional education of journalism teachers, journalists, and public relations and advertising specialists. The teaching major prepares students to teach courses and develop programs in journalism and in mass media in the schools of the state and the nation and to serve as advisers for all forms of school publications and communications programs. The departmental major prepares students to work professionally in six sequential areas : 1. News Editorial: Graduates go to work in all phases of newsroom operations of the various news media plus receiving an overall grasp of the news media. 2. Magazine: Graduates go to work in the magazine industry and also are prepared to function in the general news and feature fields as well. 3. Photojournalism: Emphasis is placed on preparing photographic journalists who can photograph and report news, feature material, and advertising. 4. Advertising: Provides the student with knowledge of the functions and operations of those departments in publications which assure circulation and/or advertising success, without which the publications could not exist. 5. Public Relations:Based on a sound journalistic foundation, graduates are prepared to go into the widely diversified field of public relations mostly in communication jobs in corporations and other organizations. 6. Radio-Television News: Graduates take work in both the Department of Journalism and the Center for Radio-Television to prepare themselves for work in electronic media newsrooms. description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Journalism in the 20th Century
description: A history of American newspapers, magazines, and press associations in the 20th century with particular emphasis on their influence on the American people, the local and national economics, culture, and politics.

title: Press and Society
description: The press in modern society, with emphasis on the press's role as social agent, recent criticisms of the press, and ethical and legal factors which guide the press today.

title: International Journalism
description: Designed to give an understanding of the journalism and mass media of the western, communist, and underdeveloped nations and continents of the world with emphasis on historical background, economics, politics, and ideology.

title: Editorials
description: Theory of newspaper editorials according to types and campaigns, with attention to opinion articles and opinion polls, staff organization, and editorial page arrangements. Prerequisite: JOURN 111 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Magazine Writing
description: Theory and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles supplemented with a study of magazine article markets.

title: Religious Journalism
description: The writing, producing and publishing of religious articles and journals coupled with practice in writing religious materials.

title: Public Affairs Reporting
description: Structures and functions of govenmental agencies and other public agencies with special attention to problems of obtaining and reporting information in appropriate articles. Prerequisite : JOURN 110.

title: Technical Writing and Editing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Familiarization with engineering and spaceage terminology, with emphasis on clarity and translation of technical terms to lay language.

title: Journalism Production Procedures
description: Acquaints the journalism student with new methods, ideas, and techniques which have been, and are in the process of being, developed in journalism printing and technology.

title: Newspaper Design and Typography
description: Theory of the design functions of journalism utilizing typographical systems with attention to their relations to communicative language. Prerequisite: JOURN 111 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Magazine Editing
description: Magazine editing, design, and production with emphasis on smaller and specialized publications. Entire production of magazines from story conception to printing processes.

title: Advanced Copy Editing
description: Advanced study of newspaper copy editing, including the development of style manuals based on underlying style systems. Prerequisite: JOURN 111, 220, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Journalism Style
description: Utilization of current developments in American grammar, including contributions of linguistics, in terms of strengthening journalism writing through adoption of these techniques. The contributions of general semantics will also be considered.

title: Journalism Law and Ethics
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the press with special attention to recent Supreme Court rulings. Discussion of codes of ethics and other extralegal considerations of the role of the press.

title: Trends and Developments in Magazine Journalism
description: An advanced course in traditional and current trends in the magazine industry. Beginning with a survey of traditionally significant periodicals, the course will trace the roots of modern magazine journalism, with particular emphasis on leading magazine editors, writers, and publishing enterprises.

title: Studies in Magazine Journalism
description: Indepth research and analysis of a selected topic in one of the major areas of magazine journalism : editing, writing, trends, management. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Magazine Management
description: A productoriented analysis of magazine editorial management, advertising, and circulation market research and development in terms of journalistic practices.

title: Editing Photographic and Illustrative Materials
description: Selection, editing, and use of photographic and other illustrative materials for newspapers, magazines, and other publications, and for other communicative purposes. Prerequisite: JOURN 230, 433, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Publication Photography
description: Photojournalism as it applies to school publications, magazines, booklets, yearbooks, and other nonnewspaper media.

title: Advertising Photography
description: Photographic methods, lighting, and photographic special effects as they apply to advertising and associated commercial photography done by media photo departments. Prerequisite: JOURN 230 or 433 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Color Photojournalism
description: An indepth study of photographic lighting procedures and equipment utilized by the media. Prerequisite: JOURN 230.

title: Lighting for Photojournalism
description: An indepth study of photographic lighting procedures and equipment utilized by the media. Prerequisite: JOURN 230.

title: Advanced Advertising for the Print Media
description: Skills required for the management of an advertising department in print media, involving the training and selection of personnel, the ethics of advertising practice, utilization of modern methods and equipment, and the development of creativity in print advertising. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Circulation and Promotion of Publications
description: Analysis of the methods and techniques for developing, maintaining, and increasing circulation of publications. Familiarization with reader participation and public school programs to maintain reader interest. Mechanics of circulation and promotion.

title: Consumerism and the Mass Media
description: Designed to analyze and catalog the relationship between the consumer movement, both amateur and professional, and the mass media, including both editorial and advertising content of mass media.

title: Advertising Copywriting
description: Journalistic skills of writing copy intended to induce favorable consideration of a service or product with the aim of selling it or increasing the consumption thereof, or to persuade persons to support or oppose a cause, morally or financially, through the medium of paid advertising. title: School Publications
