title: School Journalism
description: Actual problems in sponsoring various types of student publications and in conducting journalism classes or units, including finance, textbooks, and helpful materials. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits.

title: Journalistic Media in the Classroom

title: Individual Studies in Journalism
description: Group and individual investigations and experiences in journalistic media and techniques with special attention to social, political, and economic roles of the press in society. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematical Concepts 1
description: A general education course for students who wish to know more about the contributions of mathematics to human culture. The minimal manipulative skills necessary to understand the various concepts and topics will be developed. Such topics as the number system, simple logic, the interrelations between mathematics and history, and some interesting geometries, will be covered. Prerequisites: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry. Not open to the student with collegiate credit in mathematics except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Mathematical Concepts 2
description: Continuation of MATH 100. Topics covered include simple formulas and their applications, the concept of limit, the basic ideas of differential and integral calculus, some concepts and applications of probability, and an introduction to the computer. Prerequisite: MATH 100.

title: College Algebra 1
description: Fundamental operations of algebra through quadratics. Students who have credit for three semesters of secondary school algebra will not receive credit for this course. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra.

title: College Algebra 2
description: A brief introduction to sets and the logic of algebra, a discussion of inequalities, absolute values, functions and relations, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and mathematical induction. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary school algebra, and one year of plane geometry, or their equivalents as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied in this course if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities and equations; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers, and DeMoivre's Theorem. Prerequisite : MATH 111 or its equivalent as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Analytic Geometry
description: Use of Cartesian and polar coordinates in two and three dimensions, conic sections, transcendental curves, curve sketching, parametric equations, lines and surfaces in solid analytic geometry. Prerequisite: The equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level, or MATH 111 and 112.

title: Mathematics for Architects 1
description: Topics in analytic geometry and calculus particularly suited to the needs of the architecture major. Includes concepts of limits, differentiation, and integration. Prerequisite: MATH 112. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 161 or 170.

title: Mathematics for Architects 2
description: Continuation of MATH 123. Emphasis on applications of calculus. Prerequisite: MATH 123. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 162 or 170.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 1
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or a strong background in high school algebra.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics which are particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications in some of the above areas. Prerequisite: MATH 111 and 112 or their equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 170.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATH 161 or 170. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Calculus 1
description: Inequalities, limits, continuity, differentials and derivatives, introduction to the definite integral. Prerequisite: MATH 113.

title: Calculus 2
description: Continuation of the definite integral, differentiation and integration of elementary transcendental functions, derivatives in polar coordinates, integration by special methods, applications of integration. Prerequisite : MATH 170.

title: Calculus 3
description: Continuation of the application of the integral, elements of infinite series (convergent and divergent series), Taylor's series and theorem, partial differentiation, and multiple integration. Prerequisite : MATH 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 270.

title: Calculus 4
description: Infinite series and elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Cardinal Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: successful completion of 25 credit hours of college courses. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 205.

title: Rational Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the concept of unsigned rational numbers for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 201. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 206.

title: Geometry in the Elementary School
description: A development of geometric concepts for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 203. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 207.

title: Elementary School Enrichment Topics
description: An examination of mathematics concepts included as enrichment topics in elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 204. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman.

title: The Structure of the Real Number System
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and number systems. A systematic development of the real number system is emphasized. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 172.

title: Elements of Linear Algebra
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties, determinants, matrix inverses, rank and equivalence of matrices, and a matrix approach to the theory of systems of linear equations. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 171.

title: Topics from Linear Algebra
description: Determinants, matrices, and bilinear maps, polynomials and matrices, triangulation of matrices and linear maps, spectral theorems, multilinear products. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 412.

title: Topics from Modern Algebra
description: Basic topics from polynomial and integral domain theory, group theory, ring theory. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 313 or 411.

title: Applied Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, probability, random variables, important discrete and continuous distributions, statistical inference and testing of hypotheses, sampling theory, statistical analysis of time series, decision theory. Applications to business will be made throughout the course. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, or 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 321.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 172.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, gamma, rectuangular and normal distributions. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Statistics 1
description: Classification of data, empirical distributions, random sampling, distributions of sample mean and same variance from normal distribution, distribution of sample mean from nonnormal distributions, probability distributions for correlation and regression, empirical methods for correlation and regression, general principal of estimation and hypothesis testing. Prerequisite ; MATH 320.

title: Statistics 2
description: Testing of goodness of fit, contingency tables, small sample distributions, chisquare, t and F distributions and their applications in hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, nonparametric methods, sequential analysis, Bayesian method. Prerequisite : MATH 321.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, t, and F distributions. Some problems with moment generating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Prerequisite : MATH 221 or 321 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in synthetic geometry, closely related to the field of Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite : MATH 211.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models to problems from physics, chemistry, biology, and business. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models rather than detailed numerical results. Prerequisite : MATH 212.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nth order ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Enler equations, Laplace transforms, power series solutions, Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, first order partial differential equations, applications in business, biological, chemical, physical, and sociological sciences. Prerequisite: MATH 173. Prerequisite recommended : MATH 212.

title: Arithmetic in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching arithmetic at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Prerequisite:

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Secondary School
description: Materials and methods used in the teaching of junior and senior high school mathematics. Survey of texts, organization of materials, testing procedures, and visual aids materials. Prerequisites : MATH 211 and 340; prerequisite or parallel: EDSEC 360.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. Restricted to honors students. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra
description: The study of rings, integral domains, and fields, with emphasis on the development of integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, and polynomials. Prerequisite: MATH 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Linear Algebra
description: The study of some topics in linear algebra : matrix algebra and linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, inner product spaces, etc. Prerequisites : MATH 212 and 411.

title: Theory of Numbers 1
description: Elementary properties of integers, theory of congruences, quadratic residues, Diophantine equations, introduction to theory of groups, introduction to theory of algebraic numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Theory of Numbers 2
description: Some topics not covered in MATH 416 including elementary partition theory, quadratic residues, continued fractions, Farey fractions and irrational numbers, elementary properties of (x), Waring's problem, and density of sequences of integers. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Topics in Statistics 1
description: Includes such topics as theory of distribution, theory of statistical inference, and theory of regression analysis. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Topics in Statistics 2
description: Deals with topics mentioned in MATH 428 at an advanced level with particular reference to experimental design and analysis of variance, use of computers in statistics and Monte-Carlo methods. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or 428, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs, simple random, stratified, cluster and systematic sampling, ratio estimates, regression estimates, cost function, variarwe function. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school such as Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, Magic Squares, the Calendar Problem, Polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the Fifteen Puzzle, Nim and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers will be considered. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Advanced Analytic Geometry
description: An advanced treatment of analytic Euclidean geometry using topics from analysis and algebra as tools where helpful. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Projective Geometry
description: Properties of geometric configurations which are invariant under projection. Synthetic methods emphasized, and some use is made of analytic methods. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities certain, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, and capitalized cost. Both the discrete and the continuous approach to compound interest and annuities certain will be treated. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172.

title: Mathematics of Life Insurance
description: An introduction to the mathematics of life insurance; mortality tables ; life annuities, premiums, and reserves for basic life insurance policies; modern reserve systems. The discrete approach to contingencies of a single life will be emphasized but the continuous approach will also be introduced. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 451.

title: Topology 1
description: Set theoretic preliminaries, the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well ordering principle, topological spaces, continuity, separation axioms, nets and filters, connectedness, local connectedness, product and quotient topologies, metric spaces, metrization. Prerequisite : MATH 211. Prerequisite recommended : MATH 472.

title: Topology 2
description: Uniform spaces, paracompactness, open coverings, compactness, compactification, local compactness, function spaces, Stone-Weistrass theorem, complete spaces, Banach fixed point theorem, introductory homotopy theory. Introduction to homology theory, Jordan curve theorem, Brouwer fixed point theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 455.

title: History of Mathematics 1
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to 1600. Topics covered include number concepts and numeration, algebra, goemetry, and trigonometry. Prerequisite: MATH 211 and 340.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include: finite differences, interpolation of functions; approximation of functions, derivatives, and integrals; iterative and direct methods for solving linear systems. Prerequisite: MATH 212, CS 220 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics includes : approximate solution of nonlinear equations; numerical solution of ordinary differential equations; error analysis; difference equation; matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 173, and MATH 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 463.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation : graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, mathematical formula. Prerequisite : MATH 462 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Vector Analysis
description: An introduction to the theory and applications of vectors including the algebra, calculus, and geometry of vectors; classical theorems; applications. Prerequisite : MATH 374.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Methods of linear programming and optimization of functions of several variables with and without constraints. Geometric, algebraic, and simplex methods; duality in linear programming. Classical, optimization, search techniques, Fletcher-Powell method, and method of steepest descent. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 466.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Elements of Analysis
description: The real number system is developed through Dedekind cuts, Cauchy sequences, and complete ordered field postulation. Topology of the real line, sequences and series of real numbers, and limits and continuity. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 172.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Advanced calculus including real numbers, metric spaces, topology of R and C , continuity of functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrass theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATH 173 or 470.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics covered include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansion. Prerequisite: MATH 471.

title: Advanced Calculus 3
description: Advanced calculus of several variables. Calculus of differential forms in three dimensions. Examples from physics. Prerequisite: MATH 472.

title: Advanced Differential Equations
description: Existence and uniqueness of solution of first order nonlinear ordinary differential equations, linear systems, autonomous systems in the plane, oscillatory theory, second order partial differential equations with constant coefficients, the Cauchy problem, elements of potential theory, the Dirichlet problem. Prerequisite: MATH 374. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 467.

title: Complex Variables 1
description: Complex number systems, differentiation and integration, functions (analytic, entire, meromorphic) of one complex variable, singularities, complex integration, Cauchy's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, power series, Laurent Series, calculus of residues. Prerequisite: MATH 173. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Complex Variables 2
description: Analytic continuation, Riemann surfaces, theorem of Weirstrass and Mittag-Leffler, solution of two dimensional potential problem, conformal mapping, Schwartz-Christoffel transformations and its application to the solution of electric, magnetic field distributions and of thermal and hydraulic stationary flow problems. Prerequisite: MATH 485.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Arithmetic
description: For teachers in service who do not hold a degree. Prerequisite: teaching experience in the elementary school. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the Mathematical Sciences Department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines. Timesharing computer techniques with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. An understanding of the role of the computer in the modern world. Not open to the student with areas in mathematical or computer sciences, or with credit in ID 200, CS 210, 220, or GBA 220.

title: Commercial Data processing
description: Basic COBOL and RPG programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: ID 200 or GBA 220 or CS 200 or 220.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Computer organization and facilities. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Timesharing techniques are introduced. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or equivalent or permission of the department chairman.

title: Machine Language and Systems Programming 1
description: Introduction to computer architecture, machine language, and assembler language; fixed point and decimal arithmetic; character manipulation; subroutine linkage; looping and branching. Prerequisite: CS 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Machine Language and Systems Programming 2
description: Advanced topics in machine and assembler languages; bit manipulation, floating point arithmetic, macros, conditional assembly, core dumps and debugging, input/output using the operating system, input/output device programming, interrupt programming. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Advanced Programming Techniques
description: Topics such as structures, blocks, dynamic storage allocation, list processing and pointer variables, compile time instructions, organization and manipulation of data files, and interrupt handling are treated using the PL/1 language. Operating system features are included as required by these topics. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Computer Logic Design
description: Basic concepts used in the design and analysis of digital systems and basic principles of digital computer organization. Topics include Boolean algebra, simplification of Boolean functions by map and tabular techniques, design and analysis of combinational circuits, flipflops and synchronous clocked sequential circuits, operational and storage registers, accumulator registers. Prerequisite: CS 330, MATH 212.

title: Computer Logic and Algorithms 2
description: Mechanical formulation of algorithms, Turing machines, normal algorithms, universal machines, algorithmically unsolvable problems. Prerequisite: CS 332 and 433.

title: Computer Programming Languages
description: Emphasis is on important structural characteristics of high level programming languages. Additional languages studied are APL, ALGOL-68, LISP, and SNOBOL to show such features as dynamic array manipulation, language extensibility, list and string processing. Some compiler techniques are also considered. Prerequisite: CS 332.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Problems typical to DP centers such as file maintenance, report writing, sorting and merging are treated using COBOL. Tape oriented and direct access processing techniques. Prerequisite: CS 332. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 210.

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation and the application of simulation languages to system studies. Students will carry out simulations using examples from different fields. Prerequisite: CS 332 and MATH 221 or 321.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include: finite differences, interpolation of functions; approximation of functions, derivatives, and integrals; iterative and direct methods for solving linear systems. Prerequisite : CS 220 or permission of the department chairman; MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include : approximate solution of nonlinear equations; numerical solution of ordinary differential equations; error analysis; difference equation; matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 173, and MATH 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 463.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Methods of linear programming and optimization of functions of several variables with and without constraints. Geometric, algebraic, and simplex methods; duality in linear programming. Classical optimization, search techniques, Fletcher-Powell method, and method of steepest descent. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 466.

title: Readings and Honors
description: Special advanced work not offered in other courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Natural Resources Hibbs, Chairman; Judy, Kelling, Lowe, Mortensen, Van Meter The Department of Natural Resources is oriented toward enhancing the quality of the human experience through environmental awareness, understanding, and improvement. An interdisciplinary approach is used for the natural resources program at Ball State because the conservation of our natural resources and the concomitant improvement of our environment are areas of total university concern, requiring new ideas, diverse skills, and integrated input from many disciplines. Therefore, depending upon the individual interest of the student, programs can be developed to include work in several disciplines which will fulfill the curricular requirements. The environmental crisis has resulted from our rapidly expanding population and technology in combination with our affluent society causing accelerated resource use and abuse. There is an increasing need for both men and women with a knowledge of natural resources and their management. This course of study is designed to provide students with a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of the ecosystem and to educate them to strive toward a state of harmony between people and their environment. Students considering a professional career in natural resources should plan their high school program to include a strong background in both the sciences and the humanities. The desire and ability to work with people is also an important prerequisite. Examples of employment obtained by previous natural resources graduates include: Soil Conservation Service, Indiana state parks, city and county park boards, engineering consulting firms, Division of Reservoirs, Stream Pollution Control Board, Air Pollution Control Board, city and county health departments, Bureau of Land Management, planning commissions, Division of Water Quality Control, and commercial shooting preserves. Students may elect a general major or specialize in such areas as resource geography, fishery resources, communications, water quality, and natural resources interpretation. Although a wildlife curricula is not currently available, the University offers all of the courses required to meet the minimum recommendations of the Wildlife Society. The core requirements which all students complete includes Introduction to Natural Resources, Man and the Geologic Environment, Water Resources, Soil Resources, Mineral Resources, Air Resources, Ecology, and Integrated Resources Management. Other courses which may be elected will be determined by the option selected, the student's background, and professional employment interests. In addition to the traditional science courses, others Natural Resources 247 which may be included are political science, sociology, communications, environmental health, physical education, statistics, computer techniques, urban and regional studies, and landscape architecture. Students majoring in other departments of the University are encouraged to elect a minor in natural resources; however, it should be especially useful to accompany certain majors including biology, earth science, elementary education, geography, geology, journalism, landscape architecture, physical education, radio and television, speech, urban and regional studies, and in certain areas of the social sciences. Completion of a major or minor in natural resources also fulfills the general studies requirements in sciences and mathematics. Students who elect a major or minor in natural resources should enroll in NR 101 as their first course. The student will enroll in the Professional Arts Curriculum with a departmental major in natural resources. Inquiries of a general or specific nature are welcomed at the office of the Department of Natural Resources. title: Introduction to Natural Resources
description: The role of natural resources and their relationship to man's social and economic welfare; population growth and its impact upon resource use. The nature and interrelationships of resources with emphasis on the multipleuse concept of resource management. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to man. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 311.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as a natural resource. Hydrology, water quality, water treatment, and planning as they apply to the understanding of the resource. Prerequisite : BIO 112, CHEM 112 or 114, MATH 111, or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 211.

title: Soil Resources 1
description: The basic properties of the soil portion of the ecosystem. Prime emphasis on the genesis and resulting chemical and physical characteristics of soils. Prerequisite : BIO 112, CHEM 112 or 114, or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 221.

title: Soil Resources 2
description: Fundamental properties of soils. The classification, management, and fertility of soils will be studied in depth to develop the ability of the student to work effectively with this important resource. Prerequisite: NR 321 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources, including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, GEOG 325, or NR 101. Natural Resources 249

title: Mineral Resources
description: The relationship of minerals to renewable resources including the role of mineral fuels as a source of energy for the human ecosystem ; a descriptive and interpretive treatment of the distribution, production, and use of world mineral resources with emphasis on conservation principles, practices, and techniques. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Energy Resources
description: Extends the material on energy resources as treated in NR 331. Appraisal of the natural resource base for energy resources and analysis of the environmental impact of the development of these energy resources. Prerequisite : NR 101, 331, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Air Resources
description: The significance of the atmosphere as a resource; the important meteorological parameters in air resources and management; the economic, sociological, technical, political and biological aspects of air pollution; with special emphasis on ,basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. The interrelationships of various natural resources with emphasis directed toward multipleuse concepts of management to meet existing and projected outdoor recreation demands. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Introductory Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles as applied to the management of natural resources and related environmental problems. Prerequisite: NR 211 or 311, 221 or 321, GEOL 101, MATH 110, PHYCS 110 or 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a particular area (not to be smaller than a county) with special emphasis on the locations of these natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence these natural resources have on the environmental quality. Each time this course is conducted a specific geographic area will be specified. Laboratory and field experiences included. Prerequisite: NR 101 and permission of the department chairman. title: Integrated Resources Management
description: Integrated management of resources with emphasis on combinations of principles prerequisite to the formulation and implementation of natural resources policies and programs. title: Environmental Issues
description: An opportunity to identify and gain an understanding of selected environmental issues relevant to the local geographic area. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Environmental Quality
description: Designed to give students from the various disciplines an opportunity to relate their area of competence to current environmental problems in a meaningful way. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered spring quarter of even numbered years. Prerequisite: NR 311, BIO 480, and ZOOL 444, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Natural Resources Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis on field work and creative presentation of concepts. Prerequisite: NR 101, 221, 311, 341; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Organization and Management of Interpretive Programs
description: Develops skills and techniques relative to the sound organization and management of interpretive programs, including sites and facilities. Emphasis on planning procedures and field study of existing programs. Prerequisite: NR 101, 221, 311, 331, 341; BIO 313; GEOL 101. Prerequisite or parallel: NR 491.

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the curriculum, and the contribution teachers can make in developing a conservationconscious public. Sources of help in teaching conservation, including the use of resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources that are uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 101, 325, BIO 325, GEOG 325, or BIO 103.

title: Practicum in Natural Resources
description: Supervised practical professional experience relating theory and practice by combining instruction and work activities in natural resources, including conservation education, outdoor education, or environmental education. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; 12 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources
description: An opportunity to pursue special interests in the area of environmental quality. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; 12 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 496. Department of Philosophy Robertson, Chairman ; Andry, Annis, Foster, Miracchi, Mueller Philosophy as an Academic Discipline One of the earliest definitions of philosophy encountered by the beginning student is one that says it is the "love of wisdom." The philosopher, accordingly, is known as a "lover of wisdom." And it should be noted that this love of wisdom is not confined to any one field; indeed, most anything is grist for the philosopher's mill! Historically speaking, the above definition has resulted ever since the time of Plato in the general agreement that the traditional role of philosophy is one of synthesis and system building. To put the matter another way, the philosopher was seen to be one who knew something about each area of human experience as a result of either native genius or exhaustive investigation after which, by weaving such knowledge into a consistent and coherent whole, gives to the human race a unified picture of the universe and the individual. This general agreement about the role of philosophy both within and without the university produced about twenty or more centuries of some of the most magnificent albeit meaningless cogitations ever produced. This is not to say that these vast systems were or are without some value. As purely intellectual exercises they have their place. But surely the student has a right to note that on the assumption that synthesis is the main business of philosophy, here we are many centuries after Plato still bemused by his problems and showing very little evidence that we are any closer to solving them. Is it possible that they are not "problems" at all? In the past thirty years the role of philosophy has been changing, although not without some dire warnings as to its future if the present trend continues. Analysis has now replaced synthesis as the main job of the philosopher as a member of a university faculty. This is not to say that analysis has not always been with us, philosophically speaking, but in the past it has always been subordinated to the activity known as synthesis. It is generally agreed now that the scope of the knowledge of human beings is too large in our own century for any philosopher to pretend to carry on the timehonored function of philosophy described above. Perhaps this was possible in the small world in which Plato lived, it is not possible now. Given this change, then, just what is the role of philosophy and the philosopher in a modern university now? It is twofold, one relative to the other academic disciplines, and one relative to the students who pass through the classroom. Relative to the other academic disciplines on the campus, the philosopher can function in the role of critical analyst as a sort of catalytic agent by insisting that colleagues constantly look to the meaningfulness of their ideas. Indeed, perhaps the greatest service is that of helping others make their ideas clear regardless of the nature of their academic discipline. Relative to the students in the university, the philosopher and philosophy can serve in several ways. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all facets of life need examination if we are to get ahead with this business of living. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all values and beliefs would never have come to be except that people in the past were not afraid to question those that were then held, and that in all probability the same fate awaits values and beliefs held now. And lastly, philosophy can serve by showing the student that this succession is indeed a good thing. The alternative is stagnation. These two roles for philosophy have given rise on most university campuses to certain basic courses in philosophy designed to be of help to groups of students. The usual Philosophy 251 Introduction to Philosophy course is one of general interest which serves to do what its title implies. In this course the student becomes aware of the basic problems philosophers deal with as well as some of their answers. Logic, the study of deductive and inductive reasoning and the rule thereto, can be invaluable for prelaw students, mathematics majors, and any other persons who must reason correctly. Ethics is a course of particular interest to anyone concerned in any way with the relationships of human beings. For those occupied with the history of ideas, the three courses in the history of ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy are most valuable. These are the core courses in philosophy and form the necessary foundation for the more specialized courses which usually follow. Religious Studies as an Academic Discipline A knowledge of the religion of any culture is essential to the understanding of that culture. This is indeed true of our own culture, as well as of other cultures. Students preparing for teaching careers will be expected to deal with religious ideas, values, institutions, and practices in their teaching. Courses in religious subject matter are being expanded in public schools. A small but increasing number of students come to Ball State to prepare for theological studies. Others decide to pursue a life of religious service after entering Ball State. To meet the increasing demands of these situations, Ball State provides students with the opportunity, which compares favorably with similar programs provided by other educational institutions, to pursue religious studies. Any student may register in courses which are designed for all four years of university life. The courses are classified under the general headings of cultural settings of religion, Biblical studies, church history, and religions of the world. Any course in religious studies counts for credit as a general elective in any program of studies within the University, it counts for credit as a social science elective for general studies, or a student may acquire a departmental minor in religious studies by successfully completing the requirements in this area. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: The major types and principal problems of philosophy in terms of the most significant historical and contemporary schools and movements. Brings an awareness of the problems that constitute philosophy and their improtance to the search for truth on the part of each student.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of human thinking as far as human thinking is concerned with deduction.

title: Inductive Logic
description: An introduction to the principles and problems of inductive reasoning.

title: Ethics
description: The nature of ethical reasoning, an inquiry into the meaning of good and bad, of right and wrong. Critical analysis of leading ethical theories and their treatment of principal ethical problems in a search for criteria for an adequate ethical system for the individual and for society. The reading consists of the works of major ethical thinkers, both classical and contemporary.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of basic social concepts such as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of normative issues such as how liberty should be distributed, and how justice can be maximized.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the rise of philosophy in Greece about 600 B.C. to the fall of Rome. Emphasis is upon these theories in their relation to one another, the times in which they were produced, and the thinkers by whom they were offered.

title: History of Medieval Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the fall of Rome to the Renaissance. Consideration of the inheritance of medieval Europe from the Graeco-Romanearly Christian world and of the creative role played by medieval philosophy in the formation of the western tradition especially after the rediscovery of Aristotle.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the time of the Renaissance to the present. Emphasis is upon these theories as illustrative of the changing nature of philosophic speculation in modern times from that of synthesis to that of criticism and analysis.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A comprehensive survey beginning with post-Kantian philosophy and ending with the principal movements of twentiethcentury philosophy. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Aesthetics
description: An historical presentation of the major philosophical views on the concept of beauty and the relation of these views to the various forms of human expression.

title: Philosophy of Language
description: Examines the philosophical significance of language from any of various directions. May investigate philosophical theories of how language works, philosophical assumptions and implications of such theories in linguistics, or language as a tool for the philosophical exploration of the world. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Central Issues in Philosophy
description: Covers any number of traditional philosophical problems. These may include mind and body, freewill and determinism, knowledge and reality, and value and obligation. May be approached historically or by studying the works of current philosophers. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Open to students in the Honors Program or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Philosophies of Science
description: An investigation of the basic assumptions, methods, and logical sturcture of the various sciences. Emphasis is upon epistemological problems primarily.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: The purpose of the course is to provide superior students with an opportunity for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned if approved by the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Theories of Reality
description: A critical examination of the principal problems of metaphysics, such as the nature of reality, the problem of universals, space, time, causality, mechanism, the self, substance, and process, with particular attention to the relation of metaphysical concepts to the theory of knowledge and to the factual sciences. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Theories of Knowledge
description: Problems in the theory of knowledge: origin, nature, and validity of knowledge; critical evaluation of subjectivism and realism, dogmatism and skepticism, intuitionism, pragmatism, empiricism, rationalism, and pietism ; theories of meaning, truth, and perception as they relate to the scientific method. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Continental Rationalists
description: Critical investigation of philosophies of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman; but not more than 4 hours may be earned at one time.

title: British Empiricism
description: Philosophies of Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, their critical emphases and main arguments against rationalistic assumptions historically explored and critically examined.

title: Studies in Oriental Philosophies
description: Critical investigation in major Indian, Chinese, and Japanese philosophies and their effects.

title: Plato
description: The writings of Plato.

title: Aristotle
description: The philosophy of Aristotle based on his works in relation to his environment and life.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory
description: A variety of contemporary ethical theories.

title: Existentialism
description: Selected works of several existentialists. Philosophy 253

title: Kant
description: The philosophy of Kant with emphasis on his Critique of Pure Reason and Prolegomena.

title: Logical Empiricism
description: Early Positivism and contemporary logical Empiricism from Auguste Comte to the present.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: An introductory survey of the major religions in the United States with emphasis on their historical development, distinctive beliefs, institutions, and practices. Attention will be given to political consequences and the social significance of American religious pluralism.

title: New Religious Movements
description: A contemporary focus on nonnormative religious movements (theosophical spiritualist, occult, oriental, neopagan as upsurges of shamanism) in America, based on the three categories of religious expression : verbal, practical, social; and on the concept of religion as means for ultimate transformation.

title: Old Testament
description: The origins and developments of Hebrew-Judaic thought: its progressive expressions throughout time in personalities, theologies, and various types of Hebrew-Judaic literature.

title: New Testament
description: A basic study of the origins and developments of Christian religious thought : its Jewish environment, its early expressions, the emergence of its literature, and the various forms of its expression as found in its earliest literature.

title: Evolution of Christian Thought
description: Christian thought as it evolved in early catholicism, the orthodox creeds, the eastwest schism, the medieval age, the reformation, and the controversy between rationalism and pietism. Consideration also given to recent trends in Christian thought.

title: Paul and His Influence in Early Christianity
description: The life and thought of Paul as they relate to his letters and to the Acts of the Apostles in the context of 1st century Christianity, the development of radical Paulinism and anti-Paulinism, their influence on the formation of Christianity.

title: Problems in the Early Church
description: A consideration of problems in the early church such as resurrection, christophanies, messiahship of Jesus, conversion of Paul, Glossolalia or tongues, Sabbath versus Sunday, eucharist, baptism, Paul's missionary journeys, the Jerusalem Conference, Paul's imprisonment, early persecutions.

title: Religions of the Ancient Near East
description: The religious movements of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, and Persia as they relate to the development of Judaism and the rise of Christianity.

title: Religions of India
description: The religious heritage of India : Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism ; the ways of life they advocate, their scriptures, developments of their theologies.

title: Religions of China and Japan
description: Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, Maoism, Shintoism. Origin and developments; literature; rites and rituals.

title: North American Indian Religions
description: The major types of religious traditions of North American Indian groups, with special attention to deities, processes and problems of change, value orientations, and the contemporary viability of religious beliefs.

title: Principles of Theology
description: Consideration of traditional theological principles regarding the nature of God, of mankind, of redemption, and of the church, and an inquiry into contemporary thinking on these issues, with emphasis on the latter.

title: Black Church History and Theology
description: An analysis of the institutional structure of the black church; its contemporary functions and place in social change. Emphasis on the social conditions that shape the black church and influence redefinition of its organizational components.

title: Philosophy and Psychology of Religion
description: Investigation of mankind as religious— in experience, behavior, personality, and society. Inquiry about those realities which concern religion—tradition, traditional beliefs, institutional expression, faith, discipline, rational inquiry, and criticism. Consideration of methods and principles for investigation of religion.

title: Religious Existentialism
description: Examines both the position and effects of religious existentialists related to current religious views and movements. The contributions of men such as Kierkegaard, Tillich, and Buber will be critically analyzed in the light of orthodox Christianity.

title: Comparative Religions
description: A comparative study of the great world religions. title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting energy forms such as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physics and Sports
description: A descriptive introduction to basic physical principles and laws within a framework of applications to athletic activities and sports. Particularly suited to the student with areas or special interest in physical education. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110, 120, or 130.

title: General Physics
description: Mechanics, properties of matter, and heat. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary algebra.

title: General Physics
description: Magnetism, electricity, and atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110. *Unless given special permission by the department head, a student on the Option 2 program must complete ASTRO 100, 120, 222 before enrolling in the required courses, PHYCS 380, 382, 386. IStudents will be placed in appropriate beginning courses in mathematics.

title: General Physics
description: Sound and light. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110.

title: General Physics
description: Mechanics, properties of matter, and heat. Intended for students expecting to major or minor in the physical sciences or mathematics. Prerequisites or parallel: MATH 170.

title: General Physics
description: Electricity and magnetism. Intended for students expecting to major or minor in the physical sciences or mathematics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120. Parallel: MATH 171. 124, General Physics. (4) Sound and light, and certain modern developments in physics. Intended for students expecting to major or minor in the physical sciences or mathematics. Prerequisite : PHYCS 122.

title: Physics 1 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of mechanics and heat. Topics include particle dynamics, resolution of forces, friction, work, energy, static equilibrium, torque, properties of materials, fluids, temperature, thermal expansion, heat energy, heat transfer, phase changes in matter, and thermodynamic engines. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 124. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Physics 2 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of sound, light, and electrical power. Topics include wave phenomena, sound characteristics, sound production and absorption, human response to sound, reflection, refraction, geometrical optics, polarization, circuits, Ohms Law, Kirchoff s Laws, electromagnetic induction, transformers, meters, and power distribution systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 112 or 120.

title: Sound and Light
description: For music and art students. Sound as a basis of music and light as a basis of art. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Household Physics
description: Practical applications of physics in common everyday appliances and other devices. Topics include: why fuses blow, principles of heating and cooling, and principles of some electrical and electronic home appliances.

title: Topics in Physics
description: Discussion of a specific topic in physics. Examples are: lasers, holography, and solid state electronics. No math or science background is needed. For the nonphysics major. For the specific topics being studied during a given quarter, consult your curricular adviser, or the Department of Physics and Astronomy. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mechanics
description: Primarily a problemsolving course in kinematics and dynamics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prereqisite: PHYCS 120 and MATH 172.

title: Sound and Acoustical Art
description: A descriptive treatment of basic sound and acoustics, using a minimum of mathematics. It is especially tailored to the needs of music and other related areas such as speech. Involves pitch, wavelength, intensity levels. Not open to students with areas in physics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 184.

title: Light, Optics, and the Visual Arts
description: Principles of light and optics for students majoring in areas other than a physical science where a basic understanding of light and optics is desired. Tailored to the needs of photojournalism, art, and other students with similar interests. Not open to physics majors and minors. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 184 or JOURN 248.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
description: An introduction to classical electric and magnetic theory with introduction of vector notation. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and MATH 172.

title: Introduction to Modern Physics
description: Introduction to atomic and nuclear physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Modern Physics Laboratory
description: Experimental work involving the concepts associated with modern physics. Prerequisite or parallel: PHYCS 260.

title: Environmental Physics
description: The application of physics to environmental and societal problems. Physical principles underlying hardtechnology based industries will be discussed. Topics include: energy production, transmission, and environmental effects (including nuclear power generation and radiation); transportation problems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or the equivalent.

title: Electronics for the Life Sciences
description: Applications of electronics to the problems encountered by students in the life sciences. Electronic instruments used in biology, health, and physiology and the problems associated with their use. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 354 or 356.

title: Physical Optics
description: The electromagnetic wave theory of light, spectra, interference, diffraction, polarization, and double refraction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Electronics 1
description: Characteristics of electronic components and their circuit functions. Circuit analysis, design and construction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or 122 or permission of the department head.

title: Electronics 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 354 at a more advanced level. Prerequisite: PHYCS 354. Physics and Astronomy 257

title: Pulse and Digital Electronics
description: The function and use of pulse and digital circuitry as applied to laboratory and commercial electronic apparatus. Prerequisite : PHYCS 355 or permission of the department head.

title: Introductory Nuclear Techniques
description: Emphasis upon experimental studies of radioactive disintegrations and decay products and their relation to nuclear structure. Instrumentation in radioisotope measurements. Two lectures and two twohour laboratory periods per week. Prerequisite : PHYCS 260.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those which occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Prerequisites : PHYCS 124 and 260, or permission of the department head.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those which occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Such topics as boundary value problems (involving linear differential equations and partial differential equations), transforms, and special functions (Green's function approach, Fourier series, Legendre's equation, Bessel's equation, Hermite polynomials, etc.) of mathematical physics are covered. Prerequisites : PHYCS 124 and 260 or permission of the department head.

title: Descriptive Astronomy
description: The celestial sphere, the solar system, formation and decay of stars, instruments and basic laws of astronomy, nebulae, galactic structure, theories of the origin of the universe; constellation and telescope work.

title: Instruments and Techniques in Planetarium Operations
description: Use of planetarium instrument, console, and chamber. Organization and evaluation of planetarium programs and exhibits. Prerequisite : PHYCS 380 or 580 or permission of the department head.

title: Theories and Instruments of the Astronomer
description: The planets, stars, and nebulae as related to theories and natural laws of the universe through observatory and laboratory experiences. Prerequisite: PHYCS 380 or permission of the department head.

title: The Teaching of Physics in the Secondary School
description: Aims, nature of the subject matter, amount and nature of laboratory work, standardized tests, and textbooks used in the teaching of physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in physics. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Classical Mechanics
description: Motions of rigid bodies, moving coordinate systems, continuous media, vibrating systems and the Lagrangian formulation of classical mechanics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites : PHYCS 230 and MATH 374.

title: Celestial Mechanics
description: An application of the laws of classical mechanics to objects under the influence of inversesquare gravitational forces, leading to the theory of orbits and perturbative effects on orbits. Prerequisite : PHYCS 230. Prerequisite recommended: PHYCS 430.

title: Thermodynamics
description: Laws of thermodynamics and introduction to the kinetic theory of gases. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 230.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 1
description: Application of vector analysis to electrostatics, dipole and multipole fields, and dielectric theory. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite : PHYCS 250.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 450 with emphasis on dynamic electrical problems, alternating currents, magnetic fields, and Maxwell's equations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite : PHYCS 450.

title: Quantum Mechanics. 1
description: De Broglie's postulate, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the free particle, square well potentials, harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom, and other selected wave mechanics problems. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites : PHYCS 260 and MATH 172.

title: Solid State 1
description: An investigation of the structure and physical properties of matter in the solid state. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites : PHYCS 260 and MATH 172.

title: Independent Studies in Physics
description: Pursuit of special lines of scientific investigation in physics on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite : permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Physics Investigations in the Field
description: Investigative problems in physics which need to be pursued at other locations than at Ball State due to specialized facilities being at the specific location. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in this course is contingent upon permission of the department head.

title: Mysteries of the Sky
description: A nontechnical and nonmathematical multimedia excursion into the vast reaches of the sky including information about the sun, the moon, shooting stars, comets, supernovae, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, life on other planets.

title: Observational Astronomy
description: A continuation of ASTRO 100 providing practical experience in observing celestial objects by using telescopes and other astronomical apparatus. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100.

title: General Astronomy 1
description: Essential points of modern astronomy, emphasizing the underlying physical principles. Topics include : coordinate systems in astronomy, orbital laws, relativity, planetary physics, measurement of stellar distances, and spectral classification of stars, Prerequisite: ASTRO 100 or PHYCS 380, and MATH 111.

title: General Astronomy 2
description: A continuation of ASTRO 120. Topics include: atomic structure and stellar spectra, stellar atmospheres and interiors, multiple star systems and clusters, galactic structure, cosmology, and the origin of the universe. Prerequisite:

title: Topics in Astronomy
description: Discussion of a specific topic in astronomy. Examples are: comets, eclipses, UFO's, and interstellar travel. No math or science background is needed. For the nonphysics major. For specific topics being studied during a given quarter consult your curricular adviser, or the Department of Physics and Astronomy. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Astrophysics 1
description: An introduction to the physics of stellar structure and the theories of stellar evolution. Prerequisite: ASTRO 122 or PHYCS 124. Parallel: MATH 161 or 170.

title: Introduction to Astrophysics 2
description: Continuation of ASTRO 330 emphasizing the nuclear processes involved in stellar evolution. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330. Parallel: MATH 162 or 171.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. Open only to students with a major in elementary education. Department of Physiology and Health Science Schaller, Chairman; Bock, Carroll, Dowell, Ganion, Gowings, Harvilla, Henzlik, Jarial, Jones, Kennedy, Lesh, Paschall, Payne, Shirreffs, Siverly, Wantz, Weber, Womack, Wrestler Health Science is multidisciplinary in nature and its content is derived largely from the biological, physical, and social sciences. The fields of medicine and public health make significant contributions to the discipline of health science. Broad in scope, health science covers such areas as the nature of disease, the complexity of nutrition, effects of radiation, behavioral aspects of accident prevention, an understanding of health and medical care programs, significance of international health problems, selection of health products and services, environmental hazards of air and water pollution, community health services, foundations of mental health, family living and education for human sexuality, and drug use and abuse. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a major or minor for students who are interested in one of a variety of occupations in the health science field. Health science is known differently in some institutions; some commonly used names are: health Physiology and Health Science 259 education, health and safety education, and school and college health education. Health science teachers, coordinators, and directors are being sought by elementary and secondary schools, junior colleges, as well as universities. The department also offers a departmental minor in the field of public health. It provides basic information on public health programs, problems, and practices in the United States. Opportunities include employment with official governmental and voluntary health agencies, business, industry, and professional health associations, such as the American Medical Association. Of equal importance in the department are the subject areas of anatomy and physiology. These are vital to the health sciences and biological sciences in the broad sense and, in anticipation of future development, provide a point of departure for specialization in the respective disciplines of anatomy and physiology. The department also offers a departmental minor in physiology. One combination that is often elected by the students is the physiology minor earned in conjunction with a biology, chemistry, or psychology major. At the present time, the department contributes required and elective courses to several academic programs at Ball State, such as regional and urban planning, preprofessional programs in allied health science areas, courses for professional nurse preparation, and general education. The preprofessional programs in the allied health science area include premedical, predental, and prepharmacy programs; professional nurse preparation; and medical technology. The department provides guidance in enabling students to select a career in teaching, service, or research. Membership in Eta Sigma Gamma, the national honorary for men and women in health science, and Sigma Zeta, the national honorary in science, is offered to qualified students.
