title: Elements of Human Health
description: Human biology stressing the personal and informational aspects of current health problems. Hygiene of the basic systems of the body with emphasis on care, functions, and disorders; natural and acquired defenses against disease; elements of preventive medicine; and modern standards of sanitation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 160.

title: Fundamentals of Human Health
description: The main purpose is to promote total individual fitness. Intelligent selfmanagement, based on understanding of body functioning, is an objective. Some problems considered are the following : existing health situations; use of physicians, dentists, and public agencies; infections and body defense; in emergencies, what to do until the doctor comes; food and one's efficiency ; emotional health ; and basic understanding of human reproduction. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 150.

title: Community Health Problems
description: Organization of official and nonofficial health agencies at the various levels: international, national, state, and local. Exploration of causative community factors in disease, community diagnoses of disease, and programs being investigated to combat these conditions. Selected communicable, noncommunicable, and behaviortype problems will be the focus for the application of principles and procedures. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Emergency Health Care
description: Various emergency health problems and their management by the application of emergency health care as recommended by the American Red Cross and Civil Defense authorities. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in PPW 299 or PPM 396.

title: School Health Practice
description: Community and school health services. Practical experiences in screening for visual, auditory, and nutritional defects. Identification and control of childhood diseases. Topics included : accidents, safety, and first aid; materials for teaching health; role of the teacher and school health personnel; and effect of the total school program on the health of the child. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 150 or 160.

title: School Health Organization
description: Organization and development of school health programs. Coordination of school and community health programs, hygiene, and sanitation of the school plant, the school lunch program, school health services, and the health instructional program. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 350.

title: Health Appraisal of School Children
description: Sociological, psychological, and physiological changes that take place in school children. Prevalent health problems that occur in school children—their etiology, pathology, diagnosis, and prognosis. Experience in screening techniques for discovering these deviations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 350 or 360.

title: Teaching Health in Secondary Schools
description: Examination of the Indiana state course of study in health and safety, relation of health policies and current schoolhomecommunity problems, practice with audiovisual aids, evaluation of representative textbooks, and visits to offcampus schools. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160. Prerequisite recommended : HSC 360.

title: Health Science of Distant Areas
description: School and public health programs at local, state, and national levels. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students on elementary curricula, students with concentration areas in health science on secondary curricula, and students in public health areas. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in the course is contingent upon permission of the department chairman.

title: Health, Sexuality, and Family Life
description: The family as the basic unit in society with consideration of the health problems facing the family. Emphasis is given to tracing relationships between men and women in the areas of dating, courtship, marriage, and problems of raising children; human anatomy, physiology, and embryology; and responsibilities of the home and school in the sex education of the schoolage child. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or a major or minor in health science, home economics, biology, teacher education, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sex Education and School Health
description: Development of an understanding of how to implement and teach a positive program of sex education aimed at helping young people Physiology and Health Science 261 develop constructive attitudes, values, and practices based on sound knowledge in accordance with American Medical Association recommendation and pertinent state guidelines. Prerequisite: HSC 461 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Alcohol Problems
description: A study of alcohol as a mood modifier, its use, nonuse, and abuse in drinking societies. Critical and controversial issues relevant to alcohol ingestion will be explored for medical, economic, legal, educational, historical, physiological, and public health implications.

title: Current Progress in Disease Control
description: A critical review of pertinent research being conducted on leading causes of mortality and morbidity in the United States. A description and analysis of this current research will enable participants to gain an appreciation and understanding of current health progress in the United States. Particular emphasis upon the potential for application of this information into individual, school, and community health programs. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Drug Dependence and Abuse
description: An anlysis of the medical, psychological, sociological, and legal dimensions of drug use in the United States. The incidence and prevalence of drug abuse together with the roles played by the school and community in dealing with this health problem will be treated. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health Quackery
description: Health services and consumer protection organizations. An analysis of fradulent health practices and nostrums, available health care systems and health products. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health and Aging
description: Dynamics of later life and the aging process with specific emphasis on health. The physiological and behavioral dimensions of the aging process will be analyzed and discussed.

title: Public Health Practice
description: Public health organization and available community health resources. Recent developments and problems in the field of public health. Examination of recent literature on preventive medicine and human conservation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. prerequisites: HSC 160 and 180, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Health
description: The physical environment and its relationship to disease causation. Review of environmental health problems and their solutions. Areas of study include air and water pollution, milk and food sanitation, disposal of human excreta and waste, radiological agents in the environment, and occupational health problems. Prerequisite: HSC 480.

title: Epidemiology
description: Classic epidemics, evaluation of epidemiological principles and techniques of investigation, and epidemiological analysis of selected types of diseases. Prerequisite: HSC 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Special Studies in Physiology and Health Science
description: Designed to give undergraduate physiology and health science students who exhibit special aptitutde and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time.

title: Fundamentals of Mammalian Anatomy
description: Basic study of mammalian anatomy with detailed dissection and with examination of representative microscopic structure. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Human Embryology
description: Normal development of the human organism including germ cell formation, fertilization, implantation, and organ formation. Consideration of embryonic environment, physiology, and abnormal development. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or ANAT 201.

title: Human Neuroanatomy
description: Offers a strong background in the basic structural and functional relations of the central nervous system. Emphasis upon understanding of the location of nerve cell centers and the fiber tracts entering and leaving these centers. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or ZOOL 330. Prerequisites recommended: ANAT 320 and 430.

title: Histology
description: Microscopic structure or organisms with special emphasis on the tissues of vertebrates. Introductory microtechnique. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisites: four courses in biological science. BIO 360 and ZOOL 330 are recommended.

title: Fundamentals of Pathology
description: An introduction to the study of the principles of disease production, especially in the human body. Emphasis on basic concepts and descriptions of disease processes as seen in the human being. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 430 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Physiology
description: Vital processes with references to human functional biology. Group experimentation with recording apparatus. Prerequisites: BIO 111, or BIO 102 and 103; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Human Physiology
description: Continuation of PHYSL 210. Functions of the human organ systems. Comparisons between vertebrate systems and mechanisms in man. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210.

title: Mammalian Physiology
description: Comparative mammalian physiology with consideration of laboratory and domestic animals and their contributions to human physiology. Advanced instrumentation and animal handling techniques stressed in laboratory. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisites: one year of inorganic chemistry or BIO 111; CHEM 110; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Renal Physiology
description: A detailed study of the urinary system and excretory functions. Emphasis will be on human physiology but comparative vertebrate systems will be included. Subject matter included will be from the embryogenicanatomic level to the biochemicalpathological level. Prerequisite: general chemistry, organic chemistry; one course in anatomy; one course in physiology.

title: Cardiovascular Dynamics
description: A functional study of the mammalian circulatory system, stressing actions of homeostatic control mechanisms and applications of physical principles to a biological system, with minimal use of mathematics in developing operational concepts. Prerequisite: one course in physiology and one in physics.

title: Honors Colloquium in Science
description: Exploration of selected current issues in science, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students.

title: Life Science Statistics
description: An introduction to the practical application of statistical techniques in the life sciences. Department of Political Science Perry, Chairman; Baker, Chang, Corbett, Frankland, Gruenewald, Hamilton, Hamori, Hollands, Mast, Menez, Meyer, Rudoni, Sargent, Vasicko Political science is the study of the legal governments and relation of people thereto. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Protagoras, Gorgias, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polis or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differ from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask: What is the nature of people (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between people and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. Since comprehension of available knowledge is fundamental to intelligent valuation, emphasis must be given to teaching and learning and to continued accumulation, analysis, and organization of knowledge. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civic, and vocational. The first two, hopefully, are universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed populace. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 130) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz., political theory; American government; public law; public administration ; parties, politics, and the political process; foreign and comparative government; and international law and diplomacy. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher certification programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate level for students in other departments. On the teaching major in social studies, 60 hours, and the teaching minor in social studies, 36 hours, concentrations are required, which may be in political science. If application for admission to law school is the immediate objective after obtaining a baccalaureate degree, the student may elect to meet degree requirements on the Liberal Arts Curriculum. A departmental major of 48 hours in a social science and a departmental minor of 28 hours in a social science are specified. title: Honors Colloquium in Political Science
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in political science, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open to students on Honors Program and other outstanding students by permission of the department chairman. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in American Governments and Politics
description: The student will work part time or full time (depending on the assignment) for one quarter in the office of a public official in national, state, or local government, a candidate for public office, or a political party. Assignments will depend upon the interests of students and the convenience of sponsors. Prerequisite: 16 hours in political science including the following or their equivalents : POLS 130, 237 and 431, or 350, or 473, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do semiindependent study. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the department chairman and a professor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: basic courses in the area selected for special study, junior standing, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings in Planning
description: Reading program developed in consultation with the department chairman and a professor with special competence in planning. Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest in planning. Prerequisite: POLS 461 and permission of the department chairman. Division II: Political Theory and Methodology

title: Introduction to Politics
description: The scope and methods of the study of political science. An examination of the basic concepts and theories in the discipline. Traditions and approaches in the field and their application to the various subdivisions of political science. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Strongly recommended for students with departmental areas in political science.

title: Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of the leading political theories evolved by mankind pertaining to the state. Emphasis on the views of such thinkers as Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Grotius, Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, and Bentham.

title: Early Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of political thought of the early Mediterranean and Medieval worlds which became the foundation of modern political theories and systems of the West. Emphasis on writings of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, St. Augustine, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Machiavelli.

title: Modern Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of selected writings of leading political theorists from the Age of Reformation to the present.

title: Communist Political Thought: from Marx to Present
description: A critical analysis and evaluation of Marxism, Leninism, Stalinism, Khrushchevism, post-Khrushchev Communist ideology and Maoism as a system of theoretical propositions and as an action program of an international movement.

title: Voter Polling Techniques
description: Methods by which information is obtained on the voting behavior and attitudes of the electorate. Emphasis on producing a working knowledge of polling techniques. Includes such topics as sampling, interviewing, and questionnaire construction.

title: American Political Thought
description: American political thought from the colonial period to the present. Puritanism, nature of rights, constitutionalism and federalism, nature of the Union, democracy, liberalism, conservatism, individualism and collectivism, welfare state, isolation and internationalism, and national security and freedom.

title: Research Methods in Political Science
description: A critical examination of methodological problems and practices in the formulation, execution, evaluation, and reporting of political science research, including a comparison of data gathering techniques, their respective limitations, and appropriate application.

title: Quantitative Political Analysis
description: Introduction to data analysis computer applications in political science: minimum level of technical competence will be attained during the first two weeks; aggregate data analysis using departmental data library; formal modeling employing empirical research; intensive substantive reading. Prerequisite : POLS 425 or permission of the department chairman. Division III: American Government National Government

title: American National Government
description: The organization and operation of national government as it relates to current issues such as civil rights, welfare, ecology, consumer protection, and international relations. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS

title: The Now Politics
description: The American political system and the manner in which it deals with such problems as poverty, pollution, racism, women's rights, and the threat of nuclear war. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 130.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, and centralization will be considered. Prerequisite: POLS 130, or 237.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government. Prerequisites recommended : POLS 130 and 237.

title: Intergovernmental Relations
description: Analysis of relations among national, state, and local governments. Considerations of constitutional and legal bases, and the nature of relations, such as grantsinaid, tax immunity, education, and interstate compacts. Prerequisite:

title: Comparative State Politics
description: Major problems of states and the efforts to cope with them. Will include consideration of Indiana and its position relative to other states.

title: Urban Government in the United States
description: Structure, functions, problems, and trends in city, urban, and metropolitan governments.

title: Rural Local Government
description: Structure and functions of rural local government in the United States, including counties, townships, New England towns, and special districts. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 237.

title: State Legislatures
description: Legislative systems in American state government. External influences (constituencies, political parties, interest groups), internal influences (organizational structure, staff, norms, decisionmaking), issues confronting state legislatures and reform proposals. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Metropolitan Problems
description: Analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related aspects; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation to the entire community. Prerequisites: POLS 237 and 238, or permission of the department chairman. Division IV: Public Law and Policy

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes, and needs. Prerequisite: POLS 130 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships between government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities and finance. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 130.

title: National Defense Policy
description: An international survey of military capacity and function provides the background for analysis of the national defense policy of the United States. Special emphasis on American strategic interests and problems of weapons, technology, nuclear control, and disarmament. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
description: Significant facets of legal system's response to conflicting demands upon environmental resources. Composition of environmental problems, control issues, policy formulation, and legal remedies. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Government Protection of Consumers and Competitors
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or the equivalent. POLS 342 recommended.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and his government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content will include cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Policy Analysis
description: Equips the student with the tools of the policy analyst through systematic analysis of programs and projects. Special emphasis on problem definition, goal determination, systematic evaluation of alternatives, socioeconomic and political indicators, performance measures, and impact evaluation. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 342.

title: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies.

title: Administrative Law
description: Legal and political study of independent regulatory agencies; their powers, functions, and roles as determined by an analysis of relevant cases in which basic principals are identified and synthetized with other areas of public law. Division V: Public Administration

title: Introduction to Planning
description: A survey of problems inherent in planning for cities and regions which utilizes contributions of other disciplines such as history, geography, sociology, and economics. Required of majors in regional and urban planning; elective for others with permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration—national, state, and local. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Administrative organizations as going concerns composed of people taking action under conditions of conflict and cooperation : examination of nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisites : POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes and activities of civil service agencies ; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans ; efficiency measurements, and rewards ; training programs ; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement, and other personnel processes. Prerequisite : POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Survey of the principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances : administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, accounting of revenues, expeditures, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, management of publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Administration of American Foreign Policy
description: Deals with the process of foreign policy formulation. The course is analytic and interpretative and presents divergent views. The conception of the foreign policy process embodies the roles of the executive branch. Congress, press, public, opinion, and various nongovernmental groups.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services. Prerequisites : POLS 160.

title: Problems in Planning
description: Involves field study of selected problems in planning to emphasize the interdisciplinary character of planning and to provide an opportunity to apply political, social, economic, and a real analysis; and implementation techniques. Prerequisite : senior standing and four courses in planning.

title: Administrative Problems in State and Local Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and political interaction at the state and local level for the provision of government services. Special emphasis on the major program areas such as law enforcement, education, taxation, environmental protection, housing, recreation, and public works. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 237 or 350.

title: Problems in National Administration
description: An examination in depth of uniquely national administrative problems and activities. National administrative structures and techniques are examined in detail, including their use and application in the administration of specific national policy areas.

title: Labor-Management Relations in Government
description: Examines public employee unionization, legal provisions for collective bargaining, determination and recognition of bargaining units, bilateral negotiation, and thirdparty involvement procedures, administration of agreements, and the processes and strategies in collective bargaining negotiations in public organizations. Division VI: Politics and the Political Process

title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda.

title: Public Interest Groups and Government
description: An examination of the internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Special attention will be given to the implications of pressure group activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and to the effects of pressure groups upon political parties and the political process.

title: American Political Parties
description: Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy.

title: Women in Politics
description: A crossnational survey of women in politics with emphasis on women and public policy, the political roles of women, and the problems of women in politics within the context of contemporary public affairs.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 130.

title: Political Sociology
description: The political scientist's view of the social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Behavior
description: An analysis of the interrelation of political attitudes and public policy formation. Special attention to the substantive areas of voting behavior, political leadership, and the rise of mass political movements. Division VII: Foreign and Comparative Governments

title: Democratic and Totalitarian Political Systems
description: A comparison of modern political systems as represented by the principal nations of the world.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: Historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 279.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural area, to the government and political structures of the three major powers in Western Europe—Great Britain, France, and Germany—and to the current state of the Western European integration movement. Prerequisite : POLS 130.

title: British Government and Politics
description: The political system of the United Kingdom, including a discussion of the Commonwealth and Britain's place in an expanding European community. Emphasis also on Anglo-American relations and British contributions to American political arrangements. Prerequisite : POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 382.

title: Latin-American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin-American nations.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in the field of comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area. Prerequisite recommended : POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of Soviet Russia
description: Structure and functions of modern Russian government, including central, regional, and local units, relationships between party and government, and such functions as law enforcement, economic planning and administration, and foreign policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 315.

title: Government and Politics of China
description: A comprehensive survey of the government and politics of modern China, both of the Republic of China and Communist China. Division VIII: International Law and Diplomacy

title: Problems and Prospects of American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: Introduction to International Relations
description: A survey of the formal relations among sovereign states in the international system, emphasizing the operation of diplomacy, the factors in international relations and procedures for the settlement of disputes.

title: The United Nations
description: Concentrated study of organization and functions of the United Nations and of foreign policy of selected members of the United Nations. Prerequisite : permission of the department chairman.

title: International Relations of the USSR and the Soviet Bloc
description: The foreign policy of the USSR and her satellites and a survey of the Communist Party in international action.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the law of the international community as it developed from international customs and usage and has been developed and recognized by modern states, with special reference to the position of the Western Democracies.

title: International Organizations
description: Organizations, processes, and methods devised by the nationstate system for the preservation of international peace and security and for dealing with problems of international concern.

title: World Politics
description: Analysis of general intercourse between states; normal relations, disputes and peaceful and forceful settlements; international obligations, agreements, and problems; power relationships and dominance and balance. Particular attention will be given to contemporary problems and situations.

title: Far East in World Politics
description: A comprehensive survey of contemporary international relations in the Far East mainly from post World War II to the present.

title: Communist China in World Affairs
description: A comprehensive survey of Communist China's role in international politics, with special emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Radio and Television 269 Center for Radio and Television Tomlinson, Director; Alexander, Carnal, De Voe, Salvaggio, Smith, Wible The broadcast industries and the motion picture industries provide extremely democratic channels of information, entertainment, and communication. Ball State University has long recognized the appeals which these media have upon the mass audience, and the important part which the media play in our everyday lives. For these reasons, Ball State University and the Center for Radio and Television provide a highly selected sequence of courses which emphasize the practical applications for these media. To meet today's demands, the Center offers both graduate and undergraduate teaching and departmental majors and minors in these fields. The Ball State University program in radio, television, and motion pictures is intended for those people who are serious about career opportunities in these fast growing industries. The excellent selection of courses in the Center's curricula includes programs for those who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for instruction with the electronic media's educational aspects in the classroom, or in school administration systems which employ media. Since many positions in the broadcast and motion picture industries require a creative effort on the part of the individual, and a good understanding of teamwork, these attributes are emphasized as the student also discovers the elements of leadership and responsibility. Students working in the Center are encouraged to learn as much as possible about the function and operation of the sophisticated radio, television, and motion picture equipment planned for a "hands on" approach. Audience research, performance, production, programming, media sales, and administrative studies of the electronic and motion picture media are analyzed in the various courses. The facilities of the University radio station, WBST-FM, and the closed circuit television production facility provide additional and practical experiences for the students in the training program. Such work experiences also allow the student to build a personal resume which frequently assists in later job applications. Training on professional equipment, and the experience gained through the knowledge of operation, coupled with classroom and small group discussion, analyses, and direct study and observation of the broadcast and motion picture industries enables the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. Every effort is made to inform the student of the stringent and competitive labor marketplaces in both the broadcast and motion picture industries. At the same time while the serious student is discovering how to develop the broad based foundations needed for work in the industries, learning about the operation of equipment, and coming face to face with a faculty experience in both academics and the professional work world, the keen student discovers how to cope with the problems to be met in the industry marketplace, as well as the steps to be taken in the preparation for the future. description: An overview of the development of radio, television, and motion picture technology. title: Fundamentals of Radio Broadcasting 1

title: Fundamentals of Radio Broadcasting 2
description: An introduction to radio broadcasting program practices. The origination of the program idea, the preplanning procedures, and the execution of the radio station format. Prerequisite : RTM 230.

description: Intensive practical training in studio procedures and interpretation of radio and television copy including news, feature scripts, continuity, and commercials. Prerequisite: RTM 231.

description: This course is intended to acquaint the student with the functions of a broadcast executive as he works with program, production, and administration personnel with differing temperaments and specialties. Examination of qualitative and quantitative research information utilized by broadcasting. Prerequisite : RTM 231.

title: Broadcast Reporting 1

title: Fundamentals of Television Broadcasting 2

title: Broadcast Reporting 2
description: A continuing study and practice in the methods of gathering and reporting news at the state and national level. Reporters and their relationship to governmental officials at this level. Johnson, Martin, Moore, Morris, Neiman, Rehfeld, Royer, Stacy, Stump, Tamney, Tucker Sociology as an Academic Discipline Sociology is among the younger social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades; and especially in the period since World War II its widened inclusion in patterns of general education has resulted in exceptionally rapid growth of undergraduate enrollments. Simultaneously, quickly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge; and the concepts of the discipline are becoming widely accepted throughout society. Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. In the early years of this century, a number of persons interested in the field of sociology saw it primarily as a tool for ameliorating the various ills and problems of the society, and especially for helping groups and individuals with special needs in "adjusting" to the surrounding social order. Gradually this emphasis has come to be more identified with the special field of social work (see below), with sociology as an academic discipline being perceived more as a "pure" rather than an "applied" science. Today, however, the findings of sociology are assessed in terms of their applicability to the range of social problems as well as in terms of their relation to the furtherance of sociological knowledge. As one of the related group of social sciences, sociology focuses upon, and seeks to develop dependable generalization about human social life and the interaction patterns characteristic of human collectivities. An understanding of the bases for and influences of observable regularities—both those of harmonious existence and group conflict—in the forms of human association is fundamental to a student's knowledge about self and others as participants in structured group life, and about the groups in which such participation occurs. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to broadening of the student's perspective of the sociocultural environment, and to the individual's own relationship to it, thus helping to produce an outlook less restricted by the limitations of untested folk beliefs. As a science, sociology employs the canons of empiricism, objectivity, and ethical neutrality in its search for predictive relationships. The findings derived from such investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. The methods and concerns of sociology are functionally related to those of the other social sciences as well as to a wide range of arts (teaching, medical, expressive, correctional, etc.) which involve interactions among persons performing varied roles. The discipline of sociology thus has a significant contribution to make in the area of general (liberal) education and in professional education of widely diverse emphases, along with the preparation of scholars, to expand and transmit the body of sociological knowledge itself. Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twenthiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex social problems, has contributed to the dramatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both an art and a science. Its art cio logy 275 is the development of special skills used in working with people, either individually, in groups, or through community programs. Its science is the body of knowledge—derived from sociology, psychology, and psychiatry—about people and communities. Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare, agencies; in courts as probation officers for juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics ; in schools ; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as well as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Funds, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University provides for the needs of three groups of students : those who wish to qualify for firstlevel social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; and those who wish to prepare themselves for roles in community leadership as organization board members, in labor union leadership, in industrial social welfare relationships. After the basic twoyear general studies program at Ball State, students begin their specialization in social work within the sociology major. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, and methods of social work. Field trips in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. In the senior year students majoring in social work enroll in a course in basic social work practice. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of casework, group work, and community organization; practical experience is gained in field placement in a social agency for one quarter where the student works with individuals or groups under expert supervision. The Field of Criminal Justice and Corrections Only since the decade of the sixties have people in our society begun to take a greater interest in all facets of our system of criminal justice. A number of events in that decade have stimulated not only public interest, concern, and continuing dialogue, but also research, change in law and interpretation, publication and dissemination of information, and the growing awareness of the need for trained and qualified personnel in our criminal justice system . The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and possible employment: law enforcement, probation services in both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. In most instances, agencies, programs, and facilities operate on three levels of government: local, state, and federal. The departmental major in criminal justice and corrections has the following objectives : to provide students with the growing body of knowledge about the structure and functions of the basic elements comprising our society; to relate such problematic areas as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, to our system of criminal justice; to provide the student with a combination of theory and practical experience in the five areas listed above; and to enable the student to qualify for firstlevel employment positions in the criminal justice system or to qualify for future graduate study in this or related areas. Employment opportunities for trained men and women are increasing in our society. The general requirements include age 21, minimum physical requirements, and a thorough investigation into the candidates' background, integrity, maturity, and emotional stability. Civil service tests are frequently required for entrance into most positions on the state and federal levels. title: Principles of Sociology
description: An introductory view of the general field of sociology including basic concepts as used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, social processes, and social institutions.

title: Social Organization
description: An introduction to large scale social structures including institutions, formal organizations, communities, and society in terms of the social processes involved, such as integration, status, power, and adaptation. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: The Black Community in America
description: An examination of the major social forces influencing the structure of the contemporary black American subcommunity. Emphasis also on an exploration into the strengths and weaknesses of this structure and its relations with the large community, as bases of change in the accommodative patterns of blackwhite relations.

title: Sociology of Deviant Behavior
description: An overview of theory and research on deviant behavior. Three essential forms will be reviewed: (1) deviance arising from disability in social and physical functioning, (2) deviance arising from violation of social norms, and (3) deviance arising from membership in groups observing radical social ideologies. *Prerequisites are waived for students who are social work majors . Sociology 277 Prerequisite: SOC 100. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 242 prior to September 1, 1975.

title: Social Problems
description: A survey of the nature and range of social problems, the conditions which give rise to them, and the methods by which our society attempts to cope with them. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100.

title: Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
description: Provides students with an overview of the criminal justice system as well as a preview of vocational opportunities. Prerequisite : SOC 100 or 242.

title: Sociology of Law Enforcement
description: An examination of sociological research and theory bearing on major social factors that affect municipal police organizations as important coordinating agencies in society. Emphasis on : institutional context of police activity, bureaucratization of police professionalization, judicial decisions and the police role, police militancy, and the police and community change. Prerequisite: SOC 100, 242.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors affecting utilization of treatment programs.

title: Police-Community Relations
description: Analysis of interrelationship between police and public in the study and control of crime. Consideration is given to problems of policecommunity relations and to ways of establishing cooperation between police and various social, economic, and ethnic groups. Prerequisite: SOC 100 and 242.

title: Introduction to Sociological Research
description: Principles and techniques of organizing, conducting, and interpreting sociological research ; the appropriateness of particular methodologies for different kinds of research problems. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in the social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite recommended : SOC 100 and 380.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective on life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in honors program or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ancient and Historic Social Thought
description: A critical survey of influential views regarding the nature of society and human relations from the Greek period through the 19th century Romanticists. Social thinkers and intellectual epochs are interpreted as products of the prevailing social conditions, and are employed for purposes of illuminating contemporary social issues and sociological theories.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of sociological theories and theorists of the 19th and early 20th centuries with a view toward relating theoretical positions to contemporary social dynamics and to contemporary theoretical work in sociology. The cultural and intellectual milieu in which the theoretical works were generated will be noted. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Radical and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite recommended : SOC 100.

title: Mass Society and Culture
description: Conditions giving rise to the spreading phenomena of mass culture, current expressions of these phenomena in American society and elsewhere, and an appraisal of their implications for organizational functioning and interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: A survey of the literature, issues, and events which focus upon the nature and types of complex social organizations with particular attention to societal consequences. Prerequisite: 8 hours of sociology or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sociology of Religion
description: Examines religion as a social institution with particular attention to the societal functions of religion, the influence of social factors on the development of religion, the role of religion in the amelioration of contemporary social problems, and contemporary processes affecting the future of religion.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Medical Care Organizations
description: A sociological analysis of medical care organizations and professionals with emphasis on intraorganizational, interprofessional, and agencyclient relations. Prerequisite : SOC 100.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: A sociological analysis of the field of mental health with attention to social definitions of mental illness, selfrecognition of illness, the process of seeking care, treatment institutions, and the aftermath of treatment. Prerequisite : SOC 100.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as it is related to various sociological variables. Various sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Crime and Delinquency 1
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior; typologies of crime and criminals; the trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and current theoretical explanations. Prerequisite: SOC 100, 242.

title: Crime and Delinquency 2
description: A continuation of SOC 450. Emphasizes the juvenile and adult justice systems, their components, recent changes, and future developments. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 450.

title: Introduction to Corrections
description: A beginning course in penology with emphasis on the three major components: police, courts, and correctional institutions including their history, philosophy, and current programs, policies, and problems. Prerequisite: SOC 251 and either 450 or 451; and permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Corrections
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in correctional settings on the state and local level. Prerequisites : SOC 452 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Law Enforcement
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in police settings on the local and state levels. Prerequisite: SOC 251, 452, and permission of the department chairman.

title: Internship in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: A summer internship involving fulltime individual assignments under field supervision in a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: SOC 450 or 451 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Senior Seminar in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: Limited to majors in criminal justice and corrections, to explore in depth and to summarize current problems, theory, research, and trends in the field. Prerequisite: SOC 452.

title: Small Groups
description: Analysis of data on experimental laboratory research on small groups and field research on small group dynamics. Attention is given to the relationship between group productivity, group cohesion, size, interaction patterns, and related areas. Prerequisite: SOC 260 or GXPSY 316.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions : family, religion, stratification, and education.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historic functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis of the social dynamics of the urban core in metropolitan areas. Attention given to the development of cities and their cores, stressing ecological and demographic factors. The focus shifts to an examination of the social issues associated with the concept of the inner city, especially racism, poverty, crime, welfare, Sociology 279 and education. Finally, policy alternatives for alleviating these conditions are considered. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and utilizing sources of data; and application of survey findings to programs of community action. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 380 or 472.

title: Advanced Sociological Data Analysis
description: Deals with the selection and utilization of advanced statistical techniques and sophisticated means of calculation which have been particularly useful in analyzing sociological data. Such topics as nonparametric statistics, factor analysis, sampling statistics, and multiple regression and path analysis will be discussed in the context of sociological research. Prerequisite: SOC 382 or equivalent.

title: Independent Study in Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar in Sociology
description: An openended course offering for fourth year sociology majors. Both the focus of study and the format of the course will be determined by the students in conjunction with the instructor. Prerequisite: 24 hours in sociology and permission of the department chairman.

title: Social Welfare and Social Services 1
description: The history of private philanthropy and public welfare programs in Europe and America, including the Elizabethan poor law, the growth of public responsibility, the English background of American welfare programs and reform movements, and twentieth century developments.

title: Social Welfare and Social Services 2
description: An introductory survey of the field of social work with emphasis on twentiethcentury developments. Emphasizes contemporary agencies and services, both public and private. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200.

title: Field Observation in Social Work
description: Designed for social work participation in the Chicago Urban Field Study. It provides a coordinated, comprehensive, onthescene view of the broad range of social welfare services. Observations, seminars, and lectures will be conducted with private and public agencies in the Greater Chicago Area. Emphasis on the generic approach to social work education. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200 and permission of the department chairman. 313.Public Social Welfare. (4) An introduction to public welfare including policy, services, and administration. Tax supported income maintenance programs are examined with special emphasis on the philosophy, methods, issues, and problems of public assistance programs.

title: Child Welfare
description: An introduction to the field of child welfare, including programs, policies, problems, and services. The principles and practices of casework for children are examined with emphasis upon state and local community resources. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200 and 201.

title: Human Behavior in Social Work Practice
description: The dynamics of the sequential phases of the human life cycle as a major perspective for understanding, exploration, and treatment of variance in social functioning. Functional and dysfunctional patterns of adapting to stress and crisis are examined within the context of social work practice. Prerequisite : SOCWK 314.

title: Social Work Practice
description: Basic social work principles, values, and skills generic to social work practice. Presentation of basic concepts underlying human behavior relevant to social work practice. Emphasis on problemssolving process, systems analysis, communication skills, and a variety of intervention procedures. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200, 201, 313, 314 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Social Work Practicum
description: A field course providing basic training and practical experience in social work methods of casework, group work, and community organization through placement in social work settings. Prerequisite: SOCWK 440 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Social Work Methods of Intervention
description: Presentation of the methods of social work intervention utilized in social work agencies. Social work methods, traditional and innovative, will be examined singly or in combination which meet the needs and alleviate stresses in ways that strengthen the client system. Prerequisite: SOCWK 315 or permission of the department chairman. Department of Speech Huckleberry, Head; Artes, Benson, Bloom, Diedrich, Dorris, English, Farling, Harmon, Heady, Hemeyer, Hoops, Irving, Kramer, Lindell, Nitcavic, Olson, Pruis, Robbins, Rosentrater, Schleifer, Shawger, Shepard, Strother, Treloar General Speech The field of general speech encompasses several areas such as public address, interpersonal communication, interpretation, theatre, and speech sciences. It is a general program for undergraduate use, while persons specialize as they move toward graduate degrees. In the area of general speech, the University offers both graduate and undergraduate programs. A large proportion of those students electing a speech major plan to become teachers in the public schools. These teachers are expected to direct debating and individual events, produce theatre, and promote and direct radio and television programs. They are also asked to be in charge of special convocations. Their class work is the development of the skills of public address and participation in a democratic society. Also they must develop an appreciation and skill for interpretation and theatre as performed in school theatres or through the facilities of mass media. Another responsibility is to develop an appreciation of the artistic, an understanding of the basic issues of people, and a respect for their cultural heritage. The profession of general speech assists liberal arts graduates to develop these same skills and attitudes. In addition, the speech major and minor are especially useful to support students who enter other professions such as law, the ministry, politics, public relations, and professional radio, television, and theatre. The University offers many student activities in the areas of intercollegiate debating, individual speech events, conferences, and theatre. It is assumed that general speech majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office and from the appropriate area chairman and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Speech Pathology and Audiology The graduate with a bachelor's degree and a teaching major in speech pathology and audiology (sometimes known as speech and hearing therapy) usually works in a public school corporation. An individual with a master's degree may work in a public school, hospital speech and hearing clinic, college or university center, or communitysponsored speech and hearing agency. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers two undergraduate programs in speech pathology and audiology: a teaching major, for persons who plan to work in the public schools, and a departmental major, for persons who plan to work eventually in a hospital, community or college clinic. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology, in audiology, and in speech and hearing therapy. These are necessary for those individuals who desire professional teaching certification, for those who wish to join the American Speech and Hearing Association, and for those who desire state licensing. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs : public school therapy programs, hospital and physical therapy environment, preschool nursery programs, and the University Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. In the latter, children and adults come to the Ball State campus for clinical work for speech, language, and/or hearing problems. Theatre Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a most modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher licensing in speech for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work is available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist people to understand themselves. It also assists students to understand their dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office, and from the theatre area chairman, and should be requested early in the student's academic career.
