title: Fundamentals of Public Speaking
description: Fundamentals and techniques of organizing material and presenting that material in individual speeches. Emphasis on personal speaking improvement in the classroom and in public performances.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasis is on techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequisite: SPCH 210. 213—Beginning Collegiate Debate. (2) For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Development and composition of the debate case and consideration of factual argumentation. Prerequisite: high school speech.

title: Intermediate Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Stress on direct clash and crossquestion debate. This course involves tournament debating. Prerequisite: SPCH 213.

title: Phonetics of Speech Science
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic voice and speech science.

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Personal speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation problems.

title: Speech Practicum
description: The student works upon extemporaneous speaking, discussion, debate, oratory, or interpretive reading for intercollegiate competition, or works in theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: The development of principles of rhetorical criticism and the application of the principles to an intensified study of prominent platform, radio, and television speakers. Consideration is given also to the influence of the speaker upon our social and political life. Prerequisite recommended : SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended : SPCH 210.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Parliamentary Procedure
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Teaching of Speech in the Secondary School
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisites: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232. *Courses in statistics may be substituted for GXPSY 100 and 241 with the approval of the department head.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher.

title: Intercollegiate Forensics
description: Practical experience in speech, intercollegiate debate, discussion, oratory, extemporaneous speaking, and interpretive reading. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Studies in Persuasion
description: An intensified study and application of the principles of effective public speaking; the ideational formulation and delivery of longer speeches; the rhetorical analysis of significant speeches. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department head.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: An examination through exposure to theory, actual practice, and criticism, of the process of communication. Will include communication models of message encoding, transmission, decoding and feedback; the complexity of language, including abstracting and determination of meaning; problems in facetoface, small group, platform speaking, and mass media communication; and communication breakdowns.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of small group literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problemsolving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech pursues a particular area of study in depth on a consultative basis with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite : permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned and a total of 4 hours may be earned at one time.

title: Internship in Speech
description: The student is assigned to onthejob experience in such places as a college classroom, a hospital, a community clinic, summer camp, or summer theatre. Students will be permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the amount of college credit to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in some aspect of speech and communications, and permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned; but not more than 8 hours may be earned at one time.

title: Survey of Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to the profession of speech pathology and audiology and the professional endeavors of speech pathologists and audiologists. Not open to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Speech Science
description: An introductory study of the physical elements of sound, particularly as they apply to the communication process. Prerequisite: SPCH 216.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 261.

title: Language Development
description: Development of the phonology, grammar, content and function of language in children together with a review of the environmental and individual factors acting to influence that development.

title: Articulation Disorders
description: Designed to prepare students to diagnose and treat articulatory speech disorders, particularly in younger children. Part of the course will consist of a laboratory of observation in the treatment of defective speech. Prerequisite : SPCH 216, SPAA 260, 261. Open only to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course for the clinic student. Designed to assist the beginning clinican to develop an understanding of clinical competency, permit selfevaluation, improve phonetic testing, gain general knowledge of speech problems, develop ability to understand diagnostic principles and procedures and learning theory, and observe and evaluate therapy. Prerequisite: SPCH 216, SPAA 410. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 300.

title: Stuttering Disorders
description: Particular attention to and study of the problem of stuttering. Prerequisite: SPAA 410.

title: Organic Speech and Language Disorders
description: An introductory study of neurology and anatomy of the brain and the speech and language disorders resulting from brain damage such as cerebral palsy and aphasia. Other physical problems such as cleft palate and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 261, 410.

title: Speech Pathology and Audiology Practicum
description: The student performs observation and preprofessional participation with clients with various speech, language, and hearing disorders. A total of 8 hours of credit must be earned; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one term or quarter. Prerequisite: SPAA 410 and 411, or equivalents.

title: Introduction to Hearing Disorders
description: Review of anatomy of the ear. Nature and causes of hearing disabilities. Techniques in the conservation of hearing and in the use of residual hearing. Interpretation of audiograms. Psychological problems of persons with hearing loss. Prerequisite : SPAA 260, 261, or permission of the department head.

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in the use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for the purpose of reeducation and the necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 442.

title: Aural Rehabilitation
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for the teaching of lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite: SPAA 442. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 444.

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: An overview of the field of theatre with special reference to the origins of drama.

title: Stagecraft
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of the crafts involved in theatre production at the school, college, and community theatre levels. Three hours of lecture and three arranged hours of laboratory a week.

title: Principles of Stage Makeup
description: An investigation of the principles, techniques, and materials of stage makeup and practical experience in their application.

title: Interpretive Reading
description: Fundamentals of English speech applied to the interpretive reading of prose and poetry.

title: Acting 1
description: A lecturelaboratory class stressing the basic principles of acting. Major emphasis on stage movement.

title: Acting 2
description: A lecturelaboratory course on the principles of acting with major emphasis on character analysis and development. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Modern Drama
description: Analysis of selected dramas from the time of Ibsen to the present day and of the conditions under which they originally were produced.

title: Directing 1
description: Theory and practice of directing for the theatre. Exercises in movement, line interpretation, creation of atmosphere, and the effective use of stage areas. Prerequisite: THEAT 232 and 233.

title: Children's Theatre
description: The principles of theatre devoted to creative dramatics. Twothirds of the course is devoted to formal dramatics. A public performance will be arranged.

title: Advanced Theatre Practice
description: Students design and execute a theatre project in such areas as scenery designs, lighting, properties, acting, directing, oral interpretation, and house management. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in theatre courses and permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Theatre 1
description: The early history of theatre from its Egyptian and Grecian origins through the medieval period.

title: History of Theatre 2
description: The theatre from the Renaissance through the eighteenth century.

title: History of Theatre 3

Professional Laboratory Experiences Swafford, Director The Office of Professional Laboratory Experiences serves to integrate the laboratory experiences in the professional education programs. PARTICIPATION The purpose of participation is to familiarize teaching majors with principles of classroom management and the school environment as it relates to learning activities, and to induct students into the teaching act. Prerequisites for Participation The following are prerequisites for admission to participation : 1. Admission to the Teaching Curriculum 2. Completion of GXPSY 100 and EDPSY 250. (EDPSY 300 must be taken prior to or parallel with participation) 3. A minimum of 93 quarter hours of credit 4. A composite gradepoint average of 2.1 or above 5. Clearance from the Office of Professional Selection on such matters as speech and hearing, health, and other tests as may be required from time to time by University authorities 6. Have a TB test within twelve months prior to the time that participation occurs Organization of the Participation Program Ball State University uses a variety of facilities for providing EDEL 360 and EDSEC 360 participation experiences. These experiences are organized either as part of the program of the oncampus Burris Laboratory School or with affiliated public school systems. Burris is an open district school and provides an educational program for children from kindergarten through grade twelve. University students who are preparing to become teachers are often assigned to Burris School for participation. College seminars, which are also an integral part of the participation experience, are held at Burris or in the Teachers College on a weekly basis. Arrangements with school corporations within commuting distance and with Muncie City Schools supplement the laboratory school facility. STUDENT TEACHING The purpose of student teaching is to provide students the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Prerequisites for Student Teaching The following are prerequisites for admission to student teaching: 1. Admission to the Teaching Curriculum 2. Completion of EDEL 360 or EDSEC 360 (Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management) and special methods in the teaching major. At least one quarter or summer term must intervene between enrollment in participation and enrollment in student teaching Professional Laboratory Experiences 289 3. Completion of the senior physical examination is recommended, and TB clearance is required 4. A minimum of 140 quarter hours of credit, excepting that a student may enroll in EDEL 460 during the last quarter of the junior year 5. A gradepoint average of at least 2.1 overall in the area of concentration and in professional education courses 6. Completion of such tests in English usage, academic competence, intellectual ability, emotional adjustment, speech and hearing performance, and others as may be required from time to time by University authorities 7. Submission of an application for a student teaching assignment to the Student Teaching Office on the dates indicated The applicant who holds a baccalaureate degree from some institution other than Ball State must meet all of the above requirements and, in addition, must have completed at least 15 quarter hours on the Ball State campus, including either EDEL 360 or EDSEC 360, and must be admitted as a regular student. Application for Student Teaching Regular students make application for a student teaching assignment in the Winter Quarter of the year prior to that in which they expect to do student teaching. Students transferring to Ball State after this date, who plan to complete their certification requirements in one year, must make application in September. Official notification of the student teaching assignment will be mailed to the student after the final eligibility determination. Usually this will be in the quarter prior to student teaching. Students needing information in regard to their assignment prior to this notification may inquire at the Student Teaching Office. General Considerations The student must be free of outside commitments that might interfere with fulltime student teaching obligations. This means that students cannot be regularly employed, nor should they carry a heavy load of extracurricular activities. Enrollment for an overload during the quarter is permitted only with approval. A predetermined number of days in seminars conducted by the university supervisor, both at the beginning and the end of the quarter, are a part of the student teaching requirement. Increased demands for qualified supervising teachers resulting from increased enrollment in student teaching have made assignments more difficult in many schools throughout the state, while assignments in Muncie public schools have been difficult for several years. Therefore, students should be ready to accept assignments wherever the university supervisor can situate them for the best professional experience. Student Teaching - Secondary Student teachers preparing to teach at the secondary school level, or in special areas that include both the elementary and secondary levels, are required to spend full time for a minimum of 8 weeks in student teaching, for which they will receive 10 quarter hours of credit. They should enroll in EDSEC 460 (5 credit hours) and EDSEC 462 (5 credit hours). Usually students elect to take student teaching (EDSEC 465, 4 credit hours) for the remainder of the quarter. Students wishing junior high school endorsement should register for EDSEC 466 (10 credit hours) for the 8-week junior high school experience. When necessity demands, a student teacher may take one additional course with student teaching, providing it is scheduled after 4 : 30 p.m. or on Saturday and does not interfere with the student teaching experience. Student Teaching - Elementary Full time Students will enroll for a total of 14 quarter hours in EDEL 464 (10 credit hours) and EDEL 460 (4 credit hours). They will spend full time for the entire quarter in student teaching. If students wish to take student teaching in an area of endorsement, they must enroll in EDEL 465 in another quarter. Part time Students will enroll in EDEL 460 (4 credit hours) in the first quarter and EDEL 462 (8 credit hours) in the second quarter. The work of the first course in student teaching consists of directed observation, participation, and teaching. In the second course, students are required to attain a higher standard in their work than in the first. Under supervision of the classroom teachers, the student has full charge of the class when teaching, and is held responsible for full control and management, as well as instruction. The student spends considerable time in arranging and preparing units of work appropriate to needs and interests of pupils in the class. Special Education Students with an area major in teaching the mentally retarded or minors in teaching the deaf must enroll in SPCED 466 (10 credit hours). If they wish to earn additional elective credit, they may elect to take SPCED 465 (4 credit hours). A student with a minor in teaching the deaf must enroll in student teaching in the major area in another term. Students with minors in areas of special education other than teaching the deaf must earn credit in student teaching in their minor area. The minimum requirement is SPCED 466 (10 credit hours). It is not possible to meet this requirement during the quarter in which the student has an assignment in the major area. Elective Student Teaching The elective courses in student teaching, EDSEC 465, EDEL 465, and SPCED 465 (4 credit hours) are for students who wish to have experiences in additional or different phases of student teaching, or to meet requirements for endorsement credit. It includes principles of human development, learning, adjustment, measurement, research, and statistics as they relate to the understanding of an individual. The objectives of educational psychology--like those of other fields of psychology—are to understand, describe, predict, and guide man's behavior. These purposes are accomplished through research, service functions, and teaching about human relationships, human development, and changes in human behavior. Programs in educational psychology are specialized and offered generally on the graduate level. However, a departmental undergraduate minor in the psychology of human development is offered. Some undergraduate courses in the area are required as psychological foundations for teacher education and other undergraduate programs, and a number are offered as electives. For graduate students there are several programs : a major in educational psychology on a Master of Arts or a Master of Arts in Education degree; a certification program and a major in psychometry on a Master of Arts or a Master of Arts in Education degree; a cognate area in educational psychology for doctoral students; and a specialization in psychometry on a Specialist in Education (6th year) degree. title: Study of Selected Aspects of the Elementary School Reading Program
description: Designed to review the current thinking and approaches to teaching reading in the elementary school, and the relationship of basic psychological principles to teaching practices. Prerequisite or parallel: one term of student teaching at the elementary school level.

title: Corrective Reading in the Classroom
description: Provides prospective teachers with understanding of difficulties in reading plus practical experience in assessing reading difficulties and in study of corrective treatment. Smith, Tovatt, Veselack, Weber, Wood Burris School, the laboratory school of Ball State University, has the following responsibilities : First, the school is obligated to provide for all youth who attend the school from kindergarten through grade twelve: —an effective and sound community school which respects the worth of each individual and provides opportunities for the development of the wide range of individual potentialities found in youth; —a living and learning environment in which all youth have opportunities for cooperative living and for the development of those values and skills vital to all citizens in a free society; and —a curricular program which, in keeping abreast of contemporary problems and in strengthening the foundations of a free society, results in functional understanding of technological development, practical knowledge of economic problems, broad appreciation for world cultures, real appreciation for beauty in the arts, deep respect for human relationships, and sincere concern for the development of a workable philosophy of life coupled with respect for self. Second, the school is obligated to provide for the teacher education program at Ball State University : —a center in which both preservice and inservice teachers can observe sound educational practices; —a laboratory in which prospective teachers can gain firsthand experiences with youth in teachinglearning situations prior to student teaching; —a center for experimentation in which diverse hypotheses and methods for improving education can be formulated, studied, and tested critically, and reconstructed continuously in light of the evidence gathered ; and —a center which contributes to the improvement of educational practices in the state and nation by publicizing new practices and research findings of the laboratory school and by providing consultant and leadership services for the public schools. It is a lifelong process. Recognizing this, the Center for Lifelong Education is concerned with encompassing and unifying all stages of education. Lifelong education includes both formal and informal patterns of education and random experiential learning. Education begins with the family and moves into society as a child begins to interact with nonfamily individuals. The formal institutions of education are important but they constitute only part of many social agencies providing opportunities for individuals to learn. To promote lifelong education, Ball State University established the Center for Lifelong Education and specifically charged it with providing formal and informal programs which would prepare individuals to design, implement, and coordinate educational opportunities for individuals throughout their lives. In the formal portion of this task, the Center either offers or directs the following programs of study, mostly at the graduate level: M.A. Adult Education; M.A. Community Education; M.A. Executive Development for Public Service; M.A.E. Curriculum ; Ed.S. Curriculum; Doctoral Cognates in Curriculum; Adult and/or Community Education; and Departmental minor in Gerontology (See Interdepartmental). In addition, the Center serves as a vehicle within the Teachers College through which interdisciplinary educational services, both formal and informal, not traditionally offered by any current Teachers College department or service unit, may be developed, implemented, and coordinated. Current informal programs include: research, school curriculum studies, program evaluation, inservice professional development programs, retirement planning, and related service activities. Although professional preparation of secondary teachers is the major responsibility of this department, other departments and divisions of the University cooperate in providing methods work in subject matter fields. All students preparing to be secondary school teachers must take EDPSY 250 and 300 and a methods course in the area of their major. In addition, such students enroll in EDSEC 360, 420, 460, and 462 for a total minimum of 17 quarter hours in the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education 299 Students will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. All programs qualify graduates for provisional certification to teach in their areas of preparation. In addition to assuming major responsibility for professional preparation of junior high school and high school teachers, the Department offers the following special programs at the undergraduate level: PREPARATION OF TEACHERS FOR MULTICULTURED SECONDARY SCHOOLS (MULTICUL) The MULTICUL program at Ball State offers young people an opportunity to put words, expressions, and demonstrations into actuality which hopefully will lead toward a possible solution to one of America's most crucial problems, developing racial and cultural harmony. The program is designed not only to deal with black and white relations, but it encompasses as many ethnic groups as possible. Multiculturism is a basic characteristic of our society as well as our schools; therefore, potential teachers should prepare themselves to meet realistic situations. Three of the experiences that the MULTICUL program utilizes in the preparation of potential teachers are as follows : 1. Specialized or elective courses offered in many major departments. 2. Courses designed especially for MULTICUL students by the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. 3. Laboratory experiences in multicultural communities, social and professional organizations, and schools. Along with learning how to understand and how to coexist peacefully with fellow Americans, the participants in MULTICUL should be more employable, not only in Indiana, but across the nation. MULTICUL does not prohibit students from majoring in their areas of interest. MULTICUL is offered as a departmental minor, and it can be scheduled along with any teaching major at Ball State. Departmental minor in the preparation of teachers for multicultured secondary schools, 24 hours EDSEC 100, 200 (4 hrs.), 301, 400 16 hrs. Electives approved by the department 8 hrs. SECONDARY SCHOOL TEACHING Prospective junior high school and high school teachers wishing to gain additional professional teaching skills and understandings may do so by electing a minor in secondary school teaching. Characterized by direct contact with students in public school settings during each year of preparation, the minor in secondary school teaching also provides students with individualized counseling and advisement by fulltime regular faculty from the department. In addition to required competencies in the utilization of instructional media, students are provided with choices from such very important professional areas as high school curriculum, junior high/middle school preparation, innovations in secondary education, evaluation techniques, multi cultural dimensions of teaching, use of the total community as a resource to strengthen teaching, and other similar aspects of teaching which are not required as components in the minimum regulations for certification. Students should register for EDSEC 150, Basic Concepts of Secondary Education, during the first possible quarter on campus. The remainder of the minor in secondary school teaching will follow a pattern which includes: a) Specially designed required courses. b) Individually prescribed preteaching experiences in a variety of schools. c) Courses selected by students to build upon personal strengths and to add specially desired competencies. d) Individual professional advice and counsel. Special highlights of the minor include early and continued direct experience in classrooms, specially designed professional course work, and a total fouryear program directed toward the development of the student's potential as a member of the teaching profession. Additional direct experiences with young adolescents in school and nonschool settings, special courses relating to junior high/middle school curriculum and to effective instructional strategies, and opportunities to learn more about this age group are provided for future teachers. Such programs utilize a large block of time, such as two periods or more, in dealing with broad problems or units of work which cut across subject lines. Usually such programs are planned to provide integrative experiences primarily from the areas of language arts and social sciences. To prepare for core teaching, the student will meet requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum with professional education courses specialized for secondary teaching. BOYS' CLUB PERSONNEL PREPARATION Because of the increasing need for adequately prepared directors and other personnel of the numerous branches of Boys' Clubs of America, officials of the University have worked with the officials of the national organization of Boys' Clubs of America to evolve a pattern for preparation of such personnel. Boys' Clubs of America will provide some fouryear scholarships for selected students. Those who do not receive scholarships will proceed at their own expense. Boys' Clubs, like the public schools, are civic enterprises and are actively involved in the community. Often a staff member of a Boys' Club may also be a parttime teacher in the local secondary school. Because of this likely and desirable relationship and because the preparation for teaching is good preparation for Boys' Club work, this program has been so planned that each student who completes it satisfactorily will meet requirements for recommendation for a certificate to teach in an Indiana secondary school. For Boys' Club personnel preparation the student will meet the requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum with professional education courses specialized for secondary education. Because certain concentration areas provide education especially desirable for the personnel of Boys' Clubs, the student is advised to select a teaching major from the Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education 301 following group : art, business education (option B), English, physical education and health, and social science. Students are advised to select the departmental minor in secondary school teaching or in the preparation of teachers for multicultured secondary schools in order to gain the greatest potential professional flexibility in course selection and application to desired outcomes. Twining, Van Every, Van Tassel The philosophy of special education encompasses the right of all children to participate in educational experiences that will develop their capabilities to the fullest extent. Acceptance of this philosophy by professionally trained personnel has led to an everincreasing demand for additional personnel in the various areas of special education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to certification to teach in the areas of deaf education, mental retardation, and orthopedic and special health problems. These programs are designed in accordance with Indiana teacher certification requirements. Elective courses in special education that are open to future teachers, psychologists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, a course on the education of gifted children, a course on the education of slow learners, and a course on the education of children with learning disabilities. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE DEAF Special education for deaf children was established at Ball State University to assist at the national, state, and local levels in meeting the critical shortage of teachers for deaf children. The lack of academic instructors and professionals in related areas in residential and day schools, as well as in civic and medical centers, provides incentive enough for development of a collegiate program. The teaching area major in deaf education, as well as the teaching minor in special education with deaf children, is designed to prepare teachers for classroom instruction of the deaf. Courses include methodology in language, speech, lipreading, and basic school subjects and are designed with particular cognizance of the expressive and receptive communication barrier created by deafness. Observation of a demonstration class of preschool deaf children provides a laboratory experience early in the program. Student teaching is done at the state residential School for the Deaf in Indianapolis and/or in dayschool programs in Indiana and in neighboring states. Guidance and social counseling of deaf children are included in the program. The Ball State University program in deaf education meets approval of (1) The Indiana Teacher Training and Licensing Commission (providing certification coverage for teaching deaf children in all grades in Indiana), (2) The Conference of Executives of American Schools for the Deaf (making the qualified student eligible, upon application, to teach in the Residential Schools for the Deaf in the United States), and (3) The U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (providing the student with the opportunity to apply for federal scholarships made available to Ball State through this agency) SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE MENTALLY RETARDED Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to nationwide recognition of the special needs of mentally retarded children. To develop to the optimum of their ability, these children need a specially designed curriculum and specially prepared teachers who understand the learning process of mentally retarded children. To help alleviate the continued nationwide and statewide shortage of qualified teachers in this area of exceptionality, Ball State University prepares students to become professionally trained special class teachers. Both a teaching area major and a teaching minor are available to interested students. The teaching minor is also an endorsement for special education : teaching the mentally retarded. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR CHILDREN WITH ORTHEPEDIC AND SPECIAL HEALTH PROBLEMS Within the group of children who have special educational needs are those who are orthopedically handicapped or who have other health conditions which make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for crippled or other healthimpaired children confronts the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a special classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The program is designed to offer comprehensive, professional preparation to future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children, so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers. title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of and individual work with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children.

title: Manual Communications
description: Theory and research underlying the language of signs and fingerspelling (manual alphabet) is considered. Development of receptive and expressive skills in manual communications is required. Prerequisite: SPCED 448 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: An introductory course comparing language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Levels of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight Language for the Deaf, Barry Five- Slate, Wing Symbols, and the Natural Method. Language outlines from different schools are used as supplementary aids.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching subjects such as arithmetic and science.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Special Education
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Student Teaching: Areas of Exceptionality
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 20 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Psychology of Mental Retardation
description: Various types and degrees of retardation. The psychological, environmental, and cultural factors which contribute toward retardation. Emphasis on etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate retarded children. Prerequisites: EDPSY 300 and SPCED 201.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 1
description: Special class organization, curriculum practices and procedures, and the methods and techniques used in the instruction of the mentally retarded. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (2 hrs.), 472.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 2
description: Continuation of SPCED 474, with emphasis on the curriculum. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (4 hrs.), 474.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: This course is designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children. Topics include etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate children with physical disabilities. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 300.

title: Educational Methods with Physically Handicapped Children
description: Special class organization, curriculum, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of orthopedically handicapped children. Prerequisite: SPCED 482; prerequisite or parallel: EDEL 380 and MATH 391.

title: Education of Children with Learning Disability
description: Intensive study of the psychosocial and educational research findings pertaining to the education of children with learning disabilities. Emphasis on current research, appropriate educational methods, and behavior modifications. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, EDPSY 300. CURRICULA: BACCALAUREATE DEGREES General Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 of Curricular Information.) The General Arts Curriculum is a program in general studies and selected concentration areas. It leads to either the Bachelor of Arts or Bachelor of Science Degree. This curriculum is recommended for degree candidates who are undecided about specific educational goals in respect to graduate work, professional schools, and intensive specialization. General Studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 48 hours approved by the department or (2) two departmental minors, 24-36 hours, approved by the departments. Physical education: General courses 6 hrs. Electives: As many hours of credit in electives as are needed to increase the total of hours to 186. t Candidates for teaching licenses for secondary, junior high/middle school, and all grade (except special education and hearing impaired) must take eight hours in two different disciplines outside their major or minor areas. Liberal Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 of Curricular Information.) The Liberal Arts Curriculum provides opportunity for a search for general knowledge and for specialization primarily for development of intellectual capacities. In general studies the range is extensive; in areas of specialization the goal is depth of a sufficiency to demonstrate a degree of mastery in the selected areas. It is also possible in many cases for a student to fulfill the requirements of both the liberal arts curriculum and for teacher licensing. To do so, the student must be enrolled in and meet the requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum as approved by the Teacher Education Committee of Ball State University. Such a decision will require careful choice of courses and planning by the student and the curricular adviser. The degree to which the curriculum leads is the Bachelor of Arts. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Foreign language: One foreign language 24 hrs. f Concentration areas: (1) One departmental major of 45-60 hours and at least one departmental minor of 24-48 hours in another discipline, or (2) two departmental majors of 45-60 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statement of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Professional Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1 -6 of Curricular Information.) The Professional Arts Curriculum provides for specialization to qualify for appointments in specific professional areas or for admission to professional schools which provide more intensive preparation for the desired professional or vocational competency. The degree is the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science. If the major is architecture, the degree is the Bachelor of Architecture; and if the major is landscape architecture, the degree is Bachelor of Landscape Architecture. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 78 hours or more, or (2) a departmental major of 48-96 hours with a departmental minor of 24-36 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statements of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Teacher Education Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees; Teacher Licensing; and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The Teacher Education Curriculum is designed to prepare students for teaching in the elementary, junior high/middle, or secondary areas of the public schools of Indiana. It meets the requirements of the Teacher Training and Licensing Division of the State Board of Education of Indiana. The objectives of teacher education at Ball State University, for which preparation is made on this curriculum are — To help students acquire (a) knowledge and understanding expected of welleducated persons in our culture, (b) respect for learning and people, (c) familiarity with the value systems influencing behavior, and (d) aesthetic appreciations; To assist students in the acquisition of teaching competence in both knowledge and skills related to their areas of specialization; To enable students to understand the way learning takes place and human beings develop; To enable students to acquire a basic knowledge of the relationship between the school and its historical and contemporary settings; To help students demonstrate in their relations with others that they value highly the freedoms and responsibilities of democratic living; To promote in students the willingness and ability to experiment with effective methods of applying their intellectual, moral, aesthetic, and professional learning in practice. The degree on this curriculum is the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science. Undergraduate Programs Description of Course Identification System Each prefix has its own numbering system, with a potential of numbers from 100 through 699. Courses numbered from 100 to 199 are primarily freshman courses. Courses numbered from 200 to 299 are primarily sophomore courses. Courses numbered from 300 to 399 are primarily junior courses. Courses numbered 400 to 499 are primarily senior courses. Courses numbered from 500 up are for graduate students. Courses numbered from 600 to 699 are for graduate students with masters' degrees. In course descriptions the course number is given immediately following the prefix. If a number in parentheses follows, it is the immediately preceding number of the course. The student who has credit in a course under the parenthetical number, or any former number, may not earn credit in the course under its current number except under the terms of Course Repetition (see Credit and Grades). In the course description the number in parentheses following the descriptive title of the course is the credithour value of the course. It denotes the specific total of credit hours which may be earned in the course unless elsewhere in the description is a statement which permits the earning of a larger total of credit hours. Prerequisite refers to a course or courses which must precede the course described. Parallel indicates a course or courses which must be taken simultaneously with the described course. The letter g following the number of an undergraduate course indicates that the course is approved for the earning of graduate credit by eligible students properly registered for the course. Sappenfield The College of Architecture and Planning, established by the 1965 Indiana legislature, is dedicated to the development of professional competency in the functional, aesthetic, and humane design of the physical environment. Two fiveyear programs of study are offered: the departmental major in architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Architecture degree; and the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree. The first two years of both programs are concurrent and include a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. The Ball State general studies program is an integral part of these first two years. The last three years provide specialization in the fields of architectural or landscape design as well as providing for specialized study in areas of the student's own choosing. An environmental design major is offered on the Professional Arts Curriculum for students who have completed the first year of either the architecture or the landscape architecture program and is designed for students who wish to end their studies after four years of university work or who wish to pursue a different program at another school of environmental design. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning represent a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophy. By exposure to the variety of philosophical and technical backgrounds of creative professionals, the students are encouraged to seek their own personal philosophy within a professional teamwork situation. The curricula stress character, devotion, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility. The total program is concerned with the development of a physical environment serving the best of one's aspirations. Department of Landscape Architecture Russell, Chairman; Anderson, Benson, Cascio, Faruque, Geda Landscape Architecture involves the coordinated planning and design of land and is the art of applying scientific principles in arranging objects and spaces upon the land for human use, enjoyment, safety, health and welfare. Landscape architecture is based upon the recognition of long term ecologic, economic, social and psychological values, embracing the conservation of natural resources and the design of land for specific purposes. The landscape architect may be the prime professional consultant for a project and will be assisted by allied professionals such as architects, engineers, planners, ecologists, geologists, hydrologists, biologists, economists, sociologists, and others. Also, he/she may be a member of a site planning team coordinated by one of many allied professions. The landscape architect must be sensitive to human needs and patterns while understanding the potentials and limitations of natural systems — soils, geology, water, vegetation, wildlife, topography, and climate in the effort to solve increasingly complex problems. The undergraduate curriculum stresses a broad base of learning both within the major as well as in supportive course areas. While helping the student to develop basic skills and understanding in landscape architecture, the curriculum is structured to allow concentrations of study in particular areas of interest in allied areas. The General Studies Program in the humanities, natural sciences, social and behavioral sciences combined with opportunities in mathematics, art, directed and professional electives to play a vital part in the cultural and intellectual preparation of young men and women enrolled in this program. The program for these electives must be approved in advance by the department chairman. title: Beginning Typewriting
description: Principles of touch typewriting with emphasis upon technique and fluency. Only students with no credit in typewriting or with less than one semester of typewriting are eligible to receive credit in this course unless special permission is granted by the department head.

title: Intermediate Typewriting
description: Review of typewriting principles with emphasis on the development of speed and accuracy. Problems included on the application of typewriting skill See the professional education requirements for secondary teaching on the teacher education curriculum for the requirement of two additional courses in business education: BEOA 383 and 385. to simple business situations. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one to two semesters of typewriting. Not open to the student who has credit for more than two semesters of typewriting.

title: Advanced Typewriting
description: Advanced problems in typewriting including preparation of business letters, manuscripts, tabulations, rough drafts, legal documents, business forms, and duplicated media; continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or three or more semesters of typewriting.

title: Office Typewriting
description: Office typing problems with emphasis on preparation of materials by various typewritten media; composition of reports, memoranda, and letters; handwritten and typewritten draft copy. Opportunities for original and creative typing. Continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Touch Shorthand 1
description: Touch shorthand theory on stenograph machine. Dictation and transcription of familiar material.

title: Touch Shorthand 2
description: Touch shorthand theory review, advanced theory. Dictation and transcription including new material. Typewriter transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or equivalent and BEOA 121.

title: Touch Shorthand 3
description: Touch shorthand theory review. Advanced dictation and transcription of new material. Typewriter transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 122 and recording ability of 100 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy, and BEOA 112 or equivalent.

title: Typewriting for the Court Reporter
description: Emphasis on preparation of documents of legal offices and courts using technical, legal, and medical terminology. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or equivalent.

title: Court Reporting 1
description: Advanced theory for highspeed reporting of jury charge and twovoice testimony to minimum speeds of 140 words per minute. Prerequisite: BEOA 113, 123, and reporting ability of 120 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy.

title: Court Reporting. 2
description: Advanced reporting and transcription speed development to 180 words per minute on multiplevoice dictation, including legal and technical terminology. Prerequisite: BEOA 214, 221, 228, and reporting ability of 140 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy.

title: Court Reporting 3
description: Advanced reporting and transcription speed development to 200 words per minute on multiplevoice dictation, including legal, technical, and medical terminology. Prerequisite: BEOA 222, 229, and reporting ability of 160 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy.

title: Theory of Shorthand Court Reporting Terminology 1
description: Introduction to writing in shorthand the specialized terms encountered in the legal and technical professions and trades. Prerequisite: BEOA 123.

title: Theory of Shorthand Court Reporting Terminology 2
description: Introduction to writing in shorthand the specialized terms encountered in the medical profession. Prerequisite: BEOA

title: Machine Transcription
description: Designed to teach students to produce mailable copy from transcription equipments. Intensive drill on transcription skills with emphasis on quality production. Application of punctuation, spelling, vocabulary building, letter styles, placement, proofreading, and grammar to the transcription process. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Principles of Business Correspondence
description: Principles and basic elements of effective letter writing with emphasis on the psychological approach, reader viewpoint, positive tone, and appropriate format for personalbusiness letters and job applications.

title: Shorthand Court Reporting Procedures
description: Court reporting procedures pertaining to different court and legal proceedings. Emphasis in preparation of transcripts, marking of exhibits, and use of reference materials needed by the court reporter.

title: Law Office Administration
description: An analysis of the goals, needs, and problems in administering a legal office. Emphasis on systems for processing information and paperwork particularly in the areas of timekeeping, records administration, and word processing.

title: Internship in Court Reporting
description: Reporting in general or court proceedings verified by practicing shorthand court reporters. Prerequisite: BEOA 214, 222, 338, and GBA 263.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 1
description: Fulltime employment for a quarter in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during a quarter and the submission of various employment reports to the supervision by employer and intern. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 2
description: Fulltime employment for a quarter in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirements for BEOA 285. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of Business Education and Office Administration 103 approved, supervised, paid employment during a quarter and the submission of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisite: BEOA 285 or the equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 3
description: Fulltime employment for a quarter in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirements for BEOA 286. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during a quarter and the submission of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Prerequisite: BEOA 285 and 286 or the equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Beginning Shorthand 1
description: Special emphasis upon basic theory with stress on brief forms. Introduction to the skills of writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or the equivalent.

title: Beginning Shorthand 2
description: Completion of basic theory and increased emphasis upon development of skill in taking dictation. A student whose secondary school transcript shows credit for more than one semester of shorthand is not eligible to receive credit in this course. Prerequisite: BEOA 321.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on skill in taking dictation with some emphasis on transcription. Open to those students who have had BEOA 322 and students whose secondary school transcript shows one year of shorthand. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent.

title: Advanced Shorthand 1
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, transcription, and production of mailable copy. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and at least two years of secondary school shorthand or BEOA 323.

title: Advanced Shorthand 2
description: Special emphasis upon production of mailable copy, and continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 or the equivalent and BEOA 324.

title: Introduction to Word Processing
description: Word processing with emphasis on understanding why organizations are adopting word processing. Focus is on understanding of word processing concepts and how they fit into a total information processing network and the handling of paperwork in today's organizations. Special problems are analyzed and programmed for input to standalone text editing typewriters and on computer textprocessing systems. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or equivalent.

title: Electronic Word Processing Systems
description: Basic operation of magnetic media automated typewriters. Comparison of features and capabilities of various automatic typewriter systems. Emphasis on recording, format, editing, temporary and permanent revision, merging, proofreading, and logging. Prerequisite: BEOA 331.

title: Word Processing Applications
description: Emphasis on more sophisticated operations of magnetic media automated typewriters for production of advanced applications. Special attention to problem analysis, coding, programming, and procedures for integration with data processing and other office systems. Simulation of an actual word processing center. Prerequisite: BEOA 231 and 332.

title: Calculating Machines
description: Developing skill in using electronic calculators and other common office calculating machines as tools; emphasis is placed on developing the manipulative skills and programming abilities used to solve problems involving business data.

title: Duplicating, Machine Transcribing, and Filing
description: Preparation of ink stencils and carbon masters; operation of ink and liquid duplicators; training in machine dictation and machine transcription; indexing, coding, and filing of business correspondence; and survey of filing equipment and supplies. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems; the nature, function, and use of business papers; knowledge, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining of records of a business office and study of records administration in business and industry. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Principles of Office Supervision
description: Principles of effective office supervision with emphasis on the function of the office and the role of the office supervisor. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects A
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, typing, general business, and shorthand. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250; student will have completed the requirements in typewriting and shorthand. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option B.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects B
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, general business, typing, and related office skills. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250; student will have completed the requirements in typewriting and accounting. Not open to the student who is enrolled on the teaching major in business education, option A.

title: Methods of Teaching for the Distributive Education Teacher
description: The role of the distributive education teacher in the teaching of distributive, basic business, and bookkeeping/ accounting subjects; the courses to be taught and their objectives; teaching strategies ; instructional materials; and leson unit planing. Prerequisite: AC 31 or 31; ECON 201; EDPSY 251; and at least two courses in marketing. Restricted to students pursuing a distributive education teaching major.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Majors I and H
description: Objectives, planning, methods/techniques, devices for teaching typewriting, basic business and office machines/office practice courses. Prerequisite or parallel: BEOA 338 and completion of typewriting requirements. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Methodology of Relevant Work Experiences in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledges needed by persons who will be supervising and directing a cooperative education or a project plan program in distributive education. Prerequisite:

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Major I
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, devices in teaching accounting; the purposes of business education and its relationship to the total school program; principles, problems, issues, and trends related to program development, implementation, and evaluation. Prerequisite: ACC 202 and EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Major II
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, devices in teaching shorthand and transcription; the purposes of business education and its relationship to the total school program; principles, problems, issues, and trends related to program development, implementation, and evaluation. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum; and BEOA 323, 324, or 325.

title: Techniques of Coordinating Cooperative Distributive Education Programs
description: The special techniques and knowledges needed by a person who will be teaching and coordinating cooperative distributive education programs. Restricted to persons seeking a license as a teacher or coordinator of vocational distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of the department head.

title: The Organization, Management, and Teaching of In-School Laboratory Programs in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledges needed by a person who will be teaching and managing inschool laboratory programs in vocational distributive education. Restricted to students seeking a license as a teacher or coordinator of vocational distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of the department head.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Distributive Education
description: The principles upon which vocational distributive education is organized, administered, and supervised; the kinds of programs; federal and state regulations; relationships to programs in other vocational areas. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking a teaching license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Education
description: The principles upon which vocational education is organized, administered, and supervised; federal and state regulations; agencies which provide delivery systems for vocational education; relationship of vocational education to career education, vocational rehabilitation, and programs for persons with special needs. Prerequisite: BEOA 380, 381, or 382 ; or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 392.

title: Survey of the Vocational Education Program Areas
description: An overview of the six program areas in vocational education. For these areas, the course includes program administration and supervision, objectives, the occupations for which training is offered, curricula, equipment and facilities, student selection, inschool laboratories, field training opportunities, and youth organizations. Prerequisite: BEOA 380, 381, or 382; 393; or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 392.

title: Communications for Business Organizations
description: Techniques used in managementoriented internal and external communications. Emphasis on theory, planning, oral and written presentations, audience perceptions, data organization, media selection, and preparation techniques for business letters; and an overview of reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Business Reports: Written and Oral
description: Techniques for writing managementoriented informal and formal reports; including collecting, interpreting, summarizing, and synthesizing data. Principles for selection of tabular and graphic data presentations. Includes written and oral presentations of functional and analytical reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Employment Communications
description: Determining job requirements and writing a letter of application and resume; letters requesting reference permission, appreciation of interview, acceptance and refusal of position, and resignation. Includes interview techniques. Open to all students.

title: Secretarial Procedures
description: Operational functions of toplevel professional secretarial work through integration of basic skills, knowledges, and the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 323 or equivalent or permission of the department head.

title: Secretarial Administration
description: Administrative and supervisory aspects of toplevel professional secretarial work through planning and organizing office functions to achieve smooth and efficient work flow and with emphasis on the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 451.

title: Word Processing Management
description: Use of word processing as an integral part of the total information processing network. Development of ability to recognize when and how to use word and textprocessing to meet an organization's needs. Study of managerial problems involved in establishing and implementing word processing systems. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department head.

title: Principles of Business and Distributive Education
description: Historical development of the field of business education. Possible future trends and their effect on the entire business education program. Open only to students who have been approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Distributive Education
description: An investigation of the current status, historical development, philosophy, and principles of distributive education. Components include secondary, postsecondary, and adult distributive education, DECA, and general and specialized curricula. Prerequisite: EDPSY 251. Restricted to students pursuing a distributive education teaching major.

title: Independent Study in Business Education, Distributive Education, or Office Administration
description: For students with an excellent academic record who wish to conduct an indepth study in some phase of business education, distributive education, or office administration. The project selected, methods, and credit hours must be approved by the department head and supervising faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Economics Girgis, Chairman; Caron, Cheng, Deitsch, Hannaford, Hyclak, Jost, Keil, Lawson, Lewis, Lephardt, Lynch, McGuire, Morgan, Seeborg, Van Cott, Zegeye Economics is the scientific study of economic institutions and systems. It is a study of human wants and of efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative — relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. It is a useful study in an intellectual sense because it trains students to think carefully and logically about complex social phenomena. By such knowledge it is possible to understand the impact on economic systems and institutions of broad social and economic developments or of new economic policies and the responses of these units to them. Given the complicated economic and social problems of the modern world, an understanding of this subject is important for intelligent citizenship and for practical application in industry, government, research, and the professions. To achieve a basic comprehension of how our economy operates, the department offers a core of courses aimed at providing (1) a sound grasp of the tools of analysis and measurement, (2) an understanding of institutional development and the interrelations of economic and social factors, and (3) an ability to apply systematic analysis and understanding to problems of public policy.
