title: Economics of the Ghetto 1
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. Involved are analyses of production functions; theories of wages, rent, interest, and profits; the principles of international trade and comparative economic organizations; and a general consideration of business ethics.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Economics of the Ghetto 2
description: The economics of poverty in the United States. Includes economic concepts and analysis of poverty in the historical context, economic analysis of contemporary poverty, and analysis of current proposals dealing with poverty in the United States. Prerequisite: ECON 111 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201, MATH 110 or its equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life; surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201; MATH 131, 132 or their equivalent; and MS 320. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 524.

title: Managerial Economics
description: Application of microeconomic analysis to managerial decisionmaking. Emphasis is on the applicability of economic concepts to business decisions. Areas covered include forecasting techniques, demand measurement, production, cost, profit management, product strategy, pricing, and location analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201, MS 320, and MATH 131.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 432.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. Finance 109 At the undergraduate level, the Department of Finance offers two majors leading to either the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science degree. These majors are in finance and general business administration. Finance. Finance is a decisionoriented discipline concerned with the investment and management of money both in the present and in the future. This major is designed to provide the student with a general program in the financial aspects of business including financial management, investments, banking, insurance, real estate, and other related financial areas. Finance courses provide knowledge of concepts, processes, and institutions involved with the financing functions of the business enterprise; acquaint students with the financial instruments, institutions, and markets in the United States and the world; provide the tools and techniques of financial analysis and decision making; and expose the students to sufficient examples of financial decision making to allow them to develop expertise in applied finance. The finance major allows the student to pursue one of three options within the finance major, namely, (1) corporate financial management, (2) financial institutions, and (3) insurance and real estate. The corporate financial management option prepares the student for careers in the finance division of a business firm; such as, systems analysis, budget review analysis, financial analysis, acquisitions analysis, credit management, receivables management, and shortand longterm capital management. The financial institutions option emphasizes employment opportunities in the areas of managing stocks and bonds as a securities broker, portfolio manager, or trust department specialist and in investment banking. This option prepares an individual to work in the field of banking, savings and loan associations, loan companies, insurance companies, credit unions, pension funds, securities brokerage, and real estate brokerage. The third option, insurance and real estate, allows students to develop competence in fields leading to the various professional positions in insurance and real estate. Students also develop a background for making informed decisions relating to business and consumer purchasing in these areas. General Business Administration. This major permits students to concentrate in two of the three areas available; i.e., insurance, management, and finance. Hence, this major provides a broader diversity of vocational opportunities than the finance major but with less depth in any one area of concentration. The course of study includes an examination of the various institutions, structures, functions, organizations, operations, and environments which influence business and economic activities. The finance sequence is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activities. The management sequence is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them, as future business executives and specialists, to deal with diversity of problems which arise in the course of daytoday activities. The insurance sequence is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. Graduates in general business administration are qualified to accept positions as junior executives at the management level in finance, insurance, personnel administration, office administration, production supervision, or other areas. In addition, this degree is particularly attractive to those students who may wish to engage in a small business or who do not wish to commit themselves to a particular vocation at this time. In addition to the above, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students in other areas of the College of Business. Any student in the University may enroll in the course in personal finance, which is offered especially to provide the information necessary for the management of personal incomes, expenditures, and financial resources. The law courses are quite broad, include the fundamentals of many essential law disciplines, and are highly recommended to students in prelaw preparation. title: Estate Planning and Administration
description: An introduction to problems associated with planning for use of financial resources during working life, retirement, and after the death of the principal income producer. Included are techniques for fact gathering, tax principles, use of trusts, and will drafting.

title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law, and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law, and the effect of the law in the areas of consumer credit and economic relationships.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to corporations, partnerships and agencies, in addition to the law of bankruptcy. Prerequisite: BL 360.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principle articles of the Code including sales, commercial paper and security interests, in addition to the areas of creditor's rights and property law. Prerequisite: BL 360.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairman. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Finance 111

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the viewpoint of the consumer. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation.

title: Money and Banking
description: The role of money, credit, and financial markets in the United States financial system ; the structure and functions of commercial banks; the implementation of monetary policy through the Federal Reserve System; financial and banking system structure; international financial transactions. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Principles of Bank Operations
description: Fundamentals of bank operations. A survey of various bank functions including accounting, trusts, demand deposits, savings and time deposits, home mortgage lending, internal controls, international financial services, and public service.

title: Bank Management
description: Trends in philosophy and practice of bank management. The nature and objective of banking ; formulation of objectives and policies; organizational planning, management controls; functions of banks related to management practices policies, and procedures. 253. * Credit Administration. (4) Factors influencing and determining loan policy. Bank credit policies; credit department; sources of credit; credit correspondence; secured and unsecured loans to customers; loans to business; term loans ; interbank loans; real estate loans ; influence of the Federal Reserve System; and responsibilities of bank lending officials.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Principles underlying managerial decisions influenced by capital markets and type of ownership; problems relating to the sources of financing; the study of financial analysis and financial management ; and interrelating economic and accounting theory with other areas of business. Prerequisite: ACC 203, ECON 201, MATH 131. Not open to the student who has credit in FIN 453.

title: Consumer, Business, and Public Finance
description: The great importance in our national life of business credit, personal and consumer credit (including installment sales credit), bank credit, and public credit (federal, state, and municipal). Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: Managerial Finance
description: An analysis of working capital management. Examines the management of current assets such as cash, receivables, and inventories; a review of intermediate and shortterm credit; and a study of general working capital policy. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Problems of investment policy, including the study of types of investments risks, and introduction to security analysis, the analysis of investment requirements, and the kinds of investment policies.

title: Financial Institutions
description: The structure of financial institutions in the American economy. Financial institutions as recipients and as suppliers of funds in financial markets. The identification and analysis of many kinds of financial institutions and the administration of their loan and investment portfolios. Particular emphasis on the asset, liability, and capital management with the goal of profitability. Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some are emphasized. Prerequisite: FIN 250. Prerequisite recommended: senior standing.

title: Capital Management
description: An analysis of the management aspects relating to the inflows and outflows of permanent capital in business enterprises. Examines the management of longterm assets, intermediate and longterm credit, equity, and internal financing. Corporate expansion including mergers, acquisitions, corporate reorganization, and bankruptcies. Includes case studies. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Multinational Business Finance
description: An indepth study of the international financial institutions (central banks, International Monetary Fund, area development banks, etc.) involved with the financial decisions of multinational corporations including an overview of the new developing forces in the field of international finance. Prerequisite: FIN 452.

title: Security Analysis
description: Presents a detailed analysis of selecting securities for various investment purposes. Encompasses industry structure, volumeprice cost relationships, management, financial position, terms of security contracts and market price behavior. A research project is required. Prerequisite: FIN 355.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Finance, students majoring in finance or general business administration will work full time '1' Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business. for a quarter as an intern for a banking institution, business firm, or governmental agency. Written reports are required. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Open only to third quarter juniors or seniors.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Property Insurance
description: Study of fire and allied lines insurance, inland marine floaters, transportation, theft, and liability insurance, and employers' liability and workmen's compensation. Emphasis on management of risks in business and on the use of insurance as a tool for handling these risks. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and/or problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include no fault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, state vs. federal regulation. Prerequisite: INS 370, 371, and 372 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Real Estate
description: A survey of real estate with emphasis on the economic aspects of the development, marketing, and financing of real estate, valuation of resources, location and market analysis, and institutional influences on real estate activities. Attention is given to the growth and structure of urban areas and to emerging trends in all areas. * Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business. Management Science 113 Department of Management Science LaFollette, Chairman; Belohlav, Fleming, Green, Hill, Husain, Koehler, Lauck, Ma, McCullough, McManis, Seeborg, Swart, Terry, Wagoner, Walters, Willoughby Management involves the coordination of human and physical resources toward a purposeful goal. As this statement implies, management is germane to any type of purposive activity. Every organization has managers regardless of what they are called (e.g., managers, administrators, principals, coaches, officers, and chiefs). Therefore, a student who elects to major in management science will be preparing to assume a position of responsibility in a wide variety of profit or nonprofit organizations. The major in management science allows the student to pursue one of four management options: (1) production management, (2) personnel management, (3) information management, and (4) general management. In the production management option, the student obtains the background to assume a position of responsibility in the production of goods and services. The student is introduced to the production functions in detail, taught the methodology of making productionrelated decisions, and acquainted with modern techniques used in motivating and leading personnel in a productionoriented occupation. In the personnel management option, the student obtains the foundation for entering an occupation which relates primarily to the human component of an organization. The student is given an indepth presentation of the personnel function; that is, the student is familiarized with a conceptual framework for analyzing and solving problems involved in the selection, development, and motivation of human resources. In the information management option, the student acquires the background for a position involved in the collection, retention, and dissemination of information. Correct and timely information is needed so that an organization can plan and control its operations. The information management graduate is acquainted with a variety of data processing methods to accommodate this important function more effectively and efficiently. In the general management option, the student is introduced to a varied background in management. General management acquaints the student with the whole gamut of management: production, personnel, information, office management, small business administration, and international management. Some organizations recruit on campus for generalists such as students with the general management option. Others prefer more depth in a specific function such as production, personnel, or information management. The departmental major in management, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for a career in management. title: International Management and Multinational Operations
description: Comparative management practices around the world; international business behavior and problems confronting multinational executives and corporations; analysis of corporate structures and operations in foreign environments. Study of management functions, organizations, structures, policies, operations, and multinational practices and global strategies. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Management
description: The four major managerial functions: planning, organizing, motivation, and controlling, which are applied primarily to the process of management and the organic functions of a business enterprise. Other significant concepts stressed are the importance of leadership, problem solving techniques applied to managerial situations and the aspects of coordination, communication, human relations, and production management necessary for an individual to be successful as a manager.

title: Production/Operations Management 1
description: A basic study of functional fields of production. Decisionmaking and quantitative analysis of production problems arising in areas of methods analysis, work measurement, wage incentives, production planning and control, inventory control, plant layout, materials handling and quality control.

title: Business and Society
description: An interdisciplinary approach toward developing a philosophy concerning the role of business in society. Emphasis on contemporary issues requiring business people to reexamine their role and the role of the corporation in community and national life. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Organizational Behavior
description: Focuses on the dynamics of human behavior in business organizations, with concentration on problems of motivation and leadership. Emphasis is on the behavior of individuals and groups within organizations, and the practical interpretation and management of behavioral phenomena. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Production/Operations Management 2
description: An intermediate study of the functional areas of production. Emphasis on decisionmaking and quantitative analysis of production problems arising in the areas of incentives, production planning and control, inventory control, plant layout, materials handling and quality control. Prerequisite: MGT 383; MS 320.

title: Small Business Ventures
description: Provides essential knowledge for students interested in small business. Topics include searching for venture opportunities; economic, technical, and operational feasibility of the venture; financing; negotiations; and operations. Emphasizes characteristics of the small business enterprise. Prerequisite: BL 360, MGT 380, FIN 350, MKT 370 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Small Business Practicum
description: Teams of students consult with local small businesses. Cases are assigned by Small Business Administration. Students work on problems of the particular small business. Problems may be office administration, accounting, production, marketing, personnel, finance, insurance, legal, or information systems. Prerequisite: senior standing. Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business. Management Science 115

title: Internship in Management
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Management Science, a student majoring in management science will work full time for a quarter as an intern in an organization operating either in the private or public sector. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to third quarter juniors or seniors.

title: Personnel Planning and Selection
description: Focuses on organization and manpower planning. Includes determination of organization and manpower needs, analysis and development of job requirements and necessary qualifications for recruitment and selection, selection procedures, placement and orientation, and evaluation of selection programs. Prerequisite: MGT 481.

title: Personnel Administration
description: How to administer a personnel program in a business organization so as to deal effectively with such problems as selection, training, compensation, promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions; employee services; and industrial relations. Prerequisites recommended: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Case Problems in Personnel Management
description: Case studies depicting complex personnel issues and problems faced by organizations. Provides the student an opportunity to apply personnel policies, theories, concepts, and techniques to actual personnel situations. Prerequisite: MGT 481.

title: Problems in Production/Operations Management
description: An integration of all the production/ operations management principles, theories, and techniques gained from previous courses as applied to actual production problems. Major teaching methods include case study, discussion, and individual projects. Current topics may be discussed. Prerequisite: MGT 386 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Quality Assurance
description: Application of statistical control charts, sampling plans, and reliability analysis to problems of planning, feedback, and control of product quality, process performance, operation effectiveness, and related areas of management activities. Prerequisite: MS 320.

title: Work Design
description: The design of office and industrial jobs to meet the needs and preferences of the worker and the management. Included are methods improvement techniques, layout of work stations, incentive and motivation techniques, and the setting of output standards. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Comparative Administration
description: Comparative analysis of managing complex organizations and service industries; emphasizing environmental and organizational factors affecting the management process, firm structure, and administration functions. Study of administration crossculturally (internationally) and crossinstitutionally (service industries). Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisites recommended: ECON 200 and MGT 380.

title: Case Problems in Office Management
description: Develops skill in identifying the key problem of a complicated office situation and in formulating a practical solution to this problem. The interrelatedness of major office management activities is stressed as well as the broad scope of problems pertaining to the office. Prerequisite: MGT 488.

title: Independent Study in Management
description: An opportunity for supervised study of some phase of management. May consist of an experiment, library research, or an analysis of current management practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Business Applications of Computer Data Processing
description: An introductory course in computer data processing with special emphasis on business problem solving. Includes study of the effects of computers on business and management decisionmaking, of computer hardware and software, concepts and procedures for business systems analysis, and computer programming. Special problems in the areas of accounting, production, marketing, banking, finance, and management are analyzed and run on computers.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 220, or CS 200. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 210.

title: Interpretation of Business Data
description: An introductory course dealing with the collection, analysis, presentation, and interpretation of statistical data. Topics include frequency distributions, sampling, basic probability, decisionmaking, regression and correlation, and time series analysis. Applications are made to problems in the area of accounting, economics, finance, management, marketing, operations, and production. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Quantifying Management Decisions
description: A study and critical evaluation of operations research techniques for solving managerial problems found in business administration. Prerequisite: MS 320.

title: Simulating Management Decisions
description: A study and critical evaluation of simulation techniques for solving managerial problems found in business administration. Prerequisite: MS 220, 320.

title: Management Information Systems
description: Systems theory and practice as they are applied to satisfying information needs for management decisionmakers through the analysis and design of manual and computerbased systems. Influence of information systems upon management and organization as well as upon managerial decisionmaking. Prerequisite: MGT 380, MS 220, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Data Processing Systems and Procedures
description: Emphasizes computerbased systems and business computer applications, ranging from accounting applications to operations applications and an integration of these. Provides an awareness of the procedure in designing computer systems, characteristics, and components of business applications and interrelationships between computer applications. Prerequisite: MS 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Business Statistics
description: The more commonly used advanced statistical methods, with broad coverage of estimation and tests of hypotheses, and including chisquare tests, analysis of variance, and advanced correlation and regression analysis. Prerequisite: MS 320. Department of Marketing Lowry, Head; Baird, Battle, Brown, Moser, Riecken, Sparling, Vanderleest, Yavas Marketing is a business function concerned with the management of the flow of goods and services from the producer to the consumer. The marketing process provides an efficient way for producers to meet the needs of consumers. Marketing activities which a firm performs to satisfy its consumers include offering the right product, promoting it properly, selling it at the right price, and distributing it in the right place. Marketing courses at Ball State University are designed to allow students to develop their abilities to recognize, define, and solve creatively marketing problems. Because the majority of Ball State marketing graduates go directly into business, the marketing curriculum is career oriented. Students majoring in marketing choose one of four options within the marketing curriculum. Each option emphasizes different career opportunities. The sales and advertising management option prepares students for careers in areas such as consumer and industrial product selling, sales training, transportation, purchasing, advertising agency management, and public relations. Career opportunities for students selecting the retail management option include chain store management, merchandising, fashion coordination, small business management, and buying. The marketing planning and research option prepares students for careers in marketing analysis, marketing research management, sales forecasting, advertising research, new product research, and product planning. The general marketing option is for students who want a foundation for a career in the marketing field. After obtaining a foundation in marketing, students are qualified to pursue many different phases of the marketing process. The Department of Marketing, in cooperation with selected business firms, offers a professional practice program which allows juniors and seniors to relate classroom theory to practical experience by working for one quarter in a variety of meaningful assignments. Students who are working as interns receive from two to eight quarter hours of credit and are paid by the firm for their work experience. The Student Marketing Association (SMA) is an organization which provides opportunities for participating in marketing discussions and programs and developing friendships with students who have similar interests. In the past, the SMA has conducted a series of mini- Marketing 117 courses on career planning and has brought selected speakers to the campus to discuss job qualifications and career opportunities in various marketing fields. In cooperation with local civic organizations, the SMA has also conducted studies that have assisted in identifying the market needs of minority groups and senior citizens. The United States Department of Labor indicates that the need for individuals with college level training in marketing will continue to grow. Sales and retail store management opportunities offer the greatest potential for Ball State marketing graduates in the future. For the student interested in preparing for teaching marketing and/or distributive education, it is possible to earn a departmental major in marketing along with the teaching major in distributive education. For the student preparing for teaching business education, marketing is a part of the major and minor areas. Teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. A departmental minor in marketing is available to students with a major in any academic area other than business. title: Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 370. 202. * Salesmanship

description: Introduction to the field of advertising with emphasis on the preparation, appeal, and media selection of retail advertising. Prerequisite: GBA 101. Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 370.

title: Marketing and Consumer Issues
description: Analysis of the consumer issues which affect marketing. Includes the marketing implications of the consumer protection movement. For experience in handling consumer concerns, a practicum is available in the campus Better Business Bureau. Prerequisite: MKT 370 and junior standing.

title: Industrial Procurement Management
description: A basic course in industrial procurement management. Principal topics considered are make or buy analysis, quality and quantity control, value analysis, price determination, sources of supply, the purchasing system, and legal aspects of purchasing. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Credit Management
description: Practices of businesses in granting credit both to other business firms and to individuals. Credit limits, department operations, and collection policies are analyzed. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Buyer Behavior
description: Practical business implications of the various aspects of consumer motivation and behavior. The student is provided with information to understand how and why a buyer reacts in a purchasing situation. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Selling and Sales Management
description: Practices in recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. An analysis of the stages of a sales presentation. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Advertising Management
description: Use of advertising as a communication tool in marketing management. Analysis of media selection production and layout, measurement of effectiveness, and social and economic aspects of advertising. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Retail Management
description: An investigation of store policies, organization, location, layout, buying, stock control, pricing, and sales promotion for retail stores. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Principles of Marketing
description: A basic course that examines marketing as a productive system within our economy. Promotional activities, product policies, retail and wholesale activities, pricing policies, international marketing, and marketing's role in society are studied. Prerequisite: ECON 201 or junior standing.

title: Materials Management
description: The organizational concept that integrates the management of the flow of materials through a business enterprise into consumer markets. Content includes: anticipating, sourcing, obtaining, and monitoring the current status of materials in an enterprise. Prerequisite: MKT 370. Prerequisite recommended: MKT 310.

title: Marketing Simulation Game
description: A simulation game where students are divided into teams or companies. Management in each company makes decisions in marketing, finance, and production. Does not involve writing computer programs or utilizing information from a data processing class. Prerequisite: MKT 370 and junior standing.

title: Promotion Strategy
description: Use of cases and problems to provide experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKT 340.

title: Channel Strategy
description: An analysis of the alternative channels of distribution available to manufacturers and producers. Management decisions necessary for an effective channel organization are stressed with emphasis upon the use of retailing and wholesaling intermediaries. Prerequisite: MKT 350.

title: Survey of Transportation
description: The economics of transportation - internal waterways, railways, highways, and airways in the United States; economic development of various means of transportation and accompanying regulatory problems. Rate, traffic service, and coordination problems of our transportation system. Advantages and disadvantages, trends, and peculiarities of each of the various modes of transportation. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Physical Distribution Management
description: Physical distribution systems in the marketing environment; system components and the total cost approach; customer service objectives; physical distribution systems design and administration. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: International Marketing
description: Examines legal, economic, and cultural factors influencing marketing abroad. Commercial policies, practices, and techniques needed to locate and evaluate foreign markets, as well as the problems of pricing, promoting, and distributing products in international markets. Prerequisite: MKT 370.

title: Marketing Research
description: A basic course in marketing research. Nature and scope of marketing research; scientific method and research design; specific marketing research procedures; techniques of sampling; and research report, followup, and evaluation of research process. Selected applications in areas of motivation, advertising, and product and sales control research. Prerequisites: MKT 370 and MS 320.

title: Quantitative Marketing
description: Exploration of the various quantitative techniques that can be utilized in solving marketing problems. Principal topics considered are linear programming '1' Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business. Marketing 119 methods, game theory, Markov chains, probability theory in decision making, distribution cost analysis, and use of correlation. Prerequisite: MS 320.

title: Marketing Management
description: Marketing by manufacturers as viewed from the marketing manager's position. Principal topics are selecting channels of distribution, determining demand, pricing policies, marketing legislation, advertising policies, and methods of selling. A case study approach. Prerequisite: 12 quarter hours in marketing courses.

title: Professional Practice in Marketing
description: The student receives professional practice during a summer or a quarter as an intern on an approved program with a business firm, government agency, or nonprofit organization under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to thirdquarter juniors and seniors with a major in marketing. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

description: For students who wish to conduct independent study in some phase of marketing. May consist of an experiment, library research, or the analysis of current marketing practices and methods. The departmental programs encompass the following areas: visual communications, photography, interior/environmental design, painting, sculpture, printmaking, ceramics, metal design, weaving, and art education. The undergraduate curriculum offers a core of experiences which help prepare the graduate to enter a particular art profession or graduate school. In the preparation of art educators there is a strong emphasis on teaching methods and curriculum development as well as studio participation with the concept of the artistteacher being emphasized. Courses for the liberal arts student are also offered. These courses provide the nonart major with the opportunity for personal enrichment through the visual arts. Art majors are not required to submit an entrance portfolio but must be prepared to present a portfolio for review and evaluation upon the completion of 18-24 hours of studio courses. Students transferring art credits from other institutions are required to submit a portfolio and transcript of grades to the department for evaluation. The breadth of the field of home economics emphasizes its importance. The eleven separate, but interrelated, fields of foods, nutrition, clothing, textiles, applied art, housing, household equipment, home management, family economics, child development, and family relations provide the foundations for the good health, satisfying and successful living, psychological balance, and good management which are essential for the development of the whole personality. Needs of individuals and families in the social environment of their time are of primary concern in determining the emphases given to the various aspects of home economics. Home economics aids in helping individuals and families to make intelligent decisions concerning all aspects of family life, including the social, economic, aesthetic, managerial, health, and ethical aspects of relations, child development, foods, clothing, and housing. Home economics prepares professional personnel to carry out its objectives through education, research, social welfare and public health, dietetics, and institutional administration and business. It shares with other fields the responsibility for developing perceptive, wellinformed citizens with the ability and the initiative to further conditions favorable to effective living. title: Principles of Home Art
description: Design and color principles, with practical application to home situations. Open to all students except those who have credit in ADS 104.

title: Independent Study
description: Permits the student to select, investigate, and explore more intensively an area of home economics on an independent basis. Extensive reading and the development of research skill are emphasized. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Home Economics Field Studies
description: Designed to combine a background of reading knowledge with field experiences where students will have an opportunity to study special areas of home economics in a particular location. Open to all students with permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Home Economics
description: Involves individual or group studies and experiences. Gives the trainee actual experience under professional standards, regulations, and supervision in the type of home economicsrelated work chosen by the individual student. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Family Life and Nutrition in Early Childhood Guidance
description: Helps leaders and workers in kindergarten or preschool community groups understand the sequential growth and development of young children and the interrelationship of family meal patterns to their physical, mental, emotional, social, and motor growth. May be acquired prior to college entrance. f CHEM 225 is waived as a prerequisite for the departmental major in dietetics. BIO 112 is waived as a prerequisite for the departmental major in dietetics.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Vocational Education
description: The development of vocational education in which principles and philosophies of vocational education are related to program organization, content area, teacher qualifications, leadership preparation, curriculum design, and image. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Home Economics
description: Analysis of pupil needs and the development of a home economics program to meet these needs. Organization of teaching units, selection, and use of teaching methods, and development and use of devices for evaluating pupil growth. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Discipline oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of home economics, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of home economics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: HED 395.

title: Techniques for Implementing the Vocational Home Economics Program
description: Major emphasis on curriculum, resources, and facilities for vocational home economics programs to meet the needs of various categories of students ; management techniques, public relations activities, and professionalism included. Prerequisite: HED 392, 395 and 399.

title: Coordination of Cooperative Programs in Vocational Education
description: A study of how to coordinate class instruction and work experience ; includes selecting and recruiting students, selecting training stations, role of the coordinator, techniques of coordination, and placement and follow up of graduates. Prerequisite: HED 392, 395, 399, 492.

title: Meal Planning and Food Preparation
description: Designed for the non -home economics major. Basic principles of food buying, food preparation, and table service, along with the study of nutritive value of food. Foods and service for different social occasions. Not open to the student who has credit in HFN 110.

title: Food Preparation
description: Fundamental principles underlying the preparation of food. Correct techniques and methods of preparation stressed. Open to men and women.

title: Experimental Foods
description: Effects of different ingredients and/or methods on quality of products studied. Emphasis placed on recognition of a standard product and ability to recognize reasons for failure to achieve a standard product. Application of scientific principles to manipulative techniques of food preparation stressed.

title: Meal Management
description: Principles and fundamentals of planning, preparing, and serving nutritionally adequate, appetizing, and aesthetically appealing meals, with emphasis on resource management and on the purchase and storage of food. Attention given to foods and types of table service suitable for various occasions. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Nutrition
description: Emphasis on fundamental principles in nutrition and application to diets for children and normal adults.

title: Menu Planning for Quantity Food Service
description: Principles of nutrition applied to feeding of individuals and groups. Major emphasis is placed on menu planning for institutions with consideration given to meeting nutritional needs. Limitations or problems relating to personnel, facilities, and type of patronage also stressed.

title: Practicum in Institutional Administration and Accounting
description: Stressed are the organization structure, application of principles of scientific management, and personnel administration. Experiences in actual laboratory situation in quantity food production kitchens on campus under supervision of home economics and food production personnel.

title: Practicum in Food Service Planning—Layout and Equipment
description: Designing and equipping of food facilities for schools, colleges, hospitals, industries and commercial operations. Experiences in actual laboratory situation in quantity food production kitchens on campus under supervision of home economics and food production personnel.

title: Practicum in Quantity Food Production and Purchasing
description: Offers opportunity for insight into factors related to quantity production and purchasing of foods. Experiences in actual laboratory situation in quantity food production kitchens on campus under supervision of home economics and food production personnel.

title: Nutrition and Dietetics 1
description: A study of the nutritive value of foods and the utilization of food in the human body. The nutritional needs of people throughout the life cycle will be investigated. Prerequisite: junior/senior level standing or a major in nursing, food management, or dietetics technology, or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Community Nutrition
description: Designed to acquaint the student with nutrition problems and nutrition programs at the federal, state, and local levels. Practical experience will include Home Economics 131 investigation, observation, and participation in nutrition programs in the local community. Prerequisite: HFN 340.

title: Therapeutic Dietetics
description: Principles of dietary modification needed by individuals with certain disease conditions. Prerequisite: HFN 340. Not open to the student who has credit in HFN 441.

title: Quantity Food Production
description: Problems involved in quantity food production, distribution, and storage. Laboratory experience in university food service units. Prerequisites: HFN 220 and 340.

title: Institutional Administration and Accounting
description: Problems pertaining to school lunchrooms, hospitals, and cafeterias as to personnel, management and organization, cost control, and apportionment of labor. Field trips to institutional kitchens.

title: Institutional Equipment, Buying, and Layout
description: Stationary and small food equipment considered. Layouts of institutional kitchens planned. Field trips to institutional kitchens and equipment companies.

title: Experimental Foods
description: Experimental studies of the different foodstuffs so that their composition and physical and chemical properties can be understood. Recipes are investigated and methods of combining foods are developed and evaluated. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Nutrition and Dietetics 2
description: Advanced course in nutrition emphasizing the utilization of metabolism of nutrients at the cellular level in the human body. Current research in the field of nutrition will be included. Prerequisite: HFN 340 and CHEM 231.

title: Diet in Disease
description: Pathological conditions resulting from various nutritional diseases, with emphasis upon causes and effects of malnutrition and its treatment. Planning and preparation of diets for abnormal conditions. Hospital laboratory experience provided. Prerequisite: HFN 340.

title: Seminar in Dietetics
description: The professions involved in food service and dietetics; the roles and responsibilities of personnel and their relationships with other professionals; the standards to be attained; the code of professional ethics and the resources for continuing professional education. Prerequisite: 2 hours of credit in HE 498 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Maternal and Infant Nutrition
description: Information about maternal, prenatal, and infant (birth to 36 months) nutrition; nutritional requirements of expectant mothers and infants investigated. Emphasis is placed on readings in current periodicals. Prerequisite: HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Child Nutrition
description: Principles of child nutrition (preschool through adolescence); nutritional requirements of children and problems in nutrition will be investigated. Current professional periodicals will be researched. Prerequisite: junior standing, HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geriatric Nutrition
description: Nutritional needs of older adults will be discussed based upon physiological and social changes and research in the field. Students will review some recent literature in the field, evaluate the food intakes of elderly citizens in certain stituations, and study and evaluate nutrition programs designed for older adults in terms of meeting nutritional needs. Prerequisite: HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Quantity Food Purchasing
description: Information needed by quantity food buyers; important considerations in purchasing foods and corresponding factors that determine them. Emphasis on ethics in buying.

title: Home Care of the Sick
description: Includes concepts which affect the quality of life of individuals and families in prevention of illness, current major health problems and their costs, and procedures to follow when illness occurs.

title: Child Development
description: Emphasis on the preschool child as a member of a family group. Includes principles of natural growth and development and child guidance based on the physical, social, emotional, and intellectual needs of the preschool child. Students will participate and observe in various early childhood programs and centers. Open to all students.

title: Infant Development
description: Processes of growth and development during the first two years with various physical, social, and emotional aspects being emphasized. Open to all students.

title: Family Relations
description: Interpersonal relationships of family members, the forces impinging upon them today, and the changes that result in home and family living, courtship, and mate selection; preparation for marriage, marital adjustment, and parentchild relations. Open to all students.

title: Assisting with Family Problems
description: The major areas of adjustment in marriage and family relationships, problems of adjustment and philosophy and practice of techniques for clientcentered assistance with family problems.

title: Family Housing
description: Selection of housing to meet family needs. Evaluation of house plans for convenience, art qualities, and satisfying family life. Legal and financial aspects for home ownership. Open to all students.

title: Interior Design and Home Furnishing
description: Selection and arrangement of home furnishings to create attractive, functional interiors that are in harmony with the exterior of the home and adapted to family needs. Open to all students.

title: Home Management 1
description: Management of family and community resources to achieve desired goals in the family. Emphasis on the management problems encountered by newly married couples in establishing a home. Open to all students.

title: Household Equipment
description: Selection, use, and care of household equipment. Students will have an opportunity to plan, organize, and present demonstrations on household equipment.

title: Home Management 2
description: Residence in the home management house offers opportunity to make practical application of the principles of homemaking. Prerequisite: HHM 220.

title: Problems in Consumer Buying
description: The economic aspects of purchasing for the consumer, including marketing conditions, consumer credit, agencies that protect the consumer, and factors to consider when buying consumer goods and services. Open to all students.

title: Clothing Construction for Non-Majors
description: Fundamental techniques applied in the construction and fitting of simple garments. Not open to the student who has credit in HTC 104.

title: Clothing Selection and Construction
description: Clothing selection and wardrobe planning. Fundamental principles of construction and their application to simple garments.

title: Creative Stitchery
description: Learn creative skills in stitchery by embellishing existing fabrics or originating new ones. Techniques include macrame, crocheting, knitting, simple weaving, tie dyeing, stenciling, batik, quilting, appliqueing, trapunto, embroidery, needlepoint, rya braided and hooked rugs. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Tailoring
description: Selection and construction of tailored garments and advanced clothing problems. Prerequisite: HTC 104.

title: Motivations of Fashion
description: A history of fashion from its earliest beginnings to the present. Explores the factors — social, political, psychological, economical, technological — which have motivated what was worn at any given time. Open to all students.

title: Apparel Design by the Flat Pattern Method
description: Adaptation of standard patterns to individual porportions, designing of garments and creating an original garment by the flat pattern method. Prerequisite: HTC 104 and 203.

title: Textiles
description: Textiles and their components as they relate to care, performance, and consumer satisfaction. Open to all students.

title: Textile Testing
description: Experience in planning and conducting textile tests and in evaluating resulting data; development, present status, and importance of textile testing. Prerequisite: HTC 330 or ADS 222.

title: The Fashion Industry
description: The business of fashion through design, manufacture, distribution, merchandising, promotion, and the consumer. Explores career possibilities. Open to all students.

description: Special problems to meet students' needs in the clothing field. Unit on preparation of illustrative material for the teaching of clothing. description: A focus on the broad range of processes utilized in the construction industry. Students learn about and engage in activities related to managing, designing, building, and maintaining structures.

description: An introduction to and an understanding of our complex industrial and technological society with emphasis on modern industrial organization, materials, processes, and related socioeconomic factors, including the development of manufacturing processes from crafts to automation. Laboratory experiences of a groupproblem type developed around typical industrial processes. Open to all students except those with teaching areas in industrial education.

description: Manufacturing processes used by industries to convert raw materials into consumer products.

description: Focuses on the industrial activities of research, development, and product engineering as it relates to manufacturing enterprises. description: Advanced study of the American industrial complex with emphasis on designing and developing teaching materials and activities appropriate to class goals. Activities will be predominately studentidentified problems or research. Prerequisite: IED 361.
