title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man's place in nature is the central theme of the course. The relationship of man to other animals, especially monkeys and apes, is stressed. ANTH 100 may serve as prerequisite for departmental majors in Anthropology. Anatomy and behavior, and their interdependency, are presented within an evolutionary framework.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: The origin of man and the rise of civilization as revealed by the discovery of the antiquities of the past. Explanation of recent chronometric and established classical dating methods, how sites are excavated, and archaeological remains are interpreted.

title: Introduction to Language and Linguistics
description: The nature of human language as an object of scientific study, focusing on both the biological and sociocultural bases of language and its structure. Emphasis on language and thought, linguistic analysis of language structure, social and geographical dialects, and language families of the world.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family, kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Bio-Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological,and cultural evolution.

title: Anthropology—Culture and Women
description: The structure of women's role in various types of societies, from hunting and gathering to urban communities. In the light of these societies the western movement to liberate women from their traditional roles may be better understood. As industrialization reaches its peak the rigid sexual division of labor gives way to the female role being modeled after the male's.

title: North American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North America. Each culture is described in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: Peoples and Cultures of the World
description: An introduction to the way of life of primitive and modern peoples of the world from North America, South America, Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and the Pacific Islands. Topics discussed include religion, family life, economics, education, politics and the arts.

title: Material Culture
description: The material manifestations of culture, stressing primitive technology. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Afro-American Anthropology
description: Afro-American cultures and their relationships to the larger societies in which they are integrated. Specific problems relevant to wider questions of theory and methodology in anthropology.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Latin America
description: A general survey of the peoples of Mexico, Central America, and South America. Societies discussed range from the ancient Maya, Aztec, and Incas to modern Indians, peasants, and city dwellers. Topics discussed range from religion, family life, and the arts to modernization, urban social problems, and revolution. 390. (399). Honors Colloquium in Anthropology. (2) Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to Honors Program students only or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Osteology
description: A laboratory course dealing with the human skeleton. Topics covered are: osteological terminology, identification of whole and fragmentary bones, standardized measuring techniques, and the assessment of the age, stature, sex, and race of a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 100.

title: Races of Man
description: The present status and an historical survey of the concept of race as it applies to human populations. Ways in which human populations biologically differ from each other and the adaptive nature of such variation. The distribution and antiquity of living races. Prerequisite: ANTH 100, 120, or 160.

title: Race, Racism, and Ethnicity
description: Scientific investigation of the biological nature of race, race beliefs, and racism, an extreme expression of ethnic bias. Particular attention to the Western world, but similar attitudes in other parts of the world are also considered.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man from his nonhuman primate ancestors. The primate fossil record, with particular emphasis on those forms in the human lineage, and the human fossil record. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or 204, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs. Anthropology 201

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Summer Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation: sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Field observation and interpretation are stressed. Requires full time in the field.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Utilization of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Advanced Archeological Field Methods
description: Advanced methods of excavation and field recording studied at the excavation site. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Midwest is traced through the Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: Traces and describes the archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic to the Historic Period.

title: European Prehistory
description: The prehistory of Europe from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age with an emphasis during the later, protohistoric period on the archaeological and ethnographic evidence from the regions to the north and west of the Classical World. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: Cultural Resource Management
description: Covers the special problems of what has also been called conservation archaeology, including relevant federal and state laws, regulations, and agencies, reconnaissance and sampling methods; project budgeting; elements in the environmental impact statement; and other responsibilities of the consultant archaeologist. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120, 421 or equivalent.

title: Personality and Culture
description: Introduction to a major area of anthropological interest and investigation during the past three decades. This field of anthropology has grown out of recent efforts to unite studies of individual behavior and group, or cultural behavior. Involves discussion on the nature of human personality and its origins, both in the individual and the species. Particular stress on the phenomenon of the model personality type.

title: Peoples and Problems of Modern Africa
description: The course is intended to acquaint the student with the vast, complex, and still comparatively littleknown continent of Africa. More particularly it will enable students to acquire a systematic body of knowledge concerning the increasingly significant role which Africa plays in the modern world.

title: Religion, Culture, and Society
description: An investigation of theories of the possible origins of religious behavior and experience; various types of religious practitioners; and aspects of institutionalization and function of religion in selected societies.

title: Social Organization
description: Opportunity for depth study of man's social systems. Emphasis on the function of these systems and important grouping principles. The crosscultural method is employed extensively.

title: Anthropological Theory
description: Historical development of concept and theory in anthropology. Various theoretical viewpoints and schools of thought will be examined intensively. Prerequisites: ANTH 100, 160, and 120.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the impact of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents with European civilization.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Peoples of the South Pacific
description: A general survey of the ethnography of the peoples of Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia. Selected field studies will be examined in terms of the functional method and acculturation theories for which oceanic cultures and societies provide a most suitable and viable laboratory.

title: Field School in Ethnography and Ethnology
description: Methods of carrying out field research in cultural anthropology; techniques of establishing contact and rapport; interview and observation methods; problem formulation, data recording, and data preparation. The student may spend fullor halftime in the field. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Culture Change
description: Discussion focuses on the major processes of cultural change such as cultural evolution, revolution, ecological adaptation, conquest, diffusion, mass communications, economic aid and development, and other timely and appropriate topics.

title: The Development of Near -Eastern Cultures
description: Traces the development of cultures in the Near East as revealed by archaeology and explores the present -day cultural variability.

title: The Peoples and Culture of India
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the anthropology (social organization, cultural system) of South Asia with special stress on India.

title: Introduction to Folklore
description: An introduction to the genres of folklore with an emphasis on the anthropological study of folktales, legends, and myth; methodological and theoretical approaches to their study; their function in society; and their usefulness to anthropologists. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Anthropology
description: Focuses on that dimension of social interaction which involves the articulation and aggregation of interests within the political community. Emphasis on primitive and peasant communities (smallscale societies) drawing parallels to western society where appropriate.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to a formal) view of economic behavior. Focus on social organizational units such as lineages and clans which in primitive and peasant societies are engaged in productive and distributive activities.

title: Anthropology of the Film
description: Focuses on function and content of the ethnographic film from its inception to the present. Some contemporary documentary films will also be screened. Stress on treating the media of film both in terms of its capacity to create a visual culture in contemporary society and the direct recording of primitive and peasant lifestyles.

title: Applied Anthropology and Community Development
description: Designed for persons who might become involved in planned change situations. Offers the conceptual framework and field experience to apply anthropological concepts and field research techniques to the identification and solution of practical human problems at the local level. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 160 or SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Art and Anthropology
description: Provides a crosscultural coverage of major preliterate art traditions and introduces students to art in cultural contexts.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Acquaints the prospective teacher with basic concepts in cultural anthropology and provides the conceptual and analytical tools to understand whatever cultural setting he or she might be involved in. Examines ways in which cultural institutions, e.g., family, religion, politics, economy, might impinge on educational processes.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Field Anthropology of Distant Areas
description: Anthropological field study of distant geographical regions. Exploration and field work may be involved and travel to the staging area will probably be by airline.

title: Medical Anthropology
description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating nonwestern techniques to its western counterparts. Specific contents of this comparison involves theories of disease causation, cultural taxonomy of therapeutic techniques and cure, and analysis of the role of the medical specialists (practitioners) in selected societies. Finally, the meeting together of western and nonwestern traditional and modern medicine will be assessed in terms of cultural evolutionary theory. Department of Biology Norton, Chairman; Adalis, Allamong, Ball, Bennett, Bernhardt, Crankshaw, Eiser, Engstrom, Hale, Hendrix, Hendrickson, Kirkpatrick, List, McComish, McElhinney, Mertens, Nash, Nisbet, Olsen, Senft, Smith, Stevenson, Torke, Warnes, Welker, Wise, Zimmack The programs of the Department of Biology are designed to develop appropriate levels of competence in biology for three groups of students: (1) students who wish to prepare for positions in teaching, biological research, or particular fields of biological specialization; (2) students who are interested in obtaining a liberal education; and (3) students who need basic preparation in biology for the parabiological fields of medicine, pharmacy, veterinary medicine, dentistry, medical technology, cytotechnology, and nursing. Common background is provided for majors through a "core program in biology. - The required courses of the core are organized with three levels of emphasis. The first level is designed to develop understanding of basic principles and biological processes which are common to living organisms. The second level focuses on organisms and is concerned with problems of structure, function, and classification in specific groups of plants and animals. The third level is concerned with developing understanding of interactions and adaptations of organisms in contexts ranging from world biome organization through molecular organization. In addition to the basic background work provided by courses in the core program, the department offers specialized course work in biology, botany, zoology, and science to meet the needs of particular individuals and groups. Opportunities for research participation are available at both the advanced undergraduate and graduate levels. The student who plans a career in teaching secondary school biology should take the teaching major in science (biology primary area) or the teaching minor in biology. The student enrolled as a science (biology primary area) teaching major is encouraged to take a second major in general science or a minor in chemistry. These combinations not only greatly increase employment possibilities but also contribute significantly to the understanding of biology. Students who plan careers in college biology teaching and/or research may follow either the teaching major in science (biology primary area) or the departmental major in biology. Such students should anticipate the requirements for graduate work in biology in addition to the major in biology. In general these recommendations are: 1. Proficiency in at least one foreign language. French, German, or Russian are almost universally recommended; some institutions also accept Spanish. 2. Chemistry through the organic sequence and preferably a course in biochemistry, 3. A year of college physics. 4. Mathematics through the calculus sequence. The student who wishes to specialize in either botany or zoology may do so by following the departmental minor in botany or the departmental minor in zoology. These minors are designed to provide professional work for the student who has completed basic course work in biology and chemistry. Liberal arts students who elect to include a concentration area in biology in their curriculum will follow either the departmental major in biology or the departmental minor in biology. Nursing majors on Option I take the departmental minor in biological sciences for nurses. To prepare to do laboratory work in bacteriology, pathology, chemistry, and other scientific fields necessary in the diagnosis and treatment of disease, the student will take the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in medical technology. To prepare to work in the area of aquatic biology students should pursue the curriculum described in the departmental major. The following courses are recommended as electives: BIO 480, 481, 482, 498; BOT 481; ZOOL 332, 341, 444, 447, 483, and 484. To prepare to work in the area of wildlife biology students should pursue the curriculum described in the departmental major. The following courses are recommended as electives: BIO 498; BOT 380, 481; ZOOL 332, 340, 341, 444, 446, 447, 483. To prepare to work in the area of microbiology, students should pursue the curriculum described in the departmental major. The following courses are recommended as electives: BIO 331, 341, 344, 360, 361, 446, 457, 482; BOT 446; ZOOL 447, 480. The student who wishes to become a candidate for the National Registry of Microbiologists (ASM) should pursue the curriculum described in the departmental major. The following courses are recommended as electives: BIO 331, 341, 344; BOT 446; ZOOL 480; CHEM 225, 230, 231, 360; MATH 110. The student who wishes to become a candidate for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry at the close of three years of predental preparation but wishes also to qualify for a baccalaureate degree from Ball State University will complete the requirements for the departmental major in predental preparation. MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY The senior year (45 hours) of the major will consist of twelve months of hospital technical medical laboratory training in the ASCP approved school of medical technology. The following courses are recommended for elective credit on the major: ANAT 430; BIO 311, 344, 361; CHEM 300, 325; and PHYCS 110, 112, 114, 310. During the three years at Ball State University, the student pays the usual University fees and is subject to general regulations of the University. In the senior year students are required to pay no fees to the University. They must provide books and uniforms required by the school of medical technology. The 52 weeks course is an integrated lecture and laboratory clinical experience. Two weeks of vacation are included. The University has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with Ball Memorial Hospital, Muncie, Indiana; St. John's Hickey Memorial Hospital, Anderson, Indiana; St. Joseph's Memorial Hospital, Kokomo, Indiana; St. Francis Hospital, Beech Grove, Indiana; Lutheran Hospital and St. Joseph Hospital, Ft. Wayne, Indiana; Methodist Hospital and St. Vincent's Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana; and St. Elizabeth's Hospital, Lafayette, Indiana. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to our schools exceed the capacities of the schools. Selection of students is made entirely by the schools of medical technology — based upon several factors including scholastic standing, personal interviews, and recommendations. Premedical technology students are therefore encouraged to plan a second or alternate degree choice. To qualify for certification as a medical technologist, the student must submit evidence of successful completion of the clinical year plus an official transcript from the University indicating date of conferral of degree, with a major in medical technology, to the National Registry of Medical Technologist of the American Society of Clinical Pathologists in Chicago, Illinois. The student must then pass the national registry examination. The medical technologist is prepared to do laboratory work in any area of the clinical laboratory including bacteriology, chemistry, serology, and blood bank. There are positions calling for this preparation in hospital laboratories, physician's and surgeon's clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories. Also, there are opportunities for work in research laboratories and in commercial companies making biological products. Departmental major in medical technology, 63-65 hours ANAT 210; BIO 111, 112, 211, 213, 341; CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114), CHEM 225, 230, 231, 360; PHYSL 210; ZOOL 447; and 4 hours of credit in MATH 110, 111, or 112 63-65 hrs. PREMEDICAL PREPARATION The student who wishes to qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine at the close of three years of premedical preparation will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 142 hours of liberal arts credit in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credits earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Medicine (45 hours) to meet senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit in the first three years: SPCH 210; foreign language (12 hours in one language); BIO 311, 411; CC 214; and ZOOL 447. Except when required to complete an undergraduate major, courses in human anatomy, human physiology, bacteriology, biochemistry, pharmacology, hygiene, or public health will not be accepted by the School of Medicine as part of the 142 hours of liberal arts credit. The student who prefers to obtain a baccalaureate degree before entering Indiana University School of Medicine will do so by completing all of the work on the Professional Arts Curriculum. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in premedical preparation, it is highly recommended that the premedical student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry, or in any other area in which the student has a strong interest, because the number of applicants to a school of medicine far exceeds the capacity of the school. In following this recommendation, the student will be better prepared for graduate work in these areas in the event entrance into medical school is denied. Students contemplating a career in medicine should bear in mind the stiff competition in the field, and if they have not exhibited keen interest and aptitude in high school courses, especially in science, it will be very difficult for them to meet successfully the high standards required for premedical work and admission to medical school. The student who wishes to obtain a degree and prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will follow the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum, will elect a teaching area major or teaching major, and will combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. Thus the student prepares for teaching in the field of the elected teaching concentration. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: SPCH 210; foreign language (12 hours in one language); BIO 311, 411; CC 214; and ZOOL 447. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many medical schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other medical schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet specific requirements of the medical schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of the firstyear medical school credits on the Ball State University major is Indiana University. Students should take the Medical College Admission Test in the Spring Quarter fifteen months ahead of their expected entrance into medical school. Premedical counseling is available in the Department of Biology. Departmental major in premedical preparation, 62 -67 hours BIO 111, 112, 211, 312; CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114), CHEM 225, (230, 231, 232) or (233, 234, 235), 300; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ZOOL 330 62-67 hrs. PREDENTAL PREPARATION The student will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credit earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Dentistry (45 hours) to meet the senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: AED 200, BIO 213, CHEM 232, CC 214, SPCH 210, and courses in business management. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in predental preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many dental schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other dental schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet the specific requirements of the dental schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of firstyear dental school credits on the Ball State University majors is Indiana University. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in predental preparation, it is highly recommended that the predental student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry, or in any other area in which the student has a strong interest because the number of applicants to a school of dentistry far exceeds the capacity of the school. In following this recommendation, the student will be better prepared for graduate work in these areas in the event entrance into dental school is denied. Further, students should be aware that preference is given to applicants with four years of undergraduate work. One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory performance on the Dental admission test given by the American Dental Association. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the admission test. The test should be taken one year in advance of the student's expected entrance into dental school, but preferably only after completing the required biology and chemistry. Predental counseling is available in the Department of Biology. Departmental major in predental preparation, 57 hours ANAT 320; BIO 111, 112, 211, 311; CHEM 110, 111, 112, 230, 231; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ZOOL 330 57 hrs. PREPHARMACY PROGRAM The Prepharmacy Program is for those students who wish to apply for admission to the College of Pharmacy of Butler University or the School of Pharmacy of Purdue University. The courses designated, when completed satisfactorily, will meet the preprofessional curricular requirements of Purdue at the end of the first year or those requirements of Butler at the end of the second year. At both Purdue and Butler the prepharmacy, plus pharmacy, program is a total of five years. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to a college of pharmacy exceeds the capacity of the school and that a selection of students is therefore necessary, taking into consideration such factors as scholastic standing, character, and professional aptitude. The student's attention is directed to the admission and residence requirements set forth in the Bulletins of Butler and Purdue Universities. These prepharmacy programs do not lead to graduation from Ball State University. They merely provide a student with an approved sequence of courses for the first one or two years of the complete fiveyear program. Furthermore, physical education is not a part of this program for students who plan to transfer to Purdue, but it is for those who will go to Butler. A student who drops out of the prepharmacy program and elects to follow a degree program of Ball State University will be expected to meet the physical education and general course requirements of the elected University curriculum. A careful arrangement of the program for each year is essential in order that courses may be completed in sequence and in the allotted time. It is particularly important that the general chemistry be completed in the freshman year. Copies of the programs may be obtained from the Chairman of the Biology Department or the member of the Biology Department appointed by the chairman to serve as preprofessional adviser for students on these programs. There are minor differences in requirements between the School of Pharmacy at Purdue and the College of Pharmacy at Butler. Students planning to apply to Purdue's School of Pharmacy should make arrangements early in the Autumn Quarter to take the Pharmacy College Admission Test.

title: Man and the Life Sciences
description: Basic biological ideas and knowledge aimed at an understanding of the life processes held in common by all organisms. The physical basis of life, development, heredity, and evolution, and consideration of current biological problems confronting man. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 102 or 111.

title: Biological Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles of biology as they relate to energy requirements and reproductive processes of living organisms, including the study of plant and animal adaptation as it influences survival and natural selection. Principles of ecology and conservation with emphasis on the human role in the environment. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Field and Classroom Experiences in Biology for Teachers
description: Basic biological relationships of plants and animals as they exist in the environment and basic recognition of important members of the plant and animal kingdoms. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Principles of biology including the physical basis of life, cell structure and function, genetics, reproduction, development, evolution, ecology, and systematics. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 100 or 102.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Continuation of BIO 111. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Honors Symposium in Biology
description: An examination of some of the critical biological issues confronting contemporary society. Open only to freshmen participating in the Honors Program or others with permission of the department chairman or the director of the Honors Program.

title: Animal Biology
description: Major animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Biology
description: Major plant groups with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative protozoa, bacteria, viruses, fungi, and algae. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation with emphasis on meiosis, the mechanisms of heredity, Mendelian principles, linkage and crossingover, mutation, and the nature of the hereditary material. Some attention to human and applied genetics. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Normal development in plant and animal systems. Synthesis of current knowledge of the factors contributing to the development of a single cell into a differentiated organism in addition to the related phenomena of metamorphosis, regeneration, and growth. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212 (or permission of the department chairman); and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ecology
description: The relation of organisms to their physicalchemical environment and to each other. Plant and animal societies. Some attention to human and applied ecology. One weekend field trip required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 212, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 325, NR 101, or 325.

title: General Virology
description: Fundamentals of plant and animal virology. Physical and chemical properties of viruses; virushost interactions; pathogenesis of viral diseases. Replication, isolation, and identification of viruses with emphasis on tissue culture systems. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Bacteriology
description: Bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques in culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisites: BIO 213, and CHEM 130 or 230, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Immuno-Virology
description: General immunology and general virology with emphasis on practical experience in technique in the laboratory. The interrelationship of immunology laboratory techniques and viral growth techniques. Prerequisite: one course in microbiology and one course in organic chemistry.

title: Microtechnique 1
description: Methods and preparation of biological materials for teaching and research, including work in hematology, vital staining, photomicrography, and preparation of smears, squashes, and whole mounts. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and two courses in college chemistry.

title: Microtechnique 2
description: Preparation of sectioned tissues and histochemical treatment of materials, including the preparation of paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Recommended for students in research or in medical or laboratory fields. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213, and 12 quarter hours of college chemistry.

title: The Teaching of Biology in the Secondary School
description: Philosophy and methods in biology teaching. Emphasis on laboratory investigations. Concepts and conceptual schemes in biology. Levels of organization in secondary school biology courses. Evaluation of learning in biology. Supplies, equipment, and facilities. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum and 20 hours in biology content courses or permission of the department chairman.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Science oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of science, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of biology in the secondary school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Up to five hours experience in public schools may be required. Prerequisite or parallel: BIO 395 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 399.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Designed to integrate and enhance understanding of basic principles of biology. Recent discoveries in biology and their implications in the biological sciences are stressed. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including the nature of the organization of the cell, cell environment, plasma membrane and transport, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisites: BIO 211, 212, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Radiobiology
description: The use of radiation equipment and radioactive isotopes in the biological sciences. Experiments and projects involving living plants and animals. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212, CHEM 130 or 230, and PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Biophysics
description: The study or description of biologic phenomena in terms of contributing physical events with laboratory emphasis on physical methods of studying the structure of biologic molecules and physical forces important in biologic systems. Topics include: laws of thermodynamics, properties of macromolecular solutions, transport processes, electrophoresis, absorption and emission radiation, ultrasound, principles of various chromatographic procedures. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; CHEM 130 or 230; and MATH 112.

title: Evolution
description: The principles of evolution. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Cytology
description: Structural organization of the basic unit of living organisms in both plants and animals. The cell, cytoplasmic organelles, the nucleus, mitosis, and meiosis. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 212.

title: Applied Microbiology
description: The study of microorganisms that cause beneficial or detrimental changes in food, dairy, and industrial products. Microbiological principles involved in the study of microorganisms in food, dairy, and industrial production in addition to production methodology. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Mankind
description: Current problems in human heredity. Chromosome aberrations and developmental abnormalities. Radiation, drugs, and human chromosomal defects. DNA, genetic coding, and sickle cell anemia. Marriage of relatives and genetic defects. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems associated with genetic engineering.

title: Molecular Biology 1
description: The mechanisms which coordinate and control the activities of microorganisms. Emphasis on recent research in bacterial genetics, the nature and origin of DNA and RNA, protein synthesis, enzyme mechanisms and controls, and permease systems. Prerequisite: BIO 411 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Molecular Biology 2
description: The interrelationships of metabolic pathways, with particular emphasis on bacteria. Emphasis on the use of energy, activation processes, and biosynthetic mechanisms. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Museum Techniques
description: Methods of preparing plant and animal specimens for display. Maintenance of museum records. Use of museum materials for educational and research functions. Taxidermy not included. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Limnology
description: The dimensions of the physical, chemical, and biological factors of inland waters. One twohour laboratory per week and two or three fullday field trips will be devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 313 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Water Pollution Biology
description: Water pollution with emphasis on analysis of trophic structure in polluted and nonpolluted ecosystems. Ecological change and eutrophication as affected by pollutants from industrial, municipal, urban, and rural sources. Prerequisite: BIO 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Aquatic Microbiology
description: Microorganisms indigenous to aquatic ecosystems and their role in nutrient cycling. Emphasis on organisms involved in nitrogen, sulfur, carbon, and iron transformations. The morphology, physiology, and ecology of specific organisms will be discussed. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Marine Biology
description: Introduction to marine environments. Properties: seawater, hydrodynamics. Phytoplankton/benthic plants. Primary production, nutrient cycles. Marine animals, surveys of major taxa, food resources. Adaptations for life on the bottom, open water, intertidal zones, estuaries, abyssal regions. Population sampling and analysis. Problems of overexploitationlpollution.

title: Internship in Medical Technology
description: The fourth year of the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in medical technology consists of a fiftytwo week rotating internship, gaining theory and experience in an affiliated clinical laboratory. Approximately two thousand clock hours are spent in laboratory and classroom lectures, discussions, and demonstrations. Prerequisite: completion of the third year of the Professional Arts Curriculum with a major in medical technology. A total of 45 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Bioethical Decision -Making
description: Analysis of bioethical problems such as evolution, genetic engineering, food and famine, generated by the application of biological and biotechnological knowledge and research using a confluent, developmental methodology. Prerequisite: junior standing and the completion of Option II of the general studies science requirement or permission of the department chairman.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Anatomy
description: Origin and structure of cells, tissues, and organs of higher plants. Prerequisite: BIO 212.

title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
description: The indentification of native flowering plants. Emphasis on the distinguishing features of the major plant groups and use of manuals. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Forestry
description: Study and identification of native trees. Problems of general forestry and forest conservation. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Paleobotany
description: Morphology and anatomy of fossil plants. Correlation of extinct and living plants with emphasis on evolutionary trends. Prerequisite: BIO 212 and BOT 330 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Morphology
description: Forms, life cycles, and evolution of the major plant groups. Prerequisite: BIO .212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ornamental Plants
description: Identification and uses of ornamental trees, shrubs, and vines. Selection, special characteristics, adaptability, and maintenance of ornamentals.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the propagation and cultivation of plants in homes, schools, gardens, and greenhouses.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on pathogenic forms. Methods for identification of fungi will be discussed along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequsite: BIO 341 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants as related to plant structures and environmental influences. Prerequisites: BIO 212, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Intermediate Plant Physiology
description: A continuation of BOT 451. A treatment of selected physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BOT 451.

title: Dendrology
description: The identification and site characterization of woody plants with a n emphasis on Midwestern tre species. Utilization of botanical features and keys in field identification. Correlation of species with site factors, plant diseases, climatic parameters, associate species, and geographical distribution. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection and identification of plants from fresh water and semiaquatic habitats. The importance of the various encountered plant species in the food webs of various wildlife species. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary School
description: Recent elementary science texts, courses of study, and supplementary books are examined. Development and use of science teaching units. The use of experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and other special methods.

title: The Teaching of Science in the Junior High School
description: Recent curriculum developments in junior high school science. Science curriculum instruction related to the physical, mental, and emotional characteristics of the junior high school student. Prerequisite: 36 hours of credit in courses in the sciences.

title: History and Philosophy of Science
description: The history of natural science. Emphasis is given to the influence of science on general philosopy.

title: Comparative Vertebrate Anatomy
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and relationships of vertebrates. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Invertebrate groups. Phylogeny, comparative morphology, and life histories. Thee lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisites: BIO 211, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ornithology
description: Birds. Field identification, classification, behavior, and economic relationships. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisites: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 211.

title: Ichthyology
description: The study of fish with emphasis on identification, classification, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Indiana species will be emphasized but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The behavior of individuals and of populations. The economic relationships of mammals. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Animal Parasiotology
description: Helminth and arthropod parasites of animals. Emphasis on identification, life cycles, and hostparasite relationships. Prerequsites: BIO 211 and 213, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Field Zoology
description: The field study of animals: terrestrial and aquatic; invertebrate And vertebrate; microscopic and macroscopic; with emphasis on collection and identification of Chemistry 211 noninsect invertebrates. Three twohour fieldlaboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Protozoology
description: An introduction to aspects of the morphology, physiology, ecology, and development of protozoa. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on the terrestrial vertebrates of the United States. The management and harvest of wildlife. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identification, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasis placed on aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress. Prerequisite: ZOOL 341 or permission of the department chairman. Minor programs for prospective teachers, health scientists, and others are available, as are courses meeting the needs of students in medical technology, nursing, dietetics, natural resources, physics, predental, preengineering, prepharmacy, premedical, and other programs requiring a background in chemistry. A twoyear curriculum leading to an associate degree in chemical technology is available for those wishing to complete a less intensive program of study in preparation for industrial employment as technicians. Student research is encouraged and fostered at both undergraduate and graduate levels in six fields: analytical, biological, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry, and in chemical education. They may inquire at the Chemistry Department office concerning the procedure to be followed. title: Man and Chemistry
description: Nonmathematical treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as: organization of chemistry, language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature of matter, classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these to everyday living. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: General Chemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Description of elements and compounds; their structure, bonding, and stoichiometry with the main emphasis placed on the solution chemistry of electrolytes. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly.

title: Organic and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of both organic chemistry and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures, one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 105 or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 111.

title: General Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, and the nature of matter stressed. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 110, including properties of solutions, colloids, chemical kinetics, chemical equilibrium, and electrochemistry. Prerequisite: MATH 110 and CHEM 110 or the equivalent. Chemistry 213

title: General Chemistry 3
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemistry of metals and nonmetals, carbon compounds, nuclear structure, and radioactivity. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Prerequisite: MATH 111 and CHEM 111 or equivalents.

title: Chemical Principles 1
description: A comprehensive treatment of the fundamentals of chemistry, with emphasis on periodic relationships and stoichiometry. For science and preprofessional majors requiring more than one year of college chemistry. Class, 3 hours; prelab, 1 hour; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry or permission of the department head. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 111 or equivalent.

title: Chemical Principles 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 113, with emphasis on solutions, chemical kinetics, energetics, and equilibria. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Three lectures, two threehour laboratories weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 111 or 113.

title: Survey of Organic and Biological Chemistry
description: A broadly based introductory course suitable for life science, natural resources, and general science majors. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 2 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 111 or equivalent.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements, including gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations, ionexchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visible spectrophotometry. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 6 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: The aliphatic hydrocarbons and their derivatives, including nomenclature, chemical and physical properties, and their practical application. Three lectures, one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 230, including optical activity and the chemistry of carbohydrates and proteins. Prerequisite: CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of aromatic hydrocarbons, heterocyclic compounds, natural products, dyes, medicinals, and plastics. Prerequisite: CHEM 231.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material deals with covalent bonding, molecular structure, and the chemistry of elementary organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 233. Lecture material covers the chemistry of common functional groups, stereochemistry, and the carbohydrates. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 233 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 231.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 234. Lecture material covers the chemistry of amines and phenols. Selected advanced topics will be discussed. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 234 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 232.

title: Chemical Calculations
description: Treatment of practical chemical problems of widely varied mathematical types, including dimensional and error analysis, graphical presentation, chemical examples of simple calculus procedures, series, and symmetry. Class, 2 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 161 or 170 or equivalent.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentation: electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods. For chemical/medical technologists or departmental minors. Class, 1 hour; prelab, 1 hour; laboratory, 4 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 225.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: The thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three lectures and one fourhour laboratory weekly, including a onehour discussion period. Prerequisite: CHEM 225, MATH 172, and one year of college physics.

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 343. Prerequisite: CHEM 343.

title: Physical Chemistry 3
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 344. Prerequisite: CHEM 344.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions, and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics. Especially for chemistry minors, premedical, biology, general science majors, and chemistry teaching majors with permission of the department chairman. Three lectures and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114 and CHEM 300 or MATH 161 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 343.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry
description: Chemistry of biological compounds, their metabolism, and the regulation of metabolic processes. For students in life sciences, dietetics, or medical technology. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or equivalent. Not open to departmental majors in chemistry.

title: Scientific Glass Working
description: Laboratory work in the fundamental techniques of glass working. Prerequisite: CHEM 230 or 233 and junior standing.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for chemical technologists. Assignments equivalent to 10 clock hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of the department head. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry.

title: The Teaching of Chemistry in the Secondary School
description: A study of current chemistry curricula, laboratory safety, multimedia materials development, professional organizations, lesson planning with performance objectives and integrated sciences. Required for all teaching majors and teaching minors in chemistry. One lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: 20 hours of credit in chemistry. Prerequisite or parallel: SCI 395 or an equivalent course in another subject matter field.

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Preparation and evaluation of scientific manuscripts and their oral presentation. One twohour discussion session weekly. Prerequisite: 30 quarter hours of chemistry or permission of the department head.

title: Chemical Instrumentation
description: Theoretical principles and application of selected chromatographic, spectroscopic, and electroanalytical methods, with illustrative experiments. Class, 2 hours; prelab, 1 hour; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite or parallel: CHEM 345 or 346 or permission of the department head.

title: Analytical Chemistry
description: Analytical sampling, separations, statistical treatment of experimental data; selection of experimental methods; multicomponent analysis of complex materials: rocks, minerals, alloys, industrial mixtures; organic quantitative analysis. Class, 4 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 420 or permission of the department head.

title: Qualitative Organic Analysis
description: Theory and practice of structure determination of organic compounds by classical and spectroscopic methods, including separation and identification of components of mixtures. Prelab, 2 hours; laboratory, 8 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Physical-Organic Chemistry
description: Theoretical aspects of structure, including resonance and molecular orbital descriptions of electron distribution, aromaticity, symmetry, stereochemistry, and effects of structure on reactivity in acidbase reactions. Class, 4 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: The chemistry of the elements, including the relationships of chemical properties and atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, acidbase theories, chemical periodicity, and modern theories of coordination compounds. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or 234, and MATH 161 or 171, or CHEM 300.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 1
description: Chemistry of and techniques for isolation, purification, and identification of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. For students majoring in chemistry, life sciences, and premedicine. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 2
description: Biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolic patterns of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids; metabolic interrelationships. Three lectures and one discussion period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 463.

title: Independent Study and Research
description: Scientific investigation on an individual basis under the supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, experimental work, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. No more than 4 hours may be counted as upperdivision electives on any departmental major.

title: The Teaching of Physical-Earth Science in the Secondary School
description: Study of science instructional models, performance and objectives, testing and evaluation; science classroom and laboratory management; multimedia materials in science instruction; science education trends. Four hours of class discussion weekly. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum; and 20 hours of credit in chemistry, earth science, or physics.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Scienceoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of science, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of physicalearth science in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Up to five hours experience in public schools may be required. Prerequisite or parallel: SCI 395. Criminal Justice and Corrections 215 Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections Neiman, Chairperson; Brodt, Carlie, Clear, J. Hewitt, L. Hewitt, Martin The Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections offers a broad range of courses relevant to our system of adult and juvenile justice for both the preprofessional and the liberal arts student. The departmental major leads to a Bachelor of Science degree when combined with required and elective courses in other areas. The Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections also offers a two year Associate in Arts degree and a departmental minor. The departmental major provides the student with a body of knowledge about the organization, structure, and function of the constituent elements comprising our society. The student also gains a perspective about such areas as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, and our system of criminal justice. Additionally, the student is presented with a workable combination of theory and practical experience in the areas of law enforcement and corrections. Another objective of the criminal justice and corrections major is to give students the opportunity to prepare themselves as preprofessionals for first level positions in law enforcement, probation, parole, and institutional or community treatment settings, or for future graduate study in related areas. The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and employment: law enforcement, probation services offered by both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. Law enforcement officers are employed at three levels of government: local, state, and federal. Local law enforcement officers include municipal police men and women as well as deputy sheriffs. On the state level, all states hire officer candidates for state police departments. On the federal level, approximately forty agencies employ persons with training in law enforcement as well as in other areas of specialization. The increasing need for law enforcement in our society indicates that future employment, particularly on the local levels, will be good. Probation, which is essentially supervision of adjudicated adult criminals and juvenile delinquents, is a service offered by almost all of our adult felony and juvenile courts. Probation officers are employees of court and as such are involved in persontoperson contact with a variety of offenders. Every state maintains a variety of correctional institutions and programs for adult and juvenile offenders of both sexes. These range from open institutions with a minimum of security to maximum security institutions for adult male offenders. In addition, such facilities as youth camps, diagnostic and reception centers, and work release centers are integral parts of most state systems. Employment opportunities for both men and women range from custodial officers to caseworkers or counselors within the various settings. Parole supervision is generally a function of a state administration agency, such as a Parole Board or a Division of Parole, and may vary from state to state. Parole is essentially the supervision of offenders once they have been released from a state institution or facility. Parole officers aid the offender in his return to civilian life in a variety of ways ranging from helping with employment and living arrangements to providing counseling in personal problems which may affect the parolee's successful adjustment. In recent years there has been an increase in the number of facilities and agencies, essentially communitybased, which offer employment to persons interested in rehabilitating delinquent and criminal offenders. Group foster home, regional or local detention centers, and day treatment centers, as well as a variety of halfway houses, are just a few examples. Field Experiences The Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections has created a program which offers a maximum of choices in practical work experiences. The department offers two Practicum courses, one of which is required for graduation. The student has a choice between a placement in the field of corrections or the field of law enforcement. The choice should be made on the basis of student interest and employment goals. The Department also offers two elective internship courses. The student may elect to have four entirely different field experiences if scheduling permits. Electives in Criminal Justice and Corrections or Sociology 12 hrs. Departmental minor in criminal justice and corrections, 32 hours SOC 100 4 hrs. From: 200 level SOC courses 4 hrs.
