title: Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
description: Provides students with an overview of the criminal justice system as well as a preview of vocational opportunities. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 242. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 250.

title: Data and Theories of Crime and Delinquency
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior, typologies of crime and criminals; the trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and current theoretical explanations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 242. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 450.

title: Processing Adult and Juvenile Offenders
description: Emphasizes the juvenile and adult justice systems, their components, recent changes, and future developments. Prerequisite: CJC 210.

title: Fundamentals of Law Enforcement
description: An examination of sociological research and theory bearing on major social factors that affect municipal police organizations as important coordinating agencies in society. Emphasis on: institutional context of police activity, bureaucratization of police professionalization, judicial decisions and the police role, police militancy, and the police and community change. Prerequisite: CJC 101. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 251.

title: Introduction to Corrections
description: A beginning course in penology with emphasis on the three major components: police, courts, and correctional institutions including their history, philosophy, and current programs, policies, and problems. Prerequisite: CJC 101, 211. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 452.

title: Organized Crime
description: The nature and structure of organized crime in America with special emphasis on the history and changing images of organized crime, its operation and activities, and programs for control.

title: Criminal Law
description: Emphasis on the practical aspect of the application of Indiana criminal law for present and prospective criminal justice practitioners: purposes and functions of the substantive criminal law; historical foundations; the limits of the criminal law. Prerequisite:

title: Criminal Evidence
description: Emphasis on current Indiana criminal procedure and rules governing admissibility of evidence, as well as procedural considerations affecting arrest, search, and seizure. Focus will be on the case study approach. Prerequisite: CJC 320.

title: Criminal Investigation
description: Deals with the fundamentals of investigation; crime scene search and recording; collection and preservation of physical evidence; scientific aids; modus operandi; sources of information; interview and interrogation; followup and case preparation. Prerequisite: CJC 320.

title: Police - Community Relations
description: Analysis of interrelationship between police and public in the study and control of crime. Consideration is given to problems of policecommunity relations and to ways of establishing cooperation between police and various social, economic, and ethnic groups. Prerequisite: CJC 101. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 345.

title: Correctional Institutions
description: An indepth inquiry into the function, structure, and operations of American adult and juvenile correctional institutions. Prerequisite: CJC 260.

title: Probation and Parole
description: The organization and operation of probation and parole systems in the United States, with emphasis on Indiana. Topics will include history, law, ideologies, varieties of practice, evaluation, contemporary problems, and future trends in probation and parole. Prerequisite: CJC 101.

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: Limited to majors in criminal justice and corrections, to explore in depth and to summarize current problems, theory, research, and trends in the field. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of the department chairman. Open only to students majoring in criminal justice and corrections. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 456.

title: Police Principles and Procedures
description: Provides students with a basic understanding of police organization and management procedure. Prerequisite: CJC 230. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 340 or 350. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 346.

title: Practicum in Law Enforcement
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in police settings on the local and state levels. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. Open only to students with a major in criminal justice and corrections. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 454.

title: Internship in Law Enforcement
description: A summer internship involving fulltime individual assignments under field supervision in a variety of law enforcement settings. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in CJC courses and permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Corrections
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in correctional settings on the state and local level. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to students with a major in criminal justice and corrections. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 453.

title: Internship in Corrections
description: A summer internship involving fulltime individual assignments under field supervision in a variety of correctional settings. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in CJC courses and permission of the department chairman.

title: Independent Study in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: An individualized course of reading or limited research designed to allow majors an opportunity to explore specific topics related to the entire criminal justice system under the direction of a specific faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Open only to students majoring in criminal justice and corrections. Department of Economics Girgis, Chairman; Caron, Cheng, Deitsch, Hannaford, Hyclak, Jost, Keil, Lawson, Lewis, Lephardt, Lynch, McGuire, Morgan, Seeborg, Van Cott, Zegeye Economics is the scientific study of economic institutions and systems. It is a study of human wants and of efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative — relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. It is a useful study in an intellectual sense because it trains students to think carefully and logically about complex social phenomena. By such knowledge it is possible to understand the impact on economic systems and institutions of broad social and economic developments or of new economic policies and the responses of these units to them. Given the complicated economic and social problems of the modern world, an understanding of this subject is important for intelligent citizenship and for practical application in industry, government, research, and the professions. To achieve a basic comprehension of how our economy operates, the department offers a core of courses aimed at providing (1) a sound grasp of the tools of analysis and measurement, (2) an understanding of institutional development and the interrelations of economic and social factors, and (3) an ability to apply systematic analysis and understanding to problems of public policy. College of Business students can select the economics major, business option (see Curricula below). The business option major is designed for those choosing a professional career in business and requires 90 hours of course work, part of which satisfies the core requirements of the College of Business. The liberal arts major is comprised of 48 hours, part of which may be taken in other departments. In addition, the department offers a departmental minor which students may elect as well as an interdepartmental mathematical economics major.

title: Economics of the Ghetto 1
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. Involved are analyses of production functions; theories of wages, rent, interest, and profits; the principles of international trade and comparative economic organizations; and a general consideration of business ethics.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281. 62 hrs. 20 hrs.

title: National Income Analysis
description: The substance of the course is macroeconomic theory. Major stress will be on the meaning and measurement of national income, output and employment, the Keynesian system, inflation, and the theory of investment. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: The Price System and Resource Allocation
description: Investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing and output and resource pricing and employment in the various market structures. Graphic techniques are developed without recourse to higher mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Economics of the Ghetto 2
description: The economics of poverty in the United States. Includes economic concepts and analysis of poverty in the historical context, economic analysis of contemporary poverty, and analysis of current proposals dealing with poverty in the United States. Prerequisite: ECON 111 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201, MATH 110 or its equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life; surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201; MATH 131, 132 or their equivalent; and MS 320. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 524.

title: Managerial Economics
description: Application of microeconomic analysis to managerial decisionmaking. Emphasis is on the applicability of economic concepts to business decisions. Areas covered include forecasting techniques, demand measurement, production, cost, profit management, product strategy, pricing, and location analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201, MS 320, and MATH 131.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 432.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting.
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. In each of these areas the Department of English has definite responsibilities not only to its own majors and minors but also to all other Ball State University students. Literature provides a perspective gained only through intimacy with the thoughts and feelings of writers of all times and all cultures. To help students gain this perspective, the Department of English offers a wide variety of courses in American, British, and world literature. There are at least two good reasons for becoming better acquainted with how one's own language works. One is that a knowledge of various patterns of language should contribute to a facility in writing and speaking. Equally important, however, is the fact that the history and structure of our language are important parts of our cultural heritage. Realizing the increasing necessity for successful college graduates to express themselves clearly in writing, the Department of English requires all students to develop skill in expository writing. This is a primary purpose of both general education classes and the classes in advanced composition. For students interested in creative writing, special courses are provided on both the undergraduate and graduate levels. These students are also encouraged to contribute to the Department's literary magazine, Grub Street, and to compete for annual awards made possible through the Royalty Memorial Fund and Lambda Iota Tau, the English honorary fraternity. title: English as a Foreign Language
description: Stress on sounds, structure, and vocabulary of English in order to increase the student's facility in use of the language. In addition to class instruction, students will receive individual help in a language laboratory. Cannot be counted toward general education requirements in English. Nonnative speakers of English who wish to pursue either undergraduate or graduate studies are required to demonstrate proficiency in English by examination. Those with deficiencies will enroll in English 100 until proficiency is demonstrated. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 103 or 104.

title: Literature and Composition for Foreign Students
description: Written and oral composition through reading, discussion, and interpretation of selected pieces of literature. Continued attention to the problems of syntax, pronunciation, and vocabulary which are difficult for foreign students. (This course is the equivalent of ENG 103 for foreign students.) Prerequisite: ENG 100 or satisfactory score on proficiency test in English as a foreign language.

title: Fundamentals of English Composition
description: Special attention to the problems of grammar and mechanics. Required of all students with a score of 360 or lower on the SAT verbal examination and who ranked in the lower half of their high school class as prerequisite for ENG

title: English Composition 1
description: Introduction to composition with an emphasis on language problems, sentence and paragraph writing, the development of essays in such rhetorical modes as description, narration, and elementary exposition, and on the discussion of illustrative readings. Specific competencies will be identified at the beginning of the quarter and measured at the end of the quarter. Prerequisite: none, except for the student who is to satisfy the ENG 102 requirement.

title: English Composition 2
description: Further instruction in composition with an emphasis on such rhetorical modes as exposition, argument, and persuasion, and on the discussion of illustrative readings. Introduction to elementary research methods. Specific competencies will be identified at the beginning of the quarter and measured at the end of the quarter. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: English Composition 3
description: Continued development of composition skills through critical analysis, oral and written. Further instruction in the use of research materials. Specific competencies will be identified at the beginning of the quarter and measured at the end of the quarter. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: Honors Humanities 1: Western Thought from Homer to Dante
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and general thought of the Greek, Roman, and Christian civilizations through the Middle Ages.

title: Honors Humanities 2: Western Thought from Montaigne to Rousseau
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and science during the Renaissance and through the eighteenth century.

title: Honors Humanities 3: Western Thought from Dostoyevsky to Sartre
description: Some major writing in literature, philosophy, and science from 1800 until the present.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of world literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 206.

title: Survey of World Literature
description: A survey of the literature of western civilization, exclusive of English and American literature for students who are majors or minors in English. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 205.

title: American Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: British Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of British literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar and Usage
description: Basic course in English grammar and usage for the student whose knowledge of grammatical terminology, structure, and usage is deficient. Not to be counted as part of the total hours in a major or minor program in English.

title: Advanced Composition and Creative Writing
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for the general student, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation; and instruction in creative writing, particularly fiction and poetry. Open only to English majors and minors, except by permission of the department chairman. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent, and sophomore standing.

title: Report Writing
description: Discussion of principles of organization, structures, and style in writing reports and papers. Intensive practice in writing different types of reports and papers. Designed primarily for students pursuing the General Arts or the Professional Arts curriculum.

title: Advanced Expository Writing
description: Intensive study of the essay and guided practice in the techniques of expository writing for students not majoring or minoring in English. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206. Not open to the students with areas in English.

title: Introduction to American Literature
description: Introduction to selected American writers and their works with an emphasis on those that junior high/middle school teachers should know and be able to read skillfully. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to British Literature
description: Introduction to selected writers and periods in British literature with an emphasis on those that junior high/middle school teachers should know. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: American Literature, 1607 - 1860
description: A survey of American literature from the beginning through the middle nineteenth century. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature: Beginnings to 1780
description: A study of British poetry and non -fiction prose from their beginnings to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 260 and 270.

title: English Literature of the Middle Ages and Renaissance
description: Emphasizes major works of a number of the literary figures of the period in their historical and philosophical contexts. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature of the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries
description: An extensive study of English literature of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, or from 1600 to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds of the periods. A close reading of the works of major writers is emphasized, but not to the exclusion of the works of minor writers. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature: 1780 to the Present
description: A study of British poetry and non -fiction prose from 1780 to the present, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206, and 250.

title: Literature and Film Adaptation
description: Studies selected short stories, novels, and dramas drawn primarily from English and American literature and the films adapted from them. Designed for students preparing to teach in the junior high/middle school and secondary school. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: Selected Topics in Language and Linguistics
description: Selected works in relation to certain themes, issues, and problems. Emphasis on class discussion, student participation, and the use of appropriate media. Topics will vary from section to section, quarter to quarter. Designed especially for nonmajors and nonminors in English. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials in teaching language attitudes, habits, and skills. Consideration of written and oral expression, language usage, spelling, writing, and literature.

title: Literature for Young Children
description: An introduction to recent literature for young children. Of special interest to students of early childhood education and to parents and/or future parents.

title: Modern English Grammar
description: Modern English grammar, with emphasis on the application of the methods of uptodate descriptive linguistics to an understanding of basic grammatical terminology, relationships, and structure, including morphology (wordbuilding) and phonology (sound system).

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: The English Language: Past and Present
description: An introduction to the history and structure of the English language: a survey of important historical changes in the structure of English; a scientific study of the structure of modern English; and a survey of the dialectal variations in modern English.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of the field of children's literature and an intensive study of types at various levels. Junior or senior standing recommended.

title: American Literature, 1860- 1960
description: A survey of selected writers and the various literary movements in America during the last hundred years. Prerequisite: ENG 240. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: Nineteenth -Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinback, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth -Century American Drama
description: The themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twentieth -Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Language Arts in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching language arts in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite: EDJHM 312 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Language Arts Methods in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Discipline oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of language arts, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of language arts in the junior high/middle school. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: ENG 350.

title: Literature of Black America
description: An investigation of the literature written by black authors in the United States. Those authors to be studied will be determined by the instructor on the basis of literary merit.

title: American Indian Literature
description: A literary study of short stories, novels, and poetry by 20th century American Indian authors, with supplementary background readings in mythology, tales, and poetry from the oral traditions. The emphasis will be on works by American Indians, but some works about Indians by white authors may also be included.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to 1642
description: English drama from medieval times to the closing of the theatres in 1642, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Drama of the Restoration and Eighteenth Century
description: English drama from 1660 to 1780, including plays of Dryden, Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve, Steele, Goldsmith, and Sheridan.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenth century novels including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the Brontes, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Drama of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: A wide range of British drama, from Shelley's The Cenci, to Tennyson's Becket, to the plays of the Angry Young Men, with special attention given to the works of Shaw, Synge, Barrie, and O'Casey.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to Honors students. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching English
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in the teaching of composition, language, and literature in the secondary school. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Teaching the English Bible as Literature
description: Teaching resources and selections from the English Bible designed especially for students preparing to teach the Bible as literature in English classes in junior high, middle school, or senior high school. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: English oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of English, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of English in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: ENG 395.

title: Special Topics in World Literature
description: Special research topics in world literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Special Topics in English Education
description: Emphasis on current issues and problems at the elementary, middle, junior high, or senior high school level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or equivalent.

title: Special Topics in American Literature
description: Special research topics in American literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or equivalent.

title: Special Topics in British Literature
description: Special research topics in British literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Independent Study in English
description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in English. Prerequisite: 36 hours of credit in English on the 200-level or above at Ball State University and permission of the department chairman.

title: Creative Writing Workshop
description: The fundamentals of the short story, such as the use of language, image, and structure. Emphasis on the student's ability to write clearly and dramatically. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Fiction Writing Workshop
description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop
description: Practice, analysis, and criticism of the craft of poetry, with attention to prosody, traditional form, significant idea, the life of the poetic imagination, and the state of the art. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104.

title: Independent Study in English Education
description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in the field of English education, preschool through the secondary level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206 and permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading Literature in the English Classroom
description: Provides an overview of the process of reading, literature and the principles underlying effective reading of various types of literature. Practical suggestions for developing skills and correcting problems within the English classroom.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in the secondary school. Emphasis on the actual reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical aspects.

title: Short Story
description: The short story as a type of world literature. Not open to students with areas in English.

title: The Essay
description: Representative essays by English and American authors. Not open to students with areas in English.

title: American Folklore
description: Materials and techniques for presenting the American heritage of folklore and folk literature at the public school level. Books, films, filmstrips, recordings, and pictorial collections are among the materials studied.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 1: Theory
description: The psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in second language teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel: ENG 420 or 321.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 2: Materials and Practice
description: An application of theories of language learning to preparation of materials in English as a second language and their use in the classroom. Students will work with students of English as a foreign language in a tutorial or laboratory situation. Prerequisite: ENG 436.

title: Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of transcendentalism. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Poe, Hawthorne, Melville
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a student of the philosophical and literary implications of romanticism. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twain, James, Adams, Crane
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of the varieties of realism. Prerequisite: ENG 340.

title: American Literature, 1945 to Present
description: A survey of the works of major writers and literary trends in America since World War II. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Renaissance and Seventeenth -Century Studies
description: The nondramatic literature of the Tudor, Stuart, and Puritan periods (1485-1660), exclusive of Shakespeare and Milton. Major writers such as Spenser, Donne, and Jonson will be considered in terms of their influence and of their political and philosophical backgrounds.

title: Chaucer
description: A study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several of the minor poems. Emphasis upon the structure, the sources, and the significance of the works included. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare 1
description: An introduction to Shakespeare, consisting of an intensive study of six to eight plays (Richard II, A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Merchant of Venice, Julius Caesar, Hamlet, Measure for Measure, King Lear, The Tempest) and a selection of the sonnets.

title: Shakespeare 2
description: A study of at least eight plays (comedies, histories, tragedies), drawn from all periods in Shakespeare's artistic development, and possibly some sonnets. English majors and minors electing both Shakespeare 1 and 2 should take them in sequence.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Restoration and Augustan Periods
description: An extensive study of the nondramatic works of Dryden, Swift, and Pope, with possible supplementary readings from other British authors of the period 1660-1745. Attention will be given to philosophical, aesthetic, and political currents in the works studied and to the distinctive character of Neo-Classicism. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Milton
description: A study of Milton's family background, political service, and poetic apprenticeship, culminating in close analytical investigation of Paradise Lost and Samson Agonistes. Attention is given also to Milton's aesthetic propositions and to his social and political prose works.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Age of Johnson
description: An intensive survey of the nondramatic works of Samuel Johnson and other British authors of the later eighteenth century, 1744-1800. Prerequisites: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Romantic Studies
description: The poetry and prose of Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Keats, and Shelley.

title: Victorian Studies
description: An intensive study of the works of Carlyle, Tennyson, Browning, Ruskin, and Arnold.

title: Twentieth-Century British Studies
description: A study in depth of several significant twentiethcentury authors (such as Shaw, Conrad, Lawrence, Joyce, Woolf, Waugh, Durrell, Beckett, and Auden) and the intellectual and literary movements closely associated with them.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War I to the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Introduces the student to the cardinal features of the Greek and Roman civilization.

title: Word Origins and Vocabulary Development
description: Latin borrowings, Latin prefixes, roots, and suffixes in English. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin is required. Open to all students.

title: Scientific Terminology, the Greek Element
description: Considers the composition of Greek -based words used by the physical, biological, medical and technical sciences.

title: Scientific Terminology, the Latin Element
description: Considers the composition of Latin -based words used by the physical, biological, medical and other technical sciences.

title: Roman Private and Public Life
description: All phases of Roman customs referred to in Latin commonly read in secondary school are carefully examined and understood. No reading knowledge of Latin required. Open to all students.

title: Introduction to Mythology
description: Primarily a general education course, dealing with myths of the Greeks and Romans and their use in literature and art. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin required.

title: The Old Testament as Literature
description: Considers the Old Testament as typical of, related to, and sources of some of the major literary genres, such as: history and biography, prophetic literature, lyric poetry, dramatic literature, and short stories and tales.

title: Women in Ancient Greece and Rome
description: Famous women in literature and history are studied in this course which observes and traces the emergence of contemporary Western attitudes regarding women; the course explores and evaluates the status and role of the Greco-Roman woman as determined by social, political and legal institutions.

title: The Classical World in Film, Fiction, and Fact
description: A broad survey of life in the classical Mediterranean world through the media of motion pictures, fiction, nonfiction (such as historical, archaeological, and anthropological studies).

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selected masterpieces of classical literature; historical development of the various types of literature as a background for further study in Latin and English. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin required. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: Introduces the student to the cultural achievements of the ancient Greeks and their contribution to the modern world.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: Provides the student with a fundamental knowledge of the social, cultural, and economic framework within which the ancient Romans lived. t GER 204, 205, 206 may be substituted for 201, 202, 203.

title: German Literature in English Translation
description: Primarily a general education course. The aim of the course is to expose the non-German reader to great German writers and thinkers. The course may not be applied toward areas in German.

title: Hispanic Literature in Translation
description: Primarily a general education course, exposing the non-Spanish reader to the great writers of the Hispanic world. The course may not be applied toward areas in Spanish.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: A literary study of representative mythologies selected from Egyptian, Sumerian, Teutonic, Slavonic, and other mythologies of the world. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures through Motion Pictures
description: Presentations of the literary matter of many nations through the medium of films. Ten films will be shown. Selected ones will be compared to the works of literature. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Linguistics and the Language Teacher
description: The application of general linguistic theory to the teaching and learning of foreign and second languages. Gives the language student some basic insights into how linguistics can help in the mastery of languages.

title: Introduction to Historical Linguistics
description: An introduction to the scientific study of language for students in foreign language. An elementary survey of the methods used in historical and comparative linguistic analysis with application to language usually taught in college. Gives the language student some basic insights into the linguistic principles that underlie change in language.

title: Exotic Language
description: Beginning studies in one of the "exotic" or uncommonlytaught languages. Offered when student demand warrants and when a qualified instructor is available. May be available by guided selfinstruction. No prerequisites. May be repeated with departmental approval for a total of 12 hours per language. Not open to the student who is a native speaker in the language taught.

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and in -depth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors Program or permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Foreign Language
description: Methods current in foreign language teaching in the junior and senior high schools. Directed observation of classes, specific problems of presentation, choice of texts, and organization of teaching materials and supplementary aids are worked out in detail. Attention is given to the Report of the Foreign Language Study and to the courses of study recommended by the State Department of Education. Prerequisite: two years of college credit in French, German, Latin, or Spanish, or the equivalent and EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials in Teaching Foreign Languages
description: Discipline oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of foreign languages, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of foreign languages in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: FL 395.

title: Introduction to Romance Linguistics
description: Deals with a short history of Vulgar Latin and with the phonological, morphological, and syntactical evolution of the Romance Languages. Basic knowledge of a Romance language is desirable.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Language House Living and Learning
description: Offers students the option of earning a limited amount of credit for the language learning experience provided by the foreign language houses. A total of 3 hours of credit per language may be earned in any one house, but no more than 1 credit may be earned at one time. Offered on creditnocredit basis only.

title: The Teaching of Foreign Language in the Elementary School
description: Development of foreign language instruction in the elementary school. Curricula, training of teachers, and teaching methods; also phonemics, pronunciation, and a review of other basic language elements.

title: Beginning French
description: The first course in the French language.

title: Beginning French
description: Prerequisite: FR 101.

title: Beginning French (continued)
description: Prerequisite: FR 102 or one year of secondary school French.

title: The Language and People of France
description: A beginning course designed for students who are interested in the French language and the French culture but do not plan to take a teaching major or minor. Not open to the student who has credit in French except by permission of the department chairman.

title: The Language and People of France
description: A beginning course designed for students who are interested in the French language and the French culture but do not plan to take a teaching major or minor. Prerequisite: FR 104. Not open to the student who has credit in French except by permission of the department chairman.

title: The Language and People of France
description: A beginning course designed for students who are interested in the French language and the French culture but do not plan to take a teaching major or minor. Prerequisite: FR 105. Not open to the student who has credit in French except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Intermediate French
description: Prerequisite: one year of college French or two years of secondary school French.

title: Intermediate French (continued)
description: Prerequisites: 16 hours of college French or two and onehalf years of secondary school French.

title: Intermediate French (continued)
description: Prerequisites: 20 hours of college French or two and onehalf years of secondary school French.

title: Conversation
description: Drill on pronunciation and speech patterns, dictation, and recording. The object of the course is to train in ability to speak French. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or FR 504.

title: Composition
description: Grammar and composition. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or FR 505.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the French language and the application of phonetics to the understanding and speaking of French. Use of the phonetic alphabet. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture: Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 309 prior to September, 1973.

title: Short Story
description: A study of the short story in French literature. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Classical Drama
description: The plays of Corneille, Racine, and Moliere. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Poetry
description: A study of French poetry with emphasis on the Symbolists and on contemporary poets. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Novel
description: Extensive reading in French novel. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Drama
description: Extensive reading in French drama. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Reading
description: Contemporary prose and poetry. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Literary Heritage of France
description: Selections from various periods of French literature. A onequarter offering designed to develop an appreciation of the literary heritage of France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in two of the following courses: FR 421, 422, and 423 or the equivalent.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. Travel may be by air. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students with areas in French or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the Classical Age to 1760. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 2
description: The classical age from 1760 and the eighteenth century. Literature of the golden age of classicism and the eighteenthcentury philosophies. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 3
description: The nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The development of romanticism, realism, naturalism, and symbolism in French literature; literature of contemporary France. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Reading Course
description: Prerequisites: three years of college French or the equivalent, or permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning German
description: The first course in the German language.

title: Beginning German
description: Prerequisite: GER 101.

title: Beginning German (continued)
description: Prerequisite: GER 102 or one year of secondary school German.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Introduction to the basic German grammar needed for the reading of German texts required for science majors.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Completion of the basic German grammar needed for the reading of German texts required for science majors and some selected readings of appropriate texts. Prerequisite: GER 104 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Reading appropriate German texts to build the student's competence in reading and translating expository materials. Prerequisite: GER 105 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Basic Conversational German for Travelers
description: Beginning spoken German for travelers or those seeking employment in Germany. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The first in a three -quarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Not open to the student who has credit in German except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The second in a three -quarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Prerequisite: GER 108. description: The first course in the Latin language. description: Continued emphasis on pronunciation, accent, and syllabification. title: Beginning Latin (continued)
description: Completion of presentation of the mechanics of Latin grammar. Stress on Latin syntax; logical structure in thought patterns. Rapid short readings illustrating grammatical principles. title: Intermediate Latin

Reading of selections from Caesar, Cicero, Pliny, Livy, Seneca, Vitruvius, and others, dealing with such topics as poetry, science, agriculture, medicine, religion, business, politics, history, private life, cooking, philosophy, education, and law. The aim is to interest Latin students in literary ideas drawn from representative works. Emphasis on vocabulary, increased knowledge of Latin idiom, and practice in writing Latin. Prerequisite: one year of college Latin or two years of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin (continued)
description: Emphasis on rapid reading for comprehension. Selected passages dealing with various aspects of man's life, together with comparisons taken from later periods. Celsus, De Medicina; Horace, Ars Poetica; Vitruvius, De Aqueductis; Pliny's Natural History; Cicero's De Officiis, De Rupublica, Epistulae, De Finibus, or Pro Archia; Juvenal, Satires; Pliny's letters (concerning the Christians), Terence's and Plautus' plays; and others. Background and originality of Roman comedy; contaminatio. Play production in Rome. Comparison of Greek and Roman comedy. Aristophanes' comedies; selected plays of Terence and Plautus. title: Roman Comedy

title: Vergil: Aeneid, Books VII -XII

General and Experimental Psychology 241 Department of General and Experimental Psychology Meeker, Chairman; Clark, Deckers, Ganzhorn, Goldstone, Gordon, Hewitt, Hill, Humm, James, Martin, Mayo, McConnell, Meunier, Myers, Palacios, Poland, Renke, Wittig Psychology is the science which studies the behavior of humans as they interact with their environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. As a part of the College of Sciences and Humanities, the Department of General and Experimental Psychology is primarily concerned with the psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of human behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The Department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all areasteaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, businessincrease their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. The Department offers a departmental major and minor in the disciplinary area of psychology. These programs provide a basic background for graduate work in any one of the many fields of psychologyclinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psychology, psychometryand an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other areas such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a social studies major or minor with an area of concentration in psychology, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for instructing in psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students wishing to teach psychology should choose other primary or supporting areas for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of General and Experimental Psychology offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline, and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas on various advanced degree programs. Additionally, teachers of psychology may combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in the discipline of psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment, and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. title: The Psychology of Human Adaptation to Stress
description: Adaptation and reactions to stress as psychological phenomena; research on stress and its influence on personality development; the appraisal of threatening situations by the individual; coping and coping reaction patterns to stress; theories of adaptation to psychological stress. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Altered States of Awareness
description: An introduction to the study of normal and altered states of awareness in humans. Among the areas to be explored are: sleep and dream states, sensory deprivation, hypnosis, meditation, hallucinations, boredom, and the effect of drugs on awareness. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Applied Behavior Analysis
description: Introduction to the principles of operant psychology and application of these principles to applied situations with humans in other than formal educational settings. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Elementary Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics and statistics of inference. The computation, application, and interpretation of various elementary statistics. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Introduction to Biopsychology
description: A brief introduction to the general areas of biopsychology. Topics include: the fundamental of nervous system structure and function; consciousness and its altered states; memory, language and thought; emotionality; and personality. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Introduction to Experimental Psychology
description: An introduction to the use of the scientific method in the study of human behavior. Analysis and evaluation of experimental studies will be utilized to provide experience with research techniques using essential controls and acceptable procedures. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100 and 241.

title: Introduction to Comparative Psychology
description: A survey of the theoretical and empirical foundations of animal behavior, including that of man, considered from a comparative, biological point of view. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Introduction to Social Psychology
description: Basic understanding of the psychosocial problems involved in the functioning of an individual in society. Emphasis on various influences which help to shape the psychological patterns of interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Experimental Social Psychology
description: Emphasizes basic empirical research methods with special focus on those techniques commonly used in contemporary social psychological research. Combines the academic study of these methods with their actual application in research investigations conducted by students. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 241, and 316.

title: Psychology of Women
description: An introduction to psychological approaches to the study of women with special emphasis on achievement motivation and dependency, attitudes toward women, development of sexrole identity, biological and social influences on women's behavior, selfconcepts and psychological conflict in women, and a critical appraisal of research in the area of sex differences. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
description: Theoretical and practical foundations underlying the construction, use, and interpretation of standardized psychological tests and inventories. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Honors Colloquium in Psychology
description: Explorations of selected issues in psychology with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion of such topics as psychobiology, social psychology, learning, personality, and abnormal psychology. General and Experimental Psychology 243

title: Motivation and Emotion
description: An introduction to basic theory and research relating to motivation and emotion and applications to various aspects of human behavior. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Sensation and Perception
description: The human senses: their physiological makeup, development, and functioning. Basic principles of perception and stimulus hunger will be emphasized. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Psychology of Cognition
description: Analysis of research and theories in the psychology of cognition and thinking. Major topic areas to be covered are verbal learning, problem solving, concept formation, and psycholinguistics. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Introduction to the Study of Personality
description: A wide variety of classical and modern theories of personality and the pertinent empirical research are presented and compared. Consideration given to the components of a good theory of personality and to the applications of various personality theories. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Abnormal Psychology
description: Systematic study of behavior pathology with special reference to the psychopathology of physical illness and handicaps, psychosomatic and somatopsychic illnesses, neuroses, psychoses, character disorders, addiction, and acute and chronic brain disorders. Primary emphasis on etiology, symptomatology, prognosis, and prevention. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 421.

title: Teaching of Psychology in Secondary Schools
description: Materials and methods used in teaching psychology at the secondary school level, including instructional issues concerning psychology with a personal adjustment orientation and as an academic discipline. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in psychology.

title: Current Research and Trends in the Teaching of Psychology
description: Current research in the teaching of psychology with an emphasis on the research of new curricular and instructional approaches.

title: Psychology of Learning
description: The nature of learning processes, possible influences upon these processes and resultant behavior, and applications of the psychology of learning. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Physiological Psychology
description: A basic introduction to the physical basis of behavior, involving primarily the nervous system and its structure and function. Emphasis on the role of bodily systems in preception, learning, motivation, and conscious function. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Applied Psychology
description: Theory and application of psychological principles in various social settings. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Industrial Psychology
description: A comprehensive coverage of the application of psychological principles to personnel selection and training, worker motivation and morale, labor problems in business and industry, executive leadership, consumer behavior, engineering psychology, and personal problems in business and industry. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Organizational Development: A Psychological Perspective
description: Presentation of change techniques from a process and small group prespective with special emphasis on the limitations and logic involved in their utilization. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Psychology of Selection and Placement
description: Introduction to principles of personnel testing as applied to the selection and placement process. Focus on development of predictors and criteria, selection of an appropriate validation model, and the psychological dynamics of the interview processes. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 241 or equivalent.

title: Experimental Behavior Analysis
description: Investigation and practice in experimental behavior analysis, with emphasis on operant conditioning. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Systematic Psychology
description: The major concepts of various schools of psychological thought and contemporary theoretical systems as they have evolved historically. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241, and senior standing.

title: Seminar in Psychology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of psychology. Prerequisites: psychology major and senior standing.

title: Independent Study in Psychology
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructors with special competence in the area involved. Department of Geography and Geology Lyon, Chairman; Beatty, Carmin, Dillon, Grimes, Justham, Kane, Martinson, Orr, Pal, Peterson, Roepke, Samuelson, Schoen, Showalter, Stevenson, Sullivan Geography, geology, and the earth sciences are concerned with the study of the earth and its resources. Geography focuses attention on the spatial relationships apparent in the cultural and physical environments that have developed on the earth. The geography programs reflect these aspects of the discipline, offering general and specialized studies in methodological as well as cultural, physical, and regional fields. Curricular objectives are to educate and train geographers to assume positions in elementary and secondary schools, colleges and universities, business and industry, and governmental agencies, and to contribute to the liberal education of students. Geologists study the earth, with primary attention to its history, materials, processes, and structure. Today geologists are concerned also with the study of the moon, with the study of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, and with the discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits. The departmental major in geology on the Professional Arts Curriculum is designed to prepare geologists for immediate employment in industry and government agencies, and for graduate studies leading to research and teaching positions in industry, government, and universities. The departmental major in geology on the Liberal Arts Curriculum is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who do not wish to enter the profession. Earth science incorporates much of geology and the physical aspects of geography, meteorology, and astronomy. It provides a broad understanding of the physical environment for the student who does not expect to specialize in any one particular area of geology or geography. Earth science graduates are in increasing demand as teachers in secondary schools and colleges and universities throughout the United States. The geography faculty specialize in various aspects within the disciplines of physical and cultural geography, including such methodological specialties as urban and regional geography, transportation geography, land utilization, the structure and function of cities, cartography, meteorology and climatology, research in geography, and teacher education. Geology and earth science specialties include geomorphology, geophysics, mineralogy, petrography, paleontology, geotectonics, and oceanography. The department also provides students with training enabling them to complete undergraduate degree programs at other universities in fields related to geography, geology, and earth science. Such fields include meteorology and climatology, oceanography, geophysics, engineering geology, environmental studies, and photogrammetry. Students preparing to enter such programs at other universities should receive counseling and curriculum planning advice from department faculty members. They should understand, in addition, that a number of the science programs listed above require competence in calculus and physics and/or chemistry. Students should contact their departmental area advisers each quarter before completing their registration with the university curricular advisers. Departmental advisers help the students in developing curricular options, in selection of elective courses, and in other aspects of their major or minor program. The Department of Geography and Geology prepares students for entrance to colleges or universities which offer degrees in meteorologic and oceanographic studies. A student who desires to pursue either of these fields towards an undergraduate degree should seek the advice of the departmental adviser as soon as possible after entering Ball State University. Students wishing to complete an undergraduate degree at Ball State University, but continue meteorology or oceanography at the graduate level elsewhere, should seek this advice no later than the first quarter of the sophomore year. Basic minimum requirements to be included in first two years of undergraduate study at Ball State in preparation for study towards an undergraduate degree in meteorology elsewhere are generally 8 hours of geology, 8 hours of meteorology, 20 hours of mathematics, 12 hours of chemistry, 12 hours of physics, and 12 hours of foreign language. In addition to these 72 hours, the student who wishes to prepare for a graduate degree in meteorology elsewhere should include climatology and statistics. If the student plans to pursue a degree in agricultural meteorology at least 12 hours in biology will need to be included. Approximately 20 to 24 hours of advanced meteorology and climatology, not available at Ball State, is usually required for entrance to graduate work, and will be made up at the graduate level by assignment without credit. Acceptance into graduate work in oceanography will require a bachelor's degree in one of the sciences or mathematics, and generally including 4 hours of introductory oceanography, 23 hours of mathematics, inclusive of analytical geometry and calculus, 12 to 14 hours of general physics, and 15 to 16 hours of general chemistry. Students interested in oceanography should seek the advice of the departmental adviser. The adviser for physical and geological oceanography is located in the department of Geography and Geology; the adviser for biological oceanography, in the Department of Biology.
