title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting energy forms such as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physical Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles and concepts of the laws of nature involving mechanical, heat, light, electrical, nuclear, chemical energy, and the conservation laws associated with these forms of energy. Emphasis on applications appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Preparation of Physical Science Teaching Materials
description: A study of selected topics in physical science stressing the construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs. Prerequisite: PHYCS 101 or permission of the department head. Open only to students on the teacher education curriculum.

title: Physics and Sports
description: A descriptive introduction to basic physical principles and laws within a framework of applications to athletic activities and sports. Particularly suited to the student with areas or special interest in physical education. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110, 120, or 130.

title: General Physics
description: Mechanics, properties of matter, and heat. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary algebra.

title: General Physics
description: Magnetism, electricity, and atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110.

title: General Physics
description: Sound and light. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110.

title: Orientation Seminar for Preengineering and Beginning Physics Students
description: An overview of the fields of physics and engineering that will aid science students in effectively planning their college curriculum. Students will be introduced to career scientists and the jobs performed by persons in these professions. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 120.

title: General Physics
description: Mechanics, properties of matter, and heat. Intended for students expecting to major or minor in the physical sciences or mathematics. Prerequisites or parallel: MATH 170.

title: General Physics
description: Electricity and magnetism. Intended for students expecting to major or minor in the physical sciences or mathematics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120. Parallel: MATH

title: General Physics
description: Sound and light, and certain modern developments in physics. Intended for students expecting to major or minor in the physical sciences or mathematics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Physics 1 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of mechanics and heat. Topics include particle dynamics, resolution of forces, friction, work, energy, static equilibrium, torque, properties of materials, fluids, temperature, thermal expansion, heat energy, heat transfer, phase changes in matter, and thermodynamic engines. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH

title: Physics 2 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of sound, light, and electrical power. Topics include wave phenomena, sound characteristics, sound production and absorption, human response to sound, reflection, refraction, geometrical optics, polarization, circuits, Ohms Law, Kirchoff's Laws, electromagnetic induction, transformers, meters, and power distribution systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 112 or 120.

title: Sound and Light
description: For music and art students. Sound as a basis of music and light as a basis of art. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Household Physics
description: Practical applications of physics in common everyday appliances and other devices. Topics include: why fuses blow, principles of heating and cooling, and principles of some electrical and electronic home appliances.

title: Topics in Physics
description: Discussion of a specific topic in physics. Examples are: lasers, holography, and solid state electronics. No math or science background is needed. For the § Students will be placed in appropriate beginning courses in mathematics. Physics and Astronomy 283 nonphysics major. For the specific topics being studied during a given quarter, consult your curricular adviser, or the Department of Physics and Astronomy. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Solar Energy Technology and Applications
description: Descriptive study of various techniques and systems developed for utilizing sunlight as a nonpolluting alternative energy source. Major emphasis on the physical principles and design of solar systems for space heating, air conditioning, and hot water heating for residential and commercial buildings, and systems for the generation of electric power. Other related topics include: energy storage, agricultural and industrial applications, solar stills, solar furnaces, ocean thermal power, wind energy systems, and total energy systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or MATH 111.

title: Mechanics 1
description: Basic concepts of particle mechanics. Vector algebra and calculus. Kinematics and dynamics of a particle in two and threedimensions. Simple and dampedharmonic motion. Particle dynamics in noninertial frames of reference. Central force motion. Dynamics of a system of particles. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120 and either MATH 162 or 172.

title: Sound and Acoustical Art
description: A descriptive treatment of basic sound and acoustics, using a minimum of mathematics. It is especially tailored to the needs of music and other related areas such as speech. Involves pitch, wavelength, intensity levels. Not open to students with areas in physics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 184.

title: Introduction to Audio Engineering
description: An introductory course in the physics of the reproduction of sound. The principles involved in the operation of electroacoustical transducers such as phono cartridges, loudspeakers, and tape heads will be studied. Electronic principles as applied to the amplification process. Actual measurements of frequency response and speaker parameters conducted by the student in the laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or permission of the department head.

title: Photographic Optics in the Visual Arts
description: Principles of light and optics for students majoring in areas other than a physical science where a basic understanding of light and optics in photography is desired. Tailored to meet the needs of photojournalism, art, and other students with similar interests. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 248.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
description: An introduction to classical electric and magnetic theory with introduction of vector notation. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and MATH 172.

title: Introduction to Modern Physics
description: Introduction to atomic and nuclear physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Modern Experimental Techniques in Physics
description: Includes experimentation, instrumentation, and data analysis techniques appropriate for modern physics laboratory work. Included are experiments on electron charge and ionization potentials. Statistical treatment of experimental data is discussed including the theory of error propagation, least squares, and analysis of spectral information using Fourier techniques.

title: Environmental Physics
description: The application of physics to environmental and societal problems. Physical principles underlying hardtechnology based industries will be discussed. Topics include: energy production, transmission, and environmental effects (including nuclear power generation and radiation) ; transportation problems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or the equivalent.

title: Electronics for the Life Sciences
description: Applications of electronics to the problems encountered by students in the life sciences. Electronic instruments used in biology, health, and physiology and the problems associated with their use. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 354 or 356.

title: Physical Optics
description: The electromagnetic wave theory of light, spectra, interference, diffraction, polarization, and double refraction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Acoustics
description: Aspects of pure and applied acoustics. Topics to be discussed include: solutions to the wave equation, acoustic impedances, electromechanicalacoustic analogies, directradiator loudspeaker and enclosure theory, and a discussion of room acoustics. Prerequisite:

title: Electronics 1
description: Characteristics of electronic components and their circuit functions. Circuit analysis, design and construction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or 122 or permission of the department head.

title: Electronics 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 354 at a more advanced level. Prerequisite: PHYCS 354.

title: Pulse and Digital Electronics
description: The function and use of pulse and digital circuitry as applied to laboratory and commercial electronic apparatus. Prerequisite: PHYCS 356 or permission of the department head.

title: Introductory Nuclear Techniques
description: Emphasis upon experimental studies of radioactive disintegrations and decay products and their relation to nuclear structure. Instrumentation in radioisotope measurements. Two lectures and two twohour laboratory periods per week. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those which occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Prerequisites: PHYCS 124 and 260, or permission of the department head.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those which occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Such topics as boundary value problems (involving linear differential equations and partial differential equations), transforms, and special functions (Green's function approach, Fourier series, Legendre's equation, Bessel's equation, Hermite polynomials, etc.) of mathematical physics are covered. Prerequisites: PHYCS 124 and 260 or permission of the department head.

title: Descriptive Astronomy
description: The celestial sphere, the solar system, formation and decay of stars, instruments and basic laws of astronomy, nebulae, galactic structure, theories of the origin of the universe; constellation and telescope work.

title: Instruments and Techniques in Planetarium Operations
description: Use of planetarium instru - ment, console, and chamber. Organization and evaluation of planetarium programs and exhibits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 380 or 580 or permission of the department head.

title: Theories and Instruments of the Astronomer
description: The planets, stars, and nebulae as related to theories and natural laws of the universe through observatory and laboratory experiences. Prerequisite: PHYCS 380 or permission of the department head.

title: The Teaching of Physics in the Secondary School
description: Aims, nature of the subject matter, amount and nature of laboratory work, standardized tests, and textbooks used in the teaching of physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in physics. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 230. Dynamics of a rigid body, the moment of inertia tensor. Mechanics of deformable continua, the stress tensor. The wave equation, elasticity and rigid body vibrations. Variational techniques, virtual work, Lagrange's equations of the first and second kind. Hamiltonian mechanics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 230. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 374.

title: Celestial Mechanics
description: An application of the laws of classical mechanics to objects under the influence of inversesquare gravitational forces, leading to the theory of orbits and perturbative effects on orbits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 230. Prerequisite recommended: PHYCS 430.

title: Thermodynamics
description: Laws of thermodynamics and introduction to the kinetic theory of gases. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 230.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 1
description: Application of vector analysis to electrostatics, dipole and multipole fields, and dielectric theory. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 250.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 450 with ,e mphasis on dynamic electrical problems, alternating currents, magnetic fields, and Maxwell's equations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 450.

title: Atomic and Nuclear Physics 1
description: A study of the fundamental principles of modern physics as applied to the atom. Experimental evidence will be discussed in reference to the failures of classical physics in describing atomic phenomena and atomic structure. Special relativity an d an introduction to quantum mechanics will be followed by quantum theory applications to the atom in atomic spectra, xray spectra, and molecular spectra. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260 or permission of the department head.

title: Atomic and Nuclear Physics 2
description: A study of the nucleus and nuclear interactions. Experimental facts about nuclear processes will be emphasized in discussions on the following topics: particle accelerators, detectors, radioactivity (alpha, beta, and gamma decay), interaction of radiation with matter, nuclear reactions, nuclear structure, nuclear models, and nuclear applications in science and technology. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260 or permission of the department head.

title: Quantum Mechanics 1
description: De Broglie's postulate, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the free particle, square well potentials, harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom, and other selected wave mechanics problems. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites: PHYCS 260 and MATH 172.

title: Quantum Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 464. Course material includes perturbation theory, oneelectron atoms, magnetic moments, spin, relativistic effects, symmetric and antisymmetric eigenfunctions, the helium atom, the Thomas-Fermi theory, the Hartree theory, and transition rates. Prerequisite: PHYCS 464.

title: Solid State 1
description: An investigation of the structure and physical properties of matter in the solid state. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites: PHYCS 260 and MATH 172. Physics and ,Astronomy 285

title: Solid State Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 466. Topics include the electrical and magnetic properties of solids and the band theory of solids with special emphasis on semiconductors. Optical properties of solids and the effects of lattice defects are studied. Prerequisite: PHYCS 466.

title: Independent Studies in Physics
description: Pursuit of special lines of scientific investigation in physics on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Physics Investigations in the Field
description: Investigative problems in physics which need to be pursued at other locations than at Ball State due to specialized facilities being at the specific location. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in this course is contingent upon permission of the department head.

title: Mysteries of the Sky
description: A nontechnical and nonmathematical multimedia excursion into the vast reaches of the sky including information about the sun, the moon, shooting stars, comets, supernovae, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, life on other planets.

title: Astronomy Materials for the Teacher
description: The fundamentals of astronomy including historical aspects as well as modern astronomy concepts. Construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom are stressed. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Observational Astronomy
description: A continuation of ASTRO 100 providing practical experience in observing celestial objects by using telescopes and other astronomical apparatus. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100.

title: General Astronomy 1
description: Essential points of modern astronomy, emphasizing the underlying physical principles. Topics include: coordinate systems in astronomy, orbital laws, relativity, planetary physics, measurement of stellar distances, and spectral classification of stars. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100 or PHYCS 380, and MATH 111.

title: General Astronomy 2
description: A continuation of ASTRO 120. Topics include: atomic structure and stellar spectra, stellar atmospheres and interiors, multiple star systems and clusters, galactic structure, cosmology, and the origin of the universe. Prerequisite: ASTRO 120. Parallel: MATH 112.

title: Topics in Astronomy
description: Discussion of a specific topic in astronomy. Examples are: comets, eclipses, UFO's, and interstellar travel. No math or science background is needed. For the nonphysics major. For specific topics being studied during a given quarter consult your curricular adviser, or the Department of Physics and Astronomy. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Astrophysics 1
description: An introduction to the physics of stellar structure and the theories of stellar evolution. Prerequisite: ASTRO 122 or PHYCS 124. Parallel: MATH 161 or 170.

title: Introduction to Astrophysics 2
description: Continuation of ASTRO 330 emphasizing the nuclear processes involved in stellar evolution. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330. Parallel: MATH 162 or 171.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Lasers and Applied Electro-Optic Techniques
description: Principles of laser operation, design, and safety considered within the context of the field of electrooptic techniques. Optical detection devices such as photodetector and laser power meters, photographic techniques such as in holography, and laser applications stressed in the "handson" laboratoryoriented portion of the course. Prerequisite: PHYCS 114 or 124 or permission of the department head.

title: Fluid Mechanics 1
description: The forces and motions in fluids. Fluid characteristics and the basic theories of fluid statics and dynamics discussed. Applications in the fields of solar energy systems, hydraulics, aerodynamics, meteorology, hydrology, and fluidics will be cited. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172; PHYCS 230.

title: Fluid Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of APHYS 410. Turbulence and nonuniform flows are studied. The theories and equations of fluid mechanics are applied to areas such as environmental conditioning systems, thermal convection processes and circulation of the atmosphere, topic of tides and currents, airfoils, pipe flow, medical applications, astrophysics, and others. Computerized models are utilized by students for detailed studies of individual applications of interest. Prerequisite: APHYS 410.

title: Applied Solar Energy 1
description: The solar energy resource, the physics and engineering of solar collection, concentration, thermal conversion, and storage. Analysis of solar spectral content, attenuation, and variation; evaluation of flat plate collector efficiencies; and quantative appraisal of thermal storage materials are typical topics. Three lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: MATH 173; PHYCS 124, 434; or permission of the department head.

title: Applied Solar Energy 2
description: The engineering design, component integration, operation, and performance of solar heating and cooling systems. System modeling and sizing of residential and commercial solar space heating, water heating, and space cooling units. Control instrumentation hardware, functions, and operation. Prerequisite: APHYS 420.

title: Applied Solar Energy 3
description: Solar electric power generation, advanced solar systems, applications in industry and agriculture, the total energy concept, and the solar hydrogen economy. Physics and engineering of solar thermal power plants, solar cells, solar satellites, ocean thermal energy conversion, windmills, and bioconversion. Three onehour lectures and a twohour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: APHYS 422.

title: Heat Transfer
description: The basic heat transfer processes in nature. Conduction, convection, and radiation in applied problems are analyzed using electricalmodelanalogue, graphical, and computerized numerical methods. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172; PHYCS 124; or permission of the department head.

title: Microprocessor and Microcomputer Electronics
description: Principles and uses of microprocessors and microcomputers. Microprocessor and microcomputer timing, bus structures, inputoutput interfacing, memory interfacing, analogtodigital and digitaltoanalog conversion techniques. Prerequisite: PHYCS 358 or permission of the department head. Department of Physiology and Health Science Schaller, Chairman; Bock, Carroll, Ganion, D. C. Gobble, D. H. Gobble, Gowings, Harvilla, Henzlik, Jarial, Jones, Kennedy, Lesh, Paschall, Payne, Pinger, Wantz, Womack, Wrestler Health Science is multidisciplinary in nature and its content is derived largely from the biological, physical, and social sciences. The fields of medicine and public health make significant contributions to the discipline of health science. Broad in scope, health science covers such areas as the nature of disease, the complexity of nutrition, effects of radiation, behavioral aspects of accident prevention, an understanding of health and medical care programs, significance of international health problems, selection of health products and services, environmental hazards of air and water pollution, community health services, foundations of mental health, family living and education for human sexuality, and drug use and abuse. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a major or minor for students who are interested in one of a variety of occupations in the health science field. Health science is known differently in some institutions; some commonly used names are: health education, health and safety education, and school and college health education. Health science teachers, coordinators, and directors are being sought by elementary and secondary schools, junior colleges, as well as universities. The department also offers a departmental minor in the field of public health. It provides basic information on public health programs, problems, and practices in the United States. Physiology and Health Science 287 Opportunities include employment with official governmental and voluntary health agencies, business, industry, and professional health associations, such as the American Medical Association. Of equal importance in the department are the subject areas of anatomy and physiology. These are vital to the health sciences and biological sciences in the broad sense and, in anticipation of future development, provide a point of departure for specialization in the respective disciplines of anatomy and physiology. The department also offers a departmental minor in physiology. One combination that is often elected by the students is the physiology major earned in conjunction with a biology, chemistry, or psychology major. At the present time, the department contributes required and elective courses to several academic programs at Ball State, such as regional and urban planning, preprofessional programs in allied health science areas, courses for professional nurse preparation, and general education. The preprofessional programs in the allied health science area include premedical, predental, and prepharmacy programs; professional nurse preparation; and medical technology. The department provides guidance in enabling students to select a career in teaching, service, or research. Membership in Eta Sigma Gamma, the national honorary for men and women in health science, and Sigma Zeta, the national honorary in science, is offered to qualified students. title: Elements of Human Health
description: Human biology stressing the personal and informational aspects of current health problems. Hygiene of the basic systems of the body with emphasis on care, functions, and disorders; natural and acquired defenses against disease; elements of See the professional education requirements for secondary teaching on the Teacher Education Curriculum for the requirement of two additional courses: HSC 395, 399. preventive medicine; and modern standards of sanitation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 160.

title: Fundamentals of Human Health
description: The main purpose is to promote total individual fitness. Intelligent selfmanagement, based on understanding of body functioning, is an objective. Some problems considered are the following: existing health situations; use of physicians, dentists, and public agencies; infections and body defense; in emergencies, what to do until the doctor comes; food and one's efficiency; emotional health; and basic understanding of human reproduction. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 150.

title: Community Health Problems
description: Organization of official and nonofficial health agencies at the various levels: international, national, state, and local. Exploration of causative community factors in disease, community diagnoses of disease, and programs being investigated to combat these conditions. Selected communicable, noncommunicable, and behaviortype problems will be the focus for the application of principles and procedures. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Emergency Health Care
description: Various emergency health problems and their management by the application of emergency health care as recommended by the American Red Cross and Civil Defense authorities. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 299 or 396.

title: Introduction to Occupational Safety and Health
description: A qualitative and quantitative study of the interface between individuals, their tools, and their work environment and the methods by which the resulting health hazards can be controlled to an acceptable level. Prerequisite: HSC 250.

title: School Health Practice
description: Community and school health services. Practical experiences in screening for visual, auditory, and nutritional defects. Identification and control of childhood diseases. Topics included: accidents, safety, and first aid; materials for teaching health; role of the teacher and school health personnel; and effect of the total school program of the child. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 150 or 160.

title: School Health Organization
description: Organization and development of school health programs. Coordination of school and community health programs, hygiene, and sanitation of the school plant, the school lunch program, school health services, and the health instructional program. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 350.

title: Health Appraisal of School Children
description: Sociological, psychological, and physiological changes that take place in school children. Prevalent health problems that occur in school children — their etiology, pathology, diagnosis, and prognosis. Experience in screening techniques for discovering these deviations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 350 or 360.

title: Women and Health
description: A general overview of some current issues related to women and health: the human female, a woman's right to control her body, health problems of women, women in the health marketplace, the gynecological exam, pregnancy and childbirth, teenage pregnancies, midwifery, female sexuality, women and aging, occupational health and women, and the women's health movement.

title: Public Health Entomology
description: An examination of public health problems caused by insects and other arthropods. Emphasis will be placed on the identification, biology and control of vectors of communicable diseases, on disease transmisison cycles, and on research techniques used in solving public health entomology problems.

title: Honors Colloquium in Health Science
description: Exploration of selected current issues in health science with an emphasis upon individualized study, reporting, and discussion. Restricted to honors students.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Health and Safety
description: Examination of the Indiana state course of study in health and safety, relation of health policies and current schoolhomecommunity problems, practice with audiovisual aids, evaluation of representative textbooks, and visits to offcampus schools. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials in Health and Safety
description: Discipline oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of health and safety, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of health and safety in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: HSC 395.

title: Health Science of Distant Areas
description: School and public health programs at local, state, and national levels. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students on elementary curricula, students with concentration areas in health science on secondary Physiology and Health Science 289 curricula, and students in public health areas. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in the course is contingent upon permission of the department chairman.

title: Health, Sexuality, and Family Life
description: The family as the basic unit in society with consideration of the health problems facing the family. Emphasis is given to tracing relationships between men and women in the areas of dating, courtship, marriage, and problems of raising children; human anatomy, physiology, and embryology; and responsibilities of the home and school in the sex education of the schoolage child. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or a major or minor in health science, home economics, biology, teacher education, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sex Education and School Health
description: Development of an understanding of how to implement and teach a positive program of sex education aimed at helping young people develop constructive attitudes, values, and practices based on sound knowledge in accordance with American Medical Association recommendation and pertinent state guidelines. Prerequisite: HSC 461 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Alcohol Problems
description: A study of alcohol as a mood modifier, its use, nonuse, and abuse in drinking societies. Critical and controversial issues relevant to alcohol ingestion will be explored for medical, economic, legal, educational, historical, physiological, and public health implications.

title: Current Progress in Disease Control
description: A critical review of pertinent research being conducted on leading causes of mortality and morbidity in the United States. A description and analysis of this current research will enable participants to gain an appreciation and understanding of current health progress in the United States. Particular emphasis upon the potential for application of this information into individual, school, and community health programs. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Drug Dependence and Abuse
description: An analysis of the medical, psychological, sociological, and legal dimensions of drug use in the United States. The incidence and prevalence of drug abuse together with the roles played by the school and community in dealing with this health problem will be treated. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health Quackery
description: Health services and consumer protection organizations. An analysis of fradulent health practices and nostrums, available health care systems and health products. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health and Aging
description: Dynamics of later life and the aging process with specific emphasis on health. The physiological and behavioral dimensions of the aging process will be analyzed and discussed.

title: Death and Dying
description: An analysis of the relationship between death and health with emphasis upon the physiological, medical, psychological, legal, and consumer aspects of death and dying in contemporary America. Roles of individual, family, school, community, and various professionals examined. Problems in the meaning of death, care of dying, death ritual, bereavement, and death education investigated. Prerequisite: HSC 150 or 160 or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Internship in Health Science
description: The intern will be assigned to an approved health agency or education institution for a period of time commensurate with the hours of credit to be earned. The student will periodically and terminally report to an academic adviser and to the administrator of the participating agency(s). Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with HSC 575.

title: Public Health Practice
description: Public health organization and available community health resources. Recent developments and problems in the field of public health. Examination of recent literature on preventive medicine and human conservation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites: HSC 160 and 180, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Health
description: The physical environment and its relationship to disease causation. Review of environmental health problems and their solutions. Areas of study include air and water pollution, milk and food sanitation, disposal of human excreta and waste, radiological agents in the environment, and occupational health problems. Prerequisite: HSC 480.

title: Epidemiology
description: Classic epidemics, evaluation of epidemiological principles and techniques of investigation, and epidemiological analysis of selected types of diseases. Prerequisite: HSC 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Special Studies in Physiology and Health Science
description: Designed to give undergraduate physiology and health science students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time.

title: Fundamentals of Mammalian Anatomy
description: Basic study of mammalian anatomy with detailed dissection and with examination of representative microscopic structure. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Human Embryology
description: Normal development of the human organism including germ cell formation, fertilization, implantation, and organ formation. Consideration of embryonic environment, physiology, and abnormal development. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or ANAT 201.

title: Human Neuroanatomy
description: Offers a strong background in the basic structural and functional relations of the central nervous system. Emphasis upon understanding of the location of nerve cell centers and the fiber tracts entering and leaving these centers. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or ZOOL 330. Prerequisites recommended: ANAT 320 and 430.

title: Histology
description: Microscopic structure or organisms with special emphasis on the tissues of vertebrates. Introductory microtechnique. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisites: four courses in biological science. BIO 360 and ZOOL 330 are recommended.

title: Fundamentals of Pathology
description: An introduction to the study of the principles of disease production, especially in the human body. Emphasis on basic concepts and descriptions of disease processes as seen in the human being. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 430 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Physiology
description: Vital processes with references to human functional biology. Group experimentation with recording apparatus. Prerequisites: BIO 111, or BIO 102 and 103; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Human Physiology
description: Continuation of PHYSL 210. Functions of the human organ systems. Comparisons between vertebrate systems and mechanisms in humans. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210.

title: Mammalian Physiology
description: Comparative mammalian physiology with consideration of laboratory and domestic animals and their contributions to human physiology. Advanced instrumentation and animal handling techniques stressed in laboratory. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisites: one year of inorganic chemistry or BIO 111; CHEM 110; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Renal Physiology
description: A detailed study of the urinary system and excretory functions. Emphasis will be on human physiology but comparative vertebrate systems will be included. Subject matter included will be from the embryogenicanatomic level to the biochemicalpathological level. Prerequisite: general chemistry, organic chemistry; one course in anatomy; one course in physiology.

title: Cardiovascular Dynamics
description: A functional study of the mammalian circulatory system, stressing actions of homeostatic control mechanisms and applications of physical principles to a biological system, with minimal use of mathematics in developing operational concepts. Prerequisite: one course in physiology and one in physics.

Department of Political Science Sargent, Chairman; Baker, Chang, Corbett, Frankland, Gruenewald, Hamori, Hollands, Menez, Meyer, Perry, Rouse, Rudoni, Scheele, Vasicko Political science is the study of the legal governments and relation of people thereto. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Protagoras, Gorgias, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polls or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differ from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask: What is the nature of people (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between people and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. Since comprehension of available knowledge is fundamental to intelligent valuation, emphasis must be given to teaching and learning and to continued accumulation, analysis, and organization of knowledge. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civil, and vocational. The first two, hopefully, are universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed populace. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 101) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz., political theory; American government; public law; public administration; parties, politics, and the political process; foreign and comparative government; and international law and diplomacy. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher licensing programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate level for students in other departments. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements listed below. Teaching major in social studies, 84 hours Government primary concentration: POLS 130, 237 and one additional political science course in each of three divisions numbered II through VIII, and electives in political science 28 hrs. Electives in diversified social studies not taken from the primary or supporting areas 16 hrs. Government supporting concentration: POLS 130, 237 and one additional political science course in one of the divisions numbered II through VIII, and electives in political science 20 hrs. Teaching minor in social studies, 40 hours Government concentration: POLS 130, 237 and one additional political science course in each of three divisions numbered II through VIII, and electives in political science 24 hrs. Courses selected from three social studies areas other than government 16 hrs. Departmental major in political science, 48 hours POLS 130 or 131, one additional political science course in each of five divisions numbered II through VIII (POLS 210 strongly recommended), and electives in political science 48 hrs. Departmental minor in political science, 28 hours POLS 130 or 131, one additional political science course in each of three divisions numbered II through VIII (POLS 210 strongly recommended), and electives in political science 28 hrs. Prelaw Preparation At Ball State University the student prepares for making application for admission to law school by qualifying for a baccalaureate degree on a curriculum which provides for a broad undergraduate background in many academic areas and a strong concentration in the social sciences. If application for admission to law school is the immediate objective after obtaining a baccalaureate degree, the student may elect to meet degree requirements on the Liberal Arts Curriculum. A departmental major of 48 hours in a social science and a departmental minor of 28 hours in a social science are specified. Political science, American history, world history, sociology, and economics are disciplines especially suggested for major and minor selection. The student who wishes to prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana before making application for admission to law school may take the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum with the teaching major in social science, 60 hours, and a departmental minor, 28 hours, in social science in a field other than the fields of primary and supporting concentrations in the teaching major. Thus the student prepares for certification in the field of the teaching area(s) but not in the field of the departmental area. The prelaw student should arrange as early as possible to discuss plans with the prelaw adviser in the Department of Political Science.

title: Honors Colloquium in Political Science
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in political science, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open to students on the Honors Program and other outstanding students by permission of the department chairman. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in American Governments and Politics
description: The student will work part time or full time (depending on the assignment) for one quarter in the office of a public official in national, state, or local government, a candidate for public office, or a political party. Assignments will depend upon the interests of students and the convenience of sponsors. Prerequisite: 16 hours in political science including the following or their equivalents: POLS 130, 237 and 431, or 350, or 473, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Paralegalism
description: The internship course for the legal assistant and legal administrator programs combines the students' academic training with practical experience within a law firm, corporation, bank, or governmental agency. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141, 142 and permission of the program director.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do semiindependent study. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the department chairman and a professor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: basic courses in the area selected for special study, junior standing, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings in Planning
description: Reading program developed in consultation with the department chairman and a professor with special competence in planning. Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest in planning. Prerequisite: POLS 461 and permission of the department chairman. Division H: Political Theory and Methodology

title: Introduction to Politics
description: The scope and methods of the study of political science. An examination of the basic concepts and theories in the discipline. Traditions and approaches in the field and their application to the various subdivisions of political science. Prerequisite:

title: Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of the leading political theories evolved by mankind pertaining to the state. Emphasis on the views of such thinkers as Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Grotius, Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, and Bentham.

title: Early Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of political thought of the early Mediterranean and Medieval worlds which became the foundation of modern political theories and systems of the West. Emphasis on writings of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, St. Augustine, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Machiavelli.

title: Modern Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of selected writings of leading political theorists from the Age of Reformation to the present.

title: Communist Political Thought: from Marx to Present
description: A critical analysis and evaluation of Marxism, Leninism, Stalinsim, Khrushchevism, post-Khrushchev Communist ideology and Maoism as a system of theoretical propositions and as an action program of an international movement.

title: Voter Polling Techniques
description: Methods by which information is obtained on the voting behavior and attitudes of the electorate. Emphasis on producing a working knowledge of polling techniques. Includes such topics as sampling, interviewing, and questionnaire construction.

title: American Political Thought
description: American political thought from the colonial period to the present. Puritanism, nature of rights, constitutionalism and federalism, nature of the Union, democracy, liberalism, conservatism, individualism and collectivism, welfare state, isolation and internationalism, and national security and freedom.

title: Research Methods in Political Science
description: A critical examination of methodological problems and practices in the formulation, execution, evaluation, and reporting of political science research, including a comparison of data gathering techniques, their respective limitations, and approprite application.

title: Quantitative Political Analysis
description: Introduction to data analysis computer applications in political science: minimum level of technical competence will be attained during the first two weeks; aggregate data analysis using departmental data library; formal modeling employing empirical research; intensive substantive reading. Prerequisite: POLS 425 or permission of the department chairman. Division III: American Government National Government

title: Politics: Today and Tomorrow
description: A basic introduction to the contemporary issues of national and world politics. Emphasizes both current political events and long term trends in politics.

title: American National Government
description: The organization and operation of national government as it relates to current issues such as civil rights, welfare, ecology, consumer protection, and international relations. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 131.

title: The Now Politics
description: The American political system and the manner is which it deals with such problems as poverty, pollution, racism, women's rights, and the threat of nuclear war. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 130.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, and centralization will be considered. Prerequisite: POLS 130, or 237.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government. Prerequisites recommended: POLS 130 and 237.

title: Intergovernmental Relations
description: Analysis of relations among national, state, and local governments. Considerations of constitutional and legal bases, and the nature of relations, such as grantsinaid, tax immunity, education, and interstate compacts. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 and 238. State and Local Government

title: Comparative State Politics
description: Major problems of states and the efforts to cope with them. Will include consideration of Indiana and its position relative to other states.

title: Urban Government in the United States
description: Structure, functions, problems, and trends in city, urban, and metropolitan governments.

title: Rural Local Government
description: Structure and functions of rural local government in the United States, including counties, townships, New England towns, and special districts. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237.

title: State Legislatures
description: Legislative systems in American state government. External influences (constituencies, political parties, interest groups), internal influences (organizational structure, staff, norms, decisionmaking), issues confronting state legislatures and reform proposals. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Metropolitan Problems
description: Analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related aspects; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation to the entire community. Prerequisites: POLS 237 and 238; or permission of the department chairman. Division IV: Public Law and Policy

title: Citizen and the Law
description: To better appreciate citizen encounters with the legal system, this course explains the operation of the legal system and the political aspects of the pertinent legal issues. A variety of activities, films, and lectures employed.

title: Introduction to Legal Ethics
description: A presentation of the concepts of paralegalism with an emphasis upon legal ethics and values. The development and future of the paralegal function in our present legal environment will be employed. Prerequisite: POLS 140.

title: Litigation and Legal Writing
description: Includes an analysis of paralegalism and the common types of law suits, court procedures, and appeal procedures. Indepth examination of the various reference sources available to lawyers in determining applicable law. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141.

title: Family Law
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the legal problems in the area of domestic relations. Covers legal problems involved in marriage, separation, divorce, child custody, adoption, and nonsupport.

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrealationships, purposes, and needs. Prerequisite: POLS 130 and 237, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships between government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities and finance. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: National Defense Policy
description: An international survey of military capacity and function provides the background for analysis of the national defense policy of the United States. Special emphasis on American strategic interests and problems of weapons, technology, nuclear control, and disarmament. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
description: Significant facets of legal system's response to conflicting demands upon environmental resources. Composition of environmental problems, control issues, policy formulation, and legal remedies. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Consumers, Competition, and the Law
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or the equivalent. POLS 342 recommended.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and his government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content will include cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Policy Analysis
description: Equips the student with the tools of the policy analyst through systematic analysis of programs and projects. Special emphasis on problem definition, goal determination, systematic evaluation of alternatives, socialeconomic and political indicators, performance measures, and impact evaluation. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 342.

title: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies.

title: Administrative Law
description: Legal and political study of independent regulatory agencies; their powers, functions, and roles as determined by an analysis of relevant cases in which basic principles are identified and synthesized with other areas of public law. Division V: Public Administration

title: Introduction to Planning
description: A survey of problems inherent in planning for cities and regions which utilizes contributions of other disciplines such as history, geography, sociology, and economics. Required of majors in regional and urban planning; elective for others with permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration — national, state, and local. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Administrative organizations as going concerns composed of people taking action under conditions of conflict and cooperation: examination of nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisites: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes and activities of civil service agencies; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans; efficiency measurements, and rewards; training programs; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement, and other personnel processes. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Survey of the principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances: administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, accounting of revenues, expenditures, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, management of publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Administration of American Foreign Policy
description: Deals with the process of foreign policy formulation. The course is analytic and interpretative and presents divergent views. The conception of the foreign policy process embodies the roles of the executive branch. Congress, press, public opinion, and various nongovernmental groups.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services. Prerequisites: POLS 160.

title: Problems in Planning
description: Involves field study of selected problems in planning to emphasize the interdisciplinary character of planning and to provide an opportunity to apply political, social, economic, and a real analysis; and implementation techniques. Prerequisite: senior standing and four courses in planning.

title: Administrative Problems in State and Local Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and political interaction at the state and local level for the provision of government services. Special emphasis on the major program areas such as law enforcement, education, taxation, environmental protection, housing, recreation, and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350.

title: Problems in National Administration
description: An examination in depth of uniquely national administrative problems and activities. National administrative structures and techniques are examined in detail, including their use and application in the administration of specific national policy areas.

title: Labor-Management Relations in Government
description: Examines public employee unionization, legal provisions for collective bargaining, determination and recognition of bargaining units, bilateral negotiation, and thirdparty involvement procedures, administration of agreements, and the processes and strategies in collective bargaining negotiations in public organizations. Division VI: Politics and the Political Process

title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda.

title: Public Interest Groups and Government
description: An examination of the internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Special attention will be given to the implications of pressure group activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and to the effects of pressure groups upon political parties and the political process. 473.American Political Parties. (4) Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy.

title: Women in Politics
description: A crossnational survey of women in politics with emphasis on women and public policy, the political roles of women, and the problems of women in politics within the context of contemporary public affairs.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Political Sociology
description: The political scientist's view of the social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Behavior
description: An analysis of the interrelation of political attitudes and public policy formation. Special attention to the substantive areas of voting behavior, political leadership, and the rise of mass political movements. Division VII: Foreign and Comparative Governments

title: Democratic and Totalitarian Political Systems
description: A comparison of modern political systems as represented by the principal nations of the world.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: Historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 279.

title: Comparative Policy Problems
description: A comparative political analysis of selected contemporary domestic problems confronting modern nationstates. Emphasizes both the process of policymaking and the substance of specific public policies. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 280.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural area, to the government and political structures of the three major powers in Western Europe—Great Britain, France, and Germany—and to the current state of the Western European integration movement. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: British Government and Politics
description: The political system of the United Kingdom, including a discussion of the Commonwealth and Britain's place in an expanding European community. Emphasis also on Anglo-American relations and British contributions to American political arrangements. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 382.

title: Latin-American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin-American nations.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in the field of comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of Soviet Russia
description: Structure and functions of modern Russian government, including central, regional, and local units, relationships between party and government, and such functions as law enforcement, economic planning and administration, and foreign policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 315.

title: Government and Politics of China
description: A comprehensive survey of the government and politics of modern China, both of the Republic of China and Communist China. Division VIII: International Law and Diplomacy

title: Problems and Prospects of American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: Introduction to International Relations
description: A survey of the formal relations among sovereign states in the international system, emphasizing the operation of diplomacy, the factors in international relations and procedures for the settlement of disputes.

title: The United Nations
description: Concentrated study of organization and functions of the United Nations and of foreign policy of selected members of the United Nations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: International Relations of the USSR and the Soviet Bloc
description: The foreign policy of the USSR and her satellites and a survey of the Communist Party in international action.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the law of the international community as it developed from international customs and usage and has been developed and recognized by modern states, with special reference to the position of the Western Democracies.

title: International Organizations
description: Organizations, processes, and methods devised by the nationstate system for the preservation of international peace and security and for dealing with problems of international concern.

title: World Politics
description: Analysis of general intercourse between states; normal relations, disputes and peaceful and forceful settlements; international obligations, agreements, and problems; power relationships and dominance and balance. Particular attention will be given to contemporary problems and situations. Radio and Television 297

title: Far East in World Politics
description: A comprehensive survey of contemporary international relations in the Far East mainly from post World War II to the present.

title: Communist China in World Affairs
description: A comprehensive survey of Communist China's role in international politics, with special emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Center for Radio and Television Tomlinson, Director; Alexander, De Voe, Diaz, McMullen, Moore, Salvaggio, Smith, Wible The broadcast industries and the motion picture industries provide extremely democratic channels of information, entertainment, and communication. Ball State University has long recognized the appeals which these media have upon the mass audience, and the important part which the media play in our everyday lives. For these reasons, Ball State University and the Center for Radio and Television provide a carefully selected sequence of courses which emphasize the practical applications for these media. To meet today's demands, the Center offers both graduate and undergraduate teaching and departmental majors and minors in these fields. The Ball State University program in radio, television, and motion pictures is intended for those people who are serious about career opportunities in these fast growing industries. The excellent selection of courses in the Center's curricula includes programs for those who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for instruction with the electronic media's educational aspects in the classroom, or in school administration systems which employ media. Since many positions in the broadcast and motion picture industries require a creative effort on the part of the individual, and a good understanding of teamwork, these attributes are emphasized as the student also discovers the elements of leadership and responsibility. Students working in the Center are encouraged to learn as much as possible about the function and operation of the sophisticated radio, television, and motion picture equipment planned for a "hands on" approach. Audience research, performance, production, programming, media sales, and administrative studies of the electronic and motion picture media are analyzed in the various courses. The facilities of the University radio station, WBST-FM, and the closed circuit television production facility provide additional and practical experiences for the students in the training program. Such work experiences also allow the student to build a personal resume which frequently assists in later job applications. Training on professional equipment, and the experience gained through the knowledge of operation, coupled with classroom and small group discussion, analyses, and direct study and observation of the broadcast and motion picture industries enables the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. There are many factors which influence the future employments of individuals seeking careers in these industries. Therefore, it is not possible to guarantee employment, although the Center's records of those gainfully employed after graduation in broadcasting and motion pictures is enviable. Simultaneously, every effort is made to inform the student of the stringent and competitive labor marketplaces in both the broadcast and motion picture industries. At the same time while the serious student is discovering how to develop the broadbased foundations needed for work in the industries, learning about the operation of equipment, and coming face to face with a faculty experience in both academics and the professional work world, the keen student discovers how to cope with the problems to be met in the industry marketplace, as well as the steps to be taken in the preparation for the future. The Center's builtin Work Force programs, and summer internships allow each selected student to gain an insight into ACTUAL work situations in their respective career areas. INTERNS have been placed in all markets in Indiana, and parts of Kentucky, Ohio and Illinois. title: Foundations of Broadcasting
description: An overview of the development of radio, television, and motion picture technology. Includes the transitions that took place in the media, specifically films, video tape and audio tape, with examples. Lecturers from the various professional fields will be invited to discuss their particular field.

title: Introduction to Film
description: Develops the student's awareness of the potential of motion pictures as a means of communication and expression. Provides the opportunity for recording and extending the experience of perception, description analysis, interpretation, and selfexpression through the use of picture and sound. Prerequisite: RTM 200.

title: Writing for Radio and Television
description: Discussion and practical experience in the writing of scripts, news copy, and commercials for radio and television. Special attention is directed to style and form. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Fundamentals of Radio Broadcasting 1
description: A skillsoriented introduction to radio broadcasting production procedure. A survey of development, organization, and operation of radio broadcasting in modern society. Broadcast equipment techniques and operation.

title: Fundamentals of Radio Broadcasting 2
description: An introduction to radio broadcasting program practices. The origination of the program idea, the preplanning procedures, and the execution of radio station format. Prerequisite: RTM 230.

title: Radio and Television Announcing
description: Intensive practical training in studio procedures and interpretation of radio and television copy including news, feature scripts, continuity, and commercials. Prerequisite: RTM 231.

title: Radio and Television Management
description: Intended to acquaint students with the functions of a broadcast executive as they work with program, production, and administration personnel with differing temperaments and specialities. Students will become familiar with the steps which one takes in organizing a smooth working team. Prerequisite: RTM 231.

title: Radio and Television Time Buying
description: The relationship of the radio and television station to time buying procedures on the national, regional, and local level. Emphasis is on the role of the station, the station representative, the time buyer, the agency, client, and network. Examination of qualitative and quantitative research information utilized by broadcasting. Prerequisite: RTM 231.

title: Broadcast Reporting 1
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering and reporting news on the city and county level. The reporter's relationship to local public officials and their value to the broadcast reporter as sources of information. Practical experience in the utilization of audio tape recorders, beeper telephone recordings and other instruments found in the modern radio and television newsroom. Regular newswriting/reporting assignments in conjunction with the operations of the WBST-FM news department. Prerequisite: RTM 231.

title: Fundamentals of Television Broadcasting 1
description: Introduction to the theory and practice of television studio operation with emphasis on the factors which make up the television RTM 395 and 399 are the special methods courses required in the secondary professional education sequence. Radio and Television 299 production: the cameras, microphones, lights, setting, and performers. Students should be prepared to participate in outofclass productions and laboratory sessions. Prerequisite: RTM 231.

title: Fundamentals of Television Broadcasting 2
description: Instruction and training in the method and techniques of control room operation. Switching, audio console, assistant directing, and lighting supervision. Students should be prepared to participate in outofclass productions. Prerequisite: RTM 350.

title: Broadcast Reporting 2
description: A continuing study and practice in the methods of gathering and reporting news at the state and national level. Reporters and their relationship to governmental officials at this level. Discussion and practical experience with motion picture cameras, film editing and mechanics. Regular newswriting/reporting assignments in conjunction with the operations of WBST-FM news department. Prerequisite: RTM 341.

title: Cinema 1
description: An analysis of motion pictures beginning with their practical inception prior to the turn of the century. Depicts the production and programming highlights in the evolution of the film process. Students are expected to study feature length films during an evening schedule.

title: Cinema 2
description: A continuation of Cinema 1. The motion picture art from the early "talkie" to the present day motion picture productions. Evening schedule of film presentations continued. Prerequisite: RTM 380.

title: Trends in Film Making
description: The relationship between films as developed over the past decade and the present living experience. Experimental films, trailers, educational films, television films and film titles, as well as features. Examines how these forms have changed because of new ways of approaching the medium and the development of new technique.

title: Censorship in Cinema
description: The moral measurements and restraints which have affected the film industry almost since its inception. A chronology of events which have influenced both the direction and content of motion pictures. Governmental, legal, church, and community restraints will be examined. Prerequisite: RTM 201.

title: Fundamentals of Cinematography 1
description: An introduction to the theory and practice of motion picture production with emphasis on the function of the camera, studio lighting, and audio pickup, as well as the tools used in the editing room.

title: Fundamentals of Cinematography 2
