Department of Social Work Macy, Chairperson; Dolon, Dowery, Gildner, Holmes, Rehfeld, Stacy, Stump Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex social problems, has contributed to the dramatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both an art and a science. Its art is the development of special skills used in working with people, either individually, in groups, or through community programs. Its science is the body of knowledge — derived from social and behavioral sciences about people and communities. Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare agencies; in courts as probation officers for juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics; in schools; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as well as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Funds, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of the Council on Social Work Education. It provides for the needs of four groups of students: those who wish to qualify for first level professional social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; those who desire broad preparation for informed community participation, leadership, and world citizenship for entry into decisionmaking roles within social welfare systems; and those who desire an opportunity to test their potentialities for a career in social work and to provide knowledge for use by students in allied human service professions. During the secondyear of study, students begin to complete course work in social work which builds upon a liberal arts base including knowledge in the humanities, social, behavioral, and biological sciences. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, policies, and methods of social work. Field trips and volunteer experiences in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of work with individuals, families, small groups, organizations, and communities. Practical experience is gained in the practicum where the student works under expert supervision for one quarter in a social service agency. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. Johnson, W. Johnson, Morris, Royer, Tucker Sociology is the application of the scientific method to human relations. It is the attempt to use our collective wisdom in a systematic manner in order to have as much confidence as possible in the accuracy of our social beliefs. Science goes beyond mere opinion. Social scientists attempt to describe as objectively as possible what is really happening in the world and to understand why events have occurred in a certain way. Sociology is among the younger social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades; and especially in the period since World War II its widened inclusion in patterns of general education has resulted in exceptionally rapid growth of undergraduate enrollments. Simultaneously, quickly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge; and the concepts of the discipline are becoming widely accepted throughout society. Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. Sociology is a major part of the scientific foundation for many applied fields. Social work, the criminal justice system, personnel work, counseling management, nursing practice, and the law are all based in part on the findings of sociologists. Students interested in any of these areas would find sociology courses useful. Sociology is taught at two levels. On the one hand there is the general study of social behavior such as in courses about complex organization or social class. Ideas developed in such courses are used in the more specific social sciences such as Political Science and Economics. On the other hand, sociologists teach courses about institutions for which separate departments have not developed, such as the family, and about lifecycle stages, such as childhood or the elderly. In addition we develop research skills in our courses about methods and population. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to broadening of the student's perspective of the sociocultural environment, and to the individual's own relationship to it, thus helping to produce an outlook less restricted by the limitations of untested folk beliefs. The findings derived from sociological investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. description: An introductory view of the general field of sociology including basic concepts as used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, social processes, and social institutions.

Emphasis also on an exploration into the strengths and weaknesses of this structure and its relations with the large community, as bases of change in the accommodative patterns of blackwhite relations.

Consideration will be given to the effects of changing patterns of socialization, roles, role strain, intergroup relations, and the social process. Prerequisite: four hours of credit in sociology.

title: Sociology of Deviant Behavior

Three essential forms will be reviewed: (1) deviance arising from disability in social and physical functioning, (2) deviance arising from violation of social norms, and (3) deviance arising from membership in groups observing radical social ideologies. Prerequisite: SOC 100. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 242 prior to September 1, 1975.

title: Social Problems

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Leisure and Popular Culture
description: Discussion of issues related to the uses and distribution of nonwork time and activities. Trends in recreation folk arts, informal associations, and the growing leisure industries will be examined.

title: Blue Collar Society and Culture
description: The social realities, life styles, and selfperceptions of the bluecollar segment of society is examined. Similarly, socioeconomic and demographic patterns are investigated. Prerequisite: 4 hours of credit in sociology courses.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors affecting utilization of treatment programs.

title: Introduction to Sociological Research
description: Principles and techniques of organizing, conducting, and interpreting sociological research; the appropriateness of particular methodologies for different kinds of research problems. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in sociology.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in the social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 and 380.

description: A critical survey of influential views regarding the nature of society and human relations from the Greek period through the 19th century Romanticists. Social thinkers and intellectual epochs are interpreted as products of the prevailing social conditions, and are employed for purposes of illuminating contemporary social issues and sociological theories.

title: Classical Sociological Theory

The cultural and intellectual milieu in which the theoretical works were generated will be noted. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100.

title: Mass Society and Culture

title: Industrial Sociology

title: Sociology of Medical Care Organizations
description: A sociological analysis of medical care organizations and professionals with emphasis on intraorganizational, interprofessional, and agencyclient relations. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: A sociological analysis of the field of mental health with attention to social definitions of mental illness, selfrecognition of illness, the process of seeking care, treatment institutions, and the aftermath of treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as it is related to various sociological variables. Various sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Families in the Middle Years
description: An overview of the American family as the marital pair approach and encounter middle age. Special attention will be given to problems which Sociology 309 necessitate interaction with the criminal justice and corrections system. Prerequisite: four hours of credit in sociology.

title: Social Origins and Control of Deviant Behavior
description: Development of an acquaintance with types of family, neighborhood, and community situations which serve as pressures toward deviant behavior. Case studies and field observations. Community action in the detection, control, and treatment of behavior deviants is examined from the point of view of analyzing facilities and programs. Prerequisite: SOC 100.

title: Small Groups
description: Analysis of data on experimental laboratory research on small groups and field research on small group dynamics. Attention is given to the relationship between group productivity, group cohesion, size, interaction patterns, and related areas. Prerequisite: SOC 260 or GXPSY 316.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Methods and Materials of Population Analysis
description: Presents materials concerning the major sources of population data and elementary techniques for their analysis. Topics include population composition, mortality, natality, reproductivity, migration, and population projection. Prerequisite: SOC 382 or the equivalent or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historic functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis of the social dynamics of the urban core in metropolitan areas. Attention given to the development of cities and their cores, stressing ecological and demographic factors. The focus shifts to an examination of the social issues associated with the concept of the inner city, especially racism, poverty, crime, welfare, and education. Finally, policy alternatives for alleviating these conditions are considered. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 242.

title: Methods and Materials in Urban Social Ecology
description: An analysis of theoretical approaches to urban social ecology and presentation of recent empirical findings bearing on this topic. Attention is also given to various statistical methods for the analysis of such information. Prerequisite: SOC 382 or the equivalent or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and utilizing sources of data; and application of survey findings to programs of community action. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 380 or 472.

title: Advanced Sociological Data Analysis
description: Deals with the selection and utilization of advanced statistical techniques and sophisticated means of calculation which have been particularly useful in analyzing sociological data. Such topics as nonparametric statistics, factor analysis, sampling statistics, and multiple regression and path analysis will be discussed in the context of sociological research. Prerequisite: SOC 382 or equivalent.

title: Independent Study in Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar in Sociology
description: An openended course offering for fourth year sociology majors. Both the focus of study and the format of the course will be determined by the students in conjunction with the instructor. Prerequisite: 24 hours in sociology and permission of the department chairman. It is a general program for undergraduate use, while persons specialize as they move toward graduate degrees. In the area of general speech, the University offers both graduate and undergraduate programs. A large proportion of those students electing a speech major plan to become teachers in the public schools. These teachers are expected to direct debating and individual events, produce theatre, and promote and direct radio and television programs. They are also asked to be in charge of special convocations. Their class work is the development of the skills of public address and participation in a democratic society. Also they must develop an appreciation and skill for interpretation and theatre as performed in school theatres or through the facilities of mass media. Another responsibility is to develop an appreciation of the artistic, an understanding of the basic issues of people, and a respect for their cultural heritage. The profession of general speech assists liberal arts graduates to develop these same skills and attitudes. In addition, the speech major and minor are especially useful to support students who enter other professions such as law, the ministry, politics, public relations, and professional radio, television, and theatre. The University offers many student activities in the areas of intercollegiate debating, individual speech events, conferences, and theatre. It is assumed that general speech majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Theatre Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a most modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher licensing in speech for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work is available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist people to understand themselves. It also assists students to understand their dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office and should be requested early in the student's academic career. title: Fundamentals of Public Speaking
description: Fundamentals and techniques of organizing material and presenting that material in individual speeches. Emphasis on personal speaking improvement in the classroom and in public performances.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasis is on techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Beginning Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Development and composition of the debate case and consideration of factual argumentation. Prerequisite: high school speech.

title: Intermediate Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Stress on direct clash and crossquestion debate. This course involves tournament debating. Prerequisite: SPCH 213.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: The focus of this course is on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Will stress the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Personal speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation problems.

title: Speech Practicum
description: The student works upon extemporaneous speaking, discussion, debate, oratory, or interpretive reading for intercollegiate competition, or works in theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: The development of principles of rhetorical criticism and the application of the principles to an intensified study of prominent platform, radio, and television speakers. Consideration is given also to the influence of the speaker upon our social and political life. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Parliamentary Procedure
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher.

title: Intercollegiate Forensics
description: Practical experience in speech, intercollegiate debate, discussion, oratory, extemporaneous speaking, and interpretive reading. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminartype class focusing on various aspects of and/or problems in speech communication as they relate to individuals in their personal and professional relationships. Open to Honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; EDSEC 299, and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Deals specifically with discipline oriented classroom management techniques, an introductory involvement in the teaching of a discipline, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of a particular discipline in the secondary school curriculum. These topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: SPCH 395.

title: Studies in Persuasion
description: An intensified study and application of the principles of effective public speaking; the ideational formulation and delivery of longer speeches; the rhetorical analysis of significant speeches. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department head.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: An examination through exposure to theory, actual practice, and criticism, of the process of communication. Will include communication models of message encoding, transmission, decoding and feedback; the complexity of language, including abstracting and determination of meaning; problems in facetoface, small group, platform speaking, and mass media communication; and communication breakdowns.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of small group literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problemsolving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Business and Professional Speech
description: Concentrates on small group communication and discussion, parliamentary procedure, and on manuscript speeches for the business and professional person. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or equivalent or permission of the department head.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech and Theatre pursues a particular area of study in depth on a consultative basis with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Speech
description: The student is assigned to onthejob experience in such places as a college classroom, a political campaign or office, summer camp, or summer theatre. Students will be permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the amount of college credit to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in some aspect of speech and/or theatre and permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with SPCH 598 but no more than 8 hours may be earned at one time. Speech and Theatre 313

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: An overview of the field of threatre with special reference to the origins of drama.

title: Stagecraft
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of the crafts involved in theatre production at the school, college, and community theatre levels. Three hours of lecture and three arranged hours of laboratory a week.

title: Principles of Stage Makeup
description: An investigation of the principles, techniques, and materials of stage makeup and practical experience in their application.

title: Oral Interpretation
description: The study of prose fiction, poetry and drama through the medium of oral performance.

title: Acting 1
description: A lecturelaboratory class stressing the basic principles of acting. Major emphasis on stage movement.

title: Acting 2
description: A lecturelaboratory course on the principles of acting with major emphasis on character analysis and development. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Modern Drama
description: Analysis of selected dramas from the time of Ibsen to the present day and of the conditions under which they originally were produced.

title: Advanced Oral Interpretation
description: Literature through the medium of oral performance employing the modal approach to literary classification. Prerequisite: THEAT 230.

title: Directing 1
description: Theory and practice of directing for the theatre. Exercises in movement, line interpretation, creation of atmosphere, and the effective use of stage areas. Prerequisite: THEAT 232 and 233.

title: Children's Theatre
description: The principles of theatre devoted to creative dramatics. Twothirds of the course is devoted to formal dramatics. A public performance will be arranged.

title: Advanced Theatre Practice
description: Students design and execute a theatre project in such areas as scenery designs, lighting, properties, acting, directing, oral interpretation, and house management. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in theatre courses and permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Theatre 1
description: The early history of theatre from its Egyptian and Grecian origins through the medieval period.

title: History of Theatre 2
description: The theatre from the Renaissance through the eighteenth century.

title: History of Theatre 3
description: The modern theatre commencing with its origins in the nineteenth century.

title: Studies in American Theatre
description: An investigation of significant movements in the American professional theatre and its drama.

title: Studies in Continental Theatre
description: An intensive study of selected continental theatre movements from the turn of the century to the present day. Prerequisite: THEAT 411 or 412.

title: Studies in Contemporary European Theatre
description: An intensive study of contemporary European drama and theatres involving a field trip of three weeks to European theatre centers with appropriate side excursions. Discussions with leading theatre educators and professionals will be planned plus attendance at current productions. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department head.

title: Theatrical Design and Lighting
description: Advanced training and experience in the problems of set design and lighting for theatrical productions in many forms and styles. Some aspects of television design will be covered. Prerequisite: THEAT 220.

title: Theatre Costume Design
description: Practice in the research, design, and building techniques involved in the preparation of period costumes for use in theatre productions. Special consideration is given to the costume problems facing the elementary or secondary school teacher involved in drama.

title: Studies in Technical Theatre
description: A detailed study of technical problems of theatre production. Students must arrange to meet with the costume lab, the scenery lab, or the lighting lab. Prerequisite: 8 hours of technical theatre or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Stage Lighting
description: The design, media, instrumentation, control, and operation of stage lighting. Practical laboratory work in stage lighting on university production. Prerequisite: THEAT 220.

title: Readers Theatre
description: Theories and performance techniques relevant to group interpretation: readers theatre, chamber theatre, and choral reading.

title: Styles of Acting
description: The study and performance of the styles of acting appropriate to major types of drama from antiquity to the present. Prerequisite: THEAT 232 and 233 or permission of the department head.

title: Directing 2
description: Further investigation of the work of the director with special reference to directing the various styles, modes, and periods of theatre. Prerequisite: THEAT 350 or the equivalent.

title: Methods and Materials in School Play Production
description: For the prospective or actual directors of secondary school plays. Choice of plays, community values, casting, secondary school stages, advanced makeup, lighting, and stagecraft.

title: Creative Dramatics
description: Principles of developing original dramatizations through improvisational techniques. Students are expected to observe and work with children as well as with college adults.

title: Theatre Workshop for High School Teachers
description: Participation in the Summer High School Theatre Workshop or in the Summer Festival Theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Theatre Management
description: Study and practice in box office procedures, house management, publicity, and promotion as related to college, community, and professional theatres. Prerequisite: 12 hours of theatre. Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology Hoops, Chairman; Anderson, Artes, Farling, Harmon, Heady, Hemeyer, Kramar, Lindell, Thornburg, Updike, Wilson Until the fall of 1978, students entering the University who graduate with a bachelor's degree in speech pathology and audiology have been eligible for initial certification to work as speech and language clinicians in the public schools. Hence, most bachelor's degree graduates are employed in public school corporations. As of 1978, students entering the University who seek state teaching licensure to work in the public schools in speech pathology or audiology must acquire a master's degree as the preservice level of training. Persons with masters' degrees may also work in hospital speech and hearing clinics, rehabilitation centers, college or university centers, and communitysponsored speech and hearing agencies. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed. D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers two undergraduate majors in speech pathology and audiology. Both are departmental majors. One is a departmental major for students who are sure they wish to work eventually in a hospital, college, or community clinic and plan to proceed immediately to the master's degree without acquiring licensure to work in the public schools. The other, identified as a departmental major for those seeking licensure in school services personnel as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist, is for students who do plan to be eligible for public school employment in these positions. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology or in audiology, and completion of licensure requirements as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist is performed as part of the master's degree program. The master's degee is also required for state licensure through the Indiana Board of Health, required for all individuals who work in job environments other than the public schools, and for membership in and certification by the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate major programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs: public school speech, language, and hearing programs, hospitals, preschool nursery programs, and the University Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. In the last, children and adults come to the Ball State campus for clinical work for speech, language, and/or hearing problems. The Department also offers a departmental minor in speech pathology and audiology, for those students interested in but not committed to this profession, and a departmental minor in speech science for those students planning a career in industry or business in a research laboratory dealing with exploration of the parameters of speech or speech identification. Approval to pursue the major programs is based in part upon the student's performance in clinical practica, and is ordinarily considered early in the student's junior year. Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic Regular fulltime students enrolled in the University are administered a free speech and hearing test. This screening is performed by appointment for new fulltime students. Any speech or hearing problem which may interfere with vocational objectives is called to the attention of the student. Speech Pathology and Audiology 315 Special work for regularly enrolled students who desire to correct deficiencies in speech and voice is provided by the Clinic, located on the ground floor of the English Building. Educational work and guidance for those persons who have hearing problems are also available. Recommendations for corrective procedures are based on the needs of the individual student. Certain programs of the University, including all teaching curricula, demand various proficiency levels in regard to speech and voice. One function of the Clinic is to implement these criteria. Outpatient speech and hearing evaluation and therapy are integral parts of the clinic program, as is the education of speech pathologists and audiologists. Some classes are available for prospective classroom teachers who desire information relative to the management of speech or hearing difficulties. The work of the University Clinic is closely associated with that of the Burris School Clinic. The Clinic is equipped with the latest sound and acoustic devices, including recording machines, tape recorders, recordings, testing materials, audiometers, and other clinical equipment. Shipman The Teachers College has major responsibility for teacher education in the University. Contributions of departments in other Colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by Directors of Elementary and Secondary Teacher Education, who are responsible to the Dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by a Teacher Preparation Council which represents the total University. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers and teacher educators in early childhood education, kindergartenprimary education and elementary education, with programs at all degree levels. The Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education provides the professional education for secondary school teachers with the exception of special methods. Graduate programs in secondary and higher education and in educational foundations are also housed in this department. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate and graduate education programs for teachers of the mentally retarded, hearing impaired, the emotionally disturbed, the physically handicapped, the neurologically impaired/ learning disabled and the multiply handicapped. The Center for Lifelong Education houses programs in the areas of curriculum, adult education, and community education. The Burris Laboratory School is a center for demonstration, participation, and research in teacher education, as well as for program development and dissemination in respect to elementary and secondary schools. The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers service courses in school administration and programs at master's, specialist, and doctoral levels for students preparing for educational management and for administrative, supervisory, and collegiate positions in its areas of expertise. Two departments of the Teachers College serve students in areas of psychology. The Department of Educational Psychology offers undergraduate and graduate programs in applications of psychology to teacher education and in educational psychometry, school psychology, human development, measurement, and research. It also provides service courses as needed for related programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services offers courses and programs through the doctorate in its principal areas of specialization for people in educational and other positions. It also houses the programs for social psychology. Departments of the Teachers College, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public education and psychology; for production and dissemination of research; for innovation in instructional practices, and for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education. Courses included in the general field of education serve students on a wide variety of programs and are not appropriately assignable to a single department. Five departments in the Teachers College offer programs leading to a doctoral degree. EDUCATION: GENERAL (EDGEN)

title: Exploration of Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior in American Schools
description: Analyzes factors which influence the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in schools and educational settings. Particular emphasis will be on the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in the American schools.

title: Urban Education: Problems and Prospects
description: Explores many issues facing public education in urban areas, such as equal opportunity, federal and state aid, accountability, sociological and cultural factors, teacher unionization, busing, and community control.

title: Honors Colloquium in Education
description: The critical analysis and evaluation of selected controversial issues in American education. Restricted to honors students.

title: Contributions of Social and Cultural Minorities to American Education
description: Analysis of lifestyles of different cultural groups in terms of strengths developed by children that could be taken advantage of in school and other institutions. Flexible attitudes, bilingual/biculturalism, creativity, improvision, adjustments, and family structures will be emphasized in terms of strengths rather than weaknesses.

title: In- Service Teacher Education
description: A field course designed to provide groups of classroom teachers in a local school system an opportunity to identify and work on problems within their teaching situation. PRE-STUDENT TEACHING PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES The purpose of prestudent teaching professional laboratory experiences is to provide students on the Teacher Education Curriculum with a systematic, planned sequence of experiences in appropriate educational settings. These experiences are designed to familiarize the students with principles of classroom management and the teachinglearning process in practical and real school environments, and to induct students into the teaching act. Prerequisites for EDEL 360 (Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School) and EDSEC 290 (Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary School) The following are prerequisites for admission to EDEL 360 and EDSEC 290: 1. Admission to the Teacher Education Curriculum 2. Completion of a minimum of 93 quarter hours of credit 3. A composite grade point average of 2.1 or above 4. Clearance from the Office of Professional Selection on such matters as speech and hearing, health, and other tests as may be required from time to time by University authorities 5. Successful passage of a TB test within twelve months prior to the time of taking EDEL 360 or EDSEC 290 6. Completion of EDPSY 250 (elementary education and special education majors) or EDPSY 251 (secondary education majors) 7. EDPSY 290 (must be taken prior to or parallel with EDSEC 290 or EDEL 360) Organization of the Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management Courses (EDEL 360 and EDSEC 290) The teacher education programs of the University have been designed to include a number of planned, sequential courses which incorporate laboratory experiences in educational settings as an integral part of the curricular offerings. These prestudent teaching laboratory experiences culminate in the EDEL 360 and EDSEC 290 courses which require assignment to a classroom in an appropriate educational setting for one quarter to observe, prepare instructional presentations, and undertake other instructional tasks appropriate for students prior to student teaching. Ball State University provides laboratory settings for EDEL 360 and EDSEC 290 in the oncampus Burris Laboratory School as well as in affiliated public school systems. Burris is an open district school with an educational program for children from kindergarten through grade twelve. University students who are preparing to become teachers may have these experiences in the Burris School, in Muncie City Schools and/or in other school corporations within commuting distance. A weekly seminar with a college supervisor is an integral part of the laboratory experiences for these courses. STUDENT TEACHING The purpose of student teaching is to provide students the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professionally licensed teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Prerequisites for Student Teaching The following are prerequisite for admission to student teaching: 1. Admission to the Teacher Education Curriculum 2. Completion of EDEL 360 or EDSEC 290 (Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management) and special methods in the teaching major. At least one quarter or summer term must intervene between enrollment in EDEL 360 or EDSEC 290 and enrollment in student teaching 3. Completion of the senior physical examination is recommended and TB clearance is required 4. Completion of a minimum of 140 quarter hours of credit, excepting that a student may enroll in EDEL 460 during the last quarter of the junior year 5. A gradepoint average of at least 2.1 overall in the area of concentration and in professional education courses 6. Completion of such tests in English usage, academic competence, intellectual ability, emotional adjustment, speech and hearing performance, and others as may be required from time to time by University authorities 7. Submission of an application for a student teaching assignment to the Student Teaching Office on the dates indicated The applicant who holds a baccalaureate degree from some institution other than Ball State must meet all of the above requirements and, in addition, must have completed at least 15 quarter hours on the Ball State campus, including either EDEL 360 or EDSEC 290, and must be admitted as a regular student. Application for Student Teaching Regular students make application for a student teaching assignment in the Winter Quarter of the year prior to that in which they expect to do student teaching. Students transferring to Ball State after this date, who plan to complete their certification requirements in one year, must make application in September. Official notification of the student teaching assignment will be mailed to the student after the final eligibility determination. Usually this will be in the quarter prior to student teaching. Students needing information in regard to their assignment prior to this notification may inquire at the Student Teaching Office. General Considerations The student must be free of outside commitments that might interfere with fulltime student teaching obligations. This means that students cannot be regularly employed, nor should they carry a heavy load of extracurricular activities. Enrollment for course overload during the quarter is permitted only with approval of the Coordinator for Student Teaching. A predetermined number of days in seminars conducted by the university supervisor, both at the beginning and the end of the quarter, are a part of the student teaching requirement. Increased demands for professionally licensed supervising teachers resulting from increased enrollment in student teaching have made assignments more difficult in many schools Professional Laboratory Experiences 321 throughout the state, while assignments in Muncie public schools have been difficult for several years. title: Career and Life Planning
description: Focus is on helping the individual make career and life plans. A series of techniques (role playing, psychodrama, sociodrama, value clarification, and decision making) will be utilized to facilitate each student examining his or her interrelated value systems associated with education, work, leisure, and self expression.

title: Effective Interpersonal Relationship Development
description: An introduction to the basic psychological principles and techniques of developing interpersonal relationships. Emphasis on understanding one's self and the dynamics of interaction with others. Opportunity is provided for an individual to explore his/her strengths and weaknesses in interpersonal relationships within groups of varying ages, races, and ethnic background.

title: Fundamentals of Counseling and Guidance
description: Exploration of the principles, purposes, and nature of counseling and guidance in the public school with emphasis upon ways in which teachers can contribute to and profit from the school's guidance program.

title: Psychological Processes and Techniques of Interviewing
description: Basic psychological principles and techniques of the therapeutic interviewing process. title: Techniques of Crisis Intervention
description: Basic theory, skills, and techniques of emergency psychological intervention and counseling with persons who experience intense situational and emotional distress. Department of Educational Psychology Joy, Chairman; Annis, Bennett, Church, Fischer, Gale, Gupta, Harshbarger, Henriksen, Hosey, Hunt, Irving, Klem, Koenker, Kuo, McKee, Miller, Mitchell, Paschal, Richmond, Schurr, Sparzo, Taylor, Treloar, Trent, Van Every, Wenck Educational psychology is a social science concerned with the development of individuals. It includes the study of human development, learning, adjustment, measurement, research, and statistics as these relate to the understanding of an individual. The objectives of educational psychology — like those of other fields of psychology — are to understand, describe, predict, and guide human behavior. These purposes are accomplished through research service functions and teaching about human relationships, human development, and changes in human behavior. Programs in educational psychology are specialized and offered generally on the graduate level. However, a departmental undergraduate minor in the psychology of human development is offered. Some undergraduate courses in the area are required as psychological foundations for teacher education and other undergraduate programs, and a number are offered as electives. For graduate students there are several programs: a major in educational psychology on a Master of Arts or a Master of Arts in Education degree; a certification program and a major in psychometry on a Master of Arts or a Master of Arts in Education degree; a cognate area in educational psychology for doctoral students; a specialization in psychometry on a Specialist in Education (6th year) degree; and a Doctor of Education degree with a major in school psychology. title: Home, School, and Community Relationships in Early Childhood Education
description: Involves experiences to enrich the relationships among parents, teachers, and children in the home, school, and community environments and to acquaint and involve students with the variety of community resources concerned with the welfare of young children and their families.

title: Education of the Culturally Different Child
description: Provides students in elementary education with a broad understanding of characteristics of economically disadvantaged and culturally different children requisite to dealing realistically with their needs. Stresses consideration of teacher self attitudes towards economically disadvantaged and culturally different children as well as examination of promising instructional changes and approaches for improving learning opportunities for these children. Motivation, classroom organization, discipline, parentteacher relationships, school integration, and nonstandard dialect are emphasized. 452g. Psychology of Early Childhood. (4) Study of young children of nursery school and kindergarten age involving lectures, readings, discussions, and conferences to give individual guidance to students and help them interpret their study of the physical, mental, social, and emotional development of selected young children. Consideration is given to growth in perception, language, expression, and interests.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Elementary
description: Not open to the student who has credit in EDGEN 462.

title: Student Teaching: Pre -Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach children in prekindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Primary Grades
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in primary grades the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 468. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in kindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 467. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Practicum in Elementary Education
description: Laboratory and seminar course involving a study of progressive school practices, the philosophy of education underlying, and the possibilities of using, progressive practices in the public school. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Elementary Education
description: Independent study and research in the field of elementary education. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems in Elementary Education
description: An analysis of one's professional preparation for teaching, identifying areas in which students need to bolster weaknesses and augment strengths, and arranging for more preparation in these areas. Prerequisite: one term of student teaching. EDUCATION: READING (EDRDG)

title: Self-Improvement in Reading
description: Individualized evaluation and diagnosis of specific strengths and weaknesses in reading is followed by practice to improve comprehension skills, reading speed, vocabulary, notetaking, and content reading. Enrollment with approval of the director of reading. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Prereading Development
description: Basic understandings of environments and planned activities that foster positive attitudes and interests related to reading, procedures that stimulate prereading development, and related practical experiences with young children.

title: The Teaching of Reading in Today's Schools
description: Designed to review the current thinking, approaches, and methodology of teaching reading in today's schools. Attention is directed to readiness, word recognition and analysis, comprehension, and planning of the total developmental reading program, with emphasis on reading at the elementary level.

title: Study of Selected Aspects of the Elementary School Reading Program
description: Designed to review the current thinking and approaches to teaching reading in the elementary school, and the relationship of basic psychological principles to teaching practices. Prerequisite or parallel: one term of student teaching at the elementary school level.

title: Corrective Reading in the Classroom
description: Provides prospective teachers with understanding of difficulties in reading plus practical experience in assessing reading difficulties and in study of corrective treatment. Includes guided laboratory situations with students exhibiting reading limitations who can be aided by the regular classroom teacher. Prerequisite: EDRDG 400 or EDRDS 420 or EDRDM 421.

title: Reading Approaches and Strategies
description: Provides prospective classroom teachers (K-12) with opportunities to study and utilize various approaches and strategies used in teaching reading. Includes evaluation of related instructional materials. Prerequisite: EDRDG 430.

title: Practicum in Reading
description: Provides experiences for prospective teachers (K-12) in (1) grouping students of varying abilities in reading; (2) planning and implementing a classroom reading program appropriate for these students. Prerequisite: EDRDG 435. EDUCATION: READING SECONDARY (EDRDS)

title: Reading in Secondary School
description: See the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. EDUCATION: READING MIDDLE (EDRDM)

title: Improving General Reading Skills in Junior High/Middle Schools

It is a lifelong process. Recognizing this, the Center for Lifelong Education is concerned with encompassing and unifying all stages of education. Lifelong education includes both formal and informal patterns of education and random experiential learning. Education begins with the family and moves into society as a.child begins to interact with nonfamily individuals. The formal institutions of education are important but they constitute only part of many social agencies providing opportunities for individuals to learn. To promote lifelong education, Ball State University established the Center for Lifelong Education and specifically charged it with providing formal and informal programs which would prepare individuals to design, implement, and coordinate educational opportunities for individuals throughout their lives. In the formal portion of this task, the Center either offers or directs the following programs of study, mostly at the graduate level: M.A. Adult Education; M.A. Community Education; M.A. Executive Development for Public Service; M.A.E. Curriculum; Ed. S. Curriculum; Doctoral Cognates in Curriculum; Adult and/or Community Education; and Departmental minor in Gerontology (See Interdepartmental). In addition, the Center serves as a vehicle within the Teachers College through which interdisciplinary educational services, both formal and informal, not traditionally offered by any current Teachers College department or service unit, may be developed, implemented, and coordinated. Current informal programs include: research, school curriculum studies, program evaluation, nontraditional students, inservice professional development programs, retirement planning, and related service activities. title: Seminar in Facilitating Lifelong Learning
description: A seminar course for nontraditional students which will provide an opportunity to explore, discuss, and reenforce new changes in self as a learner and as a group participator. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on the Evolving Roles of American Men and Women
description: A course for nontraditional students which provides an indepth look at a history of rights and roles of eighteenth-, nineteenth-, and twentiethcentury American men and women. Prerequisite: EDAC 101 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on Investigation into Job Opportunities
description: A field course for nontraditional students which will provide opportunities for exploration into job opportunities or advancements through placement experiences in work settings, depth interviews and visitations, and directed readings. Emphasis is on problemsolving, acquiring firsthand knowledge in order to make realistic career decisions by older male and female students. Prerequisite: EDAC 101, 102, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Adult Education
description: The history and current status of adult education in the United States and in selected foreign countries; the nature, scope, purposes, and historical development of adult education institutions and program areas; an introduction to and overview of adult education as a field of study and practice.

title: The Adult as a Learner
description: Designed to familiarize students with implications of learning theories for education of adults in a variety of learning situations and to develop skills in use of applicable methods and techniques.

title: Adult Psychology
description: Developmental study of psychological stages of adulthood. Not open to the student who has credit in EDPSY 355.

title: Volunteers and Voluntarism
description: An analysis of the historical, theoretical, philosophical, and operational perspectives of voluntarism. Attention will be given to developing new and innovative models for volunteer programs based on field experience, readings, and course sessions.

title: The Community Educator
description: Designed to familiarize the student with the structure, purpose, and processes of community education development with emphasis on the development of skills and competencies required of a community education coordinator.

title: Workshop in Adult and/or Community Education
description: A course for persons who wish to participate in preservice or inservice training in the areas of adult and/or community education. Specific content will depend upon interests of the participants. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. EDUCATION: CURRICULUM (EDCUR)

title: Curriculum Construction
description: Principles to be used in determining the nature and content of the learner's experiences in the public school. The issue of essentialism and progressivism, teacherpupil planning, the larger use of group action in the solution of problems, and betterment of relation between problem solving and principles operative in these problems.

title: Psychology of Later Life
description: A study of the later years of life with emphasis on the adaptations required. Includes theories of aging, physical and social changes taking place, and coping strategies. Not open to the student who has credit in EDPSY 325.

title: Educational Gerontology
description: A study of education and aging with emphasis on a lifespan approach. Topics include education about aging for children and youth, career educational opportunities in gerontology, education for paraprofessionals and volunteers in the field of aging, retirement planning education, and educational opportunities for older adults.

title: Internship in Gerontology
description: Experience in one or more of the agencies, institutions, or programs now providing gerontological services or otherwise related to the field of gerontology. The internship is carried out under the joint supervision of the Institute of Gerontology and a practitioner representing the agency, institution, or program. The student chooses the internship setting with the guidance of a faculty sponsor and the approval of the practitioner. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. PREPARATION OF TEACHERS FOR MULTICULTURED SECONDARY SCHOOLS (MULTICUL) The MULTICUL program at Ball State University offers young people an opportunity to translate objectives, expressions, and demonstrations into actuality. The ultimate objectives lead toward possible solutions to one of America's crucial problems, developing racial and cultural harmony. The program is designed not only to deal with black and white relations, but it also encompasses as many ethnic groups as possible. Multiculturism is a basic characteristic of our society as well as our schools; therefore, potential teachers should prepare themselves to meet realistic situations. Three of the experiences that the MULTICUL program utilizes in the preparation of potential teachers are as follows: 1. Specialized or elective courses offered in many major departments. 2. Courses designed especially for MULTICUL students by the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. 3. Laboratory experiences in multicultural communities, social and professional organizations, and schools. Along with learning how to understand and how to coexist peacefully with fellow Americans, the participants in MULTICUL should be more employable, not only in Indiana, but across the nation. MULTICUL does not prohibit students from majoring in their areas of interest. MULTICUL is offered as a departmental minor, and it can be scheduled along with any teaching major at Ball State. title: School in the American Culture
description: An introduction to the theory, scope, organization, and functions of the public school in the United States. The student will examine the role of public education at all levels at which it operates and the responsibilities carried out by the professional teachers in their educational work.

title: International Dialogue on American Education and Life
description: Perspectives on American education and its cultural setting developed through interaction among international and American students and comparative study of educational and other social institutions as they relate to education.

title: The Role of Women in the Past, Present, and Future Development of Education
description: A survey of the role of women in education with an emphasis on analysis of career development, styles of work, and job satisfaction. EDUCATION: HIGHER (EDHI)

title: Introduction to Personnel Services in Residence Halls
description: Principles involved in understanding and working with individuals and student groups in residence halls, social forces affecting college students, and the relationship of the residence hall program to the total university. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned; a maximum of 1 credit hour per quarter.

title: Leadership and Development of Student Organizations
description: Examines philosophical bases, group processes, and skills relevant to leadership and development of student organizations in higher education. Focuses on understandings and skills requisite for effective involvement in student groups. EDUCATION: JUNIOR HIGH/MIDDLE (EDJHM)

title: Teaching in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Develops basic instructional strategies for junior high/middle schools. General methods, problems of student advisement, classroom management in light of study of the nature of junior high/middle school children, and specific laboratory experiences are emphasized. Prerequisite: EDPSY 351 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: The Junior High/Middle School Curriculum
description: Several curricular approaches appropriate for students in the age group of 10 to 14 years will be examined in relation to current research. Direct development of alternative curricular programs and appropriate use of merging structures and nontraditional materials will be emphasized. Prerequisite: EDJHM 312.

title: Foundations of Junior High/Middle School Education
description: Junior high/middle school education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from the perspective of the sociological, philosophical, historical, economic, political, and anthropological foundations of junior high/middle schools and teachers are stressed. Prerequisite: EDJHM 312.

title: Student Teaching in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Required for the Standard License in Junior High/Middle School Education. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public junior high/middle school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. EDUCATION: READING MIDDLE (EDRDM)

title: Improving Reading Skills in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: A general course for all junior high/middle school teachers which examines reading problems and provides specific methodology for improvement of reading skills in junior high/middle schools. General diagnostic teaching techniques appropriate for teachers in all curricular areas are to be achieved. Exit competencies are required. EDUCATION: READING SECONDARY (EDRDS)

title: Reading in Secondary School
description: Practical procedures for developing effective reading skills to be applied by all secondary classroom teachers. Focuses on relationships between the process of reading and learning of content, on planning to meet total range of student reading needs, and on methods and materials to enhance comprehension and study skills in all areas of secondary school curriculum. EDUCATION: SECONDARY (EDSEC)

title: Introduction to the Problems of Teaching in Cross-Cultural Environments
description: The process of education from the perspective of an educator and the varied agencies in society for formal and informal education. Provides experiences in and exposures to educational situations which will broaden student perceptions and understandings. Emphasizes experiential and problemsolving approaches to learning. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Secondary Education for Paraprofessionals
description: Study of American junior and senior high schools from the standpoint of the paraprofessional in secondary education. Prerequisite: admission to the secondary paraprofessional program. Parallel: EDSEC 111.

title: Freshman Paraprofessional Practicum
description: The organization and operation of secondary schools and the duties, procedures, and problems of secondary school faculty and staff. Provides initial experiences in assisting secondary faculty and staff. Prerequisite: admission to the secondary paraprofessional program. Parallel: EDSEC 110.

title: Basic Concepts of Secondary Education
description: Examines through classroom investigation and practical field experiences the structure, function, and development of secondary education in the United States. Designed to help students make valid decisions about preparing for and functioning in a teaching career by studying professionalism, job requirements, employment opportunities, secondary school curriculum, and the role of secondary education within the entire educational process.

title: Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Introduces prospective teachers to responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 100 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Secondary Paraprofessional and the Use of Instructional Technology
description: The use of instructional technology and the preparation of instructional materials as these skills are employed by the paraprofessional.

title: Secondary Paraprofessional Internship
description: Practical experiences in the duties, responsibilities, and related problems of the secondary school paraprofessional. The intern will be assigned to a secondary school during a regular school year for a period of one quarter. Prerequisite: EDSEC 110, 111.

title: Principles of Teaching Classroom Management: Secondary School
description: Inducts the student into the teaching act. Includes specific technical skill development, study of principles of teaching, and analysis of classroom management, organization, and discipline. Intensive inschool assignments, observations, skills, participation, and direct contact with adolescents are required. Prerequisite: EDPSY 251 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290.

title: Laboratory Experience in Secondary Education
description: Provides direct experiences in working with students, teachers, paraprofessionals, community agencies, and other appropriate assignments for undergraduate students who plan to enter secondary school teaching. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; no more than 4 hours may be taken in one quarter.

title: Instructional Strategies in Multicultured Schools
description: Theory and application of special instructional strategies of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms with special emphasis on multicultured educational situations. Prerequisite: EDSEC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: American Education: A Critical Examination
description: The complex educational system and alternatives to the traditional system, featuring an individualized, issueoriented instructional approach. Designed for students who do not plan to teach but open to those in teacher education.

title: Application of Instructional Strategies and Approaches in Junior High School
description: Factors affecting instruction in junior high schools are analyzed. Students are encouraged to develop skills which lead to more creative personal development; general instructional methods, techniques, and evaluation procedures especially appropriate for junior high schools will be the primary focus.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms.

title: Planning and Assessing Instructional Programs
description: Designed to provide secondary school teachers with methods of establishing instructional programs with feedback networks which will encourage continuous assessment and appropriate alterations of the educational environment. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Independent Study in Secondary Education
description: Independent study and research in the field of secondary education. Topics and activities to be chosen in consultation with an individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of four hours of credit may be earned.

title: Contemporary Problems in Education and Professional Concerns of the Beginning Teacher
description: Provides opportunity to examine critically and to focus educational experience and knowledge on contemporary and personally significant problems of education. Emphasizes immediate professional concerns of prospective firstyear teachers. Prerequisite: EDSEC 301 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Foundations of Secondary Education
description: Education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from the perspective of the sociological, philosophical, historical, economic, political, and anthropological foundations of secondary education. Contemporary issues such as cultural values, social class, ethnic groups, political pressure, and the role of the teachers will be stressed. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299.

title: High School Curriculum
description: General perspectives of curriculum principles, practices, and procedures common to secondary schools. Organizational structures, innovations, and intimate relationships between instruction and curriculum. Concurrently, students will choose areas of concentration or preparation as they relate to the total high school curriculum.

title: Student Activities Programs in Secondary Schools
description: Student activities will be studied in terms of historical development, philosophical foundations, objectives, functions, current role and status, principles and procedures of development, organizational patterns, and innovative programs. Accommodates needs and interests of individuals preparing to be involved in student activities programs in secondary schools.

title: The School Community and Secondary School Teaching
description: Focuses on the total school community as a broad teaching resource for every classroom teacher. Examines a variety of resources available, importance of establishing solid relationships, impact of community on classroom and classroom on community, significance of the schoolcommunity interaction both for individual teacher and total school.

title: Discipline: Practical Approaches to Improving Student Behavior in Secondary Schools
description: Designed to prepare prospective secondary teachers to cope with discipline problems in all secondary school settings. Emphasizes skills and procedures for preventing or remedying disruptive behavior by secondary students and ways to create a positive environment for learning.

title: Career Education: Content and Processes for Secondary Educators
description: Career education concepts and attitudes and their effects analyzed in relation to effective implementation of career education in secondary schools. Techniques, methods, and materials identified and developed enabling prospective teachers to see meaningful relationships between career education and secondary curricular areas. The teaching of career identification skills and development of meaningful student work values examined. Course participants will develop a model for the inclusion of career education in his/her area.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the Standard License in Secondary Education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 462 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the Standard License in Secondary Education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 460 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Secondary
description: Prerequisite or parallel: EDSEC 460, 462 or EDJHM 466; and admission to student teaching.

title: General Innovations in Secondary Education
description: Innovative practices will be identified, defined, and analyzed relative to their impact on secondary schools. Creative, innovative instructional approaches will be employed. Field trips or visitations to innovative secondary schools will be arranged when practical, and students will concentrate upon innovative practices.

title: Practicum in Boys' Club Administration
description: Offered in cooperation with Boys' Clubs of America. Students are assigned to Boys' Clubs where they are given an opportunity in all phases of program and administration with certain responsibilities for advanced problems in each of these areas. The course is largely under the direction of a visiting professor representing Boys' Clubs of America. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.
