Twining, Ulman, VanEvery, VanTassel, Wallace The philosophy of special education encompasses the right of all children, youth and adults to participate in educational and career planning experiences that will develop their capabilities to the fullest extent. Gradual acceptance of this philosophy by society has created an everincreasing demand for highly skilled personnel who are certified in the various exceptionality areas represented within special education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to teacher certification in the areas of deaf education ; mildly mentally handicapped; moderately, severely, profoundly and multiply handicapped, and physically handicapped. These programs are designed in accordance with Indiana teacher certification requirements. Elective courses in special education open to future teachers, psychologists, speech and hearing therapists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, courses in the education of gifted children, a course in the education of slow learners, and a course in the education of children with learning disabilities. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE DEAF Mandatory legislation on the rights of all children to an appropriate education has created a nation wide need for additional teachers of the hearingimpaired. The emphasis on "mainstreaming" of exceptional children in the regular classroom developed a need for teachers of the hearingimpaired with more general preparation in addition to the specialized coursework for teachers of the deaf. Also, the growth of different communication philosophies made it essential to provide additional coursework options within the majors and minors. A major in the education of the deaf is offered to those who prefer some level of elementary teaching and a minor is available for persons who wish to teach an academic subject at the junior high and high school levels. The State of Indiana, Ball State University, and the Department of Special Education have adopted more extensive requirements for licensing and, at the same time, more flexible programs which can accommodate the above needs. The Ball State University program for training teachers of the hearingimpaired meets the approval of (1) The Indiana Teacher Training and Licensing Commission, (2) The Council on the Education of the Deaf (CED), and (3) the U.S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE MENTALLY HANDICAPPED Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to the development of specialized programs for mentally handicapped children, youth and adults. These programs have provided the impetus to prepare specially trained teachers to work effectively with mildly handicapped and moderately, severely, profoundly and multiply handicapped children, youth and adults in the least restrictive instructional setting. Teachers and other interested professional personnel are taught the necessary skills to implement accepted intervention strategies for appropriately meeting the mentally handicapped individual's learning style and educational and career needs. In response to the nationwide demand for qualified teachers to serve mentally handicapped children, youth and adults, the Department of Special Education offers a teaching area major in the area of the mildly handicapped and teaching minors in both the mildly handicapped and moderately, severely, profoundly and multiply handicapped areas. The teaching minor also serves as an endorsement in each of the exceptionality areas represented within the mentally handicapped area. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR CHILDREN WITH PHYSICAL AND/OR SPECIAL HEALTH PROBLEMS Within the group of children who have special educational needs are those who are physically handicapped (mildly and severely) or those who have other health conditions which make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for these handicapped or healthimpaired children presents the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The teacher education program is designed to offer comprehensive, professional preparation to future teachers of physically handicapped (mildly and severely) or healthimpaired children so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and the area requirements given below. title: Introduction to Exceptional Children
description: A survey of the educational needs of children who deviate from the normal in mental, physical, and social characteristics. Designed as an introduction to the field of special education.

title: History of Education of the Deaf and the Psychology of Deafness
description: A brief study of educational provisions for the deaf from the beginning to the present and a survey of the social, educational, and vocational problems of deafness.

title: Education of Preschool Deaf Children
description: The development of oral communication in preschool deaf children. Directed observations of both hearing and hearingimpaired classes, home visitations, and the parenttraining program. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 261.

title: Practicum in Special Education
description: Observation and assistance of teachers in special classes for exceptional children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or may be taken parallel with

title: Psychology of Mental Retardation
description: Various types and degrees of retardation. The psychological, environmental, and cultural factors which contribute toward retardation. Emphasis on etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate retarded children. Prerequisite: EDPSY 300 arid SPCED 201.

title: Characteristics of the Moderately, Severely, and Profoundly Retarded Individuals
description: Aspects of the intellectual, perceptualmotor, communication, academic, and personal social characteristics of the moderately, severely, and profoundly retarded. Procedures for formulating realistic instructional objectives will be explained. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 372.

title: Educational Methods with Moderately, Severely, and Profoundly Retarded Individuals
description: Current instructional planning for the moderately, severely, and profoundly retarded will be reviewed and evaluated. Attention will be focused upon techniques for effecting innovative curricula for individuals at the preschool through post school levels. Prerequisite: SPCED 373.

title: Education of Gifted Children
description: Designed to help teachers in the identification of and instruction of gifted and talented children. Major topics of study are characteristics and identification of the gifted, and curriculum developments and adaptations suitable for the education of gifted children.

title: Education of Slow Learners
description: Major topics include identification, characteristics, and practices and procedures for meeting the needs of the slow learning child. Emphasis is placed on techniques and methods of instruction as well as research findings concerned with the slow learner and the culturally disadvantaged.

title: Learning Disabilities Techniques for the Regular Classroom Teacher
description: Emphasis on the role of the regular classroom teacher in relationship to legal, federal, and state mandates for identification, instruction, and programming for learning disabled students in the regular classroom. Prerequisite: senior status.

title: History of the Education of the Deaf
description: Deals with history of education of the deaf from ancient times to the present with primary emphasis on early teachers and schools in the United States. t Students are expected to meet the prerequisite for MATH 391 (MATH 204)

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for reeducation and necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA. 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 442.

title: Aural Rehabilitation
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for teaching lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite:

title: Speech Development for the Deaf
description: The International Phonetic Alphabet, Northhampton Charts, diacritical markings, and other methods and techniques used to teach speech to the deaf. Prerequisite: SPCH 216 and SPCED 240, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of an individual work with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 and 446 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Manual Communications
description: Theory and research underlying the language of signs and fingerspelling (manual alphabet) is considered. Development of receptive and expressive skills in manual communications is required. Required of students intending to student teach in schools or classes using total communication.

title: Advanced Manual Communication
description: A course in manual communication designed to improve conversational skill in signs and fingerspelling to a functional level for expressive and receptive use in a classroom for hearing impaired children. Prerequisite: SPCED 451 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: Compares language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Levels of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and SPAA 370 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight Language for the Deaf, Barry Five-Slate, Wing Symbols, and the Natural Method. Language outlines from different schools are used as supplementary aids. Prerequisite: SPCED 240, 266, and 454.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching subjects such as arithmetic and science. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and 266 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Special Education
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Student Teaching: Areas of Exceptionality
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 20 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Interpreting for the Deaf
description: A survey course to acquaint students with the fundamentals of interpreting for the deaf in special situations, familiarize them with professional behavioral guidelines unique to each setting, and develop beginning interpretive skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Expressive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Provides students who have basic manual communication skills with intensive training and practice in expressive interpreting for the deaf. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Receptive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Designed to provide students who have basic manual communication ability with professional skill for interpreting manual language in special situations. Opportunity for extensive practice and evaluation will be provided. Prerequisite: SPCED 468 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 1
description: Special class organization, curriculum practices and procedures, and the methods and techniques used in the instruction of the mentally retarded. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (2 hrs.), 372.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 2
description: Continuation of SPCED 474, with emphasis on the curriculum. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (4 hrs.) and 474.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: This course is designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children. Topics include etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate children with physical disabilities. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 300.

title: Educational Methods with Physically Handicapped Children
description: Special class organization, curriculum, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of orthopedically handicapped children. Prerequisite: SPCED 482 ; prerequisite or parallel: EDEL 380 and MATH 391.

title: Teaching Multiply Handicapped Children
description: Studies the problems of multiply handicapped children and youth. Symptomatology, assessment, and educational programming of multiply handicapped children will be emphasized. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 373, and 482.

title: Education of Children with Learning Disability
description: Intensive study of the psychosocial and educational research findings pertaining to the education of children with learning disabilities. Emphasis on current research, appropriate educational methods, and behavior modifications. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, EDPSY 300. CURRICULA: BACCALAUREATE DEGREES General Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 of Curricular Information.) The General Arts Curriculum is a program in general studies and selected concentration areas. it leads to either the Bachelor of Arts or Bachelor of Science Degree. This curriculum is recommended for degree candidates who are undecided about specific educational goals in respect to graduate work, professional schools, and intensive specialization. General Studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 48 hours approved by the department or (2) two departmental minors, 24-36 hours, approved by the departments. Physical education: General courses 6 hrs. Electives: As many hours of credit in electives as are needed to increase the total of hours to 186. 8 hrs. 4 hrs. 8 hrs. t Candidates for teaching licenses for secondary, junior high/middle school, and all grade (except special education and hearing impaired) must take eight hours in two different disciplines outside their major or minor areas. Liberal Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 of Curricular Information.) The Liberal Arts Curriculum provides opportunity for a search for general knowledge and for specialization primarily for development of intellectual capacities. In general studies the range is extensive; in areas of specialization the goal is depth of a sufficiency to demonstrate a degree of mastery in the selected areas. It is also possible in many cases for a student to fulfill the requirements of both the liberal arts curriculum and for teacher licensing. To do so, the student must be enrolled in and meet the requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum as approved by the Teacher Education Committee of Ball State University. Such a decision will require careful choice of courses and planning by the student and the curricular adviser. The degree to which the curriculum leads is the Bachelor of Arts. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Foreign language: One foreign language 24 hrs. f Concentration areas: (1) One departmental major of 45-60 hours and at least one departmental minor of 24-48 hours in another discipline, or (2) two departmental majors of 45-60 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statement of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Physical education: General courses 6 hrs. Electives: As many hours of credit in electives as are needed to increase the total of hours to 186. Professional Arts Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees and items 1 -6 of Curricular Information.) The Professional Arts Curriculum provides for specialization to qualify for appointments in specific professional areas or for admission to professional schools which provide more intensive preparation for the desired professional or vocational competency. The degree is the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science. If the major is architecture, the degree is the Bachelor of Architecture; and if the major is landscape architecture, the degree is Bachelor of Landscape Architecture; if the major is music, the degree is Bachelor of Music; and if the major is art, the degree is either Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Science, or Bachelor of Fine Arts. General studies: Courses in the program of general studies 72 hrs. Concentration areas: (1) A departmental major of 78 hours or more, or (2) a departmental major of 48-96 hours with a departmental minor of 24-36 hours (departmental majors and minors are listed in the statements of the departments of instruction within the colleges). Physical education: General courses 6 hrs. Electives: As many hours of credit in electives as are needed to increase the total of hours of 186. f See Degrees, Baccalaureate, for equivalency statement. Teacher Education Curriculum (See Baccalaureate Degrees; Teacher Licensing; and items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Curricular Information.) The Teacher Education Curriculum is designed to prepare students for teaching in the elementary, junior high/middle, or secondary areas of the public schools of Indiana. It meets the requirements of the Teacher Training and Licensing Division of the State Board of Education of Indiana. The objectives of teacher education at Ball State University, for which preparation is made on this curriculum are — To help students acquire (a) knowledge and understanding expected of welleducated persons in our culture, (b) respect for learning and people, (c) familiarity with the value systems influencing behavior, and (d) aesthetic appreciations; To assist students in the acquisition of teaching competence in both knowledge and skills related to their areas of specialization; To enable students to understand the way learning takes place and human beings develop; To enable students to acquire a basic knowledge of the relationship between the school and its historical and contemporary settings; To help students demonstrate in their relations with others that they value highly the freedoms and responsibilities of democratic living; Top romote in students the willingness and ability to experiment with effective methods of applying their intellectual, moral, aesthetic, and professional learning in practice. In addition to the specifically identified courses which have been listed as required elements of the various certification programs, many valuable electives are offered. * Students are advised by the Directors of Elementary Teacher Education and Secondary Teacher Education regarding professional program planning. Undergraduate Programs Description of Course Identification System Each prefix has its own numbering system, with a potential of numbers from 100 through 699. Courses numbered from 100 to 199 are primarily freshman courses. Courses numbered from 200 to 299 are primarily sophomore courses. Courses numbered from 300 to 399 are primarily junior courses. Courses numbered 400 to 499 are primarily senior courses. Courses numbered from 500 up are for graduate students. Courses numbered from 600 to 699 are for graduate students with masters' degrees. In course descriptions the course number is given immediately following the prefix. If a number in parentheses follows, it is the immediately preceding number of the course. The student who has credit in a course under the parenthetical number, or any former number, may not earn credit in the course under its current number except under the terms of Course Repetition (see Credit and Grades). In the course description the number in parentheses following the descriptive title of the course is the credithour value of the course. It denotes the specific total of credit hours which may be earned in the course unless elsewhere in the description is a statement which permits the earning of a larger total of credit hours. Prerequisite refers to a course or courses which must precede the course described. Parallel indicates a course or courses which must be taken simultaneously with the described course. The letter g following the number of an undergraduate course indicates that the course is approved for the earning of graduate credit by eligible students properly registered for the course. Sappenfield The College of Architecture and Planning, established by the 1965 Indiana legislature, is dedicated to the development of professional competency in the functional, aesthetic, and humane design of the physical environment. Two fiveyear programs of study are offered: the departmental major in architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Architecture degree; and the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree. The first two years of both programs are concurrent and include a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. The Ball State general studies program is an integral part of these first two years. The last three years provide specialization in the fields of architectural or landscape design as well as providing for specialized study in areas of the student's own choosing. An environmental design major is offered on the Professional Arts Curriculum for students who have completed the first year of either the architecture or the landscape architecture program and is designed for students who wish to end their studies after four years of university work or who wish to pursue a different program at another school of environmental design. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning represent a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophy. By exposure to the variety of philosophical and technical backgrounds of creative professionals, the students are encouraged to seek their own personal philosophy within a professional teamwork situation. The curricula stress character, devotion, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility. The total program is concerned with the development of a physical environment serving the best of one's aspirations. Department of Landscape Architecture Russell, Chairman; Anderson, Benson, Blumenfeld, Bremer, Faruque, Hall, Swartz Landscape Architecture involves the coordinated planning and design of land and is the art of applying scientific principles in arranging objects and spaces upon the land for human use, enjoyment, safety, health and welfare. Landscape architecture is based upon the recognition of long term ecologic, economic, social and psychological values, embracing the conservation of natural resources and the design of land for specific purposes. The landscape architect may be the prime professional consultant for a project and will be assisted by allied professionals such as architects, engineers, planners, ecologists, geologists, hydrologists, biologists, economists, sociologists, and others. Also, he/she may be a member of a site planning team coordinated by one of many allied professions. The landscape architect must be sensitive to human needs and patterns while understanding the potentials and limitations of natural systems - soils, geology, water, vegetation, wildlife, topography, and climate in the effort to solve increasingly complex problems. The undergraduate curriculum stresses a broad base of learning both within the major as well as in supportive course areas. While helping the student to develop basic skills and understanding in landscape architecture, the curriculum is structured to allow concentrations of study in particular areas of interest in allied areas. The General Studies Program in the humanities, natural sciences, social and behavioral sciences combined with opportunities in mathematics, art, directed and professional electives to play a vital part in the cultural and intellectual preparation of young men and women enrolled in this program. The program for these electives must be approved in advance by the department chairman. A core of courses including design, graphics, landscape architecture technology, plants and design, and history provides the primary focus to which supportive major and allied courses relate. While recognizing the multidisciplinary makeup of most real world decision making, the program also stresses individual problem solving and its contribution to promoting high levels of creativity and self reliance. Studio projects range from applying basic parameters of space, rhythm, movement, scale and color ; to the design of courtyards, parks, playgrounds, residences, housing projects; to large scale open space studies, river corridors, and regional resource evaluation encompassing thousands of acres. Landscape architecture is a fiveyear departmental major on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The degree received is a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture. The total hours required in Professional Arts Curriculum with landscape architecture as the major is 254. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. Departmental major in landscape architecture, 200 hours LA 101, 102, 103, 121, 161, 162, 163, 170, 201, 202, 203, 210, 220, 226, 262, 270, 301, 302, 303, 311, 312, 320, 327, 330, 341, 342, 361, 401, 402, 403, 404, 405, 406, 413, 414, 428, 429, 443, 451, 459, 460, 463, 477 MATH 148 hrs. 111, 112 ; CS 220; BIO 313 16 hrs. Art electives 12 hrs. Directed electives: select three courses from an approved list 12 hrs. Professional electives 12 hrs. Upon completion of the first year of study in the college the student shall meet with an adviser in the department to develop a tentative plan of study for his/her major in landscape architecture. This plan must have the approval of the department chairman prior to final course registration through the Curricular Advising Office. The student shall complete the following courses prior to admission into third year landscape architecture courses: all 100 and 200 level landscape architecture courses required for the major in landscape architecture ; 3 hours of art electives ; at least 8 hours of directed electives. The student shall complete the following courses prior to admission into fifth year landscape architecture courses: all 300 level landscape architecture courses; LA 401, 402, 403, 413, 428, 429, 443, 451, 463; 9 hours of art. At the end of the Spring Quarter of the third year and at the end of the Winter Quarter of the fourth year, each student shall meet with a review committee to assess the student's past Landscape Architecture 95 performance, potentials and expectations, to recognize positive achievements and to guide the student where deficiencies are apparent. A second review may be held to assess progress made in response to stated deficiencies. The student shall enroll in LA 459 during the second period of a sequence of two documented periods of employment or one documented 10-week period of employment and one documented 10-week period of creative endeavor. The student must receive prior approval from the department chairman for each 10-week experience. Employment may be under the supervision of a landscape architect or in an allied profession or trade such as architecture, contracting, nursery, surveying. In addition, the student shall participate in and document two 2-week field trips sponsored by the department during the five year period of study. All students are required to attend college and department sponsored lectures held throughout the academic year.

Johnson, Chairman; MacNair, Parker Planning is a process of social development and learning involving the designing, implementing, and evaluating of programs in order to achieve socially determined goals. The determining of those goals is itself a crucial part of the planning process. An interdisciplinary activity, planning draws upon the knowledge of such fields as economics, sociology, political science, engineering, anthropology, geography, architecture, landscape architecture, health, operations research, and natural resources among others. It involves a variety of skills. Foremost among these are skills of research, policy determination, evaluation, communication, and community organization. Urban and regional planners are employed by city, county, regional, and state planning agencies, by consulting firms, by international agencies, by industry, and by organizations dealing with planning and development issues. Planners are involved in such social matters as revitalizing the central city, improving neighborhoods, ensuring equal opportunity, determining public policies for land use and transportation, and protecting the natural environment. As these and other related problems and opportunities will continue to require public action in the future, the need for urban and regional planners will continue to grow in Indiana and elsewhere. There will, of course, always be a need for persons who seek challenge and aspire to advance the human condition and the level of social development.

Wagoner The College of Business has as its objectives the education of men and women for professional pursuits in business, industry, and education. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the University and to the service of the business community. The College recognizes the need for both breadth and depth in the total academic pattern. The curricula are designed to provide (1) a broad background in the general education areas, (2) mastery of the basic tools and an understanding of the fundamentals of business organization and procedures, and (3) specialization in a selected field of business. All curricula are designed to develop the ability to define and analyze problems, to make value judgments, and express conclusions in a cogent and concise manner. The largest responsibility of the College of Business is the training for staff and line positions in the areas of accounting, economics, finance, management, marketing, and office administration. This specialized training is preceded by a common body of knowledge that is the same for all specialties. Additionally, fouryear majors are available in four concentrations for the preparation of secondary teachers. The Associate in Arts degree is offered in Business Administration with options in (1) marketing and retailing, (2) office services, (3) midmanagement, (4) banking, and (5) insurance and real estate. The Associate in Arts degree also is available in secretarial, in court reporting and in word processing. Short courses of study are organized upon request to fit the special needs of individual employers. The College of Business is administered through six departments which are Accounting; Business Education and Office Administration ; Economics ; Finance; Management Science; and Marketing. In addition, the Bureau of Business Research offers research services and publications to the business community as well as to faculty and students. The Center for Economic Education provides economic education aids to the school systems, to business firms, and to the public in the Ball State service area. At the graduate level, the Master of Business Administration is an interdepartmental degree composed of courses from all six departments. Additionally, each department except finance and marketing offers at least one specialized degree at the masters level. Graduate programs are described in the Graduate Catalog. Department of Accounting Parkison, Head; Arndt, Barnhart, Cirtin, Hanks, Jackson, McCabe, Ounapu, Schroeder, Shivaswamy, Trowbridge, Wagoner, Walker Accounting is often described as "the language of business. - To make intelligent decisions in the effective planning and controlling of the operations of a business, management must know the effect of transactions on its financial position and its earning power. Accounting, the art by which financial results are summarized and interpreted, furnishes that necessary data. The accountant as a student of management problems endeavors to meet reporting requirements and to present data in terms of management's needs. The study of accounting is a vital part in the educational preparation of any executive and is useful in all types of business careers. Contact with all aspects and levels of business enables the accountant to acquire excellent training for executive leadership. Many and varied careers are available to the accountant both in the types of organizations and in the areas of specialization he/she may select. The future for men and women trained in accounting is almost unlimited as the continued growth in the uses of accounting is assured by further expansion and complex development of business activity. The increase of government influence in business affairs and industry's search for increased productivity through its emphasis on cost controls and efficiency cause the potential need for the services of accountants to increase more rapidly than the number of persons properly qualified to fill the need. A major in accounting provides a foundation for a career as a controller, financial officer, internal auditor, cost accountant, professional CPA, public administration officer and teacher of accounting. The departmental major in accounting, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for an interesting and rewarding career in the broad fields of accounting. title: Word Processing Management
description: Use of word processing as an integral part of the total information processing network. Development of ability to recognize when and how to use word and textprocessing to meet an organization's needs. Study of managerial problems involved in establishing and implementing word processing systems. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department head.

title: Principles of Business and Distributive Education
description: Historical development of the field of business education. Possible future trends and their effect on the entire business education program. Open only to students who have been approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Distributive Education
description: An investigation of the current status, historical development, philosophy, and principles of distributive education. Components include secondary, postsecondary, and adult distributive education, DECA, and general and specialized curricula. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299. Restricted to students pursuing a teaching major in distributive education.

title: Independent Study in Business Education, Distributive Education, or Office Administration
description: For students with an excellent academic record who wish to conduct an indepth study in some phase of business education, distributive education, or office administration. The project selected, methods, and credit hours must be approved by the department head and supervising faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Economics Deitsch, Chairman; Caron, Cheng, Dilts, Girgis, Hannaford, Jost, Keil, Lawson, Lephardt, Lynch, McGuire, Parks, Seeborg, Van Cott, Yoho, Zegeye Economics is the scientific study of economic institutions and systems. It is a study of human wants and of efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is "scarce resources of production" and scarcity is relative — relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. It is a useful study in an intellectual sense because it trains students to think carefully and logically about complex social phenomena. By such knowledge it is possible to understand the impact on economic systems and institutions of broad social and economic developments or of new economic policies and the responses of these units to them. Given the complicated economic and social problems of the modern world, an understanding of this subject is important for intelligent citizenship and for practical application in industry, government, research, and the professions. To achieve a basic comprehension of how our economy operates, the department offers a core of courses aimed at providing (1) a sound grasp of the tools of analysis and measurement, (2) an understanding of institutional development and the interrelations of economic and social factors, and (3) an ability to apply systematic analysis and understanding to problems of public policy. A number of degree programs are offered by the Department of Economics in order to provide the student with flexibility in choosing a course of study that will fit individual interest and needs. The student can choose to major in economics under either the Business or Liberal Arts Options. The Business Option is a 90-hour major designed primarily for those students choosing a professional career in business. Twothirds of the required hours are in the business core courses of accounting, finance, general business, management, and marketing. The Liberal Arts Option is comprised of 48 hours, a number of which may be taken in other departments. The Department of Economics also offers an interdepartmental major in mathematical economics as well as a minor in economics. The student may also select economics as his/her concentration area in either the Teaching Major in Social Studies or Teaching Minor in Social Studies Curricula (see Social Studies). title: Economics of the Ghetto 1
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 200 or 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Public policy relating to each area is explained and evaluated. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. Involved are analyses of production functions; theories of wages, rent, interest, and profits; the principles of international trade and comparative economic organizations; and a general consideration of business ethics. 230. -1- Survey of Industrial Relations. (4) A survey of labor economics and industrial relations. Topics covered include government regulation of the labor market, collective bargaining, security programs, and contract negotiation and administration. Designed for the student interested in the practical application of these topics. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. 231. f Introduction to Labor Market Economics. (4) Economic analysis of labor markets including a survey of theoretical and empirical analyses of wage determination, unemployment, income distribution and poverty, labor market discrimination, and effect of collective bargaining on the labor market. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. 232. f Law of Labor Relations. (4) An examination of the law governing unionmanagement relations. Primary emphasis upon the Taft-Hartley and Landrum-Griffin Acts as amended/interpreted. Extensive use of the case study. Designed to serve the needs of current/future laborrelations practitioners. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. 233. f Contract Negotiations. (4) Examines processes, techniques, and economic impact of collective bargaining. Emphasis upon what the practitioner needs to know about the negotiation, administration, and enforcement of collective bargaining agreements. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. 235. f The Economics of Dispute Settlement. (4) An economic and institutional analysis of impasses resolution. Topics covered include the causes and economic impact of labor disputes, National Labor Relations Board impasse procedures, principles of arbitration, fact finding, mediation, and conciliation, and other recent developments in dispute resolution. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
description: National income as a measure of economic activity is analyzed. Major stress is on the determination of national income, employment, price level, and the rate of growth of the economic system. Includes examination of the theories of consumption and investment spending, interaction between money and national income, and implications of alternative models for public policy. Graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses are utilized. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Intermediate Microeconomics
description: An investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing, output determination, resource pricing, and employment in various market structures. Graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses are utilized. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Economics of the Ghetto 2
description: The economics of poverty in the United States. Includes economic concepts and analysis of poverty in the historical context, economic analysis of contemporary poverty, and analysis of current proposals dealing with poverty in the United States. Prerequisite: ECON 111 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201, MATH 110 or its equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life ; surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a I Not open to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business. major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201; MATH 131, 132 or their equivalent; and MS 221. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 524.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 432.

title: Economics of Labor Market Discrimination
description: A survey of conservative, liberal and radical theories of labor market discrimination; a review of studies on the extent of economic discrimination and the effect of public policy on the economic position of women and minorities. Prerequisite: ECON 201; MS 220.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the Board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstruct or facilitate the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Internship in Economics
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Economics, a student majoring in economics works full time for one quarter as an economics intern for a private or public organization. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to third quarter juniors and seniors majoring in economics. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. Credit is not applicable toward meeting the requirements of a major in economics.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. At the undergraduate level, the Department of Finance offers two majors leading to either the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science degree. These majors are in finance and general business administration. Finance. Finance is a decisionoriented discipline concerned with the investment and management of money both in the present and in the future. This major is designed to provide the student with a general program in the financial aspects of business including financial management, investments, banking, insurance, real estate, and other related financial areas. Finance courses provide knowledge of concepts, processes, and institutions involved with the financing functions of the business enterprise; acquaint students with the financial instruments, institutions, and markets in the United States and the world; provide the tools and techniques of financial analysis and decision making; and expose the students to sufficient examples of financial decision making to allow them to develop expertise in applied finance. The finance major allows the student to pursue one of four options within the finance major, namely, (1) corporate financial management, (2) financial institutions, (3) insurance, and (4) real estate. The corporate financial management option prepares the student for careers in the finance division of a business firm; such as, systems analysis, budget review analysis, financial analysis, acquisitions analysis, credit management, receivables management, and shortand longterm capital management. The financial institutions option emphasizes employment opportunities in the areas of managing stocks and bonds as a securities broker, portfolio manager, or trust department specialist and in investment banking. This option prepares an individual to work in the field of banking, savings and loan associations, loan companies, insurance companies, credit unions, pension funds, securities brokerage, and real estate brokerage. The third option, insurance, has been designed to develop finance graduates in the areas of life, health, as well as property and casualty sales, property and casualty underwriting, insurance appraisal, and management positions with the insurance industry. The real estate option prepares a student for a sales career as well as real estate management. Finance 113 General Business Administration. This major permits students to concentrate in two of the three areas available; i.e., insurance, management, and finance. Hence, this major provides a broader diversity of vocational opportunities than the finance major but with less depth in any one area of concentration. The course of study includes an examination of the various institutions, structures, functions, organizations, operations, and environments which influence business and economic activities. The finance sequence is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activities. The management sequence is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them, as future business executives and specialists, to deal with diversity of problems which arise in the course of daytoday activities. The insurance sequence is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. Graduates in general business administration are qualified to accept positions as junior executives at the management level in finance, insurance, personnel administration, office administration, production supervision, or other areas. In addition, this degree is particularly attractive to those students who may wish to engage in a small business or who do not wish to commit themselves to a particular vocation at this time. In addition to the above, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students in other areas of the College of Business. Any student in the University may enroll in the course in personal finance, which is offered especially to provide the information necessary for the management of personal incomes, expenditures, and financial resources. The law courses are quite broad, include the fundamentals of many essential law disciplines, and are highly recommended to students in prelaw preparation. General business administration and finance courses are included in the concentration areas for the teaching of business education and distributive education. The teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. title: Legal Aspect of Real Estate
description: The elementary concepts of real estate law and practice, particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, broker's regulations, license law, and title insurance. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 232.

title: Estate Planning and Administration
description: An introduction to problems associated with planning for use of financial resources during working life, retirement, and after the death of the principal income producer. Included are techniques for fact gathering, tax principles, use of trusts, and will drafting.

title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law, and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law, and the effect of the law in the areas of consumer credit and economic relationships. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to agencies including employer and employee rights and obligations, partnerships including limited partnership, corporations including fiduciary obligations of directors, security regulations, bankruptcy and corporate reorganization in bankruptcy. Prerequisite: BL 360.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principle articles of the Code including sales, commercial paper and security interests, in addition to the areas of creditor's rights and property law. State and Federal consumer protection laws as they affect commercial law will be covered. Prerequisite: BL 360.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 360 and INS 370. Not open to the student who has credit in INS 373.

title: Current Topics in Business Law
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced business students for study of current topics and/or problems in the business law area. Topics may include current activity in the fields of property law, commercial law, and government regulation of business. Prerequisite: BL 360 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairman. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the viewpoint of the consumer. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation.

title: Money and Banking
description: The role of money, credit, and financial markets in the United States financial system ; the structure and functions of commercial banks; the implementation of monetary policy through the Federal Reserve System; financial and banking system structure; international financial transactions. Prerequisite: ECON 200; MATH 110 or equivalent. Finance 115

title: Principles of Bank Operations
description: Fundamentals of bank operations. A survey of various bank functions including accounting, trusts, demand deposits, savings and time deposits, home mortgage lending, internal controls, international financial services, and public service.

title: Bank Management
description: Trends in philosophy and practice of bank management. The nature and objective of banking; formulation of objectives and policies; organizational planning, management controls; functions of banks related to management practices, policies, and procedures.

title: Credit Administration
description: Factors influencing and determining loan policy. Bank credit policies; credit department; sources of credit; credit correspondence; secured and unsecured loans to customers; loans to business; term loans; interbank loans; real estate loans; influence of the Federal Reserve System; and responsibilities of bank lending officials.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Principles underlying managerial decisions influenced by capital markets and type of ownership; problems relating to the sources of financing; the study of financial analysis and financial management ; and interrelating economic and accounting theory with other areas of business. Prerequisite: ACC 203, ECON 201, MATH 131.

title: Consumer, Business, and Public Finance
description: The great importance in our national life of business credit, personal and consumer credit (including installment sales credit), bank credit, and public credit (federal, state, and municipal). Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: Working Capital Management
description: An analysis of working capital management. Examines the management of current assets such as cash, receivables, and inventories; a review of intermediate and shortterm credit; and a study of general working capital policy. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Problems of investment policy, including the study of types of investment risks, and introduction to security analysis, the analysis of investment requirements, and the kinds of investment policies.

title: Financial Institutions
description: The structure of financial institutions in the American economy. Financial institutions as recipients and as suppliers of funds in financial markets. The identification and analysis of many kinds of financial institutions and the administration of their loan and investment portfolios. Particular emphasis on the asset, liability, and capital management with the goal of profitability. Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some are emphasized. Prerequisite: FIN 250. Prerequisite recommended: senior standing.

title: Capital Management
description: An analysis of the management aspects relating to the inflows and outflows of permanent capital in business enterprises. Examines the management of longterm assets, intermediate and longterm credit, equity, and internal financing. Corporate expansion including mergers, acquisitions, corporate reorganization, and bankruptcies. In cludes case studies. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Multinational Business Finance
description: An indepth study of the international financial institutions (central banks, International Monetary Fund, area development banks, etc.) involved with the financial decisions of multinational corporations including an overview of the new developing forces in the field of international finance. Prerequisite: FIN 452.

title: Security Analysis
description: Presents a detailed analysis of selecting securities for various investment purposes. Encompasses industry structure, volumeprice cost relationships, management, financial position, terms of security contracts and market price behavior. A research project is required. Prerequisite: FIN 350 and 355.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Finance, students majoring in finance or general business administration will work full time for a quarter as an intern for a banking institution, business firm, or governmental agency. Written reports are required. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Open only to third quarter juniors or seniors.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Fundamentals of Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Fundamentals of Property-Liability Insurance
description: Study of fire, inland marine, liability, worker's compensation insurance. Emphasis is on commercial insurance as a method of risk management. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 360 and INS 370. Not open to the student who has credit in BL 373.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and/or problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include nofault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, state vs. federal regulations. Prerequisite: INS 370, 371, and 372 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Real Estate Practices
description: A summation of the real estate industry. Included are the business and economic aspects of real estate as well as discussions of listing statements, offer to purchase, closing statements, computation or mortgage balances, Barrett Assessments, property taxes, urban and farm zoning, properties and licensing procedures. Required for students taking the Indiana Real Estate Brokers or Sales Persons Licensing Examination. Prerequisite: RE 230 and 232.

title: Real Estate Principles
description: The economic import of real estate, real estate characteristics, land use and environmental controls, legal aspects of real estate, including ownership interests and real estate instruments, methods of valuation, real estate analysis, mortgage credit sources, secondary mortgage markets and real estate financing techniques, investment analysis, land development, and real estate operations, including brokerage, title closing, and property management.

title: Real Estate Finance
description: The contractual nature and legal implication of the instruments used in real estate finance; instrument, techniques, and strategies in the financing of real estate investment ; and the structure and operation of both primary and secondary mortgage markets. Provides the student with background in real estate law and real estate finance. Prerequisite: RE 330.

title: Real Estate Analysis
description: Will concern itself with the appraisal of real estate. In addition to the appraisal process, other analytical systems will be reviewed as they apply to the real estate industry, including the economic base analysis, feasibility studies, and investment analysis. Prerequisite: RE 330. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 230 and 231.

title: Real Estate Administration
description: An orientation of the real estate business utilizing text cases, incidents, and walking cases. Guest speakers who are experts in real estate will be invited to speak and answer questions. Prerequisite: RE 431 and senior standing or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 233. Everyorganization has managers regardless of what they are called (e.g., managers, administrators, principals, coaches, officers, or chiefs). Therefore, a student who elects to major in management science will be preparing to assume a position of responsibility in a wide variety of profit or nonprofit organizations. The major in management science allows the student to pursue one of five management options: (1) production and operations management, (2) personnel administration, (3) management information systems, (4) information and administrative management, or (5) general management. In the production and operations management option, the student obtains the background to assume a position of responsibility in the production of goods and services. The student is introduced to the production functions in detail, taught the methodology of making productionrelated decisions, and becomes acquainted with modern techniques used in motivating and leading personnel in a productionoriented occupation. In the personnel administration option, the student obtains the foundation for entering an occupation that relates primarily to the human component of an organization. The student is given an indepth presentation of the personnel function; that is, the student is familiarized with a conceptual framework for analyzing and solving problems involved in the selection, development, and motivation of human resources. In the management information systems option, the student is introduced to the concepts and techniques necessary for the development and operation of management information systems. The student receives a broad background in the role and operation of an information system in an organization. The graduate of this option is knowledgeable of the concepts and techniques of computerized information systems to accomplish this important function more effectively and efficiently. In the information and administrative management option, the student is introduced to the concepts and techniques necessary to provide an effective and efficient flow of information in an organization. The focus is more on office and records management and less on computerized information systems. The graduate of this option is knowledgeable in those concepts which are needed by an effective office manager. In the general management option, the student is introduced to a varied background in management. General management acquaints the student with the whole gamut of management: production, personnel, information, office management, small business administration, and international management. Some organizations recruit on campus for generalists such as students with the general management option. Others prefer more depth in a specific function such as production and operations, personnel, management information systems, or information and administration. description: Helps the student understand the theory, research, and applications that provide the cornerstones for the study of management within organizations. Focuses upon understanding the courses and effects of the structures within companies, the processes within firms in bringing theory to bear on the practical problems of managing organizations. 281. * Management of Human Resources. (4) Gives students an understanding of the basic operations function; gives them a viable knowledge of the systems approach to the design of operations.
