title: Earth Science Field Problems
description: A series of meteorological, geological, pedological, and geodetic problems designed for beginning students in geography, earth sciences, and geology, as an introduction to physical processes in the atmosphere and near the surface of the earth and to the procedures by which the processes may be identified from their products. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, or GEOL 101. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOL 383.

title: Seminar in Field Problems Design and Techniques
description: Discussion and identification of field problems in geography, geology, and earth science and the techniques and methods of solving these problems. Students are given the major responsibility of class plan development. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology of the National Parks and Monuments in the United States
description: Geologic description and interpretation of the national parks and monuments in the United States emphasizing geologic history and process.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments in and near the campus and visits to places of pertinent course value within the state. Normal scheduling is Saturday mornings. Prerequisite: major or minor in geography, geology, or earth science, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Geography and Earth Science
description: Methods and materials for teaching geography and earth science in secondary and junior high/middle schools. Includes a review of appropriate methods, materials, textbooks, and equipment used in these disciplines. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in geography, geology, and/or earth science or permission of the department chairman; EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Earth Physics for Teachers
description: An introduction to the major physical forces and structure of the earth. Earth's gravity and magnetic field; origin, age, radioactivity, temperature; earthquake causes, distribution, and prediction; seafloor spreading and mountain building. Prerequisite: an introductory course in physical geography, geology, earth science, or physics, or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOL 425 or 426.

title: Research Techniques
description: Basic library research and writing techniques applied to problems in geography, geology, and the earth sciences. Designed to stimulate competence in preparing research papers using library materials.

title: Quantitative Techniques
description: Application of quantitative techniques to problems in geography, geology, and the earth sciences. Special emphasis on the application of these techniques in research.

title: Fundamentals of Physical Geography and Earth Science
description: Activities of man and his relationship to the physical environment. Selected topics from astronomy, geography, geology, meteorology, and climatology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Elements of Physical Geography
description: The earth and its position in the universe, natural resources of climate, land forms, soils, vegetation, rocks and minerals, and animal life, with attention paid to the use and conservation of these resources.

title: Physical Geography/Earth Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Earthsun relationships, weather and climate, geologic processes (including earth structure and sculpturing of the earth surface); conservation principles as they pertain directly to the material taught. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 110. 4 hrs. 8 hrs. 16 hrs. 8 hrs.

title: Economic Geography and Contemporary Issues
description: A systematic approach to economic geography and current economic issues, emphasizing local, regional, national and international economic developments in the geographic setting.

title: Geography of the Cultural Environment
description: A spatial analysis of the interaction of cultural development and the physical environment. Special emphasis upon the processes of cultural change and their impact on the landscape.

title: Meteorology 1
description: Introduction to meteorology, dealing with the general planetary circulation of the atmosphere, characteristics of the weather, and an examination of weather instruments. Includes a minimum of 4 hours assignment in the university weather station.

title: Geography of the Contemporary World
description: A systematic study probing the meaning of regions and examining the geographical character of the world by regions. An analysis of regional resources and cultural patterns focusing on contemporary problems and future development.

title: Honors Seminar in Selected Studies in Geography
description: Small group discussion of geographic studies selected by the instructional staff. Studies vary according to staff assignment. For Honors Program students only.

title: Elements of Regional Geography
description: An introduction to the regional concept and regional method as related to elementary teaching. A geographic survey of the world, with selected topics and regions given detailed analysis. Prerequisite: major in elementary education or permission of the department chairman.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: The reading and interpretation of maps, charts, and diagrams, how they are used as a major tool in geography, and how their use may be applied to other areas of study; also proper care and handling of maps.

title: Map Reading for Teachers
description: An introduction to the reading and interpretation of maps, especially as maps may be used in working with school children. The use of topographic maps, special purpose maps, dot distribution maps, bar graphs, pie charts. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 240.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: A comprehensive survey of the geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Europe
description: The physical and cultural environment of Europe with emphasis on the economic and political factors involved.

title: Geography of Soils and Vegetation
description: World patterns of soils and vegetation, with emphasis on regional differences and relationships to climate and physiography; their significance in man's use of the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, GE OL 101, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Land Utilization
description: The varied uses of the land, with emphasis on the major categories of rural use, but with attention given to urban and industrial uses. Water use in respect to the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Structure and Functions of Cities
description: A critical examination of the major structural and institutional parts of the city and of how topographic and climatic forces have influenced their development. An understanding of the city as a functionally interdependent structure and as a physical monument to its contemporary culture is fostered.

title: The Urban and Regional Form
description: A survey of the origins of the urban and regional form and its relation to economic, social, and functional factors with special emphasis upon the modern American metropolis and its region. Prerequisite: GEOG 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Agricultural and Rural Geography
description: Agricultural development and the pattern of agriculture, particularly in respect to rural areas of the world. Conflict of rural and agricultural development with urbanization and industrialization.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources include minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Regularly scheduled laboratory and field work. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, NR 101, or 325.

title: Meteorology 2
description: Application of the principles of meteorology to the development and analysis of weather maps and charts and the making of weather forecasts. Includes a minimum of 6 hours assignment in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Climatology
description: Introduction to the analysis and classification of climate, with emphasis on regional distribution. Basic techniques in handling climatic data. Prerequisite: GEOG 130, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. Although the emphasis is upon graphic presentation of spatially disposed quantitative and qualitative data, the techniques and methods are applicable to a wide range of subject areas.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques. Specific projects are selected within the students' field of specialization or area of interest. Emphasis on data collection, compilation, and final drafting of projects suitable for reproduction and publication. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Geography of Caribbean America
description: Physical and cultural landscape regions of Mexico, Central America, northern South America, and the islands of the Caribbean.

title: Geography of Australia and Oceania
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of Australia, New Zealand, and the southeast Pacific area.

title: Geography of East Asia
description: A geographic survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of China, Japan, Korea, Mongolia, and coastal Asia.

title: Geography of South Asia
description: A geographic survey and analysis of the physical, economic, and human elements of the Indian subcontinent and adjacent countries to the east and west.

title: Geography of South America
description: Diverse natural and human environment of South America with special focus on the Amazon Basin, arid northeastern and industrial southern Brazil, the Argentine Pampa, and the ancient Indian cultures of Peru and Ecuador.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world as these factors contribute to domestic and foreign relations and problems.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world, and of transportation patterns.

title: Urban Geography
description: The distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention is given to the geographic factors affecting urban development and growth.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration and growth, as well as the causes and consequences of these aspects on cultural landscape.

title: Geography of Regional Development
description: Geographical factors in the identity and development of specific regions of the world, both historical and modern. Special attention given to resource and river valley development. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, 120, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geography of Industrial Location
description: An analysis of the geography of industrial location with particular emphasis given to the impact of industrial location on urban and regional economies.

title: Advanced Meteorology
description: Air mass and storm analysis, with attention given to the physical characteristics of the air layers. Detailed forecasting techniques. Prerequisites: GEOG 330, one year of college physics, and mathematics through calculus, or permission of the department chairman. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Applied Climatology
description: The practical relationships of climate to the activities of man, especially in his adjustment to the physical and cultural environment. Included are the relationships pertinent to industrial development, and to local and regional planning, and the microrelationships of climate and architecture. Prerequisite: GEOG 110, 130, 331, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Meteorological Instrumentation
description: A comprehensive study of meteorological instruments used in weather station operation. Students will actively participate in practical weather station operation. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Remote Sensing and Aerial Photo Interpretation 1
description: Introduction to the use of remote sensing techniques including aerial photo interpretation and aircraft and satellite sensors such as radar and multispectral scanners as applied to studies in the physical and social sciences.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union, and the economic development of the country.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: Topography, soils, climate, industries, commerce, and population of Indiana, with emphasis on physiography and economy.

title: Geography of Northwest Europe
description: Survey of the geography of the countries of northwestern Europe. Analysis of land use, physical landscape, and the economic and political development relationships.

title: Advanced Regional Geography
description: Advanced study of the geography of a selected region or regions of the world, with emphasis on the interrelationships of the physical, cultural, and human phenomena. Individual assignments. Prerequisite: introductory regional geography course or permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Behavioral Geography
description: Concepts derived from the behavioral sciences for understanding manenvironment relationships. Emphasis upon the cultural dimensions underlying human evaluation of the natural environment.

title: Distant Areas Field Studies
description: Study of physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Includes seminars arranged during travel. Prerequisite: major or minor in earth science, geography, or geology, or permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned, with repeated enrollment only by permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Analysis in Urban and Regional Geography
description: A consideration of the major analytical techniques used by social geographers in theoretical and applied research in urban and regional geography. Particular emphasis given to those techniques most frequently used in population projections, land use, planning, and transportation studies.

title: Readings and Special Studies in Geography and Earth Science
description: Assigned special studies in geography and earth science, including readings, research projects, teaching problems, and assignment to an undergraduate class. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: History and Philosophy of Geography
description: The development of geographic knowledge and the status of the profession as expressed in the writings of the past and present by geographers and other individuals in related fields.

title: Geographic Field Methods
description: Introduction to the techniques of field study and analysis of physical and cultural spatial patterns.

title: Man and the Geological Environment
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to mankind's environmental and resource problems. Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: An introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Emphasis on North America. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Environmental Geology
description: An examination of geologic materials and processes affecting the immediate human environment. Geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, geohealth, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Geology of Energy Resources
description: An examination of geologic processes that form and govern the distribution of oil, gas, coal, uranium ores, and geothermal energy sources; exploration strategies ; resource evaluation; and case histories studies of active energy extraction developments. Several field trips are required. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Local area field trips and field mapping. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoecologic significance. Emphasis on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to geologic problems in a specific area. Assignments include mapping projects, including a final written report and compilation of a map on general geology. Normal scheduling is first summer term (five weeks) in a selected area of western United States. Prerequisite: GEGE 382 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Regional Geology Field Study
description: The geologic history, stratigraphy, structural geology, geomorphology, and economic geology of a selected region. Students will travel through the area. Normal scheduling is second summer term in a selected area outside Indiana. Prerkuisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geomorphology of North America
description: Emphasis on the occurrence, description, and geological and geomorphological problems of the geomorphic regions of North America. Nearby area field trips. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and MATH 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans, and related problems. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to the physics of the earth and the geophysical sciences. Refraction and reflection seismology, magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods are included in lecture topics, laboratory exercises, and field investigations. Emphasis on the application of geophysical methods to energy, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, pollution detection, and other applied problems. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geotectonics
description: Plate tectonics and global geophysics; earth's origin, age, gravity, geomagnetism and paleomagnetism, geothermal heat, seismology, dynamics and internal structure; current ideas of seafloor spreading, plate tectonics and mountain building; application to locating new energy and mineral resources. Emphasis on studying the most recent developments in the science of geotectonics in the first half of the quarter and in the study of individual tectonic regions (such as the Appalachians, Rocky Mountains, Alps, and Urals) in the second half.

title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for classifying and interpreting the origins of rocks. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with the exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks for the purpose of determining their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: The structure, rocks, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Emphasis upon physical processes involved, especially Pleistocene glaciation. Designed for nonmajor students in the earth sciences, particularly teachers.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, MATH 111, NR 211, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Geochemistry
description: Composition of the earth. Distribution of elements in minerals and rocks. Principles governing migration and concentration of elements. Introduction to isotope geology and geochemical prospecting. Prerequisite: GEOL 230, CHEM 112 or 114 or permission of department chairman.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. Designed to supplement existing geoscience and computer science courses by providing opportunity to gain experience in working with Basic and Fortran programs in various geoscience data collecting, calculation, and graphic display applications. Prerequisite: open only to students with areas in geography and geology. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. T. S. Eliot, Four Quartets, "Burnt Norton" By definition, history is the record of past actions of mankind based upon surviving evidence. Thus, mankind's accumulated experience, the memory of the human race, is called history. Its study, which should lead to understanding and wisdom, indicates that all problems and patterns are the result of complex processes of growth. By shedding light on these processes, history provides a vehicle for profiting from human experience. Without a knowledge of our past, we would have no landmarks, no points of reference, and no foundations on which to build a modern world. The history major may be undertaken to attain professional, academic, or cultural objectives, including preparation for graduate study and advanced degrees, teaching licenses, prelaw or premedical preparation, qualification for appointments in business, industry, civil service, libraries, museums, art galleries, archives, and other cultural institutions. Courses in history are designed to meet the needs of students in several fields of study. The department offers a broad selection of courses in the general studies program. It offers introductory and advanced courses for students majoring in education or in liberal arts in other departments of the University. It also presents courses designed to give a broad and thorough training in the various history programs. Students majoring in Social Sciences other than History, English, Foreign Languages, Journalism, and Business, find history courses especially useful. The graduate programs are built on the foundation of undergraduate preparation. Students intending to do graduate work in history are urged to take the Bachelor of Arts degree. The masters and doctoral degrees require intensive directed study in history aimed at depth of understanding. title: Introduction to the Study of History
description: Introduction to the study of history: what history is, the uses of history, the role of historical interpretation, techniques of historical analysis, and historical methodology. A requirement for history majors. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 444 or 445.

title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: A survey of the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decisionmakers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Introduction to Civilization of Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: World Civilizations 1
description: A compact survey of the development of world civilizations from the dawn of civilization in Southwestern Asia and North Africa to the Early Modern World (ca. 1400). Open only to students with areas in architecture and planning.

title: World Civilizations 2
description: A compact survey of the development of world civilizations from the Early Modern World (ca. 1400) to the Contemporary Scene. Open only to students with areas in architecture and planning.

title: Roots of the Western Tradition
description: A survey of the principal historical and cultural developments of ancient and medieval times to 1300, with emphasis on those institutions and events of western civilization which furnish our own cultural heritage.

title: Birth of the Modern World
description: From 1300 to 1815, including such major topics as the Renaissance, Reformation, rise of modern nations, discovery and exploration, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, nationalism and the industrial revolution.

title: The World in Recent Times
description: Major world events and issues since 1815; industrialization and resulting ideologies; background, causes, and results of the two world wars; the rise and decline of the colonial empires with emerging nationalism; the impact of democratic, fascist, and communistic doctrines; nineteenth and twentieth century trends in thought; the effect of science on our age; arts; attempts at international organization and cooperation; and the revolution in expectations in the oneworld today.

title: Modern World Leaders
description: Biographical studies of key western and nonwestern men and women placed in historical perspective. Examines the leaders' characteristics, philosophies, leadership capabilities, and their resultant contributions in the field of politics, religion, military, business, and the arts.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East—the Arab world, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems; imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South Asia
description: South Asia (Afghanistan to Indonesia) since 1800: a brief description of factors influential in past history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, and eventual independence.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Foundations of the United States, 1492-1829
description: Survey of American history to 1829.

title: Development of the United States, 1829-1900
description: Survey of the history of the United States from the era of Andrew Jackson to 1900.

title: The Recent Past in the United States, 1900 to the Present
description: Political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have composed the history of the United States since 1900.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of United States resource utilization by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource utilization has shaped society.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of the negro in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing conceptions of their roles, attitudes toward women, women's ideas about themselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Designed to use documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. A complete departure from the regular lecture and textbook method. The students through their own research learn how the historian defines areas of research, selects sources, both primary and secondary, evaluates materials, and describes the findings. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Latin America, 1825 to Present
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis upon contemporary civilization of Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.

title: American Leaders
description: A biographical approach to American history. An evaluation of some of the leading Americans and their contributions in the fields of politics, business, letters, the arts, pure and applied science, and education.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American/Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Provides students with an historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others by permission of the department chairman.

title: Colonial History of the United States, 1492 - 1754
description: The ideas and institutions developed in British North America which in the course of colonial development formed a basis for American culture.

title: The United States from Colony to Nation, 1754 - 1789
description: The political, constitutional, and economic issues that developed in the thirteen British colonies of North America and culminated in revolution, independence, and the founding of a new nation in the latter part of the eighteenth century.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789 - 1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis upon the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820 - 1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis upon the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878 - 1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: From New Freedom through the New Deal
description: United States history from 1912 to 1940. The impact on the American people of the problems created by continuing industrialization at home and continued involvement in a chaotic world.

title: Recent United States History: 1941 to the Present
description: The role of the United States in World War II, the issues confronting the nation in the postwar years, and political, social, and cultural developments since that time.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the State from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Ante-Bellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum south.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans -Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers and the events which influenced their migration, and on the impact these events and the frontier had upon national development.

title: The History of Canada
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of Canada from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis will be placed on the events leading to the establishment of Canada and on United States-Canadian relations and problems.

title: History of Mexico
description: Mexico from the pre-Columbian era to the present with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Revolution of 1910.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1607 - 1865
description: Survey of history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of the history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 or 201 or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 410.

title: Historical Method and Bibliography
description: Techniques of research and documentation.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: The major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture—Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students will travel through designated areas in North America. Prior to the trip, considerable reading in various fields relative to the nature of the course will be required. At the conclusion, papers will be required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teacher education students with a concentration in U.S. history may apply 4 hours of credit in categories 1, 2, or 3.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open only to seniors of special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate investigation. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with special competence within the area involved.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1500 - 1815
description: Political, social, and economic history of Europe from the Age of Discovery to the Congress of Vienna. Emphasis on political and economic events, the rise of national states, absolutism, religious developments, and the expansion of Europe overseas.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1815 to the Present
description: Political, economic, social, and cultural history of Europe from the Congress of Vienna to the contemporary scene. Emphasis on political and economic events, the liberal and nationalist movements, industrialism, imperialism, World Wars I and II, and the conflict of national interests.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870 - 1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918- 1950
description: Survey of the origins, immediate causes, and the course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and After, 1950 to Present
description: Survey of the factors — ideological, political, economic, and social — underlying recent European history with stress on the East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, imperial decline, and the changing European role in world affairs.

title: Modern Extremist Movements
description: A survey and analysis of extremist movements in Europe since 1815 with particular attention to the growth of antidemocratic thought, workingclass movements, counterrevolution, international fascism, collaboration, and youth movements.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the Republic to approximately 500 A. D. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the Republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special stress on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Moslem worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Particular attention will be given to such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations—Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society— through varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teacher education students with a concentration in World Civilization may apply 4 hours of credit in categories I, 2, or 4.

title: France since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France — The Classical Age, 1461-1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focus on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions — the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism — and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715-1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution — the great turning point of modern civilization — and revolutions in general. Stress on the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Rise of Modern Britain, 1485-1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor, Stuart, and early Hanoverian periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain since 1763
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life since the Seven Years' War — modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of postwar government and society.

title: Constitutional History of England
description: A tracing of the development of the British constitutional system to the present time: development of the kingship, the common law, parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern British Empire and Commonwealth
description: British imperial and commonwealth history since 1815 with emphasis on the post-Napoleonic empire, the development of dominions, the problem of India, the World Wars, the shrinking empire, the Commonwealth experience, and the current controversies.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the Revolution of 1917 — stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: Modern East-Central Europe
description: Survey of the peoples of presentday Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and the Baltic States with emphasis on struggles for national independence and freedom. Developments are studied within the context of European trends and changing international conditions.

title: The Modern Middle East
description: A survey of major developments and problems in the Turkish, Persian, and Arab world in the period since 1800 — the decay of traditional life, the expansion of European influence, the modernization movements, the conflicts over Palestine, and the recent national and international crises.

title: The Modern Balkans
description: The development of the Balkans from about 1400 to the present with emphasis on the effects of the Ottoman conquest, the diversity of cultural and national patterns, and the recent history of the independent nations.

title: Modern Chinese History, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japanese History, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on factors contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Studies in Non-Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: Selected Topics in History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in the field of history with emphasis on fields, specialties, and materials not covered in established courses. Department of Journalism Popovich, Chairman; Atwell, Chaney, Conn, Heintzelman, Horney, Ingelhart, Kimble, Knott, Snyder, Walsh, Wellnitz Because the media practitioner must be a well rounded and knowledgeable person in many fields, journalism programs in the accredited schools and departments in the nation, of which Ball State University is one, stress exposure of students to the arts, humanities, sciences, and business. To study journalism in today's world is likely to mean your involvement in the purest liberal arts academic discipline. Equally important to the student's breadth and depth of knowledge is the ability to put that knowledge into words that can be understood. Besides the writing and editing classroom experiences required of journalism students, Ball State University encourages its students to participate in its extensive college student publications program and/or to seek professional experiences either during the school year or summers. Journalism students spend onefourth of their academic careers in journalism courses; threefourths in courses other than journalism, radio-TV-film, advertising, public relations, or communications media; and include the acquisition of suitable professional experience. Students are encouraged to major in another subject besides journalism, such as anthropology, economics, history, literature, management, marketing, natural resources, political science, physical education, psychology, sociology, speech, urban and regional studies, and other arts and sciences. Students who enter the Department of Journalism have the option of preparing themselves as either teaching majors or departmental majors. Teaching majors are prepared to teach journalism and mass media courses, to develop programs, and to serve as advisers for all forms of student publications and communication programs in secondary education. Students who complete the teaching major can be certified to receive an Indiana standard grade teaching license. Departmental majors have the option of career preparation in one of five sequential areas: 1. News Editorial: Students learn all phases of newsroom operations of the various news media and receive an overall grasp of the philosophy, trends, and issues in the news media. 2. Public Relations: Besides acquisition of a solid journalism foundation, students are prepared to go into public relations positions in either public or private corporations and institutions. 3. Photojournalism: Emphasis is placed on preparing students who can take and process pictures and write news, prepare features, and create advertising. 4. Advertising: Provides the student with knowledge of the functions and operations of those departments in media which insure financial successadvertising, circulation, and promotion. 5. Magazine: Students study the magazine industry and are prepared to process words and pictures either as individuals or for media organizations. Journalism courses are available to help the student who is not a major but is interested in working on special writing or editing projects or taking journalism courses to meet general studies requirements. JOURN 100, Mass Communications Media, and JOURN 120, Journalistic Writing, are selected by students as general studies requirements or as electives. In order to be certified for graduation, journalism students must earn a total of 138 quarter hours of credit in courses other than journalism, radio-TV-film, advertising, public relations, or communications media. In addition, each student will be asked to demonstrate adequate typewriting ability, pass minimum spelling and grammar requirements, and submit a portfolio of journalistic activities which can be evaluated by sequence advisers. (Portfolios are placed in the student's permanent departmental file.) Students are guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and the area requirements given below. description: Theory and practice in use of reporting skills and techniques and in newspaper writing. A total of six hours is spent in class each week, including lectures, discussions, and laboratory assignments.

description: Theory and practice of newspaperstyle writing. Not open to the student with areas in journalism.

title: History of Journalism
description: History of journalism in the United States from colonial times to the present, presenting the press as an institution against the background of the history of the nation.

title: Feature and Column Writing
description: Researching and writing feature stories and columns for newspapers and magazines, supplemented by practice assignments for student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice of researching and writing specialized stories for the news media. Emphasis on the indepth reporting approach and on coverage of special areas as government, education, sports, and reviewing the performing arts. Supplemented by practical assignments for student publications and for the University radio station. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Magazine Writing and Editing
description: Theory and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles supplemented with a study of magazine article markets, plus a study and exercises in aspects of editing general and specialized magazines.

title: Sportswriting and Reporting
description: Study and practice in covering and writing about sports events and the people connected with them. Story assignments and research combined with classroom lectures and analysis of best sports stories provide students with skills to cover a wide range of sports activities. Approved methods of presenting material, advertising data, and advertising campaigns in an interesting and effective manner. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Principles of Public Relations
description: Survey of the theory, philosophy, and function of public relations practices and programs in American institutions with special attention to public relations in various fields.

title: Honors Colloquium in Journalism
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Journalism
description: The procedures and problems in teaching journalism classes or units and the role of student publications in school journalism programs. Subjects included are curriculum, finance, textbooks, and resources. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Discipline oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of journalism, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of journalism in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experience whenever possible. Prerequisite: JOURN 395.

title: Journalism Practicum
description: Practical experience in the production of the campus student newspaper, magazine, yearbook or alternate projects with emphasis on writing and editing activities. Course work will also involve evaluations of publication management procedures and preparation of a personnel portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 110, 220, and completion of a student publications participation contract, or permission of the department head.

title: Press and Society
description: The press in modern society, with emphasis on the press's role as a social agent, recent criticisms of the press, and the ethical factors which guide the press today.

title: Editorial and Opinion Writing
description: Theory of newspaper editorials according to types and campaigns, with attention to opinion articles and opinion polls, staff organization, and editorial page planning. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Affairs Reporting and Writing
description: Structures and functions of governmental agencies and other public agencies, with special attention to problems of obtaining and reporting information in appropriate articles. Practice in writing under deadline pressure, through coverage of newsworthy events on campus or in the community. Prerequisite: JOURN 110.

title: Technical Writing and Editing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Familiarization with engineering and spaceage terminology, with emphasis on clarity and translation of technical terms to lay language.

title: Newspaper Design, Production, and Typography
description: Theory of the design functions of journalism utilizing typographical systems with attention to their relations to communicative language. Acquaints the journalism student with new methods, ideas, and techniques which have been, and are in the process of being developed in journalism printing and technology.

title: Journalism Style and Copy Editing
description: Designed to acquaint the journalism student with 20th century prose styles, stressing writing and editing. The works of various writers and editors will be analyzed as students prepare their own copy. Consideration given to writing devices and forms, encouraging the students in developing their own writing styles. In editing, the course will consider the electronic processes currently being used by publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 110, 220, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Journalism Law
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the print and broadcast media with special attention to recent Supreme Court rulings.

title: Studies in Magazine Journalism
description: Indepth research and analysis of a selected topic in one of the major areas of magazine journalism: editing, writing, trends, management.

title: Magazine Management

title: Newspaper Circulation, Promotion, and Financing

title: Newspaper Advertising Cases and Concepts
description: Designed to analyze the advertising problems of large consumer goods firms, industrial marketers, retailers, and nonprofit organizations as seen from the perspective of the media advertising manager. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Advertising Copywriting
description: Journalistic skills of writing copy intended to induce favorable consideration of a service or product with the aim of selling it or increasing the consumption thereof, or to persuade persons to support or oppose a cause, morally or financially, through the medium of paid advertising. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Publicity Writing
description: Theory and practice of producing publicity tools for various media used in campaigns to promote and interpret personal, institutional, and organizational objectives and activities. Emphasis on writing and publicity problem solving. Prerequisite recommended: JOURN 361.

title: Institutional and Industrial Publications
description: Study of the institutional and industrial publications as an important means of internal and external communications of organizations. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or 120.

title: Advertising: Public Relations Practicum
description: Practical experience in public relations or advertising projects in preparation of a senior portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 250 and 351 or 361.

title: Producing and Advising Yearbooks
description: Theories of staff organization, yearbook organization and content, illustrations, production techniques, typography, style, theme, and the role of adviser to student staff.

title: Producing and Advising School Newspapers
description: Study of the content and organization of school newspapers, production techniques, staff organization and training, and the role of the adviser. Other school publications and news bureaus considered as time permits.

title: Teaching Journalistic Media
description: The methods and materials available to teach introductory journalistic media units or courses in the secondary school. Emphasis on function, procedures, and influence of journalistic media on the public.

title: Introduction to Journalism and Communication Research
description: Issues and trends in the literature of mass communication theory and research.

title: Journalism Seminar
description: Group and individual investigations and experience in journalistic media and techniques with special attention to current trends in American and international journalism and related fields. Prerequisite: submission of a proposed study project and permission of the department chairman.

title: Journalism Internship
description: An onthejob training experience to climax classroom experience of journalism students. Students exercise assigned duties in a communications organization approved by the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.. t t Students enrolled in JOURN 230, 331, 333, 336, 434, 435 or 439 will need access to a 35mm or a 120mm camera. If students wish, they may consult with photojournalism instructors about the suitability of specific camera equipment prior to a contemplated purchase or rental. The Department of Journalism provides limited photographic chemicals. Individual students are expected to supply additional needed chemicals, supplies, film, and print paper suitable for use with these chemicals. Nelson, Owens, Parish, Partner, Perham, Petrucco, Puttaswamy, Robold, Underkoffler, Whitaker, Zage Mathematics was defined by Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777-1855) as "the queen of the sciences." This statement reflects the interdependency of mathematics and the sciences. While still true, this observation must now be extended to cover all areas of human endeavor in the second half of the twentieth century. The student considering mathematics as a career should realize that emphasis in mathematics courses will change as progress is made through undergraduate and graduate school. The early emphasis on solving problems is later subordinated to the more important tasks of formulating and dealing effectively with mathematical structures and abstract ideas. Every prospective mathematician should plan to pursue undergraduate and graduate training to the highest level of capability. To meet the need for mathematically competent graduates, several programs of study are available at the undergraduate level as either a major or a minor. The secondary teaching major is designed to prepare classroom teachers of mathematics in grades 9 through 12. The junior high/middle school mathematics primary area is designed to prepare mathematics teachers for grades 5 through 9. This primary area is accompanied by a supporting area, or another primary area, in science, social science, language arts, or foreign language on the junior high/middle school major. Prospective teachers completing the secondary teaching license may earn an endorsement for teaching in the junior high/middle school grades. All teacher preparation programs comply with the certification regulations of the Division of Teacher Education and Certification of the State Board of Education. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government as well as for further specialized study of mathematics at the graduate level. In today's complex world, problems cut across traditionally defined areas of discipline, and a departmental major offers to a student the opportunity to combine mathematics with work in other areas. The departmental major on the liberal arts curriculum is a program in the liberal arts tradition. With this liberal education, the student is well prepared for additional graduate study or for positions requiring education in breadth. Computer science, as a separate discipline, began to receive widespread attention in the last twenty years. The technological development of computers together with decreased costs which have made them available to every sector of the economy accounts for the great demand for persons knowledgeable in every phase of computer science. To meet the increasing demands of specialists in a computeroriented society, Ball State University offers a departmental major and minor in computer science, as well as a departmental major in mathematics and computer science. Actuaries are mathematically trained executives who use mathematical knowledge to analyze and solve business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. Actuaries are employed by insurance companies, state departments of insurance, management consulting firms, universities, federal agencies, and other institutions. An actuarial career promises to be a challenging and rewarding experience. A departmental major in actuarial science is offered to provide a student with the foundations for an actuarial career. An actuary gains professional recognition by passing a series of examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries. The program includes the coursework for the first three examinations, and in some cases for the fourth examination. Ball State University is an official test location for the Society of Actuaries. An applied mathematics minor is provided for those students whose primary interest lies in such fields as business, economics, biology, geography, geology, and psychology, but who recognize there is a mathematical basis for their primary field. This program is problemand applicationoriented rather than theoretical in nature. Students preparing to be elementary teachers, but with an aptitude for and an interest in mathematics, may add an endorsement for the teaching of mathematics to their elementary teaching license. This endorsement prepares them to be mathematics specialists in a departmentalized elementary school, or elementary mathematics supervisors in a school system. The prospective elementary teacher may, in addition to obtaining the mathematics endorsement, take certain additional courses and obtain the junior high/middle school endorsement in mathematics. He or she would then be licensed to teach mathematics in grades 1 through 9. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the requirements given below. The departmental offerings include courses for several curricula. Students should seek advice if they are not certain whether a particular course will apply to a certain program. Mathematics majors and minors are assigned mathematics advisers from among the departmental faculty, and should consult with these advisers before each registration after completing the first calculus course. The mathematics adviser assists the student in planning his or her program of courses on the major or minor, and can advise in such areas as careerplanning. The requirements for majors and minors on all curricula are based on a prerequisite of college preparatory mathematics in secondary school, including trigonometry. Deficiencies in secondary school mathematics must be made up before courses on the major or minor may be taken. It is strongly recommended that a student who receives a grade of D in a course such as MATH 111, 112, 113, 123, 131, 161, 170, 171, 211, or 212, which is a prerequisite for another course, consider repeating the course before proceeding in the sequence.
