title: Mathematical Concepts 1
description: A general education course for students who wish to know more about the contributions of mathematics to human culture. Includes topics particularly suited to the needs of the student who seeks a broad knowledge of mathematical ideas together with some computational skills and techniques. Prerequisite: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry. Not open to students with college credit in mathematics except by permission of the department chairman or to students with areas in mathematics or computer science.

title: Mathematical Concepts 2
description: Continuation of MATH 100. Prerequisite: MATH 100.

title: College Algebra 1
description: Fundamental operations of algebra through quadratics. Students who have credit for three semesters of secondary school algebra will not receive credit for this course. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra.

title: College Algebra 2
description: A brief introduction to sets and the logic of algebra, a discussion of inequalities, absolute values, functions and relations, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and mathematical induction. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary school algebra, and one year of plane geometry, or their equivalents as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied in this course if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities and equations ; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers, and DeMoivre's Theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or its equivalent as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Analytic Geometry
description: Use of Cartesian and polar coordinates in two and three dimensions, conic sections, transcendental curves, curve sketching, parametric equations, lines and surfaces in solid analytic geometry. Prerequisite: The equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level, or MATH 111 and 112.

title: Mathematics for Architects 1
description: Topics in analytic geometry and calculus particularly suited to the needs of the architecture major. Includes concepts of limits, differentiation, and integration. Prerequisite: MATH 112. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 161 or 170.

title: Mathematics for Architects 2
description: Continuation of MATH 123. Emphasis on applications of calculus. Prerequisite: MATH 123. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 162 or 170.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 1
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or a strong background in high school algebra.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics which are particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications in some of the above areas. Prerequisite: MATH 111 and 112 or their equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 170.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATH 161 or 170. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Calculus 1
description: Inequalities, limits, continuity, differentials and derivatives, introduction to the definite integral. Prerequisite: MATH 113.

title: Calculus 2
description: Continuation of the definite integral, differentiation and integration of elementary transcendental functions, derivatives in polar coordinates, integration by special methods, applications of integration. Prerequisite: MATH 170.

title: Calculus 3
description: Continuation of the application of the integral, elements of infinite series (convergent and divergent series), Taylor's series and theorem, partial differentiation, and multiple integration. Prerequisite: MATH 171.

title: Calculus 4
description: Infinite series and elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Cardinal Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers.

title: Rational Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the concept of unsigned rational numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 201.

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the real number system. Prerequisite: MATH 202. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 205.

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: The development and use of decimal and scientific notation through metric measurement. An extension of real number concepts including irrational numbers and integers through measurement, decimal approximations, calculator activities, coordinate graphing, and applications. MATH 203 may be substituted for

title: Geometry in the Elementary School
description: A development of geometric concepts for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 202, and MATH 203 or 205 if either course is required on the student's program.

title: Elementary School Enrichment Topics
description: An examination of mathematics concepts included as enrichment topics in elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 206. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman.

title: Structure of the Number Systems
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and selected number systems. A systematic development is emphasized. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172 or equivalent.

title: Elements of Linear Algebra
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties, determinants, matrix inverses, rank and equivalence of matrices, and a matrix approach to the theory of systems of linear equations. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 171.

title: Topics from Linear Algebra
description: Determinants, matrices, and bilinear maps, polynomials and matrices, triangulation of matrices and linear maps, spectral theorems, multilinear products. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 412.

title: Topics from Modern Algebra
description: Basic topics from polynomial and integral domain theory, group theory, ring theory. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 313 or 411.

title: Applied Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, probability, random variables, important discrete and continuous distributions, statistical inference and testing of hypotheses, sampling theory, statistical analysis of time series, decision theory. Applications to business will be made throughout the course. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, or 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 321.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Geometry
description: A revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems will be considered which deal with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by permission of the department chairman. Prerequisite: MATH 173.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 202.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Secondary School Mathematics
description: A course for the secondary teaching major designed to expose students early in their program to mathematics in a teaching environment. Prerequisite: MATH 161 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 395.

title: Computer and Enrichment Topics for the Junior High/Middle School Teacher of Mathematics
description: Designed for the junior high/middle school teacher of mathematics; includes topics in computer uses and programming and enrichment topics from such areas as topology, strategy games, number theory. Prerequisite: MATH 211 and MATH 240. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 200 or 220.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 172.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, gamma, rectangular and normal distributions. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Statistics 1
description: Classification of data, empirical distributions, random sampling, distributions of sample mean and same variance from normal distribution, distribution of sample mean from nonnormal distributions, probability distributions for correlation and regression, empirical methods for correlation and regression, general principal of estimation and hypothesis testing. Prerequisite: MATH 320.

title: Statistics 2
description: Testing of goodness of fit, contingency tables, small sample distributions, chisquare, t and F distributions and their applications in hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, nonparametric methods, sequential analysis, Bayesian method. Prerequisite: MATH

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, t, and F distributions. Some problems with moment generating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Prerequisite: MATH 221 or 321 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in synthetic geometry, closely related to the field of Euclidean geometry.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models to problems from physics, chemistry, biology, and business. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models rather than detailed numerical results. Prerequisite: MATH 212.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nth order ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Enler equations, Laplace transforms, power series solutions, Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, first order partial differential equations, applications in business, biological, chemical, physical, and sociological sciences. Prerequisite:

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematics in Early Childhood
description: Materials and methods used for teaching mathematics at prekindergarten levels. Prerequisite: MATH 204.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from kindergarten through grade three. Class ideas applied in tutoring situations. Prerequisite: MATH 204. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 391.

title: Arithmetic in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching arithmetic at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Prerequisite: MATH 204.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for the teaching of mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a tutoring situation. Prerequisite: 30 hours credit on the junior high/middle school mathematics program and junior standing.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in the teaching of senior high school mathematics. Survey of texts, organizatiOn of materials, testing procedures, and visual aids materials. Prerequisite: MATH 313, EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Deals specifically with mathematics oriented classroom management techniques, an introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: MATH 395.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 1
description: Topics from group theory, ring theory, and field theory, including integral domains and polynomial rings. Prerequisite: MATH 212.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics from MATH 411 and topics from vector spaces and module theory. Prerequisite: MATH 411.

title: Theory of Numbers 1
description: Topics from: the division algorithm, positional notation, divisibility, primes, congruences, divisibility criteria, the sigma, divisor and phi functions, diophantine equations, linear, polynomial and simultaneous congruences, theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson, primitive roots and power residues and their application to decimal expansions of rationals, Pythagorean triples, and Fermat's method of descent.

title: Theory of Numbers 2
description: Some topics not covered in MATH 416 including elementary partition theory, quadratic residues, continued fractions, Farey fractions and irrational numbers, elementary properties of (x), Waring's problem, and density of sequences of integers. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Topics in Statistics 1
description: Includes such topics as theory of distribution, theory of statistical inference, and theory of regression analysis. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Topics in Statistics 2
description: Deals with topics mentioned in MATH 428 at an advanced level with particular reference to experimental design and analysis of variance, use of computers in statistics and Monte-Carlo methods. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or 428, or permission of the

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs, simple random, stratified, cluster and systematic sampling, ratio estimates, regression estimates, cost function, variance function. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school such as Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, Magic Squares, the Calendar Problem, Polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the Fifteen Puzzle, Nim and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers will be considered. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Advanced Analytic Geometry
description: An advanced treatment of analytic Euclidean geometry using topics from analysis and algebra as tools where helpful.

title: Projective Geometry
description: Properties of geometric configurations which are invariant under projection. Synthetic methods emphasized, and some use is made of analytic methods.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities certain, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, and capitalized cost. Both the discrete and the continuous approach to compound interest and annuities certain will be treated. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172.

title: Mathematics of Life Insurance
description: An introduction to the mathematics of life insurance ; mortality tables; life anuities, premiums, and reserves for basic life insurance policies; modern reserve systems. The discrete approach to contingencies of a single life will be emphasized but the continuous approach will be introduced. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 451.

title: Topology 1
description: Set theoretic preliminaries, the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well ordering principle, topological spaces, continuity, separation axioms, nets and filters, connectedness, local connectedness, product and quotient topologies, metric spaces, metrization. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Topology 2
description: Uniform spaces, paracompactness, open coverings, compactness, compactification, local compactness, function spaces, Stone-Weierstrauss theorem, complete spaces, Banach fixed point theorem, introductory homotopy theory. Introduction to homology theory, Jordan curve theorem, Brouwer fixed point theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 455.

title: History of Mathematics 1
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to 1600. Topics covered include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, and trigonometry. Prerequisite: MATH 211 and 340.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include error analyses, solutions of nonlinear equations and systems of nonlinear equations, interpolation and approximation of functions, approximate differentiation and integration. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: CS 220 or permission of the department chairman, and MATH 124, 162, or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics covered include: numerical solutions of differential equations, matrices and approximate solutions of linear systems by both direct and iterative methods, matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: MATH 212, 162 or 173, and MATH 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 463.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, mathematical formula. Prerequisite: MATH 462 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Vector Analysis
description: An introduction to the theory and applications of vectors including the algebra, calculus, and geometry of vectors; classical theorems; applications. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Methods of linear programming and optimization of functions of several variables with and without constraints. Geometric, algebraic, and simplex methods; duality in linear programming. Classical, optimization, search techniques, Fletcher-Powell method, and method of steepest descent. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 466.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Elements of Analysis 1
description: Includes such topics as: partial derivatives, L'Hospital's Theorem, integration in polar coordinates, sequences, series, convergence, continuity, and improper integrals. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or equivalent. Open only to students with a teaching major in mathematics. Not open to the student with credit in MATH 172.

title: Elements of Analysis 2
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATH 469.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Advanced calculus including real numbers, metric spaces, topology of R and C, continuity of functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrauss theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATH 173.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics covered include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansion. Prerequisite: MATH 471.

title: Advanced Calculus 3
description: Advanced calculus of several variables. Calculus of differential forms in three dimensions. Examples from physics. Prerequisite: MATH 472.

title: Advanced Differential Equations
description: Existence and uniqueness of solution of first order nonlinear ordinary differential equations, linear systems, autonomous systems in the plane, oscillatory theory, second order partial differential equations with constant coefficients, the Cauchy problem, elements of potential theory, the Dirichlet problem. Prerequisite: MATH

title: Complex Variables 1
description: Complex number systems, differentiation and integration, functions (analytic, entire, meromorphic) of one complex variable, singularities, complex integration, Cauchy's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, power series, Laurent Series, calculus of residues. Prerequisite: MATH 173. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Complex Variables 2
description: Analytic continuation, Riemann surfaces, theorem of Weierstrauss and Mittag-Leffier, solution of two dimensional potential problem, conformal mapping, Schwartz-Christoffel transformations and its application to the solution of electric, magnetic field distributions and of thermal and hydraulic stationary flow problems. Prerequisite: MATH 485.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Arithmetic
description: For teachers in service who do not hold a degree. Prerequisite: teaching experience in the elementary school. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the Mathematical Sciences Department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines. Timesharing computer techniques with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. An understanding of the role of the computer in the modern world. Not open to the student with areas in mathematical or computer sciences, or with credit in ID 200, CS 210, 220, or MS 220.

title: Computer Science for Architects
description: An introductory course in computer science for students from the College of Architecture and Planning. Problems related to architecture are solved using timesharing and batch processing techniques. Use of the plotter is stressed. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 200, 220, or MS 220.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize application in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: CS 200 or 220 or MS 220. Not open to the student who has credit in MS 310.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Computer organization and facilities. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Timesharing techniques are introduced. Prerequisite: MATH 112 and sophomore standing; or MATH 113, 123, 132, or 161.

title: Computer Assisted Instruction
description: Explores the possible uses of the computer in the instructional process. Technological and economic problems related to selecting and designing computer assisted instruction systems considered. Students develop computerized lessons on topics of their choice. Not open to students with areas in computer science without permission of the department chairman.

title: Machine Language and Systems Programming 1
description: Introduction to computer architecture, machine language, and assembler language; fixed point and decimal arithmetic; character manipulation ; subroutine linkage; looping and branching. Prerequisite: CS 220, and MATH 124, 162, or 170, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Machine Language and Systems Programming 2
description: Advanced topics in machine and assembler languages; bit manipulation, floating point arithmetic, macros, conditional assembly, core dumps and debugging, input/output using the operating system, input/output device programming, interrupt programming. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Advanced Programming Techniques
description: Topics such as structures, blocks, dynamic storage allocation, list processing and pointer variables, compile time instructions, organization and manipulation of data files, and interrupt handling are treated using the PL/1 language. Operating system features are included as required by these topics. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Computer Hardware Systems
description: Introduction to computer logic and registertransfe r level of systems description is presented. The basic building blocks of a computer system are examined. Various computer architectures and hardware trends are studied. Microprogramming is introduced. Prerequisite: CS 330 and MATH 212.

title: Computer Programming Languages
description: Emphasis is on important structural characteristics of high level programming languages. Additional languages studied are APL, ALGOL-68, LISP, and SNOBOL to show such features as dynamic array manipulation, language extensibility, list and string processing. Some compiler techniques are also considered. Prerequisite : CS 32.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Problems typical to DP centers such as file maintenance, report writing, sorting and merging are treated using COBOL. Sequential and direct access processing techniques. Prerequisite: CS 332.

title: Systems Analysis
description: The role of and techniques used by the information processing specialist. Includes a case study laboratory. Prerequisite: CS 332.

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation and the application of simulation languages to system studies. Students will carry out simulations using examples from different fields. Prerequisite: CS 332 and MATH 221 or 321.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include error analyses, solutions of nonlinear equations and systems of nonlinear equations, interpolation and approximation of functions, approximate differentiation and integration. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: CS 220 or permission of the department chairman, and MATH 124, 162, or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics covered include: numerical solutions of differential equations, matrices and approximate solutions of linear systems by both direct and iterative methods, matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: MATH 212, 162 or 173, and MATH 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 463.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Methods of linear programming and optimization of functions of several variables with and without constraints. Geometric, algebraic, and simplex methods; duality in linear programming. Classical optimization, search techniques, Fletcher-Powell method, and method of steepest descent. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 466.

title: Minicomputer Systems
description: The minicomputer considered from the viewpoints of its architecture, operating system, and application. Topics included are processor organization, peripheral devices, I/O programming, system programs, monitor services, and file organization. The departmental minicomputer, PDP-11, will be used for handson laboratory projects. Prerequisite: CS 331.

title: Operating Systems
description: Introduction to the functions and structure of computer operating systems. I/O programming, initial program load, resource (processor, memory, device, and information) management, programming aids (compilers, linkers, dynamic debugging, editors). Prerequisite: CS 433 or 472.

description: Special advanced work not offered in other courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Natural Resources Van Meter, Chairperson; Godish, Hibbs, Lowe, Lyon, Mortensen, Siewert, Sullivan The Department of Natural Resources has as its ultimate objective the education of people to help meet the increasing demand for qualified personnel in the environmental/natural resources area. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the University by offering appropriate courses in natural resources. Through research and extension activities it also strives to provide services and otherwise contribute toward establishing and/or maintaining a state of harmony between people and their environment. Environmental problems have resulted from our rapidly expanding population and technology in combination with our affluent society causing accelerated resource use and abuse. There is an increasing need for both men and women with a knowledge of natural resources and environmental quality management. The programs offered by the department are designed to provide students with a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. Curricula offered by the Department of Natural Resources are interdisciplinary because the conservation of our natural resources and the concomitant improvement of our environment are areas of total University concern, requiring new ideas, diverse skills, and integrated input from many disciplines. Therefore, depending upon the individual interest of the student, a program may include courses in several disciplines in fulfilling the curricular requirements. Students considering a professional career in natural resources should plan their high school program to include a strong background in both the sciences and the humanities. The desire and ability to work with people (humaneering) is also an important prerequisite. Curricula offered by the department include a departmental minor and major in natural resources at both the undergraduate and graduate level and a cognate in this area for doctoral students. A teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, an area of endorsement for elementary education majors, a supporting concentration for junior high/middle school majors, and an energy resources minor are also offered. Students enrolled in the undergraduate major in natural resources may elect the general option in resource management or specialize in such areas as natural resource planning, fishery resources, communications, water quality, natural resources interpretation, soil science, environmental protection, and outdoor recreation management. Although a wildlife curricula is not currently available, the university offers all of the courses required to meet the minimum recommendations of the Wildlife Society. Common background is provided for all majors through a "core requirement" which includes Introduction to Natural Resources, Air Resources, Ecology, Man and the Geologic Environment, Mineral Resources, Soil Resources, Water Resources, and Integrated Resources Management. Other courses which may be elected will be determined by the option selected, the student's background, and professional employment interests. In addition to traditional science courses, others that may be included are communication, computer techniques, environmental health, landscape architecture, physical education, political science, sociology, statistics, and urban and regional studies. All natural resource curricula are interdisciplinary. Students majoring in other departments of the university are encouraged to elect one of the natural resource minors which compliment a variety of curricula. One of these minors should be especially useful to accompany certain majors including biology, earth science, economics, elementary education, geography, geology, journalism, landscape architecture, physical education, radio and television, sociology, speech, and urban and regional studies. Those students interested in becoming teachers are especially encouraged to elect the teaching minor, area of endorsement, or supporting concentration in conservation and environmental studies to enhance their qualifications in this area. These programs are designed to prepare future teachers to enhance the curriculum through the integration of conservation and environmental studies into existing subject areas and grade levels. They should also help prepare teachers to provide leadership in schools and school corporations in establishing and implementing environmental education programs. Completion of a minor or major in natural resources also fulfills the general studies requirements in science and mathematics. Students who elect a major or minor in natural resources should enroll in NR 101 as the first course. Providing practical or "hands on" experiences is an important part of the educational programs of students enrolled in natural resources at Ball State University. Most of the courses currently offered include a weekly twohour laboratory and field experience. Some courses even include two or threeday extended field experiences. Students are encouraged to get out where the action is by participating in practicum activities or internships extending from one to twelve weeks under the supervision of a faculty member and/or professionals working in a conservation/environmental field. If planned and approved in advance it is possible for students to earn credit while participating in this type of experience. The Department of Natural Resources is located in West Quadrangle where approximately 14,000 square feet of space is used for classrooms, laboratory/classrooms, faculty/student research labs, natural resources student reading room, faculty offices, and rooms to provide secretarial and other supporting services. In addition, educational experiences are provided by field trips to Christy Woods, local farms, Montgomery Woodlot, Irving Brothers Quarry, Muncie Water Works Plant, Muncie Wastewater Treatment Plant, local industries, and the Air Pollution Control Division of the Indiana State Board of Health. The department also utilizes the services of resource people in the community and state to enhance the educational experience provided students enrolled in natural resources classes. These include representatives of industry, local governmental units, Indiana Department of Natural Resources, Indiana State Board of Health, U.S. Soil Conservation Service, Cooperative Extension Service, and faculty from public schools and other colleges and universities. Examples of employment obtained by previous natural resources graduates include: Soil Conservation Service, Indiana State Parks, city and county park boards, engineering consulting firms, Division of Reservoirs, Stream Pollution Control Division and Air Pollution Control Division of the Indiana State Board of Health, city and county health department, Bureau of Land Management, industry, commercial shooting preserves, private recreation enterprises, Division of Water Quality Control, Planning Commissions, and U.S. Forest Service. The student will enroll in the Professional Arts curriculum with a departmental major in natural resources. Inquiries of a general or specific nature are welcomed at the office of the Department of Natural Resources, located in room 110 of West Quadrangle. Students are encouraged to consult with a departmental adviser concerning professional opportunities in natural resources and the various options available. title: Introduction to Natural Resources
description: The role of natural resources and their relationship to man's social and economic welfare; population growth and its impact upon resource use. The nature and interrelationships of resources with emphasis on the multipleuse concept of resource management. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Conservation for Teachers
description: The role and importance of natural resources and conservation in our daily life. Conservation practices needed to successfully manage natural resources discussed. Conservation and natural resources information needed by the elementary school student stressed. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 101.

title: Contemporary Environmental Problems
description: The role of science in solving environmental problems with special emphasis upon the contributions people can make in achieving a quality environment through education. Current environmental problems and possible scientific and alternate technological solutions studied.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of United States resource utilization by treating in historical perspective government policies, and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource utilization has shaped society. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 204.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to man. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 4 hours of credit in natural resources, preferably NR 101 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 311.

title: Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Food Production
description: The role of natural resources in producing food for people and the agronomic and animal science practices necessary to provide food for a growing world population. Emphasis placed on the management talents needed to successfully grow food. Two weekend field trips are included.

title: Resources for Self-Reliant Living
description: Consideration of the environmental impact of hard and soft technologies. The central focus will be divising a survival strategy based on selfreliant concepts in housing, waste material, water utilization, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation, and the role of regulatory agencies will also be studied. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 211; CHEM 111 or equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: The basic relationship between soil nutrients and plant growth will be discussed with emphasis on the factors affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Basic soil testing will be included. Prerequisite: NR 221; CHEM 111 or equivalent or permission of the department chairman.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Included will be soil genesis, morphology, classification, and survey. The relationship between soils information and the land use decisionmaking process will be stressed with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources, including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, GEOG 325, or NR 101.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts as a basis will be stressed. Management systems and individual practices will be studied with special emphasis placed on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mineral Resources
description: The relationship of minerals to renewable resources including the role of mineral fuels as a source of energy for the human ecosystem; a descriptive and interpretive treatment of the distribution, production, and use of world mineral resources with emphasis on conservation principles, practices, and techniques: One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Energy Resources
description: Appraisal of the natural resource base for energy resources, and analysis of the environmental impact of the development of these energy resources. Consideration of fossil fuels as well as solar, wind, and other alternatives. Attention also directed toward energy resource policy and research, and energy conservation.

title: Air Resources
description: The significance of the atmosphere as a resource; the important meteorological parameters in air resources and management; the economic, sociological, technical, political and biological aspects of air pollution; with special emphasis on basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Ambient Air Quality Sampling and Monitoring
description: Theory and practice of sampling, analysis, and monitoring the ambient air environment. Major gaseous and particulate air pollutants are emphasized. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114, NR 341, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Effects of Ambient Air Pollution
description: Physical, chemical, and biological effects resulting from ambient air contamination. Major emphasis is placed on the atmosphere, materials, vegetation, domestic animals, and man. Prerequisite: BIO 111, NR 341 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Turfgrass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. The identification of grass and weed species are stressed.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. The interrelationships of various natural resources with emphasis directed toward multipleuse concepts of management to meet existing and projected outdoor recreation demands. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Introductory Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles as applied to the management of natural resources and related environmental problems. Prerequisite: NR 211, 221; GEOL 101; MATH 110; PHYCS 110 or 300; or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures will be included. Prerequisite: NR 211; MATH 110 or equivalent; one college course in chemistry; or permission of the department chairman.

title: Solid Waste Management
description: Solid waste management with emphasis on delineation of the problem, disposal methods and techniques, recycling, and management of disposal systems. The relationship between solid waste disposal and other resources is stressed. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study and discussion. Restricted to honors students or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the elementary education curriculum. Sources of help in teaching conservation, including the use of resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources that are uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 101, 105, BIO 102, GEOG 111, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Environmental Conservation in the Secondary School
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating environmental conservation into the secondary school curriculum. Sources of help in teaching environmental conservation including resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources appropriate to environmental conservation. Laboratory and field work required. Prerequisite: NR 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Science oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of science, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of environmental science in the secondary school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Up to five hours experience in public schools may be required. Prerequisite or parallel: NR 395 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 399.

title: Natural Resources Agencies and Environmental Organizations
description: The development, organizational structure, responsibilities, activities, and contributions of selected local, state, regional, and federal natural resources agencies and private organizations in managing natural resources and achieving and/or maintaining a quality environment. Employment policies and career opportunities will also be considered.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a particular area (not to be smaller than a county) with special emphasis on the locations of these natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence these natural resources have on the environmental quality. Each time this course is conducted a specific geographic area will be specified. Laboratory and field experiences included. Prerequisite: NR 101 and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Natural Resources Planning
description: The application of basic planning principles, concepts and procedures in resource development and environmental management. Emphasis on the importance of natural resources in the planning process. Prerequisite: 12 hours in natural resources and POLS 160 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Integrated Resources Management
description: Integrated management of resources with emphasis on combinations of principles prerequisite to the formulation and implementation of natural resources policies and program. Attention to the economic, social, and political implications of resource development. Prerequisite: senior standing. Prerequisite or parallel: all natural resources core courses or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Issues
description: An opportunity to identify and gain an understanding of selected environmental issues relevant to the local geographic area. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Research Methodologies in Natural Resources
description: Development of concepts and skills for undergraduate students preparing for undergraduate or graduate research or research oriented professions in natural resources. Introduction to the common types of research study, research writing, research instruments, and faculty research interest and projects.

title: Seminar in Environmental Quality
description: Designed to give students from the various disciplines an opportunity to relate their area of competence to current environmental problems in a meaningful way. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Air Quality Management
description: Principles of air quality management with emphasis on control programs, regulatory strategies, and control technology. Prerequisite: NR 341, 343, 345 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered Spring Quarter of even numbered years. Prerequisite: NR 211, BIO 480, and ZOOL 444, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and utilization of natural resources for outdoor recreation. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Administration and Management of Outdoor Recreation Areas
description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to implement outdoor recreation plans to provide quality outdoor recreation experiences. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairman. Philosophy 287

title: Wilderness and Society
description: Concerned with defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. Integral to the course will be a study of research in user perception and use, and a weekend trip to a potential Indiana wilderness area. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Principles of Natural Resources Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis on field work and creative presentation of concepts. Prerequisite: NR 101, 211, 221; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Organization and Management of Interpretive Programs
description: Develops skills and techniques relative to the sound organization and management of interpretive programs, including sites and facilities. Emphasis on planning procedures and field study of existing programs. Prerequisite: NR 101, 211, 221; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Resident Environmental Education
description: Philosophy and techniques of resident environmental education and an analysis of exemplary programs. Emphasis on the practical aspects of using resident environmental education facilities, curriculum planning, outdoor class management, evaluation, and administration including staffing, financing, and related activities. Prerequisite: NR 101 or 105 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Resource Manager's Role in Information and Education Programs
description: The contributions natural resource managers can make in communicating their knowledge to individuals, schools, service clubs, agencies, governmental units, and other organizations. The role of resource managers in developing a conservationconscious public is discussed. Adult education techniques and methodologies are developed. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Natural Resources
description: Supervised practical professional experience relating theory and practice by combining instruction and work activities in natural resources, including conservation education, outdoor education, or environmental education. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; 12 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources
description: An opportunity to pursue special interests in the area of environmental quality. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; 12 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 496.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Participation in original research under faculty guidance. Research will include: problem definition, literature review, data collection, analysis, and a summary report. Preparatory or parallel course work in research methodologies, statistics, or computer science may be required. Prerequisite: faculty sponsor and permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Philosophy Annis, Chairperson; Andry, Barker, Foster, Houston, Mueller, Robertson Philosophy as an Academic Discipline One of the earliest definitions of philosophy encountered by the beginning student is one that says it is the "love of wisdom. - The philosopher, accordingly, is known as a "lover of wisdom. - And it should be noted that this love of wisdom is not confined to any one field; indeed, most anything is grist for the philosopher's mill! Historically speaking, the above definition has resulted ever since the time of Plato in the general agreement that the traditional role of philosophy is one of synthesis and system building. To put the matter another way, the philosopher was seen to be one who knew something about each area of human experience as a result of either native genius or exhaustive investigation after which, by weaving such knowledge into a consistent and coherent whole, gives to the human race a unified picture of the universe and the individual. This general agreement about the role of philosophy both within and without the university produced about twenty or more centuries of some of the most magnificent albeit meaningless cogitations ever produced. This is not to say that these vast systems were or are without some value. As purely intellectual exercises they have their place. But surely the student has a right to note that on the assumption that synthesis is the main business of philosophy, here we are many centuries after Plato still bemused by his problems and showing very little evidence that we are any closer to solving them. Is it possible that they are not "problems" at all? In the past thirty years the role of philosophy has been changing, although not without some dire warnings as to its future if the present trend continues. Analysis has now replaced synthesis as the main job of the philosopher as a member of a university faculty. This is not to say that analysis has not always been with us, philosophically speaking, but in the past it has always been subordinated to the activity known as synthesis. It is generally agreed now that the scope of the knowledge of human beings is too large in our own century for any philosopher to pretend to carry on the timehonored function of philosophy described above. Perhaps this was possible in the small world in which Plato lived, it is not possible now. Given this change, then, just what is the role of philosophy and the philosopher in a modern university now? It is twofold, one relative to the other academic disciplines, and one relative to the students who pass through the classroom. Relative to the other academic disciplines on the campus, the philosopher can function in the role of critical analyst as a sort of catalytic agent by insisting that colleagues constantly look to the meaningfulness of their ideas. Indeed, perhaps the greatest service is that of helping others make their ideas clear regardless of the nature of their academic discipline. Relative to the students in the university, the philosopher and philosophy can serve in several ways. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all facets of life need examination if we are to get ahead with this business of living. Philosophy can serve by equipping the student with the attitude that all values and beliefs would never have come to be except that people in the past were not afraid to question those that were then held, and that in all probability the same fate awaits values and beliefs held now. And lastly, philosophy can serve by showing the student that this succession is indeed a good thing. The alternative is stagnation. These two roles for philosophy have given rise on most university campuses to certain basic courses in philosophy designed to be of help to groups of students. The usual Introduction to Philosophy course is one of general interest which serves to do what its title implies. In this course the student becomes aware of the basic problems philosophers deal with as well as some of their answers. Logic, the study of deductive and inductive reasoning and the rule thereto, can be invaluable for prelaw students, mathematics majors, and any other persons who must reason correctly. Ethics is a course of particular interest to anyone concerned in any way with the relationships of human beings. For those occupied with the history of ideas, the three courses in the history of ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy are most valuable. These are the core courses in philosophy and form the necessary foundation for the more specialized courses which usually follow. Religious Studies as an Academic Discipline A knowledge of the religion of any culture is essential to the understanding of that culture. This is indeed true of our own culture, as well as of other cultures. Students preparing for teaching careers will be expected to deal with religious ideas, values, institutions, and practices in their teaching. Courses in religious subject matter are being expanded in public schools. A small but increasing number of students come to Ball State to prepare for theological studies. Others decide to pursue a life of religious service after entering Ball State. To meet the increasing demands of these situations, Ball State provides students with the opportunity, which compares favorably with similar programs provided by other educational institutions, to pursue religious studies. Any student may register in courses which are designed for all four years of university life. The courses are classified under the general headings of cultural settings of religion, Biblical studies, church history, and religions of the world. Any course in religious studies counts for credit as a general elective in any program of studies within the University, it counts for credit as a social science elective for general studies, or a student may acquire a departmental major or minor in religious studies by successfully completing the requirements in this area. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: The major types and principal problems of philosophy in terms of the most significant historical and contemporary schools and movements. Brings an awareness of the problems that constitute philosophy and their importance to the search for truth on the part of each student.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of human thinking as far as human thinking is concerned with deduction.

title: Inductive Logic
description: An introduction to the principles and problems of inductive reasoning.

title: Ethics
description: The nature of ethical reasoning, an inquiry into the meaning of good and bad, of right and wrong. Critical analysis of leading ethical theories and their treatment of principal ethical problems in a search for criteria for an adequate ethical system for the individual and for society. The reading consists of the works of major ethical thinkers, both classical and contemporary.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of basic social concepts such as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of normative issues such as how liberty should be distributed, and how justice can be maximized.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Investigation of mankind as religious—in experience, behavior, personality, and society. Philosophical inquiry about the nature and meaning of those realities which concern religion—traditional beliefs, institutional expression, faith, and religious experience.

title: Introduction to Existentialism
description: The philosophies of major existentialists will be pursued with a view to understanding both what philosophical existentialism opposes and also attempts to correct as a proper philosophical endeavor. Not open to the student who has credit in PHIL 421.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the rise of philosophy in Greece about 600 B.C. to the fall of Rome. Emphasis is upon these theories in their relation to one another, the times in which they were produced, and the thinkers by whom they were offered.

title: History of Medieval Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the fall of Rome to the Renaissance. Consideration of the inheritance of medieval Europe from the Graeco-Romanearly Christian world and of the creative role played by medieval philosophy in the formation of the western tradition especially after the rediscovery of Aristotle.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophic theories from the time of the Renaissance to the present. Emphasis is upon these theories as illustrative of the changing nature of philosophic speculation in modern times from that of synthesis to that of criticism and analysis.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics discussed may include: the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of the department head.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A comprehensive survey beginning with post-Kantian philosophy and ending with the principal movements of twentiethcentury philosophy. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Students selecting these courses are advised to check with the director of the program and Catalog concerning prerequisites.

title: Aesthetics
description: An historical presentation of the major philosophical views on the concept of beauty and the relation of these views to the various forms of human expression.

title: Introduction to Legal Philosophy
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of basic concepts such as action, interaction, causation, responsibility.

title: Philosophy of Language
description: Examines the philosophical significance of language from any of various directions. May investigate philosophical theories of how language works, philosophical assumptions and implications of such theories in linguistics, or language as a tool for the philosophical exploration of the world. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Central Issues in Philosophy
description: Covers any number of traditional philosophical problems. These may include mind and body, freewill and determinism, knowledge and reality, and value and obligation. May be approached historically or by studying the works of current philosophers. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Philosophies of Science
description: An investigation of the basic assumptions, methods, and logical structure of the various sciences. Emphasis is primarily upon epistemological problems.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Open to students in the Honors College or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: The purpose of the course is to provide superior students with an opportunity for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned if approved by the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Theories of Reality
description: A critical examination of the principal problems of metaphysics, such as the nature of reality, the problem of universals, space, time, causality, mechanism, the self, substance, and process, with particular attention to the relation of metaphysical concepts to the theory of knowledge and to the factual sciences. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Theories of Knowledge
description: Problems in the theory of knowledge: origin, nature, and validity of knowledge ; critical evaluation of subjectivism and realism, dogmatism and skepticism, intuitionism, pragmatism, empiricism, rationalism, and pietism; theories of meaning, truth, and perception as they relate to the scientific method. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Rationalism and Empiricism
description: Emphasis upon the classical theories of one or more of such distinguished philosophers as Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume.

title: Studies in Oriental Philosophies
description: Critical investigation in major Indian, Chinese, and Japanese philosophies and their effects.

title: Plato and Aristotle
description: The writings of Plato and Aristotle. Specific topics may include Plato's theory of ideas and Aristotle's ethics.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory
description: A variety of contemporary ethical theories.

title: Advanced Existentialism
description: Indepth study of the writings of a particular major existentialist, or the instructor may elect to examine selected works of more than one existentialist examining a specific topic such as freedom or authenticity. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Kant
description: The philosophy of Kant with emphasis on his Critique of Pure Reason and Prolegomena.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: An introductory survey of the major religions in the United States with emphasis on their historical development, distinctive beliefs, institutions, and practices. Attention will be given to political consequences and the social significance of American religious pluralism.

title: The Long Search
description: A series of thirteen videotape programs plus class discussions about man's religious experiences, a series of encounters with men and women around the world who are living their faiths in the face of real life situations, overpopulation, materialism, inflation, H-bombs, pollution.

title: New Religious Movements
description: A contemporary focus on nonnormative religious movements (theosophical spiritualist, occult, oriental, neopagan as upsurges of shamanism) in America, based on the three categories of religious expression: verbal, practical, social ; and on the concept of religion as means for ultimate transformation.

title: Old Testament
description: The origins and developments of Hebrew-Judaic thought: its progressive expressions throughout time in personalities, theologies, and various types of Hebrew- Judaic literature.

title: New Testament
description: A basic study of the origins and developments of Christian religious thought: its Jewish environment, its early expressions, the emergence of its literature, and the various forms of its expression as found in its earliest literature.

title: Evolution of Christian Thought
description: Christian thought as it evolved in early catholicism, the orthodox creeds, the eastwest schism, the medieval age, the reformation, and the controversy between rationalism and pietism. Consideration also given to recent trends in Christian thought.

title: Christian Ethics
description: Reflection upon life and morality from the standpoint of Christian faith and fundamental Christian convictions. Discussion of contemporary ethical issues in the light of important theological presuppositions; good and evil, divine law, sin and redemption, freedom, conscience, love.

title: Religion in a Scientific World
description: Dialogue between religion and science: areas of conflict and modes of similarity. Differing perspectives on the nature and meaning of life. Theological implications in new areas of technological advance; genetic control, cybernetics, new artificial means of prolonging life.

title: Paul and His Influence in Early Christianity
description: The life and thought of Paul as they relate to his letters and to the Acts of the Apostles in the context of 1st century Christianity, the development of radical Paulinism and anti-Paulinism, their influence on the formation of Christianity.

title: Jesus and the Gospel Traditions
description: Jesus and the types of tradition about him; their origins, development, and functions in early Christianity as reflected in the early Christian writings, with special interest in the Gospels.

title: Problems in the Early Church
description: A consideration of problems in the early church such as resurrection, christophanies, messiahship of Jesus, conversion of Paul, Glossolalia or tongues, Sabbath versus Sunday, eucharist, baptism, Paul's missionary journeys, the Jerusalem Conference, Paul's imprisonment, early persecutions.

title: Religions of the Ancient Near East
description: The religious movements of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, and Persia as they relate to the development of Judaism and the rise of Christianity.

title: Religions of India
description: The religious heritage of India: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism; the ways of life they advocate, their scriptures, developments of their theologies.

title: Religions of China and Japan
description: Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, Maoism, Shintoism. Origin and developments; literature; rites and rituals.

title: North American Indian Religions
description: The major types of religious traditions of North American Indian groups, with special attention to deities, processes and problems of change, value orientations, and the contemporary viability of religious beliefs.

title: Principles of Theology
description: Consideration of traditional theological principles regarding the nature of God, of mankind, of redemption, and of the church, and an inquiry into contemporary thinking on these issues, with emphasis on the latter.

title: Black Church History and Theology
description: An analysis of the institutional structure of the black church; its contemporary functions and place in social change. Emphasis on the social conditions that shape the black church and influence redefinition of its organizational components

title: Religious Existentialism
description: Examines both the position and effects of religious existentialists related to current religious views and movements. The contributions of men such as Kierkegaard, Tillich, and Buber will be critically analyzed in the light of orthodox Christianity.

title: Comparative Religions
description: A comparative study of the great world religions. Department of Physics and Astronomy Hults, Chairman; Burgess, Cosby, Errington, Howes, Koltenbah, Ober, Place, Thomas, Watson The Department of Physics and Astronomy offers courses intended to provide a thorough background in physics, both pure and applied, and a moderate background in astronomy. Programs are designed specifically for different groups of students such as those planning to make physics or astronomy a career, those planning to teach, and others needing work in physics, applied physics, or astronomy to complement their major field. This diversification is evident in the course descriptions. It is recommended that students planning to go to graduate school in physics or related areas take PHYCS 430, 434, 450, 452, and 464. It is suggested that students planning to go into industry, government laboratories, or other fields of work with a bachelor's degree in physics take PHYCS 354, 356, 358, 360, and APHYS 454. Physics and astronomy students planning to go to graduate school should take CS 220. It is also recommended that German, French, or Russian be studied if the graduate school that will be attended requires a foreign language for Ph.D. or M. S. candidacy. Physics major and minor programs are available both for those students planning to make physics a career and those planning to teach. An astronomy minor is available with two options, one for those who want to pursue astronomy as a career taking further advanced work at another university and another option designed specifically for those whose goal is to have expertise in presenting planetarium programs and becoming planetarium directors. A minor in applied physics is available for students wanting to learn modern electronics and the use of electronics in instrumentation and computers. Courses in selected areas of applied physics such as heat transfer, fluid mechanics, solar energy, and microprocessor electronics may be taken by the student. Courses having the APHYS or PHYCS prefix but not listed in the requirements (see below) as allowed electives may be taken by the interested student and substituted for listed electives upon written approval of the department head or departmental adviser. Physics and astronomy courses have two hours of regularly scheduled laboratory a week during the regular school year unless designated otherwise. In evening and Saturday classes and in the summer terms a ratio of lecture and laboratory experiences equivalent to the quarter dayclass ratio is maintained. PRE-ENGINEERING MAJOR This departmental major is intended for students interested in preparing themselves for admission to a school of engineering. Specifically, the program is offered in cooperation with the Purdue University School of Engineering so that courses taken at Ball State on the preengineering curriculum parallel courses the student would take at Purdue during the first several years of study. Although the courses taken at Ball State on the preengineering curriculum are similar or identical to those taken by students at many institutions offering engineering programs, the School of Engineering at Purdue is the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program whereby the student attends Ball State for three years then transfers to Purdue to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of such a program the student is eligible to receive a bachelor's degree from Ball State and the engineering degree from Purdue. It is possible to complete the degree requirements for both institutions in less than five years if summer sessions are attended. The student may, of course, elect to transfer to Purdue or some other engineering school before completing the full preengineering course of study at Ball State. In such a case, the student will be eligible to receive only the degree at the institution to which he or she may transfer. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not mean automatic admission to the Purdue University School of Engineering. The student must contact Purdue and apply for admission when he or she wants to transfer. In order to succeed in being admitted to the School of Engineering at Purdue as a transfer student, it is expected that the applicant have no less than a 2.5 overall GPA with grades in math, physics, chemistry, and computer science at Ball State being very important. Three options on the preengineering major are available. The options for, students interested in chemical or metallurgical engineering are specifically listed. For other areas of engineering such as electrical, mechanical, civil, etc., the student should elect the General Engineering option.
