title: Elements of Human Health
description: Human biology stressing the personal and informational aspects of current health problems. Hygiene of the basic systems of the body with emphasis on care, functions, and disorders; natural and acquired defenses against disease; elements of preventive medicine; and modern standards of sanitation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 160.

title: Fundamentals of Human Health
description: The main purpose is to promote total individual fitness. Intelligent selfmanagement, based on understanding of body functioning, is an objective. Some problems considered are the following: existing health situations; use of physicians, dentists, and public agencies; infections and body defense; in emergencies, what to do until the doctor comes; food and one's efficiency; emotional health; and basic understanding of human reproduction. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 150.

title: Community Health Problems
description: Organization of official and nonofficial health agencies at the various levels: international, national, state, and local. Exploration of causative community factors in disease, community diagnoses of disease, and programs being investigated to combat these conditions. Selected communicable, noncommunicable, and behaviortype problems including traffic safety will be the focus for the application of principles and procedures. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course. f The following courses are prerequisite to this program: BIO 111; CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114). CHEM 231 required if this course is elected. Prerequisite waived for students admitted to the physical therapy major.

title: Emergency Health Care
description: Various emergency health problems and their management by the application of emergency health care as recommended by the American Red Cross and Civil Defense authorities. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 299 or 396.

title: Introduction to Occupational Safety and Health
description: A qualitative and quantitative study of the interface between individuals, their tools, and their work environment and the methods by which the resulting health hazards can be controlled to an acceptable level. Prerequisite: HSC 250.

title: School Health Practice
description: Community and school health services. Practical experiences in screening for visual, auditory, and nutritional defects. Identification and control of childhood diseases. Topics included: accidents, safety, and first aid; materials for teaching health; role of the teacher and school health personnel; and effect of the total school program on the health of the child. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: School Health Organization
description: Organization and development of school health programs. Coordination of school and community health programs, hygiene, and sanitation of the school plant, the school lunch program, school health services, and the health instructional program. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 350.

title: Health Appraisal of School Children
description: Sociological, psychological, and physiological changes that take place in school children. Prevalent health problems that occur in school children — their etiology, pathology, diagnosis, and prognosis. Experience in screening techniques for discovering these deviations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 350 or 360.

title: Women and Health
description: A general overview of some current issues related to women and health: the human female, a woman's right to control her body, health problems of women, women in the health marketplace, the gynecological exam, pregnancy and childbirth, teenage pregnancies, midwifery, female sexuality, women and aging, occupational health and women, and the women's health movement.

title: Public Health Entomology
description: An examination of public health problems caused by insects and other anthropods. Emphasis will be placed on the identification, biology, and control of vectors of communicable diseases; on disease transmisison cycles; and on research techniques used in solving public health entomology problems.

title: Honors Colloquium in Health Science
description: Exploration of selected current issues in health science with an emphasis upon individualized study, reporting, and discussion. Restricted to honors students.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Health and Safety
description: Examination of the Indiana state course of study in health and safety, relation of health policies and current schoolhomecommunity problems, practice with audiovisual aids, evaluation of representative textbooks, and visits to offcampus schools. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials in Health and Safety
description: Discipline oriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of health and safety, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of health and safety in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: HSC 395.

title: Health Science of Distant Areas
description: School and public health programs at local, state, and national levels. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students on elementary curricula, students with concentration areas in health science on secondary curricula, and students in public health areas. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in the course is contingent upon permission of the department chairman.

title: Health, Sexuality, and Family Life
description: The family as the basic unit in society with consideration of the health problems facing the family. Emphasis is given to tracing relationships between men and women in the areas of dating, courtship, marriage, and problems of raising children; human anatomy, physiology, and embryology; and responsibilities of the home and school in the sex education of the schoolage child. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or a major or minor in health science, home economics, biology, teacher education, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sex Education and School Health
description: Development of an understanding of how to implement and teach a positive program of sex education aimed at helping young people develop constructive attitudes, values, and practices based on sound knowledge in accordance with American Medical Association recommendation and pertinent state guidelines. Prerequisite: HSC 461 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Alcohol Problems
description: A study of alcohol as a mood modifier, its use, nonuse, and abuse in drinking societies. Critical and controversial issues relevant to alcohol ingestion will be explored for medical, economic, legal, educational, historical, physiological, and public health implications

title: Current Progress in Disease Control
description: A critical review of pertinent research being conducted on leading causes of mortality and morbidity in the United States. A description and analysis of this current research will enable participants to gain an appreciation and understanding of current health progress in the United States. Particular emphasis upon the potential for application of this information into individual, school, and community health programs. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Drug Dependence and Abuse
description: An analysis of the medical, psychological, sociological, and legal dimensions of drug use in the United States. The incidence and prevalence of drug abuse together with the roles played by the school and community in dealing with this health problem will be treated. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health Quackery
description: Health services and consumer protection organizations. An analysis of fradulent health practices and nostrums, available health care systems and health products. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health and Aging
description: Dynamics of later life and the aging process with specific emphasis on health. The physiological and behavioral dimensions of the aging process will be analyzed and discussed.

title: Death and Dying
description: An analysis of the relationship between death and health with emphasis upon the physiological, medical, psychological, legal, and consumer aspects of death and dying in contemporary America. Roles of individual, family, school, community, and various professionals examined. Problems in the meaning of death, care of dying, death ritual, bereavement, and death education investigated. Prerequisite: HSC 150 or 160 or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Internship in Health Science
description: The intern will be assigned to an approved health agency or education institution for a period of time commensurate with the hours of credit to be earned. The student will periodically and terminally report to an academic adviser and to the administrator of the participating agency(s). Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with HSC 575.

title: Public Health Practice
description: Public health organization and available community health resources. Recent developments and problems in the field of public health. Examination of recent literature on preventive medicine and human conservation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites: HSC 160 and 180, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Health
description: The physical environment and its relationship to disease causation. Review of environmental health problems and their solutions. Areas of study include air and water pollution, milk and food sanitation, disposal of human excreta and waste, radiological agents in the environment, and occupational health problems. Prerequisite: HSC 480.

title: Epidemiology
description: Classic epidemics, evaluation of epidemiological principles and techniques of investigation, and epidemiological analysis of selected types of diseases. Prerequisite: HSC 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Health Education
description: Basic functions of public educators in various settings. Emphasis will also be placed upon (1) need for public health education, (2) current settings for health education, (3) forces and movements that influence health education, (4) and the historical development of public health education. Prerequisite: HSC 180, 480.

title: Public Health Education: Planning and Evaluation
description: Intended for persons planning to work in public health agencies. Emphasis will be placed upon (1) the need for planning, (2) current settings for public health education, (3) techniques used to identify health education components of health programs, (4) program planning techniques, and (5) evaluation methodologies. Prerequisite: HSC 480, 484 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Studies in Health Science
description: Designed to give undergraduate health science students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamentals of Mammalian Anatomy
description: Basic study of mammalian anatomy with detailed dissection and with examination of representative microscopic structure. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Human Embryology
description: Normal development of the human organism including germ cell formation, fertilization, implantation, and organ formation. Consideration of embryonic environment, physiology, and abnormal development. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or ANAT 201.

title: Human Anatomy
description: Regional study of the structural and functional relations of the human body by means of dissection. Consideration of normal and abnormal development and microscopic structure of tissues and organs. Prerequisite: admission to the Physical Therapy program.

title: Human Anatomy
description: A continuation of ANAT 330. Regional study of the structural and functional relations of the human body by means of dissection. Consideration of normal and abnormal development and microscopic structure of tissues and organs. Prerequisite: ANAT 330.

title: Human Neuroanatomy
description: Offers a strong background in the basic structural and functional relations of the central nervous system. Emphasis upon understanding of the location of nerve cell centers and the fiber tracts entering and leaving these centers. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or ZOOL 330. Prerequisites recommended: ANAT 320 and 430.

title: Histology
description: Microscopic structure or organisms with special emphasis on the tissues of vertebrates. Introductory microtechnique. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisites: four courses in biological science. BIO 360 and ZOOL 330 are recommended.

title: Fundamentals of Pathology
description: An introduction to the study of the principles of disease production, especially in the human body. Emphasis on basic concepts and descriptions of disease processes as seen in the human being. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 430 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Special Studies in Anatomy
description: Designed to give undergraduate anatomy students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Essentials of Human Physiology
description: A basic human physiology course designed primarily for science teaching majors and minors in secondary education with stress on the major function of each organ system. Laboratory exercises designed so that they can be used to demonstrate physiological principles to high school students. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or BIO 111 and 112. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYSL 210.

title: Human Physiology
description: Vital processes with references to human functional biology. Group experimentation with recording apparatus. Prerequisites: BIO 111, or BIO 102 and 103; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Human Physiology
description: Continuation of PHYSL 210. Functions of the human organ systems. Comparisons between vertebrate systems and mechanisms in humans. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210.

title: Mammalian Physiology
description: Comparative mammalian physiology with consideration of laboratory and domestic animals and their contributions to human physiology. Advanced instrumentation and animal handling techniques stressed in laboratory. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisites: one year of inorganic chemistry or BIO 111; CHEM 110; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Renal Physiology
description: A detailed study of the urinary system and excretory functions. Emphasis will be on human physiology but comparative vertebrate systems will be included. Subject matter included will be from the embryogenicanatomic level to the biochemicalpathological level. Prerequisite: general chemistry, organic chemistry; one course in anatomy; one course in physiology.

title: Cardiovascular Dynamics
description: A functional study of the mammalian circulatory system, stressing actions of homeostatic control mechanisms and applications of physical principles to a biological system, with minimal use of mathematics in developing operational concepts. Prerequisite: one course in physiology and one in physics.

title: Special Studies in Physiology
description: Designed to give undergraduate physiology students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Introduction to Physical Therapy
description: Various responsibilities and occupational opportunities; student's aptitude for this type of work evaluated.

title: Medical Sciences
description: Principles of surgery, orthopedics, medicine, pediatrics, neurology, neurosurgery, psychiatry, and dermatology. Prerequisite: admission to the Physical Therapy program or permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit must be earned.

title: Physical Therapy Procedures
description: Theory and practice of principles and procedures of : patient care, and use of masage, water, heat, light, electricity, therapeutic exercise, and rehabilitation procedures; evaluation; planning and correlation of hospital and community health services in the total care of patients. Prerequisite: admission to the Physical Therapy program. A total of 10 hours of credit must be earned.

title: Physical Therapy Directed Experience
description: Supervised practicum in physical therapy in s selected patient carenvironments; interprofesional planing and participation in program concerned with total patient care. Prerequisite: admision to the Physical Therapy program.

title: Medical Sciences
description: A continuation of PT 304. Principles of surgery, orthopedics, medicine, pediatrics, neurology, neurosurgery, psychiatry, and dermatology. Prerequisite: PT

title: Principles of Professional Practice and Administration
description: Ethics, interprofessional relationships, organization, and administration of physical therapy services and departments in various situations and types of institutions. Prerequisite: admission to the Physical Therapy program or permission of the department chairman.

title: Physical Therapy Procedures
description: A continuation of PT 320. Theory and practice of principles and procedures of patient care, and use of massage, water, heat, light, electricity, therapeutic exercise, and rehabilitation procedures; evaluation; planning and correlation of hospital and community health services in the total care of patients. Prerequisite: PT 320. A total of 12 hours of credit must be earned.

title: Physical Therapy Directed Experience
description: A continuation of PT 340. Supervised practicum in physical therapy in selected patient care environments; interprofessional planning and participation in programs concerned with total patient care. Prerequisite: PT 340. A total of 11 hours of credit must be earned.

title: Physical Therapy Seminar
description: An introduction to scientific methodology; presentation and critical discussion of current literature; discussion of current problems, new developments, and research in the field. Prerequisite: admission to the Physical Therapy program or permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit must be earned.

title: Life Science Statistics
description: An introduction to the practical application of statistical techniques in the life sciences. Department of Political Science Sargent, Chairman; Baker, Chang, Corbett, Cranor, Frankland, Gruenewald, Hamori, Hollands, Menez, Meyer, Perry, Rouse, Rudoni, Scheele, Vasicko Political science is the study of the legal governments and relation of people thereto. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Protagoras, Gorgias, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polis or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differ from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask: What is the nature of people (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between people and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. Since comprehension of available knowledge is fundamental to intelligent valuation, emphasis must be given to teaching and learning and to continued accumulation, analysis, and organization of knowledge. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civil, and vocational. The first two, hopefully, are universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed populace. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 101) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz. , political theory; American government; public law; public administration; parties, politics, and the political process; foreign and comparative government; and international law and diplomacy. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher licensing programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate level for students in other departments. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements listed below. Teaching major in social studies, 84 hours * Primary area: government POLS 130, 237 and one additional political science course in each of three divisions numbered II through VIII, and electives in political science 28 hrs. Electives in diversified social studies not taken from the primary or supporting areas 16 hrs. Supporting area: government POLS 130, 237 and one additional political science course in one of the divisions numbered II through VIII, and electives in political science 20 hrs. Teaching minor in social studies, 40 hours Government concentration: POLS 130, 237 and one additional political science course in each of three divisions numbered II through VIII, and electives in political science 24 hrs. Courses selected from three social studies areas other than government 16 hrs. Departmental major in political science, 48 hours POLS 130, one additional political science course in each of five divisions numbered II through VIII (POLS 210 strongly recommended), and electives in political science 48 hrs. Departmental minor in political science, 28 hours POLS 130, one additional political science course in each of three divisions numbered II through VIII (POLS 210 strongly recommended), and electives in political science 28 hrs Prelaw Preparation At Ball State University the student prepares for making application for admission to law school by qualifying for a baccalaureate degree on a curriculum which provides for a broad undergraduate background in many academic areas and a strong concentration in the social sciences. If application for admission to law school is the immediate objective after pbtaining a baccalaureate degree, the student may elect to meet degree requirements on the Liberal Arts Curriculum. A departmental major of 48 hours in a social science and a departmental minor of 28 hours in a social science are specified. Political science, American history, world history, sociology, and economics are disciplines especially suggested for major and minor selection. The student who wishes to prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana before making application for admission to law school may take the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum with the teaching major in social science, 60 hours, and a departmental minor, 28 hours, in social science in a field other than the fields of primary and supporting concentrations in the teaching major. Thus the student prepares for certification in the field of the teaching area(s) but not in the field of the departmental area. The prelaw student should arrange as early as possible to discuss plans with the prelaw adviser in the Department of Political Science.

title: Honors Colloquium in Political Science
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in political science, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open to students on the Honors Program and other outstanding students by permission of the department chairman. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in American Governments and Politics
description: The student will work part time or full time (depending on the assignment) for one quarter in the office of a public official in national, state, or local government, a candidate for public office, or a political party. Assignments will depend upon the interests of students and the convenience of sponsors. Prerequisite: 16 hours in political science including the following or their equivalents: POLS 130, 237 and 431, or 350, or 473, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Paralegalism
description: The internship course for the legal assistant and legal administrator programs combines the students' academic training with practical experience within a law firm, corporation, bank, or governmental agency. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141, 142 and permission of the program director.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do semiindependent study. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the department chairman and a professor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: basic courses in the area selected for special study, junior standing, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings in Planning
description: Reading program developed in consultation with the department chairman and a professor with special competence in planning. Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest in planning. Prerequisite: POLS 461 and permission of the department chairman. Division II: Political Theory and Methodology

title: Introduction to Politics
description: The scope and methods of the study of political science. An examination of the basic concepts and theories in the discipline. Traditions and approaches in the field arid their application to the various subdivisions of political science. Prerequisite:

title: Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of the leading political theories evolved by mankind pertaining to the state. Emphasis on the views of such thinkers as Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Grotius, Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, and Bentham.

title: Early Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of political thought of the early Mediterranean and Medieval worlds which became the foundation of modern political theories and systems of the West. Emphasis on writings of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, St. Augustine, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Machiavelli.

title: Modern Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of selected writings of leading political theorists from the Age of Reformation to the present.

title: Communist Political Thought: from Marx to Present
description: A critical analysis and evaluation of Marxism, Leninism, Stalinism, Khrushchevism, post-Khrushchev Communist ideology and Maoism as a system of theoretical propositions and as an action program of an international movement.

title: Voter Polling Techniques
description: Methods by which information is obtained on the voting behavior and attitudes of the electorate. Emphasis on producing a working knowledge of polling techniques. Includes such topics as sampling, interviewing, and questionnaire construction.

title: American Political Thought
description: American political thought from the colonial period to the present. Puritanism, nature of rights, constitutionalism and federalism, nature of the Union, democracy, liberalism, conservatism, individualism and collectivism, welfare state, isolation and internationalism, and national security and freedom.

title: Research Methods in Political Science
description: A critical examination of methodological problems and practices in the formulation, execution, evaluation, and reporting of political science research, including a comparison of data gathering techniques, their respective limitations, and approprite application. Division HI: American Government National Government

title: Politics: Today and Tomorrow
description: A basic introduction to the contemporary issues of national and world politics. Emphasizes both current political events and long term trends in politics.

title: American National Government
description: The organization and operation of national government as it relates to current issues such as civil rights, welfare, ecology, consumer protection, and international relations. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 131.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, and centralization will be considered. Prerequisite: POLS 130, or 237.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government. Prerequisites recommended: POLS 130 and 237.

title: Intergovernmental Relations
description: Analysis of relations among national, state, and local governments. Considerations of constitutional and legal bases, and the nature of relations, such as grantsinaid, tax immunity, education, and interstate compacts. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 and 238. State and Local Government

title: Comparative State Politics
description: Major problems of states and the efforts to cope with them. Will include consideration of Indiana and its position relative to other states.

title: Urban Government in the United States
description: Structure, functions, problems, and trends in city, urban, and metropolitan governments.

title: Rural Local Government
description: Structure and functions of rural local government in the United States, including counties, townships, New England towns, and special districts. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237.

title: State Legislatures
description: Legislative systems in American state government. External influences (constituencies, political parties, interest groups), internal influences (organizational structure, staff, norms, decisionmaking), issues confronting state legislatures and reform proposals. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 and 237, or permission of the department chairman. 438, Metropolitan Problems. (4) Analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related aspects; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation to the entire community. Prerequisites: POLS 237 and 238; or permission of the department chairman. Division IV: Public Law and Policy

title: Citizen and the Law
description: To better appreciate citizen encounters with the legal system, this course explains the operation of the legal system and the political aspects of the pertinent legal issues. A variety of activities, films, and lectures employed.

title: Introduction to Legal Ethics
description: A presentation of the concepts of paralegalism with an emphasis upon legal ethics and values. The development and future of the paralegal function in our present legal environment will be employed. Prerequisite: POLS 140.

title: Litigation and Legal Writing
description: Includes an analysis of paralegalism and the common types of law suits, court procedures, and appeal procedures. Indepth examination of the various reference sources available to lawyers in determining applicable law. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141.

title: Family Law
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the legal problems in the area of domestic relations. Covers legal problems involved in marriage, separation, divorce, child custody, adoption, and nonsupport.

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes, and needs. Prerequisite : POLS 130 and 237, or permision of the department chairman.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships between government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities and finance. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: National Defense Policy
description: An international survey of military capacity and function provides the background for analysis of the national defense policy of the United States. Special emphasis on American strategic interests and problems of weapons, technology, nuclear control, and disarmament. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
description: Significant facets of legal system's response to conflicting demands upon environmental resources. Composition of environmental problems, control issues, policy formulation, and legal remedies. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or 131 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Consumers, Competition, and the Law
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or the equivalent. POLS 342 recommended.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and his government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content will include cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Policy Analysis
description: Equips the student with the tools of the policy analyst through systematic analysis of programs and projects. Special emphasis on problem definition, goal determination, systematic evaluation of alternatives, socialeconomic and political indicators, performance measures, and impact evaluation. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 342.

title: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies.

title: Administrative Law
description: Legal and political study of independent regulatory agencies; their powers, functions, and roles as determined by an analysis of relevant cases in which basic principles are identified and synthesized with other areas of public law. Division V: Public Administration

title: Introduction to Planning
description: A survey of problems inherent in planning for cities and regions which utilizes contributions of other disciplines such as history, geography, sociology, and economics. Required of majors in regional and urban planning; elective for others with permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration — national, state, and local. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Administrative organizations as going concerns composed of people taking action under conditions of conflict and cooperation: examination of nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisites: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes and activities of civil service agencies; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans; efficiency measurements, and rewards; training programs ; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement, and other personnel processes. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Survey of the principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances: administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, accounting of revenues, expenditures, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, management of publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Politics and Administration of Local Government Budgets
description: Local government budgeting with emphasis on political and administrative issues in budget preparation and accountability. Topics include revenue development including tax and nontax sources, capital expenditure programming, financing pensions, contracting for services, cost/benefit analysis and federal and state grant mechanisms.

title: The Administration of American Foreign Policy
description: Deals with the process of foreign policy formulation. The course is analytic and interpretative and presents divergent views. The conception of the foreign policy process embodies the roles of the executive branch. Congress, press, public opinion, and various nongovernmental groups.

title: Public Works Administration
description: An overview of public works administrative techniques and problems. Designed to provide a general awareness of management, policy, and decisionmaking concerns on such topics as water, street, solid waste, pollution control systems.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services. Prerequisites: POLS 160.

title: Problems in Planning
description: Involves field study of selected problems in planning to emphasize the interdisciplinary character of planning and to provide an opportunity to apply political, social, economic, and a real analysis; and implementation techniques. Prerequisite: senior standing and four courses in planning.

title: Problems in National Administration
description: An examination in depth of uniquely national administrative problems and activities. National administrative structures and techniques are examined in detail, including their use and application in the administration of specific national policy areas.

title: Labor-Management Relations in Government
description: Examines public employee unionization, legal provisions for collective bargaining, determination and recognition of bargaining units, bilateral negotiation, and thirdparty involvement procedures, administration of agree ments, and the processes and strategies in collective bargaining negotiations in public organi- - zations.

title: Administrative Problems in State Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and organizational behavior at the state level. Special emphasis on the provision of government services and functions in the major areas of budgeting and taxation, education, environmental protection, public health and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 463.

title: Administrative Problems in Local Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and organizational behavior at the local level. Special emphasis on intergovernmental aspects of program administration in the major areas of taxing and spending, education, personnel and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 463.

title: The Politics of Public Sector Productivity
description: A literature review of the contemporary political issues in local, state and federal government productivity. Emphasis will be placed on the political and attitudinal problems associated with proposals for improved productivity and effectiveness in governmental administration. Prerequisite: POLS 350.

title: Career Development and Training in the Public Sector
description: The focus of this course is on the politics and administration of public personnel development programs especially as they have emerged within the last decade. Emphasis will be given to personnel needs assessment and training programs in government agencies at the federal, state and local levels. Emphasis will also be placed on the politics and public policy implications of CETA training efforts. Division VI: Politics and the Political Process

title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda.

title: Public Interest Groups and Government
description: An examination of the internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Special attention will be given to the implications of pressure group activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and to the effects of pressure groups upon political parties and the political process.

title: Political Campaigns
description: As the linkage between citizens and the government in a representative democracy, political campaigns will be considered from theoretical and practical perspectives. The course will answer questions on the why (theory), what (strategies), and how (techniques) of political campaigns.

title: American Political Parties
description: Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy.

title: Women in Politics
description: A crossnational survey of women in politics with emphasis on women and public policy, the political roles of women, and the problems of women in politics within the context of contemporary public affairs.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Political Sociology
description: The political scientist's view of the social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effect of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Behavior
description: An analysis of the interrelation of political attitudes and public policy formation. Special attention to the substantive areas of voting behavior, political leadership, and the rise of mass political movements. Division VII: Foreign and Comparative Governments

title: Democratic and Totalitarian Political Systems
description: A comparison of modern political systems as represented by the principal nations of the world.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: Historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 279.

title: Comparative Policy Problems
description: A comparative political analysis of selected contemporary domestic problems confronting modern nationstates. Emphasizes both the process of policymaking and the substance of specific public policies. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 280.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural area, to the government and political structures of the three major powers in Western Europe—Great Britain, France, and Germany—and to the current state of the Western European integration movement. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: British Government and Politics
description: The political system of the United Kingdom, including a discussion of the Commonwealth and Britain's place in an expanding European community. Emphasis also on Anglo-American relations and British contributions to American political arrangements. Prerequisite: POLS 130. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 382.

title: Latin -American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin-American nations.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in the field of comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Government and Politics of Soviet Russia
description: Structure and functions of modern Russian government, including central, regional, and local units, relationships between party and government, and such functions as law enforcement, economic planning and administration, and foreign policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130 and 315.

title: Government and Politics of China
description: A comprehensive survey of the government and politics of modern China, both of the Republic of China and Communist China. Division VIII: International Law and Diplomacy

title: Problems and Prospects of American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: Introduction to International Relations
description: A survey of the formal relations among sovereign states in the international system, emphasizing the operation of diplomacy, the factors in international relations and procedures for the settlement of disputes.

title: The United Nations
description: Concentrated study of organization and functions of the United Nations and of foreign policy of selected members of the United Nations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: International Relations of the USSR and the Soviet Bloc
description: The foreign policy of the USSR and her satellites and a survey of the Communist Party in international action.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the law of the international community as it developed from international customs and usage and has been developed and recognized by modern states, with special reference to the position of the Western Democracies. Psychological Science 311

title: International Organizations
description: Organizations, processes, and methods devised by the nationstate system for the preservation of international peace and security and for dealing with problems of international concern.

title: World Politics
description: Analysis of general intercourse between states; normal relations, disputes and peaceful and forceful settlements; international obligations, agreements, and problems; power relationships and dominance and balance. Particular attention will be given to contemporary problems and situations.

title: Far East in World Politics
description: A comprehensive survey of contemporary international relations in the Far East mainly from post World War II to the present.

title: Communist China in World Affairs
description: A comprehensive survey of Communist China's role in international politics, with special emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Prerequisite: POLS 494 or 594 or permission of the department chairman. Department of Psychological Science Meeker, Chairman; Clark, Cook, Davidson, Deckers, Ganzhorn, Goldstone, Gordon, Hill, Humm, James, Martin, McConnell, Meunier, Myers, Pisano, Poland, Thomas, Wittig Psychology is the science which studies the behavior of humans as they interact with their environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. As a part of the College of Sciences and Humanities, the Department of Psychological Science is primarily concerned with the psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of human behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The Department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all areas—teaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, business—increase their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. The Department offers a departmental major and minor in the disciplinary area of psychology. These programs provide a basic background for graduate work in any one of the many fields of psychology—clinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psychology, psychometry—and an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other areas such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a social studies major or minor with an area of concentration in psychology, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for instructing in psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students wishing to teach psychology should choose other primary or supporting areas for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of Psychological Science offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline, and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas on various advanced degree programs. Additionally, teachers of psychology may combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in the discipline of psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment, and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. title: The Psychology of Human Adaptation to Stress
description: Adaptation and reactions to stress as psychological phenomena; research on stress and its influence on personality development; the appraisal of threatening situations by the individual; coping and coping reaction patterns to stress; theories of adaptation to psychological stress. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Altered States of Awareness
description: An introduction to the study of normal and altered states of awareness in humans. Among the areas to be explored are: sleep and dream states, sensory deprivation, hypnosis, meditation, hallucinations, boredom, and the effect of drugs on awareness. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Applied Behavior Analysis
description: Introduction to the principles of operant psychology and application of these principles to applied situations with humans in other than formal educational settings. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Elementary Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics and statistics of inference. The computation, application, and interpretation of various elementary statistics. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Introduction to Biopsychology
description: A brief introduction to the general areas of biopsychology. Topics include: the fundamental of nervous system structure and function; consciousness and its altered states; memory, language and thought; emotionality; and personality. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Introduction to Experimental Psychology
description: An introduction to the use of the scientific method in the study of human behavior. Analysis and evaluation of experimental studies will be utilized to provide experience with research techniques using essential controls and acceptable procedures. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100 and 241.

title: Introduction to Comparative Psychology
description: A survey of the theoretical and empirical foundations of animal behavior, including that of man, considered from a comparative, biological point of view. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Introduction to Social Psychology
description: Basic understanding of the psychosocial problems involved in the functioning of an individual in society. Emphasis on various influences which help to shape the psychological patterns of interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241, or permission of the department chairman. Psychological Science 313

title: Experimental Social Psychology
description: Emphasizes basic empirical research methods with special focus on those techniques commonly used in contemporary social psychological research. Combines the academic study of these methods with their actual application in research investigations conducted by students. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 241, and 316.

title: Psychology of Women
description: An introduction to psychological approaches to the study of women with special emphasis on achievement motivation and dependency, attitudes toward women, development of sexrole identity, biological and social influences on women's behavior, selfconcepts and psychological conflict in women, and a critical appraisal of research in the area of sex differences. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
description: Theoretical and practical foundations underlying the construction, use, and interpretation of standardized psychological tests and inventories. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Honors Colloquium in Psychology
description: Explorations of selected issues in psychology with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion of such topics as psychobiology, social psychology, learning, personality, and abnormal psychology.

title: Motivation and Emotion
description: An introduction to basic theory and research relating to motivation and emotion and applications to various aspects of human behavior. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Sensation and Perception
description: The human senses: their physiological makeup, development, and functioning. Basic principles of perception and stimulus hunger will be emphasized. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Psychology of Cognition
description: Analysis of research and theories in the psychology of cognition and thinking. Major topic areas to be covered are verbal learning, problem solving, concept formation, and psycholinguistics. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Introduction to the Study of Personality
description: A wide variety of classical and modern theories of personality and the pertinent empirical research are presented and compared. Consideration given to the components of a good theory of personality and to the applications of various personality theories. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Abnormal Psychology
description: Systematic study of behavior pathology with special reference to the psychopathology of physical illness and handicaps, psychosomatic and somatopsychic illnesses, neuroses, psychoses, character disorders, addiction, and acute and chronic brain disorders. Primary emphasis on etiology, symptomatology, prognosis, and prevention. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 421.

title: Teaching of Psychology in Secondary Schools
description: Materials and methods used in teaching psychology at the secondary school level, including instructional issues concerning psychology with a personal adjustment orientation and as an academic discipline. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in psychology.

title: Current Research and Trends in the Teaching of Psychology
description: Current research in the teaching of psychology with an emphasis on the research of new curricular and instructional approaches.

title: Psychology of Learning
description: The nature of learning processes, possible influences upon these processes and resultant behavior, and applications of the psychology of learning. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Physiological Psychology
description: A basic introduction to the physical basis of behavior, involving primarily the nervous system and its structure and function. Emphasis on the role of bodily systems in preception, learning, motivation, and conscious function. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Applied Psychology
description: Theory and application of psychological principles in various social settings. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Industrial Psychology
description: A comprehensive coverage of the application of psychological principles to personnel selection and training, worker motivation and morale, labor problems in business and industry, executive leadership, consumer behavior, engineering psychology, and personal problems in business and industry. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

title: Organizational Development: A Psychological Perspective
description: Presentation of change techniques from a process and small group prespective with special emphasis on the limitations and logic involved in their utilization. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100.

title: Psychology of Selection and Placement
description: Introduction to principles of personnel testing as applied to the selection and placement process. Focus on development of predictors and criteria, selection of an appropriate validation model, and the psychological dynamics of the interview processes. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 241 or equivalent.

title: Experimental Behavior Analysis
description: Investigation and practice in experimental behavior analysis, with emphasis on operant conditioning. Prerequisite: GXPSY 100, 213, and 241.

Center for Radio and Television Alexander, Acting Director; Gehring, Smith, Tomlinson, Wible The broadcast industries and the motion picture industries provide extremely democratic channels of information, 'entertainment, and communication. Ball State University has long recognized the appeals which these media have upon the mass audience, and the important part which the media play in our everyday lives. For these reasons, Ball State University and the Center for Radio and Television provide a carefully selected sequence of courses which emphasize the practical applications for these media. To meet today's demands, the Center offers both graduate and undergraduate teaching and departmental majors and minors in these fields. The Ball State University program in radio, television, and motion pictures is intended for those people who are serious about career opportunities in these fast growing industries. The excellent selection of courses in the Center's curricula includes programs for those who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for instruction with the electronic media's educational aspects in the classroom, or in school administration systems which employ media. Since many positions in the broadcast and motion picture industries require a creative effort on the part of the individual, and a good understanding of teamwork, these attributes are emphasized as the student also discovers the elements of leadership and responsibility. Students working in the Center are encouraged to learn as much as possible about the function and operation of the sophisticated radio, television, and motion picture equipment planned for a "hands on" approach. Audience research, performance, production, programming, media sales, and administrative studies of the electronic and motion picture media are analyzed in the various courses. The facilities of the University radio station, WBST-FM, and the closed circuit television production facility provide additional and practical experiences for the students in the training program. Such work experiences also allow the student to build a personal resume which frequently assists in later job applications. Training on professional equipment, and the experience gained through the knowledge of operation, coupled with classroom and small group discussion, analyses, and direct study and observation of the broadcast and motion picture industries enables the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. There are many factors which influence the future employments of individuals seeking careers in these industries. Therefore, it is not possible to guarantee employment, although the Center's records of those gainfully employed after graduation in broadcasting and motion pictures is enviable. Simultaneously, every effort is made to inform the student of the stringent and competitive labor marketplaces in both the broadcast and motion picture industries. At the same time while the serious student is discovering how to develop the broadbased foundations needed for work in the industries, learning about the operation of equipment, and coming face to face with a faculty experience in both academics and the professional work world, the keen student discovers how to cope with the problems to be met in the industry marketplace, as well as the steps to be taken in the preparation for the future. Department of Social Work Macy, Chairman; Dolon, Dowery, Gildner, Holmes, Stump Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex social problems, has contributed to the dramatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both an art and a science. Its art is the development of special skills used in working with people, either individually, in groups, or through community programs. Its science is the body of knowledge — derived from social and behavioral sciences about people and communities. Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare agencies; in courts as probation officers for juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics; in schools; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as well as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Funds, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of the Council on Social Work Education. It provides for the needs of four groups of students: those who wish to qualify for first level professional social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; those who desire broad preparation for informed community participation, leadership, and world citizenship for entry into decisionmaking roles within social welfare systems; and those who desire an opportunity to test their potentialities for a career in social work and to provide knowledge for use by students in allied human service professions. During the secondyear of study, students begin to complete course work in social work which builds upon a liberal arts base including knowledge in the humanities, social, behavioral, and biological sciences. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, policies, and methods of social work. Field trips and volunteer experiences in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of work with individuals, families, small groups, organizations, and communities. Practical experience is gained in the practicum where the student works under expert supervision for one quarter in a social service agency. Johnson, W. Johnson, Morris, Royer, Tucker Sociology is the application of the scientific method to human relations. It is the attempt to use our collective wisdom in a systematic manner in order to have as much confidence as possible in the accuracy of our social beliefs. Science goes beyond mere opinion. Social scientists attempt to describe as objectively as possible what is really happening in the world and to understand why events have occurred in a certain way. Sociology is among the younger social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades. Quickly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge; and the concepts of the discipline are becoming widely accepted throughout society. Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. Sociology is a major part of the scientific foundation for many applied fields. Social work, the criminal justice system, personnel work, counseling management, nursing practice, and the law are all based in part on the findings of sociologists. Students interested in any of these areas would find sociology courses useful. Sociology is taught at two levels. On the one hand there is the general study of social behavior such as in courses about complex organization or social class. Ideas developed in such courses are used in the more specific social sciences such as Political Science and Economics. On the other hand, sociologists teach courses about institutions for which separate departments have not developed, such as the family, and about lifecycle stages, such as childhood or the elderly. In addition we develop research skills in our courses about methods and population. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to broadening of the student's perspective of the sociocultural environment, and to the individual's own relationship to it, thus helping to produce an outlook less restricted by the limitations of untested folk beliefs. The findings derived from sociological investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives.
