title: Principles of Sociology
description: An introduction to sociology including basic concepts used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, and social institutions. This course is for students unfamiliar with sociology.

title: Contemporary American Society
description: The sociology of contemporary society with emphasis on social institutions: the family, the political structure, religious groups and movements, medicine, the economy, and education. Dynamics, change, and institutional interrelationships will be assessed.

title: The Black Community in America
description: An examination of the major social forces influencing the structure of the contemporary black American subcommunity. Emphasis also on an exploration into the strengths and weaknesses of this structure and its relations with the large community, as bases of change in the accommodative patterns of blackwhite relations.

title: Sociology of the Future
description: Examination of probable nearfuture (30-50 years) social states and social forms. Particular attention to trends in social institutions, longterm social trends, and culture change. Emphasis on basic principles of sociological analysis, demography, societal indexes, and social ecology.

title: Sociology of Women
description: A critical examination of the nature of women's roles and their impact on social organization. Consideration will be given to the effects of changing patterns of socialization, roles, role strain, intergroup relations, and the social process.

title: Sociology of Deviant Behavior
description: An overview of theory and research on deviant behavior. Three essential forms will be reviewed: deviance arising from disability in social and physical functioning, deviance arising from violation of social norms, and deviance arising from membership in groups observing radical social ideologies.

title: Social Problems
description: A survey of the nature and range of social problems, the conditions which give rise to them, and the methods by which our society attempts to cope with them.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociological Research Design
description: A basic course in principles and techniques for organizing, conducting, and analyzing sociological research; research strategies and selection of appropriate techniques for a variety of research problems. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 380.

title: Leisure and Popular Culture
description: Discussion of issues related to the uses and distribution of nonwork time and activities. Trends in recreation, folk arts, and the growing leisure industries. The impact of leisure activities on the natural environment and other "quality of life" issues.

title: Blue Collar Society and Culture
description: The social realities, life styles, and selfperceptions of the bluecollar society and culture is examined. Similarly, socioeconomic and demographic patterns are investigated. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. Sociology 325

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors affecting utilization of treatment programs.

title: Introduction to Social Research
description: The research process and research design; ethics of research; stress on use of research to assess needs and evaluate programs. Familiarization with statistics; critical analysis of selected articles in the student's field of specialization. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in the social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. Not open to the student who has credit in GXPSY 241.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective on life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors Program.

title: Ancient and Historic Social Thought
description: A critical survey of influential views regarding the nature of society and human relations from the Greek period through the 19th century Romanticists. Social thinkers and intellectual epochs are interpreted as contemporary social issues and sociological theories. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of sociological theories and theorists of the 19th and early 20th centuries with a view toward relating theoretical positions to contemporary social dynamics and to contemporary theoretical work in sociology. The cultural and intellectual milieu in which the theoretical works were generated will be noted. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Stratification
description: An analysis of theories and practices related to social stratification; examples of caste and class systems with special emphasis on the contemporary American scene. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Trends in Mass Society
description: An introduction to the major trends of mass society and changes in those trends. Students are encouraged to perform their own analyses of changing trends using existing information. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: The sociological aspects of organizational life. Special attention will be given to organizational structure, change, and strategies for planned change. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effects of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Religion
description: Examines religion as a social institution with particular attention to the societal functions of religion, the influence of social factors on the development of religion, the role of religion in the amelioration of contemporary social problems, and contemporary processes affecting the future of religion.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Medical Care Organizations
description: A sociological analysis of medical care organizations and professionals with emphasis on intraorganizational, interprofessional, and agencyclient relations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: A sociological analysis of the field of mental health with attention to social definitions of mental illness, selfrecognition of illness, the process of seeking care, treatment institutions, and the aftermath of treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as related to various sociological variables. Various sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Families in the Middle Years
description: An overview of the American family as the marital pair approach and encounter middle age. Special attention will be given to problems which necessitate interaction with the criminal justice and corrections system. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Origins and Control of Deviant Behavior
description: Development of an acquaintance with types of family, neighborhood and community situations which serve as pressures toward deviant behavior. Case studies and field observations. Community action in the detection, control, and treatment of behavior deviants is examined from the point of view of analyzing facilities and programs. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Changing Societies
description: Analysis of social change processes within societies in the modern world. Attention will be given to social movement; institutional change; and organizational change. Implementing, controlling, and measuring change will be discussed. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 or equivalent.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures, and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Methods and Materials of Population Analysis
description: Presents materials concerning the major sources of population data and elementary techniques for their analysis. Topics include population composition, mortality, natality, reproductivity, migration, and population projection. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 382 or the equivalent.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historical functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis of the social dynamics of the urban core in metropolitan areas. Attention given to the development of cities and their cores, stressing ecological and demographic factors. Examines the social issues associated with the concept of the inner city, especially racism, poverty, crime, welfare, and education. Finally, policy alternatives for alleviating these conditions are considered. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Methods and Materials in Urban Social Ecology
description: An analysis of theoretical approaches to urban social ecology and presentation of recent empirical findings bearing on this topic. Attention is also given to various statistical methods for the analysis of such information. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 382 or the equivalent.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and utilizing sources of data; and application or survey findings to programs of community action. The student will participate directly in the various phases of a survey research project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 382 or the equivalent; prerequisite recommended: SOC 472.

title: Advanced Sociological Data Analysis
description: The selection and utilization of advanced statistical techniques and sophisticated means of calculation which have been particularly useful in analyzing sociological data. Such topics as nonparametric statistics, factor analysis, sampling statistics, and multiple regression and path analysis will be discussed in the context of sociological research. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 382 or equivalent.

title: Fieldwork in Sociology
description: The research process will be reviewed. Students will learn how to use observation, interviewing, and official documents in sociological research through practical exercises. The relation between these techniques and the survey method will be discussed. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Internship in Sociology
description: Supervised field experience in a public agency. Training would involve reseach, evaluation, and implementation of agency programs. Prerequisite: SOC major with 24 hours of credit in sociology. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar in Sociology
description: An openended course offering for fourth year sociology majors. Both the focus of study and the format of the course will be determined by the students in conjunction with the instructor. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 16 hours at 300 or 400 level. Speech and Theatre 327 Department of Speech and Theatre Strother, Head; Anderson, Benson, Bloom, Diedrich, Dorris, English, Hardin, Heady, Irving, Nitcavic, Robbins, Shawger, Shepard, Yordon General Speech The field of general speech encompasses several areas such as public address, interpersonal communication, interpretation, theatre and some speech sciences. It is a general program for undergraduate use, while persons specialize as they move toward graduate degrees. In the area of general speech, the University offers both graduate and undergraduate programs. A large proportion of those students electing a speech major plan to become teachers in the public schools. These teachers are expected to direct debating and individual events, produce theatre, and promote and direct radio and television programs. They are also asked to be in charge of special convocations. Their class work is the development of the skills of public address and participation in a democratic society. Also they must develop an appreciation and skill for interpretation and theatre as performed in school theatres or through the facilities of mass media. Another responsibility is to develop an appreciation of the artistic, an understanding of the basic issues of people, and a respect for their cultural heritage. The profession of general speech assists liberal arts graduates to develop these same skills and attitudes. In addition, the speech major and minor are especially useful to support students who enter other professions such as law, the ministry, politics, public relations, and professional radio, television, and theatre. The University offers many student activities in the areas of intercollegiate debating, individual speech events, conferences, and theatre. It is assumed that general speech majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. Information concerning these activities is available in the departmental office and should be requested early in the student's academic career. Theatre Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a most modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher licensing in speech for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work is available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist people to understand themselves. It also assists students to understand their dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it. The variety and amount of participation is taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. title: Fundamentals of Public Speaking
description: Fundamentals and techniques of organizing material and presenting that material in individual speeches. Emphasis on personal speaking improvement in the classroom and in public performances.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasis is on techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Beginning Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Development and composition of the debate case and consideration of factual argumentation. Prerequisite: high school speech.

title: Intermediate Collegiate Debate
description: For students who have had previous high school speech experience. Stress on direct clash and crossquestion debate. This course involves tournament debating. Prerequisite: SPCH 213.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: The focus of this course is on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Will stress the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Personal speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation problems.

title: Speech Practicum
description: The student works upon extemporaneous speaking, discussion, debate, oratory, or interpretive reading for intercollegiate competition, or works in theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: The development of principles of rhetorical criticism and the application of the principles to an intensified study of prominent platform, radio, and television speakers. Consideration is given also to the influence of the speaker upon our social and political life. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210. Speech and Theatre 329

title: Interviewing
description: The principles and types of interviews, with application of the principles in informational, employment, appraisal and counseling interviews. Consideration of the following aspects of employment seeking: resume, placement papers, job application, interview, and followup.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Parliamentary Procedure
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher.

title: Intercollegiate Forensics
description: Practical experience in speech, intercollegiate debate, discussion, oratory, extemporaneous speaking, and interpretive reading. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminartype class focusing on various aspects of and/or problems in speech communication as they relate to individuals in their personal and professional relationships. Open to Honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; EDSEC 299, and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Deals specifically with discipline oriented classroom management techniques, an introductory involvement in the teaching of a discipline, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of a particular discipline in the secondary school curriculum. These topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: SPCH 395.

title: Studies in Persuasion
description: An intensified study and application of the principles of effective public speaking; the ideational formulation and delivery of longer speeches; the rhetorical analysis of significant speeches. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department head.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: An examination through exposure to theory, actual practice, and criticism, of the process of communication. Will include communication models of message encoding, transmission, decoding and feedback; the complexity of language, including abstracting and determination of meaning; problems in facetoface, small group, platform speaking, and mass media communication; and communication breakdowns.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of small group literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problemsolving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Business and Professional Speech
description: Concentrates on small group communication and discussion, parliamentary procedure, and on manuscript speeches for the business and professional person. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or equivalent or permission of the department head.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech and Theatre pursues a particular area of study in depth on a consultative basis with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Speech
description: The student is assigned to onthejob experience in such places as a college classroom, a political campaign or office, summer camp, or summer theatre. Students will be permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the amount of college credit to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in some aspect of speech and/or theatre and permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with SPCH 598 but no more than 8 hours may be earned at one time.

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: An overview of the field of threatre with special reference to the origins of drama.

title: Stagecraft
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of the crafts involved in theatre production at the school, college, and community theatre levels. Three hours of lecture and three arranged hours of laboratory a week.

title: Principles of Stage Makeup
description: An investigation of the principles, techniques, and materials of stage makeup and practical experience in their application.

title: Oral Interpretation
description: The study of prose fiction, poetry and drama through the medium of oral performance.

title: Acting 1
description: A lecturelaboratory class stressing the basic principles of acting. Major emphasis on stage movement.

title: Acting 2
description: A lecturelaboratory course on the principles of acting with major emphasis on character analysis and development. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Modern Drama
description: Analysis of selected dramas from the time of Ibsen to the present day and of the conditions under which they originally were produced.

title: Advanced Oral Interpretation
description: Literature through the medium of oral performance employing the modal approach to literary classification. Prerequisite: THEAT 230.

title: Directing 1
description: Theory and practice of directing for the theatre. Exercises in movement, line interpretation, creation of atmosphere, and the effective use of stage areas. Prerequisite: THEAT 232 and 233.

title: Children's Theatre
description: The principles of theatre devoted to creative dramatics. Twothirds of the course is devoted to formal dramatics. A public performance will be arranged.

title: Advanced Theatre Practice
description: Students design and execute a theatre project in such areas as scenery designs, lighting, properties, acting, directing, oral interpretation, and house management. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in theatre courses and permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Theatre 1
description: The early history of theatre from its Egyptian and Grecian origins through the medieval period.

title: History of Theatre 2
description: The theatre from the Renaissance through the eighteenth century.

title: History of Theatre 3
description: The modern theatre commencing with its origins in the nineteenth century.

title: Studies in American Theatre
description: An investigation of significant movements in the American professional theatre and its drama.

title: Studies in Continental Theatre
description: An intensive study of selected continental theatre movements from the turn of the century to the present day. Prerequisite: THEAT 411 or 412.

title: Studies in Contemporary European Theatre
description: An intensive study of contemporary European drama and theatres involving a field trip of three weeks to European theatre centers with appropriate side excursions. Discussions with leading theatre educators and professionals will be planned plus attendance at current productions. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department head.

title: Scene Design
description: Advanced training and experience in the problems of set design and lighting for theatrical productions in many forms and styles. Some aspects of television design will be covered. Prerequisite: THEAT 220.

title: Theatre Costume Design
description: Practice in the research, design, and building techniques involved in the preparation of period costumes for use in theatre productions. Special consideration is given to the costume problems facing the elementary or secondary school teacher involved in drama.

title: Studies in Technical Theatre
description: A detailed study of technical problems of theatre production. Students must arrange to meet with the costume lab, the scenery lab, or the lighting lab. Prerequisite: 8 hours of technical theatre or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Stage Lighting
description: The design, media, instrumentation, control, and operation of stage lighting. Practical laboratory work in stage lighting on university productions. Prerequisite: THEAT 220.

title: Readers Theatre
description: Theories and performance techniques relevant to group interpretation: readers theatre, chamber theatre, and choral reading.

title: Styles of Acting
description: The study and performance of the styles of acting appropriate to major types of drama from antiquity to the present. Prerequisite: THEAT 232 and 233 or permission of the department head.

title: Directing 2
description: Further investigation of the work of the director with special reference to directing the various styles, modes, and periods of theatre. Prerequisite: THEAT 350 or the equivalent. Speech Pathology and Audiology 331

title: Methods and Materials in School Play Production
description: For the prospective or actual directors of secondary school plays. Choice of plays, community values, casting, secondary school stages, advanced makeup, lighting, and stagecraft.

title: Creative Dramatics
description: Principles of developing original dramatizations through improvisational techniques. Students are expected to observe and work with children as well as with college adults.

title: Theatre Workshop for High School Teachers
description: Participation in the Summer High School Theatre Workshop or in the Summer Festival Theatre. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Theatre Management
description: Study and practice in box office procedures, house management, publicity, and promotion as related to college, community, and professional theatres. Prerequisite: 12 hours of theatre. Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology Hoops, Chairman; Artes, Farling, Harmon, Hemeyer, Kramer, Lindell, Updike Until the fall of 1978, students entering the University who graduate with a bachelor's degree in speech pathology and audiology have been eligible for initial certification to work as speech and language clinicians in the public schools. Hence, most bachelor's degree graduates are employed in public school corporations. As of 1978, students entering the University who seek state teaching licensure to work in the public schools in speech pathology or audiology must acquire a master's degree as the preservice level of training. Persons with masters' degrees may also work in hospital speech and hearing clinics, rehabilitation centers, college or university centers, and communitysponsored speech and hearing agencies. Persons with Ph. D. or Ed. D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers two undergraduate majors in speech pathology and audiology. Both are departmental majors. One is a departmental major for students who are sure they wish to work eventually in a hospital, college, or community clinic and plan to proceed immediately to the master's degree without acquiring licensure to work in the public schools. The other, identified as a departmental major for those seeking licensure in school services personnel as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist, is for students who do plan to be eligible for public school employment in these positions. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology or in audiology, and completion of licensure requirements as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist is performed as part of the master's degree program. Completion of clinical practicum hours is required as part of master's degree requirements. The master's degree is also required for state licensure through the Indiana Board of Health, required for all individuals who work in job environments other than the public schools, and for membership in and certification by the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate major programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs: public school speech, language, and hearing programs, hospitals, preschool nursery programs, and the University Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. Educational work and guidance for those persons who have hearing problems are also available. Recommendations for corrective procedures are based on the needs of the individual student. Certain programs of the University, including all teaching curricula, demand various proficiency levels in regard to speech and voice. One function of the Clinic is to implement these criteria. Outpatient speech and hearing evaluation and therapy are integral parts of the clinic program, as is the education of speech pathologists and audiologists. Some classes are available for prospective classroom teachers who desire information relative to the management of speech or hearing difficulties. The work of the University Clinic is closely associated with that of the Burris School Clinic. The Clinic is equipped with the latest sound and acoustic devices, including recording machines, tape recorders, recordings, testing materials, audiometers, and other clinical equipment. Shipman The Teachers College has major responsibility for teacher education in the University. Contributions of departments in other Colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by Directors of Elementary and Secondary Teacher Education, who are responsible to the Dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by a Teacher Preparation Council which represents the total University. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers and teacher educators in early childhood education, kindergartenprimary education and elementary education, with programs at all degree levels. The Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education provides the professional education for junior high/middle and secondary school teachers with the exception of special methods. Graduate programs in these areas as well as in higher education and educational foundations are also housed in this department. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate and graduate education programs for teachers of the mentally retarded, hearing impaired, the emotionally disturbed, the physically handicapped, the neurologically impaired/learning disabled and the multiply handicapped. The Center for Lifelong Education houses programs in the areas of curriculum, adult education, and community education. The Burris Laboratory School is a center for demonstration, participation, and research in teacher education, as well as for program development and dissemination in respect to elementary, junior high/middle, and secondary schools. The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers service courses in school administration and programs at master's, specialist, and doctoral levels for students preparing for educational management and for administrative, supervisory, and collegiate positions in its areas of expertise. Two departments of the Teachers College serve students in areas of psychology. The Department of Educational Psychology offers undergraduate and graduate programs in applications of psychology to teacher education and in educational psychometry, school psychology, human development, measurement, and research. It also provides service courses as needed for related programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services offers courses and programs at all graduate levels in its principal areas of specialization for people in educational and other positions. It also houses the programs for social psychology. Doctoral programs are offered by the Departments of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services; Educational Administration and Supervision; Educational Psychology; Elementary Education (including reading); and Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. Departments of the Teachers College, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public education and psychology; for production and dissemination of research ; for innovation in instructional practices, and for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education. Institute for Education of Teachers of the Disadvantaged Sciara, Director The Institute for Education of Teachers of the Disadvantaged (TOD) was organized in the Teachers College at Ball State University to prepare students for teaching at the elementary school level in economically disadvantaged, racially integrated, and multiethnic schools. It also provides inservice programs for teachers already working in these areas. The TOD Institute was formed when it was discovered that more than half of the graduates in elementary education began teaching careers with economically disadvantaged children. Other influential factors were the rising rate of school integration that has created a need for teachers prepared to teach multicultural groups, the rapid movement of populations from more rural to urban areas which has created a large group of economically disadvantaged people, and the growing demand for teachers with special preparation for service in underprivileged communities. Students with a teaching major in early childhood, kindergartenprimary, elementary, special, or all grade education may earn a departmental minor in teaching the disadvantaged through successful completion of a series of specially planned experiences and course work in this program. Students with a teaching major in elementary education, special education, or other approved majors with K-12 certification may earn a departmental minor in teaching the disadvantaged through successful completion of a series of specially planned experiences and course work in this program. Students interested in further information regarding this special teacher preparation program and school districts wishing to establish special inservice programs for teachers in economically disadvantaged or racially integrated teaching assignments should contact the Director of the Institute for Education of Teachers of the Disadvantaged. This means that students cannot be regularly employed, nor should they carry a heavy load of extracurricular activities. Emphasis is placed on understanding one's self and the dynamics of interaction with others. Opportunity is provided for an individual to explore his/her own strengths and weaknesses in interpersonal relationships within groups of varying ages, races, and ethnic backgrounds. Department of Educational Psychology Fischer, Chairman; Annis, Bennett, Church, Gale, Gupta, Harshbarger, Henriksen, Hosey, Hunt, Irving, Joy, Klem, Kuo, McKee, Miller, Paschal, Richmond, Schurr, Sparzo, Taylor, Treloar, Trent, Van Every, Wenck Educational psychology is a social science concerned with the development of individuals. It includes the study of human development, learning, adjustment, measurement, research, and statistics as these relate to the understanding of an individual. The objectives of educational psychology — like those of other fields of psychology — are to understand, describe, predict, and guide human behavior. These purposes are accomplished through research service functions and teaching about human relationships, human development, and changes in human behavior. Williams, Wolpert The Department of Elementary Education provides courses and programs for the professional preparation of teachers for early childhood, kindergartenprimary and elementary school children, and specialized supervisory and administrative personnel. Although the professional preparation of elementary teachers is the major responsibility of this department, other departments within the university cooperate in providing courses required on various programs. The department provides elective courses for students throughout the university. Required courses on majors outside the department are also provided. The Reading Laboratory, its services and related programs and courses, preschool through university, is an administrative part of the Department of Elementary Education. Early Childhood (prekindergarten) Laboratories, courses, and programs reside in the department. The twoyear paraprofessional program prepares paraprofessionals for early elementary and prekindergarten teachers. It leads to the Associate in Science degree. The department provides an experimental program called EXEL. Students selecting this program are assigned to work in elementary classrooms in conjunction with most of the required professional courses beginning the freshman year. Interested students should contact the Elementary Education Department immediately after starting their first quarter of work. Students will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the requirements listed under each program heading. All programs qualify graduates for standard certification to teach in their areas of preparation. EDUCATION: ELEMENTARY (EDEL)

title: Introduction to Teaching in the Elementary School: Seminar and Laboratory
description: Work with elementary schoolage children of a variety of cultural and ethnical backgrounds with opportunities through seminars and counseling to plan and evaluate experiences and to begin to develop skills, attitudes, and understandings necessary for successful communication with children as an orientation to teaching in the elementary school. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Lower Division Laboratory Experience in Early Childhood Education
description: Supervised field experience for staff working in educational settings for young children. Open only to students enrolled on the twoyear early elementary education program. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Interaction Skills for the Young Child
description: Introduces students to basic skills which each young child needs to acquire in order to use language competently in society. Deals with materials, methods, principles of learning, and conditions necessary for optimum learning.

title: Lower Division Practicum in Early Childhood Education
description: Focuses on the young child and his/her learning environment and how adults apply this knowledge in early childhood education. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Elementary School Classroom Organization and Management: Laboratory and Seminar
description: The role of the teacher as the facilitator for learning in the elementary classroom with particular attention to understanding the child as a growing, learning person and to affirming and expediting his/her growth and learning goals. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Writing
description: Development of skills in manuscript and cursive writing, methods of teaching handwriting in the elementary school, and relationship of manuscript and cursive writing to the language arts.

title: Human Relations in School
description: Development of understandings and skills needed for effective teacherpupil, teacherparent, and teacherteacher relationships in school settings for young children. Open to students enrolled on the twoyear elementary education program, or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Child Care Services 1
description: Selection and organization of learning experiences appropriate for individual children. Need identification, identification of appropriate child care facilities, and the students' roles as members of a staffing team. Open only to students on the twoyear elementary education program.

title: Child Care Services 2
description: Selection and organization of learning experiences appropriate for individual children. Need identification, identification of appropriate child care facilities and the students' roles as members of a staffing team. Prerequisite: EDEL 240. Open only to students on the twoyear early elementary education program.

title: Creative Experiences for Young Children
description: Designed to develop awareness of, and skill in, providing creative experiences for the young child. Working with children is an integral part of the course.

title: Lower Division Laboratory Experience in Early Elementary Education 2
description: Provides experience in assisting the classroom teacher in the implementation of educational opportunities for young children under supervision of a university faculty member and/or an agency representative. Emphasizes evaluation of the child and the program in conjunction with the classroom teacher. Role differentiation is stressed. Prerequisite: minimum of 36 hours in early elementary education courses, always including EDEL 160.

title: Materials and Techniques for Teaching Children of Multiethnic Backgrounds
description: Designed to offer multisensory approaches to learning. Attempts will be made to identify learning methods and materials best suited to the student's style of learning.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in elementary school classrooms.

title: Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School
description: Problems of school organization, management, control, and environment in relation to the learning activities of children. Legal rights and responsibilities of teachers and use of instructional media are stressed. Prerequisite: approval to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290, except for majors in Special Education.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Lower Elementary Grades
description: Development of language arts skills — listening, speaking, reading, and writing in the primary grades.

title: The Social, Historical, and Philosophical Foundations of Elementary Education
description: Emphasizes historical, and social derivations of contemporary educational ideas, philosophical foundations for educational practices, alternatives for ethical decisions in education, and formulation of a personal philosophical position related to educational issues in elementary education.

title: Discipline and Classroom Management: Some Practical Approaches
description: Designed to help beginning elementary school teachers create and maintain effective learning environments. Emphasizes practical approaches to prevention and remediation of disruptive classroom behavior.

title: The Parent in Early Childhood Education
description: Explores important and complex roles of parents and parent substitutes in the educational development of young children. Factors affecting parent/child interactions and skills needed for effective parenting are studied and related to the educational process. Parent involvement as a significant factor in early childhood education is included. 440g. Kindergarten Education. (4) Development of the kindergartenprimary curriculum with special emphasis on kindergarten children and procedures to be used in their development. 442g. Nursery School Education. (4) Guidance of young children. Observation and evaluation of the activities of children between the ages of two and six. Organization, administration, and educational program of nursery schools. Child development and parent education as parts of nursery school education. Use of the physician, nurse, and nutritionist.

title: Home, School, and Community Relationships in Early Childhood Education
description: Involves experiences to enrich the relationships among parents, teachers, and children in the home, school, and community environments and to acquaint and involve students with the variety of community resources concerned with the welfare of young children and their families.

title: Education of the Culturally Different Child
description: Provides students in elementary education with a broad understanding of characteristics of economically disadvantaged and culturally different children requisite to dealing realistically with their needs. Stresses consideration of teacher self attitudes towards economically disadvantaged and culturally different children as well as examination of promising instructional changes and approaches for improving learning opportunities for these children. Motivation, classroom organization, discipline, parentteacher relationships, school integration, and nonstandard dialect are emphasized. 452g. Psychology of Early Childhood. (4) Study of young children of nursery school and kindergarten age involving lectures, readings, discussions, and conferences to give individual guidance to students and help them interpret their study of the physical, mental, social, and emotional development of selected young children. Consideration is given to growth in perception, language, expression, and interests.

title: Student Teaching: Elementary School
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 460 (4) and EDEL 464 (10) for a total of 14 quarter hours, requiring 11 weeks of fulltime student teaching. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Elementary School
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 464 (10) and EDEL 460 (4) for a total of 14 quarter hours, requiring 11 weeks of fulltime student teaching. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Elementary
description: Parttime student teaching for 11 weeks in an area of endorsement. Taken in a different quarter and in addition to the regular student teaching requirement for elementary education. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Pre-Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach children in prekindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Prerequisite: E DEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Primary Grades
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in primary grades the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University in the student teaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 468. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in kindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the University' in the student teaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 467. Prerequisite: EDEL 360. Laboratory School 347

title: Practicum in Elementary Education
description: Laboratory and seminar course involving a study of progressive school practices, the philosophy of education underlying, and the possibilities of using, progressive practices in the public school. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Elementary Education
description: Independent study and research in the field of elementary education. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems in Elementary Education
description: An analysis of one's professional preparation for teaching, identifying areas in which students need to bolster weaknesses and augment strengths, and arranging for more preparation in these areas. Prerequisite: one term of student teaching. EDUCATION: READING (EDRDG)

title: Self-Improvement in Reading
description: Individualized evaluation and diagnosis of specific strengths and weaknesses in reading is followed by practice to improve comprehension skills, reading speed, vocabulary, notetaking, and content reading. Enrollment with approval of the director of reading. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Prereading Development
description: Basic understandings of environments and planned activities that foster positive attitudes and interests related to reading, procedures that stimulate prereading development, and related practical experiences with young children.

title: The Teaching of Reading in Today's Schools
description: Designed to review the current thinking, approaches, and methodology of teaching reading in today's schools. Attention is directed to readiness, word recognition and analysis, comprehension, and planning of the total developmental reading program, with emphasis on reading at the elementary level.

title: Study of Selected Aspects of the Elementary School Reading Program
description: Designed to review the current thinking and approaches to teaching reading in the elementary school, and the relationship of basic psychological principles to teaching practices. Prerequisite or parallel: one term of student teaching at the elementary school level.

title: Corrective Reading in the Classroom
description: Provides prospective teachers with understanding of difficulties in reading plus practical experience in assessing reading difficulties and in study of corrective treatment. Includes guided laboratory situations with students exhibiting reading limitations who can be aided by the regular classroom teacher. Prerequisite: EDRDG 400 or EDRDS 420 or EDRDM 421.

title: Reading Approaches and Strategies
description: Provides prospective classroom teachers (K-12) with opportunities to study and utilize various approaches and strategies used in teaching reading. Includes evaluation of related instructional materials. Prerequisite: EDRDG 430.

title: Practicum in Reading
description: Provides experiences for prospective teachers (K-12) in (1) grouping students of varying abilities in reading ; (2) planning and implementing a classroom reading program appropriate for these students. Prerequisite: EDRDG 435. EDUCATION: READING SECONDARY (EDRDS)

title: Reading in Secondary School
description: See the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. EDUCATION: READING MIDDLE (EDRDM)

title: Improving General Reading Skills in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: See the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. Smith, Swanger, Veselack, Watson, Weber, Wickersham, Wimmer Burris School, the laboratory school of Ball State University, has the following responsibilities: First, the school is obligated to provide for all youth who attend the school from kindergarten through grade twelve: —an effective and sound community school which respects the worth of each individual and provides opportunities for the development of the wide range of individual potentialities found in youth; —a living and learning environment in which all youth have opportunities for cooperative living and for the development of those values and skills vital to all citizens in a free society; and —a curricular program which, in keeping abreast of contemporary problems and in strengthening the foundations of a free society, results in functional understanding of technological development, practical knowledge of economic problems, broad appreciation for world cultures, real appreciation for beauty in the arts, deep respect for human relationships, and sincere concern for the development of a workable philosophy of life coupled with respect for self. Second, the school is obligated to provide for the teacher education program at Ball State University: —a center in which both preservice and inservice teachers can observe sound educational practices; —a laboratory in which prospective teachers can gain firsthand experiences with youth in teachinglearning situations prior to student teaching; —a center for experimentation in which diverse hypotheses and methods for improving education can be formulated, studied, and tested critically, and reconstructed continuously in light of the evidence gathered; and —a center which contributes to the improvement of educational practices in the state and nation by publicizing new practices and research findings of the laboratory school and by providing consultant and leadership services for the public schools. Burris School maintains a working relationship with all of the colleges of the University. Center for Lifelong Education Craddock, Chairman; Atwood, Bailey, Danglade, Fallon, Fisher, Foster, Greenwood, Hatton, Hoyt, Janove, Kaluzynski, Lucas, McElhinney, McGinnis, Murk, Nisbet, Ratliff, Rawlings, Thompson, Van Ness Learning neither starts nor terminates with formal education. It is a lifelong process. Recognizing this, the Center for Lifelong Education is concerned with encompassing and unifying all stages of education. Lifelong education includes both formal and informal patterns of education and random experiential learning. Education begins with the family and moves into society as a child begins to interact with nonfamily individuals. The formal institutions of education are important but they constitute only part of many social agencies providing opportunities for individuals to learn. To promote lifelong education, Ball State University established the Center for Lifelong Education and specifically charged it with providing formal and informal programs which would prepare individuals to design, implement, and coordinate educational opportunities for individuals throughout their lives. In the formal portion of this task, the Center either offers or directs the following programs of study, mostly at the graduate level: M.A. Adult Education; M.A. Appled Gerontology; M.A. Community Education; M.A. Executive Development for Public Service; M.A. E. Curriculum; Ed. S. Curriculum; Doctoral Cognates in Curriculum; Adult and/or Community Education; Departmental Minor in Gerontology (see Interdepartmental); and Seminars for the older returning undergraduate students. In addition, the Center serves as a vehicle within the Teachers College through which interdisciplinary educational services, both formal and informal, not traditionally offered by any current Teachers College department or service unit, may be developed, implemented, and coordinated. Current informal programs include: research, school curriculum studies, program evaluation, nontraditional students, inservice professional development programs, retirement planning, and related service activities. title: Seminar in Facilitating Lifelong Learning
description: A seminar course for nontraditional students which will provide an opportunity to explore, discuss, and reenforce new changes in self as a learner and as a group participator. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on the Evolving Roles of American Men and Women
description: A course for nontraditional students which provides an indepth look at a history of rights and roles of eighteenth-, nineteenth-, and twentiethcentury American men and women. Prerequisite: EDAC 101 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on Investigation into Job Opportunities
description: A field course for nontraditional students which will provide opportunities for exploration into job opportunities or advancements through placement experiences in work settings, depth interviews and visitations, and directed readings. Emphasis is on problemsolving, acquiring firsthand knowledge in order to make realistic career decisions by older male and female students. Prerequisite: EDAC 101, 102, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on Comprehensive Programming for Lifelong Learning
description: Assist nontraditional students to prepare portfolios on learnings obtained through life experiences and to develop comprehensive plans for continuous learning throughout their life spans.

title: Adult Education
description: The history and current status of adult education in the United States and in selected foreign countries; the nature, scope, purposes, and historical development of adult education institutions and program areas; an introduction to and overview of adult education as a field of study and practice.

title: The Adult as a Learner
description: Designed to familiarize students with implications of learning theories for education of adults in a variety of learning situations and to develop skills in use of applicable methods and techniques.

title: Adult Psychology
description: Developmental study of psychological stages of adulthood. Not open to the student who has credit in EDPSY 355.

title: Volunteers and Voluntarism
description: An analysis of the historical, theoretical, philosophical, and operational perspectives of voluntarism. Attention will be given to developing new and innovative models for volunteer programs based on field experience, readings, and course sessions.

title: The Community Educator
description: Designed to familiarize the student with the structure, purpose, and processes of community education development with emphasis on the development of skills and competencies required of a community education coordinator.

title: Workshop in Adult and/or Community Education
description: A course for persons who wish to participate in preservice or inservice training in the areas of adult and/or community education. Specific content will depend upon interests of the participants. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. EDUCATION: CURRICULUM (EDCUR)

title: Curriculum Construction
description: Principles to be used in determining the nature and content of the learner's experiences in the public school. The issue of essentialism and progressivism, teacherpupil planning, the larger use of group action in the solution of problems, and betterment of relation between problem solving and principles operative in these problems.

title: Psychology of Later Life
description: A study of the later years of life with emphasis on the adaptations required. Includes theories of aging, physical and social changes taking place, and coping strategies. Not open to the student who has credit in EDPSY 325.

title: Educational Gerontology
description: A study of education and aging with emphasis on a lifespan approach. Topics include education about aging for children and youth, career educational opportunities in gerontology, education for paraprofessionals and volunteers in the field of aging, retirement planning education, and educational opportunities for older adults.

title: Workshop in Applied Gerontology
description: Preservice or inservice education in selected areas of applied gerontology using a workshop format of concentrated study, presentation, demonstrations, and practice. Specific content will depend upon the problems or interest area to which the workshop is addressed. The learner is encouraged to work out a program of personal study with help from other workshop participants and resource persons. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Credit may be applied to the minor in gerontology only with permission of the Director of the Institute of Gerontology.

title: Topical Seminar in Applied Gerontology
description: Individual and group investigation of topics, problems, or issues in applied gerontology with discussion of them by all seminar participants under the guidance of the instructor. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. Credit may be applied to the minor in gerontology only with permission of the Director of the Institute of Gerontology.

title: Internship in Gerontology
description: Experience in one or more of the agencies, institutions, or programs now providing gerontological services or otherwise related to the field of gerontology. The internship is carried out under the joint supervision of the Institute of Gerontology and a practitioner representing the agency, institution, or program. The student chooses the internship setting with the guidance of a faculty sponsor and the approval of the practitioner. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. PREPARATION OF TEACHERS FOR MULTICULTURED SECONDARY SCHOOLS (MULTICUL) The MULTICUL program at Ball State University offers young people an opportunity to translate objectives, expressions, and demonstrations into actuality. The ultimate objectives lead toward possible solutions to one of America's crucial problems, developing racial and cultural harmony. The program is designed not only to deal with black and white relations, but it also encompasses as many ethnic groups as possible. Multiculturism is a basic characteristic of our society as well as our schools; therefore, potential teachers should prepare themselves to meet realistic situations. Three of the experiences that the MULTICUL program utilizes in the preparation of potential teachers are as follows: 1. Specialized or elective courses offered in many major departments. 2. Courses designed especially for MULTICUL students by the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. 3. Laboratory experiences in multicultural communities, social and professional organizations, and schools. Along with learning how to understand and how to coexist peacefully with fellow Americans, the participants in MULTICUL should be more employable, not only in Indiana, but across the nation. MULTICUL does not prohibit students from majoring in their areas of interest. MULTICUL is offered as a departmental minor, and it can be scheduled along with any teaching major at Ball State.
