title: School in the American Culture
description: An introduction to the theory, scope, organization, and functions of the public school in the United States. The student will examine the role of public education at all levels at which it operates and the responsibilities carried out by the professional teachers in their educational work.

title: International Dialogue on American Education and Life
description: Perspectives on American education and its cultural setting developed through interaction among international and American students and comparative study of educational and other social institutions as they relate to education.

title: The Role of Women in the Past, Present, and Future Development of Education
description: A survey of the role of women in education with an emphasis on analysis of career development, styles of work, and job satisfaction. EDUCATION: HIGHER (EDHI)

title: Introduction to Personnel Services in Residence Halls
description: Principles involved in understanding and working with individuals and student groups in residence halls, social forces affecting college students, and the relationship of the residence hall program to the total university. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned; a maximum of 1 credit hour per quarter.

title: Leadership and Development of Student Organizations
description: Examines philosophical bases, group processes, and skills relevant to leadership and development of student organizations in higher education. Focuses on understandings and skills requisite for effective involvement in student groups. EDUCATION: JUNIOR HIGH/MIDDLE (EDJHM) 205. (EDGEN 205) Exploration of Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior in American Junior High/Middle Schools. (4) Analyzes factors which influence the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in schools and educational settings. Particular emphasis will be on the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in the American junior high/middle schools. Not open to the student with credit in EDSEC 205.

title: Teaching in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Develops basic instructional strategies for junior high/middle schools. General methods, problems of student advisement, legal considerations, classroom management, instructional media, in light of study of the nature of junior high/middle school children, and specific laboratory experiences are emphasized. Prerequisite: EDPSY 351 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: The Junior High/Middle School Curriculum
description: Several curricular approaches appropriate for pupils in the age group 10 to 14 years will be examined in relation to current research. Legal rights and the significance of positive human relations are studied. Direct development of alternative curricular programs and appropriate use of merging structures and nontraditional materials will be emphasized. Prerequisite: EDJHM 312.

title: Foundations of Junior High/Middle School Education
description: Junior high/middle school education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from the perspective of the sociological, philosophical, historical, legal, economic, political, and anthropological foundations of junior high/middle schools and teachers are stressed. Prerequisite: EDJHM 312.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Junior High/Middle School
description: This elective student teaching experience will enable a student to complete a full quarter assignment in fullday student teaching assignments in a public junior high/middle school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. Parallel: EDJHM 466.

title: Student Teaching in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Required for the Standard License in Junior High/Middle School Education. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public junior high/middle school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. EDUCATION: READING MIDDLE (EDRDM)

title: Improving Reading Skills in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: A general course for all junior high/middle school teachers which examines reading problems and provides specific methodology for improvement of reading skills in junior high/middle schools. General diagnostic teaching techniques appropriate for teachers in all curricular areas are to be achieved. Exit competencies are required. EDUCATION: READING SECONDARY (EDRDS)

title: Reading in Secondary School
description: Practical procedures for developing effective reading skills to be applied by all secondary classroom teachers. Focuses on relationships between the process of reading and learning of content, on planning to meet total range of student reading needs, and on methods and materials to enhance comprehension and study skills in all areas of secondary school curriculum. EDUCATION: SECONDARY (EDSEC)

title: Introduction to the Problems of Teaching in Cross-Cultural Environments
description: The process of education from the perspective of an educator and the varied agencies in society for formal and informal education. Provides experiences in and exposures to educational situations which will broaden student perceptions and understandings. Emphasizes experiential and problemsolving approaches to learning. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Introduction to Secondary Education for Paraprofessionals
description: Study of American junior and senior high schools from the standpoint of the paraprofessional in secondary education. Prerequisite: admission to the secondary paraprofessional program. Parallel: EDSEC 111.

title: Freshman Paraprofessional Practicum
description: The organization and operation of secondary schools and the duties, procedures, and problems of secondary school faculty and staff. Provides initial experiences in assisting secondary faculty and staff. Prerequisite: admission to the secondary paraprofessional program. Parallel: EDSEC 110.

title: Basic Concepts of Secondary Education
description: Examines through classroom investigation and practical field experiences the structure, function, and development of secondary education in the United States. Designed to help students make valid decisions about preparing for and functioning in a teaching career by studying professionalism, job requirements, employment opportunities, secondary school curriculum, and the role of secondary education within the entire educational process.

title: Introduction to Cross -Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Introduces prospective teachers to responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Intermediate Cross -Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Continued study of responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 200 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Advanced study of responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 201 or permission of the department chairman. 205. (EDGEN 205) Exploration of Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior in American Secondary Schools. (4) Analyzes factors which influence the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in schools and educational settings. Particular emphasis will be on the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in the American secondary schools. Not open to students with credit in EDJHM 205.

title: Laboratory Experience in Secondary Education
description: Provides direct experiences in working with students, teachers, paraprofessionals, community agencies, and other appropriate assignments for undergraduate students who plan to enter secondary school teaching. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; no more than 4 hours may be taken in one quarter.

title: The Secondary Paraprofessional and the Use of Instructional Technology
description: The use of instructional technology and the preparation of instructional materials as these skills are employed by the paraprofessional.

title: Secondary Paraprofessional Internship
description: Practical experiences in the duties, responsibilities, and related problems of the secondary school paraprofessional. The intern will be assigned to a secondary school during a regular school year for a period of one quarter. Prerequisite: EDSEC 110, 111.

title: Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary School
description: Inducts the student into the teaching act. Includes specific technical skill development, legal implications, study of principles of teaching, application of instructional media, curriculum development and organization, classroom management, and discipline. Intensive inschool assignments, observations, skills, participation, and direct contact with adolescents are required. Prerequisite: EDPSY 251 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290.

title: Instructional Strategies in Multicultured Schools
description: Theory and application of special instructional strategies of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms with special emphasis on multicultured educational situations. Prerequisite: EDSEC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: American Education: A Critical Examination
description: The complex educational system and alternatives to the traditional system, featuring an individualized, issueoriented instructional approach. Designed for students who do not plan to teach but open to those in teacher education.

title: Application of Instructional Strategies and Approaches in Junior High School
description: Factors affecting instruction in junior high schools are analyzed. Students are encouraged to develop skills which lead to more creative personal development; general instructional methods, techniques, and evaluation procedures especially appropriate for junior high schools will be the primary focus.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms.

title: Planning and Assessing Instructional Programs
description: Designed to provide secondary school teachers with methods of establishing instructional programs with feedback networks which will encourage continuous assessment and appropriate alterations of the educational environment. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Independent Study in Secondary Education
description: Independent study and research in the field of secondary education. Topics and activities to be chosen in consultation with an individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of four hours of credit may be earned.

title: Contemporary Problems in Education and Professional Concerns of the Beginning Teacher
description: Provides opportunity to examine critically and to focus educational experience and knowledge on contemporary and personally significant problems of education. Emphasizes immediate professional concerns of prospective firstyear teachers. Prerequisite: EDSEC 301 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Foundations of Secondary Education
description: Education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from the perspective of the sociological, philosophical, historical, economic, political, and anthropological foundations of secondary education. Contemporary issues such as cultural values, social class, legal aspects, ethnic groups, political pressure, and the role of the teachers will be stressed. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299.

title: High School Curriculum
description: General perspectives of curriculum principles, practices, and procedures common to secondary schools. Organizational structures, innovations, and intimate relationships between instruction and curriculum. Concurrently, students will choose areas of concentration or preparation as they relate to the total high school curriculum.

title: Student Activities Programs in Secondary Schools
description: Student activities will be studied in terms of historical development, philosophical foundations, objectives, functions, current role and status, principles and procedures of development, organizational patterns, and innovative programs. Accommodates needs and interests of individuals preparing to be involved in student activities programs in secondary schools.

title: The School Community and Secondary School Teaching
description: Focuses on the total school community as a broad teaching resource for every classroom teacher. Examines a variety of resources available, importance of establishing solid relationships, impact of community on classroom and classroom on community, significance of the schoolcommunity interaction both for individual teacher and total school.

title: Discipline: Practical Approaches to Improving Student Behavior in Secondary Schools
description: Designed to prepare prospective secondary teachers to cope with discipline problems in all secondary school settings. Emphasizes skills and procedures for preventing or remedying disruptive behavior by secondary students and ways to create a positive environment for learning.

title: Career Education: Content and Processes for Secondary Educators
description: Career education concepts and attitudes and their effects analyzed in relation to effective implementation of career education in secondary schools. Techniques, methods, and materials identified and developed enabling prospective teachers to see meaningful relationships between career education and secondary curricular areas. The teaching of career identification skills and development of meaningful student work values examined. Course participants will develop a model for the inclusion of career education in his/her area.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the Standard License in Secondary Education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 462 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the Standard License in Secondary Education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 460 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Secondary
description: Prerequisite or parallel: EDSEC 460, 462 or EDJHM 466; and admission to student teaching.

title: General Innovations in Secondary Education
description: Innovative practices will be identified, defined, and analyzed relative to their impact on secondary schools. Creative, innovative instructional approaches will be employed. Field trips or visitations to innovative secondary schools will be arranged when practical, and students will concentrate upon innovative practices.

title: Practicum in Boys' Club Administration
description: Offered in cooperation with Boys' Clubs of America. Students are assigned to Boys' Clubs where they are given an opportunity in all phases of program and administration with certain responsibilities for advanced problems in each of these areas. The course is largely under the direction of a visiting professor representing Boys' Clubs of America. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Twining, Ulman, VanEvery, VanTassel, Wallace The philosophy of special education encompasses the right of all children, youth and adults to participate in educational and career planning experiences that will develop their capabilities to the fullest extent. Gradual acceptance of this philosophy by society has created an everincreasing demand for highly skilled personnel who are certified in the various exceptionality areas represented within special education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to teacher certification in the areas of deaf education; mentally handicapped; moderately, severely, profoundly, and multiply handicapped; and physically handicapped. Graduate programs are offered in areas of learning disabled and emotionally disturbed as well as in the area of undergraduate preparation. These programs are designed in accordance with Indiana teacher licensure requirements. Elective courses in special education open to future teachers, psychologists, speech and hearing therapists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, courses in the education of gifted children, a course in the education of slow learners, and a course in the education of children with learning disabilities. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE HEARING IMPAIRED Mandatory legislation on the rights of all children to an appropriate education has created a nation wide need for additional teachers of the hearingimpaired. The emphasis on "mainstreamingof exceptional children in the regular classroom developed a need for teachers of the hearingimpaired with more general preparation in addition to the specialized coursework for teachers of the deaf. Also, the growth of different communication philosophies made it essential to provide additional coursework options within the majors and minors. A major in the education of the deaf is offered to those who prefer some level of elementary teaching and a minor is available for persons who wish to teach an academic subject at the junior high and high school levels. The State of Indiana, Ball State University, and the Department of Special Education have adopted mare extensive requirements for licensing and, at the same time, more flexible programs which can accommodate the above needs. The Ball State University program for training teachers of the hearingimpaired meets the approval of (1) The Indiana Teacher Training and Licensing Commission, (2) The Council on the Education of the Deaf (CED), and (3) the U.S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE MENTALLY HANDICAPPED Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to the development of specialized programs for mentally handicapped children, youth and adults. These programs have provided the impetus to prepare specially trained teachers to work effectively with mildly handicapped and moderately, severely, profoundly and multiply handicapped children, youth and adults in the least restrictive instructional setting. Teachers and other interested professional personnel are taught the necessary skills to implement accepted intervention strategies for appropriately meeting the mentally handicapped individual's learning style and educational and career needs. In response to the nationwide demand for qualified teachers to serve mentally handicapped children, youth and adults, the Department of Special Education offers a teaching area Special Education 359 major in the area of the mildly handicapped and teaching minors in both the mildly handicapped and moderately, severely, profoundly and multiply handicapped areas. The teaching minor also serves as an endorsement in each of the exceptionality areas represented within the mentally handicapped area. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR CHILDREN WITH PHYSICAL AND/OR SPECIAL HEALTH PROBLEMS Within the group of children who have special educational needs are those who are physically handicapped (mildly and severely) or those who have other health conditions which make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for these handicapped or healthimpaired children presents the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The teacher education program is designed to offer comprehensive, professional preparation to future teachers of physically handicapped (mildly and severely) or healthimpaired children so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers. description: A survey of the educational needs of children who deviate from the normal in mental, physical, and social characteristics. Designed as an introduction to the field of special education.

title: History of Education of the Deaf and the Psychology of Deafness
description: A brief study of educational provisions for the deaf from the beginning to the present and a survey of the social, educational, and vocational problems of deafness.

title: Education of Preschool Deaf Children

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 261.

title: Practicum in Special Education
description: Observation and assistance of teachers in special classes for exceptional children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or may be taken parallel with

title: Psychology of Mental Retardation

title: Characteristics of the Moderately, Severely, and Profoundly Retarded Individuals
description: Aspects of the intellectual, perceptualmotor, communication, academic, and personal social characteristics of the moderately, severely, and profoundly retarded. Procedures for formulating realistic instructional objectives will be explained. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 372.

title: Educational Methods with Moderately, Severely, and Profoundly Retarded Individuals
description: Current instructional planning for the moderately, severely, and profoundly retarded will be reviewed and evaluated. Attention will be focused upon techniques for effecting innovative curricula for individuals at the preschool through post school levels. Prerequisite: SPCED 373.

title: Education of Gifted Children
description: Examination of definitions, characteristics, and identification procedures relating to gifted and talented children in school and society. Research findings pertaining to these topics will be reviewed and analyzed.

title: Education of Slow Learners
description: Major topics include identification, characteristics, and practices and procedures for meeting the needs of the slow learning child. Emphasis is placed on techniques and methods of instruction as well as research findings concerned with the slow learner and the culturally disadvantaged.

title: Learning Disabilities Techniques for the Regular Classroom Teacher
description: Emphasis on the role of the regular classroom teacher in relationship to legal, federal, and state mandates for identification, instruction, and programming for learning disabled students in the regular classroom. title: Aural Rehabilitation
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for teaching lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation, Prerequisite:

title: Speech Development for the Deaf
description: The International Phonetic Alphabet, Northhampton Charts, diacritical markings, and other methods and techniques used to teach speech to the deaf. Prerequisite: SPCH 216 and SPCED 240, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of an individual working with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 and 446 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Manual Communications
description: Theory and research underlying the language of signs and fingerspelling (manual alphabet) is considered. Development of receptive and expressive skills in manual communications is required. Required of students intending to student teach in schools or classes using total communication.

title: Advanced Manual Communication
description: A course in manual communication designed to improve conversational skill in signs and fingerspelling to a functional level for expressive and receptive use in a classroom for hearing impaired children. Prerequisite: SPCED 451 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: Compares language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Levels of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and SPAA 370 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight Language for the Deaf, Barry Five-Slate, Wing Symbols, and the Natural Method. Language outlines from different schools are used as supplementary aids. Prerequisite: SPCED 240, 266, and 454.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching subjects such as arithmetic and science. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and 266 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Special Education
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Student Teaching: Areas of Exceptionality
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 20 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Interpreting for the Deaf
description: A survey course to acquaint students with the fundamentals of interpreting for the deaf in special situations, familiarize them with professional behavioral guidelines unique to each setting, and develop beginning interpretive skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Expressive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Provides students who have basic manual communication skills with intensive training and practice in expressive interpreting for the deaf. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Receptive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Designed to provide students who have basic manual communication ability with professional skill for interpreting manual language in special situations. Opportunity for extensive practice and evaluation will be provided. Prerequisite: SPCED 468 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 1
description: Special class organization, curriculum practices and procedures, and the methods and techniques used in the instruction of the mentally retarded. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (2 hrs.), 372.

title: Educational Methods with the Mentally Retarded 2
description: Continuation of SPCED 474, with emphasis on the curriculum. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (4 hrs.) and 474.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: This course is designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired children. Topics include etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate children with physical disabilities. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290 for majors other than in Special Education.

title: Educational Methods with Physically Handicapped Children
description: Special class organization, curriculum, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of orthopedically handicapped children. Prerequisite: SPCED 482; prerequisite or parallel: EDEL 380 and MATH 391.

title: Teaching Multiply Handicapped Children
description: Studies the problems of multiply handicapped children and youth. Symptomatology, assessment, and educational programming of multiply handicapped children will be emphasized. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 373, and 482. description: Readings, group discussions, individual research, and investigation of topics in the history of architecture, preservation, planning, and landscape architecture.

title: Philosophy, History, and Theory of Historic Preservation
description: Survey of the philosophy, history, and theory of historic preservation primarily in Europe and North America. title: Preservation Techniques and Policies
description: Planning and programming for preservation, restoration, and neighborhood conservation; economic and legal consideration in federal, state, and private programs in preservation and restoration. Not open to the student who has credit in LA 441.

title: Documentation of Historic Sites and Buildings
description: Methods of documenting historic sites and buildings using various survey and inventory forms. Extensive oral and written descriptive analysis of historic buildings. Not open to the student who has credit in LA 442.

title: Field Workshop in Preservation
description: Exercises in surveying and the use of state inventory forms, National Register material, and environmental impact studies; field trips. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

description: Significant historic styles and periods of architecture in Europe and their interpretation in America and an analysis of significant aesthetic characteristics, building materials, and technology. Landscape architecture is based upon the recognition of longterm ecologic, economic, social and psychological values, embracing the conservation of natural resources and the design of land for specific purposes. The landscape architect may be the prime professional consultant for a project and will be assisted by allied professionals such as architects, engineers, planners, ecologists, geologists, hydrologists, biologists, economists, sociologists, and others. Also, he/she may be a member of a site planning team coordinated by one of many allied professions. The landscape architect must be sensitive to human needs and patterns while understanding the potentials and limitations of natural systemssoils, geology, water, vegetation, wildlife, topography, and climatein the effort to solve increasingly complex problems. The undergraduate curriculum stresses a broad base of learning both within the major and in supportive course areas. While helping the student to develop basic skills and understanding in landscape architecture, the curriculum is structured to allow concentrations of study in particular areas of interest in allied areas. The General Studies Program in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences combined with opportunities in mathematics, art, and directed and professional electives play a vital part in the cultural and intellectual preparation of young men and women enrolled in this program. The program for these electives must be approved in advance by the department chairman. A core of courses including design, graphics, landscape architecture technology, plants and design, and history provides the primary focus to which supportive major and allied courses relate. Studio projects range from applying basic parameters of space, rhythm, movement, scale, and color to the design of courtyards, parks, playgrounds, residences, and housing projects to largescale openspace studies, river corridors, and regional resource evaluation encompassing thousands of acres. The professional planning degree is offered at the graduate level only, and the urban studies major is offered at the undergraduate level. Dr. Mitchell is director of urban studies. The urban studies program is the undergraduate component of the Department of Urban Studies and Planning. It is based on the belief that meaningful analysis of the dynamic complexities of urban areas requires collaboration among experts with different backgrounds. This orientation has resulted in a thoroughly interdisciplinary program involving courses offered by twelve departments in three of the university's colleges. Urban studies students examine the forces that have led to development of urban areas, the economic, social, political, and spatial structure that evolves when human populations aggregate in cities, the advantages and disadvantages that result, and the application of various social disciplines to overcoming or ameliorating these disadvantages. Students are exposed to the body of knowledge and receive instruction in the use of various analytical tools. One goal of the program is to prepare students for entrylevel or preprofessional positions in planning, public service, community development, social agencies, or related private firms. The curriculum is designed primarily to educate rather than train students, for regular training in these professions is normally at the graduate level. Nonetheless, urban studies graduates have successfully launched related careers directly after graduation. A second goal is to provide an educational foundation for those students who desire to pursue graduate training in planning, law, social work, public administration, business, or other related disciplines. A third goal is to encourage student involvement in community activities and to provide learning experiences outside the classroom. Students participate in various projects. They also gain valuable work experiences through internships with planning commissions, community development agencies, local governments, and the like. A fourth goal is to provide a general background, through either the departmental major or, more likely, the departmental minor for those students having a more casual interest in urban affairs. This general background gives students a degree of understanding about the urban environment which may be reflected in their future civic and professional activities. A fifth goal is to provide a departmental minor designed to add new skills and enhance and focus knowledge gained in the student's departmental major. description: Basic concepts of cost accounting. Methods used to record and control costs of materials, labor, and overhead by manufacturing firms. Prerequisite: ACC 203.

title: Advanced Cost Accounting

title: Individual Income Tax Problems
description: Federal income and Indiana adjusted gross income tax laws as they affect the individual with some emphasis upon concepts of taxation, including history and development, and a review of statutes, regulations and court decisions.

title: Business Income Tax Problems
description: Federal income tax laws as they affect businesses, especially partnerships and corporations. Study of statutes, regulations, tax forms, and court decisions pertaining to such topics as depreciation, bad debts, inventory, and recognition of income. Prerequisite: ACC 203 and 441.

title: Auditing Principles and Practices
description: The principles underlying the practice of auditing. Prerequisite: ACC 312.

title: Financial Statement Analysis and Interpretation
description: Financial statements and reports of various types of businesses and industries, methods of constructing, comparing, and analyzing these statements and reports and the various uses of such analyses. Prerequisite: ACC 203.

title: Internship in Accounting
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Accounting, a student majoring in accounting will work full time for one quarter as an accounting intern for a public accountant, a business firm, or a governmental agency. title: Beginning Typewriting
description: Principles of touch typewriting with emphasis upon technique and fluency. Only students with no credit in typewriting or with less than one semester of typewriting are eligible to receive credit in this course unless special permission is granted by the department head. These are the professional methods courses which are prerequisite to student teaching. § To teach data processing in a reimbursed program, holder must also have an endorsement in Vocational Business Education.

title: Intermediate Typewriting
description: Review of typewriting principles with emphasis on the development of speed and accuracy. Problems included on the application of typewriting skill to simple business situations. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one to two semesters of typewriting. Not open to the student who has credit for more than two semesters of typewriting.

title: Advanced Typewriting
description: Advanced problems in typewriting including preparation of business letters, manuscripts, tabulations, rough drafts, legal documents, business forms, and duplicated media; continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or three or more semesters of typewriting.

title: Office Typewriting
description: Office typing problems with emphasis on preparation of materials by various typewritten media; composition of reports, memoranda, and letters; handwritten and typewritten draft copy. Opportunities for original and creative typing. Continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Touch Shorthand 1
description: Touch shorthand computercompatible theory for the stenograph machine. Dictation and transcription of familiar material. Prerequisite: permission of the department head and the ability to typewrite at 40 net words per minute for five minutes.

title: Touch Shorthand 2
description: Continuation of touch shorthand computercompatible theory for the stenograph machine. Review and advanced theory. Dictation and transcription on both familiar and new material. Typewritten transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 121 or permission of the department head and the ability to typewrite at 40 net words per minute for five minutes.

title: Touch Shorthand 3
description: Touch shorthand computercompatible theory review. Theory abbreviations. Advanced dictation and transcription of new material. Typewritten transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 122 or permission of the department head; the ability to typewrite at 40 net words per minute for five minutes; and reporting ability of 90 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy for three minutes.

title: Typewriting for the Court Reporter
description: Development of speed and accuracy to meet reporting transcription requirements. Preparation of documents used in legal offices and in courts. Emphasis on depositions. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 and the ability to typewrite at 50 net words per minute for five minutes.

title: Introduction to Touch Shorthand Court Reporting
description: Emphasis on theory shortcuts for highspeed reporting. Introduction to reporting and transcription of jury charge, twovoice testimony, and literary. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 and the ability to typewrite at 50 net words per minute for five minutes; BEOA 123 and reporting ability of 110 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy for three minutes.

title: Touch Shorthand Court Reporting 1
description: Advanced theory for highspeed reporting. Reporting of jury charge, twovoice testimony, and literary. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 and the ability to typewrite at 50 net words per minute for five minutes; BEOA 220 and reporting ability of 130 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy for four minutes.

title: Touch Shorthand Court Reporting 2
description: Advanced reporting and transcription speed development. Dictation to include jury charge, multiplevoice testimony, and literary. Vocabulary will include legal, technical, and medical terminology. Prerequisite: BEOA 214, 221, 228, 229, and reporting ability of 150 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy for five minutes.

title: Touch Shorthand Court Reporting 3
description: Advanced reporting and transcription speed development. Dictation to include jury charge, multiplevoice testimony, and literary. Vocabulary will include legal, technical, and medical terminology. Prerequisite: BEOA 222 and reporting ability of 170 words per minute at 95 percent accuracy for five minutes.

title: Court Reporting 4
description: Advanced reporting and transcription speed development toward 225 words per minute on multiplevoice dictation. Dictation will include jury charge, testimony, and literary material. Prerequisite: BEOA 223 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Theory of Shorthand Court Reporting Terminology 1
description: Introduction to writing in shorthand the specialized terms encountered in the legal and technical professions, and trades. Prerequisite: BEOA 123.

title: Theory of Shorthand Court Reporting Terminology 2
description: Introduction to writing in shorthand the specialized terms encountered in the medical profession. Prerequisite: BEOA 123.

title: Introduction to Transcription
description: Designed to teach transcription skills as they apply to the typewritten production of business documents. Application of punctuation, number usage, word choice, spelling, proofreading, and use of reference sources through machine transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or two semesters of typewriting.

title: Machine Transcription
description: Designed to teach students to produce mailable copy from transcription equipment. Intensive drill on transcription skills with emphasis on quality production. Application of punctuation, spelling, vocabulary building, letter styles, placement, proofreading, and grammar to the transcription process. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Principles of Business Correspondence
description: Principles and basic elements of effective letter writing with emphasis on the psychological approach, reader viewpoint, positive tone, and appropriate format for personalbusiness letters and job applications.

title: Shorthand Court Reporting Procedures
description: Court reporting procedures pertaining to different court and legal proceedings. Emphasis on preparation of transcripts, marking of exhibits, and use of reference materials needed by the court reporter.

title: Law Office Administration
description: An analysis of the goals, needs, and problems in administering a legal office. Emphasis on systems for processing information and paperwork particularly in the areas of timekeeping, records administration, and word processing.

title: Internship in Court Reporting
description: Reporting of general or court proceedings verified by practicing shorthand court reporters. Evidence of a minimum of forty (40) verified clock hours of court reporting is required. title: Internship in Distributive Education 1
description: Fulltime employment for a quarter in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations. Required: a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during a quarter and the submission of various employment reports to the supervisor by employer and intern. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 2
description: Fulltime employment for a quarter in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Opportunity for the intern to perform a wide variety of duties for a broad view of distributive occupations of a higher level than those fulfilling the requirements for BEOA 285. title: Internship in Distributive Education 3
description: Fulltime employment for a quarter in an approved distributive occupation under department supervision. Prerequisite: BEOA 285 and 286 or the equivalent. Restricted to persons seeking license as a distributive education teachercoordinator.

title: Beginning Shorthand 1
description: Basic symbolic theory fundamentals with emphasis on abbreviated forms. Introduction to the skills of writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one semester of typewriting.

title: Beginning Shorthand 2
description: Completion and/or review of basic theory with increased emphasis upon development of skill in taking dictation and transcribing. Prerequisite: BEOA 321 or student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing; and BEOA 112 or two semesters of typewriting.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on skill in taking dictation with emphasis on transcribing. Prerequisite: BEOA 322 or student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing; and BEOA 113 or four semesters of typewriting.

title: Advanced Shorthand 1
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, transcription, and production of mailable copy. Prerequisite: BEOA 323 or student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing; and BEOA 113 or four semesters of typewriting.

title: Advanced Shorthand 2
description: Special emphasis upon production of mailable copy, and continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 324.

title: Introduction to Word Processing
description: Word processing with emphasis on understanding why organizations are adopting word processing. Focus is on understanding of word processing concepts and how they fit into a total information processing network and the handling of paperwork in today's organizations. Special problems are analyzed and programmed for input in standalone text editing typewriters and on computer textprocessing systems. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or two semesters of typewriting.

title: Calculating Machines

title: Principles of Office Supervision

title: Integrating Word Processing/Data Processing Systems
description: Explores the evolutionary changes within the office. An introduction to the considerations involved in integrating text and data from word processing and data processing input to enhance the information processing output. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 200 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in MS 362.

title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects A
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. title: Methods of Teaching Business Subjects B
description: History and development, objectives, methods of approach and presentation, and special methods and devices in classroom procedures; lesson planning. Business subjects included are bookkeeping, general business, typing, and related office skills. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250; student will have completed the requirements in typewriting and accounting. title: Methods of Teaching for the Distributive Education Teacher
description: The role of the distributive education teacher in the teaching of distributive, basic business, and bookkeeping/accounting subjects; courses to be taught and their objectives, teaching strategies, instructional materials, and lesson and unit planning. title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Majors 1 and 2
description: Objectives, planning methods/techniques, devices for teaching typewriting, basic business and office machines/office practice courses. Prerequisite: BEOA 113, EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: BEOA 338.

title: Methodology of Relevant Work Experiences in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by persons who will be supervising and directing a cooperative education or a project plan program in distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Major 2

description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and coordinating cooperative distributive education programs. description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and managing inschool laboratory programs in vocational distributive education. title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Distributive Education
description: The principles upon which vocational distributive education is organized, administered, and supervised; the kinds of programs; federal and state regulations; relationships to programs in other vocational areas. title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Education
description: The principles upon which vocational education is organized, administered, and supervised; federal and state regulations; agencies which provide delivery systems for vocational education; relationship of vocational education to career education, vocational rehabilitation, and programs for persons with special needs. description: An overview of the six program areas in vocational education. title: Computerized Business Document Generation
description: An introduction to text editing capabilities of the computer for designing and processing business documents for the modern office. Development of an understanding of the use of the generalpurpose computer for text processing. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 200.

title: Communications for Business Organizations
description: Techniques used in managementoriented internal and external communications. Emphasis on theory, planning, oral and written presentations, audience perceptions, data organization, media selection, and preparation techniques for business letters; and an overview of reports. description: Techniques for writing managementoriented informal and formal reports, including collecting, interpreting, summarizing, and synthesizing data. title: Employment Communications
description: Determining job requirements and writing a letter of application and resume; letters requesting reference permission, appreciation of interview, acceptance and refusal of position, and resignation. Includes interview techniques. Open to all students.

title: Secretarial Procedures
description: Operational functions of toplevel professional secretarial work through integration of basic skills, knowledge, and the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 241 and sophomore standing.

title: Secretarial Administration
description: Administrative and supervisory aspects of toplevel professional secretarial work through planning and organizing office functions to achieve smooth and efficient work flow and with emphasis on the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 451.

title: Internship in Office Systems Administration
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Business Education and Office Administration Department, students majoring in office systems administration will serve during a summer or a quarter in an office environment in a public or private organization. Written reports are required. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

description: Use of word processing as an integral part of the total information processing network. Development of ability to recognize when and how to use word and text processing to meet an organization's needs. Study of managerial problems involved in establishing and implementing word processing systems. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department head.

description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments Economics 111 of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 200 and

description: Develops skill in identifying the key problem of a complicated office situation and in formulating a practical solution to this problem. Not open to the student who has credit in MGT 489.

description: Historical development of the field of business education. Possible future trends and their effect on the entire business education program. Open only to students who have been approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

Components include secondary, postsecondary, and adult distributive education, DECA, and general and specialized curricula. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299. Restricted to students pursuing a teaching major in distributive education.

Department of Economics Keil, Chairman; Bohanon, Caron, Carter, Cheng, Deitsch, Girgis, Hannaford, Jost, Koch, Lawson, Lynch, McGuire, Seeborg, Talafuse, Van Cott, Yoho, Zegeye Economics is the scientific study of economic institutions and systems. It is a study of human wants and of efforts to satisfy those wants through alternative uses of the scarce resources of production. The key phrase is -scarce resources of production," and scarcity is relative to human wants. The discipline of economics is dominated by a comprehensive body of theory that interrelates human wants and the means for their fulfillment. Economic theory is founded upon a set of assumptions that permit rigorous analysis of the use of all resources or of any one category of them. It is a useful study in an intellectual sense because it trains students to think carefully and logically about complex social phenomena. By such knowledge it is possible to understand the impact on economic systems and institutions of broad social and economic developments or of new economic policies and the responses of these units to them. Given the complicated economic and social problems of the modern world, an understanding of this subject is important for intelligent citizenship and for practical application in industry, government, research, and the professions. To achieve a basic comprehension of how our economy operates, the department offers a core of courses aimed at providing (1) a sound grasp of the tools of analysis and measurement, (2) an understanding of institutional development and the interrelations of economic and social factors, and (3) an ability to apply systematic analysis and understanding to problems of public policy. A number of degree programs are offered by the Department of Economics in order to provide the student with flexibility in choosing a course of study that will fit individual interests and needs. The student can choose to major in economics under either the Business or Liberal Arts Options. The Business Option is a 90-hour major designed primarily for those students choosing a professional career in business. Twothirds of the required hours are in the business core courses of accounting, finance, general business, management, and marketing. The Liberal Arts Option is composed of 48 hours, a number of which may be taken in other departments. The Department of Economics also offers an interdepartmental major in mathematical economics as well as a minor in economics. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. 232.t Law of Labor Relations. (4) An examination of the law governing unionmanagement relations. Primary emphasis upon the Taft-Hartley and Landrum-Griffin Acts as amended/interpreted. Extensive use of the case study. Designed to serve the needs of current/future laborrelations practitioners. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. 233.t Contract Negotiations. (4) Examines processes, techniques, and economic impact of collective bargaining. Emphasis upon what the practitioner needs to know about the negotiation, administration, and enforcement of collective bargaining agreements. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economics of Dispute Settlement
description: An economic and institutional analysis of impasse resolution. Topics covered include the causes and economic impact of labor disputes, National Labor Relations Board impasse procedures, principles of arbitration, fact finding, mediation, and conciliation, and other recent developments in dispute resolution. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
description: National income as a measure of economic activity is analyzed. Major stress is on the determination of national income, employment, price level, and the rate of growth of the economic system. Includes examination of the theories of consumption and investment spending, interaction between money and national income, and implications of alternative models for public policy. Graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses are utilized. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Intermediate Microeconomics
description: An investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involved are analyses of product pricing, output determination, resource pricing, and employment in various market structures. Graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses are utilized. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and thq advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Economics of the Ghetto 2
description: The economics of poverty in the United States. Includes economic concepts and analysis of poverty in the historical context, economic analysis of contemporary poverty, and analysis of current proposals dealing with poverty in the United States. Prerequisite: ECON 111 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Quantitative Methods in Economics
description: The development of mathematical concepts and tools, including a brief treatment of the calculus, most useful in economics. At each stage the concepts developed are applied to problems in economic theory. Designed to provide preparation for ECON 421 and 521 for students who lack the necessary background in mathematics. Prerequisite: ECON 201, MATH 110 or its equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Growth rates of various countries will be compared and analyzed. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. t Not open to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economi c life; surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from Biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite : ECON 20 and 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201; MATH 131, 132 or their equivalent; and MS 221.

title: Managerial Economics
description: Application of microeconomic analysis to managerial decision making. Emphasis is on the applicability of economic concepts to business decisions. Areas covered include forecasting techniques, demand measurement, production, cost, profit management, product strategy, pricing, and location analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201, MS 221, and MATH 131.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analysis of the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 432.

title: Economics of Labor Market Discrimination
description: A survey of conservative, liberal, and radical theories of labor market discrimination; a review of studies on the extent of economic discrimination and the effect of public policy on the economic position of women and minorities. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasis on economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy are presented. Institutional factors of the society are viewed as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. This is followed by a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture investigated. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201. Finance 115

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstructs or facilitates the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Internship in Economics
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Economics, a student majoring in economics works full time for one quarter as an economics intern for a private or public organization. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to thirdquarter juniors and seniors majoring in economics. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. Credit is not applicable toward meeting the requirements of a major in economics.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses, thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. At the undergraduate level, the Department of Finance offers two majors leading to either the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science degree. These majors are in finance and general business administration. Finance. Finance is a decisionoriented discipline concerned with the investment and management of money both in the present and in the future. This major is designed to provide the student with a general program in the financial aspects of business including financial management, investments, banking, insurance, real estate, and other related financial areas. Finance courses provide knowledge of concepts, processes, and institutions involved with the financing functions of the business enterprise; acquaint students with the financial instruments, institutions, and markets in the United States and the world; provide the tools and techniques of financial analysis and decision making; and expose the students to sufficient examples of financial decision making to allow them to develop expertise in applied finance. The finance major allows the student to pursue one of five options within the finance major: (1) corporate financial management, (2) financial institutions, (3) insurance, (4) real estate, and (5) international business. The corporate financial management option prepares the student for such careers in the finance division of a business firm as systems analysis, budget review analysis, financial analysis, acquisitions analysis, credit management, receivables management, and shortand longterm capital management. The financial institutions option emphasizes employment opportunities in the areas of managing stocks and bonds as a securities broker, portfolio manager, or trust department specialist and in investment banking. This option prepares an individual to work in the field of banking, savings and loan associations, loan companies, insurance companies, credit unions, pension funds, securities brokerage, and real estate brokerage. The third option, insurance, has been designed to develop finance graduates in the areas of life and health, as well as property and casualty sales, property and casualty underwriting, insurance appraisal, and management positions with the insurance industry. The real estate option prepares a student for a sales career as well as real estate management. The international business option prepares a student for a career in multinational business fields and for the importexport business. General Business Administration. This major permits students to concentrate in two of the three areas available, i.e., insurance, management, and finance. Hence, this major provides a broader diversity of vocational opportunities than the finance major but with less depth in any one area of concentration. The course of study includes an examination of the various institutions, structures, functions, organizations, operations, and environments which influence business and economic activities. The finance sequence is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activities. The management sequence is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them, as future business executives and specialists, to deal with diversity of problems which arise in the course of daytoday activities. The insurance sequence is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. Graduates in general business administration are qualified to accept positions as junior executives at the management level in finance, insurance, personnel administration, office administration, production supervision, or other areas. In addition, this degree is particularly attractive to those students who may wish to engage in a small business or who do not wish to commit themselves to a particular vocation at this time. In addition to the above, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students in other areas of the College of Business. Any student in the university may enroll in the course in personal finance, which is offered especially to provide the information necessary for the management of personal incomes, expenditures, and financial resources. The law courses are quite broad, include the fundamentals of many essential law disciplines, and are highly recommended to students in prelaw preparation. General business administration and finance courses are included in the concentration areas for the teaching of business education and distributive education. The teaching areas are listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration.
