title: Estate Planning and Administration
description: An introduction to problems associated with planning for use of financial resources during working life, retirement, and after the death of the principal income producer. Included are techniques for fact gathering, tax principles, use of trusts, and will drafting.

title: Legal Aspect of Real Estate
description: The elementary concepts of real estate law and practice, particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, brokers' regulations, license law and title insurance. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 332 (232).

title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law, and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law, and the effect of the law in the areas of consumer credit and economic relationships. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to agencies including employer and employee rights and obligations, partnerships including limited partnership, corporations including fiduciary obligations of directors, security regulations, bankruptcy and corporate reorganization in bankruptcy. Prerequisite: BL 360.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principal articles of the code including sales, commercial paper and security interests, in addition to the areas of creditors' rights and property law. State and federal consumer protection laws as they affect commercial law will be covered. Prerequisite: BL 360.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 360 and INS 370. Not open to the student who has credit in INS 373.

title: Current Topics in Business Law
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced business students for study of current topics and/or problems in the business law area. Topics may include current activity in the fields of property law, commercial law, and government regulation of business. Prerequisite: BL 360 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairman. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the viewpoint of the consumer. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation. Not open to juniors and seniors majoring in business.

title: Money and Banking
description: The role of money, credit, and financial markets in the United States financial system; the structure and functions of commercial banks; the implementation of monetary policy through the Federal Reserve System; financial and banking system structure ; international financial transactions. Prerequisite: ECON 20; MATH 10 or equivalent.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Designed to study different areas of financial decision making in a business firm. Specific topics include: financial objectives of the firm, sources of funds, working capital management, capital budgeting, investment decisions under uncertainty, valuation, capital structure decisions, and dividend policy. Prerequisite: ACC 203, ECON 201, MS 221.

title: Consumer, Business, and Public Finance
description: The great importance in our national life of business credit, personal and consumer credit (including installment sales credit), bank credit, and public credit (federal, state, and municipal). Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: Working Capital Management
description: An analysis of working capital management. Examines the management of current assets such as cash, receivables, and inventories; a review of intermediate and shortterm credit; and a study of general working capital policy. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Designed to introduce the student to areas of investment: securities markets, transaction of stocks and bonds, valuation and timing, fundamental and technical indicators, money markets, and funds. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Financial Institutions
description: The structure of financial institutions in the American economy. Financial institutions as recipients and as suppliers of funds in financial markets. The identification and analysis of many kinds of financial institutions and the administration of their loan and investment portfolios. Particular emphasis on the asset, liability, and capital management with the goal of profitability. Prerequisite: FIN 250.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some are emphasized. Prerequisite: FIN 250. Prerequisite recommended: senior standing.

title: Capital Management
description: An analysis of the management aspects relating to the inflows and outflows of permanent capital in business enterprises. Examines the management of longterm assets, intermediate and longterm credit, equity, and internal financing. Corporate expansion including mergers, acquisitions, corporate reorganization, and bankruptcies. Includes case studies. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Multinational Business Finance
description: An indepth study of the international financial institutions (central banks, International Monetary Fund, area development banks, etc.) involved with the financial decisions of multinational corporations including an overview of the new developing forces in the field of international finance. Prerequisite: FIN 452.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Theory
description: An indepth analysis of valuation theory, capital market theory, and portfolio theory. Prerequisite: FIN 350 and 355.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Finance, students majoring in finance or general business administration will work full time for a quarter as interns for a banking institution, business firm, or governmental agency. Written reports are required. Open only to thirdquarter juniors or seniors. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Fundamentals of Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Fundamentals of Property-Liability Insurance
description: Study of fire, inland marine, liability, worker's compensation insurance. Emphasis is on commercial insurance as a method of risk management. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 360 and INS 370. Not open to the student who has credit in BL 373.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and/or problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include nofault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, state vs. federal regulations. Prerequisite: INS 370, 371, and 372 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Real Estate Principles
description: The economic import of real estate, real estate characteristics, land use and environmental controls, legal aspects of real estate, including ownership interests and real estate instruments, methods of valuation, real estate analysis, mortgage credit sources, secondary mortgage markets and real estate financing techniques, investment analysis, land development, and real estate operations, including brokerage, title closing, and property management.

title: Real Estate Finance
description: The contractual nature and legal implication of the instruments used in real estate finance; instrument, techniques, and strategies in the financing of real estate investment; and the structure and operation of both primary and secondary mortgage markets. Provides the student with background in real estate law and real estate finance. Prerequisite: RE 330. 332 (232).t Legal Aspect of Real Estate. (4) The elementary concepts of real estate law and practice particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, brokers' regulations, license law, and title insurance. Not open to the student who has credit in BL 332 (232).

title: Real Estate Analysis
description: Will concern itself with the appraisal of real estate. In addition to the appraisal process, other analytical systems will be reviewed as they apply to the real estate industry, including the economic base analysis, feasibility studies, and investment analysis. Prerequisite: RE 330. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 230 and 231.

title: Real Estate Administration
description: An orientation of the real estate business utilizing text cases, incidents, and walking cases. Guest speakers who are experts in real estate will be invited to speak and answer questions. Prerequisite: RE 431 and senior standing or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 233. Department of Management Science LaFollette, Chairman; Ahmed, Ault, Baird, Green, Guild, Jeffers, Koehler, Lauck, Lorette, Ma, Montagno, Mumtaz, Necessary, Seeborg, Silbey, Swart, Walters, Walton Management involves the coordination of human and physical resources toward an objective or goal. As this statement implies, management is germane to any type of purposive activity. Every organization has managers regardless of what they are called (e.g. , managers, administrators, principals, coaches, officers, or chiefs). Therefore, a student who elects to major in management science will be preparing to assume a position of responsibility in a wide variety of profit or nonprofit organizations. t Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business. The major in management science allows the student to pursue one of four management options: (1) production and operations management, (2) personnel administration, (3) management information systems, or (4) general management. In the production and operations management option, the student acquires the background to assume a position of responsibility in the production of goods and services. The student is introduced to the production functions in detail, is taught the methodology of making productionrelated decisions, and becomes acquainted with modern techniques used in motivating and leading personnel in a productionoriented occupation. In the personnel administration option, the student acquires the foundation for entering an occupation that relates primarily to the human component of an organization. The student is given an indepth presentation of the personnel function; that is, the student is familiarized with a conceptual framework for analyzing and solving problems involved in the selection, development, and motivation of human resources. In the management information systems option, the student is introduced to the concepts and techniques necessary for the development and operation of management information systems. The student receives a broad background in the role and operation of an information system in an organization. The graduate of this option is knowledgeable about the concepts and techniques of computerized information systems to accomplish this important function more effectively and efficiently. In the general management option, the student is introduced to a varied background in management. General management acquaints the student with the whole gamut of management: production, personnel, management information systems, and other managerial topics. Some organizations recruit on campus for generalists such as students with the general management option. Others prefer more depth in a specific function such as production and operations, personnel, or management information systems. The student will be guided by the curricular statement (see Professional Arts Curricula) and by the area requirements listed below. The departmental major in management, on the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for a career in management. Departmental major in management, 96 hours. title: Management of Human Resources
description: Deals directly with persons having responsibility in organizations and faced with a wide range of problems in which people are the principal subjects. Attention to the individual personality; group and intergroup relations, environmental factors, business and social responsibilities, and leadership as a critical factor in organizations.

title: Operations Management
description: Gives students an understanding of the basic operations function; gives them a viable knowledge of the systems approach to the design of operations. Covers all important activities of the manufacturing enterprise with the exception of finance and general accounting. Prerequisite: MGT 280.

title: Industrial Supervision
description: For practicing or potential firstline supervisors and managers who hold or who will hold positions up to middlelevel management positions. Knowledge of sound job control techniques, disciplinary techniques, verbal and nonverbal communications, supervisorunion relationships, and other topics which are the common denominator of all supervisors and bases for the course. Prerequisite: MGT 280.

title: International Management and Multinational Operations
description: Comparative management practices around the world; international business behavior and problems confronting multinational executives and corporations; analysis of corporate structures and operations in foreign environments. Study of management functions, organizations, structures, policies, operations, and multinational practices and global strategies. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Management
description: This course examines in detail the four major managerial functions: planning, organizing, motivating, and controlling as they are applied to the process of management and the organic functions of a business enterprise. Other significant concepts stressed are the importance of leadership and problemsolving techniques applied to managerial situations and the aspects of coordination, communication, human relations, and production/operations management necessary for an individual to be successful as a manager. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Production/Operations Management 1
description: A basic study of functional fields of production. Decision making and quantitative analysis of production problems arising in areas of methods analysis, work measurement, wage incentives, production planning and control, inventory control, plant layout, materials handling, and quality control. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Business and Society
description: An interdisciplinary approach toward developing a philosophy concerning the role of business in society. Emphasis on contemporary issues requiring business people to reexamine their role and the role of the corporation in community and national life. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Organizational Behavior
description: Focuses on the dynamics of human behavior in business organizations, with concentration on problems of motivation and leadership. Emphasis is on the behavior of individuals and groups within organizations, and the practical interpretation and management of behavioral phenomena. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Production/Operations Management 2
description: An intermediate study of the functional areas of production. Emphasis on decision making and quantitative analysis of production problems arising in the areas of incentives, production planning and control, inventory control, plant layout, materials handling, and quality control. Prerequisite: MGT 383; MS 221.

title: Small Business Ventures
description: Provides essential knowledge for students interested in small business. Topics include searching for venture opportunities; economic, technical, and operational feasibility of the venture; financing; negotiations; and operations. Emphasizes characteristics of the small business enterprise. Prerequisite: BL 360, MGT 380, FIN 350, MKG 300, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Small Business Practicum
description: Teams of students consult with local small businesses. Cases are assigned by Small Business Administration. Students work on problems of the particular small business. Problems may be office administration, accounting, production, marketing, personnel, finance, insurance, legal, or information systems. Prerequisite: senior standing and MGT 380 or permission of the department head. * Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Internship in Management
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Management Science, a student majoring in management science will work full time for a quarter as an intern in an organization operating in either the private or public sector. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to thirdquarter juniors or seniors.

title: Internship in Computer Management
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Management Science, a student majoring in management science will work halftime two quarters as an intern in Ball State University Computer Services. Prerequisite: MS 220, 382, four hours of experience working in the Ball State University Computer Services, or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Personnel Planning and Selection
description: Focuses on organization and manpower planning. Includes determination of organization and manpower needs, analysis and development of job requirements and necessary qualifications for recruitment and selection, selection procedures, placement and orientation, and evaluation of selection programs. Prerequisite: MGT 481.

title: Personnel Administration
description: How to administer a personnel program in a business organization so as to deal effectively with such problems as selection, training, compensation, promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions; employee services; and industrial relations. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Case Problems in Personnel Management
description: Case studies depicting complex personnel issues and problems faced by organizations. Provides the student an opportunity to apply personnel policies, theories, concepts, and techniques to actual personnel situations. Prerequisite: MGT 481.

title: Problems in Production/Operations Management
description: An integration of all the production/operations management principles, theories, and techniques gained from previous courses as applied to actual production problems. Major teaching methods include case study, discussion, and individual projects. Current topics may be discussed. Prerequisite: MGT 386 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Quality Assurance
description: Application of statistical control charts, sampling plans, and reliability analysis to problems of planning, feedback, and control of product quality, process performance, operation effectiveness, and related areas of management activities. Prerequisite: MS 221.

title: Work Design
description: The design of office and industrial jobs to meet the needs and preferences of the worker and the management. Included are methods improvement techniques, layout of work stations, incentive and motivation techniques and the setting of output standards. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Comparative Administration
description: Comparative analysis of managing complex organizations and service industries; emphasizing environmental and organizational factors affecting the management process, firm structure, and administration functions. Study of administration crossculturally (internationally) and crossinstitutionally (service industries). Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Case Problems in Office Management
description: Develops skill in identifying the key problem of a complicated office situation and in formulating a practical solution to this problem. The interrelatedness of major office management activities is stressed as well as the broad scope of problems pertaining to the office. Prerequisite: MGT 488.

title: Independent Study in Management
description: An opportunity for supervised study of some phase of management. May consist of an experiment, library research, or an analysis of current management practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Management
description: Explores in depth current problems, theory, research, and trends in the management field. The topics of the seminar will vary depending upon the current status of managerial research, the instructor, and the needs and desires of the students. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Business Applications of Computer Data Processing
description: An introductory course in computer data processing with special emphasis on business problem solving. Includes study of the effects of computers on business and management decision making, of computer hardware and software, concepts and procedures for business systems analysis, and computer programming. Special problems in the areas of accounting, production, marketing, banking, finance, and management are analyzed and run on computers.

title: Interpretation of Business Data
description: An introductory course dealing with the collection, presentation, analysis, and interpretation of statistical data. Topics include descriptive statistics, basic probability, probability distributions, sampling, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, regression, and correlation. Prerequisite: MATH 131 and 132 or permission of the department head. Prerequisite recommended: MS 220.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 220 or CS 200. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 210.

title: Business Computer Systems and Applications
description: Acquaints students with current business use of computer. Deals with selected properties of systems design and file design. Presents a general framework from singlepurpose to integrated business applications, such as accounting, operationscontrol, production scheduling, personnel, and marketing. Prerequisite: MS 220.

title: Quantifying Management Decisions
description: A study and critical evaluation of operations research techniques for solving managerial problems found in business administration. Prerequisite: MS 220 and 221.

title: Simulating Management Decisions
description: A study and critical evaluation of simulation techniques for solving managerial problems found in business administration. Prerequisite: MS 220 and 221.

title: Integrating Word Processing/Data Processing Systems
description: Explores the evolutionary changes within the office. An introduction to the considerations involved in integrating text and data from word processing and data processing input to enhance the information processing output. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 200 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 362.

title: Management Information Systems
description: Systems theory and practice as they are applied to satisfying information needs for management decision makers through the analysis and design of manual and computerbased systems. Influence of information systems upon management and organization as well as upon managerial decision making. Prerequisite: MGT 380, MS 220, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Data Base: Structures and Management
description: Logical and physical organization of data. Describes data description, command and interrogation languages. Examines function of data bases in information systems. Prerequisite: MS 220 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Administration of Management Information Systems
description: Topics include equipment selection, equipment acquisition, computer operations management, project management, computer personnel management, financial control, systems security and control, and the relationship of the information systems functions to the organization as a whole. Prerequisite: MS 382 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Communications Based Information Systems
description: Describes computerrelated communication equipment, transmission services, and protocols. Studies the uses, features, control, benefits, and costs of online and realtime information systems. Prerequisite: MS 220 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business Systems Analysis and Design
description: An introductory course in business systems analysis and design. Introduces elementary systems techniques and tools. Explains in detail the key steps in the systems development cycle. Deals with some of the practical applications and considerations in systems within the business environment. Prerequisite: MS 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Business Statistics
description: The application to business problems of the most commonly used advanced statistical methods including goodnessoffit, contingency tables, analysis of variance, nonparametric techniques, advanced regression and correlation as applied to time series, and index numbers. Prerequisite: MS 221. Prerequisite recommended: MS 220.

title: Getting and Keeping a Job in Business
description: Indepth discussions involving personal goals in business, business opportunities, and management evaluations. Preparations and techniques for personal interviews in the business setting. Particular focus on personal discipline early in the business career.

title: Business Administration Policy
description: An integration at the senior level of the administrative processes of the operation of organizations producing goods and services in the private enterprise system. Emphasis on the case study method in solving problems (accounting, finance, management, marketing, production, economics, etc.) under conditions of uncertainty including overall analysis and policy determination pertaining to decision making. Also included is the relationship of a code of ethics as a control device for policy decisions. Prerequisite: senior standing, MKG 300, MGT 380, FIN 350, or permission of the department head. Department of Marketing Lowry, Head; Baird, Brown, Clabaugh, Fox, Greicus, Kuieck, Miller, Moser, Riecken, Sparling, Talafuse, Vanderleest, Wallace, Yavas (on leave 1981-83) Marketing is a business function concerned with the management of the flow of goods and services from the producer to the consumer. The marketing process provides an efficient way for enlightened producers to meet the needs of discerning consumers. Important marketing activities include providing the right product, promoting it properly, selling it at the right price, and distributing it in the right place. Marketing courses at Ball State University are designed to allow students to develop their abilities to recognize and define marketing problems and solve them creatively. Because the majority of Ball State marketing graduates go directly into business, the marketing curriculum is careeroriented. Students majoring in marketing choose one of five options within the marketing curriculum. Each option emphasizes different career opportunities. The sales and promotion option prepares students for careers in areas such as consumer and industrial product selling, sales training, advertising agency management, public relations, and product or brand management. Career opportunities for students selecting the retailing option include chainstore management, merchandising, fashion coordination, small business management, and buying. For students interested in the physical distribution option, career opportunities include the areas of materials management, industrial procurement, transportation, and physical distribution. After acquiring a foundation in marketing, students in the general marketing option are qualified to pursue many different phases of the marketing process. Some of the careers that are available to students in the general marketing option include international marketing, bank marketing, consumer affairs, and service organizations. Students choosing the shopping center administration -option receive career preparation in such areas as shopping center planning and development, shopping center administration, and retail management. The Department of Marketing, in cooperation with selected business firms, offers a professional practice program which allows juniors and seniors to relate classroom theory to practical experience by working for one quarter in a variety of meaningful assignments. Students who are working as interns receive from 2 to 8 quarter hours of credit and are paid by the firm for their work experience. The Student Marketing Association (SMA) is an organization which provides opportunities for participating in marketing discussions and programs and developing friendships with students who have similar interests. In the past, the SMA has conducted a series of minicourses on career planning and has brought selected speakers to the campus to discuss job qualifications and career opportunities in various marketing fields. In cooperation with local civic organizations, the SMA has also conducted studies that have assisted in identifying the market needs of minority groups and senior citizens. A departmental honors program is available to academically superior students. MKG 475, Marketing Simulation, has been designated as an honors course. The United States Department of Labor indicates that the need for persons with collegelevel training in marketing will continue to grow. Nearly 30 percent of employment in this country is in the marketing field. Sales and retail store management opportunities offer the greatest potential for Ball State marketing graduates in the future. Marketing 125 Students in the Marketing Department operate the Ball State University Better Business Bureau, a branch of the Indianapolis Better Business Bureau. These students usually either are enrolled in or have completed MKG 380, Marketing and Consumer Issues. There are several Positions of responsibility in the bureau that offer students unusual learning experiences. The activities of the bureau include resolving consumerbusiness grievances, providing consumer buying information, alerting consumers to deceptive business practices, and preparing media releases on consumerbusiness problems. For the student interested in preparing for teaching marketing and/or distributive education, it is possible to earn a departmental major in marketing along with the teaching major in distributive education. A departmental minor in marketing is available to students with a major in any academic area other than business. The minor consists of 24 quarter hours in marketing and is intended to provide a valuable supplement to students majoring in nonbusiness fields. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements listed below. title: Principles of Marketing
description: A basic course that examines marketing as a productive system within our economy. Promotional activities, product policies, retail and wholesale activities, pricing policies, international marketing, and marketing's role in society are studied. Prerequisite: ECON 201 or junior standing.

title: Consumer Relations/Training Orientation
description: Practicum involvin g administrative and operational activities esential to the Bal State University Beter Busines Bureau. A broad spectrum of activities including handbook examinations, training, and evaluation of operatives' performance level would be involved in this consumer relations operation. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department head. Offered first summer term only. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 380.

title: Marketing and Controversial Issues
description: Reading, research, and discussion course focusing on corporate citizenship. Myriad topics such as cost effectiveness of regulations, deceptive advertising, health impact of products, and safety/product liability are addressed. Prerequisite: MKG 301 or permission of department head. Offered during second summer term only. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 380.

title: Buyer Behavior
description: Practical business implications of the various aspects of consumer motivation and behavior. The student is provided with information to understand how and why a buyer reacts in a purchasing situation. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Advertising Management
description: Use of advertising as a communication tool in marketing management. Analysis of media selection production and layout, measurement of effectiveness, and social and economic aspects of advertising. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Personal Selling
description: Provides a detailed introduction to and application of the principles of personal selling as applied to individuals pursuing any vocation, as well as those aspiring to careers in the marketing area of business. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 334.

title: Sales Management
description: Policies and practices in organizing, recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Not open to the student who has credit in MKT 334.

title: Retail Management
description: An investigation of store policies, organization, location, layout, buying, stock control, pricing, and sales promotion for retail stores. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Survey of Transportation
description: The economics of transportationinternal waterways, railways, highways, and airwaysin the United States; economic development of various means of transportation and accompanying regulatory problems. Rate, traffic service, and coordination problems of our transportation system. Advantages and disadvantages, trends, and peculiarities of each of the various modes of transportation. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Research
description: A basic course in marketing research. Nature and scope of marketing research; scientific method and research design; specific marketing research procedures; techniques of sampling; and research report, followup, and evaluation of research process. Selected applications in areas of motivation, advertising, and product and sales control research. Prerequisite: MATH 131, 132; MKG 300; and MS 221.

title: Marketing and Consumer Issues
description: Analysis of the consumer issues which affect marketing. Includes the marketing implications of consumerism, ecology, and the disadvantaged consumers. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Credit Management
description: Practices of businesses in granting credit both to other business firms and to individuals. Credit limits, department operations, and collection policies are analyzed. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Promotion Strategy
description: Use of cases and problems to provide experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKG 320.

title: Retail Strategy
description: Advanced course in retailing management utilizing case studies and special projects to examine current topics and problems in the field of retailing. Prerequisite: MKG 330.

title: Physical Distribution Management
description: Physical distribution systems in the marketing environment; system components and the total cost approach; customer service objectives; physical distribution systems design and administration. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Industrial Procurement Management
description: A basic course in industrial procurement management. Principal topics considered are make or buy analysis, quality and quantity control, value analysis, price determination, sources of supply, the purchasing system, and legal aspects of purchasing. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Materials Management
description: The organizational concept that integrates the management of the flow of materials through a business enterprise into consumer markets. Marketing 127 Content includes: anticipating, sourcing, obtaining, and monitoring the current status of materials in an enterprise. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 460. 4 70 (MKT 466). International Marketing. (4) Examines legal, economic, and cultural factors influencing marketing abroad. Commercial policies, practices, and techniques needed to locate and evaluate foreign markets, as well as the problems of pricing, promoting, and distributing products in international markets. Prerequisite: MKG 300. 47 5 (MKT 430). Marketing Simulation Game. (4) A simulation game in which students are divided into teams or companies. Management in each company makes decisions in marketing, finance, and production. Does not involve writing computer programs or utilizing information from a data processing class. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and junior standing.

title: Shopping Center Seminar
description: A study of the managerial activities that are important in the operation of a shopping center. Subjects include layout, promotions, financing, merchandising, and regulation. Prerequisite: MKG 330, 431.

title: Marketing Management
description: Marketing by manufacturers as viewed from the marketing manager's position. Principal topics are selecting channels of distribution, determining demand, pricing policies, marketing legislation, advertising policies, and methods of selling. A case study approach. Prerequisite: 20 quarter hours in marketing, including MKG 350, and senior standing, or permission of the department head.

title: Professional Practice in Marketing
description: The student receives professional practice during a summer or a quarter as an intern on an approved program with a business firm, government agency, or nonprofit organization under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to thirdquarter juniors and seniors with a major in marketing. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Product Innovation
description: The evolution of a new product—essentially a disorderly process—receives systematic study. The framework comprises newproduct policies, creativity, idea screening and business analysis, physicalproduct development and marketing planning, applied research including testmarketing, and commercialization. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Commercial Pricing Strategies and Administration
description: The focus is on the pricing function for industrial and consumer products as part of the marketing mix. Psychological, financial, legal, economic, and managerial influences on price setting in business receive treatment in depth. Prerequisite: MKG 300, ACC 203, ECON 201.

title: Independent Study in Marketing
description: For students who wish to conduct independent study in some phase of marketing. May consist of an experiment, library research, or the analysis of current marketing practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing, a scholastic ratio of 3.0 and permission of the department head. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Practicum in the Better Business Bureau
description: Provides practical experience in mediating businessconsumer problems. Students utilize personnel skills in organizing and administering a Better Business Bureau. Prerequisite: MKG 301, 302, or 380. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 3 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 497.

title: Introduction to Business
description: Emphasizes the vital role of business in our society through a discussion of both the external environment of business and the internal environment of the business enterprise. Recognition is given to the contribution of the social and behavioral sciences in decision making. Open only to freshmen or sophomores except by permission of the department chairman. Hoyt The College of Fine and Applied Arts is dedicated to the education of professional personnel in the various areas represented, and also contributes to the cultural development of students throughout the university. The programs of the college are administered through its six departments and two schools: the Departments of Art, Home Economics, Industrial Education and Technology, Library Science, Military Science, and Nursing, the School of Music, and the School of Physical Education and Athletics. While, traditionally, teaching has been the objective of most of the students enrolled in the college, curricula for other professional preparation in each of the schools and departments are increasingly popular. The Department of Nursing, for example, is totally devoted to professional preparation of men and women for service in the field of nursing. In recent years, the leadership and direction for the fine arts in America are emanating from college and university campuses. Therefore, at Ball State as elsewhere, outstanding artists and musicians are to be found on the faculties. The departments in the College of Fine and Applied Arts may be thought of as the "doing" or "performing" departments; thus the faculty and students are frequently engaged in displaying, demonstrating, or performing their skills and achievements before numerous publics attracted to them. Graduate offerings of the departments in the College of Fine and Applied Arts are described in the Graduate Catalog. The responsibility of the Art Department is to prepare art educators and professional artists as well as to offer general art courses to liberal arts students. The departmental programs encompass the following areas: visual communications, photography, drawing, design, interior/environmental design, painting, sculpture, printmaking, ceramics, metal design, weaving, and art education. The undergraduate curriculum offers a core of experiences which help prepare the graduate to enter a particular art profession or graduate school. In the preparation of art educators there is a strong emphasis on teaching methods and curriculum development as well as studio participation, emphasizing the concept of the artistteacher. Courses for the liberal arts student are also offered. These courses provide the nonart major with the opportunity for personal enrichment through the visual arts. Art majors are not required to submit an entrance portfolio but must be prepared to present a portfolio for review and evaluation upon the completion of 18-24 hours of studio courses. Students transferring art credits from other institutions are required to submit a portfolio and transcript of grades to the department for evaluation. The Art Department reserves the right to retain examples of student work for exhibition purposes. title: Weaving 1
description: Fundamentals of loom and offloom weaving. Emphasis on technique, design, and threedimensional forms. Prerequisite: for students with areas in art, ADS 102; for others, permission of the department head. 202, 303, 304. Weaving 2, 3, 4. (3) Continuation of loom weaving with emphasis on technique and design in color, texture, and threedimensional form. Courses must be taken in sequence. Prerequisite: ACR 201.

title: Ceramics 1
description: A study of basic handbuilding techniques. Glazes, slips, bisque and glaze firing will be part of the studio experience. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 101.

title: Ceramics: Throwing 1
description: Beginning throwing. A basic study of the use of the potter's wheel and continued study of form, glaze, and idea. Prerequisite: ACR 211.

title: Ceramics: Technical Problems
description: A technical study of ceramic materials and processes as related to art forms. Prerequisite: ACR 212 and 313.

title: Metal Design 1
description: An introduction to jewelry making with a strong emphasis on design. The techniques of sawing, soldering, finishing, and other basic processes used in constructed jewelry. Prerequisite: ADS 101, 102.

title: Metal Design 2
description: An introduction to metal smithing with a strong emphasis on design. The basic techniques of forming metal along with further introduction to decorative processes used in metal. Prerequisite: ACR 221.

title: Weaving 3
description: (See ACR 202.) 304. Weaving 4. (3) (See ACR 202.)

title: Ceramics: Hand 1
description: A continued study of hand building techniques, form, glaze, and idea. Prerequisite: ACR 211. 314. Ceramics: Throwing 2. (3) Production techniques using the potter's wheel and continued study of form, glaze, and ideas. Prerequisite: ACR 212.

title: Ceramics: Hand 2
description: Individual problems in ceramic hand building based on students' needs. Continued study of form, glaze, and idea. Prerequisite: ACR 313. 323, 324, 425, 426. Metal Design 3, 4, 5, 6. (3) A further study in the techniques used in the art of metal smithing and jewelry design. Strong emphasis on design along with research in historical metal work. Courses must be taken in sequence. Prerequisite: ACR 222.

title: Metal Design 4
description: (See ACR 323.) 405, 406, 407. Weaving 5, 6, 7. (3) Advanced study and application of contemporary techniques in weaving. Emphasis on personal expression in twoand threedimensional form. Courses must be taken in sequence. Prerequisite: ACR 304.

title: Independent Study in Crafts
description: Designed for professionally oriented students allowing them to select and explore more intensively a special area. Prerequisite: sponsorship of an art faculty member and permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Ceramics: Throwing 3

Department of Home Economics Smith, Chairperson; Carr, Caylor, Finn, Harmon, Kim, Lacey, Miller, Nixon, Quesenberry, Rendina, Roepke, Spangler, Steele, Whitaker, Wittig Home economics is the field of knowledge and service that is fundamentally concerned with strengthening home and family life through educating the individuals for family living; improving the services and goods used by families; conducting research to discover the changing needs of individuals and families and to determine means of satisfying these needs; and furthering community, national, and world conditions favorable to family living. The profession of home economics synthesizes knowledge drawn from its own research from the physical, biological, and social sciences and the arts and applies this knowledge to improving the lives of families and individuals. The breadth of the field of home economics emphasizes its importance. The eleven separate, but interrelated, fields of foods, nutrition, clothing, textiles, applied art, housing, household equipment, home management, family economics, child development, and family relations provide the foundations for the good health, satisfying and successful living, psychological balance, and good management which are essential for the development of the whole personality. Needs of individuals and families in the social environment of their time are of primary concern in determining the emphases given to the various aspects of home economics. Home economics aids in helping individuals and families to make intelligent decisions concerning all aspects of family life, including the social, economic, aesthetic, managerial, health, and ethical aspects of relations, child development, foods, clothing, and housing. Home economics prepares professional personnel to carry out its objectives through education, research, social welfare and public health, dietetics, and institutional administation and business. It shares with other fields the responsibility for developing perceptive, wellinformed citizens with the ability and the initiative to further conditions favorable to effective living. description: Selected experiences related to quantity food equipment use, sanitation, and employee training in a quantity food service setting. Gives the student experiences under professional standards and supervision. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. Parallel: HFN 262 and 362.

title: Quantity Food Service Personnel Management Practicum
description: Selected experiences in personnel management in the quantity food service setting. Gives the student experiences under professional standards and supervision. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Parallel: HFN 263 and 363.

title: Quantity Menu Planning and Purchasing Practicum
description: Selected experiences related to quantity menu planning and purchasing in a variety of quantity food service organizations. Gives the student experiences under professional standards and supervision. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. Parallel: HFN 364 and 367.

title: Therapeutic Dietetics
description: Principles of dietary modifications needed by individuals with certain disease conditions. Prerequisite: HFN 340. Parallel: HFN 282 for Dietetic Technology students. Not open to the student who has credit in HFN 441.

title: Community Nutrition
description: Designed to acquaint the student with nutrition problem s and nutrition programs athe federal, state, and localevels. Practical experience wil include investigation and observation of and participation in nutrition programs in the local community. Prerequisite: HFN 340.

title: Quantity Food Production
description: Problems involved in quantity food production, distribution, and storage. Laboratory experience in university food service units. Prerequisite : HFN 20. Prerequisite or paralel: 340.

title: Institutional Equipment, Buying, and Layout
description: Stationary and small food equipment considered. Layouts of quantity food production kitchens planned. Field trips to quantity food kitchens and equipment companies. Dietetic Technology and Food Management majors must take this course parallel with HFN 262. In addition, Dietetic Technology students must take this course parallel with HFN 292.

title: Institutional Administration
description: Concepts of quantity food service in restaurants, schools, hospitals, and cafeterias. Emphasis is placed on personnel, management, organization, cost control, and apportionment of labor. Field trips to institutional kitchens. Dietetic Technology and Food Management majors must take this course parallel with HFN 263. In addition Dietetic Technology students must take this course parallel with HFN 293.

title: Menu Planning for Quantity Food Service
description: Principles of nutrition applied to feeding individuals and groups. Major emphasis is placed on menu planning for food services with consideration given to meeting nutritional needs. Limitation or problems relating to personnel, facilities, and type of patronage also stressed. Prerequisite: HFN 220 and 340. Parallel: HFN 294 and 367 for Dietetic Technology students.

title: Quantity Food Purchasing
description: Information needed by quantity food buyers and important considerations in purchasing foods. Emphasis on ethics in buying. Parallel: HFN 294 and 364 for Dietetic Technology students.

title: Experimental Foods
description: Experimental studies of foods in relation to their composition, physical and chemical properties, and factors affecting food quality. Recipes are investigated and methods of combining ingredients are developed and evaluated. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Advanced Nutrition
description: An advanced course in nutrition emphasizing the utilization of metabolism of nutrients at the cellular level in the human body. Current research in the field of nutrition will be included. Prerequisite: HFN 340 and CHEM 231.

title: Diet in Disease
description: Pathological conditions resulting from various nutritional diseases, with emphasis upon causes and effects of malnutrition and its treatment. Planning and preparation of diets for abnormal conditions. Hospital laboratory experience provided. Prerequisite: HFN 440 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Nutrition Assessment
description: A didactic and laboratory course employing the techniques needed to identify persons at risk of nutritional deficiency, to estimate the nutrient content of the diet and to evaluate anthropometric measures and tissue and excretory levels of certain nutrients, functional proteins, and metabolites used as indicators of nutrition status, and determine appropriate nutrition therapies. Prerequisite: HFN 340 and 342 or 441, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Dietetics
description: The professions involved in food service and dietetics; the roles and responsibilities of personnel and their relationships with other professionals; the standards to be attained; the code of professional ethics and the resources for continuing professional education. Prerequisite: 2 hours of credit in HE 498 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Nutrition, Weight Control, and Athletics
description: Designed for students in dietetics, physical education, biology (especially those specializing in human bioenergetics), and related fields, to provide information needed for nutrition counseling of individuals involved in weight control and exercise/athletics training programs. Prerequisite: HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Maternal and Infant Nutrition
description: Information about maternal, prenatal, and infant (birth to 36 months) nutrition; nutritional requirements of expectant mothers and infants investigated. Emphasis is placed on readings in current periodicals. Prerequisite: HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Child Nutrition
description: Principles of child nutrition (preschool through adolescence); nutritional requirements of children and problems in nutrition will be investigated. Current professional periodicals will be researched. Prerequisite: junior standing, HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geriatric Nutrition
description: Nutritional needs of older adults will be discussed based upon physiological and social changes and research in the field. Students will review some recent literature in the field, evaluate the food intake of elderly citizens in certain situations, and study and evaluate nutrition programs designed for older adults in terms of meeting nutritional needs. prerequisite: HFN 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Nutrition Counseling Practicum
description: Students will provide nutrition counseling for pregnant women; families with infants; young and teenage children; and persons seeking guidance for weight control and special problems. Students will be supervised by a member of the American Dietetic Association. Prerequisite: HFN 340 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours credit may be earned in this course but no more than 4 credit hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Food Service Management Practicum
description: Student will gain experience in a food service organization, either in the private or public sector. Practicum approved and supervised by the Department of Home Economics. Emphasis placed on developing food management expertise. Prerequisite: junior standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Home Care of the Sick
description: Includes concepts which affect the quality of life of individuals and families in prevention of illness, current major health problems and their costs, and procedures to follow when illness occurs.

title: Parent-Infant Development
description: Growth and development during first two years. Emphasizes practical aspects of infant caregiving and resources and information for developing confidence and competence in parenting. Limited to parents with infants under one year and those expecting baby in 8 months or less. Parents bring infants to class.

title: Infant Development
description: Growth and development from conception through the second year of life including physical, social, emotional, cognitive aspects of development. Students observe and interact with infants and parents. Open to all students.

title: Child Development
description: Emphasis on the preschool child as a member of a family group. Includes principles of natural growth and development and child guidance based on the physical, social, emotional, and intellectual needs of the preschool child. Students will participate and observe in various early childhood programs and centers. Open to all students.

title: Marriage
description: The dynamics of the marital relationship, the changes influencing marriages today. Emphasis is focused on the following: the individual and marriage, dating, mate selection and singlehood, marital communication, sexual adjustment in marriage, marriage adjustment, choosing parenthood, marriage dissolution, and marital growth.

title: Family Relations
description: Dynamics of family relationships and changes influencing family life and structure. Emphasis is placed on marriage, family life cycle, family problems, parent education, family enrichment.

title: Assisting with Family Problems
description: The major areas of adjustment in marriage and family relationships, problems of adjustment and philosophy and practice of techniques for clientcentered assistance with family problems.

title: Family Housing
description: Selection of housing to meet family needs. Evaluation of house plans for convenience, art qualities, and satisfying family life. Legal and financial aspects of home ownership. Open to all students.

title: Interior Design and Home Furnishing
description: Selection and arrangement of home furnishings to create attractive, functional interiors that are in harmony with the exterior of the home and adapted to family needs. Open to all students.

title: Home Management 1
description: Management of family and community resources to achieve desired goals in the family. Emphasis on the management problems encountered by newly married couples in establishing a home. Open to all students.

title: Household Equipment
description: Selection, use, and care of household equipment. Students will have an opportunity to plan, organize, and present demonstrations on household equipment.

title: Home Management 2
description: Residence in the home management house offers opportunity to make practical application of the principles of homemaking. Prerequisite: HFN 220. Prerequisite or parallel: HHM 340.

title: Problems in Consumer Buying
description: The economic aspects of purchasing for the consumer, including marketing conditions, consumer credit, agencies that protect the consumer, and factors to consider when buying consumer goods and services. Open to all students.

title: Clothing Construction
description: Fundamental techniques applied in the construction and fitting of simple garments. Not open to the student who has credit in HTC 104.

title: Introduction to Clothing
description: Provides basic knowledge of garment construction, clothin g selection, the aparel industry, and social psychological aspects of clothing.

title: Creative Stitchery
description: Learn creative skills in stitchery by embellishing existing fabrics or originating new ones. Techniques include macrame, crocheting, knitting, quilting, appliquein g, trapunto, embroidery, nedlepoint, rya, braided, and hoked rugs. A total of 6 hours credit may be earned.

title: Tailoring
description: Selection and construction of tailored garments and advanced clothing problems. Prerequisite: HTC 104 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Costume History
description: A history of costume from its earliest beginnings to the present. Emphasis on the motivating influences of each period as well as on the costume itself. Open to all students.

title: The Fashion Industry
description: A survey of the business of fashion through design, manufacture, distribution, and promotion. Explores career possibilities. Open to all students.

title: Apparel Design by the Flat Pattern Method
description: Adaptation of standard patterns to individual proportions, designing of garments and creating an original garment by the flat pattern method. Prerequisite: HTC 104 and 203.

title: Textiles
description: Textiles and their components as they relate to care, performance, and consumer satisfaction. Open to all students.

title: Textile Testing
description: Experience in planning and conducting textile tests and in evaluating resulting data; development, present status, and importance of textile testing. Prerequisite: HTC 330 or ADS 222.

title: Household Textiles
description: The selection, use, care of drapery and curtain fabric, upholstery fabrics, household linens, carpets and rugs. Including thermal comfort of selected household textiles and energy conservation.

title: Clothing Problems
description: Special problems to meet students' needs in clothing construction. Includes units in machine attachments and adjustments, draperies, career projects, problem fabrics. Prerequisite: HTC 104.

title: Fashion Merchandising Practicum
description: Gives the trainee actual experience under professional standards, regulations, and supervision in an establishment chosen by the student. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Department of Industrial Education and Technology Wagner, Head; Barella, David, DeKeyser, Edwards, Folls, Gurbach, Henak, Kirkwood, Middleton, Nelson, Poucher, Reams, Ridgeway, Shackleford, Smith, South, Steczak, Steele, Tang, Tomlinson, Tucker, Wright The programs of the Department of Industrial Education and Technology are designed to meet the needs of students who are (1) qualifying for the teaching profession or allied professions of business and industry, (2) exploring the industrial world for possible occupations or vocations, or (3) seeking knowledge and understanding of our industrial society. A wide variety of industryrelated courses offers students many opportunities to explore occupational choices in the following industries: construction, manufacturing, communications, and power. Courses in the above areas will also be of interest to students as part of their general studies program. Students who intend to pursue a concentration in teaching industrial education should take the following courses during their first year: IED 150, 151, 152, 154, 156, 158, and 198. Students who intend to pursue a concentration in one of the several technological programs should contact the department head to obtain recommendations for courses to take the first year. Students who have no intention of concentrating in the Department of Industrial Education and Technology are encouraged to take IED 161 as an elective. For those who earn credit in IED 161 and later choose to take a concentration within the department, credit will count toward their concentration area as recommended by the department head. NOTE: Students are required to wear industrial safety glasses in all classes where they are exposed to sparks, flying chips, hot materials, and other hazardous substances. In addition to the baccalaureate degree programs, the Department of Industrial Education and Technology has two associate degree programs, Manufacturing Technology and Printing Technology. The Manufacturing Technology program has three options: Manufacturing Design, Metals Manufacturing, and Plastics Manufacturing. For a description of associate degree programs, see the Academic Programs section of this catalog.
