title: Intermediate Badminton
description: Presents skills in badminton beyond the beginning level and is designed to provide opportunities to learn advanced technique and strategy. Prerequisite: PEG 124 or PEP 173 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 122.

title: Intermediate Bowling
description: Designed to give the student knowledge and experience in bowling on a team or in a league, keeping league records, team standings, and computing and figuring handicaps as well as review of basic fundamentals.

title: Bicycle Touring
description: Designed to develop touring physical fitness and camping skills associated with the touring aspects of bicycling. Prerequisite: PEG 130 or equivalent. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Golf
description: Designed to offer the golfing student an opportunity to learn and practice the finer points of the game.

title: Intermediate Horsemanship
description: Work toward perfecting form in the three gaits: walk, trot, and canter. Harness driving. Stable management.

title: Intermediate Tennis
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 128.

title: Intermediate Hatha Yoga
description: Designed for the student wishing to perfect previously learned asanas and to learn new ones. Prerequisite: PEG 119 or permission of the department head.

title: Intermediate Basketball (Women's Rules)
description: An intermediate course in basketball designed to include a review of fundamental skills, further development of these skills, and the introduction of advanced skills and strategies. Prerequisite: PEG 137 or equivalent.

title: Intermediate Power Volleyball (Women's Rules)
description: Instruction in intermediate techniques, terminology, strategy, rules, and competition. Includes individual and team offensive and defensive techniques, offensive and team game strategies, and competition. Prerequisite: PEG 131 or PEP 183 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 140.

title: Intermediate Fencing
description: Prerequisite: beginning fencing or equivalent.

title: Intermediate Snow Skiing
description: Designed to teach intermediate skiers the skills necessary to become advancedlevel skiers; affords them the opportunity to ski on longer, higher open and trail slopes provided by ski areas in the west (Rocky Mountains) or the east (White Mountains). Prerequisite: PEG 142 or permission of the department head.

title: Intercollegiate Athletics
description: Actual participation in the organized practice sessions and competitions during the regular season for the varsity sport as directed by the coach for that sport. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Seasonal Sports Activities
description: Designed to be offered only at an offcampus location with a great deal of flexibility in course content in order to accommodate the needs of individuals and to adapt to the facilities available and the weather conditions existing at the time the course is being offered. Students will be provided activity and instruction in physical fitness activities and two lifetime sports activities.

title: Sport Scuba Diving
description: Provides opportunities for refining techniques and skills for using selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus. Prerequisite: PEG 206 or permission of the department head.

title: White Water Canoeing
description: Designed to assist students to develop skills and gain knowledge necessary for white water canoeing and portaging. Field trips may involve overnight camping. Prerequisite: PEG 209 or permission of the department head.

title: Advanced Tennis
description: Designed for the student wishing to perfect previously learned skills and to learn more indepth strokes and playing strategies. Prerequisite: PEG 227 or 128 or permission of the department head.

title: General Safety Education
description: Designed to prepare prospective teachers for the comprehensive general safety education program.

title: Conditioning and Exercise
description: An exercise course designed to maintain and/or increase physical fitness and aid in weight control. Designed to aid the student to develop a fitness philosophy, to structure physical fitness programs, and to recognize individual physiological limitations.

title: Gymnastics (Balance Beam and Floor Exercise)
description: Prerequisite: PEP 157 or permission of the department head.

title: Gymnastics (Trampoline, Vaulting, Uneven Bars)
description: Instruction in the basic stunts and creative routines on the following pieces of apparatus: trampoline, balance beam, flying rings, and uneven parallel bars. Prerequisite: PEP 157 or permission of the department head.

title: Studio of Contemporary Dance Theatre
description: Provides training toward the act of performance, through varied choreographic dance experiences. Students plan, rehearse, and perform in studio hour presentations. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Folk Dance Studio Theatre
description: The third course in folk dance. Designed to emphasize the different styles existing in folk dance. Introduces the student to elements of folk dance choreography. Prerequisite: PEG 112, 212 or PEG 262. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned

title: Foundations of Physical Education
description: An introductory course for professional physical education students that covers the psychomotor, cognitive, and affective scope of physical education and its relationship to education. An attempt is made to assist students in assessing those qualities of motor and physical fitness expected of physical education majors as they commence their vocational study.

title: Driver and Traffic Safety Education 1
description: Content, methods, materials, organization, and administration of the classroom and laboratory phase of the secondary school program.

title: Developmental Game Activities
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the application of the principles of movement and to provide a knowledge of basic skills and appropriate activities for the development of these skills as applied to game activities. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Principles and Problems of Coaching Sports for Girls and Women
description: Introduces students to the following: the principles and problems of coaching girls' team and individual sports at the junior and senior high school level; the philosophies and principles which underlie the development of such a program.

title: Coaching Observation (Girls'/Women's Athletics)
description: Guided observation of coaching techniques and practices with analysis of teaching/coaching philosophies for competitive sports in schools. Prerequisite: PEP 231.

title: Practicum in Aquatics
description: An internship in aquatics at Ball State or other approved aquatic programs. Prerequisite: PEP 353 and permission of the department chairman. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Officiating Competitive Aquatic Sports
description: Introduces the student to officiating practices, the decisionmaking role of the official, and laboratory experience in officiating. Opportunities exist for certification in various aquatic areas.

title: Gymnastics for Children
description: Designed to acquaint the student with teaching methodology, developmental skills, and activities for gymnastics at the elementary school level. Prerequisite: PEP 157.

title: Tumbling and Apparatus (Women's Events)
description: Prerequisite: PEP 158 and 159 or permission of the department head.

title: Gymnastic Performance Techniques
description: Not open to the student who has 2 hours of credit in PEP 256 or 258.

title: Contemporary Dance Theatre
description: Provides the dance student with experience in performing with a company of dancers who plan, rehearse, and perform both informal and forma] dance performances. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Folk Dance
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 112.

title: The Teaching of Folk Dance
description: Materials and techniques of teaching folk dance in the secondary schools. Prerequisite: PEP 262 or equivalent.

title: Folk Dance Theatre
description: Provides opportunities and experiences in participating with a company of dancers who plan and perform in both informal and formal folk dance presentations. Prerequisite: PEG 112 and permission of the department head. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Teaching of Square Dance
description: The development of teaching skills for beginning and intermediate classes in square dancing. The development of techniques of calling square dance (patter and singing). Prerequisite: PEP 263.

title: Teaching of Recreational Dance
description: An introduction to folk, square, round, and other types of recreational dance, and methods of teaching recreational dance.

title: Dance Composition 1
description: Principal elements of dance composition. Simple compositional forms for small groups and solo work. Prerequisite: PEG 215 or the equivalent.

title: Intermediate Badminton
description: Prerequisite: PEP 173 or permission of the department head.

title: Folk and Square Dance Methods for Elementary School Children
description: Movement experiences in the forms of folk and square dance for the elementary school child. Emphasis is on the selection of dance materials and methods of teaching dance for the elementary school child.

title: Intermediate Tennis
description: Prerequisite: PEP 177 or permission of the department head.

title: Baseball/Softball Performance Techniques
description: . Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 179.

title: Track and Field Performance Techniques
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 180.

title: Games and Activities for the Handicapped
description: Designed to familiarize the student with games and activities commonly used with the handicapped. Prerequisite: SPCED 201.

title: Recreation Playground Activities
description: Provides a knowledge of playground operation, equipment, and supplies. Presentation of a wide variety of activities for effective playground leadership.

title: Practicum in Elementary School Physical Education
description: Offers the student supervised experience in basic movementoriented activities generally included in elementary school physical education programs (suggested range K-6). Course work will be contracted among the student, the department, and the school/agency through the appropriate campus office. Prerequisite: PEP 230 or permission of the department head. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Anatomy
description: Basic concepts in anatomy for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching.

title: Physiology
description: Basic concepts in physiology for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching. Prerequisite: PEP 292, or permission of the department head.

title: Kinesiology
description: The mechanics of motion as applied to the human body. Development of the ability to analyze activity for the purpose of improving physical skills. Prerequisite: PEP 292.

title: First Aid
description: First Aid as outlined by the American Red Cross, leading to standard certification. Designed for the student pursuing a major or minor program in the School of Physical Education and Athletics. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 250.

title: First Aid Instructor
description: Instructor's course in Standard First Aid and Personal Safety, and including the instructor's course in Multimedia First Aid as established by the American Red Cross. Designed for the professional student pursuing a major or minor in physical education. Prerequisite: PEP 299 or HSC 250, or valid certification in Standard First Aid and Personal Safety, Standard First Aid and Multimedia, or Advanced First Aid and Emergency Care.

title: Camping
description: Acquaints the student with various aspects of organized and individual camping. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Simulation in Driver and Traffic Safety Education
description: Designed to meet the needs of prospective teachers in the simulation phase of driver and traffic safety education. Prerequisite: PEP 124.

title: Strategies and Techniques in Coaching Gymnastics, Volleyball, and Track and Field
description: Coaching techniques involved in gymnastics, volleyball, and track and field. Strategies are presented, discussed, and practiced. Prerequisite: four skill courses from directed list.

title: Strategies and Techniques in Coaching Volleyball, Basketball, and Softball
description: Coaching techniques involved in volleyball, basketball, and softball. Strategies are presented, discussed, and practiced. Prerequisite: four skill courses from directed list.

title: Strategies and Techniques in Coaching Swimming, Golf, Gymnastics, and Tennis
description: Coaching techniques involved in swimming, golf, gymnastics, and tennis. Strategies are presented, discussed, and practiced. Prerequisite: four skill courses from directed list.

title: Organization and Management of Women's Athletics
description: Understanding and appreciation of the responsibilities and desirable characteristics of competent officials; organizing and managing competitive events and tournaments; relationships among coach, officials, players, and spectators; local, state, and national organizations involved in officiating and management.

title: Sports Information 1
description: Designed primarily for the sports information student. Develops the student's knowledge and background in the terminology, basic strategy, scoring, and officiating in gymnastics (men's), basketball, golf, ice hockey, boxing, wrestling, horseracing, billiards, crosscountry, baseball, and football. Not open to the student with teaching areas in physical education.

title: Sports Information 2
description: Designed for the sports information student. Includes the following sport areas: gymnastics (women's), volleyball, tennis, track and field, swimming, lacrosse, field hockey, softball, soccer, badminton, and bowling. Geared to increase the students' knowledge in these sports especially in regard to terminology, basic rules, strategy, scoring, and officiating, which will assist them in covering these activities. Not open to physical education majors or minors.

title: Aquatic Art Production
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of management and staging activities involved in an aquatic art production at the high school and college levels.

title: Teaching and Coaching Swimming
description: Prerequisite: PEG 201, or permission of the department head.

title: American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor
description: Students have the opportunity to earn the American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor Certificate. Prerequisite: an unexpired American National Red Cross advanced lifesaving certificate.

title: Instructional Techniques and Analysis of Aquatic Performance
description: Selected learning theories, teaching strategies, and physical laws which affect learning and performance in the aquatic medium. Analysis of basic safety skills and stroke and diving techniques receive major emphasis.

title: Field and/or Laboratory Experience
description: Permits the student to receive credit for aquatic experiences in categories of leadership, administration, and/or operation of aquatic programs or facilities. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching and Coaching Gymnastics
description: Prerequisite: PEP 259.

title: Teaching and Coaching Wrestling
description: Prerequisite: PEP 261.

title: Dance for Children
description: Basic rhythms, exploration of movement, and creative dance for the lower level of the elementary school.

title: History of Dance
description: Basic dance forms and functions from the primitive era into the 20th century.

title: Accompaniment for Modern Dance
description: Exploration and the use of accompaniment in dance. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or equivalent.

title: Dance Production 1
description: Designed to acquaint the student with various technical and performance aspects of dance production. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or equivalent.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator (Techniques)
description: Fundamental modern dance techniques, elements of rhythmic patterns, materials or space, design, and improvisation.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator (Composition)
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques. Emphasis on composition. Prerequisite: PEP 365.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator (Methodology)
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques. Emphasis on teaching modern dance in the public schools, camps, and others. Dance composition. Prerequisite: PEP 366.

title: Aquatics for the Elementary School Child
description: Introduces the student to safety factors, developmental strokes, diving sequences, and teaching strategies for aquatic instruction of the young child. Prerequisite: PEP 353 or equivalent certificate from a nationally recognized organization such as the Young Men's Christian Association or the Boy Scouts of America.

title: Diagnostic Techniques and Athletic Injury Mechanisms
description: An introduction to predisposing anatomical, kinesiological, growth stress, and other such factors that contribute to athletic injuries. Procedures for accurate recognition and evaluation of not only these factors, but also the extent of an athletic injury are presented. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Administration and Organization of Programs for the Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries
description: Problems, principles, and objectives in the designing, planning, and operation of a program for the prevention and care of athletic injuries. There will also be an examination of the code of ethics of the National Athletic Trainers Association. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Athletic Training Modalities and Therapeutic Techniques
description: An introduction to mechanical therapies, thermal therapy, cryotherapy, hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, and therapeutic exercise. Only those modalities and their clinical uses that have special implications for the athletic trainer in the treatment of injuries to the athlete will be considered. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Methods of Teaching Team Sports
description: Methods, materials, and organizational techniques in the following team sports: basketball, field hockey, flag football, soccer, softball, speedball, team handball, volleyball. Prerequisite: beginning courses or equivalency in team sports included.

title: Methods of Teaching Individual Sports
description: Methods, materials, and organizational techniques in the following individual sports: archery, badminton, bowling, golf, tennis, track. Prerequisite: beginning courses or equivalency in individual sports included.

title: Teaching and Coaching Tennis
description: Prerequisite: PEP 276.

title: Teaching and Coaching Baseball and Softball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 279.

title: Teaching and Coaching Track and Field
description: . Prerequisite: PEP 280.

title: Teaching and Coaching Football
description: Prerequisite: PEP 281.

title: Teaching and Coaching Basketball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 282.

title: Teaching and Coaching Volleyball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 283.

title: Teaching and Coaching Soccer
description: Prerequisite: PEP 284.

description: The development of gymnastics judging techniques with the opportunity for obtaining an IHSAA and/or NAGWS (Class) official's rating. Prerequisite: PEP 157, 158, 159.

title: Track and Field Officiating
description: The development of track and field officiating techniques with the opportunity for obtaining an IHSAA and/or NAGWS official's rating. Prerequisite: PEP 180.

title: Softball Umpiring
description: The development of softball umpiring techniques with the opportunity for obtaining an IHSAA, ASA, and/or NAGWS official's rating. Prerequisite: PEP 179.

title: Volleyball Officiating
description: The development of volleyball officiating techniques with the opportunity for obtaining an IHSAA and/or NAGWS official's rating. Prerequisite: PEP 183.

title: Basketball Officiating
description: The development of basketball officiating techniques with the opportunity for obtaining an IHSAA and/or NAGWS official's rating. Prerequisite: PEP 182.

title: Principles of Physical Education
description: General concepts based upon the scientific facts and philosophic judgments which underlie physical education.

title: Motor Development of Young Children
description: Human motor development theory and practice for early childhood and primary school children emphasizing behaviors related to nonlocomotor, locomotor, transitory, and manipulatory motor patterns as they emerge and become controlled, utilizing task analysis, assessment, program planning, physical activities, and evaluation. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department head.

title: Neurophysiological Approach to Physical Education for the Handicapped
description: Designed to provide the student with an understanding of the theoretical basis of selected neurophysiological programs for treatment of motor decrements of various handicapping conditions and to teach the student how to administer such programs.

title: Teaching of Physical Education in the Elementary School
description: Methods and consideration for teaching physical education in the elementary school that include the factors of purpose, growth and development, motor learning, program planning, and evaluation.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Physical Education in the Secondary School
description: Designed to analyze and develop teaching methods that enable the student to successfully plan, implement, and evaluate an array of teaching strategies that would be utilized in creating a freesafe environment for a public school physical education program. Prerequisite: PEP activity sequence and EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries
description: Principles; practice of athletic training principles and techniques necessary for care and prevention of athletic injuries.

title: Remedial Exercises and Rehabilitation
description: An introduction to the objectives and principles involved in designing and planning conditioning programs for the athlete. Therapeutic exercises essential in planning the rehabilitation program of the injured athlete are introduced and developed. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials for Physical Education in the Secondary School
description: Designed as a practicum that involves comprehensive planning of instruction, designing teaching implementation strategies, classroom management techniques, and evaluation of teaching behaviors and materials in physical education. Opportunities for students to work with children in a classroom setting. Prerequisite: PEP 395 and juniorlevel status.

title: Exercise Technician and Leader Practicum
description: To provide training for potential leaders of physical fitness programs, emphasis will be on administering exercise tests in the laboratory and in field situations, prescribing exercise based on test results and scientific principles, and leading exercise sessions. Prerequisite: PEP 293 or equivalent course or permission of the department head.

title: Practicum in Recreation
description: Supervised, practical, professional leadership experienc e designed for the recreationoriented person. Experiences include: work activities in federal, state, county, or community parks or with private camps. Close supervision supplied by the university and the participating agency. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Driver and Traffic Safety Education 2
description: Presentation of materials and information designed to prepare for teaching driver education in the secondary schools.

title: Motorcycle Safety Education
description: Will prepare prospective teachers to conduct motorcycle rider education courses.

Sargent The College of Sciences and Humanities provides courses and programs for either a liberal education or for specialized and professional curricula. The liberal arts programs permit the student to elect more freely and to explore the "idea" subject matter. "Liberal" stems from the Latin liber, free. By definition, a liberal arts education should free people from ignorance by providing them an intelligent grasp of the experiences of the past and an understanding of the interrelationship of branches of knowledge. The individual is educated to think objectively, critically, and creatively. The liberal arts include the study of foreign languages, the physical and social environment, the evolution of Western civilization, the foundations of modern science, and the classical works. The wide range of courses offered by the College of Sciences and Humanities provides the basis for specialized and professional curricula—offered both within the college and in the other colleges requiring service courses. Within the college, preprofessional programs are specified—for medicine, dentistry, engineering, and law. A variety of specialist programs is offered, including medical technology and social work. Also, the departments within the college have programs designed for those planning graduate study in the field of their choice. The college includes the following departments: Anthropology, Biology, Chemistry, Criminal Justice and Corrections, English, Foreign Languages (French, German, Greek, Latin, Portuguese, Spanish), Geography, Geology, History, Journalism, Mathematical Sciences, Natural Resources, Philosophy, Physics and Astronomy, Physiology and Health Science, Political Science, Psychological Science, Social Work, Sociology, Speech and Theatre, Speech Pathology and Audiology, and Telecommunications. Department of Anthropology Glenn, Chairperson; Coffin, Flores-Meiser, Hicks, Izmirlian, Scruton, Swartz, Whitehead The question of questions for mankind . . . is the ascertainment of the place which Man occupies in nature and of his relations to the universe of things. — T. H. Huxley Anthropology means literally "the study of man, Unlike the other social, behavioral, and life sciences, anthropology does not concentrate on only one aspect of human existence, but rather assumes we can achieve a true understanding of the workings of individuals and groups only by an integrated study of biology and culture, past and present, primitive and complex, as a whole. As the discipline has grown it has transcended its original goals. There are four major subdivisions of anthropology: cultural anthropology, archaeology, physical anthropology, and linguistics. Central to ethnology, the basic ingredient of cultural anthropology is the idea of "culture" as the sum of all things we learn as members of groups. Among the many topics of interest to cultural anthropologists are kinship and community social organization, child rearing practices, individual statuses and roles, ideology, economic and political organization, the interactions between societies and their environments, material goods, and how and why cultures change. The courses in cultural anthropology stress how people make culture and, conversely, how culture shapes people. Hence, humans are studied as products of specific cultures. The reasons for and results of people conforming to or conflicting with their cultures' ideals are also considered. Archaeologyprovides time depth for anthropology, particularly for those societies for which there are no written records. Archaeologists are interested in many of the same questions as cultural anthropologists, but the type of evidence they study is different. Cultural anthropology depends heavily on living informants, but archaeologists have only the physical remains left behind, which are much more difficult to interpret. Thus while archaeologists do gather information about social organization, they devote greater attention to subsistence practices, settlement patterns, technology, and to the questions of why and how cultures change. The courses in archaeology attempt to show the students what issues archaeology can investigate, how we go about carrying out those investigations, and what we have learned so far. Through the work of archaeologists on culture history we now know far more about the lives of our ancient ancestors than was thought possible a century ago. Physical anthropology pays particular attention to the biological nature not only of humans but also of our nearest relatives, the other primates— prosimians, monkeys, and apes. Within physical anthropology there are further subspecialties: primate paleontology, which tries to trace the development of Homo sapiens and the other primates through fossil studies; primatology, which compares the anatomy, physiology, and behavior of the various primate species; and human biology, which studies growth and development, racial and other genetic differences, and the ways our bodies adapt to our natural and cultural environments. Anthropological linguistics concerns itself with the nature and history of language, an especially complex part of our cultural heritage. The influence of social situations on language performance is studied, as is language's role in the transmission of culture. By combining the studies of these four divisions we are able to see human nature as a whole, a system of interrelated parts. The nature of this system is often made clearest by comparative studies, by stepping outside our own culture or race or time to see how others are constituted. Courses in anthropology form part of the university's general studies program, and even students who have no professional interest in anthropology benefit from the breadth of perspective about our own and other cultures that anthropology provides. There are both introductory and advanced courses pertinent to students majoring in education, business, or in liberal arts in other departments. There is also a special teaching major in anthropology as well as anthropology courses that meet part of the requirements for Ancient Studies, Latin American Studies, Afro-American Studies, Medieval and Renaissance Area Studies, Asian Studies, and Native American Studies (which is based in the department). An undergraduate major or minor in anthropology can be an invaluable background for students going into law school, medical school, or studies in such areas as public health, international business, public administration, or urban and regional planning. For those students who wish to become professional anthropologists, graduate study is usually required and can lead to a career in either academic teaching and research or to work in a more applied field such as planning and development, environmental assessment, cultural or archaeological preservation, public health, or medical research. The structure of the anthropology major is flexible and thus can accommodate the academic and professional goals of the individual student. Special programs available within the department include opportunities for field experience in archaeological resources management and summer field schools in Indiana archaeology and in ethnography in Jamaica and among the Indians of the American Southwest. Arrangements can be made for field studies anywhere in the world. description: The origin of man and the rise of civilization as revealed by the discovery of the antiquities of the past. Explanation of recent chronometric and established classical dating methods, how sites are excavated, and archaeological remains are interpreted.

title: Introduction to Language and Linguistics
description: The nature of human language as an object of scientific study, focusing on both the biological and sociocultural bases of language and its structure. Emphasis on language and thought, linguistic analysis of language structure, social and geographical dialects, and language families of the world.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Bio-Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological and cultural evolution. * See Social Science and Social Studies section for total requirements for this area. ANTH 100 may serve as prerequisite for departmental major in anthropology.

title: Black Africa's Contribution to Western Civilization
description: The African cultural and historical roots of the American black will be investigated. The origins of the human race, plant and animal domestication, metallurgy, art, and state formation are covered, focusing on West Africa, the source of black population in the United States. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 154.

title: Anthropology—Culture and Women
description: The structure of women's role in various types of societies, from hunting and gathering to urban communities. In the light of these societies the western movement to liberate women from their traditional roles may be better understood. As industrialization reaches its peak the rigid sexual division of labor gives way to the female role being modeled after the male's.

title: North American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North America. Each culture is described in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: Peoples and Cultures of the World
description: An introduction to the way of life of primitive and modern peoples of the world from North America, South America, Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and the Pacific Islands. Topics discussed include religion, family life, economics, education, politics and the arts.

title: Material Culture
description: The material manifestations of culture, stressing primitive technology. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Latin America
description: A general study of the peoples of Mexico, Central America, and South America. Societies discussed range from the ancient Maya, Aztec, and Incas to modern Indians, peasants, and city dwellers. Topics discussed range from religion, family life, and the arts to modernization, urban social problems, and revolution.

title: Contemporary Problems of the American Indian
description: A multivariate analysis of significant political, ecological, economic, and educational problems confronting particular American Indian tribes today. Individual and group responses to these problems will be studied within pertinent psychological, historical, political, and sociocultural theoretical frameworks.

title: Indians of the American Southwest
description: Surveys: prehistoric, historic, and contemporary cultures of selected Southwest Indian groups with an emphasis on culturespecific solutions to common problems caused by their social and natural environment.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to Honors College students only or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Osteology
description: A laboratory course dealing with the human skeleton. Topics covered are: osteological terminology, identification of whole and fragmentary bones, standardized measuring techniques, and the assessment of the age, stature, sex, and race of a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 100.

title: Races of Man
description: The present status and a historical survey of the concept of race as it applies to human populations. Ways in which human populations biologically differ from each other and the adaptive nature of such variation. The distribution and antiquity of living races. Prerequisite: ANTH 100,120, or 160.

title: Race, Racism, arid Ethnicity
description: Scientific investigation of the biological nature of race, race beliefs, and racism, an extreme expression of ethnic bias. Particular attention to the Western world, but similar attitudes in other parts of the world are also considered.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man from his nonhuman primate ancestors. The primate fossil record, with particular emphasis on those forms in the human lineage, and the human fossil record. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or 204, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs.

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Suinrner Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation; sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Field observation and interpretation are stressed. Requires full time in the field. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Utilization of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Advanced Archeological Field Methods
description: Advanced methods of excavation and field recording studied at the excavation site. Prerequisite: ANTH 421. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Midwest is traced through the Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: Traces and describes the archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic to the Historic Period.

title: European Prehistory
description: The prehistory of Europe from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age with an emphasis during the later, protohistoric period on the archaeological and ethnographic evidence from the regions to the north and west of the Classical World. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: Cultural Resources Management
description: Covers the special problems of what has also been called conservation archaeology, including relevant federal and state laws, regulations, and agencies, reconnaissance, and sampling methods; project budgeting; elements in the environmental impact statement; and other responsibilities of the consultant archaeologist. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120, 421 or equivalent.

title: History and Philosophy of Archaelogical Theory
description: Examination of the theoretical trends in archaeology. Survey of the areas of taxonomic, spatiotemporal, and cultural archaeology. Comparison of the tenets of historical or traditional and processual or "new" archaeology, Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Seminar in Archaeological Interpretation
description: A reading seminar designed to familiarize the student with the literature of archaeological theory with an emphasis on more recent work. Such topics as culture change, spatial analysis, social structure, demography, subsistence, ethnographic analogy, sampling, and experimental archaeology will be covered. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: Seminar on Scientific Techniques in Archaeology
description: A reading seminar designed to familiarize the student with the literature on the application of scientific techniques to archaeological problems. Topics to be covered include dating methods; soil, faunal, botanical, ceramic, and lithic analysis; geophysical surveying; photogrammetry; and others. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: Historical Archaeology
description: Covers the major themes and philosophies of historical archaeology as well as the related literature and sources of information on architectural features and items of material culture likely to be encountered in the course of excavation.

title: Scope of Cultural Anthropology
description: General survey of the comparative study of human cultures and social processes that influence behavior designed for upperlevel undergraduate students with little or no background. The holistic application of the basic data, concepts, and premises of cultural anthropology will be emphasized.

title: Personality and Culture
description: Introduction to a major area of anthropological interest and investigation during the past three decades. This field of anthropology has grown out of recent efforts to unite studies of individual behavior and group, or cultural behavior. Involves discussion of the nature of human personality and its origins, both in the individual and the species. Particular stress on the phenomenon of the model personality type.

title: Peoples and Problems of Modern Africa
description: The course is intended to acquaint the student with the vast, complex, and still comparatively little known continent of Africa. More particularly it will enable students to acquire a systematic body of knowledge concerning the increasingly significant role which Africa plays in the modern world.

title: Witchcraft, Magic, and Religion
description: An anthropological study of mankind's ageold concern with life, death, sickness, the unknown. Shows how men have attempted to control their lives through supernatural beings, prayer, sacrifice, and techniques of magic and witchcraft. Discusses the possible origins of religious beliefs and shows how these are part of the fabric of social life in primitive and contemporary societies.

title: Social Organization
description: Opportunity for indepth study of man's social systems. Emphasis on the function of these systems and important grouping principles. The crosscultural method is employed extensively.

title: Anthropological Theory
description: Historical development of concept and theory in anthropology. Various theoretical viewpoints and schools of thought will be examined intensively. Prerequisites: ANTH 100, 160, and 120.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the impact of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents with European civilization.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Peoples of the South Pacific
description: A general survey of the ethnography of the peoples of Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia. Selected field studies will be examined in terms of the fu nctional method and acculturation theories for which oceanic cultures and societies provide a most suitable and viable laboratory.

title: Field School in Ethnography and Ethnology
description: Methods of carrying out field research in cultural anthropology; techniques of establishing contact and rapport; interview and observation methods; problem formulation, data recording, and data preparation. The student may spend fullor halftime in the field. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Culture Change
description: Discussion focuses on the major processes of cultural change such as cultural evolution, revolution, ecological adaptation, conquest, diffusion, mass communications, economic aid and development and other timely and appropriate topics.

title: The Development of Near-Eastern Cultures
description: Traces the development of cultures in the Near East as revealed by archaeology and explores the presentday cultural variability.

title: The Peoples and Cultures of India
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the anthropology (social organization, cultural system) of South Asia with special stress on India.

title: Introduction to Folklore
description: An introduction to the genres of folklore with an emphasis on the anthropological study of folktales, legends, and myth; methodological and theoretical approaches to their study; their function in society; and their usefulness to anthropologists. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: Political Anthropology
description: Focuses on that dimension of social interaction which involves the articulation and aggregation of interests within the political community. Emphasis on primitive and peasant communities (smallscale societies) drawing parallels to western society where appropriate.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to a formal) view of economic behavior. Focus on social organizational units such as lineages and clans which in primitive and peasant societies are engaged in productive and distributive activities.

title: Anthropology of the Film
description: Focuses on function and content of the ethnographic film from its inception to the present. Some contemporary documentary films will also be screened. Stress on treating the medium of film both in terms of its capacity to create a visual culture in contemporary society and the direct recording of primitive and peasant lifestyles.

title: Applied Anthropology and Community Development
description: Designed for persons who might become involved in planned change situations. Offers the conceptual framework and field experience to apply anthropological concepts and field research techniques to the identification and solution of practical human problems at the local level. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 160 or SOC 100 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Art and Anthropology
description: Provides a crosscultural coverage of major preliterate art traditions and introduces students to art in cultural contexts.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Acquaints the prospective teacher with basic concepts in cultural anthropology and provides the conceptual and analytical tools to understand whatever cultural setting he or she might be involved in. Examines ways in which cultural institutions, e.g., family, religion, politics, economy, might impinge on educational processes.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Field Anthropology of Distant Areas
description: Anthropological field study of distant geographical regions. Exploration and field work may be involved and travel to the staging area will probably be by airline.

title: Medical Anthropology
description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating nonwestern techniques to western counterparts. Specific contents of this comparison involve theories of disease causation, cultural taxonomy of therapeutic techniques and cure, and analysis of the role of the medical specialists (practitioners) in selected societies. Finally, the meeting together of western and nonwestern traditional and modern medicine will be assessed in terms of cultural evolutionary theory. Common background is provided for majors through a "core program in biology." The required courses of the core are organized with three levels of emphasis. The first level is designed to develop understanding of basic principles and biological processes which are common to living organisms. The second level focuses on organisms and is concerned with problems of structure, function, and classification in specific groups of plants and animals. The third level is concerned with developing understanding of interactions and adaptations of organisms in contexts ranging from world biome organization through molecular organization. In addition to the basic background work provided by courses in the core program, the department offers specialized course work in biology, botany, zoology, and science to meet the needs of particular individuals and groups. MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY The senior year (45 hours) of the major will consist of twelve months of hospital clinical medical laboratory training in an approved school of medical technology. All students are required to take a course in immunology prior to admission to the clinical year. This requirement can be met by taking Biology 344. § Prerequisite of ECON 201 waived for biology majors. Strongly recommended electives are BIO 453 or 311, and CHEM 325. Other electives are: ANAT 430, BIO 361, CHEM 300, and PHYCS 110, 112, 114. During the three years at Ball State University, the student pays the usual university fees and is subject to general regulations of the university. In the senior year students are required to pay no fees to the university. (The school of medical technology may require fees.) They must Provide books and uniforms required by the school of medical technology. The 52-week course is an integrated lecture and laboratory clinical experience. Two weeks of vacation are included. The university has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with Ball memorial Hospital, Muncie, Indiana; St. John's Hickey Memorial Hospital, Anderson, Indiana; St. Joseph's Memorial Hospital, Kokomo, Indiana; St. Francis Hospital, Beech Grove, Indiana; Lutheran Hospital and St. Joseph Hospital, Ft. Wayne, Indiana; Methodist Hospital and St. Vincent's Hospital, Indianapolis, Indiana. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to our schools exceeds the capacities of the schools. Selection of students is made entirely by the schools of medical technologY—based upon several factors including scholastic standing, personal interviews, and recommendations. Premedical technology students are therefore encouraged to plan a second or alternate degree choice. To qualify for certification as a medical technologist, the student must submit evidence of successful completion of the clinical year plus an official transcript from the university indicating date of conferral of degree, with a major in medical technology to the National Registry of Medical Technologists of the American Society of Clinical Pathologists in Chicago, Illinois. The student must then pass the national registry examination. The medical technologist is prepared to do laboratory work in any area of the clinical laboratory including bacteriology, chemistry, serology, and blood bank. There are positions calling for this preparation in hospital laboratories, physicians' and surgeons' clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories. Also, there are opportunities for work in research laboratories and in commercial companies making biological products. In addition students are required to earn four hours of credit in MATH 110, 111, or 112. PREMEDICAL PREPARATION Although approximately 90 percent of the students entering medical school will have had four years of premedical work, those with outstanding qualifications may be admitted after only three years. The student who wishes to qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine at the close of three years of premedical preparation will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 142 hours of liberal arts credit in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credits earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Medicine (45 hours) to meet senioryear course requirements on the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit in the first three years: Mathematics; CHEM 360 or 463; SPCH 210; BIO 311, 411, 492; CC 215; and ZOOL 447. Except when required to complete an undergraduate major, courses in human anatomy, human physiology, medical bacteriology, medical biochemistry, or medical pharmacology will not be accepted by the School of Medicine as part of the 142 hours of liberal arts credit. The student who prefers to obtain a baccalaureate degree before entering Indiana University School of Medicine will do so by completing all of the work on the Professional Arts Curriculum. Although it is possible to graduate with a departmental major in premedical preparation, it is highly recommended that the premedical student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry, or in any other area in which the student has a strong interest, because the number of applicants to a school of medicine far exceeds the capacity of the school, and an alternate goal is important. Students contemplating a career in medicine should bear in mind the stiff competition, and if they have not exhibited keen interest and aptitude in high school courses, especially in science, it will be very difficult for them to meet successfully the high standards required for admission to medical school. The student who wishes to obtain a degree and prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will follow the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum, will elect a teaching area major or teaching major, and will combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. Thus the student prepares for teaching in the field of the elected teaching concentration. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: BIO 311, 411, 492; CC 215; CHEM 360 or 463; SPCH 210; and ZOOL 447. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many medical schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other medical schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet specific requirements of the medical schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of the firstyear medical school credits on the Ball State University major is Indiana University. Students should take the Medical College Admission Test in the Spring Quarter fifteen months ahead of their expected entrance into medical school and should complete the formal application during the following summer, twelve months ahead. Premedical counseling is available in the Department of Biology. One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory performance on the Dental Admission Test given by the American Dental Association. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the admission test. The test should be taken in the Spring Quarter, fifteen months in advance of the student's expected entrance into dental school, but preferably only after completing the required biology and chemistry.
