The courses designated, when completed satisfactorily, will meet the preprofessional curricular requirements of Purdue at the end of the first year or those requirements of Butler at the end of either the first or second year. At both Purdue and Butler the prepharmacy, plus pharmacy, program is a total of five years. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to a college of pharmacy exceeds the capacity of the school and that a selection of students is therefore necessary, taking into consideration such factors as scholastic standing, character, and professional aptitude. The student's attention is directed to the admission and residence requirements set forth in the bulletins of Butler and Purdue Universities. These prepharmacy programs do not lead to graduation from Ball State University. They merely provide a student with an approved sequence of courses for the first one or two years of the complete fiveyear program. Furthermore, physical education is not a part of this program for students who plan to transfer to Purdue, but it is for those who will go to Butler. A student who drops out of the prepharmacy program and elects to follow a degree program of Ball State University will be expected to meet the physical education and general course requirements of the elected university curriculum. A careful arrangement of the program for each year is essential in order that courses may be completed in sequence and in the allotted time. It is particularly important that the general chemistry be completed in the freshman year. Mathematics, including calculus, is highly desirable. Copies of the programs may be obtained from the chairman of the Biology Department or the member of the Biology Department appointed by the chairman to serve as preprofessional adviser for students on these programs. There are minor differences in requirements between the School of Pharmacy at Purdue and the College of Pharmacy at Butler. Students planning to apply to Purdue's School of Pharmacy should make arrangements early in the Autumn Quarter to take the Pharmacy College Admission Test.

title: Man and the Life Sciences
description: An introductory course designed for the nonscience major. Topic emphasis is on the human and social aspects of biology: reproduction, birth control, genetic counseling, behavior, evolution, pollution, radiation, and energy. Course activities include study in a selfpaced, aurally guided multimedia learning center. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 102 or 112.

title: Biological Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles of biology as they relate to energy requirements and reproductive processes of living organisms, including the study of plant and animal adaptation as it influences survival and natural selection. Principles of ecology and conservation with emphasis on the human role in the environment. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Field and Classroom Experiences in Biology for Teachers
description: Basic biological relationships of plants and animals as they exist in the environment and basic recognition of important members of the plant and animal kingdoms. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Principles of biology including the physical basis of life, cell structure and function, energy flow in living systems, nutrition, drugs and drug abuse, cellular regulation and control, genetics, reproduction, development, biosystematics, evolution, and ecology.

title: Principles of Biology
description: Continuation of BIO 111. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Honors Symposium in Biology
description: An examination of some of the critical biological issues confronting contemporary society. Open only to freshmen participating in the Honors Program or others with permission of the department chairman or the director of the Honors Program.

title: Animal Biology
description: Major animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification, and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Biology
description: Major plant groups with emphasis on structure, function, classification and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative protozoa, bacteria, viruses, fungi, and algae. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation with emphasis on meiosis, Mendelian inheritance and probability considerations, sex and gene transmission and expression, linkage and crossingover, the nature of the hereditary material, and gene action. Som e atention to human and aplied genetics. Prerequisite: BIO 12.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Analysis of development concepts and phenomena, using current theories of biological information usage. Descriptive vertebrate embryology is emphasized in the laboratory work. Some attention is given to metamorphosis, regeneration, and neoplasia. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairman. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 211, 311; CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ecology
description: The relationships of organisms to physical, chemical, and biotic factors. Interactions are examined at the population and community levels of organization. Aquatic, saline, and terrestrial ecosystems are considered in terms of species composition, dominant organisms, climatic factors, and land use patterns. One twoday field trip required in addition to regular lab periods.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 101 or 325.

title: General Virology
description: Fundamentals of plant and animal virology. Physical and chemical properties of viruses; virushost interactions; pathogenesis of viral diseases. Replication, isolation, and identification of viruses with emphasis on tissue culture systems. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Bacteriology
description: Bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques in culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisites: BIO 213, and CHEM 130 or 230, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Immuno-Virology
description: General immunology and general virology with emphasis on practical experience in technique in the laboratory. The interrelationship of immunology laboratory techniques and viral growth techniques. Prerequisite: one course in microbiology and one course in organic chemistry.

title: Biometry
description: Principles and application of statistics to biological problems. The use of parametric and nonparametric tests of significance in solving biological problems. Practice in the analysis of data and the interpretation of biological experiments. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or equivalent.

title: Microtechnique 1
description: Methods and preparation of biological materials for teaching and research, including work in hematology, vital staining, photomicrography, and preparation of smears, squashes, and whole mounts. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and two courses in college chemistry.

title: Microtechnique 2
description: Preparation of sectioned tissues and histochemical treatment of materials, including the preparation of paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Recommended for students in research or in medical or laboratory fields. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213, and 12 quarter hours of college chemistry.

title: Honors Colloquium in Biology
description: Exploration of selected issues in biology with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Restricted to honors students or by permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Biology
description: Practical application of biology in a variety of situations including biology instruction as undergraduate teaching assistants and discussion leaders, arid practical experience in government or industrial laboratories and field stations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Designed to integrate and enhance understanding of basic principles of biology. Recent discoveries in biology and their implications in the biological sciences are stressed. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including the nature of the organization of the cell, basic bioenergetics and enzyme function, cell environment, membrane structure and function, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisite: CHEM 130 or 230 and BIO 213 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Radiobiology
description: Familiarizes the student with the nature of radiation, its effect on living tissue, the ways in which the isotopes can be used in research projects, and problems related to the use of nuclear power and radiation in the environment. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212, CHEM 130 or 230 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Biophysics
description: The study or description of biologic phenomena in terms of contributing physical events with laboratory emphasis on physical methods of studying the structure of biological molecules and physical forces important in biologic systems. Topics include: laws of thermodynamics, properties of macromolecular solutions, transport processes, electrophoresis, absorption and emission radiation, ultrasound, principles of various chromatographic procedures. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; CHEM 130 or 230; and MATH 112.

title: Evolution
description: The principles of evolution. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Cytology
description: Recent developments and methodologies concerning the structural organization of plant and animal cells and cellular organelles. Prerequisite: BIO 311. Prerequisite recommended: chemistry courses through organic.

title: Applied Microbiology
description: The study of microorganisms that cause beneficial or detrimental changes in food, dairy, and industrial products. Microbiological principles involved in the study of microorganisms in food, dairy, and industrial production in addition to production methodology. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Advanced Genetics
description: A second course in genetics with emphasis on recent advances. Prerequisite: BIO 311, CHEM 230. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 411.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Mankind
description: Current problems in human heredity. Chromosome aberrations and developmental abnormalities. DNA, the genetic code, and sickle cell anemia. Consanguineous marriages and genetic defects. Mendelian principles applied to humans. Pedigrees and probability. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems associated with recent advances in genetics.

title: Molecular Biology
description: The structure and function of macromolecules found in living things. Emphasis will be placed on the threedimensional structure of molecules and biological control mechanism. Various recent models for enzyme mechanisms, DNA replication, protein synthesis, and membrane structure and function will be investigated. Prerequisite: BIO 411 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Molecular Biology 2
description: Recent developments in DNA and RNA research, membrane biology, protein processing, and cellular control mechanisms. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Bioenergetics
description: The study of flow of energy in biological systems with emphasis on application of laws of thermodynamics to biological processes, energy production metabolism in chemotrophs and phototrophs, and the major uses of energy in biological systems. Prerequisite: BIO 411, its equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Museum Techniques
description: Methods of preparing plant and animal specimens for display. Maintenance of museum records. Use of museum materials for educational and research functions. Taxidermy not included. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Limnology
description: The dimensions of the physical, chemical, and biological factors of inland waters. One twohour laboratory per week and two or three fullday field trips will be devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 313 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Water Pollution Biology
description: Water pollution with emphasis on analysis of trophic structure in polluted and nonpolluted ecosystems. Ecological change and eutrophication as affected by pollutants from industrial, municipal, urban, and rural sources. Prerequisite: BIO 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Aquatic Microbiology
description: Microorganisms indigenous to aquatic ecosystems and their role in nutrient cycling. Emphasis on organisms involved in nitrogen, sulfur, carbon, and iron transformations. The morphology, physiology, and ecology of specific organisms will be discussed. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Marine Biology
description: Introduction to marine environments. Properties: seawater, hydrodynamics. Phytoplankton/benthic plants. Primary production, nutrient cycles. Marine animals, surveys of major taxa, food resources. Adaptations for life on the bottom, open water, intertidal zones, estuaries, abyssal regions. Population sampling and analysis. Problems of overexploitation /pollution.

title: Bioethical Decision-Making
description: Analysis of bioethical problems such as evolution, genetic engineering, food and famine, generated by the application of biological and biotechnological knowledge and research using a confluent, developmental methodology. Prerequisite: junior standing and the completion of Option II of the general studies science requirement or

title: Research Techniques in Biology
description: Principles and applications of laboratory procedure s used in biological research. Emphasis on methods of determining population growths, rates of enzymatic reactions, effects of the environment on biological processes, and interpretation of results. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with spe cial aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours credit may be taken at one time. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Anatomy
description: Origin and structure of cells, tissues, and organs of higher plants. Prerequisite: BIO 212.

title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
description: The identification of native flowering plants. Emphasis on the distinguishing features of the major plant groups and use of manuals. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Forestry
description: A survey course in forestry which includes a consideration of the major areas in that discipline. Emphasis is on management, problems, and use of midwestern wood lots. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods should be anticipated.

title: Plant Morphology
description: Forms, life cycles, and evolution of the major plant groups. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ornamental Plants
description: Identification and uses of ornamental trees, shrubs, vines, and annuals. Selection, special characteristics, adaptability, and maintenance of ornamentals.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the propagation and cultivation of plants in homes, schools, gardens, and greenhouses.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on pathogenic forms. Methods for identification of fungi will be discussed along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BIO 212 and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Intermediate Plant Physiology
description: A continuation of BOT 451 with emphasis on independent study of detailed physiological mechanisms. Prerequisite: BOT 451.

title: Dendrology
description: The identification and site characterization of woody plants with an emphasis on Midwestern tree species. Utilization of botanical features and keys in field identification. Correlation of species with site factors, plant diseases, climatic parameters, associate species, and geographical distribution. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection, identification, and preservation of plants from freshwater ecosystems. The morphology, physiology, and ecology of these plants will be stressed in order to better understand their distributions in nature. Techniques for measuring the growth and abundance of aquatic plants will also be studied. One or two weekend field trips will be made to study aquatic plants in their natural habitats. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary Schools
description: Methods of teaching science concepts, process skills, and scientific attitudes are developed through direct experiences. Recent elementary science tests, courses of study, and curricular materials are examined and utilized. Experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and special methods are utilized.

title: The Teaching of Science in the Junior High School
description: Recent curriculum developments in junior high school science. Science curriculum instruction related to the physical, mental, and emotional characteristics of the junior high school student. Prerequisite: 36 hours of credit in courses in the sciences.

title: Teaching Science in the Early Childhood and Primary Grades
description: Analysis of the cognitive, psychomotor, and affective processes inherent in science investigations for young children. Handson activities with science materials appropriate for early childhood and primary children. Designed primarily for students on early childhood/primary education programs. Prerequisite: 12 hours of science or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Teaching of Science in the Secondary School
description: Philosophy and methods in science teaching. Emphasis on laboratory investigations. Concepts and conceptual schemes in science. Levels of organization in secondary school science courses. Evaluation of learning in science. Supplies, equipment, and facilities. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum and 20 hours in biology, chemistry, earth science, or physics content courses or permission of the department chairman.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials.
description: Scienceoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of science, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of science in the secondary school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Up to five hours' experience in public schools may be required. Prerequisite or parallel: SCI 395 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 399 .

title: History and Philosophy of Science
description: The history of science. Consideration is given to the impact of science on mankind, the part science plays in bringing about general knowledge, and how science influences decision making.

title: Comparative Vertebrate Anatomy
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and relationships of vertebrates. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Invertebrate groups. Phylogeny, comparative morphology, and life histories. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisites: BIO 211, and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ornithology
description: Birds. Field identification, classification, behavior, and economic relationships. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisites: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 211.

title: Herpetology
description: The natural history, identification, systematics, and distribution of amphibians and reptiles. Field work required. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Ichthyology
description: The study of fish with emphasis on identification, classification, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Indiana species will be emphasized but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The behavior of individuals and of populations. The economic relationships of mammals. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth and arthropod parasites of animals. Emphasis on identification, life cycles, and hostparasite relationships. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Field Zoology
description: The field study of animals; terrestrial and aquatic; invertebrate and vertebrate; microscopic and macroscopic: with emphasis on collection and identification of noninsect invertebrates. Three twohour fieldlaboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Protozoology
description: An introduction to aspects of the morphology, physiology, ecology, and development of protozoa. Prerequisites: BIO 211 and 213.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on the terrestrial vertebrates of the United States. The management and harvest of wildlife. Additional field work, including one extended field trip, may be required.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identification, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasis placed on aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress. Prerequisite: ZOOL 341 or permission of the department chairman. title: Man and Chemistry
description: Nonmathematical treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as: organization of chemistry, language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature of matter, classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevance of these to everyday living. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 110 or 113.

title: General Chemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Description of elements and compounds; their structure, bonding, and stoichiometry with the main emphasis placed on the solution chemistry of electrolytes. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly.

title: Organic and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of both organic chemistry and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures, one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 105 or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 111.

title: General Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, and the nature of matter stressed. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 113.

title: General Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 110, including properties of solutions, colloids, chemical kinetics, chemical equilibrium, and electrochemistry. Prerequisite: MATH 110 and CHEM 110 or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 114.

title: General Chemistry 3
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemistry of metals and nonmetals, carbon compounds, nuclear structure, and radioactivity. Laboratory work includes qualitative analysis. Prerequisite: MATH 111 and CHEM 111 or equivalents. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 115.

title: Chemical Principles 1
description: A comprehensive treatment of the fundamentals of chemistry, with emphasis on periodic relationships and stoichiometry. For science and preprofessional majors requiring more than one year of college chemistry. Class, 3 hours; prelab, 1 hour; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry or permission of the department head. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH Hi or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 110. 1 14. Chemical Principles 2. (5) Continuation and extension of CHEM 113, with emphasis on solutions, chemical kinetics, energetics, and equilibria. Laboratory work includes qualitativ e analysis. Thre lectures, two threhour laboratories wekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 13 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 111.

title: Chemical Principles 3
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 114, with emphasis on thermodynamics, ionic equilibria, chemistry of metals, and nuclear chemistry. Prerequisite : CHEM 14. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 12.

title: Survey of Organic and Biological Chemistry
description: A broadly based introductory course suitable for life science, natural resources, and general science majors. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 2 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 111 or equivalent.

title: Fundamentals of Chemical Analysis
description: Theory, techniques, and applications of quantitative analytical chemical measurements. Acquisition, evaluation, and statistical treatment of experimental data. Class, 1 hour; prelab, 1 hour; laboratory, 4 hours per week. Prerequisite or parallel: CHEM 115. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 225.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements, including gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations, ionexchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visible spectrophotometry. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 6 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 223.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: The aliphatic hydrocarbons and their derivatives, including nomenclature, chemical and physical properties, and their practical application. Three lectures, one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 115. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 233.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 230, including optical activity and the chemistry of carbohydrates and proteins. Prerequisite: CHEM 230. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 234.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of aromatic hydrocarbons, heterocyclic compounds, natural products, dyes, medicinals, and plastics. Prerequisite: CHEM 231. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 235.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material deals with covalent bonding, molecular structure, and the chemistry of elementary organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 115. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 230.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 233. Lecture material covers the chemistry of common functional groups, stereochemistry, and the carbohydrates. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 233 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 231.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 234. Lecture material covers the chemistry of amines and phenols. Selected advanced topics will be discussed. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 234 or permission of the department head. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 232.

title: Chemical Calculations
description: Treatment of practical chemical problems of widely varied mathematical types, including dimensional and error analysis, graphical presentation, chemical examples of simple calculus procedures, series, and symmetry. Class, 2 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 115. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 161 or 170 or equivalent.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentation: electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods. For chemical/medical technologists or departmental minors. Class, 1 hour; prelab, 1 hour; laboratory, 4 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 223 or 225.

title: Analytical Chemistry in Foods and Nutrition
description: Modern methods of chemical analysis applied to selected foodstuffs and biochemical samples, with particular emphasis on spectrophotometric and chromatographic techniques. Class, 2 hours; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite or parallel: CHEM 360.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: The thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three lectures and one fourhour laboratory weekly, including a onehour discussion period. Prerequisite: CHEM 223 or 225, MATH 172, and one year of college physics. Chemistry 233

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 343. Prerequisite: CHEM 343.

title: Physical Chemistry 3
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 344. Prerequisite: CHEM 344.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions, and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and, kinetics. Especially for chemistry minors, premedical, biology, general science majors, and chemistry teaching majors with permission of the department chairman. Three lectures and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 115 and CHEM 300 or MATH 161 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 343.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry
description: Chemistry of biological compounds, their metabolism, and the regulation of metabolic processes. For students in life sciences, dietetics, or medical technology. Class, 3 hours; laboratory, 3 hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or equivalent. Not open to departmental majors in chemistry.

title: Specialized Topics in Chemistry
description: Discussion and/or experimentation in specialized topics in and related to chemistry (such as environmental chemistry, glassworking, water analysis, computer interfacing, chemistry in industry, and other specialty areas). Information concerning specific topics offered during a given quarter may be obtained from the departmental office. Lecture/discussion and/or laboratory schedules appropriate to the topics offered. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned in this course but no more than 2 hours may be counted toward departmental major or minor requirements.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for chemical technologists. Assignments equivalent to ten clock hours per week. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of the department head. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry.

title: The Teaching of Chemistry in the Secondary School
description: A study of current chemistry curricula, laboratory safety, multimedia materials development, professional organizations, lesson planning with performance objectives, and integrated sciences. Required for all teaching majors and teaching minors in chemistry. One lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: 20 hours of credit in chemistry. Prerequisite or parallel: SCI 395 or an equivalent course in another subject matter field.

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Preparation and evaluation of scientific manuscripts and their oral presentation. One twohour discussion session weekly. Prerequisite: 30 quarter hours of chemistry or permission of the department head.

title: Chemical Instrumentation

Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections Brodt, Chairperson; Carlie, Hendricks, Hewitt, Marting, Mickish, Neiman The Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections offers a broad range of courses relevant to our system of adult and juvenile justice for both the preprofessional and the liberal arts student. The departmental major leads to a Bachelor of Science degree when combined with required and elective courses in other areas. The Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections also offers a two year Associate in Arts degree and a departmental minor. The departmental major provides the student with a body of knowledge about the organization, structure, and function of the constituent elements comprising our society. The student also gains a perspective about such areas as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, and our system of criminal justice. Additionally, the student is presented with a workable combination of theory and practical experience in the areas of law enforcement and corrections. Another objective of the criminal justice and corrections major is to give students the opportunity to prepare themselves as preprofessionals for firstlevel positions in law enforcement, probation, parole, and institutional or community treatment settings, or for future graduate study in related areas. The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and employment: law enforcement, probation services offered by both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. Law enforcement officers are employed at three levels of government: local, state, and federal. Local law enforcement officers include municipal policemen and policewomen as well as deputy sheriffs. On the state level, all states hire officer candidates for state police departments. On the federal level, approximately forty agencies employ persons with training in law enforcement as well as in other areas of specialization. The increasing need for law enforcement in our society indicates that future employment, particularly on the local levels, will be good. Probation, which is essentially supervision of adjudicated adult criminals and juvenile delinquents, is a service offered by almost all of our adult felony and juvenile courts. Probation officers are employees of court and as such are involved in persontoperson contact with a variety of offenders. Every state maintains a variety of correctional institutions and programs for adult and juvenile offenders of both sexes. These range from open institutions with a minimum of security to maximum security institutions for adult male offenders. In addition, such facilities as youth camps, diagnostic and reception centers, and work release centers are integral parts of most state systems. Employment opportunities for both men and women range from custodial officers to caseworkers or counselors within the various settings. Parole supervision is generally a function of a state administration agency, such as a Parole Board or a Division of Parole, and may vary from state to state. Parole is essentially the supervision of offenders once they have been released from a state institution or facility. Parole officers aid the offender in his return to civilian life in a variety of ways ranging from helping with employment and living arrangements to providing counseling in personal problems which may affect the parolee's successful adjustment. Criminal Justice and Corrections 235 In recent years there has been an increase in the number of facilities and agencies, essentially communitybased, which offer employment to persons interested in rehabilitating delinquent and criminal offenders. Group foster homes, regional or local detention centers, and day treatment centers, as well as a variety of halfway houses, are just a few examples. Field Experiences The Department of Criminal Justice and Corrections has created a program which offers a maximum of choices in practical work experiences. The department offers two practicum courses, one of which is required for graduation. The student has a choice between placement in the field of corrections or the field of law enforcement. The choice should be made on the basis of student interest and employment goals. The department also offers two elective internship courses. The student may elect to have four entirely different field experiences if scheduling permits. title: Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
description: Provides students with an overview of the criminal justice system as well as a preview of vocational opportunities.

title: Data and Theories of Crime and Delinquency
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior, typologies of crime and criminals; the trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and current theoretical explanations.

title: Processing Adult and Juvenile Offenders
description: Emphasizes the juvenile and adult justice systems, their components, recent changes, and future developments.

title: Fundamentals of Law Enforcement
description: An examination of sociological research and theory bearing on major social factors that affect municipal police organizations as important coordinating agencies in society. title: Introduction to Corrections

description: The role of security in crime prevention and the criminal justice system; standards for private security in relation to administrative, personnel, and physical aspects of the security fields; methods of reducing property loss by security in proprietary and governmental institutions.

title: Women and Crime
description: An examination of traditional and contemporary explanations of female delinquency and criminality, the differential treatment accorded female defendants and victims, and the nature of state and federal correctional systems for women.

title: Domestic Violence
description: An examination of criminal justice aspects of domestic violence in contemporary America.

title: Organized Crime
description: The nature and structure of organized crime in America with special emphasis on the history and changing images of organized crime, its operation and activities, and programs for control.

title: White Collar Crime
description: An examination of the criminological aspects of white collar crime in American society. * No more than a total of 8 hours in field experience may be counted toward the major.

title: Victims of Crime
description: A criminological examination of the victims of crime in contemporary America.

title: Criminal Law
description: Emphasis on the practical aspect of the application of Indiana crimi nal law for present and prospective criminal justice practitioners; purposes and functions of the substantive criminal law; historical foundations; the limits of the criminal law. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 340 or 350.

title: Sex and the Law
description: A review of the development and present status of laws governing sex offenses and their impact on the criminal justice system.

title: Criminal Evidence
description: Emphasis on current Indiana criminal procedure and rules governing admissibility of evidence, as well as procedural considerations affecting arrest, search, and seizure. Focus will be on the casestudy approach.

title: Criminal Investigation
description: Deals with the fundamentals of investigation; crime scene search and recording; collection and preservation of physical evidence; scientific aids; modus operandi; sources of information; interview and interrogation; followup and case preparation.

title: Police-Community Relations
description: Analysis of interrelationship between police and public in the study and control of crime. Consideration is given to problems of policecommunity relations and to ways of establishing cooperation between police and various social, economic, and ethnic groups.

title: Correctional Institutions
description: An indepth inquiry into the function, structure, and operations of American adult and juvenile correctional institutions.

title: Probation and Parole
description: The organization and operation of probation and parole systems in the United States, with emphasis on Indiana. Topics will include history, law, ideologies, varieties of practice, evaluation, contemporary problems, and future trends in probation and parole.

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice and Corrections
description: Limited to majors in criminal justice and corrections, to explore in depth and to summarize current problems, theory, research, and trends in the field. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of the department chairman. Open only to students majoring in criminal justice and corrections.

title: Police Principles and Procedures
description: Provides students with a basic understanding of police organization and management procedure. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 340 or 350.

title: Practicum in Law Enforcement
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in police settings on the local and state levels. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. Open only to students with a major in criminal justice and corrections.

title: Internship in Law Enforcement

title: Practicum in Corrections
description: A field work course combining practical experience and theoretical orientations in correctional settings on the state and local level. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to students with a major in criminal justice and corrections.

title: Internship in Corrections
description: An internship involving fulltime individual assignments under field supervision in a variety of correctional settings. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in CJC courses and permission of the department chairman.

description: An individualized course of reading or limited research designed to allow majors an opportunity to explore specific topics related to the entire criminal justice system under the direction of a specific faculty member. title: English for Non-Native Speakers of English
description: Stress on sounds, structure, and vocabulary of English in order to increase the student's facility in use of the language. Students will receive individual help in language laboratory. description: Continued attention to the problems of syntax, pronunciation, and vocabulary that are difficult for foreign students. Emphasis on written composition. Undergraduate nonnative students registering for ENG 101 will be required to complete the course with credit before being granted permission to proceed to

description: Introduction to composition with an emphasis on writing short essays. Assigned readings. Specific competencies will be identified at the beginning of the quarter and measured at the end of the quarter. Prerequisite: ENG 103 or the equivalent.

description: Continued instruction in composition skills through oral and written work. Assigned readings. Further instruction in research techniques. title: Honors English Composition 2
description: Instruction in composition with emphasis on writing essays. Assigned readings. Introduction to basic research methods. title: Honors Humanities 2: Western Thought from Montaigne to Rousseau

title: Honors Humanities 3: Western Thought from Dostoyevsky to Sartre
description: Some major writing in literature, philosophy, and science from 1800 until the present.

description: Introduction to selected pieces of world literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 206.

title: World Literature Masterpieces
description: Selected major works of world literature, exclusive of English and American literature, for students who are majors or minors in English. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 205.

title: American Literature
description: Instruction to selected pieces of American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: British Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of British literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for those who are not English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar and Usage
description: Basic course in English grammar and usage for the student whose knowledge of grammatical terminology, structure, and usage is deficient. Not to be counted as part of the total hours in a major or minor program in English.

title: Advanced Composition and Creative Writing
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for the general student, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation; and instruction in creative writing, particularly fiction and poetry. Open only to English majors and minors, except by permission of the department chairman. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent, and sophomore standing.

title: Professional Writing
description: Discussion of principles of organization, structures, and style in writing reports and papers. Intensive practice in writing different types of reports and papers. Designed primarily for students pursuing the General Arts or the Professional Arts curriculum.

title: Advanced Expository Writing
description: Intensive study of the essay and guided practice in the techniques of expository writing for students not majoring or minoring in English. Prerequisite : ENG 205 or 206. Not open to students with areas in English.

title: Introduction to American Literature
description: Introduction to selected American writers and their works with an emphasis on those that junior high/middle school teachers should know and be able to read skillfully. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to British Literature
description: Introduction to selected writers and periods in British literature with an emphasis on those that junior high/middle school teachers should know. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: American Literature, 1607-1860
description: A survey of American literature from its beginning through the middle nineteenth century, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent.

title: English Literature of the Middle Ages and Renaissance
description: Emphasizes major works of a number of the literary figures of the period in their historical and philosophical contexts. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature of the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries
description: An extensive study of English literature of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, or from 1600 to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds of the periods. A close reading of the works of major writers is emphasized, but not to the exclusion of the works of minor writers. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Literature: 1780 to the Present
description: British literature from 1780 to the present, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Literature and the Narrative Media
description: A consideration of the ways in which the narrative media have been used to develop fictional and nonfictional literature. Special attention to works which have been adapted from one medium to another and to works which have lasting significance. Attention will be given to the narrative media and the language arts curriculum in junior high/middle and secondary schools.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials in teaching language attitudes, habits, and skills. Consideration of written and oral expression, language usage, spelling, writing, and literature.

title: Literature for Young Children
description: An introduction to recent literature for young children. Of special interest to students of early childhood education and to parents and future parents.

title: Modern English Grammar
description: Modern English grammar, with emphasis on the application of the methods of uptodate descriptive linguistics to an understanding of basic grammatical terminology, relationships, and structure, including morphology (wordbuilding) and phonology (sound system).

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: The English Language: Past and Present
description: An introduction to the history and structure of the English language: a survey of important historical changes in the structure of English; a scientific study of the structure of modern English; and a survey of the dialectal variations in modern English.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of the field of children's literature and an intensive study of types at various levels. Junior or senior standing recommended.

title: Linguistic Phonetics
description: Speech sounds and the linguistic methods employed in their description, classification, and analysis as elements in language systems.

title: American Literature, 1860-1960
description: A survey of selected American writers and the various literary movements since 1860, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: An intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Literature of Black America

title: American Indian Literature

The emphasis will be on works by American Indians, but some works about Indians by white authors may also be included.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to the Restoration

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century

title: English Drama from the Restoration to the Present
description: English drama from 1700 to the present. Special attention is given to the plays of Steele, Goldsmith, Sheridan, Wilde, Shaw, Synge, O'Casey, Osborne, Beckett, and Pinter.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century

title: Studies in British Drama

description: Special research topics in British literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religiou s atitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or thequivalent.

description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the department chairman.

description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in the field of English education, preschool through the secondary level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206 and permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading Printed Materials in the English Classroom
description: Provides an overview of the process of reading printed materials with practical suggestions for developing analytic skills for reading and interpreting written communications, including literary and popular materials used in the English classroom.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Emphasis on the actual reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical aspects.

title: Old English
description: An introduction to Old English with readings in representative texts.

title: American Indian Folklore
description: The stories, tales, and rituals from American Indian oral traditions, selected to represent major themes, types, and culture areas. Not to be counted as part of the total hours in a major or minor program in English.

title: American Folklore
description: Materials and techniques for presenting the American heritage of folklore and folk literature at the public school level. Books, films, filmstrips, recordings, and pictorial collections are among the materials studied.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 1: Theory
description: The psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in second language teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel: ENG 420 or 321.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 2: Materials and Practices
description: An application of theories of language learning to preparation of materials in English as a second language and their use in the classroom. Students will work with students of English as a foreign language in an actual teaching situation. Prerequisite: ENG 436. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Contrastive Analysis
description: Language universals and a comparison of the structural systems of language. Examines and compares languages to note the differing ways in which meaning can be expressed. Students may work on a general topic in the area or on a comparison of two or more languages of their choice.

title: Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of transcendentalism. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Poe, Hawthorne, Melville
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of romanticism. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twain, James, Adams, Crane
description: An intensive reading of their principal works, and a study of the philosophical and literary implications of the varieties of realism. Prerequisite: ENG 340.

title: American Literature, 1945 to Present
description: A survey of the works of major writers and literary trends in America since World War II. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Renaissance and Seventeenth-Century Studies
description: The nondramatic literature of the Tudor, Stuart, and Puritan periods (1485-1660), exclusive of Shakespeare and Milton. Major writers such as Spenser, Donne, and Jonson will be considered in terms of their influence and of their political and philosophical backgrounds.

title: Chaucer
description: A study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several of the minor poems. Emphasis upon the structure, the sources, and the significance of the works included. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare
description: An introductory study of representative plays (comedies, histories, tragedies) and some selections from the sonnets by Shakespeare.

title: Studies in Shakespeare
description: Special topics in a selection of Shakespeare's tragedies, comedies, and histories. Open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Studies in English Literature of the Restoration and Eighteenth Century
description: An extensive study of the nondramatic works of Dryden, Swift, Pope, and Johnson, with possible supplementary readings from other British authors of the period 1660-1800. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Milton
description: A study of Milton's family background, political service, and poetic apprenticeship, culminating in close analytical investigation of Paradise Lost and Samson Agonistes. Attention is given also to Milton's aesthetic propositions and to his social and political prose works.

title: Romantic Studies
description: The poetry and prose of Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Keats, and Shelley.

title: Victorian Studies
description: An intensive study of the works of Carlyle, Tennyson, Browning, Ruskin, and Arnold.

title: Women in Literature
description: An investigation of the various ways in which women have been portrayed in the literature of the Western world. Not to be counted as part of the total hours in a major or minor program in English.

title: Twentieth-Century British Studies
description: A study in depth of several significant twentiethcentury authors (such as Shaw, Conrad, Lawrence, Joyce, Woolf, Waugh, Durrell, Beckett, and Auden) and the intellectual and literary movements closely associated with them.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War I to the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. Department of Foreign Languages Gardiol, Chairperson; Barnette, Brown, Coen, Fritz, Gilman, Goertz, Hightower, Johnson, Kadletz, Kasparek, Magrath, Sotiropoulos, Warner The Department of Foreign Languages is equipped to offer a varied program of quality instruction in both ancient and modern foreign languages. Close cooperation with other departments on campus makes possible the combining of foreign language training with other disciplines. Classroom and librarytype foreign language laboratories are designed for class instruction as well as for selfinstruction. Such programs as exchanges with schools of other countries, academic summers and study opportunities abroad, and foreign language houses with pleasant, hometype living accommodations and native speakers in French, German, and Spanish as directors offer intensified language practice and cultural enrichment. Language proficiency tests make possible the awarding of credit based on prior language study and placement in classes at appropriate levels. The Department of Foreign Languages offers indepth training for all types of language oriented students: —for those desiring to enrich their professional preparedness by acquiring a knowledge of a foreign language; —for those desiring a broad liberal education; —for preprofessional students in such areas as law, medicine, library science, and business; —for graduatelevel students who need a reading competency in foreign language to meet program requirements; —for students on the teaching program seeking permanent certification for teaching at the elementary and secondary levels; -for students planning to acquire skills for further study at other graduate schools offering the Ph.D. in languages; -for those desiring to improve their abilities in English through the transfer value of classical and modern foreign languages; -for those desiring practical training in translation skills. Students who begin their study of a foreign language at Ball State University will start with the initial course in the 100-level sequence. Students with secondary school credit in a foreign language or other previous noncollege language training will be placed in appropriate courses through the placement examination administered by the Department of Foreign Languages. No placement credit is given for 101, but students placed in 103 or any higherlevel course may receive Ball State University credit for 102 and each higherlevel course thereafter by earning a grade of or better in the course in which they are placed. Both undergraduate and graduate students should regularly consult with foreign language departmental advisers about sequencing of courses in accordance with individual needs. Additionally, students will be guided by the statements in the Curricula section of the catalog and by the area requirements given below. For a statement of the foreign language requirements for the Bachelor of Arts degree, see Degrees, Baccalaureate. The lowerdivision courses in foreign language are highly sequential and should be taken in order except in special cases. Entry into 200-level courses requires the successful completion of the 101-2-3 courses or equivalents as determined by the departmental placement program.
