title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Introduces the student to the cardinal features of the Greek and Roman civilization.

title: Word Origins and Vocabulary Development
description: Latin borrowings, Latin prefixes, roots, and suffixes in English. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin is required. Open to all students.

title: Scientific Terminology, the Greek Element
description: Considers the composition of Greekbased words used by the physical, biological, medical, and technical sciences.

title: Scientific Terminology, the Latin Element
description: Considers the composition of Latinbased words used by the physical, biological, medical, and other technical sciences.

title: Roman Private and Public Life
description: All phases of Roman customs referred to in Latin commonly read in secondary school are carefully examined and understood. No reading knowledge of Latin required. Open to all students.

title: Introduction to Mythology
description: Primarily a general education course, dealing with myths of the Greeks and Romans and their use in literature and art. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin required.

title: The Old Testament as Literature
description: Considers the Old Testament as typical of, related to, and source of some of the major literary genres, such as history and biography, prophetic literature, lyric poetry, dramatic literature, and short stories and tales.

title: Women in Ancient Greece and Rome
description: Famous women in literature and history are studied in this course which observes and traces the emergence of contemporary Western attitudes regarding women; the course explores and evaluates the status and role of the Greco- Roman woman as determined by social, political, and legal institutions.

title: The Classical World in Film, Fiction, and Fact
description: A broad survey of life in the classical Mediterranean world through the media of motion pictures, fiction, nonfiction (such as historical, archaeological, and anthropological studies). It is strongly recommended that all candidates for endorsements take FL 496 The Teaching of Foreign Languages in the Elementary School.

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selected masterpieces of classical literature; historical development of the various types of literature as a background for further study in Latin and English. No reading knowledge of Greek and Latin required. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: Introduces the student to the cultural achievements of the ancient Greeks and their contribution to the modern world.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: Provides the student with a fundamental knowledge of the social, cultural, and economic framework within which the ancient Romans lived.

title: German Literature in English Translation
description: Primarily a general education course. The aim of the course is to expose the non-German reader to great German writers and thinkers. The course may not be applied toward areas in German.

title: Hispanic Literature in Translation
description: Primarily a general education course, exposing the non-Spanish reader to the great writers of the Hispanic world. The course may not be applied toward areas in Spanish.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: A literary study of representative mythologies selected from Egyptian, Sumerian, Teutonic, Slavonic, and other mythologies of the world. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures through Motion Pictures
description: Presentations of the literary matter of many nations through the medium of films. Ten films will be shown. Selected ones will be compared to the works of literature. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Historical Linguistics
description: An introduction to the scientific study of language for students in foreign language. An elementary survey of the methods used in historical and comparative linguistic analysis with application to language usually taught in college. Gives the language student some basic insights into the linguistic principles that underlie change in language.

title: Guided Self-Instruction Studies in Less Commonly Taught Languages
description: Languages such as Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, Hebrew (Modern), Greek (Modern), Russian, and Portuguese are offered at basic spoken levels by Guided Self-Instruction (GSI). Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in one language and as many as 12 hours may be earned in any one quarter or term. Not open to the student who is a native speaker.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Foreign Language in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and applications of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching foreign language in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite: EDJHM 312 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College or permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Foreign Language
description: Methods current iv foreign language teaching in the senior high school. Directed observation of classes, specific problems of presentation, choice of texts, and organization of teaching materials and supplementary aids are worked out in detail. Attention is given to the Report of the Foreign Language Study and to the courses of study recommended by the State Department of Education. Prerequisite: two years of college credit in French, German, Latin, or Spanish, or the equivalent; EDSEC 299; and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials in Teaching Foreign Languages
description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of foreign languages, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of foreign languages in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: FL 395.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Language House Living and Learning
description: Offers students the option of earning a limited amount of credit for the language learning experience provided by the foreign language houses. A total of 3 hours of credit per language may be earned in any one house, but no more than 1 credit may be earned at one time. Offered on credit/nocredit basis only.

title: The Teaching of Foreign Language in the Elementary School
description: Development of foreign language instruction in the elementary school. Curricula, training of teachers, and teaching methods; also phonemics, pronunciation, and a review of other basic language elements.

title: Beginning French
description: The first course in the French language.

title: Beginning French
description: Prerequisite: FR 101.

title: Beginning French (continued)
description: Prerequisite: FR 102 or one year of secondary school French.

title: Basic Conversational French for Travelers
description: Beginning spoken French for travelers to Frenchspeaking countries, not applicable to a major or minor in French. Not open to the student who has credit in any collegelevel French course.

title: Intermediate French
description: Prerequisite: one year of college French or two years of secondary school French.

title: Intermediate French (continued)
description: Prerequisites: 16 hours of college French or two and onehalf years of secondary school French.

title: Intermediate French (continued)
description: Prerequisites: 20 hours of college French or two and onehalf years of secondary school French.

title: Conversation 1
description: Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Students wishing additional instruction should register for FR 404 or 504.

title: Composition 1
description: Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent. Students wishing additional instruction should register for FR 405.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the French language and the application of phonetics to the understanding and speaking of French. Use of the phonetic alphabet. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Business French
description: Designed to familiarize the advanced French student with commercial forms and terminology used in business, banking, and industry. Prerequisite: FR 203 or the equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture: Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 309 prior to September, 1973.

title: Short Story
description: A study of the short story in French literature. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Classical Drama
description: The plays of Corneille, Racine, and Moliere. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Poetry
description: A study of French poetry with emphasis on the Symbolists and on contemporary poets. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Novel
description: Extensive reading in French novel. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Modern Drama
description: Extensive reading in French drama. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Contemporary French Civilization
description: Presentday France and French institutions viewed in the context of French perception of the family, education, politics, the judicial system, the economy, and religion. Supplementary readings in current newspapers and periodicals. Lectures in English; readings in French and English. Prerequisite: FR 203 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Modern Reading
description: Contemporary prose and poetry. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Literary Heritage of France
description: Selections from various periods of French literature. A onequarter offering designed to develop an appreciation of the literary heritage of France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in two of the following courses: FR 421, 422, and 423 or the equivalent.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. Travel may be by air. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students with areas in French or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: Conversation 2
description: A continuation of FR 304. Prerequisite: FR 304.

title: Composition 2
description: A continuation of FR 305. Prerequisite: FR 305.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the Classical Age to 1760. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 2
description: The classical age from 1760 and the eighteenth century. Literature of the golden age of classicism and the eighteenthcentury philosophies. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 3
description: The nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The development of romanticism, realism, naturalism, and symbolism in French literature; literature of contemporary France. Prerequisites: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Reading Course
description: Prerequisites: three years of college French or the equivalent, or permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning German
description: The first course in the German language.

title: Beginning German
description: Prerequisite: GER 101.

title: Beginning German (continued)
description: Prerequisite: GER 102 or one year of secondary school German.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Introduction to the basic German grammar needed for the reading of German texts required for science majors.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Completion of the basic German grammar needed for the reading of German texts required for science majors and some selected readings of appropriate texts. Prerequisite: GER 104 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Beginning German for Science Majors
description: Reading appropriate German texts to build the student's competence in reading and translating expository materials. Prerequisite: GER 105 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Basic Conversational German for Travelers
description: Beginning spoken German for travelers or those seeking employment in Germany. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The first in a threequarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Not open to the student who has credit in German except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The second in a threequarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Prerequisite: GER 108. Not open to the student who has credit in German other than GER 108 except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Guten Tag: Learning German with Films
description: The third in a threequarter course in conversational German entailing work with twentysix German language films and accompanying textbook. The film episodes give the American student interesting and meaningful insights into the culture of a foreign land and people. Prerequisite: GER 108 and

title: Guten Tag: German Language Television Course
description: Affords the student who is unable to attend a regular language course on campus the opportunity to do independent study. Gives the student a fundamental knowledge of basic conversational German. Not open to the student who has credit in GER 101, 102, and 103 or GER 108, 109, 110.

title: Intermediate German
description: Reading of representative German authors of moderate difficulty. Vocabulary, increased knowledge of German idiom, and practice in writing German are emphasized. Prerequisite: one year of college German or two years of secondary school German.

title: Intermediate German (continued)
description: Prerequisites: 16 hours of college German or two and onehalf years of secondary school German.

title: Intermediate German (continued)
description: Extensive reading of German authors in class. Prerequisites: 20 hours of college German or two and onehalf years of secondary school German.

title: Conversation
description: To increase fluency in speaking and ease of comprehension through conversation. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or GER 504.

title: Composition
description: To familiarize students with the fine points of German grammar and to train them to express themselves in the correct idiom. Prerequisites: two years of college Germ an or the equivalent. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or GER 505.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the German language and the application of phonetics and phonemics in the understanding and speaking of German. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Contemporary German Culture
description: A variety of lectures, readings, and audiovisual materials introducing the student to presentday social mores of Germany. Employing American culture as a frame of reference, it will deal with numerous areas of cultural similarities and differences.

title: Civilization and Culture
description: Civilization and cultural development of the Germans from ancient times to the present. Taught in German. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Masterpieces
description: Classical and Romantic periods. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Drama
description: Drama and theories of the drama of Goethe, Schiller, Grillparzer, and Hebbel. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Poetry
description: Introduction to German lyric poetry and survey of historical development of this literary genre. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Modern Prose
description: Growth and significance of modern prose writing in Germany. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Modern Drama
description: Extensive reading in recent German drama. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Modern Masterpieces
description: Realism, naturalism, and recent German literary periods. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Goethe
description: Intensive study of the life and of one or more of the works of Johann Wolfgang Goethe. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: German Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced German language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where German is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. Travel may be by air. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students with areas in German or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairman.

title: History of German Literature 1
description: From its beginnings to 1750. A survey of German literary trends from the earliest times to the Classical Period, with illustrative readings from selected writers. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: History of German Literature 2
description: From 1750 to 1850. A survey of the classical and romantic German literature, with illustrative readings from selected writers. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: History of German Literature 3
description: From 1850 to the present. A survey of recent German literature, with illustrative readings from selected writers, such as Moerike, Keller, Storm, Stifter, Thomas Mann, Hermann Hesse, and others. Prerequisites: two years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Romanticism
description: Philosophical and historical background of German romanticism, the development of romantic poetry and prose. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Poetic Realism
description: Emphasis on major works representative of Poetic Realism in German literature, including works of Adalbert Stifter, Annette von Droste-Hulshoff, Gottfried Keller, C. F. Meyer, and Theodor Storm.

title: Practical Materials and Techniques
description: Presentation and development of materials of practical value in special interest areas. Various topics of current interest will be covered in miniworkshop situations. Prerequisite: Two years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading Course
description: Prerequisites: three years of college German or the equivalent, or permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Greek

title: Beginning Greek (continued)

title: Introduction to New Testament Greek
description: Beginning course in New Testament Greek. The alphabet, pronunciation, basic grammar, and vocabulary. Not open to the student who has credit in GRK 101, 102, 103.

title: Introduction to New Testament Greek
description: A review of grammar, vocabulary building, and development of reading skills in the Greek of the New Testament. Prerequisite: GRK 104. Not open to the student who has credit in GRK 101, 102, 103.

title: Beginning Latin
description: The first course in the Latin language. Elements of Latin pronunciation, alphabet, rules of accent, syllabification, basic Latin grammar with oral and written exercises, reading of easy short selections from Latin authors, exercises in English derivatives, and consideration of the close connection of Latin and English vocabularies.

title: Beginning Latin
description: Continued emphasis on pronunciation, accent, and syllabification. Oral and written exercises of greater difficulty, reading of short selections from various Latin authors, exercises in dictation, practice in comprehension, with exercises requiring comprehension of speech patterns rather than memorization of single words, and presentation of more grammatical principles. Prerequisite: LAT 101.

title: Beginning Latin (continued)
description: Completion of presentation of the mechanics of Latin grammar. Stress on Latin syntax; logical structure in thought patterns. Rapid short readings illustrating grammatical principles. Emphasis on mastery of grammar through usage; oral and written exercises. Reading of relatively long essays, orations, and letters of Cicero, Pliny's letters, short poems of Horace, Catullus, and Vergil, longer reading selections chosen for importance in history of civilization rather than for illustration of grammatical principles. Prerequisite: LAT 102 or one year of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin
description: Rapid review of Latin grammar with oral and written exercises. Reading of selections from Caesar, Cicero, Pliny, Livy, Seneca, Vitruvius, and others, dealing with such topics as poetry, science, agriculture, medicine, religion, business, politics, history, private life, cooking, philosophy, education, and law. The aim is to interest Latin students in literary ideas drawn from representative works. Emphasis on vocabulary, increased knowledge of Latin idiom, and practice in writing Latin. Prerequisite: one year of college Latin or two years of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin (continued)
description: Emphasis on rapid reading for comprehension. Selected passages dealing with various aspects of man's life, together with comparisons taken from later periods. Celsus, De Medicina; Horace, Ars Poetica; Vitruvius, De Aqueductis; Pliny's Natural History; Cicero's De Officiis, De Republica, Epistulae, De Finibus, or Pro Archia; Juvenal, Satires; Pliny's letters (concerning the Christians), Terence's and Plautus' plays; and others. Prerequisites: 16 hours of college Latin or two and onehalf years of secondary school Latin.

title: Intermediate Latin (continued)
description: Extensive reading of Roman comedies in class. . Stress on rapid reading of Latin, particularly of the dramatists, Plautus and Terence. Introduction to colloquial Latin and everyday idiomatic language. Development of plot, characterization, and artistic unity of Roman comedies. Background and originality of Roman comedy; contaminatio. Play production in Rome. Comparison of Greek and Roman comedy. Aristophanes' comedies; selected plays of Terence and Plautus. Prerequisites: 20 hours of college Latin or two and onehalf years of secondary school Latin.

title: Prose Composition
description: For advanced students who are preparing to teach Latin. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course and/or LAT 505.

title: Suetonius: Lives of the Caesars
description: Reading with special reference to life and times of Suetonius.

title: Horace: Odes
description: Selections from the Odes, with emphasis on metrical forms, grammatical construction, and mythology.

title: The Latin Elegiac Poets
description: The elegies of Catullus, Tibullus, Propertius, and Ovid.

title: Ovid: The Metamorphoses
description: Selected readings from the Metamorphoses of Ovid, with special reference to the life and times of Ovid, and the poetic traditions of Classical Latin. Prerequisites: two years of college Latin or the equivalent.

title: Livy: History
description: Selected readings from Livy's Ab Urbe Condita, with a study of Livy's historical concept, and contrasted with the other greater Roman historians. Prerequisite: two years of college Latin or the equivalent.

title: Roman Comedy
description: Selected plays of Plautus and Terence with attention to influence on French and English literature.

title: Survey of Latin Literature
description: A comprehensive study of Latin literature through the reading of selections from Livius Andronicus to the church fathers. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Lucretius: De Rerum Natura
description: Selected readings from Lucretius' De Rerum Natura, with collateral studies in development in philosophic attitudes in classical times. Prerequisites: two years of college Latin or the equivalent.

title: Vergil: Aeneid, Books I-VI
description: Readings from Books I-VI of the Aeneid of Vergil, with collateral studies in epic genre and the relationship to Homeric epic. Prerequisites: three years of college Latin or the equivalent.

title: Vergil: Aeneid, Books VII-XII

title: Cicero: The Philosophic Works

title: Caesar: The Civil War

title: Martial: Epigrams

title: Juvenal: The Satires

title: Medieval Latin Literature

description: Acquaints the student with the major literary works in all genres which reflect the changing currents of Spanish life and thought during the nineteenth century: romanticism, costumbrism, naturalism, and realism. Prerequisite: three years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

Department of Geography Showalter, Chairman; Beatty, Grimes, Haack, Justham, Lyon, Martinson, Peterson, Schoen, Sullivan, Wheeler Geography is concerned with man and his interaction with the environment. Geography focuses attention on the spatial relationships of our cultural and physical environments. The geography programs reflect these aspects of the discipline, offering general and specialized studies in methodological as well as cultural, physical, and regional fields. Curricular objectives are to educate and train geographers to assume positions in elementary and secondary schools, colleges and universities, business and industry, and governmental agencies. Geography definitely contributes to the liberal education of students. The geography faculty specialize in various aspects within the disciplines of cultural and physical geography, including social, urban, economic, and regional geography, the structure and function of cities, cartography and remote sensing, meteorology and climatology, research methodology, and teacher education. Earth science incorporates the physical aspects of geography, geology, meteorology, and astronomy. It provides a broad understanding of the physical environment for the student who chooses not to specialize in one particular aspect of geography or geology. Earth science students are employed in business, industry, and government, as well as in educational institutions. The Department of Geography prepares students for entrance to colleges or universities which offer degrees in meteorologic studies. A student who desires to pursue this field towards an undergraduate degree should seek the advice of the departmental adviser as soon as possible upon entering Ball State University. Those who plan to continue in meteorology at the graduate level elsewhere should seek this advice no later than the first quarter of the sophomore year. Basic minimum requirements to be included in the first two years of undergraduate study at Ball State in preparation for study towards an undergraduate degree in meteorology elsewhere are generally 8 hours of geology, 8 hours of meteorology, 20 hours of mathematics, 12 hours of chemistry, 12 hours of physics, and 12 hours of foreign language. In addition to these 72 hours, the student who wishes to prepare for a graduate degree in meteorology elsewhere should include climatology, statistics, and computer science. Additional work not available at Ball State may have to be made up at the graduate level. description: Discussion and identification of field problems in geography, geology, and earth science and the techniques and methods of solving these problems. Students are given the major responsibility of class plan development. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman.

Earth's gravity and magnetic field; origin, age, radioactivity, temperature ; earthquake causes, distribution, and prediction; seaflor spreading and mountain building. description: Basic library research and writing techniques applied to problems in geography, geology, and the earth sciences. Designed to stimulate competence in preparing research papers using library materials.

title: Quantitative Techniques
description: Application of quantitative techniques to problems in geography, geology, and the earth sciences. Special emphasis on the application of these techniques in research.

title: Fundamentals of Physical Geography and Earth Science
description: Activities of man and his relationship to the physical environment. Selected topics from astronomy, geography, geology, meteorology, and climatology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Elements of Physical Geography
description: The earth and its position in the universe, natural resources of climate, land forms, soils, vegetation, rocks and minerals, and animal life, with attention paid to the use and conservation of these resources.

title: Physical Geography/Earth Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Earthsun relationships, weather and climate, geologic processes (including earth structure and sculpturing of the earth surface); conservation principles as they pertain directly to the material taught. title: Economic Geography and Contemporary Issues
description: A systematic approach to economic geography and current economic issues, emphasizing local, regional, national and international economic developments in the geographic setting.

title: Geography of the Cultural Environment
description: A spatial analysis of the interaction of cultural development and the physical environment. Special emphasis upon the processes of cultural change and their impact on the landscape.

title: Meteorology 1
description: Introduction to meteorology, dealing with the general planetary circulation of the atmosphere, characteristics of the weather, and an examination of weather instruments. Includes a minimum of 4 hours' assignment in the university weather station.

title: Geography of the Contemporary World
description: A systematic study probing the meaning of regions and examining the geographical character of the world by regions. An analysis of regional resources and cultural patterns focusing on contemporary problems and future development.

title: Honors Seminar in Selected Studies in Geography
description: Smallgroup discussion of geographic studies selected by the instructional staff. Studies vary according to staff assignment. For Honors Program students only.

title: Elements of Regional Geography
description: An introduction to the regional concept and regional method as related to elementary teaching. A geographic survey of the world, with selected topics and regions given detailed analysis. Prerequisite: major in elementary education or permission of the department chairman.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: The reading and interpretation of maps, charts, and diagrams, how they are used as a major tool in geography, and how their use may be applied to other areas of study; also proper care and handling of maps.

title: Map Reading for Teachers
description: An introduction to the reading and interpretation of maps, especially as maps may be used in working with school children. The use of topographic maps, special purpose maps, dot distribution maps, bar graphs, pie charts. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 240.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: A comprehensive survey of the geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Europe
description: The physical and cultural environment of Europe with emphasis on the economic and political factors involved. Geography 257

title: Geography of Soils and Vegetation
description: World patterns of soils and vegetation, with emphasis on regional differences and relationships to climate and physiography; their significance in man's use of the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, GEOL 101, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Land Utilization
description: The varied uses of the land, with emphasis on the major categories of rural use, but with attention given to urban and industrial uses. Water use in respect to the land. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Structure and Functions of Cities
description: A critical examination of the major structural and institutional parts of the city and of how topographic and climatic forces have influenced their development. An understanding of the city as a functionally interdependent structure and as a physical monument to its contemporary culture is fostered.

title: The Urban and Regional Form
description: A survey of the origins of the urban and regional form and its relation to economic, social, and functional factors with special emphasis upon the modern American metropolis and its region. Prerequisite: GEOG 322 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Agricultural and Rural Geography
description: Agricultural development and the pattern of agriculture, particularly in respect to rural areas of the world. Conflict of rural and agricultural development with urbanization and industrialization.

title: Meteorology 2
description: Application of the principles of meteorology to the development and analysis of weather maps and charts and the making of weather forecasts. Includes a minimum of 6 hours' assignment in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Climatology
description: Introduction to the analysis and classification of climate, with emphasis on regional distribution. Basic techniques in handling climatic data. Prerequisite: GEOG 130, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques. Specific projects are selected within the student's field of specialization or area of interest. Emphasis on data collection, compilation, and final drafting of projects suitable for reproduction and publication. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Geography of Latin America and the Caribbean
description: Physical and cultural patterns in a diverse world region. Emphasis on population and settlement, agriculture, and environmental hazards in the context of development.

title: Geography of Africa
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of Africa.

title: Geography of Australia and Oceania
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environment of Australia, New Zealand, and the southeast Pacific area.

title: Geography of Asia
description: The geography of South, Southwest, Southeast, and East Asia. A survey and analysis of the physical geographic patterns, bases of cultural diversity, and changing spatial aspects of political organization.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world as these factors contribute to domestic and foreign relations and problems.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world, and of transportation patterns.

title: Urban Geography
description: The distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention is given to the geographic factors affecting urban development and growth.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration and growth, as well as the causes and consequences of these aspects on cultural landscape.

title: Geography of Regional Development
description: Geographical factors in the identity and development of specific regions of the world, both historical and modern. Special attention given to resource and river valley development. Prerequisite: GEOG 101, 110, 120, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geography of Industrial Location
description: An analysis of the geography of industrial location with particular emphasis given to the impact of industrial location on urban and regional economies.

description: Air mass and storm analysis, with attention given to the physical characteristics of the air layers. Detailed forecasting techniques. description: The practical relationships of climate to human activities, especially in adjustment to the physical and cultural environment. Included are the relationship s pertinento industrial development, and to local regional planing, and the microrelationships of climate and architecture. Prerequisite: GEOG 110, 130, 331, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Meteorological Instrumentation
description: A comprehensive study of meteorological instrument s used in weather station operation. Students wil actively participate in practical weather station operation. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOG 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Remote Sensing and Aerial Photo Interpretation 1
description: Introduction to the use of remote sensing techniques including aerial photo interpretation and aircraft and satellite sensors such as radar and multispectral scanners as applied to studies in the physical and social sciences.

description: Additional instruction and practice in the use of remote sensing techniques including manual and computer analysis of aircraftand satelliteobtained data as applied to studies in the physical and social sciences. Prerequisite : GEOG 42 or permision of the department chairman.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union, and the economic development of the country.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: Topography, soils, climate, industries, commerce, and population of Indiana, with emphasis on physiography and economy.

title: Geography of Northwest Europe
description: Survey of the geography of the countries of northwestern Europe. Analysis of land use, physical landscape, and the economic and political development relationships.

title: Advanced Regional Geography

title: Behavioral Geography

title: Quantitative Analysis in Urban and Regional Geography
description: A consideration of the major analytical techniques used by social geographers in theoretical and applied research in urban and regional geography. Particular emphasis given to those techniques most frequently used in population projections, land use, planning, and transportation studies.

title: History and Philosophy of Geography

Geology 259 Department of Geology Orr, Acting Chairman; Kane, Pierce, Roepke, Samuelson, Sans Geologists study the earth with primary attention to its history, materials, processes, and structure. Today geologists are concerned also with the study of the moon, with the study of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, and discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits. The departmental major in geology on the Professional Arts Curriculum is designed to prepare geologists for immediate employment in industry and government agencies, and for graduate studies leading to research and teaching positions in industry, government, and universities. The departmental major in geology on the Liberal Arts Curriculum is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who do not wish to enter the profession. Geology specialties within the department include geomorphology, geophysics, mineralogy, petrography/petrology, paleontology, geotectonics, oceanography, and stratigraphy. Students should contact the departmental advisers immediately upon electing to major or minor in geology. Thereafter, it is important to maintain contact with the advisers before completing registration with the university curricular advisers. Departmental advisers help the student in developing curricular options, selecting appropriate elective courses toward career objectives, and in other aspects of his or her major and minor. The Department of Geology also prepares students for entrance to colleges or universities which offer degrees in oceanographic studies. A student who desires to pursue this field towards an undergraduate degree should seek the advice of the departmental adviser as soon as possible upon entering Ball State University. Those who plan to continue oceanography at the graduate level elsewhere should seek this advice no later than the first quarter of the sophomore year. Acceptance into graduate work in oceanography will require a bachelor's degree in one of the sciences or mathematics and will generally include 4 hours of introductory oceanography, 28 hours of mathematics inclusive of analytical geometry and calculus, 12 to 14 hours of general physics, and 15 to 16 hours of general chemistry. Students interested in physical and geological oceanography should seek the advice of the adviser in the Department of Geology. title: Man and the Geological Environment
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to mankind's environmental and resource problems. Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: An introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Emphasis on North America. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Environmental Geology
description: An examination of geologic materials and processes affecting the immediate human environment. Geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, geohealth, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Geology of Energy Resources
description: An examination of geologic processes that form and govern the distribution of oil, gas, coal, uranium ores, and geothermal energy sources; exploration strategies; resource evaluation; and case history studies of active energy extraction developments. Several field trips are required. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Local area field trips and field mapping. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoecologic significance. Emphasis on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman. Geology 261

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects, the use of field instruments in and near the campus, and visits to places of pertinent course value within the state. Normal scheduling is Saturday mornings. Prerequisite: major or minor in geography, geology, or earth science, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to geologic problems in a specific area. Assignments include mapping projects, including a final written report and compilation of a map on general geology. Normal scheduling is first summer term (five weeks) in a selected area of western United States. Prerequisite: GEOL 382 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Regional Geology Field Study
description: The geologic history, stratigraphy, structural geology, geomorphology, and economic geology of a selected region. Students will travel through the area. Normal scheduling is second summer term in a selected area outside Indiana. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geomorphology of North America
description: Emphasis on the occurrence, description, and geological and geomorphological problems of the geomorphic regions of North America. Nearby area field trips. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and MATH 112 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans, and related problems. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to the physics of the earth and the geophysical sciences. Refraction and reflection seismology, magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods are included in lecture topics, laboratory exercises, and field investigations. Emphasis on the application of geophysical methods to energy, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, pollution detection, and other applied problems. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geotectonics
description: Plate tectonics and global geophysics; earth's origin, age, gravity, geomagnetism and paleomagnetism, geothermal heat, seismology, dynamics, and internal structure; current ideas of seafloor spreading, plate tectonics, and mountain building; application to locating new energy and mineral resources. Emphasis on studying the most recent developments in the science of geotectonics in the first half of the quarter and in the study of individual tectonic regions (such as the Appalachians, Rocky Mountains, Alps, and Urals) in the second half.

title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for classifying and interpreting the origins of rocks. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with the exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks for the purpose of determining their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: The structure, rocks, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Emphasis upon physical processes involved, especially Pleistocene glaciation. Designed for nonmajor students in the earth sciences, particularly teachers.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, MATH 111, NR 211, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Geochemistry
description: Composition of the earth. Distribution of elements i n minerals and rocks. Principles governing migration and concentration of elements. Introduction to isotope geology and geochemical prospecting. Prerequisite: GEOL 230, CHEM 112 or 114, or permission of department chairman.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. Designed to supplement existing geoscience and computer science courses by providing opportunity to gain experience in working with Basic and Fortran programs in various geoscience data collecting, calculation, and graphic display applications. Open only to students with areas in geography and geology. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Department of History Eidson, Chairman; Aquila, Backor, Barber, Bohler, Burkhardt, Chase, Edmonds, Grossman, Hoover, Huston, Koumoulides, Mackey, Marek, Mayfield, Mitchell, Peterson, Rosenberg, Schreiber, Schroeder, Seager, Somers, Vander Hill, Weakland, White, Wires, Yuhas, Zimmerman Time present and time past Are both perhaps present in time future, And time future contained in time past. T.S. Eliot, Four Quartets, "Burnt Norton" By definition, history is the record of past actions of mankind based upon surviving evidence. Thus, mankind's accumulated experience, the memory of the human race, is called history. Its study, which should lead to understanding and wisdom, indicates that all problems and patterns are the result of complex processes of growth. By shedding light on these processes, history provides a vehicle for profiting from human experience. Without a knowledge of our past, we would have no landmarks, no points of reference, and no foundations on which to build a modern world. The history major may be undertaken to attain professional, academic, or cultural objectives, including preparation for graduate study and advanced degrees, teaching licenses, prelaw or premedical preparation, qualification for appointments in business, industry, civil service, libraries, museums, art galleries, archives, and other cultural institutions. Courses in history are designed to meet the needs of students in several fields of study. The department offers a broad selection of courses in the general studies program. It offers introductory and advanced courses for students majoring in education or in liberal arts in other departments of the university. It also presents courses designed to give a broad and thorough training in the various history programs. Students majoring in social sciences other than history, English, foreign languages, journalism, and business find history courses especially useful. The graduate programs are built on the foundation of undergraduate preparation. Students intending to do graduate work in history are urged to take the Bachelor of Arts degree. The master's and doctoral degrees require intensive directed study in history aimed at depth of understanding. title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: A survey of the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decision makers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Introduction to Civilization of Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: World Civilizations 1
description: A compact survey of the development of world civilizations from the dawn of civilization in Southwestern Asia and North Africa to the Early Modern World (ca. 1400). Open only to students in the College of Architecture and Planning.

title: World Civilizations 2
description: A compact survey of the development of world civilizations from the Early Modern World (ca. 1400) to the Contemporary Scene. Open only to students in the College of Architecture and Planning.

title: Roots of the Western Tradition
description: A survey of the principal historical and cultural developments of ancient and medieval times to 1300, with emphasis on those institutions and events of Western civilization which furnish our own cultural heritage.

title: Birth of the Modern World
description: From 1300 to 1815, including such major topics as the Renaissance, Reformation, rise of modern nations, discovery and exploration, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, nationalism, and the industrial revolution.

title: The World in Recent Times
description: Major world events and issues since 1815; industrialization and resulting ideologies; background, causes, and results of the two world wars; the rise and decline of the colonial empires with emerging nationalism; the impact of democratic, fascist, and communistic doctrines; nineteenthand twentiethcentury trends in thought; the effect of science on our age; arts; attempts at international organization and cooperation; and the revolution in expectations in the oneworld today.

title: Black Africa's Contribution to Western Civilization
description: The African cultural and historical roots of the American black will be investigated. The origins of the human race, plant and animal domestication, metallurgy, art, and state formation are covered focusing on West Africa, the source of black population in the United States. Not open to the student who has credit in ANTH 270 (370).

title: Modern World Leaders
description: Biographical studies of key western and nonwestern men and women placed in historical perspective. Examines the leaders' characteristics, philosophies, leadership capabilities, and their resultant contributions in the field of politics, religion, military, business, and the arts.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East—the Arab world, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems; imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South Asia
description: South Asia (Afghanistan to Indonesia) since 1800: a brief description of factors influential in past history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, and eventual independence.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Foundations of the United States, 1492-1829
description: Survey of American history to 1829.

title: Development of the United States, 1829-1900
description: Survey of the history of the United States from the era of Andrew Jackson to 1900.

title: The Recent Past in the United States, 1900 to the Present
description: Political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have composed the history of the United States since 1900.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of United States resource utilization by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource utilization has shaped society.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of the negro in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing conceptions of their roles, attitudes toward women, women's ideas about themselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Designed to use documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. A complete departure from the regular lecture and textbook method. The students through their own research learn how the historian defines areas of research, selects sources, both primary and secondary, evaluates materials, and describes the findings. A tot al of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The History of American Popular Culture
description: Historical overview of the development of American popular culture. Basic theories, approaches, and topics in popular culture will be studied, with special attention given to amusements, movies, pop music, magazines, pulp novels, and television. The focus will be on the relationship of popular culture to American cultural and social history.

title: History of Latin America, 1825 to Present
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis upon contemporary civilization of Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.

title: Introduction to Public History
description: An overview of opportunities for nonteaching historyrelated careers in areas such as historic preservation, archival work, records management, museology, historical editing, living history and public parks programs, and corporate history. Student contact with working professionals will be made. Students will make a concentrated study of at least one field of public history. Open to all students interested in investigating nonteaching historyrelated careers.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to the history profession. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies such as the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or with private institutions such as historical galleries and business firms. Prerequisite: permission of department chairman. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: American Leaders
description: A biographical approach to American history. An evaluation of some of the leading Americans and their contributions in the fields of politics, business, letters, the arts, pure and applied science, and education.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American/Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Provides students with an historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Selected Topics in Military History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular period, topic, or issue in the field of military history with emphasis on materials not covered in established courses. Exact content announced in advance of each offering. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others by permission of the department chairman.

title: Colonial History of the United States, 1492-1754
description: The ideas and institutions developed in British North America which in the course of colonial development formed a basis for American culture.

title: The United States from Colony to Nation, 1754-1789
description: The political, constitutional, and economic issues that developed in the thirteen British colonies of North America and culminated in revolution, independence, and the founding of a new nation in the latter part of the eighteenth century.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis upon the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis upon the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820- 1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economi c problems entailed therein, and various eforts at reform.

title: From New Freedom through the New Deal
description: United States history from 1912 to 1940. The impact on the American people of the problems created by continuing industrialization at home and continued involvement in a chaotic world.

title: Recent United States History: 1941 to the Present
description: The role of the United States in World War II, the issues confronting the nation in the postwar years, and political, social, and cultural developments since that time.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the state from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Ante-Bellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum south.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans-Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers and the events which influenced their migration, and on the impact these events and the frontier had upon national development.

title: Indians in U.S. History
description: Survey of Indian and white relations from 1492 to the present, focusing on the Indian wars, treaty making, various types of Indian and white interaction, and the development of federal and state Indian policy.

title: The History of Canada
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of Canada from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis will be placed on the events leading to the establishment of Canada and on United States-Canadian relations and problems.

title: History of Mexico
description: Mexico from the pre-Columbian era to the present with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Revolution of 1910.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1607-1865
description: Survey of history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu.

title: Social and Intellectual History of the United States, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of the history of the ideas, knowledge, and values developed in philosophy, religion, literature, education, and science, and relationships to the total social milieu.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisites: ECON 200 or 201 or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 410.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: The major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture-Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students will travel through designated areas in North America. Prior to the trip, considerable reading in various fields relative to the nature of the course will be required. At the conclusion, papers will be required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teacher education students with a concentration in U.S. history may apply 4 hours of credit in categories 1, 2, or 3.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open only to seniors of special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do pregraduate investigation. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with special competence within the area involved.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1500-1815
description: Political, social, and economic history of Europe from the Age of Discovery to the Congress of Vienna. Emphasis on political and economic events, the rise of national states, absolutism, religious developments, and the expansion of Europe overseas.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1815 to the Present
description: Political, economic, social, and cultural history of Europe from the Congress of Vienna to the contemporary scene. Emphasis on political and economic events, the liberal and nationalist movements, industrialism, imperialism, World Wars I and II, and the conflict of national interests.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870-1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918-1950
description: Survey of the origins, immediate causes, and the course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and After, 1950 to Present
description: Survey of the factors—ideological, political, economic, and social—underlying recent European history with stress on the East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, imperial decline, and the changing European role in world affairs.

title: Modern Extremist Movements
description: A survey and analysis of extremist movements in Europe since 1815 with particular attention to the growth of antidemocratic thought, workingclass movements, counterrevolution, international fascism, collaboration, and youth movements.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the Republic to approximately 500 A.D. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the Republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special stress on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Moslem worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Particular attention will be given to such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations—Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society— through varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teacher education students with a concentration in World Civilization may apply 4 hours of credit in categories 1, 2, or 4.

title: France since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France—The Classical Age, 1461-1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focus on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715-1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization—and revolutions in general. Stress on the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Rise of Modern Britain, 1485-1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor, Stuart, and early Hanoverian periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain since 1763
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life since the Seven Years' War—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of postwa r government and society.

title: Constitutional History of England
description: A tracing of the development of the British constitutional system to the present time: development of the kingship, the common law, parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern British Empire and Commonwealth
description: British imperial and commonwealth history since 1815 with emphasis on the post-Napoleonic empire, the development of dominions, the problem of India, the World Wars, the shrinking empire, the Commonwealth experience, and the current controversies.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the Revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: Modern East-Central Europe and the Balkans
description: Studies in the modern history of peoples living in this exposed area of Europe, with stress on their struggles for national independence, ethnic, religious, cultural, socioeconomic, and political diversities. Problems are examined within the context of European trends and developments, especially interference of the Great Powers.

title: The Modern Middle East
description: A survey of major developments and problems in the Turkish, Persian, and Arab world in the period since 1800—the decay of traditional life, the expansion of European influence, the modernization movements, the conflicts over Palestine, and the recent national and international crises.

title: Modern Chinese History, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japanese History, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on factors contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Studies in Non-Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: Selected Topics in History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in the field of history with emphasis on fields, specialties, and materials not covered in established courses.
