Department of Journalism Popovich, Chairman; Atwell, Chaney, Conn, Costa, Harrison, Hatfield, Lleintzelman, Forney, Ingelhart, Kimble, Knott, Sharpe, Ware, Weaver, Wellnitz Because the media practitioner must be a wellrounded and knowledgeable person in many fields, journalism programs in the accredited schools and departments in the nation, of which Ball State is one, stress exposure of students to the arts, humanities, sciences, and business. To study journalism in today's world is likely to mean involvement in the purest liberal arts academic discipline. Equally important to the student's breadth and depth of knowledge is the ability to put that knowledge into words that can be understood. Besides the writing and editing classroom experiences required of journalism students, Ball State University encourages its students to participate in its extensive college student publications program and/or to seek professional experiences either during the school year or summers. Journalism students spend onefourth of their academic careers in journalism courses; threefourths in courses other than journalism, radio-TV-film, advertising, public relations, or communications media. Students are encouraged to major in another subject besides journalism, such as anthropology, economics, history, literature, management, marketing, natural resources, political science, physical education, psychology, sociology, speech, urban and regional studies, and other arts and sciences. Students who enter the journalism department have the option of preparing themselves as either teaching majors or departmental majors. Teaching majors are prepared to teach journalism and mass media courses, to develop educational programs, and to serve as advisers for all forms of student publications and communication programs in secondary education. Students who pursue the teaching major are certified to receive an Indiana standard grade teaching license. JOURN 395 and 399 are the methods courses for the teaching major in journalism (see the professional education requirements on the curriculum). Students earning a teaching major in journalism are advised to earn a teaching minor in English or, if possible, a teaching major in English. Teaching majors or minors in the social sciences or business are also particularly recommended. Departmental majors have the option of career preparation in one of six sequential areas. 1. News Editorial: Students learn all phases of newsroom operations of the various news media and receive an overall grasp of the philosophy, trends, and issues in the news media. 2. Public Relations: Besides acquisition of a sound journalism foundation, students are prepared to go into public relations positions in either public or private corporations and institutions. 3. Photojournalism: Emphasis is placed on preparing students who can take and process pictures and write news, prepare features, and create advertising. 4. Advertising: This option provides students with knowledge and practical experiences in the functions and operations of those departments in media which ensure financial success— advertising, circulation, and promotion. 5. Magazine: Students study the magazine industry and are prepared to process words and pictures either as individuals or for media organizations. 6. Sports Information: Both men and women learn journalistic and public relations techniques in order to interpret for the public organized athletic endeavor, either amateur or professional. Graduate work is available in all these fields and students can professionalize teaching licenses if they wish. Journalism courses are available to help the student who is not a major but is interested in working on special writing or editing projects or taking journalism courses to meet general studies requirements. JOURN 100, Mass Communications Media, and JOURN 120, Journalistic Writing, are selected by students as general studies requirements or as electives. During the freshman or sophomore year, students will be required to demonstrate adequate typewriting ability and pass minimum spelling and grammar requirements. If students are unable to pass the proficiency tests, remedial courses may be required to sharpen basic skills. By the end of the sophomore year, students should have taken and successfully completed the work in JOURN 110, 220, 230, and 250. Students should contact their sequence advisers by the end of the sophomore year for a midcareer review of their academic work. In order to be certified for graduation, journalism students must earn a total of 138 quarter hours of credit in courses other than journalism, radio-TV-film, advertising, public relations, or communications media. In addition, students will be asked to submit a recent photo, a college resume, and a portfolio of examples of journalistic work to be placed in their permanent files. A senior interview with the appropriate sequence adviser, preferably in the student's last quarter on campus, will help qualify the student for graduation. This statement reflects the interdependency of mathematics and the sciences. While still true, this observation must now be extended to cover all areas of human endeavor in the second half of the twentieth century. The student considering mathematics as a career should realize that emphasis in mathematics courses will change as progress is made through undergraduate and graduate school. The early emphasis on solving problems is later subordinated to the more important tasks of formulating and dealing effectively with mathematical structures and abstract ideas. Every prospective mathematician should plan to pursue undergraduate and graduate training to the highest level of capability. To meet the need for mathematically competent graduates, several programs of study are available at the undergraduate level as either majors or minors, The secondary teaching major is designed to prepare classroom teachers of mathematics in grades 9 through 12. The junior high/middle school mathematics primary area is designed to prepare mathematics teachers for grades 5 through 9. This primary area is accompanied by a supporting area, or another primary area, in science, social science, language arts, or foreign language on the junior high/middle school major. Prospective teachers completing the secondary teaching license may earn an endorsement for teaching in the junior high/middle school grades. All teacher preparation programs comply with the certification regulations of the Division of Teacher Education and Certification of the State Board of Education. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government, as well as for further specialized study of mathematics at the graduate level. In today's complex world, problems cut across traditionally defined areas of discipline, and a departmental major offers to a student the opportunity to combine mathematics with work in other areas. The departmental major on the liberal arts curriculum is a program in the liberal arts tradition. With this liberal education, the student is well prepared for additional graduate study or for positions requiring education in breadth. Computer science, as a separate discipline, began to receive widespread attention in the last twenty years. The technological development of computers together with decreased costs which have made them available to every sector of the economy accounts for the great demand for persons knowledgeable in every phase of computer science. To meet the increasing demands of specialists in a computeroriented society, Ball State University offers a departmental major and minor in computer science, a departmental major in mathematics and computer science, and a statistics and computer science option. A cooperative education (workstudy) program is available to majors in computer science, mathematics and computer science, and mathematics with an option in statistics. Students with the majors specified above may apply for this program after the completion of three academic quarters (minimum 45 quarter hours) in which minimum cumulative gradepoint averages of 3.0 in computer science and mathematics courses and 2.5 in all courses have been earned. The university cannot guarantee work assignments for all students. Additional information concerning the Cooperative program may be obtained from the mathematical sciences departmental office. Actuaries are mathematically trained executives who use mathematical knowledge to analyze and solve business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. Actuaries are employed by insurance companies, state departments of insurance, management consulting firms, universities, federal agencies, and other institutions. An actuarial career promises to be a c hallenging and rewarding experience. A departmental major in actuarial science is offered to provide a student with the foundations for an actuarial career. An actuary gains professional recognition by passing a series of examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries. The program includes the coursework for the first three examinations, and in some cases for the fourth and fifth examinations. Ball State University is an official test location for the Society of Actuaries. title: Mathematical Concepts 1
description: A general education course for students who wish to know more about the contributions of mathematics to human culture. Includes topics particularly suited to the needs of the student who seeks a broad knowledge of mathematical ideas together with some computational skills and techniques. Prerequisite: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry. Not open to students with college credit in mathematics except by permission of the department chairman or to students with areas in mathematics or computer science.

title: Mathematical Concepts 2
description: Continuation of MATH 100. Prerequisite: MATH 100.

title: College Algebra 1
description: Fundamental operations of algebra through quadratics. students who have credit for three semesters of secondary school algebra will not receive credit for this course. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra.

title: College Algebra 2
description: A brief introduction to sets and the logic of algebra, a discussion of inequalities, absolute values, functions and relations, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and mathematical induction. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary school algebra, and one year of plane geometry, or their equivalents as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied in this course if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities and equations; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers, and DeMoivre's Theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or its equivalent as determined by the department chairman. Credit is denied if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairman.

title: Analytic Geometry
description: Use of Cartesian and polar coordinates in two and three dimensions, conic sections, transcendental curves, curve sketching, parametric equations, lines and surfaces in solid analytic geometry. Prerequisite: The equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level, or MATH 111 and 112.

title: Mathematics for Architects 1
description: Topics in analytic geometry and calculus particularly suited to the needs of the architecture major. Includes concepts of limits, differentiation, and integration. Prerequisite: MATH 112. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 161 or 170.

title: Mathematics for Architects 2
description: Continuation of MATH 123. Emphasis on applications of calculus. Prerequisite: MATH 123. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 162 or 170.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 1
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or a strong background in high school algebra.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics which are particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite : MATH 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications in some of the above areas. Prerequisite : MATH 1 and 12 or their equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 170.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATH 161 or 170. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 171.

title: Calculus 1
description: Inequalities, limits, continuity, differentials and derivatives, introduction to the definite integral. Prerequisite: MATH 113.

title: Calculus 2
description: Continuation of the definite integral, differentiation and integration of elementary transcendental functions, derivatives in polar coordinates, integration by special methods, applications of integration. Prerequisite: MATH 170.

title: Calculus 3
description: Continuation of the application of the integral, elements of infinite series (convergent and divergent series), Taylor's series and theorem, partial differentiation, and multiple integration. Prerequisite: MATH 171.

title: Calculus 4
description: Infinite series and elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Cardinal Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers.

title: Rational Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the concept of unsigned rational numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 201.

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the real number system. Prerequisite: MATH 202. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 205.

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: The development and use of decimal and scientific notation through metric measurement. An extension of real number concepts including irrational numbers and integers through measurement, decimal approximations, calculator activities, coordinate graphing, and applications. MATH 203 may be substituted for MATH 205. It is recommended that students preparing to teach in upper elementary grades substitute MATH 203 for MATH 205. Prerequisite: MATH 202. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 203.

title: Geometry in the Elementary School
description: A development of geometric concepts for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 202 and MATH 203 or 205 if either course is required on the student's program.

title: Elementary School Enrichment Topics
description: An examination of mathematics concepts included as enrichment topics in elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 206. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education. Other students by permission of the department chairman.

title: Structure of the Number Systems
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and selected number systems. A systematic development is emphasized. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172 or equivalent.

title: Elements of Linear Algebra
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties, determinants, matrix inverses, rank and equivalence of matrices, and a matrix approach to the theory of systems of linear equations. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 171.

title: Topics from Linear Algebra
description: Determinants, matrices, and bilinear maps, polynomials and matrices, triangulation of matrices and linear maps, spectral theorems, multilinear products. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 412.

title: Applied Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, probability, random variables, important discrete and continuous distributions, statistical inference and testing of hypotheses, sampling theory, statistical analysis of time series, decision theory. Applications to business will be made throughout the course. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, or 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 321.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Geometry
description: A revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems will be considered which deal with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by Permission of the department chairman. Prerequisite: MATH 173.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 202.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Secondary School Mathematics
description: A course for the secondary teaching major designed to expose students early in their program to mathematics in a teaching environment. Prerequisite: MATH 161 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 395.

title: Computer and Enrichment Topics for the Junior High/Middle School Teacher of Mathematics
description: Designed for the junior high/middle school teacher of mathematics; includes topics in computer uses and programming and enrichment topics from such areas as topology, strategy games, number theory. Prerequisite: MATH 211 and MATH 240. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 200 or 220.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATH 211; prerequisites for students preparing for the elementary endorsement in mathematics: MATH 172.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, gamma, rectangular, and normal distributions. Prerequisite: MATH 172.

title: Statistics 1
description: Classification of data, empirical distributions, random sampling, distributions of sample mean and same variance from normal distribution, distribution of sample mean from nonnormal distributions, probability distributions for correlation and regression, empirical methods for correlation and regression, general principle of estimation and hypothesis testing. Prerequisite: MATH 320.

title: Statistics 2
description: Testing of goodness of fit, contingency tables, small sample distributions, chisquare, t and F distributions and their applications in hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, nonparametric methods, sequential analysis, Bayesian method. Prerequisite: MATH 321.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, t, and F distributions. Some problems with moment generating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Prerequisite: MATH 221 or 321 or permission of the department chairman. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in synthetic geometry, closely related to the field of Euclidean geometry.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models to problems from physics, chemistry, biology, and business. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models rather than detailed numerical results. Prerequisite: MATH 212.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nthorder ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Enler equations, Laplace transforms, power series solutions, Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, firstorder partial differential equations, applications in business, biological, chemical, physical, and sociological sciences. Prerequisite:

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematics in Early Childhood
description: Materials and methods used for teaching mathematics at prekindergarten levels. Prerequisite: MATH 206.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from kindergarten through grade three. Class ideas applied in tutoring situations. Prerequisite: MATH 206. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 391.

title: Teaching Mathematics in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Each student will plan and teach seven onetoone sessions with an elementary school child. Prerequisite: MATH 206.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for the teaching of mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a tutoring situation. Prerequisite: 30 hours credit on the junior high/middle school mathematic s program and junior standing.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in the teaching of senior high school mathematics. Survey of texts, organization of materials, testing procedures, and visual aids materials. Prerequisite: MATH 313, EDSEC 299 and identificatio n to pursue a teaching curiculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Deals specifically with mathematicsoriented classroom management techniques, an introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: MATH 395.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 1
description: Topics from group theory, ring theory, and field theory, including integral domains and polynomial rings. Prerequisite: MATH 212.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics from MATH 411 and topics from vector spaces and module theory. Prerequisite: MATH 411.

title: Theory of Numbers 1
description: Topics from: the division algorithm, positional notation, divisibility, primes, congruences, divisibility criteria, the sigma, divisor, and phi functions, diophantine equations, linear, polynomial, and simultaneous congruences, theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson, primitive roots and power residues and their application to decimal expansions of rationale, Pythagorean triples, and Fermat's method of descent.

title: Theory of Numbers 2
description: Some topics not covered in MATH 416, including elementary partition theory, quadratic residues, continued fractions, Farey fractions and irrational numbers, elementary properties of (x), Waring's problem, and density of sequences of integers. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Topics in Statistics 1
description: Includes such topics as theory of distribution, theory of statistical inference, and theory of regression analysis. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or MS 421 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Topics in Statistics 2
description: Deals with topics mentioned in MATH 428 at an advanced level with particular reference to experimental design and analysis of variance, use of computers in statistics, and Monte-Carlo methods. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or 428 or MS 421, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs, simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling, ratio estimates, regression estimates, cost function, variance function. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or MS 421 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school such as Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, Magic Squares, the Calendar Problem, Polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the Fifteen Puzzle, Nim, and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers will be considered. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Advanced Analytic Geometry
description: An advanced treatment of analytic Euclidean geometry using topics from analysis and algebra as tools where helpful.

title: Projective Geometry
description: Properties of geometric configurations which are invariant under projection. Synthetic methods emphasized, and some use is made of analytic methods.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities certain, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, and capitalized cost. Both the discrete and the continuous approach to compound interest and annuities certain will be treated. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172.

title: Mathematics of Life Insurance
description: An introduction to the mathematics of life insurance; mortality tables; life annuities, premiums, and reserves for basic life insurance policies; modern reserve systems. The discrete approach to contingencies of a single life will be emphasized but the continuous approach will be introduced. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 451.

title: Topology 1
description: Set theoretic preliminaries, the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well ordering principle, topological spaces, continuity, separation axioms, nets and filters, connectedness, local connectedness, product and quotient topologies, metric spaces, metrization. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Topology 2
description: Uniform spaces, paracompactness, open coverings, compactness. compactification, local compactness, function spaces, Stone-Weierstrauss theorem, complete spaces, Banach fixedpoint theorem, introductory homotopy theory. Introduction to homology theory, Jordan curve theorem, Brouwer fixedpoint theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 455.

title: History of Mathematics 1
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to 1600. Topics covered include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, and trigonometry. Prerequisite: MATH 211 and 340. Mathematical Sciences 28.1

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include error analyses, solutions of nonlinear equations and systems of nonlinear equations, interpolation and approximation of functions, approximate differentiation and integration. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: CS 220 or permission of the department chairman, and MATH 124, 162, or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics covered include: numerical solutions of differential equations, matrices and approximate solutions of linear systems by both direct and iterative methods, matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: MATH 212, 162 or 173, and MATH 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 463.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, mathematical formula. Prerequisite: MATH 462 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Vector Analysis
description: An introduction to the theory and applications of vectors including the algebra, calculus, and geometry of vectors; classical theorems; applications. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Methods of linear programming and optimization of functions of several variables with and without constraints. Geometric, algebraic, and simplex methods; duality in linear programming. Classical, optimization, search techniques, Fletcher-Powell method, and method of steepest descent. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 466.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Elements of Analysis 1
description: Includes such topics as: partial derivatives, L'Hospital's Theorem, integration in polar coordinates, sequences, series, convergence, continuity, and improper integrals. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or equivalent. Open only to students with a teaching major in mathematics. Not open to the student with credit in MATH 172.

title: Elements of Analysis 2
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATH 469.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Advanced calculus including real numbers, metric spaces, topology of R and C, continuity of functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrauss theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATH 173.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics covered include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansion. Prerequisite: MATH 471.

title: Advanced Calculus 3
description: Advanced calculus of several variables. Calculus of differential forms in three dimensions. Examples from physics. Prerequisite: MATH 472.

title: Advanced Differential Equations
description: Existence and uniqueness of solution of firstorder nonlinear ordinary differential equations, linear systems, autonomous systems in the plane, oscillatory theory, secondorder partial differential equations with constant coefficients, the Cauchy problem, elements of potential theory, the Dirichlet problem. Prerequisite: MATH 374. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 467.

title: Complex Variables 1
description: Complex number systems, differentiation and integration, functions (analytic, entire, meromorphic) of one complex variable, singularities, complex integration, Cauchy's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, power series, Laurent Series, calculus of residues. Prerequisite: MATH 173. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Complex Variables 2
description: Analytic continuation, Riemann surfaces, theorem of Weierstrauss and Mittag-Leffler, solution of two dimensional potential problem, conformal mapping, Schwartz-Christoffel transformations and its application to the solution of electric, magnetic field distributions and of thermal and hydraulic stationary flow problems. Prerequisite: MATH 485.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Arithmetic
description: For teachers in service who do not hold a degree. Prerequisite: teaching experience in the elementary school. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the Mathematical Sciences Department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Coop Orientation
description: Seminar for students entering the coop program in computer science. Topics covered are: responsibilities of the coop student and employer, resum e preparation, job interview training, types of placement available, general cooprogram administration and requirements. Open only to students majoring in computer science. 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107. Coop Professional Experience. (0) Students register for one course (in sequence) during each coop work period. Requires satisfactory work performance and a written coop report at the end of each work period. Open only to students majoring i n computer science on the coperative program. Prerequisite: CS 10.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines. Timesharing computer techniques with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. An understanding of the role of the computer in the modern world. Not open to the student with areas in mathematical or computer sciences, or with credit in CS 210, 220, or MS 220.

title: Computer Science for Architects
description: An introductory course in computer science for students from the College of Architecture and Planning. Problems related to architecture are solved using timesharing and batch processing techniques. Use of the plotter is stressed. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 200, 220, or MS 220.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize application in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: CS 200 or 220 or MS 220. Not open to the student who has credit in MS 310.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Computer organization and facilities. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Timesharing techniques are introduced. Prerequisite: MATH 112 and sophomore standing; or MATH 113, 123, 132, or 161.

title: Computer-Assisted Instruction
description: Explores the possible uses of the computer in the instructional process. Technological and economic problems related to selecting and designing computerassisted instruction systems considered. Students develop computerized lessons on topics of their choice. Not open to students with areas in computer science without permission of the department chairman.

title: Applied Combinatorics
description: Techniques of network and combinatorial analysis with applications to algorithms and structures in computer and information science. Course assignments will include analysis, design, and implementation of various algorithms and structures. Prerequisite: MATH 212 and CS 220.

title: Machine Language and Systems Programming 1
description: Introduction to computer architecture, machine language, and assembler language; fixedpoint and decimal arithmetic; character manipulation; bit manipulation; floatingpoint arithmetic; looping and branching, and internal subroutines. Prerequisite: CS 220, and MATH 124, 162, or 170, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Machine Language and Systems Programming 2
description: Advanced topics in machine and assembler languages; bit manipulation, floatingpoint arithmetic, macros, conditional assembly, core dumps and debugging, input/output using the operating system, input/output device programming, interrupt programming. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Advanced Programming Techniques
description: Topics such as structures, blocks, dynamic storage allocation, list processing and pointer variables, compile time instructions, organization and manipulation of data files, and interrupt handling are treated using the PL/1 language. Operating system features are included as required by these topics. Prerequisite: CS 330.

title: Computer Hardware Systems
description: Introduction to computer logic and registertransfer level of systems description is presented. The basic building blocks of a computer system are examined. Various computer architectures and hardware trends are studied. Microprogramming is introduced. Prerequisite: CS 331, 332 and MATH 212.

title: Computer Programming Languages
description: Emphasis is on important structural characteristics of highlevel programming languages. Additional languages studied are APL, ALGOL-68, LISP, and SNOBOL to show such features as dynamic array manipulation, language extensibility, list and string processing. Some compiler techniques are also considered. Prerequisite: CS 332.

title: Information Structures
description: Data structures used in computer storage to represent the information involved in solving problems. Emphasis is placed on data structures independently of applications in which they are embedded. Storage structures are described according to their characteristics. Prerequisite: CS 331.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Problems typical to DP centers such as file maintenance, report writing, sorting and merging are treated using COBOL. Sequential and direct access processing techniques. Prerequisite: CS 332.

title: Systems Analysis
description: The role of and techniques used by the information processing specialist. Includes a case study laboratory. Prerequisite: CS 332.

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation and the application of simulation languages to system studies. Students will carry out simulations using examples from different fields. Prerequisite: CS 332 and MATH 221 or 321.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics covered include error analyses, solutions of nonlinear equations and systems of nonlinear equations, interpolation and approximation of functions, approximate differentiation and integration. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: CS 220 or permission of the department chairman, and MATH 124, 162, or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics covered include: numerical solutions of differential equations, matrices and approximate solutions of linear systems by both direct and iterative methods, matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Programming of numerical algorithms studied is included. Prerequisite: MATH 212, 162 or 173, and MATH 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 463.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Methods of linear programming and optimization of functions of several variables with and without constraints. Geometric, algebraic, and simplex methods; duality in linear programming. Classical optimization, search techniques, Fletcher-Powell method, and method of steepest descent. Prerequisite: MATH 212 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 466.

title: Minicomputer Systems
description: The minicomputer considered from the viewpoints of its architecture, operating system, and application. Topics included are processor organization, peripheral devices, I/O programming, system programs, monitor services, and file organization. The departmental minicomputer, PDP-11, will be used for handson laboratory projects. Prerequisite: CS 331.

title: Operating Systems
description: Introduction to the functions and structure of computer operating systems. I/O programming, initial program load, resource (processor, memory, device, and information) management, programming aids (compilers, linkers, dynamic debugging, editors). Prerequisite: CS 433 or 472.

title: Computer Software Laboratory
description: A software system will be designed, developed, and implemented in an environment simulating a software development organization. The latest methods and discipline of software engineering will be used. Prerequisite: CS 440, 441.

title: Readings and Honors
description: Special advanced work not offered in other courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairman. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Natural Resources Van Meter, Chairperson; Godish, Hibbs, Lowe, Lyon, Mortensen, Siewert, Sullivan The Department of Natural Resources has as its ultimate objective the education of people to help meet the increasing demand for qualified personnel in the environmental/natural resources area. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the university by offering appropriate courses in natural resources. Through research and extension activities it also strives to provide services concerning environmental quality and resource management for Indiana citizens. Environmental problems have resulted from our rapidly expanding population and technology in combination with our affluent society causing accelerated resource use and abuse. There is need for both men and women with a knowledge of natural resources and environmental quality management. The programs offered by the department are designed to provide students with a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. Curricula offered by the Department of Natural Resources are interdisciplinary because the conservation of our natural resources and the concomitant improvement of our environment are areas of total university concern, requiring new ideas, diverse skills, and integrated input from many disciplines. Therefore, depending upon the individual interest of the student, a program may include courses in several disciplines in fulfilling the curricular requirements. Students considering a professional career in natural resources should plan their high school program to include a strong background in both the sciences and the humanities. The desire and ability to work with people is also an important prerequisite. Curricula offered by the department include a departmental minor and major in natural resources at both the undergraduate and graduate level and a cognate in this area for doctoral students. A teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, an area of endorsement for elementary education majors, a supporting concentration for junior high/middle school majors, and an energy resources minor are also offered. Students enrolled in the undergraduate major in natural resources may elect the general option in resource management or specialize in such areas as natural resource planning, fishery resources, communications, water quality, natural resources interpretation, soil science, environmental protection, and outdoor recreation management. Common background is provided for all majors through a "core requirement" which includes Introduction to Natural Resources, Air Resources, Ecology, Man and the Geologic Environment, Mineral Resources, Soil Resources, Water Resources, and Integrated Resources Management. Other courses which may be elected will be determined by the option selected, the student's background, and professional employment interests. In addition to traditional science courses, others that may be included are communication, computer techniques, environmental health, landscape architecture, physical education, political science, sociology, statistics, and urban and regional studies. All natural resource curricula are interdisciplinary. Students majoring in other departments of the university are encouraged to elect one of the natural resource minors which complement a variety of curricula. One of these minors should be especially useful to accompany certain majors including biology, earth science, economics, elementary education, geography, geology, journalism, landscape architecture, physical education, radio and television, sociology, speech, and urban studies and planning. Students interested in becoming teachers are especially encouraged to elect the teaching minor, area of endorsement, or supporting concentration in conservation and environmental studies to enhance their qualifications in this area. These programs are designed to prepare future teachers to enhance the curriculum through the integration of conservation and environmental studies into existing subject areas and grade levels. They should also help prepare teachers to provide leadership in schools and school corporations in establishing and implementing environmental education programs. Completion of a minor or major in natural resources also fulfills the general studies requirements in science and mathematics. Students who elect a major or minor in natural resources should enroll in NR 101 as the first course. Providing practical or "hands on" experiences is an important part of the educational programs of students enrolled in natural resources at Ball State University. Most of the courses currently offered include a weekly twohour laboratory and field experience. Some courses even include twoor threeday extended field experiences. Students are encouraged to get out where the action is by participating in practicum activities or internships extending from one to twelve weeks under the supervision of a faculty member and/or professionals working in a conservation/environmental field. If planned and approved in advance it is possible for students to earn credit while participating in this type of experience. The Department of Natural Resources is located in West Quadrangle where approximately 14,000 square feet of space is used for classrooms, laboratory/classrooms, faculty/student research labs, natural resources student reading room, faculty offices, and rooms to provide secretarial and other supporting services. In addition, educational experiences are provided by field trips to Christy Woods, local farms, Montgomery Woodlot, Irving Brothers Quarry, Muncie Water Works Plant, Muncie Wastewater Treatment Plant, local industries, and the Air Pollution Control Division of the Indiana State Board of Health. The department also utilizes the services of resource people in the community and state to enhance the educational experience provided students enrolled in natural resources classes. These include representatives of industry, local governmental units, Indiana Department of Natural Resources, Indiana State Board of Health, U.S. Soil Conservation Service, Cooperative Extension Service, and faculty from public schools and other colleges and universities. title: Introduction to Natural Resources
description: The role of natural resources and their relationship to man's social and economic welfare; population growth and its impact upon resource use. The nature and interrelationships of resources with emphasis on the multipleuse concept of resource management. Laboratory and field work included. 1 05. Conservation for Teachers. (3) The role and importance of natural resources and co nservation in our daily life. Conservation practices needed to successfully manage natural resources discussed. Conservation and natural resources information needed by the elementary school student stressed. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 101.

title: Contemporary Environmental Problems
description: The role of science in solving environmental problems with special emphasis upon the contributions people can make in achieving a quality environment through education. Current environmental problems and possible scientific and alternate technological solutions studied.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of United States resource utilization by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource utilization has shaped society. Not open to the student who has credit in JUST 204.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to man. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 4 hours of credit in natural resources, preferably NR 101 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 311.

title: Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Food Production
description: The role of natural resources in producing food for people and the agronomic and animal science practices necessary to provide food for a growing world population. Emphasis placed on the management talents needed to successfully grow food. Two weekend field trips are included.

title: Resources for Self-Reliant Living
description: Consideration of the environmental impact of hard and soft technologies. The central focus will be devising a survival strategy based on selfreliant concepts in housing, waste material, water utilization, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation and the role of regulatory agencies will also be studied. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 211; CHEM 111 or equivalent, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: The basic relationship between soil nutrients and plant growth will be discussed with emphasis on the factors affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Basic soil testing will be included. Prerequisite: NR 221; CHEM 111 or equivalent or permission of the department chairman.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Included will be soil genesis, morphology, classification, and survey. The relationship between soils information and the land use decisionmaking process will be stressed with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, utilization, management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources, including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Laboratory and field work included. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, GEOG 325, or NR 101.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts as a basis will be stressed. Management systems and individual practices will be studied with special emphasis placed on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Mineral Resources
description: The relationship of minerals to renewable resources including the role of mineral fuels as a source of energy for the human ecosystem; a descriptive and interpretive treatment of the distribution, production, and use of world mineral resources with emphasis on conservation principles, practices, and techniques. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Energy Resources
description: Appraisal of the natural resource base for energy resources and analysis of the environmental impact of the development of these energy resources. Consideration of fossil fuels as well as solar, wind, and other alternatives. Attention also directed toward energy resource policy and research and energy conservation.

title: Air Resources
description: The significance of the atmosphere as a resource; the important meteorological parameters in air resources and management; the economic, sociological, technical, political, and biological aspects of air pollution; with special emphasis on basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Ambient Air Quality Sampling and Monitoring
description: Theory and practice of sampling, analysis, and monitoring the ambient air environment. Major gaseous and particulate air pollutants are emphasized. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114, NR 341, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Effects of Ambient Air Pollution
description: Physical, chemical, and biological effects resulting from ambient air contamination. Major emphasis is placed on the atmosphere, materials, vegetation, domestic animals, and man. Prerequisite: BIO 111, NR 341 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Turfgrass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. The identification of grass and weed species is stressed.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. The interrelationships of various natural resources with emphasis directed toward multipleuse concepts of management to meet existing and projected outdoor recreation demands. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods. 38 1. Introductory Environmental Engineering. (4) Engineering principles as applied to the management of natural resources and related environmental problems. Prerequisite: NR 211, 221; GEOL 101; MATH 110; PHYCS 110 or 300; or permission of the department chairman.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures will be included. Prerequisite: NR 211; MATH 110 or equivalent; one college course in chemistry; or permission of the department chairman. 38 7. Solid Waste Management. (4) Solid waste management with emphasis on delineation of the problem, disposal methods and techniques, recycling, and management of disposal systems. The relationship between solid waste disposal and other resources is stressed. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairman.

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Restricted to honors students or by permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the elementary education curriculum. Sources of help in teaching conservation, including the use of resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources that are uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 101, 105, BIO 102, GEOG 111, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Environmental Conservation in the Secondary School
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating environmental conservation into the secondary school curriculum. Sources of help in teaching environmental conservation including resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources appropriate to environmental conservation. Laboratory and field work required. Prerequisite: NR 101 or

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Scienceoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of science, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of environmental science in the secondary school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Up to five hours experience in public schools may be required. Prerequisite or parallel: NR 395 or permission of the department chairman. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 399.

title: Natural Resources Agencies and Environmental Organizations
description: The development, organizational structure, responsibilities, activities, and contributions of selected local, state, regional, and federal natural resources agencies and private organizations in managing natural resources and achieving and/or maintaining a quality environment. Employment policies and career opportunities will also be considered.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: Natural resources of a particular area with special emphasis on location of natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence these natural resources have on the regional environmental quality. Each time the course is offered the specific geographic area will be studied. Laboratory and field experience included. Prerequisite: NR 101 or equivalent and permission of department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Natural Resources Planning
description: The application of basic planning principles, concepts and procedures in resource development and environmental management. Emphasis on the importance of natural resources in the planning process. Prerequisite: 12 hours in natural resources and POLS 160 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Integrated Resources Management
description: Integrated management of resources with emphasis on combinations of principles prerequisite to the formulation and implementation of natural resources policies and programs. Attention to the economic, social, and political implications of resource development. Prerequisite: senior standing. Prerequisite or parallel: all natural resources core courses or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Issues
description: An opportunity to identify and gain an understanding of selected environmental issues relevant to the local geographic area. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Research Methodologies in Natural Resources
description: Development of concepts and skills for undergraduate students preparing for undergraduate or graduate research or researchoriented professions in natural resources. Introduction to the common types of research study, research writing, research instruments, and faculty research interest and projects.

title: Seminar
description: Formal reports and discussion of selected natural resource topics, current events, and special articles in naturalresourcerelated professional and scientific journals. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Air Quality Management
description: Principles of air quality management with emphasis on control programs, regulatory strategies, and control technology. Prerequisite: NR 341, 343, 345 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered Spring Quarter of evennumbered years. Prerequisite: NR 211, BIO 480, and ZOOL 444, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and utilization of natural resources for outdoor recreation. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Administration and Management of Outdoor Recreation Areas
description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to implement outdoor recreation plans to provide quality outdoor recreation experiences. One weekend field trip may be required in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Wilderness and Society
description: Concerned with defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. Integral to the course will be a study of research in user perception and use, and a weekend trip to a potential Indiana wilderness area. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Principles of Natural Resources Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis on field work and creative presentation of concepts. Prerequisite: NR 101, 211, 221; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Organization and Management of Interpretive Programs
description: Develops skills and techniques nd relative to the sound organization and management of interpretive programs, including sites a facilities. Emphasis on planning procedures and field study of existing programs. Prerequisite: NR 101, 211, 221; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Resident Environmental Education
description: Philosophy and techniques of resident environmental education and an analysis of exemplary programs. Emphasis on the practical aspects of using resident environmental education facilities, curriculum planning, outdoor class management, evaluation, and administration including staffing, financing, and related activities. Prerequisite: NR 101 or 105 or permission of the department chairman.

title: The Resource Manager's Role in Information and Education Programs
description: The contributions natural resource managers can make in communicating their knowledge to individuals, schools, service clubs, agencies, governmental units, and other organizations. The role of resource managers in developing a conservationconscious public is discussed. Adult education techniques and methodologies are developed. Laboratory and field work included. Prerequisite: NR 10] or permission of the department chairman.

title: Practicum in Natural Resources
description: Supervised practical professional experience relating theory and practice by combining instruction and work activities in natural resources, including conservation education, outdoor education, or environmental education. Prerequisite : permision of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours credit may bearned; 12 of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources
description: An opportunity to pursue special interests in the area of environmental quality. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned; 12 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 496.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Participation in original research under faculty guidance. Research will include: problem definition, literature review, data collection, analysis, and a summary report. Preparatory or parallel course work in research methodologies, statistics, or computer science may be required. Prerequisite: faculty sponsor and permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Philosophy Annis, Chairperson; Andry, Barker, Foster, Mitchell, Mueller, Robertson Philosophy as an Academic Discipline Philosophy is the attempt to arrive at reasoned answers to important questions that fall outside the scope of any particular science, either because they are normative, or especially general, or more fundamental than the questions the sciences raise. The major areas within philosophy include: 1. Logic—the study of techniques of critical reasoning. This is a primary tool for resolving philosophical issues. 2. Metaphysics—examines questions concerning the ultimate nature of reality—for example, is there a Supreme Being, are all our actions causally determined, do machines think, etc. 3. Epistemology—deals with the theory of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism. 4. Ethics—the study of such problems as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as contemporary moral problems including abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, and famine relief. Other important areas in philosophy include the history of philosophy, social philosophy, existentialism, and oriental philosophy. Examining a philosophical question involves the clarification of basic concepts in order to improve one's understanding of the issues, as well as a critical evaluation of the arguments given to support different positions. By critically evaluating basic philosophical questions, students improve their critical thinking ability as well as their communication skills. They learn how to evaluate an argument and how to express an issue clearly. Philosophy 291 Students desiring a professional career in philosophy generally consider teaching at the college or university level. A number teach at junior colleges, and some high schools are now introducing courses in philosophy. Philosophy is an excellent major or minor for students preparing for vocations requiring a liberal education, plus skills in critical thinking, conceptual analysis, problem solving, and skills in communication. Thus it is appropriate preparation for careers in law, public service, governmental agencies, writing, as well as any religionoriented vocation. Religious Studies as an Academic Discipline A knowledge of the religion of any culture is essential to the understanding of that culture. This is indeed true of our own culture, as well as of other cultures. Students preparing for teaching careers will be expected to deal with religious ideas, values, institutions, and practices in their teaching. Courses in religious subject matter are being expanded in public schools. A small but increasing number of students come to Ball State to prepare for theological studies. Others decide to pursue a life of religious service after entering Ball State. To meet the increasing demands of these situations, Ball State provides students with the opportunity to pursue religious studies. Any student may register in courses which are designed for all four years of university life. The courses are classified under the general headings of cultural settings of religion, Biblical studies, church history, and religions of the world. Any course in religious studies counts for credit as a general elective in any program of studies within the university, it counts for credit as a humanities elective for general studies, or a student may acquire a departmental major or minor in religious studies by successfully completing the requirements in this area.
