title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: An introduction to important philosophical problems. Typical topics include the existence of God, whether ethical values are subjective, the extent of our freedom. These problems and others may be approached by examining the ideas of great philosophers or current thinkers.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of human thinking as far as human thinking is concerned with deduction.

title: Inductive Logic
description: An introduction to the principles and problems of inductive reasoning.

title: Ethics
description: A discussion of some of the central problems in ethics such as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as a discussion of current moral issues.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of basic social concepts such as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of normative issues such as how liberty should be distributed and how justice can be maximized. Students selecting these courses are advised to check with the director of the program and the Catalog concerning prerequisites.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Critical analysis of selected problems such as the nature and existence of God, the problem of evil, the justification of religious belief, and the significance of religious experience. Not open to the student who has credit in RELST 391.

title: Introduction to Existentialism
description: A discussion of major existentialists includin g Kierkegard, Nietzsche, Sartre, as wel importanthemes in existentialism such as alienation, subjectivism, the meaning of life, and freedom. Not open to the student who has credit i n PHIL 421.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophical theories and ideas from the rise of philosophy in Greece about 600 B.C. to the fall of Rome. Emphasis is upon these theories in their relation to one another, the times in which they were produced, and the thinkers by whom they were offered.

title: History of Medieval Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophical theories and ideas from the fall of Rome to the Renaissance. Consideration of the inheritance of medieval Europe from the Graeco-Romanearly Christian world and of the creative role played by medieval philosophy in the formation of the Western tradition especially after the rediscovery of Aristotle.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: History of the development of philosophical theories and ideas from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Emphasis is upon these theories in relation to one another, the times in which they were produced, and the thinkers by whom they were offered.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics discussed may include: the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of the department head.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading philosophers and movements in the twentieth century. May concentrate on selected philosophers such as Russell, Wittgenstein, Husserl or may concentrate on contemporary treatments of selected philosophical problems.

title: Aesthetics
description: Exploration of philosophical views on the nature, interpretation, and criticism of art. Readings and discussion may range from classical to contemporary thinkers and issues.

title: Introduction to Legal Philosophy
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of basic concepts such as action, intention, causation, responsibility.

title: Philosophy of Language
description: Study of philosophical theories of language and the role of language in the treatment of philosophical problems. Issues investigated may include views of truth, linguistic paradoxes, and other problems related to language, its interpretation and structure.

title: Current Issues in Philosophy
description: Selected current and important issues in philosophy. Topics may include social and ethical problems, recent work on traditional philosophical problems, and other issues of concern.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: An examination of central philosophical problems in the sciences such as the nature of scientific explanation and the testing of hypotheses, as well as a discussion of ethical issues arising from science such as the use of human subjects, prolonging life.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Prerequisite: students in the Honors College or by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Provides superior students with an opportunity for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Metaphysics
description: A study of the principal problems of metaphysics including the nature of reality, the relation of mind and body, the issue of freedom and determinism.

title: Introduction to Theory of Knowledge
description: A critical discussion of leading theories and problems of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge and rational belief, the different kinds of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism.

title: Oriental Philosophy
description: Philosophical exploration of Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, and Confucianism.

title: Plato and Aristotle
description: An indepth examination of selected works of Plato or Aristotle and their influence in the history of philosophy. Philosophy 293

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory and Problems
description: A critical examination of recent ethical theories and their application to contemporary problems.

title: Advanced Existentialism
description: Indepth study of the writings of a particular major existentialist; or the instructor may elect to examine selected works of more than one existentialist examining a specific topic such as freedom or authenticity.

title: Kant
description: The philosophy of Kant with emphasis on his Critique of Pure Reason and Prolegomena.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: An introductory survey of the major religions in the United States with emphasis on their historical development, distinctive beliefs, institutions, and practices. Attention will be given to political consequences and the social significance of American religious pluralism.

title: The Long Search
description: A series of thirteen videotape programs plus class discussions about man's religious experiences, a series of encounters with men and women around the world who are living their faiths in the face of real life situations, overpopulation, materialism, inflation, H-bombs, pollution.

title: New Religious Movements
description: A contemporary focus on nonnormative religious movements (theosophical spirtualist, occult, oriental, neopagan as upsurges of shamanism) in America, based on the three categories of religious expression: verbal, practical, social; and on the concept of religion as means for ultimate transformation.

title: Old Testament
description: The origins and developments of Hebrew-Judaic thought: its progressive expressions throughout time in personalities, theologies, and various types of Hebrew-Judaic literature.

title: New Testament
description: A basic study of the origins and developments of Christian religious thought: its Jewish environment, its early expressions, the emergence of its literature, and the various forms of its expression as found in its earliest literature.

title: Evolution of Christian Thought
description: Christian thought as it evolved in early catholicism, the orthodox creeds, the eastwest schism, the medieval age, the reformation, and the controversy between rationalism and pietism. Consideration also given to recent trends in Christian thought.

title: Christian Ethics
description: Reflection upon life and morality from the standpoint of Christian faith and fundamental Christian convictions. Discussion of contemporary ethical issues in the light of important theological presuppositions; good and evil, divine law, sin and redemption, freedom, conscience, love.

title: Religion in a Scientific World
description: Dialogue between religion and science: areas of conflict and modes of similarity. Differing perspectives on the nature and meaning of life. Theological implications in new areas of technological advance; genetic control, cybernetics, new artificial means of prolonging life.

title: Paul and His Influence in Early Christianity
description: The life and thought of Paul as they relate to his letters and to the Acts of the Apostles in the context of firstcentury Christianity, the development of radical Paulinism and anti-Paulinism, their influence on the formation of Christianity.

title: Jesus and the Gospel Traditions
description: Jesus and the types of tradition about him; their origins, development, and functions in early Christianity as reflected in the early Christian writings, with special interest in the Gospels.

title: Problems in the Early Church
description: A consideration of problems in the early church such as resurrection, christophanies, messiahship of Jesus, conversion of Paul, Glossolalia or tongues, Sabbath versus Sunday, eucharist, baptism, Paul's missionary journeys, the Jerusalem Conference, Paul's imprisonment, early persecutions.

title: Religions of the Ancient Near East
description: The religious movements of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, and Persia as they relate to the development of Judaism and the rise of Christianity.

title: Religions of India
description: The religious heritage of India: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism; the ways of life they advocate, their scriptures, developments of their theologies.

title: Religions of China and Japan
description: Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, Maoism, Shintoism. Origin and developments; literature; rites and rituals.

title: Principles of Theology
description: Consideration of traditional theological principles regarding the nature of God, of mankind, of redemption, and of the church, and an inquiry into contemporary thinking on these issues, with emphasis on the latter.

title: Religious Existentialism
description: Examines both the position and effects of religious existentialists related to current religious views and movements. The contributions of men such as Kierkegaard, Tillich, and Buber will be critically analyzed in the light of orthodox Christianity.

title: Comparative Religions
description: A comparative study of the great world religions. Department of Physics and Astronomy Hults, Chairman; Burgess, Cosby, Errington, Howes, Koltenbah, Mrozowski, Ober, Pitts, Place, Robertson, Scott, Thomas, Watson The Department of Physics and Astronomy offers courses intended to provide a thorough background in physics, both pure and applied, and a moderate background in astronomy. Programs are designed specifically for different groups of students such as those planning to make physics or astronomy a career, those planning to teach, and others needing work i n physics, aplied or astronomy to complementheir major field. This diversification is evident in the course descriptions. It is recommended that students planning to go to graduate school in physics or related areas take PHYCS 430, 434, 450, 452, and 464. It is suggested that students planning to go into industry, government laboratories, or other fields of work with a bachelor's degree in physics take PHYCS 354, 356, 358, 360, and APHYS 454. Physics and astronomy students planning to go to graduate school should take CS 220, It is also recommended that German, French, or Russian be studied if the graduate school that will be attended requires a foreign language for Ph.D. or M.S. candidacy. Physics major and minor programs are available both for those students planning to make physics a career and those planning to teach. An astronomy minor is available with two options, one for those who want to pursue astronomy as a career taking further advanced work at another university and another option designed specifically for those whose goal is to have expertise in presenting planetarium programs and becoming planetarium directors. A minor in applied physics is availably for students wanting to learn modern electronics and the use of electronics in instrumentation and computers. Courses in selected areas of applied physics such as heat transfer, fluid mechanics, solar energy, and microprocessor electronics may be taken by the student. Courses having the APHYS or PHYCS prefix but not listed in the requirements (see below) as allowed electives may be taken by the interested student and substituted for listed electives upon written approval of the department head or departmental adviser. Physics and astronomy courses have two hours of regularly scheduled laboratory a week during the regular school year unless designated otherwise. In evening and Saturday classes and in the summer terms a ratio of lecture and laboratory experiences equivalent to the quarter dayclass ratio is maintained. PRE-ENGINEERING MAJOR This departmental major is intended for students interested in preparing themselves for admission to a school of engineering. Specifically, the program is offered in cooperation with the Purdue University School of Engineering so that courses taken at Ball State on the preengineering curriculum parallel courses the student would take at Purdue during the first several years of study. Although the courses taken at Ball State on the preengineering curriculum are similar or identical to those taken by students at many institutions offering engineering programs, the School of Engineering at Purdue is the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program whereby the student attends Ball State for three years then transfers to Purdue to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of such a program the student is eligible to receive a bachelor's degree from Ball State and the engineering degree from Purdue. It is possible to complete the degree requirements for both institutions in less than five years if summer sessions are attended. The student may, of course, elect to transfer to Purdue or some other engineering school before completing the full preengineering course of study at Ball State. In such a case, the student will be eligible to receive only the degree at the institution to which he or she may transfer. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not mean automatic admission to the Purdue University School of Engineering. The student must contact Purdue and apply for admission when he or she wants to transfer. The student should have completed at least a full year of physics (PIIYCS 120, 122, 124) and a year of calculus prior to transfer. Three options on the preengineering major are available. title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting energy forms such as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physical Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles and concepts of the laws of nature involving mechanical, heat, light, electrical, nuclear, and chemical energy and the conservation laws associated with these forms of energy. Emphasis on applications appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Preparation of Physical Science Teaching Materials
description: A study of selected topics in physical science stressing the construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs. Prerequisite: PHYCS 101 or permission of the department head. Open only to students on the teacher education curriculum.

title: Physics and Sports
description: A descriptive introduction to basic physical principles and laws within a framework of applications to athletic activities and sports. Particularly suited to the student with areas or special interest in physical education. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110, 120, or 130.

title: General Physics
description: Mechanics, properties of matter, and heat. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary algebra.

title: General Physics
description: Magnetism, electricity, and atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110.

title: General Physics
description: Sound and light. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110,

title: Orientation Seminar for Preengineering and Beginning Physics Students
description: An overview of the fields of physics and engineering that will aid science students in effectively planning their college curriculum. Students will be introduced to career scientists and the jobs performed by persons in these professions. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 120.

title: General Physics 1
description: A first course in calculusbased physics for students with areas in preengineering, the physical sciences, or mathematics. Topics studied include Newtonian Mechanics (statics and dynamics), motion in a plane, the workenergy principle, impulse and momentum (linear and rotational), elasticity and harmonic motion, and hydrostatics and hydrodynamics. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 161 or 170.

title: General Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 120. Topics studied include Coulomb's Law and the electric field, Gauss's Law, dc circuits and instruments, the magnetic field, Ampere's Law, Faraday's Law, the magnetic properties of matter, the integral form of Maxwell's equation, alternatingcurrent circuits, impedance, and electromagnetic waves. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120. Parallel: MATH 162 or 171.

title: General Physics 3
description: Topics studied include waves, acoustic phenomena, the nature and propagation of light, reflection, refraction, image formation by lenses and mirrors, interference and diffraction, polarization, heat flow, thermal properties of matter, the laws of thermodynamics, the kinetic theory of gases, and introductory atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120, MATH 162 or 171. Students having a major or minor in mathematics or computer science may substitute MATH 170, 171 for these courses. § Students will be placed in appropriate beginning courses in mathematics.

title: Physics 1 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of mechanics and heat. Topics include particle dynamics, resolution of forces, friction, work, energy, static equilibrium, torque, properties of materials, fluids, temperature, thermal expansion, heat energy, heat transfer, phase changes in matter, and thermodynamic engines. Prerequisite: MATH 112 or equivalent secondary school mathematics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Physics 2 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of sound, light, and electrical power. Topics include wave phenomena, sound characteristics, sound production and absorption, human response to sound, reflection, refraction, geometrical optics, polarization, circuits, Ohm's Law, Kirchoff's Laws, electromagnetic induction, transformers, meters, and power distribution systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 112 or 120.

title: Sound and Light
description: For music and art students. Sound as a basis of music and light as a basis of art. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Household Physics
description: Practical applications of physics in common everyday appliances and other devices. Topics include: why fuses blow, principles of heating and cooling, and principles of some electrical and electronic home appliances.

title: Topics in Physics
description: Discussion of a specific topic in physics. Examples are: lasers, holography, and solidstate electronics. No math or science background is needed. For the nonphysics major. For the specific topics being studied during a given quarter, consult your curricular adviser, or the Department of Physics and Astronomy. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Solar Energy Technology and Applications
description: Descriptive study of various techniques and systems developed for utilizing sunlight as a nonpolluting alternative energy source. Major emphasis on the physical principles and design of solar systems for space heating, air conditioning, and hot water heating for residential and commercial buildings, and systems for the generation of electric power. Other related topics include: energy storage, argicultural and industrial applications, solar stills, solar furnaces, ocean thermal power, wind energy systems, and total energy systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or MATH 111.

title: Sound and Acoustical Art
description: A descriptive treatment of basic sound and acoustics, using a minimum of mathematics. It is especially tailored to the needs of music and other related areas such as speech. Involves pitch, wavelength, intensity levels. Not open to students with areas in physics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 184.

title: Introduction to Audio Engineering
description: An introductory course in the physics of the reproduction of sound. The principles involved in the operation of electroacoustical transducers such as phono cartridges, loudspeakers, and tape heads will be studied. Electronic principles as applied to the amplification process. Actual measurements of frequency response and speaker parameters conducted by the student in the laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or permission of the department head.

title: Photographic Optics in the Visual Arts
description: Principles of light and optics for students majoring in areas other than a physical science where a basic understanding of light and optics in photography is desired. Tailored to meet the needs of photojournalism, art, and other students with similar interests.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
description: An introduction to classical electric and magnetic theory with introduction of vector notation. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and MATH 172.

title: Introduction to Modern Physics
description: Introduction to atomic and nuclear physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Modern Experimental Techniques in Physics
description: Includes experimentation, instrumentation, and data analysis techniques appropriate for modern physics laboratory work. Included are experiments on electron charge and ionization potentials. Statistical treatment of experimental data is discussed including the theory of error propagation, least squares, and analysis of spectral information using Fourier techniques.

title: Environmental Physics
description: The application of physics to environmental and societal problems. Physical principles underlying hardtechnology based industries will be discussed. Topics include: energy production, transmission, and environmental effects (including nuclear power generation and radiation); transportation problems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or the equivalent.

title: Electronics for the Life Sciences
description: Applications of electronics to the problems encountered by students in the life sciences. Electronic instruments used in biology, health, and physiology and the problems associated with their use. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 354 or 356.

title: Mechanics 1
description: Basic concepts of particle mechanics. Vector algebra and calculus. Kinematics and dynamics of a particle in two and three dimensions. Simple and dampedharmonic motion. Particle dynamics in noninertial frames of reference. Central force motion. Dynamics of a system of particles. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120 and either MATH 162 or 172.

title: Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 330. Dynamics of a rigid body the moment of inertia tensor. Mechanics of deformable continua, the stress tensor. The wave equation, elasticity, and rigid body vibrations. Variational techniques, virtual work, Lagrange's equations of the first and second kind. Hamiltonian mechanics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330.

title: Physical Optics
description: The electromagnetic wave theory of light, spectra, interference, diffraction, polarization, and double refraction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Acoustics
description: Aspects of pure and applied acoustics. Topics to be discussed include solutions to the wave equation, acoustic impedances, electro - mechanicalacoustic analogies, direct- PHYCS 122. radiator loudspeaker and enclosure theory, and a discussion of room acoustics. Prerequisite:

title: Electronics 1
description: Characteristics of electronic components and their circuit functions. Circuit analysis, design, and construction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 or permission of the department head.

title: Electronics 2
description: The function and use of integrated circuitry as applied to pulse and digital circuits found in laboratory and computer apparatus. Prerequisite: PHYCS 354 or permission of department head.

title: Pulse and Digital Electronics
description: The function and use of pulse and digital circuitry as applied to laboratory and commerical electronic apparatus. Prerequisite: PHYCS 356 or permission of the department head.

title: Introductory Nuclear Techniques
description: Emphasis upon experimental studies of radioactive disintegrations and decay products and their relation to nuclear structure. Instrumentation in radioisotope measurements. Two lectures and two twohour laboratory periods per week. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those which occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Prerequisites: PHYCS 124 and 260, or permission of the department head.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those which occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Such topics as boundary value problems (involving linear differential equations and partial differential equations), transforms, and special functions (Green's function approach, Fourier series, Legendre's equation, Bessel's equation, Hermite polynomials, etc.) of mathematical physics are covered. Prerequisites: PHYCS 124 and 260 or permission of the department head.

title: Descriptive Astronomy
description: The celestial sphere, the solar system, formation and decay of stars, instruments and basic laws of astronomy, nebulae, galactic structure, theories of the origin of the universe; constellation and telescope work.

title: The Teaching of Physics in the Secondary School
description: Aims, nature of the subject matter, amount and nature of laboratory work, standardized tests, and textbooks used in the teaching of physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in physics. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Celestial Mechanics
description: An application of the laws of classical mechanics to objects under the influence of inversesquare gravitational forces, leading to the theory of orbits and perturbative effects on orbits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 332.

title: Thermodynamics
description: Laws of thermodynamics and introduction to the kinetic theory of gases. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 1
description: Application of vector analysis to electrostatics, dipole and multipole fields, and dielectric theory. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 450 with emphasis on dynamic electrical problems, alternating currents, magnetic fields, and Maxwell's equations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 450.

title: Elementary Particles
description: The nature and behavior of elementary particles through the study of the symmetries and dynamics responsible for their production, reactions, and decays. Prerequisite: PHYCS 465.

title: Nuclear Physics
description: Nucleus and nuclear interactions. Experimental facts about nuclear processes will be emphasized in discussions on the following topics: particle accelerators, detectors, radioactivity (alpha, beta, and gamma decay), interaction of radiation with matter, nuclear reactions, nuclear structure, nuclear models, and nuclear applications in science and technology. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 1
description: De Broglie's postulate, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the free particle, square well potentials, harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom, and other selected wave mechanics problems. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites: PIIYCS 260 and MATH 172.

title: Quantum Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 464. Course material includes perturbation theory, oneelectron atoms, magnetic moments, spin, relativistic effects, symmetric and antisymmetric eigenfunctions, the helium atom, the Thomas-Fermi theory, the Hartree theory, and transition rates. Prerequisite: PHYCS 464.

title: Solid State Physics 1
description: An investigation of the structure and physical properties of matter in the solid state. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisites: PHYCS 260 and MATH 172.

title: Solid State Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 466. Topics include the electrical and magnetic properties of solids and the band theory of solids with special emphasis on semiconductors. Optical properties of solids and the effects of lattice defects are studied. Prerequisite: PHYCS 466.

title: Independent Studies in Physics
description: Pursuit of special lines of scientific investigation in physics on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Physics Investigations in the Field
description: Investigative problems in physics which need to be pursued at other locations than at Ball State due to specialized facilities being at the specific location. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in this course is contingent upon permission of the department head.

title: Mysteries of the Sky
description: A nontechnical and nonrnathematical multimedia excursion into the vast reaches of the sky including information about the sun, the moon, shooting stars, comets, supernovae, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, life on other planets.

title: Astronomy Materials for the Teacher
description: The fundamentals of astronomy including historical aspects as well as modern astronomy concepts. Construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom are stressed. Designed primarily for students on elementary education programs.

title: Observational Astronomy
description: A continuation of ASTRO 100 providing practical experience in observing celestial objects by using telescopes and other astronomical apparatus. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100.

title: General Astronomy 1
description: Essential points of modern astronomy, emphasizing the underlying physical principles. Topics include: coordinate systems in astronomy, orbital laws, relativity, planetary physics, measurement of stellar distances, and spectral classification of stars. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100 or PHYCS 380, and MATH 111.

title: General Astronomy 2
description: A continuation of ASTRO 120. Topics include atomic structure and stellar spectra, stellar atmospheres and interiors, multiple star systems and clusters, galactic structure, cosmology, and the origin of the universe. Prerequisite: ASTRO 120. Parallel: MATH 112.

title: Topics in Astronomy
description: Discussion of a specific topic in astronomy. Examples are: comets, eclipses, UFO's, and interstellar travel. No mathor science background is needed. For the nonphysics major. For specific topics being studied during a given quarter consult your curricular adviser, or the Department of Physics and Astronomy. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 1
description: An indepth study of the solar system starting with earliest concepts and extending to modern space explorations. Topics will include the celestial sphere, theories of planetary motions, the earth and moon, celestial mechanics, the origin of the solar system, and the sun's planets as habitats for life. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120, 122, 124.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 2
description: Introduction to the basic properties of stars. Topics covered will include stellar distances and motions, stellar magnitudes, luminosities and colors, the H-R diagram, stellar evolution and energy production, double and variable stars, and nebulae. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 3
description: A detailed survey of the Milky Way Galaxy and the general structure of the Universe as a whole. Topics covered will include the structure and dynamics of the Milky Way, other galaxies, quasistellar objects (quasars), and cosmology. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330 and 332.

title: Seminar in Modern Astronomy
description: Seminar covering selected topics in contemporary astronomy. Extensive use of library facilities including current journals and periodicals in astronomy. Topics for study may include ongoing astronomical research, and such esoteric subjects as UFO's and extraterrestrial life. Prerequisite: ASTRO 334.

title: Instruments and Techniques in Planetarium Operations
description: Use of planetarium s instrum ents, console, and chamber. Creation presentation of planetarium program tracks. including slide duplicating techniques, opaquing, and the production of sound Prerequisite: permission of the planetarium director. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 382.

title: Theories and Instruments of the Astronomer
description: Reviews of various atlases, catalogs, ephemerides, and charts. The development of methods used to compute and update stellar positions. Astronomical instruments will be discussed in the context of their use by research astronomers. An analysis will be made of the specific techniques employed in astronomical photometry, spectroscopy, and photography. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330, 332, and 334.

title: Advanced Astrophysics
description: A detailed investigation of the frontier areas of modern astrophysics. Possible topics will include stellar structure, nucleosynthesis, stellar evolution, stellar atmospheres, and the interstellar material. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330, 332, and 334.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Lasers and Applied Electro-Optic Techniques
description: Principles of laser operation, design, and safety considered within the context of the field of electrooptic techniques. Optical detection devices such as photodetector and laser power meters, photographic techniques such as in holography, and laser applications stressed in the "handson" laboratoryoriented portion of the course. Prerequisite: PHYCS 114 or 124 or permission of the department head.

title: Fluid Mechanics 1
description: The forces and motions in fluids. Fluid characteristics and the basic theories of fluid statics and dynamics discussed. Applications in the fields of solar energy systems, hydraulics, aerodynamics, meteorology, hydrology, and fluidics will be cited. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172; PHYCS 330.

title: Fluid Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of APHYS 410. Turbulence and nonuniform flows are studied. The theories and equations of fluid mechanics are applied to areas such as environmental conditioning systems, thermal convection processes and circulation of the atmosphere, topic of tides and currents, airfoils, pipe flow, medical applications, astrophysics, and others. Computerized models are utilized by students for detailed studies of individual applications of interest. Prerequisite: APHYS 410.

title: Applied Solar Energy 1
description: The solar energy resource, the physics and engineering of solar collection, concentration, thermal conversion, and storage. Analysis of solar spectral content, attenuation, and variation; evaluation of flat plate collector efficiencies; and quantitative appraisal of thermal storage materials are typical topics. Three lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: MATH 172 or 162, PHYCS 122, 124.

title: Applied Solar Energy 2
description: The engineering design, component integration, operation, and performance of solar heating and cooling systems. System modeling and sizing of residential and commercial solar space heating, water heating, and space cooling units. Control instrumentation hardware, functions, and operation. Prerequisite: APHYS 420.

title: Applied Solar Energy 3
description: Solar electric power generation, advanced solar systems, applications in industry and agriculture, the total energy concept, and the solar hydrogen economy. Physics and engineering of solar thermal power plants, solar cells, solar satellites, ocean thermal energy conversion, windmills, and bioconversion. Three onehour lectures and a twohour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: APHYS 422.

title: Heat Transfer
description: The basic heat transfer processes in nature. Conduction, convection, and radiation in applied problems are analyzed using electricalmodelanalogue, graphical, and computerized numerical methods. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 172; PHYCS 124; or permission of the department head.

title: Microprocessor and Microcomputer Electronics
description: Principles and uses of microprocessors and microcomputers. Microprocessor and microcomputer timing, bus structures, inputoutput interfacing, memory interfacing, analogtodigital and digitaltoanalog conversion techniques. Gobble, Gowings, Griffin, Grigsby, Hahn, Henzlik, Jarial, Jones, Kennedy, Lesh, Marini, Paschall, Payne, Pinger,INantz, Womack The Department of Physiology and Health Science represents a multidisciplinary study of the life sciences and their application to health promotion and disease prevention. Physiology is the study of life forms in terms of vital functions of cells, tissues, organs, and systems and their several life processes in relation to both internal and external environments. Anatomy is the specialized investigation of the structure of cells, tissues, organs, and systems, as these constitute the basic units which experience life, health, disease, and death. A relatively new discipline, Health Science involves the application of scientific health principles to human life, primarily through programs of health education based in schools, community health agencies, health care facilities, and industrial settings. The goals of Health Science are to help individuals make intelligent decisions in solving personal, family, and community health problems, and to assist persons in leading personally satisfying and socially constructive, healthy lives. Derived primarily from anatomy, physiology, psychology, and sociology, Health Science has important reciprocal relationships with chemistry, physics, home economics, physical education, philosophy, logic, and education. Applied to the human conditions of wellness and lifestyling in the promotion of health status, Health Science includes such areas as drug dependence and abuse, human sexuality, lack of exercise in a sedentary society, health care delivery, selfmedication and consumer health education, health and disease throughout the human life cycle, community health problems, and emergency health care. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers both a teaching major and teaching minor designed to meet Indiana state licensing requirements for teaching Health and Safety in grades 7-12. Additionally, an endorsement for teaching Health Science and Safety in the elementary school provides elementary education majors with specific competencies for promoting students' health status through the school health program in grades K-6. Students who are interested in community health education programs rather than school health consult with the departmental chairperson. The department also offers a major in physical therapy, a professional program of study including coursework in the theory and clinical practice of physical therapy and related sciences. Two departmental minors are also administered by the department: (1) the physiology minor provides the necessary background for application to appropriate professional schools or to graduate education in anatomy and/or physiology; and (2) the public health minor prepares candidates for entrylevel positions in community health agencies, both governmental and private. At the present time, the department contributes required and elective courses to several academic programs at Ball State, including preprofessional programs in allied health science areas, courses for professional nurse preparation, and general education. The department provides guidance to students who are interested in teaching, research, or service careers related to life science, and health promotion. Membership in Sigma Zeta, the national honorary in science and mathematics, and in Eta Sigma Gamma, the national honorary in health science, is offered to qualified students who earn high scholastic honors. title: Elements of Human Health
description: Human biology stressing the personal and informational aspects of current health problems. Hygiene of the basic systems of the body with emphasis on care, functions, and disorders; natural and acquired defenses against disease; elements of preventive medicine; and modern standards of sanitation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 160.

title: Fundamentals of Human Health
description: The main purpose is to promote total individual fitness. Intelligent selfmanagement, based on understanding of body functioning, is an objective. Some problems considered are the following: existing health situations; use of physicians, dentists, and public agencies; infections and body defense; in emergencies, what to do until the doctor comes; food and one's efficiency; emotional health; and basic understanding t The following courses are prerequisite to this program: BIO 111; CHEM (110, 111, 112) or (113, 114), CHEM 231 required if this course is elected. 2 Prerequisite waived for student admitted to the physical therapy major. of human reproduction. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 150.

title: Community Health Problems
description: Organization of official and nonofficial health agencies at the various levels; international, national, state, and local. Exploration of causative community factors in disease, community diagnoses of disease, and programs being investigated to combat these conditions. Selected communicable, noncommunicable, and behaviortype problems including traffic safety will be the focus for the application of principles and procedures. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Emergency Health Care
description: Various emergency health problems and their management by the application of emergency health care as recommended by the American Red Cross and Civil Defense authorities. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 299 or 396.

title: Introduction to Occupational Safety and Health
description: A qualitative and quantitative study of the interface between individuals, their tools, and their work environment and the methods by which the resulting health hazards can be controlled to an acceptable level. Prerequisite: HSC 250.

title: School Health Practice
description: Community and school health services. Practical experiences in screening for visual, auditory, and nutritional defects. Identification and control of childhood diseases. Topics included: accidents, safety, and first aid; materials for teaching health; role of the teacher and school health personnel; and effect of the total school program on the health of the child. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: School Health Organization
description: Organization and development of school health programs. Coordination of school and community health programs, hygiene, and sanitation of the school plant, the school lunch program, school health services, and the health instructional program. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 350.

title: Health Appraisal of School Children
description: Sociological, psychological, and physiological changes that take place in school children. Prevalent health problems that occur in school children—their etiology, pathology, diagnosis, and prognosis. Experience in screening techniques for discovering these deviations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 350 or 360.

title: Insects and Human Health
description: A survey of diseases caused or transmitted by insects and other arthropods. Emphasis is given to the recognition of medically important insects and to their biology as it relates to human disease. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: Honors Colloquium in Health Science
description: Exploration of selected current issues in health science with an emphasis upon individualized study, reporting, and discussion. Restricted to honors students.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Health and Safety
description: Examination of the Indiana state course of study in health and safety, relation of health policies and current schoolhomecommunity problems, practice with audiovisual aids, evaluation of representative textbooks, and visits to offcampus schools. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials in Health and Safety
description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of health and safety, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of health and safety in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: HSC 395.

title: Health Science of Distant Areas
description: School and public health programs at local, state, and national levels. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students on elementary curricula, students with concentration areas in health science on secondary curricula, and students in public health areas. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Repeated enrollment in the course is contingent upon permission of the department chairman.

title: Health, Sexuality, and Family Life
description: The family as the basic unit in society with consideration of the health problems facing the family. Emphasis is given to tracing relationships between men and women in the areas of dating, courtship, marriage, and problems of raising children; human anatomy, physiology, and embryology; and responsibilities of the home and school in the sex education of the schoolage child. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or a major or minor in health science, home economics, biology, teacher education, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Sex Education and School Health
description: Development of an understanding of how to implement and teach a positive program of sex education aimed at helping young people develop constructive attitudes, values, and practices based on sound knowledge in accordance with American Medical Association recommendation and pertinent state guidelines. Prerequisite: HSC 461 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Patient Education: A Team Approach
description: Theories of client education and application of the education process to individuals and groups in a variety of health care settings. Emphasis on the multidisciplinary team concept in planning, implementing, and evaluating client education. Application of knowledge of growth and development in meeting learning needs of clients from a variety of age and intellectual levels.

title: Alcohol Problems
description: A study of alcohol as a mood modifier, its use, nonuse, and abuse in drinking societies. Critical and controversial issues relevant to alcohol ingestion will be explored for medical, economic, legal, educational, historical, physiological, and public health implications.

title: Current Progress in Disease Control
description: A critical review of pertinent research being conducted on leading causes of mortality and morbidity in the United States. A description and analysis of this current research will enable participants to gain an appreciation and understanding of current health progress in the United States. Particular emphasis upon the potential for application of this information into individual, school, and community health programs. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Drug Dependence and Abuse
description: An analysis of the medical, psychological, sociological, and legal dimensions of drug use in the United States. The incidence and prevalence of drug abuse together with the roles played by the school and community in dealing with this health problem will be treated. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health Quackery
description: Health services and consumer protection organizations. An analysis of fraudulent health practices and nostrums, available health care systems and health products. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Health and Aging
description: Dynamics of later life and the aging process with specific emphasis on health. The physiological and behavioral dimensions of the aging process will be analyzed and discussed.

title: Death and Dying
description: An analysis of the relationship between death and health with emphasis upon the physiological, medical, psychological, legal, and consumer aspects of death and dying in contemporary America. Roles of individual, family, school, community, and various professionals examined. Problems in the meaning of death, care of dying, death ritual, bereavement, and death education investigated. Prerequisite: HSC 150 or 160 or by permission of the department chairman.

title: Women and Health
description: A general overview of some current issues related to women and health: the human female, a woman's right to control her body, health problems of women, women in the health marketplace, the gynecological examination, pregnancy and childbirth, teenage pregnancies, midwifery, female sexuality, women and aging, occupational health and women, and the women's health movement.

title: Internship in Health Science
description: The intern will be assigned to an approved health agency or education institution for a period of time commensurate with the hours of credit to be earned. The student will periodically and terminally report to an academic adviser and to the administrator of the participating agency or agencies. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with HSC 575.

title: Public Health Practice
description: Public health organization and available community health resources. Recent developments and problems in the field of public health. Examination of recent literature on preventive medicine and human conservation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160 and 180, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Health
description: The physical environment and its relationship to disease causation. Review of environmental health problems and their solutions. Areas of study include air and water pollution, milk and food sanitation, disposal of human excreta and waste, radiological agents in the environment, and occupational health problems. Prerequisite: HSC 480.

title: Epidemiology
description: Classic epidemics, evaluation of epidemiological principles and techniques of investigation, and epidemiological analysis of selected types of diseases. Prerequisite: HSC 480 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Health Education
description: Basic functions of public educators in various settings. Emphasis will also be placed upon (1) need for public health education, (2) current settings for health education, (3) forces and movements that influence health education, and (4) the historical development of public health education. Prerequisite: HSC 180, 480.

title: Public Health Education: Planning and Evaluation
description: Intended for persons planning to work in public health agencies. Emphasis will be placed upon (1) the need for planning, (2) current settings for public health education, (3) techniques used to identify health education components of health programs, (4) program planning techniques, and (5) evaluation methodologies. Prerequisite: HSC 480, 484 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Studies in Health Science
description: Designed to give undergraduate health science students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamentals of Mammalian Anatomy
description: Basic study of mammalian anatomy with detailed dissection and with examination of representative microscopic structure. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Human Embryology
description: Normal development of the human organism including germ cell formation, fertilization, implantation, and organ formation. Consideration of embryonic environment, physiology, and abnormal development. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or ANAT 201.

Prerequisites recommended: ANAT 320 and 430.

title: Fundamentals of Pathology
description: An introduction to the study of the principles of disease production, especially in the human body. title: Special Studies in Anatomy
description: Designed to give undergraduate anatomy students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. description: A detailed study of the urinary system and excretory functions. Emphasis will be on human physiology but comparative vertebrate systems will be included. description: Designed to give undergraduate physiology students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Department of Political Science Perry, Chairman; Baker, Chang, Corbett, Cranor, Frankland, Hamori, Hollands, Menez, Meyer, Rouse, Rudoni, Sargent, Scheele, Vasicko Political science is the study of politics and government. Political science has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Aristotle, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions which continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polis or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differs from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask: What is the nature of people (which makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship between people and the state? The only substantial aspect added later was relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data which has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continuous testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civil, and vocational. The first two may be considered universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed citizenry. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study arid experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group utilizing the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations which draw heavily on the disciplin e are law, journalism, busines, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 130) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The total pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz, political theory and methodology, American government, public law and policy, public administration, foreign and comparative government, and international politics. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher licensing programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate levels for students in other departments. title: Honors Colloquium in Political Science
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in political science, with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open to students on the Honors Program and other outstanding students by permission of the department chairman. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in American Government and Politics
description: The student will work part time or full time (depending on the assignment) for one quarter in the office of a public official in national, state, or local government, a candidate for public office, or a political party. Assignments will depend upon the interests of students and the convenience of sponsors. Prerequisite: 16 hours in political science including the following or their equivalents: POLS 130, 237 and 431, or 350, or 473, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Paralegalism
description: The internship course for the legal assistant and legal administrator programs combines the students' academic training with practical experience within a law firm, corporation, bank, or governmental agency. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141, 142 and permission of the program director.

title: Issues in Political Science
description: Investigation of a particular topic, problem or issue in the field with emphasis on subfields, specialties, and materials not covered in established courses. Open to upperclass students with special interest in politics. The content is announced prior to each offering.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest which qualify them to do semiindependent study. Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the department chairman and a professor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: basic courses in the area selected for special study, junior standing, and permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings in Planning
description: Reading program developed in consultation with the department chairman and a professor with special competence in planning. Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest in planning. Prerequisite: POLS 461 and permission of the department chairman.

title: Workshop in Political Science
description: Intensive study of selected problems in political science. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Division II: Political Theory and Methodology

title: Introduction to Politics
description: The scope and methods of the study of political science. An examination of the basic concepts and theories in the discipline. Traditions and approaches in the field and their application to the various subdivisions of political science. Strongly recommended for students with departmental areas in political science.

title: Early Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of political thought of the early Mediterranean and medieval worlds which became the foundation of modern political theories and systems of the West. Emphasis on writings of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, St. Augustine, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Machiavelli.

title: Modern Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of selected writings of leading political theorists from the Age of Reformation to the present.

title: Communist Political Thought: from Marx to Present
description: A critical analysis and evaluation of Marxism, Leninism, Stalinism, Khrushchevism, post-Khrushchev Communist ideology and Maoism as a system of theoretical propositions and as an action program of an international movement.

title: Voter Polling Techniques
description: Methods by which information is obtained on the voting behavior and attitudes of the electorate. Emphasis on producing a working knowledge of polling techniques. Includes such topics as sampling, interviewing, and questionnaire construction.

title: American Political Thought
description: American political thought from the colonial period to the present. Puritanism, nature of rights, constitutionalism and federalism, nature of the Union, democracy, liberalism, conservatism, individualism and collectivism, welfare state, isolation and internationalism, and national security and freedom.

title: Research Methods in Political Science
description: A critical examination of methodological problems and practices in the formulation, execution, evaluation, and reporting of political science research, including a comparison of data gathering techniques, their respective limitations, and appropriate application.

title: Political Socialization and Behavior

Special attention given to the areas of political belief systems, political participation, political leadership, and the distribution of power in society. title: American National Government
