title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda.

title: Political Campaigns
description: As the linkage between citizens and the government in a represerA,ative democracy, political campaigns will be considered from theoretical and practical perspectives. The course will answer questions on the why (theory), what (strategies), and how (techniques) of political campaigns.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, and centralization will be considered.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government.

title: Intergovernmental Relations
description: Analysis of relations among national, state, and local governments. Considerations of constitutional and legal bases and the nature of relations, such as grantsinaid, tax immunity, education, and interstate compacts.

title: American Political Parties
description: Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy. State and Local Government

title: State and Local Politics
description: Practices, politics, and structures of state and local governments in the United States with an emphasis on the Indiana experience.

title: Urban Government in the United States
description: Structure, functions, problems, and trends in city, urban, and metropolitan governments.

title: State Legislatures
description: Legislative systems in American state government. External influences (constituencies, political parties, interest groups), internal influences (organizational structure, staff, norms, decision making), issues confronting state legislatures and reform proposals.

title: Metropolitan Problems
description: Analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related aspects; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation to the entire community. Division IV: Public Law and Policy

title: Citizen and the Law
description: To better appreciate citizen encounters with the legal system, this course explains the operation of the legal system and the political aspects of the pertinent legal issues. A variety of activities, films, and lectures employed. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman or the paralegal program coordinator.

title: Introduction to Legal Ethics
description: A presentation of the concepts of paralegalism with an emphasis upon legal ethics and values. The development and future of the paralegal function in our present legal environment will be employed. Prerequisite: POLS 140.

title: Litigation and Legal Writing
description: Includes an analysis of paralegalism and the common types of lawsuits, court procedures, and appeal procedures. Indepth examination of the various reference sources available to lawyers in determining applicable law. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141.

title: Family Law
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the legal problems in the area of domestic relations. Covers legal problems involved in marriage, separation, divorce, child custody, adoption, and nonsupport.

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes, and needs.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships between government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities, and finance.

title: National Defense Policy
description: An international survey of military capacity and function provides the background for analysis of the national defense policy of the United States. Special emphasis on American strategic interests and problems of weapons, technology, nuclear control, and disarmament.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
description: Significant facets of legal system's response to conflicting demands upon environmental resources. Composition of environmental problems, control issues, policy formulation, and legal remedies.

title: Public Interest Groups and Government
description: An examination of the internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Special attention will be given to the implications of pressuregroup activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and to the effects of pressure groups upon political parties and the political process.

title: Consumers, Competition, and the Law
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and his government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content will include cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Policy Analysis
description: Equips the student with the tools of the policy analyst through systematic analysis of programs and projects. Special emphasis on problem definition, goal determination, systematic evaluation of alternatives, socialeconomic and political indicators, performance measures, and impact evaluation. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 342.

title: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies.

title: Women in Politics
description: A crossnational survey of women in politics with emphasis on women and public policy, the political roles of women, and the problems of women in politics within the context of contemporary public affiars.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130. Division V: Public Administration

title: Introduction to Planning
description: A survey of problems inherent in planning for cities and regions which utilizes contributions of other disciplines such as history, geography, sociology, and economics. Required of majors in urban studies and planning; elective for others with permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration—national, state, and local.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Administrative organizations as going concerns composed of people taking action under conditions of conflict and cooperation; examination of nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisites: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes, and activities of civil service agencies; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans; efficiency measurements and rewards; training programs; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement. and other personnel processes. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Survey of the principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances; administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, accounting of revenues, expenditures, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, management of publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairman.

title: Politics and Administration of Local Government Budgets
description: Local government budgeting with emphasis on political and administrative issues in budget preparation and accountability. Topics include revenue development including tax and nontax sources, capital expenditure programming, financing pensions, contracting for services, cost/benefit analysis, and federal and state grant mechanisms.

title: Administrative Law
description: Legal and political study of independent regulatory agencies; their powers, functions, and roles as determined by an analysis of relevant cases in which basic principles are identified and synthesized with other areas of public law.

title: Public Works Administration
description: An overview of public works administrative techniques and problems. Designed to provide a general awareness of management, policy, and decisionmaking concerns on such topics as water, street, solid waste, pollution control systems.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services.

title: Problems in National Administration
description: An examination in depth of uniquely national administrative problems and activities. National administrative structures and techniques are examined in detail, including their use and application in the administration of specific national policy areas.

title: Labor-Management Relations in Government
description: Examines public employee unionization, legal provisions for collective bargaining, determination and recognition of bargaining units, bilateral negotiation, and thirdparty involvement procedures, administration of agreements, and the processes and strategies in collective bargaining negotiations in public organizations.

title: Administrative Problems in State Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and organizational behavior at the state level. Special emphasis on the provision of government services and functions in the major areas of budgeting and taxation, education, environmental protection, public health, and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350 Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 463.

title: Administrative Problems in Local Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and organizational behavior at the local level. Special emphasis on intergovernmental aspects of program administration in the major areas of taxing and spending, education, personnel and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 463.

title: The Politics of Public Sector Productivity
description: A literature review of the contemporary political issues in local, state, and federal government productivity. Emphasis will be placed on the political and attitudinal problems associated with proposals for improved productivity and effectiveness in governmental administration.

title: Career Development and Training in the Public Sector
description: The focus of this course is on the politics and administration of public personnel development programs especially as they have emerged within the last decade. Emphasis will be given to personnel needs assessment and training programs in government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. Emphasis will also be placed on the politics and public policy implications of CETA training efforts. Division VI: Foreign and Comparative Governments

title: Comparative Political Systems
description: A comparison of modern political systems as represented by the principal nations of the world.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: Historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 280. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 279.

title: Comparative Policy Problems
description: A comparative political analysis of selected contemporary domestic problems confronting modern nationstates. Emphasizes both the process of policymaking and the substance of specific public policies.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural area, to the government and political structures of the three major Psychological Science 313 powers in Western Europe—Great Britain, France, and Germany—and to the current state of the Western European integration movement.

title: British Government and Politics
description: The political system of the United Kingdom, including a discussion of the Commonwealth and Britain's place in an expanding European community. Emphasis also on Anglo-American relations and British contributions to American political arrangements.

title: Latin-American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin-American nations.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in the field of comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area.

title: Government and Politics of the Soviet Union
description: A survey of the modes, methods and policies by which communist philosophy is put into action by the Communist Party and by its authoritative extension, the Soviet government. Includes those peculiar governmental roles— economic planning, indoctrination, and purges—that are special trademarks of a communist political system.

title: Government and Politics of China
description: A comprehensive survey of the government and politics of modern China, both of the Republic of China and Communist China. Division VII: International Politics

title: American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: International Relations
description: A survey of the formal relations among sovereign states in the international system, emphasizing the operation of diplomacy, the factors of power, the procedures for the settlement of disputes, and the various modes of conflict resolution.

title: The United Nations and International Organization
description: Concentrated study of international organizations and the structure, functions, and current issues facing the United Nations. Students participate in a mock Security Council at Ball State and may have an opportunity to participate in the National Model United Nations Conference.

title: International Relations in Asia
description: A survey of contemporary international relations in Asia with a special emphasis on the role of China, Japan, United States of America, and Union of Soviet Socialist Republics in this area.

title: International Relations of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and the Soviet Bloc
description: The role of the Soviet Union as a world power and the examination of Soviet strategic concepts in foreign policy.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the Law of Nations by the analysis of prominent decisions of international tribunals, examination of representative legal principles, the briefing of appropriate cases, and the conducting of mock court trials.

title: World Politics
description: Theories of contemporary interactions among states, especially the major powers. Particular attention will be given to conflict resolution.

title: Communist China's Foreign Policy
description: A comprehensive analysis of Communist China's role in international politics, with specific emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Department of Psychological Science Meeker, Chairman; Balough, Butler, Caplan, Clark, Davidson, Deckers, Fischer, Ganzhorn, Goldstone, Hill, Hines, Humm, McConnell, Meunier, Myers, Pisano, Poland, Warnick, Wittig Psychology is the science which studies the behavior of humans as they interact with their environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is that of better understanding of human beings. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. As a part of the College of Sciences and Humanities, the Department of Psychological Science is primarily concerned with the psychological realms not necessarily or specifically related to the area of education. The basic objective of contributing to the increased understanding of human behavior is pursued by means of teaching, research, and service. The department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundation s and programs apropriate to its function, and helping students in al areasteaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, businessincrease their understanding of the forces and influences which shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribut e to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology wil make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. The department offers a departmental major and minor in the disciplinary area of psychology. These programs provide a basic backgound for graduate work in any one of the many fields of psychologyclinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psychology, psychometryand an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other areas such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a social studies major or minor with an area of concentration in psychology, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for instructing in psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students wishing to teach psychology should choose other primary or supporting areas for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of Psychological Science offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas on various advanced degree programs. Additionally, teachers of psychology may combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in the discipline of psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. title: The Psychology of Human Adaptation to Stress
description: Adaptation arid reactions to stress as psychological phenomena; research on stress and its influence on personality development; the appraisal of threatening situations by the individual; coping and coping reaction patterns to stress; theories of adaptation to psychological stress. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Altered States of Awareness
description: An introduction to the study of normal and altered states of awareness in humans. Among the areas to be explored are sleep and dream states, sensory deprivation, hypnosis, meditation, hallucinations, boredom, and the effect of drugs on awareness. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Applied Behavior Analysis
description: Introduction to the principles of operant psychology and application of these principles to applied situations with humans in other than formal educational settings. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Elementary Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics and statistics of inference. The computation, application, and interpretation of various elementary statistics. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Intermediate Statistics for Psychological Research
description: Inferential statistics and research design, computation and interpretation of statistics in the context of psychological research design issues. Critical analysis of published research literature. Prerequisite: PSYSC 241.

title: Introduction to Biopsychology
description: A brief introduction to the general areas of biopsychology. Topics include: the fundamentals of nervous system structure and function; consciousness and its altered states; memory, language, and thought; emotionality; and personality. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Introduction to Experimental Psychology
description: An introduction to the use of the scientific method in the study of human behavior. Analysis and evaluation of experimental studies will be utilized to provide experience with research techniques using essential controls and acceptable procedures. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Introduction to Comparative Psychology
description: A survey of the theoretical and empirical foundations of animal behavior, including that of man, considered from a comparative, biological point of view. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Introduction to Social Psychology
description: Basic understanding of the psychosocial problems involved in the functioning of an individual in society. Emphasis on various influences which help to shape the psychological patterns of interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Experimental Social Psychology
description: Emphasizes basic empirical research methods with special focus on those techniques commonly used in contemporary social psychological research. Combines the academic study of these methods with their actual application in research investigations conducted by students. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 316.

title: Psychology of Women
description: An introduction to psychological approaches to the study of women with special emphasis on achievement motivation and dependency, attitudes toward The prerequisite of PSYSC 213 will he waived for students pursuing Option 2. women, development of sexrole identity, biological and social influences on women's behavior, selfconcepts and psychological conflict in women, and a critical appraisal of research in the area of sex differences. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, 241, or permission of the department chairman.

title: Environmental Psychology
description: To present the current knowledge and research i n environmental psychology, and study its relevance to psychological planing for special neds of individuals. It is also the intent of the course to investigate the psychological impact of selected factors in various kinds of environments on individuals and groups. Prerequisite: PSYSC 316 or permission of the department chairman. NR 101 is strongly recommended.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
description: Theoretical and practical foundations underlying the construction, use, and interpretation of standardized psychological tests and inventories. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Honors Colloquium in Psychology
description: Explorations of selected issues in psychology with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion of such topics as psychobiology, social psychology, learning, personality, and abnormal psychology.

title: Motivation and Emotion
description: An introduction to basic theory and research relating to motivation and emotion and applications to various aspects of human behavior. Prerequisite : PSYSC 10, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Sensation and Perception
description: The human senses: their physiological makeup, development, and functioning. Basic principles of perception and stimulus hunger will be emphasized. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Psychology of Cognition
description: Analysis of research and theories in the psychology of cognition and thinking. Major topic areas to be covered are verbal learning, problem solving, concept formation, and psycholinguistics. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Introduction to the Study of Personality
description: A wide variety of classical and modern theories of personality and the pertinent empirical research are presented and compared. Consideration given to the components of a good theory of personality and to the applications of various personality theories. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Abnormal Psychology
description: Systematic study of behavior pathology with special reference to the psychopathology of physical illness and handicaps, psychosomatic and somatopsychic illnesses, neuroses, psychoses, character disorders, addiction, and acute and chronic brain disorders. Primary emphasis on etiology, symptomatology, prognosis, and prevention. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, 241, and 421.

title: Survey of Clinical Psychology
description: Introduction to the roles and functions of personnel in the area of clinical psychology. Prerequisite: PSYSC 421 and 432.

title: Child Personality and Psychopathology
description: The factors and research directed toward the understanding of personality and psychopathology in children and youth. Prerequisite: PSYSC 421 and 432.

title: Teaching of Psychology in Secondary Schools
description: Materials and methods used in teaching psychology at the secondary school level, including instructional issues concerning psychology with a personal adjustment orientation and as an academic discipline. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in psychology.

title: Current Research and Trends in the Teaching of Psychology
description: Current research in the teaching of psychology with an emphasis on the research of new curricular and instructional approaches.

title: Psychology of Learning
description: The nature of learning processes, possible influences upon these processes and resultant behavior, and applications of the psychology of learning. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, 241, and 284.

title: Physiological Psychology
description: A basic introduction to the physical basis of behavior, involving primarily the nervous system and its structure and function. Emphasis on the role of bodily systems in perception, learning, motivation, and conscious function. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Applied Psychology
description: Theory arid application of psychological principles in various social settings. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Industrial Psychology
description: A comprehensive coverage of the application of psychological principles to personnel selection and training, worker motivation and morale, labor problems in business and industry, executive leadership, consumer behavior, engineering psychology, and personal problems in business and industry. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Organizational Development: A Psychological Perspective
description: Presentation of change techniques from a process and small group perspective with special emphasis on the limitations and logic involved in their utilization. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Psychology of Selection and Placement
description: Introduction to principles of personnel testing as applied to the selection and placement process. Focus on development of predictors and Science 317 criteria, selection of an appropriate validation model, and the psychological dynamics of the interview processes. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241 or equivalent.

title: Psychological Factors in Workplace Design
description: The influences of job design on worker productivity and satisfaction. Contributions made in engineering psychology, industrial psychology, job enrichment, and quality of worklife literatures are covered. Considers aspects of both physical and social work environments. Prerequisite: PSYSC 241 or equivalent, and PSYSC 473.

title: Psychology of Sexual Behavior
description: An examination of the determinants of human sexual behavior, focusing especially on the development of sexual identity and attitudes. Utilizes perspectives from the fields of social psychology, personality theory, and physiological psychology to build an understanding of this most complex behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 316, 421, 468. 48 1. Experimental Behavior Analysis. (4) Investigation and practice in experimental behavior analysis, with emphasis on operant conditioning. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Systematic Psychology
description: The major concepts of various schools of psychological thought and contemporary theoretical systems as they have evolved historically. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241, and senior standing.

title: Seminar in Psychology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of psychology. Prerequisites: psychology major and senior standing.

title: Supervised Empirical Research Experience
description: Experience in the actual collection of behavioral data in the field or laboratory setting. Students would work closely with a supervising faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Psychology
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructors with special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairman. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. description: Materials and procedure for teaching social studies from kindergarten through grade six. Emphasis on behavioral objectives; inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation.

description: Provides more experience in methods used in teaching elementary social studies and an opportunity to utilize materials available to teachers. Prerequisite: SS 391 or permission of the department chairman.

description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of social studies, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of social studies in the secondary school curriculum. description: Directed study of special problems or research in the field of social science education by individuals or groups of students. Social Work 321 Department of Social Work Macy, Chairman; Brown, Dolon, Dowery, Gildner, Holmes, Miller, Stacy Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession. Before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for the training of social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex social problems, has contributed to the dramatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both an art and a science. Its art is the development of special skills used in working with people, either individually, in groups, or through community programs. Its science is the body of knowledge derived from social and behavioral sciences about people and communities. Social workers are concerned with helping people solve their social problems in order to achieve more satisfying ways of living. They practice in a wide variety of settings. Some work with individuals in family service, child welfare, and public welfare agencies; in courts as probation officers for juveniles as well as adults; in hospitals, both medical and mental; in child guidance clinics; in schools; and with handicapped persons. Some work with groups in the Y's, Boys' Clubs, Scouts, and community centers, as well as with street gangs and poverty programs. And some work in community organizations such as United Fund, Community Chests, and Community Welfare Councils, where their skills are used in planning for social services. All social workers serve the needy, or the young, or the aged, or the handicapped in public or voluntary agencies. The undergraduate program in social work at Ball State University is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of the Council on Social Work Education. It provides for the needs of four groups of students: those who wish to qualify for firstlevel professional social work positions upon graduation; those who wish to continue their education in graduate schools of social work; those who desire broad preparation for informed community participation, leadership, and world citizenship for entry into decisionmaking roles within social welfare systems; and those who desire an opportunity to test their potentialities for a career in social work and to provide knowledge for use by students in allied human service professions. During the secondyear of study, students begin to complete course work in social work which builds upon a liberal arts base including knowledge in the humanities, social, behavioral, and biological sciences. Specific social work courses acquaint them with the philosophy, development, policies, and methods of social work. Field trips and volunteer experiences in conjunction with these courses enable the students to visit places in which social work is practiced. In the classroom they learn the theory of social work methods of work with individuals, families, small groups, organizations, and communities. Practical experience is gained in the practicum where the student works tinder expert supervision for one quarter in a social service agency. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the area requirements given below. title: Introduction to Social Work
description: A view of traditional and innovative social work practice. Focuses on the role of the social worker within the various social work service delivery system s and practice setings.

title: Social Welfare and Services 1
description: A descriptive, historical, and evolutionary study of the institution of social welfare, including social welfare programs, policies, and services. The factors influencing the development of social services as a societal response to social problems are explored. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 220, 242, ECON 200, and sophomore standing.

title: Social Welfare and Services 2
description: Introduction to social work practice at the generalist level and social work as a major profession within the social welfare institution in American society. The roles and functions of practitioners in various settings and the overall framework for the problemsolving approach used by social workers in the planned change process are studied. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200.

title: Internship in Social Welfare
description: Provides exposure to and beginning confrontation with the general nature of social work. Provides students opportunity to apply previously learned social work knowledge, as either a volunteer or staff member in a social service agency. Prerequisite : SOCWK 20, 201, 35, and permision of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in SOCWK 459.

title: Public Social Welfare
description: The impact of public social welfare policies on social service client systems is studied. Effects of social policies on various economic, ethnic, racial, and sex groups are given special emphasis. Prerequisite: SOCWK 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Welfare Services in Developing and Overdeveloped Countries
description: Survey and comparison of selected social welfare services in developing and overdeveloped countries. Social policies underlying the services, the cultural and traditional value basis, and the role of the profession of social work are explored. Special emphasis is placed on health, family planning, community development, and income maintenance programs.

title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment 1
description: Emphasis is on understanding the behavior of the macro social systems and the influence of these systems on human behavior. Prerequisite: SOCWK 201 and 313 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment 2
description: Emphasis is on the individual and family as social systems, their developmental stages and the social services needed at stages throughout the life cycle of these social systems. Prerequisite: SOCWK 201 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Helping Skills
description: Examines the ways in which social work skills may be used to develop and codify areas of social work practice theory. Materials on interviewing, reporting, and recording as means of helping others will be reviewed as background for analyzing social workerclient relationships and interactions. Prerequisite: SOCWK 321 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Services for Allied Professions
description: Acquaints professionals in allied fields with the social work profession and fields of social work profession. Emphasis placed upon community resources and interdisciplinary approaches to social welfare problems. Not open to students majoring in social work.

title: Supervision of Social Workers
description: For students who plan to enter a supervisory position in a social service organization. Emphasis on administrative practices within social service settings, the building and maintenance of work relationships, and the development of supervisory techniques.

title: Social Work Practice 1
description: Focus is on the application of social work generalist practice methods to micro level systems. Emphasis on individual, family, and small group contexts of practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200, 201, 313, 321, 327 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Practice 2
description: Focus is on the application of social work generalist practice methods to macro level systems. Emphasis is on the task group, organization, and community contexts of practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200, 201, 313, 327 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Practicum
description: The course is a 400 clockhour field placement in a social service setting selected and approved by the Department of Social Work. Social work assignments provide learning opportunities to integrate social work theory. professional ethics, and practice skills corroborated by professional evaluation. Prerequisite: SOCWK 450, 454, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Social Work
description: This course promotes an indepth examination of research studies, social work literature, and current practice issues of special concern to the profession, Sociology 323 students, and instructors. Open only to senior students with majors in social work. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Social Work
description: Topic to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor with special competence within the area involved. Johnson, W. Johnson, Kulman, Morris, Nelsen, Polansky, Robertson, Royer, Tucker Sociology is the application of the scientific method to human relations. It is the attempt to use our collective wisdom in a systematic manner in order to have as much confidence as possible in the accuracy of our social beliefs. Science goes beyond mere opinion. Social scientists attempt to describe as objectively as possible what is really happening in the world and to understand why events have occurred in a certain way. Sociology is among the younger social sciences. Although introduced into a handful of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades. Quickly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge, and the concepts of the discipline are becoming widely accepted throughout society. Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. Sociology is a major part of the scientific foundation for many applied fields. Social work, the criminal justice system, personnel work, counseling management, nursing practice, and the law are all based in part on the findings of sociologists. Students interested in any of these areas would find sociology courses useful. Sociology is taught at two levels. On the one hand there is the general study of social behavior such as in courses about complex organization or social class. Ideas developed in such courses are used in the more specific social sciences such as Political Science and Economics. On the other hand, sociologists teach courses about institutions for which separate departments have not developed, such as the family, and about lifecycle stages, such as childhood or old age. In addition we develop research skills in our courses about methods and population. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to broadening the student's perspective of the sociocultural environment, and to the individual's own relationship to it, thus helping to produce an outlook less restricted by the limitations of untested folk beliefs. The findings derived from sociological investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. title: Principles of Sociology
description: An introduction to sociology including basic concepts used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, and social institutions. This course is for students unfamiliar with sociology.

title: Contemporary American Society
description: The sociology of contemporary society with emphasis on social institutions: the family, the political structure, religious groups and movements, medicine, the economy, and education. Dynamics, change, and institutional interrelationship s wil be asesed.

title: The Black Community in America
description: An examination of the major social forces influencing the structure of the contemporary black American subcommunity. Emphasis also on an exploration into the strengths and weaknesses of this structure and its relations with the large community, as bases of change in the accommodative patterns of blackwhite relations.

title: Sociology of the Future
description: Examination of probable nearfuture (30-50 years) social states and social forms. Particular attention to trends in social institutions, longterm social trends, and culture change. Emphasis on basic principles of sociological analysis, demography, societal indexes, and social ecology.

title: Sociology of Women
description: A critical examination of the nature of women's roles and their impact on social organization. Consideration will be given to the effects of changing patterns of socialization, roles, role strain, intergroup relations, and the social process.

title: Sociology of Deviant Behavior
description: An overview of theory and research on deviant behavior. Three essential forms will be reviewed: deviance arising from disability in social and physical functioning, deviance arising from violation of social norms, and deviance arising from membership in groups observing radical social ideologies.

title: Social Problems
description: A survey of the nature and range of social problems, the conditions which give rise to them, and the methods by which our society attempts to cope with them.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociological Research Design
description: A basic course in principles and techniques for organizing, conducting, and analyzing sociological research; research strategies and selection of appropriate techniques for a variety of research problems. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 380.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Leisure and Popular Culture
description: Discussion of issues related to the uses and distribution of nonwork time and activities. Trends in recreation, folk arts, and the growing leisure industries. The impact of leisure activities on the natural environment and other "quality of life" issues.

title: Social Stratification and Inequality
description: An analysis of United States and world stratification systems with attention to the unequal distribution of wealth, status, and power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: The Sociology of Modernization
description: The sociology of social change and industrial change— modernization in the non-Western world. Study of the reasons for change: demographicurban, family social, and international pressures. Discussion of thirdworld social problems and the social change models and ideologies for changing societies. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Blue Collar Society and Culture
description: The social realities, life styles, and selfperceptions of the bluecollar society and culture are examined. Similarly, socioeconomic and demographic patterns are investigated. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and factors affecting utilization of treatment programs. Sociology 325

title: Introduction to Social Research
description: The research process and research design; ethics of research; stress on use of research to assess needs and evaluate programs. Familiarization with statistics; critical analysis of selected articles in the student's field of specialization. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective on life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors Program.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of sociological theories and theorists of the 19th and early 20th centuries with a view to relating theoretical positions to contemporary social dynamics and to contemporary theoretical work in sociology. The cultural and intellectual milieu in which the theoretical works were generated will be noted. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Trends in Mass Society
description: An introduction to the major trends of mass society and changes in those trends. Students are encouraged to perform their own analyses of changing trends using existing information. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: The sociological aspects of organizational life. Special attention will be given to organizational structure, change, and strategies for planned change. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effects of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Religion
description: Examines religion as a social institution with particular attention to the societal functions of religion, the influence of social factors on the development of religion, the role of religion in the amelioration of contemporary social problems, and contemporary processes affecting the future of religion.

title: The Sociology of Modernization
description: Emphasis on specific sociological theories and findings that pertain to social change/modernization in nonindustrialized societies, such as Dependency Theory and Human Resources Theory. The application of these models is to specific concerns of sociologists as they deal with lessdeveloped countries, demographicurban, racialethnic tensions, and family. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Medical Care Organizations
description: A sociological analysis of medical care organizations and professionals with emphasis on intraorganizational, interprofessional, and agencyclient relations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: A sociological analysis of the field of mental health with attention to social definitions of mental illness, selfrecognition of illness, the process of seeking care, treatment institutions, and the aftermath of treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as related to various sociological variables. Various sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Families in the Middle Years
description: An overview of the American family as the marital pair approach and encounter middle age. Special attention will be given to problems which necessitate interaction with the criminal justice and corrections system. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Seminar in the Family
description: An analysis and critique of published research studies of marriage and the family. The nature and complexity of the family as well as its future. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220,424, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Origins and Control of Deviant Behavior
description: Development of an acquaintance with types of family, neighborhood, and community situations which serve as pressures toward deviant behavior. Community action in the detection, control, and treatment of deviance is examined from the point of view of analyzing facilities, programs, and the legal system, Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Changing Societies
description: Analysis of social change processes within societies in the modern world. Attention will be given to social movement; institutional change; and organizational change. Implementing, controlling, and measuring change will be discussed. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 or equivalent.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historical functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis of the social dynamics of the urban core in metropolitan areas. Attention given to the development of cities and their cores, stressing ecological and demographic factors. Examines the social issues associated with the concept of the inner city, especially racism, poverty, crime, welfare, and education. Finally, policy alternatives for alleviating these conditions are considered. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Seminar on Middletown
description: Two works by the Lynds, Middletown and Middletown in Transition, are sociological classics about Muncie. Updates by teams of scholars have been undertaken. Students participate in an ongoing sociological project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and utilizing sources of data; and application of survey findings to programs of community action. The student will participate directly in the various phases of a survey research project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 282 or the equivalent; prerequisite recommended: SOC 472.

title: Evaluation Research
description: Considerations and problems in developing and conducting research for the purpose of evaluating social action programs. Topics include the unique nature of evaluation research, operationalizing and assessing variables, goal attainment measures, needs assessments, and development of guidelines for programmatic change.

title: Advanced Sociological Data Analysis
description: The selection and utilization of advanced statistical techniques and sophisticated means of calculation which have been particularly useful in analyzing sociological data. Such topics as nonparametric statistics, factor analysis, sampling statistics, and multiple regression and path analysis will be discussed in the context of sociological research. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 282 or equivalent.

title: Fieldwork in Sociology
description: The research process will be reviewed. Students will learn how to use observation, interviewing, and official documents in sociological research through practical exercises. The relation between these techniques and the survey method will be discussed. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Internship in Sociology
description: Internship in sociology, supervised field experience in a public agency. Training would involve research, evaluation, and the implementation of agency programs. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study of Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Topics in Sociology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of sociology. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. The department offers undergraduate and graduate degrees in speech communication. The major includes courses in theory and practice in rhetoric and public address, interpersonal communication, business communication, persuasion, and argumentation and debate. The undergraduate speech communication minor may be especially useful to the student in prelaw, public relations, or radiotelevision. Many speech communications graduates are in law, politics, and the ministry. The teaching major in speech communication and theatre meets the requirements established in Rule 46-47 by the Department of Public Instruction: high school teachers are expected to direct theatre productions, to direct debate and individual events, to direct radiotelevision programs and special convocations. For these reasons, teaching majors are expected to participate in activities sponsored by the department: theatre, debate, and individual events. The graduate degree in speech communication and theatre permits the public school teacher to professionalize his or her teaching license. Public speaking and theatre are, along with mathematics and philosophy, the oldest of the liberal arts disciplines. The courses help one to develop an understanding of the basic issues of society and a respect for our cultural heritage. Theatre. Ball State has, for many years, produced plays for the enjoyment of its student body. Large numbers of students have taken part in the dramatic productions now being produced in a modern and attractive theatre. The department offers a departmental major and minor in theatre. The theatre courses at Ball State emphasize both professional and liberal education. Professional training leads to teacher licensing in speech, communication, and theatre for those who plan to direct school theatre, while adequate experience and course work are available for those who plan to enter the professional theatre. The content of theatre courses is important in the liberal education of any student. Theatre is an art which attempts to assist people to understand themselves. It also assists students to understand their dramatic heritage and the several related arts including music, dance, and design. It is assumed that theatre majors and minors are active in their profession from the time they enter it.The variety and amount of participation are taken into account as one applies for approval to follow this curriculum. title: Fundamentals of Public Speaking
description: Fundamentals and techniques of organizing material and presenting that material in individual speeches. Emphasis on personal speaking improvement in the classroom and in public performances.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasis is on techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: The focus of this course is on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Will stress the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Speech improvement dealing with voice and articulation.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: The development of principles of rhetorical criticism and the application of the principles to an intensified study of prominent platform, radio, and television speakers. Consideration is given also to the influence of the speaker upon our social and political life. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210 or 240.

title: Interviewing
description: The principles and types of interviews, with application of the principles in informational, employment, appraisal, and counseling interviews. Consideration of the following aspects of employment seeking: resume, placement papers, job application, interview, and followup.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Meeting Management
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher. Speech and Theatre 329

title: Speech Practicum
description: Practical experience in speech, intercollegiate debate, discussion, oratory, extemporaneous speaking, and interpretive reading. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminartype class focusing on various aspects of and/or problems in speech communication as they relate to individuals in their personal and professional relationships. Open to Honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; EDSEC 299, and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Deals specifically with disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, an introductory involvement in the teaching of a discipline, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of a particular discipline in the secondary school curriculum. These topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: SPCH 395.

title: Studies in Persuasion
description: An intensified study and application of the principles of effective public speaking; the ideational formulation and delivery of longer speeches; the rhetorical analysis of significant speeches. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department head.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: An examination through exposure to theory, actual practice, and criticism, of the process of communication. Will include communication models of message encoding, transmission, decoding and feedback; the complexity of language, including abstracting and determination of meaning; problems in facetoface, small group, platform speaking, and mass media communication; and communication breakdowns.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of small group literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problem solving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Business and Professional Speech
description: Concentrates on small group communication and discussion, parliamentary procedure, and on manuscript speeches for the business and professional person. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or 240 or equivalent, or permission of the department head.

title: Communication in Organizations
description: The oral communication processes in organizations, with special emphasis upon causes of communication problems and correctives for the problems. Examination of the systems of oral communication within organizations.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech and Theatre pursues a particular area of study in depth on a consultative basis with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department head. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Speech
description: The student is assigned to onthejob experience in such places as a college classroom, a political campaign or office, summer camp, or summer theatre. Students will be permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the amount of college credit to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in some aspect of speech and/or theatre and permission of the department head. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with SPCH 598 but no more than 8 hours may be earned at one time.

title: Introduction to Theatre
description: An overview of the field of theatre with special reference to the origins of drama.

title: Stagecraft
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of the crafts involved in theatre production at the school, college, and community theatre levels. Three hours of lecture and three arranged hours of laboratory a week.

title: Principles of Stage Makeup
description: An investigation of the principles, techniques, and materials of stage makeup and practical experience in their application.

title: Acting 1
description: A lecturelaboratory class stressing the basic principles of acting. Major emphasis on stage movement.

title: Acting 2
description: A lecturelaboratory course on the principles of acting with major emphasis on character analysis and development. Prerequisite: THEAT 232.

title: Modern Drama
description: Analysis of selected dramas from the time of Ibsen to the present day and of the conditions under which they originally were produced.

title: Directing 1

Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology Hoops, Chairman; Artes, Farling, Harmon, Heady, Hemeyer, Hull, Kramer, Lindell, Updike Until the fall of 1978, students entering the university who graduated with a bachelor's degree in speech pathology and audiology were eligible for initial certification to work as speech and language clinicians in the public schools. Hence, most bachelor's degree graduates are employed in public school corporations. As of 1978, students entering the university who seek state teaching licensure to work in the public schools in speech pathology or audiology must acquire a master's degree as the preservice level of training. Persons with master's degrees may also work in hospital speech and hearing clinics, rehabilitation centers, college or university centers, and communitysponsored speech and hearing agencies. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers two undergraduate majors in speech pathology and audiology. Both are departmental majors. One is a departmental major for students who are sure they wish to work eventually in a hospital, college, or community clinic and plan to proceed immediately to the master's degree without acquiring licensure to work in the public schools. The other, identified as a departmental major for those seeking licensure in school services personnel as speech, language, and hearing clinicians or as educational audiologists, is for students who do plan to be eligible for public school employment in these positions. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology or in audiology, and completion of licensure requirements as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist is performed as part of the master's degree program. Completion of clinical practicum hours is required as part of master's degree requirements. The master's degree is also required for state licensure through the Indiana Board of Health, for all individuals who work in job environments other than the public schools, and for membership in and certification by the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate major programs are given clinical experiences in four kinds of programs: public school speech, language, and hearing programs, hospitals, preschool nursery programs, and the University Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. In the last, children and adults come to the Ball State campus for clinical work for speech, language, and/or hearing problems. The department also offers a departmental minor in speech pathology and audiology, for those students interested in but not committed to this profession, and a departmental minor in speech science for those students planning a career in industry or business in a research laboratory dealing with exploration of the parameters of speech or speech identification. Approval to pursue the major programs is based in part upon the student's performance in clinical practica, and is ordinarily considered early in the student's junior year. Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. Regular fulltime students enrolled in the university are administered a speech and hearing test free of charge. This screening is perfoi.med by appointment for new fulltime students. Any speech or hearing problem which may interfere with vocational objectives is called to the attention of the student. Special work for regularly enrolled students who desire to correct deficiencies in speech and voice is provided by the clinic, located on the ground floor of the English Building. Educational work and guidance for those persons who have hearing problems are also available. Recommendations for corrective procedures are based on the needs of the individual student. Certain programs of the university, including all teaching curricula, demand various proficiency levels in regard to speech and voice. One function of the clinic is to implement these criteria. Outpatient speech and hearing evaluation and therapy are integral parts of the clinic program, as is the education of speech pathologists and audiologists. Some classes are available for prospective classroom teachers who desire information relative to the management of speech or hearing difficulties. The work of the university clinic is closely associated with that of the Burris School clinic. The clinic is equipped with the latest sound and acoustic devices, including recording machines, tape recorders, recordings, testing materials, audiometers, and other clinical equipment. Department of Telecommunications Kurtz, Chairman; Alexander, DeVoe, Gehring, Heuser, Smith, Tomlinson, Wible The broadcast industries and the motion picture industries provide extremely democratic channels of information, entertainment, and communication. Ball State University has long recognized the appeal which these media have to the mass audience, and the important part which they play in our everyday lives. For these reasons, Ball State University and the Department of Telecommunications provide a carefully selected sequence of courses which emphasize the practical applications of these media. To meet today's demands, the department offers both graduate and undergraduate departmental majors and minors in these fields, as well as a teaching minor. The Ball State University program in radio, television, and motion pictures is intended for those people who are serious about career opportunities in these fastgrowing industries. The excellent selection of courses in the curriculum includes programs for those who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for instruction with the educational aspects of the electronic media in the classroom, or in school administration systems which employ the media. Since many positions in the broadcast and motion picture industries require a creative effort on the part of the individual, and a good understanding of teamwork, these attributes are emphasized as the student also discovers the elements of leadership and responsibility. Students working in the department are encouraged to learn as much as possible about the function and operation of the sophisticated radio, television, and motion picture equipment planned for a "hands on" approach. Audience research, performance, production, programming, news, media sales, and administrative studies of the electronic and motion picture media are analyzed in the various courses. The facilities of the university radio station. WBST-FM, and the closedcircuit television production facility provide additional practical experiences for the students in the training program. Such work experiences also allow the student to build a personal resume which frequently assists in later job applications. Familiarity with professional equipment and the experience gained through the knowledge of operation, coupled with classroom and smallgroup discussion, analyses, and direct study and observation of the broadcast and motion picture industries enable the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. There are many factors which influence the future employment of individuals seeking careers in these industries. Therefore, it is not possible to guarantee employment, although the department's record of those gainfully employed after graduation in broadcasting and motion pictures is excellent. Simultaneously, every effort is made to inform the student of the stringent and competitive labor marketplaces in both the broadcast and motionpicture industries. At the same time while the serious student is discovering how to develop the broadbased foundations needed for work in the industries, learning about the operation of equipment, and coming face to face with a faculty experience in both academics and the professional work world, the keen student discovers how to cope with the problems to be met in the industry marketplace, as well as the steps to be taken in the preparation for the future. The department's builtin workforce programs and summer internships allow each selected student to gain an insight into actual work situations in their respective career areas. Interns have been placed in many markets in Indiana and in parts of Kentucky, Ohio, and Illinois. In addition to the EDEL 360 course (Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School), EDJHM 312 course (Teaching in Junior High/Middle Schools), the EDSEC 299 course (Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary School), and the student teaching programs, requests for observations, individual research projects and studies involving professional laboratory experiences, and tutoring opportunities are administered through this office. Burris Laboratory School is a department in the Teachers College of Ball State University and provides an educational program from kindergarten through grade twelve. Observations, individual studies, tutoring, testing, and similar projects can be arranged directly through the office of the principal. The Office of Professional Laboratory Experiences provides assistance in placing students for such activities in all other educational settings for laboratory or field experiences in conjunction with course work or individual selfenhancement for development of teaching skills. PRE-STUDENT TEACHING PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES The purpose of prestudent teaching professional laboratory experiences is to provide students on the Teacher Education Curriculum with a systematic, planned sequence of experiences in appropriate educational settings. These experiences are designed to familiarize the students with principles of classroom management and the teachinglearning process in practical and real school environments, and to induct students into the teaching act. Prerequisites for: EDEL 360, Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School (4) EDJHM 312, Teaching in Junior High/Middle Schools (4) EDSEC 299, Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary Schools (4) The following prerequisites apply: 1. Admission to Teacher Education Curriculum 2. Completion of a minimum of 75 quarter hours for EDSEC 299 and EDJHM 312; 90 hours for EDEL 360 3. A composite gradepoint average of 2.1 or above 4.
