title: Topics in. Economics
description: This course is used for students wishing to earn general studies social science credit for television courses offered through the School of Continuing Education, Contact the School of Continuing Education or the Department at least five weeks before the beginning of each term for topics and instructions for registration. Does not apply toward business or economics majors or minors. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Economics of the Ghetto 1
description: The causes of segregation of residences according to income and race. The reasons for the level of income of ghetto residents and for the lack of efficiency with which society serves their economic needs. The effect of ghetto life on economic motivation. Not applicable toward major or minor concentrations in economics.

title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of modern economics are surveyed along with the general lines of thinking upon which those conclusions are founded. Especially designed to serve the needs and interest of the general education student. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 200 or 201.

title: Elements of Economics
description: A survey of the major institutions, of the theoretical explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions, of money and banking, and a brief introduction to the market determination of output and prices. Explains and evaluates the public policy relating to each area. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or credit in ECON 116.

title: Elements of Economics
description: Intensive study of the theory of price determination in various kinds of markets. Includes analyses of production functions; theories of wages, rent, interest, and profits; the principles of international trade and comparative economic organizations; and a general consideration of business ethics.

title: Economic and. Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Conditions related to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: Honors Colloquium in Economics
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honor students; others by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
description: Analyzes national income as a measure of economic activity. Major stress is on the determination of national income, employment, and price level, and the rate of growth of the economic system. Includes examination of the theories of consumption and investment spending, interaction between money and national income, and implications of alternative models for public policy. Includes graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Intermediate Microeconomics
description: An investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involves analyses of product pricing, output determination, resource pricing, and employment in various market structures. Includes graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 8 hours of credit in natural resources including NR 101 or 325 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Managerial Economics
description: Application of microeconomic analysis to managerial decision making. Emphasis on the applicability of economic concepts to business decisions. Forecasting techniques, demand measurement, production, cost, profit, management, product strategy, pricing, and location analysis. Prerequisite: junior standing; ECON 200, 201; MATH 132; MS 221.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Compares and analyzes growth rates of various countries. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201, or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 436.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life; surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Utilization of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201 and MATH 162 or 171.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201; MATH 131, 132 or their equivalent; and MS 221.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Labor Law
description: Origins and status of the major aspects of law as the law concerns the relations of unions and management. Major emphasis is on federal law as derived from the Management Labor Relations Act of 1947 and its interpretation by the National Labor Relations Board.

title: Economics and Practice of Collective Bargaining
description: Analyzes the interaction of the trade union, the employer, and the government. The legal, economic, and social framework of collective bargaining, negotiation, administration, and enforcement of the labor agreement. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Economics of Labor Market Discrimination
description: A survey of conservative, liberal, and radical theories of labor market discrimination; a review of studies on the extent of economic discrimination and the effect of public policy on the economic position of women and minorities. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the Board of ,Governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate, and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasizes economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives as regards provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: EC ON 200 and 201.

title: Economic Cycles and Forecasting
description: Techniques for forecasting the trend of activity for the entire economy. Analyzes institutional factors of the society as the determinants of total spending within the theoretical framework. Includes a seminar exercise and forecast for one sector of the economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Economics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
description: Evaluation of economic growth and efficiency of the Soviet economy and its pattern of evolution from 1917 to the present. Investigation of planning mechanism in industry as well as contributions and problems of agriculture. Examination of Soviet significance for other nations. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 200 and 201.

title: National Income and Capital Formation in China
description: Examines and compares basic concepts and methodology concerning national income accounting and capital formation in Communist China. Utilizes a combination of computation methods, growth theory, and a case study of modern Chinese economy. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and 300, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstructs or facilitates the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Internship in Economics
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Economics, a student majoring in economics works full time for one quarter as an economics intern for a private or public organization. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to thirdquarter juniors and seniors majoring in economics. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Credit is not applicable toward meeting the requirements of a major in economics.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 8 hours of credit in economics. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 hours may be earned in any one quarter.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses, thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 200, 201, and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. Department of Finance J. Hoban, Chairperson; Black, Caslan, Creviston, Engber, Faulhaber, Groeber, Hammer, G. Hoban, Howard, Johns, Mantripragada, Matsumoto, Sweeney, Wells, Williams, Zemedkun Programs in the Department of Finance provide opportunities for students to acquire a specialized or a broad business background. At the undergraduate level, the Department of Finance offers two majors leading to either the Bachelor of Arts or the Bachelor of Science degree. These majors are in finance and general business administration. Finance . Finance is a decisionoriented discipline concerned with the investment and management of money both in the present and in the future. This major is designed to provide the student with a general program in the financial aspects of business including financial management, investments, banking, insurance, real estate, and other related financial areas. Finance courses provide knowledge of concepts, processes, and institutions involved with the financing functions of the business enterprise; acquaint students with the financial instruments, institutions, and markets in the United States and the world; provide the tools and techniques of financial analysis and decision making; and expose the students to enough examples of financial decision making to allow them to develop expertise in applied finance. The finance major allows the student to pursue one of five options within the finance major: corporate financial management, financial institutions, risk management, real estate, and international business. The corporate financial management option prepares students for careers in the finance division of a business firm such as systems analysis, budget review analysis, financial analysis, acquisitions analysis, credit management, receivables management, and shortand longterm capital management. The financial institutions option emphasizes employment opportunities in managing stocks and bonds as a securities broker, portfolio manager, or trust department specialist and in investment banking. This option prepares the student to work in banking, savings and loan associations, loan companies, insurance companies, credit unions, pension funds, securities brokerage, and real estate brokerage. The risk management option has been designed to develop finance graduates in life and health, as well as property and casualty sales, property and casualty underwriting, insurance appraisal, and management positions with the insurance industry. The real estate option prepares a student for a sales career as well as real estate management. The international business option prepares a student for a career in multinational business fields and for the importexport activities of business firms. The departmental major in finance, in the Professional Arts Curriculum, is designed for students who want a foundation for a career in finance. General Business Administration . This major permits students to concentrate in two of the three areas available, i.e., insurance, management, and finance. Thus, this major provides a broader diversity of vocational opportunities than the finance major but with less depth in any one area of concentration. The course of study includes an examination of the various institutions, structures, functions, organizations, operations, and environments that influence business and economic activities. The finance sequence is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activities. The management sequence is designed to develop in students the necessary abilities to enable them, as future business executives and specialists, to deal with the diversity of problems that arise in the course of daytoday activities. The insurance sequence is designed to provide students with a survey of the major areas of insurance and with more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. Depending on the areas elected, graduates in general business administration are qualified to accept positions as junior executives at the management level in finance, insurance, personnel administration, office administration, production supervision, or other areas. In addition, this degree is particularly attractive to those students who may wish to engage in a small business or who do not wish to commit themselves to a particular vocation at this time. In addition to the above, the department provides certain basic background courses needed by students in other areas of the College of Business. title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law and the effect of the law in consumer credit and economic relationships. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Legal Aspect of Real Estate
description: The elementary concepts of real estate law and practice, particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, brokers' regulations, license law, and title insurance. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 332.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to agencies including employer and employee rights and obligations, partnerships including limited partnership, corporations including fiduciary obligations of directors, security regulations, bankruptcy, and corporate reorganization in bankruptcy. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principle articles of the code including sales, commercial paper, and security interests, in addition to creditors' rights and property law. Includes state and federal consumer protection laws as they affect commercial law. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Law for Small Business
description: Analysis of the laws affecting the small business. Emphasis on the legal aspects and legal implications of formation of a business, employeremploye e relationships, consumer protection laws, creditorights, and closing the busines. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Estate Planning and Administration
description: An introduction to problems associated with planning of financial resources during working life, retirement, and after the death of the principal income producer. Included are techniques for fact gathering, tax principles, use of trusts, and will drafting. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 260 and INS 370. Not open to the student who has credit in INS 373.

title: Current Topics in Business Law
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced business students for study of current topics and problems in business law. Topics may include current activity in property law, commercial law, and government regulation of business. Prerequisite: BL 260 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairperson. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the consumer's point of view. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation. Not open to juniors and seniors majoring in business.

title: Money, Banking, and Financial Institutions
description: The role of money, credit, and financial institutions in the U.S. financial system; deposit creation; the structure and functions of commercial banks, financial institutions and their regulatory agencies; domestic and international aspects of monetary policy; competition and regulation of financial institutions. Prerequisite: ACC 203; ECON 200, 201; MATH 132.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Designed to study different areas of financial decision making in a business firm. Specific topics include financial objectives of the firm, sources of funds, working capital management, capital budgeting, investment decisions under uncertainty, valuation, capital structure decisions, and dividend policy. Prerequisite: ACC 203; ECON 201; MS 221; and junior standing.

title: Consumer, Business, and Public Finance
description: The great importance in our national life of business credit, personal and consumer credit (including installment sales credit), bank credit, and public credit (federal, state, and municipal). Prerequisite: FIN 310.

title: Theory of Finance
description: A course devoted to the study of the current theory of finance. Topics include the nature and methodology of finance, efficient market hypothesis, portfolio theory and market equilibrium, optimal investment and financing decisions under certainty and uncertainty. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Designed to introduce the student to areas of investment: securities markets, transaction of stocks and bonds, valuation and timing, fundamental and technical indicators, money markets, and funds. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Financial Markets and the Economy
description: Nature and functions of financial markets; classification and interrelation of domestic and international financial markets; determination of the level and structure of interest rates; impact of monetary policy on financial markets and the economy. Prerequisite: FIN 310 and 350.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Quantitative Analysis in Financial Management
description: Studies the techniques for the selection and application of quantitative tools that aid the financial manager in the decisionmaking process. Stresses financial theory in practical applications faced by financial managers; a quantitative analysis of longand shortterm assets; and the strengths and weaknesses involved with the use of quantitative techniques. Prerequisite: FIN 354.

title: Multinational Business Finance
description: An indepth study of international financial institutions such as central banks, International Monetary Fund, and area development banks involved with the financial decisions of multinational corporations. Includes an overview of the new developing forces in international finance. Prerequisite: FIN 452.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Theory
description: An indepth analysis of valuation theory, capital market theory, and portfolio theory. Prerequisite: FIN 350 and 355.

title: Managerial Decision Making in Finance
description: A summary course devoted to the compilation of knowledge and the application of financial analysis to decision making in various subareas of finance. The course is structured on the case study approach. Prerequisite: FIN 457.

title: Operations of Financial Institutions
description: To integrate the various topics of finance with a view toward applications to the management of financial institutions in the following decision areas: assetliability management, cost control, profitability, capital adequacy, business development. Cases will be integrated in the method of instruction. Prerequisite: FIN 354, 355, 356.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Finance, students majoring in finance or general business administration work full time for a quarter as interns for a banking institution, business firm, or governmental agency. Requires written reports. Open only to thirdquarter juniors or seniors. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, researching, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Fundamentals of Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Fundamentals of Property -Liability Insurance
description: Study of fire, inland marine, liability, worker's compensation insurance. Emphasis on commercial insurance as a method of risk management. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 260 and INS 370. Not open to the student who has credit in BL 373.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include nofault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, state vs. federal regulations. Prerequisite: INS 370, 371, and 372 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Insurance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of insurance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various insurance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Real Estate Principles
description: The economic import of real estate, real estate characteristics, land use and environmental controls, legal aspects of real estate, methods of valuation, mortgage credit sources, secondary mortgage markets and financing techniques, investment analysis, land development, and real estate operations.

title: Real Estate Finance
description: The contractual nature and legal implication of the instruments used in real estate finance; instrument, techniques, and strategies in the financing of real estate investment; and the structure and operation of both primary and secondary mortgage markets. Provides the student with background in real estate law and real estate finance. Prerequisite: RE 330.

title: Legal Aspect of Real Estate
description: Elementary concepts of real estate law and practice particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, brokers' regulations, license law, and title insurance. Not open to the student who has credit in BL 332.

title: Real Estate Analysis
description: The appraisal of real estate. In addition to the appraisal process, other analytical systems will be reviewed as they apply to the real estate industry, including the economic base analysis, feasibility studies, and investment analysis. Prerequisite:

title: Real Estate Administration
description: An orientation of the real estate business using test cases, incidents, and walking cases. Guest speakers who are experts in real estate will be invited to speak and answer questions. Prerequisite: RE 431 and senior standing or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in RE 233. Department of Management Science LaFollette, Chairperson; Ahmed, Ault, Baird, Green, Harris, Kuratko, Lauck, Ma, Montagno, Mumtaz, Necessary, Seeborg, Swart, Walters, Yoo Management involves the coordination of human and physical resources toward an objective or goal. As this statement implies, management is germane to any type of purposive activity. Every organization has managers, regardless of what they are called (e. g. , managers, administrators, principals, coaches, officers, or chiefs). Therefore, a student who elects to major in management science will be preparing to assume a position of responsibility in a wide variety of profit and nonprofit organizations. The major in management science allows the student to pursue one of five management options: production and operations management, personnel administration, management information systems, or general management. In the production and operations management option, the student acquires the background to assume a position of responsibility in the production of goods and services. The student is introduced to the production functions in detail, is taught the methodology of making productionrelated decisions, and becomes acquainted with modern techniques used in motivating and leading personnel in a productionoriented occupation. In the personnel administration option, the student acquires the foundation for entering an occupation that relates primarily to the people in an organization. The student is given an indepth presentation of the personnel function, becoming familiar with a conceptual framework for analyzing and solving problems involved in the selection, development, and motivation of human resources. In the management information systems option, the student is introduced to the concepts and techniques necessary for the development and operation of management information systems. The student acquires a broad background in the role and operation of an information system in an organization. The graduate of this option is knowledgeable about the concepts and techniques of computerized information systems necessary to accomplish this important function effectively and efficiently. The entrepreneurship and small business option is designed to provide the student with the knowledge needed to work in a small business environment. The student learns how to formulate a plan for a small business and how to implement that plan, becoming acquainted with management information systems and business law tailormade for the small business. Finally, the student is provided with the opportunity to help a small business as a consultant in a team practicum. In the general management option, the student is introduced to a varied background in management. General management acquaints the student with the whole gamut of management: production, personnel, management information systems, and other managerial topics. Some organizations recruit on campus for generalists; students with the general management options fulfill this need. Other recruiters prefer more depth in a specific function such as production and operations, personnel, or management information systems. title: Management Principles
description: Helps the student understand the theory, research, and applications that provide the cornerstones for the study of management within organizations. Focuses on structures within companies and the processes within firms to bring theory to bear on the practical problems of managing organizations. Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Management of Human Resources
description: Deals directly with persons having responsibility in which people are the principal subjects. Attention to the individual personality; group and intergroup relations, environment factors, business and social responsibilities, and leadership as a critical factor in organizations. Prerequisite: MGT 280. Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Operations Management
description: Gives students an understanding of the basic operations function and a viable knowledge of the systems approach to the design of operations. Covers all important activities of the manufacturing enterprise with the exception of finance and general accounting. Prerequisite: MGT 280. Not open to the B. S . or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Industrial Supervision
description: For practicing or potential firstline supervisors and managers holding management positions up to middlelevel. Sound job control techniques, disciplinary techniques, verbal and nonverbal communications, supervisorunion relationships, and other problems common to all supervisors. Prerequisite: MGT 280. Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Small Business Ventures
description: Provides essential knowledge for students interested in small business. Topics include searching for venture opportunities; economic, technical, and operational feasibility of the venture; financing; negotiations; and operations. Emphasizes characteristics of the small business enterprise. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Entrepreneurship 1
description: Development and management of an entrepreneurial organization. Explains the function of entrepreneurs. Assesses the causes of failure and success. Small business management during prestartup, start up, survival, growth, and the transition from entrepreneurial to professional management, including franchising and partnering. Prerequisite: MGT 301 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Survey of Production/Operations Management
description: A basic study of functional fields of production. Decision making and quantitative analysis of production problems arisin g ng in areas of methods analysis, work measurement, wage incentives, production plani and control, inventory plant layout, materials handling and quality control. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Principles of Production/Operations Management
description: An intermediate study of the functional topics of production. Topics of MGT 351 are further defined and quantified to enable the student not only to acquire an indepth understanding of Production/OM but also to perform elementary decision making based on various management strategies. Prerequisite: MGT 351, MS 220 and 221.

title: Aggregate Planning and Scheduling
description: Examines in detail different aspects of production and inventory control systems covering such topics as forecasting, inventory decisions, materialrequirements planning, operations sequencing and balancing, jobshop scheduling, project scheduling and management of production and inventory control systems. Prerequisite: MGT 383, MS 220, and 221. 361. (481). Personnel Administration. (4) Administration of personnel programs in businesss organizations so as to deal effectively with such problems as selection, training, compensation, promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions, employee services, and industrial relations. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: International Management and Multinational Operations
description: Comparative management practices around the world; problems confronting multinational executives and corporations ; analysis of corporate structures and operations in foreign environments. Study of management functions, policies, global strategies. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Principles of Management
description: Examines planning, organizing, motivating, and controlling as they apply to managing a business organization. Discusses the functional field of production/operations management. Stresses leadership, problemsolving techniques, and the coordination, communication, and human relations necessary for successful management. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business and Society
description: An interdisciplinary approach toward developing a philosophy concerning the role of business in society. Emphasis on contemporary issues requiring business people to reexamine their roles and the role of the corporation in community and national life. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Organizational Behavior
description: Focuses on the dynamics of human behavior in business organizations, with concentration on problems of motivation and leadership. Emphasis is on the behavior of individuals and groups within organizations, and the practical interpretation and management of behavioral phenomena. Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Small Business Practicum
description: Teams of students consult with local small businesses. Cases are assigned by Small Business Administration. Students work on problems of the particular small businesses in office administration, accounting, production, marketing, personnel, finance, insurance, legal, or information systems. Prerequisite: MGT 301 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Management Information Systems for Small Businesses
description: The role of computer -based applications for smallbusiness operations without access to an internal specialist. Emphasis placed on microcomputers and purchased software. Prerequisite: MGT 301 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Entrepreneurship 2
description: Advanced smallbusiness management course using case approach to study situations and approaches. Includes thorough research project culminating in the development of a finished business or venture plan for a small business. Prerequisite: MGT 302, FIN 350, and M KG 300 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Internship in Management
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Management Science, a student majoring in management science will work full time for a quarter as an intern in an organization operating in either the private or public sector. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to thirdquarter juniors or seniors.

title: Techniques of Production/Operations Management
description: Emphasis on decision making and quantitative analysis of production problems arising in incentives, production planning and control, inventory control, plant layout, materials handling and quality control. Prerequisite: MGT 352.

title: Internship in Computer Management
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Management Science, a student majoring in management science will work halftime two quarters as an intern in Ball State University Computing Services. Management Science 165 Prerequisite: MS 220, 312, four hours of experience working in the Ball State University Computing Services, or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Compensation Administration
description: Reviews basic compensation issues including internal, external, and individual equity, as well as benefits administration. The design and implementation of compensation systems are addressed. Prerequisite: MGT 361.

title: Problems in Personnel Management
description: Case studies depicting complex personnel issues and problems faced by organizations. Provides the student an opportunity to apply personnel policies, theories, concepts, and techniques to actual personnel situations. Prerequisite: MGT 361.

title: Personnel Planning and Selection
description: Focuses on organization and manpower planning. Includes determination of organization and manpower needs, analysis and development of job requirements and necessary qualifications for recruitment and selection, selection procedures, placement and orientation, and evaluation of selection programs. Prerequisite: MGT 463 and MS 421.

title: Problems in Production/Operations Management
description: An integration of all the production/ operations management principles, theories, and techniques gained from previous courses as applied to actual production problems. Major teaching methods include case study, discussion, and individual projects. Current topics may be discussed. Prerequisite: MGT 452.

title: Quality Assurance
description: Application of statistical control charts, sampling plans, and reliability analysis to problems of planning, feedback, and control of product quality, process performance, operation effectiveness, and related areas of management activities. Prerequisite: MS 221, MGT 351.

title: Work Design
description: The design of office and industrial jobs to meet the needs and preferences of the worker and the management. Included are methods improvement techniques, layout of work stations, incentive and motivation techniques, and the setting of output standards. Prerequisite: MGT 351 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Comparative Administration
description: Comparative analysis of managing complex organizations and service industries; emphasizing environmental and organizational factors affecting the management process, firm structure, and administration functions. Study of administration crossculturally (internationally) and crossinstitutionally (service industries). Prerequisite: MGT 380 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisite: MGT 380.

title: Independent Study in Management
description: An opportunity for supervised study of some phase of management. May consist of an experiment, library research, or an analysis of current management practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Management
description: Explores in depth current problems, theory, research, and trends in the management field. The topics of the seminar will vary depending upon the current status of managerial research, the instructor, and the needs and desires of the students. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business Applications of Computer Data Processing
description: An introductory course in computer data processing with special emphasis on business problem solving. Discusses the effects of computers on business and management decision making, hardware and software, business systems analysis, and computer programming. Analyzes problems in account- Mg, production, marketing, banking, finance, and management. Prerequisite: open only to business majors and minors or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Interpretation of Business Data
description: Deals with the collection, presentation, analysis, and interpretation of statistical data. Topics include descriptive statistics, basic probability, probability distributions, sampling, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, regression, and correlation. Class, four hours, laboratory one hour per week. Prerequisite: MATH 131 and 132 or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: MS 220. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 221.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics which emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 220, or CS 200. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 210.

title: Information Systems Analysis
description: Systems theory and practice as they apply to satisfying information needs for management decision makers through the analysis and design of manual and computer based systems. Influence of information systems upon management and organizations as well as upon managerial decision making. Prerequisite: MGT 380; MS 220; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business COBOL Data Processing Applications
description: COBOL programming techniques to solve business data processing problems such as file maintenance, report writing, sorting, and merging. Coverage of techniques for sequential and direct access devices. Prerequisite: MS 310 and 312.

title: Business Computer Systems and Applications
description: Acquaints students with current business use of computer. Deals with selected properties of systems design and file design. Presents a general framework from singlepurpose to integrated business applications, such as accounting, operationscontrol, production scheduling, personnel, and marketing. Fortran programming skills are developed. Prerequisite: MS 220, 312.

title: Quantifying Management Decisions
description: A study and critical evaluation of operations research techniques for solving managerial problems found in business administration. Prerequisite: MS 220 and 221.

title: Simulating Management Decisions
description: A study and critical evaluation of simulation techniques for solving managerial problems found in business administration. Prerequisite: MS 220 and 221.

title: Advanced Business Statistics
description: The application to business problems of the most commonly used advanced statistical methods including goodnessoffit, contingency tables, analysis of variance, nonparametric techniques, advanced regression and correlation as applied to time series, and index numbers. Prerequisite: MS 220 and 221.

title: Integrating Word Processing/Data Processing Systems
description: Explores the evolutionary changes within the office. An introduction to the considerations involved in integrating text and data from word processing and data processing input to enhance the information processing output. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 200 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 362.

title: Business Systems Analysis and Design
description: An introductory course in business systems analysis and design. Introduces elementary systems techniques and tools. Explains in detail the key steps in the systems development cycle. Deals with some of the practical applications and considerations in systems within the business environment. Prerequisite: MS 321 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Data Base: Structures and Management
description: Logical and physical organization of data. Describes data description, command and interrogation languages. Examines function of data bases in information systems. Prerequisite: MS 310 and 312 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Administration of Management Information Systems
description: Topics include equipment selection, equipment acquisition, computer operations management, project management, computer personnel management, financial control, systems security and control, and the relationship of the information systems functions to the organization as a whole. Prerequisite: MS 410 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Getting and Keeping a Job in Business
description: Indepth discussions involving personal goals in business, business opportunities, and management evaluations. Preparations and techniques for personal interviews in the business setting. Particular focus on personal discipline early in the business career.

title: Business Administration Policy
description: An integration of the administrative processes of the operation of organizations producing goods and services in the private enterprise system. Emphasizes the case study method in solving problems under conditions of uncertainty. Includes the relationship of a code of ethics as a control device for policy decisions. Prerequisite: senior standing, M KG 300, MGT 380, FIN 350, or permission of the department chairperson. Marketing 167 Department of Marketing Lowry, Chairperson; Baird, Brown, Emamalizadeh, Fox, Kumcu, Moser, Sparling, Vanderleest, Wunder Marketing is a dynamic business function concerned with the "customeroriented" management of the flow of goods and services from the producer to the customer/consumer. The marketing process attempts to provide an efficient way for enlightened producers to meet the needs of discerning consumers profitably. Important marketing activities include developing a wanted product, promoting it efficiently, selling it at an economically logical price, and distributing it in the right places. Marketing courses at Ball State University are designed to allow students to develop their abilities to recognize and define marketing problems and solve them creatively. The marketing curriculum is career oriented. Students majoring in marketing choose at least one of five options within the curriculum. Each option focuses on the unique activities and career opportunities within the professional field of marketing. The sales and promotion option prepares students for careers such as consumer and industrial product selling, sales training, advertising agency management, public relations, and product or brand management. Career opportunities for students selecting the retailing option include chainstore management, merchandising, fashion coordination, small business management, and buying. For students choosing the physical distribution option, career opportunities include materials management, industrial procurement, transportation, and physical distribution. After acquiring a foundation in marketing, students taking the general marketing option are qualified to pursue many different phases of the marketing process. Some of the careers available to students with the general marketing option are international marketing, bank marketing, consumer relations, and service marketing. Students choosing the shopping center administration option prepare for such careers as shopping center planning and development, shopping center administration, and retail management. The Department of Marketing, in cooperation with selected business firms and commercial institutions, administers a professional practice program that allows juniors and seniors to relate classroom theory to practical experience by working for one quarter in a variety of relevant assignments. Students who work as interns receive from 2 to 8 quarter hours of credit, and most are paid by the firm for their work experience. Students are responsible for finding their own internships; they will be assisted by marketing department administrators in this process. Students in the marketing department coordinate and administer, with the participation of students from other departments, the Ball State University Better Business Bureau, a branch of the Indianapolis Better Business Bureau. Students interested in BSU/BBB are advised to enroll in MKG 380, Marketing and Consumer Issues, or its summer equivalents (MKG 301 and 302) during their junior year. There are several positions of responsibility in the bureau that offer students unusual learning experiences. The activities of the bureau include resolving consumerbusiness grievances, providing buying information to consumers, alerting consumers to deceptive business practices, and preparing media releases on consumerbusiness problems. The Ball State University collegiate chapter of the American Marketing Association (BSU/AMA) is a professionally oriented organization that exposes students to professional contacts and programs. The organization also coordinates and promotes participation in various personal development programs for students who have similar interests in marketing careers. The BSU/AMA has conducted a series of "mini courses" focused on career planning, bringing speakers to the campus to discuss job qualifications and career opportunities in various areas of marketing. In cooperation with local civic organizations, the BSU/AMA has also conducted studies to assist in the identification of the market needs of minority groups and senior citizens. A departmental honors program is available to academically superior students. MKG 475, Marketing Simulation, has been designated as an honors course. For students interested in preparing for teaching marketing or distributive education, it is possible to earn a departmental major in marketing along with the teaching major in distributive education. title: Retail Merchandising
description: An introduction to the retail industry with a concentration, on the merchandising activities of buying, selling, pricing, and inventory controlling. Prerequisite:

title: Salesmanship
description: Fundamentals of retail, wholesale, outside, and service selling. Emphasizes sales approaches, presentation, closings, and postsale service. Prerequisite: GBA

title: Retail Advertising
description: Introduction to the field of advertising with emphasis on the preparation, appeal, and media selection of retail advertising. Prerequisite: GBA 101. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 300 or to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the the College of Business.

title: Principles of Marketing
description: Examines marketing as a productive system within our economy. Studies promotional activities, product policies, retail and wholesale activities, pricing policies, international marketing, and the role of marketing in society. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Consumer Relations/Training Orientation
description: Practicum involving administrative and operational activities essential to the Ball State University Better Business Bureau. A broad spectrum of activities including handbook examinations, training, and evaluation of operatives' performance level in a consumer relations operation. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department chairperson. Offered first summer term only. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 380.

title: Marketing and Controversial Issues
description: Reading, research, and discussion course focusing on corporate citizenship. Addresses many topics such as cost effectiveness of regulations, Marketing 169 deceptive advertising, health impact of products, and safety/product liability. Prerequisite: MKG 301 or permission of department chairperson. Offered during second summer term only. Not open to the student who has credit MKG 380.

title: Consumer Behavior
description: Practical business implications of the various aspects of consumer motivation and behavior. The student is provided with information to understand how and why a buyer reacts in a purchasing situation. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Advertising Management
description: Use of advertising as a communication tool in marketing management. Analysis of media selection production and layout, measurement of effectiveness, and social and economic aspects of advertising. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 310.

title: Personal Selling
description: Provides a detailed introduction to and application of the principles of personal selling as applied to persons pursuing any vocation, as well as those aspiring to careers in the marketing area of business. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 327.

title: Sales Management
description: Policies and practices in organizing, recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and 325 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Retail Management
description: An investigation of store policies, organization, location, layout, buying, stock control, pricing, and sales promotion for retail stores. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Survey of Transportation
description: The economics of transportationinternal waterways, railways, highways, and airwaysin the United States; economic development of various means of transportation and accompanying regulatory problems. Rate, traffic service, and coordination problems; advantages and disadvantages, trends, and peculiarities of the various modes. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Research
description: The basic nature and scope of marketing research; scientific method and research design; specific marketing research procedures; techniques of sampling; and research report, followup, and evaluation of research process. Selected applications in motivation, advertising, and product and sales control research. Prerequisite: MATH 131, 132; MKG 300; and MS 221.

title: Marketing and Consumer Issues
description: Analysis of the consumer issues that affect marketing. Includes the marketing implications of consumerism, ecology, and the disadvantaged consumers. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Promotion Strategy
description: Use of cases and problems to provide experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKG 320.

title: Retail Strategy
description: Advanced course in retailing management using case studies and special projects to examine current topics and problems in the field of retailing. Prerequisite: MKG 330.

title: Physical Distribution Management
description: Physical distribution systems in the marketing environment: system components and the total cost approach; customer service objectives; physical distribution systems design and administration. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Industrial Procurement Management
description: A basic course in industrial procurement management. Principal topics include make or buy analysis, quality and quantity control, value analysis, price determination, sources of supply, the purchasing system, and legal aspects of purchasing. Prerequisite: M KG 300.

title: Materials Management
description: The organizational concept that integrates the management of the flow of materials through a business enterprise into consumer markets. Content includes anticipating, sourcing, obtaining, and monitoring the current status of materials in an enterprise. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 460.

title: International Marketing
description: Examines legal, economic, and cultural factors influencing marketing abroad. Commercial policies, practices, and techniques needed to locate and evaluate foreign markets, as well as the problems of pricing, promoting, and distributing products in international markets. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Simulation Game
description: A simulation game in which students are divided into teams or companies. Management in each company makes decisions in marketing, finance, and production. Does not involve writing computer programs or using information from a data processing class. Prerequisite: M KG 300 and junior standing.

title: Shopping Center Seminar
description: A study of the managerial activities that are important in the operation of a shopping center. Subjects include layout, promotions, financing, merchandising, and regulation. Prerequisite: MKG 330, 431.

title: Marketing Management
description: Marketing by manufacturers as viewed from the marketing manager's position. Principal topics are selecting channels of distribution, determining demand, pricing policies, marketing legislation, advertising policies, and methods of selling. A case study approach. Prerequisite: 20 quarter hours in marketing, including MKG 350 and senior standing, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Professional Practice in Marketing
description: Professional practice during a summer or a quarter as an intern on an approved program with a business firm, government agency, or nonprofit organization under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Requires periodic written reports of job experiences. Open only to thirdquarter juniors and seniors with a major in marketing. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Product Innovation
description: A systematic study of the evolution of a new product. The framework comprises newproduct policies, creativity, idea screening and business analysis, physicalproduct development and marketing planning, applied research including testmarketing, and commercialization. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Commercial Pricing Strategies and Administration
description: Focuses on the pricing function for industrial and consumer products as part of the marketing mix. Indepth analysis of psychological, financial, legal, economic, and managerial influences on price setting in business. Prerequisite: MKG 300; ACC 203; ECON 201.

title: Independent Study in Marketing
description: Independent study in some phase of marketing that may consist of an experiment, library research, or the analysis of current marketing practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing, a scholastic ratio of 3.0 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Practicum in the Better Business Bureau
description: Provides practical experience in mediating businessconsumer problems. Students utilize personnel skills in organizing and administering a Better Business Bureau. Prerequisite: MKG 301, 302, or 380. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 3 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 497.

title: Introduction to Business
description: Emphasizes the vital role of business in our society through a discussion of both the external environment of business and the internal environment of the business enterprise. Assesses the contribution of the social and behavioral sciences in the decision making process. Open only to freshmen or sophomores except by permission of the department chairman.

title: International Business Decision Making—A Managerial Approach
description: Practical application of the management decision making process as applied to planning, organizing, implementing, and controlling international business operations. This capstone course is designed to prepare the student for a career in international business management. Urice The College of Fine Arts centers on the commonalities of its constituent departments in making symbols of the culture concrete and formal to create aesthetic experiences. Each of the departments provides technical mastery and depth of understanding within its own discipline, while the college unites them in recognition of the interrelationship of the arts with one another and with other areas of the university. The faculty is committed to the practice, teaching, and encouragement of professions that have the arts as their primary focus and to humanistic study of the arts and their place in society. They aspire to impart mastery of their own disciplines, as well as to explore interdisciplinary relationships, develop aesthetic judgment and a sense of pleasure in beauty, lead students to an understanding of the theory and history of the arts, and embody those principles in research and creative work of the highest possible quality. This commitment is expressed through professional programs dedicated to academic excellence, intensive laboratory experiences, and directed work with faculty models. Curricular opportunities are also available for the general student to understand the arts through study and participation so that college graduates can learn to understand our artistic heritage and value its future. The larger community, too, has access to the many possibilities for personal enrichment that the college provides as an outgrowth of its programs. All aspects of the curriculum are designed to contribute to the creation of a salutary climate for the practice and appreciation of the fine arts. Inherent in this ideal are the opportunity and the obligation for students and faculty to play a significant role in the intellectual and cultural life of the university, the state, and the broader community of the arts. Department of Art Minkler, Chairperson; Arndt, Bertrand, Davis, Dorethy, Easton, Foster, Graham, Griner, Hill, Murphy, Nelson, Parish, Preston, Repp, Spoerner Education in the visual arts brings a third dimension to the academic program of the school through the personal dimensions of feeling, sensitivity, empathy, and expression. The visual arts specifically seek to involve the student in perceiving the world he lives in, reacting to the things seen and felt, and interpreting emotions, feelings, and insights through a variety of visual materials. The making of works of art involving various materials and processes, knowledge of art objects in relation to cultural meaning, and the critical evaluation of art products are the basic aspects of the visual art program. The ordering of these areas of learning is determined both by the properties inherent in the subject and the varying abilities, interests, and social needs of art students. Studio experience is the foundation upon which each of these aspects of the program is based. From the technical and creative aspects of art production flow the various functions, meaning, and special knowledge of education in the visual arts. The primary purpose of the art program is to develop professional artists, designers, teachers, and educated consumers of fine art and commercial imagery. Professional Opportunities in Art Programs in the department prepare students for careers in the visual arts, interior and environmental design, graphic and advertising design, and teaching. Some graduates with degrees in art are employed in commercial and private firms, government, industry, and education; others are selfemployed artists and craftsmen. Other employment possibilities are as museum and art program directors, crafts directors, studio artists, and public school and university teachers. Recommended High School Preparation For students entering all art department programs, courses in art and drafting are highly recommended. In addition, for students planning to enter the professional art and design B. F.A. programs or the teaching field, four years of English composition, one year of algebra, and two years of science are recommended. Curricula in the Art Department Students have a variety of curricula from which to choose. Each curriculum is unique, yet there are many courses common to all programs before specialization. The major difference found among programs is the course work specifically related to the career or area of emphasis. Many of the programs are accredited by professional agencies. Each area provides a curriculum guide specifying the exact art requirements for graduation to assist students in planning their programs. Students may use their electives to broaden their education, to strengthen their area or specialization, or in some cases to meet the requirements for two programs of study. The undergraduate curricula and specialty areas are Drawing Photography Weaving Graphic Design Metals Interior/Environmental Design Ceramics Art History Sculpture Art Education Printmaking Painting Requirements for Basic Programs in the Art Department Students are advised to seek departmental advising about majoring in art and design before undertaking the following course groupings, which are normally completed during the first year: Art Core; Design and Drawing Foundations (ADS 101, 102; AFA 101, 202); Painting (AFA 211); and Art History Survey (AHS 101, 102). After completion of the 20-credit core requirements, students seeking the B. F.A. degree take an additional 8-credit art history core and 16 credits in area support courses. Students preparing for the B. S. degree program take 12 credits in area support courses. Area support courses are usually completed before the major specialization art or design courses. Courses for Non—Art Majors Courses for the liberal arts student are also offered (see course descriptions and prerequisites). These courses provide the nonart major with the opportunity for personal enrichment through the visual arts. Entry Level and Transfer Student Requirements Art majors are not required to submit an entrance portfolio but must be prepared to present a portfolio for review and evaluation periodically throughout the program. Students transferring art credits from other institutions are required to submit a portfolio and transcript of grades to the department for evaluation. title: Weaving 1
description: Basic instruction in loom weaving with an emphasis on tapestry technique and color experimentation. Prerequisite: ADS 102.

description: Beginning throwing; use of the potter's wheel to develop skills in throwing. A continued study of form, glaze, and idea. Prerequisite: ACR 211.

description: Exploration of woven fiber techniques and application of these techniques to a project. Techniques introduced will vary from quarter to quarter.
