title: Mathematical Concepts 1
description: A general education course for students who wish to know more about the contributions of mathematics to human culture. Includes topics particularly suited to the needs of the student who seeks a broad knowledge of mathematical ideas together with some computational skills and techniques. Prerequisite: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry. Not open to students with college credit in mathematics except by permission of the department chairperson or to students with areas in mathematics or computer science.

title: Mathematical Concepts 2
description: Continuation of MATH 100. Prerequisite: MATH 100.

title: College Algebra 1
description: Fundamental operations of algebra through quadratics. Students who have credit for three semesters of secondary school algebra will not receive credit for this course. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra.

title: College Algebra 2
description: A brief introduction to sets and the logic of algebra, a discussion of inequalities, absolute values, functions and relations, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and mathematical induction. Prerequisite: MATH 110 or three semesters of secondary school algebra and one year of plane geometry, or their equivalent as determined by the department chairperson. Credit is denied in this course if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities, and equations; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers, and Demoivre's Theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or its equivalent as determined by the department chairperson. Credit is denied if credit has been earned in any greaternumbered mathematics course or its equivalent except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Elementary Analytic Geometry
description: The coordinate plane, straight lines and circles, conic sections, elementary transcendental functions, curve sketching, polar coordinates, and parametric equations. Prerequisite: the equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level, or MATH 111 and 112. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 113.

title: Mathematics for Architects 1
description: Topics in analytic geometry and calculus particularly suited to the needs of the architecture major. Includes concepts of limits, differentiation, and integration. Prerequisite: MATH 112. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 161, 165, or 170.

title: Mathematics for Architects 2
description: Continuation of MATH 123. Emphasis on applications of calculus. Prerequisite: MATH 123. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 162, 165, or 170.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 1
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 111 or a strong background in high school algebra.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics that are particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATH 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications in some of the above areas. Prerequisite: MATH 111 and 112 or their equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 123, 165, or 170.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATH 161, 165, or 170. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 124, 166, or 171.

title: Calculus 1
description: Differential calculus and its applications. Advanced topics from analytic geometry will be introduced as needed. Prerequisite: elements of analytic geometry from high school, or MATH 113 or 114. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 123, 161, or 170.

title: Calculus 2
description: Antidifferentiation and the Riemann integral. Elementary transcendental functions. Standard techniques of integration and applications of the integral. Prerequisite: MATH 165 or 170. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 124, 162, or 171.

title: Calculus 3
description: Infinite series. Further development and applications of integral calculus. Vectors. Partial differentiation. Prerequisite: MATH 166 or 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 172.

title: Cardinal Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the number concept from sets through cardinal numbers.

title: Rational Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the concept of unsigned rational numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 201.

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: A development of the real number system. Prerequisite: MATH 202. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 205.

title: Real Numbers in the Elementary School
description: The development and use of decimal and scientific notation through metric measurement. An extension of real number concepts including irrational numbers and integers through measurement, decimal approximations, calculator activities, coordinate graphing, and applications. It is recommended that students preparing to teach in upper elementary grades substitute MATH 203 for MATH 205. Prerequisite:

title: Geometry in the Elementary School
description: A development of geometric concepts for elementary school teachers. Prerequisite: MATH 202, and MATH 203 or 205 if either course is required in the student's program.

title: Elementary School Enrichment Topics
description: An examination of mathematics concepts included as enrichment topics in elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 206. Open only to students with areas in elementary education and special education, except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Structure of the Number Systems
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and selected number systems. A systematic development is emphasized. Prerequisite: MATH 162, 166, 171, or equivalent.

title: Elements of Linear Algebra
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties, determinants, matrix inverses, rank and equivalence of matrices, and a matrix approach to the theory of systems of linear equations. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, 166, or 171.

title: Topics From Linear Algebra
description: Determinants, matrices, and bilinear maps, polynomials and matrices, triangulation of matrices and linear maps, spectral theorems, multilinear products. Prerequisite: MATH 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 412.

title: Applied Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, probability, random variables, important discrete and continuous distributions, statistical inference and testing of hypotheses, sampling theory, statistical analysis of time series, decision theory. Considers the application of these topics to business. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, 166, or 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 321.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Geometry
description: A revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Calculus 4
description: Multidimensional calculus and its applications. Multiple integration. Elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATH 167 or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 173,

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems dealing with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite: MATH 173 or 268.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 202.

title: Computer Topics for Elementary and Junior High/Middle School Mathematics
description: Includes topics in computer uses and programming; also enrichment topics from areas such as topology, strategy games, and number theory. Prerequisite: MATH 206 or 240. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 200 or 220.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATH 211.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, gamma, rectangular, and normal distributions. Prerequisite: MATH 167 or 172.

title: Statistics 1
description: Classification of data, empirical distributions, random sampling, distributions of sample mean and same variance from normal distribution, distribution of sample mean from nonnormal distributions, probability distributions for correlation and regression, empirical methods for correlation and regression, general principle of estimation and hypothesis testing. Prerequisite: MATH 320.

title: Statistics 2
description: Testing of goodness of fit, contingency tables, small sample distributions, chisquare, t and F distributions and their applications in hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, nonparametric methods, sequential analysis, Bayesian method. Prerequisite: MATH 321.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, t, and F distributions. Some problems with moment generating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Prerequisite: MATH 221 or 321 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in synthetic geometry, closely related to the field of Euclidean geometry.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models to problems from physics, chemistry, biology, and business. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models rather than detailed numerical results. Prerequisite: MATH 212.

title: Intermediate Calculus
description: Topics include vector functions, displacement, velocity and acceleration of particles in twoand threespace, curvature, torsion and Frenet's formulas, divergence, curl, line integrals, work, surface integrals, Gauss's Theorem, Green's Theorem, Stokes's Theorem, orthogonal curvilinear coordinates. Prerequisite: MATH 173 or 268.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nthorder ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Enler equations. Laplace transforms, power series solutions. Method of kryloff and Bogolinboff, firstorder partial differential equations. Prerequisites: MATH 173 or 268. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 212.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematics in Early Childhood
description: Materials and methods used for teaching mathematics at prekindergarten levels. Prerequisite: MATH 206.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from kindergarten through grade three. Class ideas applied in tutoring situations. Prerequisite; MATH 206. Not open to the student who has credit in MATH 391.

title: Teaching Mathematics in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Each student will plan and teach seven onetoone sessions with an elementary school child. Prerequisite: MATH 206.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for the teaching of mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a tutoring situation. Prerequisite: 30 hours credit in the junior high/middle school mathematics program and junior standing.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in teaching senior high school mathematics. Survey of texts, organization of materials, testing procedures, and visual aids materials. Prerequisite: MATH 313 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: E DS EC 299.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Mathematics -oriented classroom management techniques ; introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics; evaluation of instructional activities; and rationale for including mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: MATH 395.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 1
description: Topics from group theory, ring theory, and field theory, including integral domains and polynomial rings. Prerequisite: MATH 212.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics from MATH 411 and topics from vector spaces and module theory. Prerequisite: MATH 411.

title: Theory of Numbers 1
description: Topics include the division algorithm ; positional notation; divisibility; primes; congruences; divisibility criteria; the sigma, divisor, and phi functions; diophantine equations ; linear, polynomial, and simultaneous congruences; theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson.

title: Theory of Numbers 2
description: Some topics not covered in MATH 416, including elementary partition theory, quadratic residues, continued fractions, Farey fractions and irrational numbers, elementary properties of (x), Waring's problem, and density of sequences of integers. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Topics in Statistics 1
description: Includes such topics as theory of distribution, theory of statistical inference, and theory of regression analysis. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or MS 421 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Topics in Statistics 2
description: Deals with topics mentioned in MATH 428 at an advanced level with particular reference to experimental design and analysis of variance, use of computers in statistics, and Monte Carlo methods. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or MS 421, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling ; ratio estimates; regression estimates; cost function; variance function. Prerequisite: MATH 322 or MS 421 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school include Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, magic squares, the Calendar Problem, polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the Fifteen Puzzle, Nim, and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers. Prerequisite: MATH 416.

title: Advanced Analytic Geometry
description: An advanced treatment of analytic Euclidean geometry using topics from analysis and algebra as tools as needed.

title: Projective Geometry
description: Properties of geometric configurations that are invariant under projection. Synthetic methods emphasized, and some use is made of analytic methods.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities certain, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, and capitalized cost. Both the discrete and the continuous approach to compound interest and annuities certain. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, 167, or 171.

title: Mathematics of Life Insurance
description: An introduction to the mathematics of life insurance; mortality tables; life annuities, premiums, and reserves for basic life insurance policies; modern reserve systems. Emphasizes the discrete approach to contingencies of a single life and introduces the continuous approach. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 451.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 1
description: Advanced treatment of the contingencies of a single life using both discrete and continuous functions. Topics include measurement of mortality, life annuities, life insurance, net annual premiums, net level premium reserves, and the expense factor. Prerequisite: MATH 452.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 2
description: Advanced treatment of the contingencie s of both single and multiple lines. Topics include population theory, the jointlife status, lastsurvivor and general multistatuses, contingent functions, compound contingent functions, reversionary annuities, multipledecrement tables, tables with secondary decrements, and a generalized model. Prerequisite: MATH 453.

title: Topology 1
description: Set theoretic preliminaries, the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well ordering principle, topological spaces, continuity, separation axioms, nets and filters, connectedness, local connectedness, product and quotient topologies, metric spaces, metrization. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Topology 2
description: Uniform spaces, paracompactness, open coverings, compactness, compactification, local compactness, function spaces, Stone-Weierstrauss theorem, complete spaces, Banach fixedpoint theorem. Introduction to homology theory, Jordan curve theorem, Brouwer fixedpoint theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 455.

title: History of Mathematics 1
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to 1600. Topics include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, and trigonometry. Prerequisite: MATH 124, 162, 166 or 171.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analyses, solutions of nonlinear equations and systems of nonlinear equations, interpolation and approximation of functions, approximate differentiation and integration. Includes programming of the numerical algorithms being studied. Prerequisite: CS 220 or permission of the department chairperson, and MATH 124, 162, 167 or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 462.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include numerical solutions of differential equations, matrices and approximate solutions of linear systems by both direct and iterative methods, matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Includes programming of the numerical algorithms being studied. Prerequisite: MATH 212 and 462 or CS 462. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 463.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, mathematical formula. Prerequisite: MATH 462 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Optimization techniques of linear, dynamic, and integer programming. Optimal solutions of PERT-CPM networks. Optimal decision strategies. Prerequisite: MATH 212 and 221 or 320 and a working knowledge of FORTRAN (CS 220 or equivalent).

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATH 374.

title: Elements of Analysis 1
description: Topics include partial derivatives, L'Hospital's Theorem, integration in polar coordinates, sequences, series, convergence, continuity, and improper integrals. Prerequisite: MATH 162 or 166. Open only to students with a teaching major in mathematics. Not open to the student with credit in MATH 167 or 172.

title: Elements of Analysis 2
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives, and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATH 469.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Advanced calculus including real numbers, metric spaces, topology of R and C, continuity of functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrauss theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATH 173 or 268.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics covered include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansion. Prerequisite: MATH 471.

title: Advanced Calculus 3
description: Advanced calculus of several variables. Calculus of differential forms in three dimensions. Examples from physics. Prerequisite: MATH 472.

title: Advanced Differential Equations
description: Existence and uniqueness of solution of firstorder nonlinear ordinary differential equations, linear systems, autonomous systems in the plane, oscillatory theory, secondorder partial differential equations with constant coefficients, the Cauchy problem, elements of potential theory, the Dirichlet problem. Prerequisite: MATH

title: Diagnostic Techniques in Mathematics Education
description: Provides prospective teachers with an understanding of difficulties in learning mathematics and practical experience in accessing these difficulties and methods of corrective treatment. Each student will diagnose children in mathematics and prepare an informal diagnostic instrument. Prerequisite: MATH 390, 391, 393, or 399. Prerequisite recommended EDPSY 345.

title: Complex Variables 1
description: Complex number systems, differentiation and integration, functions (analytic, entire, meromorphic) of one complex variable, singularities, complex integration, Cauchy's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, power series, Laurent Series, calculus of residues. Prerequisite: MATH 173 or 268. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 472.

title: Complex Variables 2
description: Analytic continuation, Riemann surfaces, theorem of Weierstrauss and Mittag-Leffler, solution of twodimensional potential problem, conformal mapping, Schwartz-Christoffel transformations and its application to the solution of electric, magnetic field distributions and of thermal and hydraulic stationary flow problems. Prerequisite: MATH 485.

title: Problems in the Teaching of Arithmetic
description: For teachers in service who do not hold a degree. Prerequisite: teaching experience in the elementary school. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the mathematical sciences department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 level. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Natural Resources Van Meter, Chairperson; Godish, Hibbs, Lowe, Lyon, Mortensen, Siewert, Sullivan The Department of Natural Resources has as its ultimate objective the education of people to help meet the demand for qualified personnel in environmental and natural resources. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the university by offering appropriate courses in natural resources. Through research and extension activities it also strives to provide services concerning environmental quality and resource management for Indiana citizens. Our expanding population and technology in combination with our affluent society and its accelerated use and abuse of resources have placed severe stress on the environment. There is an urgent need for men and women with a knowledge of natural resources and environmental quality management. The programs offered by the department are designed to give students a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. Curricula offered by the Department of Natural Resources are interdisciplinary because the conservation of our natural resources and the concomitant improvement of our environment are areas of total university concern, requiring new ideas, diverse skills, and the contributions of many disciplines. Therefore, depending upon the special interest of the student, a program may include courses in several disciplines in fulfilling the curricular requirements. Students considering professional careers in natural resources should plan their high school programs to include a strong background in both the sciences and the humanities. The desire and ability to work with people is also an important prerequisite. Curricula offered by the department include a departmental minor and major in natural resources at both the undergraduate and graduate levels and a cognate for doctoral students. A teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, an area of endorsement for elementary education majors, a supporting concentration for junior high/middle school majors, and an energy resources minor are also offered, Students enrolled in the undergraduate major in natural resources may elect the general option in resource management or specialize in such subjects as natural resource planning, fishery resources, communications, water quality, natural resources interpretation, soil science, environmental protection, and outdoor recreation management. Common background is provided for all majors through a "core requirement" that includes Introduction to Natural Resources, Air Resources, Ecology, Man and the Geologic Environment, Mineral Resources, Soil Resources, Water Resources, and Integrated Resources Management. Other courses that may be elected will be determined by the option selected, the student's background, and professional employment interests. In addition to traditional science courses, others that may be included are communication, computer techniques, environmental health, landscape architecture, physical education, political science, sociology, statistics, and urban and regional studies. Students majoring in other departments of the university are encouraged to elect one of the natural resource minors that complement a variety of curricula. Students interested in becoming teachers are especially encouraged to elect the teaching minor, area of endorsement, or supporting concentration in conservation and environmental studies to enhance their qualifications. These programs are designed to prepare future teachers to enhance the curriculum by integrating conservation and environmental studies into existing subject areas and grade levels. They should also help prepare teachers to provide leadership in schools and school corporations in establishing and implementing environmental education programs. Completion of a minor or major in natural resources also fulfills the general studies requirements in science and mathematics. Students who elect a major or minor in natural resources should enroll in NR 101 as the first course. Providing practical or "hands on" experiences is an important part of the educational programs of students enrolled in natural resources at Ball State University. Most of the courses currently offered include a weekly twohour laboratory and field experience. Some courses even include twoor threeday extended field experiences. Students are encouraged to participate in practicum activities or internships extending from one to twelve weeks under the supervision of a faculty member or professionals working in a conservation/environmental field. If planned and approved in advance it is possible for students to earn credit while participating in this type of experience. The Department of Natural Resources is in West Quadrangle, where approximately 14,000 square feet of space is used for classrooms, laboratoryclassrooms, facultystudent research labs, natural resources student reading room, faculty offices, and rooms for secretarial and other supporting services. Additional educational experiences are provided by field trips. The department uses the services of resource people in the community and state to enhance the educational experience of students enrolled in natural resources classes. These include representatives of industry, local governmental units, Indiana Department of Natural Resources, Indiana State Board of Health, U.S. Soil Conservation Service, Cooperative Extension Service, and faculty from public schools and other colleges and universities. Examples of employment obtained by previous natural resources graduates include Soil Conservation Service, Indiana State Parks, city and county park boards, engineering consulting firms, Division of Reservoirs, Stream Pollution Control Division and Air Pollution Control Division of the Indiana State Board of Health, city and county health departments, Bureau of Land Management, industry, commercial shooting preserves, private recreation enterprises, Division of Water Quality Control, Planning Commissions, and U.S. Forest Service. The student will enroll in the Professional Arts curriculum with a departmental major in natural resources. Inquiries are welcomed at the office of the Department of Natural Resources in room 110 of West Quadrangle. Students are encouraged to consult with a departmental adviser concerning professional opportunities in natural resources and the various options available. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 68-71) and by the concentration areas listed below. title: Introduction to Natural Resources
description: The role of natural resources and their relationship to man's social and economic welfare; population growth and its impact upon resource use. The nature and interrelationships of resources with emphasis on the multipleuse concept of resource management. Laboratory and field work included.

title: Conservation for Teachers
description: The role and importance of natural resources and conservation in our daily life. Conservation practices needed to successfully manage natural resources; conservation and natural resources information needed by the elementary school student. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 101.

title: Contemporary Environmental Problems
description: The role of science in solving environmental problems with special emphasis upon the contributions people can make in achieving a quality environment through education. Current environmental problems and possible scientific and alternate technological solutions.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of United States resource use by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource use has shaped society. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 204.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to man. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Includes laboratory and field work.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Includes laboratory and field work.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 4 hours of credit in natural resources, preferably NR 101 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 311.

title: Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Food Production
description: The role of natural resources in producing food for people and the agronomic and animal science practices necessary to provide food for a growing world population. Emphasis on the management talents needed to grow food successfully. Two weekend field trips.

title: Resources for Self-Reliant Living
description: Considers the environmental impact of hard and soft technologies. Focuses on devising a survival strategy based on selfreliant concepts in housing, waste material, water use, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation, and the role of regulatory agencies. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 211; CHEM 111 or equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: The basic relationship between soil nutrients and plant growth with emphasis on the factors affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Includes basic soil testing. Prerequisite: NR 221; CHEM 111 or equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Includes soil genesis, morphology, classification, and survey. Stresses the relationship between soils information and the land use decisionmaking process with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Conservation
description: Distribution, use, and management of the natural resources with emphasis on the United States. Natural resources, including minerals, air, soils, water, plants, animals, and man. Includes laboratory and field work. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 325, GEOG 325, or NR 101.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Stresses principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts. Studies management systems and individual practices with special emphasis on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mineral Resources
description: The relationship of minerals to renewable resources including the role of mineral fuels as a source of energy for the human ecosystem; distribution, production, and use of world mineral resources with emphasis on conservation principles, practices, and techniques. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Energy Resources
description: Appraisal of the natural resource base for energy resources and analysis of the environmental impact of the development of these energy resources. Consideration of fossil fuels as well as solar, wind, and other alternatives; energy resource policy; and research and energy conservation.

title: Air Resources
description: Significance of the atmosphere as a resource; important meteorological parameters in air resources and management; economic, sociological, technical, political, and biological aspects of air pollution; special emphasis on basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Ambient Air Quality Sampling and Monitoring
description: Theory and practice of sampling, analysis, and monitoring the ambient air environment. Major gaseous and particulate air pollutants are emphasized. Prerequisite: CHEM 112 or 114, NR 341, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Effects of Ambient Air Pollution
description: Physical, chemical, and biological effects resulting from ambient air contamination. Major emphasis on the atmosphere, materials, vegetation, domestic animals, and man. Prerequisite: BIO 111, NR 341 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Turfgrass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. Identification of grass and weed species.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. Emphasizes multipleuse concepts of management to meet outdoor recreation demands. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Introductory Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles as applied to the management of natural resources and related environmental problems. Prerequisite: NR 211, 221; GEOL 101; MATH 110; PHYCS 110 or 300; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures. Prerequisite: NR 211; MATH 110 or equivalent; one college course in chemistry; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Solid Waste Management
description: Solid waste management with emphasis on delineation of the problem, disposal methods and techniques, recycling, and management of disposal systems. Stresses the relationship between solid waste disposal and other resources. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students; others with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned,

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the elementary education curriculum. Reviews sources helpful in teaching conservation like resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 101, 105, BIO 102, GE OG 111, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Methods and Materials: Environmental Conservation in the Secondary School
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating environmental conservation into the secondary school curriculum. Reviews sources helpful in teaching environmental conservation like resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources appropriate to environmental conservation. Requires laboratory and field work. Prerequisite NR 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Science -oriented classroom management techniques; introductory involvement in the teaching of science; evaluation of instructional activities; rationale for including environmental science in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. May require up to five hours of experience in public schools. Prerequisite or parallel: NR 395 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in SCI 399.

title: Natural Resources, Environmental Agencies, and Organizations
description: Development, organizational structure, responsibilities, activities, and contributions of selected natural resources, agencies, and environmental organizations in managing natural resources. Formulation, implementation, and evaluation of natural resource policies and programs. Discussion of career opportunities.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area

description: Introduction to strategies used in environmental planning and resource management in contemporary society. Stresses use of data analysis and its role in the decisionmaking process by conceptually centering on natural and manmade systems. May require/field trips. title: Research Methodologies in Natural Resources
description: Development of concepts and skills needed for undergraduate or graduate research or for researchoriented professions in natural resources. Introduction to research study, designs, data gathering techniques, data analysis, and projects planning. Special emphasis on interpreting relevant research in scientific journals.

description: Formal reports and discussion of selected natural resource topics, current events, and special articles in natural resourcerelated professional and scientific journals. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may

title: Air Quality Management
description: Principles of air quality management with emphasis on control programs, regulatory strategies, and control technology. Prerequisite: NR 341, 343, 345 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics offish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered Spring Quarter of evennumbered years. Prerequisite: NR 211, BIO 480, and ZOOL 444, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and use of natural resources for outdoor recreation. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to implement outdoor recreation plans to provide quality outdoor recreation experiences. description: Concerned with defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis on field work and creative presentation of concepts. Prerequisite: NR 101, 211, 221; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

description: Develops skills and techniques relative to the sound organization and management of interpretive programs, including sites and facilities. Emphasis on planning procedures and field study of existing programs. Prerequisite: NR 101, 211, 221; GEOL 101; BIO 313.

title: Resident Environmental Education
description: Philosophy and techniques of resident environmental education and an analysis of exemplary programs. description: The con tributions of natural resource managers to individuals, schools, service clubs, agencies, gov- - ernmental units, and other organizations. description: Supervised practical professional experience relating theory and practice by combining instruction and work activities in natural resources, including conservation education, outdoor education, or environmental education. Department of Philosophy Annis, Chairperson; Andry, Barker, Foster, Mitchell, Mueller, Robertson Philosophy as an Academic Discipline Philosophy is the attempt to arrive at reasoned answers to important questions that fall outside the scope of any particular science, either because they are normative, or especially general, or more fundamental than the questions the sciences raise. The major branches of philosophy are 1. Logic—the study of techniques of critical reasoning. This is a primary tool for resolving philosophical issues. 2. Metaphysics—examines questions concerning the ultimate nature of reality—for example, Is there a Supreme Being? Are all our actions casually determined? Do machines think? etc. 3. Epistemology—deals with the theory of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism. 4. Ethics—the study of such problems as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as contemporary moral problems including abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, and famine relief. Other important subjects in philosophy are the history of philosophy, social philosophy, existentialism, and oriental philosophy. Examining a philosophical question involves the clarification of basic concepts in order to improve one's understanding of the issues, as well as a critical evaluation of the arguments given to support different positions. By critically evaluating basic philosophical questions, students improve their critical thinking ability as well as their communication skills. They learn how to evaluate an argument and how to express an issue clearly. Students desiring a professional career in philosophy generally consider teaching at the college or university level. A number teach at junior colleges, and some high schools are now introducing courses in philosophy. Philosophy is an excellent major or minor for students preparing for vocations requiring a liberal education and skills in critical thinking, conceptual analysis, problem solving, and communication. Thus it is appropriate preparation for careers in law, public service, governmental agencies, and writing, as well as any religionoriented vocation. Students preparing for teaching careers will be expected to deal with religious ideas, values, institutions, and practices in their teaching. Courses in religious subject matter are being expanded in public schools. A small but increasing number of students come to Ball State to prepare for theological studies. Others decide to pursue a life of religious service after entering Ball State. To meet the increasing demands of these situations, Ball State provides students with the opportunity to pursue religious studies. Any student may register in courses designed for all four years of university life. The courses are classified under the general headings of cultural settings of religion, biblical studies, church history, and religions of the world. Any course in religious studies counts for credit as a general elective in any program of studies within the university, as a humanities elective for general studies, or toward a departmental major or minor in religious studies when the student successfully completes the requirements in this area. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: An introduction to such important philosophical problems as the existence of God, whether ethical values are subjective, and the extent of our freedom. These topics and others may be approached by examining the ideas of great philosophers or current thinkers.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of deduction.

title: Inductive Logic
description: An introduction to the principles and problems of inductive reason ing.

title: Ethics
description: A discussion of some of the central problems in ethics such as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as a discussion of current moral issues.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of basic social concepts such as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of normative issues such as how liberty should be distributed and how justice can be maximized.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Critical analysis of selected topics such as the nature and existence of God, the problem of evil, the justification of religious belief, and the significance of religious experience.

title: Introduction to Existentialism
description: A discussion of major existentialists, including Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Sartre, and important themes in existentialism such as alienation, subjectivism, the meaning of life, and freedom. Not open to the student who has credit in PHIL 421.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the rise of philosophy in Greece about 600 B.C. to the fall of Rome. Emphasis on these theories in their relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: History of Medieval Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the fall of Rome to the Renaissance. The inheritance of medieval Europe from the Graeco-Romanearly Christian world and the creative role played by medieval philosophy in the formation of the Western tradition especially after the rediscovery of Aristotle.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Emphasis on these theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics may include the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading philosophers and movements in the twentieth century. May concentrate on selected philosophers such as Russell, Wittgenstein, and Husserl, or may concentrate on contemporary treatments of selected philosophical problems.

title: Aesthetics
description: Exploration of philosophical views on the nature, interpretation, and criticism of art. Readings and discussion may range from classical to contemporary thinkers and issues.

title: Introduction to Legal Philosophy
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, and justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of basic concepts such as action, intention, causation, and responsibility.

title: Philosophy of Language
description: Study of philosophical theories of language and the role of language in the treatment of philosophical problems. Issues investigated may include views of truth, linguistic paradoxes, and other problems related to language, its interpretation, and its structure.

title: Current Issues in Philosophy
description: Selected current and important issues in philosophy. Topics may include social and ethical problems, recent work on traditional philosophical problems, and other issues of concern.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: An examination of central philosophical problems in the sciences such as the nature of scientific explanation and the testing of hypotheses; a discussion of ethical issues arising from science, for example, the use of human subjects and prolonging life.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Prerequisite: students in the Honors College or permission of the department chairperson. A total of4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: An opportunity for superior students to do guided reading and investigation in branches of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Metaphysics
description: A study of the principal problems of metaphysics including the nature of reality, the relation of mind and body, and the issue of freedom and determinism.

title: Introduction to Theory of Knowledge
description: A critical discussion of leading theories and problems of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge and rational belief, the different kinds of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism.

title: Oriental Philosophy
description: Philosophical exploration of Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, and Confucianism.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory and Problems
description: A critical examination of recent ethical theories and their application to contemporary problems.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: Traditional religious groups in the United States with attention to developments, institutions, and distinctive practices and beliefs. The groups and the subjects treated will be adjusted to the interests of the students .

title: Religions of the World
description: An introductory survey of the major religions of the world (Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Islam, Christianity and others), emphasizing how people live out their faiths in their daily lives.

title: New Religious Movements
description: A study of recent religious developments in the United States, both inside and outside the Judeo-Christian tradition, such as Children of God, I Am, Eckankar, Scientology, TM, Western Zen, and others; what these groups mean to their followers and to America.

title: Old Testament
description: Our Hebrew-Judaic religious heritage as reflected in various personalities and their religious expressions as found in the literature of the Old Testament.

title: New Testament
description: Our early Christian heritage in relation to its Jewish-Greek background as reflected by various personalities in the literature of the New Testament.

title: Early Christian Thought
description: The development of Christian thought in relation to its various ethnic backgrounds beginning with Old Catholicism, through the Gnostic crisis, Constantine, and the church councils.

title: Christian Ethics
description: Reflection upon life and morality from the point of view of Christian faith and fundamental Christian convictions. Discussion of contemporary ethical issues in the light of important theological presuppositions; good and evil, divine law, sin and redemption, freedom, conscience, love.

title: Religion in a Scientific World
description: A study of the dialogue between religion and science; their views of the world, differences and similarities; interpretations leading to conflict and those opening up possibilities for reconciliation. Topics include technology, medicine, creation/ evolution, environment, computer science, and others.

title: Religions of the Ancient Near East
description: The religious movements of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, and Persia as they relate to the development of Judaism and the rise of Christianity.

title: Religions of India
description: The religious heritage of India: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism; the ways of life they advocate, their scriptures, developments of their theologies.

title: Religions of China and Japan
description: Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, Maoism, Shintoism. Origin and developments; literature; rites and rituals.

title: Principles of Theology
description: A study of basic theological principles (God, the person and work of Jesus Christ, human being, the church, others) from both traditional and contemporary points of view (Protestant, Roman Catholic, and Jewish, liberation theology, black theology, feminist theology, others).

title: Paul and His Influence on Early Christianity
description: Paul and his contributions to early Christianity as they relate to his letters and the Acts of the Apostles in the context of firstcentury Christianity (with attention also to his influence on later Western Christianity).

title: Jesus and the Gospel Tradition
description: Jesus and the traditions that developed about him among the firstand early secondcentury Christians as reflected by the four evangelists in their Gospels.

title: Problems in Early Christianity
description: Problems the earliest Christians faced—birthplace of Jesus, birth year, virgin birth, genealogy, miracles, Last Supper, betrayal, arrest, trial, Crucifixion, burial, Resurrection, Christophanies, and others. The choice of topics is determined by the interests of the students.

title: Methods in the Study of Religion
description: An exploration of the many ways to approach the study of religion, its origins, nature, and functions in human society.

title: Comparative Religion
description: An indepth investigation, analysis, and comparison of selected major religious traditions, with attention to their underlying structures. Particular attention is given to the comparison of Eastern and Western traditions.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: To provide superior students with an opportunity for guided investigation in areas of religion not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson and instructor. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Special Topics in Religion
description: Indepth focus on a selected issue of central importance. Topics vary from quarter to quarter, but include such subjects as American Indian religions, women and religion, and the Pentecostal and charismatic movements. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. PRE-ENGINEERING MAJOR This departmental major is intended for students interested in preparing for admission to a school of engineering. Specifically, the program is offered in cooperation with the Purdue University School of Engineering so that courses taken at Ball State in the preengineering curriculum parallel courses the student would take at Purdue during the first several years of study. Although the courses taken at Ball State in the preengineering curriculum are similar or identical to those taken by students at many institutions offering engineering programs, the School of Engineering at Purdue is the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program in which the student attends Ball State for three years then transfers to Purdue to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of such a program the student is eligible to receive a bachelor's degree from Ball State and the engineering degree from Purdue. It is possible to complete the degree requirements for both institutions in less than five years by attending summer sessions. The student may, of course, elect to transfer to Purdue or some other engineering school before completing the full preengineering course of study at Ball State. If so, the student will be eligible to receive only the degree at the institution to which he or she transfers. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not mean automatic admission to the Purdue University School of Engineering. The student must apply to Purdue for admission when he or she wants to transfer. The student should have completed at least a full year of physics (PHYCS 120, 122, 124) and a year of calculus before transferring. Three options within the preengineering major are available. The options for students interested in chemical or metallurgical engineering are specifically listed. For other kinds of engineering such as electrical, mechanical, civil, etc. , the student should elect the General Engineering option. title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting energy forms such as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physical Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles and concepts of the laws of nature involving mechanical, heat, light, electrical, nuclear, and chemical energy and the conservation laws associated with these forms of energy. Emphasis on applications appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Preparation of Physical Science Teaching Materials
description: Selected topics in physical science stressing the construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Prerequisite: PHYCS 101 or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students in the teacher education curriculum.

title: Physics and Sports
description: A descriptive introduction to basic physical principles and laws within a framework of applications to athletic activities and sports. Particularly suited to the student with areas or special interest in physical education. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110, 120, or 130.

title: Basic Physics for the Allied Health Sciences
description: A condensed study of basic physics with special emphasis on principles and applications pertinent to the health sciences. Three lectures and one twohour laboratoryrecitation weekly. Prerequisite: one year high school algebra and one year high school geometry or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students on the allied health sciences program in the areas of respiratory therapy, radiologic technology, nuclear therapy, and ultrasound technology or permission of the department chairperson.

title: General Physics 1
description: Studies the laws of mechanics including kinematics, dynamics, work and energy relationships, torque, rotational energy, angular momentum, stress and strain, elastic moduli, and introductory topics in fluid statics and dynamics. Prerequisite:

title: General Physics 2
description: The study of static and current electricity including Ohm's law, DC and AC circuit concepts, electric and magnetic field basics, and introductory concepts in modern physics (relativity, atomic and nuclear physics). Prerequisite: PHYCS 110.

title: General Physics 3
description: A study of the laws of thermal physics including calorimetry, heat transfer, and introductory thermodynamics concepts. title: Orientation Seminar for Pre -engineering and Beginning Physics Students
description: An overview of the fields of physics and engineering that will aid science students in effectively planning their college curriculum. Students will be introduced to career scientists and the jobs performed by persons in these professions. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 120.

title: General Physics 1
description: A first course in calculusbased physics for students with areas in preengineering, the physical sciences, or mathematics. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 161 or 170.

title: General Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 120. Topics include Coulomb's Law and the electric field, Gauss's Law, DC circuits and instruments, the magnetic field, Ampere's Law, Faraday's Law, the magnetic properties of matter, the integral form of Maxwell's equation, alternatingcurrent circuits, impedance, and electromagnetic waves.
