title: Survey of Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to speech pathology and audiology with a survey of speech and hearing disorders in relation to etiology, incidence, and management.

title: Clinical Phonetics
description: Study of speech sounds as applied to communication disorders. Transcription practice of normal and abnormal speech and the informational, perceptual aspects of phonetics. Relationship and application of distinctive features and phonological analysis to speech remediation. Open only to SPAA majors and minors.

title: Acoustics of Speech
description: An introductory study of the physical elements of sound, particularly as they apply to the communication process. Prerequisite: SPAA 201.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Vocal Mechanism
description: Study of the anatomy and physiology of the parts of the body involved in speech production, including respiratory, phonatory, articulatoryresonance, and neurological mechanisms. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 261.

title: Language Development
description: Development of the phonology, grammar, content, and function of language in children together with a review of environmental and personal conditions acting to influence that development.

title: Introduction to Research in Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Develops the student's capabilities to read and conduct research. Includes research writing style, experimental design, instrumentation, and basic statistics. Emphasis on research methods and instrumentation most commonly used in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Articulation Disorders
description: Designed to prepare students to diagnose and treat articulatory speech disorders, particularly in younger children. Includes laboratory observation in the treatment of defective speech. Prerequisite: SPAA 201, 260, 261. Open only to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course to assist the beginning clinician in developing an understanding of clinical competency; improves phonetic testing; increases general knowledge of speech problems; develops ability to understand diagnostic principles, procedures, and learning theory; observes and evaluates therapy; and permits selfevaluation. Prerequisite: SPAA 201, 410.

title: Stuttering 1: Research and Theory
description: An introduction to the disorder of stuttering with attention directed to its symptoms and development. Reviews the research and theoretical formulations regarding stuttering. Prerequisite: SPAA 410.

title: Organic Speech and Language Disorders
description: An introductory study of neurology and anatomy of the brain and speech and language disorders resulting from brain damage such as cerebral palsy and aphasia. Other physical problems such as cleft palate and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 261, 410.

title: Speech Pathology and Audiology Practicum
description: The student performs observation and preprofessional participation with clients with various speech, language, and hearing disorders. A total of 8 hours of credit must be earned; not more than 2 hours of credit may be earned in any one term or quarter. Prerequisite: SPAA 410 and 411, or equivalent.

title: Hearing: Anatomy, Physiology, and Disorders
description: Study of the anatomy and physiology of the hearing mechanisms and the nature, causes, treatment, and effects of hearing disorders. Audiogram interpretation. Prerequisite: SPAA 260, 261, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Hearing: Assessment and Diagnostics
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in the use of various types of audiometers. Interpretation of test results for the purpose of reeducation and the necessary followup measures in an educational hearing program. Prerequisite: SPAA 261 or SPCED 261, SPAA 440 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 442.

title: Aural Rehabilitation
description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for teaching lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite:

title: Directed Study in Speech Pathology or Audiology
description: The student with a major or minor in speech pathology and audiology pursues a specific subject of study in depth in consultation with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned: Telecommunications 335 Department of Telecommunications Kurtz, Chairperson; Alexander, DeVoe, Gehring, Gemignani, Richardson, Smith, Wible The broadcast industries and the motion picture industries provide extremely democratic channels of information, entertainment, and communication. Ball State University has long recognized the appeal that these media have for the mass audience, and the important part media play in our everyday lives. For these reasons, Ball State University and the Department of Telecommunications provide a carefully selected sequence of courses that emphasize the practical applications of these media. To meet today's demands, the department offers both graduate and undergraduate departmental majors and minors in these fields, as well as a teaching minor. The Ball State University program in radio, television, and motion pictures is intended for people who are serious about career opportunities in these fastgrowing industries. The excellent selection of courses in the curriculum includes programs for those who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for instruction with the educational aspects of the electronic media in the classroom, or in school administration systems that employ media. Audience research, performance, production, programming, news, media sales, and administrative studies of the electronic and motion picture media are analyzed in the various courses. Since many positions in the broadcast and motion picture industries require a creative effort and a good understanding of teamwork, these attributes are emphasized as the student also discovers the elements of leadership and responsibility. Students working in the department are encouraged to learn as much as possible about the function and operation of the sophisticated radio, television, and motion picture equipment through a handson approach. Training with professional equipment and the experience gained through the knowledge of operation, coupled with classroom and smallgroup discussion, analyses, and direct study and observation of the broadcast and motion picture industries enable the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. The facilities of the university radio station, WBST-FM, and the closedcircuit television production facility provide additional practical experiences for the students in the training program. Such work experiences also allow the student to build a personal résumé that frequently assists in later job applications . Many factors influence the future employment of persons seeking careers in these industries. Therefore, it is not possible to guarantee employment, although the department's record of those gainfully employed after graduation in broadcasting and motion pictures is excellent. Simultaneously, every effort is made to inform the student of the stringent and competitive labor marketplaces in both the broadcast and motionpicture industries. While the serious student is developing the broadbased foundations needed for work in the industries, learning about the operation of equipment, and coming face to face with a faculty experienced in both academics and the professional work world, the keen student discovers how to cope with the problems to be met in the industry marketplace, as well as the steps to be taken in preparation for the future. The department's builtin workforce programs and summer internships allow each student selected to gain an insight into actual work in his or her chosen career. Interns have been placed in markets in Indiana, Kentucky, Ohio, and Illinois. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 68-71) and by the concentration areas listed below. title: Developments in Telecommunications
description: An overview of the development of the telecommunications industry. Emphasis on the interrelatedness of historical and contemporary forces in a social setting. Development of cable television, satellite communication, videocassettes, and videodiscs, as well as radio and television. Prerequisite: sophomore standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Production/Performance in Telecommunications
description: Introduces the production equipment used in radio, television, and film courses. Emphasizes skills students need to learn the use of equipment they will operate in future courses. Students also learn fundamental performance techniques. Prerequisite: sophomore standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Writing for Telecommunications
description: Designed to give students understanding of styles and techniques used in writing for telecommunications. Students write extensively, producing scripts for news, commercials, and productions in all media. Prerequisite: TCOM 200 and 201, 8 hours of credit in ENG 102, 103, or 104, and a satisfactory score on the typing proficiency examination.

title: Law of Telecommunications
description: Familiarizes students with the legal foundation of telecommunications. Legal history of telecommunications from 1910 to the present. Major actions by the Congress and pertinent actions by the state and federal court systems, including the U. S. Supreme Court. Emphasis onthe legal issues that most affect daily system operation. Prerequisite: TCOM 200 and 201 .

title: Programs and Audiences
description: Appreciation of the complexity of programming decision making by investigating programming concepts, strategies, and techniques to understand better the objectives of presentday programming at national and local levels. Understanding existing methods of audience research and designing audience research studies. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 201, and 240.

title: Program Analysis and Media Criticism
description: Stimulates understanding of and sensitivity to broadcasting production techniques. Sharpens student's desire to analyze logically and state creatively evaluations of contemporary practices in electronic communication. Promotes recognition and appreciation of constructive and creative critical writing. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: Radio and Television Announcing
description: Practical training in studio and control room procedures. Interpretive training in the delivery and performance of radio and television copy, including news, scripts, continuity, and commercials. Special attention given to the preparation of an audition tape. Prerequisite: TCOM 201.

title: Audio Production
description: A practical skillsoriented course in audio production. Emphasizes production for radio broadcasting, but examines all uses of audio in the media. Students learn skills and techniques of audio production in practical applications to media production situations. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: Video Production
description: A skillsoriented course in the theory and practice of television production. Students learn techniques necessary for camera operation, studio set up, lighting, and control room operations. A number of miniproductions give students experience in the basic television programs and formats. Prerequisite: TCOM 210. Telecommunications 337

title: News Writing
description: Practical experience in writing news copy for radio and television. Students may have the opportunity to gain this experience through an arrangement with BSU radio station WBST. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: News Performance
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering and reporting broadcast news. Practical experience in the use of audio tape recorders, telephone recording, electronic news gathering (ENG) equipment, and other equipment found in the radio and television newsroom. Newswritingreporting assignments may be performed in conjunction with BSU radio station WBST and BSU television station WIPB. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: Electronic News Gathering
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering and reporting news with ENG equipment. Practical experience in the techniques of recording and editing with ENG equipment. Prerequisite: TCOM 342.

title: Advertising, Sales, and Promotion for Radio
description: Functions of advertising, sales, and promotion unique to radio; develops skills in using available tools and techniques in creating effective advertising campaigns. Use of Radio Advertising Bureau and Broadcast Promotion Association material. Emphasis on retail advertising and sales. Prerequisite: TCOM 300.

title: Advertising, Sales, and Promotion for Television
description: Functions of advertising, sales, and promotion unique to television; develops skills in using available tools and techniques for creating effective advertising campaigns. Use of Television Bureau of Advertising and Broadcast Promotion Association material. Application of rating services to campaigns. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 201, 240, and 300.

title: Promotion in Telecommunications
description: Developing promotional concepts and methodologies available for carrying out strategies and campaigns, identifying an image, and planning image campaigns. Coordinating and using various media. Prerequisite: TCOM 300.

title: World Film History 1
description: History of world cinema from its beginning until World War II. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as key movements in other national cinemas before 1941, such as German Expressionism and the Soviet Montage School. Prerequisite: TCOM 305.

title: World Film History 2
description: Continuation of TCOM 380, from World War II until the present. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as post-1945 national cinema movements, such as Italian Neorealism and the French New Wave. Prerequisite: TCOM 380

title: Film Genres
description: Broad genres, or forms, of film expression identifiable with a specific tradition, such as westerns, screwball comedies, gangster films, musicals, and so on. Offered twice each academic year, with the focus genre changing each time. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Film Censorship
description: Moral measurements and restraints affecting the film industry almost since its inception. A chronology of events influencing both the direction and content of motion pictures. Examines governmental, legal, church, and community restraints. Prerequisite: TCOM 201.

title: Honors Colloquium in Telecommunications
description: Exploration of selected issues in telecommunications, with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Open only to honors students. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Film Production 1
description: A basic introduction to super-8 film production, as well as the theory behind the technique. Prerequisite: TCOM 305.

title: Film Production 2
description: A continuation ofTCOM 391. Prerequisite: TCOM 391.

title: Social Responsibility in Telecommunications
description: Political, economic, social, and governmental elements that interact with telecommunications. Major contemporary issues in broadcasting and other electronic media. Ethics involved in decision making as well as definition of standards and responsibilities involved in electronic communication. Prerequisite: senior standing; TCOM 300 and 305.

title: Directing and Producing
description: Duties and responsibilities of the director and the producer of programs. Examines the artistic and practical decisions made in producing a finished product from the script. Students assist in departmental productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 315 and 316.

title: Public Affairs Programming
description: Examines and discusses the role of the professional broadcaster in public affairs programming: news, editorials, political events, documentaries, and indepth reports. Students make practical application of class content in departmental productions on WBST and on television. Prerequisite: TCOM 300.

title: Advanced Audio-Video Production
description: Follows TCOM 315, 316, and 410. Students make practical application of theory and techniques learned in the production of fulllength programs in radio and television. Students are assigned to work the production of individual programs or series on WBST or university television, or individual creative projects. Prerequisite: TCOM 410.

title: Management of Telecommunications
description: Acquaints students with the problems and responsibilities of management in the telecommunications industry. Guest lecturers, class discussions, and management roleplaying familiarize students with administrative practices in the industry. Prerequisite: senior standing; TCOM 360 and 361.

title: Non-Broadcast Television Operations
description: An examination of the special requirement s of busines, industrial, and medical uses of television for nonbroadcast purposes, e.g., instruction, information, promotion, public relations. Special emphasis on management and budgeting. Prerequisite: TCOM 200,201, and 210. Prerequisite or parallel: TCOM 316.

title: Non-Broadcast Television Production
description: Video production that meets special requirements of business, industry, and medicine. Planning, identifying needs, executing and evaluating productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 316,475.

title: Independent Study
description: A special service course. Students enroll with the intent of special study or research on some specific aspect of telecommunications or with the objective of producing a specific program or production. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson, after written submission and approval of the topic of study. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term. May be repeated only once.

title: Internship in Telecommunications
description: Provides opportunity for the student to gain practical onthejob experience with a radio or television station or a company in allied field. Attempt will be made to place the student in a position of interest to him or her. Prerequisite: junior standing; permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Documentary Film
description: A survey introduction to various techniques, purposes, devices, functions, definitions, qualities, material use, development, and critical approaches found in the documentaries studied. Students study the documentary in its many forms: historical, commercial, informational, educational, and propaganda. Prerequisite : TCOM 380 and 381.

title: Seminar in Film and Culture
description: A close examination of the interaction between film and culture at different times and places in world history, for example, the chaos of Germany's Weimar Republic in the 1920s or depression America in the 1930s. May be team taught with faculty from foreign languages, art, and history. Prerequisite: TCOM 380 and 381.

title: Seminar in Film Theory
description: An analysis of the key theorists in the history of world cinema, as well as some influential critics. Prerequisite: TCOM 380 and 381.

title: Research in Telecommunications
description: Acquaints students with principles and methods of scholarly research; illustrates applications of research within electronic communication, both for scholarly investigation and for use in support of the functions of broadcasting. Provides principles and practice in writing about results of research. Prerequisite: senior standing; TCOM 200 and 201. Teachers College Dean, Theodore Kowalski Acting Associate Dean, Roy Weaver Assistant Dean, Charles D. Shipman The Teachers College has major responsibility for teacher education in the university. Contributions of departments in other colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by directors of Elementary and Secondary Teacher Education, who are responsible to the dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by the Teacher Preparation Council, which represents the university as a whole. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers and teacher educators in early childhood education, kindergartenprimary education, and elementary education, with programs at all degree levels. The Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education provides the professional education for junior high/middle and secondary school teachers with the exception of special methods. Graduate programs in these areas as well as in higher education and educational foundations are also offered by this department. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate and graduate education programs for teachers of the mentally retarded, the hearing impaired, the emotionally disturbed, the physically handicapped, the neurologically impaired/learning disabled, and the multiply handicapped. The Center for Lifelong Education offers programs in curriculum, adult education, and community education. The Burris Laboratory School is a center for demonstration, participation, and research in teacher education, as well as for program development and dissemination in respect to elementary, junior high/middle, and secondary schools. The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers service courses in school administration and programs at master's, specialist, and doctoral levels for students preparing for educational management and for administrative, supervisory, and collegiate positions in its subjects of expertise. Two departments of the Teachers College serve students in psychology. The Department of Educational Psychology offers undergraduate and graduate programs in applications of psychology to teacher education and in educational psychometry, school psychology, human development, measurement, and research. It also provides service courses as needed for related programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services offers courses and programs at all graduate levels in its principal areas of specialization for people in educational and other positions. It also offers programs in social psychology. Doctoral programs are offered by the Center for Lifelong Education and the departments of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services, Educational Administration and Supervision, Educational Psychology, Elementary Education (including early childhood education and reading), and Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education. Departments of the Teachers College, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public education and psychology, for production and dissemination of research, for innovation in instructional practices, for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education, and for direct human services programs. Courses included in the general field of education serve students in a wide variety of programs and are not appropriately assignable to a single department. EDUCATION: GENERAL (EDGEN)

title: All -Grade Program Development
description: Provides students seeking allgrade licensure with knowledge of the K-12 school curriculum and organization needed by teachers of special areas in a total school system. Parallel: EDSEC 299. Prerequisite: EDPSY 251 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290.

title: Urban Education: Problems and Prospects
description: Explores many issues facing public education in urban areas, such as equal opportunity, federal and state aid, accountability, sociological and cultural factors, teacher unionization, busing, and community control.

title: Applied Research Techniques in Education
description: Acquaints students with data collection and participation in educational research. Emphasizes small group work as part of specific teacher education faculty research projects. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Bilingual-Bicultural Education
description: A survey of linguistic, cognitive, and cultural characteristics of bilingualism with emphasis on the effects these languagerelated features have on bilingual/bicultural education in the United States. Emphasizes program design, model programs in operation, and legislative mandates. Parallel: EDGEN 371.

title: Bilingual/Bicultural Materials and Methods
description: Considers the educational needs of bilingual students with specific regard to the evaluation of existing materials, the development of materials, and appropriate bilingual classroom methodology. Parallel: EDGEN 370.

title: Honors Colloquium in Education
description: The critical analysis and evaluation of selected controversial issues in American education. Restricted to honors students.

title: Contributions of Social and Cultural Minorities to American Education
description: Analysis of lifestyles of different cultural groups in terms of strengths developed by children that could be taken advantage of in school and other institutions. Flexible attitudes, bilingual/biculturalism, creativity, improvisation, adjustments, and family structures will be emphasized in terms of strengths rather than weaknesses.

title: In-Service Teacher Education
description: A field course designed to provide groups of classroom teachers in a local school system an opportunity to identify and work on problems within their teaching situations. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. All teaching assignments as professional teachers in the state of Indiana require a teaching license based upon the recommendation of the teacher preparation institution. All such applications involving Ball State University undergraduate teacher education programs and any letters verifying qualification for teacher licensing based upon these programs require the signature of the teacher certification adviser in the Office of Advising and Scheduling. Professional Laboratory Experiences Swafford, Director The Office of Professional Laboratory .Experiences coordinates all laboratory experiences for professional education programs in which educational settings are used. In addition to EDEL 360, Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School; EDJHM 312, Teaching in Junior High/Middle Schools; EDSEC 299, Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary School; and the student teaching programs, the office also administers requests for observations, individual research projects and studies involving professional laboratory experiences, and tutoring opportunities. Burris Laboratory School is a department in the Teachers College of Ball State University and provides an educational program from kindergarten through grade twelve. Observations, individual studies, tutoring, testing, and similar projects can be arranged directly through the office of the principal. The Office of Professional Laboratory Experiences provides assistance in placing students for such activities in all other educational settings for laboratory or field experiences in conjunction with course work or individual selfenhancement for development of teaching skills. To be accepted into the teacher education curriculum and to remain in the program, students must meet the established criteria of various areas that monitor their progress, such as the departments that offer the teaching programs, the Speech and Hearing Clinic, and the Office of Student Affairs. For detailed descriptions of the selection and retention standards for the teaching curricula, see Department of Elementary Education, p. 351; Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education, p. 360; and Department of Special Education, p. 373. Students whose approval has been denied or withdrawn may consult the Office of the Associate Provost regarding the establishment of a teacher education review committee. The committee is chaired by the appropriate director of Elementary, Secondary, or Special Education and consists of the director, the associate provost, a representative of the student Professional Laboratory Experiences 345 teaching office, two representatives of the major department, and when appropriate one representative of the minor department. PRE—STUDENT TEACHING PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES The purpose of pre—student teaching professional laboratory experiences is to provide students pursuing the Teacher Education Curriculum with a systematic, planned sequence of experiences in appropriate educational settings. These experiences are designed to make students familiar with principles of classroom management and the teachinglearning process in practical and real school environments, and to induct students into the teaching act. The pre—student teaching laboratory experiences culminate in EDEL 360, EDJHM 312, or EDSEC 299, which requires assignment to classrooms in appropriate educational settings for one quarter to observe, prepare instructional presentations, and undertake other instructional tasks appropriate for students before student teaching. The university provides laboratory settings for EDEL 360, EDJHM 312, and EDSEC 299 in the oncampus Burris Laboratory School, as well as in affiliated public school systems in Muncie City Schools and in other school corporations within commuting distance. Weekly seminars with a college supervisor are an integral part of the laboratory experience for these courses. STUDENT TEACHING Student teaching provides students an opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professionally licensed teachers cooperating with the university in the student teaching program. Application for Student Teaching Students should make application for a student teaching assignment in the Winter Quarter of the year before that in which they expect to do student teaching. Students transferring to Ball State after this date who plan to complete their certification requirements in one year must make application in September. Official notification of the student teaching assignment will be mailed to the student after the final eligibility determination, usually during the quarter before student teaching. Students needing information about their assignments before this notification may inquire at the student teaching office. General Consideration The student must be free of outside commitments that might interfere with fulltime student teaching obligations. This means that students cannot be regularly employed, nor should they carry a heavy load of extracurricular activities. Enrollment for course overload during the quarter is permitted only with approval of the coordinator for student teaching. Requirements for student teaching also include a predetermined number of days in seminars conducted by the university supervisor, at both the beginning and the end of the quarter. Students should be prepared to accept student teaching assignments wherever the university can place them for the best professional experience. Although requests for particular supervising teachers, schools, or school systems are considered, the placement process requires close cooperation with the public school systems, and there are instances when circumstances within the local school system prohibit a specific placement request. Therefore, students should be willing to accept assignments that the university supervisor arranges for them. Student Teaching: Secondary and All-Grade License Student teachers preparing to teach at the secondary school level are required to spend full time for a minimum of nine weeks in student teaching. They must enroll for 10 credit hours in EDSEC 460 (5 credit hours) and EDSEC 462 (5 credit hours). Usually students take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching (4 credit hours), to complete the rest of the quarter. Student Teaching: Junior High/Middle School Standard License Student teachers pursuing the junior high/middle school licensure program are required to spend full time for a minimum of nine weeks in student teaching. They must enroll in EDJHM 466 for a total of 10 credit hours. It is recommended that students take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching, for 4 credit hours to complete the rest of the quarter. Student Teaching: Elementary Standard License Students seeking licensure in elementary education must enroll for 14 credit hours in EDEL 460 (4 credit hours) and EDEL 464 (10 credit hours) and spend full time for the entire quarter in student teaching. Students who wish to take elective credits in student teaching may enroll for 4 credit hours in EDEL 465, Elective Student Teaching, during another quarter. Student Teaching: Early Childhood Standard License Students seeking licensure in early childhood education must enroll in EDEL 466 for 14 credit hours and spend full time for the entire quarter in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten-Primary Standard License Students seeking licensure in kindergartenprimary education must enroll for 14 credit hours in EDEL 467 (7 credit hours) and EDEL 468 (7 credit hours) and spend full time for the entire quarter in student teaching. In addition, students must enroll in a second area of exceptionality for 14 credit hours in either SPCED 490, Teaching the Physically/Multiply Handicapped, or SPCED 492, Teaching the Moderately Mentally Handicapped, Severely/ Profoundly Mentally Handicapped, and Multiply Handicapped, for a second quarter of fulltime student teaching. Students with an allgrade major in special education: hearing impaired will complete SPCED 465 (4 credit hours) and SPCED 466 (10 credit hours) for a total of 14 credit hours for one quarter of fulltime student teaching. Students pursuing a teaching minor or teaching endorsement in the area of special education must complete 14 credit hours of fulltime student teaching in the area of concentration. Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services Hayes, Chairperson; Barke, Beyerl, Cartwright, Daly, Dimick, Donn, Duckworth, Hendrickson, Hutchinson, Krause, Mitchell, Nunnelly, Randolph, White, Zimmerman The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services is one of two psychology departments within the Teachers College. The department offers an undergraduate minor in interpersonal relations. The minor is available for students seeking a combination and integration of didactic and experiential work dealing with basic psychological principles and techniques for understanding and developing interpersonal relationships. Emphasis is placed on understanding oneself and the dynamics of interaction with others. Opportunity is provided for an individual to explore his or her own strengths and weaknesses in interpersonal relationships within groups of varying ages, races, and ethnic backgrounds. The focus is applied and interdisciplinary. The program focuses also on strategies for gaining life satisfaction and meaning. Undergraduate courses are offered to students as electives or as courses applicable toward a certification program as a school counselor. The department offers graduate programs in counseling psychology and counseling and guidance, with emphasis on the interdisciplinary approach and with depth in psychology. Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services 347 Programs are designed for students wishing to qualify for positions as counselors, directors of counseling and guidance programs, and counseloreducators, as well as for those pursuing degrees in counseling psychology. The department also offers courses and programs in social psychology. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 68-71) and by the concentration area listed below. Departmental minor in interpersonal relations, 24 hours From CPSY 130, 220, 230, 400, 405, 432, 490 (4 or 8 hrs.) 24 hrs. Students may take all 24 hours from the Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services or up to 8 hours of directed electives.

title: Career and Life Planning
description: Focuses on helping the individual to make career and life plans. Uses a series of such techniques as role playing, psychodrama, sociodrama, value clarification, and decision making to help students examine interrelated value systems associated with educatio n , work, leisure, and self expression. Not open to juniors and seniors except with permission of the department chairperson.

title: Career and Life Planning for Women
description: Focus on helping the individual student consider the special problems confronting women in making career and life plans. Is also helpful for males associated with women who are in nontraditional roles. Uses a series of such techniques as role playing, group interaction, value clarification, and decisionmaking strategies to help students examine interrelated value systems associated with education, career, family, leisure, and selfexpression.

title: Intrapersonal Relationships
description: An introduction to the examination of one's thoughts and feeling about self and how these internal processes relate to behavior. Particular attention will be given to understanding selflimiting behaviors such as anxiety, shyness, and selfdoubt and potential strategies for change. The course will assist students in understanding how they limit their own accomplishments, thus freeing them for a more successful academic career.

title: Interrelational Aspects of Sexuality
description: Emphasizes the psychological aspects of human sexuality, especially in relation to emotions, attitude, and values. Stresses the psychological importance of responsibility for self in the area of sexuality. Considers the psychological aspects of human sexual development, adjustment, dysfunction, and remediation. Designed to increase the students' understanding and acceptance of their own sexuality and that of others.

title: Effective Interpersonal Relationship Development
description: An introduction to the basic psychological principles and techniques of developing interpersonal relationships. Emphasis on understanding oneself and the dynamics of interaction with others. Opportunity is provided for an individual to explore his/her strengths and weaknesses in interpersonal relationships within groups of varying ages, races, and ethnic backgrounds.

title: Fundamentals of Counseling and Guidance
description: Exploration of the principles, purposes, and nature of counseling and guidance in the public school with emphasis upon ways in which teachers can contribute to and profit from the school's guidance program.

title: Psychological Processes and Techniques of Interviewing
description: Basic psychological principles and techniques of the therapeutic interviewing process. Intended primarily as an exploratory didactic and experiential course for undergraduate students planning to do graduate work in counseling and related areas, or for those in other fields requiring skills in interviewing,

title: Techniques of Crisis Intervention
description: Basic theory, skills, and techniques of emergency psychological intervention and counseling with persons who experience intense situational and emotional distress. Emphasis placed on anxiety reactions, psychology of suicide, suicide prevention, special crisis situations, psychology of referral, community resources, use of listening and responding skills, and techniques of training crisis counselors.

title: Problems in Counseling
description: Intensive study in selected areas of student need and interest within the field of counseling. Opportunity for students to choose particular areas for indepth study under faculty supervision. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Interdisciplinary Issues in Social Psychology and History
description: A unified approach through social psychology and history relating to selected areas of current interest. Deals with contemporary research and publications from both foreign and American cultures. Department of Educational Administration and Supervision Riegle, Chairperson; Ballou, Drake, Linson, Lyon, Marconnit, Nesper, Patton, Pole, Shipman, Swafford, Wagner The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers courses and programs designed to serve the needs of elementary and secondary schools and higher education. Present programs are designed to prepare competent persons for such central office administrative and supervisory positions in public schools as those of superintendent, elementary principal, junior high/middle school principal, secondary principal, business manager, director of buildings and grounds, personnel director, and information officer. Other programs prepare specialized personnel for administrative and supervisory responsibilities in fields of education, administrative positions in junior colleges and other collegiate institutions, and administrative positions in educational programs in private industries and foundations. title: Legal Aspects of Education for Future Teachers
description: Special attention will focus on legal foundations of education, on rights and responsibilities of teachers (employment, tenure, fringe benefits, liability, and negotiations), and on rights and responsibilities of students (attendance, discipline, and due process). Department of Educational Psychology Fischer, Chairperson; Annis, Bennett, Church, Gupta, Harshbarger, Henriksen, Hunt, Irving, Joy, Klem, Kuo, McKee, Miller, Paschal, Richmond, Schurr, Sparzo, Taylor, Treloar, Trent, Van Every-Filson, Wenck Educational psychology is a social science concerned with the development of individuals. It includes the study of human development, learning, adjustment, measurement, research, and statistics as these relate to the understanding of an individual. The objectives of educational psychologylike those of other fields of psychologyare to understand, describe, predict, and guide human behavior. These purposes are accomplished through research service functions and teaching about human relationships, human development, and changes in human behavior. Programs in educational psychology are specialized and offered generally on the graduate level. However, a departmental undergraduate minor in the psychology of human development is offered. Some undergraduate courses in the area are required as psychological foundations for teacher education, nursing, and other undergraduate programs, and a number are offered as electives. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 68-71) and by the concentration area listed below. title: Study Skills for College Students
description: Provides empirically supported study strategies and skills to increase the probability of university success. Emphasizes scientific approach to techniques for successful study and test taking. For students who need additional help with study skills. AOP students must have permission of the Director of the Academic Opportunity Program before enrollment.

title: Becoming a Planetary Citizen
description: Designed to promote global and crosscultural awareness and consciousness of the significant and necessary knowledge of the numerous psychological facets and networks that compose the merging human family of our world. Explores the dimensions and challenges for living, learning, and coping as planetary citizens in the dawning of a new civilization that will make multiple demands upon our survival and enhancement needs in the coming decades of our world community.

title: Human Growth and Development
description: Development of personality in the Western world from birth through adolescence and application to life in the family, school, community, and broader social situations. Emphasis on physical, motor, social, emotional, and cognitive development and their interweaving relationships, particularly as they apply to the school setting. Should be taken during the sophomore year. PSYSC 100 is a highly recommended elective. 251.. Human Growth and Development. (4) Development of personality in the Western world, beginning at birth, but placing special emphasis upon the period from preadolescence through adolescence. Emphasis on physical, motor, social, emotional, and cognitive development and their interweaving relationships, particularly as they apply to the school setting. Should be taken during the sophomore year and is intended for students planning to teach in secondary schools. PSYSC 100 is a highly recommended elective.

title: Educational Psychology
description: Psychological principles underlying learning and the improvement of teaching, tests, and measurements. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250 or 251, except for students with a departmental major in dietetics or junior high/middle school education. PSYSC 100 is a highly recommended elective.

title: Independent Study: Educational Psychology
description: Individually planned experiences, extensive study in independent research in educational psychology. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Behavior Analysis in Education
description: Assists students to translate learning principles into teaching practices, to design and implement behavior analysis procedures which enhance motivation and learning in educational settings and decrease behavior problems, and to assess the effects of such instructional techniques.

title: Psychology of Later Life
description: A study of the later years of life with emphasis on the adaptations required. Includes theories of aging, physical and social changes taking place, and coping strategies. Not open to the student who has credit in EDGER 325.

title: Educational Tests and Measurement
description: Standard educational tests and the use of such tests as instruments for the evaluation of learning. Techniques of test construction.

title: Individual and Group Intelligence Testing
description: Nature of intelligence and its measurement. Study of selected tests for normal and exceptional persons with special emphasis on development of elementary psychometric skills.

title: Applications of Biofeedback to School Psychology and the Educational Setting
description: The relationship of biofeedback to intelligence, learning, behavior, and creativity within the classroom will be particularly stressed.

title: Child Psychology
description: Study of the psychology of childhood, with special emphasis on various psychological influences contributing to child development.

title: Adolescent Psychology
description: A study of childhood influences upon the adolescent period, of the psychology of the adolescent period, and of the effects of that development during young adulthood. Emphasis on various psychological influences contributing to adolescent development.

title: Adult Psychology
description: Developmental study of psychological stages of adulthood. Not open to the student who has credit in E DAC 355.

title: Honor Colloquium in Educational Psychology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with concepts and issues in educational psychology. Emphasis on independent study to culminate in a product representative of the student with honors. Prerequisite: open only to students participating in the Honors Program except by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mental Hygiene
description: Psychological principles underlying mental health and the application of these principles in and out of the classroom. Prerequisite: 8 hours of psychology.

title: Seminar in Educational Psychology
description: Group or individual investigation and study of current issues, problems, and developments in human development, classroom learning, and evaluation. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. title: Introduction to Teaching in the Elementary School: Seminar and Laboratory
description: Work with elementary schoolage children of a variety of cultural and ethnical backgrounds with opportunities through seminars and counseling to plan and evaluate experiences and to begin to develop skills, attitudes, and understanding necessary for successful communication with children as an orientation to teaching in the elementary school. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Lower -Division Laboratory Experience in Early Childhood Education
description: Supervised field experience for staff working in educational settings for young children. Prerequisite: permission of the coordinator of early childhood education or the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Interaction Skills for the Young Child
description: Introduces students to basic skills every young child needs to acquire in order to use language competently in society. Deals with materials, methods, principles of learning, and conditions necessary for optimum learning.

title: Lower -Division Practicum in Early Childhood Education
description: Focuses on the young child and his/her learning environment and how adults apply this knowledge in early childhood education. Prerequisite: EDEL 160 and permission of the coordinator of early childhood education or department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Elementary School Classroom Organization and Management
description: The role of the teacher as the facilitator for learning in the elementary classroom with opportunites through seminars and counseling to plan and evaluate experiences and to begin to develop skills, attitudes, and understanding necessary for successful communication with children as an orientation to teaching in the elementary school. Prerequisite: EDEL 101. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Writing
description: Development of skills in manuscript and cursive writing, methods of teaching handwriting in the elementary school, and relationship of manuscript and cursive writing to the language arts.

title: Human Relations in School
description: Development of understanding and skills needed for effective teacherpupil, teacherparent, and teacherteacher relationships in school settings for young children. Open to students enrolled in the twoyear elementary education program, or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Child Care Services 1
description: Selection and organization of learning experiences appropriate for individual children. Need identification, identification of appropriate child care facilities, and the students' roles as members of a staffing team. Prerequisite: permission of the coordinator of early childhood education or the department chairperson.

title: Child Care Services 2
description: Selection and organization of learning experiences appropriate for individual children. Need identification, identification of appropriate child care facilities, and the students' roles as members of a staffing team. Prerequisite: EDEL 240 and permission of the coordinator of early childhood education or the department chairperson. Open only to students on the twoyear early elementary education program.

title: Creative Experiences for Young Children
description: Designed to develop awareness of, and skill in, providing creative experiences for the young child. Working with children is an integral part of the course.

title: Lower Division Laboratory Experience in Early Elementary Education 2
description: Provides experience in assisting the classroom teacher in the implementation of educational opportunities for young children under supervision of a university faculty member or an agency representative. Emphasizes evaluation of the child and the program in conjunction with the classroom teacher. Role differentiation is stressed. Prerequisite: minimum of 36 hours in early elementary education courses, always including EDEL 160.

title: Materials and Techniques for Teaching Children of Multiethnic Backgrounds
description: Designed to offer multisensory approaches to learning. Attempts will be made to identify learning methods and materials best suited to the student's style of learning.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in elementary school classrooms.

title: Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School
description: Problems of school organization, management, control, and environment in relation to the learning activities of children. Stresses legal rights and responsibilities of teachers and use of instructional media. Prerequisite: EDEL 101, 201, and approval to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: E DPSY 290, except for majors in special education.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Lower Elementary Grades
description: Development of language arts skills—listening, speaking, reading, and writing—in the primary grades.

title: The Social, Historical, and Philosophical Foundations of Elementary Education
description: Emphasizes historical and social derivations of contemporary educational ideas, philosophical foundations for educational practices, alternatives for ethical decisions in education, and formulation of a personal philosophical position related to educational issues in elementary education.

title: Computer Literacy in the Elementary School Classroom
description: Develops computer literacy and application for elementary school instruction. Introduces programming in BASIC, evaluation of software, and methods of developing literacy in children. Handson experience with microcomputers is provided.

title: Discipline and Classroom Management: Some Practical Approaches
description: Designed to help beginning elementary school teachers create and maintain effective learning environments. Emphasizes practical approaches to prevention and remediation of disruptive classroom behavior.

title: The Parent in Early Childh000d Education
description: Explores important and complex roles of parents and parent substitutes in the educational development of young children. Factors affecting parent/child interactions and skills needed for effective parenting are studied and related to the educational process. Parent involvement as a significant factor in early childhood education is included.

title: Kindergarten Education
description: Development of the kindergartenprimary curriculum with special emphasis on kindergarten children and procedures to be used in their development.

title: Nursery School Education
description: Guidance of young children. Observation and evaluation of the activities of children between the ages of two and six. Organization, administration, and educational program of nursery schools. Child development and parent education as parts of nursery school education. Use of the physician, nurse, and nutritionist.

title: Home, School, and Community Relationships in Early Childhood Education
description: Involves experiences to enrich the relationships among parents, teachers, and children in the home, school, and community environments and to acquaint and involve students with the variety of community resources concerned with the welfare of young children and their families.

title: Education of the Culturally Different Child
description: Provides students in elementary education with a broad understanding of characteristics of economically disadvantaged and culturally different children requisite to dealing realistically with their needs. Stresses consideration of teacher self attitudes toward economically disadvantaged and culturally different children as well as examination of promising instructional changes and approaches for improving learning opportunities for these children. Motivation, classroom organization, discipline, parentteacher relationships, school integration, and nonstandard dialect are emphasized.

title: Psychology of Early Childhood
description: Study of young children of nursery school and kindergarten age involving lectures, readings, discussions, and conferences to give individual guidance to students and help them interpret their study of the physical, mental, social, and emotional development of selected young children. Consideration is given to growth in perception, language, expression, and interests.

title: Student Teaching: Elementary School
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 460 (4) and EDEL 464 (10) for a total of 14 quarter hours, requiring eleven weeks of fulltime student teaching. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Elementary School
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 464 (10) and EDEL 460 (4) for a total of 14 quarter hours, requiring eleven weeks of fulltime student teaching. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Elementary
description: Parttime student teaching for eleven weeks in an area of endorsement. Taken in a different quarter and in addition to the regular student teaching requirement for elementary education. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Pre-Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach children in prekindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the university in the student teaching program. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Primary Grades
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in primary grades the oppportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the university in the student teaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 468. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in kindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the university in the student teaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 467. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Practicum in Elementary Education
description: Laboratory and seminar course involving a study of progressive school practices, the philosophy of education underlying, and the possibilities of using, progressive practices in the public school. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Elementary Education
description: Independent study and research in the field of elementary education. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems in Elementary Education
description: An analysis of one's professional preparation for teaching, identifying areas in which students need to bolster weaknesses and augment strengths, and arranging for more preparation in these areas. Prerequisite: one term of student teaching. EDUCATION: READING (EDRDG)

title: Self Improvement in Reading
description: A remedial course designed to improve comprehension skills, reading speed, vocabulary, notetaking, and content reading. Students who do not achieve the 30th percentile in comprehension on the Diagnostic Reading Tests or a selected reading test administered by Reading Programs and Services must repeat the course. The course is offered on a credit/no credit basis and credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements. This course may be taken twice.

title: College Reading Skills
description: Emphasizes development of the ability to critically read collegelevel materials from a variety of subject areas and to develop flexibility of rate.

title: Prereading Development
description: Basic understanding of environments and planned activities that foster positive attitudes and interests related to reading, procedures that stimulate prereading development, and related practical experiences with young children.

title: The Teaching of Reading in Today's Schools
description: Designed to review the current thinking, approaches, and methodology of teaching reading in today's schools. Attention is directed to readiness, word recognition and analysis, comprehension, and planning of the total developmental reading program, with emphasis on reading at the elementary level.

title: Study of Selected Aspects of the Elementary School Reading Program
description: Designed to review the current thinking and approaches to teaching reading in the elementary school, and the relationship of basic psychological principles to teaching practices. Prerequisite or parallel: one term of student teaching at the elementary school level.

title: Corrective Reading in the Classroom
description: Provides prospective teachers with understanding of difficulties in reading and practical experience in assessing reading difficulties and in study of corrective treatment. Includes guided laboratory situations with students exhibiting reading limitations who can be aided by the regular classroom teacher. Prerequisite: EDRDG 400 or EDRDS 420 or EDRDM 421.

title: Reading Approaches and Strategies
description: Provides prospective classroom teachers (K-12) with opportunities to study and use various approaches and strategies in teaching reading. Includes evaluation of related instructional materials. Prerequisite: EDRDG 430.

title: Practicum in Reading
description: Provides experiences for prospective teachers (K-12) in grouping students of varying reading abilities and in planning and implementing a classroom reading program appropriate for these students. Prerequisite: EDRDG 435.

title: Independent Study in Reading
description: Designed to meet the needs of students wishing to study in individually selected areas of reading education. Prerequisite: 8 hours of credit in reading education and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. Center for Lifelong Education McElhinney, Chairperson; Danglade, Fallon, Fisher, Foster, Greenwood, Hoyt, Janove, Kaluzynski, Kowalski, Lucas, Murk, Ratliff, Thompson, Van Ness, Weaver, Wood Learning neither starts nor ends with formal education. It is a lifelong process. Recognizing this, the Center for Lifelong Education is concerned with encompassing and unifying all stages of education. Lifelong education includes both formal and informal patterns of education and experiential learning. Education begins with the family and moves into society as a child begins to interact with people outside the family. The formal institutions of education are important but they constitute only part of many social agencies providing opportunities for people to learn. To promote lifelong education, Ball State University established the Center for Lifelong Education and specifically charged it with providing formal and informal programs that would prepare people to design, implement, and coordinate educational opportunities throughout their lives. In the formal portion of this task, the center either offers or directs the following programs of study, mostly at the graduate level: M.A. in adult education; M.A. in applied gerontology; M.A. in community education; M.A. in executive development for public service; M. A.E. in curriculum; Ed. S. in curriculum ; doctoral cognates in curriculum; Ed. D. in adult and community education; departmental minor in gerontology (see Interdepartmental); and seminars for the older returning undergraduate students. In addition, the center serves as a vehicle within the Teachers College through which interdisciplinary educational services, both formal and informal, not traditionally offered by any current Teachers College department or service unit, may be developed, implemented, and coordinated. Current informal programs include research, school curriculum studies, program evaluation, nontraditional students, inservice professional development programs, retirement planning, and related service activities. EDUCATION: ADULT AND COMMUNITY (EDAC)

title: Seminar in Facilitating Lifelong Learning
description: A seminar course for nontraditional students that provides an opportunity to explore, discuss, and reinforce new changes in self as a learner and as a group participator. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on the Evolving Roles of American Men and Women
description: A course for nontraditional students that provides an indepth look at a history of rights and roles of eighteenth-, nineteenth-, and twentiethcentury American men and women. Prerequisite: EDAC 101 and permission of the department chairperson .

title: Seminar on Investigation into Job Opportunities
description: A field course for nontraditional students to explore job opportunities or advancements through placement experiences in work settings, depth interviews and visitations, and directed readings. Emphasis on problem solving, acquiring firsthand knowledge in order for older students to make realistic career decisions. Prerequisite: EDAC 101, 102, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar on Comprehensive Programming for Lifelong Learning
description: Assists nontraditional students to prepare portfolios on learning acquired through life experiences and to develop comprehensive plans for continuous learning throughout their life spans.

title: The Adult Learner in the Undergraduate Classroom
description: A seminar for the adult learner that provides an opportunity to examine the university setting, values expressed in the classroom by faculty and students, and the dynamics of higher education in terms of the student's own developing values.

title: Assertive Behavior and the Adult Learner
description: A seminar that focuses on the specific need to express oneself openly and fully without fear of ridicule, rejection, or guilt. Emphasizes assertive behavior as a means of accomplishing this end.

title: Adult Education
description: The history and current status of adult education in the United States and in selected foreign countries; the nature, scope, purposes, and historical development of adult education institutions and program areas; an introduction to and overview of adult education as a field of study and practice.

title: The Adult as a Learner
description: Designed to familiarize students with implications of learning theories for education of adults in a variety of learning situations and to develop skills in use of applicable methods and techniques.

title: Adult Psychology
description: Developmental study of psychological stages of adulthood. Not open to the student who has credit in EDPSY 355.

title: Volunteers and Voluntarism
description: An analysis of the historical, theoretical, philosophical, and operational perspectives of voluntarism. Attention will be given to developing new and innovative models for volunteer programs based on field experience, readings, and course sessions.

title: The Community Educator
description: Designed to familiarize the student with the structure, purpose, and processes of community education development with emphasis on the development of skills and competencies required of a community education coordinator.

title: Workshop in Adult and/or Community Education
description: A course for persons who wish to participate in preservice or inservice training in the areas of adult and/or community education. Specific content will depend upon interests of the participants. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. EDUCATION: CURRICULUM (EDCUR)

title: Curriculum Construction
description: Principles to be used in determining the nature and content of the learner's experiences in the public school. The issue of essentialism and progressivism, teacherpupil planning, the larger use of group action in the solution of problems, and betterment of the relationships between problem solving and principles operative in these problems.

title: Psychology of Later Life
description: A study of the later years of life with emphasis on the adaptations required. Includes theories of aging, physical and social changes taking place, and coping strategies. Not open to the student who has credit in EDPSY 325.

title: Educational Gerontology
description: A study of education and aging with emphasis on a lifespan approach. Topics include education about aging for children and youth, career educational opportunities in gerontology, education for paraprofessionals and volunteers in the field of aging, retirement planning education, and educational opportunities for older adults.

title: Workshop in Applied Gerontology
description: Preservice or inservice ediication in selected areas of applied gerontology using a workshop format of concentrated study, presentation, demonstrations, and practice. Specific content will depend upon the problems or interest area to which the workshop is addressed. The learner is encouraged to work out a program of personal study with help from other workshop participants and resource persons. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. Credit may be applied to the minor in gerontology only with permission of the director of the Institute of Gerontology.

title: Topical Seminar in Applied Gerontology
description: Individual and group investigation of topics, problems, or issues in applied gerontology with discussion of them by all seminar participants under the guidance of the instructor. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned. Credit may be applied to the minor in gerontology only with permission of the director of the Institute of Gerontology.

title: Internship in Gerontology
description: Experience in one or more of the agencies, institutions, or programs now providing gerontological services or otherwise related to the field of gerontology. The internship is carried out under the joint supervision of the Institute of Gerontology and a practitioner representing the agency, institution, or program. The student chooses the internship setting with the guidance of a faculty sponsor and the approval of the practitioner. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. The director will be responsible for student advising and will function with an advisory committee consisting of one representative from each of the following: elementary education, English, foreign language, secondary education, and the Institute for International Studies. PREPARATION OF TEACHERS FOR MULTICULTURED SECONDARY SCHOOLS (MULTICUL) The MULTICUL program offers students an opportunity to study possible solutions to one of America's most crucial problems: developing racial and cultural harmony. The program is not designed to deal only with black and white relations, but rather with as many ethnic groups as possible. Multiculturalism is a basic characteristic of our society as well as of our schools; therefore, potential teachers should prepare themselves to meet realistic situations. Three of the experiences that the MULTICUL program uses in the preparation of potential teachers are 1. Specialized or elective courses offered in many major departments 2. Courses designed especially for MULTICUL students by the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education 3. Laboratory experiences in multicultural communities, social and professional organizations, and schools Departmental minor in the preparation of teachers for multicultured secondary schools, 24 hours EDSEC 200 (4 hrs.), 206, 301, 400 15 hrs . Electives approved by the department 9 hrs. Secondary School Teaching (Minor) Prospective high school teachers wishing to gain additional professional teaching skills may do so by electing a minor in secondary school teaching. This minor helps students develop competencies in the use of instructional media and provides additional study in such professional areas as high school curriculum, classroom discipline, innovations in secondary education, student activity programs, and other similar aspects of teaching. These experiences go beyond required minimum regulations for certification. In addition the minor includes a. Specially designed required courses b. Individually prescribed preteaching experiences in a variety of schools c. Courses selected by students to build upon personal strengths and to add specially desired competencies d. Individual professional advice and counsel by fulltime regular faculty from the department Students should register for EDSEC 148, Introduction to Basic Elements of Teaching in Secondary and Junior High/Middle Schools, or 150, Basic Concepts of Secondary Education, during the first quarter possible. Departmental minor in secondary school teaching, 36 hours EDSEC 148 and 149 or 150, 299, 350, 420, 460, and 462; EDRDS 420 . . . 29 hrs. Electives from the following to equal a minimum of 36 hours: EDPSY 351; EDJHM 313; EDSEC 210, 431, 432, 434, 470; or other appropriate courses with the approval of the department chairperson. Boys' Club Personnel Preparation Boys' Clubs of America, like the public schools, are civic enterprises and are actively involved in the community. Often a staff member of a Boys' Club may also be a parttime teacher in the local secondary school. Because of this relationship and because the preparation for teaching is good preparation for Boys' Club work, this program has been planned so that students who complete it satisfactorily will meet requirements for recommendation for a certificate to teach in an Indiana secondary school. Students will meet the requirements of the Teacher Education Curriculum. Because certain concentration areas provide education especially desirable for the personnel of Boys' Clubs, the students are advised to select a teaching major from art, business education I, English, health and safety, physical education, or social studies.
