description: Designed to teach the basic tap steps and combinations along with their rhythmic analysis and style to be used in composition. Intended for the student with no experience in tap dancing.

title: Hatha Yoga
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through yoga exercises and yoga relaxation techniques.

title: Beginning Badminton
description: Introductory skills for playing singles and doubles badminton. Stresses basic strategy, rules, and courtesy.

title: Beginning Horsemanship
description: Schooling in three gaits: walk, trot, and canter.

title: Beginning Tennis
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 128.

title: Bicycling
description: Bicycling techniques involving maintenance of equipment; city, open country, and endurance riding primarily to introduce the student to family bicycling for lifetime use. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 130.

title: Cross Country Snow Skiing
description: Designed to teach the beginning skier the skills necessary to reach the more advanced level of cross country skiing. Takes the skier from short, closein trails to longer, more challenging trails offered at several Indiana State Parks.

title: Field Handball
description: An international team field sport similar to soccer.

title: Distance Running
description: Designed for people who like to run for physical fitness. Students are expected to start at one to two mile distances and progress to as much as thirtyfive to forty minutes of running. Prerequisite: must be in condition to run two miles on first day. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 135.

title: Flag Football
description: Introduction to fundamentals and rules of football through flag football; instruction in techniques, terminology, strategies, and rules.

title: Beginning Basketball
description: Information, practice, and experience in basic skills, strategies, and knowledge. Course includes passing, shooting, dribbling, offense, and defense.

title: Beginning Fencing
description: Basic techniques, terminology, strategy, rules, and courtesies. Includes positions, footwork, parries, and lunges.

title: Volleyball (Coed Rules)
description: Provides the beginner with an understanding of rules and skills underlying optimal enjoyment for power volleyball. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 131.

title: Snow Skiing
description: Designed to teach the beginner the mechanics of snow skiing, equipment choice, and care of equipment; also offers a field experience of several days of skiing on available slopes. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Orienteering
description: Introduces the student to the activity of orienteering, a sport in which the participant uses such land navigation skills as mapand compassreading. Circulorespiratory fitness is emphasized in distance running for time.

title: Beginning Gymnastics (Apparatus)
description: Instruction in beginning skills leading to stunts on balance beam, rings, pommel horse, horizontal bars, parallel bars, uneven bars, and vaulting horse. Prerequisite: PEG 107 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Beginning Weight Training
description: Development of a basic personalized program for building and maintaining strength for both general conditioning and activities.

title: Rhythmic Aerobics
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through aerobic exercise routines performed to music. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 148.

title: Individualized Physical Education
description: Limited to nontraditional students with special problems that may keep them from enrolling in conventional physical education classes. Registration is by permission of the department. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Swimming 1
description: Phase two of a program designed to help the student to become an efficient swimmer. Open only to students who can swim in deep water. During the regular school year (September through May) the course is administered as either a learning or a testout program. Students enroll at the aquatics office of the Lewellen Aquatics Center. After students meet the skill performance standards, further attendance is not required, and they may register for credit and grade in either the current quarter or a future quarter; however, registration must be completed at least two weeks before the end of the quarter chosen. Summer students use the same procedures to register for swimming class as they do for other classes.

title: Swimming 2
description: Students who are interested in advancing their swimming skills or are preparing to specialize in aquatics should consider this course. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Lifeguarding
description: A preparatory course for students who are highly skilled swimmers and are interested in becoming lifeguards. The American National Red Cross certification in lifesaving can be earned in this course. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Synchronized Swimming Techniques
description: Introduces the student to stroke modifications, standard figures, sculling techniques, and floating patterns. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Beginning Springboard Diving
description: Designed to assist the student in developing the basic skills used in dives from a onemeterhigh springboard. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Scuba
description: Selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus techniques and the scientific laws pertaining to that activity. Nationally recognized association diver's certification can be earned in this class. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Basic Canoeing
description: An introduction to movement control of a canoe as a type of small craft. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Folk Dance
description: Prerequisite: PEG 112.

title: Intermediate Square Dance
description: Mainstream movements of contemporary square dance. Prerequisite: PEG 113 or equivalent.

title: Advanced Judo
description: Emphasis placed on understanding and practicing intermediate judo techniques, international contest rules and skills, and teaching methods that will enable one to teach beginning judo. Prerequisite: PEG 210.

title: Intermediate Modern Dance
description: A progression of technical skills in modern dance movement beyond the beginning level and in preparation for an advanced level of movement skill. Prerequisite: PEG 115.

title: Fitness Swimming
description: Designed to improve cardiovascular and muscular endurance and stroke efficiency through swimming and land conditioning. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 217.

title: Racquetball
description: Instruction in the basic skills, strategies, and knowledge required to play racquetball.

title: Bicycle Touring
description: Designed to develop touring physical fitness and camping skills associated with bicycle touring. Prerequisite: PEG 130 or equivalent. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Golf
description: Designed to offer the golfing student an opportunity to learn and practice the finer points of the game.

title: Intermediate Horsemanship
description: Work toward perfecting form in three gaits: walk, trot, and canter. Harness driving. Stable management.

title: Intermediate Tennis
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 128.

title: Intermediate Hatha Yoga
description: Designed for the student wishing to perfect previously learned asanas and to learn new ones. Prerequisite: PEG 119 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Fencing
description: Prerequisite: beginning fencing or equivalent.

title: Intermediate Volleyball—Coed Rules
description: Designed to provide the intermediate player with an opportunity to improve and expand individual volleyball skills and become knowledgeable about intermediatelevel tactics and strategies. Prerequisite: PEG 131, 140, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Snow Skiing
description: Designed to teach intermediate skiers the skills necessary to become advanced skiers; affords them the opportunity to ski on longer, higher open and trail slopes provided by ski areas in the west (Rocky Mountains) or the east (White Mountains). Prerequisite: PEG 142 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Rhythmic Aerobics
description: Designed to further enhance the student's fitness level through aerobic exercise routines performed to music. Prerequisite: PEG 148. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 148.

title: Selected Seasonal Sports Activities
description: Designed to be offered only at an offcampus location with a great deal of flexibility in course content in order to accommodate the needs of individual students and to adapt to the facilities available and the weather conditions existing at the time the course is being offered. Provides activity and instruction in physical fitness activities and two lifetime sports activities.

title: Sport Scuba Diving
description: Provides opportunities for refining techniques and skills for using selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus. Prerequisite: PEG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: White Water Canoeing
description: Designed to assist students in developing skills and gaining knowledge necessary for white water canoeing and portaging. Field trips may involve overnight camping. Prerequisite: PEG 209 or permission of the department chairperson. PHYSICAL EDUCATION, GENERAL—FITNESS (PEGF)

title: Physical Conditioning
description: Designed to help students become aware of their present fitness and to appreciate the role of exercise in everyday life. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 100.

title: Jogging
description: Designed to increase cardiovascular fitness through jogging. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture emphasizing common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 104.

title: Swimnastics
description: Physical conditioning through water exercise, using high potential fitness activities that can be used in a small pool or in a limited area of a crowded instructional pool. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Prerequisite: ability to put face in water, ability to float on front or back in shallow water, and ability to regain standing position after floating. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 117.

title: Bicycling
description: Bicycling techniques involving maintenance of equipment; city, open country, and endurance riding for lifetime fitness. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 130.

title: Distance Running
description: Designed for people who like to run for physical fitness. Students are expected to progress to as much as thirtyfive to forty minutes of running. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture per quarter concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Prerequisite: students must be in condition to run two miles on the first day. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 135.

title: Rhythmic Aerobics
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through aerobic exercise routines performed to music. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 148 or 248.

title: Fitness Swimming
description: Designed to improve cardiovascular and muscular endurance and stroke efficiency through swimming and land conditioning. Includes a total of ten hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 217. PHYSICAL EDUCATION, GENERAL—RECREATION (PEGR)

title: Beginning Bowling
description: Introductory skills for enjoyment of bowling.

title: Pocket Billiards
description: The rudimentary skills and knowledge of the sport.

title: Casting and Angling
description: An introduction to the basic principles of casting and angling along with the practical application of how to cast for fish.

title: Intermediate Bowling
description: Designed to give the student knowledge and experience in bowling on a team; in a league; and keeping league records, team standings, and computing and figuring handicaps. Includes a review of the fundamentals of bowling.

title: General Safety Education
description: Designed to prepare prospective teachers for the comprehensive general safety education program.

title: Conditioning and Exercise
description: An exercise course designed to maintain or increase physical fitness and aid in weight control. Designed to help the student to develop a fitness philosophy, to structure physical fitness programs, and to recognize individual physiological limitations.

title: Gymnastics (Balance Beam and Floor Exercise)
description: Prerequisite: PEP 157 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Gymnastics (Trampoline, Vaulting, Uneven Bars)
description: Instruction in the basic stunts and creative routines on the following equipment: trampoline, balance beam, flying rings, and uneven parallel bars. Prerequisite: PEP 157 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Studio of Contemporary Dance Theatre
description: Provides training for performance through varied choreographic dance experiences. Students plan, rehearse, and perform in studio hour presentations. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Folk Dance Studio Theatre
description: The third course in folk dance. Designed to emphasize the different styles existing in folk dance. Introduces the elements of folk dance choreography. Prerequisite: PEG 212 or PEP 262. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Volleyball
description: Beginning professional preparation course in volleyball including the basic skills, rules, and courtesies associated with the game.

title: Field Hockey
description: Introduction to a team sport played with a hooked stick that challenges the participant to dribble or pass a ball down a field into the opponent's goal. Positioning and strategies of field hockey are similar to the game of soccer.

title: Foundations of Physical Education
description: Introduces professional physical education students to the psychomotor, cognitive, and affective scope of physical education and its relationship to education. Assists students in assessing the qualities of motor and physical fitness expected of physical education majors as they begin their vocational study.

title: Games and Activities for the Older Adult
description: Designed to acquaint the student with a variety of recreational activities suitable for the older adult.

title: Driver and Traffic Safety Education 1
description: Content, methods, materials, organization, and administration of the classroom and laboratory phase of the secondary school program.

title: Developmental Game Activities
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the application of the principles of movement and to provide a knowledge of basic skills and appropriate activities for the development of these skills as applied to game activities. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Principles and Problems of Coaching Sports for Girls and Women
description: Introduces the principles and problems of coaching girls' team and individual sports at the junior and senior high school levels. Considers the philosophies and principles that underlie the development of such a program.

title: Coaching Observation (Girls'/Women's Athletics)
description: Guided observation of coaching techniques and practices with analysis of teaching and coaching philosophies for competitive sports in schools. Prerequisite: PEP 231.

title: Practicum in Aquatics
description: An internship in aquatics at Ball State or another approved aquatic program. Prerequisite: PEP 353 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Officiating Competitive Aquatic Sports
description: Introduces the student to officiating practices, the decisionmaking role of the official, and laboratory experience in officiating. opportunities exist for certification in various aquatic areas.

title: Gymnastics for Children
description: Designed to acquaint the student with teaching methodology, developmental skills, and activities for gymnastics at the elementary school level. Prerequisite: PEP 157.

title: Tumbling and Apparatus (Women's Events)
description: Prerequisite: PEP 158 and 159 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Gymnastic Performance Techniques
description: Not open to the student who has 2 hours of credit in PEP 257 or 258.

title: Folk Dance
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 112.

title: The Teaching of Folk Dance
description: Materials and techniques of teaching folk dance in the secondary schools. Prerequisite: PEP 262 or equivalent.

title: The Teaching of Square Dance
description: Develops teaching skills for beginning and intermediate classes in square dancing and develops techniques of calling square dance (patter and singing). Prerequisite: PEP 263.

title: Teaching of Recreational Dance
description: An introduction to folk, square, round, and other types of recreational dance, and methods of teaching recreational dance.

title: Dance Composition 1
description: Principal elements of dance composition. Simple compositional forms for small groups and solo work. Prerequisite: PEG 215 or the equivalent.

title: Folk and Square Dance Methods for Elementary School Children
description: Movement experiences in the forms of folk and square dance for the elementary school child. Emphasis on the selection of appropriate dance materials and teaching methods for the elementary school child.

title: Contemporary Sport Activities
description: Introduces selected emerging sport activities with emphasis on both skill development and teaching methodology. Presents five activities such as weight training, cycling, hockey, martial arts, team handball, and ultimate frisbee.

title: Baseball/Softball Performance Techniques
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 179.

title: Track and Field Performance Techniques
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 180.

title: Lacrosse (Women's Game)
description: Introduction to an aerial game played on an outdoor field with a netted stick or "crosse" and a hard rubber ball. This team sport challenges the physical endurance and manipulative skills of the player.

title: Games and Activities for the Handicapped
description: Designed to familiarize the student with games and activities commonly used with the handicapped. Prerequisite: SPCED 201.

title: Recreation Playground Activities
description: Provides a knowledge of playground operation, equipment, and supplies. Presentation of a wide variety of activities for effective playground leadership.

title: Practicum in Elementary School Physical Education
description: Offers the student supervised experience in basic movementoriented activities generally included in elementary school physical education programs (suggested range: K-6). Course work is contracted among the student, the department, and the school or agency. Prerequisite: PEP 230 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foundations of Exercise Leadership
description: Designed to provide basic knowledge in physical fitness and related areas for students pursuing nonteaching areas, such as corporate fitness programs, private fitness centers, and YMCA's. Prerequisite: PEP 190.

title: Anatomy
description: Basic concepts of anatomy for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching.

title: Physiology
description: Basic concepts of physiology for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching. Prerequisite: PEP 292 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Kinesiology
description: The mechanics of motion as applied to the human body. Development of the ability to analyze activity for the purpose of improving physical skills. Prerequisite: PEP 292.

title: First Aid
description: First aid as outlined by the American Red Cross, leading to standard certification. Designed for the student pursuing a major or minor program in the School of Physical Education and Athletics. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 250.

title: First Aid Instructor
description: Instructor's course in Standard First Aid and Personal Safety, including also the instructor's course in Multimedia First Aid as established by the American Red Cross. Designed for the professional student pursuing a major or minor in physical education. Prerequisite: PEP 299 or HSC 250, or valid certification in Standard First Aid and Personal Safety, Standard First Aid and Multimedia, or Advanced First Aid and Emergency Care.

title: Teaching Physical Activity to the Older Adult
description: Designed to teach the student to recognize the characteristics of the older adult and to successfully plan, implement, and evaluate a program of physical activity based upon the special needs of the older adult. Prerequisite: PEP 150 or PEG 100.

title: Camping
description: Acquaints the student with various aspects of organized and individual camping. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Simulation in Driver and Traffic Safety Education
description: Designed to meet the needs of prospective teachers in the simulation phase of driver and traffic safety education. Prerequisite: PEP 124.

title: Strategies and Techniques in Coaching Gymnastics; Volleyball; Track and Field
description: Coaching techniques involved in gymnastics, volleyball, and track and field. Strategies are presented, discussed, and practiced. Prerequisite: four skill courses from directed list.

title: Strategies and Techniques in Coaching Volleyball, Basketball, and Softball
description: Coaching techniques involved in volleyball, basketball, and softball. Strategies are presented, discussed, and practiced. Prerequisite: four skill courses from directed list.

title: Physical Therapy Kinesiology
description: The mechanics of motion as applied to the human body. Development of the ability to analyze "normal" motor performance. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ANAT 330, 331, 405.

title: Organization and Management of Women's Athletics
description: Explores the concepts and practices inherent in the organization and management of a women's athletic program.

title: Sports Information 1
description: Designed primarily for the sports information student. Develops the student's knowledge and background in the terminology, basic strategy, scoring, and officiating in gymnastics (men's), basketball, golf, ice hockey, boxing, wrestling, horseracing, billiards, cross country, baseball, and football. Not open to the student with teaching areas in physical education.

title: Sports Information 2
description: Designed for the sports information student. Includes the following sport areas: gymnastics (women's), volleyball, tennis, track and field, swimming, lacrosse, field hockey, softball, soccer, badminton, and bowling. Geared to increase the student's knowledge in these sports, especially in regard to terminology, basic rules, strategy, scoring, and officiating, which will assist them in reporting on these activities. Not open to physical education majors or minors.

title: Teaching and Coaching Weight Training
description: Designed for the professional student pursuing a career in teaching physical education, in coaching, as an exercise science and fitness specialist, or in related areas. Not intended to be a personal weight training course. Prerequisite: PEG 151 or 152 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Art Production
description: A practical introduction to the fundamentals of management and staging activities involved in aquatic art productions at the high school and college levels.

title: Teaching and Coaching Swimming
description: Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor
description: Provides the opportunity for students to earn the American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor certificate. Prerequisite: an unexpired American National Red Cross Advanced Lifesaving certificate.

title: Instructional Techniques and Analysis of Aquatic Performance
description: Selected learning theories, teaching strategies, and physical laws that affect learning and performance in the aquatic medium. Emphasis on analysis of basic safety skills and stroke and diving techniques.

title: Field and Laboratory Experience
description: Permits the student to receive credit for aquatic experiences in categories of leadership, administration, and operation of aquatic programs or facilities. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching and Coaching Gymnastics
description: Prerequisite: PEP 259.

title: Teaching and Coaching Wrestling
description: Prerequisite: PEP 261.

title: Dance for Children
description: Basic rhythms, exploration of movement, and creative dance for the early grades of the elementary school.

title: Accompaniment for Modern Dance
description: Exploration and the use of accompaniment in dance. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or equivalent.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator (Techniques)
description: Fundamental modern dance techniques, elements of rhythmic patterns, materials of space, design, and improvisation. Accompaniment for Modern Dance. (2) Exploration and the use of accompaniment in dance. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or equivalent.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator (Composition)
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques. Emphasis on composition. Prerequisite: PEP 365.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator (Methodology)
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques. Emphasis on teaching modern dance in the public schools, camps, and others. Dance composition. Prerequisite: PEP 366.

title: Aquatics for the Elementary School Child
description: Introduces the student to safety factors, developmental strokes, diving sequences, and teaching strategies for aquatic instruction of the young child. Prerequisite: PEP 353 or equivalent certificate from a nationally recognized organization such as the Young Men's Christian Association or the Boy Scouts of America.

title: Diagnostic Techniques and Athletic Injury Mechanisms
description: An introduction to predisposing anatomical, kinesiological, growth stress, and other such conditions that contribute to athletic injuries. Presents the procedures needed to accurately recognize and evaluate these conditions and the extent of an athletic injury. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Administration and Organization for Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries
description: Problems, principles, and objectives in the designing, planning, and operation of a program for the prevention and care of athletic injuries. Examines the code of ethics of the National Athletic Trainers' Association. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Athletic Training Modalities and Therapeutic Techniques
description: Introduces mechanical therapies, thermal therapy, cryotherapy, hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, and therapeutic exercise. Considers only those modalities and their clinical uses that have special implications for the athletic trainer in the treatment of athletic injuries. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Methods of Teaching Sports
description: Methods, materials, and organizational techniques in selected team and individual sports. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing.

title: Teaching and Coaching Tennis
description: Prerequisite: PEP 276.

title: Teaching and Coaching Baseball and Softball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 279.

title: Teaching and Coaching Track and Field
description: Prerequisite: PEP 280.

title: Teaching and Coaching Football
description: Prerequisite: PEP 281.

title: Teaching and Coaching Basketball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 282.

title: Teaching and Coaching Volleyball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 283.

title: Teaching and Coaching Soccer
description: Prerequisite: PEP 284.

title: Gymnastics Judging (Women's Events)
description: The development of gymnastics judging techniques with the opportunity for obtaining IHSAA and NAGWS (Class) officials' ratings. Prerequisite: PEP 157, 158, 159.

title: Softball Umpiring
description: The development of softball umpiring techniques with the opportunity for obtaining IHSAA, ASA, and NAGWS officials' ratings. Prerequisite: PEP 179.

title: Volleyball Officiating
description: The development of volleyball officiating techniques with the opportunity for obtaining IHSAA and NAGWS officials' ratings. Prerequisite: PEP 183.

title: Basketball Officiating
description: The development of basketball officiating techniques with the opportunity for obtaining IHSAA and NAGWS officials' ratings. Prerequisite: PEP 182.

title: Principles of Physical Education
description: General concepts based upon the scientific facts and philosophic judgments that underlie physical education.

title: Motor Learning
description: Introduction to principles and factors related to the teaching, learning, and performance of motor skills. Emphasis on the application of this knowledge to teaching and learning strategies for motor skill acquisition. For undergraduate students who plan to teach motor skills to people in all age ranges.

title: Motor Development of Young Children
description: Human motor development theory and practice for early childhood and primary school children, emphasizing behaviors related to nonlocomotor, locomotor, transitory, and manipulatory motor patterns as they emerge and become controlled, using task analysis, assessment, program planning, physical activities, and evaluation. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Neurophysiological Approach to Physical Education for the Handicapped
description: Designed to give the student an understanding of the theoretical basis of selected neurophysiological programs for treatment of various handicaps and to teach the student how to administer such programs.

title: Teaching of Physical Education in the Elementary School
description: Methods and consideration for teaching physical education in the elementary school that include purpose, growth and development, motor learning, program learning, and evaluation.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Physical Education in the Secondary School
description: Designed to analyze and develop teaching methods that enable the student to plan, implement, and evaluate an array of teaching strategies that would be used in creating a safe environment for a public school physical education program. Prerequisite: PEP activity sequence and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries
description: Principles; practice of athletic training principles and techniques necessary for care and prevention of athletic injuries.

title: Remedial Exercises and Rehabilitation
description: Introduces the objectives and principles involved in designing and planning conditioning programs for the athlete. Introduces and develops therapeutic exercises essential in planning the rehabilitation program of the injured athlete. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Methods and Materials for Physical Education in the Secondary School
description: Designed as a practicum that involves comprehensive planning of instruction, designing teaching implementation strategies, classroom management techniques, and evaluation of teaching behaviors and materials in physical education. Opportunities for students to work with children in a classroom setting. Prerequisite: PEP 395 and junior status.

title: Exercise Leader Internship
description: An indepth practical experience in the application of exercise leadership knowledge and skills as related to fitness and rehabilitation programs owned and operated by private and corporate business firms, as well as municipal organizations. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Exercise Technician and Leader Practicum
description: To provide training for potential leaders of physical fitness programs, emphasis will be on administering exercise tests in the laboratory and in field situations, prescribing exercise based on test results and scientific principles, and leading exercise sessions. Prerequisite: PEP 293 or equivalent course or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Practicum in Recreation
description: Supervised, practical, professional leadership experience designed for the recreationoriented person. Experiences include work activities in federal, state, county, or community parks or with private camps. Close supervision supplied by the university and the participating agency. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Exercise Programs for the Older Adult
description: A practical experience in leading physical activities for older adults in health care centers, senior citizen centers, retirement centers, or other places where older adults engage in exercise. Prerequisite: PEP 312 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Driver and Traffic Safety Education 2
description: Presentation of materials and information designed to prepare for teaching driver education in the secondary schools.

title: Driver Education for Special Populations
description: Designed to provide information for prospective teachers of special populations. Prerequisite: PEP 424.

title: Motorcycle Safety Education
description: Will prepare prospective teachers to conduct motorcycle rider education courses.

title: Coaching Internship
description: Students assist in coaching competitive sports in schools. Includes internship in coaching and indepth classroom discussions centering on selfawareness and the teachingcoaching process. May not be taken parallel with student teaching. Prerequisite: PEP 231.

title: Sports Information Statistics
description: Designed for the sports information student. Consists of the identification, computation, practical application, and communication of statistics in selected sports, such as ERA, match play, difficulty rating, and percentages. Not open to students with teaching areas in physical education.

title: Athletic Governance
description: Directed mainly toward the sports information student. Designed to discuss the various organizations that govern amateur and professional sports in the United States. Emphasis on the sports information student's role in shaping sports in this country and in international competition. Not recommended for physical education majors and minors.

title: Swimming Pool Operation and Maintenance
description: Emphasizes water circulation and filtration, chemical treatment for disease control, sanitation, and administrative procedures for personal safety.

title: Teaching Modern Dance for the Secondary Schools
description: Methods and materials for teaching modern dance in the secondary schools. Prerequisite: PEG 215 or equivalent.

title: Advanced Studio in Contemporary Dance
description: Advanced techniques in contemporary dance. Designed for students interested in improving skills in contemporary dance technique beyond those developed in the regular college classes. Choreographic forms, performance, and production, using such allied fields as costuming, lighting, and accompaniment. Prerequisite: some previous study of modern dance or ballet. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Implementation of Elementary School Physical Education Programs
description: Designed for advanced students, giving an overview of educationally sound elementary physical education programs; history, curriculum, assessment, objectives, methodology, planning, progressions, and evaluations. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mainstreaming in Elementary School Physical Education
description: Designing physical education programs to meet the requirements of Public Law 94-142 mandating that all handicapped children have an individualized physical education program.

title: Teaching the Handicapped in Aquatics
description: Adaptation of swimming strokes for people with physical limitations. Provides swimming as a rehabilitation program. Analyzes facilities and pool design adaptations. Prerequisite: an unexpired American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor certificate.

title: Practicum in Physical Education for the Handicapped
description: Designed to provide the student with practical experience in working with handicapped children in a physical education setting. Prerequisite: PEP 488 and 494.

title: History, Philosophy, Administration, and Coaching of a Modern Athletic Program
description: Explores the historical development of modern athletics. Students develop a philosophical relationship to the total school program and learn to deal with everyday coaching and administration problems.

title: Program Development for Intramural and Recreational Activities
description: Initiation, organization, and administration of intramural and recreational programs in the secondary school.

title: Teaching Physical Education for the Developmentally Disabled
description: A study of people with developmental disabilities, including mental retardation, learning disabilities, and emotional disturbance, that affect motor performance. Considers the characteristics, limitations, and special needs of these people, with implications for selection of activities in physical education.

title: History and Philosophy of Recreation
description: The history of recreation in the United States from the first settlers in America to modern times. A study of various philosophies that have influenced the development of the new leisure principles.

title: Skill Analysis, Theory and Practice of Play
description: Scientific principles involved in movement as they apply to specific skills in elementary school physical education. Prerequisite: PEP 292, 293, 294.

Fisher The College of Architecture and Planning, established by the 1965 Indiana legislature, is dedicated to the development of professional competency in the functional, aesthetic, and humane design of the physical environment. Three fiveyear programs of study are offered: the departmental major in architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Architecture degree, the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree, and the departmental major in urban planning, leading to a Bachelor of Urban Planning and Development degree. The first year of all three programs includes a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences. Demonstrated proficiency in collegelevel algebra and trigonometry is a prerequisite for admission to the college. An environmental design major is offered for students who have completed the first three years of either the architecture or the urban planning and development program; it is designed for students who wish to end their studies after four years of university work or who wish to pursue graduate study in a different subject. This program leads to the Bachelor of Science degree. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning have a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophies. The curricula stress character, dedication, initiative, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility.

This accredited professional degree is the first step in pursuing a professional career as an architect. The general educational objective of the program is to foster the creativity and professional skills necessary to become a responsible and contributing member of the profession. The curriculum provides a framework within which fundamental courses are logically presented, beginning with the first year in which architecture, landscape architecture, and planning students are introduced to the three environmental design disciplines in a common curriculum, through the fifth year where students pursue specific professional interests and abilities. Design reviews at the end of the second and fourth year further serve to determine progress in the program. A twentyweek internship experience occurs at the end of the third year. Studios in each of the years afford the student the opportunity to synthesize and integrate the subject matter of other courses into the development of design skills. Lectures and seminars offer the opportunity for indepth study of specific topics. Approval to pursue the departmental major in architecture entails a selection process in addition to admission to the university. For more information regarding this process contact the Office of Admissions. Architecture is a departmental major within the Professional Arts Curriculum. A student receiving two consecutive grades below C in any two sequential architecture courses must repeat both courses in order to receive credit toward a major in environmental design or a Bachelor of Architecture degree. Department of Landscape Architecture Spangler, Chairperson; Benson, Dorsey, Faruque, Hall, Pardee, Russell, Smith, Young Landscape architecture involves coordinated planning and design of land. It applies aesthetic and scientific principles in arranging objects and spaces on the landscape for human use, enjoyment, safety, and health and welfare. Landscape architecture is based on recognition of longterm ecologic, economic, social, and psychological values. It embraces the conservation of natural resources and the design of land for specific purposes. Landscape architects provide professional services for site planning, landuse projects, and feasibility studies, and may be assisted by such allied professionals as architects, engineers, planners, ecologists, geologists, geographers, hydrologists, biologists, economists, and sociologists. Understanding the potentials and limitations of natural systems (soils, water, vegetation, wildlife, and climate) provides the basis for responding to complex problems of land use. The undergraduate curriculum stresses basic skills and understanding within the department while allowing study in allied areas. The general studies program and general and directed electives offer opportunities for the study of art and ecology and other cultural and intellectual preparations. The core courses focus on design, graphics, engineering and construction, plants, philosophy and history, and computer technology. The program includes problemsolving experiences to promote self reliance, decisionmaking skills, and creativity. Studio activities range from applying basic considerations of space, form, rhythm, movement, scale, and color to the designing of sites for recreation, business, industry, and housing, increasing in scale to include entire cities, regional studies, open space and river basin planning, mining operations, land management, reclamation, and resource evaluation studies encompassing thousands of acres. After completing the first year of study in the college, students must meet with their departmental advisers to develop a tentative plan of study for the major. This plan must have the approval of the department adviser before final course registration through the Office of Advising and Scheduling. To be admitted to the fifthyear courses, students must complete all 100-, 200-, and 300- level landscape architecture courses required for the major, and LA 401, 402, 413, and 415. The directed elective must be approved by the department adviser before registration. Students are required to attend collegeand departmentsponsored lectures held throughout the academic year. Landscape architecture offers a fiveyear departmental major in the professional arts curriculum. The degree received is a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture with a total of 246 hours required. Department of Urban Studies and Planning Parker, Chairperson; Mitchell, Schoen The Department of Urban Studies and Planning offers two undergraduate degrees: the fiveyear professional planning degree program and the fouryear environmental design major. The fiveyear Bachelor of Urban Planning and Development degree prepares students for professional planning positions in the public and private sectors. Planners work for city, county, state, and federal agencies concerned with orderly urban growth, with economic and community revitalization, and with development of effective transportation, recreation, and other urban infrastructure systems. They work for private consulting firms, for chambers of commerce, and for private development companies. The fouryear departmental major in environmental design prepares students for nonprofessional entrylevel positions in public and private planning offices and provides background for graduate work in urban planning or in related subjects. Students seeking admission to either program are admitted first to the College of Architecture and Planning, where they share a common first year of basic design principles and an introduction to planning, architecture, and landscape architecture. Students begin to specialize in planning in their second year. Course work in the second through fourth years includes a core of planning studios and lecture courses, selected planning electives, and required urban background courses from other departments. Each student in the fiveyear professional degree program will also complete a thesis, a required minor, and an internship in a planning or development office. Transfer students or Ball State students interested in pursuing a planning degree program after their freshman year should inquire about the summer accelerated entry program, which condenses the firstyear design and introduction courses into an intense summer program, thereby permitting entry into the secondyear sequence in the fall. Degree requirements for the major in urban planning and development and the departmental major in environmental design are given below. Arndt The College of Business is a professional school and has as its objective the education of men and women for pursuits in business, industry, and education. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the university and to the service of the business community. The college ranks tenth in the nation in undergraduate enrollment. Its undergraduate programs are accredited by the American Assembly of Collegiate Schools of Business. The college recognizes the need for both breadth and depth in the total academic pattern. The curricula are designed to provide a broad background in general education, mastery of the basic tools and an understanding of the fundamentals of business organization and procedures, and specialization in a selected field of business. All curricula are designed to develop the ability to define and analyze problems, to make value judgments, and to express conclusions in a cogent and concise manner. The largest responsibility of the College of Business is the training for staff and line positions in accounting, economics, finance, management, marketing, and office administration. This specialized training is preceded by the acquisition of a body of knowledge that is common to all specialties. Baccalaureate programs are also available in four concentrations for the preparation of secondary teachers. The Associate in Arts degree is offered in business administration with options in marketing and retailing, office services, midmanagement, and labor relations. The Associate in Arts degree is also available in secretarial studies and in word processing. Short courses of study are organized upon request to fit the special needs of individual employers. The College of Business is administered through six departments: accounting, business education and office administration, economics, finance, management science, and marketing. In addition, the Bureau of Business Research offers research services and publications to the business community as well as to faculty and students. The Center for Economic Education provides economic education aids to the school systems, to business firms, and to the public in the Ball State service area. The Better Business Bureau, serving the campus and Delaware County, is administered by the Department of Marketing and its students. At the graduate level, the Master of Business Administration is an interdepartmental degree composed of courses from all six departments. The departments of Business Education and Office Administration and Economics offer at least one specialized degree at the master's level. Graduate programs are described in the Graduate Catalog. The 3/2 Program The 3/2 program is designed to give a small, select group of Ball State University students an opportunity to combine their undergraduate liberal arts studies with graduate study in the College of Business. Students who successfully complete the program earn both a bachelor's degree and Master of Business Administration degree (M.B.A.) within a fiveyear period. To be eligible for this option, all requirements must be completed for the General Studies Program and the liberal arts departmental major by the conclusion of the third year of academic work. Therefore, students should begin to prepare during the freshman year, planning each quarter's course load with this goal in mind. During the fourth year, students who gain admission to the 3/2 program take course work that represents the first year of the twoyear M.B.A. curriculum. While enrolled in M.B.A. course work during the senior year, students are officially undergraduate students fulfilling undergraduate requirements. Students who successfully complete a subsequent year of fulltime graduate study will be granted the M.B.A. degree. The following departments are participating in the 3/2 program: anthropology, biology, chemistry, computer science, economics, English, foreign languages, geography, history, journalism, philosophy, political science, psychological science, sociology, social work, and speech communication. Preadmission Students interested in the 3/2 program should consult their advisers to determine requirements for their liberal arts majors. Students should also become acquainted with the programs that coordinate their majors with the 3/2 program. Each participating department will provide sample programs. Additionally, students should consult with an adviser in the College of Business, who will assist in the review of admission standards. Students must complete MATH 131 and 132 before beginning the fourth year of study. Admission Students apply for admission to the 3/2 program during the Winter Quarter of their junior years. Students will take the Graduate Management Admissions Test (GMAT) during the Winter Quarter of their junior years. To be admitted, a student must have a gradepoint ratio of 3.2 or higher based on at least 109 credit hours earned and a score of 1100 or higher using the AACSB formula of GMAT + (GPA x 200). Students are admitted to the program during the Spring Quarter of their junior years and begin study the Autumn Quarter of their senior years. Admission to the 3/2 program in the College of Business does not guarantee admission to fulltime graduate study in the college in the fifth year. When admitted, students are advised within the College of Business. Fourth Year During the fourth year, students will take graduatenumbered courses that make up the common body of knowledge and that are prerequisites for the M.B.A. Credit in these courses will apply to the credit hours required for the baccalaureate degree. At the end of the fourth year of study, students will normally have completed 186 credit hours, the minimum credit hours required for a baccalaureate degree. Assuming that all requirements are met, students may choose to leave the 3/2 program and take a bachelor's degree with a major in the College of Sciences and Humanities and a minor in foundations of business. Fifth Year Students in the 3/2 program are expected to meet all university requirements for admission to the graduate program in business administration. M.B.A. study will be fulltime study beginning the Autumn Quarter of the fifth year. Department of Accounting Parkison, Chairperson; Arndt, Barnhart, Cirtin, Foss, Hanks, Matthew, McCabe, Ounapu, Schmutte, Shivaswamy, Trowbridge, Van Alst, Wagoner, Walker, White Accounting is often described as "the language of business." To make intelligent decisions in the effective planning and controlling of the operations of a business, management must know the effect of transactions on its financial position and its earning power. Accounting, the method by which financial results are summarized and interpreted, furnishes the necessary data. The accountant as a student of management problems endeavors to meet reporting requirements and to present data in terms of management's needs. The study of accounting is a vital part of the educational preparation of any executive and is useful in all types of business careers. Contact with all aspects and levels of business enables the accountant to acquire excellent training for executive leadership. Many and varied careers may be available to the accountant both in the types of organizations and in the areas of specialization he or she may select. The future for men and women trained in accounting is almost unlimited, since the continued growth in the uses of accounting is assured by further expansion and complex development of business activity. The increase of government influence in business affairs and industry's search for increased productivity through its emphasis on cost controls and efficiency cause the need for the services of accountants to increase more rapidly than the number of persons properly qualified to fill the need. A major in accounting provides a foundation for careers as certified public accountants, controllers, financial officers, internal auditors, cost accountants, public administration officers, and teachers of accounting. The departmental major in accounting, within the Professional Arts Curriculum, is for students who want a foundation for an interesting and rewarding career in the broad fields of accounting. Students who wish to prepare for the teaching of accounting in the secondary school will complete the Teacher Education Curriculum with the business education teaching major I. This teaching area is listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. Through graduate study students may improve their abilities as business teachers, prepare to advance to positions in the administration of departments of business education, or advance to teaching positions in institutions of higher education. Second, students may prepare for service as office supervisors or for professional and administrative positions in business communications, general office administration, secretarial capacities, and administrative and office systems. Office systems administration encompasses the advising and facilitating services necessary for effectively planning, organizing, and supervising activities related to office functions. title: Keyboarding for Information Processing
description: Basic keyboarding skills needed for using computer terminals and other office machines with typewriters, tenkey keyboards, or both. For students entering fields in computer science, data processing, information processing, journalism, printing technology, and education. Course will be taught on a credit/nocredit basis. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 111 or equivalent.

title: Beginning Typewriting
description: Principles of touch typewriting with emphasis upon technique and fluency. Only students with no credit in typewriting or with less than one semester of high school typewriting are eligible to receive credit in this course unless special permission is granted by the department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Typewriting
description: Review of typewriting principles with emphasis on the development of speed and accuracy. Focus on problems involved in the application of typewriting skill to simple business situations. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one to two semesters of high school typewriting. Not open to the student who has credit for more than two semesters of high school typewriting.

title: Advanced Typewriting
description: Advanced problems in typewriting including preparation of business letters, manuscripts, tabulations, rough drafts, legal documents, business forms, and duplicated media; continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or three or more semesters of high school typewriting.

title: Office Typewriting
description: Office typing problems with emphasis on preparation of materials by various typewritten media; composition of reports, memoranda, and letters; handwritten and typewritten draft copy. Opportunities for original and creative typing. Continuation of speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Microcomputer Programming for Business Applications
description: Developing skill on microcomputers with display and hard copy capabilities; emphasis on skills to manipulate and program business applications on the microcomputer. Prerequisite: typewriting or keyboarding ability. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 225 and MS 120.

title: Microcomputer Applications for Business
description: Operation of microcomputers in processing business applications using commercial software packages including spread sheet, data base manipulation, and text creation and editing.

title: Introduction to Transcription
description: Designed to teach transcription skills as they apply to the typewritten production of business documents. Application of punctuation, number usage, word choice, spelling, proofreading, and use of reference sources through machine transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or two semesters of high school typewriting.

title: Machine Transcription
description: Designed to teach students to produce mailable copy from transcription equipment. Intensive drill on transcription skills with emphasis on quality production. Application of punctuation, spelling, vocabulary building, letter styles, placement, proofreading, and grammar to the transcription process. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 and 230.

title: Principles of Business Correspondence
description: Principles and basic elements of effective letter writing with emphasis on the psychological approach, reader point of view, positive tone, and appropriate format for personalbusiness letters and job applications.

title: Law Office Administration
description: An analysis of the goals, needs, and problems of administering a legal office. Emphasis on systems for processing information and paperwork, particularly in timekeeping, records administration, and word processing. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 1
description: Fulltime employment in an approved distributive occupation under departmental supervision according to a formal training agreement between the employer and the department. Provides experience in areas in which distributive education teachers instruct. Requires a minimum of 500 hours of approved, supervised, paid employment during a quarter and submission by employer and intern of various employment reports to the supervisor. Open only to students seeking licenses as distributive education teachercoordinators.

title: Internship in Distributive Education 2
description: Full -time employment in an approved distributive occupation under departmental supervision according to a formal training agreement between the employer and the department. Experiences exceed those included in

title: Internship in Distributive Education 3
description: Fulltime employment in an approved distributive occupation under departmental supervision according to a formal training agreement between the employer and the department. Experience exceeds those included in

title: Beginning Shorthand 1
description: Basic symbolic theory fundamentals with emphasis on abbreviated forms. Introduction to the skills of writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one semester of typewriting.

title: Beginning Shorthand 2
description: Completion and/or review of basic theory with increased emphasis on development of skill in taking dictation and transcribing. Prerequisite: BEOA 321 or student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing: and BEOA 112 or two semesters of high school typewriting.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on skill in taking dictation with emphasis on transcribing. Prerequisite: BEOA 322 or student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing; and BEOA 113 or four semesters of high school typewriting.

title: Advanced Shorthand 1
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, transcription, and production of mailable copy. Prerequisite: BEOA 323 or student placement based on departmental advising and/or placement testing; and BEOA 113 or four semesters of high school typewriting.

title: Advanced Shorthand 2
description: Special emphasis on production of mailable copy, and continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 324.

title: Personal Use Word Processing
description: Designed to acquaint nonmajors with basic word processing capabilities of microcomputers. Handson instruction in basic text editing and concepts of information processing. Cannot be substituted for BEOA 331. Prerequisite: BEOA 110 or 111 or high school typing credit.

title: Introduction to Word/Information Processing
description: An introductory course in word/information processing emphasizing why organizations adopt word processing. Focuses on understanding word processing concepts, how they fit into a total information processing network, and the handling of paperwork in today's organizations. Handson experience on electronic typewriters and computer text processing systems. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Electronic Word/Information Processing Systems
description: Studies basic operations of microprocessor visual display systems. Compares features and capabilities of various text processing systems with emphasis on recording, formatting, editing, temporary and permanent storage, revising, merging, proofreading, and logging. Prerequisite: BEOA 114, 231, and 331.

title: Word/Information Processing Applications
description: Emphasizes a more sophisticated operation of microprocessor visual display systems for production of advanced applications. Focuses on problem analysis and coding, programming, and procedures for integration with data processing and other systems. Simulates working conditions in an actual word processing center. Prerequisite: MS 220 and BEOA 332.

title: Electronic Records Processing
description: Procedures for establishing and maintaining numeric and alphanumeric files used in electronic information systems. Handson laboratory experience with office automation software for records processing and data base management. Prerequisite: BEOA 332, 353; MS 220, and permission of department chairperson.

title: Teleprocessing and Office Information Systems
description: Integration of electronic office equipment interconnected through telecommunications including concepts of data communications, electronic mail, and networks. Handson laboratory experience with communicating word processors or microcomputers. Prerequisite: BEOA 332; MS 220, and permission of department chairperson.

title: Reprographics, Voicewriting, and Filing
description: Preparation of impression and multi copy on reproduction machines; comparative costs and appropriateness of reprographic methods; training in machine dictation and transcription; alphabetic filing of business correspondence; and survey of filing methods, equipment, and supplies. Prerequisite: BEOA 113.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems; the nature, function, and use of business papers; knowledge, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining of records of a business office and study of records administration in business and industry. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Principles of Office Supervision
description: Principles of effective office supervision with emphasis on the function of the office and the role of the office supervisor. Prerequisite: MGT 280 or 300.

title: Integrating Word Processing/Data Processing Systems
description: Explores the evolutionary changes within the office. An introduction to the considerations involved in integrating text and data from word processing and data processing input to enhance the information processing output. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 116 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in MS 362.

title: Methods of Teaching for the Distributive Education Teacher
description: The role of the distributive education teacher in the teaching of distributive, basic business, and bookkeeping/ accounting subjects; courses to be taught and their objectives, teaching strategies, instructional materials, and lesson and unit planning. Prerequisite: ACC 202, ECON 201, EDPSY 251, and at least two courses in marketing. Restricted to students with an area in distributive education.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Majors 1 and 2
description: Objectives, planning, methods, techniques, devices for teaching typewriting, basic business, and office machines and office procedures courses. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: BEOA 338. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Methodology of Relevant Work Experiences in Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by persons who will be supervising and directing a cooperative education or a project plan program in distributive education. Prerequisite:

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Accounting, Major 1
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, and devices for teaching accounting. Prerequisite: ACC 202 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Must be taken concurrently with BEOA 490. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Shorthand and Transcription, Major 2
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, and devices for teaching shorthand and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 113 and 323 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Must be taken concurrently with BEOA 490. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Techniques of Coordinating Cooperative Distributive Education Programs
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and coordinating cooperative distributive education programs. Restricted to persons seeking licenses as teachers or coordinators of vocational distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or per mission of the department chairperson.

title: Organization, Management, and Teaching: Vocational Distributive Education
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and managing inschool laboratory programs in vocational distributive education. Restricted to students seeking licenses as teachers or coordinators of vocational distributive education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration: Vocational Distributive Education
description: The principles upon which vocational distributive education is organized, administered, and supervised; the kinds of programs; federal and state regulations; relationships to programs in other vocational areas. Prerequisite: BEOA 382. Restricted to students seeking teaching licenses as distributive education teachers or coordinators.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Education
description: The principles upon which vocational education is organized, administered, and supervised; federal and state regulations; agencies that provide delivery systems for vocational education; rela.- tionship of vocational education to career education, vocational rehabilitation, and programs for persons with special needs. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or 383; or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 392.

title: Survey of the Vocational Education Program Areas
description: An overview of the six program areas in vocational education. Includes program administration and supervision, objectives, the occupations for which training is offered, curricula, equipment and facilities, student selection, inschool laboratories, field training opportunities, and youth organizations. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or 383; 393; or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 392.

title: Microcomputers in Business Education
description: A handson approach to the use of microcomputers in the business education classroom; use of business software; analysis and design of programs for business education courses. Prerequisite: open only to students pursuing a teaching major in business or distributive teacher education or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Computerized Business Document Generation
description: An introduction to text editing capabilities of the computer for designing and processing business documents for the modern office. Development of an understanding of the use of the generalpurpose computer for text processing. Prerequisite: MS 220 or CS 116.

title: Communications for Business Organizations
description: Techniques used in managementoriented internal and external communications. Emphasis on theory, planning, oral and written presentations, audience perceptions, data organization, media selection, and preparation techniques for business letters; and an overview of reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Business Reports: Written and Oral
description: Techniques used in writing both formal and informal managementoriented reports, including collecting, interpreting, summarizing, and synthesizing data. Principles for selection of tabular and graphic data presentations. Includes written and oral presentations of functional reports with an overview of analytical reports. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Employment Communications
description: Determining job requirements and writing a letter of application and résumé; letters requesting reference permission, appreciation of interview, acceptance and refusal of position, and resignation. Includes interview techniques. Open to all students.

title: Secretarial Procedures
description: Operational functions of toplevel professional secretarial work through integration of basic skills, knowledge, and the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 241 and sophomore standing.

title: Secretarial Administration
description: Administrative and supervisory aspects of toplevel professional secretarial work through planning and organizing office functions to achieve smooth and efficient work flow. Emphasizes the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 451.

title: Internship in Office Systems Administration
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Business Education and Office Administration, students majoring in office systems administration will serve during a summer or a quarter in an office environment in a public or private organization. Written reports are required. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Word/Information Processing Management
description: Use of word processing as an integral part of the total information processing network. Development of ability to recognize when and how to use word/information processing to meet an organization's needs. Study of managerial problems involved in establishing and implementing appropriate office systems. Prerequisite: MGT 300 or equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 200 and MGT 300. Not open to the student who has credit in MGT 488.

title: Case Problems in Office Management
description: Develops skill in identifying the key problem of a complicated office situation and in formulating a practical solution to this problem. Stresses the interrelatedness of major office management activities as well as the broad scope of problems pertaining to the office. Prerequisite: BEOA 488 or MGT 488.

title: Principles of Business Education
description: The analysis of a total business education program and the integration of various facets that leads to sound instruction. The impact of past, present, and future legislative and societal developments. Parallel: BEOA 385 or 386. Open only to students approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Distributive Education
description: An investigation of the current status, historical development, philosophy, and principles of distributive education. Components include secondary, postsecondary, and adult distributive education, DECA, and general and specialized curricula. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299. Open only to students pursuing a teaching major in distributive education.

title: Independent Study: Business or Distributive Education; Office Administration
description: For students with excellent academic records who wish to conduct an indepth study in some phase of business education, distributive education, or office administration. The project selected, methods, and credit hours must be approved by the department head and supervising faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.
