Van Meter The College of Sciences and Humanities provides courses and programs for either a liberal education or specialized and professional curricula. The liberal arts programs permit the student to elect more freely and to explore the "idea" subject matter. Liberal stems from the Latin liber, free. By definition, a liberal arts education should free people from ignorance by allowing them to acquire an intelligent grasp of the experiences of the past and an understanding of the interrelationship of branches of knowledge. The individual is educated to think objectively, critically, and creatively. The liberal arts include the study of foreign languages, the physical and social environment, the evolution of Western civilization, the foundations of modern science, and the classical works. The wide range of courses offered by the College of Sciences and Humanities provides the basis for specialized and professional curricula—offered both within the college and in the other colleges requiring service courses. Within the college, preprofessional programs are specified—for medicine, dentistry, engineering, and law. A variety of specialist programs is offered, including medical technology and social work. Also, the departments within the college have programs designed for those planning graduate study in the fields of their choice. The college includes the following departments: Anthropology, Biology, Chemistry, Computer Science, Criminal Justice and Criminology, English, Foreign Languages (Chinese, French, German, Greek, Latin, Spanish), Geography, Geology, History, Journalism, Mathematical Sciences, Natural Resources, Philosophy, Physics and Astronomy, Physiology and Health Science, Political Science, Psychological Science, Social Work, Sociology, Speech Communication, Speech Pathology and Audiology, and Telecommunications. Department of Anthropology Scruton, Chairperson; Coffin, Flores-Meiser, Glenn, Hicks, Izmirlian, Swartz, Whitehead The question of questions for mankind .. . is the ascertainment of the place which Man occupies in nature and of his relations to the universe of things. T. H. Huxley Anthropology means literally "the study of man." Unlike the other social, behavioral, and life sciences, anthropology does not concentrate on only one aspect of human existence, but rather assumes we can achieve a true understanding of the workings of individuals and groups only by an integrated study of biology and culture, past and present, primitive and complex, as a whole. As the discipline has grown it has transcended its original goals. There are four major subdivisions of anthropology: cultural anthropology, archaeology, physical anthropology, and linguistics. Central to ethnology, the basic ingredient of cultural anthropology, is the idea of "culture" as the sum of all things we learn as members of groups. Among the many topics of interest to cultural anthropologists are kinship and community so- Anthropology 195 cial organization, child rearing practices, individual status and roles, ideology, economic and political organization, the interactions between societies and their environments, material goods, and how and why cultures change. The courses in cultural anthropology stress how people make culture and, conversely, how culture shapes people. Hence, humans are studied as products of specific cultures. The results when people conform to or conflict with their cultures' ideals, as well as the reasons for such behavior, are also considered. Archaeology provides time depth for anthropology, particularly for those societies for which there are no written records. Archaeologists are interested in many of the same questions as cultural anthropologists, but the type of evidence they study is different. Cultural anthropology depends heavily on living informants, but archaeologists have only the physical remains left behind, which are much more difficult to interpret. Thus while archaeologists do gather information about social organization, they devote greater attention to subsistence practices, settlement patterns, technology, and the questions of why and how cultures change. The courses in archaeology attempt to show the students what issues archaeology can investigate, how we go about carrying out those investigations, and what we have learned so far. Through the work of archaeologists on culture history we now know far more about the lives of our ancient ancestors than was thought possible a century ago. Physical anthropology pays particular attention to the biological nature not only of humans but also of our nearest relatives, the other primates—prosimians, monkeys, and apes. Within physical anthropology there are further subspecialties: primate paleontology, which tries to trace the development of Homo sapiens and the other primates through fossil studies; primatology, which compares the anatomy, physiology, and behavior of the various primate species; and human biology, which studies growth and development, racial and other genetic differences, and the ways our bodies adapt to our natural and cultural environments. Anthropological linguistics concerns itself with the nature and history of language, an especially complex part of our cultural heritage. The influence of social situations on language performance is studied, as is language's role in the transmission of culture. By combining the studies of these four divisions we are able to see human nature as a whole, a system of interrelated parts. The nature of this system is often made clearest by comparative studies, by stepping outside our own culture or race or time to see how others are constituted. Courses in anthropology form part of the university's general studies program, and even students who have no professional interest in anthropology benefit from the breadth of perspective about our own and other cultures that anthropology provides. There are both introductory and advanced courses pertinent to students majoring in education, business, or liberal arts in other departments. There is also a special teaching major in anthropology as well as anthropology courses that meet part of the requirements for Ancient Studies, Latin American Studies, Afro- American Studies, Medieval and Renaissance Area Studies, Asian Studies, and Native American Studies (based in the department). An undergraduate major or minor in anthropology can be an invaluable background for students going into law school or medical school, or for studies of such subjects as public health, international business, public administration, or urban and regional planning. For students who wish to become professional anthropologists, graduate study is usually required and can lead either to a career in academic teaching and research or to work in a more applied field such as planning and development, environmental assessment, cultural or archaeological preservation, public health, or medical research. The structure of the anthropology major is flexible and thus can accommodate the academic and professional goals of the individual student. Special programs available within the department include opportunities for field experience in archaeological resources management and summer field schools in Indiana archaeology and in ethnography in Jamaica and among the Indians of the American Southwest. Arrangements can be made for field studies anywhere in the world. The student will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 66-69) and by the concentration areas listed below. title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man's place in nature and the relationship of man to other animals, especially monkeys and apes. Anatomy and behavior and their interdependency are presented within an evolutionary framework.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: The origin of man and the rise of civilization as revealed by the discovery of the antiquities of the past. Explanation of recent chronometric and established classical dating methods; methods of excavating sites; interpretation of archaeological remains.

title: Introduction to Language and Linguistics
description: The nature of human language as an object of scientific study, focusing on both the biological and sociocultural bases of language and its structure. Emphasis on language and thought, linguistic analysis of language structure, social and geographical dialects, and language families of the world.

title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Cultures, Languages, and Races of the World
description: An anthropological survey of the peoples of the world and their cultures. Focuses on such major social institutions as economics, religion, the family, and government, presented in terms of major culturegeographic areas. Includes linguistic and racial features.

title: Bio- Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Processes of biological and cultural evolution. The relationship between biological and cultural evolution.

title: Black Africa's Contribution to Western Civilization
description: The African cultural and historical roots of the American black. The origins of the human race, plant and animal domestication, metallurgy, art, and state formation; focus is on West Africa, the source of black population in the United States. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 154.

title: Anthropology-Culture and Women
description: The structure of women's roles in various types of societies from hunting and gathering to urban communities. Examines the relationship of the women's liberation movement in Western cultures to the changing role of women in the industrialized labor forces.

title: Special Topics in Anthropology
description: Detailed analysis of a special problem area in cultural anthropology, archaeology, or physical anthropology. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 hours in one quarter or term.

title: North American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North America. Describes each culture in terms of its major social and economic institutions. Anthropology 197

title: History of Method and Theory in Anthropology
description: Survey of the major ideas and issues of anthropology. Methods and theories from the subfields of archaeology, physical anthropology, linguistics, and cultural anthropology that have been interrelated through the years.

title: Material Culture
description: The material manifestations of culture, stressing primitive technology Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Latin America
description: A general study of the peoples of Mexico, Central America, and South America. Societies discussed range from the ancient Maya, Aztec, and Incas to modern Indians, peasants, and city dwellers. Topics range from religion, family life, and the arts to modernization, urban social problems, and revolution.

title: Contemporary Problems of the American Indian
description: A multivariate analysis of significant political, ecological, economic, and educational problems confronting American Indian tribes today. Individual and group responses to these problems will be studied within pertinent psychological, historical, political, and sociocultural theoretical frameworks.

title: Indians of the American Southwest
description: Surveys prehistoric, historic, and contemporary cultures of selected Southwest Indian groups with an emphasis on culturespecific solutions to common problems caused by their social and natural environment.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to Honors College students only except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Osteology
description: A laboratory course dealing with the human skeleton. Osteological terminology, identification of whole and fragmentary bones, standardized measuring techniques, and the assessment of the age, stature, sex, and race of a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 100.

title: Races of Man
description: The present status and a historical survey of the concept of race as it applies to human populations. Ways in which human populations differ biologically and the adaptive nature of such variation. The distribution and antiquity of living races. Prerequisite: ANTH 100, 120, or 160.

title: Race, Racism, and Ethnicity
description: Scientific investigation of the biological nature of race, race beliefs, and racism, an extreme expression of ethnic bias. Devotes particular attention to the Western world, but also considers similar attitudes in other parts of the world.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man from his nonhuman primate ancestors. The primate fossil record, with particular emphasis on those forms in the human lineage, and the human fossil record. Prerequisite: ANTH 100 or 204, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the Old World from the beginnings of cultural development to the appearance of societies with writing systems. Prerequisite: ANTH 120.

title: New World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. General cultural and specific regional development, with attention to the accomplishments of the Inca, Maya, and Aztecs.

title: Field Methods in Archaeology (Summer Field School)
description: Methods of excavation and field recording studies at the excavation site. Site surveying; principles of excavation: sampling and control, exposing techniques, recording, mapping, and field cataloging. Stresses field observation and interpretation. Requires full time in the field. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Use of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies. Prerequisite: ANTH 421.

title: Advanced Archeological Field Methods
description: Advanced methods of excavation and field recording at the excavation site. Prerequisite: ANTH 421. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Midwest traced through the Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic to the historic period.

title: European Prehistory
description: The prehistory of Europe from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age with an emphasis during the later, protohistoric period on archaeological and ethnographic evidence from the regions to the north and west of the Classical world. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Cultural Resources Management
description: The special problems of what has also been called conservation archaeology, including relevant federal and state laws, regulations, and agencies, reconnaissance and sampling methods; project budgeting; elements in the environmental impact statement; and other responsibilities of the consultant archaeologist. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120. 421, or equivalent.

title: History and Philosophy of Archaeological Theory
description: Examination of the theoretical trends in archaeology. Survey of the areas of taxonomic, spatiotemporal. and cultural archaeology. Comparison of the tenets of historical or traditional and processual or "new" archaeology. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 120.

title: Historical Archaeology
description: Covers the major themes and philosophies of historical archaeology as well as the related literature and sources of information on architectural features and items of material culture likely to be encountered in the course of excavation.

title: Personality and Culture
description: Introduction to a major area of anthropological interest and investigation during the past three decades. Studies a field of anthropology that has grown out of recent efforts to unite studies of individual behavior and group or cultural behavior. Discussion of the nature of human personality and its origins, both in the individual and the species. Particular stress on the phenomenon of the model personality type.

title: Witchcraft, Magic, and Religion
description: An anthropological study of mankind's ageold concern with life, death, sickness, and the unknown. Discusses man's attempt to control his life through supernatural beings, prayer, sacrifice, and techniques of magic and witchcraft. Examines possible origins of religious beliefs and how these are part of the fabric of social life in primitive and contemporary societies.

title: Social Organization
description: Opportunity for indepth study of man's social systems. Emphasis on the function of these systems and important grouping principles. The crosscultural method is employed extensively.

title: Anthropological Theory
description: Historical development of concept and theory in anthropology. Various theories and schools of thought will be examined intensively. Prerequisite: ANTH 100, 120, and 160.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the effect of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents and European civilization.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Field School in Ethnography and Ethnology
description: Methods of carrying out field research in cultural anthropology; techniques of establishing contact and rapport; interview and observation methods; problem formulation, data recording, and data preparation. The student may spend full or half time in the field. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Culture Change
description: Discussion focuses on the major processes of cultural change such as cultural evolution, revolution, ecological adaptation, conquest, diffusion, mass communications, economic aid and development, and other timely and appropriate topics.

title: The Development of Near-Eastern Cultures
description: Traces the development of cultures in the Near East as revealed by archaeology and explores the presentday cultural variability.

title: The Peoples and Cultures of India
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the anthropology (social organization, cultural system) of South Asia with special stress on India.

title: Introduction to Folklore
description: An introduction to the genres of folklore with an emphasis on the anthropological study of folktales, legends, and myth; methodological and theoretical approaches to their study; their function in society; and their usefulness to anthropologists. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Political Anthropology
description: Focuses on the dimension of social interaction involving the articulation and aggregation of interests within the political community. Emphasis on primitive and peasant communities (smallscale societies), drawing parallels to Western society where appropriate.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to a formal) view of economic behavior. Focus on social organizational units such as lineages and clans that in primitive and peasant societies are engaged in productive and distributive activities.

title: Anthropology of the Film
description: Focuses on function and content of the ethnographic film from its inception to the present, including some contemporary documentary films. Stress on the capacity of the film medium to create a visual culture in contemporary society and to record primitive and peasant lifestyles.

title: Art and Anthropology
description: Provides a crosscultural coverage of major preliterate art traditions and introduces students to art in cultural contexts.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Acquaints the prospective teacher with basic concepts in cultural anthropology and provides the conceptual and analytical tools to understand various cultural settings. Examines ways in which cultural institutions—e.g., family, religion, politics, economy—might impinge on educational processes.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar in Anthropology
description: Designed to familiarize students with current theoretical and methodological issues in anthropology. Demands active participation in the discussion of those issues. Provides the setting for students to explore their own theoretical interests and present them coherently. Prerequisite: ANTH 364.

title: Field Anthropology of Distant Areas
description: Anthropological field study of distant geographical regions. Exploration and field work may be involved, and travel to the staging area will probably be by airline.

description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating non Western techniques to Western counterparts. MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY This programs leads to a B.S. degree with a major in medical technology. The major outlined below is completed in the first three years. The senior year consists of a twelvemonth clinical laboratory program in an accredited hospital school of medical technology. Fortyfive quarter hours of credit are granted for the successful completion of the senior year. General studies, physical education, and elective courses added to the above must total 186 hours for graduation. Therefore, the student must have completed a minimum of 141 hours before beginning the clinical year. Minimum (national) requirements for admission to the clinical year are 24 hours of biology (including microbiology and immunology), 24 hours of chemistry (including organic or biochemistry, or both), and 4 hours of math. These are included in the departmental major outlined below. Strongly recommended electives are CS 116 and PHYSL 211. Other helpful electives are BIO 361, CHEM 300, MGT 280, PHYCS 110, 112, 114. The university has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with the following Indiana hospitals: Ball Memorial Hospital (Muncie); St. Joseph's Memorial Hospital (Kokomo); St. Francis Hospital (Beech Grove); Parkview Hospital, Lutheran Hospital, and St. Joseph Hospital (Fort Wayne); Methodist Hospital, Community Hospital, and St. Vincent's Hospital (Indianapolis); and St. Mary Medical Center (Gary). For information about any specific hospital program students may write to the Education Coordinator, School of Medical Technology, of the preferred hospital. The number of applicants to any school of medical technology usually exceeds the capacity of the school. Selection of students is made entirely by the school of medical technology and is based upon several considerations, including scholastic standing, personal interviews, and recommendations. Completion of the first three years does not guarantee admission to the clinical year; students are therefore encouraged to plan an alternative degree choice that may be completed in the fourth year. Reapplication for a clinical year may then be made if the student wishes. To qualify for certification as a medical technologist, the student may apply to any recognized certification agency. Documentation requirements (transcripts, etc.) vary among these agencies. The student must then pass a national certification examination. Conferral of the B.S. degree does not depend on the certification exam. The medical technologist is prepared to do laboratory work of many kinds in the clinical laboratory, including bacteriology, chemistry, serology, and blood bank technology. There are positions calling for this preparation in hospital laboratories, physicians' and surgeons' clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories. There are also opportunities for work in research laboratories and in commercial companies making biological products. PRE-FORESTRY PROGRAM The preforestry program offered by the Department of Biology is designed for students who wish to major in forestry and prefer to satisfy the preprofessional requirements at Ball State University. Students at Purdue enrolled in the preforestry program in the Department of Forestry and Natural Resources apply to the professional program at the end of their sophomore year. Preforestry students at Ball State may also apply during their sophomore year for admission when they have completed 98 credit hours. To be considered for admission to the Purdue program, Ball State students will be expected to complete successfully the following courses. BIO 111, 112, 211, 212, 313, 448; BOT 380, 470; CHEM 110, 111, 112; CS 118; ECON 200; ENG 103, 104; LA 217; MATH 108, 112, 114, 165, 166; NR 221; SPCH 210; and additional humanities electives in such subjects as English, foreign languages, history, philosophy, and political science. Applications for admission into the twoyear professional program at Purdue should be filed before December 1 for consideration for admission the following fall. The application letter should include a Purdue Office of Admissions form, a Department of Forestry and Natural Resources application form, and a transcript of courses taken at Ball State. The student who wishes to earn a degree and prepare for teaching in the secondary schools of Indiana as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will follow the secondary pattern of the Teacher Education Curriculum, will elect a teaching area major or teaching major, and will combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. Thus the student prepares for teaching in the field of the elected teaching concentration. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: BIO 311, 314, 492; CC 215; CHEM 360 or 463; SPCH 210; and ZOOL 447. Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in premedical preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many medical schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other medical schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet specific requirements of the medical schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of the firstyear medical school credits of the Ball State University major is Indiana University. Students should take the Medical College Admission Test in the Spring Quarter fifteen months before their expected entrance into medical school and should complete the formal application during the following summer, twelve months in advance. Premedical counseling is available in the Department of Biology. Departmental major in premedical preparation, 63-67 hours BIO 111, 112, 211, 312; CHEM (110, 111, 112, 225) or (113, 114, 115, 223), CHEM (230, 231, 232) or (233, 234, 235), 300; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ZOOL 330 63-67 hrs. PREDENTAL PREPARATION Although approximately 90 percent of the students entering dental school will have had four years of predental work, those with outstanding qualifications may be admitted after only three years. The student who wishes to qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry at the close of three years of predental preparation will elect the Professional Arts Curriculum, will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum in three years at Ball State University, and will use the credit earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Dentistry (45 hours) to meet the senioryear course requirements of the Professional Arts Curriculum. The following courses are recommended for elective credit: AED 200; ANAT 430; BIO 213, 314; CHEM 232, 360; CC 215; SPCH 210; and courses in business management. In addition to the basic science requirements, students entering the Indiana University School of Dentistry will be required to have credit in three quarters of English, including two quarters of composition; one quarter of interpersonal communication (SPCH 240 is recommended); one quarter of introductory psychology; and one quarter of business management or personnel management (MGT 380 is recommended). Since the first three years of the Professional Arts Curriculum with the departmental major in predental preparation cover all or most of the basic requirements of many dental schools, that much of the curriculum may be taken by students with other dental schools as their objectives. Modifications will be made to enable students to meet the specific requirements of the dental schools of their choice. However, the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation for the use of the firstyear dental school credits of the Ball State University major is Indiana University-. Although it is possible for the student to graduate with a departmental major in predental preparation, it is highly recommended that the predental student take the additional courses required to qualify for a departmental major in biology or chemistry, or in any other area in which the student has a strong interest, because the number of applicants to any school of dentistry far exceeds the capacity of the school and an alternative goal is important. One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory performance on the Dental Admission Test given by the American Dental Association. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the admission test. The test should be taken in the Spring Quarter, fifteen months before the student's expected entrance into dental school, but preferably only after completing the required biology and chemistry courses. Application for admission to dental school should be completed in the summer, twelve months in advance. Predental counseling is available in the Department of Biology. Departmental major in predental preparation, 57 hours ANAT 320; BIO 111, 112, 211, 311; CHEM 110, 111, 112, 230, 231; PHYCS 110, 112, 114; ZOOL 330 57 hrs. PREPHARMACY PROGRAM The Prepharmacy Program is for students who wish to apply for admission to the Butler University College of Pharmacy or the Purdue University School of Pharmacy'. The courses designated, when completed satisfactorily, will meet the preprofessional curricular requirements of Purdue at the end of the first year or those requirements of Butler at the end of either the first or second year. At both Purdue and Butler the combined prepharmacypharmacy program requires five years. The student is advised, however, that the number of applicants to any college of pharmacy exceeds the capacity of the school and that a selection of students is therefore necessary, taking into consideration such qualifications as scholastic standing, character, and professional aptitude. The student should become familiar with the admission and residence requirements set forth in the bulletins of Butler and Purdue universities. These prepharmacy programs do not lead to graduation from Ball State University. They merely provide a student with an approved sequence of courses for the first one or two years of the complete fiveyear program. Furthermore, physical education is not a part of this program for students who plan to transfer to Purdue, but it is for those who will go to Butler. A student who drops out of the prepharmacy program and elects to follow a degree program of Ball State University will be expected to meet the physical education and general course requirements of the university curriculum chosen. A careful arrangement of the program for each year is essential so that courses may be completed in sequence and in the allotted time. It is particularly important that general chemistry be completed in the freshman year. Mathematics, including calculus, is highly desirable. Copies of the programs may be obtained from the chairperson of the biology department or the member of the biology department appointed by the chairperson to serve as preprofessional adviser for students enrolled in these programs. There are minor differences in requirements between the School of Pharmacy at Purdue and the College of Pharmacy at Butler. Students planning to apply to Purdue's School of Pharmacy should make arrangements early in the Autumn Quarter to take the Pharmacy College Admission Test.

title: Man and the Life Sciences
description: An introductory course designed for students not majoring in science. Emphasizes the human and social aspects of biology: reproduction, birth control, genetic counseling, behavior, evolution, pollution, radiation, and energy. Course activities include study in a selfpaced, aurally guided multimedia learning center. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 102 or 112.

title: Biological Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles of biology as they relate to energy requirements and reproductive processes of living organisms, including the study of plant and animal adaptation as it influences survival and natural selection. Principles of ecology and conservation with emphasis on the human role in the environment. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Field and Classroom Experiences in Biology
description: Study of living things, their growth patterns, responses, and adaptations. Open to students interested in direct experience with living things with special emphasis on activities in the woods and greenhouse that can be duplicated in elementary classrooms. No regularly scheduled laboratory. 111.Principles of Biology 1. (4) Designed for biology, allied health, and other science majors. Emphasis at cellular level: chemical and physical organization of life; cell structure and function; bioenergetics; cell division; genetics and the molecular basis of inheritance, gene expression, and protein synthesis. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry, one quarter of college chemistry, or equivalent.

title: Principles of Biology 2
description: Continuation of Biology 111. Emphasis at organism, population, and community levels: population genetics, evolution of species; prokaryotes, eukaryotes; plant and animal diversity stressing tissues, systems, and physiology of land plants and vertebrates; ecology, including human ecology and environmental biology. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Symposium in Biology
description: An examination of some of the critical biological issues confronting contemporary society. Open only to freshmen participating in the Honors Program except by permission of the department chairperson or the director of the Honors Program.

title: Animal Biology
description: Major animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification, and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. May require field work in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Plant Biology
description: Major plant groups with emphasis on structure, function, classification, and phylogenetic relationships. Some consideration is given to local forms. May require field work in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative protozoa, bacteria, viruses, fungi, and algae. Two lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation emphasizing meiosis, Mendelian inheritance and probability, sex and gene transmission and expression, linkage and crossingover, the nature of the hereditary material, and gene action. Some attention to human and applied genetics. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Analysis of developmental concepts and phenomena, using current theories of biological information usage. Descriptive vertebrate embryology is emphasized in the laboratory work. Some attention is given to metamorphosis, regeneration, and neoplasia. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 211, 311; CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ecology
description: The relationships of organisms to physical, chemical, and biotic factors. Interactions are examined at the population and community levels of organization. Aquatic, saline, and terrestrial ecosystems are considered in terms of species composition, dominant organisms, climatic factors, and land use patterns. One twoday field trip required in addition to regular lab periods.

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including the nature of the organization of the cell, basic bioenergetics and enzyme function, cell environment, membrane structure and function, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisite: CHEM 130 or 230 and BIO 213 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Laboratory Techniques in Biological Research
description: Principles and applications of procedures used in biological research. Emphasizes methods of preparation of solutions, using standard curves, determination of rates of enzyme reactions, separation and identification of cell organelles, identification of cell metabolites, and separation of macromolecules. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Immunology
description: Indepth examination of basic immunology and the immune system, including subjects such as immunoglobulins, macrophages, lymphocytes and other lymphoid cells, regulatory interactions, tolerance, immunity, autoimmunity, immunogenetics, and clinical immunology. Emphasizes practical experience in techniques in the laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and one course in organic chemistry.

title: Honors Colloquium in Biology
description: Exploration of selected issues in biology with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students except by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Biology
description: Practical application of biology in a variety of situations including biology instruction as undergraduate teaching assistants and discussion leaders, and practical experience in government or industrial laboratories and field stations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Designed to integrate and enhance understanding of basic principles of biology. Stresses recent discoveries in biology and their implications in the biological sciences. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned with permission of the department chairperson.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Radiobiology
description: Familiarizes the student with the nature of radiation, its effect on living tissue, the ways in which the isotopes can be used in research projects, and problems related to the use of nuclear power and radiation in the environment. Prerequisite: BIO 211, 212; CHEM 130 or 230; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Biophysics
description: The study of biologic phenomena with laboratory emphasis on physical methods of studying the structure of biological molecules and physical forces important in biologic systems. Topics include laws of thermodynamics, properties of macromolecular solutions, transport processes, electrophoresis, absorption and emission radiation, ultrasound, principles of various chromatographic procedures. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; CHEM 130 or 230; and MATH 112.

title: Evolution
description: The principles of evolution. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111.

title: Bacteriology
description: Study of bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques in culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisites: BIO 213, and CHEM 130 or 230, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Cytology
description: Recent developments and methodologies concerning the structural organization of plant and animal cells and cellular organelles. Prerequisite: BIO 311. Prerequisite recommended: chemistry courses through organic.

title: Applied Microbiology
description: The study of microorganisms that cause beneficial or detrimental changes in food, dairy, and industrial products. Microbiological principles involved in the study of microorganisms in food, dairy, and industrial production in addition to production methodology. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Biometry
description: Principles and application of statistics to biological problems. The use of parametric and nonparametric tests of significance in solving biological problems. Practice in the analysis of data and the interpretation of biological experiments. Prerequisite: MATH 108 or equivalent.

title: Advanced Genetics
description: A second course in genetics with emphasis on recent advances. Prerequisite: BIO 311, CHEM 230. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 314.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Mankind
description: Current problems in human heredity. Chromosome aberrations and developmental abnormalities. DNA, the genetic code, and sickle cell anemia. Consanguineous marriages and genetic defects. Mendelian principles applied to humans. Pedigrees and probability. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems associated with recent advances in genetics.

title: Molecular Biology
description: The structure and function of macromolecules found in living things. Emphasizes the threedimensional structure of molecules and biological control mechanisms. Investigates various recent models for enzyme mechanisms, DNA replication, protein synthesis, and membrane structure and function. Prerequisite: BIO 314 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Cellular and Molecular Biology
description: Study of recent developments in cell development and differentiation, DNA and RNA research, membrane biology, cellular and molecular evolution, and cellular control mechanisms. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Bioenergetics
description: The study of flow of energy in biological systems with emphasis on application of laws of thermodynamics to biological processes, energy production metabolism in chemotrophs and phototrophs, and the major uses of energy in biological systems. Prerequisite: BIO 314, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Microtechnique 1
description: Methods and preparation of biological materials for teaching and research, including work in hematology, vital staining, photomicrography, and preparation of smears, squashes, and whole mounts. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and two courses in college chemistry.

title: Microtechnique 2
description: Preparation of sectioned tissues and histochemical treatment of materials, including the preparation of paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Recommended for students in research or in medical or laboratory fields. Three twohour laboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and 12 quarter hours of college chemistry.

title: Museum Techniques
description: Methods of preparing plant and animal specimens for display. Maintenance of museum records. Use of museum materials for educational and research functions. Taxidermy not included. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Limnology
description: The dimensions of the physical, chemical, and biological aspects of inland waters. One twohour laboratory per week and two or three fullday field trips devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 313 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Water Pollution Biology
description: Water pollution with emphasis on analysis of trophic structure in polluted and nonpolluted ecosystems. Ecological change and eutrophication as affected by pollutants from industrial, municipal, urban, and rural sources. Prerequisite: BIO 480 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Microbiology
description: Microorganisms indigenous to aquatic ecosystems and their role in nutrient cycling. Emphasizes organisms involved in nitrogen, sulfur, carbon, and iron transformations. The morphology, physiology, and ecology of specific organisms. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Marine Biology
description: Introduction to marine environments. Properties: seawater, hydrodynamics. Phytoplankton/benthic plants. Primary production, nutrient cycles. Marine animals, surveys of major taxa, food resources. Adaptations for life on the bottom, open water, intertidal zones, estuaries, abyssal regions. Population sampling and analysis. Problems of overexploitation and pollution.

title: Bioethical Decision Making
description: Analysis of bioethical problems such as evolution, genetic engineering, and food and famine, generated by the application of biological and biotechnological knowledge and research using a confluent, developmental methodology. Prerequisite: junior standing and the completion of option 2 of the general studies science requirement or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned; as much as 4 hours of credit may be taken at one time. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Forestry
description: A survey course in forestry with emphasis on management, problems, and use of midwestern wood lots. May include field work in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Plant Anatomy
description: Origin and structure of cells, tissues, and organs of higher plants. Prerequisite: BIO 212.

title: Plant Morphology
description: Forms, life cycles, and evolution of the major plant groups. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
description: The identification of native flowering plants. Emphasis on the distinguishing features of the major plant groups and use of manuals. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Economic Botany
description: The cultivation, processing, environmental requirements, and use of plants and plant derivatives for food, drugs, dwellings, clothing, and power.

title: Ornamental Plants
description: Identification and uses of ornamental trees, shrubs, vines, and annuals. Selection, special characteristics, adaptability, and maintenance of ornamentals.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the propagation and cultivation of plants in homes, schools, gardens, and greenhouses.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on pathogenic forms. Discusses methods for identification of fungi along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BIO 212 and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Intermediate Plant Physiology
description: A continuation of BOT 451 with emphasis on independent study of detailed physiological mechanisms. Prerequisite: BOT 451.

title: Dendrology
description: The identification and site characterization of woody plants with an emphasis on midwestern tree species. Use of botanical features and keys in field identification. Correlation of species with site factors, plant diseases, climatic parameters, associate species, and geographical distribution. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection, identification, and preservation of plants from freshwater ecosystems. Stresses the morphology, physiology, and ecology of these plants to explain their distribution in nature. Studies techniques for measuring the growth and abundance of aquatic plants. Includes one or two weekend field trips to study aquatic plants in their natural habitats. Prerequisite: BIO 212 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Comparative Vertebrate Anatomy
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and relationships of vertebrates. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Invertebrate groups. Phylogeny, comparative morphology, and life histories. Three lecture periods and two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisite: BIO 211 and CHEM 130 or 230.

title: Ornithology
description: Field identification, classification, behavior, and economic relationships of birds. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 211.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 211.

title: Ichthyology
description: The study of fish with emphasis on identification, classification, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Emphasizes Indiana species, but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Herpetology
description: The natural history, identification, systematics, and distribution of amphibians and reptiles. Field work required. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The behavior of individuals and of populations. The economic relationships of mammals. May require additional field work, including one extended field trip.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth and arthropod parasites of animals. Emphasis on identification, life cycles, and hostparasite relationships. Prerequisite: BIO 211 and 213, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ethology
description: The introductory study of animal behavior, its evolution and ecological adaptiveness. The functional role of animal signals and strategies in their environment. Development of research hypotheses, collection and analysis of ethological data. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Field Zoology
description: The field study of animals—terrestrial and aquatic, invertebrate and vertebrate, microscopic and macroscopic—with emphasis on collection and identification of noninsect invertebrates. Three twohour fieldlaboratorylecture periods per week. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Protozoology
description: An introduction to aspects of the morphology, physiology, ecology, and development of protozoa. Prerequisite: BIO 211 and 213. 483. Wildlife Biology. (4) The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on the terrestrial vertebrates of the United States. The management and harvest of wildlife. May require additional field work, including one extended field trip.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identification, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasis on aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress. Prerequisite: ZOOL 441 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary School
description: Methods of teaching science concepts, process skills, and scientific attitudes are developed through direct experiences. Recent elementary science texts, courses of study, and curricular materials are examined and used as are experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and special methods.

title: The Teaching of Science in the Junior High School
description: Recent curriculum developments in junior high school science. Science curriculum instruction related to the physical, mental, and emotional characteristics of the junior high school student. Prerequisite: 36 hours of credit in courses in the sciences.

title: Teaching Science in the Early Childhood and Primary Grades
description: Analysis of the cognitive, psychomotor, and affective processes inherent in science investigations for young children. Handson activities with science materials appropriate for early childhood and primary children. Designed primarily for students in early childhood/primary education programs. Prerequisite: 12 hours of science or permission of the department chairperson.

title: The Teaching of Science in the Secondary School
description: Philosophy and methods in science teaching. Emphasis on laboratory investigations. Concepts and conceptual schemes in science. Levels of organization in secondary school science courses. Evaluation of learning in science. Supplies, equipment, and facilities. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum and 20 hours in biology, chemistry, earth science, or physics content courses or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Scienceoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of science, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of science in the secondary school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Up to five hours of experience in public schools may be required. Prerequisite or parallel: SCI 395 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 399.

title: History and Philosophy of Science
description: The history of science. Consideration is given to the impact of science on mankind, the part science plays in bringing about general knowledge, and how science influences decision making. Department of Chemistry Joyner, Chairperson; Ault, Behforouz, Bock, Johnson, Kruger, Meiser, Pyle, Rybarczyk, Sousa, Storhoff, Warnes The Department of Chemistry offers a broad program to meet the diverse needs of students. title: Man and Chemistry
description: Introductory treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as organization and language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature and classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these to everyday living. Four class meetings weekly. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 105, 110, 113.

title: General Chemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Description of elements and compounds; their structure, bonding, and stoichiometry with the main emphasis on the solution chemistry of electrolytes. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 110.

title: Organic and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of both organic chemistry and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences or related areas. Three lectures, one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 105 or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, and the nature of matter stressed. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or the equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 113. 111.General Chemistry. description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 233. Lecture material covers the chemistry of common functional groups, stereochemistry, and the carbohydrates. title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 234. Lecture material covers the chemistry of amines and phenols with discussion of selected advanced topics. description: Treatment of practical chemical problems of widely varied mathematical types, including dimensional and error analysis, graphical presentation, chemical examples of simple calculus procedures, series, and symmetry. title: Analytical Chemistry in Foods and Nutrition

title: Physical Chemistry 1

Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology Brodt, Chairperson; Hendricks, Hewitt, Neiman, Smith The Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology offers a broad range of courses relevant to our system of adult and juvenile justice for both the preprofessional and the liberal arts student. The departmental major leads to a Bachelor of Science degree when combined with required and elective courses in other disciplines. The Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology also offers a twoyear Associate in Arts degree and a departmental minor. The student gains a perspective about such subjects as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, and our system of criminal justice. The student is also given a workable combination of theory and practical experience in law enforcement and corrections. Another objective of the criminal justice and criminology major is to give students the opportunity to prepare themselves as preprofessionals for firstlevel positions in law enforcement, probation, parole, and institutional or community treatment settings, or for future graduate study in related areas. The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and employment: law enforcement, probation services offered by both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, Parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. Law enforcement officers are employed at three levels of government: local, state, and federal. Local law enforcement officers include municipal policemen and policewomen as well as deputy sheriffs. On the state level, all states hire officer candidates for state police departments. On the federal level, approximately forty agencies employ persons with training in law enforcement as well as in other areas of specialization. The increasing need for law enforcement in our society indicates that future employment, particularly on the local levels, will be good. Probation, which is essentially supervision of adjudicated adult criminals and juvenile delinquents, is a service offered by almost all of our adult felony and iuveniie courts. Realizing the increasing necessity for successful college graduates to express themselves clearly in writing, the Department of English requires all students to develop skill in expository writing. This is a primary purpose of both general education classes and the classes in advanced composition. For students interested in creative writing, special courses are provided on both the undergraduate and graduate levels. These students are also encouraged to contribute to the department's literary magazine, Prism Light, and to compete for annual awards made possible through the Rocking Horse competition and Lambda Iota Tau, the English honorary fraternity. The English Qualifying Test is a requirement for students whose major or minor is English and must be passed in order to receive departmental approval for continuation with an area in English. Students should contact the director of undergraduate studies about this requirement early in their programs. Students receiving credit for ENG 103 and/or ENG 104, based upon the scores obtained on ACT, APP, CEEB, SAT, and/or departmental examinations, will be notified by their curricular advisers and will begin their sequences with the proper courses. Honors students pursuing English curricula may substitute credit in ENG 201, 202, or 203 for ENG 206. title: Level 3 Grammar
description: Oral and written practice in graded grammatical exercises. Review of elementary grammar. Prerequisite: ENEFL 122 or approval of program director.

title: Level 3 Readings
description: Readings in intermediate EFL texts. Emphasis on linguistic and cultural problems of readings in English as a foreign language. Prerequisite: ENEFL 123 or approval of program director.

title: Level 3 Conversation
