title: Man and the Geological Environment
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to mankind's environmental and resource problems. Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Geology 245

title: Historical Geology
description: An introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Emphasis on North America. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Geology of the National Parks and Monuments in the United States
description: Geologic description and interpretation of the national parks and monuments in the United States emphasizing geologic history and process.

title: Geology of Energy Resources
description: An examination of geologic processes that form and govern the distribution of oil, gas, coal, uranium ores, and geothermal energy sources; exploration strategies; resource evaluation; and case history studies of active energy extraction developments. Several field trips are required. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Environmental Geology
description: Examines geologic materials and processes affecting the human environment. Discusses geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, surface water hydrology, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Local area field trips and field mapping. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoecologic significance. Emphasis on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, and MATH 112 (or high school equivalent) or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments in and near the campus and visits to places of pertinent course value within the state. Normal scheduling is Saturday mornings. Prerequisite: major or minor in geography, geology, or earth science, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to the resolution of geologic problems. Assignments include accumulation and interpretation of field observations and preparation of geologic maps, crosssections, and stratigraphic sections. Requires a report of investigations for one of the mapping projects. The course is conducted during a fiveweek period in June and July in South Dakota and Wyoming. Prerequisite: GEOL 230 and 382 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Regional Geology Field Study
description: The geologic history, stratigraphy, structural geology, geomorphology, and economic geology of a selected region. Students will travel through the area. Normal scheduling is second summer term in a selected area outside Indiana. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 and 102 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geomorphology of North America
description: Emphasis on the occurrence, description, and geological and geomorphological problems of the geomorphic regions of North America. Nearby area field trips. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite : GEOL 101 and MATH 12 or permision of the department chairperson.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans and related topics. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to refraction and reflection seismology; magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods. Emphasis on applying geophysical methods to such problems as energy resources, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, and pollution detection. Includes laboratory exercises and field investigations. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geotectonics
description: Plate tectonics and global geophysics; Earth's origin, age, gravity, geomagnetism and paleomagnetism, geothermal heat, seismology, dynamics, and internal structure; current ideas of seafloor spreading, plate tectonics and mountain building; application to finding new energy and mineral resources. Emphasizes recent developments in geotectonics and the study of individual tectonic regions such as the Appalachians, Rocky Mountains, Alps, and Urals.

title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for classifying and interpreting the origins of rocks. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks for the purpose of determining their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: The structure, rocks, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Emphasis upon physical processes involved, especially Pleistocene glaciation. Designed for nonearth science majors, particularly teachers.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, MATH 108, NR 211, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Principles of Geochemistry
description: Composition of the earth. Distribution of elements in minerals and rocks. Principles governing migration and concentration of elements. Introduction to isotope geology and geochemical prospecting. Prerequisite: GEOL 230, CHEM 112 or 114 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. Designed to supplement existing geoscience and computer science courses using BASIC and FORTRAN programs in various geoscience data collecting, calculation, and graphic display applications. Prerequisite: open only to students with areas in geography and geology. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Without a knowledge of our past, we would have no landmarks, no points of reference, and no foundations on which to build a modern world. The history major may be undertaken to attain professional, academic, or cultural objectives, including preparation for graduate study and advanced degrees, teaching licenses; prelaw or premedical preparation; and qualification for appointments in business, industry, civil service, libraries, museums, art galleries, archives, and other cultural institutions. Courses in history are designed to meet the needs of students in several fields of study. The department offers a broad selection of courses in the general studies program. It offers introductory and advanced courses for students majoring in education or in liberal arts in other departments of the university. It also presents courses designed to give a broad and thorough training in the various history programs. Students majoring in any of the social sciences find history courses especially useful. The graduate programs are built on the foundation of undergraduate preparation. Students intending to do graduate work in history are urged to take the Bachelor of Arts degree. The master's and doctoral degrees require intensive directed study in history aimed at depth of understanding. title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: Surveys the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decision makers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Introduction to Civilization of Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: Western Civilization
description: A survey of the major themes and developments in the evolution of Western civilization from its origins to the present with emphasis on key problems, critical turningpoints, recurring issues, and cultural growth and heritage. Special stress on the character and crises confronting the Western world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. 151.Roots of the Western Tradition. (4) A survey of the principal historical and cultural developments of ancient and medieval times to 1300, with emphasis on those institutions and events of Western civilization that furnish our own cultural heritage.

title: Birth of the Modern World
description: From 1300 to 1815, explores such major topics as the Renaissance, the Reformation, the rise of modern nations, discovery and exploration, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, nationalism, and the Industrial Revolution.

title: The World in Recent Times
description: Major world events and issues since 1815; industrialization and resulting ideologies; background, causes, and results of the two world wars; the rise and decline of the colonial empires with emerging nationalism; the impact of democratic, fascist, and communistic doctrines; nineteenthand twentiethcentury trends in thought; attempts at international organization and cooperation.

title: Black Africa's Contribution to Western Civilization
description: Investigates the African cultural and historical roots of American blacks. Origins of the human race, plant and animal domestication, metallurgy, art, and state formation, focusing on West Africa, the source of the black population of the United States. Not open to the student who has credit in ANTH 270.

title: Modern World Leaders
description: Biographical studies of key Western and non Western men and women in historical perspective. Examines the leaders' characteristics, philosophies, leadership capabilities, and their resultant contributions to politics, religion, the military, business, and the arts.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stresses nineteenthand twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East—the Arab World, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems: imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South and Southeast Asia
description: South Asia (Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka) and Southeast Asia (Burma, Thailand, Laos, Kampuchea (Cambodia), Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines) since 1800: a brief description of factors influential in past history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, independence, and modernization.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Studies in Non Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: Foundations of the United States, 1492-1829
description: Survey of American history to 1829.

title: Development of the United States, 1829-1900
description: Survey of the history of the United States from the era of Andrew Jackson to 1900.

title: The Recent Past in the United States, 1900 to the Present
description: Political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have composed the history of the United States since 1900.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of resource use in the United States by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource use has shaped society.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of the Negro in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing con -ceptions of theiroles, atitudes toward women, women's ideas abouthemselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Uses documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research instead of the regular lecture and textbook method. Students through their own research learn how the historian defines areas of research; selects sources, both primary and secondary; evaluates materials; and describes the findings. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The History of American Popular Culture
description: Historical overview of the development of American popular culture. Basic theories, approaches, and topics in popular culture with special attention to amusements, movies, pop music, magazines, pulp novels, and television. Focuses on the relationship of popular culture to American cultural and social history.

title: History of Latin America, 1825 to Present
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis upon contemporary Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.

title: Introduction to Public History
description: An overview of opportunities for nonteaching historyrelated careers in preservation, archival work, records management, museology, historical editing, living history and public parks programs, corporate history, and others. Students make a concentrated study of at least one field of public history and have contact with working professionals. Open to all students.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to the history profession. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or with private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: American Leaders
description: A biographical approach to American history. An evaluation of some of the leading Americans and their contributions in the fields of politics, business, letters, the arts, pure and applied science, and education.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American/Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Provides students with a historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Selected Topics in Military History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular period, topic, or issue in the field of military history with emphasis on materials not covered in established courses. Exact content announced in advance of each offering. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others may enroll by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Colonial History of the United States, 1492-1756
description: The ideas and institutions developed in British North America that in the course of colonial development formed a basis for American culture.

title: The American Revolution, 1756-1789
description: Transformation of American society and politics in the era of the American Revolution with emphasis on the origins of the revolution, the development of a democratic society, and the Constitution of the United States.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis on the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism Versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis on the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: The United States from World War I through World War II
description: An examination of the reaction of the American people to a society changing rapidly under the impact of two major wars, the Great Depression, and continuing industrialization and urbanization.

title: Recent United States History: 1945 to the Present
description: A study of the role of the United States in the modern world and an examination of the efforts of America to preserve a society that is prosperous and humane while adjusting to technological change and continuing social and intellectual ferment. 415.History of Indiana. (4) Exploration, colonization, and development of the state from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Antebellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum South.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans -Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers and the events that influenced their migration, and the effect of these events and the frontier on national development.

title: Indians in U.S. History
description: Survey of Indian and white relations from 1492 to the present, focusing on the Indian wars, treaty making, various types of Indian and white interaction, and the development of federal and state Indian policy.

title: The History of Canada
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of Canada from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasizes the events leading to the establishment of Canada and United States-Canadian relations and problems.

title: History of Mexico
description: Mexico from the pre-Columbian era to the present with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Revolution of 1910.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History Since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I.

title: American Life and Thought, 1607 -1865
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from the colonial period to the Civil War, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American Life and Thought, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from Reconstruction to the present, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisite: ECON 200 or 201 or a combination of ECON 200 and 4 hours of credit in United States history, or 8 hours of credit in United States history. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 410.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: the major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students travel through designated areas in North America. Requires considerable reading before the trip and papers at the conclusion. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teacher education students with a concentration in U.S. history may apply 4 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 3. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1500 -1815
description: Political, social, and economic history of Europe from the Age of Discovery to the Congress of Vienna. Emphasis on political and economic events, the rise of national states, absolutism, religious developments, and the expansion of Europe overseas.

title: Rise of Modern Europe, 1815 to the Present
description: Political, economic, social, and cultural history of Europe from the Congress of Vienna to the contemporary scene. Emphasis on political and economic events, the liberal and nationalist movements, industrialism, imperialism, World Wars I and II, and the conflict of national interests.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements i n the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870 -1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918 -1945
description: The origins, immediate causes, and course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and Europe Since 1945
description: European origin of the Cold War and rebirth of a "new" but divided Europe with stress on East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, and temporary decline of European influence; ideological, political, economic, and social development, including competition between Western and Sovietized Eastern Europe.

title: Modern Extremist Movements
description: A survey and analysis of extremist movements in Europe since 1815 with particular attention to the growth of antidemocratic thought, workingclass movements, counterrevolution, international fascism, collaboration, and youth movements.

title: History of Medicine in Western Society
description: A survey of the ideas, attitudes, and institutions of medicine and public health in the Western world from antiquity to modern times. Special attention given to social forces influencing medical knowledge and health care. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 460.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the Republic to approximately A.D. 500. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the Republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social, and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socio -economic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special emphasis on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Moslem worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300 -1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Emphasizes such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, and political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations—Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society— through varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teacher education students with a concentration in World Civilization may apply 4 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 4.

title: France Since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France—The Classical Age, 1461 -1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focuses on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715 -1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization—and revolutions in general. Stresses the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of a uthorityin the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Rise of Modern Britain, 1485 -1763
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor, Stuart, and early Hanoverian periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain since 1763
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life since the Seven Years' War—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of postwar government and society.

title: Constitutional History of England
description: A tracing of the development of the British constitutional system to the present time: development of the kingship, the common law, Parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern British Empire and Commonwealth
description: British imperial and commonwealth history since 1815 with emphasis on the post-Napoleonic empire, the development of dominions, the problem of India, the world wars, the shrinking empire, the Commonwealth experience, and the current controversies.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the Revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: Modern East- Central Europe and the Balkans
description: Studies in the modern history of peoples living in this exposed area of Europe, with stress on their struggles for national independence, ethnic, religious, cultural, socioeconomic, and political diversities. Problems are examined within the context of European trends and developments, especially interference of the Great Powers.

title: The Modern Middle East
description: A survey of major developments and problems in the Turkish, Persian, and Arab world in the period since 1800—the decay of traditional life, the expansion of European influence, the modernization movements, the conflicts over Palestine, and the recent national and international crises.

title: Selected Topics in Non -Western History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in non-Western history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern China, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japan, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on conditions contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Selected Topics in European History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in European history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Topics in American History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Studies for the Primary Grades and Early Childhood
description: Materials and procedures for teaching social studies for nursery school through grade three. Emphasis on behavioral objectives, inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation. Required of persons in the twoyear early elementary education program.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Social Studies in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate f or teaching social studies in junior high/midle schols. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDJHM 312.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Materials and procedure for teaching social studies from kindergarten through grade six. Emphasis on behavioral objectives; inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Provides more experience in methods used in teaching elementary social studies and an opportunity to use materials available to teachers. Prerequisite: SS 391 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Urban Elementary School
description: Specialized preparation for teaching social studies in urban elementary schools. Methods, strategies, and materials specifically designed for urban schools. Observations and field experiences in urban schools are an important part of the course.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Social Studies
description: The theory and practice of teaching the social studies in secondary schools with emphasis on methodology, materials, and specific application in the secondary classroom. Prerequisite: 28 hours of credit in social science and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended : EDSEC 29.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Social studiesoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of social studies, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of social studies in the secondary school curriculum. Topics are developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: SS 395.

title: Independent Study
description: Directed study of special problems or research in social science education by individuals or groups of students. Topics to be investigated are chosen after consultation with an instructor with special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Journalism Conn, Chairperson; Chaney, Duncan, Hatfield, Heintzelman, Knott, Nuwer, Pitts, Popovich, Sharpe, Ware, Weaver, Woodress Because the media practitioner must be a wellrounded and knowledgeable person in many fields, journalism programs in the accredited schools and departments in the nation, of which Ball State is one, stress exposure of students to the arts, the humanities, the sciences, and business. To study journalism in today's world is likely to mean involvement in the liberal arts academic tradition. Equally important to the student's breadth and depth of knowledge is the ability to put that knowledge into words that can be understood. Besides the writing and editing classroom experience required of journalism students, Ball State University encourages its students to participate in its extensive college student publications program and to seek professional experience either during the school year or summers. Journalism students spend onefourth of their academic careers in journalism courses and threefourths in courses other than journalism, radio-TV-film, advertising, public relations, or communications media. Students are encouraged to major in another subject in addition to journalism, such as anthropology, economics, history, literature, management, marketing, natural resources, political science, physical education, psychology, sociology, speech, urban and regional studies, and other arts and sciences. Students who enter the journalism department have the option of preparing themselves as either teaching majors or departmental majors. Teaching majors are prepared to teach journalism and mass media courses, to develop educational programs, and to serve as advisers for all forms of student publications and communication programs in secondary education. Students who pursue the teaching major are certified to receive an Indiana standard grade teaching license. JOURN 395 is the methods course for the teaching major in journalism (see the professional education requirements of the curriculum). Students earning a teaching major in journalism are advised to earn a teaching minor in English or, if possible, a teaching major in English. Teaching majors or minors in the social sciences or business are also recommended. Departmental majors have the option of career preparation in one of six sequential areas. 1. News-Editorial: Students learn all phases of newsroom operations of the various news media and acquire an overall grasp of the philosophy, trends, and issues in the news media. 2. Public Relations: Besides acquisition of a sound journalism foundation, students are prepared to go into public relations positions in public and private corporations and institutions. 3. Photojournalism: Emphasis is placed on preparing students who can take and process pictures and write news, prepare features, and create advertising. 4. Advertising: This option provides students with knowledge and practical experience in the functions and operations of the departments in media that ensure financial success—advertising, circulation, and promotion. 5. Magazine: Students study the magazine industry and are prepared to process words and pictures either freelance or for media organizations. 6. Sports Information: Students learn journalistic and public relations techniques in order to interpret for the public organized athletic events, either amateur or professional. Journalism courses are available to help the student who is not a major but is interested in working on special writing or editing projects or taking journalism courses to meet general studies requirements. JOURN 100, Mass Communications Media, and JOURN 120, Journalistic Writing, are selected by students as general studies requirements or as electives. During the freshman or sophomore year, students will be required to demonstrate adequate typing ability and meet minimum spelling and grammar requirements. If students are unable to pass the proficiency tests, remedial courses may be required to sharpen basic skills. By the end of the sophomore year, students should have taken and successfully completed the work in JOURN 110, 130, 220, and 250. Students should contact their sequence advisers by the end of the sophomore year for a midcareer review of their academic work. In order to be certified for graduation, journalism students must earn a total of 138 quarter hours of credit in courses other than journalism, radio-TV-film, advertising, public relations, or communications media. In addition, students will be asked to submit a recent photo, a college résumé, and a portfolio of examples of journalistic work to be placed in their permanent files. A senior interview with the appropriate sequence adviser, preferably during the student's last quarter on campus, will help qualify the student for graduation. ASSOCIATE DEGREE Associate in Arts—Journalism The twoyear journalsim curriculum offers an Associate in Arts degree to students who wish to prepare for work on a newspaper or in allied fields of communications such as advertising and public relations. Students enrolled in this curriculum will meet the standards of Ball State University with respect to admission, orientation, residence, scholastic ratio, and scholastic standards. Those who wish to continue their education may transfer to a curriculum leading to a baccalaureate degree. General studies: ENG 103, 104 8 hrs. From introductory or colloquium courses in social and behavioral sciences or in sciences and mathematics 20 hrs. Concentration area: JOURN 110, 130, 220, 250, 325, 402 24 hrs. From JOURN 275 and 475 or 469 or 498 4 hrs. From newseditorial, photojournalism, public relations, advertising, or magazine journalism courses 8 hrs. From ACC 201; BEOA 111, 112, 241; ITE 180, 181, 182, 281, 282, 285, 385, 481; MKG 300 20 hrs. Physical education 2 hrs. Electives 7 hrs. 93 hrs. title: Mass Communications Media
description: An overview of mass communications media, with emphasis on their historical development, structure, contemporary function, and operating methods.

title: Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice in use of reporting skills and techniques and in newspaper writing. Six hours are spent in class each week, including lectures, discussions, and laboratory assignments.

title: Introduction to Journalistic Writing
description: Theory and practice of newspaper -style writing. Not open to the student with areas in journalism.

title: Introduction to Photojournalism
description: An introduction to planning, shooting, and processing pictures for newspapers, magazines, and other print media. Designed for the working wordjournalist with little or no background in news photography. Students must provide a 35mm or 120mm camera and may consult a photojournalism instructor for advice about specific camera equipment before they buy or rent it. The department provides limited photographic chemicals, but students must furnish other needed supplies, such as additional chemicals, film, and print paper. Not open to students with previous news photo background.

title: Publication Design and Production
description: Publication design theory with emphasis on preparation of material for newspapers, magazines, and brochures. Lectures and projects focus on type selection, copy fitting, photo and illustration use, pasteup skills, and printing processes.

title: Copy Editing
description: Theory and practice of newspaper copy editing, headline writing, and page layout, with instruction in electronic editing processes. Prerequisite: JOURN 110.

title: Advanced Photojournalism Printing
description: Advanced studies of camera exposure techniques (including the zone system) affecting the photographic negative and advanced photographic printing to meet the highquality print requirements of all types of publications. Students must provide a 35mm or 120mm camera and may consult a photojournalism instructor for advice about specific camera equipment before they buy or rent it. The department provides limited photographic chemicals, but students must furnish other needed supplies, such as additional chemicals, film, and print paper. Prerequisite: JOURN 130.

title: Photographic Lighting
description: An indepth study of photographic lighting procedures and equipment as used by media photographers. Students must provide a 35mm or 120mm camera and may consult a photojournalism instructor for advice about specific camera equipment before they buy or rent it. The department provides limited photographic chemicals, but students must furnish other needed supplies, such as additional chemicals, film, and print paper. Prerequisite: JOURN 130.

title: Introduction to Advertising
description: A survey of the advertising communication process. Focuses on communication research, creative strategy, campaign planning, function of mass media as carriers of advertising, and evaluation of advertising effectiveness.

title: Principles of Public Relations
description: Survey of the theory, philosophy, and function of public relations practices and programs in American institutions with special attention to public relations in various fields.

title: Journalism Practicum
description: Introductory practical experiences in the production of the campus newspaper, magazine, yearbook, or alternative projects with emphasis on writing, editing, or photographic activities. Course work will involve demonstrating mastery of spelling, grammar, and typing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 110, 130, and 220. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 469 or 475.

title: History of Journalism
description: History of journalism in the United States from colonial times to the present, presenting the press as an institution against the background of the history of the nation.

title: Feature and Column Writing
description: Researching and writing feature stories and columns for newspapers and magazines, supplemented by practice assignments for student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice of researching and writing specialized stories for the news media. Emphasis on the indepth reporting approach and on coverage of such special areas as government, education, sports, and reviewing the performing arts. Supplemented by practical assignments for student publications and for the university radio station. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Magazine Writing and Editing
description: Theory of and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles. Includes a study of markets for magazine articles and exercises in various aspects of editing general and specialized magazines.

title: Sportswriting and Reporting
description: Study and practice in covering and writing about sports events and the people connected with them. Story assignments and research combined with classroom lectures and analysis of best sports stories provide students with skills to cover a wide range of sports activities. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Journalism Law
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the print and broadcast media with special attention to recent Supreme Court rulings.

title: Advanced Photojournalism
description: An extended study of the theory and practice of making photographs and using photography as communicative art. Students must provide a 35mm or 120mm camera and may consult a photojournalism instructor for advice about specific camera equipment before they buy or rent it. The department provides limited photographic chemicals, but students must furnish other needed supplies, such as additional chemicals, film, and print paper. Prerequisite: JOURN 130, 233, and 236, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advertising Media
description: Strategy and procedures for planning, executing, and controlling the placement of advertising. Examines characteristics of media, techniques of media budgeting and selection, and methods of evaluating media effectiveness. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Advertising Copy and Layout
description: Instruction in preparing copy for mass media advertising. Major emphasis on creative thinking and basic writing skills. Students prepare copy strategies, write copy, prepare layouts and storyboards. Discussion of fundamentals of consumer motivation and selecting target audiences. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Publicity Writing
description: Theory and practice of producing publicity tools for various media used in campaigns to promote and interpret personal, institutional and organizational objectives and activities. Emphasis on writing and publicity problem solving. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 and 261.

title: Institutional and Industrial Publications
description: Institutional and industrial publications as an important means of internal and external communications of organizations. Prerequisite: JOURN 110 or 120.

title: Honors Colloquium in Journalism
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Journalism
description: The procedures and problems in teaching journalism classes or units and the role of student publications in school journalism programs. Subjects included are curriculum, finance, textbooks, and resources. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Press and Society
description: The press in modern society, with emphasis on the press's role as a social agent, recent criticisms of the press, and the ethical considerations that guide the press today.

title: The Editorial Function
description: Theory and practice of the editorial function of the press with attention to editorials and opinion writing, editorial types and campaigns, page design, staff organization, and reader relations.

title: Public Affairs Reporting and Writing
description: Structures and functions of governmental and other public agencies, with special attention to problems of obtaining and reporting infor- 'nation in appropriate articles. Practice in writing under deadline pressure through coverage of newsworthy events on campus or in the community. Prerequisite: JOURN 110.

title: Scientific and Technical Writing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Familiarization with engineering and spaceage terminology, with emphasis on clarity and translation of technical terms to lay language.

title: Newspaper Design
description: Theory of the design functions of journalism using typographical systems with attention to their relations to communicative language. Acquaints the journalism student with new methods, ideas, and techniques that have been and are in the process of being developed in journalism printing and technology.

title: Journalism Styles
description: Acquaints students with twentiethcentury prose styles, stressing writing and editing. Students analyze the works of various writers and editors as they prepare their own copy and consider various writing devices and forms to help them develop their own writing styles. Discussion of electronic processes currently being used by publications for editing. Prerequisite: JOURN 110, 220, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Magazine Writing
description: A workshop in writing and marketing magazine articles with emphasis on targeting markets for freelance articles, analyzing trends in major national magazines, and developing story ideas. Prerequisite: JOURN 315, 424, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Magazine Management
description: A productoriented analysis of magazine editorial management, advertising, and circulation market research and development in terms of journalistic practices.

title: Picture Editing
description: Selection, editing, and use of photographic and other illustrative materials for newspapers, magazines, and other publications and for other communicative purposes.

title: Advertising Photography
description: Photographic methods, lighting, and photographic special effects as they apply to advertising and associated commercial photography done by media photo departments. Students must provide a 35mm or 120mm camera and may consult a photojournalism instructor for advice about specific camera equipment before they buy or rent it. The department provides limited photographic chemicals, but students must furnish other needed supplies, such as additional chemicals, film, and print paper. Prerequisite: JOURN 130 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Color Photojournalism
description: The principles, techniques, and materials of color photography as they apply to the publishing of color art work and photographs in printed publications. Students must provide a 35mm or 120mm camera and may consult a photojournalism instructor for advice about specific camera equipment before they buy or rent it. The department provides limited photographic chemicals, but students must furnish other needed supplies, such as additional chemicals, film, and print paper. Prerequisite: JOURN 130 or 337.

title: Direct Response Advertising
description: An introduction to and application of the principles of direct media advertising. Emphasizes target selection, copy and layout, media selecting, and response evaluation. Prerequisite: JOURN 250; MKG 300, 310, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advertising Communication Case Studies
description: Designed to analyze and solve advertising problems based on actual situations. Cases focus on consumer goods companies, industrial marketers, and nonprofit organizations. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 352, 354; MKG 300, 310; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Copy Writing
description: Advanced studies in the strategy and creation of advertising for the mass media. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 354.

title: Advertising Campaigns
description: Synthesis of skills and concepts acquired in the specialized advertising courses. Students research, plan, write, schedule, budget, and evaluate a complete advertising campaign. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 352, 354; MKG 300, 310; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advertising: Public Relations Practicum
description: Practical experience in public relations or advertising projects in preparation of a senior portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 250 and 261 or 456.

title: Producing and Advising Yearbooks
description: Theories of staff organization, yearbook organization and content, illustrations, production techniques, typography, style, theme, and the role of adviser to student staff.

title: Producing and Advising School Newspapers
description: Study of the content and organization of school newspapers, production techniques, staff organization and training, and the role of the adviser. Other school publications and news bureaus considered as time permits.

title: Teaching Journalistic Media
description: The methods and materials available to teach introductory journalistic media units or courses in the secondary school. Emphasis on function, procedures, and influence of journalistic media on the public.

title: Journalism Practicum
description: Practical experiences in the production of the campus newspaper, magazine, yearbook, or alternate projects with emphasis on writing, editing, photography, and management. Includes preparation of portfolios of journalistic materials. Prerequisite: JOURN 110, 130, 220, and 275. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 469.

title: Introduction to Journalism and Communication Research
description: Issues and trends in the literature of mass communication theory and research.

title: Individual Studies in Journalism
description: Group and individual investigations and experiences in journalistic media and techniques with special attention to social, political, and economic roles of the press in society. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Journalism Internship
description: Onthejob training that synthesizes classroom experiences of journalism or public relations students. Involves assigned duties in an offcampus communications organization with appropriate compensation. Prerequisite: JOURN 110, 130, 220, 250, and permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students with credit in Journ 469 or 275 and 475. Department of Mathematical Sciences Whitaker, Chairperson; Ali, Avila, Beekman, Brumbaugh, Deal, Dugan, Farris, Garnett, Hoelzer, Jones, Joshi, Kallman, Lee, Ludwig, R. B. Nelson, R. S. Nelson, Parish, Partner, Perham, Petrucco, Puttaswamy, Robold, Umbach Mathematics was defined by Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777-1855) as "the queen of the sciences." This statement reflects the interdependency of mathematics and the sciences. While still true, this observation must now be extended to cover all areas of human endeavor in the second half of the twentieth century. The student considering mathematics as a career should realize that emphasis in mathematics courses will change as progress is made through undergraduate and graduate school. The early emphasis on solving problems is later subordinated to the more important tasks of formulating and dealing effectively with mathematical structures and abstract ideas. Every prospective mathematician should plan to pursue undergraduate and graduate training to the highest level of capability. To meet the need for mathematically competent graduates, several programs of study are available at the undergraduate level as either majors or minors. The secondary teaching major is designed to prepare classroom teachers of mathematics in grades 9 through 12. The junior high/middle school mathematics primary area is designed to prepare mathematics teachers for grades 5 through 9. This primary area is accompanied by a supporting area or another primary area in science, social science, language arts, or a foreign language for the junior high/middle school major. Prospective teachers completing the secondary teaching license may earn an endorsement for teaching in the junior high/ middle school grades. All teacher preparation programs comply with the certification regulations of the Division of Teacher Education and Certification of the State Board of Education. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government, as well as for further specialized study of mathematics at the graduate level. In today's complex world, problems cut across traditionally defined areas of discipline, and a departmental major offers a student the opportunity to combine mathematics with work in other subjects. The departmental major in the liberal arts curriculum is a program in the liberal arts tradition. With this liberal education, the student is well prepared for additional graduate study or for positions requiring education in breadth. Actuaries are mathematically trained executives who use mathematical knowledge to analyze and solve business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. Actuaries are employed by insurance companies, state departments of insurance, management consulting firms, universities, federal agencies, and other institutions. An actuarial career promises to be a challenging and rewarding experience. A departmental major in actuarial science is offered to give students the foundation for an actuarial career. An actuary gains professional recognition by passing a series of examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries. The program includes the course work for the first three examinations, and in some cases for the fourth and fifth examinations. Ball State University is an official test site for the Society of Actuaries. An applied mathematics minor is provided for students whose primary interests lie in such fields as business, economics, biology, geography, geology, and psychology, but who recognize that there is a mathematical basis for their primary fields. This program is problem and application oriented rather than theoretical in nature. Students preparing to be elementary teachers, but with an aptitude for and an interest in mathematics, may add the endorsement for the teaching of mathematics to their elementary teaching license. The endorsement prepares them to be mathematics specialists in a departmentalized elementary school, in a teamteaching situation, or in other situations calling for persons who are well prepared in both elementary school teaching and in mathematics. The student who earns the mathematics endorsement may also earn certification to teach mathematics in the junior high/middle school, as well as in the elementary school, by taking certain additional professional education courses. He or she is then licensed to teach mathematics in grades 1 through 9. The student will be guided by the curricular statements (see Curricula) and by the requirements given below. The departmental offerings include courses for several curricula. Students should seek advice if they are not certain whether a particular course will apply to a certain program. Mathematics majors and minors are assigned mathematics advisers from among the departmental faculty, and should consult with these advisers before each registration after completing the first calculus course. The mathematics adviser assists the student in planning his or her program of courses for the major or minor, and can advise in career planning. The requirements for majors and minors for all curricula are based on a prerequisite of college preparatory mathematics in secondary school. Deficiencies in secondary school mathematics must be made up before courses in the major or minor program may be taken.
