title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting energy forms such as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physical Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles and concepts of the laws of nature involving mechanical, heat, light, electrical, nuclear, and chemical energy and the conservation laws associated with these forms of energy. Emphasis on applications appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Preparation of Physical Science Teaching Materials
description: Selected topics in physical science stressing the construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Prerequisite: PHYCS 101 or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students in the teacher education curriculum.

title: Physics and Sports
description: A descriptive introduction to basic physical principles and laws within a framework of applications to athletic activities and sports. Particularly suited to the student with areas or special interest in physical education. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110, 120, or 130.

title: Basic Physics for the Allied Health Sciences
description: A condensed study of basic physics with special emphasis on principles and applications pertinent to the health sciences. Three lectures and one twohour laboratoryrecitation weekly. Prerequisite: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students in the allied health sciences program in respiratory therapy, radiologic technology, nuclear therapy, and ultrasound technology or with permission of the department chairperson.

title: General Physics 1
description: The laws of mechanics including kinematics, dynamics, work and energy relationships, torque, rotational energy, angular momentum, stress and strain, elastic moduli, and introductory topics in fluid statics and dynamics. Prerequisite: MATH 108. Prerequisite recommended: MATH 112 (trigonometry).

title: General Physics 2
description: The study of static and current electricity including Ohm's law, DC and AC circuit concepts, electric and magnetic field basics, and introductory concepts in modern physics (relativity, atomic and nuclear physics). Prerequisite: PHYCS 110.

title: General Physics 3
description: A study of the laws of thermal physics including calorimetry, heat transfer, and introductory thermodynamics concepts. Includes harmonic motion and sound, as well as the study of geometrical (lenses and mirrors) and physical (interference and diffraction) optics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112.

title: Orientation Seminar for Pre -engineering and Beginning Physics Students
description: An overview of the fields of physics and engineering that will aid science students in effectively planning their college curriculum. Students will be introduced to career scientists and the jobs performed by persons in these professions. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 120.

title: General Physics 1
description: A first course in calculusbased physics for students with areas in preengineering, the physical sciences, or mathematics. Topics include Newtonian Mechanics, motion in a plane, the workenergy principle, impulse and momentum, elasticity and harmonic motion, and hydrostatics and hydrodynamics. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 161.

title: General Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 120. Topics include Coulomb's Law and the electric field, Gauss's Law, DC circuits and instruments, the magnetic field, Ampere's Law, Faraday's Law, the magnetic properties of matter, the integral form of Maxwell's equation, alternatingcurrent circuits, impedance, and electromagnetic waves. Prerequisite:

title: General Physics 3
description: Topics include waves, acoustic phenomena, the nature and propagation of light, reflection, refraction, image formation by lenses and mirrors, interference and diffraction, polarization, heat flow, thermal properties of matter, the laws of thermodynamics, the kinetic theory of gases, and introductory atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120, MATH 162.

title: Physics 1 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of mechanics and heat. Topics include particle dynamics, resolution of forces, friction, work, energy, static equilibrium, torque, properties of materials, fluids, temperature, thermal expansion, heat energy, heat transfer, phase changes in matter, and thermodynamic engines. Prerequisite: MATH 112 or equivalent secondary school mathematics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Physics 2 for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of sound, light, and electrical power. Topics include wave phenomena, sound, reflection, refraction, geometrical optics, polarization, circuits, Ohm's Law, Kirchoff's Laws, electromagnetic induction, transformers, meters, and power distribution systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 130. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 112 or 120.

title: Sound and Light
description: For music and art students. Sound as a basis of music and light as a basis of art. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Household Physics
description: Practical applications of physics in common everyday appliances and other devices. Topics include principles of heating and cooling and principles of some electrical and electronic home appliances. Study of fuses and why they blow.

title: Topics in Physics
description: Discussion pf specific topics in physics, such as lasers, holography, and solidstate electronics. Designed for the nonphysics major, the course requires no math or science background. Students may consult their curricular advisers or the Department of Physics and Astronomy for the specific topics being studied during a given quarter. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Solar Energy Technology and Applications
description: Descriptive study of various techniques and systems using sunlight as a nonpolluting alternative energy source. Principles and design of solar systems for space heating, air conditioning, and heating water for residential and commercial buildings, and systems for the generation of electric power. Includes other related topics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or MATH 108.

title: Sound and Acoustical Art
description: A descriptive treatment of basic sound and acoustics, using a minimum of mathematics. Especially tailored to the needs of music and other related areas such as speech. Involves pitch, wavelength, intensity levels. Not open to students with areas in physics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 184.

title: Introduction to Audio Engineering
description: Introduction to the reproduction of sound. Principles of operating electroacoustical transducers such as phono cartridges, loudspeakers, and tape heads. Applies electronic principles to the amplification process. Students measure frequency response and speaker parameters in the laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Photographic Optics in the Visual Arts
description: Principles of light and optics for students majoring in areas other than the physical sciences that require a basic understanding of light and optics in photography. Tailored to meet the needs of photojournalism, art, and other students with similar interests.

title: Introduction to Modern Physics
description: The underlying principles and theories of modern physics. Topics include introductory relativity, atomic and nuclear structure, quantum theory, and the theory of solids. A regularly scheduled laboratory is included. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Environmental Physics
description: The application of physics to environmental and societal problems. Physical principles underlying industries based on hard technology. Topics include energy production, transmission, and environmental effects (including nuclear power generation and radiation); transportation problems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or the equivalent.

title: Observational Astronomy Workshop for Teachers
description: A laboratoryoriented course that prepares secondary teachers to explain celestial events and patterns. Emphasizes development of skills for selection of resource materials, planning of observing sessions, and use of star charts and telescopes. Projects involving application of these subjects in an educational setting will be required.

title: Physical Foundations of Astronomy Workshop for Teachers
description: A lecture/laboratory course designed to teach secondary teachers the basic physical principles of modern astronomy and space science. Discusses the fundamentals of mechanics and celestial mechanics, optics, and structure of matter in the context of the development of astronomical theories.

title: Stellar Evolution and Black Holes Workshop for Teachers
description: Prepares secondary teachers to explain current theories regarding stellar properties and stellar evolution. Includes discussions of pulsars, neutron stars, and black holes. Instructional projects relating to course topics will be required. Prerequisite: PHYCS 304 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Electronics for the Life Sciences
description: Applications of electronics to the problems encountered by students in the life sciences. Electronic instruments used in biology, health, and physiology and the problems associated with their use. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 354 or 356.

title: Mechanics 1
description: Basic concepts of particle mechanics. Vector algebra and calculus. Kinematics and dynamics of a particle in two and three dimensions. Simple and dampedharmonic motion. Particle dynamics in noninertial frames of reference. Central force motion. Dynamics of a system of particles. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120 and MATH 162.

title: Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 330. Dynamics of a rigid body, the moment of inertia tensor. Mechanics of deformable continua, the stress tensor. The wave equation, elasticity, and rigid body vibrations. Variational techniques, virtual work, Lagrange's equations of the first and second kind. Hamiltonian mechanics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330.

title: Physical Optics
description: The electromagnetic wave theory of light, spectra, interference, diffraction, polarization, and double refraction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Laser and Holography Workshop for Teachers
description: A laboratory -oriented course designed for junior high and high school science teachers that presents the field of lasers and holography. Reviews basic geometrical optics, physical optics, and atomic theory phenomena in relation to laser operation and hologram making. Emphasizes laser safety and the use of lasers for demonstrating optical phenomena in the classroom. Prerequisite: PHYCS 114 or 124 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 340 or APHYS 340.

title: Acoustics
description: Aspects of pure and applied acoustics. Topics include solutions to the wave equation, acoustic impedances, electromechanicalacoustic analogies, directradiator loudspeaker and enclosure theory, and a discussion of room acoustics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Electronics 1
description: Characteristics of electronic components and their circuit functions. Circuit analysis, design, and construction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introductory Integrated Circuit Electronics Workshop for Teachers
description: A laboratoryoriented course designed for students who do not have a strong background in electronics to acquaint them with the uses of modern integrated circuitry. Emphasizes the construction and use of circuits that can be used in the classroom. Introduces analog, digital, and microprocessor electronics topics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or 122 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 354, 356; APHYS 454.

title: Electronics 2
description: The function and use of integrated circuitry as applied to pulse and digital circuits found in laboratory and computer apparatus. Prerequisite: PHYCS 354 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Applications of Nuclear Techniques Workshop for Teachers
description: A laboratoryoriented course designed for junior high and high school science teachers. Emphasizes the applications of nuclear techniques in research, medicine, the environment, energy production, and industry with instruction on the use of radiation detection devices and radiation safety procedures. Prerequisite: PHYCS 114 or 124 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 360.

title: Introductory Nuclear Techniques
description: Emphasis on experimental studies of radioactive disintegrations and decay products and their relation to nuclear structure. Instrumentation in radioisotope measurements. Two lectures and two twohour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those that occur in classical physics and elementary quantum mechanics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124 and 260, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems. Topics include boundary value problems, transforms, and special functions of mathematical physics (Green's function approach, Fourier series, Legendre's equation, Bessel's equation, Hermite polynomials, etc.). Prerequisite: PHYCS 124 and 260 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Descriptive Astronomy
description: The celestial sphere, the solar system, formation and decay of stars, instruments and basic laws of astronomy, nebulae, galactic structure, theories of the origin of the universe; constellation and telescope work.

title: Honors Colloquium in Physics
description: Exploration of selected topics in physics, with emphasis on individual projects, study and discussion. Open only to honors students or students with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Teaching of Physics in the Secondary School
description: Aims, nature of the subject matter, calculus concepts and applications in the teaching of physics, amount and nature of laboratory work, standardized tests, and textbooks used in the teaching of physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in physics or permission of the , department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Celestial Mechanics
description: An application of the laws of classical mechanics to objects under the influence of inversesquare gravitational forces, leading to the theory of orbits and perturbative effects on orbits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 332.

title: Thermodynamics
description: Laws of thermodynamics and introduction to the kinetic theory of gases. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 1
description: Application of vector analysis to electrostatics, dipole and multipole fields, and dielectric theory. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 450 with emphasis on dynamic electrical problems, alternating currents, magnetic fields, and Maxwell's equations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 450.

title: Elementary Particles
description: The nature and behavior of elementary particles through the study of the symmetries and dynamics responsible for their production, reactions, and decays. Prerequisite: PHYCS 465.

title: Nuclear Physics
description: Nucleus and nuclear interactions. Emphasizes experimental facts about nuclear processes in discussions of particle accelerators, detectors, radioactivity (alpha, beta, and gamma decay), interaction of radiation with matter, nuclear reactions, nuclear structure, nuclear models, and nuclear applications in science and technology. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 1
description: De Broglie's postulate, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the free particle, square well potentials, harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom, and other selected wave mechanics problems. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 464. Course material includes perturbation theory, oneelectron atoms, magnetic moments, spin, relativistic effects, symmetric and antisymmetric eigenfunctions, the helium atom, the Thomas-Fermi theory, the Hartree theory, and transition rates. Prerequisite: PHYCS 464.

title: Solid State Physics 1
description: An investigation of the structure and physical properties of matter in the solid state. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Solid State Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 466. Topics include the electrical and magnetic properties of solids and the band theory of solids with special emphasis on semiconductors. Examines the optical properties of solids and the effects of lattice defects. Prerequisite: PHYCS 466.

title: Independent Studies in Physics
description: Pursuit of special lines of scientific investigation in physics on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Physics Investigations in the Field
description: Investigative problems in physics that need to be pursued at places other than Ball State because of their specialized facilities. No regularly scheduled laboratory. This course may be repeated with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mysteries of the Sky
description: A nontechnical and nonmathematical multimedia excursion into the vast reaches of the sky including information about the sun, the moon, shooting stars, comets, supernovae, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, life on other planets.

title: Astronomy Materials for the Teacher
description: The fundamentals of astronomy including historical aspects and modern astronomy concepts. Emphasis on construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Observational Astronomy
description: A continuation of ASTRO 100 providing practical experience in observing celestial objects by using telescopes and other astronomical apparatus. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100.

title: General Astronomy 1
description: Essential points of modern astronomy, emphasizing the underlying physical principles. Topics include coordinate systems in astronomy, orbital laws, relativity, planetary physics, measurement of stellar distances, and spectral classification of stars. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100 or PHYCS 380, and MATH 108.

title: General Astronomy 2
description: A continuation of ASTRO 120. Topics include atomic structure and stellar spectra, stellar atmospheres and interiors, multiple star systems and clusters, galactic structure, cosmology, and the origin of the universe. Prerequisite: ASTRO 120. Parallel: MATH 112.

title: Topics in Astronomy
description: Discussion of specific topics in astronomy, such as comets, eclipses, UFOs, and interstellar travel. Designed for nonphysics majors, the course requires no math or science background. Students may consult their curricular advisers or the Department of Physics and Astronomy for specific topics being studied during a given quarter. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 1
description: An indepth study of the solar system, starting with man's earliest concepts and extending to modern space explorations. Topics include the celestial sphere, theories of planetary motions, the earth and moon, celestial mechanics, the origin of the solar system, and the sun's planets as habitats for life. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120, 122, and 124.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 2
description: Introduction to stellar astronomy. Topics include stellar distances and motions; stellar magnitudes, luminosities, and colors; the H-R diagram; stellar evolution and energy production; double and variable stars; nebulae; structure and dynamics of the Milky Way. Other galaxies, quasistellar objects (quasars), and cosmology. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 3
description: A detailed survey of the Milky Way galaxy and the general structure of the universe as a whole. Topics covered will include structure and dynamics of the Milky Way, other galaxies, quasistellar objects (quasars), and cosmology. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330 and 332.

title: Seminar in Modern Astronomy
description: Selected topics in contemporary astronomy. Extensive use of library facilities including current journals and periodicals in astronomy. Topics for study may include astronomical research in progress and such esoteric subjects as UFOs and extraterrestrial life. Prerequisite: PHYCS 124 and permission of department chairperson.

title: Instruments and Techniques in Planetarium Operations
description: Use of planetarium instruments, console, and chamber. Creation and presentation of planetarium programs including slideduplicating techniques, slide opaquing, and the production of sound tracks. Prerequisite: permission of the planetarium director.

title: Theories and Instruments of the Astronomer
description: Reviews of various atlases, catalogs, ephemerides, and charts. The development of methods used to compute and update stellar positions. Discusses astronomical instruments in the context of their use by research astronomers. Analysizes specific techniques employed in astronomical photometry, spectroscopy, and photography. Prerequisite: ASTRO 332.

title: Advanced Astrophysics
description: A detailed investigation of the frontier areas of modern astrophysics. Possible topics include stellar structure, nucleosynthesis, stellar evolution, stellar atmospheres, and the interstellar material. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330, 332, and 334.

title: Specialized Imaging Modalities
description: Overview of special computerized imaging techniques and radiologic applications to include tomography, nuclear magnetic resonance, and digital vascular imaging. Prerequisite: AHSC 226. Parallel: AHSC 234.

title: Principles of Radiography 1
description: An overview of radiation physics to include properties of radiation, biological effects, xray production and interaction, and radiation protection. Prerequisite: PHYCS 106.

title: Introduction to Radioactivity
description: Mechanisms and characteristics of nuclear decay and interaction of radiation with matter. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in nuclear medicine.

title: Radiopharmaceuticals
description: Preparation, quality control, and the diagnostic and therapeutic application of radiopharmaceuticals in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 247.

title: Radionuclide Measurements
description: An introduction to the mechanisms of detection and measurement of radioactive materials and descriptive and inductive statistics used in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 247.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation
description: An indepth study of the components and performance characteristics of equipment commonly used in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 250. Parallel: APHYS 252.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation Lab
description: A weekly laboratory for nuclear medicine technology students enrolled in APHYS 251.

title: Lasers and Applied Electro - Optic Techniques
description: Principles of laser operation, design, and safety considered within the context of the field of electrooptic techniques. Optical detection devices, photographic techniques, and laser applications stressed in the handson l aboratoryoriented portion of the course. Prerequisite: PHYCS 114 or 124 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Fluid Mechanics 1
description: The forces and motions in fluids. Fluid characteristics and the basic theories of fluid statics and dynamics. Applications of solar energy systems, hydraulics, aerodynamics, meteorology, hydrology, and fluidics. Prerequisite: MATH 162, PHYCS 330.

title: Fluid Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of APHYS 410. Turbulence and nonuniform flows. Applies the theories and equations of fluid mechanics to environmental conditioning systems, thermal convection processes and circulation of the atmosphere, tides and currents, airfoils, pipe flow, medicine, astrophysics, and other subjects. Uses computerized models for studies of individual interest. Prerequisite: APHYS 410.

title: Applied Solar Energy 1
description: The solar energy resource, the physics and engineering of solar collection, concentration, thermal conversion, and storage. Analysis of solar spectral content, attenuation, and variation; flat plate collector efficiencies; and thermal storage materials. Three lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: MATH 162, PHYCS 122, 124.

title: Applied Solar Energy 2
description: The engineering design, component integration, operation, and performance of solar heating and cooling systems. System modeling and sizing of residential and commercial solar space heating, water heating, and space cooling units. Control instrumentation hardware, functions, and operation. Prerequisite: APHYS 420.

title: Applied Solar Energy 3
description: Solar electric power generation, advanced solar systems, applications in industry and agriculture, and the solar hydrogen economy. Physics and engineering of solar thermal power plants, solar cells, solar satellites, ocean thermal energy conversion, windmills, and bioconversion. Three onehour lectures and a twohour laboratory each week. Prerequisite: APHYS 422.

title: Heat Transfer
description: The basic heat transfer processes in nature. Conduction, convection, and radiation in applied problems using electricalmodelanalogue, graphical, and computerized numerical methods. Prerequisite: MATH 162; PHYCS 124; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Microprocessor and Microcomputer Electronics
description: Principles and uses of microprocessors and microcomputers. Microprocessor and microcomputer timing, bus structures, inputoutput interfacing, memory interfacing, analogtodigital and digitaltoanalog conversion techniques. Prerequisite: PHYCS 356 or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: CS 230.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals. Open only to students majoring in elementary education.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. Open only to students majoring in elementary education. Department of Physiology and Health Science Schaller, Chairperson; Amschler, Bock, Carroll, Ellis, Ganion, Gobble, Griffin, Hahn, Henzlik, Jarial, Jones, Kennedy, Lesh, Marini, Paschall, Payne, Pinger, Wantz, Womack The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a multidisciplinary study of the life sciences and their application to health promotion, disease prevention, and therapeutic intervention through specific allied health science programs. Physiology is the study of life forms in terms of vital functions of cells, tissues, organs, and systems and their several life processes in relation to both internal and external environments. Anatomy is the specialized investigation of the structure of cells, tissues, organs, and systems, as these constitute the basic units that experience life, health, disease, and death. A relatively new discipline, health science involves the application of scientific health principles to human life, primarily through programs of health education based in schools, community health agencies, health care facilities, and industrial settings. The goals of health science are to help people make intelligent decisions in solving personal, family, and community health problems and to assist them in leading personally satisfying, socially constructive, healthy lives. Derived primarily from anatomy, physiology, psychology, and sociology, health science has important reciprocal relationships with chemistry, physics, home economics, physical education, philosophy, logic, and education. Applied to the human conditions of wellness and lifestyling in the promotion of health status, health science includes such subjects as drug dependence and abuse, human sexuality, lack of exercise in a sedentary society, health care delivery, selfmedication and consumer health education, health and disease throughout the human life cycle, community health problems, and emergency health care. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers both a teaching major and a teaching minor designed to meet Indiana state licensing requirements for teaching health and safety in grades 7-12. An endorsement for teaching health science and safety in the elementary school provides elementary education majors with specific competencies for promoting students' health status through the school health program in grades K-6. Students who are interested in community health education programs rather than school health should consult the departmental chairperson. Two departmental minors are also administered by the department: the physiology minor provides the necessary background for application to appropriate professional schools or to graduate education in anatomy and physiology; the public health minor prepares candidates for entrylevel positions in community health agencies, both governmental and private. At the present time, the department contributes required and elective courses to several academic programs at Ball State, including preprofessional programs in allied health science areas, courses for professional nurse preparation, and general education. The department provides guidance to students who are interested in teaching, research, or service careers related to life science, and health promotion. Membership in Sigma Zeta, the national honorary in science and mathematics, and in Eta Sigma Gamma, the national honorary in health science, is offered to qualified students who earn high scholastic honors. ASSOCIATE DEGREE Associate in Arts—General Arts The department offers courses in allied health science that lead to an associate in arts in general arts degree with electives in nuclear medicine technology, radiography, and respiratory therapy technology. This program is offered in conjunction with Methodist Hospital of Indiana, Inc., and several central Indiana hospitals. Students are required to undergo a selection process for admission to the program and may contact the department chairperson or the appropriate curricular adviser for information. Contact the department or curricular advising for the outline of the general arts associate degree. title: Elements of Human Health
description: Human biology stressing the personal and informational aspects of current health problems. Hygiene of the basic systems of the body with emphasis on care, functions, and disorders; natural and acquired defenses against disease; elements of preventive medicine; and modern standards of sanitation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 160.

title: Fundamentals of Human Health
description: Emphasizes total individual fitness and intelligent selfmanagement, based on understanding body functioning. Topics include existing health conditions; use of physicians, dentists, and public agencies; infections and body defense; emergencies; food and one's efficiency; emotional health; and human reproduction. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 150.

title: Community Health Problems
description: Organization of official and nonofficial health agencies at international, national, state, and local levels. Exploration of causative community factors and diagnoses of disease and programs to combat these conditions. Focuses on selected communicable and noncommunicable diseases and behavior problems including traffic safety. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Introduction to Health Education
description: Intended for majors and minors as an introduction to generic health education and health promotion. Basic philosophy and practice in health education; historical events, significant persons, current literature, professional organizations, role delineation process, and ethical concerns.

title: Emergency Health Care
description: Various emergency health problems and their management by the application of emergency health care as recommended by the American Red Cross and Civil Defense authorities. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 299 or 396.

title: Health, Sexuality, and Family Life
description: Health aspects of human sexuality and family life with a focus on human reproduction, physiology of sexual response, sexual disorders and dysfunctions, sexually transmitted diseases, promotion of sexual health, and the family's role in sex education. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Occupational Safety and Health
description: A qualitative and quantitative study of the interfaces among individuals, their tools, and their work environment and the methods by which the resulting health hazards can be reduced to an acceptable level. Prerequisite: HSC 250.

title: School Health Practice
description: Community and school health services. Practical experiences in screening for visual, auditory, and nutritional defects. Identification and control of childhood diseases. Topics include safety, first aid, materials for teaching health, and effect of the school program on the health of the child. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: School Health Organization
description: Organization and development of school health programs. Coordination of school and community health programs, hygiene, sanitation of the school plant, the school lunch program, school health services, and the health instructional program. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 350.

title: Health Appraisal of School Children
description: Sociological, psychological, and physiological changes that take place in school children. Prevalent health problems in school children— their etiology, pathology, diagnosis, and prognosis. Experience in screening techniques for discovering these deviations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 350 or 360.

title: Insects and Human Health
description: A survey of diseases caused or transmitted by insects and other arthropods. Emphasis is given to the recognition of medically important insects and to their biology as it relates to human disease. Three onehour lectures and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: Honors Colloquium in Health Science
description: Exploration of selected current issues in health science with an emphasis upon individualized study, reporting, and discussion. Restricted to honors students.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Health and Safety
description: Examination of the Indiana state course of study in health and safety. Relation of health policies and current schoolhomecommunity problems. Students practice with audiovisual aids, evaluate representative textbooks, and visit offcampus schools. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Classroom Use of Methods and Materials in Health and Safety
description: Emphasizes promoting health through schools, disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, and learner motivation in health education. Supportive role of community agencies, justification and evaluation of health instruction, and enhancement of school and public interaction. Prerequisite: HSC 200.

title: Health Science of Distant Areas
description: School and public health programs at local, state, and national levels. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Open to students in elementary curricula, students with concentration areas in health science in secondary curricula, and students in public health areas. No regularly scheduled laboratory. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned. May be repeated with permission of the department chairperson.

title: History of Medicine in Western Society
description: A survey of the ideas, attitudes, and institutions of medicine and public health in the Western world from antiquity to modern times, with special attention to social forces influencing medical knowledge and health care. Not open to students who have credit in HIST 460.

title: Sex Education and School Health
description: Development of an understanding of how to implement and teach a positive program of sex education aimed at helping young people develop constructive attitudes, values, and practices based on sound knowledge in accordance with American Medical Association recommendations and pertinent state guidelines. Prerequisite: HSC 261 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Patient Education: A Team Approach
description: Theories of client education and application of the education process to individuals and groups in health care settings. Emphasis on the multidisciplinary team concept in planning, implementing, and evaluating client education. Application of knowledge of growth and development in meeting learning needs of clients.

title: Alcohol Problems
description: A study of alcohol as a mood modifier, its use, nonuse, and abuse in drinking societies. Critical and controversial issues relevant to alcohol ingestion will be explored for medical, economic, legal, educational, historical, physiological, and public health implications.

title: Current Progress in Disease Control
description: A critical review of research on leading causes of mortality and morbidity in the United States. Designed to enable students to appreciate and understand current health progress in the United States. Emphasizes the potential application of this information to individual, school, and community health programs. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Drug Dependence and Abuse
description: Analyzes the medical, psychological, sociological, and legal dimensions of drug use in the United States. Examines the incidence and prevalence of drug abuse together with the roles played by school and community in dealing with this health problem. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Health Quackery
description: Health services and consumer protection organizations. An analysis of fraudulent health practices and nostrums, available health care systems, and health products. Prerequisite: HSC 150, 160, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Health and Aging
description: Dynamics of later life and the aging process with specific emphasis on health. The physiological and behavioral dimensions of the aging process will be analyzed and discussed.

title: Death and Dying
description: Analyzes the relationship between death and health with emphasis upon the physiological, medical, psychological, legal, and consumer aspects of dying in contemporary America. Investigates problems that relate to the meaning of death, care of the dying, death ritual, bereavement, and death education. Prerequisite: HSC 150 or 160 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Women and Health
description: A general overview of issues related to women and health: the human female, a woman's right to control her body, health problems, women in the health marketplace, the gynecological examination, pregnancy and childbirth, teenage pregnancies, midwifery, female sexuality, women and aging, occupational health and women, and the women's health movement.

title: Internship in Health Science
description: The intern will be assigned to an approved health agency or educational institution for a period of time commensurate with the hours of credit to be earned. The student will periodically and terminally report to an academic adviser and to the administrator of the participating agency or agencies. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with HSC 575.

title: Public Health Practice
description: Public health organization and available community health resources. Recent developments and problems in public health. Examination of recent literature on preventive medicine and human conservation. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: HSC 160 and 180, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Environmental Health
description: The physical environment and its relationship to disease causation. Review of environmental health problems and their solutions. Areas of study include air and water pollution, milk and food sanitation, disposal of human excreta and waste, radiological agents in the environment, and occupational health problems. Prerequisite: HSC 480.

title: Epidemiology
description: Classic epidemics, evaluation of epidemiological principles and techniques of investigation, and epidemiological analysis of selected types of diseases. Prerequisite: HSC 480 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Public Health Education
description: Basic functions of public educators in various settings. Emphasizes the need for public health education, current settings for health education, forces and movements that influence health education, and the history of public health education. Prerequisite: HSC 180, 480.

title: Public Health Education: Planning and Evaluation
description: Intended for persons planning to work in public health agencies. Emphasizes the need for planning, current settings for public health education, techniques used to identify health education components of health programs, program planning techniques, and evaluation methodologies. Prerequisite: HSC 480, 484 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Quantitative Methods in Health Science
description: An introduction to practical applications of quantitative methods in health. Various approaches to identify, evaluate, compare, and report existing and potential health problems in community settings. One twohour laboratory period weekly emphasizes data manipulation by advanced technology.

title: Special Studies in Health Science
description: Designed to give undergraduate health science students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. -Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamentals of Mammalian Anatomy
description: Basic study of mammalian anatomy with detailed dissection and with examination of representative microscopic structure. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course.

title: Human Embryology
description: Normal development of the human organism including germ cell formation, fertilization, implantation, and organ formation. Consideration of embryonic environment, physiology, and abnormal development. Prerequisite: BIO 211 or ANAT 201.

title: Human Anatomy
description: Regional study of the structural and functional relations of the human body by means of dissection. Consideration of normal and abnormal development and microscopic structure of tissues and organs. Prerequisite: admission to the physical therapy program.

title: Human Anatomy
description: A continuation of ANAT 330. Regional study of the structural and functional relations of the human body by means of dissection. Consideration of normal and abnormal development and microscopic structure of tissues and organs. Prerequisite: ANAT 330.

title: Human Neuroanatomy
description: Offers a strong background in the basic structural and functional relations of the central nervous system. Emphasis on understanding the location of nerve cell centers and the fiber tracts entering and leaving these centers. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or ZOOL 330. Prerequisite recommended: ANAT 320 and 430. Prerequisites waived for physical therapy students.

title: Histology
description: Microscopic structure of organisms with special emphasis on the tissues of vertebrates. Introductory microtechnique. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: four courses in biological science. BIO 460 and ZOOL 330 are recommended.

title: Special Studies in Anatomy
description: Designed to give undergraduate anatomy students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Essentials of Human Physiology
description: Basic human physiology with stress on the major function of each organ system including aspects of nutrition, drugs, and drug abuse. Intended primarily for science teaching majors and minors in secondary education. Includes laboratory exercises designed to demonstrate physiological principles to high school students. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYSL 210.

title: Human Physiology
description: Vital processes with references to human functional biology. Group experimentation with recording apparatus. Prerequisite: BIO 102 and 103, BIO 111; and ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Human Physiology
description: Continuation of PHYSL 210. Functions of the human organ systems. Comparisons between vertebrate systems and mechanisms in humans. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210.

title: Neurophysiology
description: The function of the nervous system. Emphasis on electrical properties of excitable cells, synaptic transmissions, sensory and motor mechanisms, reflexes, higher sensory functions, and motor control. Laboratory exercises to demonstrate basic principles in neurophysiology. Prerequisite: admission to the physical therapy program or ANAT 405 with permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Physiology—Selected Systems
description: Human organsystem functions with consideration of laboratory animals and their contributions to human physiology. Advanced instrumentation and animal handling techniques stressed in laboratory. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: one year of inorganic chemistry; BIO 111; ANAT 201 or BIO 211.

title: Endocrinology
description: Endocrine functions in humans and mammals with special emphasis on mechanisms. Normal hormone regulation and pathophysiological principles. Laboratory experience with small mammal surgery and endocrine testing. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201; PHYSL 210 and 211; one year of general chemistry.

title: Cellular Physiology
description: The cell as the basic unit of function in all organisms. Ultrastructure of cell organelles and their metabolic processes. Physicochemical phenomena of membrane dynamics. Laboratory work on cell mechanisms and processes. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: one course in general chemistry; BIO 111, 112; ANAT 201; PHYSL 210.

title: Renal Physiology
description: A detailed study of the urinary system and excretory functions. Emphasizes human physiology but also includes comparative vertebrate systems. Subject matter ranges from the embryogenicanatomic level to the biochemicalpathological level. Laboratory study includes gross and microscopic anatomy, physiologic demonstrations, and clinical testing procedures. One threehour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: general chemistry, organic chemistry; one course in anatomy; one course in physiology.

title: Cardiovascular Dynamics
description: A functional study of the mammalian circulatory system, stressing actions of homeostatic control mechanisms and applications of physical principles to a biological system, with minimal use of mathematics in developing operational concepts. Experience in seminar style presentations with discussion of current research and recent literature. Prerequisite: one course in physiology and one in physics.

title: Human Toxicology
description: A survey of chemical, physical, zoological, and botanical toxicoses in human health. The implications and methodology of dealing with hazardous substances and poisons will be considered in detail. Prerequisite: one year of chemistry; one year of biology; one course in physiology; one course in anatomy.

title: Pathophysiology
description: The physiologic pathology of selected disease processes and dysfunctions. The pathogenesis of certain derangements with broad applicability. Underlying chemical, biological, and physical mechanisms will be studied. Laboratory experience will include demonstrations, specimen study, and visitations. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: a course in anatomy, physiology, and chemistry.

title: Special Studies in Physiology
description: Designed to give undergraduate physiology students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned but no more than 4 hours may be earned in one quarter or term.

title: Introduction to Patient Care
description: Designed as an introduction to the hospital setting and patient care. Instruction in nursing skills and basic medical technology. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in respiratory therapy.

title: Cardiopulmonary-Renal Anatomy and Physiology
description: Designed to give the student an indepth knowledge of the respiratory, circulatory, and renal systems. Emphasis on the respiratory system and how it interrelates with the other two systems. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210.

title: Basic Respiratory Care
description: Designed to familiarize the student with all types of basic respiratory care and equipment in preparation for clinical practice. Prerequisite: PHYCS 106.

title: Pharmacology
description: Designed to familiarize the respiratory therapy student with the indications and hazards of all commonly encountered drugs and to provide an indepth understanding of drugs used in respiratory care. Prerequisite: CHEM 105.

title: General Pathology
description: Designed to give respiratory therapy students an overview of human pathology.

title: Life Support
description: Designed to familiarize the student with aspects of resuscitation and the management of cardiorespiratory emergencies. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Diseases of the Chest
description: Designed to give respiratory therapy students an indepth study of diseases of the chest. Topics include acute and chronic pulmonary diseases and thoracic trauma. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Respiratory Specialties 1
description: Designed to familiarize the student with the specialty areas of respiratory therapy, including pulmonary function studies, pulmonary rehabilitation, and basic supervision. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Clinical Practice 1
description: Designed to introduce the student to patient care and respiratory therapy. Introduction to oxygen therapy, aerosol therapy, cleaning and sterilization of respiratory equipment, and intermittent therapy. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Mechanical Ventilation
description: Designed to familiarize the student with mechanical ventilation, including evaluation of the patient, selection of therapy, patient management, and the equipment used for these tasks. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Pediatric Respiratory Care
description: Designed to provide the student with the necessary knowledge for pediatric and neonatal respiratory care. Indepth presentation of oxygen therapy, mechanical ventilation, resuscitation, and treatment modalities. Prerequisite: permission of the program director. 211.Respiratory Specialties 2. (3) Provides the student with advanced knowledge in pulmonary care with emphasis on critical care. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Clinical Practice 2
description: Provides opportunity for the student to master techniques practiced in the previous quarter. Introduces critical respiratory care, airway care, and pulmonary function studies. Prerequisite: permission of the director.

title: Clinical Practice 3
description: Provides opportunity for the student to master techniques practiced in the previous quarter in the general care area and to increase proficiency in providing therapy to children. The major portion of the student's time is spent in critical care areas mastering ventilator therapy for adults and neonates. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Introduction to Radiography
description: Overview of radiography and its role in health care delivery. Includes general program information, student responsibilities, and an introduction to the radiology department and the hospital.

title: Medical Terminology
description: Provides the student with an understanding of the origins of medical terms, components of word building, abbreviations and symbols, terminology relating to the human body, and the use of medical terminology in understanding radiographi c orders and reports.

title: The American Health Care System
description: Overview of the health care system to include history and structure, providers, current issues, medical economics, and the organization and administration of hospitals.

title: The Principles of Patient Care
description: Overview of the concepts of patient care including considerations of physical and psychological conditions, routine and emergency procedures, medical ethics, and legal aspects. Prerequisite: ANAT 201; PHYSL 205.

title: Radiographic Procedures 1
description: A comprehensive study of skeletal radiographic positioning procedures to include radiographic terminology, procedural orientation, and an indepth description of the bony structures of the human body. Prerequisite: ANAT 201; PHYSL 205. Parallel AHSC 231.

title: Radiographic Procedures 2
description: A continuation of AHSC 224, including special procedures performed with and without contrast materials and the equipment used for these advanced imaging techniques. Prerequisite: AHSC 224. Parallel: AHSC 232.

title: Radiographic Procedures 3
description: A continuation of AHSC 225, including additional special procedures and the equipment used for advanced imaging techniques. Prerequisite:

title: Specialized Imaging Modalities
description: Overview of special computerized imaging techniques and radiologic applications to include tomography, nuclear magnetic resonance, and digital vascular imaging. Prerequisite: AHSC 226. Parallel: AHSC 234.

title: Principles of Radiography 2
description: A study of radiographic film and processing to include exposure factors and their effects and special equipment used to perform diagnostic procedures. Prerequisite: APHYS 228.

title: Principles of Radiography 3
description: A study of clinical diseases and their effects on radiographs to include technical adjustments, film evaluation, and quality control. Prerequisite: AHSC 229.

title: Clinical Applications 1
description: Practical experience in the performance of radiographic procedures through a rotational system correlated with didactic coursework. General radiography, stomachs, colons, IVPs, pediatrics, chest, bedsides, surgery, nuclear xray, evenings, myelograms, and emergency room. Parallel: AHSC 224.

title: Clinical Applications 2
description: Practical experience in the performance of radiographic procedures, through a rotational system correlated with didactic coursework. General radiography, stomachs, colons, IVPs, pediatrics, chest, bedsides, surgery, nuclear xray, evenings, myelograms, and emergency room. Prerequisite: AHSC 224, 231. Parallel: AHSC 225.

title: Clinical Applications 3
description: Practical experience in the performance of radiographic procedures through a rotational system correlated with didactic coursework. Stomachs, colons, IVPs, general radiography, emergency room, pediatrics, bedsides, myelograms, surgery, nuclear xray, float, mammograms, tomograms, and reading room. Includes rotation through an outside affiliate and an elective in either ultrasound, nuclear medicine, radiation therapy, or cardiac cath. Prerequisite: AHSC 225, 232. Parallel: AHSC 226.

title: Clinical Applications 4
description: Practical experience in the performace of radiographic procedures through a rotational system correlated with didactic coursework. Stomachs, colons, IVPs, general radiography, emergency room, pediatrics, bedsides, myelograms, surgery, nuclear xray, float, mammograms, tomograms, and reading room. Includes rotation through an outside affiliate and an elective in either ultrasound, nuclear medicine, radiation therapy, or cardiac cath. Prerequisite: AHSC 226, 233. Parallel: APHYS 227.

title: Clinical Applications 5
description: Practical experience in the performance of radiographic procedures through a rotational system correlated with didactic coursework. Computerized tomography, special procedures, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Includes an approved internship in an outside hospital or clinic by prior arrangement. Prerequisite: AHSC 234 and AHSC 227 or APHYS 227.

title: Special Topics in Radiography
description: Overview of basic principles of radiology management, education, and research. Includes the registration procedure for radiographers and legal implications on the state and national levels. Prerequisite: AHSC 220.

title: Clinical Internship 1
description: An orientation to the field of nuclear medicine technology. Emphasizes elementary patient care procedures and professional ethics. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in nuclear medicine.

title: Clinical Internship 2
description: Introduction to nursing care in the nuclear medicine clinic and patient processing. Prerequisite: AHSC 240.

title: Clinical Internship 3
description: Directed learning experiences in special areas of the nuclear medicine clinic. Introduction to scintillation camera and rectilinear imaging, in addition to related instrumentation, hot lab procedures, and dose preparation and administration. Prerequisite: AHSC 241.

title: Clinical Internship 4
description: Directed learning experiences in nuclear medicine clinical procedures to include imaging, quality control of instrumentation, radiopharmaceuticals, and in vitro techniques. Prerequisite: AHSC 242.

title: Clinical Internship 5
description: Directed learning experiences in nuclear medicine clinical procedures to include imaging, quality control of instrumentation, radiopharmaceuticals, and in vitro techniques. Prerequisite: AHSC 243.

title: Clinical Theory and Administration 1
description: Indepth study of the clinical theory of nuclear medicine technology as it applies to examinations performed in a nuclear medicine clinic. Introduces administrative and recordkeeping procedures required by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the operation of a nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in nuclear medicine.

title: Clinical Theory and Administration 2
description: Continuation of AHSC 245. Indepth study of the clinical theory of nuclear medicine technology as it applies to examinations performed in nuclear medicine clinics. Basic introduction to the types of film and film processing used in nuclear medicine clinics. Prerequisite: AHSC 245.

title: Radiopharmaceuticals
description: Preparation, quality control, and the diagnostic and therapeutic application of radiopharmaceuticals in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 247.

title: Radiation, Biology, and Safety
description: Somatic and genetic effects of radiation and the procedures for radiological control and safety. Prerequisite: APHYS 247.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation
description: An indepth study of the components and performance characteristics of equipment commonly used in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 250. Parallel: AHSC 252.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation Lab
description: A weekly laboratory for nuclear medicine technology students enrolled in AHSC 251. Parallel: AHSC 251.

title: In Vitro Nuclear Medicine Procedures
description: An introduction to the basic principles of radioimmunoassay and in vitro nuclear medicine procedures. Prerequisite: APHYS 250 and AHSC 248 or APHYS 248.

title: Topics in Nuclear Medicine
description: Designed to provide the student with academic credit for the completion of a scientific project. Parallel: AHSC 243.

title: Principles of Health Care Management
description: Basic introduction to principles of managing health care services for students preparing for supervisory and middlemanagement positions. Includes the hospital as a workplace; hospital organization, management; job design, performance appraisals, compensation; finance, budgeting; planning, evaluation; and management information systems. Prerequisite: major or minor in subject relating to course.

title: Advanced Concepts in Allied Health Sciences
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with instructor with competence in the subject to be studied. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Research Seminar
description: Knowledge and skills required to conduct clinical, educational, and managerial research in the health care setting. Prerequisite: health science major and senior class standing.

title: Independent Study in Allied Health
description: Designed to allow the student to increase his or her knowledge and skills in both the technical and patient care aspects of allied health. Students may complete one of Methodist Hospital's "Adda-Comp" programs to earn credit in this course. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Department of Political Science Vasicko, Chairperson; Baker, Chang, Corbett, Cranor, Crawley, Frankland, Hamori, Hollands, Menez, Meyer, Perry, Rouse, Rudoni, Sargent, Scheele Political science, the study of politics and government, has been a subject of formal intellectual inquiry since classical antiquity. Aristotle, Socrates, and Plato developed the fundamental questions that continue to form the core of the discipline. They observed that all societies have political systems (polis or state), that polities differ in form and functions, that the relationship of individuals to the state differs from one society to another, and that differences among polities lead to war. Those observations led them to ask, What is the nature of people (that makes government inevitable and affects the nature of the political system)? What is the nature of the state (legal political system)? What is the nature of the relationship betwee n people and the state? The only substantial question aded later was about relationships among states (international relations). These questions are at once the basis for political theory and the construct for the mass of normative and empirical data that has been accumulated through the centuries. The primary goals of political science are (1) transmission of established knowledge through lectures, discussion, scholarly writing, textbooks, and commentary and (2) research. These goals assume a scientific study of available data and a continual testing and evaluation of relevant social norms. Political science does not seek to give students values, but to develop their talents for valuation. The principal utilities of political science are intellectual, civil, and vocational. The first two may be considered universal in that serious study of the discipline results in a more informed citizenry. The last is more particular in that it applies chiefly to those in occupations involving a degree of expertise derived from study and experience in the discipline. Teachers of civics, government, and political science at all school levels constitute a major group using the peculiar contributions of political science. The growing numbers of government officers and employees constitute another. Increasing professionalism in government service and the gradual passing of Jacksonian standards for public service have increased the demand for knowledge of political science. Among the numerous related occupations that draw heavily on the discipline are law, journalism, business, economics, medicine, agriculture, and labor. The political science program at Ball State University is designed to facilitate pursuit of the primary goals of the discipline and realization of its principal utilities. The basic course (POLS 130) is an introduction to national government, upon which all the other courses are based. The pattern of courses is organized into the subareas generally recognized by the discipline, viz., political theory and methodology, American government, public law and policy, public administration, foreign and comparative government, and international politics. Political science courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in political science, teacher licensing programs, urban and regional studies, master of arts, master of public administration, as a cognate field in the social science doctoral program, and at both the undergraduate and graduate levels for students in other departments.
