title: Politics: Today and Tomorrow
description: An introduction to the contemporary issues of national and world politics. Emphasizes both current political events and longterm trends in politics.

title: American National Government
description: The organization and operation of national government as it relates to current issues such as civil rights, welfare, ecology, consumer protection, and international relations.

title: Citizen and the Law
description: To help students understand citizen encounters with the legal system, this course explains the operation of the legal system and the political aspects of the pertinent legal issues. Uses a variety of activities, films, and lectures. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson or the paralegal program coordinator.

title: Introduction to Paralegalism
description: Provides students with concepts of paralegalism with emphasis on legal ethics and values, the development and future of the paralegal function in our present legal environment, and a presentation of the concepts of litigation and legal procedure. Prerequisite: POLS 140.

title: Legal Research and Writing
description: Provides students with an analysis of court procedures and appeal procedures, an indepth examination of reference sources available to attorneys, and improvement of research and writing skills. Prerequisite: POLS 141.

title: Introduction to Planning
description: A survey of problems inherent in planning for cities and regions that uses contributions of other disciplines such as history, geography, sociology, and economics. Required for majors in urban studies and planning; elective for others with permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Politics
description: The scope and methods of the study of political science. An examination of the basic concepts and theories in the discipline. Traditions and approaches in the field and their application to the various subdivisions of political science. Strongly recommended for students with departmental areas in political science.

title: Introduction to Western Political Thought
description: A topical exploration of perennial themes and issues raised within the tradition of Western political thought. Explores points of view of prominent Western theorists by examining various dimensions of the political concepts of equality, justice, freedom, and authority.

title: State and Local Politics
description: Practices, politics, and structures of state and local governments in the United States with an emphasis on the Indiana experience.

title: Urban Government in the United States
description: Structure, functions, problems, and trends in city, urban, and metropolitan governments.

title: Family Law
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the legal problems in domestic relations. Covers legal problems involved in marriage, separation, divorce, child custody, adoption, and nonsupport.

title: Comparative Political Systems
description: A comparison of modern political systems as represented by the principal nations of the world.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: Historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors contributing to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 280. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 279.

title: American Foreign Policy
description: A survey of major factors in foreign policy formulation, an introduction to the process of making U.S. foreign policy, and an analysis of relevant American strategic doctrines.

title: International Relations
description: A survey of the formal relations among sovereign states in the international system, emphasizing the operation of diplomacy, the elements of power, the procedures for the settlement of disputes, and the various modes of conflict resolution.

title: Early Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of political thought of the early Mediterranean and medieval worlds that became the foundation of modern political theories and systems of the West. Emphasis on writings of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, St. Augustine, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Machiavelli.

title: Modern Western Political Thought
description: Analysis of selected writings of leading political theorists from the Age of Reformation to the present.

title: Communist Political Thought: From Marx to Present
description: A critical analysis and evaluation of Marxism, Leninism, Stalinism, Khrushchevism, post-Khrushchev Communist ideology, and Maoism as a system of theoretical propositions and as an action program of an international movement.

title: Voter Polling Techniques
description: Methods by which information is obtained on the voting behavior and attitudes of the electorate. Emphasis on producing a working knowledge of polling techniques. Includes such topics as sampling, interviewing, and questionnaire construction.

title: Introduction to Law and Enforcement
description: Survey of the development of law and contemporary law enforcement in the United States with special attention to various components of law enforcement systems, their interrelationships, purposes, and needs.

title: Problems in Public Policy
description: Current political, economic, and social problems in the United States. Consideration of relationships between government and elements of our free enterprise system, including agriculture, small and large firms, labor, public utilities, and finance.

title: National Defense Policy
description: An international survey of military capacity and function provides the background for analysis of the national defense policy of the United States. Special emphasis on American strategic interests and problems of weapons, technology, nuclear control, and disarmament.

title: Environmental Law and Policy
description: Significant facets of the legal system's response to conflicting demands upon environmental resources. Composition of environmental problems, control issues, policy formulation, and legal remedies.

title: Public Administration
description: Organization, personnel, and functions of the various agencies of administration—national, state, and local.

title: Public Opinion and the Political Process
description: The nature of public opinion, instruments, techniques, and institutions involved in formation of public opinion; and the political uses and implications at home and abroad of public opinion and propaganda. 371.Public Interest Groups and Government. (4) Internal government and external political strategy of private associations, such as trade associations, unions, and professional, church, and patriotic organizations. Implications of pressure group activities for constitutionalism, majoritarianism, and constituency, and the effects of pressure groups on the political process.

title: Political Campaigns
description: Considers political campaigns from theoretical and practical perspectives as the linkage between citizens and the government in a representative democracy. Designed to answer questions on the theory, strategies, and techniques of political campaigns.

title: Comparative Policy Problems
description: A comparative political analysis of selected contemporary domestic problems confronting modern nationstates. Emphasizes both the process of policy making and the substance of specific public policies.

title: Governments and Politics of Western Europe
description: An introduction to the concept of Europe as a political and cultural entity, to the government and political structures of the three major powers in Western Europe—Great Britain, France, and Germany—and to the current state of the Western European integration movement. 384, British Government and Politics. (4) The political system of the United Kingdom, including a discussion of the Commonwealth and Britain's place in an expanding European community. Emphasis also on Anglo-American relations and British contributions to American political arrangements.

title: Honors Colloquium in Political Science
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in political science, with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Open to students in the Honors College and to other outstanding students by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The United Nations and International Organization
description: Concentrated study of international organizations and the structure, functions and current issues facing the United Nations. Students participate in a mock Security Council at Ball State and may have an opportunity to participate in the National Model United Nations Conference.

title: International Relations in Asia
description: A survey of contemporary international relations in Asia with a special emphasis on the roles of China, Japan, the United States, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics in this area.

title: International Relations: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics/Soviet Bloc
description: The role of the Soviet Union as a world power and the examination of Soviet strategic concepts in foreign policy.

title: Internship in American Government and Politics
description: The student works either parttime or fulltime for one quarter in the office of a public official in national, state, or local government; a candidate for public office; or a political party. Assignments depend upon the interests of students and the convenience of sponsors. Prerequisite: 16 hours in political science including the following or their equivalents: POLS 130, 237, and 431, or 350, or 473 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Paralegalism
description: The internship course for the legal assistant and legal administration programs combines the student's academic training with practical experience within a law firm, corporation, bank, or governmental agency. Prerequisite: POLS 140, 141, 142, permission of the program director, and approval of the supervising employer.

title: Issues in Political Science
description: Investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in the field with emphasis on subfields, specialties, and materials not covered in established courses. Open to upperclass students with special interest in politics. The content is announced before each offering.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Topics are chosen and investigated in consultation with the department chairperson and a professor with special competence in the area involved. Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interests that qualify them to do semiindependent study. Prerequisite: basic courses in the area selected for special study and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings in Planning
description: Reading program developed in consultation with the department chairperson and a professor with special competence in planning. Open to juniors and seniors with special aptitude and interest in planning. Prerequisite: POLS 461 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Workshop in Political Science
description: Intensive study of selected problems in political science. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: American Political Thought
description: American political thought from the colonial period to the present. Puritanism, nature of rights, constitutionalism and federalism, nature of the Union, democracy, liberalism, conservatism, individualism and collectivism, welfare state, isolation and internationalism, and national security and freedom.

title: Research Methods in Political Science
description: A critical examination of methodological problems and practices in the formulation, execution, evaluation, and reporting of political science research, including a comparison of datagathering techniques, their respective limitations, and appropriate application.

title: Legislation
description: A functional study of legislative bodies and lawmaking, covering organization of legislative bodies, operation of the committee system, relations with interest groups, executive branches, bill drafting, legislative aids, controls over legislation, and movement for reform.

title: The American Chief Executive
description: An examination of the American concept of a political chief executive as a coordinate member, with legislature and courts, of a government team. Problems of jurisdiction, leadership, authority, public relations, and centralization.

title: The American Judicial System
description: The nature and functions of state and federal judicial systems, including the role of courts in relation to individuals and the executive and legislative branches of government.

title: State Legislatures
description: Legislative systems in American state government. External influences (constituencies, political parties, interest groups), internal influences (organizational structure, staff, norms, decision making), issues confronting state legislatures, and reform proposals.

title: Intergovernmental Relations
description: Analysis of relations among national, state, and local governments. Considerations of constitutional and legal bases and the nature of relations, such as grantsinaid, tax immunity, education, and interstate compacts.

title: Metropolitan Problems
description: Analysis of cities and metropolitan communities; examines the nature, characteristics, functions, governmental structure, intergovernmental relations, social makeup and problems, economic base, decisionmaking structure, and other related topics; considers the present and future role of planning and citizen participation.

title: Consumers, Competition, and the Law
description: Legal and political aspects of commercial and industrial regulation with emphasis upon antitrust policy and consumer protection.

title: American Constitutional Law
description: The Constitution of the United States, its development and interpretations through principal statutes and judicial decisions. Congressional policies embodied in socioeconomic legislation and doctrines developed by the Supreme Court. Prerequisite: POLS 130.

title: Constitutional Liberties
description: Relations between the individual and the government as revealed through cases in constitutional law. Content includes cases involving the Bill of Rights and the Fourteenth Amendment. Prerequisite: POLS 130 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Policy Analysis
description: Equips the student with the tools of the policy analyst through systematic analysis of programs and projects. Special emphasis on problem definition,• goal determination, systematic evaluation of alternatives, socioeconomic and political indicators, performance measures, and impact evaluation. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 342.

title: Land Use Regulation
description: An analysis of the legislative and constitutional aspects of the regulation of land use at various levels of government, including zoning, subdivision regulations, urban renewal, codes, enforcement, eminent domain, conservation, reclamation, interstate compacts, and metropolitan and regional agencies.

title: Administrative Organization and Management in Government
description: Examines the nature and role of administrative organization and management, growth and impact on government of the scientific management movement, formal and informal organization of administrative authority, operational problems and processes, and criteria for evaluation of administration. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Public Personnel Administration
description: The organization, purposes, and activities of civil service agencies; recruitment policies and procedures; classification and compensation plans; efficiency measurements, and rewards; training programs; morale, discipline, and rights of public employees; and promotion, transfer, retirement, and other personnel processes. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Public Financial Administration
description: Principles and practices of administration of national, state, and local finances; administrative financial organization, budgetary procedure, preaudit and postaudit, assessment and collection of taxes, purchasing, letting of contracts, publicly owned undertakings, public debt, and grantsinaid. Prerequisite: POLS 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Politics and Administration of Local Government Budgets
description: Local government budgeting with emphasis on political and administrative issues in budget preparation and accountability. Topics include revenue development including tax and nontax sources, capital expenditure programming, financing pensions, contracting for services, costbenefit analysis, and federal and state grant mechanisms.

title: Administrative Law
description: Legal and political study of independent regulatory agencies; their powers, functions, and roles as determined by an analysis of relevant cases in which basic principles are identified and synthesized with other areas of public law.

title: Public Works Administration
description: An overview of public works administrative techniques and problems. Designed to provide a general awareness of management, policy, and decisionmaking concerns on such topics as water, street, solid waste, pollution control systems.

title: Community Planning and Its Administration
description: Planning and development of improved land use and service activities of cities and predominantly urban communities. Consideration of scope, legal basis, implementation, and problems of planning for streets, utilities, education, recreation, transportation, zoning, and related community services.

title: Problems in National Administration
description: An examination in depth of uniquely national administrative problems and activities. National administrative structures and techniques are examined in detail, including their use and application in the administration of specific national policy areas.

title: Labor-Management Relations in Government
description: Examines public employee unionization, legal provisions for collective bargaining, determination and recognition of bargaining units, bilateral negotiation, and thirdparty involvement procedures, administration of agreements, and the processes and strategies in collective bargaining negotiations in public organizations.

title: Administrative Problems in State Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and organizational behavior at the state level. Special emphasis on the provision of government services and functions in the major areas of budgeting and taxation, education, environmental protection, public health, and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350.

title: Administrative Problems in Local Government
description: An analysis of administrative procedures and organizational behavior at the local level. Special emphasis on intergovernmental aspects of program administration in the major areas of taxing and spending, education, personnel, and public works. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 237 or 350.

title: The Politics of Public Sector Productivity
description: Reviews literature concerned with contemporary political issues in local, state, and federal government productivity. Emphasis on the political and attitudinal problems associated with proposals for improved productivity and effectiveness in governmental administration.

title: Career Development and Training in the Public Sector
description: Administration of public personnel development programs especially as they have emerged within the last decade. Emphasis on personnel needs assessment and training programs in government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels and on the political implications of CETA training efforts.

title: American Political Parties
description: Organization and functions of political parties in the United States and their role in a representative democracy.

title: Women in Politics
description: A crossnational survey of women in politics with emphasis on women and public policy, the political roles of women, and the problems of women in politics within the context of contemporary public affairs.

title: Minority Group Politics
description: Deals with political impact of ethnic groups on American politics. Emphasis on both legal and extralegal means by which ethnic groups become involved in and influence public policy. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 130.

title: Political Socialization and Behavior
description: The political scientist's view of the sociological and psychological bases of political attitudes and behavior with emphasis on political belief systems, political participation, political leadership, and the distribution of power in society.

title: Latin American Political Systems
description: Underlying principles and institutional development of government and politics in selected Latin American nations.

title: Government and Politics of the Middle East
description: The Middle East as a case study in comparative politics. The application of conceptual tools in political science to the investigation and analysis of political systems in non-Western cultures. The role of foreign powers in the government and politics of the area.

title: Government and Politics of the Soviet Union
description: A survey of the modes, methods, and policies by which communist philosophy is put into action by the Communist Party and by its authoritative extension, the Soviet government. Includes those peculiar governmental roles—economic planning, indoctrination, and purges—that are special trademarks of a communist political system.

title: Government and Politics of China
description: A comprehensive survey of the government and politics of modern China, both the Republic of China and Communist China.

title: International Law
description: A survey of the Law of Nations by the analysis of prominent decisions of international tribunals, examination of representative legal principles, the briefing of appropriate cases, and the conducting of mock court trials.

title: World Politics
description: Theories of contemporary interactions among states, especially the major powers. Particular attention will be given to conflict resolution.

title: Communist China's Foreign Policy
description: A comprehensive analysis of Communist China's role in international politics, with specific emphasis on the impact of Communist China's foreign policy and the response to it. Department of Psychological Science Hines, Chairperson; Balogh, Barr, Butler, Caplan, Clark, Davidson, Deckers, Fischer, Goldstone, Hill, Hines, Humm, Meeker, Meunier, Perkins, Pisano, Stevenson, Whitley, Wittig Psychology is the science that studies the behavior of humans as they interact with their environment. Lower forms of animal life may also be studied, but the ultimate purpose is to understand human beings better. As a behavioral science, psychology shares with the other sciences the objectives of description, understanding, prediction, and control. The department carries out its purposes by developing and communicating psychology as a specialized area of knowledge, providing general education courses in psychological foundations and programs appropriate to its function, and helping students in all disciplines— teaching, law, medicine, engineering, art, music, business—increase their understanding of the forces and influences that shape their behavior and society. For many students, the role of psychology in the university curriculum will be to contribute to their general education; but for an increasing number of students, psychology will make more detailed and specific contributions to their programs. The department offers a departmental major and minor in the discipline of psychology. These programs provide a basic background for graduate work in any one of the many branches of psychology—clinical, industrial, social, experimental, counseling, school psy- Psychological Science 301 chology, psychometryand an appropriate supplemental background for advanced work in other disciplines such as law, the ministry, or medicine. Students interested in teaching psychology at the high school level may complete a social studies major or minor with an area of concentration in psychology, organized to ensure that they, as teachers, will have an appropriate and sufficient background for teaching psychology at the secondary level. Although an increasing number of high schools offer psychology, the number of courses taught in high school psychology is rather limited. For this reason, students wishing to teach psychology should choose other primary or supporting areas for which there is a reasonable demand in the public schools. Graduate courses and programs in the Department of Psychological Science offer advanced work in the study of psychology as an academic discipline and provide programs applicable to advanced degrees in specialized areas of psychology. Also, offerings provide electives for general education and serve as appropriate concentration areas in various advanced degree programs. Teachers of psychology may also combine graduate study in professional education with graduate study in psychology. Such combined study may enlarge the sphere of potential employment and add permanence to previously temporary or provisional teacher licensing and certification. title: General Psychology
description: Introduction to various branches of psychology and the contributions of each to an understanding of the behavior of people as they interact with their en, vironment. Prerequisite: EXEL students can take this course in two consecutive 2-hour segments. All other students must complete a single 4-hour offering of the course.

title: The Psychology of Human Adaptation to Stress
description: Adaptation and reactions to stress as psychological phenomena; research on stress and its influence on personality development; the appraisal of threatening situations by the individual; coping and coping reaction patterns to stress; theories of adaptation to psychological stress. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Not open to the student who has credit in PSYSC 421 or 432.

title: Applied Behavior Analysis
description: Introduction to the principles of operant psychology and application of these principles to applied situations with humans in other than formal educational settings. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Not open to the student who has credit in PSYSC 481.

title: Elementary Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics and statistics of inference. The computation, application, and interpretation of various elementary statistics. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Intermediate Statistics for Psychological Research
description: Inferential statistics and research design, computation and interpretation of statistics in the context of psychological research design issues. Critical analysis of published research literature. Prerequisite: PSYSC 241.

title: Introduction to Biopsychology
description: A brief introduction to the general subject of biopsychology. Topics include the fundamentals of nervous system structure and function; consciousness and its altered states; memory, language, and thought; emotionality and personality. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Psychology of Sexual Behavior
description: An examination of the determinants of human sexual behavior, focusing especially on the development of sexual identity and attitudes. Uses perspectives from social psychology, personality theory, and physiological psychology to build an understanding of this most complex behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Introduction to Experimental Psychology
description: An introduction to the use of the scientific method in the study of human behavior. Students analyze and evaluate experimental studies to gain experience with research techniques while using essential controls and acceptable procedures. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Introduction to Comparative Psychology
description: A survey of the theoretical and empirical foundations of animal behavior, including that of man, considered from a comparative, biological point of view. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Introduction to Social Psychology
description: Basic understanding of the psychosocial problems involved in the functioning of an individual in society. Emphasis on various influences that help to shape the psychological patterns of interpersonal relationships. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Experimental Social Psychology
description: Emphasizes basic empirical research methods with special focus on techniques commonly used in contemporary social psychological research. Combines the academic study of these methods with their actual application in research investigations conducted by students. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 316.

title: Experimental Child Psychology
description: A survey of theory and research in children's perception, memory, learning, cognition, and language. Prerequisites: PSYSC 100, 241, 284.

title: Psychology of Women
description: Psychological study of women with emphasis on achievement motivation and dependency, attitudes toward women, sexrole identity, biological and social influences on women's behavior, selfconcepts and psychological conflicts, and a study of research in sex differences. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, or permission of the department Psychological Science 303

title: Environmental Psychology
description: Presents the current knowledge and research in environmental psychology, and studies its relevance to psychological planning for special needs of individuals. Investigates the psychological impact of selected factors in various kinds of environments on individuals and groups. Prerequisite: PSYSC 316 or permission of the department chairperson. NR 101 is strongly recommended.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
description: Theoretical and practical foundations underlying the construction, use, and interpretation of standardized psychological tests and inventdories. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Honors Colloquium in Psychology
description: Explorations of selected issues in psychology with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion of such topics as psychobiology, social psychology, learning, personality, and abnormal psychology.

title: Motivation and Emotion
description: An introduction to basic theory and research relating to motivation and emotion and applications to various aspects of human behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 284 or 317.

title: Sensation and Perception
description: The human senses: their physiological makeup, development, and functioning. Emphasizes basic principles of perception and stimulus hunger. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 284 or 317.

title: Psychology of Cognition
description: Analysis of research and theories in the psychology of cognition and thinking. Major topics are verbal learning, problem solving, concept formation, and psycholinguistics. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 284 or 317.

title: Introduction to the Study of Personality
description: Presents and compares a wide variety of classical and modern theories of personality and pertinent empirical research. Considers the components of a good theory of personality and the applications of various personality theories. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Abnormal Psychology
description: Systematic study of behavior pathology with special reference to the psychopathology of physical illness and handicaps, psychosomatic and somatopsychic illnesses, neuroses, psychoses, character disorders, addiction, and acute and chronic brain disorders. Primary emphasis on etiology, symptomatology, prognosis, and prevention. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 421.

title: Hereditary Influences on Human Behavior
description: Hereditary influences on the development of cognitive and intellectual abilities, personality, mental illness, and biopsychological characteristics with emphasis on data pertaining to humans. No biological or genetic expertise is assumed. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241 or permission of the chairperson.

title: Organically Based Behavioral Disorders
description: Investigates behavioral abnormalities associated with neurological dysfunction. Topics include epilepsy, senility, drug effects, sleep disorders, and the violent personality. Explores theoretical views concerning schizophrenia and affective disorders. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 267; junior or senior standing.

title: Survey of Clinical Psychology
description: Introduction to the roles and functions of personnel in clinical psychology. Prerequisite: PSYSC 421 and 432.

title: Child Personality and Psychopathology
description: Research directed toward the understanding of personality and psychopathology in children and youth. Prerequisite: PSYSC 421 and 432.

title: Teaching of Psychology in Secondary Schools
description: Materials and methods used in teaching psychology at the secondary school level, including instructional issues concerning psychology with a personal adjustment orientation and as an academic discipline. Prerequisite: 12 hours of credit in psychology.

title: Current Research and Trends in the Teaching of Psychology
description: Current research in the teaching of psychology with an emphasis on the research of new curricular and instructional approaches.

title: Psychology of Learning
description: The nature of learning processes, possible influences upon these processes and resultant behavior, and applications of the psychology of learning. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 284 or 317.

title: Physiological Psychology
description: An introduction to the physical basis of behavior, involving primarily the nervous system and its structure and function. Emphasis on the role of bodily systems in perception, learning, motivation, and conscious function. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Industrial Psychology
description: The application of psychological principles to personnel selection and training, worker motivation and morale, labor problems in business and industry, executive leadership, consumer behavior, engineering psychology, and personal problems in business and industry. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Organizational Development: A Psychological Perspective
description: Presentation of change techniques from a process and small group perspective with special emphasis on the limitations and logic involved in their use. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Psychology of Selection and Placement
description: Introduction to principles of personnel testing as applied to the selection and placement process. Focus on development of predictors and criteria, selection of an appropriate validation model, and the psychological dynamics of the interview processes. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241 or equivalent.

title: Human Factors Psychology
description: Influences of job design on worker productivity and satisfaction. Includes topics such as engineering psychology, industrial psychology, job enrichment, and quality of work life. Considers aspects of both physical and social work environments. Prerequisite: PSYSC 241 or equivalent.

title: Experimental Behavior Analysis
description: Investigation and practice in experimental behavior analysis, with emphasis on operant conditioning. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 213, and 241.

title: Systematic Psychology
description: The major concepts of various schools of psychological thought and contemporary theoretical systems as they have evolved historically. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and senior standing.

title: Honors Seminar in Psychology
description: Explores possibilities for and development of a research project. Prerequisite: acceptance to the departmental honors program.

title: Seminar in Psychology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of psychology. Prerequisite: psychology major and senior standing.

title: Seminar in Psychology
description: Investigates topics of interest in the current literature of psychology.

title: Supervised Empirical Research Experience
description: Experience in the collection of behavioral data in the field or laboratory setting. Students work closely with a supervising faculty member. The credit hours may be accumulated in more than one quarter. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Psychology
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with instructors with special competence in the area involved. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. The credit hours may be accumulated in more than one quarter. Department of Social Work Macy, Chairperson; Brown, Dolon, Dowery, Gildner, Holmes, Miller Social Work as a Professional Discipline Social work is truly a twentiethcentury profession: before 1900 there were no professional schools of social work, graduate or undergraduate, for preparing social workers. The rapidly changing industrial society of the United States, accompanied by the increasing number and variety of complex social problems, has contributed to the dramatic growth of the profession in recent decades. Social work is both a science and an art concerned with meeting human and social welfare needs. Its science is the body of knowledge, derived from social and behavioral sciences, about individuals, families, organizations, groups, and communities. Its art is the blending of that knowledge with professional values and skills to meet human and social welfare needs. The practice of social work requires not only the intellectual capacity to absorb a substantial body of knowledge but also the ability to master skills in interpersonal relationships and in effecting social change. It requires commitment to ethical values, concern for people, regard for human dignity, selfdiscipline, selfknowledge, independence, and integrity. Social work is practiced in a variety of settings, both public and private, with many client groups, including youth, developmentally disabled, emotionally disturbed, chemically dependent, older persons, and the poor. The baccalaureate social work program prepares students for entry into beginning social work practice. The program, which has been accredited by the Council on Social Work Education since 1974, also provides an appropriate background for advanced study in social work. Throughout the program, students complete social work courses that build upon a liberal arts base including the humanities and the social, behavioral, and biological sciences. An orientation to the philosophy, history, settings, and professional practice of social work is provided, as are opportunities to implement classroom content in actual agency and community settings. Specific social work courses, field trips, practicums, and volunteer experiences help students develop an understanding of the knowledge, values, and skills required for entrylevel professional practice. Social Work 305 The department maintains a formal advising program for social work majors. This program, which is required for accreditation, is designed to help each student evaluate his or her potential for completing the social work major. Registration for upperdivision social work courses requires permission of the department chairperson. Students who are admitted to the major are given academic and professional advising by social work faculty. description: A descriptive, historical, and evolutionary study of the institution of social welfare, including social welfare programs, policies, and services. title: Social Work Practice 1
description: Introduction to social work practice at the generalist level and social work as a general profession within the social welfare institution in American society. title: Internship in Social Welfare
description: Exposure to and beginning confrontation with the general nature of social work. Opportunity for students to apply previously learned social work knowledge, either as volunteers or as staff members in a social service agency. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200, 201, 355, and permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in SOCWK 459.

title: Social Welfare and Services 2
description: The effect of public social welfare policies on social service client systems. The effect of social policies on various economic, ethnic, racial, and sex groups. Prerequisite: SOCWK 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Welfare Services in Developing and Overdeveloped Countries
description: Survey and comparison of selected social welfare services in developing and overdeveloped countries. Social policies underlying the services, the cultural and traditional value basis, and the role of the profession of social work. Special emphasis on health, family planning, community development, and income maintenance programs.

title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment 1
description: The behavior of the macro social systems and the influence of these systems on human behavior. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200 and 201.

description: The individual and the family as social systems, their developmental stages and the social services needed at stages throughout the life cycle of these social systems. Prerequisite: SOCWK 321 and permission of the department chairperson

description: The use of social work skills to develop and codify social work practice theory. Materials on interviewing, reporting, and recording as means of helping others are reviewed as background for analyzing relationships and interactions between social workers and clients. Prerequisite: SOCWK 200 and 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Selected Aspects of Social Work Practice
description: Examines specialized issues, methodologies, and professional concerns confronting social work practitioners in contemporary American society. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Services for Allied Professions
description: Designed for the non -social work major preparing for a career in an allied human service profession. Emphasizes social work practice skills useful for work with individuals, families, and support and task groups. Social work practice principles are core themes of the course. Not open to students majoring in social work.

title: Supervision for Social Workers
description: For students who plan to enter a supervisory position in a social service organization. Emphasis on administrative practices within social service settings, the building and maintenance of work relationships, and the development of supervisory techniques.

title: Social Work Practice 2
description: The application of practice methods of the social work generalist to microlevel systems. Emphasizes individual, family, and small group practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 313, 327, 355; SOC 380 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Practice 3
description: The application of practice methods of the social work generalist to macrolevel systems. Emphasizes the task group, organization, and community aspects of practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 313, 327, 355; SOC 380 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Practicum
description: The course is a 400-clockhours field placement in a social service setting selected and approved by the Department of Social Work. Social work assignments provide learning opportunities to integrate social work theory, professional ethics, and practice skills corroborated by professional evaluation. Prerequisite: SOCWK 450, 454, and permission of the department chairperson.

Johnson, Morris, Tamney, Tucker Sociology is the application of the scientific method to human relations. It is the attempt to use our collective wisdom in a systematic manner in order to have as much confidence as possible in the accuracy of our social beliefs. Science goes beyond mere opinion. Social scientists attempt to describe as objectively as possible what is really happening in the world and to understand why events have occurred in a certain way. Sociology is among the younger social sciences. Although introduced into a small number of universities before the close of the nineteenth century, its development as a recognized academic discipline has occurred chiefly within the past few decades. Quickly expanding research activities have vastly extended the body of sociological knowledge, and the concepts of the discipline are becoming widely accepted throughout society. Increasingly, these concepts as well as an understanding of the sociological perspective are being introduced at the high school level. Sociology is a major part of the scientific foundation for many applied fields. Social work, the criminal justice system, personnel work, counseling management, nursing practice, and the law are all based in part on the findings of sociologists. Students interested in any of these areas would find sociology courses useful. Sociology is taught at two levels. On the one hand there is the general study of social behavior, in courses about complex organization or social class. Ideas developed in such courses are used in the more specific social sciences such as political science and economics. On the other hand, sociologists teach courses about institutions for which separate departments have not developed, such as the family, and about lifecycle stages, such as childhood or old age. In addition sociologists develop research skills in courses about methods and population. As a liberal discipline, sociology contributes to broadening the student's perspective of the sociocultural environment, and to the individual's own relationship to it, thus helping to produce an outlook less restricted by the limitations of untested folk beliefs. The findings derived from sociological investigations may serve as guidelines for intelligent social action in the pursuit of shared human objectives. title: Sociology of World Society
description: Study of the world as a single society. Topics include world population, worldwide economic and political arrangements, and attempts to create a world culture by transnational organizations.

title: Introduction to Social Organization
description: Principles of sociology for the more advanced student. The sociology of contemporary societies with emphasis on social institutions: the family, the political structure, religious groups and movements, medicine, the economy, and education. Dynamics, change, and institutional interrelationships will be assessed. 221.The Black Community in America. title: Sociology of the Future
description: Examination of probable nearfuture (thirty to fifty years) social states and social forms. Particular attention to trends in social institutions, longterm social trends, and culture change. Emphasis on basic principles of sociological analysis, demography, societal indexes, and social ecology.

title: Sociology of Women
description: A critical examination of the nature of women's roles and their impact on social organization. Considers the effects of changing patterns of socialization, roles, role strain, intergroup relations, and the social process.

title: Sociology of Deviant Behavior
description: An overview of theory and research on deviant behavior. Reviews three essential forms: deviance arising from disability in social and physical functioning, deviance arising from violation of social norms, and deviance arising from membership in groups observing radical social ideologies.

title: Social Problems
description: A survey of the nature and range of social problems, the conditions that give rise to them, and the methods by which our society attempts to cope with them.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contem_ porary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociological Research Design
description: A basic course in principles and techniques for organizing, conducting, and analyzing sociological research; research strategies and selection of appropriate techniques for a variety of research problems. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. Not open to the student who has credit in SOC 380.

title: Basic Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Leisure and Popular Culture
description: Discussion of issues related to the uses and distribution of nonwork time and activities. Trends in recreation, folk arts, and the growing leisure industries. The impact of leisure activities on the natural environment and other "quality of life" issues.

title: Social Stratification and Inequality
description: An analysis of United States and world stratification systems with attention to the unequal distribution of wealth, status, power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: The Sociology of Modernization
description: The sociology of social and industrial changemodernization in the non-Western world. Study of reasons for change, for example, demographicurban, familysocial, and international pressures. Discussions of thirdworld social problems and the social change models and ideologies for changing societies. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Blue- Collar Society and Culture
description: Examines the social realities, lifestyles, and selfperceptions of bluecollar society and culture. Investigates socioeconomic and demographic patterns. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, and conditions affecting use of treatment programs.

title: Introduction to Social Research
description: Problem selection, hypothesis formation, conceptualization, operationalization, data collection designs; data reduction and analysis; report writing; and the ethics of research. Includes research experience in laboratory sessions as well as in the field. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective of life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
description: An intensive study of sociological theories and theorists of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with a view to relating theoretical positions to contemporary social dynamics and to contemporary theoretical work in sociology. Examines the cultural and intellectual milieu in which the theoretical works were created. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions, and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Trends in Mass Society
description: An introduction to the major trends of mass society and changes in those trends. Students are encouraged to perform their own analyses of changing trends using existing information. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family life cycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Complex Social Organizations
description: The sociological aspects of organizational life. Special attention given to organizational structure, change, and strategies for planned change. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Political Sociology
description: The social basis of political behavior and beliefs, the effects of consensus and cleavage on the political process, the social foundations of political institutions, and the distribution of power. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Religion
description: Examines religion as a social institution with particular attention to the societal functions of religion, the influence of social factors on the development of religion, the role of religion in the amelioration of contemporary social problems, and contemporary processes affecting the future of religion. Sociology 309

title: Social Gerontology
description: Survey of social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Medical Care Organizations
description: A sociological analysis of medical care organizations and professionals with emphasis on intraorganizational, interprofessional, and agencyclient relations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: A sociological analysis of the field of mental health with attention to social definitions of mental illness, selfrecognition of illness, the process of seeking care, treatment institutions, and the aftermath of treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as related to various sociological variables. Various sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Families in the Middle Years
description: An overview of the American family as the marital pair approach and encounter middle age. Discussion of problems that necessitate interaction with the criminal justice and corrections system. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Seminar in the Family
description: An analysis and critique of published research studies of marriage and the family. The nature and complexity of the family as well as its future. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220, 424, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Changing Societies
description: Analysis of social change processes within societies in the modern world with attention to social movement, institutional change, and organizational change. Discussion of implementing, controlling, and measuring change. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 or equivalent.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historical functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis of the social dynamics of the urban core in metropolitan areas. Attention given to the development of cities and their cores, stressing ecological and demographic factors. Examines the social issues associated with the concept of the inner city and policy alternatives for alleviating undesirable conditions. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Seminar on Middletown
description: Focuses on two works by the Lynds, Middletown and Middletown in Transition, sociological classics about Muncie. Examines followup studies that teams of scholars have undertaken. Students participate in a continuing sociological project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and using sources of data; and application of survey findings to programs of community action. Students participate directly in the various phases of a survey research project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 282 or equivalent. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 472.

title: Evaluation Research
description: Considerations and problems in developing and conducting research for the purpose of evaluating social action programs. Topics include the unique nature of evaluation research, operationalizing and assessing variables, goal attainment measures, needs assessments, and development of guidelines for programmatic change.

title: Advanced Sociological Data Analysis
description: The selection and use of advanced statistical techniques and sophisticated means of calculation particularly useful in analyzing sociological data. Discusses topics such as nonparametric statistics, factor analysis, sampling statistics, and multiple regression and path analysis in the context of sociological research. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and 282 or equivalent.

title: Fieldwork in Sociology
description: Review of the research process. Students learn how to use observation, interviewing, and official documents in sociological research through practical exercises. Emphasizes the relation between these techniques and the survey method. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Internship in Sociology
description: Supervised field experience in a public agency or in the Department of Sociology. Training involves research, evaluation, and implementation of agency programs under the supervision of the agency and the Department of Sociology. Prerequisite: permission of director of Sociological Research Center. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study of Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor with special competence in the subject involved. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Topics in Sociology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of sociology. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. Department of Speech Communication Nitcavic, Acting Chairperson; Benson, Crouse, Diedrich, Dorris, Ely, Nothstine, Semmel, Shepard If all my possessions and powers were to be taken from me with one exception, I would choose to keep the power of speech, for by it I could soon recover all the rest. —Daniel Webster Communication, as old as the human race, has always played a central role in the personal, social, and political affairs of men and women. People have looked for centuries to find specific reasons underlying their communicative successes and failures—reasons that could guide their future communicative efforts. There are two central reasons to study human communication. First, the study of communication enables us to understand more about ourselves and our world. Communication is fundamental to all human activity. It is through our ability to communicate, to assign meaning to verbal and nonverbal symbols, that we individually and collectively create and order our lives, relationships, and society. The second and perhaps strongest argument for studying communication arises from its central role in our lives. Communication lies at the core of all human affairs. We cannot begin to probe individual behavior, social structures, political activity, artistic creation, language and culture, or any other human concern without considering communication. Speech communication courses are available to students on the following bases: general education, departmental major or minor in speech communication, teacher licensing programs, master of arts, and as a cognate field for students in other departments. Within the discipline of speech communication there are several areas of specialization, including rhetorical theory and public communication, interpersonal communication, organizational communication, and communication education. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare graduates for careers in business, government, politics, education, public affairs, public relations, and the media as well as advanced study of speech communication at the graduate level. The undergraduate speech communication minor is particularly useful to students in prelaw, business, telecommunications, political science, history, and journalism. The student will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 66-69) and by the concentration areas listed below. title: Fundamentals of Public Communication
description: Principles and practice of effective oral communication; analysis and evaluation of the speakinglistening process; preparation in message construction, emphasizing the selection, organization, and delivery of materials.

title: Public Speaking 2
description: Preparation and presentation of longer speeches based upon the purposes and occasions of speaking. Emphasizes techniques of persuasion and careful construction of speeches based upon analysis of actual audiences. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: Focus on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Stresses the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: Speechmaking as a force in political and intellectual history; critical analysis of selected speeches in relation to political, social, and economic issues. Analysis of issues dealing with problems of progress, reform, and revolution. Emphasis on public address in American social and political institutions. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210 or 240.

title: Contemporary Forms of Persuasion
description: Examines the modes of persuasion reflected in dimensions of American popular culture. Attention focuses on the persuasive appeals employed in forms of popular culture and methods for evaluating their persuasive potential and impact. Stresses the importance of applying communication theory in everyday transactions.

title: Interviewing
description: The principles and types of interviews, with application of the principles in informational, employment, appraisal, and counseling interviews. Consideration of the following aspects of employment seeking: résumé, placement papers, job application, interview, and followup.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Topics in Speech Communication
description: Critical examination of selected topics and issues in speech communication. Designed to familiarize students with current trends, theoretical and methodological issues in the discipline. May be repeated once by permission of instructor and department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Meeting Management
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Business and Professional Communication
description: The communication activities in business and the professions: oral reports, persuasive presentations, interpersonal skills, and communication problemsolving strategies.

title: Professional Speechwriting
description: A blend of persuasive theory and the pragmatics of speechwriting and training for persons who write speeches and public presentations for business, industry, education, and government. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or 240 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Nonverbal Communication in Human Interaction
description: The nature, forms, and functions of nonverbal codes in human speech communication. Focuses on understanding one's own nonverbal communication and that of others.

title: Presentational Communication
description: A blended approach of principles and applications formulated to meet the needs of managers, executives, and other professionals who submit proposals, ideas, and recommendations to the scrutiny of peers and superiors. Focus on unique nature and strategies of presentational communication.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher.

title: Practicum in Speech Communication
description: Practical experience in intercollegiate debate, individual events, applied communication research, or alternative speech communication projects. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminar focusing on various aspects and problems of speech communication as they relate to people in their personal and professional relationships. Open to honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 299.

title: Classroom Utilization of Methods and Materials
description: Classroom management techniques, an introductory involvement in the teaching of a discipline, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of speech communication in the secondary school curriculum. These topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: SPCH 395.

title: The Rhetoric of Political Campaigns
description: Examines the nature, forms, and effects of persuasion in organized political campaigns that seek to influence mass publics. Focuses on the skills needed to describe, analyze, and evaluate persuasive uses of language and to understand better the role of campaign persuasion in influencing voter behavior. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 372.

title: Studies in Persuasion
description: Examination and analysis of current theories and research in persuasion and social influence. Variables affecting implementation of persuasive principles and strategies. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: Examines theories, concepts, models, and research related to communication in relatively unstructured facetoface settings. Emphasis on understanding message exchanges between people. Focuses on social interaction with attention to communication models, perception, symbols, systems, self concept, attitudes, meaning, and nonverbal message cues.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of smallgroup literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problem solving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Communication in Organizations
description: The oral communication processes in organizations, with special emphasis upon causes of communication problems and correctives for the problems. Examination of the systems of oral communication within organizations.

title: Communication Consultation
description: The role and obligations of the communication consultant. Emphasizes interpersonal and team decisionmaking skills as well as developing Speech Pathology and Audiology 313 breadth of knowledge, theoretical coherence, and the capacity to employ practical communication analysis and intervention consistent with organizational goals. Prerequisite: SPCH 451.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech Communication pursues a specific subject of study in depth in consultation with some member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Speech
description: Onthejob experience in such places as a college classroom, a political campaign or office, summer camp, or summer theater. Students are permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the credit hours to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in speech and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned in this course or in combination with SPCH 598 but no more than 8 hours may be earned at one time. Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology Hoops, Chairperson; Artes, Farling, Heady, Hemeyer, Kramer, Lindell, Martin, Updike Until the fall of 1978, students entering the university who graduated with a bachelor's degree in speech pathology and audiology were eligible for initial certification to work as speech and language clinicians in the public schools. Thus, most bachelor's degree graduates are employed in public school corporations. As of 1978, students entering the university who seek state teaching licensure to work in the public schools in speech pathology or audiology must acquire a master's degree as the preservice level of training. Persons with master's degrees may also work in hospital speech and hearing clinics, rehabilitation centers, college or university centers, and communitysponsored speech and hearing agencies. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers two undergraduate majors in speech pathology and audiology. Both are departmental majors. One is a departmental major for students who are sure they wish to work eventually in a hospital, college, or community clinic and plan to proceed immediately to the master's degree without acquiring licensure to work in the public schools. The other, identified as a departmental major for those seeking licensure in school services personnel as speech, language, and hearing clinicians or as educational audiologists, is for students who do plan to be eligible for public school employment in these positions. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology or in audiology, and completion of licensure requirements as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist is performed as part of the master's degree program. Completion of clinical practicum hours is a part of master's degree requirements. The master's degree is also required for state licensure through the Health Professions Bureau, for all persons who work in job environments other than the public schools, and for membership in and certification by the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate major programs are given clinical experience in four kinds of programs: public school speech, language, and hearing programs; hospitals; preschool nursery programs; and the university Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic, to which children and adults come for clinical work for speech, language, and hearing problems. The department also offers a departmental minor in speech pathology and audiology, for students interested in but not committed to this profession, and a departmental minor in speech science for students planning a career in industry or business or in a research laboratory dealing with exploration of the parameters of speech or speech identification. Approval to pursue the major programs is based in part upon the student's performance in clinical practicums, and is ordinarily considered early in the student's junior year. Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. Fulltime students enrolled in some major programs of the university are administered a speech and hearing test free of charge. This screening is performed by appointment for new fulltime students. Any speech or hearing problem that may interfere with vocational objectives is called to the attention of the student. Special work for regularly enrolled students who desire to correct deficiencies in speech and voice is provided by the clinic, situated on the ground floor of the Arts and Communication Building. Educational work and guidance for persons who have hearing problems are also available. Recommendations for corrective procedures are based on the specific needs of the student. Certain programs of the university, including all teaching curricula, demand various proficiency levels in regard to speech and voice. One function of the clinic is to implement these criteria. Outpatient speech and hearing evaluation and therapy are integral parts of the clinic program, as is the education of speech pathologists and audiologists. Some classes are available for prospective classroom teachers who desire information relative to the management of speech or hearing difficulties. The work of the university clinic is closely associated with that of the Burris School clinic. The clinic is equipped with the latest sound and acoustic devices, including recording machines, tape recorders, recordings, testing materials, audiometers, and other clinical equipment.
