title: Introduction to Teaching in Secondary and Junior High/Middle School
description: Examines the structure, function, and development of schools in the United States. Designed to help students make valid decisions about career choices and about preparing for a teaching career. Focuses on professionalism, job requirements, and employment opportunities. Specific planning for the Ball State University program is included. Not open to the student who has credit in EDSEC 150.

title: Basic Concepts of Secondary Education
description: Examines through classroom investigation and practical field experiences the structure, function, and development of secondary education in the United States. Designed to help students make valid decisions about preparing for and functioning in a teaching career by studying professionalism, job requirements, employment opportunities, secondary school curriculum, and the role of secondary education within the entire educational process.

title: Introduction to Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Introduces prospective teachers to responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Continued study of responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, supporting personnel, and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 200 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Advanced study of responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, supporting personnel, and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior in American Secondary Schools
description: Analyzes factors that influence the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in schools and educational settings. Particular emphasis on the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in the American secondary schools. Not open to students with credit in EDJHM 205.

title: Advanced Study of Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior
description: Focuses on indepth analyses of many of the concepts introduced in EDSEC 205. Particular emphasis on variables that contribute to the development and maintenance of prejudice, stereotypes, racism, and oppressive conditions. Equal emphasis on instructional strategies for combating such behaviors. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 or EDJHM 205 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Microcomputers in the Secondary School
description: A basic understanding of the functions and application of microcomputers in the classroom setting. Topics include evaluation and use of available software, introduction to the development of teachermade software, and the availability and selection of hardware.

title: Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary'School
description: Inducts the student into the teaching act. Includes specific technical skill development, legal implications, study of principles of teaching, application of instructional media, curriculum development and organization, classroom management, and discipline. Intensive inschool assignments, observation, skills, participation, and direct contact with adolescents are required. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205, EDPSY 251, and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290.

title: Instructional Strategies in Multicultural Schools
description: Theory and application of special instructional strategies of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms with special emphasis on multicultural educational situations. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 or EDJHM 205 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms.

title: Planning and Assessing Instructional Programs
description: Designed to provide secondary school teachers with methods of establishing instructional programs with feedback networks that will encourage continuous assessment and appropriate alterations of the educational environment. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Intermediate Study of Microcomputers in the Secondary School
description: Designed to help students understand and develop the application of computer technology to their disciplines as computerassisted instruction. Prerequisite: EDGEN 320 for students pursuing the computer endorsement. EDSEC 255 for all others.

title: Problems in Education and Professional Concerns of the Beginning Teacher
description: Provides opportunity to examine critically and to focus educational experience and knowledge on contemporary and personally significant problems of education. Emphasizes immediate professional concerns of prospective firstyear teachers. Prerequisite: EDSEC 301 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Foundations of Secondary Education
description: Education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from sociological, philosophical, historical, economic, political, and anthropological perspectives. Such contemporary issues as cultural values, social class, legal aspects, ethnic groups, political pressure, and the role of teachers will be stressed. Prerequisite: EDSEC 299.

title: High School Curriculum
description: General perspectives of curriculum principles, practices, and procedures common to secondary schools. Organizational structures, innovations, and intimate relationships between instruction and curriculum. Concurrently, students will choose areas of concentration or preparation as they relate to the total high school curriculum.

title: Discipline: Improving Student Behavior in Secondary Schools
description: Designed to prepare prospective secondary teachers to cope with discipline problems in all secondary school settings. Emphasizes skills and procedures for preventing or remedying disruptive behavior by secondary students and ways to create a positive environment for learning.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the Standard License in Secondary Education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 462 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the Standard License in Secondary Education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 460 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for nine weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

description: Prerequisite or parallel: EDSEC 460, 462 or EDJHM 466; and admission to student teaching.

description: Innovative practices will be identified, defined, and analyzed relative to their impact on secondary schools. Creative, innovative instructional approaches will be employed. Field trips or visitations to innovative secondary schools will be arranged when practical, and students will concentrate on innovative practices. Twining, Ulman, VanEvery, VanTassel The philosophy of special education encompasses the right of all children, youth, and adults to participate in educational and career planning experiences that will develop their capabilities to the fullest extent. Gradual acceptance of this philosophy by society has created an everincreasing demand for highly skilled personnel who are certified in the various exceptionality areas represented within special education. The Department of Special Education offers undergraduate programs leading to teacher certification in deaf education; mentally handicapped; moderately, severely, profoundly, and multiply handicapped; and physically handicapped. Graduate programs are offered in teaching of learningdisabled and emotionally disturbed in addition to undergraduate preparation. These programs are designed in accordance with Indiana teacher licensure requirements. Elective courses in special education open to future teachers, psychologists, speech and hearing therapists, and social workers include a survey course of exceptional children, courses in the education of gifted children, a course in the education of slow learners, and a course in the education of children with learning disabilities. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE HEARING -IMPAIRED The legal right of all children to an appropriate education has created a need for teachers of the hearingimpaired. The emphasis on "mainstreaming" exceptional children into the regular classroom developed a need for teachers of the hearingimpaired with more general preparation in addition to the specialized course work for teachers of the deaf. The growth of different communication philosophies made it essential to provide additional course work options within the majors and minors. A major in the education of the deaf is offered to those who prefer some level of elementary teaching, and a minor is available for persons who wish to teach an academic subject at the junior high and high school levels. The state of Indiana, Ball State University, and the Department of Special Education have adopted extensive requirements for licensing and have developed flexible programs that can accommodate the above needs. The Bali State University program for training teachers of the hearingimpaired meets the approval of the Indiana Teacher Training and Licensing Commission, the Council on the Education of the Deaf (CED), and the U.S. Department of Education. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR THE MENTALLY HANDICAPPED Acceptance of the philosophy of special education has led to the development of specialized programs for mentally handicapped children, youth, and adults. These programs have provided the impetus to prepare specially trained teachers to work effectively with mildly handicapped and moderately, severely, profoundly, and multiply handicapped children, youth, and adults in the least restrictive instructional setting. Teachers and other interested professional personnel are taught the necessary skills to implement accepted intervention strategies for appropriately meeting the mentally handicapped person's learning style and educational and career needs. In response to the nationwide demand for qualified teachers to serve mentally handicapped children, youth, and adults, the Department of Special Education offers a major in the teaching of the mildly handicapped and minors in the teaching of the mildly handicapped and moderately, severely, profoundly, and multiply handicapped. The teaching minor also serves as an endorsement in each of the exceptionality areas represented within the Mentally handicapped area. SPECIAL EDUCATION FOR CHILDREN WITH PHYSICAL OR SPECIAL HEALTH PROBLEMS Among children who have special educational needs are the physically handicapped (mildly and severely) and those who have other health conditions that make special class placement necessary. A typical classroom for these handicapped or healthimpaired children presents the teacher with a challenging variety of physical impairments as well as learning difficulties. To profit from their educational experience, these children are in need of specially prepared teachers with an understanding of the physical, psychological, and educational problems encountered in such a classroom, as well as knowledge of curriculum and methodology to meet these problems. The teacher education program is designed to offer comprehensive professional preparation to future teachers of physically handicapped (mildly and severely) or healthimpaired children so that these children will have the opportunity to learn and grow to the best of their ability under the guidance of competent, special teachers. title: Introduction to Exceptional Children
description: A survey of the educational needs of children who deviate from the normal in mental, physical, and social characteristics. Designed as an introduction to special education.

title: Strategies for Developing Positive Concepts in Preschool Handicapped Children
description: Examines instructional methodology and curricular practices for developing the preschool handicapped child's social and emotional stability. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or equivalent.

title: Child Management Strategies for Preschool Handicapped Children
description: Examines instructional methodology and curricular practices for more effectively managing the preschool handicapped child's home and preschool learning environments. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or equivalent.

title: Individualizing Learning Opportunities for Preschool Handicapped Children
description: Examines instructional methodology and curricular practices for serving preschool handicapped children in the least restrictive learning environment. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or equivalent.

title: Practicum-Teaching Young Handicapped Children
description: Student works with handicapped children six years of age or younger in a supervised practicum to acquire practical skills for planning and organizing activities to meet the needs of handicapped children in the classroom. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fostering Developmental Competence of Preschool Handicapped Children
description: Examines instructional methodology and curricular practices for developing the preschool handicapped child's cognitive, language, and general learning environments. These developmental components will be studied based on current instructional practices with preschool handicapped children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or equivalent.

title: Microcomputers and the Exceptional Learner
description: Introduces students to uses of microcomputers with exceptional children. Includes uses of microcomputers in special education; elements of programming with emphasis on computerassisted instruction; and direct programming experience with exceptional children. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. 1. Students are expected to meet the prerequisite for MATH 391.

title: Microcomputers and the Exceptional Learner 2
description: The use of advanced BASIC programming techniques to increase the usefulness of teachermade educational software. Explores topics related to adapting computers for exceptional learners and strategies for integrating the computer into the special education classroom. Prerequisite: EDGEN 320 for students pursuing the computer endorsement. SPCED 230 (4 hrs.) for all others.

title: History of Education of the Deaf and the Psychology of Deafness
description: A brief study of educational provisions for the deaf from the beginning to the present and a survey of the social, educational, and vocational problems of deafness.

title: Education of Preschool Hearing/Language-Impaired Children
description: The development of oral communication in preschool hearingimpaired children. Directed observations of both hearing and hearingimpaired classes, home visitations, and the parenttraining program. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Ear and Vocal Mechanism
description: Physical structure of the parts of the body used in speech and hearing. An equal stress on related physical defects and how they affect speech and understanding. Not open to the student who has credit in SPAA 261.

title: Practicum in Special Education
description: Observation and assistance of teachers in special classes for exceptional children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or may be taken parallel with

title: Psychology of Mental Retardation
description: Studies various types and degrees of retardation, the psychological, environmental, and cultural factors that contribute to retardation. Emphasizes etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate retarded students. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, BIO 453 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Characteristics of Moderately, Severely, and Profoundly Retarded Individuals
description: Aspects of the intellectual, perceptualmotor, communication, academic, and personal social characteristics of the moderately, severely, and profoundly retarded. Procedures for formulating realistic instructional objectives will be explained. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 372.

title: Educational Methods with Moderately, Severely, and Profoundly Mentally Handicapped
description: Current instructional planning for the moderately, severely, and profoundly mentally handicapped will be reviewed and evaluated. Focuses on techniques for effecting innovative curricula for students at the preschool through postschool levels. Prerequisite: SPCED 372.

title: Education of Gifted Children
description: Examination of definitions, characteristics, and identification procedures relating to gifted and talented children in school and society. Research findings pertaining to these topics will be reviewed and analyzed.

title: Education of Slow Learners
description: Major topics include identification, characteristics, and practices and procedures for meeting the needs of the slowlearning child. Emphasis on techniques and methods of instruction as well as research findings concerned with the slow learner and the culturally disadvantaged.

title: Learning Disabilities Techniques for the Regular Classroom Teacher
description: Emphasis on the role of the regular classroom teacher in relationship to legal, federal, and state mandates for identification, instruction, and programming for learningdisabled students in the regular classroom. Prerequisite: senior status.

title: Basic Audiology
description: Methods of measuring hearing. Practice in use of various types of audiometers. description: Fundamentals of the visible movements involved in speech and the various methods, techniques, and materials for teaching lipreading to the deaf and the hardofhearing. Use of auditory training and hearing aids for rehabilitation. Prerequisite:

title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of an individual working with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 and 446 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Manual Communications
description: Theory and research underlying the language of signs and fingerspelling (manual alphabet) is considered. Development of receptive and expressive skills in manual communications is required. Required of students intending to student teach in schools or classes using total communication.

title: Advanced Manual Communication
description: A course in manual communication designed to improve conversational skill in signs and fingerspelling to a functional level for expressive and receptive use in a classroom for hearingimpaired children. Prerequisite: SPCED 451 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: Compares language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Level of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and SPAA 370 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight Language for the Deaf, Barry Five-Slate, Wing Symbols, and the Natural Method. Language outlines from different schools are used as supplementary aids. Prerequisite: SPCED 240, 266, and 454.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary. School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching subjects such as arithmetic and science. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and 266 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Student Teaching: Areas of Exceptionality
description: May be repeated by students fulfilling requirements for certification in a second exceptionality area. A total of 20 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Interpreting for the Deaf
description: A survey course to acquaint students with the fundamentals of interpreting for the deaf in special situations, familiarize them with professional behavioral guidelines unique to each setting, and develop beginning interpretive skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Expressive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Provides students who have basic manual communication skills with intensive training and practice in expressive interpreting for the deaf. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Receptive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Designed to provide students who have basic manual communication ability with professional skill for interpreting manual language in special situations. Opportunity for extensive practice and evaluation will be provided. Prerequisite: SPCED 468 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Diagnostic/Prescriptive Teaching of the Mildly Handicapped
description: Continuation of SPCED 474, emphasizing curriculum modifications and prescriptive teaching. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (2 hrs.) and 474.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: Designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired students. Includes etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate students with physical disabilities. Prerequisite: SPCED 372.

title: Educational Methods with Physically/Multiply Handicapped Children
description: Special class organization, curriculum, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of multiply handicapped and/or orthopedic and special health problem children. Prerequisite: SPCED

description: Studies the problems of multiply handicapped children and youth. Symptomatology, assessment, and educational programming of multiply handicapped children will be emphasized. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 373, and 482.

description: Required for licensure in Special Education: Mildly Mentally Handicapped. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. A total of 14 hours of credit may be earned. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 465, 466.

Students gain knowledge of social and intellectual history and an understanding of American beliefs, customs, art, and patterns of behavior. The focus on folk, popular, and high culture provides a unique view of the nation's social fabric and history and equips students with knowledge and skills applicable to careers in business, liberal arts, education, journalism, advertising sales, and other fields. Departmental minor in American culture, 36 hours Society and culture ANTH 160 or SOC 100 4 hrs. Historical foundations From HIST 201, 202, 203 8 hrs. High culture ENG 240 or 340 4 hrs. ANCIENT STUDIES Maxima est enim vis vetustatis et consuetudinis (Great is the power of antiquity and of custom) Cicero, De Amicitia, XIX, 68. The university offers a departmental minor in ancient studies designed to provide students with a broad experience in various aspects of ancient life. Members of the faculty and courses in the ancient studies minor are drawn from the departments of Anthropology (which also offers courses in archaeology), Foreign Languages, History, and Philosophy. The university library has extensive printed sources for every branch of ancient studies in which courses are offered. Students interested in the ancient studies minor may concentrate in anthropology, foreign languages, history, or philosophy. HUMANITIES This interdepartmental minor is designed for academically talented students (students admitted with distinction or maintaining an overall gradepoint ratio of 3.0). In addition to expanding the humanities studies for liberal arts students, this minor may serve as a valuable adjunct for students pursuing teaching majors in one of the departments of the humanities. Departmental minor in humanities, 36 hours ENG 201, 202, 203 12 hrs. HIST 453 4 hrs. From ENG 240, 260, 270, 280, 340 4 hrs. From CC 217, 218 4 hrs. From PHIL 100, 202, 302 4 hrs. In addition to a core of courses, students will study the law as an evolutionary concept based upon the experience and needs of society and will be confronted with ethical problems involved in their jobs, as well as legal and administrative problems. An internship with a legal firm, bank, or corporation will be required. The minor is also an initial preparation for professional careers in personnel and public relations, in planning agencies for humanistic social programs, in libraries, in museums, and in institutions of higher education. title: Colloquium in Humanities
description: Guided experiences in the arts and humanities. An investigation of the major ideas and themes of specific works of art that are available and an attempt to demonstrate the interrelationships among the arts. Entails informed attendance at concerts, plays, art exhibits, and lectures.

title: Colloquium in Social and Behavioral Sciences
description: Students participate directly in the formulation and investigation of questions about man and society so that they can better understand human affairs now and in the future. The interrogations deal with matters such as violence, dissent and rebellion, university life, the cities, race relations, environmental pollution, people and political processes, and fundamental human traits.

title: Colloquium in Science and Mathematics
description: A study of "New Perspectives in the Sciences" designed to sensitize students to the implications of scientific thought for the student who is not pursuing a special area of science. One twohour lecture and two hours arranged weekly.

title: Colloquium in Business, Technology, and Applied Fields
description: A consideration of the interrelationships among business, technology, and other applied fields, and the major forces affecting the world at the present and in the future. Discussion of ways individuals may or should influence a more effective society in the United States and the world in order to live with meaning, purpose, and identity.

title: Colloquium in the Arts
description: Guided experiences in the arts and humanities. An investigation of the major ideas and themes of specific works of art that are available and an attempt to demonstrate the interrelationships among the arts. Entails informed attendance at concerts, plays, art exhibits, and lectures. Not open to the student who has credit in GENED 200.

title: Honors Symposium in Contemporary Civilization
description: An examination of some of the critical issues that confront contemporary civilization. Open only to freshmen participating in the Honors College.

title: Introduction to Sport in American Life
description: A thorough 'examination of the various historical, sociological, and psychological aspects of sport in our society. Not sportappreciation oriented, but rather an examination of what occurs to both competitors and spectators as they become involved with a sport activity. Open to all undergraduate students.

title: Women's Studies
description: An analysis of the role of American women in sociology, history, and literature, and an attempt to define the woman biologically and psychologically.

title: Related Field Experiences
description: Departments may use this course to grant students university credit for programs under their jurisdiction for field experiences meeting departmental crediting criteria. Students must apply formally to the department chairperson for such credit and supply supporting documentation. The department determines the amount of credit to be granted and notifies the Office of Admissions and the registrar accordingly. The Office of Advising and Scheduling is informed how the credit is to be applied to the student's program. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Study
description: Foreign study provides a means of granting Ball State University credit for course work undertaken abroad at institutions of higher learning (e.g., universities, centers, and institutes) as part of approved study programs. Applicable toward majors, minors, or general education with departmental approval. Prerequisite: acceptance into a Ball State exchange program or approved studyabroad program. A total of 48 hours of credit may be earned. The course is offered for credit/no credit only.

title: Honors Candidate
description: May be taken each quarter by the honors candidate who has already registered in previous quarters for all his or her undergraduate course work, including ID 499, but has not yet completed his or her senior honors project. Enrollment in this course entitles the enrollee to ordinary undergraduate student use of library, health, and other university facilities.

title: Senior Honors Project
description: An inquiry culminating in an honors paper prepared in accordance with accepted standards of documentation and presentation under the supervision of a faculty member. Open only to seniors participating in the Honors College or completing the requirements for departmental honors. title: Introduction to Home Economics
description: Career opportunities available in home economics; introduction to Ball State home economics programs, facilities, staff; development of home economics as a profession. Activityoriented class involving field trips, using practicing home economists as resource persons, with indepth exploration of one topic in the profession.

title: Home Economics Field Studies
description: Combines reading knowledge with field experiences in which students study special topics in home economics in a particular location. Open to all students with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Home Economics
description: Individual or group studies and experiences. Experience with professional standards, regulations, and supervision in the type of home economicsrelated work chosen by the student. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester.

title: Workshop: Home Economics
description: Activityoriented study of one topic in home economics. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester.

title: Independent Study in Home Economics
description: Independent investigation and exploration of a topic in home economics. Emphasizes extensive reading and the development of research skills. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester.

title: Seminar in Home Economics
description: Student presentations and discussions on selected topics of current interest in home economics. Focuses on a different topic in home economics each semester offered. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Professional Development in Home Economics
description: Examines the skills needed in getting a job, emphasizing résumé writing, interviewing, and dress. Explores such topics as adjusting, succeeding, and growing as a professional in one's chosen career. Prerequisite: senior standing.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Vocational Education
description: Applies the principles and philosophies of vocational education to program organization, content area, teacher qualifications, leadership preparation, curriculum design, and image.

title: Home Economics Presentation Techniques
description: Analysis of audience and business needs and the development of presentations and projects to meet these needs. Includes selection and use of presentation methods, development and use of devices, and professional roles and expectations. Open to all departmental majors in home economics and dietetics. Not open to students with teaching majors in vocational home economics.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Home Economics
description: Organization of teaching units and lesson plans; selection and use of teaching methods and materials. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Practicum in Home Economics
description: Individual or group studies and experiences. Experience with professional standards, regulations, and supervision in the type of home economicsrelated work chosen by the student. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester.

title: Implementation of Vocational Education Programs
description: Emphasis on techniques for implementing vocational education programs, including applications to management, public relations, and professionalism in vocational home economics. Prerequisite: HED 392, 395.

title: Coordination of Cooperative Programs in Vocational Education
description: A study of how to coordinate class instruction and work experience; includes selecting and recruiting students, selecting training stations, role of the coordinator, techniques of coordination, and placement and followup of graduates. Prerequisite: HED 392, 395.

title: Food Preparation and Meal Planning
description: Designed for students not majoring in home economics. Fundamentals of planning, preparing, and serving nutritionally adequate, appetizing, and aesthetically appealing meals with emphasis on correct techniques and methods of food preparation. Not open to the student who has credit in HFN 110.

title: Principles of Food Preparation
description: Fundamental principles underlying the preparation of food. Correct techniques and methods of food preparation.

title: Food Experimentation and Comparison
description: Effects of different ingredients and methods of determining quality of products. Emphasizes recognition of standard products Home Economics 73 and ability to recogni ze reasons for failure to achieve standard products. Application of scientific principles to manipulative techniques of food preparation. Prerequisite: HFN 110. Not open to the student who has credit in HFN 430.

title: Meal Management
description: Principles and fundamentals of planning, preparing, and serving nutritionally adequate, appetizing, and aesthetically appealing meals, with emphasis on resource management and the purchase and storage of food. Attention given to foods and types of table service suitable for various occasions. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Nutrition
description: Emphasis on fundamental principles of nutrition and application to diets of children and normal adults.

title: Practicum in Food Service Planning —Layout and Equipment
description: Designing and equipping food facilities for schools, colleges, hospitals, industry, and commercial operations. Experiences in quantity foodproduction kitchens under supervision of home economics and food production personnel. Parallel: HFN 360 for dietetic or food management majors. HFN 292 for dietetic technology students.

title: Practicum in Institutional Administration
description: Emphasis on organizational structure, scientific management, and personnel administration. Experiences in quantity foodproduction kitchens under supervision of home economics and food production personnel. Parallel: HFN 363 for dietetic or food management majors. HFN 293 for dietetic technology students.

title: Normal and Therapeutic Nutrition Supervised Field Experience
description: Experience with professional standards and supervision related to normal and therapeutic nutrition in clinical and community settings. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Parallel: HFN

title: Equipment Use and Sanitation, and Employee Training Supervised Field Experience
description: Selected experiences related to foodequipment use, sanitation, and employee training in a quantity foodservice setting. Experience with professional standards and supervision. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Parallel: HFN 262 and 360.

title: Quantity Food-Service Personnel Management Supervised Field Experience
description: Selected experience in personnel management in a quantity foodservice setting. Experience with professional standards and supervision. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Parallel: HFN 263 and 363.

title: Quantity Menu Planning and Purchasing Supervised Field Experience
description: Selected experiences related to menu planning and purchasing in a variety of quantity foodservice organizations. Experience with professional standards and supervision. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Parallel: HFN 364.

title: Nutrition
description: Nutritive value of foods and the use of food by the human body. Nutritional needs of people throughout the life cycle. Prerequisite: junioror seniorlevel standing; a major in nursing, food management, or dietetic technology; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Therapeutic Dietetics
description: Dietary modifications needed by people with certain disease conditions. Prerequisite: HFN 340. Parallel: HFN 282 for dietetic technology students. Not open to the student who has credit in HFN 441.

title: Community Nutrition
description: Nutrition problems and programs at the federal, state, and local levels. Investigation and observation of and participation in nutrition programs in the local community. Prerequisite: HFN 340.

title: Quantity Food Production and Equipment
description: Problems involved in quantity food production, distribution, and storage. Stationary and small equipment for food preparation. Layouts of kitchens. Prerequisite: HFN 110 and 220. Parallel: HFN 262 for dietetic and food management majors. HFN 292 for dietetic technology students.

title: Institutional Administration
description: Concepts of quantity food service in restaurants, schools, hospitals, and cafeterias. Emphasis on personnel, management, organization, cost control, and apportionment of labor. Field trips to institutional kitchens. Parallel: HFN 263 for dietetic and food management majors. HFN 293 for dietetic technology students.

title: Quantity Food Purchasing and Menu Planning
description: Information needed by quantity food buyers and important considerations in purchasing foods. Emphasizes menu planning with consideration given to meeting nutritional needs. Prerequisite: HNF 220, 340. Parallel: HFN 294 for dietetic technology students.

title: Experimental Foods
description: Experimental studies of foods in relation to their composition, physical and chemical properties, and circumstances affecting food quality. Investigates recipes and develops and evaluates methods of combining ingredients. Prerequisite: HFN 110.

title: Advanced Nutrition
description: Advanced course in nutrition, emphasizing the use and metabolism of nutrients at the cellular level in the human body. Current research in the field of nutrition. Includes laboratory experiences. Prerequisite: HFN 340 and CHEM 231; senior standing.

title: Diet in Disease and Nutrition Assessment
description: Dietary modifications and the planning of therapeutic diets for treating various nutritional diseases and problems. Techniques needed to identify persons at risk of nutritional deficiency. Includes laboratory experiences. Prerequisite: HFN 292 or 440 or permission of department chairperson; senior standing.

title: Seminar in Dietetics
description: The professions involved in food service and dietetics; the roles and responsibilities of personnel, their relationships with other professionals, and standards to be attained; the code of professional ethics and the resources for continuing professional education. Prerequisite: 2 hours of credit in HE 490 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Nutrition, Weight Control, and Exercise
description: Designed for students in dietetics, physical education and healthrelated fields. Information and experience for students preparing to provide nutrition counseling to people in weightcontrol and exercisetraining programs. Prerequisite: HFN 340 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Nutrition Counseling Practicum
description: Students provide nutrition counseling for pregnant women, families with infants, young and teenage children, and people seeking guidance for weight control and special problems. Students are supervised by a member of the American Dietetic Association. Prerequisite: HFN 340 and permission of department chairpersons. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Food Service Management Practicum
description: Experience in a foodservice organization, either in the private or public sector. Emphasizes development of food management expertise. Practicum approved and supervised by the Department of Home Economics. Prerequisite: HFN 360, 364; senior standing; permission of department chairperson; and documented completion of at least 500 hours of appropriate foodservice experience.

title: Seminar in Foods and Nutrition
description: Student presentations and discussions on specific topics of current interest in foods and nutrition. Prerequisite: senior standing; permission of department chairperson.

title: Infant Development
description: Growth and development from conception through the second year of life. Includes physical, social, emotional, and cognitive aspects of development. Students observe and interact with infants and toddlers. Open to all students.

title: Child Development
description: Emphasis on the preschool child as a member of a family group. Includes principles of natural growth and development and child guidance based on the physical, social, emotional, and intellectual needs of the preschool child. Students will participate in and observe various early childhood programs and centers. Open to all students.

title: Marriage
description: The dynamics of the marital relationship and the changes influencing marriages today. Emphasizes the individual and marriage, dating, mate selection, marital communication, sexual adjustment, choosing parenthood, marriage dissolution, and marital growth. Open to juniors and seniors or by permission of department chairperson.

title: Family Relations
description: Dynamics of family relationships and changes influencing family life and structure. Emphasizes marriage, family life cycle, family problems, parent education, family enrichment. Open to juniors and seniors or by permission of department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Family Relations
description: History and recent trends and developments in familylife education, career opportunities involved in familylife education, professional organizations, and ethical standards. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson and senior standing.

title: Consumer Housing
description: Selection of housing to meet family needs. Evaluation of house plans for convenience, aesthetic qualities, and satisfying family life. Legal and financial aspects of home ownership. Open to all students.

title: Interior Design and Home Furnishing
description: Selection and arrangement of home furnishings to create attractive, functional interiors that are in harmony with the exterior of the home and adapted to family needs. Open to all students.

title: Life Management
description: Management of family and community resources to achieve desired goals in the family. Practical application of management principles to daily experience. Open to all students.

title: Energy and Equipment in the Home
description: The study of energy and equipment in the home. Current legislation, methods of conservation, cost and energy concerns of the future. Selection, use, and care of household equipment. Demonstrations by instructor, students, and guests.

title: Home Management
description: Practical applications of the principles of life management. Prerequisite: HFN 220. Prerequisite or parallel: HHM 340.

title: Problems in Consumer Buying
description: The economic aspects of purchasing including marketing conditions, consumer credit, agencies that protect the consumer, and points to consider when buying consumer goods and services. Open to all students.

title: Functional Home Design Practicum
description: Gives the student onthejob work experience with professional supervision in functional home design. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Clothing
description: Basics of garment construction, clothing selection, the apparel industry, and social and psychological aspects of clothing.

title: Creative Stitchery
description: Creative skills in stitchery used to embellish existing fabrics or to create new ones. Techniques include macrame, crocheting, knitting, quilting, appliqueing, trapunto, embroidery, and needlepoint; rya, braided, and hooked rugs. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Tailoring
description: Selection and construction of tailored garments and advanced clothing problems. Prerequisite: HTC 104 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Textiles
description: Textiles and their components as they relate to care, performance, and consumer satisfaction. Open to all students.

title: Evolution of Costume
description: A study of Western costume from its beginning to the present. Emphasis on motivating influences of each period as well as on the costume itself. Prerequisite: HTC 230 or permission of department chairperson.

title: The Fashion Industry
description: A survey of the business of fashion through design, manufacture, distribution, and promotion. Explores career possibilities. Open to all students.

title: Apparel Design by the Flat Pattern Method
description: Adapting standard patterns to individual proportions, designing garments, and creating an original garment by the flat pattern method. Prerequisite: HTC 104 and 203.

title: Household Textiles
description: Raw materials, quality, performance, and comparative cost of textiles used in home furnishing. Planning and conducting tests with household textiles and evaluating results.

title: Fashion Merchandising Practicum
description: Experience with professional standards, regulations, and supervision in an establishment chosen by the student. Prerequisite: HTC 270 and permission of department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Fashion
description: Problems and issues facing the modern fashion merchandiser. Working and consulting with fashion merchandisers. Prerequisite: HTC 270 and senior standing or permission of department chairperson. Department of Industry and Technology Smith, Chairperson; Baldwin, Byers, Cornwall, DeKeyser, Ross, Gurbach, Henak, Kirkwood, Kovac, Middleton, Ridgeway, Seymour, Shackleford, Snader, South, Steele, Thomasser, Thompson, Tomlinson, Vickery, Wright The programs of the Department of Industry and Technology are designed to meet the needs of students who are qualifying for the teaching profession or technical or managerial positions in business and industry, exploring the industrial world for possible occupations or vocations, or seeking knowledge and understanding of our technological society. A wide variety of industryrelated courses offers students many opportunities to explore occupational choices in manufacturing, communications, and computer applications. In addition to the baccalaureate degree programs, the Department of Industry and Technology has three associate degree programs: manufacturing technology, printing technology, and supervision. The manufacturing technology program has four options: computerintegrated manufacturing (CIM), manufacturing design, metals manufacturing, and plastics manufacturing. Note: Students are required to wear industrial safety glasses in all classes where they are exposed to sparks, flying chips, hot materials, and other hazardous substances. ASSOCIATE DEGREES ASSOCIATE IN SCIENCE—MANUFACTURING TECHNOLOGY This associate degree program prepares students for careers in computerintegrated manufacturing (CIM), drafting and design, and the metals and plastics industries. Students will meet the standards of the university with respect to admission, orientation, residence, and scholastic standards. Upon completion of this degree students may transfer to the fouryear industrial technology curriculum with little or no loss of credit. General requirements: CHEM 111; CS 118 or 120; ENG 103; MATHS 108, 115, and 117 or 161; PHYCS 110 .25 hrs. Physical education (from PEG or PEGF) 1 hr. Electives 5 hrs. Concentration area, 33 hours Core requirements: ITMFG 105, 161, 205, 225, 233, 270, 340, 362 24 hrs. Complete one option 9 hrs. Option 1: Computerintegrated manufacturing (CIM), 9 hours ITMFG 301, 308, 372 9 hrs. Option 2: Manufacturing design, 9 hours ITMFG 206, 305, 306 9 hrs. Option 3: Metals manufacturing, 9 hours ITMFG 333, 334, 336 9 hrs. Option 4: Plastics manufacturing, 9 hours ITMFG 325, 326, 327 9 hrs. 64 hrs. Students qualifying for exemption from ENG 103 will receive credit for the course. ASSOCIATE IN SCIENCE—PRINTING TECHNOLOGY This associate degree program offers preparation for entrance into salaried technical positions in the printing industry. Emphasis is placed on new techniques and on developments taking place in the printing industry. General requirements: CHEM 100; ENG 103, 104 9 hrs. PSYSC 100 or SOC 100 3 hrs. From HIST 150; HSC 160; MATHS 125; SPCH 210 3 hrs. Physical education (from PEG or PEGF) 1 hr. Electives 2 hrs. Concentration area, 45 hours CS 116 or ITGRA 381 3 hrs. ITGRA 180, 181, 182, 183, 282, 286, 287, 288, 385, 387, 388, 488 36 hrs. Electives from ACC, ADS, BEOA, ITGRA, ITMFG, and JOURN 6 hrs. 63 hrs. Students qualifying for exemption from ENG 103 and 104 will receive credit for the course(s). ASSOCIATE IN SCIENCE—INDUSTRIAL SUPERVISION This associate degree program is designed primarily for people in industrial occupations who wish to gain the professional knowledge needed to be successful industrial supervisors. The program is designed for those who are currently supervisors as well as those desiring to move into supervisory roles. General requirements: ENG 103, 104; MATHS 108; SPCH 210 12 hrs. CHEM 111 or PHYCS 110 4 hrs. From ECON 202; PSYSC 100; SOC 100 6 hrs. Physical education (PEG or PEGF) 1 hr. Concentration area, 40 hours Core requirements: ITMFG 161, 265, 360, 390; MGS 200, 251 18 hrs. Technical skills (courses are planned and approved according to the student's individual needs) 12 hrs. From ITMFG 105, 225, 233, 262, 270, 362; ACC 201, 202: CS 116, 118; ECON 332; MATHS 115 10 hrs. 63 hrs. Students qualifying for exemption from ENG 103 and 104 will receive credit for the course(s). BACCALAUREATE DEGREES Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 56-58) and by the concentration areas listed below. INDUSTRIAL TECHNOLOGY To prepare for management or technical positions in industry, the student will take a departmental major in industrial technology with an option in either management or manufacturing technology. Students in the manufacturing technology option can specialize in computerintegrated manufacturing (CIM), drafting and design, factory electronics, metals, and plastics. Students in the management option take a sequence of courses in business administration from the College of Business. Cooperative work experience (industrial internship) is open to selected industrial technology students. Students pursue coop jobs through the program coordinator; however, the university does not guarantee industrial coop assignments. Students who complete three or more cooperative work semesters may enroll in ITMFG 365 for a maximum of 3 hours of elective credit. The time normally required for completing the curriculum ranges from four years for students with adequate high school preparation who spend fulltime on campus to five years for students following the cooperative work experience (industrial internship) option. Departmental major in industrial technology, 69-78 hours Core requirements, 51 hours CHEM 111; CS 118 or 120: ITMFG 105, 161, 205, 225, 233, 262, 270, 331, 340, 362, 363, 463; PHYCS 110, 112 51 hrs. Complete one option 18-27 hrs. Option 1: Manufacturing technology, 27 hours MATHS 117, 161, 162 9 hrs. Approved electives 18 hrs. Option 2: Management, 18 hours BEOA 444; MATHS 131; MGS 300 9 hrs. From MGS 210, 221, 352, 361, 455 9 hrs. Industrial technology majors must have the equivalent of or complete MATHS 115. Students in the management option must take MATHS 132 if they wish to enroll in MGS 221. Departmental minor in industrial technology, 18 hours For students majoring in management with options in production management or general management whose career goals relate to management in industrial enterprises. The purpose of this minor is to provide an understanding of industrial materials, manufacturing processes, production systems, and industrial computer applications. ITMFG 105, 161, 205 9 hrs. Complete one option 9 hrs. Option 1: Computer applications in manufacturing, 9 hours From ITMFG 233, 270, 301, 331, 372 9 hrs. Option 2: Manufacturing systems, 9 hours From ITMFG 262, 360, 362, 363, 463 9 hrs. Departmental minor in industrial technology, 15 hours For students majoring in marketing with options in sales and advertising management whose career goals relate to industrial advertising and sales. The purpose of this minor is to provide an understanding of industrial materials, manufacturing processes, and product development. ITMFG 161, 262, 362 9 hrs. From ITEDU 152; ITGRA 180; ITMFG 225 6 hrs. GRAPHIC ARTS MANAGEMENT Departmental major in graphic arts management, 59 hours Students preparing for management positions in the graphic arts industry will complete a departmental major in graphic arts management and a minor in one of three specialized business administration areas: management, marketing and advertising, or accounting and cost control (see College of Business for the minor patterns). Internships give students educational work experience in the graphic arts industry. Plans for internship credit may be arranged with the assistance and approval of the program coordinator, who also supervises the interns; however, the university is not obligated to provide internships.
