INDUSTRIAL EDUCATION The curricula for industrial education teachers prepares students to teach industrial arts at the elementary, junior high, and senior high school levels, vocationalindustrial education at the secondary and posthigh school levels, and technical education at the college level. Teaching programs require additional courses in educational methods. See the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education for the listing of these courses and other professional requirements of the teacher education curriculum. Teaching major in industrial arts, 54 hours ITEDU 150, 152, 153, 154, 158, 253, 254, 258, 298, 352, 357, 358, 361, 394 42 hrs. From ITEDU 352, 452, 453, 454, 458, 490; ITMFG 363, 450 12 hrs. Teaching major in vocational trade, industrial and technical laboratory, 52 hours Interested students should consult the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Woods
description: A basic course in wood processing for persons interested in consumer information related to wood products and how wood can be worked to produce a desired effect or product. A portion of the class time will be set aside for studentdesigned product construction so that each student can receive individual assistance. Not open to the student who has credit in ITEDU 352.

title: Cabinetry Design and Fabrication
description: Application of design and fabrication principles as they relate to residential, business, and industrial cabinetry. Activities will include the design and detailing of typical cabinets and the construction and finishing of a studentdesigned product. Prerequisite: ADS 205 and ARCH 217.

title: Maintaining a Home
description: Includes opportunities to learn basic terminology, to perform routine preventive maintenance, and to make simple modifications and installations in plumbing, electrical circuits, general carpentry, painting, and climatecontrol systems of the home.

title: Private Pilot Ground Training
description: Designed to qualify the student for the Federal Aviation Agency written examination for the Private Pilot Certificate. Not open to persons currently holding any FAA certificates or ratings.

title: Industrial Arts for Elementary Grades
description: Industrial arts emphasizing the use of tools, materials, and industrial processes that provide an enrichment of the elementary program. Examines and evaluates methods of planning and developing individual and group activity units.

title: Technical Communication Systems
description: The elements, relationships, and operations of technical communication systems. Major emphasis on communication systems with laboratory experiences in the design, production, and transmission of various messages.

title: Construction Technology
description: Focuses on construction and management practices used to design, engineer, and construct residential, commercial, industrial, and civil structures.

title: Manufacturing Materials and Processes
description: Properties of ceramic, metallic, polymeric, and composite materials and techniques used to convert these materials into products.

title: Product and Structure Design
description: Introduces the design process and methodology used to create and transmit technical ideas using graphic methods. Major emphasis on technical designing, sketching, pictorial drawing, orthographic projection, charting and graphing, and reprographics as applied to developing products and structures. Prerequisite: ITEDU 150.

title: Energy Systems
description: Focuses on inputs, processes, and outputs associated with energy systems. Emphasis on the sources of energy; methods of controlling, converting, and transmitting energy; and the use of energy conversion systems.

title: Building Diagnostics
description: Overview of building construction and energy systems, energy audit techniques, principles of heat transfer, and air movement. Field and laboratory work to include pressurization and remote heatsensing devices to measure energy loss in building systems and thermal envelopes. A total of 15 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Manufacturing Material Processing
description: Provides experiences necessary to develop essential competencies required to perform common manufacturing processes with ceramic, metallic, polymeric, and composite materials. Prerequisite: ITEDU 153 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Graphic Communication Systems
description: Focuses on visual communication media as a technical communication system. Major laboratory activities emphasize design, development, production, and dissemination of graphic messages. Prerequisite: ITEDU 154.

title: Transportation Systems
description: Focuses on powered transportation systems used to move people and goods. Emphasizes land, water, air, and space vehicles and and transportation systems. Prerequisite: ITEDU 158.

title: Student Organizations Practicum
description: A practicum in the organization, maintenance, and evaluation of student vocational organizations. A total of 3 semesters hours must be taken by persons seeking certification as teachers of vocational trade, industrial, and technical laboratory programs and endorsements as cooperative coordinators. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Vocational Education
description: Introduction to the foundation and operation of various vocational educational programs. Analyzes legislation in the light of past and present issues of vocational education and its function as a vital component of the educational system.

title: Exploring Industrial Technology Education
description: Teaching of contemporary industrial technology education as a career. Students learn about the development and kinds of industrial technology programs and engage in activities that emphasize the curriculumdevelopment process.

title: Constructing Structures
description: Comprehensive study of the activities involved in preparing to build, construct, and complete residential, commercial, industrial, and civil structures. Prerequisite: ITEDU 152, 154, and 253 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Electronic Communication Systems
description: Introduces the principles, components, and operation of electronic communication systems. Emphasizes design production and transmission in telecommunication, informationprocessing, and acoustical systems. Prerequisite: ITEDU 150, 158.

title: Industrial Control Systems
description: Overview of the various methods used in controlling power in the industrial setting. Emphasis on the application of computers and other controlling devices and systems within the manufacturing, construction, communication, and transportation industries. Prerequisite: ITEDU 158, 357.

title: Manufacturing Enterprise
description: Introduces students to the managed activities used to design, engineer, produce, and market products with additional emphasis on providing financial and personnel support for these activities. Prerequisite: ITEDU 154, 253.

title: Trade and Occupational Analysis
description: A study of the fundamentals of analyzing trades and occupations. Techniques of identifying occupations by breakdown into jobs, tasks, and processes.

title: Vocational Related Class Content
description: A study of the sources of related materials and techniques of developing and using these materials.

title: Vocational Guidance
description: Principles, purposes, and practices of guidance by the teacher. Examines and evaluates educational and occupational information, testing programs, school records, occupational trends, and jobtraining programs.

title: Curriculum Laboratory in Industrial Technology Education
description: Emphasizes contemporary approaches to curriculum development and the preparation of instructional materials for use in industrial technology education. Students plan and execute a teaching unit in a public school setting. Prerequisite: ITEDU 298.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Industrial Education
description: Problems in developing and implementing instructional strategies; preparing evaluation instruments; planning, specifying, and managing the physical environment; and establishing and maintaining a cooperative classroom environment. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: ITEDU 298, 394.

title: Community Planning
description: Activities involved in planning communities. Emphasizes construction, demand, and site factors as related to developing housing, streets, utilities, schools, transportation systems, parks, shopping areas, and recreational centers for public needs. Prerequisite: ITEDU 152, 154.

title: Technical Experiences in Material Processing
description: Development of advanced competencies in casting and molding, forming, separating, conditioning, assembling, and finishing processes. Prerequisite: ITEDU 253.

title: Advanced Technical Experience in Communication
description: Development of advanced competencies in the graphic, photographic, and electronic areas of communication technology. Prerequisite: ITEDU 254, 357.

title: Design and Evaluation of Transportation Systems
description: Design and operation of transportation systems. Emphasizes technical aspects typical of transportation systems: control, guidance, suspension, propulsion, structure, and support. Prerequisite: ITEDU 258.

title: Study in Industrial Technology Education
description: Special investigation in industrial technology education on an independent basis. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Organization and Coordination of Vocational Education
description: The organizational structure, responsibilities, and roles recognized in the operation of vocational education programs. Major emphasis on state functions.

title: Introduction to Graphic Arts
description: A comprehensive study of the graphic arts industry that focuses on products, reproduction processes, materials, equipment, and graphic arts careers. Related areas of instruction include design, relief printing, photooffset lithography, screen printing, color reproduction, and finishing operations. 181.Relief Printing and Bindery. (3) A general applications course in relief printing and basic bindery operations found in the graphic arts industries. Major areas of instruction include copy preparation, typesetting, camerawork, conventional and photopolymer platemaking, presswork, paper, and ink.

title: Photo-Offset Lithography 1
description: Introductory course in photooffset lithography that includes planning and layout, copy preparation, phototypesetting, line and halftone camerawork, platemaking, presswork, and introduction to fourcolorprocess printing.

title: Screen Printing
description: The screen printing process as it relates to the graphic arts and printing industry and as an auxiliary manufacturing process in other industries. Topics include products, materials, equipment, techniques, inksubstrate relationships, estimating, and product design.

title: Photo -Offset Lithography 2
description: Study of contemporary applications of photooffset lithography in commercial printing and publishing. Reviews layout and planning, pasteup, camera, stripping, plates, and press. Emphasis is on camera, stripping, and single and multicolor press operations. Prerequisite: ITGRA 182 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Photography
description: Emphasizes camera types, exposure techniques, film characteristics and selection, blackandwhite and color film processing, printmaking, print finishing, and composition. Related areas include special photographic applications and introduction to color photography.

title: Typesetting and Copy Preparation
description: The use, operation, and application of machine principles and mechanisms as related to typesetting. Typography, copy preparation, and copyfitting are emphasized in addition to various methods of type generation.

title: Printing Estimating 1
description: Introductory course in contemporary estimating practices. Emphasizes production planning, development of hourly cost and production rate standards, cost of materials and outside services, sheetfed and web presses, and bindery operations. Prerequisite: ITGRA 180 and 182, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Graphic Arts Practicum
description: Emphasizes internal or external placement of students in a graphic arts setting selected and approved by the department. Provides opportunities to integrate and expand on theory gained during course work. Prerequisite: ITGRA 180, 181, 182 and 183.

title: Quality Control in the Graphic Arts
description: Explores the basic professional practices of quality control for printed products. Focuses on instrumentation used in evaluating material and products, inspection and sampling techniques, manufacturing specification, analysis techniques, and control systems found in the graphic arts industries. Prerequisite: ITGRA 180, 181, 182 and 183, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Commercial Printing
description: Studies the organization and production systems of commercial printing and publishing. Emphasizes management and production systems, quality control, material control, scheduling, and production specifications. Class organizes a system and manufactures production jobs during semester. Prerequisite: ITGRA 180, 181, 182 and 183, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Techniques of Color Photography
description: Color as it relates to photography with emphasis on additive and subtractive color processes, color films, color film processing, color printmaking (additively and subtractively), color measurement, color design and composition principles. Prerequisite: ITGRA 286 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Color Separation and Process Printing
description: A study of color reproduction procedures in the graphic arts industries. Emphasizes additive and subtractive processes of color, direct and indirect separation procedures, color measurement, registration systems, and quality control procedures for color reproduction. Prerequisite: ITGRA 182, 387, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Colloquium and Senior Project in Graphic Arts Management
description: The study and application of concepts, issues, and technological developments unique to the graphic arts. Topics include flexography, computer applications, electronic pagination, color scanning, and intaglio printing. Prerequisite: ITGRA 385 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Printing Management
description: Examines planning, organizing, controlling, and motivation as it relates to managing a business. Emphasis is on human relations, decision making, problem solving, and coordination of management, sales, and production for successful management. Prerequisite: ITGRA 381, 385, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Printing Estimating 2
description: Sheetfed and web estimating. Emphasizes obtaining and interpretation of specifications, pricing for profit margin, preparing quotations, printing trade customs, multicolor presses and signaturerelated bindery operations, application of the computer to estimating. Prerequisite: ITGRA 288 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Production Control in the Printing Industry
description: Production control systems used in contemporary graphic arts industries. Includes such topics as organization, systems approach, decision making, production planning and control, purchasing, inventory control, quality control, work measurement, and cost analysis. Prerequisite: ITGRA 385 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Technical Drawing and Print Reading
description: The theory and practice of basic production drawings and print reading. Topics include graphics language and design, instrumental drawing, lettering, geometric constructions, sketching and shape description, multiview projection, sectional views, pictorial views, dimensioning, fasteners, working drawings, and computer graphics.

title: Introduction to Manufacturing Industries
description: Introduction to manufacturing and its managed activities of research and development, production, marketing, industrial relations, and finance in manufacturing industries. Laboratory experiences involve organizing, staffing, and operating a model manufacturing enterprise. Open to all students except teaching majors in industrial education.

title: Computer-Aided Drafting and Computer -Applied Technology
description: Introduces computer drafting using an interactive software package on a microcomputer. Word processing and spreadsheet software packages are used to prepare and analyze technical reports. Prerequisite: ITMFG 105 or equivalent.

title: Advanced Technical Drawing
description: The theory and practice of preparing productionrelated detail and assembly drawings in selected specialized areas and indepth study of geometric dimensioning. Topics include auxiliary views, cams, machine components, and welding drawings. Prerequisite: ITMFG 105.

title: Industrial Plastics
description: Study of industrial plastics processes and materials. Subjects will include injection molding, extrusion, blow molding, compression and transfer molding, thermoforming, rotational molding, dip coating and casting, decorating and finishing processes. Polymer chemistry is included. Laboratory activities for all processes.

title: Machine Tool Processing
description: Metal separation with lathes, shapers, milling and grinding machines, bandsawing, and EDM. Discussions include tool design, precision measuring, metallurgy, heat treating, and safety.

title: Industrial Materials
description: Study of tests used to characterize properties of ceramic, polymeric, and metallic materials and how material properties influence their use and manufacturing. Laboratory exercises involve testing procedures recommended by ASTM and currently used by industry. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 and CHEM 112.

title: Applied Quality Control
description: Variables, procedures, and processes of total quality control within the manufacturing industries. Topics include instrumentation for material evaluation, attribute inspection and sampling, supervising for organizational quality improvements, and statistical control. Emphasizes directed laboratory experiences.

title: DC Circuit Analysis
description: Study of theories, measurement, and applications of direct current. Topics include electron theory, components, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuit analysis, voltage and current dividers, electromagnetism, and mesh analysis. Laboratories include basic measurement in electric circuits using VOM and DVM. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 and PHYCS 110.

title: Computer-Integrated Manufacturing Systems
description: A survey of computer - aided design (CAD) and computeraided manufacturing (CAM) and their integration into a complete manufacturing system. Prerequisite: ITMFG 161 and 233.

title: Manufacturing Design with CAD
description: Emphasizes creating product and tooling drawings using a major computeraided design (CAD) system. Topics include twodimensional drafting, threedimensional wireframe and surface models, test, dimensioning, flat pattern development, section and mass properties, and component libraries. Prerequisite: ITMFG 205 and 233.

title: Three-Dimensional Modeling
description: Theory of surface and solid geometric models with applications in the manufacturing industries. Prerequisite: ITMFG 305 and MATHS 117.

title: Programming Computer Graphics
description: Programming in FORTRAN and a graphics language such as Tektronix Interactive Graphics Language (IGL). Emphasis is placed on writing programs to create technical drawings and other graphical representations. Prerequisite: ITMFG 205 and a computer programming language.

title: Plastic Product Design and Mold Making
description: Plastic product design and moldmaking techniques. Individual problemsolving approach. Studies construction of the injection molds for thermoplastics. Appropriate moldmaking equipment demonstrated and used. Prerequisite: ITMFG 105, 225, and 233.

title: Plastic Production Systems
description: Plastics processing with automatic production equipment. Emphasizes injection molding, extrusion, and thermoforming. Appropriate quality control and flowanalysis tests performed on production parts. Charts, graphs, and reports on products are prepared. Includes field trips to local plastics industries. Prerequisite: ITMFG 225, 325.

title: Advanced Plastics Mold Making
description: Designing and building automatic molds and dies for injection, extrusion, and compression molding. Ejection pins, water cooling lines, stripper plates, and interchangeable inserts are included in the mold design and construction. Automated machining equipment is used. Field trips to mold and die shops.

title: Numerical Control Systems
description: The fundamentals of NC and CNC processes. Activities include programming of NC and CNC equipment and preparing tapes both manually and with computers. Prerequisite: ITMFG 205 and 233, MATHS 115.

title: Manufacturing Machine Tool Processing
description: Focuses on factors that influence the control of metal manufacturing processes. Laboratory activities emphasize the significance of locators, power requirements, feeds, speeds, microstructure, coolants, and other variables. Complex operations are covered on grinding, milling, EDM, and other multifunctional machine tools. Prerequisite: ITMFG 233.

title: Casting and Bending Metals
description: Flatposition welding with electric and oxyacetylene equipment. Limited work with tungsten inert gas (TIG) and metal inert gas (MIG) equipment. Emphasizes various casting methods, gating, sands, pattern design, cores, automated foundry practices, pouring, and furnace techniques. Prerequisite: ITMFG 233, 333.

title: Applied Mechanics
description: Applications of statics and dynamics. Strength of materials with applications to problems in manufacturing. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 and PHYCS 110.

title: Fixture Design for Metal Machining
description: Study of fixture design and other partholding systems used with metal machining. Discussion of common problems associated with fixtures when machining. Laboratory activities reinforce design concepts. Prerequisite: ITMFG 233, 333.

title: Fluid Power: Hydraulic Systems
description: An overview of the fundamentals of hydraulic systems with a review of basic equations regarding force, pressure, area, velocity, horsepower, volume, etc.; component types and designs; simplified hydraulic circuitry analysis; and basic maintenance and troubleshooting procedures. Prerequisite: ITMFG 270.

title: Industrial Safety and Health
description: Provides an awareness of the regulations governing health and safety and the methods and practices used in industry in general and industrial education specifically to comply with these regulations. Designed primarily for students choosing concentration areas in the Department of Industry and Technology.

title: Manufacturing Materials and Processes
description: The study of principal manufacturing processes, the parameters required for their control, and factors influencing product tolerances and quality. Laboratory provides direct process experience, with field trips to observe local manufacturing operations. Prerequisite: ITMFG 262.

title: Manufacturing Operations
description: Focuses on analyzing product designs and the design, engineering, and operation of industrial production systems through classroom and laboratory activities. Prerequisite: ITEDU 361 or ITMFG 105 and 161.

title: Industrial Internship
description: Student works in an industry related to his or her curriculum with the approval of the program coordinator. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: AC Circuit Analysis
description: Studies the behaviors of inductors and capacitors under DC and AC, RLC circuits, series and parallel resonance, diodes and transistors, and power supplies and filters. Includes handson experience and project construction. Prerequisite: ITMFG 270 and MATHS 115.

title: Digital Electronics
description: Digital technology and its applications. Laboratory activities include digital circuit construction using mediumscale integration (MSI) and largescale integration (LSI) chips.

title: Industrial Robots
description: The technology, applications, and management of industrial robots. Topics include classifications, controls, sensors, programming, machine vision, robot workcell design, coordinates transformation, and feasibility study in robotics. Prerequisite: ITMFG 161, 270, and computer programming experience.

title: Training and Development in Industry
description: Training and development in industry and their relationship to the job and the organization. Emphasizes skills needed to systematically plan, implement, evaluate, and revise training and development programs. Provides opportunities for practical application and practice.

title: Computer Design of Plastics Molds
description: Design of molds for plastics products by computer. Plastics flowanalysis, cooling analysis, part shrinkage, and cost analysis using computer programs. Use of electroniccomponent and database catalogs. Prerequisite: ITMFG

title: Research and Development in Plastics 1
description: Extensive study and experimentation in industrial plastics. May include mold making, materials testing, and equipment design. Prerequisite: ITMFG 326, 327.

title: Research and Development in Plastics 2
description: A continuation of ITMFG 425. Development of the research started in ITMFG 425. Material or process tests made, equipment or molds developed, and equipment installed. Prerequisite: ITMFG 425.

title: Research and Development in Metals
description: Research and development of problems related to metals manufacturing. Prerequisite: ITMFG 333 and 334, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Industrial Research and Development
description: Focuses on the methodology and practices of technical research and development as conducted in an industrial setting. Laboratory activities allow students to perform basic tasks associated with product and process research and development. Prerequisite: ITEDU 361.

title: Industrial Seminar
description: Guest lectures on contemporary topics in manufacturing. Student presentations on capstone projects. Information and guidance in seeking employment in manufacturing. Prerequisite or parallel: ITMFG 473. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Manufacturing Controls
description: Studies the controls of manufacturing. Topics include cost estimation and control, manufacturing resources planning (MRP), justintime (JIT), group technology, production and inventory controls, statistical process control, management information systems (MIS), and other advanced control technology.

title: Industrial Programmable Controls
description: Emphasizes programmable controls in industry. Topics include relay controls, programmable controller controls, and incremental motion controls. Laboratory activities involve control applications using motor control panel, programmable controller panel, and stepper and servo control trainers. Prerequisite: ITMFG 370.

title: Microprocessor and Microcomputer Systems
description: The architecture, programming, interfacing, and applications of microprocessor and microcomputer systems. Laboratories involve programming in assembly codes for basic operations and interfacing applications. Prerequisite: ITMFG 371 and computer programming experience.

title: Electric Machines and Controls
description: Principles and applications of power transformers, DC and AC generators, and DC and AC motors; controls and testing of various machines. Laboratory experiments. Prerequisite: ITMFG 370.

title: Projects in Computer -Aided Manufacturing
description: Individual project applying CNC, CAD, CAM, robotics, and other computerbased technology in manufacturing systems. Prerequisite: senior status and at least two of the following: ITMFG 301, 305, 306, 325, 326, 333, 334, 371, 372, 470.

title: Industrial Electronics
description: Study semiconductor devices, rectifiers, SCR, frequency conversion, digital and analog transducers, optoelectronics, operational amplifiers, and the industrial applications of these devices. Prerequisite: ITMFG 370.

title: Industrial Electronics Fabrication
description: Focuses on printed circuit board design, development, fabrication, and production. Electronic inventory and component assembly are studied as they relate to the manufacturing process. Prerequisite: ITMFG 475 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Problems in Industrial Technology
description: Individual advanced study and experimentation in one or more of the areas of concentration: metals, plastics, design, or factory electronics. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Military Science Flynn, Chairperson; Fields, Fountain, Gaiter, Hart, Johnson, Kelley, Kirby, Tooley The mission of the Department of Military Science is to commission future officers of the United States Army. The Army ROTC program gives qualified students an opportunity to obtain commissions as second lieutenants in the United States Army and its reserve components. Students may obtain these commissions by enrolling in the Army ROTC program along with their regular undergraduate studies. The program consists of basic and advanced courses. The basic course, normally taken during the freshman and sophomore years, provides essential background information concerning organization and operations of the U.S. defense establishment. Students do not incur any military obligations by enrolling in the basic classes. The advanced course, normally taken during the junior and senior academic years, provides students with leadership and management skills not available in other curricula and with concepts of military tactics, operations, and organizations. Contracted advancedcourse students are obligated to attend an advanced summer camp (six weeks) and to accept commissions as officers, if tendered; these students receive subsistence and pay of about $2,800 during the two years. All necessary equipment and books are furnished by the Department of the Army at no cost to the student. Credits earned in the military science (AROTC) program may apply toward degree requirements. The U.S. Army offers financial assistance in the form of two-, three-, and fouryear scholarships. Each scholarship covers tuition, textbooks, laboratory fees, and supplies in addition to subsistence pay of $100 a month for the period the scholarship is in effect. Most graduates who have completed the advanced course will be called upon to serve a threeyear tour of active duty and three years in the U.S. Army Reserve. Others will serve three months active duty for training in lieu of three years active duty and be required to participate in the Ready Reserve until the eighth anniversary date of the initial appointment in the Army Reserve. Entry to active duty may be deferred to obtain an advanced degree. Departmental minor in military science, 16 hours MIL 101, 102, 201, 202, 301, 302, 401, 402 16 hrs. Nursing 85

title: U.S. Defense Establishment
description: Introduction to ROTC and ROTC scholarship programs. The role of the U.S. Army, Army Reserve, and National Guard in peacetime and during mobilization. Examination of current threats to world peace.

title: Leadership
description: A study of human relations within the military environment. Training, counseling, communication skills, power and influence, and management skills are discussed as they apply to the military leader.

title: Small Unit Tactics and Operations
description: Introduction to troopleading procedures; mission, organization, and composition of basic military units; the conduct of offensive and defensive operations, and military first aid.

title: Land Navigation
description: Basic cartographic principles emphasizing terrain analysis, map reading, military map use, and azimuths and coordinates plotting.

title: The Military Team
description: Introduction to drill and ceremonies, role of the noncommissioned officer, logistics, intelligence, the Soviet army, principles of war, and tactics. Prerequisite: MIL 202 or approval of department chairperson.

title: Advanced Military Leadership
description: Analysis of leadership and management problems. Military tactics at squad and platoon level, military skills including advanced land navigation, and radio communications. Prerequisite: MIL 301 or approval of department chairperson.

title: The Military Profession
description: Seminar on ethics and professionalism, discussion and practical exercises in preparing military correspondence and conducting briefings. Prerequisite: MIL 302 or approval of department chairperson.

title: Taking Command
description: Continued study of leadership with emphasis on duties of an officer; introduction to laws of war and military justice system; discussion of training management. Prerequisite: MIL 401 or approval of department chairperson. School of Nursing Hodson, Acting Director; Allen, Arndt, Baldwin, Bennett, Berning, Brown, Caldwell, Cekarmis, Cheatham, Dillard, Elliott, Foster, Gaston, Gibas, Guendling, Hakes, Hanson, Heifner, Jones, Judy, Mahoney, Marhoefer, Marine, Miller, Myton, Nelson, Ryan, Wantz, Wilhoite, Wolfe The purpose of the N.L.N.-accredited baccalaureate program of studies in nursing is the preparation of professional nurse generalists who work independently and interdependently with people and with healthteam members in a variety of hospital and community settings. Graduates have the background knowledge and skill needed for entrylevel administrative positions and graduate study. Graduates earn bachelor of science degrees and are eligible to take the State Board Test Pool Examination for licensure as registered nurses. Classroom and laboratory instruction is provided by the university. The program also uses hospital facilities adjacent to campus and other nearby community health agencies. A student indicating an intent to major in nursing must complete approximately two years of academic work in humanities and behavioral and biological sciences. The major in nursing is concentrated in the student's junior and senior years. A professional nursing program is available for registered nurses wishing to obtain baccalaureate degrees. The program, designed for either fulltime or parttime students, is flexible and takes into account past educational endeavors and work experience. ADMISSION STANDARDS Clearance from the Health Center, which usually takes two to three weeks, is required before taking NUR 212. In order to be admitted to NUR 212, students must have completed 45 semester hours, including credit in ANAT 201, BIO 111, CHEM 101, PHYSL 210, PSYSC 100, SOC 100, MATHS 125, SPCH 240, and NUR 211. Furthermore, a grade of C or better is required in NUR 211, ANAT 201, PHYSL 210, and if taken, in BIO 113, CHEM 101, and PHYSL

description: Additional information about nursing assessments and interventions that will help clients and families cope with sexual problems related to a variety of stressors. Encompasses a broad range of clinically pertinent topics amenable to nursing approaches. title: Pharmacotherapeutics
description: Applies the problemsolving process to the nurse's role in administering medication using knowledge from previous science and nursing courses. Prerequisite: NUR 211, 212. Parallel: NUR 312.

title: Seminar on Professional Practice
description: Examines historical, legal, political, and ethical developments in nursing as well as trends in health care. Prerequisite: NUR 312, 314.

title: Physical Assessment
description: Enhancement of skills in performing total physical assessment with clients of diverse ages. Learning experiences include lecture, demonstration, and practice in clinical laboratory. Prerequisite: NUR 312. 427. *Emergency Nursing. (2) Nursing process of clients who need emergency treatment. Medicalsurgical and emergency nursing concepts. Clinical experiences in a variety of emergencycare settings, focusing on client assessment as a basis for emergency nursing. Prerequisite: NUR 312, 314. 456. *Gerontological Nursing. Involves the application of the nursing process to attain the appropriate level of independence and wellness. Prerequisite: NUR 312 or equivalent.

title: Patient Education: A Multidisciplinary Approach
description: Theories of client education and application of the educational process to individuals and groups in a variety of healthcare settings. Emphasis on the multidisciplinary team concept in planning, implementing, and evaluating client education. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 464.

title: Independent Study
description: Designed for students who want to pursue independent study in nursing under the direction of a faculty adviser. Prerequisite: NUR 312. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. title: Physical Conditioning
description: Designed to help students become aware of their present fitness status and to appreciate the role of physical exercise in everyday life. Students will engage in a program of exercise to maintain and increase physical fitness and aid in weight control. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 100.

title: Water Adjustment for Swimming
description: Phase one of a program designed to help the nonswimmer to become an efficient swimmer. Open only to students who cannot swim in deep water. During the regular school year (September through May) the course is administered as either a learning or a testout program. Students enroll at the aquatics office of the Lewellen Aquatics Center. After students meet the skillperformance standards, further attendance is not required and they may register for credit and grade in either the current semester or a future semester; however, registration must be completed at least two weeks before the end of the semester chosen. Summer students use the same procedures to register for swimming class as they do for other classes.

title: Fitness Walking
description: Designed to increase cardiovascular fitness through brisk walking. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 103.

title: Jogging
description: Designed to increase cardiovascular fitness through jogging. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 104.

title: Adapted Physical Education
description: Intended for students with physical handicaps or limiting conditions that would prevent full and unlimited participation as determined by the University Health Service. Students consult with a physical education faculty member and are assigned according to their interests, needs, and qualifications. Regular course requirements are adjusted for the individual. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Tai Chi Ch'uan
description: Designed to teach basic skills and knowledge of Tai Chi Ch'uan and to increase physical fitness through Chi Ch'uan exercises.

title: Beginning and Intermediate Judo
description: Designed to give the student an appreciation of judo, both as a sport and an art. Emphasis on understanding basic judo techniques and the development of selfconfidence and selfdefense.

title: Beginning Karate
description: Introductory skills for enjoyment of karate.

title: Beginning Modern Dance
description: Basic skills of modern dance through movement techniques and creative projects.

title: Beginning Modern Jazz Dance
description: Understanding and skill in basic techniques arid styles (cool, hot, blues, urban, primitive) of the jazz dance.

title: Swimnastics
description: Physical conditioning through water exercise, using high potential fitness activities that can be used in a small pool or in a limited area of a crowded instructional pool. Prerequisite: ability to put face in water, to float on front or back in shallow water, and to regain standing position after floating. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 117.

title: Beginning Tap Dance
description: Designed to teach the basic tap steps and combinations along with their rhythmic analysis and style to be used in composition. Intended for the student with no experience in tap dancing.

title: Hatha Yoga
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through yoga exercises and yoga relaxation techniques.

title: Bowling
description: Introductory and intermediate skills designed to give the student knowledge in bowling on a team, in a league, keeping league records, team standings, and computing and figuring handicaps as well as concentration on basic fundamentals.

title: Beginning Badminton
description: Introductory skills for playing singles and doubles badminton. Stresses basic strategy, rules, and courtesy.

title: Horsemanship
description: Schooling and work toward perfecting form in three gaits: walk, trot, and canter. Harness driving and stable management are also emphasized.

title: Bicycling
description: Bicycling techniques involving maintenance of equipment; city, open country, and endurance riding primarily to introduce the student to family bicycling for lifetime use. Not open to the student who has credit in PELF 130.

title: Cross - Country Snow Skiing
description: Designed to teach the beginning skier the skills necessary to reach the more advanced level of crosscountry skiing. Takes the skier from short, closein trails to longer, more challenging trails offered at several Indiana state parks.

title: Distance Running
description: Designed for people who like to run for physical fitness. Students are expected to start at oneto twomile distances and progress up to thirtyfive to forty minutes of running. Prerequisite: must be in condition to run two miles on first day.

title: Flag Football
description: Introduction to fundamentals and rules of football through flag football; instruction in techniques, terminology, strategies, and rules.

title: Beginning Basketball
description: Information, practice, and experience in basic skills, strategies, and knowledge. Course includes passing, shooting, dribbling, offense, and defense.

title: Fencing
description: Basic techniques, terminology, strategy, rules, and courtesies. Includes positions, footwork, parries, and lunges.

title: Volleyball
description: Provides the beginner with an understanding of rules and skills underlying optimal enjoyment for power volleyball.

title: Orienteering
description: Introduces the student to the activity of orienteering, a sport in which the participant uses such landnavigation skills as mapand compassreading. Circulorespiratory fitness is emphasized in distance running for time.

title: Beginning Gymnastics
description: Instruction in beginning skills leading to various stunts on balance beam, rings, pommel horse, horizontal bars, parallel bars, uneven bars, and vaulting horse. Prerequisite: PEG 107 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Weight Training
description: Development of a basic personalized program for building and maintaining strength for both general conditioning and activities.

title: Rhythmic Aerobics
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through aerobic exercise routines performed to music. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 148.

title: Individualized Physical Education
description: Limited to nontraditional students with special problems that may keep them from enrolling in conventional physical education classes. Registration is by permission of the department. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Swimming 1
description: Phase two of a program designed to help the student to become an efficient swimmer. Open only to students who can swim in deep water. During the regular school year (September through May) the course is administered as either a learning or a testout program. Students enroll at the aquatics office of the Lewellen Aquatics Center. After students meet the skill performance standards, further attendance is not required and they may register for credit and grade in either the current semester or a future semester; however, registration must be completed at least two weeks before the end of the semester chosen. Summer students use the same procedures to register for swimming class as they do for other classes.

title: Swimming 2
description: Students who are interested in advancing their swimming skills or are preparing to specialize in aquatics should consider this course. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Lifeguarding
description: A preparatory course for students who are highly skilled swimmers and are interested in becoming lifeguards. The American National Red Cross certification in lifesaving can be earned in this course. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Beginning Springboard Diving
description: Designed to assist the student in developing the basic skills used in dives from a onemeterhigh springboard. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Scuba
description: Selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus techniques and the scientific laws pertaining to that activity. Provides opportunities for refining techniques and skills for using selfcontained underwater breathing apparatus. Nationally recognized association diver's certification can be earned in this class. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Basic Canoeing
description: An introduction to movement control of a canoe as a type of small craft. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Fitness Swimming
description: Designed to improve cardiovascular and muscular endurance and stroke efficiency through swimming and land conditioning. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PEGF 217.

title: Racquetball
description: Instruction in the basic skills, strategies, and knowledge required to play racquetball.

title: Intermediate Golf
description: Designed to offer the golfing student an opportunity to learn and practice the finer points of the game.

title: Intermediate Tennis
description: Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 127.

title: Intermediate Hatha Yoga
description: Designed for the student wanting to perfect previously learned asanas and to learn new ones. Prerequisite: PEG 119 or permission of department chairperson. PHYSICAL EDUCATION, GENERAL—FITNESS (PEGF)

title: Physical Conditioning
description: Designed to help students become aware of their present fitness and to appreciate the role of exercise in everyday life. Includes a total of fifteen hours of lecture concerning physical fitness, health, and related aspects. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 100.

title: Fitness Walking
description: Designed to increase cardiovascular fitness through brisk walking. Includes fifteen hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and other related wellness topics. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 103.

title: Jogging
description: Designed to increase cardiovascular fitness through jogging. Includes a total of fifteen hours of lecture emphasizing common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related aspects. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 104.

title: Swimnastics
description: Physical conditioning through water exercise, using high potential fitness activities that can be used in a small pool or in a limited area of a crowded instructional pool. Includes a total of fifteen hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Prerequisite: ability to put face in water, to float on front or back in shallow water, and to regain standing position after floating. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 117.

title: Bicycling
description: Bicycling techniques involving maintenance of equipment; city, open country, and endurance riding for lifetime fitness. Includes a total of fifteen hours of lecture per semester concerning physical fitness, health, and related aspects. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 130.

title: Rhythmic Aerobics
description: Designed to increase physical fitness through aerobic exercise routines performed to music. Includes a total of fifteen hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 148.

title: Fitness Swimming
description: Designed to improve cardiovascular and muscular endurance and stroke efficiency through swimming and land conditioning. Includes a total of fifteen hours of lecture emphasizing a common core of knowledge concerning physical fitness, health, and related topics. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 217.

title: Pocket Billiards
description: Assists the student in the rudimentary skills and knowledge of the sport.

title: Conditioning, Fitness, and Exercise
description: Designed to emphasize the role of fitness; introduction to various activity forms and principles that underlie the development of fitness and wellness programs. Prerequisite: any PELF course.

title: Contemporary Activities 1
description: Designed to introduce the physical education student to a series of recreational and leisure activities that reflect changing needs.

title: Contemporary Activities 2
description: Designed to continue to add to the instructional options of the physical educator. Prerequisite: PEP 151.

title: Practicum 1
description: An introduction to the classroom setting for physical education students. Emphasis on observation, exploration, and interpersonal skills.

title: Movement Exploration
description: Introduction to theories of movement and strategies to enhance creative teaching.

title: Gymnastics 1
description: Introduction to basic techniques and progressions in tumbling and apparatus.

title: Gymnastics 2
description: Personal technique development; safety, instructional strategies, and principles of movement. Prerequisite: PEP 157.

title: Gymnastics 3
description: Continued study of the role of gymnastics K-12 in the public schools. Oriented to the physical educator. Prerequisite: 157, 158.

title: Studio of Contemporary Dance Theatre
description: Provides training for performance through varied choreographic dance experiences. Students plan, rehearse, and perform in studiohour presentations. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or permission of department chairperson. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foundations and Principles of Physical Education
description: Introduction to physical education and the role of the physical educator with emphasis on the educational process. Not open to the student who has credit in PEP 390.

title: Ethnic Dance Studio Theatre
description: Designed to emphasize the different styles existing in ethnic dance. Introduces the elements of ethnic dance choreography. Prerequisite: PEG 112 or PEP 262. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Badminton and Contemporary Activities 2
description: Elements of strategy, skill, and methodology in badminton; leisure and current activities for curricular variety.

title: Tennis and Contemporary Activities 3
description: Elements of tennis skill, methodology, and strategy; continued exploration of various leisure and recreational activities.

title: Softball and Volleyball
description: Beginning professional preparation in volleyball and softball including skills, rules, strategies, and teaching methods.

title: Volleyball
description: Beginning professional preparation course in volleyball including the basic skills, rules, and courtesies associated with the game.

title: Soccer and Contemporary Activities 1
description: Course designed to introduce pre - professional students to the elements of soccer, strategy, skills, and methods of teaching; introduction to a series of recreational and leisure activities.

title: Basketball; Field Hockey or Wrestling
description: Designed for pre - professional students with elements of skill and methodology included. Student selects either field hockey or wrestling; all students participate in basketball portion.

title: Foundations of Physical Education
description: Introduces professional physical education students to the psychomotor, cognitive, and affective scope of physical education and its relationship to education. Assists students in assessing the qualities of motor and physical fitness expected of physical education majors as they begin their vocational study.

title: Introduction to Sports Medicine and Athletic Training
description: Discussion of responsibilities and occupational opportunities in athletic training and sports medicine. Includes evaluation of the student's aptitude for this type of work.

title: Games and Activities for the Older Adult
description: Designed to acquaint the student with a variety of recreational activities suitable for the older adult.

title: Beginning Swimming for the Physical Educator
description: Introduces the nonswimmer or novice to basic skills and strokes of swimming and diving. Not open to deep water swimmers.

title: Aquatics for the Physical Educator
description: Designed to teach advanced beginners the skills, strokes, and basic dives necessary to become intermediate swimmers. Introduction to basic knowledge of water performance, terminology and safety, and instructional aquatic programs. Open to students who can swim in deep water. Students who are proficient in the aquatic skills, strokes, and dives taught in PEP 215 should see an adviser for alternate aquatic courses to meet aquatic requirement of 3 credit hours.

title: Aqua-Fitness for the Physical Educator
description: Designed to introduce physical education majors and minors to the benefits of an exercise program conducted in water. Major emphasis will be given to conditioning through water exercise.

title: Developmental Game Activities
description: Designed to acquaint the student with the application of the principles of movement and to provide a knowledge of basic skills and appropriate activities for the development of these skills as applied to game activities. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Principles and Problems of Coaching Sports
description: Introduces the principles and problems of coaching team and individual sports at the junior and senior high school levels. Considers the philosophies and principles that underlie the development of such a program.

title: Coaching Observation
description: Guided observation of coaching techniques and practices with analysis of teaching and coaching philosophies for competitive sports in schools. Prerequisite: PEP 231.

title: Practicum in Aquatics
description: An internship in aquatics at Ball State or another approved aquatic program. Prerequisite: PEP 353 and permission of department chairperson.

title: Tumbling and Apparatus
description: Prerequisite: PEP 157, 158.

title: Dance Composition 1
description: Principal elements of dance composition. Simple compositional forms for small groups and solo work. Prerequisite: PEG 215.

title: Lacrosse (Women's Game)
description: Introduction to an aerial game played on an outdoor field with a netted stick or "crosse" and a hard rubber ball. This team sport challenges the physical endurance and manipulative skills of the player.

title: Games and Activities for the Handicapped
description: Designed to familiarize the student with games and activities commonly used with the handicapped. Prerequisite: SPCED 201.

title: Practicum in Elementary School Physical Education
description: Offers the student supervised experience in basic movementoriented activities generally included in elementary school physical education programs (suggested range: K-6). Course work is contracted among the student, the department, and the school or agency. Prerequisite: PEP 230 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Anatomy
description: Basic concepts of anatomy for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching.

title: Physiology
description: Basic concepts of physiology for students with concentration areas in physical education and coaching. Prerequisite: PEP 292 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Kinesiology
description: The mechanics of motion as applied to the human body. Development of the ability to analyze activity for improving physical skills. Prerequisite: PEP 292.

title: Sports Officiating
description: Officiating techniques in a variety of sports. Different sport emphasis by semesters. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: First Aid
description: First aid as outlined by the American Red Cross, leading to standard certification. Designed for the student pursuing a major or minor program in the School of Physical Education. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 250.

title: Foundations of Exercise Leadership
description: Designed to provide basic knowledge in physical fitness and related areas for students not pursuing teaching majors, such as corporate fitness programs, private fitness centers, and YMCA's. Prerequisite: PEP 190.

title: Applied Methods of Exercise Leadership
description: Emphasizes practical experiences associated with designing, promoting, and implementing exercise and wellness programs. Introduces the basic principles and interpretation of the E.K.G. and includes presentation, activity participation, and fitness testing. Prerequisite: PEP 292, 293, 294, 301 and permission of department chairperson.

title: Practicum 2
description: Laboratory and classroom course involving the study and implementation of instructional strategies, growth and development factors, teaching progressions, and basic movement patterns.

title: Dance 1
description: Introduction to dance formsbasic styles, rhythms, technique. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 112.

title: Dance 2
description: Expansion of basic rhythmic activities, including technique, patterns, principles of movement, and instructional strategies. Prerequisite: PEP 306. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 113.

title: Dance 3
description: Advanced forms of dance for dance educators with emphasis on advanced technique and style, teaching strategies, progressions. Prerequisite: PEP 306, 307. Not open to the student who has credit in PEG 114.

title: Developmental Activities
description: Introduction to psychomotor activities (locomotor, nonlocomotor, manipulative) that are fundamental to the elementary curriculum and enhance middle school and upperlevel programs.

title: Evaluation in Physical Education
description: Measurement and evaluation in physical education with emphasis on underlying philosophy, tests, construction, and use of test results.

title: Teaching Physical Activity to the Older Adult
description: Designed to teach the student to recognize the characteristics of the older adult and to successfully plan, implement, and evaluate a program of physical activity based upon the special needs of the older adult. Prerequisite: PEP 150 or PEG 100.

title: Physical Therapy Kinesiology
description: The mechanics of motion as applied to the human body. Development of the ability to analyze - normal" motor performance. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110, 112; ANAT 330, 405.

title: Sports Information
description: Designed primarily for the sports information student. Develops the student's knowledge and background in the terminology, strategy, scoring, and officiating of a variety of sports. Not open to physical education majors.

title: Teaching and Coaching Swimming
description: Learning theories, teaching strategies, and physical laws that affect learning and performance in the water. Emphasis on analysis and technique. Prerequisite: PEG 201 or permission of department chairperson.

title: American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor
description: Opportunity for students to earn the American National Red Cross Water Safety Instructor certificate. Prerequisite: an unexpired American National Red Cross Advanced Lifesaving certificate.

title: Field and Laboratory Experience
description: Permits the student to receive credit for aquatic experiences in leadership, administration, and operation of aquatic programs or facilities. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching and Coaching Gymnastics
description: Prerequisite: PEP 157.

title: Teaching and Coaching Wrestling
description: Prerequisite: PEP 261.

title: Dance for Children
description: Basic rhythms, exploration of movement, and creative dance for the early grades of the elementary school.

title: Accompaniment for Modern Dance
description: Exploration and the use of accompaniment in dance. Prerequisite: PEG 115 or equivalent.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator 1
description: Fundamental modern dance techniques, elements of rhythmic patterns, materials of space, design, and other elements of composition.

title: Modern Dance for the Physical Educator 2
description: Continued development of modern dance techniques with emphasis on teaching. Prerequisite: PEP 365.

description: An introduction to predisposing anatomical, kinesiological, growth stress, and other problems that contribute to athletic injuries. Presents the procedures needed to accurately recognize and evaluate these problems and the extent of an athletic injury. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Athletic Training Modalities and Therapeutic Techniques
description: Introduces mechanical therapies, thermal therapy, cryotherapy, hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, and therapeutic exercise. Considers only treatments and their clinical uses that are of value to the athletic trainer in attending to athletic injuries. Prerequisite: PEP 396.

title: Methods of Teaching Sports
description: Methods, materials, and organizational techniques in selected team and individual sports. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing.

title: Teaching and Coaching Tennis
description: Prerequisite: PEP 177.

title: Teaching and Coaching Baseball and Softball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 179.

title: Teaching and Coaching Track and Field
description: Prerequisite: PEP 180.

title: Teaching and Coaching Football
description: Prerequisite: PEP 281.

title: Teaching and Coaching Basketball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 182.

title: Teaching and Coaching Volleyball
description: Prerequisite: PEP 183.

title: Teaching and Coaching Soccer
description: Prerequisite: PEP 184.

title: Prevention and Care of Athletic Injuries

description: An indepth practical experience in the application of exercise leadership knowledge and skills to fitness and rehabilitation programs owned and operated by private and corporate businesses, and by municipal organizations. title: Seminar
description: Capstone experience for the preprofessional including but not limited to curriculum development, current trends, futures in physical education.

title: Internship in Exercise Programs for the Older Adult
description: A practical experience in leading physical activities for older adults in healthcare centers, senior citizen centers, retirement centers, or other places where older adults engage in exercise. Prerequisite: PEP 312 and permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Coaching Internship
description: Students assist in coaching competitive sports in schools. Includes internship in coaching and indepth classroom discussions centering on selfawareness and the teachingcoaching process. May not be taken parallel with student teaching. Prerequisite: PEP 231.

description: Directed mainly toward the sports information student. Designed to discuss the various organizations that govern amateur and professional sports in the United States. description: Designed to provide the student with practical experience in working with handicapped children in a physical education setting. Prerequisite: PEP 488 and 494.

description: Explores the historical development of modern athletics. Students develop a philosophical relationship to the total school program and learn to deal with everyday coaching and administration problems.

title: Teaching Physical Education to the Developmentally Disabled
description: A study of people with developmental disabilities, including mental retardation, learning disabilities, and emotional disturban ces that affect motor performance. description: Scientific principles involved in movement as they apply to specific skills in elementary school physical education. Prerequisite: PEP 292, 293, 294.

description: Fundamental play needs of children; research into the play interests of children; and evaluation of space, equipment, and supervision. description: The effect of exercise on the human body. Prerequisite: PEP 292, 293, 294, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Teaching Physical Education for the Handicapped
description: Recognition of various abnormalities and physical handicaps and the limitation each causes. Physical education and recreational activities for each type.

description: An introduction to the practical application of athletic training methods such as bandaging, adhesive strapping, massage, and other therapeutic techniques used by the athletic trainer in the prevention and care of athletic injuries. Prerequisite: PEP 370, 372, and 396.

title: Clinical Experience in Athletic Training
description: Students receive on - thejob experience as student athletic trainers in conjunction with their studentteaching assignments in an Indiana high school that is qualified to provide students with both experiences. Prerequisite: PEP 370, 372 and 396.

description: An opportunity to investigate an area of particular interest to the student, under supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, research, analysis, and writing. Fisher The College of Architecture and Planning, established by the 1965 Indiana legislature, is dedicated to the development of professional competency in the functional, aesthetic, and humane design of the physical environment. Three fiveyear programs of study are offered: the departmental major in architecture, leading to a bachelor of architecture degree; the departmental major in landscape architecture, leading to a bachelor of landscape architecture degree; and the departmental major in urban planning, leading to a bachelor of urban planning and development degree. The first year of all three programs includes a sound foundation in the humanities, natural sciences, and social and behavioral sciences; the first year of professional course work is the same for all three programs. An environmental design major is offered for students who have completed the first three years of either the architecture or the urban planning and development program; it is designed for students who wish to end their studies after four years of university work or who wish to pursue graduate study in a different subject. This program leads to the bachelor of science degree. The faculty of the College of Architecture and Planning have a variety of backgrounds, education, experience, qualifications, and philosophies. The curricula stress character, dedication, initiative, and a strong commitment to creativity, technical skill, and social and professional responsibility.

title: History of Architecture 3

title: History of Architecture, Planning, and Engineering in the Midwest Region

title: History of Architecture, Preservation, Planning, and Landscape Architecture

title: History of Housing in Architecture
description: Analysis of various types of housing in the history of architecture, from primitive detached units to sophisticated complexes of multifamily dwellings. Emphasis on planning, materials, structure, and aesthetics. Prerequisite: ARCH 223, 224, 429.

title: Historic Preservation Restoration and Adaptive Use Cost Benefits

title: Internship in Preservation and Restoration
description: Ten weeks of employment during the summer with a federal, state, or private organization engaged in preservation or restoration.

title: Architectural Design Internship
description: Preparation for the internship experience; supplements the experience gained during the internship and serves as the basis for evaluation of student growth. Prerequisite: ARCH 302.

title: Architectural Research
description: Experience in architectural inquiry: the contexts, definitions, and processes of design creativity; relationships to scientific and environmental design and behavior research; technologyrelated research; strategies in building and testing concepts, assumptions, hypotheses, empirical evaluation; methods and procedures. description: Problems, theories, and methods leading to development of individual and group requirements and their translation into conventional and nonconventional performance criteria. Programming of thesis project. Prerequisite: admission to fifth year by the Faculty Design Review Panel.

description: Problems, processes, and philosophies of architectural practice. Emphasis on applied organizational and management theories, processes, tools. Includes offcampus laboratory. Prerequisite: ARCH 450.

description: A study of archaeological methods applied to architectural remains. Principles of stratigraphic excavation, dating methods, and techniques for surveying and recording; technical and comparative analysis of building elements for dating, interpreting, and reconstructing.

title: History of Urban Form
description: Analysis of urban centers and city planning, emphasizing spatial organization, order, and philosophy of planning in architecture. Prerequisite: ARCH 224.

title: Life Safety in Architecture and Environmental Design
description: Survey of topics relevant to life safety encompassing wind, fire, ground motions; environmental factors including noise, criminal activity, and home accidents; and matters pertaining to the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA). Prerequisite: senior standing.

title: Advanced Graphic Techniques
description: Advanced graphic explorations of architectural subject matter, stressing fullcolor rendering. title: Landscape Architecture History 2

title: Environmental Systems and Structures

title: Philosophy of Landscape Architecture

Arndt The College of Business is a professional school and has as its objective the education of men and women for pursuits in business, industry, and education. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the university and to the service of the business community. The college ranks tenth in the nation in undergraduate enrollment. Its undergraduate programs are accredited by the American Assembly of Collegiate Schools of Business. The college recognizes the need for both breadth and depth in the total academic pattern. The curricula are designed to provide a broad background in general education, mastery of the basic tools and an understanding of the fundamentals of business organization and procedures, and specialization in a selected field of business. All curricula are designed to develop the ability to define and analyze problems, to make value judgments, and to express conclusions in a cogent and concise manner. The largest responsibility of the College of Business is the training for staff and line positions in accounting, economics, finance, management, marketing, and office administration. This specialized training is preceded by the acquisition of a body of knowledge that is common to all specialties. Baccalaureate programs are also available in four concentrations for the preparation of secondary teachers. The associate in arts degree is offered in business administration with options in marketing and retailing, office services, and midmanagement. The associate in arts degree is also available in secretarial studies and in word processing. The College of Business is administered through six departments: accounting, business education and office administration, economics, finance, management science, and marketing. In addition, the Bureau of Business Research offers research services and publications to the business community as well as to faculty and students. The Center for Economic Education provides economic education aids to the school systems, to business firms, and to the public in the Ball State service area. The Better Business Bureau, serving the campus and Delaware County, is administered by the Department of Marketing and its students. The 3/2 Program The 3/2 program is designed to give a select group of students an opportunity to combine their undergraduate liberal arts studies with graduate study in the College of Business. Students who successfully complete the program earn both a bachelor's degree and master of business administration degree (M.B.A.) within a fiveyear period. To be eligible for this option, all requirements must be completed for the program in general studies and the liberal arts departmental major by the conclusion of the third year of academic work. Therefore, students should begin to prepare during the freshman year, planning each semester's course load with this goal in mind. During the fourth year, students who gain admission to the 3/2 program take course work that represents the first year of the twoyear M.B.A. curriculum. While enrolled in M.B.A. course work during the senior year, students are officially undergraduate students fulfilling undergraduate requirements. Students who successfully complete a subsequent year of fulltime graduate study will be granted the M.B.A. degree. The following departments participate in the 3/2 program: anthropology, biology, chemistry, computer science, economics, English, foreign languages, geography, history, journalism, philosophy, political science, psychological science, sociology, social work, and speech communication. Preadmission Students interested in the 3/2 program should consult their advisers to determine requirements for their liberal arts majors. Students should also become acquainted with the programs that coordinate their majors with the 3/2 program. Each participating department will provide sample programs. Additionally, students should consult with an adviser in the College of Business, who will assist in the review of admission standards. Students must complete the College of Business math requirement before beginning the fourth year of study. Admission Students apply for admission to the 3/2 program during the spring semester of their junior years. Students will take the Graduate Management Admissions Test (GMAT) during the fall semester of their junior years. To be admitted, students must have a gradepoint ratio of 3.2 or higher based on at least 78 credit hours earned and a score of 1100 or higher using the AACSB formula of GMAT + (GPA x 200). Students are admitted to the program during the spring semester of their junior years and begin study the fall semester of their senior years. Admission to the 3/2 program in the College of Business does not guarantee admission to fulltime graduate study in the college in the fifth year. When admitted, students are advised within the College of Business. Fourth Year During the fourth year, students will take graduatenumbered courses that make up the common body of knowledge and that are prerequisites for the M.B.A. Credit in these courses will apply to the credit hours required for the baccalaureate degree. At the end of the fourth year of study, students will normally have completed 126 semester hours, the minimum credit hours required for a baccalaureate degree. Assuming that all requirements are met, students may choose to leave the 3/2 program and take a bachelor's degree with a major in the College of Sciences and Humanities and a minor in foundations of business. Fifth Year Students in the 3/2 program are expected to meet all university requirements for admission to the graduate program in business administration. M.B.A. study will be fulltime study beginning the fall semester of the fifth year. Accounting, the method by which financial results are summarized and interpreted, furnishes the necessary data. The accountant as a student of management problems endeavors to meet reporting requirements and to present data in terms of management's needs. The study of accounting is a vital part of the educational preparation of any executive and is useful in all types of business careers. Contact with all aspects and levels of business enables the accountant to acquire excellent training for executive leadership. Many and varied careers may be available to the accountant both in the types of organizations and in the areas of specialization selected. The future for students trained in accounting is almost unlimited, since the continued growth in the uses of accounting is assured by further expansion and complex development of business activity both in government and industry. A major in accounting provides a foundation for careers as certified public accountants, controllers, financial officers, internal auditors, cost accountants, public administration officers, and teachers of accounting. The departmental major in accounting is for students who want a foundation for an interesting and rewarding career in the broad fields of accounting. Students who wish to prepare for the teaching of accounting in the secondary school will complete the teacher education curriculum with the business education teaching major I. This teaching area is listed in the statement of the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate programs (pp. 56-58) and by the concentration areas listed below.
