title: Principles of Accounting 1
description: An introduction to accounting with emphasis on the basic principles underlying the accounting cycle. Includes the preparation of reports to management and external users of financial statements.

title: Principles of Accounting 2
description: A continuation of ACC 201 with emphasis on financial statement analysis and managerial and cost accounting concepts. Prerequisite: ACC 201.

title: Accounting for the Industrial Technologist
description: Concepts and procedures in accounting with emphasis on an understanding of double entry bookkeeping, financial statements, budgeting, and cost accounting. Not open to the student who has credit in ACC 202 or is a major in the College of Business.

title: Tax Law for Paralegals
description: The law of income and estate taxation, including preparation of income tax returns and related materials. Includes a survey of the various administrative and judicial tribunals, and their jurisdiction, involved in the determination of tax controversies. Prerequisite: ACC 201. Not open to the student who has credit in ACC 401 or 405 or who is majoring in accounting.

title: Intermediate Accounting 1
description: The theoretical framework for accounting principles and procedures, the application of generally accepted accounting principles, and the preparation of financial statements. Prerequisite: ACC 202.

title: Intermediate Accounting 2
description: A continuation of ACC 301. Includes such topics as accounting theory, external reporting, and accounting for partnerships. Prerequisite: ACC 301.

title: Cost Accounting
description: Basic concepts of cost accounting including methods used to record and control costs of materials, labor, and overhead by manufacturing firms. Prerequisite: ACC 202.

title: Advanced Cost Accounting
description: Advanced situations and techniques with emphasis on managerial use of cost accounting data and management information systems. Prerequisite: ACC 305.

title: Income Tax Accounting
description: A study of the basic features of the federal income tax. Emphasis is placed on the determination of taxable income of individuals and corporations. Prerequisite: ACC 201.

title: Tax Research and Advanced Topics
description: A study of federal taxes on business income of corporations and partnerships. Includes emphasis on tax research and planning and the use of tax reference materials and services. Prerequisite: ACC 202 and 401.

title: Advanced Accounting
description: Special accounting problems related to business combinations, consolidated financial statements, governmental and nonprofit accounting, and fiduciary accounting. Prerequisite: ACC 302.

title: C.P.A. Problems
description: Advanced accounting practices and procedures intended to prepare students for Certified Public Accountant Examination. Emphasis on application of accounting principles to problems given in recent examinations and on working under substantially the same conditions as in the examination room. Prerequisite: ACC 420.

title: Auditing Principles and Practices
description: Auditing of financial data by internal auditors and independent public accountants. The role of the auditor, the code of professional ethics, and auditing standards and procedures are studied. Prerequisite: ACC 302.

title: Internship in Accounting
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Accounting, a student majoring in accounting will work fulltime for one semester as an accounting intern for a public accountant, a business firm, or a governmental agency. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Accounting
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some phase of accounting. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours must be approved by the department. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. title: Beginning Keyboarding/Typewriting
description: Principles of basic keyboarding and touchtypewriting skills needed for using computer terminals or other office machines with typewriterstyle keyboards. For all students, particularly those entering fields in business education, computer science, data processing, information processing, journalism, printing technology, and education. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson required for those students with two or more semesters of high school or college keyboarding/typewriting credit.

title: Intermediate Keyboarding/Typewriting
description: A refinement of basic keyboarding and touchtypewriting techniques, development of speed and accuracy, and the preparation of business letters, manuscripts, and tables. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one to two semesters of high school or college keyboarding/typewriting.

title: Advanced Keyboarding/Typewriting
description: Advanced problems in keyboarding/typewriting, including reports, memoranda, letters, statistical tables, rough drafts, legal documents, and business forms. Continued speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or three or more semesters of high school or college keyboarding/typewriting.

title: Microcomputer Programming for Business Applications
description: Developing skill on microcomputers with display and hard copy capabilities; emphasis on skills to manipulate and program business applications on the microcomputer. Prerequisite: typewriting or keyboarding ability. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 225.

title: Microcomputer Applications for Business
description: Operation of microcomputers in processing business applications using commercial software packages including spreadsheet, database manipulation, and text creation and editing. Prerequisite: MGS 210 and keyboarding ability or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Transcription
description: Designed to teach transcription skills as they apply to the typewritten production of business documents. Application of punctuation, number usage, word choice, spelling, proofreading, and use of reference sources through machine transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or two semesters of typewriting.

title: Machine Transcription
description: Designed to teach students to produce mailable copy from transcription equipment. Intensive drill on transcription skills with emphasis on quality production. Application of punctuation, spelling, vocabulary building, letter styles, placement, proofreading, and grammar to the transcription process. Prerequisite: BEOA 230.

title: Principles of Business Correspondence
description: Principles and basic elements of effective letter writing with emphasis on the psychological approach, reader point of view, positive tone, and appropriate format for personal and business letters and job applications.

title: Internship in Distributive Education
description: Fulltime employment in an approved marketing occupation under departmental supervision according to a formal training agreement with the employer. Provides experience in areas in which distributive education teachers instruct. Each hour of credit requires 375 hours of approved employment and submission of various reports by the intern and employer. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to students seeking licenses as distributive education teachers.

title: Beginning Shorthand
description: Basic symbolic theory fundamentals with emphasis on abbreviated forms. Introduction to skills in writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement based on departmental advising and placement testing. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or two semesters of high school or college keyboarding/typewriting.

title: Intermediate Shorthand
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on skill in taking dictation and developing transcription skills. Prerequisite: BEOA 322 or student placement based on departmental advising, placement testing, or both; and BEOA 113 or three semesters of high school or college keyboarding/typewriting.

title: Advanced Shorthand
description: A continuation of theory, dictation, and transcription, wit 1 special emphasis on the production of mailable copy. Prerequisite: BEOA 323 or student placement based on departmental advising, placement testing, or both; and BEOA 113 or three or more semesters of high school or college keyboarding/typewriting.

title: Personal Word Processing and Graphics
description: Designed to acquaint nonmajors with word processing and graphics capabilities of microcomputers. Handson instruction in information processing and presentation graphics. Cannot be substituted for BEOA 331. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or high school typing credit. Not open to the student who has credit in BEOA 331.

title: Introduction to Word/Information Processing
description: An introductory course in word/information processing focusing on understanding word processing concepts and how they fit into a total information processing system. Some handson experience with microcomputers. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Electronic Word/Information Processing Systems
description: Studies basic operations of microprocessor visual display systems. Compares features and capabilities of various word processing systems with emphasis on recording, formatting, editing, temporary and permanent storage, revising, merging, proofreading, and logging. Prerequisite: BEOA 112, 230, 331.

title: Word/Information Processing Applications
description: Emphasizes a more sophisticated operation of microprocessor visual display systems for production of advanced applications. Special attention to problem analysis, software comparison and evaluation, and procedures for integration with graphics, data processing, and other systems. Prerequisite: BEOA 231, 332, and MGS 210.

title: Teleprocessing and Office Information Systems
description: Integration of electronic office equipment interconnected through telecommunications including concepts of data communications, electronic mail, and networks. Some handson laboratory experience with communicating word processors and microcomputers. Prerequisite: BEOA 331 or MGS 210 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Reprographics
description: Preparation of materials for desktop publishing combining word processing and graphics based upon principles of page layout; comparative costs and appropriateness of various reprographic methods, software, and equipment. Some handson experience with microcomputers and laser printers. Prerequisite: BEOA 330 or 331 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems; knowledge, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining records in business and industry. Some handson laboratory experience with office automation software for records processing and database management. Prerequisite: sophomore standing and BEOA 331 or MGS 210 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Principles of Office Supervision
description: Principles of effective office supervision with emphasis on the function of the office and the role of the office supervisor. Prerequisite: MGS 200 or 300.

title: Methods of Teaching for the Marketing Education Teacher
description: The role of the marketing education teacher in the teaching of marketing, basic business, and bookkeeping/ accounting subjects; courses to be taught and their objectives, teaching strategies, instructional materials, and lesson and unit planning. Prerequisite: ACC 201, ECON 201, EDPSY 251, and at least two courses in marketing. Open only to students with an area in marketing education.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects, Majors 1 and 2
description: Objectives, planning, methods, techniques, devices for teaching typewriting, basic business, and office machines and office procedures courses. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280. Parallel: BEOA 338.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Accounting, Major 1
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, devices for teaching accounting. Prerequisite: ACC 201 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Must be taken concurrently with BEOA 490. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Shorthand and Transcription, Major 2
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, devices for teaching shorthand and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 and 322 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Must be taken concurrently with BEOA 490. Prerequisite: EDSEC 280.

title: Techniques of Coordinating Cooperative Marketing Education Programs
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and coordinating cooperative marketing education programs. Restricted to persons seeking licenses as teachers or coordinators of vocational marketing education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Organization, Management, and Teaching: Vocational Marketing Education
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and managing inschool laboratory programs in vocational marketing education. Restricted to students seeking licenses as teachers or coordinators of vocational marketing education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Education
description: The principles upon which vocational education is organized, administered, and supervised; federal and state regulations; agencies that provide delivery systems for vocational education; relationship of vocational education to career education, vocational rehabilitation, and programs for persons with special needs. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or 383; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Survey of the Vocational Education Program Areas
description: An overview of the six program areas in vocational education. Includes program administration and supervision, objectives, the occupations for which training is offered, curricula, equipment and facilities, student selection, inschool laboratories, fieldtraining opportunities, and youth organizations. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or 383; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Microcomputers in Business Education
description: A handson approach to the use of microcomputers in the business education classroom; use of business software; analysis and design of programs for business education courses. Prerequisite: open only to students pursuing teaching majors in business or marketing teacher education or by permission of department chairperson.

title: Computerized Business Document Generation
description: An introduction to text editing capabilities of the computer for designing and processing business documents for the modern office. Development of an understanding of the use of the generalpurpose computer for text processing. Prerequisite: MGS 210 or CS 116.

title: Communications for Business Organizations
description: Techniques used in managementoriented internal and external communications. Emphasis on theory, planning, oral and written presentations, audience perceptions, data organization, media selection, and preparation techniques for business letters; and an overview of reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Business Reports: Written and Oral
description: Techniques used in writing both formal and informal managementoriented reports, including collecting, interpreting, summarizing, and synthesizing data. Principles for selection of tabular and graphic data presentations. Includes written and oral presentations of functional reports with an overview of analytical reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Employment Communications
description: Determining job requirements and writing a letter of application and résumé; letters requesting reference permission, appreciation of interview, acceptance and refusal of position, and resignation. Includes interview techniques. Open to all students.

title: Secretarial Procedures
description: Operational functions of toplevel professional secretarial work through integration of basic skills, knowledge, and the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 241 and sophomore standing.

title: Secretarial Administration
description: Administrative and supervisory aspects of toplevel professional secretarial work through planning and organizing office functions to achieve smooth and efficient work flow. Emphasizes the human relations aspects of office work. Prerequisite: BEOA 451.

title: Internship in Office Systems Administration
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the business education and office administration department, students majoring in office systems administration will work in an office environment in a public or private organization. Written reports are required. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Office Information Systems Management
description: Implementation and management of integrated office information systems. Study of managerial problems involved with people, procedures, and technology. Prerequisite: MGS 300 or equivalent, BEOA 331 or MGS 210 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the several other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 202 and MGS 300.

title: Principles of Business Education
description: The analysis of a total business education program and the integration of various facets that lead to sound instruction. The impact of past, present, and future legislative and societal developments. Parallel: BEOA 385 or 386. Open only to students approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Marketing Education
description: An investigation of the current status, historical development, philosophy, and principles of marketing education. Components include secondary, postsecondary, and adult marketing education, DECA, and general and specialized curricula. Prerequisite: EDSEC 280. Open only to students pursuing the teaching major in marketing education.

title: Independent Study: Business or Marketing Education; Office Administration
description: For students with excellent academic records who wish to conduct an indepth study in some phase of business education, marketing education, or office administration. The project selected, methods, and credit hours must be approved by the department chairperson and supervising faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of economics are surveyed and applied to topics chosen by the instructor. Especially valuable to students with no high school background in economics. Not applicable to a major or minor in economics. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 201 or 202.

title: Elementary Microeconomics
description: A study of why people specialize as producers and exchange what they produce with others. Includes analysis of how market structure affects prices. Discusses the issue of whether selfinterested economic behavior promotes or hinders society.

title: Elementary Macroeconomics
description: A survey of the major explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions. The focus is how the private sector's economic behavior is affected by various governmental policies and institutions. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Factors contributing to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to the student who has credit in POLS 281.

title: Honors Colloquium in Economics
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others by permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 in any semester.

title: Intermediate Microeconomics
description: An investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involves analyses of product pricing, output determination, resource pricing, and employment in various market structures. Includes graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
description: Analyzes national income as a measure of economic activity. Emphasizes the determination of national income, employment, and price level and the rate of growth of the economic system. Includes examination of the theories of consumption and investment spending, interaction between money and national income, and implications of alternative models for public policy. Includes graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202 or a combination of ECON 201 and 3 hours of credit in United States history, or 6 hours of credit in United States history.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 6 hours of credit in natural resources, NR 101 or permission of department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 303.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Labor Relations and Law
description: Study of collective bargaining, the joint determination by employers and employees (through their representatives) of the problems of the employment relationship--encompassing both the negotiation and administration of the labor agreement with primary emphasis upon the rules governing these processes. Prerequisite: EGON 201 and 202 or permission of department chairperson.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasizes economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives regarding provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Compares and analyzes growth rates of various countries. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how mankind has looked at its economic life; surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Use of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202, and MATHS 132 or its equivalent.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202; MATHS 132 or its equivalent; MGS 221.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the board of governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstructs or facilitates the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Internship in Economics
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Economics, a student majoring in economics works fulltime for one semester as an economics intern for a private or public organization. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Open only to second semester juniors and seniors majoring in economics. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Credit is not applicable toward meeting the requirements of a major in economics.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 6 hours of credit in economics. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses, thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202, and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester. Finance is a decisionoriented discipline concerned with the investment and management of money both in the present and in the future. This major is designed to pro- Finance 121 vide students with a general program in the financial aspects of business including financial management, investments, banking, insurance, real estate, and other related financial areas. The finance major allows students to pursue one of the following five options: The corporate financial management option prepares students for careers in the finance division of a business firm such as systems analysis, budget review analysis, financial analysis, acquisitions analysis, credit management, receivables management, and shortand longterm capital management. The financial institutions option emphasizes employment opportunities in investment banking and in managing stocks and bonds as a securities broker, portfolio manager, or trust department specialist. This option prepares the student to work in banking, savings and loan associations, loan companies, insurance companies, credit unions, pension funds, securities brokerage, and real estate brokerage. The risk management option has been designed to develop finance graduates in life and health as well as property and casualty sales, property and casualty underwriting, insurance appraisal, and management positions with the insurance industry. The real estate option prepares a student for a sales career as well as real estate management. The international business option prepares a student for a career in multinational business fields and for the importexport activities of business firms. General Business Administration. This major permits students to concentrate in two of the three areas available, i.e., insurance, management, and finance, providing a broader diversity of vocational opportunities than the finance major but with less depth in any one area of concentration. The course of study includes an examination of the various institutions, structures, functions, organizations, operations, and environments that influence business and economic activities. The finance sequence is designed to provide familiarity with the institutions and instruments of finance and with the operation of the financial system. It is intended to develop understanding of the problems of financing business activities. The management sequence is designed to develop abilities to enable students, as future business executives and specialists, to deal with the diversity of problems that arise in the course of daytoday activities. The insurance sequence is designed to give students a survey of the major areas of insurance and more specific study in the fields of life and property insurance. title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law and the effect of the law in the areas of consumer credit and economic relationships. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of department chairperson.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to agencies including employer and employee rights and obligations, partnerships including limited partnership, corporations including fiduciary obligations of directors, security regulations, bankruptcy, and corporate reorganization in bankruptcy. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principal articles of the code including sales, commercial paper, and security interests, in addition to creditors' rights and property law. Includes state and federal consumer protection laws as they affect commercial law. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Law for Small Business
description: Analysis of the laws affecting the small business. Emphasis on the legal aspects and legal implications of formation of a business, employeremployee relationships, consumer protection laws, creditor rights, and closing the business. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Estate Planning and Administration
description: An introduction to problems associated with planning of financial resources during working life, retirement, and after the death of the principal income producer. Included are techniques for fact gathering, tax principles, use of trusts, and will drafting. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Current Topics in Business Law
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced business students for study of current topics and problems in business law. Topics may include current activity in property law, commercial law, and government regulation of business. Prerequisite: BL 260 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairman. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the consumer's point of view. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation. Not open to juniors and seniors majoring in business.

title: Money, Banking, and Financial Institutions
description: The role of money, credit, and financial institutions in the U.S. financial system; deposit creation; the structure and functions of commercial banks, financial institutions and their regulatory agencies; domestic and international aspects of monetary policy; competition and regulation of financial institutions. Prerequisite: ACC 202; ECON 201, 202; MATHS 132.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Designed to study different areas of financial decision making in a business firm. Specific topics include financial objectives of the firm, sources of funds, working capital management, capital budgeting, investment decisions under uncertainty, valuation, capital structure decisions, and dividend policy. Prerequisite: ACC 202; ECON 201; MGS 221; and junior standing. Finance 123

title: Theory of Finance
description: A course devoted to the study of the current theory of finance. Topics include the nature and methodology of finance, efficient market hypothesis, portfolio theory and market equilibrium, optimal investment and financing decisions under certainty and uncertainty. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Designed to introduce the student to areas of investment: securities markets, transaction of stocks and bonds, valuation and timing, fundamental and technical indicators, money markets, and funds. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Financial Markets and the Economy
description: Nature and functions of financial markets; classification and interrelation of domestic and international financial markets; determination of the level and structure of interest rates; impact of monetary policy on financial markets and the economy. Prerequisite: FIN 250, 350.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance, import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Multinational Business Finance
description: An indepth study of international financial institutions such as central banks, International Monetary Fund, and area development banks involved with the financial decisions of multinational corporations. Includes an overview of the new developing forces in international finance. Prerequisite: FIN 452.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Theory
description: An indepth analysis of valuation theory, capital market theory, and portfolio theory. Prerequisite: FIN 350, 355.

title: Managerial Decision Making in Finance
description: A summary course devoted to the compilation of knowledge and the application of financial analysis to decision making in various subareas of finance. The course is structured on the casestudy approach. Prerequisite: FIN 354.

title: Operations of Financial Institutions
description: To integrate the various topics of finance with a view toward applications to the management of financial institutions in the following decision areas: assetliability management, cost control, profitability, capital adequacy, business development. Cases will be integrated in the method of instruction. Prerequisite: FIN 354, 355, 356.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Finance, students majoring in finance or general business administration work fulltime for a semester as interns for a banking institution, business firm, or governmental agency. Requires written reports. Open only to secondsemester juniors or seniors. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, researching, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major areas of insurance, such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Fundamentals of Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Fundamentals of Property- Liability Insurance
description: Study of fire, inland marine, liability, worker's compensation insurance. Emphasis on commercial insurance as a method of risk management. Prerequisite: INS 370.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry, emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 260 and INS 370.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include nofault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, state vs. federal regulations. Prerequisite: INS 370, 371, and 372 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Insurance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who wish to study some phase of insurance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various insurance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Real Estate Principles
description: The economic import of real estate, real estate characteristics, land use and environmental controls, legal aspects of real estate, methods of valuation, mortgage credit sources, secondary mortgage markets and financing techniques, investment analysis, land development, and real estate operations.

title: Real Estate Finance
description: The contractual nature and legal implication of the instruments used in real estate finance; instrument, techniques, and strategies in the financing of real estate investment; and the structure and operation of both primary and secondary mortgage markets. Provides the student with background in real estate law and real estate finance. Prerequisite: RE 330.

title: Legal Aspects of Real Estate
description: Elementary concepts of real estate law and practice particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, brokers' regulations, license law, and title insurance.

title: Real Estate Analysis
description: The appraisal of real estate. Other analytical systems will be reviewed as they apply to the real estate industry, including the economic base analysis, feasibility studies, and investment analysis. Prerequisite: RE 330.

title: Real Estate Administration
description: An orientation of the real estate business using text cases, incidents, and walking cases. Guest speakers who are experts in real estate will be invited to speak and answer questions. Prerequisite: RE 431 and senior standing or permission of department chairperson. Department of Management Science Gupta, Chairperson; Ahmed, Baird, Green, Harris, Hornsby, Kuratko, LaFollette, Lyles, Ma, Montagno, Necessary, Seeborg, Swart, Walters Management involves the coordination of human and physical resources toward an objective or goal. Every organization has managers, regardless of what they are called (e.g., managers, administrators, principals, coaches, officers, or chiefs). Therefore, a student who elects to major in management will be preparing to assume a position of responsibility in a wide variety of profit and nonprofit organizations. The major in management allows the student to pursue one of the following five management options: The production and operations management option prepares students to assume positions of responsibility in the production of goods and services. Students are introduced to the production functions in detail, are taught the methodology of making productionrelate , ' decisions, and become acquainted with modern techniques used in motivating and leading personnel in a productionoriented occupation. The personnel administration option prepares students to enter occupations that relate primarily to the people in an organization. Students are given an indepth presentation of the personnel function needed to become familiar with a conceptual framework for analyzing and solving problems involved in the selection, development, and motivation of human resources. The management information systems option introduces students to the concepts and techniques necessary for the development and operation of management information systems. Students acquire a broad background in the role and operation of an information system in an organization. Graduates of this option are knowledgeable about the concepts and techniques of computerized information systems necessary to accomplish this function effectively and efficiently. The entrepreneurship and small business option is designed to provide students with the knowledge needed to work in a small business environment. Students learn how to formulate a plan for a small business and how to implement that plan, becoming acquainted with management information systems and business law tailormade for the small business. Students are also given the opportunity to help small businesses as consultants in team practicums. The general management option introduces students to a varied background in management. General management acquaints students with the whole gamut of management: production, personnel, management information systems, and other managerial topics. title: Management Principles
description: Introduction to the basic concepts and principles of management. Focuses on structures within companies and processes within firms to bring principles to bear on the practical problems of managing organizations. Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Business Information Systems
description: Basic concepts of information processing systems with emphasis on computer skills for generating business information including computing concepts and procedures in business, computer programming, text editing, file processing, and use of commercial software packages on mainframe computers and microprocessors. Prerequisite:

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: MGS 210 or CS 116. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 210.

title: Business Statistics
description: Statistical analysis and interpretation of data. Probability and random variables, statistical frequency distributions and summary measures, estimation and hypothesis testing. Applications to business problems. Prerequisite: MATHS 131 and 132; MGS 210 recommended. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 181.

title: Introductory Operations Management
description: Introduction to the tools and techniques of management with practical applications to the production of goods and services. Prerequisite:

title: Personnel and Supervision
description: Introduction to the personnel and supervisory functions in organizations. Focuses on employee and union relationships; environmental, business, and social responsibilities; and leadership and supervision techniques, especially for the firstline supervisors. Prerequisite: MGS 200. Not open to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Principles of Management
description: Explores current management principles and practices including planning, organizing, motivating, and controlling. Discusses leadership, problemsolving techniques and communication, coordination, and human relations skills required for managerial success. Prerequisite: junior standing. Not open to the student who has credit in MGS 200.

title: Getting and Keeping a Job in Business
description: Explores students' personal goals in business, business opportunities, and management evaluations with preparations and techniques for personal interviews in the business setting. Focuses on personal discipline early in the business career.

title: Information System Analysis
description: Explores the applications of satisfying information needs of management decision makers including information flows, needs assessment analysis of computerbased information systems, and organizational influence of information systems. Prerequisite: MGS 210 and 300.

title: Computer Systems Applications
description: Business use of computerbased information and telecommunication systems. Presents a general framework from singlepurpose to integrated and distributed business applications, such as accounting, operationscontrol, production scheduling, personnel, and marketing. Prerequisite: MGS 210 and 311.

title: Advanced Business Statistics
description: Business applications of the most commonly used advanced statistical methods including goodnessoffit, contingency tables, analysis of variance, nonparametric techniques, advanced regression and correlation, time series, and index numbers. Prerequisite: MGS 210 and 221.

title: Systems Simulation
description: Concepts and techniques of system modeling and simulation using computers. Includes computer simulation languages, industrial dynamics, variance reduction techniques, and applications of computer simulation to various practical business situations. Prerequisite: MGS 210 and 221.

title: Small Business Venture
description: Provides essential knowledge for students interested in small business including search for venture opportunities; economic, technical, and operational feasibility of ventures; financing, marketing, and legal operations; and franchising and partnering. Prerequisite: MGS 300.

title: Entrepreneurship
description: Development and management of an entrepreneurial organization including prestartup, startup, survival, growth, and the transition from entrepreneurial to professional management. Explains the function of entrepreneurship and corporate entrepreneurship. Prerequisite: MGS 341.

title: Introductory Production Management
description: Various functional fields of production and operations management including product analysis, work design and measurement, forecasting, production planning, scheduling and inventory control, facility location and layout, material handling, plant safety and maintenance, and quality control. Prerequisite: MGS 210, 221, and 300.

title: Production Management in Service Sector
description: Various techniques for the design, operation, and control of service operations including service design and process selection, facility location and layout determination, staffing, equipment selection and operations, and scheduling of service operations. Prerequisite: MGS 351.

title: Managing Human Resources
description: Administration of personnel programs in business organizations so as to deal effectively with such problems as selection, training, compensation, promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions; employee services; and industrial relations. Prerequisite: MGS 300.

title: Organizational Behavior
description: Dynamics of human behavior in business organizations with emphasis on problems of motivation and leadership. Examines the behavior of individuals and groups within organizations and the practical interpretation and management of behavioral phenomena. Prerequisite: MGS 300.

title: Business and Society
description: The interrelationships between business and its external environment and the multiple and complex ways business organizations are affected by governmental and societal expectations. Emphasizes contemporary issues through discussions and case analysis. Prerequisite: MGS 300.

title: Business Systems Analysis and Design
description: Various systems analysis and design concepts and techniques, including the key steps in the systems design and development cycle. Emphasizes the consideration of practical applications within the business environment. Prerequisite: MGS 213 and 311.

title: Database: Structures and Management
description: Logical and physical organization of data. Describes data description, command and interrogation languages. Examines function of databases in information systems. Prerequisite: MGS 213 and 311.

title: Information Systems of Small Business
description: Computerbased information systems in small business operations without access to an internal specialist. Includes the identification of information requirements and the use of mainframe and microcomputers and purchased software to satisfy the information needs in small business. Prerequisite: MGS 210 and 341.

title: Information System Management
description: Equipment selection, equipment acquisition, computer operations management, project management, computer personnel management, financial control, systems security and control, and the relationship of the information systems function to an organization. Prerequisite: MGS 412.

title: Small Business Practicum
description: Teams of students consult with local small businesses recommended by the Small Business Development Center. Students work on problems in Management Science 127 such areas as accounting, production, marketing, personnel, finance, insurance, law, or information systems. Prerequisite: MGS 346.

title: New Venture Creation
description: Advanced smallbusiness management entrepreneurship. Requires thorough research project culminating in the development of a finished plan for a smallbusiness venture to be approved by an outside board of professional experts. Prerequisite: MGS 346; FIN 350; MKG 300; and senior standing.

title: Production Planning and Inventory Management
description: Production planning and inventory control in manufacturing and service industries, including capacity planning, resourcerequirements planning, production activity control, and related management models and systems. Prerequisite: MGS 351.

title: Current Topics in Production Management
description: Various current and emerging concepts and techniques of production and operations management with emphasis on flexible manufacturing, computeraided manufacturing, justintime production techniques, international operations, and other recent developments. Prerequisite: MGS 351.

title: Quality Assurance
description: Study of assuring and controlling the quality of goods and services, including the application of statistical techniques to problems of planning, feedback, and enhancement of process performance and operation effectiveness. Prerequisite: MGS 351.

title: Problems in Production/Operations Management
description: An integration of various production/ operations management principles, theories, and techniques as applied to the solution of actual production problems including the use of computers in production control activities. Requires the completion of a major individual project. Prerequisite: completion of all required courses for the production and operations management option.

title: Compensation Administration
description: Reviews basic compensation issues including internal, external, and individual equity, as well as benefits administration. Emphasis on design and implementation of compensation systems. Prerequisite: MGS 361.

title: Problems in Personnel Management
description: Case studies depicting complex personnel issues and problems faced by organizations. Presents opportunities for students to apply personnel policies, theories, concepts, and techniques to actual personnel situations. Prerequisite: MGS 361.

title: Personnel Planning and Selection
description: Focuses on organization and manpower planning, including determination of organization and manpower needs, analysis and development of job requirements and necessary qualifications for recruitment and selection procedures, placement and orientation, and evaluation of selection programs. Prerequisite: MGS 321, 463.

title: Business Policy and Strategic Management
description: Integration of various functional areas of business. Development and administration of strategy and policy in private and public sector organizations. Case studies focus on strategic decisions that enable an organization to relate effectively to its industrial, national, and international environments. Normally taken during the last semester of the student's program. Prerequisite: senior standing; FIN 350; MGS 300; and MKG 300.

title: Special Topics in Management Sciences
description: Exploration of special topics in management science of interest to faculty and students. May be repeated for credit for different topics. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Independent Study
description: Supervised study of some phase of management. May consist of an experiment, library research, or an analysis of current management practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Management Science
description: Explores current problems, theory, research, and trends in the management field. Will vary depending upon the current status of managerial research, the instructor, and the needs and interests of the students. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Management Science Internship
description: Job experience in an organization with a continuing innovative management program. Requires periodic written progress reports that will be evaluated by the assigned faculty member and the intern's supervisor. Thpic selected will depend on student's option. Prerequisite: second semester junior or senior standing and permission Department of Marketing Lowry, Chairperson; Avila, Baird, Borna, Brown, Chapman, Kumcu, Moser, Vanderleest, Vann, Wunder Marketing is concerned with the "customeroriented" management of the flow of goods and services from the producer to the consumer. The marketing process attempts to provide an efficient way for producers to meet the needs of consumers profitably. Marketing activities include developing a wanted product, promoting it efficiently, selling it at an economically logical price, and distributing it in the right places. Marketing courses are designed to allow students to develop their abilities to recognize and define marketing problems and solve them creatively. The marketing curriculum is career oriented and offers the following five options. The sales and promotion option prepares students for such careers as consumer and industrial product selling, sales training, advertising agency management, public relations, and product or brand management. The retailing option prepares students for careers in chainstore management, merchandising, fashion coordination, small business management, franchised organizations, and buying. For students choosing the physical distribution option, career opportunities include materials management, industrial procurement, transportation, and physical distribution. Students taking the general marketing option may pursue many different phases of the marketing process. Some of the careers available to students with this option are international marketing, bank marketing, consumer relations, and service marketing. The shopping center administration option prepares students for such careers as shopping center planning and development, shopping center administration, and retail management. The insurance marketing option is designed for students who seek careers with local insurance agencies or branch offices of large insurance companies. The Department of Marketing, in cooperation with selected business firms and commercial institutions, administers a professional practice program that allows juniors and seniors to relate classroom theory to practical experience by working for one semester in a variety of relevant assignments. Students who work as interns receive from 3 to 6 semester hours of credit, and most are paid by the firm for their work experience. Students are responsible for finding their own internships; they will be assisted by marketing department administrators in this process. Students in the marketing department coordinate and administer, with the participation of students from other departments, the Ball State University Better Business Bureau, a branch of the Indianapolis Better Business Bureau. Students interested in BSU/BBB are advised to enroll in MKG 380, Marketing and Consumer Issues, during their junior year. The activities of the bureau include resolving consumerbusiness grievances, providing buying information to consumers, alerting consumers to deceptive business practices, and preparing media releases on consumerbusiness problems. For students interested in teaching marketing education, it is possible to earn a departmental major in marketing along with the teaching major. The marketing education major is offered by the Department of Business Education and Office Administration. Such minors as applied mathematics, a foreign language, geography, industrial technology, journalism, and telecommunications are available for tailoring educational development to students' preferences and needs. title: Retail Merchandising
description: An introduction to the retail industry with a concentration on the merchandising activities of buying, selling, pricing, and inventory control. Prerequisite:

title: Salesmanship
description: Fundamentals of retail, wholesale, outside, and service selling. Emphasizes sales approaches, presentation, closings, and postsale service. Prerequisite: GBA

title: Retail Advertising
description: Introduction to advertising with emphasis on the preparation, appeal, and media selection of retail advertising. Prerequisite: GBA 101. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 300 or to the B.S. or B.A. candidate for a major or minor in the the College of Business.

title: Principles of Marketing
description: Examines marketing as a productive system within our economy. Studies promotional activities, product policies, retail and wholesale activities, pricing policies, international marketing, and the role of marketing in society. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and junior standing or permission of department chairperson.

title: Consumer Behavior
description: Practical business implications of the various aspects of consumer motivation and behavior. The student is provided with information to understand how and why a buyer reacts in a purchasing situation. Prerequisite: junior standing. Parallel recommended: MKG 300.

title: Advertising Management
description: Use of advertising as a communication tool in marketing management. Analysis of media selection, production and layout, measurement of effectiveness; and social and economic aspects of advertising. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 310.

title: Personal Selling
description: Provides a detailed introduction to and application of the principles of personal selling as applied to persons pursuing any vocation, as well as those aspiring to careers in the marketing area of business. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 327.

title: Sales Management
description: Policies and practices in organizing, recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and 325 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Retail Management
description: An investigation of store policies, organization, location, layout, buying, stock control, pricing, and sales promotion for retail stores. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Transportation: An International Focus
description: The economics of transportation with an international focus; economic development of various means of transportation and accompanying regulatory problems. Rate, traffic service, and coordination problems; advantages and disadvantages, trends, and peculiarities of the various modes. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Research
description: The basic nature and scope of marketing research; scientific method and research design; specific marketing research procedures; techniques of sampling; and research report, followup, and evaluation of research process. Selected applications in motivation, advertising, and product and sales control research. Prerequisite: MKG 300; MATHS 132; and MGS 221.

title: Marketing and Consumer Issues
description: Analysis of the consumer issues that affect marketing. Includes the marketing implications of consumerism, ecology, and the disadvantaged consumers. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Promotion Management
description: Uses cases and problems to provide experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKG 320.

title: Retail Strategy
description: Advanced course in retailing management using case studies and special projects to examine current topics and problems in retailing. Prerequisite: MKG 330.

title: Industrial Procurement Management
description: A basic course in industrial procurement management. Principal topics include make or buy analysis, quality and quantity control, value analysis, price determination, sources of supply, the purchasing system, and legal aspects of purchasing. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Materials Management
description: The organizational concept that integrates the management of the flow of materials through a business enterprise into consumer markets. Content includes anticipating, sourcing, obtaining, and monitoring the current status of materials in an enterprise. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 460.

title: International Marketing
description: Examines legal, economic, and cultural factors influencing marketing abroad. Commercial policies, practices, and techniques needed to identify and evaluate foreign markets, as well as the problems of pricing, promoting, and distributing products in international markets. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Simulation Game
description: A simulation game in which students are divided into teams or companies. Management in each company makes decisions in marketing, finance, and production. Does not involve writing computer programs or using information from a dataprocessing class. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and junior standing.

title: Marketing Management
description: Marketing by manufacturers as viewed from the marketing manager's position. Principal topics are selecting channels of distribution, determining demand, pricing policies, marketing legislation, advertising policies, and methods of selling. A casestudy approach. Prerequisite: 15 semester hours in marketing, including MKG 350 and senior standing, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Professional Practice in Marketing
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program with a business firm, government agency, or nonprofit organization under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Requires periodic written reports of job experiences. Open only to secondsemester juniors and seniors with majors in marketing. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Marketing
description: Independent study in some phase of marketing that may consist of an experiment, library research, or the analysis of current marketing practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing, scholastic ratio of 3.0, and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Practicum in the Better Business Bureau
description: Provides practical experience in mediating businessconsumer problems. Students use personnel skills in organizing and administering a Better Business Bureau. Prerequisite: MKG 380. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester. Not open to the student who has credit in MKG 497.

title: Introduction to Business
description: Emphasizes the vital role of business in our society through a discussion of both the external environment of business and the internal environment of the business enterprise. Assesses the contribution of the social and behavioral sciences in the decisionmaking process. Open only to freshmen or sophomores except by permission of department chairperson.

title: International Business Decision Making —A Managerial Approach
description: Practical application of the management decisionmaking process as applied to planning, organizing, implementing, and controlling international business operations. This capstone course is designed to prepare the student for a career in international business management. Prerequisite: any one of the following courses: ECON 351, 461; FIN 452, 458; MKG 470. Urice Associate Dean, Margaret Merrion The College of Fine Arts, consisting of the Department of Art, the Department of Theatre, the School of Music, and the University Art Gallery, exists to provide unity and focus to education in the arts at Ball State University. Its mission is to promote awareness of, appreciation for, and expertise in the fine arts within its three constituencies: student body, university community, and city and surrounding region. Faculty members of the College of Fine Arts are dedicated to providing technical mastery and depth of understanding within individual disciplines as well as interdisciplinary sensitivity to the place of the arts within society. Because of the college commitment to enhancing the intellectual and cultural life of the university and the region, faculty members and students act as advocates for the arts in a variety of ways, ranging from performance and exhibition to consultation.

title: The Computer in the Fine Arts
description: An interdisciplinary approach to the philosophy, use, and limits of the computer in the visual arts, music, dance, and theatre; includes background on and implications for the computer as a functional tool in the arts. Department of Art Repp, Chairperson; Ahmad, Arndt, Chanda, Cunningham, Davis, Foster, Gee, Graham, Griner, Johnson, Lizza, Marin-Carle, Marshall, Maul, Minkler, Nelson, Preston, Skau, Spoerner, Tauser, Zack The Department of Art educates artists, designers, and teachers. In pursuing a visual arts education, students will be expected to do more than aspire to personal expression and meaning through form. Students will explore the diversity of meaning in society and attempt to clarify and explain those meanings and their differences through visual interpretation. A student's educational experience within the department helps identify the role of visual art as an instrument and a record of cultural change. The faculty members in the department are dedicated to refining students' skills as well as developing their artistic independence and emotional maturity. The emphasis of the program in the Department of Art is upon the professional bachelor of fine arts (B.F.A.) degree in the studio and design areas and the bachelor of science or bachelor of arts in art education. The philosophical commitment to a freshman core stresses all the disciplines in the department; thus, students majoring in the department must complete the freshman foundation year, which includes fundamental design, drawing, painting, and an art history survey. Thereafter, students may choose from one of the following areas of specialization: Art Education Interior/Environmental Design Art History Metals Design Ceramics Painting Drawing Photography Fibers Printmaking Graphic Design Sculpture Entrance and Program Standards Students declaring majors in art may enroll in the freshman foundation courses. After the freshman foundation year the department uses selection guidelines for specific programs. Students in the design programs must undergo portfolio reviews after the completion of the sophomore design sequence. Admission to the junior interior/environmental design sequence and junior graphic design sequence also requires successful completion of a portfolio review. All students in the department undergo periodic portfolio reviews throughout their undergraduate education. The studio areas require a senior thesis and exhibition and the design areas require an exit portfolio evaluation. Transfer students from other universities are required to submit portfolios and transcripts for evaluation. Transfer students should be aware that design programs involve a threeyear sequence beyond the freshman foundations, and it is unusual for a student to be admitted at any point other than at the beginning of the sequence.
