title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduction to human social life as an object of scientific study and to the nature and origins of culture, showing the biological foundations of man's social interaction. Emphasis on such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, the family kinship systems, social control, aesthetics, and religion.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: The origin of man and the rise of civilization as revealed by the discovery of the antiquities of the past. Explanation of recent chronometric and established classical dating methods; methods of excavating sites; interpretation of archaeological remains.

title: Introduction to Physical Anthropology
description: Man's place in nature and the relationship of man to other animals, especially monkeys and apes. Anatomy and behavior and their interdependency are presented within an evolutionary framework.

title: Cultures, Languages, and Races of the World
description: An anthropological survey of the peoples of the world and their cultures. Focuses on major social institutions, such as Anthropology 163 economics, religion, the family, and government, presented in terms of major culture and geographic areas. Discusses linguistic and racial features of cultures.

title: Races of Man
description: The present status and a historical survey of the concept of race as it applies to human populations. Ways in which human populations differ biologically and the adaptive nature of such variation. The distribution and antiquity of living races. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, 103, or 105.

title: Race, Racism, and Ethnicity
description: Scientific investigation of the biological nature of race, race beliefs, and racism, an extreme expression of ethnic bias. Devotes particular attention to the Western world, but also considers similar attitudes in other parts of the world.

title: Introduction to Folklore
description: An introduction to the genres of folklore with an emphasis on the anthropological study of folktales, legends, and myths; methodological and theoretical approaches to their study; their function in society; and their usefulness to anthropologists.

title: Black Africa's Contribution to Western Civilization
description: The African cultural and historical roots of the American black. The origins of the human race, plant and animal domestication, metallurgy, art, and state formation; focus is on West Africa, the source of most of the black population of the United States.

title: History of Method and Theory in Anthropology
description: Survey of the major ideas and issues of anthropology. Methods and theories from archaeology, physical anthropology, linguistics, and cultural anthropology.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Acquaints the prospective teacher with basic concepts in cultural anthropology and discusses the conceptual and analytical tools used to understand various cultural settings. Examines ways in which cultural institutions—e.g., family, religion, politics, economy—might impinge on educational processes.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: The archaeological development of the Mediterranean and European areas from the Paleolithic era to the historic period.

title: Bio- Cultural Evolutionary Theory
description: The place of evolutionary theory in anthropology. Process of and relationship between biological and cultural evolution.

title: North American Indians
description: Culture areas of pre-Columbian North America. Describes each culture in terms of its major social and economic institutions.

title: Human Evolution
description: The emergence of man from his nonhuman primate ancestors. The primate fossil record, with particular emphasis on those forms in the human lineage, and the human fossil record. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 304, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Topics in Old World Prehistory
description: The prehistory of various Old World regions and time periods. Topics will vary from semester to semester: Europe, the paleolithic, general survey. May be repeated for different topics.

title: Topics in New World Archaeology
description: The prehistory of the New World from the time of its populating to European exploration. Topics will vary from semester to semester: the Midwest, Meso-America, the Southwest, etc. May be repeated for different topics.

title: Special Topics in Native American Cultures
description: A detailed analysis of contemporary issues facing the American Indian or a focus on the Indian cultures of a particular area, such as the Southwest, the Great Lakes, etc. May be repeated for different topics.

title: Anthropology—Culture and Women
description: The structure of women's role in various types of societies, from hunting and gathering to urban communities. Examines the relationship of the women's liberation movement in Western cultures to the changing role of women in the industrialized labor forces.

title: Laboratory Methods in Archaeology
description: Laboratory analysis of archaeological materials. Cataloging, restoring, describing, photographing, typing, and mode plotting. Use of archaeological literature for comparison and distribution studies.

title: Special Topics in Anthropology
description: Detailed analysis of a special problem in cultural anthropology, archaeology, or physical anthropology. May be repeated for different topics.

title: Culture Areas of the World
description: An anthropological survey of the culture patterns of a selected continent or region. Examples are Latin America, India, China, and Africa. May be repeated for different areas.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis on individual study and development of results. Open to Honors College students only by permission of department chairperson.

title: History and Philosophy of Archaeological Theory
description: Examination of the theoretical trends in archaeology. Survey of the areas of taxonomic, spatiotemporal, and cultural archaeology. Comparison of the tenets of historical or traditional and processual or "new" archaeology.

title: Medical Anthropology
description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating non-Western techniques to Western counterparts. Studies theories of disease causation, cultural taxonomy of therapeutic techniques and cure, and analysis of the role of the medical specialists (practitioners) in selected societies. Assesses Western and non-Western traditional and modern medicine in terms of cultural evolutionary theory.

title: Primatology
description: A survey of nonhuman primates, with particular emphasis on behavioral patterns of groups in their natural settings. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Human Osteology
description: A laboratory course dealing with the human skeleton. Osteological terminology, identification of whole and fragmentary bones, standardized measuring techniques, and the assessment of the age, stature, sex, and race of a skeleton. Prerequisite: ANTH 105.

title: Historical Archaeology
description: Covers the major themes and philosophies of historical archaeology as well as the related literature and sources of information on architectural features and items of material culture likely to be encountered in the course of excavation.

title: Archaeological Resources Management
description: The special problems of what has also been called conservation archaeology, including relevant federal and state laws, regulations, and agencies, reconnaissance and sampling methods; project budgeting; elements in the environmental impact statement; and other responsibilities of the consultant archaeologist. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: The Development of Near -Eastern Cultures
description: Traces the development of cultures in the Near East as revealed by archaeology and explores the presentday cultural variability.

title: Anthropological Field Studies
description: Methods of carrying out field research in ethnography, archaeology, and physical anthropology. Stresses problem formulation, field observation, data recording, interpretation, and data preparation. Taught at field location. Topics and areas will vary. May be repeated for different topics. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Witchcraft, Magic, and Religion
description: An anthropological study of mankind's ageold concern with life, death, sickness, and the unknown. Discusses man's attempts to control his life through supernatural beings, prayer, sacrifice, and techniques of magic and witchcraft. Examines possible origins of religious beliefs and how these are part of the fabric of social life in primitive and contemporary societies.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland Southeast Asia. Specific emphasis on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory with particular application to the effect of contacts of traditional ethnographic groups in the American continents and European civilization.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to a formal) view of economic behavior. Focuses on such social organizational units as lineages and clans that in primitive and peasant societies are engaged in productive and distributive activities.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor with competence in the area involved. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar in Anthroplogy
description: Designed to make students familiar with current theoretical and methodological issues in anthropology. Demands active participation in the discussion of those issues. Provides a setting for students to explore their own theoretical interests and present them coherently. MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY This program leads to a bachelor of science degree with a major in medical technology. The medical technologist is prepared for such laboratory work as bacteriology, chemistry, serology, and blood bank technology in hospital laboratories, physicians' and surgeons' clinics, and federal, state, and municipal health laboratories as well as research laboratories and commercial companies making biological products. The departmental major in medical technology along with the general studies requirements and elective courses, all of which must total at least 94 semester hours, are to be completed in the first three years. The fourth, or senior, year consists of a twelvemonth clinical laboratory program in an accredited hospital school of medical technology. Thirtytwo semester hours are granted for the successful completion of this year. The minimum total for the degree is 126 semester hours. Selection of students to a school of medical technology is made entirely by the school where the student applies and is based on such considerations as scholastic standing, personal interviews, and recommendations. Completion of the first three years does not guarantee admission to the clinical year; students are therefore advised to plan an alternative program that may be completed in the fourth year. Reapplication for a clinical year may then be made if the student wishes. The university has established affiliations for preparation of medical technologists with the following Indiana hospitals: Ball Memorial Hospital in Muncie; St. Joseph's Memorial Hospital in Kokomo; St. Francis Hospital in Beech Grove; Parkview Hospital and Lutheran Hospital in Fort Wayne; Methodist Hospital and St. Vincent's Hospital in Indianapolis; and St. Mary Medical Center in Gary. Strongly recommended electives are CS 116 and PHYSL 211. Other recommended electives are BIO 460; MGS 200; and PHYCS 110, 112. Departmental major in medical technology, 45 hours ANAT 201; BIO 111, 213, 341, 344; CHEM 111, 112, 225, 231, 325, 360; PHYSL 210; ZOOL 447 45 hrs. PREFORESTRY PROGRAM The preforestry program is designed for students who wish to major in forestry and prefer to satisfy the preprofessional requirements at Ball State University. Upon completion of the preforestry curriculum application may be made for admission to the professional forestry program at Purdue University, which is the only state university in Indiana with a curriculum leading to a baccalaureate degree in forestry. Admission to the professional program at Purdue is not guaranteed. Students at Purdue enrolled in the preforestry program in the Department of Forestry and Natural Resources apply to the professional program at the end of their sophomore year. Preforestry students at Ball State may also apply during their sophomore year for admission when they have completed 68 semester hours. Applications for admission into the twoyear professional program at Purdue should be filed before December 1 for consideration for admission the next fall. Before enrolling at Ball State, students should consult with the preforestry program adviser or the chairperson of the Department of Biology. Preforestry program, 62 hours BIO 111, 112, 216, 448; BOT 380, 470; CHEM 111, 112; CS 118; ECON 202; EN G 103, 104; LA 217; MATHS 108, 115, 117, 171; SPCH 210 62 hrs. Additional electives in such subjects as English, foreign languages, history, philosophy, and political science. PREMEDICAL PREPARATION Although most students entering medical school will have completed four years of premedical work, those with outstanding qualifications may be admitted after only three years. To qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine at the close of three years of premedical preparation, students will complete the major and specific courses and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 94 semester hours at Ball State University and will use the credits earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Medicine (32 semester hours) to meet senioryear course requirements for the baccalaureate degree. The student who wishes to earn a degree and prepare for teaching in secondary schools as well as apply for admission to the Indiana University School of Medicine will choose a teaching area major or teaching major and combine with it the departmental major in premedical preparation. The following courses are recommended for elective credit in the first three years: mathematics; CHEM 360 or 463; BIO 214, 215, 492; CC 103; and ZOOL 347. Except when required to complete an undergraduate major, courses in human anatomy, human physiology, medical bacteriology, medical biochemistry, or medical pharmacology will not be accepted by the School of Medicine as part of the 94 hours of liberal arts credit. Students should take the Medical College Admission Test in the spring semester fifteen months before their expected entrance into medical school and should complete the formal application during the following summer, twelve months in advance. Departmental major in premedical preparation, 40-42 hours BIO 111, 112; CHEM 111, 112, 225; CHEM (231, 232) or (234, 235); PHYCS 110, 112; ZOOL 330 40-42 hrs. PREDENTAL PREPARATION Although most students entering dental school will have completed four years of predental work, those with outstanding qualifications may be admitted after only three years. To qualify for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry at the close of three years of predental preparation, students will complete the major and specific course and scholastic requirements of the curriculum with a minimum of 94 semester hours at Ball State University and will use the credit earned in the first year in the Indiana University School of Dentistry (32 semester hours) to meet the senioryear course requirements for the baccalaureate degree. In addition to the basic science requirements, students entering the Indiana University School of Dentistry will be required to have credit in two semesters of English, including one semester of composition; one semester of interpersonal communication (SPCH 240 is recommended); one semester of introductory psychology; and one semester of business management or personnel management (MGS 300 is recommended). The following courses are recommended for elective credit: AED 100; ANAT 430; BIO 213, 215; CHEM 232, 360; CC One of the requirements for admission to the Indiana University School of Dentistry is a satisfactory performance on the Dental Admission Test given by the American Dental Association. It is the student's responsibility to make application to the dental school and to make arrangements for taking the admission test. The test should be taken in the spring semester fifteen months before the student's expected entrance into dental school, but preferably only after completing the required biology and chemistry courses. Application for admission to dental school should be completed in the summer, twelve months in advance. Predental counseling is available in the Department of Biology. Departmental major in predental preparation, 37 hours BIO 111, 112, 214; CHEM 111, 112, 231; PHYCS 110, 112; ZOOL 330 37 hrs. PREPHARMACY PROGRAM The prepharmacy program is for students who wish to apply for admission to the Butler University College of Pharmacy or the Purdue University School of Pharmacy. The courses designated, when completed satisfactorily, will meet the preprofessional curricular requirements of Purdue at the end of the first year or those requirements of Butler at the end of either the first or second year. At both Purdue and Butler the combined prepharmacypharmacy program requires five years. Students are advised, however, that the number of applicants to any college of pharmacy exceeds the capacity of the school and that a selection of students is therefore necessary, taking into consideration such qualifications as scholastic standing, character, and professional aptitude. Students should become familiar with the admission and residence requirements set forth in the bulletins of Butler and Purdue universities. These prepharmacy programs do not lead to graduation from Ball State University. They merely provide a student with an approved sequence of courses for the first one or two years of the complete fiveyear program. Furthermore, physical education is not a part of this program for students who plan to transfer to Purdue, but it is for those who will go to Butler. Students who drop out of the prepharmacy program and elect to follow degree programs of Ball State University will be expected to meet the physical education and other degree requirements. Careful arrangement of the program for each year is essential so that courses may be completed in sequence and in the allotted time. It is particularly important that general chemistry be completed in the freshman year. Mathematics, including calculus, is highly desirable. Copies of the programs may be obtained from the chairperson of the biology department. There are minor differences in requirements between the School of Pharmacy at Purdue and the College of Pharmacy at Butler.

title: Man and the Life Sciences
description: Introductory course designed for students not majoring in science. Emphasizes human and social aspects of biology: reproduction, birth control, genetic counseling, behavior, evolution, pollution, radiation and energy. Not open to the student who has credit in BIO 102, 111, or 112.

title: Biological Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles of biology as they relate to energy requirements and reproductive processes of living organisms, including the study of plants and conservation with emphasis on the human role in the environment. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Principles of Biology 1
description: Designed for biology, allied health, and other science majors. Emphasis at cellular level: chemical and physical organization of life; prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell structure and function; bioenergetics; cell division; genetics, gene expression, protein synthesis, and evolution. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry, one semester of college chemistry or equivalent.

title: Principles of Biology 2
description: Emphasis at organism, population, and community levels: major plant and animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification, and phylogenetic relationships; ecology, including human ecology and environmental biology. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 111 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Microbiology for the Health Sciences
description: Introductory course for students in applied health curricula. Presents biomolecules of life, enzyme interaction, physiology and structure of representative microorganisms. Emphasis on bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa of health significance and the hostparasite relationship. Microbiological techniques emphasized in laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 101 or equivalent.

title: Honors Symposium in Biology
description: A general studies science course. Focus is on developing genetic awareness to enable students to apply personal knowledge toward the solution of some critical biological issues confronting contemporary society. Open only to freshmen participating in the Honors Program except by permission of department chairperson or the director of Honors Program.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and fungi. Emphasis placed on morphology, physiology, genetics, and control. Some consideration of applied aspects of microbiology. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 111.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation emphasizing meiosis, Mendelian inheritance and probability considerations, sex and gene transmission arid expression, linkage and crossingover, the nature of the hereditary material, gene action and genetic control of development. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 .

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including cell differentiation and growth, the nature of the organization of the cell, basic bioenergetics and enzyme function, cell environment, membrane structure and function, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; CHEM 231 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Ecology
description: The relationships of organisms to physical, chemical, and biotic factors. Interactions are examined at the population, community, aid biome levels of organization. Aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems are considered in terms of species composition, dominant organisms, climatic factors, and use patterns. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112.

title: Pathogenic Bacteriology
description: Study of pathogenic bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques in culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisite: BIO 213, CHEM 130 or 231.

title: Laboratory Techniques in Biological Research
description: Principles and applications of procedures used in biological research. Emphasis on methods of preparation of solutions, using standard curves, determination of rates of enzyme reactions, separation and identification of cell organelles, identification of cell metabolites, and separation of macromolecules. Prerequisite: BIO 112 and permission of department chairperson.

title: Immunology-Virology
description: Examination of the basic principles of immunology and virology. Topics include the immune system, the variety of immune responses, immunoregulation, and characteristics of viruses. Emphasis will be placed on virushost interactions and serological diagnosis of viral infections. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and one course in organic chemistry.

title: Honors Colloquium in Biology
description: Exploration of selected issues in biology with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students except by permission of department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Biology
description: Practical application of biology in a variety of situations including biology instruction as undergraduate teaching assistants and discussion leaders, and practical experience in government or industrial laboratories and field stations. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned in this course.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Stresses recent discoveries in biology and integrates and enhances understanding of basic principles of the discipline. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Biophysics
description: The study of biologic phenomena in terms of contributing physical events. Transport processes. Absorption and emission radiation. Ionizing radiation; its effects on living tissue; use of isotopes in research projects. Prerequisite: BIO 215.

title: Evolution
description: Principles, evidence, and the historical context of modern evolution theory. Some attention given to the origin of life and the evolution of plants and animals. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Applied Microbiology
description: The study of microorganisms that are beneficial or detrimental to changes in foods (including milk and milk products) and industrial fermentations. This is a lecture/lab course. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Biometry
description: Principles and application of statistics to biological problems. The use of parametric and nonparametric tests of significance in the analysis of data and the interpretation of experiments. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advanced Genetics
description: Course in bacterial and eukaryotic genetics with emphasis on recent developments in molecular genetics. Topics include alternative structures of DNA, mechanisms of DNA replication, mutagenesis, DNA rearrangements, regulation of gene expression, RNA processing, molecular and mutagenetic analysis of cell cycle. Prerequisite: BIO 214, CHEM 231. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 215.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Mankind
description: Current problems in human heredity. Human chromosome aberrations. DNA, the genetic code, and mutations. Consanguineous marriages and genetic defects. Mendelian principles applied to humans. Pedigrees and probability. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems and advances in genetics.

title: Molecular Biology
description: Structure and function of macromolecules in living things. Emphasizes threedimensional structures; models for enzyme mechanisms; DNA replication; protein synthesis and membrane function; and applications of biotechnology. Prerequisite: BIO 215 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advanced Cellular and Molecular Biology
description: Study of recent developments in cell growth and differentiation, DNA and RNA research, membrane biology, cellular and molecular evolution, and cellular control mechanisms. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Bioenergetics
description: The study of flow of energy in biological systems with emphasis on application of laws of thermodynamics to biological processes, energy production metabolism in chemotrophs and phototrophs, and the major uses of energy in biological systems. Prerequisite: BIO 215, its equivalent, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Microtechniques
description: A lecture/lab course in the preparation of biological material for microscopic examination in teaching, research, and clinical applications. Emphasis on preparation of smears, squashes, whole mounts, paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112, 213 and one course of college chemistry.

title: Limnology
description: The physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of inland waters. Laboratory and several field trips will be devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Microbiology
description: Microorganisms indigenous to nonpolluted and polluted aquatic ecosystems. Emphasis on nutrient cycling and use of microorganisms as indicators of pollution. Morphology, physiology, and ecology of specific organisms. Lecture/laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Marine Biology
description: Introduction to marine environments. Properties of seawater, hydrodynamics. Phytoplankton and benthic plants. Primary production, nutrient cycles. Marine animals, surveys of major taxa. Adaptations for life on the bottom, open water, intertidal zones, estuaries, abyssal regions.

title: Bioethical Decision Making
description: Development of decisionmaking skills through the analysis and personal resolution of bioethical problems created by the application of new biological and biomedical knowledge and technologies. Prerequisite: completion of general studies science component.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Forestry
description: A survey course in forestry with emphasis on management, problems, and use of midwestern wood lots. May include field work in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Plant Anatomy and Morphology
description: Forms, life cycles, and evolution of the major plant groups with emphasis on the origin and structure of cells, tissues, and organs in higher plants. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Taxonomy of Vascular Plants
description: Identification, use, and care of native and ornamental trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plant material. The use of botanical keys, manuals, and texts in the identification of the plant taxa. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Economic Botany
description: The cultivation, processing, environmental requirements, and use of plants and plant derivatives for food, drugs, dwellings, clothing, and power.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the different methods of plant propagation, care, and cultivation for use in the home, school, garden, and greenhouse. Also, some emphasis on diseases, pathogens, and pests of the plant.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on pathogenic forms. Discusses methods for identification of fungi along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BIO 112 and CHEM 231.

title: Dendrology
description: The identification and site characterization of woody plants with an emphasis on midwestern tree species. Use of botanical features and keys in field identification. Correlation of species with site factors, plant diseases, climatic parameters, associate species, and geographical distribution. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection and identification of nonvascular and vascular plants from fresh water ecosystems. Emphasizes the morphology, physiology, and ecology of these plants to explain their distribution in nature. Class project and field trips may be used to demonstrate ecological relationships. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Structure and Development of Vertebrates
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and evolutionary relationships of vertebrates. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth, protozoan, and arthropod parasites of animals and man. Emphasizes identification, life cycles, hostparasite relationships and physiology of common species. Some emphasis on medical and clinical aspects of parasites in man, and tropical forms. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Comparative morphology, physiology, ecology, life histories, and phylogeny of invertebrate animal phyla. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Ornithology
description: The study of birds including identification, systematics, anatomy, physiology, life histories, ecological relationships, and conservation. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Ichthyology
description: The study of fish with emphasis on identification, classification, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Emphasizes Indiana species but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The economic relationships of mammals. The collection and preservation of specimens. May require additional field work. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on those of the United States. The harvest and management of wildlife. May require additional field work. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identification, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasis on aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress. Prerequisite: ZOOL 441 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals. Open only to students with majors in elementary education.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. Open only to students with a major in elementary education.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary School
description: Methods of teaching science concepts, process skills, and scientific attitudes are developed through direct experiences. Recent elementary science texts, courses of study, and curricular materials are examined and used as are experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and special methods. Prerequisite: 8 hours of science courses or permission of department chairperson.

title: Teaching of Science in the Junior High School
description: Recent curriculum developments in junior high school science. Science curriculum instruction related to the physical, mental, and emotional characteristics of the junior high school student. Experiences in public schools may be required. Prerequisite: 24 hours of science courses or permission of department chairperson.

title: Teaching Science in the Early Childhood and Primary Grades
description: Analysis of the cognitive, psychomotor, and affective processes inherent in science investigations for young children. Handson activities with science materials appropriate for early childhood and primary children. Designed primarily for students in early childhood/primary education programs. Prerequisite: 8 hours of science or permission of department chairperson.

title: Teaching of Science in the Secondary School
description: Philosophy and methods in science teaching. Emphasis on laboratory investigations, concepts and conceptual schemes, scienceoriented classroom management, evaluation of instructional activities, supplies, equipment, facilities, curriculum materials. Experiences in public schools may be required. Prerequisite: 13 hours in biology, chemistry, earth science, or physics content courses or permission of department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280. title: Man and Chemistry
description: Introductory treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as organization and language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature and classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these to everyday living. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 101, 111.

title: General, Organic, and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of general chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences and related areas. Four hours of lecture and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 111. 111.General Chemistry 1. (4) Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, properties of solutions, and nature of matter. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitation/ laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or equivalent.

title: General Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemical kinetics, electrochemistry, chemical equilibrium, chemistry of metals and nonmetals, and radioactivity. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitation/laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 111, MATHS 108.

title: Survey of Organic and Biochemistry
description: A broadly based introductory course suitable for life science, natural resources, and general science majors. Three hours of lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Lecture and intensive laboratory treatment of the theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements, including gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations, ion exchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visible spectrophotometry. One and onehalf hours of lecture and four and onehalf hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: Nomenclature, structure, bonding, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory Chemistry 175 period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of natural products and biomolecules. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 235.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material includes nomenclature, covalent bonding, molecular structure, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Laboratory experience includes spectroscopy and syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: A continuation of CHEM 234, including the properties of carbohydrates, proteins, and other natural products. Laboratory experience includes qualitative organic analysis and multistep syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 234.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentation: electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods. For chemical/ medical technologists or departmental minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: Thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232, MATHS 172, one year of college physics.

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 344, including theoretical aspects of quantum mechanics and spectroscopy. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 344.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics. Especially for premedical, biology, and general science majors, chemistry teaching majors, and chemistry minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitation/laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225, MATHS 161. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 344.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry
description: Organic chemistry of carboxylic acids, amines, and their derivatives; biochemistry of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids; metabolism and the regulation of metabolic processes. For students in life sciences, dietetics, and medical technology. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory session weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or equivalent. Not open to departmental majors in chemistry.

title: Specialized Topics in Chemistry
description: Discussion, experimentation, or both in specialized topics in and related to chemistry. Information concerning specific topics offered during a given semester may be obtained from the departmental office. Lecture, discussion, and laboratory schedules appropriate to the topic offered. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 hour may be counted toward departmental major or minor requirements.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for chemical technologists. Assignments equivalent to four clock hours a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of department chairperson. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry.

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Prerequisite: 20 hours of chemistry or permission of department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 1
description: Theoretical principles and application of selected spectroscopic and nuclear methods, with illustrative experiments. Two hours of lecture and one threehour lab period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 345 or 346 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 2
description: Theoretical principles and application of selected chromatographic, electroanalytical, and mass spectroscopic methods. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 420 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Qualitative Organic Analysis
description: Laboratory intensive study of the theory and practice of structure determination of organic compounds by classical and spectroscopic methods, including separations and identification of components in mixtures. Six hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232.

title: Physical -Organic Chemistry
description: Theoretical aspects of structure, including resonance and molecular orbital descriptions of electron distribution, aromaticity, symmetry, stereochemistry, and effects of structure on reactivity in acidbase reactions. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements, including the relationships of chemical properties and atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, acidbase theories, chemical periodicity, and modern theories of coordination compounds. Four hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235, MATHS 161 or 171.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 1
description: Chemistry and techniques for isolation, purification, and identification of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. For students majoring in chemistry, life sciences, and premedicine. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitation/laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 463 including biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids; and regulation of metabolic processes. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 463.

title: Independent Study and Research
description: Scientific investigation on an individual basis under the supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, experimental work, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward any departmental major. The technological development of computers, together with decreased costs that have made them available to every sector of the economy, has resulted in a demand for persons knowledgeable in every aspect of computer science. To meet the increasing demands for specialists in a computeroriented society, Ball State University offers a departmental major and minor in computer science. Students may enter this program after the completion of two semesters (minimum 30 semester hours) in which they have earned minimum cumulative gradepoint averages of 3.0 in the required computer science and mathematics courses and at least 2.5 in all courses. The cooperative director in the Department of Computer Science advises students in this program and assists in the work placement of each student. The university cannot guarantee work assignments for all students. Additional information about the cooperative program may be obtained from the Department of Computer Science. title: Coop Orientation
description: Seminar for students entering the coop program in computer science. Topics include responsibilities of the coop student and the employer, résumé preparation, job interview training, types of job placement available, general coop program administration and requirements. May be taken for credit/nocredit only. Prerequisite: major in computer science in progress and permission of department chairperson. Open only to computer science majors.

title: Introduction to Programming 1
description: Problems of programming in a structured language emphasizing topdown design and modular structure. Designed primarily for students in the computer endorsement program. Prerequisite: MATHS 125, 201, or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 120 or equivalent.

title: Introduction to Programming 2
description: An introduction to files and their applications. An introduction to a LOGO environment. Prerequisite: CS 110 or equivalent. Open only to noncomputer science majors.

title: Computer Literacy for Non -Programmers
description: Presents the computer as a tool for students majoring in other disciplines to solve problems arising in their subjects. The student will use such software as spreadsheets, databases, and word processing, and will develop vocabulary. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 121.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines other than computer science. Timesharing computer techniques using BASIC with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 118, 120, 121, 210, or MGS 210.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Programming in FORTRAN. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Introduces timesharing techniques. Prerequisite: MATHS 117. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 120.

title: Computer Programming 1
description: Introductory programming in PASCAL in a timesharing environment. Covers topics such as concepts of computers and programming, data types, statements, expressions, input and output of data, basic control structures, procedures and functions, arrays, files, and editing. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161.

title: Computer Programming 2
description: Advanced programming in PASCAL. Includes such topics as Boolean variables, files, linked lists, pointer variables, stacks, hashing, recursion, and binary searching. Prerequisite: CS 120 and MATHS 161.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize application in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: CS 120 or 116 or 118 or MGS 210. Not open to the student who has credit in MGS 213 or CS 240.

title: Discrete Structures
description: Introduction to topics in discrete structures that are needed by computer science majors. Topics will emphasize applications of structures to a computer environment. Sample topics: array manipulation, Karnaugh maps, finite state machines, analysis as applied to software development. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Introduction to Computer Systems
description: Introduction to computer architecture, IBM JCL, machine and assembly languages. Includes fixedpoint, floatingpoint, and decimal arithmetic, character and bit manipulation, looping, branching, macros, and subroutines. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Use of COBOL to solve problems in file maintenance, report writing, and sorting. Emphasizes directaccess processing techniques including development of interactive screens. Further study of IBM JCL. Prerequisite: CS 121, 230.

title: Combinatorial Algorithms
description: A study of the analysis, design, and complexity of combinatorial algorithms with applications to computer and information science. Course assignments include the implementation of various algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 121, 224, and MATHS 212.

title: Data Structures
description: Data structures including stacks, queues, trees, tables, lists, strings, arrays, and files. Studies implementation techniques and algorithms for the management of these structures. Prerequisite: CS 121, 224, 230.

title: Computer Hardware Systems
description: Introduction to computer logic and registertransfer level of systems description. Examines the basic building blocks of a computer system and studies various computer architectures and hardware trends. Develops a general methodology for computer selection and introduces microprogramming. Prerequisite: CS 224, 230 and MATHS 212.

title: Programming Language Seminar
description: Indepth study of a computer language taught in a seminar format. Advanced postings of topics(s) will be made in the department before registration. Six hours of elective credit may be earned in this course by computer science majors. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester. Open only to computer science majors.

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation. Use of higher level languages and simulation languages in system studies. Students use examples from different subjects to carry out simulation. Prerequisite: CS 121 and MATHS 181 or equivalent.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analyses, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 118 or 121 and MATHS 162. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and CS 362 or MATHS 362. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 363.

title: Professional Experience
description: Professional computing experience in an approved program with computing facilities in business and industry. Requires periodic reports. Credit/nocredit only. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 15 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester. Open only to computer science majors.

title: Systems Programming
description: Considers the computer system from the points of view of its architecture, operating system, and applications. Topics include processor organization, peripheral devices, I/O programming, system programs, monitor services, file organization, and realtime applications. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Programming Languages
description: A comparative study of programming languages. Emphasizes syntactic specification of programming languages and important features, structures, and compile and runtime characteristics of various higher level languages. Prerequisite: CS 230, 332.

title: Database Design
description: An introduction to database design, including physical representation, modeling, database systems, and implementation. Prerequisite: CS 332 and knowledge of C or COBOL or FORTRAN.

title: An Introduction to the Design of Computer Graphics Systems
description: An introduction to various graphics hardware devices and software packages for both mainframe and microcomputers. Requires students to develop and execute graphics programs. Includes some twodimensional graphics algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 332 and MATHS 212.

title: Operating Systems
description: The functions and structure of computer operating systems, processors, memory, and device management. Concurrency and process synchronization. Input/ output handling, device drivers, and disk scheduling. File systems, operating system design philosophy. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Software Engineering 1-Systems Analysis
description: Software life cycle, software engineering concepts, systems analysis phase of life cycle. Introduces and applies structured methods to a project. The output of the project is a systems specification from which a software system can be designed and developed. Prerequisite: CS 332, 333.

title: Software Engineering 2-Design and Development
description: Studies the design and development phases of the software life cycle. Introduces the latest appropriate structured methods and applies them to a software project. This project will take a system specification and develop software from it. Prerequisite: CS 240, 497.

Criminal Justice and Criminology 179 Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology Brodt, Chairperson; Daane, Farrell, Hendricks, Hewitt, Hickey, Koch, Smith The Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology offers a broad range of courses relevant to our system of adult and juvenile justice for both the preprofessional and the liberal arts student. The departmental major leads to a baccalaureate degree. The department also offers a twoyear associate in arts degree and a departmental minor. The student gains a perspective about such subjects as crime and delinquency, their prevention and control, and our system of criminal justice. The department presents a combination of theory and practical experience in law enforcement and corrections and offers students the opportunity to prepare themselves as preprofessionals for firstlevel positions in law enforcement, probation, parole, and institutional or community treatment settings, or for future graduate study in related areas. The criminal justice system in our society covers five main areas of study and employment: law enforcement, probation services offered by both adult and juvenile courts, correctional institutions and programs, parole supervision for both adult and juvenile offenders, and community rehabilitative agencies and organizations. Law enforcement officers are needed at three levels of government: local, state, and federal. Local law enforcement officers include municipal policemen and policewomen as well as deputy sheriffs. On the state level, all states hire officer candidates for state police departments. On the federal level, approximately forty agencies employ persons with training in law enforcement as well as in other areas of specialization. Probation, which is essentially supervision of adjudicated adult criminals and juvenile delinquents, is a service offered by almost all our adult felony and juvenile courts. Probation officers are employees of the court and as such are involved in persontoperson contact with a variety of offenders. The federal government and all states maintain a variety of correctional institutions and programs for adult and juvenile offenders of both sexes. These range from open institutions with a minimum of security to maximum security institutions for adult male offenders. In addition, such facilities as youth camps, diagnostic and reception centers, and work release centers are incorporated into most state systems. Both men and women may work as custodial officers, caseworkers, or counselors within the various settings. Parole supervision is generally a function of a state administration agency, such as a parole board or a division of parole, and may vary from state to state. Parole is essentially the supervision of offenders once they have been released from a state institution or facility. Parole officers aid offenders in their return to civilian life in a variety of ways ranging from helping with employment and living arrangements to providing counseling for personal problems that may affect a parolee's successful adjustment. Field Experience A semester internship is required for all criminal justice and criminology majors; it may be taken during the fall, spring, or summer semester, and enrollment is generally limited to seniors. The program is supervised by agency personnel and a member of the department faculty and offers practical experience. Students may choose an internship in corrections or law enforcement, depending upon their interests and goals. title: Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
description: An overview of the criminal justice system and a summary of vocational opportunities.

title: Data and Theories of Crime and Delinquency
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior, typologies of crime and criminals; the trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and current theoretical explanations.

title: Processing Adult and Juvenile Offenders
description: Emphasizes the juvenile and adult justice systems, their components, recent changes, and anticipated future developments.

title: Policing in. American Society
description: Examination and analysis of the development of the police in America in the past, present, and future. Emphasizes institutional context of police activity, bureaucratization of the police, professionalization, the role of the police, and the police and community change.

title: Women and Crime
description: An examination of traditional and contemporary explanations of female delinquency and criminality, the differential treatment accorded female defendants and victims, and the nature of state and federal correctional systems for women.

title: Organized Crime
description: The nature and structure of organized crime in America with special emphasis on the history and changing images of organized crime, its operation and activities, and programs for control.

title: Victimology
description: A criminological examination of the victims of crime in contemporary America.

title: Criminal. Law
description: Emphasis on the practical aspect of the application of Indiana criminal law for present and prospective criminal justice practitioners: purposes and functions of the substantive criminal law; historical foundations; the limits of the criminal law. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 340 or 350.

title: Criminal Evidence and Investigation
description: Legal, ethical, and theoretical issues surrounding policies, procedures, and standards of criminal evidence and investigation.

title: Institutional Corrections
description: An indepth inquiry into the function, structure, and operations of American adult and juvenile correctional institutions.

title: Community Corrections
description: The organization and operation of communitybased correctional programs throughout the United States. Topics include probation, parole, halfway houses, group homes, diversion, restitution, and community service programs, with an emphasis on the most popular programs and practices.

title: Honors Colloquium in Criminal Justice
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in criminal justice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Open only to honors students; others by permission of department chairperson.

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in criminal justice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Topics may include crisis intervention, historical criminology, white collar crime, and others of current interest. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in one semester.

title: Practicum in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Part - time individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of department chairperson.

title: Internship in Criminal Justice and Criminology

In each of these areas the department has definite responsibilities not only to its own majors and minors but also to other students. Literature provides a perspective gained only through intimacy with the thoughts and feelings of writers of all times and all cultures. To help students gain this perspective, the department offers a wide variety of courses in American, British, and world literature. There are at least two good reasons for becoming better acquainted with how one's own language works. One is that a knowledge of various patterns of language should contribute to facility in writing and speaking. Equally important is the fact that the history and structure of our language are important parts of our cultural heritage. Realizing the increasing necessity for successful college graduates to express themselves clearly in writing, the Department of English requires all students to develop skill in expository writing. This is a primary purpose of both general education classes and the classes in advanced composition. For students interested in creative writing, special courses are provided on both the undergraduate and graduate levels. These students are also encouraged to contribute to the department's literary magazine, Riverbend, and to compete for annual awards made possible through the Rocking Horse competition and Lambda Iota Tau, the English honorary fraternity.
