description: Note taking, impromptu writing in English as a foreign language, preparing for tests, and using library resources. Prerequisite: ENEFL 133 and 135 or permission of program director.

title: Writing 4
description: Paragraph and essay writing. Practice in rhetorical modes of American English. Prerequisite: ENEFL 141 or permission of program director.

title: Grammar 4
description: Focus on individual grammatical problems with grammatical variants and rhetorical devices. General grammar review. Prerequisite: ENEFL 142 or permission of program director.

title: Reading 4
description: Reading in unadapted selections from general and technical literature and current publications. Prerequisite: ENEFL 143 or permission of program director.

title: Cross- Cultural Studies 2
description: Topics include U.S. and international politics, civil and human rights, individual freedom and responsibility, and academic and cultural issues. Prerequisite: ENEFL 147 or permission of program director.

title: Study Skills for Foreign Students 2
description: Indepth library research methods and research paper writing. Advanced study techniques. Prerequisite: ENEFL 148 or permission of program director.

title: TOUT Preparation
description: Review of English grammar and vocabulary with special practice in aural and written comprehension to prepare for the Test of English as a Foreign Language. Prerequisite: permission of program director.

title: Fundamentals of English Composition
description: Focuses on the fundamentals of composition with special attention to the problems of grammar and mechanics. Required of all students with an SAT (V) score of 360 or lower or a TSWE score of 36 or lower. The course is offered on a credit/no credit basis and credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements.

title: English Composition 1
description: Introduction to composition with an emphasis on writing short essays. Includes assigned readings. Specific competencies are measured by the English department at the beginning and end of the semester. Prerequisite: SAT (V) above 360, TSWE above 36, ACT English score above 15, ENG 099, or placement according to a test administered by the Department of English.

title: English Composition 2
description: Further instruction in composition with an emphasis on writing longer essays. Includes assigned readings. Introduction to basic research methods. Specific competencies are identified at the beginning of the semester and measured at the end of the semester. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Honors English Composition 2
description: Instruction in composition with emphasis on writing essays. Assigned readings. Introduction to basic research methods. Specific competencies will be identified at the beginning of the semester and measured at the end of the semester. Prerequisite: SAT Verbal score of 530 or above. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 104.

title: Honors Humanities 1: Western Thought from Homer to Dante
description: Some major texts in the literature, philosophy, history, and general thought of the Greek, Roman, and Christian civilizations through the Middle Ages.

title: Honors Humanities 3: Western Thought from Dostoyevsky to Sartre
description: Some major writing in literature, philosophy, and science from 1800 until the present.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of world, British, and American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for non- English majors or minors. Section content will be identified each semester. Prerequisite:

title: World Literature Masterpieces
description: Selected major works of world literature, exclusive of English and American literature, for students who are majors or minors in English. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 205.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar and Usage
description: Basic course in English grammar and usage for the student who is underprepared. A grade of C or better will satisfy the grammar component of the English Qualifying Test for English majors or minors. Not counted as part of major or minor programs in English.

title: Advanced Composition and Creative Writing
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for the general student, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation; and instruction in creative writing, particularly fiction and poetry. Open only to English majors and minors except by permission of department chairperson. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or equivalent, and sophomore standing.

title: Professional Writing
description: Intensive study of the essay and guided practice in the techniques of expository writing. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or equivalent.

title: Introduction to American Literature
description: Introduction to selected American writers and their works with an emphasis on those that junior high/middle school teachers should know and be able to read skillfully. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to British Literature
description: Introduction to selected writers and periods in British literature with an emphasis on those that junior high/middle school teachers should know. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: American Literature, 1607 -1860
description: A survey of American literature from its beginning through the middle nineteenth century, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or the equivalent.

title: British Literature 1: The Beginnings to 1780
description: Major works of a number of writers and genres with attention to the historical, social, and philosophical background of the times. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: British Literature 2: 1780 to the Present
description: British literature from 1780 to the present, with attention to the historical, social, and philosophical background of the times. Prerequisite: ENG 260.

title: Literature and the Narrative Media
description: A consideration of the ways in which the narrative media have been used to develop fictional and nonfictional literature. Special attention to works that have been adapted from one medium to another and to works of lasting significance. Attention will be given to the narrative media and the language arts curriculum in junior high/middle and secondary schools.

title: Practicum in Peer Tutoring
description: Offers strategies for working with grammar, mechanics, and the larger rhetorical elements, practice in peer evaluation, and a forum for discussing the role and responsibilities of peer tutors. Credit in this course does not apply to a major or minor in English. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to students assigned to tutor at the Writing Center.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials for teaching written and oral expression, language use, spelling, handwriting, and literature. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: Literature for Young Children
description: An introduction to literature for young children. Designed for elementary and early childhood education programs and endorsements and for parents and future parents. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: English Linguistics
description: Modern English grammar with emphasis on the application of uptodate descriptive linguistics to an understanding of basic grammatical structure, relationship, and terminology, including morphology and phonology. Prerequisite: a standard score of 75 percent or higher on a competency examination in English grammar, diction, usage, and mechanics or C or better in ENG 221. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 323.

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: The English Language: Past and Present
description: An introduction to the history and structure of the English language: a survey of important historical changes in the structure of English; a scientific study of the structure of modern English; and a survey of the dialectal variations in modern English. Designed for elementary and junior high/middle school education programs and endorsements. Cannot be counted as an elective in other major or minor programs in English. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 321 or 322.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of children's literature and an intensive study of various types. Designed for elementary education programs and endorsements. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English. Junior or senior standing recommended.

title: Linguistic Phonetics
description: Speech sounds and the linguistic methods employed in their description, classification, and analysis as elements in language systems.

title: American Literature 2, 1860-1960
description: A survey of selected American writers and the various literary movements since 1860, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or equivalent.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: Intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: Intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period, such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: The themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Language Arts in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching language arts in junior high/middle schools. Cannot be counted as an elective in other major or minor programs in English. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDJHM 280.

title: Literature of Black America
description: An investigation of the literature written by black authors in the United States. Authors to be studied will be determined by the instructor on the basis of literary merit.

title: American Indian Literature
description: A literary study of short stories, novels, and poetry by twentiethcentury American Indian authors, with supplementary background readings in mythology, tales, and poetry from the oral traditions. The emphasis will be on works by American Indians, but some works about Indians by white authors may also be included.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to the Restoration
description: English drama from medieval times to 1700, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to The Second Shepherds' Play and Everyman, and to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, Webster, Dryden, and Congreve.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Drama from the Restoration to the Present
description: English drama from 1700 to the present. Special attention is given to the plays of Steele, Goldsmith, Sheridan, Wilde, Shaw, Synge, O'Casey, Osborne, Beckett, and Pinter.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenthcentury novels including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the Brontes, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Studies in British Drama
description: Special topics in contemporary British drama. Open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open only to honors students. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Junior- Level Writing Competency Examination
description: Open to students who have completed ENG 103 and ENG 104 with a grade of C or better. Students must have juniorlevel standing, having earned at least 63 semester hours and fewer than 96 semester hours.

title: Junior-Level Writing Competency Remediation
description: Open to students who have not completed ENG 392 after two attempts.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching English
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in teaching composition, language, and literature in the secondary school. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Special Topics in World and British Literature
description: Special research topics in world or British literature with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or equivalent.

title: Special Topics in English Education
description: Emphasis on current issues and problems at the elementary, middle, junior high, or senior high school level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Special Topics in American Literature
description: Special research topics in American literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Independent Study in English
description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in English. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in English at the 200 level or above at Ball State University and permission of department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Creative Writing Workshop
description: The fundamentals of the short story, such as the use of language, image, and structure. Emphasis on the student's ability to write clearly and dramatically. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Fiction -Writing Workshop
description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Poetry-Writing Workshop
description: Practice, analysis, and criticism of the craft of poetry, with attention to prosody, traditional form, significant idea, the life of the poetic imagination, and the state of the art. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104.

title: Independent Study in English Education
description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in English education, preschool through the secondary level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206 and permission of department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading Printed Materials in the English Classroom
description: Provides an overview of the process of reading printed materials with practical suggestions for developing analytic skills for reading and interpreting written communications, including literary and popular materials used in the English classroom.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Emphasis on the actual reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical aspects.

title: Teaching English as a Foreign Language 1: Theory
description: The psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in second language teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Methods and Materials in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Study and practice of a variety of methods in teaching English as a foreign language. Discussion of pedagogical issues in language teaching. Topics vary each semester; consult the English department for schedule of offerings. Prerequisite: ENG 420 or permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: American Literature, 1945 to Present
description: A survey of the works of major writers and literary trends in America since World War II. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Chaucer
description: A study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several of the minor poems. Emphasis on the structure, the sources, and the significance of the works included. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare
description: An introductory study of representative plays (comedies, histories, tragedies) and some selections from the sonnets by Shakespeare.

title: Studies in Shakespeare
description: Special topics in a selection of Shakespeare's tragedies, comedies, and histories. Prerequisite: open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Milton
description: Indepth, analytical study of Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, Samson Agonistes, Lycidas, and Areopagitica, as well as a brief study of "The Christian Doctrine" and other selected poems and prose by John Milton.

title: Women in Literature
description: Investigation of various ways that women have been portrayed in the literature of the Western world.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War I to the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. Department of Foreign Languages Gardiol, Chairperson; Barnette, Brown, Finney, Fritz, Gilman, Hightower, Johnson, Kadletz, King, Magrath, Moskalew, Shea, Sotiropoulos, Warner The Department of Foreign Languages offers a varied program of instruction in both ancient and modern foreign languages. Close cooperation with other departments on campus makes possible the combining of foreign language training with other disciplines. Classroom and library language laboratories provide for class instruction as well as selfinstruction. Opportunities exist for exchanges with schools in other countries, academic summer study abroad, and foreign language house residence with homelike accommodations and directors who are native speakers of French, German, and Spanish. Language proficiency tests make it possible to award credit for secondlanguage study and to place students in classes at appropriate levels. The Department of Foreign Languages offers indepth training for languageoriented students, including • those desiring to enrich their professional preparedness by acquiring a knowledge of a foreign language; • those desiring a broad liberal education; • those in the teaching program seeking permanent certification for teaching at the elementary and secondary levels; • those planning to travel, live, or work abroad • those desiring practical training in translation skills. Students who begin their study of a foreign language at Ball State University will start with the initial course in the 100-level sequence. Students with secondary school credit in a foreign language or other previous noncollege secondlanguage training will be placed in appropriate courses through the placement examination administered by the department. No placement credit is given for 101, but students placed in 102 or any higherlevel course may receive credit for 102 and each higherlevel course up to 301 by earning a grade of C or better in the course in which they are placed. Students should consult with foreign language faculty advisers about sequencing of courses to meet individual needs. The 100- and 200-level courses in foreign languages are sequential and should be taken in order except in special cases. Entry into 200-level courses requires the successful completion of 101 and 102 or equivalents as determined by the departmental placement program. title: Word Origins and Vocabulary Development
description: English vocabulary derived from Latin and Greek, emphasizing wordformation as a means of expanding and enriching the student's vocabulary. No knowledge of Greek and Latin is required.

title: Scientific Terminology: Greek
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Greek commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Greek is required.

title: Scientific Terminology: Latin
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Latin commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Latin is required.

title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Main features of the civilization of the Greeks and Romanstheir history, political institutions, art, literature, and philosophy. Explores through lectures, readings, and audiovisual materials the nature of the ancients' contribution to Western civilizations.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: A close, interpretive view of Greek cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as individualism, ideals of beauty, social experimentation, competitiveness, and intellectual curiosity, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: A close, interpretive view of Roman cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as respect for tradition, rule of law, social responsibility, and technical expertise, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: The Classical World in Film
description: Aspects of ancient civilization depicted in film (such as Roman history, Greek mythology, etc.). An examination of the accuracy of such portrayals through comparison with ancient sources. The place of such films in the history of cinema. Topics will vary.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: Classical mythology (Greek and Roman) will represent Western tradition in a comparative study with other mythologies of the world. Emphasis on understanding mythologies as symbolic cultural systems expressing societal values. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selections from the major works of Greek and Roman literature and their continuing influence on Western literature. Emphasis on prose and poetry in alternate terms. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned,

title: Women in Antiquity
description: The study of women in ancient Greece and Rome, based on evidence from literary and nonliterary sources. Explores the influence of social, political, and legal institutions on the status of women and on their relationships with men.

title: Greek and Roman Cults
description: Introduces the religions of the ancient Greeks and Romans and examines the nature of their cult activities and theological speculations. Topics include prayer, sacrifice, feasting, ritual, scripture, myth, clergy, etc,

title: The Ancient City
description: Life of the ancient city as mirrored in archaeological and literary sources. The concept of the city, its art and architecture, with special emphasis on Periclean Athens and Augustan Rome.

title: Classical Myth and Theory
description: Major themes of classical myths: creation, the divine and human family, life of the hero, the quest, monsters, etc. Study and employment of modern theories of analysis: mythritual, psychological, structuralist, etc. Prerequisite recommended: CC 205.

title: Readings
description: Individualized course of reading or limited research to allow students to explore special topics in classical antiquity. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Chinese 1
description: The first course in the Chinese language.

title: Beginning Chinese 2
description: The second course in the Chinese language. Prerequisite: CH 101.

title: Intermediate Chinese 1
description: Designed to build on a foundation of firstyear Chinese to help students achieve greater fluency in oral expression and to emphasize the reading of Chinese character texts containing both old and simplified character forms. Grammar will be taught through the use of sentence patterns, and character writing will be practiced. Traditional and contemporary aspects of Chinese culture will also be taught. Prerequisite: CH 102.

title: Intermediate Chinese 2
description: Designed to build on the foundation laid thus far in Chinese and to help students achieve greater fluency in the four basic skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will read newspapers, short stories, and essays by modern authors with the help of a dictionary and will write short compositions in Hanzi on their readings. Prerequisite: CH 201.

title: Beginning Readings in Chinese
description: A course designed to develop skills in reading simple Chinese essays, short stories, and newspaper articles, using approximately 2,000 characters and the help of a dictionary. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Chinese Literature in English Translation
description: A brief overview of major Chinese literary trends and works using selections from traditional masterpieces in poetry, myth, legend, short story, and novel and also contemporary essay, short story, and novel. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Beginning Guided Self-Instruction in Common Languages
description: Guided selfinstruction in beginning French, German, Greek, Latin, or Spanish using audiovisual materials, texts, workbooks, tests, and tutors on an arranged basis. Designed to meet the needs of students who cannot otherwise study languages. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Not open to native speakers. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Guided Self-Instruction in Common Languages
description: Guided selfinstruction in intermediate French, German, Greek, Latin, or Spanish using audiovisual materials, texts, workbooks, tests, and tutors on an arranged basis. Designed to meet the needs of students who cannot otherwise study these languages. Not open to native speakers. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures in Translation
description: Readings in English translation of selected works of major writers in one of the foreign languages taught in this department. Topics and works may vary. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Foreign Culture through Films
description: Study of cultures of the countries whose languages are taught in this department through the medium of foreign contemporary and classic films. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Indochina: Traditions and Languages of Laos and Vietnam
description: A survey of the high traditions and values of the peoples of Indochina. World view through folklore, literature, arts, and language. Conducted in Lao and Vietnamese. Prerequisite: conversational knowledge of Lao or Vietnamese. A total of 9 hours may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester.

title: Guided Self-Instruction Studies in Less Common Languages
description: Offers languages such as Japanese, Arabic, modern Hebrew, modern Greek, Chinese, and Portuguese at basic spoken levels by guided selfinstruction. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in one language. Not open to native speakers.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Foreign Language in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and applications of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching foreign language in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite: EDJHM 280 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and in -depth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College or permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Foreign Language
description: Current methods in foreign language teaching in the senior high school. Presentation, texts, teaching materials, CAI, and other supplementary aids. Reviews current professional literature, trends, requirements. Prerequisite: two years of college credit or equivalent in a modern language and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Foreign Language Trends and CAI
description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of foreign languages, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of foreign languages in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: FL 395.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Language House Living and Learning
description: Offers students the option of earning a limited amount of credit for the languagelearning experience provided by the foreign language houses. A total of 3 hours of credit per language may be earned in any one house, but no more than 1 credit may be earned in one semester. Offered on credit/nocredit basis only.

title: Beginning French 1
description: The first course in the French language.

title: Beginning French 2
description: Prerequisite: FR 101.

title: Intermediate French 1
description: Prerequisite: FR 102.

title: Intermediate French 2
description: Prerequisite: FR 201.

title: Conversation
description: Practice in oral French to increase fluency and authenticity through activities and conversation. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Composition
description: Practice in written French with review of grammatical structures. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent.

title: Grammar
description: An advanced study of French grammar, stressing creative expression in the language. Prerequisite: FR 302 or equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Civilization and Culture: Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the French language and the application of phonetics to the understanding and speaking of French. Use of the international phonetic alphabet. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Business French
description: Designed to make the advanced French student familiar with commericial forms and terminology used in business, banking, and industry. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introduction to French Literature 1
description: Selections from various periods of French literature, designed to develop an appreciation of the literary heritage of France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 401 or equivalent.

title: Introduction to French Literature 2
description: Modern prose and poetry. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 402 or equivalent.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the Classical Age to 1760. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent.

The bachelor's degree program emphasizes both the content and the method of geography. The department specializes in remote sensing and cartographic analysis, geographic education, and travel and tourism. The remote sensing and cartographic analysis program emphasizes computer and satellite technology in the study of land uses, vegetation, the environment, resources, and urban and economic phenomena expressed on the surface of the earth. The display of geographic informationmanual, photo, and computeris the primary focus of the cartographic analysis program. Geographic education remains a strong emphasis within the department, particularly with reference to earth science education. The department maintains a National Weather Service station and has special interest and competency in meteorological sciences, physical geography, and earth science for teachers. The Department of Geography offers a concentration of travel and tourism courses for students wishing to specialize in and enter into the travel and tourism business after graduation. Majors are encouraged to take strong minors in such related subjects as marketing, foreign languages, and general business. title: Earth, Sea, and Sky: A Geographic View
description: Selected aspects of the physical environment and their relationship to human occupancy of the earth. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 111.

title: Global Geography for Teachers
description: Introduction to the regional concept and regional method as related to elementary teaching. Geographic survey of the world. Selected topics and regions given detailed analysis. title: Physical Geography and Earth Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Earthsun relationships, weather and climate, geologic processes (including earth structure and sculpturing of the earth's surface); conservation principles as they pertain directly to the material taught. title: Economic Geography and Contemporary Issues
description: A systematic approach to economic geography and current economic issues emphasizing local, regional, national, and international economic developments in the geographic setting.

title: Geography of the Cultural Environment
description: A spatial analysis of the interaction of cultural development and the physical environment. Special emphasis upon the processes of cultural change and their impact on the landscape.

description: A basic survey course emphasizing geographic facts and interdependencies between the developed and developing world. Particular emphasis is given to physical and social environmental interdependencies. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 105.

title: Weather 1
description: How and why the weather changes, the characteristics of weather, and an examination of weather instruments.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation

title: Geography of Travel and Tourism
description: Introduction to travel and tourism, including study of its geographic, economic, cultural, and social dimensions. Topics include basic principles of travel and tourism; industry organization; how, where, and why people travel; spatial aspects.

title: Urban Geography
description: Distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention given to the geographic factors affecting urban development and growth.

title: Weather 2
description: Introduction to weather forecasting using applied examples. Students may gain practical experience by working in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 230.

title: Climate
description: Introduction to climate with emphasis on regional distribution. How and why climates differ across the earth. Prerequisite: GEOG 230, its equivalent, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. Although the emphasis is on graphic presentation of spatially disposed quantitative and qualitative data, the techniques and methods apply to a wide range of subject areas.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques, including an introduction to computer graphics. Projects are selected within the student's specialization or topic of interest. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Remote Sensing 1
description: Principles of photo interpretation, satellite scanners, and radar. Characteristic features of remotely sensed data, classification processes, and algorithms.

title: Remote Sensing 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in remote sensing, including digital data analysis, image enhancement technique as applied to natural resources, urban analysis, soil studies, geology, and other applied branches. Prerequisite: GEOG 342.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: Comprehensive survey of geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Latin America and the Caribbean
description: Physical and cultural patterns in a diverse world region. Emphasis on population and settlement, agriculture, and environmental hazards in the context of development.

description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environments of Africa.

description: A geographic examination of the physical, cultural, and economic diversity of the state. Field experiences supplement classroom activities.

title: Geography of Asia
description: The geography of South, Southwest, Southeast, and East Asia. A survey and analysis of the physical geographic patterns, bases of cultural diversity, and changing spatial aspects of political organization.

title: Geography of Europe
description: The physical and cultural environment of Europe with emphasis on the economic and political conditions involved.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union and the economic development of the country.

title: Geography of Transportation

description: Introduction to the use of automation in the travel industry as it applies to information management and task functions like reservation and ticketing systems. Includes laboratory experience. Prerequisite: GEOG 361. Open to majors only.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the contribution of physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world to domestic and foreign relations problems.

description: Physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Open to students in geography, earth science, and allied subjects. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in one semester.

Department of Geology Samuelson, Chairperson; Fluegeman, Orr, Roepke, Snow Geologists study the earth with primary attention to its history, materials, structure, and the active processes that continue to change the landscape. Geologists are concerned also with the investigation of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, the evaluation of groundwater resources, the discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits, and the study of the moon and planets. The department offers two departmental majors in geology. One is designed to prepare students for some geological positions in industry and government agencies upon completion of the undergraduate degree and for graduate studies that lead to research, teaching, management, and many other positions in industry, government, and universities. The other departmental major is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who have related interests and do not wish to enter the profession directly. Geology specialties within the department include geomorphology, geophysics, mineralogy, petrography/petrology, paleontology, geotectonics, geohydrology, environmental geology, and stratigraphy. The department also prepares students for entrance into graduate programs that offer degrees in oceanographic studies. Students should contact the departmental advisers immediately upon choosing to major or minor in geology. The advisers help students to develop curricular options and select appropriate elective courses beneficial for optimum career preparation. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 56-58) and by the concentration areas listed below. title: Man and the Geological Environment
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to mankind's environmental and resource problems. Localarea field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: Introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Environmental Geology
description: Examines geologic materials and processes affecting the human environment. Discusses geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, surface water hydrology, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the Geology 201 laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Localarea field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Localarea field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 115 (or high school equivalent) or permission of department chairperson.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments near the campus and visits to places within the state of value to the course. Prerequisite: major or minor in geology, earth science, or geography, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to the resolution of geologic problems. Assignments include accumulation and interpretation of field observations and preparation of geologic maps, cross sections, and stratigraphic sections. Requires a report of investigations for one of the mapping projects. The course is conducted during a fiveweek period in June and July in South Dakota and Wyoming. Prerequisite: GEOL 230 and 382 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Localarea field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoecologic significance. Emphasis on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 115 (or high school equivalent) or permission of department chairperson.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans and related topics. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to refraction and reflection seismology; magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods. Emphasis on applied geophysical methods to such problems as energy resources, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, and pollution detection. Includes laboratory exercises and field investigations. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for classifying and interpreting the origins of rocks. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks to determine their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 108 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: Surveys the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decision makers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Western Civilization
description: A survey of the major themes and developments in the evolution of Western civilization from its origins to the present with emphasis on key problems, critical turningpoints, recurring issues, and cultural growth and heritage. Special stress on the character and crises confronting the Western world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: World Civilization 1
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the dawn on civilization in Southwestern Asia and North Africa to the early modern world.

title: World Civilization 2
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the early modern world to the present.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stresses nineteenth and twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East—the Arab World, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems: imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South and Southeast Asia
description: South Asia (Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka) and Southeast Asia (Burma, Thailand, Laos, Kampuchea, Cambodia, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines) since 1800; a brief description of factors influential in history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, independence, and modernization.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Studies in Non Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: American History, 1492-1876
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States to 1876.

title: American History, 1877 to Present
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States since 1877.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of resource use in the United States by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource use has shaped society.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of blacks in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing conceptions of their roles, attitudes toward women, women's ideas about themselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Uses documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. Students through their own research learn how the historian defines topics of research; selects sources, both primary and secondary; evaluates materials; and describes the findings.

title: The History of American Popular Culture
description: Historical overview of the development of American popular culture. Basic theories, approaches, and topics in popular culture with special attention to amusements, movies, pop music, magazines, pulp novels, and television. Focuses on the relationship of popular culture to American cultural and social history.

title: Early Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: Modern Latin America
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis on Mexico, Chile, Cuba, and Central America.

title: Introduction to Public History
description: An overview of opportunities for nonteaching historyrelated careers in preservation, archival work, records management, museology, historical editing, living history and public parks programs, corporate history, and others. Students make a concentrated study of at least one field of public history and have contact with working professionals. Open to all students.

title: History of the European Family
description: A survey of the changing social, economic, and political roles of the European family from antiquity to the present. Topics include the distribution of authority, marriage and inheritance, childrearing, domestic labor, and the impact of industrialization.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American--Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Gives students a historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Selected Topics in Military History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular period, topic, or issue in military history with emphasis on materials not covered in established courses. Exact content announced in advance of each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others may enroll by permission of department chairperson.

title: Colonial America 1492-1756
description: The settlement of North America by the British and the evolution of the distinctive colonial societies that formed the foundation of the United States.

title: The American Revolution, 1756 -1789
description: Transformation of American society and politics in the era of the American Revolution with emphasis on the origins of the revolution, the development of a democratic society, and the Constitution of the United States.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789 -1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis on the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism Versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820 -1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis on the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878 -1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: The United States from World War I through World II
description: An examination of the reaction of the American people to a society changing rapidly under the impact of two major wars, the Great Depression, and continuing industrialization and urbanization.

title: Recent United States History: 1945 to the Present
description: A study of the role of the United States in the modern world and an examination of the efforts of America to preserve a society that is prosperous and humane while adjusting to technological change and continuing social and intellectual ferment.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the state from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Antebellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum South.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans-Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers, and the events that influenced their migration, and on the effect of these events and the frontier on national development.

title: Indians in U.S. History
description: Survey of Indian and white relations from 1492 to the present, focusing on the Indian wars, treaty making, various types of Indian and white interaction, and the development of federal and state Indian policy.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History Since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I. 433, American Life and Thought, 1607-1865. (3) Sur\ ey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from the colonial period to the Civil War, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American Life and Thought, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from Reconstruction to the present, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: the major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students travel through designated areas in North America. Requires considerable reading before the trip and papers at the conclusion With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in U.S. history may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, 3. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870-4918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918-1945
description: The origins, immediate causes, and the course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and Europe Since 1945
description: European origin of the Cold War and rebirth of a "new" but divided Europe with stress on East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, and temporary decline of European influence; ideological, political, economic, and social development, including competition between Western and Sovietized Eastern Europe.

title: History of Medicine in Western Society
description: A survey of the ideas, attitudes, and institutions of medicine and public health in the Western world from antiquity to modern times. Special attention given to social forces influencing medical knowledge and health care. Not open to the student who has credit in IISC 460.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the republic to approximately A.D. 500. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social, and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special emphasis on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Muslim worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Emphasizes such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, and political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations -Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and societythrough varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in world civilization may apply 4 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 4.

title: France since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France--The Classical Age, 1461 -1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focuses on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Galilean Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715 -1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization—and revolutions in general. Stresses the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Britain, 1485 -1714
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor and Stuart periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain, 1714 to the Present
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life from the Hanoverian period to the present—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of government and society since World War II.

title: Topics in English Constitutional History
description: Selected topics concerning the constitutional history of England, such as the development of the kingship, the common law, Parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: The Modern Middle East
description: A survey of major developments and problems in the Turkish, Persian, and Arab world in the period since 1800—the decay of traditional life, the expansion of European influence, the modernization movements, the conflicts over Palestine, and the recent national and international crises.

title: Selected Topics in Non Western History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in non-Western history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern China, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japan, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on conditions contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Selected Topics in European History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in European history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Topics in American History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Studies for the Primary Grades and Early Childhood
description: Materials and procedures for teaching social studies for nursery school through grade three. Emphasis on behavioral objectives, inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation. Required of persons in the twoyear early elementary education program.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Social Studies in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching social studies in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDJHM 280.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Materials and procedure for teaching social studies from kindergarten through grade six. Emphasis on behavioral objectives; inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Provides more experience in methods used in teaching elementary social studies and an opportunity to use materials available to teachers. Prerequisite: SS 391 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Social Studies
description: Theory and practice of teaching secondary school social studies. Emphasis on methodology, materials, and specific application in the secondary classroom. Includes introductory involvement in the teaching of social studies with a focus on rationale, planning, teaching, and evaluation. Prerequisite: 18 hours of credit in social science and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Independent Study
description: Directed study of special problems or research in social science education by individuals or groups of students. Topics to be investigated are chosen after consultation with the instructor with special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.
