title: Mass Media in Society
description: Study of mass media in their historical and societal contexts with emphasis on practitioner issues including ethics, state of the art, and future.

title: Communications Graphics
description: Theory of publication and visual communication emphasizing preparation of material for newspapers, magazines, and brochures. Lectures and projects focus on type selection, copy fitting, photo and illustration selection and use, pasteup skills, and printing processes.

title: Introduction to Photojournalism
description: Emphasis on preparing students to take, process, and caption photographs for newspapers, magazines, public relations, and advertising purposes. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies.

title: Newswriting, Reporting, and Editing 1
description: Theory and practice in newsstyle writing, gathering news, and editing for publication. Emphasis on newspaper writing skills. Includes one hour of lab per week.

title: Newswriting, Reporting, and Editing 2
description: Theory and practice in newsstyle writing, reporting, and editing. Emphasis on developing reporting and editing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 210.

title: Photographic Lighting
description: An indepth study of photographic lighting procedures and equipment for studio and field use by media photographers. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 130 or other basic photography class. Journalism 211

title: Introduction to Advertising
description: A survey of the advertising communication process. Focuses on communication research, creative strategy, campaign planning, function of mass media as carriers of advertising, and evaluation of advertising effectiveness.

title: Principles of Public Relations
description: Survey of the theory, philosophy, and function of public relations practices and programs in American institutions with special attention given to public relations in various fields.

title: History of Journalism
description: History of journalism in the United States from colonial times to the present, presenting the press as an institution against the background of the history of the nation.

title: Feature and Column Writing
description: Researching and writing feature stories and columns for newspapers and magazines, supplemented by practice assignments for student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 211.

title: Magazine Writing and Editing
description: Theory and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles. Includes a study of markets for magazine articles and exercises in various aspects of editing general and specialized magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Open only to magazinesequence majors or to others with permission of department chairperson.

title: Sportswriting and Reporting
description: Study and practice in covering and writing about sports events and the people connected with them. Story assignments and research combined with classroom lectures and analysis of best sports stories provide students with skills to cover a wide range of sports activities. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Journalism Prose Styles
description: Writing and editing for students interested in publishing their work in newspapers, magazines, and public relations organizations. Emphasizes works of contemporary prose writers. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 315.

title: Journalism Law
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the print and broadcast media with special attention given to recent Supreme Court rulings.

title: Advanced Photojournalism
description: An extended study of the theory and practice of making photographs and using photography as communicative art. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advertising Media
description: Strategy and procedures for planning, executing, and controlling the placement of advertising. Examines characteristics of media, techniques of media budgeting and selection, and methods of evaluating media effectiveness. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Advertising Copy and Layout
description: Instruction in preparing copy for mass media advertising. Major emphasis on creative thinking and basic writing skills. Students prepare copy strategies, write copy, prepare layouts and storyboards. Discussion of fundamentals of consumer motivation and selecting target audiences. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Public Relations Writing and Publicity Techniques
description: Theory and practice of producing publicity tools for various media used in campaigns to promote and interpret personal, institutional, and organizational objectives and activities. Emphasis on writing and publicity problem solving. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 and 261.

title: Public Relations Publication Design and Production
description: Institutional and industrial publications as an important means of internal and external communications. Design and production techniques. Includes one hour of lab per week. Prerequisite: JOURN 125, 211, 360.

title: Editorial Practicum
description: Introductory practical experience in the production of the campus newspaper, magazine, yearbook, or alternative projects with emphasis on writing, editing, or photographic activities. Emphasizes mastery of spelling, grammar, and typing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 469 or

title: Honors Colloquium in Journalism
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Journalism
description: The procedures and problems in teaching journalism classes or units and the role of student publications in school journalism programs. Subjects included are curriculum, finance, textbooks, and resources. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Advanced Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice in reporting and writing specialized new stories. Emphasis on indepth reporting and coverage of specialized areas ineluding public affairs, government, education, and business. Assignments designed for use in student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 211.

title: Scientific and Technical Writing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Students become familiar with engineering and spaceage terminology, with emphasis on clarity and translation of technical terms to lay language.

title: Newspaper Design
description: Theory of the design functions of journalism using typographical systems with attention to their relations to communicative language. Acquaints the journalism student with new methods, ideas, and techniques that have been and are in the process of being developed in journalism printing and technology. Prerequisite: JOURN 125 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advanced Magazine Writing
description: A workshop in writing articles with emphasis on targeting markets for freelance articles. The emphasis is upon writing for magazines that publish articles of 2,500 words or more. Prerequisite: JOURN 315 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Magazine Management
description: Analysis of all facets of magazine management: editorial, advertising, circulation, and art. Designed for students interested in working for professional magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 315 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Picture Editing
description: Selecting, editing, and using photographic and other illustrative graphic materials. Includes layout and design of picture pages for newspapers, magazines, books, brochures, and pamphlets.

title: Advertising Photography
description: Advertising, commercial, and concept illustration photography for the print media. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Color Photojournalism
description: Principles, techniques, and materials of color photography as they apply to color art work and photographs in printed publications. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 337 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advertising Case Studies
description: Designed to analyze and solve advertising problems based on actual situations. Cases focus on consumer goods companies, industrial marketers, and nonprofit organizations. Prerequisite: JOURN 352, 354.

title: Advanced Copy Writing
description: Advanced studies in the strategy and creation of advertising for the mass media. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 354.

title: Advertising Campaigns
description: Synthesis of skills and concepts acquired in the specialized advertising courses. Students research, plan, write, schedule, budget, and evaluate a complete advertising campaign. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 352, 354; MKG 300, 310; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advertising: Public Relations Practicum
description: Practical experience in public relations or advertising projects in preparation of a senior portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 352 and 354 or 368; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advising High School Publications
description: Theories of staff organization and content of high school yearbooks, newspapers, and magazines. Emphasizes the role of the adviser, financial management, staff motivation, and trends in scholastic publications.

title: Introduction to Journalism and Communication Research
description: Issues and trends in the literature of mass communication theory and research.

title: Individual Studies in Journalism
description: Group and individual investigations and experiences in journalistic media and techniques with special attention to social, political, and economic roles of the press in society. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Journalism Internship
description: Onthejob training in which journalism or public relations students get practical experience in applying what they have learned in the classroom. Involves assigned duties in an offcampus communications organization with appropriate compensation. Prerequisite: JOURN 130, 210, 211, 250, and permission of department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 375 and 469. An actuary gains professional recognition by passing a series of examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries. title: Intermediate Algebra
description: Review of factoring; quadratic equations and inequalities, relations and functions, rational exponents, systems of linear equations, exponential and logarithmic functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 099 or appropriate score on mathematics placement examination or permission of department chairperson.

title: Algebra and Trigonometry
description: Such topics as theory of polynomial equations, matrices and determinants, systems of equalities and inequalities, mathematical induction, binomial theorem, permutations and combinations. Trigonometric functions, identities, and equations; inverse functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, complex numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or its equivalent as determined by department chairperson. Credit is denied if credit has been earned in any highernumbered coarse or its equivalent except by permission of department chairperson.

title: Pre-Calculus Mathematics
description: The coordinate plane, straight lines and circles, conic sections, elementary transcendental functions, curve sketching, polar coordinates, parametric equations, sequences and series. Prerequisite: the equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondary school level or MATHS 115.

title: Mathematics and Its Applications
description: A general studies course including such topics as mathematical modeling, problem solving, geometrical concepts, growth patterns, and appli- ,cations to the physical sciences, social sciences, and economics. Prerequisite: MATHS 099 or appropriate score on mathematics placement examination or permission of department chairperson.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 1
description: Thpics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or a strong background in high school algebra.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics that are particularly suited to the needs of the student with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATHS 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications in some of the above areas. Prerequisite: MATHS 115 or its equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 171.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 171. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 172.

title: Calculus 1
description: Differential calculus and its applications. Advanced topics from analytic geometry will be introduced as needed. Antidifferentiation and the Reimann integral. Elementary transcendental functions. Prerequisite: elements of analytic geometry from high school or MATHS 117.

title: Calculus 2
description: Standard techniques of integration and applications of the integral. Infinite series. Further development of applications of integral calculus. Vectors. Partial differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 171.

title: Elementary Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, measures of central tendency and dispersion, basic probability concepts, random variables, binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression, considers various applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 115 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 320.

title: Number Concepts in the Elementary School
description: A development of cardinal and unsigned rational number concepts and properties interfaced with selected models and computer software from elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite: MATHS 099 or appropriate score on mathematics placement examination or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geometry and Measurement in the Elementary School
description: A development of geometry and measurement concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite: MATHS 201. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 203.

title: Geometry and Measurement in the Primary Grades
description: A development of measurement and geometry concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from K-3 mathematics programs. Prerequisite: MATHS 201. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 202.

title: Structure of the Number Systems
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and selected number systems. A systematic development is emphasized. Prerequisite: MATHS 162, 171, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Linear Algebra 1
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties and applications, determinants, rank and equivalence of matrices. Introduction to vector spaces and linear transformation. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 171.

title: Linear Algebra 2
description: A continuation of topics from MATHS 212 including transformation of coordinates, diagonalization of matrices, and introduction to canonical forms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 412.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Geometry
description: A revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Computer applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 211 and one year of secondary school geometry.

title: Calculus 3
description: Multidimensional calculus and its applications. Topics include vectorvalued functions, partial derivatives, multiple integrals in rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates, and some vector analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems dealing with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by permission of department chairperson. Prerequisite: MATHS 273.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 201.

title: Introduction to Polynomials
description: Consideration of polynomials as extensions, equations, and functions over rings, integral domains, and fields, particularly the real and complex number systems. Prerequisite: MATHS 211.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, moment generating functions, common distributions, sampling Mathematical Sciences 217 distribution theory, central limit theorem, t, chisquare, and F distributions. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Mathematical Statistics
description: Point and interval estimation, maximum likelihood, Neyman-Pearson Lemma, likelihood ratio tests, classical tests of significance, goodnessoffit, contingency tables, correlation, regression, nonparametric methods, Bayesian methods. Prerequisite: MATHS 320.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, and other distributions. Some problems with moment generating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Actuarial review class. Prerequisite: MATHS 321.

title: Computer and Mathematics Enrichment Topics
description: Topics for elementary and junior high/middle school in computer uses and programming, and enrichment topics from such areas as topology, strategy games, and number theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 202. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 116 or 118.

title: Computer Applications in the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Emphasizes the use of computers in the teaching of mathematics. Students whose area of licensure is mathematics may apply credit in this course toward the undergraduate computer endorsement. Prerequisite: MATHS 240 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models for use with problems in physics, chemistry, biology, and economics. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models. Existing computer software will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in analytic, synthetic, transformational, and vector geometry, closely related to Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 240 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities, equations of value, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, current actuarial topics in finance. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analysis, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 118 or 121 and MATHS 162 or 172. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 362. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 363.

title: Intermediate Calculus
description: Topics include vector functions; displacement; velocity and acceleration of particles in twoand threedimensional space; curvature; torsion and Frenet's formulas; divergence; curl; line integrals; work; surface integrals; theorems of Gauss, Green, and Stokes; orthogonal curvilinear coordinates. Prerequisite: MATHS 273.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nthorder ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equations. Laplace transforms, power series solutions. Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, firstorder partial differential equations. Use of standard computer software for elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood and Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from early childhood through grade three. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. One hour lecture, one hour teaching, and one hour laboratory per week. Prerequisite: MATHS 202 or

title: Teaching Mathematics in the Elementary School
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels throughout the elementary school. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Two onehour lectures and one hour teaching per week. Prerequisite: MATHS 202 or 203.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for the teaching of mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a smallgroup teaching siutation. Prerequisite: 20 hours credit in the junior high/middle school mathematics program and junior standing.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in teaching secondary mathematics. Survey of texts, organization of materials, evaluation procedures, instructional aids, and classroom observations. Prerequisite: MATHS 211, 240.

title: Classroom Use of Methods and Materials
description: Classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics, evaluation of instructional activities, and rationale for including mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences, whenever appropriate. Prerequisite: MATHS 313, 340, 395.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 1
description: An introduction to group theory, ring theory through the first isomorphism theorems. Polynomial rings, integral domains and elementary field theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Algebra 2
description: A continuation of the study of abstract algebra. Topics from series of groups, Burnside and Polya counting, Sylow theorems, group presentations, field extensions and geometric constructions, module theory, algebraic coding theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 411.

title: Theory of Numbers
description: Topics include the division algorithm; positional notation; divisibility; primes; congruences; divisibility criteria; the sigma, divisor, and phi functions; diophantine equations; linear, polynomial, and simultaneous congruences; theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson; quadratic reciprocity. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school include Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, magic squares, the calendar problem, polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the fifteen puzzle, Nim, and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 416.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling; ratio estimates; regression estimates; cost and variance functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or equivalent.

title: Topics in Statistics
description: Includes such topics as oneand twoway ANOVA, multiple comparisons, regression analysis, time series analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or equivalent.

title: Analysis of Variance in Experimental Design Models
description: Multivariate normal distribution; quadratic forms; linear models; simple random, randomized block, Latin squares, factorial, splitplot, balanced incomplete block design; analysis of covariance; confounding; multiple comparison tests. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or equivalent.

title: Geometry and Topology 1
description: Introduction to Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometries and the surfaces admitting these geometries. Basic topological notions, such as the boundary operator, continuity, and connectedness, underlying the development of these topics. Elements of linear geometry leading to basic ideas of differential geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 273.

title: Geometry and Topology 2
description: A continuation of MATHS 441 culminating in the treatment of selected advanced topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 441.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 1
description: Survival distributions, life tables; the mathematics of life insurance, life annuities, net premiums, and net premium reserves. Prerequisite: MATHS 351.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 2
description: Mathematics of multiple life functions, multiple decrement models, valuation theory for pension plans, insurance models including expenses, nonforfeiture benefits, acid dividends. Prerequisite: MATHS 452.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, math formula. Prerequisite: MATHS 362.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Optimization techniques of linear, dynamic, and integer programming. Optimal solutions of PERT-CP/M networks. Optimal decision strategies. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 321, and a working knowledge of FORTRAN (CS 118 or equivalent).

title: History of Mathematics
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to the seventeenth century. Topics may include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, and calculus. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 171.

title: Elements of Analysis
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives, and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 172 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Metric spaces, topological concepts in IR and C leading to consideration of connectedness, compactness and completeness, continuous functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrass theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 273.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansions. Prerequisite: MATHS 471.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace's equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATHS 374. Natural Resources 219

Department of Natural Resources Mortensen, Chairperson; Godish, Hibbs, Lowe, Lyon, Pichtel, Siewert, Van Meter The Department of Natural Resources has as its ultimate objective the education of people to help meet the demand for qualified personnel in environmental science and natural resources. It is further dedicated to contributing to the general education of students throughout the university by offering appropriate courses in natural resources. Through research and extension activities it also strives to provide services concerning environmental quality and resource management for Indiana citizens. The programs offered by the department are designed to give students a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. Curricula are interdisciplinary because the conservation of our natural resources and the concomitant improvement of our environment require the contributions of many disciplines. Therefore, depending upon the special interest of the student, a program may include courses in several disciplines. Curricula offered by the department include a departmental major and minor in natural resources and a teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, an area of endorsement for elementary education majors, a supporting concentration for junior high/middle school majors, and an energy resources minor. Students enrolled in the major in natural resources may elect the general option in resource studies or specialize in such subjects as natural resource planning, land resource management, communications/public information, water quality, natural resources interpretation, soil science, environmental protection, and outdoor recreation management. Common background is provided for all majors through a core requirement. In addition to traditional science courses, others that may be included are communication, environmental health, landscape architecture, physical education, political science, sociology, and urban and regional studies. Giving students practical or "handson" experience is an important part of the educational programs in natural resources. Most of the courses include a laboratory as well as field experience. Some courses include indepth twoweek field studies in the North, West, and Southeast. Students are encouraged to participate in practicums or internships under the supervision of a faculty member or professionals working in a conservation/environmental field. The department uses the services of resource people in the community and state to enhance the educational experience of students enrolled in natural resources classes. These include representatives of industry, local governmental units, Indiana Departments of Natural Resources and Environmental Management, Indiana State Board of Health, U.S. Soil Conservation Service, Cooperative Extension Service, and faculty from public schools and other colleges and universities. title: Natural Resources: Environment, Conservation, and Society
description: Study of natural resources (air, energy, minerals, soil, vegetation, water, wildlife) and the impact of population and technology on environmental systems. Role of resource management, conservation, and outdoor recreation in achieving an environment of high quality. Laboratory and field activities included.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of United States resource use by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource use has shaped society. Not open to the student who has credit in HIST 204.

title: International Natural Resources: Development and Conservation
description: An analysis of problems occurring as a result of development and use of natural resources worldwide. The role of resource management and conservation to enhance the carrying capacity of earth. A casestudy approach to the management of global environmental problems.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to man. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Includes laboratory and field work.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Includes laboratory and field work.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 3 semester hours in NR, preferably NR 101, or permission of department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in ECON 311.

title: Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Food Production
description: The role of natural resources in producing food for people and the agronomic and animal science practices necessary to provide food for a growing world population. Emphasis placed on the management talents needed to grow food successfully. Two weekend field trips.

title: Resources for Self-Reliance Living
description: Considers the environmental impact of hard and soft technologies. Focuses on devising a survival strategy based on selfreliance concepts in housing, waste material, water use, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation, and the role of regulatory agencies. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 211; CHEM 111 or equivalent, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: The basic relationship between soil nutrients and plant growth with emphasis on the factors affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Includes basic soil testing. Prerequisite: NR 221; CHEM 111 or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Includes soil genesis, morphology, classification, and survey. Stresses the relationship between soils information and the landuse decisionmaking process with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Stresses principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts. Studies management systems and individual practices with special emphasis on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Energy and Mineral Resources: Issues and Choices
description: Appraisal of the problems, prospects, and societal and technical issues surrounding the use of energy and mineral resources. Emphasis on environmental problems and ecoenergetics, consideration of the natural resource base, distribution and production problems, conservation, alternative energy systems, resource policy, and research.

title: Air Resources
description: Significance of the atmosphere as a resource; important meteorological parameters in air resources and management; economic, sociological, technical, political, and biological aspects of air pollution; special emphasis on basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Indoor Air Quality Management
description: Indoor air pollution problems of residential and nonresidential environments. Features discussions of pollutants like asbestos, radon, and formaldehyde as well as combustiongenerated pollutants. Topics include energy conservation, building design, modeling, measurement techniques, and mitigation measures. Lab and field experiments.

title: Turfgrass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. Identification of grass and weed species.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. Emphasizes multipleuse concepts of management to meet outdoor recreation demands. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Introductory Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles as applied to the management of natural resources and related environmental problems. Prerequisite: NR 211, 221; GEOL 101, PHYCS 110 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures. Prerequisite: NR 211; one college course in chemistry; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Solid Waste Management
description: Solid waste management with emphasis on delineation of the problem, disposal methods and techniques, recycling, and management of disposal systems. Stresses the relationship between solid waste disposal and other resources. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students; others with permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the elementary education curriculum. Reviews sources helpful in teaching conservation like resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 101, BIO 102, GEOG 111, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Methods and Materials: Environmental Conservation in the Secondary School
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating environmental conservation into the secondary school curriculum. Reviews sources helpful in teaching environmental conservation like resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources appropriate to environmental conservation. Requires laboratory and field work. Prerequisite NR 101 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a specific area with special emphasis on location of natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence they have on the regional environ- Philosophy 223 mental quality. Each time the course is offered a specific geographic area is studied. Includes laboratory and field experience. Prerequisite: NH 101 or equivalent and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Integrated Resources Planning and Management
description: Introduction to strategies used in environmental planning and resource management in contemporary society. Stresses use of data analysis and its role in the decisionmaking process by conceptually centering on natural and manmade systems. May require field trips. Prerequisite: all natural resources core courses or concurrent enrollment and senior standing. Students in related disciplines may seek permission from department chairperson.

title: Seminar
description: Formal reports and discussion of selected natural resource topics, current events, and special articles in natural resourcerelated professional and scientific journals. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered spring semester of evennumbered years. Prerequisite: NR 211, BIO 480, and ZOOL 444, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and use of natural resources for outdoor recreation. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Administration and Management of Outdoor Recreation Areas
description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to implement outdoor recreation plans to provide outdoor recreation experiences of high quality. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Wilderness and Society
description: Concerned with defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. Integral to the course will be a study of research in user perception and use and a weekend trip to a potential Indiana wilderness area. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Environmental Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis on field work and creative presentation of concepts. Additional emphasis on the organization and management of interpretive programs including sites and facilities. Prerequisite: NR 101 or equivalent, BIO 216.

title: Practicum in Natural Resources
description: Supervised practical professional experience relating theory and practice by combining instruction and work activities in natural resources, including conservation education, outdoor education, or environmental education. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources
description: An opportunity to pursue special interests in environmental quality. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 496.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Participation in original research under faculty guidance. Research includes problem definition, literature review, data collection, analysis, and a summary report. May require preparatory or parallel course work in research methodologies, statistics, or computer science. Prerequisite: faculty sponsor and permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. Department of Philosophy Annis, Chairperson; Barker, Corbett, Fears, Foster, Landini, Miller Philosophy as an Academic Discipline Philosophy attempts to arrive at reasoned answers to important questions that fall outside the scope of any particular science, either because they are normative, or especially general, or more fundamental than the questions the sciences raise. The major branches of philosophy are • Logic—the study of techniques of critical reasoning. • Metaphysics—the examination of questions concerning the ultimate nature of reality. • Epistemology—the investigation of the theory of knowledge. • Ethics--the study of such problems as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as contemporary moral problems including abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, and famine relief. Other important subjects in philosophy are the history of philosophy, social philosophy, aesthetics, and philosophy of science. Students wanting professional careers in philosophy generally consider teaching at the junior college, college, or university level. Philosophy also prepares students for vocations requiring a liberal education and skills in critical thinking, conceptual analysis, problem solving, and communication. Thus it is appropriate preparation for careers in law, public service, governmental agencies, and writing, as well as any religionoriented vocation. Religious Studies as an Academic Discipline The program of religious studies seeks to enable students to appreciate various religions and to cultivate a better awareness and understanding of themselves and openness toward others. Throughout the program, students will grapple with the deepest questions of human existence from a religious point of view. Persons with a background in religious studies may apply to work in hospitals, community agencies, correctional institutions, and other public service offices. Publishing, editing, Christian education, guidance and counseling, social work, youth organizations, and adult education programs are other career possibilities. The program of religious studies also prepares students to enter seminaries and the professional ministry and for further studies at the graduate level. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: An introduction to such important philosophical problems as the existence of God, whether ethical values are subjective, and the extent of our freedom. These topics and others may be approached by examining the ideas of great philosophers or current thinkers.

title: Introduction to Techniques of Critical Reasoning
description: Introduction to basic techniques of critical reasoning in deductive and inductive logic, and strategies for decision making and problem solving.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of deduction.

title: Ethics
description: A discussion of some of the central problems in ethics such as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as a discussion of current moral issues.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of such basic social concepts Philosophy 225 as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of such normative issues as how liberty should be distributed and how justice can be maximized.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Critical analysis of such selected topics as the nature and existence of God, the problem of evil, the justification of religious belief, and the significance of religious experience.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the rise of philosophy in Greece through the medieval period. Emphasis on the theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Emphasis on these theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics may include the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading philosophers and movements in the twentieth century. May concentrate on such selected philosophers as Russell, Wittgenstein, and Husserl, or may concentrate on contemporary treatments of selected philosophical problems.

title: Aesthetics
description: Exploration of philosophical views on the nature, interpretation, and criticism of art. Readings and discussion may range from classical to contemporary thinkers and issues.

title: Philosophy of Law
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, and justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of such basic concepts as action, intention, causation, and responsibility.

title: Current Issues in Philosophy
description: Selected current and important issues in philosophy. Topics may include social and ethical problems, recent work on traditional philosophical problems, and other issues of concern.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: An examination of such central philosophical problems in the sciences as the nature of scientific explanation and the testing of hypotheses; a discussion of ethical issues arising from science, for example the use of human subjects and prolonging life.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Prerequisite: students in the Honors College or permission of department chairperson.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Provides superior students with opportunities for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Introduction to Metaphysics
description: A study of the principal problems of metaphysics including the nature of reality, the relation of mind and body, and the issues of freedom and determinism.

title: Introduction to Theory of Knowledge
description: A critical discussion of leading theories and problems of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge and rational belief, the different kinds of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory and Problems
description: A critical examination of recent ethical theories and their application to contemporary problems.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: Traditional religious groups in the United States with attention to developments, institutions, distinctive practices and beliefs. The groups and the subjects treated will be adjusted to the interests of the students.

title: Religions of the World
description: An introductory survey of the major religions of the world (Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Islam, Christianity, and others), emphasizing how people live out their faiths in their daily lives.

title: Old Testament
description: Our Hebrew-Judaic religious heritage as reflected in various personalities and their religious expressions as found in the literature of the Old Testament.

title: New Testament
description: Our early Christian heritage in relation to its Jewish-Greek background as reflected by various personalities in the literature of the New Testament.

title: Jesus, Paul, and Early Christianity
description: The traditions that developed about Jesus among the early Christians as reflected in the Gospels, and the Pauline tradition as reflected in the Book of Acts and the letters attributed to Paul.

title: Problems of the Early Church
description: Problems of understanding and interpretation that arose in the early church surrounding the place and year of Jesus' birth, virgin birth, miracles, last supper, betrayal, arrest, trial, crucifixion, burial, resurrection, appearances, and other events.

title: Methods in the Study of Religion
description: An exploration of the many ways to approach the study of religion, its origins, nature, and functions in human society

title: Seminar in Eastern Religions
description: An intensive seminarformat study of the religions of India, China, and Japan, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Shinto, and contemporary Japanese religions.

title: Comparative Religion
description: Investigation, analysis, and comparison of selected major religious traditions with attention to their underlying structures. Particular attention is given to the comparison of Eastern and Western traditions.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: For superior students: an opportunity for guided investigation in aspects of religion not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Special Topics in Religion
description: Indepth focus on a selected issue of central importance. Topics vary each semester and include such subjects as American Indian religions, women and religion, the Pentecostal and charismatic movements. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester. PRE-ENGINEERING MAJOR This departmental major is intended for students interested in preparing for admission to a school of engineering. Specifically, the program is offered in cooperation with the Purdue University School of Engineering so that courses taken at Ball State in the preengineering curriculum parallel courses the student would take at Purdue during the first years of study. Although the courses taken at Ball State in the preengineering curriculum are similar or identical to those taken by students at many institutions offering engineering programs, the School of Engineering at Purdue is the only institution with which Ball State University has an affiliation. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program in which the student attends Ball State for three years then transfers to Purdue to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of such a program the student is eligible to receive a bachelor's degree from Ball State and the engineering degree from Purdue. It is possible to complete the degree requirements for both institutions in less than five years by attending summer sessions. Students may, of course, elect to transfer to Purdue or some other engineering school before completing the full preengineering course of study at Ball State. If so, students will be eligible to receive only the degrees at the other institutions. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not mean automatic admission to the Purdue University School of Engineering. Students must apply to Purdue for admission and should have completed at least a full year of physics (PHYCS 120, 122) and a year of calculus before transferring. Three options within the preengineering major are available. The options for students interested in chemical or metallurgical engineering are specifically listed. For other kinds of engineering such as electrical, mechanical, civil, etc., the student should elect the general engineering option. Approved electives from PHYCS, APHYS, CS, and MATHS 8 hrs. Option 2: Metallurgical, 11 hours CHEM 225, 344, 345 11 hrs. Option 3: Chemical, 21 hours CHEM 225, 234, 235, 344, 345 21 hrs. title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting such energy forms as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physical Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles and concepts of the laws of nature involving mechanical, heat, light, electrical, nuclear, and chemical energy and the conservation laws associated with these forms of energy. Emphasis on applications appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Preparation of Physical Science Teaching Materials
description: Selected topics in physical science stressing the construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Prerequisite: PHYCS 101 or permission of department chairperson. Open only to students in the teachereducation curriculum.

title: Basic Physics for the Allied Health Sciences
description: A condensed study of basic physics with special emphasis on principles and applications pertinent to the health sciences. Three lectures and one twohour laboratoryrecitation weekly. Prerequisite: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry or permission of department chairperson. Open only to students in the allied health sciences program in respiratory therapy, radiologic technology, nuclear therapy, and ultrasound technology or by permission of department chairperson.

title: General Physics 1
description: Studies the laws of Newtonian mechanics. Introductory fluid statics and dynamics, heat and thermodynamics, and wave motion and sound. Prerequisite:

title: General Physics 2
description: Static and current electricity, magnetism, light and optics, and an introduction to modern physics including relativity and elements of atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110 or 130.

title: General Physics 1
description: A first course in calculusbased physics for students in preengineering, the physical sciences, or mathematics. Topics include Newtonian mechanics, work and energy, motion, impulse and momentum, elasticity and wave motion, sound, and hydrostatics and hydrodynamics. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161.

title: General Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 120. Topics include heat and laws of thermodynamics, Coulomb's law and the electric field, Ampere's law and the magnetic field, introduction to Maxwell's equation, DC and AC circuits; the nature, propagation, and properties of light; and lens systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120. Parallel: MATHS 162.

title: Physics for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of mechanics and heat. Topics include particle dynamics, resolution of forces, friction, work, energy, static equilibrium, torque, properties of materials, fluids, temperature, thermal expansion, heat energy, heat transfer, phase changes in matter, and thermodynamic engines. Prerequisite: MATHS 115 or equivalent secondary school mathematics. Not open to the student who has credit in PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Sound and Light
description: For music and art students. Sound as a basis of music and light as a basis of art. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Topics in Physics
description: Discussion of specific topics in physics, such as lasers, holography, and solidstate electronics. Designed for students not majoring in physics, the course requires no math or science background. Students may consult their curricular advisers or the Department of Physics and Astronomy for the specific topics being studied during a given semester. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Solar Energy Technology and Applications
description: Descriptive study of various techniques and systems using sunlight as a nonpolluting alternative energy source. Principles and design of solar systems for space heating, air conditioning, and heating water for residential and commercial buildings, and systems for the generation of electric power. Includes other related topics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or MATHS 108.

title: Introduction to Modern Physics
description: The underlying principles and theories of modern physics. Topics include introductory relativity, atomic and nuclear structure, quantum theory, and the theory of solids. A regularly scheduled laboratory is included. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Mechanics
description: Basic concepts of particle mechanics. Simple and damped harmonic motion. Particle dynamics in noninertial frames of reference, central forces. Dynamics of a system of particles. Dynamics of a rigid body and the moment of inertia tensor. The wave equation, elasticity, and rigid body vibrations. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120 and MATHS 162.

title: Physical Optics
description: The electromagnetic wave theory of light, spectra, interference, diffraction, polarization, and double refraction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Acoustics
description: Aspects of pure and applied acoustics. Topics include solutions to the wave equation, acoustic impedances, electromechanicalacoustic analogies, directradiator loudspeaker and enclosure theory, and a discussion of room acoustics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Electronics 1
description: Introductory DC and AC circuit theory, semiconductor components, power supplies, transistor amplification; integrated circuit operational amplifiers, active filters, oscillators and function generators. Basic combinational logic circuits and Boolean algebra. Emphasizes applications of integrated circuits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Electronics 2
description: Sequential logic circuits including scalars, displays, memories, shift registers, analogtodigital and digitaltoanalog conversion techniques. Microprocessor architecture and support electronics for microcomputer design. IC chips and circuits for experiment to microcomputer interfacing. Use of a microprocessor development system. Prerequisite: PHYCS 354 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introductory Nuclear Techniques
description: Emphasis on experimental studies of radioactive disintegrations and decay products and their relation to nuclear structure. Instrumentation in radioisotope measurements. Two lectures and two twohour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics 1
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those that occur in classical mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetic theory and in quantum mechanics. Topics include vector methods, generalized coordinates, and methods of applications of differential equations in physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and 260 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics 2
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems. Topics include boundary value problems. Transforms, special functions of mathematical physics, and applications of tensor analysis in physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122, 260 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Descriptive Astronomy
description: The celestial sphere, the solar system, formation and decay of stars, instruments and basic laws of astronomy, nebulae, galactic structure, theories of the origin of the universe; constellation and telescope work.

title: Honors Colloquium in Physics
description: Exploration of selected topics in physics, with emphasis on individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students or students with permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Teaching of Physics in the Secondary School
description: Aims, nature of the subject matter, calculus concepts, and applications in the teaching of physics, amount and nature of laboratory work, standardized tests, and textbooks used in the teaching of physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in physics or permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Thermodynamics
description: Laws of thermodynamics and introduction to the kinetic theory of gases. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Celestial Mechanics
description: An application of the laws of classical mechanics to objects under the influence of inversesquare gravitational forces, leading to the theory of orbits and perturbative effects on orbits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 1
description: Application of vector analysis to electrostatics, dipole and multipole fields, and dielectric theory. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 450 with emphasis on dynamic electrical problems, alternating currents, magnetic fields, and Maxwell's equations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 450.

title: Elementary Particles
description: The nature and behavior of elementary particles through the study of the symmetries and dynamics responsible for their production, reactions, and decays. Prerequisite: PHYCS 465.

title: Nuclear Physics
description: Nucleus and nuclear interactions. Emphasizes experimental facts about nuclear processes in discussions of particle accelerators, detectors, radioactivity (alpha, beta, and gamma decay), interaction of radiation with matter, nuclear reactions, nuclear structure, nuclear models, and nuclear applications in science and technology. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 1
description: De Broglie's postulate, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the free particle, square well potentials, harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom, and other selected wave mechanics problems. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 464. Course material includes perturbation theory, oneelectron atoms, magnetic moments, spin, relativistic effects, symmetric and antisymmetric eigenfunctions, the helium atom, the Thomas-Fermi theory, the Hartree theory, and transition rates. Prerequisite: PHYCS 464.

title: Solid State Physics 1
description: An investigation of the structure and physical properties of matter in the solid state. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Solid State Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 466. Topics include the electrical and magnetic properties of solids and the band theory of solids with special emphasis on semiconductors. Examines the optical properties of solids and the effects of lattice defects. Prerequisite: PHYCS 466.

title: Independent Studies in Physics
description: Pursuit of special lines of scientific investigation in physics on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mysteries of the Sky
description: A nontechnical and nonmathematical multimedia excursion into the vast reaches of the sky including information about the sun, the moon, shooting stars, comets, supernovae, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, life on other planets.

title: Astronomy Materials for the Teacher
description: The fundamentals of astronomy including historical aspects and modern astronomy concepts. Emphasis on construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Observational Astronomy
description: A continuation of ASTRO 100 providing practical experience in observing celestial objects by using telescopes and other astronomical apparatus. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100.

title: General Astronomy 1
description: Essential points of modern astronomy, emphasizing the underlying physical principles. Topics include coordinate systems in astronomy, orbital laws, relativity, planetary physics, measurement of stellar distances, and spectral classification of stars. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100 or PHYCS 380, and MATHS 108.

title: General Astronomy 2
description: A continuation of ASTRO 120. Topics include atomic structure and stellar spectra, stellar atmospheres and interiors, multiple star systems and clusters, galactic structure, cosmology, and the origin of the universe. Prerequisite: ASTRO 120.

title: Topics in Astronomy
description: Discussion of specific topics in astronomy, such as comets, eclipses, UFOs, and interstellar travel. Designed for students not majoring in physics, the course requires no math or science background. Students may consult their curricular advisers or the Department of Physics and Astronomy for specific topics being studied during a given semester. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 1
description: A review of mechanics, electromagnetic radiation, and atomic structure in the context of modern observational astrophysics. Solar system astrophysicsincluding an introduction to celestial mechanics and astronomical coordinate and time systemsare surveyed, and astronomical instruments are discussed. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120, 122.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 2
description: An examination of observational stellar astronomy with applications to the study of stellar structure and evolution, and a review of the physics of stellar systems such as star clusters, galaxies, and clusters of galaxies. Prerequisite: ASTRO

title: Seminar in Modern Astronomy
description: Selected topics in contemporary astronomy. Extensive use of library facilities including current journals and periodicals in astronomy. Topics for study may include astronomical research in progress and such esoteric subjects as UFOs and extraterrestrial life. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and permission of department chairperson.

title: Instruments and Techniques in Planetarium Operations
description: Use of planetarium instruments, console, and chamber. Creation and presentation of planetarium programs including slideduplicating techniques, slide opaquing, and the production of sound tracks. Prerequisite: permission of planetarium director.

title: Theories and Instruments of the Astronomer
description: Reviews of various atlases, catalogs, ephemerides, and charts. The development of methods used to compute and update stellar positions. Discusses astronomical instruments in the context of their use by research astronomers. Analyzes specific techniques employed in astronomical photometry, spectroscopy, and photography. Prerequisite: ASTRO 332.

title: Advanced Astrophysics
description: A detailed investigation of the frontier areas of modern astrophysics. Possible topics include stellar structure, nucleosynthesis, stellar evolution, stellar atmospheres, and the interstellar material. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330, 332.

title: Principles of Radiography 1
description: An overview of radiation physics to include properties of radiation, biological effects, xray production and interaction, and radiation protection. Prerequisite: MATHS 108, PHYCS 106.

title: Introduction to Radioactivity
description: Mechanisms and characteristics of nuclear decay and interaction of radiation with matter. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in nuclear medicine.

title: Radiopharmaceuticals
description: Preparation, quality control, and the diagnostic and therapeutic application of radiopharmaceuticals in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 247.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation
description: An indepth study of the components and performance characteristics of equipment commonly used in the nuclear medicine clinic. Parallel: APHYS 252.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation Lab
description: A weekly laboratory for nuclear medicine technology students enrolled in APHYS 251.

title: Lasers and Applied Electro-Optic Techniques
description: Principles of laser operation, design, and safety considered within the context of the field of electrooptic techniques. Optical detection devices, photographic techniques, and laser applications stressed in the handson laboratoryoriented portion of the course. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or 122 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Fluid Mechanics
description: The forces and motions in fluids. Fluid characteristics and the basic theories of fluid statics and dynamics. Applications of solar energy systems, hydraulics, aerodynamics, meteorology, hydrology, and fluidics, environmental conditioning systems, and other subjects. Prerequisite: MATHS 162, PHYCS 330.

title: Applied Solar Energy 1
description: A study of physics and engineering aspects of the solar energy resource, solar collection, concentration, thermal conversion, energy storage, and the design and performance of solar thermal energy systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and MATHS 172 or 162.

title: Applied Solar Energy 2
description: Physics and engineering of solar electric power generation with emphasis on properties of solar cells and design, operation, and performance of photovoltaic systems. Prerequisite: APHYS 420.

title: Heat Transfer
description: The basic heat transfer processes in nature. Conduction, convection, and radiation in applied problems using electricalmodelanalogue, graphical, and computerized numerical methods. Prerequisite: MATHS 162; PHYCS 122; or permission of department chairperson. Department of Physiology and Health Science Schaller, Chairperson; Amschler, Bock, Carroll, Ellis, Ganion, Gobble, Hahn, Henzlik, Jarial, Jones, Kennedy, Lesh, Lindsay, Marini, Paschall, Payne, Pinger, Taylor, Wantz, Womack The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a multidisciplinary study of the life sciences and their application to health promotion, disease prevention, and therapeutic intervention through specific allied health science programs. Physiology is the study of life forms in terms of vital functions of cells, tissues, organs, and systems and their several life processes in relation to both internal and external environments. Anatomy is the specialized investigation of the structure of cells, tissues, organs, and systems, as these constitute the basic units that experience life, health, disease, and death. Health science involves the application of scientific health principles to human life, primarily through programs of health education based in schools, community health agencies, health care facilities, and industrial settings. The goals of health science are to help people make intelligent decisions in solving personal, family, and community health problems and to assist them in leading personally satisfying, socially constructive, healthy lives. The Department of Physiology and Health Science offers a departmental major in health science with options in community health education, health services supervision, and allied health science (for students who have earned associate degrees with electives in nuclear medicine, radiography, or respiratory therapy). In addition, the department offers both a teaching major and a teaching minor designed to meet Indiana state licensing requirements for teaching health and safety in grades 7-12. An endorsement for teaching health science and safety in the elementary school emphasizes competencies for teachers in grades K-6. Two departmental minors are also administered by the department: the physiology minor provides the necessary background for application to appropriate professional schools or to graduate education in anatomy and physiology; the public health minor prepares candidates for entrylevel positions in community health agencies, both governmental and private. BACCALAUREATE DEGREES Associate in Arts—General Arts The department offers courses in allied health science that lead to an associate in arts in general arts degree with electives in nuclear medicine technology, radiography, and respiratory therapy technology. This program is offered in conjunction with Methodist Hospital of Indiana, Inc., and several central Indiana hospitals. Students are required to undergo a selection process for admission to the program and may contact the department chairperson or the appropriate academic adviser for information.
