title: Fundamentals of Public Communication
description: Principles and practice of effective oral communication; analysis and evaluation of the speakinglistening process; preparation in message construction, emphasizing the selection, organization, and delivery of materials.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: Focus on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Stresses the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: Speechmaking as a force in political and intellectual history; critical analysis of selected speeches in relation to political, social, and economic issues. Analysis of issues dealing with problems of progress, reform, and revolution. Emphasis on public address in American social and political institutions. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210 or 240.

title: Contemporary Forms of Persuasion
description: Examines the modes of persuasion reflected in dimensions of American popular culture. Attention focuses on the persuasive appeals employed in forms of popular culture and methods for evaluating their persuasive potential and impact. Stresses the importance of applying communication theory in everyday transactions.

title: Interviewing
description: The principles and types of interviews, with application of the principles in informational, employment, appraisal, and counseling interviews. Consideration of the following aspects of employment seeking: résumé, placement papers, job application, interview, and followup.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Topics in Speech Communication
description: Critical examination of selected topics and issues in speech communication. Designed to help students become familiar with current trends and theoretical and methodological issues in the discipline. May be repeated once by permission of instructor and department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Meeting Management
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Business and Professional Communication
description: Focuses on the communication activities in business and the professions: oral reports, persuasive presentations, interpersonal skills, and communication problemsolving strategies.

title: Nonverbal Communication in Human Interaction
description: Examines the nature, forms, and functions of nonverbal codes in human speech communication. Focuses on understanding one's own nonverbal communication and that of others.

title: Presentational Communication
description: Preparation and delivery of presentations and longer speeches. Examination and analysis of current theories and research in persuasion as they pertain to managers, executives, and other professionals who submit proposals, ideas, and recommendations to the scrutiny of clients, peers, and superiors. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher. A total of 3 hours of credit

title: Practicum in Speech Communication
description: Practical experience in intercollegiate debate, individual events, applied communication research, or alternate speech communication projects. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminartype class focusing on various aspects and problems of speech communication as they relate to people in their personal and professional relationships. Open to honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: The Rhetoric of Political Campaigns
description: Examines the nature, forms, and effects of persuasion in organized political campaigns that seek to influence mass publics. Focuses on the skills needed to describe, analyze, and evaluate persuasive uses of language and to understand better the role of campaign persuasion in influencing voter behavior. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 372.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: Examines contemporary theories, concepts, models, and pertinent research related to the communication process in relatively unstructured facetoface settings. Particular emphasis on understanding message exchanges between people and how they affect the people involved. Introduces students to the approaches, variables, and topics that influence social interaction. Special attention to communication models, perception, symbols, systems, selfconcept, attitudes, meaning, and nonverbal message cues.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of smallgroup literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problem solving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Communication in Organizations
description: The oral communication processes in organizations, with special emphasis upon causes of communication problems and correctives for the problems. Examination of the systems of oral communication within organizations.

title: Communication Consultation
description: Focuses on the role and obligations of the communication consultant. Emphasis is placed upon interpersonal and team decisionmaking skills as well as developing breadth of knowledge, theoretical coherence, and the capacity to employ practical communication analysis and intervention consistent with organizational goals. Prerequisite: SPCH 451.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech Communication pursues a specific subject in depth in consultation with a member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Speech
description: Onthejob experience in such places as college classrooms, political campaigns or offices, summer camps, or summer theaters. Students are permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the credit hours to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in speech and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester. Speech Pathology and Audiology 255 Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology Hoops, Chairperson; Artes, Farling, Heady, Hemeyer, Kramer, Lindell, Martin, Updike Students entering the university who seek state teaching licensure to work in the public schools in speech pathology or audiology must acquire a master's degree as the preservice level of training. Persons with master's degrees may also work in hospital speech and hearing clinics, rehabilitation centers, college or university centers, and communitysponsored speech and hearing agencies. Persons with Ph.D. or Ed.D. degrees usually work in college or university speech and hearing clinics, although many have private practices or serve as consultants to industrial firms. Ball State University offers two undergraduate majors in speech pathology and audiology. Both are departmental majors. One is a departmental major for students who are sure they wish to work eventually in a hospital, college, or community clinic and plan to proceed immediately to the master's degree without acquiring licensure to work in the public schools. The other, identified as a departmental major for those seeking licensure in school services personnel as speech, language, and hearing clinicians or as educational audiologists, is for students who do plan to be eligible for public school employment in these positions. Ball State also offers programs for the master's degree in speech pathology or in audiology, and completion of licensure requirements as a speech, language, and hearing clinician or as an educational audiologist is performed as part of the master's degree program. Completion of clinical practicum hours is a part of master's degree requirements. The master's degree is also required for state licensure through the Health Professions Bureau, for all persons who work in job environments other than the public schools, and for membership in and certification by the American Speech and Hearing Association. Students who participate in the undergraduate and graduate major programs are given clinical experience in four kinds of programs: public school speech, language, and hearing programs; hospitals; preschool nursery programs; and the university Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic, to which children and adults come for clinical work for speech, language, and hearing problems. The department also offers a departmental minor in speech pathology and audiology for students interested in but not committed to this profession, and a departmental minor in speech science for students planning careers in industry or business or in research laboratories dealing with exploration of the parameters of speech or speech identification. Approval to pursue the major programs is based in part upon the student's performance in clinical practicums and is ordinarily considered early in the student's junior year. Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic. Fulltime students enrolled in some major programs of the university are administered a speech and hearing test free of charge. This screening is performed by appointment for new fulltime students. Any speech or hearing problem that may interfere with vocational objectives is called to the attention of the student. Special work for regularly enrolled students who want to correct deficiencies in speech and voice is provided by the clinic, situated on the ground floor of the Arts and Communication Building. Educational work and guidance for persons who have hearing problems are also available. Recommendations for corrective procedures are based on the specific needs of the student. Outpatient speech and hearing evaluation and therapy are integral parts of the clinic program, as is the education of speech pathologists and audiologists. Some classes are available for prospective classroom teachers who want information relative to the management of speech or hearing difficulties. The work of the university clinic is closely associated with that of the Burris School clinic. The clinic is equipped with the latest sound and acoustic devices, including recording machines, tape recorders, recordings, testing materials, audiometers, and other clinical equipment. title: Survey of Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to speech pathology and audiology with a survey of speech and hearing disorders in relation to etiology, incidence, and management.

title: Clinical Phonetics
description: Study of speech sounds as applied to communication disorders. Transcription practice of normal and abnormal speech and the informational, perceptual aspects of phonetics. Relationship and application of distinctive features and phonological analysis to speech remediation. Open only to SPAA majors and minors.

title: Speech Acoustics
description: Introduction to the physical elements of sound, particularly as they apply to communication. Prerequisite: SPAA 201.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of Speech and Hearing
description: Study of the anatomy and physiology of the parts of the body involved in speech production, including respiratory, phonatory, articulatoryresonance, and neurological mechanisms. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 261.

title: Language Development
description: Development of the phonology, grammar, content, and function of language in children together with a review of environmental and personal conditions acting to influence that development.

title: Articulation Disorders
description: Designed to prepare students to diagnose and treat articulatory speech disorders, particularly in younger children. Includes laboratory observation in the treatment of defective speech. Prerequisite: SPAA 201, 261. Open only to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course to assist the beginning clinician in developing an understanding of clinical competency; improves phonetic testing; increases general knowledge of speech problems; develops ability to understand diagnostic principles, procedures, and learning theory; observes and evaluates therapy; and permits selfevaluation. Prerequisite: SPAA 201, 410.

title: Introduction to Diagnosis and Appraisal
description: Techniques in the diagnosis of speech, language, and hearing disorders. Recognizing and understanding the components of differential diagnosis. Prerequisite: SPAA 410. Open only to speech pathology and audiology majors except by permission of department chairperson.

title: Stuttering 1: Research and Theory
description: An introduction to the disorder of stuttering with attention directed to its symptoms and development. Reviews the research and theoretical formulations regarding stuttering and its treatment. Prerequisite: SPAA 410.

title: Organic Speech and Language Disorders
description: An introductory study of neurology and anatomy of the brain and speech and language disorders resulting from brain damage such as Telecommunications 257 cerebral palsy and aphasia. Other physical problems such as cleft palate and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 261, 410.

title: Speech Pathology and Audiology Practicum
description: The student performs observation and preprofessional participation with clients with various speech, language, and hearing disorders. Prerequisite: SPAA 410, 411. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to SPAA majors.

title: Hearing 1: Anatomy, Disorders, and Assessment
description: An overview of the anatomy and physiology of hearing disorders; hearing assessment. The management of school screening programs will be included in the assessment section. Practice in the use of various types of audiometers. Prerequisite: SPAA 260 and 261, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Hearing 2: Aural Habilitation
description: An overview of aural habilitation. The practical implications of various types of hearing losses and appropriate habilitative procedures. Amplification, auditory training, speechreading, education and vocational considerations, and psychosocial implications of hearing loss. Prerequisite: SPAA 443.

title: Directed Study in Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: The student with a major or minor in speech pathology and audiology pursues a specific subject in depth in consultation with a member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to SPAA majors or minors. Department of Telecommunications Kurtz, Chairperson; DeVoe, Gehring, McConnell, Richardson, Wible, Wilhelm The broadcast industries and the motion picture industries provide democratic channels of information, entertainment, and communication. Ball State University has long recognized the appeal that these media have for the mass audience and the important part media play in our everyday lives. For these reasons, the Department of Telecommunications offers a sequence of courses that emphasize the practical applications of these media. The department offers an undergraduate departmental major and minor in these fields. The program in radio, television, film, and corporate video is intended for people pursuing careers in these industries. The selection of courses in the curriculum includes programs for those who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for instruction with the educational aspects of the electronic media in the classroom, or in school administration systems that employ media. Training with professional equipment and the experience gained through the knowledge of operation, coupled with classroom and smallgroup discussion, analyses, and direct study and observation of the broadcast and motion picture industries enable the student to develop advanced skills and knowledge. The facilities of the university radio station, WBST-FM, and the closedcircuit television production facility provide additional practical experiences for the students in the training program. The department's builtin workforce programs and summer internships allow students selected to gain an insight into actual work in their chosen careers. Interns have been placed in markets throughout the United States. The Letterman Telecommunications Scholarships are open to majors and minors in telecommunications as a means to demonstrate their potential of becoming professionals in the industry. One fully funded scholarship (tuition, room and board, personal expenses, and transportation) for one year is awarded each year. The specific amount will be determined by the Office of Student Financial Assistance. A number of partially funded scholarships also are awarded each year. The scholarships are awarded on the basis of a creative endeavor. Grades are not a criterion, and only fulltime, firstsemester juniors through firstsemester seniors are eligible. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 56-58) and by the concentration areas listed below. Standards for selection Telecommunications programs begin with TCOM 200 and 201. To be eligible for either of these courses students must have attained sophomore standing and completed two courses from ENG 099, 103, and 104 with a grade of C or better. Before taking any telecommunications courses other than TCOM 200 and 201, students must have completed BEOA 111 or 112 with a grade of C or better or must have passed a typ_ ing proficiency examination demonstrating the ability to type accurately at least thirtyfive words a minute. Departmental major in telecommunications, 42-45 hours TCOM 200, 210, 240, 300, 400 15 hrs. Complete one option 9-12 hrs. Option 1: Production, 9 hours TCOM 315, 316, and 460 or 477 9 hrs. Option 2: News, 9 hours TCOM 342, 343 6 hrs. From JOURN 210; SPCH 250; POLS 237 3 hrs. Option 3: Sales and management, 12 hours TCOM 360, 362, 463; MKG 300 12 hrs. Option 4: Film, 12 hours TCOM 380, 381, 485 9 hrs. From TCOM 383, 384, 391, 484 3 hrs. One course from each of the options not chosen 9 hrs. Electives in TCOM 9 hrs. Departmental minor in telecommunications, 24 hours TCOM 200, 210, 240, 300, 400 15 hrs. From TCOM 315, 316, 342, 362, 380 9 hrs. Departmental minor in film, 21 hours TCOM 200, 210, 380, 381, 383, 391, 485 21 hrs. (This minor is not open to telecommunications majors.)

title: Developments in Telecommunications
description: An overview of the development of the telecommunications industry. Emphasizes the historical growth of telecommunications as a system in a social setting. Special attention is given to the technological advances that affect the industry. Prerequisite: sophomore standing; grade of C or better in both ENG 103 and

title: Writing for Telecommunications
description: Designed to give students understanding of styles and practice with the styles and techniques used in writing for telecommunications. Students will write extensively, producing scripts for news, commercials, and programs in all media. Prerequisite: TCOM 200 and must have met typing requirement.

title: Law of Telecommunications
description: Familiarizes students with the legal foundations of telecommunications. The course deals with the legal history from 1910 to the present. It covers actions by Congress, U.S. Supreme Court, federal courts, and the states. Special emphasis is given to cases that most affect daily system operations. Prerequisite: TCOM 200.

title: Analysis of Programs and Audiences
description: The course objective is to analyze and appreciate the complexity of programming decision making through examination of concepts, strategies, and techniques in order to better understand the objectives of present day programming at the national and local levels. Students will conduct case studies in programming and audience research. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 210, 240.

title: Multimedia Production 1
description: Basic knowledge and laboratory work in the development of multimedia materials for teaching and presentation. Provides laboratory experience in various mounting, laminating, lettering, coloring, and transparencymaking techniques.

title: Multimedia Production 2
description: Basic photographic and cinematographic techniques. Advanced transparencymaking using photographic processes.

title: Radio and Television Announcing
description: Course concentrates on the practical training and the interpretive vocal skills necessary for announcing. Students will be exposed to use of the vocal system, analysis of copy, and delivery of verbal messages in both radio and television. Presentations focus on news, commercials, and continuity. Prerequisite: TCOM 200.

title: Audio Production
description: A practical skillsoriented course in audio production. Emphasizes production for radio broadcasting, but examines all uses of audio in the media. Students learn skills and techniques of audio production in practical applications to media production situations. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: Video Production
description: A skillsoriented course in the theory and practice of basic television production. Students learn through practicing skills and techniques for crew work in the Telecommunications 259 studio and in the control room. A number of miniproductions, some written by the instructor, some by the student, will give the student experience in basic program formats. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: News Writing and Performance
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering, writing, and reporting broadcast news. Students get practical experience in the uses of audio tape recorders and telephone recording, electronic news gathering (ENG), and other similar equipment used by radio and television news reporters. Prerequisite: TCOM 210.

title: Electronic News Gathering
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering and reporting news with ENG equipment. Practical experience in the techniques of recording and editing with ENG equipment. Prerequisite: TCOM 342.

title: Advertising, Sales, and Promotion in Telecommunications
description: Emphasizes the functions of advertising, sales, and promotion that are unique to broadcasting. Students will study the tools available and develop skills in using them to create effective campaigns. Students will make extensive use of Radio Advertising Bureau, TV Bureau of Advertising, and Broadcast Promotion Association materials as they produce individual projects. Prerequisite: TCOM 240, 300.

title: Promotion in Telecommunications
description: Students develop an understanding of promotional concepts, strategies, and methodologies available for carrying out efficient campaigns in the medium. Students will experience the process of identifying an image and planning an image campaign coordinated with various media. Prerequisite: TCOM 240, 300.

title: World Film History 1
description: History of world cinema from the beginning until World War II. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as key movements in other national cinemas before 1941, such as German Expressionism and the Soviet Montage School. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: World Film History 2
description: Continues the study of world cinema from World War II until the present time. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as the post- 1945 national cinema movements exemplified by Italian Neo-Realism and the French New Wave films. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Film Genres
description: Study of the general types and forms of film expression, each identified with a specific tradition. Film genres include Westerns, screwball comedies, gangster films, musicals, etc. Offered twice each academic year, with a different genre each semester. May be repeated once. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Film Censorship
description: Emphasizes the moral measurements and restraints that have affected the film industry almost since its inception. A chronology of events influencing both the direction and content of motion pictures. Examines governmental, legal, church, and community pressures and restraints. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Telecommunications
description: Exploration of selected issues in telecommunications, with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Open only to honors students. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Film Production
description: A basic introduction to super-8 film production, as well as the theory behind the technique. Students will plan, write, and produce minifilms. Prerequisite: TCOM 300.

title: Social Responsibility in Telecommunications
description: Political, economic, social, and governmental elements that interact with telecommunications. Discussion of major contemporary issues that confront broadcasters and other electronic media operators. Examines the role of ethics involved in the broadcasters' decisionmaking processes. Prerequisite: senior standing and TCOM 240, 300.

title: Advanced Audio -Video Production
description: Provides the student with the opportunity to make practical application of production theory and techniques in the presentation of original audio and video programs. Students serve as producers, writers, and directors of their own projects. Prerequisite: TCOM 315, 316.

title: Management of Telecommunications
description: Acquaints students with the problems and responsibilities of management in the telecommunications industry. Guest lecturers, class discussions, and management roleplaying help students to become familiar with administrative practices in the industry. Prerequisite: senior standing and TCOM 360, 362.

title: Non- Broadcast Television Operations
description: An examination of the special requirements of business, industry', and medicine as they use video production. Special emphasis on management and budgeting productions aimed at instruction, information, promotion, and public relations. Prerequisite: TCOM 210. Prerequisite or parallel: TCOM 316.

title: Non-Broadcast Television Production
description: Video production that meets special requirements of business, industry, and medicine. Planning, identifying needs, executing and evaluating productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 316, 475.

title: Independent Study
description: A special service course. Students enroll with the intent of special study or research on some specific aspect of telecommunications or with the objective of producing a specific program or production. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson after written submission and approval of the topic of study. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester.

title: Internship in Telecommunications
description: Provides opportunity for the student to gain practical onthejob experience with a radio or television station or a company in an allied field. An attempt will be made to place the student in a position of interest to him or her. Prerequisite: junior standing; permission of department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Film and Culture
description: Examines the interaction of film and culture at different times and places in world history, such as the chaos of Germany's Weimar Republic in the 1920s or depression America in the 1930s. May be team taught with faculty from foreign languages, art, and history. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Film Theory
description: An analysis of the key theorists in the history of world cinema, as well as some influential critics of film. A special focus of this course is on the documentary film. The course examines many dimensions of the documentary film: historical, commercial, informational, educational, and propaganda applications. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson and TCOM 380, 381.

title: Research in Telecommunications
description: Acquaints students with principles and methodologies of scholarly research; illustrates applications of research within electronic communication, both for scholarly investigation and for use in support of the functions of broadcasting. Provides principles and practice in writing about results of research. Prerequisite: senior standing. Teachers College Dean, Theodore Kowalski Associate Dean, Roy Weaver The Teachers College has major responsibility for teacher education in the university. Contributions of departments in other colleges to the professional preparation of teachers are coordinated by chairpersons of elementary education and special education and the coordinator of secondary teaching programs, who are responsible to the dean of the Teachers College. Overall policies on teacher education are processed by the Teacher Education Committee, which represents the university as a whole. The Department of Elementary Education prepares teachers and teacher educators in early childhood education, kindergartenprimary education, and elementary education, with programs at all degree levels. The Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education provides the professional education for junior high/middle and secondary school teachers with the exception of special methods. The Department of Special Education offers programs for teachers of the mentally retarded, the hearing impaired, the emotionally disturbed, the physically handicapped, the neurologically impaired/learning disabled, and the multiply handicapped. The Center for Lifelong Education offers programs in curriculum, adult education, and community education. The Burris Laboratory School is a center for demonstration, participation, and research in teacher education, as well as for program development and dissemination in respect to elementary, junior high/middle, and secondary schools. The Department of Educational Psychology offers a program in applications of psychology to teacher education. It also provides service courses as needed for related programs. The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services offers courses and a minor program. Departments in the college, in addition to providing programs for enrolled students, assume active responsibility for field services related to public education and psychology, for production and dissemination of research, for innovation in instructional practices, for demonstration of effective leadership in public and higher education, and for direct human services programs. Courses included in the general field of education serve students in a wide variety of programs and are not appropriately assignable to a single department. title: All- Grade Program Development
description: Provides students seeking allgrade licensure with knowledge of the K-12 school curriculum and organization needed by teachers of special areas in a total school system. Parallel: EDSEC 280. Prerequisite: EDPSY 251 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290.

title: Teachers as Community Leaders
description: Practice in community leadership skills by working in a community agency as a volunteer.

title: Introduction to Computers for Teachers K -12
description: Designed to provide prospective teachers with a basic understanding of the computer curriculum and of computer applications in grades K-12.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in elementary and secondary schools. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Bilingual Theory and Program Development
description: A survey of linguistic, cognitive, and cultural characteristics of bilingualism emphasizing the effects of these languagerelated features on bilingual/bicultural education in the United States. Emphasizes program design, model programs in operation, and legislative mandates.

title: Bilingual Evaluation and Methods
description: Considers the educational needs of bilingual students with specific regard to the evaluation of existing materials, the development of materials, and appropriate bilingual classroom methodology. Prerequisite: EDGEN 370.

title: Honors Colloquium in Education
description: The critical analysis and evaluation of selected controversial issues in American education. Restricted to honors students.

title: Contributions of Social and Cultural Minorities to American Education
description: Analysis of lifestyles of different cultural groups in terms of strengths developed by children that could be taken advantage of in school and other institutions. Flexible attitudes, bilingual/biculturalism, creativity, improvisation, adjustments, and family structures will be emphasized in terms of strengths rather than weaknesses. Approval to Continue a Teaching Curriculum To continue in a teaching curriculum, students must • earn 30 credit hours with an overall gradepoint ratio of at least 2.2. • earn a grade of C or better in EDEL 101 or 160 and 201; or EDSEC 150 (if elected) and EDSEC or EDJHM 205; or SPCED 201. • obtain clearance from the Office of Student Affairs. Burris Laboratory School, a department in the Teachers College of Ball State University, provides an educational program from kindergarten through grade twelve. Observations, individual studies, tutoring, testing, and similar projects can be arranged by contacting the Office of Professional Laboratory Experiences. The office provides assistance in placing students for such activities in all other educational settings for laboratory or field experiences in conjunction with course work or individual selfenhancement for development of teaching skills. To be accepted into a teacher education program and to remain in the program, students must meet the established criteria of various areas that monitor their progress, such as the departments that offer the teaching programs, the Speech and Hearing Clinic, and the Office of Student Affairs. For detailed descriptions of the selection and retention standards for a teaching program, see Selective Retention in Teacher Education above. Students whose approval has been denied or withdrawn may consult the Office of the Associate Provost for Academic Programs and Faculty Development regarding the establishment of a teacher education review committee. The committee is chaired by the dean of Teachers College or the dean's designee. The committee consists of the chair, either the chairperson of elementary education or special education or the coordinator of secondary teaching programs, the associate provost, a representative of the office of professional laboratory experiences (when appropriate), two representatives of the major department, and when appropriate one representative of the minor department. PRE-STUDENT TEACHING PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES The purpose of prestudent teaching professional laboratory experiences is to give students pursuing teacher education a systematic, planned sequence of experiences in appropriate educational settings. These experiences are designed to make students familiar with principles of classroom management and the teachinglearning process in practical and real school environments, and to induct students into the teaching act. The prestudent teaching laboratory experiences culminate in EDEL 360, EDJHM 280, or EDSEC 280, all of which require assignment to classrooms in appropriate educational settings for one semester to observe, prepare instructional presentations, and undertake other instructional tasks appropriate for students before student teaching. The university provides laboratory settings for EDEL 360, EDJHM 280, and EDSEC 280 in the oncampus Burris Laboratory School, as well as in affiliated public school systems in Muncie City Schools and in other school corporations within commuting distance. Weekly seminars with a college supervisor are an integral part of the laboratory experience for these courses. STUDENT TEACHING Student teaching affords students an opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professionally licensed teachers cooperating with the university in the studentteaching program. Application for Student Teaching Students should make application for a studentteaching assignment in January of the year before that in which they expect to do student teaching. Students transferring to Ball State after this date who plan to complete their certification requirements in one year must make application in September. Official notification of the studentteaching assignment will be mailed to the student after the final eligibility determination, usually during the semester before student teaching. Professional Laboratory Experiences 269 Students needing information about their assignments before this notification may inquire at the studentteaching office. General Consideration The student must be free of outside commitments that might interfere with fulltime studentteaching obligations. This means that students cannot be regularly employed, nor should they carry a heavy load of extracurricular activities. Enrollment for course overload during the semester is permitted only with approval of the coordinator for student teaching. Requirements for student teaching also include a predetermined number of days in seminars conducted by the university supervisor, at both the beginning and the end of the semester. Students should be prepared to accept studentteaching assignments wherever the university can place them for the best professional experience. Although requests for particular supervising teachers, schools, or school systems are considered, the placement process requires close cooperation with the public school systems, and there are instances when circumstances within the local school system prohibit a specific placement request. Student Teaching: Secondary and All - Grade License Student teachers preparing to teach at the secondary school level are required to spend full time for a minimum of ten weeks in student teaching. They must enroll for 7 semester hours in EDSEC 460 (4 semester hours) and EDSEC 462 (3 semester hours). Students may take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching (1-5 semester hours), to complete the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: Junior High/Middle School Standard License Student teachers pursuing the junior high/middle school licensure program are required to spend full time for a minimum of ten weeks in student teaching. They must enroll in EDJHM 460 (4 semester hours) and EDJHM 462 (3 semester hours). It is recommended that students take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching, for 1-5 semester hours to complete the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: Elementary Standard License Students seeking licensure in elementary education must enroll for 9 semester hours in EDEL 463 (3 semester hours) and EDEL 464 (6 semester hours) and spend full time for ten weeks in student teaching. Students who wish to take elective credits in student teaching may enroll for up to 3 semester hours in EDEL 465, Elective Student Teaching. Student Teaching: Early Childhood Standard License Students seeking licensure in early childhood education must enroll in EDEL 461 for 6 semester hours and EDEL 462 for 3 semester hours and spend full time for ten weeks in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten -Primary Standard License Students seeking licensure in kindergartenprimary education must enroll for 12 semester hours in EDEL 467 (6 semester hours) and EDEL 468 (6 semester hours) and spend the entire semester in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten Endorsement Students completing the kindergarten endorsement on the standard license for early childhood or elementary education must enroll in EDEL 465 for 3 semester hours for student teaching in the kindergarten. Student Teaching: Special Education Students with an allgrade major in special education will complete SPCED 488 for 9 semester hours in the first area of exceptionality, Teaching the Mildly Mentally Handicapped, for ten weeks of fulltime student teaching. In addition, students must enroll in a second area of exceptionality for 4-9 semester hours in either SPCED 490, Teaching the Physically/Multiply Handicapped, or SPCED 492, Teaching the Moderately Mentally Handicapped, Severely/ Profoundly Mentally Handicapped, and Multiply Handicapped, for another ten weeks of fulltime student teaching. Students with an allgrade major in special education: hearing impaired will complete SPCED 466 (1-12 semester hours) for a minimum of 9 semester hours for ten weeks of fulltime student teaching. Students pursuing a teaching minor or teaching endorsement in special education must complete 6-9 semester hours for ten weeks of fulltime student teaching in the area of exceptionality. Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services Dixon, Chairperson; Barke, Beyerl, Brown, Cartwright, Daly, Dimick, Donn, Duckworth, Gerstein, Hayes, Hendrickson, Hutchinson, Mitchell, Nicholas, Nunnelly, White, Zimmerman The Department of Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services is one of two psychology departments within the Teachers College. The department offers an undergraduate minor in interpersonal relations. The minor is available for students seeking a combination and integration of didactic and experiential work dealing with basic psychological principles and techniques for understanding and developing interpersonal relationships. Emphasis is placed on understanding oneself and the dynamics of interaction with others. Opportunity is provided for students to explore their strengths and weaknesses in interpersonal relationships. The focus is on strategies for gaining life satisfaction and meaning. Courses are also offered to students as electives. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 56-58) and by the concentration area listed below. Departmental minor in interpersonal relations, 15 hours To qualify for admission to CPSY 300- and 400-level courses, students must have earned an accumulative gradepoint ratio of a least 2.6. From CPSY 230, 360, 400, 420, 490 15 hrs. Student may include 6-9 hours of approved electives.

title: Career and Life Planning
description: Focuses on helping the individual to make career and life plans. A series of such techniques as role playing, psychodrama, sociodrama, values clarification, and decision making are used to help students examine interrelated value systems associated with education, work, leisure, and selfexpression. Not open to juniors and seniors except with permission of department chairperson.

title: Human Relationship Development
description: An introduction to the basic psychological principles and techniques of enhancing relationships with self and others. Emphasis given to understanding selflimiting behavior, selfunderstanding, and skill development and knowledge in the dynamics of interaction with others.

title: Interrelational Aspects of Sexuality
description: Emphasizes the psychological aspects of human sexuality, especially in relation to emotions, attitude, and values. Stresses the psychological importance of responsibility for self in sexuality. Considers the psychological aspects of human sexual development, adjustment, dysfunction, and remediation. Designed to increase the students' understanding and acceptance of their own sexuality and that of others.

title: Fundamentals of Counseling
description: Introduces the principles, purposes, and nature of counseling including a review of basic counseling theories and the history of counseling, an exposure to research, and a discussion of issues in the practice of counseling.

title: Techniques of Psychological Interventions
description: Basic psychological principles and techniques of counseling. Intended as an exploratory didactic and experimental course for students planning to do graduate work in counseling and related areas or for those in other fields requiring skills in interviewing.

title: Issues in Counseling
description: Intensive study in selected areas of student need and interest in counseling. Opportunity for students to choose particular areas for indepth study under faculty supervision. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. Educational Psychology 271 Department of Educational Administration and Supervision Riegle, Chairperson; Ballou, Drake, Marconnit, Patton, Swafford, Wagner The Department of Educational Administration and Supervision offers courses and programs designed to serve the needs of elementary and secondary schools and higher education. Programs are designed to prepare persons for such central office administrative and supervisory positions in public schools as those of superintendent, elementary principal, junior high/middle school principal, secondary principal, business manager, director of buildings and grounds, personnel director, and information officer. Other programs prepare specialized personnel for administrative and supervisory responsibilities in fields of education, administrative positions in junior colleges and other collegiate institutions, and administrative positions in educational programs in private industries and foundations. EDUCATION: ADMINISTRATION (EDAD)

title: Legal Aspects of Education for Future Teachers
description: Special attention will focus on legal foundations of education, on rights and responsibilities of teachers (employment, tenure, fringe benefits, liability, and negotiations), and rights and responsibilities of students (attendance, discipline, and due process). Department of Educational Psychology Fischer, Chairperson; Annis, Church, Dean, Glover, Gupta, Henriksen, Hunt, Irving, Joy, Kiem, Kuo, McKee, Paschal, Schurr, Sparzo, Taylor, Treloar, Van Every-Filson, Wenck Educational psychology is a social science concerned with the development of individuals. It includes the study of human development, learning, adjustment, measurement, research, and statistics as these relate to the understanding of an individual. The objectives of educational psychology—like those of other fields of psychology—are to understand, describe, predict, and guide human behavior. These purposes are accomplished through research service functions and teaching about human relationships, human development, and changes in human behavior. Programs in educational psychology are specialized and offered generally on the graduate level. However, a departmental undergraduate minor in the psychology of human development is offered. Some undergraduate courses in the area are required as psychological foundations for teacher education, nursing, and other undergraduate programs, and a number are offered as electives. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (pp. 56-58) and by the concentration area listed below. Departmental minor in psychology of human development, 17 hours From EDPSY 325, 350, 351, 355, 430 8-9 hrs. Approved electives 8-9 hrs.

title: Study Skills for College Students
description: Provides empirically supported study strategies and skills to increase the probability of university success. Focuses on techniques for successful study and test taking. Includes laboratory experiences.

title: Human Growth and Development
description: Development of personality in the Western world from birth through adolescence and application to life in the family, school, community, and broader social situations. Emphasis on physical, motor, social, emotional, and cognitive development and their interweaving relationships, particularly as they apply to the school setting. Should be taken during the sophomore year. PSYSC 100 is a highly recommended elective.

title: Human Growth and Development
description: Development of personality in the Western world, beginning at birth, but placing special emphasis upon the period from preadolescence through adolescence. Emphasis on physical, motor, social, emotional, and cognitive development and their interweaving relationships, particularly as they apply to the school setting. Should be taken during the sophomore year and is intended for students planning to teach in secondary schools. PSYSC 100 is a highly recommended elective.

title: Educational Psychology
description: Psychological principles underlying learning and the improvement of teaching, tests, and measurements. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250 or 251, except for students with a departmental major in dietetics or junior high/middle school education. PSYSC 100 is a highly recommended elective.

title: Independent Study: Educational Psychology
description: Individually planned experiences, extensive independent research in educational psychology. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Behavior Analysis in Education
description: Helps students to translate learning principles into teaching practices, to design and implement behavior analysis procedures that enhance motivation and learning in educational settings and decrease behavior problems, and to assess the effects of such instructional techniques.

title: Psychology of Later Life
description: A study of the later years of life with emphasis on the adaptations required. Includes theories of aging, physical and social changes taking place, and coping strategies. Not open to the student who has credit in EDGER 325.

title: Educational Tests and Measurement
description: Standard educational tests and the use of such tests as instruments for the evaluation of learning. Techniques of test construction.

title: Child Psychology
description: Study of the psychology of childhood, with special emphasis on various psychological influences contributing to child development.

title: Adolescent Psychology
description: A study of childhood influences upon the adolescent period, of the psychology of the adolescent period, and of the effects of that development during young adulthood. Emphasis on various psychological influences contributing to adolescent development.

title: Adult Psychology
description: Developmental study of psychological stages of adulthood. Not open to the student who has credit in EDAC 355.

title: Mental Hygiene
description: Psychological principles underlying mental health and the application of these principles in and out of the classroom. Prerequisite: 6 hours of psychology.

title: Seminar in Educational Psychology
description: Group or individual investigation and study of current issues, problems, and developments in human development, classroom learning, and evaluation. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may earned. title: Introduction to Teaching in the Elementary School: Seminar and Laboratory
description: Work with elementary schoolage children of a variety of cultural and ethnic backgrounds with opportunities through seminars and counseling to plan and evaluate experiences and to begin to develop skills, attitudes, and understanding necessary for successful communication with children as an orientation to teaching in the elementary school. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 2 in one semester.

title: Laboratory Experiences: Multiethnic Young Children
description: A lab -seminar working with preschoolaged children of a variety of cultural and ethnic backgrounds with opportunities through seminars and conferences to begin to develop skills, attitudes, and understanding necessary for successful communication with children as an orientation to teaching preschool children. Prerequisite: permission of the coordinator of early childhood education or department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Interaction Skills for the Young Child
description: Introduces students to basic skills every young child needs to acquire in order to use language competently in society. Deals with materials, methods, principles of learning, and conditions necessary for optimum learning.

title: Curriculum and Lab Experiences in Early Childhood Education 1
description: A field and seminar experience focusing on the young child and his or her learning environment and how adults apply this knowledge in early childhood education. Open to students enrolled in the twoyear early elementary education program. Prerequisite: EDEL 160 and permission of the coordinator of early childhood education or department chairperson.

title: Organization and Management of the Multicultural Classroom
description: The role of the teacher as the facilitator for learning in the elementary classroom with opportunites through seminars and counseling to plan and evaluate experiences and to begin to develop skills, attitudes, and understanding necessary for successful communication with children of various ethnic and cultural groups. Prerequisite: EDEL 101. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Writing
description: Development of skills in manuscript and cursive writing, methods of teaching handwriting in the elementary school, and relationship of manuscript and cursive writing to the language arts.

title: Principles of Organization and Management in Early Childhood
description: Development of understanding and skills needed for effective teacherpupil, teacherparent, and teacherteacher relationships in school settings for young children.

title: Curriculum and Lab Experiences in Early Childhood 2
description: A field and seminar experience focusing on the selection and organization of learning experiences appropriate for individual children. Need identification, identification of appropriate childcare facilities, and the students' role as members of a staffing team. Open only to students in the twoyear elementary education program. Prerequisite: EDEL 190 and permission of coordinator of early childhood education or department chairperson.

title: Creative Experiences for Young Children
description: Designed to develop awareness of and skill in providing creative experiences for the young child. Working with children is an integral part of the course.

title: Curriculum and Lab Experiences in Early Childhood 3
description: A field and seminar experience to assist the classroom teacher in the implementation of educational opportunities for young children under supervision of a university faculty member or agency representative. Prerequisite: minimum of 36 hours in early elementary education courses, always including EDEL 160, 190, 241, and permission of the early childhood coordinator or department chairperson.

title: Materials and Techniques for Teaching Children of Multiethnic Backgrounds
description: Designed to offer multisensory approaches to learning. Attempts will be made to identify learning methods and materials best suited to the students' style of learning.

title: Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Elementary School
description: Problems of school organization, management, control, and environment in relation to the learning activities of children. Stresses legal rights and responsibilities of teachers and use of instructional media. Prerequisite: EDEL 101, 20I, and approval to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290, except for majors in special education.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Lower Elementary Grades
description: Development of language arts skills—listening, speaking, reading, and writing—in the primary grades.

title: The Social, Historical, and Philosophical Foundations of Elementary Education
description: Emphasizes historical and social derivations of contemporary educational ideas, philosophical foundations of educational practices, alternatives for ethical decisions in education, and formulation of a personal philosophical position related to educational issues in elementary education.

title: Computer Literacy in the Elementary School Classroom
description: Develops computer literacy and application for elementary school instruction. Introduces programming in BASIC, evaluation of software, and methods of developing literacy in children. Handson experience with microcomputers.

title: Discipline and Classroom Management: Some Practical Approaches
description: Designed to help beginning elementary school teachers create and maintain effective learning environments. Emphasizes practical approaches to prevention and remediation of disruptive classroom behavior.

title: Parent and Community Relations
description: Explores important and complex roles of parents and parent substitutes in the educational development of young children. Factors affecting parentchild interactions and skills needed for effective parenting are studied and related to the educational process. Parent involvement as a significant factor in early childhood education.

title: Kindergarten Education
description: Development of the kindergartenprimary curriculum with special emphasis on kindergarten children and procedures to be used in their development.

title: Educational Programs for Pre -Kindergarten
description: Activities of young children in prekindergarten. Organization, administration, and educational program of prekindergarten care. Child development and parent education as part of prekindergarten education.

title: Foundations of Early Childhood Education
description: Involves experiences to enrich the relationships among parents, teachers, and children in the home, school, and community environments and to acquaint and involve students with the variety of community resources concerned with the welfare of young children and their families.

title: Psychology of Early Childhood
description: Study of young children of nursery school and kindergarten age involving lectures, readings, discussions, and conferences to give individual guidance to students and help them interpret their study of the physical, mental, social, and emotional development of selected young children. Consideration is given to growth in perception, language, expression, and interests.

title: Student Teaching: Pre - Kindergarten
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 461 (6) and EDEL 462 (3) for a total of 9 semester hours. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Pre - Kindergarten
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 462 (3) and EDEL 461 (6) for a total of 9 semester hours. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Elementary School
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 463 (3) and EDEL 464 (6) for a total of 9 semester hours. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Elementary School
description: Students enroll simultaneously for EDEL 464 (6) and EDEL 460 (3) for a total of 9 semester hours. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Elementary
description: Part - time student teaching for ten weeks in an area of endorsement. Taken in a different semester and in addition to the regular student teaching requirement for elementary education. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Student Teaching: Primary Grades
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in primary grades the oppportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the university in the studentteaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 468. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Student Teaching: Kindergarten
description: Designed to provide students preparing to teach in kindergarten the opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professional teachers cooperating with the university in the studentteaching program. Must be taken in conjunction with EDEL 467. Prerequisite: EDEL 360.

title: Practicum in Elementary Education
description: Laboratory and seminar course involving a study of progressive school practices; the philosophy of education underlying and the possibilities of using progressive practices in the public school. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Elementary Education
description: Independent study and research in elementary education. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems in Elementary Education
description: An analysis of one's professional preparation for teaching, identifying areas in which students need to bolster weaknesses and augment strengths, and arranging for more preparation in these areas. Prerequisite: one term of student teaching. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned. EDUCATION: READING (EDRDG)

title: Self-Improvement in Reading
description: A remedial course designed to improve comprehension skills, reading speed, vocabulary, notetaking, and content reading. Students who do not achieve the 30th percentile in comprehension on the Diagnostic Reading Tests or a selected reading test administered by Reading Programs and Services must repeat the course. The course is offered on a credit/nocredit basis, and credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: College Reading Skills
description: Emphasizes development of the ability to read collegelevel materials critically from a variety of subject areas and to develop flexibility of rate.

title: Rapid Reading Techniques
description: Rapid reading techniques of previewing, skimming, and scanning will be practiced. Machines available. Rate of comprehension and flexibility of rate will be emphasized. Techniques will be applied to student's reading assignments. Open to all graduate and undergraduate students who have basic mastery of reading skills.

title: Prereading Development
description: Basic understanding of environments and planned activities that foster positive attitudes and interests related to reading, procedures that stimulate prereading development, and related practical experiences with young children.

title: Teaching of Reading in Elementary School
description: Designed to review the current thinking, approaches, and methodology of teaching reading in today's schools. Attention is directed to readiness, word recognition and analysis, comprehension, and planning of the total developmental reading program, with emphasis on reading at the elementary level. Prerequisite: EDEL 380, or permission of director of reading.

title: Developmental and Corrective Reading
description: Designed to review current thinking, approaches, and methodology of teaching developmental reading in the elementary schools. Provides prospective teachers with understanding of difficulties in reading and practical experiences in assessing reading difficulties and in study of corrective treatment. Includes guided laboratory experience. Prerequisite: EDRDG 400 or EDRDS 320 or EDRDG 321.

title: Using Computers in Reading Instruction
description: Prepares the prospective elementary school teacher to make appropriate and effective use of the computer in a classroom reading program. Includes attention to commercially prepared courseware and teacherdeveloped applications. Prerequisite: EDGEN 320 for students pursuing the computer endorsement. EDRDG 400 or equivalent for all others.

title: Reading Strategies and Practicum
description: Provides prospective classroom teachers (K-12) with opportunities to study and try various approaches and strategies in teaching reading. Provides experience in grouping students of varying reading abilities and in planning and implementing a classroom reading program appropriate for these students. Prerequisite : EDRDG 40 or 430.

title: Independent Study in Reading
description: Designed to meet the needs of students wishing to study in individually selected areas of reading education. Prerequisite: 6 hours of credit in reading education and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. PREPARATION OF TEACHERS FOR MULTICULTURAL SECONDARY SCHOOLS (MULTICUL) The MULTICUL program offers students an opportunity to study possible solutions to the problem of developing racial and cultural harmony. The program is not designed to deal only with black and white relations, but rather with as many ethnic groups as possible. Multiculturalism is a basic characteristic of our society as well as of our schools; therefore, potential teachers should prepare themselves to meet realistic situations. Three of the experiences that the MULTICUL program uses in the preparation of potential teachers are • specialized or elective courses offered in many major departments • courses designed especially for MULTICUL students by the Department of Secondary, Higher, and Foundations of Education • laboratory experiences in multicultural communities, social and professional organizations, and schools. title: Discipline: Improving Student Behavior in Junior High/Middle School
description: Designed to prepare prospective junior high/middle school educators to cope with discipline problems in all junior high/middle school settings. description: An introduction to microcomputers and information systems in library automation.

title: Online Information Retrieval Techniques
description: Provides overview of online information services and principles of information retrieval. Students develop search strategies to meet client's information needs and conduct online searches in a supervised laboratory.

title: Methods and Materials for School Library Media Centers
description: Methods and materials for teaching students skills necessary for successful completion of assignments using resources of school library media centers and libraries. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Selection of Audiovisual Materials and Microcomputer Software
description: Selection and evaluation of audiovisual materials and microcomputer software for instructional and management use in libraries. Systematic identification of sources and selection tools. Practice in selection and evaluation.

title: Production of Audiovisual Media
description: A project course that meets the individual needs of undergraduate students in the production of such instructional media as 8 and 16 mm films, filmstrips, slide sets, and tape recordings.

title: Selection of Library Materials
description: Fundamental principles and objectives of selection of library materials. Development of skill in using reliable aids for selection and evaluation of materials for public, academic, and school libraries.

title: Materials for Children
description: Reading and examining books and other materials for the enrichment of library programs for preschool through upper elementary.

title: Materials for Young Adults
description: Reading and examining books and other materials for young adult programs. EDUCATION: READING MIDDLE (EDRDM)

title: Improving General Reading Skills in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: A general course for all junior high/middle school teachers that examines reading problems and provides specific methodology for improvement of reading skills in junior high/middle schools. General diagnostic teaching techniques appropriate for teachers in all curricular areas are to be achieved. Exit competencies are required. EDUCATION: READING SECONDARY (EDRDS)

title: Reading in Secondary School
description: Practical procedures for developing effective reading skills to be applied by all secondary classroom teachers. Focuses on relationships between the process of reading and learning of content, on planning to meet total range of student reading needs, and on methods and materials to enhance comprehension and study skills in all areas of secondary school curriculum. EDUCATION: SECONDARY (EDSEC)

title: Basic Concepts of Secondary Education
description: Using classroom investigation and practical field experiences, examines the structure, function, and development of secondary education in the United States. Designed to help students make valid decisions about preparing for and functioning in teaching careers by studying professionalism, job requirements, employment opportunities, secondary school curricula, and the role of secondary education within the entire educational process.

title: Introduction to Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Introduces prospective teachers to responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 206 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Advanced study of responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, supporting personnel, and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 200.

title: Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior in American Secondary Schools
description: Analyzes factors that influence the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in schools and educational settings. Particular emphasis on the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in the American secondary schools. Not open to students with credit in EDJHM 205. Laboratory included.

title: Advanced Study of Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior
description: Focuses on indepth analyses of many of the concepts introduced in EDSEC 205. Particular emphasis on variables that contribute to the development and maintenance of prejudice, stereotypes, racism, and oppressive conditions. Equal emphasis on instructional strategies for combating such behaviors. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 or EDJHM 205 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Laboratory Experience in Secondary Education
description: Provides direct experiences in working with students, teachers, paraprofessionals, community agencies, and other appropriate assignments for undergraduate students who plan to enter secondary school teaching. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Microcomputers in the Secondary School
description: Provides a basic understanding of the functions and applications of microcomputers in the classroom setting. Topics include evaluation and use of available software, introduction to the development of teachermade software, and the availability and selection of hardware.

title: Principles of Teaching and Classroom Management: Secondary School
description: Inducts the student into the teaching act. Includes specific technical skill development, legal implications, study of principles of teaching, application of instructional media, curriculum development and organization, classroom management, and discipline. Intensive inschool assignments, observation, skills, participation, and direct contact with adolescents are required. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205, EDPSY 251, and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290.

title: Instructional Strategies in Multicultured Schools
description: Theory and application of special instructional strategies of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms with special emphasis on multicultured educational situations. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 or EDJHM 205 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Planning and Assessing Instructional Programs
description: Designed to provide secondary school teachers with methods of establishing instructional programs with feedback networks that will encourage continuous assessment and appropriate alterations of the educational environment. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Intermediate Study of Microcomputers in the Secondary School
description: Designed to help students understand and develop the application of computerassisted instruction to their respective disciplines. Prerequisite: EDGEN 320 for students pursuing the computer endorsement. EDSEC 255 for all others.

title: Independent Study in Secondary Education
description: Independent study and research in secondary education. Topics and activities to be chosen in consultation with an instructor with competence in the subject involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems in Education and Professional Concerns of the Beginning Teacher
description: Provides opportunity to examine critically and to focus educational experience and knowledge on contemporary and personally significant problems of education. Emphasizes immediate professional concerns of prospective firstyear teachers. Prerequisite: EDSEC 301 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Social Foundations of Secondary Education
description: Education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from sociological, philosophical, historical, economic, political, and anthropological perspectives. Such contemporary issues as cultural values, social class, legal aspects, ethnic groups, political pressure, and the role of the teachers will be stressed. Prerequisite: EDSEC 280.

title: High School Curriculum
description: General perspectives of curriculum principles, practices, and procedures common to secondary schools. Organizational structures, innovations, and intimate relationships between instruction and curriculum. Concurrently, students will choose areas of concentration or preparation as they relate to the total high school curriculum.

title: Discipline: Improving Student Behavior in Secondary Schools
description: Designed to prepare prospective secondary teachers to cope with discipline problems in all secondary school settings. Emphasizes skills and procedures for preventing or remedying disruptive behavior by secondary students and ways to create a positive environment for learning.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the standard license in secondary education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 462 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for ten weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching: Secondary School
description: Required for the standard license in secondary education. Simultaneous registration in EDSEC 460 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for ten weeks in a public secondary school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Secondary
description: Parallel: EDSEC 460, 462 or EDJHM 460, 462 and admission to student teaching. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned.

title: General Innovations in Secondary Education
description: Innovative practices will be identified, defined, and analyzed relative to their impact on secondary schools. Creative, innovative instructional approaches will be used. Field trips or visitations to innovative secondary schools will be arranged when practical, and students will concentrate on innovative practices.
