title: People and Chemistry
description: Introductory treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as organization and language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature and classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these to everyday living. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 101, 111.

title: General, Organic, and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of general chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences and related areas. Four hours of lecture and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 111.

title: General Chemistry 1
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, properties of solutions, and nature of matter. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or equivalent.

title: General Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemical kinetics, electrochemistry, chemical equilibrium, chemistry of metals and nonmetals, and radioactivity. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 111, MATHS 108.

title: Survey of Organic and Biochemistry
description: A broadly based introductory course suitable for life science, natural resources, and general science majors. Three hours of lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Lecture and intensive laboratory treatment of the theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements, including gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations, ion exchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visible spectrophotometry. One and onehalf hours of lecture and four and onehalf hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: Nomenclature, structure, bonding, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 234.

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of natural products and biomolecules. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 235.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material includes nomenclature, covalent bonding, molecular structure, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Laboratory experience includes spectroscopy and syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: A continuation of CHEM 234, including the properties of carbohydrates, proteins, and other natural products. Laboratory experience includes qualitative organic analysis and multistep syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 234.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentation: electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods. For chemical/medical technologists or departmental minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: Thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Chemistry 185 Prerequisite: CHEM 232, MATHS 172, one year of college physics.

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 344, including theoretical aspects of quantum mechanics and spectroscopy. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 344.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics. Especially for premedical, biology, and general science majors, chemistry teaching majors, and chemistry minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225, MATHS 161. Not open to the student who has credit in CHEM 344.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry
description: Organic chemistry of carboxylic acids, amines, and their derivatives; biochemistry of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids; metabolism and the regulation of metabolic processes. For students in life sciences, dietetics, and medical technology. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory session weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or equivalent. Not open to departmental majors in chemistry.

title: Practical Experience in Chemistry
description: Paid work and learning experience as a practicing chemist. Practical problemsolving experience will be gained through such programs as internships, practicums, cooperative education programs, and the Department of Chemistry summer research program. Prerequisite: application, recommendation of the program selection committee, and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. One hour may be counted toward the associate in science in chemical technology degree. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward the departmental major.

title: Specialized Topics in Chemistry
description: Discussion, experimentation, or both in specialized topics in and related to chemistry. Information concerning specific topics offered during a given semester may be obtained from the departmental office. Lecture, discussion, and laboratory schedules appropriate to the topic offered. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 hour may be counted toward departmental major or minor requirements.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for chemical technologists. Assignments equivalent to four clock hours a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of department chairperson. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry.

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Prerequisite: 20 hours of chemistry or permission of department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 1
description: Theoretical principles and application of selected spectroscopic and nuclear methods, with illustrative experiments. Two hours of lecture and one threehour lab period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 345 or 346 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 2
description: Theoretical principles and application of selected chromatographic, electroanalytical, and mass spectroscopic methods. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 420 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Qualitative Organic Analysis
description: Laboratory intensive study of the theory and practice of structure determination of organic compounds by classical and spectroscopic methods, including separations and identification of components in mixtures. Six hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232.

title: Physical -Organic Chemistry
description: Theoretical aspects of structure, including resonance and molecular orbital descriptions of electron distribution, aromaticity, symmetry, stereochemistry, and effects of structure on reactivity in acidbase reactions. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements, including the relationships of chemical properties and atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, acidbase theories, chemical periodicity, and modern theories of coordination compounds. Four hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235, MATHS 161 or 171.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 1
description: Chemistry and techniques for isolation, purification, and identification of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. For students majoring in chemistry, life sciences, and premedicine. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 463 including biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids; and regulation of metabolic processes. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 463.

title: Independent Study and Research
description: Scientific investigation on an individual basis under the supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, experimental work, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward any departmental major. DEPARTMENT OF COMPUTER SCIENCE C. Fuelling, Chairperson; K. Bagga, K. Keil, R. McCormick, J. McGrew, E. McKinney, C. Nelson, F. Owens, R. Place, C. Tzeng, M. Underkoffler, W. Zage Computer science is concerned with collection, storage, retrieval, and processing of data and information, as well as with the data structures, algorithms, and computer programs used to perform these tasks. The departmental major in computer science with its special emphasis on software is accredited by the Computer Science Accreditation Board. A cooperative education program is available to majors in computer science. Students may enter this program after the completion of two semesters (minimum 30 credits) in which they have earned minimum cumulative gradepoint averages of 3.0 in the required computer science and mathematics courses and at least 2.5 in all courses. The cooperative director in the Department of Computer Science advises students in this program and assists in the work placement of each student. The university cannot guarantee work assignments for all students. To be admitted to a major or minor program in computer science, students must have a mathematical background strong enough to take the first required calculus course, MATHS 161. Transfer students applying for admission to the computer science program must submit transcripts of credits and catalog course descriptions of the computer science courses for which they want to transfer credit. To remain in the computer science program, students must earn combined gradepoint averages of at least 2.5 in MATHS 161, 162; CS 120, 121, 230, and 332 with grades of at least C in each course. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (p. 21), the program of general studies (p. 23) and the concentration areas listed below. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN COMPUTER SCIENCE, 68-86 hours Option 1, 68-70 hours

title: Coop Orientation
description: Seminar for students entering the coop program in computer science. Topics include responsibilities of the coop student and the employer, résumé preparation, job interview training, types of job placement available, general coop program administration and requirements. May be taken only for credit/nocredit. Prerequisite: major in computer science in progress and permission of department chairperson. Open only to computer science majors.

title: Introduction to Microcomputers
description: Covers computer literacy topics including a brief history of computing, current trends in the use of microcomputers, and the impact of computers on society. To understand microcomputers better, students work through an integrated software package and write and debug a number of short BASIC programs. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 114.

title: Introduction to Programming 1
description: Problems of programming in a structured language emphasizing topdown design and modular structure. Designed primarily for students in the computer endorsement program. Prerequisite: MATHS 125, 201, or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 120 or equivalent.

title: Introduction to Programming 2
description: An introduction to files and their applications. An introduction to a LOGO environment. Prerequisite: CS 110 or equivalent. Open only to students not majoring in computer science.

title: Computer Literacy for Nonprogrammers
description: Presents the computer as a tool for students majoring in other disciplines to solve problems arising in their subjects. The student will use such software as spreadsheets, databases, and word processing and will develop vocabulary. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 121.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines other than computer science. Timesharing computer techniques using BASIC with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 118, 120, 121, 210, or BEOA 210.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Programming in FORTRAN. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Introduces timesharing techniques. Prerequisite: MATHS 117. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 120.

title: Computer Programming 1
description: Introductory programming in PASCAL in a timesharing environment. Covers topics such as concepts of computers and programming, data types, statements, expressions, input and output of data, basic control structures, procedures and functions, arrays, files, and editing. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161.

title: Computer Programming 2
description: Advanced programming in PASCAL. Includes such topics as Boolean variables, files, linked lists, pointer variables, stacks, hashing, recursion, and binary searching. Prerequisite: CS 120 and MATHS 161.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and CR HRS topics that emphasize application in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: CS 110 or 116 or 118 or 120. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 240 or MGS 213.

title: Discrete Structures
description: Introduction to topics in discrete structures for computer science majors. Topics include propositional and predicate logic, sets, induction, recursion, relations, functions, combinatorial enumeration, Boolean algebra, and finite state machines. Applications of these topics to computer science are discussed. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Assembler Language Programming
description: Introduction to computer architecture, machine and assembly languages. Includes fixedpoint, floatingpoint, and decimal arithmetic, character and bit manipulation, looping, branching, macros, and subroutines. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Microcomputer System Architecture
description: Elements of microcomputer system architecture and organization. Topics to be discussed include processors, primary and secondary memory systems, and networking principles. Prerequisite: CS 110 or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 333.

title: Microcomputer Database
description: Considers how database techniques may be used in personal computer applications, how to design and develop database applications, and how to select a database product for a personal computer. Prerequisite: CS 104. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 436.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Use of COBOL to solve problems in file maintenance, report writing, and sorting. Emphasizes directaccess processing techniques including development of interactive screens. Further study of IBM JCL. Prerequisite: CS 121, 230.

title: Micrcomputer Operating Systems
description: Introduction to operating systems for the microcomputer. Topics related to concurrency, process and resource management, input/output control, and design problems are discussed. Comparisons of current microcomputer operating systems will be studied. Prerequisite: CS 233. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 476.

title: Recent Computer-Related Developments
description: Current topics related to the development and uses of the computer in society are discussed. Topics covered will vary as the discipline of computer science changes. Prerequisite: CS 276.

title: Combinatorial Algorithms
description: A study of the analysis, design, and complexity of combinatorial algorithms with applications to computer and information science. Course assignments include the implementation of various algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 121, 224, and MATHS 212.

title: Data Structures
description: Data structures including stacks, queues, trees, tables, lists, strings, arrays, and files. Studies implementation techniques and algorithms for the management of these structures. Prerequisite: CS 121, 224, 230.

title: Computer Hardware Systems
description: Introduction to computer logic and registertransfer level of systems description. Examines the basic building blocks of a computer system and studies various computer architectures and hardware trends. Develops a general methodology for computer selection and introduces microprogramming. Prerequisite: CS 224, 230 and MATHS 212.

title: Introduction to Computer Graphics Systems
description: An introduction to computer graphics software and hardware including computerassisted design systems, interface programming, user interfaces, and presentation graphics programming. Prerequisite: proficiency in a highlevel programming language like PASCAL, FORTRAN, or C (CS 118 or CS 121 or equivalent).

title: Advanced Topics Seminar
description: Indepth study of a topic taught in a seminar format. Advanced postings of topics will be made in the department before registration. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Computer Science 189

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation. Use of higher level languages and simulation languages in system studies. Students use examples from different subjects to carry out simulation. Prerequisite: CS 121 and MATHS 181 or equivalent.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analyses, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 118 or 121 and MATHS 162. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and CS 362 or MATHS 362. Not open to the student who has credit in MATHS 363.

title: Professional Experience
description: Professional computing experience in an approved program with computing facilities in business and industry. Requires periodic reports. Credit/nocredit only. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 in any one semester or term.

title: Systems Programming
description: Considers the computer system from the points of view of its architecture, operating system, and applications. Topics include processor organization, peripheral devices, I/O programming, system programs, monitor services, file organization, and realtime applications. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Programming Languages
description: A comparative study of programming languages. Emphasizes syntactic specification of programming languages and important features, structures, and compile and runtime characteristics of various higher level languages. Prerequisite: CS 230, 332

title: Database Design
description: An introduction to database design, including physical representation, modeling, database systems, and implementation. Prerequisite: CS 332 and knowledge of C, COBOL, or FORTRAN.

title: Computer Graphics
description: Methods of developing, modifying, and rendering graphics displays. Emphasizes the design and writing of graphics software for both twoand threedimensional displays. Knowledge of a structured highlevel language is required. Prerequisite: CS 332 and MATHS 212.

title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
description: Introduction to basic programming techniques of artificial intelligence (Al). Primary contents are symbol manipulations and Al problemsolving techniques. Topics include LISP primitives, LISP objects and evaluation, recursion and iteration, data abstraction (association lists, properties, and DESTRUCT), macros, objectcentered programming, symbolic pattern matching, and basic problemsolving methods. Prerequisites: CS 324, 435.

title: Principles of Computer Vision and Machine Intelligence
description: Laboratory based, dealing with the basic principles of acquisition and analysis of visual images by means of the computer. Studies the incorporation of vision in machine (robot) operation. Artificial intelligence techniques applied to task planning are used in integrating visual images with manipulator actions. Prerequisite: CS 333 or permission of instructor.

title: Theory of Computation 1
description: Mathematical logic; alphabets and languages; finite automata, regular and nonregular languages, Kleene's theorem; regular grammars; pushdown automata and contextfree grammars; Turing and Post machines; recursive and recursively enumerable languages; the Chomsky Hierarchy. Prerequisite: CS 324, 435.

title: Operating Systems
description: The functions and structure of computer operating systems, processors, memory, and device management. Concurrency and process synchronization. Input/output handling, device drivers, and disk scheduling. File systems, operating system design philosophy. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Software Engineering 1 —Systems Analysis
description: Software life cycle, software engineering concepts, systems analysis phase of life cycle. Introduces and applies structured methods to a project. The output of the project is a systems specification from which a software system can be designed and developed. Prerequisite: CS 332, 333.

title: Software Engineering 2—Design and Development
description: Studies the design and development phases of the software life cycle. Introduces the latest appropriate structured methods and applies them to a software project. This project will take a system specification and develop software from it. Prerequisite: CS 240, 497.

title: Readings and Honors
description: Special advanced studies of computer science topics not taught in other courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. DEPARTMENT OF CRIMINAL JUSTICE AND CRIMINOLOGY D. Smith The Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology offers a variety of courses that help students understand the dimensions and causes of crime and delinquency, theories of crime prevention and control, the structure and philosophy of the American criminal justice system, the operation of criminal courts at the local, state, and federal levels, the techniques and theories of law enforcement, and the philosophies and practices of various correctional programs. Students are prepared for entrylevel professional positions in the criminal justice system as well as for graduate study in related subjects. title: Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
description: An overview of the criminal justice system and a summary of vocational opportunities.

title: Research Methods in Criminal Justice
description: An introduction to research methods pertinent to the study of crime, criminality, and the criminal justice system. Criminal Justice and Criminology 191 Emphasis will be on computer applications in the design, development, interpretation, and use of both quantitative and qualitative research. Prerequisite: CJC 101.

title: Data and Theories of Crime and Delinquency
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior, typologies of crime and criminals; the trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and current theoretical explanations.

title: Processing Adult and Juvenile Offenders
description: Emphasizes the juvenile and adult justice systems, their components, recent changes, and anticipated future developments.

title: Policing in American Society
description: Examination and analysis of the development of the police in America in the past, present, and future. Emphasizes institutional context of police activity, bureaucratization of the police, professionalization, the role of the police, and the police and community change.

title: Women and Crime
description: An examination of traditional and contemporary explanations of female delinquency and criminality, the differential treatment accorded female defendants and victims, and the nature of state and federal correctional systems for women.

title: Organized Crime
description: The nature and structure of organized crime in America with special emphasis on the history and changing images of organized crime, its operation and activities, and programs for control.

title: Victimology
description: A criminological examination of the victims of crime in contemporary America.

title: Criminal Law
description: Emphasis on the practical aspect of the application of Indiana criminal law for present and prospective criminal justice practitioners: purposes and functions of the substantive criminal law; historical foundations; the limits of the criminal law. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 340 or 350.

title: Criminal Evidence and Investigation
description: Legal, ethical, and theoretical issues surrounding policies, procedures, and standards of criminal evidence and investigation.

title: Institutional Corrections
description: An indepth inquiry into the function, structure, and operations of American adult and juvenile correctional institutions.

title: Community Corrections
description: The organization and operation of communitybased correctional programs throughout the United States. Topics include probation, parole, halfway houses, group homes, diversion, restitution, and community service programs, with an emphasis on the most popular programs and practices.

title: Paid Internship in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Paid fulltime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. Not open to the student who has credit in CJC 472. Open only to senior criminal justice majors.

title: Honors Colloquium in Criminal Justice
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in criminal justice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Open only to honors students; others by permission of department chairperson.

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in criminal justice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Topics may include crisis intervention, historical criminology, whitecollar crime, and others of current interest. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in one semester or term.

title: Practicum in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Parttime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of department chairperson.

title: Internship in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Fulltime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: An individualized course of reading or limited research designed to allow majors an opportunity to explore specific topics related to the criminal justice system under the direction of a specific faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Open only to students majoring in criminal justice and criminology. title: Grammar 1
description: Oral and written practice in graded grammatical exercises. Prerequisite: permission of program director.

title: Reading 1
description: Reading in basic EFL texts with emphasis on linguistic and cultural problems of reading in English as a foreign language. Prerequisite: permission of program director.

title: Speaking 1
description: Speaking practice with emphasis on building vocabulary and developing oral fluency. Prerequisite: permission of program director.

title: Listening Comprehension 2
description: Continued practice in comprehension of normal spoken American English. Prerequisite: ENEFL 115 or permission of program director.

title: Writing 2
description: Practice in increasingly advanced grammatical structures with emphasis on vocabulary and idiom building. Prerequisite: ENEFL 121 or permission of program director.

title: Grammar 2
description: Oral and written practice in graded grammatical exercises. Review of elementary grammar. Prerequisite: ENEFL 122 or permission of program director.

title: Reading 2
description: Reading in intermediate EFL texts with emphasis on linguistic and cultural problems or readings in English as a foreign language. Prerequisite: ENEFL 123 or permission of program director.

title: Speaking 2
description: Speaking practice with emphasis on building vocabulary and developing oral fluency. Increasing use of newspaper and magazine articles as sources of topics. Prerequisite: ENEFL 124 or permission of program director.

description: Continued practice in comprehension of

title: Pronunciation
description: American English segmental and prosodic systems. Practice for accuracy in production of diphthongs, unstressed syllables, and reduced segments. Prerequisite: permission of program director.

title: Writing 3
description: Development of paragraph forms with emphasis on logic and coherence, grammatical variations, diction, and idiom. Prerequisite: ENEFL 131 or permission of program director.

title: Grammar 3
description: Development of grammatical variants and increasingly complex and specialized structures. Prerequisite: ENEFL 132 or permission of program director.

title: Reading 3
description: Reading in both prepared and unadapted English. Selections from general English as well as from technical fields with emphasis on linguistic and cultural problems and critical response. Prerequisite: ENEFL 133 or permission of program director.

title: Speaking 3
description: Continued speaking practice with emphasis on speaking for academic purposes. Student presentations and discussion. Examination of issues of current interest. Prerequisite: ENEFL 134 or permission of program director.

title: Cross-Cultural Studies 1
description: Topics include U.S. and international politics, civil and human rights, individual freedom and responsibility, academic and cultural issues. Prerequisite: ENEFL 134 or permission of program director.

title: Study Skills for Foreign Students 1
description: Note taking, impromptu writing in English as a foreign language, preparing for tests, and using library resources. Prerequisite: ENEFL 133 and 135 or permission of program director.

title: Writing 4
description: Paragraph and essay writing. Practice in rhetorical modes of American English. Prerequisite: ENEFL 141 or permission of program director.

title: Grammar 4
description: Focus on individual grammatical problems with grammatical variants and rhetorical devices. General grammar review. Prerequisite: ENEFL 142 or permission of program director.

title: Reading 4
description: Reading in unadapted selections from general and technical literature and current publications. Prerequisite: ENEFL 143 or permission of program director.

title: Cross-Cultural Studies 2
description: Topics include U.S. and international politics, civil and human rights, individual freedom and responsibility, and academic and cultural issues. Prerequisite: ENEFL 147 or permission of program director.

title: Study Skills for Foreign Students 2
description: Indepth library research methods and researchpaper writing. Advanced study techniques. Prerequisite: ENEFL 148 or permission of program director.

title: TOEFL Preparation
description: Review of English grammar and vocabulary with special practice in aural and written comprehension to prepare for the Test of English as a Foreign Language. Prerequisite: permission of program director.

title: Fundamentals of English Composition
description: Focuses on the development of effective composing, revising, and editing strategies. Required of all students with TSWE of 27 or below; a TSWE of 28-31 and high school rank of 75 percent or below; a TSWE of 32-35 and high school rank of 66 percent or below; a TSWE of 36-41 and high school rank of 50 percent or below; a TSWE of 42 or above and high school rank of 33 percent or below. Offered on a credit/no credit basis; credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements.

title: English Composition 1
description: Introduction to composition with an emphasis on writing short essays. Includes assigned readings. Introduction to basic research methods. Prerequisite: a combination of TSWE scores and high school rank that would not require enrolling in ENG 099 or allow enrolling in ENG 104; ENG 099; or placement according to a test administered by the Department of English.

title: English Composition 2
description: Further instruction in composition with an emphasis on writing longer essays. Includes assigned readings. Further instruction and practice in research methods. Prerequisite: ENG 103 or TSWE of 45 and above with high school rank of 85 percent or above.

title: Honors English Composition 2
description: Instruction in composition with emphasis on writing essays. Includes assigned readings. Instruction and practice in research methods. Prerequisite: TSWE of 45 and above with high school rank of upper 10 percent and acceptance into the Honors program. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 104.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of world, British, and American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for students not majoring or minoring in English. Section content will be identified each semester. Prerequisite: ENG 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 206.

title: World Literature Masterpieces
description: Selected major works of world literature, exclusive of English and American literature, for students who are majoring or minoring in English. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104. Not open to the student who has credit in ENG 205.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar and Usage
description: Basic course in English grammar and usage for the student who is underprepared. A grade of C or higher will satisfy the grammar component of the English Qualifying Test for English majors or minors. Not counted as part of major or minor programs in English.

title: Advanced Composition and Creative Writing
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for the general student, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation; and instruction in creative writing, particularly fiction and poetry. Open only to English majors and minors except by permission of department chairperson. Prerequisite: ENG 104,114, or equivalent.

title: Professional Writing
description: Practice in writing effective, professional prose with particular attention to the writing tasks often required in students' careers. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or equivalent.

title: American Literature, 1607-1860
description: A survey of American literature from its beginning through the middle nineteenth century, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 205,206, or the equivalent.

title: British Literature of the Middle Ages through the Eighteenth Century
description: Extensive survey of British literature from the Middle Ages through the eighteenth century, or from about 450 to 1780, with attention to social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds, including issues of gender, class, and race. Close reading of major works is emphasized. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: British Literature 2: 1780 to the Present
description: British literature from 1780 to the present, with attention to the historical, social, and philosophical background of the times. Prerequisite: ENG 260.

title: Literature and the Narrative Media
description: A consideration of the ways in which the narrative media have been used to develop fictional and nonfictional literature. Special attention to works that have been adapted from one medium to another and to works of lasting significance. Attention will be given to the narrative media and the language arts curriculum in junior high/middle and secondary schools.

title: Practicum in Peer Tutoring
description: Offers strategies for working with grammar, mechanics, and the larger rhetorical elements, practice in peer evaluation, and a forum for discussing the role and responsibilities of peer tutors. Credit in this course does not apply to a major or minor in English. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to students assigned to tutor at the Writing Center.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials for teaching written and oral expression, language use, spelling, handwriting, and literature. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: Literature for Young Children
description: An introduction to literature for young children. Designed for elementary and early childhood education programs and endorsements and for parents and future parents. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: English Linguistics
description: Modern English grammar with emphasis on the application of uptodate descriptive linguistics to an understanding of basic grammatical structure, relationship, and terminology, including morphology and phonology. Prerequisite: a standard score of 75 percent or higher on a competency examination in English grammar, diction, usage, and mechanics or C or higher in ENG 221.

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of children's literature and an intensive study of various types. Designed for elementary education programs and endorsements. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English. Junior or senior standing recommended.

title: Linguistic Phonetics
description: Speech sounds and the linguistic methods employed in their description, classification, and analysis as elements in language systems.

title: American Literature 2, 1860 -1960
description: A survey of selected American writers and the various literary movements since 1860, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or equivalent.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: Intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: Intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period, such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: The themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: The themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Language Arts in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching language arts in junior high/middle schools. Cannot be counted as an elective in other major or minor programs in English. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDJHM 280.

title: Literature of Black America
description: A survey of the literature written by Black authors in the United States.

title: American Indian Literature
description: A literary study of short stories, novels, and poetry by twentiethcentury American Indian authors, with supplementary background readings in mythology, tales, and poetry from the oral traditions. The emphasis will be on works by American Indians, but some works about Indians by Caucasian authors may also be included.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to the Restoration
description: English drama from medieval times to 1660, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to The Second Shepherds' Play and Everyman, and to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: English Internship
description: Supervised onthejob training and work experiences in which English majors and minors apply what they have learned. Involves assigned duties in an organization, agency, corporation, bank, or professional office, with appropriate monetary compensation for services rendered. Prerequisite: ENG 230 or 231, 221 or 321; junior standing; and permission of the internship program director. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. Three hours of credit may be earned toward the elective requirement of the preprofessional minor. Six hours of credit may be applied toward the elective requirement in the preprofessional major.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: English Drama from the Restoration to the Present
description: English drama from 1700 to the present. Special attention is given to the plays of Steele, Goldsmith, Sheridan, Wilde, Shaw, Synge, O'Casey, Osborne, Beckett, and Pinter.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenthcentury novels including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the Brontes, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Studies in British Drama
description: Special topics in contemporary British drama. Open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open only to honors students. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Writing Competency Examination
description: Open to students who have completed ENG 103 and ENG 104 with a grade of C or better. Students must have juniorlevel standing, having earned at least 63 semester hours, and must register through the English department three weeks before the examination period. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. This course is offered on a credit/no credit basis.

title: Writing Competency Course
description: Required of all students who have not completed ENG 392 after two attempts. This course is offered on a credit/no credit basis, and credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements.

title: Teaching English in Secondary Schools
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in teaching composition, language, and literature. Required for teaching majors; may be an elective for teaching minors; may not be applied toward any other departmental program. Prerequisite: ENG 350.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Special Topics in World and British Literature
description: Special research topics in world or British literature with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or equivalent.

title: Special Topics in English Education
description: Emphasis on current issues and problems at the elementary, middle, junior high, or senior high school level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Special Topics in American Literature
description: Special research topics in American literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or the equivalent.

title: Independent Study in English
description: Designed for the student who wants to conduct independent study and research in English. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in English at the 200 level or above at Ball State University and permission of department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Creative Writing Workshop
description: The fundamentals of the short story, such as the use of language, image, and structure. Emphasis on the student's ability to write clearly and dramatically. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Fiction-Writing Workshop
description: Open to students who already have had some experience with the short story, the novel, or the play. Primary emphasis on instructor evaluation and class discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Poetry-Writing Workshop
description: Practice, analysis, and criticism of the craft of poetry, with attention to prosody, traditional form, significant idea, the life of the poetic imagination, and the state of the art. Prerequisite: ENG 103 and 104.

title: Independent Study in English Education
description: Designed for the student who wishes to conduct independent study and research in English education, preschool through the secondary level. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206 and permission of department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading Printed Materials in the English Classroom
description: Provides an overview of the process of reading printed materials with practical suggestions for developing analytic skills for reading and interpreting written communications, including literary and popular materials used in the English classroom.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Emphasis on the actual reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical aspects.

title: Sociolinguistics
description: A detailed examination of the relationship between language variety and social class, including recent studies in urban social dialectology. Basic issues in the study of bilingualism. Prerequisite: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Theory and Research in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in secondlanguage teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Methods and Materials in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Study and practice of a variety of methods in teaching English as a second or foreign language. Discussion of pedagogical issues in language teaching. Topics vary each semester; consult the English department for schedule of offerings. Prerequisite: ENG 420 or permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: American Literature, 1945 to Present
description: A survey of the works of major writers and literary trends in America since World War II. Prerequisite: ENG 205 or 206.

title: Practicum in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Practical experience in observation, teaching, and analysis of teaching English as a second or foreign language. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Parallel: ENG 436 or 437. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Chaucer
description: Study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several minor poems. Emphasizes structure, sources, and significance of the works. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works considered.

title: Shakespeare
description: An introductory study of representative plays (comedies, histories, tragedies) and some selections from the sonnets by Shakespeare.

title: Studies in Shakespeare
description: Special topics in a selection of Shakespeare's tragedies, comedies, and histories. Prerequisite: open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Milton
description: Indepth, analytical study of Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, Samson Agonistes, Lycidas, and Areopagitica, as well as a brief study of "The Christian Doctrine" and other selected poems and prose by John Milton.

title: Women in Literature
description: Investigation of various ways that women have been portrayed in the literature of the Western world.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War Ito the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. DEPARTMENT OF FOREIGN LANGUAGES R. Gardiol, Chairperson; B. Anderson, D. Barnette, J. Brown, R. Fritz, D. Gilman, J. Hightower, L. Johnson, E. Kadletz, A. King, W. McGrath, W. Moskalew, C. Shea, R. Warner The Department of Foreign Languages offers programs in both ancient and modern foreign languages and works closely with other programs and departments to combine foreign language training with other subjects. Language laboratory practice, computer applications, and opportunities for foreign exchange programs and summer study abroad enhance classroom instruction. The department offers foreign language training for students who want to acquire a broad liberal education; enrich their preparation for their careers; seek certification for teaching at the elementary or secondary level; plan to travel, live, or work abroad; or work as translators. Students may earn credit for previous language study through either advanced placement tests or departmentally administered proficiency tests. These exams also help determine the appropriate classes in which students are placed. Placement credit is not given for the firstlevel (101) course. Students placed in any higherlevel course may receive up to a maximum of 10 credit hours for the courses they test out of by earning grades of C or higher in the course into which they are placed. Native speakers who have completed high school studies in their native countries are not eligible for credit in the first or second year of their native languages. Students should consult with foreign language faculty advisors about arranging courses to meet their individual needs. The 100- and 200-level courses in foreign languages are sequential and must be taken in order. Only work at the 200 level and above will apply toward any major or minor in foreign languages except those in Chinese and Japanese, where firstyear courses may be counted. description: English vocabulary derived from Latin and Greek, emphasizing wordformation as a means of expanding and enriching the student's

title: Scientific Terminology: Greek
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Greek commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Greek is required.

title: Scientific Terminology: Latin
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Latin commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Latin is required.

title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Main features of the civilization of the Greeks and Romans—their history, political institutions, art, literature, and philosophy. Explores through lectures, readings, and audiovisual materials the nature of the ancients' contribution to Western civilizations.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: A close, interpretive view of Greek cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as individualism, ideals of beauty, social experimentation, competitiveness, and intellectual curiosity, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: A close, interpretive view of Roman cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as respect for tradition, rule of law, social responsibility, and technical expertise, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: The Classical World in Film
description: Aspects of ancient civilization depicted in film (such as Roman history, Greek mythology, etc.). An examination of the accuracy of such portrayals through comparison with ancient sources. The place of such films in the history of cinema. Topics will vary.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: Classical mythology (Greek and Roman) will represent Western tradition in a comparative study with other mythologies of the world. Emphasis on understanding mythologies as symbolic cultural systems expressing societal values.

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selections from the major works of Greek and Roman literature and their continuing influence on Western literature. Emphasis on prose and poetry in alternate terms. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Women in Antiquity
description: The study of women in ancient Greece and Rome, based on evidence from literary and nonliterary sources. Explores the influence of social, political, and legal institutions on the status of women and on their relationships with men.

title: Greek and Roman Cults
description: Introduces the religions of the ancient Greeks and Romans and examines the ii

title: The Ancient City
description: Life of the ancient city as mirrored in archaeological and literary sources. The concept of the city, its art and architecture, with special emphasis on Periclean Athens and Augustan Rome.

title: Classical Myth and Theory
description: Major themes of classical myths: creation, the divine and human family, life of the hero, the quest, monsters, etc. Study and employment of modern theories of analysis: mythritual, psychological, structuralist, etc. Prerequisite recommended: CC 205.

title: Readings
description: Individualized course of reading or limited research to allow students to explore special topics in classical antiquity. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Chinese 1
description: The first course in the Chinese language.

title: Beginning Chinese 2
description: The second course in the Chinese language. Prerequisite: CH 101.

title: Intermediate Chinese 1
description: Designed to build on a foundation of firstyear Chinese to help students achieve greater fluency in oral expression and to emphasize the reading of Chinese character texts containing both old and simplified character forms. Grammar will be taught through the use of sentence patterns, and character writing will be practiced. Traditional and contemporary aspects of Chinese culture will also be taught. Prerequisite: CH 102.

title: Intermediate Chinese 2
description: Designed to build on the foundation laid thus far in Chinese and to help students achieve greater fluency in the four basic skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will read newspapers, short stories, and essays by modern authors with the help of a dictionary and will write short compositions in Hanzi on their readings. Prerequisite: CH 201.

title: Beginning Readings in Chinese
description: A course designed to develop skills in reading simple Chinese essays, short stories, and newspaper articles, using approximately 2,000 characters and the help of a dictionary. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Chinese Literature in English Translation
description: A brief overview of major Chinese literary trends and works using selections from traditional masterpieces in poetry, myth, legend, short story, and novel and also contemporary essay, short story, and novel. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Beginning Guided Self-Instruction in Common Languages
description: Guided selfinstruction in beginning French, German, Greek, Latin, or Spanish using audiovisual materials, texts, workbooks, tests, and tutors on an arranged basis. Designed to meet the needs of students who cannot otherwise study languages. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. Not open to native speakers. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Guided Self-Instruction in Common Languages
description: Guided selfinstruction in intermediate French, German, Greek, Latin, or Spanish using audiovisual materials, texts, workbooks, tests, and tutors on an arranged basis. Designed to meet the needs of students who cannot otherwise study these languages. Not open to native speakers. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures in Translation
description: Readings in English translation of selected works of major writers in one of the foreign languages taught in this department. Topics and works may vary. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Foreign Culture through Films
description: Study of cultures of the countries whose languages are taught in this department through the medium of foreign contemporary and classic films. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Indochina: Traditions and Languages of Laos and Vietnam
description: A survey of the high traditions and values of the peoples of Indochina. World view through folklore, literature, arts, and language. Conducted in Lao and Vietnamese. Prerequisite: conversational knowledge of Lao or Vietnamese. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Guided Self-Instruction Studies in Less Common Languages
description: Offers languages such as Japanese, Arabic, modern Hebrew, modern Greek, Chinese, and Portuguese at basic spoken levels by guided selfinstruction. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in one language. Not open to native speakers.

title: Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and applications of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching foreign language in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite: EDJHM 280 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Cooperative Education in Foreign Languages
description: A partnership program that unites foreign language students with employers. The program integrates foreign and classical language skills with incomeproducing, careerrelated positions in international firms, the travel industry, and local, state, and federal agencies. Prerequisite: minimum of two years of universitylevel foreign language study, permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College or permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Foreign Language
description: Current methods in foreign language teaching in the senior high school. Presentation, texts, teaching materials, CAI, and other supplementary aids. Reviews current professional literature, trends, requirements. Prerequisite: two years of college credit or equivalent in a modern language and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Foreign Language Trends and CAI
description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of foreign languages, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of foreign languages in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: FL 395.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with individual instructor. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Language House Living and Learning
description: Offers students the option of earning a limited amount of credit for the languagelearning experience provided by the foreign language houses. A total of 3 hours of credit per language may be earned in any one house, but no more than 1 credit may be earned in one semester or term. Offered on credit/nocredit basis only.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Civilization and Culture: Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introduction to French Literature 1
description: Selections from various periods of French literature, designed to develop an appreciation of the literary heritage of France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 401 or equivalent.

title: Introduction to French Literature 2
description: Modern prose and poetry. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent. Not open to the student who has credit in FR 402 or equivalent.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the Classical Age to 1760. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 2
description: From the classical age to the present. The development of eighteenthcentury philosophies, romanticism, realism, naturalism, and symbolism in French literature; literature of modern France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent.

title: Seminar in French Literature
description: Seminar studies by author, genre, period, or theme; topic to be announced. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in French Language or Civilization
description: Seminar studies in grammar, stylistics, conversation, or civilization; topic to be announced. Prerequisite: two years of college French or equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings

Wheeler The Department of Geography offers three options to meet the varied needs of its students. Option 1 is a general survey of physical and cultural geography and is selected by students seeking a broad education leading to careers in education, government, and business. Option 2 is a specialized program in travel and tourism. Students selecting this option are encouraged to take minors in foreign languages and business. Option 3, geographic information sciences (remote sensing, geographic information systems, computer cartography), is a technical specialization selected by students who seek to study various geographic problems through the use of computer technology. Graduates with this option often go on to graduate school or find employment with private or public agencies.
