title: Earth, Sea, and Sky: A Geographic View
description: Selected aspects of the physical environment and their relationship to human occupancy of the earth. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 111.

title: Physical Geography and Earth Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Earthsun relationships, weather and climate, geologic processes (including earth structure and sculpturing of the earth's surface); conservation principles as they pertain directly to the material taught. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Not open to the student who has credit in GEOG 101.

title: Economic Geography and Contemporary Issues
description: A systematic approach to economic geography and current economic issues emphasizing local, regional, national, and international economic developments in the geographic setting.

title: Geography of the Cultural Environment
description: A spatial analysis of the interaction of cultural development and the physical environment. Special emphasis upon the processes of cultural change and their impact on the landscape.

title: Global Geography
description: A basic survey course emphasizing geographic facts and interdependencies between the developed and developing world. Particular emphasis is given to physical and social environmental interdependencies.

title: The American Landscape: A Historical Geography of the United States
description: Geography of American landscape in earlier times. Selected PREFIX GEOG GEOL GEOG GEOG GEOL GEOL ASTRO PHYCS GEOG GEOL regions examined to understand geographical influences on transformation of the wilderness. Emphasis placed on exploration, discovery, migration routes, settlement, adjustments to the land, and means of securing a livelihood.

title: Weather 1
description: How and why the weather changes, the characteristics of weather, and an examination of weather instruments.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: Introduction to skills needed to use and appreciate maps as a form of communication and as a research tool. Topics include elements and sources of maps, history of map making, techniques of analysis, and introduction to aerial photography and remote sensing.

title: Introduction to Travel and Tourism
description: A survey of the travel and tourism industry; its various components, dimensions, organization, and structure. Topics include economic, social, cultural, and environmental implications; motivations for travel, and the past and future of the industry.

title: Geography of Travel and Tourism
description: An emphasis upon the spatial interaction arising from the movement of people engaged in travel for leisure and other purposes. Models of tourism, measuring spatial variations, patterns of domestic and international flows (regions), and spatial organization are examined.

title: Urban Geography
description: Distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention given to the geographic factors affecting urban development and growth.

title: Urban Geography: Trends in Theory and Research
description: Survey of the contribution of Weberian, Marxist, and "managerialist" theory to the interpretation of urban spatial organization and change. In the light of these theories, current research trends and techniques are examined.

title: Weather 2
description: Introduction to weather forecasting using applied examples. Students may gain practical experience by working in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 230.

title: Climate
description: Introduction to climate with emphasis on regional distribution. How and why climates differ across the earth. Prerequisite: GEOG 230, its equivalent, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. Although the emphasis is on graphic presentation of spatially disposed quantitative and qualitative data, the techniques and methods apply to a wide range of subject areas.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques, including an introduction to computer graphics. Projects are selected within the student's specialization or topic of interest. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Remote Sensing 1
description: Principles of photo interpretation, satellite scanners, and radar. Characteristic features of remotely sensed data, classification processes, and algorithms.

title: Remote Sensing 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in remote sensing, including digital data analysis, image enhancement technique as applied to natural resources, urban analysis, soil studies, geology, and other applied branches. Prerequisite: GEOG 342.

title: Geographic Information Systems Analysis
description: Methods of analysis provided by geographic information systems (GIS). Operations on spatial and attribute information including basic functions (e.g., map overlay) and special functions (e.g., network analysis). Exposure to raster and vector software. Review capabilities of currently available GIS software. Prerequisite: GEOG 240, 340, and 341 or permission of the instructor.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: Comprehensive survey of geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Latin America and the Caribbean
description: Physical and cultural patterns in a diverse world region. Emphasis on population and settlement, agriculture, and environmental hazards in the context of development.

title: Geography of Africa
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environments of Africa.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: A geographic examination of the physical, cultural, and economic diversity of the state. Field experiences supplement classroom activities.

title: Geography of Asia
description: The geography of South, Southwest, Southeast, and East Asia. A survey and analysis of the physical geographic patterns, bases of cultural diversity, and changing spatial aspects of political organization.

title: Geography of Europe
description: The physical and cultural environment of Europe with emphasis on the economic and political conditions involved.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union and the economic development of the country.

title: Domestic and International Travel and Tourism
description: Examination of the technical aspects of domestic and international travel and tourism. Develops skills by using professionally prepared materials related to travel planning, regulations, tariffs, services, and ticketing. Prerequisite: GEOG 261 and 262. Open to option 2 majors only.

title: Geography Internship
description: Paid fullor parttime work experiences with an organization allied to the student's area of specialization. Assignments depend on the student's interest and the sponsor's convenience. Used for paid work experiences only. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world and of transportation patterns.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration, and growth, as well as their causes and the effects they produce on the cultural landscape.

title: Seminar in Geography or Earth Science
description: Advanced study of a selected topic in geography or earth science. Prerequisite: an introductory geography or earth science course or permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Advanced Techniques in Remote Sensing
description: Advanced Geography 213 techniques applied to remotely sensed data using stateoftheart software. Review of current methods of computer and manual interpretation techniques. Includes active participation in classroom presentations. Prerequisite: GEOG 342 and 343.

title: Advanced Cartography
description: Application of computerassisted design (CAD) to computerassisted cartography. Introduction to relational databases for maps. Interfacing of graphic files to thematic mapping software. Prerequisite: GEOG 340 and 341.

title: Applications of Geographic Information Systems
description: Practical experience applying geographic information system (GIS) tools to analyze spatial data. Workshop format requires studentmotivated projects; diverse disciplines encouraged. Project work involves proposal, work plan, presentation, and final report. Prerequisite: GEOG 344 or permission of the instructor.

title: Automation and the Travel Industry
description: Introduction to the use of automation in the travel industry as it applies to information management and task functions like reservation and ticketing systems. Includes laboratory experience. Prerequisite: GEOG 360. Open to majors only.

title: Internship in Geography
description: Fullor parttime work experience with an organization allied to the student's area of specialization. Assignments depend upon the student's interest and the sponsor's convenience. Used for unpaid work experience only.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the contribution of physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world to domestic and foreign relations problems.

title: Distant Areas Field Studies
description: Physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Open to students in geography, earth science, and allied subjects. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Travel and Tourism
description: Advanced study exploring problems and issues, theory and research related to travel and tourism. Topics will vary depending upon the instructor, and needs and interests of students. Prerequisite: GEOG 360. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Geograph!,‘; Research Methods
description: An introduction to the use of statistics and quantitative techniques in geographic research. Topics include research design, statistical testing, and geographic modeling.

title: Readings and Special Studies in Geography and Earth Science
description: Assigned special studies in geography and earth science, including readings, research projects, teaching problems, or assignment to an undergraduate class. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Thesis
description: The formulation and writing of a researchoriented thesis. Student working with a faculty advisor will write a research paper on a geographic theme or topic of his or her choice. Papers will be evaluated for geographic content and compositional skills. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geographic Field Methods
description: Introduction to the techniques of field study and analysis of physical and cultural spatial patterns. DEPARTMENT OF GEOLOGY A. Samuelson, Chairperson; R. Fluegeman, R. Orr, H. Roepke, R. Snow Geologists study the earth with primary attention to its history, materials, and structure and the active processes that continue to change the landscape. Geologists are also concerned with the investigation of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, the evaluation of groundwater resources, the discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits, and the study of the moon and planets. The department offers two departmental majors in geology. The professional arts major is designed to prepare graduates for some geological careers in industry and government agencies and for graduate studies that lead to research, teaching, management, and many other positions in industry, government, and universities. The liberal arts major is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who have related interests, want to pursue double majors, or do not want to enter the geological profession directly. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN GEOLOGY, 61 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS It is expected that students will have completed mathematics through MATHS 117 or high school equivalent.

title: People and the Geological Environment
description: An introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to human environmental and resource problems. Localarea field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: Introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Oceans and Nations
description: Worldwide human interactions with the oceans and international conflicts of interest related to the ocean environment. Introduction to physical and biological characteristics of the oceans. Marine law, resource conflicts, pollution, cooperation for oceanographic research and hazard response, and other topics.

title: Environmental Geology
description: Examines geologic materials and processes affecting the human environment. Discusses geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, surface water hydrology, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Localarea field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 115 (or high school equivalent) or permission of department chairperson.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geology Internship
description: A paid work and learning experience arranged for each student in an approved geological or environmental agency or geological division of a private business for a time commensurate with the credit to be earned. Assignments include activity log, selfanalysis, and final summary report. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson and coordinator of internships. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments near the campus and visits to places within the state of value to the course. Prerequisite: major or minor in geology, earth science, or geography, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to the resolution of geologic problems. Assignments include accumulation and interpretation of field observations and preparation of geologic maps, cross sections, and stratigraphic sections. Requires a report of investigations for one of the mapping projects. The course is conducted during a fiveweek period in June and July in South Dakota and Wyoming. Prerequisite: GEOL 230 and 382 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Localarea field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoecologic significance. Emphasis on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 115 (or high school equivalent) or permission of department chairperson.

title: Oceanography
description: Description of the physical and organic environments of the oceans and related topics. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to refraction and reflection seismology; magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods. Emphasis on applied geophysical methods to such problems as energy resources, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, and pollution detection. Includes laboratory exercises and field investigations. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of textures and mineralogies of rocks, together with a review of experimental and field data, provide the basis for classifying and interpreting the origins of rocks. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Sedimentology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and sedimentary rocks determine their depositional environments. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 320 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: Rocks, structure, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Fieldtrip oriented with collection of rock, mineral, and fossil specimens. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 108 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. Designed to supplement existing geoscience and computer science courses by providing opportunity to gain experience in working with BASIC and FORTRAN programs in various geoscience datacollecting, calculation, and graphic display applications. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 in one semester or term. DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY A. Edmonds, Chairperson; A. Alves, R. Aquila, J. Barber, L. Birkin, W. Eidson, M. title: Introduction to American Studies
description: Survey of American studies as a field and as an interdisciplinary approach to the study of American civilization. Methods and theories of American studies will be discussed, along with major themes and topics of American life and thought. Not open to the student who has credit in AMSTU 101.

title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: Surveys the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decision makers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Western Civilization
description: A survey of the major themes and developments in the evolution of Western civilization from its origins to the present with emphasis on key problems, turning points, recurring issues, and cultural growth and heritage. Special stress on the character and crises confronting the Western world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: World Civilization 1
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the dawn of civilization in Southwestern Asia and North Africa to the early modern world.

title: World Civilization 2
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the early modern world to the present.

title: Introduction to Modern Africa
description: Designed to give the student a general knowledge of modern Africa. Stresses nineteenthand twentiethcentury Africa with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: Introduction to the Middle East
description: Provides the student with general knowledge and understanding of the recent Middle East—the Arab World, Israel, Turkey, Iran, and other states. Stress on nineteenthand twentiethcentury problems: imperialism, nationalism, reform, wars, development.

title: Introduction to South and Southeast Asia
description: South Asia (Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka) and Southeast Asia (Burma, Thailand, Laos, Kampuchea, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines) since 1800; a brief description of factors influential in history and concentration on problems, leaders, and issues of imperialism, nationalism, independence, and modernization.

title: Introduction to the Far East
description: Survey of China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and contiguous areas in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with emphasis on their relations with Europe and America, nationalism, modernization, and contemporary issues.

title: Studies in Non-Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: American History, 1492 -1876
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States to 1876.

title: American History, 1877 to Present
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States since 1877.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give the student knowledge of resource use in the United States by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis on the way resource use has shaped society. Not open to the student who has credit in NR 204.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of Blacks in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis on the impact of Blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing conceptions of their roles, attitudes toward women, women's ideas about themselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Uses documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. Students through their own research learn how the historian defines topics of research; selects sources, both primary and secondary; evaluates materials; and describes the findings.

title: The History of American Popular Culture
description: Historical overview of the development of American popular culture. Basic theories, approaches, and topics in popular culture with special attention to amusements, movies, pop music, magazines, pulp novels, and television. Focuses on the relationship of popular culture to American cultural and social history.

title: Early Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: Modern Latin America
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis on Mexico, Chile, Cuba, and Central America.

title: Introduction to Public History
description: An overview of opportunities for nonteaching historyrelated careers in preservation, archival work, records management, museology, historical editing, living history and public parks programs, corporate history, and others. Students make a concentrated study of at least one field of public history and have contact with working professionals. Open to all students.

title: History of the European Family
description: A survey of the changing social, economic, and political roles of the European family from antiquity to the present. Topics include the distribution of authority, marriage and inheritance, childrearing, domestic labor, and the impact of industrialization.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American-Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Gives students a historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Selected Topics in Military History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular period, topic, or issue in military history with emphasis on materials not covered in established courses. Exact content announced in advance of each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Paid Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. This course is designed for paid work and learning experiences on or off campus. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others may enroll by permission of department chairperson.

title: Colonial America 1492 -1756
description: The settlement of North America by the British and the evolution of the distinctive colonial societies that formed the foundation of the United States.

title: The American Revolution, 1756-1789
description: Transformation of American society and politics in the era of the American Revolution with emphasis on the origins of the revolution, the development of a democratic society, and the Constitution of the United States.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis on the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism Versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis on the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: The United States from World War I through World II
description: An examination of the reaction of the American people to a society changing rapidly under the impact of two major wars, the Great Depression, and continuing industrialization and urbanization.

title: Recent United States History: 1945 to the Present
description: A study of the role of the United States in the modern world and an examination of the efforts of America to preserve a society that is prosperous and humane while adjusting to technological change and continuing social and intellectual ferment.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the state from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Antebellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum South.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans -Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's impact upon the settler in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans- Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers, the events that influenced their migration, and the effect of these events and the frontier on national development.

title: Indians in U.S. History
description: Survey of Indian and white relations from 1492 to the present, focusing on the Indian wars, treaty making, various types of Indian and white interaction, and the development of federal and state Indian policy.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History Since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I.

title: American Life and Thought, 1607-1865
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from the colonial period to the Civil War, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American Life and Thought, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from Reconstruction to the present, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: the major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students travel through designated areas in North America. Requires considerable reading before the trip and papers at the conclusion. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in U.S. history may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 3. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870-1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918-1945
description: The origins, immediate causes, and the course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and Europe since 1945
description: European origin of the Cold War and rebirth of a "new" but divided Europe with stress on East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, and temporary decline of European influence; ideological, political, economic, and social development, including competition between Western and Sovietized Eastern Europe.

title: History of Medicine in Western Society
description: A survey of the ideas, attitudes, and institutions of medicine and public health in the Western world from antiquity to modern times. Special attention given to social forces influencing medical knowledge and health care. Not open to the student who has credit in HSC 460.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the republic to approximately A.D. 500. Emphasis on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social, and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special emphasis on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Muslim worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Emphasizes such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, and political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations—Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society—through varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in world civilization may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 4.

title: France since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France—The Classical Age, 1461 -1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focuses on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715-1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization—and revolutions in general. Stresses the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Britain, 1485-1714
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor and Stuart periods. Emphasis on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain, 1714 to the Present
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life from the Hanoverian period to the present—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of government and society since World War II.

title: Topics in English Constitutional History
description: Selected topics concerning the constitutional history of England, such as the development of the kingship, the common law, Parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: The Modern Middle East
description: A survey of major developments and problems in the Turkish, Persian, and Arab world in the period since 1800—the decay of traditional life, the expansion of European influence, the modernization movements, the conflicts over Palestine, and the recent national and international crises.

title: Selected Topics in Non -Western History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in non- Western history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern China, 1800 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's response to the West, disintegration of the traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant aspects of Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japan, 1850 to Present
description: A descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on conditions contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Selected Topics in European History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in European history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Topics in American History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Studies for the Primary Grades and Early Childhood
description: Materials and procedures for teaching social studies for nursery school through grade three. Emphasis on behavioral objectives, inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation. Required of persons in the twoyear early elementary education program.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Junior High/Middle School
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching social studies in junior high/ middle schools. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Materials and procedure for teaching social studies from kindergarten through grade six. Emphasis on behavioral objectives; inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Provides more experience in methods used in teaching elementary social studies and an opportunity to use materials available to teachers. Prerequisite: SS 391 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Secondary Schools
description: Theory and practice of teaching secondary school social studies. Emphasis on methodology, materials, and specific application in the secondary classroom. includes introductory involvement in the teaching of social studies with a focus on rationale, planning, teaching, and evaluation. Prerequisite: 18 hours of credit in social science, identification to pursue a teaching curriculum, and SS 350.

title: Independent Study
description: Directed study of special problems or research in social science education by individuals or groups of students. Topics to be investigated are chosen after consultation with the instructor with special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. CENTER FOR INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SCIENCES R. Steele, Director; R. Bellaver, J. Dickey, E. Kaminski, R. Stowe, R. Students use stateoftheart writing and magazine, newseditorial, photojournalism editing, graphics, and photojournalism equipment. They are encouraged to gain experience on national awardwinning student publications including the Daily News, a daily newspaper; the Orient, the university's yearbook; Expo, the student magazine; and Limited Edition, the studentoperated public relations and advertising agency. The Department of Journalism is accredited by the national journalism accrediting body, the Accrediting Council on Education in Journalism and Mass Communication. Students must complete JOURN 101, 125, 210, and 211 by the end of their sophomore year. title: Mass Media in Society
description: Study of mass media in their historical and societal contexts with emphasis on practitioner issues including ethics, state of the art, and future.

title: Communications Graphics
description: Theory of publication and visual communication emphasizing preparation of material for newspapers, magazines, and brochures. Lectures and projects focus on type selection, copy fitting, photo and illustration selection and use, pasteup skills, and printing processes.

title: Introduction to Photojournalism
description: Emphasis on preparing students to take, process, and caption photographs for newspapers, magazines, public relations, and advertising purposes. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies.

title: Newswriting, Reporting, and Editing 1
description: Theory and practice in newsstyle writing, gathering news, and editing for publication. Emphasis on newspaper writing skills. Includes one hour of lab a week.

title: Newswriting, Reporting, and Editing 2
description: Theory and practice in newsstyle writing, reporting, and editing. Emphasis on developing reporting and editing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 210.

title: Photographic Lighting
description: An indepth study of photographic lighting procedures and equipment for studio and field use by media photographers. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 130 or other basic photography class.

title: Introduction to Advertising
description: A survey of the advertising communication process. Focuses on communication research, creative strategy, campaign planning, function of mass media as carriers of advertising, and evaluation of advertising effectiveness.

title: Principles of Public Relations
description: Survey of the theory, philosophy, and function of public relations practices and programs in American institutions with special attention given to public relations in various fields.

title: History of Journalism
description: History of journalism in the United States from colonial times to the present, presenting the press as an institution against the background of the history of the nation.

title: Feature, Column, and Opinion Writing
description: Researching and writing feature stories, columns, and editorials for newspapers and magazines. Discussion of feature, column, and editorial types and campaigns. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Magazine Writing and Editing
description: Theory and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles. Includes a study of markets for magazine articles and exercises in various aspects of editing general and specialized magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Open only to magazinesequence majors or to others with permission of department chairperson.

title: Sportswriting and Reporting
description: Study and practice in covering and writing about sports events and the people connected with them. Story assignments and research combined with classroom lectures and analysis of best sports stories provide students with skills to cover a wide range of sports activities. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Journalism Prose Styles
description: Writing and editing for students interested in publishing their work in newspapers, magazines, and public relations organizations. Emphasizes works of contemporary prose writers. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 315. CR HRS

title: Journalism Law
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the print and broadcast media with special attention given to recent Supreme Court rulings.

title: Magazine Management
description: Analysis of all facets of magazine management: editorial, advertising, circulation, and art. Designed for students interested in working for professional magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 315 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Photojournalism
description: An extended study of the theory and practice of making photographs and using photography as communicative art. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advertising Media
description: Strategy and procedures for planning, executing, and controlling the placement of advertising. Examines characteristics of media, techniques of media budgeting and selection, and methods of evaluating media effectiveness. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Advertising Copy and Layout
description: Instruction in preparing copy for mass media advertising. Major emphasis on creative thinking and basic writing skills. Students prepare copy strategies, write copy, prepare layouts and storyboards. Discussion of fundamentals of consumer motivation and selecting target audiences. Prerequisite: JOURN 250.

title: Public Relations Writing and Publicity Techniques
description: Theory and practice of producing publicity tools for various media used in campaigns to promote and interpret personal, institutional, and organizational objectives and activities. Emphasis on writing and publicity problem solving. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 and 261.

title: Public Relations Publication Design and Production
description: Institutional and industrial publications as an important means of internal and external communications. Design and production techniques. Includes one hour of lab a week. Prerequisite: JOURN 125, 211, 360.

title: Journalism Internship
description: Onthejob training in which journalism or public relations students get practical experience in applying what they have learned in the classroom. Involves assigned duties in an offcampus communications organization with appropriate compensation. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson, JOURN 211, and required 300-level sequence courses. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 375 or 469. May be taken for credit/no credit only.

title: Editorial Practicum
description: Introductory practical experience in the production of the campus newspaper, magazine, yearbook, or alternative projects with emphasis on writing, editing, or photographic activities. Emphasizes mastery of spelling, grammar, and typing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to the student who has credit in JOURN 369 or 469.

title: Electronic Journalistic Production Techniques
description: Theory, principles, and handson experience in camera and videocassette recorder operation; microphones and audio recording; electronic editing; studio production; field production and delivery systems. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Open only to journalism majors and minors.

title: Honors Colloquium in Journalism
description: Readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Journalism
description: The procedures and problems in teaching journalism classes or units and the role of student publications in school journalism programs. Subjects included are curriculum, finance, textbooks, and resources. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Advanced Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice in reporting and writing specialized news stories. Emphasis on indepth reporting and coverage of specialized areas including public affairs, government, education, and business. Assignments designed for use in student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 211.

title: Scientific and Technical Writing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Students become familiar with engineering and spaceage terminology, with emphasis on clarity and translation of technical terms to lay language.

title: Newspaper Design
description: Theory of the design functions of journalism using typographical systems with attention to their relations to communicative language. Acquaints students with new methods, ideas, and techniques that have been and are in the process of being developed in journalism printing and technology. Prerequisite; JOURN 125 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Authors as Journalists
description: Survey of the works written by American journalists who became major literary figures of their time. Examines their styles, techniques, and theories as writers and reporters and analyzes their journalistic writings. Prerequisite: JOURN 315 or 324 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Magazine Writing
description: A workshop in writing articles. Emphasizes targeting markets for freelance articles and writing for magazines that publish articles of 2,500 words or more. Prerequisite: JOURN 315 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Picture Editing
description: Selecting, editing, and using photographic and other illustrative graphic materials. Includes layout and design of picture pages for newspapers, magazines, books, brochures, and pamphlets.

title: Advertising Photography
description: Advertising, commercial, and concept illustration photography for the print media. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Color Photojournalism
description: Principles, techniques, and materials of color photography as they apply to color art work and photographs in printed publications. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 337 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advertising Case Studies
description: Designed to analyze and solve advertising problems based on actual situations. Cases focus on consumer goods companies, industrial marketers, and nonprofit organizations. Prerequisite: JOURN 352, 354.

title: Advanced Copy Writing
description: Advanced studies in the strategy and creation of advertising for the mass media. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 354.

title: Advertising Campaigns
description: Synthesis of skills and concepts acquired in the specialized advertising courses. Students research, plan, write, schedule, budget, and evaluate a complete advertising campaign. Prerequisite: JOURN 250, 352, 354; MKG 300, 310; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Public Relations Campaigns
description: Allows the public relations major to apply research and problemsolving techniques to actual or simulated public relations case problems using all of the methodologies learned previously. Prerequisite: JOURN 261, 360, and 368.

title: Advertising and Public Relations Practicum
description: Practical experience in public relations or advertising projects in preparation of a senior portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 352 and 354 or 368; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Advising High School Publications
description: Theories of staff organization and content of high school yearbooks, newspapers, and magazines. Emphasizes the role of the adviser, financial management, staff motivation, and trends in scholastic publications.

title: Introduction to Journalism and Communication Research
description: Issues and trends in the literature of mass communication theory and research.

title: Individual Studies in Journalism
description: Group and individual investigations and experiences in journalistic media and techniques with special attention to social, political, and economic roles of the press in society. Robold, D. Umbach The Department of Mathematical Sciences offers general studies course work to help all students understand the role that mathematics plays in today's world. The department also offers specialized programs to prepare mathematically oriented students for a variety of careers. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government as well as for more intense study of mathematics at the graduate level. The applied mathematics minor is designed for students whose primary interests lie in such subjects as business, economics, biology, geography, geology, and psychology. The major in actuarial science provides training for careers that involve analyzing and solving business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. The program includes course work for the first three examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries and in some cases for the fourth and fifth examinations. The teaching major and minor satisfy state certification requirements for students preparing to teach mathematics in junior high/middle school or high school. Students preparing to be elementary teachers may add the endorsement for teaching mathematics to their elementary teaching licenses and may also earn certification to teach mathematics in junior high/middle schools. For information on the major in mathematical economics, see Interdepartmental Programs, p. 41. Unless otherwise noted, all students enrolling in courses in the Department of Mathematical Sciences are expected to have completed at least three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school, including two years of algebra and one year of geometry. To begin all programs (except the endorsement for teaching a subject field: mathematics), it is expected the student will have completed high school mathematics courses equivalent to the prerequisite for MATHS 171 (161 for the minor in applied mathematics). In addition, for all programs (except the actuarial science major and the endorsement), it is expected the student will have had some computer programming experience.
