title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of processes involved in the interaction between person and group, including the dynamics of group influence on personal behavior and the impact of personal variables on the functioning of primary and secondary groups in contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociological Research Design
description: A basic course in principles and techniques for organizing, conducting, and analyzing sociological research; research strategies and selection of appropriate techniques for a variety of research problems. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Statistics
description: The calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Leisure and Popular Culture
description: Discussion of issues related to the uses and distribution of nonwork time and activities. Trends in recreation, folk arts, and the growing leisure industries. The impact of leisure activities on the natural environment and other "quality of life" issues.

title: Social Stratification and Inequality
description: An analysis of United States and world TEACHER EDUCATION TEACHING MAJOR IN SOCIAL STUDIES, 54 hours (See Teaching Major in Social Studies, College of Sciences and Humanities, p. 168, for total requirements for this area.) Primary area: sociology, 18 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE

title: The Sociology of Modernization
description: The sociology of social and industrial change—modernization in the non- Western world. Study of reasons for change, for example, demographicurban, familysocial, and international pressures. Discussions of Third-World social problems and the social change models and ideologies. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Blue Collar Society and Culture
description: Examines the social realities, lifestyles, and selfperceptions of bluecollar society and culture. Investigates socioeconomic and demographic patterns. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Aspects of Illness
description: Analysis of the social components of illness and its treatment; social factors in differential disease incidence, social problems experienced and presented by patients, conditions affecting use of treatment programs, and interaction patterns within healthcare institutions.

title: Sociological Internship Experience
description: Paid supervised field experience in a public agency or business setting. Training involves data analysis, evaluation research, and implementation of agency programs under the supervision of the employer and the Department of Sociology. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective of life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College.

title: Classical Sociological Theory
description: Study of sociological theories and theorists in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and relating these theories to contemporary social dynamics and theories in sociology. Examines the cultural and intellectual milieux in which the theories were created. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: The nature of minority groups and their distribution in American society; expressions, causes, and consequences of intergroup tensions and proposals for their reduction. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Social Trends in Mass Society
description: Major trends of mass society and changes in those trends. Students are encouraged to perform their own analyses of changing trends using existing information. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Industrial Sociology
description: The social aspects of modern, largescale industrial and business organization, social and technological factors contributing to its development, and its implications for the individual worker, the community, and society. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: The Family
description: The role of the family in contemporary society, factors influencing trends in family structure, functions, roles, stability, and their implications for both the community and individuals at varying stages of the family lifecycle. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Religion
description: Examines why people are religious, the consequences of religiosity, and the future of religion.

title: Social Gerontology
description: Social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: A sociological analysis of mental health with attention to social definitions of mental illness, selfrecognition of illness, the process of seeking care, treatment institutions, and the aftermath of treatment. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Sociology of Human Sexual Behavior
description: Human sexuality (behavior and attitudes) as related to sociological variables. Sociological correlates of human sexuality (premarital, marital, and nonmarital). Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Changing Societies
description: Analysis of social change processes within societies in the modern world with attention to social movement, institutional change, and organizational change. Discussion of implementing, controlling, and measuring change. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 or equivalent.

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Population Problems
description: An examination of population trends and their implications for social problems and social policy, with special attention to the American scene. Factors influencing the quality and quantity, composition, distribution, growth, and movement of populations. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historical functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems, especially the inner city. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century.

title: Sociology of the Inner City
description: Analysis of the social dynamics of the urban core in metropolitan areas. Attention given to the development of cities and their cores, stressing ecological and demographic factors. Examines the social issues associated with the concept of the inner city and policy alternatives for alleviating undesirable conditions. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220.

title: Seminar on Middletown
description: Focuses on two works by the Lynds, Middletown and Middletown in Transition, sociological classics about Muncie. Updates by teams of scholars have been undertaken. Students participate in a continuing sociological project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 or equivalent.

title: Evaluation Research
description: Considerations and problems in developing and conducting research to evaluate social action programs. Topics include the unique nature of evaluation research, operationalizing and assessing variables, goal attainment measures, needs assessments, and development of guidelines for programmatic change.

title: Internship in Sociology
description: Supervised field experience in a business, industrial, governmental, educational, or other setting. Training involves data analysis, research, evaluation, or other applications of sociological theories and methods. Supervision will be jointly provided by the employer and the Department of Sociology. Prerequisite: permission of sociology internship coordinator and the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent Study of Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with instructor with special competence in the subject involved. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220 and permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Topics in Sociology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of sociology. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 220. DEPARTMENT OF SPEECH COMMUNICATION R. Nitcavic, Chairperson; D. Diedrich, R. Dowling, L. Flint, W. Powers Speech communication offers programs in rhetorical theory, public, interpersonal, and organizational communication, and communication education. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare students for careers in business, government, politics, education, public affairs, public relations, and the media as well as for graduate study. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN SPEECH COMMUNICATION, 33 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS

title: Fundamentals of Public Communication
description: Principles and practice of effective oral communication; analysis and evaluation of the speakinglistening process; preparation in message construction, emphasizing the selection, organization, and delivery of materials.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: The theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: Focus on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Stresses the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation.

title: Intercultural Communication
description: Critical survey of major concepts in crosscultural and intercultural interaction. Examines the effects of customs, behaviors, and values on the interpersonal communication process.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: Speechmaking as a force in political and intellectual history; critical analysis of selected speeches in relation to political, social, and economic issues. Analysis of issues dealing with problems of progress, reform, and revolution. Emphasis on public address in American social and political institutions. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210.

title: Persuasion
description: The use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 210 or 240.

title: Contemporary Forms of Persuasion
description: Examines the modes of persuasion reflected in dimensions of American popular culture. Attention focuses on the persuasive appeals used in forms of popular culture and methods for evaluating their persuasive potential and impact. Stresses the importance of applying communication theory in everyday transactions.

title: Interviewing
description: The principles and types of interviews, with application of the principles in informational, employment, appraisal, and counseling interviews. Consideration of the following aspects of employment seeking: résumé, placement papers, job application, interview, and followup.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participant as well as the leader.

title: Topics in Speech Communication
description: Critical examination of selected topics and issues in speech communication. Designed to help students become familiar with current trends and theoretical and methodological issues in the discipline. May be repeated once by permission of instructor and department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Meeting Management
description: The study and practice of parliamentary procedure for business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations.

title: Business and Professional Communication
description: Focuses on the communication activities in business and the professions: oral reports, persuasive presentations, interpersonal skills, and communication problemsolving strategies.

title: Paid Internship
description: Supervised internships with business firms or public agencies offering work experience relating tocareers in speech communication. The job description may include research, training, organization, and planning of informative or persuasive campaigns, problem solving, and conflict management. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 240, and 350 or 451 and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Nonverbal Communication in Human Interaction
description: Examines the nature, forms, and functions of nonverbal codes in human speech communication. Focuses on understanding one's own nonverbal communication and that of others.

title: Presentational Communication
description: Preparation and delivery of presentations and longer speeches. Examination and analysis of current theories and research in persuasion as they pertain to managers, executives, and other professionals who submit proposals, ideas, and recommen- Speech Communication 277 dations to the scrutiny of clients, peers, and superiors. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Phonetics, dramatics, storytelling, speech correction, and public speaking for the elementary classroom teacher. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Speech Communication
description: Practical experience in intercollegiate debate, individual events, applied communication research, or alternate speech communication projects. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminartype class focusing on various aspects and problems of speech communication as they relate to people in their personal and professional relationships. Open to honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping the student acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: The Rhetoric of Political Campaigns
description: Examines the nature, forms, and effects of persuasion in organized political campaigns that seek to influence mass publics. Focuses on the skills needed to describe, analyze, and evaluate persuasive uses of language and to understand better the role of campaign persuasion in influencing voter behavior. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 372.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: Examines contemporary theories, concepts, models, and pertinent research related to the communication process in relatively unstructured facetoface settings. Particular emphasis on understanding message exchanges between people and how they affect the people involved. Introduces students to the approaches, variables, and topics that influence social interaction. Special attention to communication models, perception, symbols, systems, selfconcept, attitudes, meaning, and nonverbal message cues.

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of smallgroup literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual vs. group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problem solving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems.

title: Communication in Organizations
description: The oral communication processes in organizations, with special emphasis upon causes of communication problems and correctives for the problems. Examination of the systems of oral communication within organizations.

title: Communication Consultation
description: Focuses on the role and obligations of the communication consultant. Emphasis is placed upon interpersonal and team decisionmaking skills as well as developing breadth of knowledge, theoretical coherence, and the capacity to employ practical communication analysis and intervention consistent with organizational goals. Prerequisite: SPCH 451.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: The student with an area in the Department of Speech Communication pursues a specific subject in depth in consultation with a member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship in Speech
description: Onthejob experience in such places as college classrooms, political campaigns or offices, summer camps, or summer theaters. Students are permitted to earn some payment for their work in addition to the college credit, the amount depending upon the credit hours to be earned. Prerequisite: major or minor in speech and permission of department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one DEPARTMENT OF SPEECH PATHOLOGY AND AUDIOLOGY T. Hemeyer, Chairperson; L. Heady, R. Hoops, J. Johnson, W. Kramer, G. Lindell, C. Martin, T. Powell, C. Updike Speechlanguage pathologists provide diagnostic services and therapy to people with speech or language problems. Audiologists provide testing, hearingaid, and other rehablitative services to people with hearing problems. Speechlanguage pathologists and audiologists work in medical settings, schools, private practice, community and university clinics, nursing homes, and industrial settings. The Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology's programs are accredited by the American Speech-Language- Hearing Association. To become speech pathologists or audiologists, students must complete both bachelor's and master's degrees. As part of their work, students obtain extensive clinical practicum experience working with patients who have speech, language, and hearing problems. The department offers two undergraduate majors and two undergraduate minors. The 57-credit major, combined with an appropriate graduate program, leads to a state professional license, national certification, and school certification. The 48-credit major, combined with an appropriate graduate program, leads to a state professional license and national certification. The department operates the Ball State University Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic to provide an oncampus facility where students can have their initial practicum experience under the supervision of the department's faculty. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN SPEECH PATHOLOGY AND AUDIOLOGY, 57 hours

title: Survey of Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to speech pathology and audiology with a survey of speech and hearing disorders in relation to etiology, incidence, and management.

title: Clinical Phonetics
description: Study of speech sounds as applied to communication disorders. Transcription practice of normal and abnormal speech and the informational, perceptual aspects of phonetics. Relationship and application of distinctive features and phonological analysis to speech remediation. Open only to SPAA majors and minors.

title: Speech Acoustics
description: Introduction to the physical elements of sound, particularly as they apply to communication. Prerequisite: SPAA 201.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of Speech and Hearing
description: Study of the anatomy and physiology of the parts of the body involved in speech production, including respiratory, phonatory, articulatoryresonance, and neurological mechanisms. Not open to the student who has credit in SPCED 261.

title: Language Development
description: Development of the phonology, grammar, content, and function of language in children together with a review of environmental and personal conditions acting to influence that development.

title: Articulation Disorders
description: Designed to prepare students to diagnose and treat articulatory speech disorders, particularly in younger children. Includes laboratory observation in the treatment of defective speech. Prerequisite: SPAA 201, 261. Open only to students with areas in speech pathology and audiology.

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course to assist the beginning clinician in developing an understanding of clinical competency;

title: Introduction to Diagnosis and Appraisal
description: Techniques in the diagnosis of speech, language, and hearing disorders. Recognizing and understanding the components of differential diagnosis. Prerequisite: SPAA 410. Open only to speech pathology and audiology majors except by permission of department chairperson.

title: Stuttering 1: Research and Theory
description: An introduction to the disorder of stuttering with attention directed to its symptoms and development. Reviews the research and theoretical formulations regarding stuttering and its treatment. Prerequisite: SPAA 410.

title: Organic Speech and Language Disorders
description: An introductory study of neurology and anatomy of the brain and speech and language disorders resulting from brain damage such as cerebral palsy and aphasia. Other physical problems such as cleft palate and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 261, 410.

title: Speech Pathology and Audiology Practicum
description: The student performs observation and preprofessional participation with clients with various speech, language, and hearing disorders. Prerequisite: SPAA 410, 411. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to SPAA majors.

title: Hearing 1: Anatomy, Disorders, and Assessment
description: An overview of the anatomy and physiology of hearing disorders; hearing assessment. The management of school screening programs will be included in the assessment section. Practice in the use of various types of audiometers. Prerequisite: SPAA 260 and 261, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Hearing 2: Aural Habilitation
description: An overview of aural habilitation. The practical implications of various types of hearing losses and appropriate habilitative procedures. Amplification, auditory training, speechreading, education and vocational considerations, and psychosocial implications of hearing loss. Prerequisite: SPAA 443.

title: Directed Study in Speech Pathology and Audiology
description: The student with a major or minor in speech pathology and audiology pursues a specific subject in depth in consultation with a member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to SPAA majors or minors. DEPARTMENT OF TELECOMMUNICATIONS J. Misiewicz, Chairperson; N. Carlson, R. De Voe, W. Gehring, R. McConnell, A. Richardson, D. Smith, D. Wible, D. Wilhelm, G. Yeamans The program in radio, television, film, and corporate video includes curricula for students who intend to enter the broadcast and motion picture industries, as well as opportunities for working with electronic media in the classroom or in school administration systems that use media. The facilities of the university radio station, WBST-FM, and the closedcircuit television production facility offer additional practical experiences for students. The department's summer internships allow selected students to gain an insight into actual work in their chosen careers. Interns have been placed in markets throughout the United States. The Letterman Telecommunications Scholarships are offered to majors and minors in telecommunications. One fully funded scholarship (tuition, room and board, personal expenses, and transportation) for one year is awarded each year. The specific amount will be determined by the Office of Scholarships and Financial Aid. A number of partially funded scholarships also are awarded each year. The scholarships are awarded on the basis of creative endeavor. Grades are not a criterion, and only fulltime firstsemester juniors through firstsemester seniors are eligible. To be admitted to the department, a student must 1. Submit a typed application no later than five weeks before the first sophomore term of study. (Applications are available from the department office; these may be submitted toward the end of the freshman year, but not before.) 2. When returning the application, make an appointment with the assistant to the department chairperson for an entry interview. The student must bring his or her most recent DAPR to the interview. 3. Complete ENG 103 and 104 with a combined gradepoint average of 2.5 or higher (or the universityestablished equivalent). 4. Achieve an overall gradepoint average of 2.25 or higher (or the universityestablished equivalent). 5. Satisfy the typing proficiency requirement by completing either BEOA 111 or 112 with a grade of C or higher, or by passing the Department of Telecommunications Typing Test (a threeminute test with an error penalty) with a speed of least thirty words a minute. The test is usually offered during the first four weeks of a term. Completing these requirements results in conditional admission to the department; the student will be assigned a faculty advisor. To be granted regular status in the department, the student must confer with the faculty advisor, bringing a recent DAPR, to show the achievement of the following: 1. A gradepoint average of 2.33 or higher in ENG 103, 104 and TCOM 200, 202. 2. An overall gradepoint average of 2.25 or higher. A student whose overall gradepoint average falls below 2.25 will be placed on departmental probation. Failure to raise the overall gradepoint average to 2.25 during the next semester will result in dismissal from the program. Students whose overall gradepoint averages fall below 2.0 will be dismissed from the program. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (p. 21), the program of general studies (p. 23), and the concentration areas listed below. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN TELECOMMUNICATIONS, 43-45 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS Common core, 17 hours

title: Developmental History of Telecommunications
description: Historical review of the development of telecommunications as an industry. Emphasis on growth of radio and television as a communication system in a social setting. Special attention is given to technological advances that have occurred and are occurring in the industry. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors. The Edmund F Ball Telecommunications Building features stateoftheart audio and video equipment and recording and broadcast facilities.

title: Writing for Telecommunications
description: Designed to give the student an understanding of and practice with the styles and techniques used in writing for the media in telecommunications. Students will write extensively, producing scripts for commercials, news, and programs presented using electronic media. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Research: Writing and Reporting
description: Covers recently published research in telecommunications. Includes conducting some original research, learning the writing styles of various formats, and experiencing written and oral presentations of research. Prerequisite: TCOM 202.

title: Regulations of Telecommunications
description: Legal regulations that are foundations of telecommunications. Legal history from 1910 to the present. Actions by Congress, the Supreme Court, federal courts, and the states. Case study of rulings that most affect daily broadcasting. Prerequisite: TCOM 302. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Programs: Evaluation and Analysis
description: Analysis and appreciation of the complexity of programming decisions through examination of concepts, strategies, and techniques practiced by broadcasters. In addition, students will examine programmatic content in order to evaluate program quality. Prerequisite: TCOM 302. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Organizational Video Production
description: Video production that meets the requirements of business, industry, medicine, and special interest organizations. Identifying needs; planning, executing, and evaluating productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 310, 332. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: News Writing and Performance
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering, writing, and reporting broadcast news. Practical experience in the uses of audio tape recorders and telephone recording, electronic news gathering (ENG) equipment, and other similar equipment used by radio and television news reporters. Prerequisite: TCOM 330, 332. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Electronic News Gathering
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering, shooting, editing, and reporting news with electronic news gathering (ENG) video equipment. Students will plan, shoot, edit, and produce a varied series of news reports. Prerequisite: TCOM 320. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Audio Production
description: Emphasizes techniques and skills needed for audio production. Typical experiences in radio broadcasting. A practical test is part of the final examination, and students are expected to maintain a record of their productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 202. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Video Production
description: The student learns the basic skills of equipment operation in miniproductions that simulate television station programming. A practical test is part of the final examination, and students must maintain records of their course work. Prerequisite: TCOM 202. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Radio Sales
description: Study and practice of the skills for selling radio time. Both salesmanship and the use of marketing research tools are emphasized. Students will have practice in preparing sales presentations for clients. Prerequisite: TCOM 304. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Broadcast Promotion
description: Promotional concepts, strategies, and methodologies available for carrying out efficient and effective promotional campaigns for broadcast stations. Students will have practice designing and executing audience, image, and sales promotions. Prerequisite: TCOM 340 and 345. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Television Sales
description: Skills needed for selling television time. Emphasizes the use of quantitative audience research tools. Students will have practice in preparing sales presentations for clients. Prerequisite: TCOM 304.

title: World Film History 1
description: History of world cinema from its beginning until World War II. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as Telecommunications 283 key movements in other national cinemas before 1941, such as German Expressionism and the Soviet Montage School. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: World Film History 2
description: Continues the study of world cinema from World War II until the present. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema as well as the post-1945 national cinema movements exemplified by Italian Neo-Realism and the French New Wave films. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Film Genres
description: Study of the general types and forms of film expression, each identified with a specific tradition. Film genres include Westerns, screwball comedies, gangster films, musicals, etc. Offered twice each academic year, with a different genre each semester. May be repeated once. Prerequisite: permission of instructor. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Announcing
description: Concentrates on training and practice in the vocal interpretive skills necessary for speech presentation. Students study the structure and use of the human vocal system; analysis of copy; and delivery of verbal messages in radio, television, and recording. Prerequisite: TCOM 302 and SPCH 250. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Sports Announcing
description: Research, writing, production, and performance with emphasis on the remote broadcast. Study of rules, organization and planning, promotion and selling, techniques of playbyplay, and color description of major sports. Lab includes onsite practical experience. Prerequisite: permission of instructor. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 2 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent study
description: A special service course. Student will be directed by a faculty member or an approved representative of an outside agency directly related to the subject. Term project is a written report. Prerequisite: junior standing and departmental approval. A written proposal for a project in telecommunications must be submitted to the department four weeks before term of study begins. A total of 6 hours may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Internship Study
description: Presents an opportunity for the student to gain practical applied onthejob experience with an approved agency directly related to the business. Students must make written application to the department and meet criteria before enrollment. Prerequisite: junior standing and departmental approval. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Practicum
description: Production of an audio or audiovideo project. Requires submittal of detailed outlined proposal of the project to the faculty member who will direct the project. Prerequisite: permission and approval of instructor directing student after review of student's work. A written proposal for a project must be submitted four weeks before the term of study.

title: Honors Colloquium in Telecommunications
description: Exploration of selected issues in telecommunications, with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Prerequisite: permission of instructor. Open only to Honors students.

title: Social Responsibility
description: Political, economic, social, and governmental influences on telecommunications. Students will examine the contemporary issues and the ethics surrounding them that confront broadcasters today. Prerequisite: senior standing and TCOM 306. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Organizational Media Management
description: An examination of the special requirements of business, industrial, medical, and other uses of television for instruction, information, public relations, etc. Special emphasis on budgeting and management. Corporate program sources are considered. Prerequisite: TCOM 312. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Television News
description: Planning, gathering, writing, and presenting a television newscast. Discussion of current events; evaluation of commercial station newscasts; onair production of typical news programs. The productionclass periods are two hours in length. Prerequisite: TCOM 323 and 332.

title: Advanced Video Production
description: Advanced course in television production in which the student does more original and longer productions. Format for programs written and produced duplicates typical programming in the commercial broadcast operation. The student is required to keep a record of produced projects. Prerequisite: TCOM 332. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Management of Telecommunications
description: Problems and responsibilities of management in the telecommunications industry. Consists largely of guest lecturers, class discussion, management roleplaying, and computer projects to make students familiar with administrative practices in the industry. Prerequisite: TCOM 344 and senior standing. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Film Censorship
description: Emphasizes the moral measurements and restraints that have affected the film industry almost since its inception. A chronology of events influencing both the direction and content of motion pictures. Examines governmental, legal, church, and community pressures and restraints. Prerequisite: permission of instructor. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Seminar in Film Theory
description: An analysis of the key theorists in the history of world cinema as well as some influential critics of film. A special focus of this course is on the documentary film. The course examines many dimensions of the documentary film: historical, commercial, informational, educational, and propaganda applications. Prerequisite: TCOM 360 and 361. Open only to telecommunications majors and minors.

title: Film Production

title: Seminar in Documentary Film

title: Advanced Script Writing

title: Communications Technologies
description: Explores technologies beyond the conventional broadcast and organizational systems. title: Seminar in Television Production
description: Requires planning, writing, and producing a major project in television. Each project, as it develops, will serve as a case study for the class to discuss and evaluate. Prerequisite: departmental permission after review of student's work.

title: Video Graphics Technology
description: Provides working knowledge of video computer graphic programs using Cubicomp graphics generators. Students will manipulate DOS files, draw backgrounds with True Color Paint, create threedimensional objects with Build, and combine Draw and Build for animation images in Motion program. title: Research in Telecommunications
description: Acquaints students with principles and methodologies of scholarly research; illustrates applications of research within electronic communication, both for scholarly investigation and for use in support of the functions of broadcasting. description: Considers the educational needs of bilingual students with specific regard to the evaluation of existing materials, the development of materials, and appropriate bilingual classroom methodology. Parallel: EDGEN 370.

PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES PRE-STUDENT TEACHING PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES The purpose of prestudent teaching professional laboratory experiences is to give students pursuing teacher education a systematic, planned sequence of experiences in appropriate educational settings. These experiences are designed to make students familiar with principles of classroom management and the teachinglearning process in practical and real school environments, and to help them learn how to teach. The prestudent teaching laboratory experiences culminate in EDEL 360, EDJHM 285, or EDSEC 280, which require assignment to classrooms in appropriate educational settings for the semester to observe, prepare instructional presentations, and undertake other instructional tasks appropriate for students before student teaching. The university provides laboratory settings for EDEL 360, EDJHM 285, and EDSEC 280 in the oncampus Burris Laboratory School as well as in affiliated public school systems in Muncie and others within commuting distance. Weekly seminars with a college supervisor are an integral part of the laboratory experience for these courses. STUDENT TEACHING Student teaching gives students an opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professionally licensed teachers cooperating with the university in the studentteaching program. Application for Student Teaching Students should apply for studentteaching assignments in January of the year before that in which they expect to do student teaching. Students transferring to Ball State after this date who plan to complete their certification requirements in one year must make application in April (for fall) or September (for spring). Official notification of the studentteaching assignment will be mailed to the student after the final eligibility determination, usually during the semester before student teaching. Students needing information about their assignments before this notification may inquire at the studentteaching office. General Consideration The student must be free of outside commitments that might interfere with fulltime studentteaching obligations. Students should not be regularly employed, nor should they carry heavy loads of extracurricular activities. Enrollment for course overload during the semester is permitted only with approval of the coordinator for student teaching. Student teaching requirements also include a set number of days in seminars conducted by the university supervisor at the beginning and end of the semester. Students should be prepared to accept studentteaching assignments wherever the university can place them for the best professional experience. Although requests for particular supervising teachers, schools, or school systems are considered, the placement process requires close cooperation with the public school systems, and there are instances when circumstances within the local school system prohibit a specific placement request. Student Teaching: Senior High, Junior High/Middle School License, grades 5-12 Student teachers preparing to teach at the senior high, junior high, and middle school levels are required to spend full time for a minimum of ten weeks in student teaching. They must enroll in EDSEC 460 (4 hours) and EDSEC 462 (3 hours). Students may take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching (3-5 hours), to complete an additional part or the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: All-Grade License Student teachers preparing to teach at the allgrade level are required to spend full time for a minimum of ten weeks in student teaching. They must enroll in EDALG 470 (4 hours) and EDALG 472 (3 hours). Students may take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching (3-5 hours), to complete part or the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: Elementary Standard License Students seeking licensure in elementary education must enroll for 9 semester hours in EDEL 463 (3 hours) and EDEL 464 (6 hours) and spend full time for ten weeks in student teaching. Students who want to take elective credits in student teaching may enroll for up to 3 hours in EDEL 465, Elective Student Teaching, for assignment for the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: Early Childhood Standard License Students seeking licensure in early childhood education must enroll in EDEL 461 for 6 hours and EDEL 462 for 3 hours and spend full time for ten weeks in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten-Primary Standard License Students seeking licensure in kindergartenprimary education must enroll for 12 hours in EDEL 467 (6 hours) and EDEL 468 (6 hours) and spend the entire semester in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten Endorsement Students completing the kindergarten endorsement on the standard license for early childhood or elementary education Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services 293 must enroll in EDEL 465 for 3 hours for students teaching in kindergarten for six weeks, all day. Student Teaching: Special Education Students with allgrade majors in special education will complete 12 hours in either SPCED 489 (Mild Disabilities) or SPCED 491 (Serious Emotional Handicaps) or SPCED 492 (Severe Disabilities). Students with allgrade majors in special education: hearing impairments will complete SPCED 466 (1-12 hours) for a minimum of 12 hours for sixteen weeks of fulltime student teaching. Students pursing teaching minors or endorsements in special education must complete student teaching requirements in the area of concentration as follows: mildly mentally handicapped, 8 hours (eight weeks); severe disabilities, 12 hours (sixteen weeks); hearing impairments, 6-9 hours (six to nine weeks). title: International Dialogue on American Education and Life
description: Perspectives on American education and its cultural setting developed through interaction among international and American students and comparative study of educational and other social institutions as they relate to education. EDUCATION: HIGHER (EDHI)

title: Introduction to Personnel Services in Residence Halls
description: 9-12 Principles involved in selfawareness, developing interand intrapersonal skills, and examining the development of community within the residence hall. Prerequisite: sophomore standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Leadership and Development of Student Organizations
description: Examines philosophical bases, group processes, and skills relevant to leadership and development of student organizations in higher education. title: Principles of Teaching, Curriculum and Classroom Management: Middle School
description: Combines the theory and practice of teaching at the middle school level. Includes direct teaching experiences with early adolescents in public school settings; seminars concerned with such topics as curriculum, instructional strategies, legal aspects, discipline, and advanced microteaching. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205; EDPSY 250 or 251, and approval to pursue a teaching curriculum. Parallel: EDSEC 280.

title: Independent Study in Junior High/Middle School Education
description: Independent study and research in junior high/middle school topics and activities to be chosen in consultation with an instructor with competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Instructional Strategies and Approaches in Junior High/Middle School
description: Factors affecting the total instructional responsibilities in junior high/middle schools are studied. Students are required to develop skills in individualizing instruction to serve the full range of students, the ability to work cooperatively with other professional personnel, and instructional techniques and evaluation procedures especially appropriate for junior high/middle school teaching. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 and EDPSY 251 or 351.

title: Discipline: Improving Student Behavior in Junior High/Middle School
description: Designed to prepare prospective junior high/middle school educators to cope with discipline problems in all junior high/middle school settings. Emphasizes skills and procedures in preventing or remedying disruptive behavior by junior high/middle school students and ways to create positive environments for learning.

title: Student Teaching in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Required for the standard license in junior high/middle school education. Simultaneous registration in EDJHM 462 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for ten weeks in a public junior high/middle school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Student Teaching in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Required for the standard license in junior high/middle school education. Simultaneous registration in EDJHM 460 is required. Involves a fullday assignment for ten weeks in a public junior high/middle school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

title: Elective Student Teaching: Junior High/Middle School
description: Elective studentteaching experience enables a student to complete a fullsemester assignment in a fullday student teaching assignment in a public junior high/middle school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. Parallel: EDJHM 460 and 462. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Advanced Undergraduate Practicum in Junior High/Middle School Education
description: Provides direct, supervised experiences for students wanting to gain increased skill and knowledge regarding junior high/middle school teaching. Prerequisite: EDSEC 280. EDUCATION: LIBRARY (EDLIB)

title: Information Resources in Libraries
description: An examination of the most essential information sources in libraries, such as dictionaries, encyclopedias, periodical indexes, and special reference works in subject areas. Open to all students who desire a better understanding of the library as an information center.

title: Reference Materials for Information Centers and Libraries
description: Examines the role and function of the information specialist in information centers and libraries. Evaluation and selection of information resources, and directed experience using representative materials essential to information centers and libraries.

title: Selection and Management of Audiovisual Equipment
description: Sources and principles of selection and management of audiovisual equipment and related devices. Preparation of bid specifications.

title: School Media Center and Library Administration
description: Principles of planning, organizing, supervising, and evaluating schoolmediacenter and public library services. Includes originating model program plans.

title: Technical Processing: Cataloging and Classification
description: Accepted procedures for systematic organization of book, audiovisual, computer, and other materials by use of the Dewey Decimal Classification and the construction of a library catalog. Working knowledge of OCLC terminal for searching, input, and manipulation of cataloging data.

title: Technical Processing: On -line and Automation
description: Practice in cataloging and organization of materials of all types. Study of principles of online systems and microcomputerbased technical processing.

title: Media Design and Production
description: Basic knowledge and laboratory work concerning production of materials and maintenance of audiovisual equipment. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Media Practicum
description: Supervised field experience for students in school media centers or libraries. Prerequisite: EDLIB 280 and approval of program coordinator or department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Microcomputers and Library Automation
description: An introduction to microcomputers and information systems in library automation.

title: Online Information Retrieval Techniques
description: Provides overview of online information services and principles of information retrieval. Students develop search strategies to meet client's information needs and conduct online searches in a supervised laboratory.

title: Methods and Materials for School Library Media Centers
description: Methods and materials for teaching skills necessary for successful completion of assignments using resources of school library media centers and libraries.

title: Selection of Audiovisual Materials and Microcomputer Software
description: Selection and evaluation of audiovisual materials and microcomputer software for instructional and management use in libraries. Systematic identification of sources and selection tools. Practice in selection and evaluation.

title: Production of Audiovisual Media
description: A project course that meets the individual needs of undergraduate students in the production of such instructional media as 8- and 16-mm films, filmstrips, slide sets, and tape recordings.

title: Selection of Library Materials
description: Fundamental principles and objectives of selection of library materials. Development of skill in using reliable aids for selection and evaluation of materials for public, academic, and school libraries.

title: Materials for Children
description: Reading and examining books and other materials for the enrichment of library programs for preschool through upper elementary.

title: Materials for Young Adults
description: Reading and examining books and other materials for young adult programs. EDUCATION: READING MIDDLE (EDRDM)

title: Improving General Reading Skills in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: A general course for all junior high/middle school teachers that examines reading problems and provides specific methodology for improvement of reading skills in junior high/middle schools. General diagnostic teaching techniques appropriate for teachers in all curricular areas are to be achieved. Exit competencies are required. Lab included. EDUCATION: READING SECONDARY (EDRDS)

title: Reading in Secondary School
description: Practical procedures for developing effective reading skills to be applied by all secondary classroom teachers. Focuses on relationships between the process of reading and learning of content, on planning to meet total range of student reading needs, and on methods and materials to enhance comprehension and study skills in all areas of secondary school curriculum. Lab included. EDUCATION: SECONDARY (EDSEC)

title: Basic Concepts of Secondary Education
description: Using classroom investigation and practical field experiences, examines the structure, function, and development of secondary education in the United States. Designed to help students make valid decisions about preparing for and functioning in teaching careers by studying professionalism, job requirements, employment opportunities, secondary school curricula, and the role of secondary education within the entire educational process.

title: Introduction to Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Introduces prospective teachers to responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, and supporting personnel and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 206 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Intermediate Cross-Role Experiences in Secondary Schools
description: Advanced study of responsibilities assigned to various educational personnel in secondary schools through direct contact with teachers, counselors, administrators, supporting personnel, and students. Role differentiation will be explored. Prerequisite: EDSEC 200.

title: Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior in American Secondary Schools
description: Analyzes conditions that influence the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in schools and educational settings. Particular emphasis on the behavior of ethnic and cultural group members in the American secondary schools. Lab included.

title: Advanced Study of Ethnic and Multicultural Group Behavior
description: Focuses on indepth analyses of many of the concepts introduced in EDSEC 205. Particular emphasis on variables that contribute to the development and maintenance of prejudice, stereotypes, racism, and oppressive conditions. Equal emphasis on instructional strategies for combating such behaviors. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Laboratory Experience in Secondary Education
description: Provides direct experiences in working with students, teachers, paraprofessionals, community agencies, and other appropriate assignments for undergraduate students who plan to enter secondary school teaching. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Microcomputers in the Secondary School
description: Provides a basic understanding of the functions and applications of microcomputers in the classroom setting. Topics include evaluation and use of available software, introduction to the development of teachermade software, and the availability and selection of hardware.

title: Secondary School
description: Inducts the student into the teaching act. Includes specific technical skill development, study of principles of teaching and evaluation, use of instructional media equipment, curriculum development and organization, and classroom management. Intensive inschool assignments, observation skills, participation, and direct contact with adolescents are required. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205; EDPSY 250 or 251, and approval to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel: EDPSY 290. Parallel: EDJHM 285.

title: Instructional Strategies in Multicultured Schools
description: Theory and application of special instructional strategies of teaching and learning in secondary school classrooms with special emphasis on multicultured educational situations. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Planning and Assessing Instructional Programs
description: Designed to provide secondary school teachers with methods of establishing instructional programs with feedback networks that will encourage continuous assessment and appropriate alterations of the educational environment. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Intermediate Study of Microcomputers in the Secondary School
description: Designed to help students understand and develop the application of computerassisted instruction to their respective disciplines. Prerequisite: EDGEN 320 for students pursuing the computer endorsement. EDSEC 255 for all others.

title: Independent Study in Secondary Education
description: Independent study and research in secondary education. Topics and activities to be chosen in consultation with an instructor with competence in the subject involved. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be

title: Problems in Education and Professional Concerns of the Beginning Teacher
description: Opportunity to examine critically and to focus educational experience and knowledge on contemporary and personally significant problems of education. Emphasizes immediate professional concerns of prospective firstyear teachers. Prerequisite: EDSEC 301 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Social Foundations of Secondary and Middle School Education
description: Education as an institution in society and its relationship to the individual and American culture from sociological, philosophical, historical, economic, political, and anthropological perspectives. Such contemporary issues as cultural values, social class, legal aspects, ethnic groups, political pressure, and the role of the teacher will be stressed. Prerequisite: EDSEC 280.

title: High School Curriculum
description: General perspectives of curriculum principles, practices, and procedures common to secondary schools. Organizational structures, innovations, and intimate relationships between instruction and curriculum. Concurrently, students will choose areas of concentration or preparation as they relate to the total high school curriculum.

title: Discipline: Improving Student Behavior in Secondary Schools
description: Designed to prepare prospective secondary teachers to cope with discipline problems in all secondary school settings. Emphasizes skills and procedures for preventing or remedying disruptive behavior by secondary students and ways to create a positive environment for learning.

description: Involves a fullday assignment for either three or six weeks in a public school. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. Parallel: EDSEC 460, 462 or EDALG 470, 472. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned.

title: General Innovations in Secondary Education
description: Innovative practices will be identified, defined, and analyzed relative to their impact on secondary schools. Creative, innovative instructional approaches will be used. Field trips or visitations to innovative secondary schools will be arranged when practical, and students will concentrate on innovative practices. DEPARTMENT OF SPECIAL EDUCATION J. description: An introduction to definitions, characteristics, and educational needs of children who deviate from normal in mental, physical, social, and emotional ways. Examines federal and state legal bases for education of exceptional children.

description: Examines instructional methodology and curricular practices for more effective management of the preschool handicapped child's home and preschool learning environments. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 or equivalent.

title: Developmental Methods with Preschool Handicapped
description: Examines instructional methodology and curricular practices for developing the preschool handicapped child's cognitive, language, creative, and physical environments. These developmental components will be studied based on current instructional practices with preschool handicapped children.

title: Practicum—Teaching Young Handicapped Children
description: Student works with handicapped children in a supervised teaching practicum to acquire practical skills for planning and organizing activities to meet the needs of handicapped children. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Microcomputers and the Exceptional Learner
description: Introduction to microcomputer applications in special education through orientation to hardware, programming experience, word processing, and special purpose software. Also emphasizes teaching strategies for introducing microcomputers to children in the classroom.

title: History of Education of the Deaf and Psychology of Deafness
description: Brief study of educational provisions for the deaf from the beginning to the present and a survey of the social, educational, and vocational problems of deafness.

title: Education of Preschool Hearingand Language-Impaired Children
description: The development of oral communication in preschool hearingimpaired children. Directed observations of both hearing and hearingimpaired classes, home visitations, and the parenttraining program. Prerequisite: EDPSY 250.

title: Practicum in Special Education
description: Observation and assistance of teachers in special classes for exceptional children. Prerequisite: SPCED 201. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Human Relations and Consulting Skills for Special Educators
description: Examines human relations strategies and skills that will help teachers of exceptional children build trust and understanding with other professionals and parents of the child. Skills are acquired through simulation and practicum modules. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 with a minimum grade of C or permission of department chairperson.

title: Legal and Procedural Foundations of Special Education
description: Studies court cases, statelevel legislation, and related historical events that preceded passage of PL 94-142. Covers definitions, procedural requirements, and legal safeguards of PL 94-142 and PL 99-457 as implemented in Indiana Rule 5-1. Prerequisite: SPCED 201 with a minimum grade of C.

title: Principles of Behaviorology in Special Education
description: Intermediatelevel course designed to enable special education professionals to increase their contributions to the field by virtue of adding the scientific foundations of behaviorology to their repertoires. Prerequisite: EDPSY 306 or equivalent.

title: Introduction of Behavior Disorders
description: Introduction to the history of educating children with behavior disorders; the problems of defining, assessing, and treating behavior disorders; and types and causes of disordered behavior. Prerequisite: SPCED 201.

title: Educating Elementary Students with Behavior Disorders
description: Educational assessments, methods, materials, and programs for seriously emotionally handicapped elementary school children. For future teachers of students with behavior disorders. Prerequisite: SPCED 332 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Educating Secondary Students with Behavior Disorders
description: Educational assessments, methods, materials, and programs for seriously emotionally handicapped youth. For future teachers of students with behavior disorders. Prerequisite: SPCED 332, 334; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Psychology and Physiology of Physical Disability
description: Designed for future teachers of crippled or other healthimpaired students. Includes etiology, assessment, and understanding necessary to educate students with physical disabilities. Prerequisite: SPCED 372.

title: Introduction to Mild Disabilities
description: Studies psychological, environmental, and cultural factors that contribute to mild disabilities. Compares and differentiates historical and contemporary definitions of mental retardation and learning disabilities. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 301; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Persons with Mental Retardation
description: Studies various types and degrees of retardation; the psychological, environmental, and cultural factors that contribute to retardation. Emphasizes etiology, assessment, and issues. Prerequisite: SPCED 201; BIO 453 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Developmental Language Skills for Persons with Mild Disabilities
description: Compares and contrasts the language development of exceptional children with that of nonhandicapped children. Language difficulties are viewed as they relate to the teaching of listening skills, oral expression, written expression, reading, and other academic subject areas. Prerequisite: SPCED 201; SPAA 370.

title: Assessment in Special Education
description: Educational assessment practices with exceptional children with emphasis on curriculumbased assessment and informal tests. Role of the special educator on the multidisciplinary evaluation team. Prerequisite: SPCED 201, 371; EDPSY 345.

title: Method of Teaching the Mildly Disabled
description: Studies techniques of teaching children and adults with mild disabilities. Emphasis is placed on the process by which content is taught to students of all age levels within the least restrictive environment. Prerequisite: SPCED 266, 301, 371, 375; MATHS 125; EDRDG 400.

title: Educating Persons with Severe Disabilities
description: Studies persons with moderate, severe, or profound mental retardation, orthopedic or other health impairments, or autism. Topics include assessment strategies, instructional planning, and research on education in the least restrictive environment. Prerequisite: SPCED 372.

title: Educational Methods for Persons with Physical and Multiple Handicaps
description: Examines environmental adaptations, curriculum, and teaching and management methods for the instruction of persons with orthopedic handicaps or special health problems. Emphasizes multidisciplinary practices and procedures based on research in education and allied fields. Prerequisite: SPCED 372, 377, 378.

title: Educating Youth and Adults with Severe Disabilities
description: Introduction to the concept of lifelong educational needs of persons with severe disabilities. Topics include career education, vocational and employment programming, transition from school to work, and other educational issues for youth and adults. Prerequisite: SPCED 372, 377, 378, 379; or permission of department chairperson.

title: Education of Gifted Children
description: Examination of psychological characteristics and educational needs of gifted and talented children in the schools. Definitions of giftedness and identification procedures are studied; review of current and past practices in the field.

title: Speech Development for the Deaf
description: The International Phonetic Alphabet, Northhampton Charts, diacritical markings, and other methods and techniques used to teach speech to the deaf. Prerequisite: SPCH 216 and SPCED 240, or permission of department chairperson.

title: Practicum in Speech for the Deaf
description: Observation of a person working with preschool children in developmental speech. Time will also be devoted to speech improvement for older children. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 and 446 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Manual Communications
description: Theory and research underlying the language of signs and fingerspelling (manual alphabet) is considered. Development of receptive and expressive skills in manual communications is required. Required of students intending to student teach in schools or classes using total communication.

title: Advanced Manual Communication
description: A course in manual communication designed to improve conversational skill in signs and fingerspelling to a functional level for expressive and receptive use in a classroom for hearingimpaired children. Prerequisite: SPCED 451 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Language for the Deaf
description: Compares language development of hearing children with that of deaf children. Levels of abstraction and the difficulty encountered in both receptive and expressive language are examined. The philosophy underlying various methods of language teaching is studied. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and SPAA 370 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Language Methods for the Deaf
description: Language systems are studied and used in practice situations. Includes Fitzgerald Straight Language for the Deaf, Barry Five- Slate, Wing Symbols, and the Natural Method. Language outlines from different schools are used as supplementary aids. Prerequisite: SPCED 240, 266, and 454.

title: Teaching Reading and Elementary School Subjects to the Deaf
description: Principles and methods of teaching reading to deaf children in the lower and higher grades; methods of teaching such subjects as arithmetic and science. Prerequisite: SPCED 240 and 266 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Student Teaching: Hearing Impaired
description: Required preservice teaching practica for students seeking licensure in special education hearingimpaired. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. A total of 6 hours of credit must be earned, but a student may earn up to 12.

title: Expressive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Provides students who have basic manual communication skills with intensive training and practice in expressive interpreting for the deaf. Prerequisite: permission of department chairperson.

title: Receptive Interpreting for the Deaf
description: Designed to provide students who have basic manual communication ability with professional skill for interpreting manual language in special situations. Opportunity for extensive practice and evaluation will be provided. Prerequisite: SPCED 468 or permission of department chairperson.

title: Methods and Materials for the Mildly Mentally Handicapped
description: Special class organization, instructional materials, and methods and techniques used in the instruction of the mildly mentally handicapped. Using the individualized education plan (IEP) and mainstreaming are incorporated. Prerequisite: SPCED 266 (1 hr.), 372; EDRDG 430; and MATHS 391.

title: Diagnostic and Prescriptive Teaching of the Mildly Handicapped
description: Continuation of methods and materials for the mildly handicapped, begun in SPCED 474, with emphasis on use of the diagnosticprescriptive model to determine the learner's special needs and prescription of required curricular modifications in the IEP. Prerequisite: SPCED 266, 474 or 376.

description: Required for licensure in special education: mildly mentally handicapped. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. A total of 9 hours of credit must be earned, but a student may earn up to 12

description: Required for licensure in special education: mild disabilities. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

description: Required for licensure in special education: physically/multiply handicapped. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Student Teaching: Seriously Emotionally Handicapped
description: Required for licensure in special education: seriously emotionally handicapped. Prerequisite: admission to student teaching.

description: Required for licensure in special education: moderately mentally handicapped, severely/profoundly mentally handicapped, and multiply handicapped. Margenau, J. Nemitz The Indiana Academy for Science, Mathematics, and Humanities is a residential school for three hundred of Indiana's most academically gifted high school juniors and seniors. In addition to core courses required for all students, the exploratory curriculum gives students the opportunity to sample advanced courses from the university's curriculum and to pursue individualized research and experiential education opportunities in cooperation with businesses, university faculty members, and practicing professionals. Students are also required to donate time to both academy and community service. The academy also offers opportunities for outstanding educators from throughout Indiana to teach in and study at the academy for a semester or a year. An interactive telecommunications system delivers selected academy classes to gifted pupils in other schools. In addition, academy faculty members will develop and distribute curriculum materials for the gifted and organize regular workshops for teachers of the gifted. Experiential Education Students are more likely to achieve their potential if they can apply what they are learning in an educational program that gives them experience in the world beyond the boundaries of the campus. Such experiences can also enhance students' personal and career development. Therefore, the university's goal is to offer each student the opportunity to participate in some form of experiential education. This experience may include such noncredit oncampus opportunities as working with Student Voluntary Services, becoming a research assistant, or providing tutorial services. Students may also receive academic credit through their major or minor areas of study for cooperative education or internship experiences.

title: Alternating Cooperative Education
description: For the student participating in a paid careerrelated work experience alternating periods of fulltime work with semesters of academic study, but who for a variety of reasons is unable to earn academic credit. A $50 affiliation fee will be charged. Prerequisite: permission of instructor.

title: Parallel Cooperative Education
description: For the student participating in a paid careerrelated work experience while enrolled in university courses halftime (for at least 6 credit hours), but who for a variety of reasons is unable to earn academic credit.
