title: People and Chemistry
description: Introductory treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as organization and language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature and classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these topics to everyday living. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 101, 111.

title: General, Organic, and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of general chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences and related areas. Four hours of lecture and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 111.

title: General Chemistry 1
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic an'd molecular structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, properties of solutions, and nature of matter. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemical kinetics, electrochemistry, chemical equilibrium, chemistry of metals and nonmetals, and radioactivity. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 111; MATHS 108.

title: Survey of Organic and Biochemistry
description: A broadly based introductory course suitable for life science, natural resources, and general science majors. Three hours of lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Lecture and intensive laboratory treatment of the theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements, including gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations, ion exchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visible spectrophotometry. One and onehalf hours of lecture and four and onehalf hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: Nomenclature, structure, bonding, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 234.

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of natural products and biomolecules. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 235.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material includes nomenclature, covalent bonding, molecular structure, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Laboratory experience includes spectroscopy and syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: A continuation of CHEM 234, including the properties of carbohydrates, proteins, and other natural products. Laboratory experience includes qualitative organic analysis and multistep syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 234. CR HRS CR HRS Chemistry 191 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentation: electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods. For chemical/medical technologists or departmental minors. Two hours of iecture and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics. Especially for premedical, biology, and general science majors, chemistry teaching majors, and chemistry minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitation/laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225; MATHS 161. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 344.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: Thermodynamic and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 235 or 232; MATHS 172; one year of college physics.

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 344. Topics include reaction kinetics, theoretical aspects of quantum mechanics, and spectroscopy. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 344.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry
description: Organic chemistry of carboxylic acids, amines, and their derivatives; biochemistry of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids; metabolism and the regulation of metabolic processes. For students in life sciences, dietetics, and medical technology. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory session weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or its equivalent. Not open to departmental majors in chemistry.

title: Practical Experience in Chemistry
description: Paid work and learning experience as a practicing chemist. Practical problemsolving experience will be gained through such programs as internships, practicums, cooperative education programs, and the Department of Chemistry summer research program. Prerequisite: application, recommendation of the program selection committee, and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. One hour may be counted toward the associate in science in chemical technology degree. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward the departmental major.

title: Specialized Topics in Chemistry
description: Discussion, experimentation, or both in specialized topics in and related to chemistry. Information concerning specific topics offered during a given semester is available from the departmental office. Lecture, discussion, and laboratory schedules appropriate to the topic offered. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 hour may be counted toward departmental major or minor requirements.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for chemical technologists. Assignments equivalent to four clock hours a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of the department chairperson. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry.

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Prerequisite: 20 hours of chemistry or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 1
description: Theoretical principles and applications of selected spectroscopic, electrochemical, and chromatographic methods, with illustrative experiments. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225 and 344 or 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 2
description: Advanced treatment of selected topics in spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and chromatography. Introduction to mass spectroscopy, nuclear methods, thermal and surface analysis. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 420 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Organic Laboratory Techniques
description: Laboratory course that includes multistep syntheses of organic compounds, their isolation, purification, and characterization using modern spectroscopic and chromatographic techniques. Six hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or its equivalent.

title: Physical-Organic Chemistry
description: Theoretical aspects of structure, including resonance and molecular orbital descriptions of electron distribution, aromaticity, symmetry, stereochemistry, and effects of structure on reactivity in acidbase reactions. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements, including the relationships of chemical properties and atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, acidbase theories, chemical periodicity, and modern theories of coordination compounds. Four hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235 or 360; MATHS 161 or 171.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 1
description: Chemistry and techniques for isolation, purification, and identification of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. For students majoring in chemistry, life sciences, and premedicine. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 463 including biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids; and regulation of metabolic processes. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 463.

title: Independent Study and Research
description: Scientific investigation on an individual basis under the supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, experimental work, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward any departmental major. DEPARTMENT OF COMPUTER SCIENCE C. Fuelling, Chairperson; K. Bagga, P. Buis, K. Keil, R. McCormick, J. McGrew, E. McKinney, C. Nelson, F. Owens, R. Place, C. Tzeng, M. Underkoffler, W. Zage Computer science is concerned with collection, storage, retrieval, and processing of data and information, as well as with the data structures, algorithms, and computer programs used to perform these tasks. The departmental major in computer science with its special emphasis on software is accredited by the Computer Science Accreditation Board. A cooperative education program is available to majors in computer science. Students may enter this program after the completion of two semesters (minimum 30 credits) in which they have earned minimum cumulative gradepoint averages of 3.0 in the required computer science and mathematics courses and at least 2.5 in all courses. The cooperative director in the Department of Computer Science advises students in this program and assists in the work placement of each student. The university cannot guarantee work assignments for all students. To be admitted to a major or minor program in computer science, students must have a mathematical background strong enough to take the first required calculus course, MATHS 161. Transfer students applying for admission to the computer science program must submit transcripts of credits and catalog course descriptions of the computer science courses for which they want to transfer credit. To remain in the computer science program, students must earn combined gradepoint averages of at least 2.5 in MATHS 161, 162; CS 120, 121, 224, and 230 with grades of at least C in each course. Students will be guided by the outline of baccalaureate degrees (p. 25), the program of general studies (p. 29) and the concentration areas listed below. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN COMPUTER SCIENCE, 75-90 hours Option 1, 75-78 hours

title: Introduction to Microcomputers
description: Covers computer literacy topics including a brief history of computing, current trends in the use of microcomputers, and the effects of computers on society. To understand microcomputers better, students work through an integrated software package and write and debug a number of short BASIC programs. Not open to students who have credit in CS 114.

title: Introduction to Programming 1
description: Problems of programming in a structured language emphasizing topdown design and modular structure. Designed primarily for students in the computer endorsement program. Prerequisite: MATHS 125, 201, or the equivalent. Not open to students who have credit in CS 120 or the equivalent.

title: Introduction to Programming 2
description: An introduction to files and their applications. An introduction to a LOGO environment. Prerequisite: CS 110 or its equivalent. Open only to students not majoring in computer science.

title: Computer Literacy for Nonprogrammers
description: Presents the computer as a tool for students majoring in other disciplines to solve problems arising in their subjects. Students will use such software as spreadsheets, databases, and word processing and will develop vocabulary. Not open to students who have credit in CS 121.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines other than computer science. Timesharing computer techniques using BASIC with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. Not open to students who have credit in CS 118, 120, 121, 210; or BEOA 210.

title: Computer Programming for Technology (C)
description: Programming in C. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and projects that emphasize applications in industry and technology. Introduces realtime input/output device programming. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161.

title: Scientific Computer Programming
description: Programming in FORTRAN. Basic computer programming skills using examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize applications in mathematics and science. Introduces timesharing techniques. Prerequisite: MATHS 117. Not open to students who have credit in CS 120.

title: Computer Science 1
description: Introduction to programming using a structured, strongly typed language such as PASCAL. Topics include basic control structures, input/output, procedures and functions, arrays, textfiles, sets, records, introduction to software engineering, and ethics of computing. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161.

title: Computer Science 2
description: Continuation of Computer Science 1. Topics include pointer variables, linked lists, stacks, queues, binary trees, binary search and its complexity, recursion, sorting algorithms and their complexity, binary files and file organization, and software development tools. Prerequisite: CS 120 and MATHS 161.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize application in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: CS 110 or 116 or 118 or 120. Not open to students who have credit in CS 240 or MGT 213.

title: Discrete Structures
description: Introduction to topics in discrete structures for computer science majors. Topics include propositional and predicate logic, sets, induction, recursion, relations, functions, combinatorial enumeration, Boolean algebra, and finite state machines. Applications of these topics to computer science are discussed. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Assembler Language Programming
description: Introduction to computer architecture, machine and assembly languages. Includes fixedpoint, floatingpoint, and decimal arithmetic, character and bit manipulation, looping, branching, macros, and subroutines. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Microcomputer System Architecture
description: Elements of microcomputer system architecture and organization. Topics to be discussed include processors, primary and secondary memory systems, and networking principles. Prerequisite: CS 110 or the equivalent. Not open to students who have credit in CS 333.

title: Microcomputer Database
description: Considers how database techniques may be used in personal computer applications, how to design and develop database applications, and how to select a database product for a personal computer. Prerequisite: CS 104. Not open to students who have credit in CS 436.

title: Micrcomputer Operating Systems
description: Introduction to operating systems for the microcomputer. Topics related to concurrency, process and resource management, input/output control, and design problems are discussed. Comparisons of current microcomputer operating systems will be studied. Prerequisite: CS 233. Not open to students who have credit in CS 476. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Recent Computer-Related Developments
description: Current topics related to the development and uses of the computer in society are discussed. Topics covered will vary as the discipline of computer science changes. Prerequisite: CS 276.

title: Combinatorial Algorithms
description: Topics include analysis of algorithms, selected graph algorithms and their complexity, pattern matching, geometric algorithms, fast Fourier transform, introduction to the classes P and NP, introduction to parallel algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 121, 224; and MATHS 212.

title: Data Structures
description: Topics include abstract data structures, trees and graphs and their traversal, priority queues, algorithm design techniques, external storage and sorting, hashing, data compression, memory management. Prerequisite: CS 121, 224, 230.

title: Computer Hardware Systems
description: Introduction to computer logic and registertransfer level of systems description. Examines the basic building blocks of a computer system and studies various computer architectures and hardware trends. Develops a general methodology for computer selection and introduces microprogramming. Prerequisite: CS 224, 230; and MATHS 212.

title: Introduction to Computer Graphics Systems
description: An introduction to computer graphics software and hardware including computerassisted design systems, interface programming, user interfaces, and presentation graphics programming. Prerequisite: proficiency in a highlevel programming language like PASCAL, FORTRAN, or C (CS 118 or CS 121 or the equivalent). Computer Science 195

title: Advanced Topics Seminar
description: Indepth study of a topic taught in a seminar format. Advanced postings of topics will be made in the department before registration. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Use of COBOL to solve problems in file maintenance, report writing, and sorting. Emphasizes directaccess processing techniques including development of interactive screens. Further study of IBM Job Control Language. Prerequisite: CS 121, 230.

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation. Use of higher level languages and simulation languages in system studies. Students use examples from different subjects to carry out simulation. Prerequisite: CS 121 and MATHS 181 or the equivalent.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analyses, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, and orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 118 or 120 and MATHS 162 or 172. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and CS 362 or MATHS 362. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 363.

title: Professional Experience
description: Professional computing experience in an approved program with computing facilities in business and industry. Paid positions only. Experience may be through coop, internship, or parttime employment. Requires term activity report. Offered on a credit/no credit basis only. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 in any one semester or term.

title: Systems Programming
description: Considers the computer system from the points of view of its architecture, operating system, and applications. Topics include processor organization, peripheral devices, I/O programming, system programs, monitor services, file organization, and realtime applications. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Programming Languages
description: A comparative study of programming languages. Emphasizes syntactic specification of programming languages and important features, structures, and compile and runtime characteristics of various higher level languages. Prerequisite: CS 230, 332

title: Database Design
description: An introduction to database design, including physical representation, modeling, database systems, and implementation. Prerequisite: CS 332 and knowledge of C, COBOL, or FORTRAN.

title: Computer Graphics
description: Methods of developing, modifying, and rendering graphics displays. Emphasizes the design and writing of graphics software for both twoand threedimensional displays. Knowledge of a structured highlevel language is required. Prerequisite: CS 332 and MATHS 212.

title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
description: Introduction to basic programming techniques of artificial intelligence (Al). Primary contents are symbol manipulations and Al problemsolving techniques. Topics include LISP primitives, LISP objects and evaluation, recursion and iteration, data abstraction (association lists, properties, and DESTRUCT), macros, objectcentered programming, symbolic pattern matching, and basic problemsolving methods. Prerequisites: CS 324, 435.

title: Principles of Computer Vision and Machine Intelligence
description: Laboratory based, dealing with the basic principles of acquisition and analysis of visual images by means of the computer. Studies the incorporation of vision in machine (robot) operation. Artificial intelligence techniques applied to task planning are used in integrating visual images with manipulator actions. Prerequisite: CS 333 or permission of the instructor.

title: Theory of Computation 1
description: Mathematical logic; alphabets and languages; finite automata, regular and nonregular languages, Kleene's theorem; regular grammars; pushdown automata and contextfree grammars; Turing and Post machines; recursive and recursively enumerable languages; the Chomsky Hierarchy. Prerequisite: CS 324, 435.

title: Operating Systems
description: The functions and structure of computer operating systems, processors, memory, and device management. Concurrency and process synchronization. Input/output handling, device drivers, and disk scheduling. File systems, operating system design philosophy. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Software Engineering 1—Systems Analysis
description: Software life cycle, software engineering concepts, systems analysis phase of life cycle. Introduces and applies structured methods to a project. The output of the project is a systems specification from which a software system can be designed and developed. Prerequisite: CS 332, 333.

title: Software Engineering 2—Design and Development
description: Studies the design and development phases of the software life cycle. Introduces the latest appropriate structured methods and applies them to a software project. This project will take a system specification and develop software from it. Prerequisite: CS 497.

title: Readings and Honors
description: Special advanced studies of computer science topics not taught in other courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors. DEPARTMENT OF CRIMINAL JUSTICE AND CRIMINOLOGY G. Webb, Chairperson; S. Brodt, B. Carson, D. Daane, J. Hendricks, M. Meagher, F. Reddington, J. Smith, D. Stead The Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology offers a variety of courses that help students understand the dimensions and causes of crime and delinquency, theories of crime prevention and control, the structure and philosophy of the American criminal justice system, the operation of criminal courts at the local, state, and federal levels, the techniques and theories of law enforcement, and the philosophies and practices of various correctional programs. Students are prepared for entrylevel professional positions in the criminal justice system as well as for graduate study in related subjects. title: Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
description: Overview of the criminal justice system including its historical and philosophical background, structure, functions, the interrelation of agencies, and an introduction to the study of crime.

title: Data and Theories of Crime and Delinquency
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior, typologies of crime and criminals; the trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and current theoretical explanations.

title: Processing Adult and Juvenile Offenders
description: Emphasizes the juvenile and adult justice systems, their components, recent changes, and anticipated future developments.

title: Research Methods in Criminal Justice
description: Introduction to research methods used in criminology and criminal justice. Emphasizes the design, implementation, interpretation, and evaluation of qualitative and quantitative research. Use of the computer is required. Prerequisite: CJC 101, 210, or permission of the instructor.

title: Policing in American Society
description: Examination and analysis of the development of the police in America in the past, present, and future. Emphasizes institutional context of police activity, bureaucratization of the police, professionalization, the role of the police, and police and community relations. Prerequisite: CJC 101, 220, or permission of the instructor.

title: Women and Crime
description: Examination of female delinquency and criminality, and the differential treatment accorded females in the criminal justice system, focusing on females as offenders, victims, and professionals. Prerequisite: CJC 101 or WMNST 210 or permission of the instructor.

title: Organized Crime
description: The nature and structure of organized crime in America with special emphasis on the history and changing images of organized crime, its operation and activities, and programs for control.

title: Victimology
description: A criminological examination of the victims of crime in contemporary America.

title: Criminal Law
description: Study of the historical foundations, development, limitations, and application of substantive criminal law in the United States. Indiana statutory law and case law are compared with common law and modern criminal law from other states. Prerequisite: CJC 101 or POLS 140 or permission of the instructor. Prerequisite recommended: CJC 211.

title: Criminal Evidence
description: Rules of evidence as they apply in criminal investigation and criminal court are examined with discussion of relevant ethical issues. Prerequisite: CJC 211 or POLS 140 or permission of the instructor.

title: Institutional Corrections
description: Indepth inquiry into the function, structure, and operations of American adult and juvenile correctional institutions. Prerequisite: CJC 210, 211, or permission of the instructor.

title: Community Corrections
description: Organization and operation of communitybased correctional programs throughout the United States. Topics include probation, parole, halfway houses, group homes, diversion, restitution, and community service programs. Prerequisite: CJC 210, 211, or permission of the instructor.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid fulltime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: senior standing, 2.2 G.P.A., and permission of the instructor. Not open to students who have credit in CJC 479. Open only to criminal justice majors.

title: Honors Colloquium in Criminal Justice
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in criminal justice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Open only to honors students; others by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Current Issues in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Exploration of selected issues and topics in criminal justice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Topics may include crisis intervention, historical criminology, white collar crime, and others of current interest. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to criminal justice majors. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in any one semester or term.

title: Practicum in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: Parttime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Practical Experience
description: Unpaid fulltime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: senior standing, 2.2 G.P.A., and permission of the instructor. Not open to students who have credit in CJC 369. Open only to criminal justice majors.

title: Independent Study in Criminal Justice and Criminology
description: An individualized course of reading or limited research designed to allow majors an opportunity to explore specific topics related to the criminal justice system under the direction of a specific faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students majoring in criminal justice and criminology. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. Schumacher, H. Stahlke, T. Thornburg, J. Trimmer, M. VanCamp, B. Weaver, V. White, R. Whitworth English includes three interdependent disciplines: literature, language, and composition. Literature gives students a perspective gained only through intimacy with the thoughts and feelings of writers of various times and cultures; to that end, the department offers a wide variety of courses in American, British, and world literature. Historic and descriptive linguistics offer insight into our linguistic heritage and, by making students aware of various patterns of language, contribute to understanding the way people use language. Composition gives all students the opportunity to become competent as writers. English education prepares students to teach these interdependent disciplines. The minimum gradepoint average for all English courses for graduation with a major in English is 2.5. The lowest acceptable grade in a course for credit toward a major or minor in English is C. For information about the minors in humanities and in medieval and Renaissance studies, see Interdepartmental Programs, p. 43. Course Withdrawal Students may withdraw only once from any of the following composition courses: ENG 101, 102, 103, 104, 114. Any exception to this regulation must be approved by the chairperson of the English department. title: Reading 2

title: Listening Comprehension 3
description: Continued practice in comprehension of normal spoken English. Increased use of recorded unadapted materials and radio, television, and film. Prerequisite: ENEFL 125 or permission of the program director.

title: Pronunciation
description: American English segmental and prosodic systems. Practice for accuracy in production of diphthongs, unstressed syllables, and reduced segments. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Writing 3

title: Grammar 3

title: Speaking 3
description: Continued speaking practice with emphasis on speaking for academic purposes. Student presentations and discussion. Examination of issues of current interest. Prerequisite: ENEFL 134 or permission of the program director.

title: Cross-Cultural Studies 1
description: Topics include U.S. and international politics, civil and human rights, individual freedom and responsibility, academic and cultural issues. Prerequisite: ENEFL 134 or permission of the program director.

title: Study Skills for Foreign Students 1
description: Note taking, impromptu writing in English as a foreign language, preparing for tests, and using library resources. Prerequisite: ENEFL 133 and 135 or permission of the program director.

title: Writing 4
description: Paragraph and essay writing. Practice in rhetorical modes of American English. Prerequisite: ENEFL 141 or permission of the program director.

title: Grammar 4
description: Focus on individual grammatical problems with grammatical variants and rhetorical devices. General grammar review. Prerequisite: ENEFL 142 or permission of the program director.

title: Reading 4
description: Reading in unadapted selections from general and technical literature and current publications. Prerequisite: ENEFL 143 or permission of the program director.

title: Cross-Cultural Studies 2

title: Fundamentals of English Composition 1
description: The first of two consecutive semesters composing a portfoliobased course focusing on the development of effective composing, revising, and editing strategies. Introduction to basic research methods. Prerequisite: appropriate combination TSWE score and high school rank.

title: Fundamentals of English Composition 2
description: The second of two consecutive semesters composing a portfoliobased course focusing on the development of effective composing, revising, and editing strategies. Introduction to basic research methods. Prerequisite: ENG 101.

title: English Composition 1
description: Introduction to composition with an emphasis on writing short essays. Includes assigned readings. Introduction to basic research methods. Prerequisite: appropriate combination of TSWE score and high school rank.

title: English Composition 2
description: Further instruction in composition with an emphasis on writing longer essays. Includes assigned readings. Further instruction and practice in research methods. Prerequisite: ENG 101 and 102, ENG 103, or appropriate combination of TSWE score and high school class rank.

title: Honors English Composition 2
description: Instruction in composition with emphasis on writing essays. Includes assigned readings. Instruction and practice in research methods. Prerequisite: appropriate combination of TSWE score and high school rank and acceptance into the Honors program. Not open to students who have credit in ENG 104.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to selected pieces of world, British, and American literature for class and individual oral and written interpretation and evaluation for non-English majors or minors. Section content will be identified each semester. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or 114.

title: World Literature Masterpieces
description: Selected major works of world literature, exclusive of English and American literature, for English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or 114.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar and Usage
description: Basic course in English grammar and usage for the underprepared. Cannot be counted as part of major or minor programs in English.

title: Advanced Composition and Creative Writing
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for general students, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation. Instruction in creative writing, particularly fiction and poetry. Prerequisite: ENG 206 and sophomore standing or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to English majors and minors except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Professional Writing
description: Practice in writing effective, professional prose with of particular attention to the writing tasks often required in students' careers. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or its equivalent.

title: American Literature, 1607-1860
description: Survey of American literature from its beginning through the middle nineteenth century, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 206, 230, or the equivalent required for English majors and minors.

title: British Literature 1: The Beginnings to 1780
description: British literature from about 450 to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds. Prerequisite: ENG 206, 230, or the equivalent required for English minors.

title: British Literature 2: 1780 to the Present
description: British literature from 1780 to the present, with attention to the historical, social, and philosophical background of the times. Prerequisite: ENG 206, 230, or the equivalent required for English majors and minors.

title: Introduction to Creative Writing: Prose
description: Development of the creative process and writing techniques for selfexpression and for exploration of ideas to enhance personal and professional life, such forms as journal, meditation, sketch, vignette, personal and descriptive essay. Prerequisite: ENG 103. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Introduction to Creative Writing: Poetry
description: Introduction to the creative process in the writing of poetry, including the use of traditional and contemporary forms and devices. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the researchpaper writing. Advanced study techniques. Prerequisite: ENEFL 148 or permission of the program director.

title: TOEFL Preparation
description: Review of English grammar and vocabulary with special practice in aural and written comprehension to prepare for the Test of English as a Foreign Language. Prerequisite: permission of the program director.

title: Literature and the Narrative Media
description: Consideration of the ways in which the narrative media have been used to develop fictional and nonfictional literature. Special attention to works adapted from one medium to another and to works of lasting significance. Attention will be given to the narrative media and the language arts curriculum in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Prerequisite: ENG 206, 230, or the equivalent required for English majors and minors.

title: Practicum in Peer Tutoring
description: Offers strategies for working with grammar, mechanics, and the larger rhetorical elements, practice in peer evaluation, and a forum for discussing the role and responsibilities of peer tutors. Credit in this course does not apply to a major or minor in English. Open only to students assigned to tutor at the Writing Center. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Creative Writing: Personal Essay
description: Instruction in the theory and techniques of writing the personal essay. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or its equivalent.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop 1
description: Practice and critique of the art of poetry in a workshop format, with instruction in the use of poetic forms and devices. Prerequisite: ENG 288 and permission of the instructor.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials for teaching written and oral expression, language use, spelling, handwriting, and literature. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: Literature for Young Children
description: An introduction to literature for young children. Designed for elementary and early childhood education programs and endorsements and for parents and future parents. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: English Linguistics
description: Modern English grammar with emphasis on the application of uptodate descriptive linguistics, leading to an understanding of basic grammatical structure, relationship, and terminology, including morphology and phonology.

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Prerequisite: ENG 321. Prerequisite waived for departmental majors in English, option 2, and for departmental minors in English. 33$ Children's Literature. (3) An overview of children's literature and an intensive study of various types. Designed for elementary education programs and endorsements. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English. Junior or senior standing recommended.

title: Linguistic Phonetics
description: Speech sounds and the linguistic methods employed in their description, classification, and analysis as elements in language systems.

title: American Literature 2,1860-1960
description: Survey of selected American writers and the various literary movements since 1860, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 206, 230, or the equivalent required for English majors and minors.

title: Nineteenth-Century American Fiction
description: Intensive reading in the works of two or three major writers of the period, such as Irving, Cooper, Hawthorne, Melville, Twain, and James.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: Intensive reading in the works of three major writers of the period, such as Anderson, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Wolfe, and Dos Passos.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: Themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: Themes and techniques of selected American poets with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Language Arts in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching language arts in junior high/middle schools. Cannot be counted as an elective in other major or minor programs in English. Prerequisite: identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDJHM 280.

title: Literature of Black America
description: A survey of the literature written by Black authors in the United States.

title: American Indian Literature
description: A literary study of short stories, novels, and poetry by twentiethcentury American Indian authors, with supplementary background readings in mythology, tales, and poetry from the oral traditions. The emphasis will be on works by American Indians, but some works about Indians by Caucasian authors may also be included.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to the Restoration
description: English drama from medieval times to 1660, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to The Second Shepherds' Play and Everyman, and to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid, supervised work experience in which classroomlearned skills are applied in research, critical thinking, and professional writing. Work assignments may be partor fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs in organizations, agencies, corporations, banks, or professional offices. Prerequisite: junior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: English Drama from the Restoration to the Present
description: English drama from 1700 to the present. Special attention is given to the plays of Steele, Goldsmith, Sheridan, Wilde, Shaw, Synge, O'Casey, Osborne, Beckett, and Pinter.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenthcentury novels, including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the BrontOs, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Studies in British Drama
description: Special topics in contemporary British drama. Open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open only to honors students. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Writing Competency Examination
description: Open to students who have completed ENG 103 and ENG 104 with grades of C or better. Students must have juniorlevel standing, having earned at least 63 semester hours, and must register through the English department three weeks before the examination period. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. This course is offered on a credit/no credit basis.

title: Writing Competency Course
description: Required of all students who have not completed ENG 392 after two attempts. This course is offered on a credit/no credit basis, and credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements.

title: Teaching English in Secondary Schools
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in teaching composition, language, and literature. Required for teaching majors; may be an elective for teaching minors; may not be applied toward any other departmental program. Prerequisite: ENG 350.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, James, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in World and British Literature
description: Special research topics in world or British literature with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in English Education
description: Emphasis is on current issues and problems at the elementary, middle, junior high, or senior high school level. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in American Literature
description: Special research topics in American literature, with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in Composition
description: Special research topics in composition and rhetoric. Prerequisite: ENG 230.

title: Independent Study in English
description: Designed for students who want to conduct independent study and research in English. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in English at the 200 level or above at Ball State University and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fiction Writing Workshop 1
description: Practice and critique of fiction writing, in a workshop format, with instruction in the fundamentals of the short story such as plot, character, and setting. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Essay Writing Workshop
description: Advanced instruction in writing the personal and literary essay in a workshop format. Prerequisite: ENG 306 or permission of the instructor.

title: Fiction-Writing Workshop
description: Open to students who have had some experience with shortstory or novel writing. Primary emphasis iis on instructor evaluation and student discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop 2
description: Advanced practice and criticism of the art of poetry in a workshop format, with attention to contemporary poetics and the current state of the art. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent Study in English Education
description: Designed for students who wish to conduct independent study and research in English education, preschool through secondary level. Prerequisite: ENG 206 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading Printed Materials in the English Classroom
description: An overview of the process of reading printed materials with practical suggestions for developing analytic skills for reading and interpreting written communications, including literary and popular materials used in the English classroom.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Emphasis is on reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical functions.

title: Sociolinguistics
description: A detailed examination of the relationship between language variety and social class, including recent studies in urban social dialectology. Basic issues in the study of bilingualism. Prerequisite: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Theory and Research in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in secondlanguage teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Methods and Materials in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Study and practice of a variety of methods in teaching English as a second or foreign language. Discussion of pedagogical issues in language teaching. Topics vary each semester; consult the English department for a schedule of offerings. Prerequisite: ENG 420 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: American Literature, 1945 to the Present
description: Survey of the works of major writers and literary trends in America since World War II. Prerequisite: 206 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Practicum in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Practical experience in observation, teaching, and analysis of teaching English as a second or foreign language. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Parallel: ENG 436 or 437. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Chaucer
description: Study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several minor poems. Emphasizes structure, sources, and significance of the works. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare
description: An introductory study of representative plays (comedies, histories, tragedies) and some selections from the sonnets by Shakespeare.

title: Studies in Shakespeare
description: Special topics in a selection of Shakespeare's tragedies, comedies, and histories. Prerequisite: open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Milton
description: Indepth, analytical study of Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, Samson Agonistes, Lycidas, and Areopagitica, as well as a brief study of "The Christian Doctrine" and other selected poems and prose by John Milton.

title: Practical Experience
description: Nonpaid, supervised work experience in which classroomlearned skills are applied in research, critical thinking, and professional writing. Work assignments may be partor fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs in organizations, agencies, corporations, banks, or professional offices. Prerequisite: junior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Creative Writing
description: Directed independent writing of poetry, fiction, or essay. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one

title: Women in Literature
description: Investigation of various ways women have been portrayed in the literature of the Western world. Examination of significant writing by women.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War Ito the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY E. Lyon, Chairperson; C. Airriess, T. Grimes, G. Showalter, J. Slack, M. Sullivan, K. Turcotte, G. Venugopal, D. Wheeler The Department of Geography offers three options to meet the varied needs of its students. Option 1, a general survey of physical and cultural geography, is selected by students seeking a broad education leading to careers in education, government, and business. Option 2 is a specialized program in travel and tourism. Students selecting this option are encouraged to take minors in foreign languages and business. Option 3, geographic information sciences (remote sensing, geographic information systems, computer cartography), is a technical specialization selected by students who seek to study various geographic problems through the use of computer technology. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN GEOGRAPHY, 48-57 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE Core requirements, 18 hours

title: Earth, Sea, and Sky: A Geographic View
description: Selected aspects of the physical environment and their relationship to human occupancy of the earth. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to students who have credit in GEOG 111.

title: Physical Geography and Earth Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Earthsun relationships, weather and climate, geologic processes (including earth structure and sculpturing of the earth's surface); conservation principles as they pertain directly to the material taught. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Not open to students who have credit in GEOG 101.

title: Economic Geography and Contemporary Issues
description: A systematic approach to economic geography and current economic issues emphasizing local, regional, national, and international economic developments in the geographic setting.

title: Geography of the Cultural Environment
description: A spatial analysis of the interaction of cultural development and the physical environment. Special emphasis upon the processes of cultural change and their effect on the landscape.

title: Global Geography
description: A basic survey course emphasizing geographic facts and interdependencies between the developed and developing world. Particular emphasis is given to physical and social environmental interdependencies.

title: The American Landscape: A Historical Geography of the United States
description: Geography of American landscape in earlier times. Selected regions examined to understand geographical influences on transformation of the wilderness. Emphasis is placed on exploration, discovery, migration routes, settlement, adjustments to the land, and means of securing a livelihood.

title: Weather 1
description: How and why the weather changes, the characteristics of weather, and an examination of weather instruments.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: Introduction to skills needed to use and appreciate maps as a form of communication and as a research tool. Topics include elements and sources of maps, history of map making, techniques of analysis, and introduction to aerial photography and remote sensing.

title: Introduction to Travel and Tourism
description: A survey of the travel and tourism industry; its various components, dimensions, organization, and structure. Topics include economic, social, cultural, and environmental implications; motivations for travel, and the past and future of the industry.

title: Geography of Travel and Tourism
description: An emphasis upon the spatial interaction arising from the movement of people engaged in travel for leisure and other purposes. Models of tourism, measuring spatial variations, patterns of domestic and international flows (regions), and spatial organization are examined. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Urban Geography
description: Distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention is given to the geographic conditions affecting urban development and growth.

title: Urban Geography: Trends in Theory and Research
description: Survey of the contribution of Weberian, Marxist, and "managerialist" theory to the interpretation of urban spatial organization and change. In the light of these theories, current research trends and techniques are examined.

title: Weather 2
description: Introduction to weather forecasting using applied examples. Students may gain practical experience by working in the university weather station. Prerequisite: GEOG 230.

title: Climate
description: Introduction to climate with emphasis on regional distribution. 6 hours from GEOG 331 GEOL 207 ASTRO 382 Geography 209 How and why climates differ across the earth. Prerequisite: GEOG 230, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. Although the emphasis is on graphic presentation of spatially disposed quantitative and qualitative data, the techniques and methods apply to a wide range of subject areas.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques, including an introduction to computer graphics. Projects are selected within students' specializations or topics of interest. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Remote Sensing 1
description: Principles of photo interpretation, satellite scanners, and radar. Characteristic features of remotely sensed data, classification processes, and algorithms.

title: Remote Sensing 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in remote sensing, including digital data analysis, image enhancement technique as applied to natural resources, urban analysis, soil studies, geology, and other applied branches. Prerequisite: GEOG 342.

title: Geographic Information Systems Analysis
description: Methods of analysis provided by geographic information systems (GIS). Operations on spatial and attribute information including basic functions (e.g., map overlay) and special functions (e.g., network analysis). Exposure to raster and vector software. Review capabilities of currently available GIS software. Prerequisite: GEOG 240, 340, and 341 or permission of the instructor.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: Comprehensive survey of geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Latin America and the Caribbean
description: Physical and cultural patterns in a diverse world region. Emphasis is on population and settlement, agriculture, and environmental hazards in the context of development.

title: Geography of Africa
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environments of Africa.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: A geographic examination of the physical, cultural, and economic diversity of the state. Field experiences supplement classroom activities.

title: Geography of Asia
description: The geography of South, Southwest, Southeast, and East Asia. A survey and analysis of the physical geographic patterns, bases of cultural diversity, and changing spatial aspects of political organization.

title: Geography of Western Europe
description: Treats the spatial elements of the physical and cultural environment of Western Europe. Using a thematic approach, primary emphasis is given to the United Kingdom, Ireland, Scandinavia, France, Benelux countries, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, and the Iberian and Italian peninsulas.

title: Geography of the Soviet Union
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural features of the Soviet Union and the economic development of the country.

title: Geography of Central Europe
description: Treats the spatial elements of the physical and human environments of seven Central European countries: Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Yugoslovia, and what was formerly East Germany. Attention is given to physiographic, climatological, and sociocultural processes.

title: Domestic and International Travel and Tourism
description: Examination of the technical aspects of domestic and international travel and tourism. Develops skills by using professionally prepared materials related to travel planning, regulations, tariffs, services, and ticketing. Prerequisite: GEOG 261 and 262. Open to option 2 majors only.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid fullor parttime work experiences with an organization allied to a student's area of specialization. Assignments depend on student interests and the sponsor's convenience. Used for paid work experience only. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world and of transportation patterns.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration, and growth, as well as their causes and the effects they produce on the cultural landscape.

title: Seminar in Geography or Earth Science
description: Advanced study of a selected topic in geography or earth science. Prerequisite: an introductory geography or earth science course or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Advanced Techniques in Remote Sensing
description: Advanced techniques applied to remotely sensed data using stateoftheart software. Review of current methods of computer and manual interpretation techniques. Includes active participation in classroom presentations. Prerequisite: GEOG 342 and 343.

title: Advanced Cartography
description: Application of computerassisted design (CAD) to computerassisted cartography. Introduction to relational databases for maps. Interfacing of graphic files to thematic mapping software. Prerequisite: GEOG 340 and 341.

title: Applications of Geographic Information Systems
description: Practical experience applying geographic information system (GIS) tools to analyze spatial data. Workshop format requires studentmotivated projects; diverse disciplines encouraged. Project work involves proposal, work plan, presentation, and final report. Prerequisite: GEOG 344 or permission of the instructor.

title: Automation and the Travel Industry
description: Introduction to the use of automation in the travel industry as it applies to information management and task functions like reservation and ticketing systems. Includes laboratory experience. Prerequisite: GEOG 360. Open to majors only.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the contribution of physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world to domestic and foreign relations problems.

title: Practical Experience
description: Fullor parttime work experience with an organization allied to a student's area of specialization. Assignments depend upon student interests and the sponsor's convenience. Used for unpaid work experience only. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Distant Areas Field Studies
description: Physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Open to students in geography, earth science, and allied subjects. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in any one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Travel and Tourism
description: Advanced study exploring problems and issues, theory and research related to travel and tourism. Topics will vary depending upon the instructor and needs and interests of students. Prerequisite: GEOG 360. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Geographic Research Methods
description: An introduction to the use of statistics and quantitative techniques in geographic research. Topics include research design, statistical testing, and geographic modeling.

title: Readings and Special Studies in Geography and Earth Science
description: Assigned special studies in geography and earth science, including readings, research projects, teaching problems, or assignment to an undergraduate class. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Thesis
description: The formulation and writing of a researchoriented thesis. Student working with a faculty advisor will write a research paper on a geographic theme or topic of his or her choice. Papers will be evaluated for geographic content and compositional skills. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geographic Field Methods
description: Introduction to the techniques of field study and analysis of physical and cultural spatial patterns. DEPARTMENT OF GEOLOGY A. Samuelson, Chairperson; R. Fluegeman, R. Orr, H. Roepke, G. Scarbrough, R. Snow Geologists study the earth with primary attention to its history, materials, and structure and the active processes that continue to change the landscape. Geologists are also concerned with the investigation of geologic hazards and other environmental problems, the evaluation of groundwater resources, the discovery of new mineral and petroleum deposits, and the study of the moon and planets. The department offers two departmental majors in geology. The professional arts major is designed to prepare graduates for some geological careers in industry and government agencies and for graduate studies that lead to research, teaching, management, and many other positions in industry, government, and universities. The liberal arts major is designed to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who have related interests, want to pursue double majors, or do not want to enter the geological profession directly. Geology 211 DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN GEOLOGY (PROFESSIONAL ARTS), 65-66 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS Students are expected to have completed GEOL 101 or GEOG 101 and mathematics through MATHS 117 or the high school equivalent as approved by the primary departmental advisor.

title: Physical Geology
description: Introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to humankind's environmental and resource problems. Localarea field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: Introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or GEOG 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Oceans and Nations
description: Worldwide human interactions with the oceans and international conflicts of interest related to the ocean environment. Introduction to physical and biological characteristics of the oceans. Marine law, resource conflicts, pollution, cooperation for oceanographic research and hazard response, and other topics.

title: Environmental Geology
description: Examines geologic materials and processes affecting the human environment. Discusses geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, surface water hydrology, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Hand Specimen Petrography
description: Principles concerning the formation, occurrence, and classification of rocks in the earth's crust. Description and identification of rocks in the laboratory and field. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Localarea field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 112 (or the high school equivalent) or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Optical Mineralogy
description: Optical theory as it applies to the polarizing microscope and procedures for identification of minerals by oil immersion and in thin section. Laboratory practice will be emphasized. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid professional work and learning experience arranged during one or more semesters or summers. Eligible students will be placed in an approved agency or private business. Assignments, including activity log, selfanalysis, and summary report, are supervised by the department. Geology 213 Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson and the coordinator of internships. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Field Methods
description: Methods and techniques of collecting, compiling, and analyzing geographic and geologic field data. Assignments include mapping projects and the use of field instruments near the campus and visits within the state to places of value to the course. Prerequisite: major or minor in geology, earth science, or geography or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Extended application of field techniques to the resolution of geologic problems. Assignments include accumulation and interpretation of field observations and preparation of geologic maps, cross sections, and stratigraphic sections. Requires a report of investigations for one of the mapping projects. The course is conducted during a fiveweek period in June and July in South Dakota and Wyoming. Prerequisite: GEOL 230 and 382 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Stratigraphy
description: Principles, nomenclature, and practices of stratigraphy. The genesis and history of stratified rocks, sedimentation, induration, weathering, and methods of correlation. Localarea field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoecologic significance. Emphasis is on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 112 (or the high school equivalent) or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geological and Physical Oceanography
description: Description of geological and physical characteristics of the oceans, marine processes, and related topics. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to refraction and reflection seismology; magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods. Emphasis is on geophysical methods applied to such problems as energy resources, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, and pollution detection. Includes laboratory exercises and field investigations. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
description: Microscopic analysis of mineralogies and textures, together with a review of field and laboratory data, for the purpose of classifying and interpreting the origins of the two groups of rocks. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 230.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 315 or 405 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Sedimentary Petrology
description: Qualitative and quantitative description and statistical analysis of sediments and the description of mineralogies and textures of sedimentary rocks in thin section as the basis for determining environments of deposition and lithification. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 230.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: Rocks, structure, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Fieldtrip oriented with collection of rock, mineral, and fossil specimens. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Geohydrology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 108 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. Designed to supplement existing geoscience and computer science courses by providing opportunity to gain experience in working with BASIC and FORTRAN programs in various geoscience datacollecting, calculation, and graphic display applications.
