title: Introduction to American Studies
description: Survey of American studies as a field and as an interdisciplinary approach to the study of American civilization. Methods and theories of American studies will be discussed, along with major themes and topics of American life and thought. Not open to students who have credit in AMSTU 101.

title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: Surveys the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decision makers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Western Civilization
description: A survey of the major themes and developments in the evolution of Western civilization from its origins to the present with emphasis on key problems, turning points, recurring issues, and cultural growth and heritage. Special stress on the character and crises confronting the Western world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: World Civilization 1
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the dawn of civilization in Southwestern Asia and North Africa to the early modern world.

title: World Civilization 2
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the early modern world to the present.

title: Studies in Non-Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: American History, 1492-1876
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States to 1876.

title: American History, 1877 to the Present
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States since 1877.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give students knowledge of resource use in the United States by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis is on the way resource use has shaped society. Not open to students who have credit in NR 204.

title: Introduction to Sport in American Life
description: A thorough examination of the various historical, sociological, and psychological features of sports in our society. Not sportappreciation oriented, but rather an examination of what occurs to both competitors and spectators as they become involved with a sport activity. Open to all undergraduate students except students who have credit in PEP 205.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of Blacks in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis is on the effects of Blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing conceptions of their roles, attitudes toward women, women's ideas about themselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Uses documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. Students through their own research learn how the historian defines topics of research; selects sources, both primary and secondary; evaluates materials; and describes the findings.

title: The History of American Popular Culture
description: Historical overview of the development of American popular culture. Basic theories, approaches, and topics in popular culture with special attention to amusements, movies, pop music, magazines, pulp novels, and television. Focuses on the relationship of popular culture to American cultural and social history.

title: Early Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: Modern Latin America
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis on Mexico, Chile, Cuba, and Central America.

title: Introduction to Public History
description: An overview of opportunities for nonteaching historyrelated careers in preservation, archival work, records management, museology, historical editing, living history and public parks programs, corporate history, and others. Students make a concentrated study of at least one field of public history and have contact with working professionals. Open to all students.

title: History of the European Family
description: A survey of the changing social, economic, and political roles of the European family from antiquity to the present. Topics include the distribution of authority, marriage and inheritance, childrearing, domestic labor, and the effects of industrialization. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The United States and the Vietnam War
description: Historical analysis of American involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1975, with discussions of the military, political, diplomatic, and social effects of the war. Includes background information on Vietnamese history as well as its continuing legacy.

title: Introduction to Peace Studies and Conflict Resolution
description: Interdisciplinary study of methods of achieving peace within communities and among nations; history of peace movements and the causes of conflict; and analysis of principles to resolve conflict using case studies.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American-Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and their place in the history of the United States. Gives students a historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Selected Topics in Military History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular period, topic, or issue in military history with emphasis on materials not covered in established courses. Exact content will be announced in advance of each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Paid Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. This course is designed for paid work and learning experience on or off campus. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foundations of Asian Civilization
description: Survey of South, Southeast, and East Asian history from earliest times to roughly A.D. 1600, with special focus on the development of Asian societies and cultures before any significant European presence.

title: Tradition, Conflict, and Change in Modern Asia
description: Survey of South, Southeast, and East Asian history from roughly A.D. 1600 to the present, with concentration on the problems, leaders, and issues that resulted from Western presence, nationalism, independence, and modernization as well as contemporary issues.

title: Africa Since 1500
description: Stresses the emergence of modern African civilization from roughly 1500 to the present, with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: History of the Middle East
description: Provides indepth knowledge and understanding of the Middle East—today's Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Turkey, and other states—since Muhammed. Stresses indigenous societies and how they have dealt with Islam, imperialism, nationalism, development, and wars.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others may enroll by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Colonial America 1492-1756
description: The settlement of North America by the British and the evolution of the distinctive colonial societies that formed the foundation of the United States.

title: The American Revolution, 1756- 1789
description: Transformation of American society and politics in the era of the American Revolution with emphasis on the origins of the revolution, the development of a democratic society, and the Constitution of the United States.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis on the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism Versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis on the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: The United States from World War I through World War II
description: An examination of the reaction of the American people to a society changing rapidly under the impact of two major wars, the Great Depression, and continuing industrialization and urbanization.

title: Recent United States History: 1945 to the Present
description: A study of the role of the United States in the modern world and an examination of the efforts of America to preserve a society that is prosperous and humane while adjusting to technological change and continuing social and intellectual ferment.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the state from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Antebellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum South.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans-Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis is on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's effect upon the settlers in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers, the events that influenced their migration, and the effect of these events and the frontier on national development.

title: Indians in U.S. History
description: Survey of Indian and white relations from 1492 to the present, focusing on the Indian wars, treaty making, various types of Indian and white interaction, and the development of federal and state Indian policy.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History Since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I.

title: American Life and Thought, 1607- 1865
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from the colonial period to the Civil War, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American Life and Thought, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from Reconstruction to the present, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American History through Film
description: Introduces techniques to analyze films as primary documents in U. S. history. Focuses on the most significant feature and documentary films of American society. Compares and contrasts filmic and historical reality.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: the major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students travel through designated areas in North America. Requires considerable reading before the trip and papers at the conclusion. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in U.S. history may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 3. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870-1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918-1945
description: The origins, immediate causes, and the course of the Second World War with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and Europe since 1945
description: European origin of the Cold War and rebirth of a "new" but divided Europe with stress on East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, and temporary decline of European influence; ideological, political, economic, and social development, including competition between Western and Sovietized Eastern Europe.

title: The Jews in Europe and the Middle East. 1098 to the Present
description: Survey of the Jewish role in European and Middle Eastern history and society. Focus will be on the commonalities and differences between Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, and changing attitudes toward the Jewish community in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: History of Medicine in Western Society
description: A survey of the ideas, attitudes, and institutions of medicine and public health in the Western world from antiquity to modern times. Special attention given to social forces influencing medical knowledge and health care. Not open to students who have credit in HSC 460.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis is on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the republic to approximately A.D. 500. Emphasis is on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social, and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special emphasis on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Muslim worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Emphasizes such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and Northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, and political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations—Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society—through varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in world civilization may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 4.

title: France since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis is on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France—The Classical Age, 1461- 1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism, classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focuses on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715-1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization—and revolutions in general. Stresses the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Britain, 1485-1714
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor and Stuart periods. Emphasis is on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain, 1714 to the Present
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life from the Hanoverian period to the present—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of government and society since World War II.

title: Topics in English Constitutional History
description: Selected topics concerning the constitutional history of England, such as the development of the kingship, the common law, Parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, the Second World War, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Cultural History of the Celtic Peoples from Prehistory to the Present
description: Surveys the cultural history of the six modern Celtic countries (Brittany, Cornwall, Ireland, Isle of Man, Scotland, and Wales) and their ancient continental forebears, including major political events, literature, social organization, and traditional oral culture.

title: Irish History
description: Covers all of Irish history from pre-Christian Celtic times to the present, including political events, literature (both oral and written), the role of language, music, folklore, and other elements of Irish cultural history.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: History of South Asia
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of the subcontinent of South Asia, comprising India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka, from early times to the present.

title: History of Southeast Asia
description: History of the region from earliest times to the present, with special attention to the formation of the earliest civilizations, the influence of Indian, Chinese, and European cultures upon the people of Southeast Asia, and the processes of synthesis that have taken place within these civilizations through the centuries.

title: Economic History of Asia
description: Study of the implications of Asia's economic evolution for the development of Asian civilization, the stimulus of international maritime routes through time, indigenous productive patterns, the effects of imperialism, and Asia's role in the world economy of the twentieth century.

title: Topics in Middle Eastern History
description: Selected issues and problems in the Middle Eastern world since Muhammed. Topics may include the expansion of Islam, slavery in the Middle East, the economic and social history and the Ottoman empire, the Arab/Israeli dispute, and recent national and international crises.

title: History of China to 1600
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of China's history from earliest times to roughly A.D. 1600, with emphasis on the development of the dynastic tradition, Confucianbased society and culture, and China's focal point status in the pre-1600 world order.

title: History of Premodern Japan
description: Analytical survey of premodern Japanese history to c. A.D. 1600, focusing on the ideological, political, social, economic, and cultural developments that build a foundation for the understanding of modern Japan.

title: Selected Topics in Non-Western History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in non- Western history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content will be announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern China, 1600 to the Present
description: Descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's changing role as a member of the world community, its response to increased Western contacts, disintegration of traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant elements of contemporary Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japan, 1600 to the Present
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on conditions contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Selected Topics in European History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in European history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content will be announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Topics in American History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Exact content will be announced before each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Studies for the Primary Grades and Early Childhood
description: Materials and procedures for teaching social studies for nursery school through grade three. Emphasis is on behavioral objectives, inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation. Required of persons in the twoyear early elementary education program.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Junior High/Middle School
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching social studies in junior high/ middle schools. Prerequisite or parallel: EDJHM 285; EDSEC 280. Open only to social studies teaching majors.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Materials and procedure for teaching social studies from kindergarten through grade six. Emphasis is on behavioral objectives; inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Provides more experience in methods used in teaching elementary social studies and an opportunity to use materials available to teachers. Prerequisite: SS 391 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Secondary Schools
description: Theory and practice of teaching secondary school social studies. Emphasis is on methodology, materials, and specific application in the secondary classroom. Includes introductory involvement in the teaching of social studies with a focus on rationale, planning, teaching, and evaluation. Prerequisite: SS 350; EDJHM 285; EDSEC 280; and 18 hours of credit in social science. Open only to social studies teaching majors.

title: Independent Study
description: Directed study of special problems or research in social science education by individuals or groups of students. Topics to be investigated are chosen after consultation with the instructor with special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. CENTER FOR INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SCIENCES R. Steele, Director; R. Bellaver, D. Hibner, E. Kaminski, R. Stowe, M. Wise, R. Yadon The Center for Information and Communication Sciences, an interdisciplinary and handson managementoriented graduate professional program designed to prepare students for careers in information and communications in various industries, offers a master of science degree in information and communication sciences. DEPARTMENT OF JOURNALISM E. Conn, Chairperson; R. Heintzelman, D. Knott, T. Kumbula, A. Marin-Carle, B. McDonald, B. Pitts, M. Popovich, M. Sharpe, D. Sumner, R. Ware, M. Weaver, W. Willis The Department of Journalism offers professional programs in advertising, journalism graphics, magazine, newseditorial, photojournalism, public relations, and teacher education. Students use stateoftheart writing and editing, graphics, and photojournalism equipment. They are encouraged to gain experience on national awardwinning student publications including the Daily News, a daily newspaper; the Orient, the university's yearbook; Expo, the student magazine; and Limited Edition, the studentoperated public relations and advertising agency. The Department of Journalism is accredited by the national journalism accrediting body, the Accrediting Council on Education in Journalism and Mass Communication. Journalism students must demonstrate adequate keyboard skills and competence in grammar and spelling. If students lack these skills, they may be required to take remedial courses. Computer terminals are used in writing, editing, and graphics classes. Students first complete a prejournalism program consisting of five courses before applying for the professional journalism program. They must earn at least C grades and 2.25 G.RA.'s in the prejournalism courses and at least C grades and 2.5 G.P.A.'s in all journalism courses to graduate. Prerequisites for all courses are rigidly enforced. The department's curricular advisor and the six sequence coordinators can assist students in selecting courses and other majors and minors to complement their journalism programs as well as provide career counseling. An exit interview with a sequence coordinator is required before graduation. ASSOCIATE DEGREE ASSOCIATE IN ARTS—JOURNALISM, 63 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS General education, 19 hours

title: Mass Media in Society
description: Study of mass media in their historical and societal contexts with emphasis on practitioner issues including ethics, state of the art, and future.

title: Communications Graphics
description: Theory of publication and visual communication emphasizing preparation of material for newspapers, magazines, and brochures. Lectures and projects focus on type selection, copy fitting, photo and illustration selection and use, pasteup skills, and printing processes. Includes one hour of lab each week. Open only to students enrolled in a journalism area.

title: Mass Media Writing and Editing 1
description: Theory and practice in writing and editing for journalistic media publications. Includes one hour of lab each week.

title: Editorial Presentation
description: Survey of journalistic visual/verbal relationships and analysis needed to train news editors. Introduces the concept of journalistic visual reporting, visual editing, and journalistic graphics technology. Preparatory for journalism graphics sequence students. Prerequisite: JOURN 125 and enrollment in the journalism graphics prejournalism program. Recommended parallel: JOURN 211. 2-3 230 (130) Introduction to Photojournalism. (3) Emphasis is on preparing students to take, process, and caption photographs for newspapers, magazines, public relations, and advertising purposes. Students must rovide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies.

title: Photographic Lighting
description: An indepth study of photographic lighting procedures and equipment for studio and field use by media photographers. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 230 or other basic photography class.

title: Introduction to Advertising
description: A survey of the advertising communication process. Focuses on communication research, creative strategy, campaign planning, function of mass media as carriers of advertising, and evaluation of advertising effectiveness.

title: Principles of Public Relations
description: Survey of the theory, philosophy, and function of public relations practices and programs in American institutions with special attention given to public relations in various fields.

title: Introduction to Newspaper Journalism
description: Analysis of daily and weekly newspapers. Examination of reporting and editing functions and orientations brought to the newswriting profession. Brief look at newspaper management principles and history of newspapers will be included.

title: Magazines in American Life
description: History and significance of magazines in American society. Examination of editorial, production, circulation, and advertising functions, as well as current market conditions and job opportunities. Special study of magazines in a field chosen from students' particular interests. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Journalism
description: History of journalism in the United States from colonial times to the present, presenting the press as an institution against the background of the history of the nation.

title: Feature, Column, and Opinion Writing
description: Researching and writing feature stories, columns, and editorials for newspapers and magazines. Discussion of feature, column, and editorial types and campaigns. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Magazine Article Writing
description: Theory and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles. Includes a study of markets for magazine articles and exercises in various facets of writing for general and specialized magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to magazine sequence majors.

title: Sportswriting and Reporting
description: Study and practice in covering and writing about sports events and the people connected with them. Story assignments and research combined with classroom lectures and analysis of best sports stories provide students with skills to cover a wide range of sports activities. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Journalism Prose Styles
description: Writing and editing for students interested in publishing their work in newspapers, magazines, and public relations organizations. Emphasizes works of contemporary prose writers. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students or magazinesequence majors. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Journalism Law
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the print and broadcast media with special attention given to recent Supreme Court rulings.

title: Magazine Editing and Production
description: Analysis of all facets of magazine publishing: editorial, advertising, circulation, and art. Designed for students interested in working for professional magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 315. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Photojournalism
description: An extended study of the theory and practice of making photographs and using photography as communicative art. Students must have their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236. Not open to prejournalism students or magazinesequence majors. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Journalistic Visual Reporting
description: Examination of the facets of informational graphics and the job of the modernday graphics reporter. Experience gained in creating and researching explanatory charts, diagrams, maps, and graphics editing. Computers are an integral tool. Prerequisite: JOURN 225, 211. Not open to students in prejournalism. Open only to students with other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Media
description: Strategy and procedures for planning, executing, and controlling the placement of advertising. Examines characteristics of media, techniques of media budgeting and selection, and methods of evaluating media effectiveness. Prerequisite: JOURN 250. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Copy and Layout
description: Instruction in preparing copy for mass media advertising. Major emphasis is on creative thinking and basic writing skills. Students prepare copy strategies, write copy, prepare layouts and storyboards. Discussion of fundamentals of consumer motivation and selecting target audiences. Prerequisite: JOURN 250. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas and minors in campaign communication.

title: Public Relations Writing and Publicity Techniques
description: Theory and practice of producing publicity tools for various media used in campaigns to promote and interpret personal, institutional, and organizational objectives and activities. Emphasis is on writing and publicity problem solving. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 and 261. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Public Relations Publication Design and Production
description: Institutional and industrial publications as an important means of internal and external communications. Design and production techniques. Includes one hour of lab each week. Prerequisite: JOURN 225 or 360. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Journalism Internship
description: Onthejob training in which journalism or public relations students get practical experience in applying what they have learned in the classroom. Involves assigned duties in an offcampus communications organization with appropriate compensation. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson, JOURN 211, and required 300-level sequence courses. Not open to students who have credit in JOURN 375 or 469. May be taken for credit/no credit only.

title: Editorial Practicum
description: Introductory practical experience in the production of the campus newspaper, magazine, yearbook, or alternative projects with emphasis on writing, editing, or photographic activities. Emphasizes mastery of spelling, grammar, and typing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to students who have credit in JOURN 369 or 469.

title: Electronic Journalistic Production Techniques
description: Theory, principles, and handson experience in camera and videocassette recorder operation; microphones and audio recording; electronic editing; studio production; field production and delivery systems. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Open only to journalism majors and minors.

title: Honors Colloquium in Journalism
description: Readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Journalism
description: The procedures and problems in teaching journalism classes or units and the role of student publications in school journalism programs. Subjects included are curriculum, finance, textbooks, and resources. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Advanced Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice in reporting and writing specialized news stories. Emphasis is on indepth reporting and coverage of specialized areas including public affairs, government, education, and business. Assignments are designed for use in student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: World Press Systems
description: Survey of the international news media, with particular attention to the four press theories; ownership, structure, and access to the media; the political, economic, and social environment in which the media operate; governmentmedia relations. Comparison with the American media.

title: Scientific and Technical Writing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Students become familiar with engineering and spaceage terminology, with emphasis on clarity and translation of technical terms to lay language.

title: Newspaper Design
description: Theory of the design functions of journalism using typographical systems with attention to their relations to communicative language. Acquaints students with new methods, ideas, and techniques that have been and are in the process of being developed in journalism printing and technology. Prerequisite: JOURN 125. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Magazine Composition and Layout
description: Study of magazine layout and production from an editor's point of view. Explores journalistic visual literacy, visual/verbal interpretation, and composition unique to magazines and newspaper magazine supplements. Prerequisite: JOURN 225, 211, or JOURN 125, 328. Not open to students in prejournalism. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Magazine Writing
description: A workshop in writing articles. Emphasizes targeting markets for freelance articles and writing for magazines that publish articles of 2,500 words or more. Prerequisite: JOURN 315. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Picture Editing
description: Selecting, editing, and using photographic and other illustrative graphic materials. Includes layout and design of picture pages for newspapers, magazines, books, brochures, and pamphlets.

title: Advertising Photography
description: Advertising, commercial, and concept illustration photography for the print media. Students must have their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Color Photojournalism
description: Principles, techniques, and materials of color photography as they apply to color art work and photographs in printed publications. Students must have their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 337. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Case Studies
description: Designed to analyze and solve advertising problems based on actual situations. Cases focus on consumer goods companies, industrial marketers, and nonprofit organizations. Prerequisite: JOURN 352, 354. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Copy Writing
description: Advanced studies in the strategy and creation of advertising for the mass media. Prerequisite: JOURN 354. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Campaigns
description: Synthesis of skills and concepts acquired in the specialized advertising courses. Students research, plan, write, schedule, budget, and evaluate a complete advertising campaign. Prerequisite: JOURN 352, 354; MKG 300, 310. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Public Relations Campaigns
description: Allows public relations majors to apply research and problemsolving techniques to actual or simulated public relations case problems using all of the methodologies learned previously. Prerequisite: JOURN 368. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising and Public Relations Practicum
description: Practical experience in public relations or advertising projects in preparation of a senior portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 352 and 354 or 368 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advising High School Publications
description: Theories of staff organization and content of high school yearbooks, newspapers, and magazines. Emphasizes the role of the advisor, financial management, staff motivation, and trends in scholastic publications.

title: Introduction to Journalism and Communication Research
description: Issues and trends in the literature of mass communication theory and research.

title: Individual Studies in Journalism
description: Group and individual investigations and experiences in journalistic media and techniques with special attention to social, political, and economic roles of the press in society. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF MATHEMATICAL SCIENCES D. Whitaker, Chairperson; M. Ali, J. Anderson, R. Avila, J. Zhang The Department of Mathematical Sciences offers General Studies course work to help all students understand the role that mathematics plays in today's world. The department also offers specialized programs to prepare mathematically oriented students for a variety of careers. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government as well as for more intense study of mathematics at the graduate level. The applied mathematics minor is designed for students whose primary interests lie in such subjects as business, economics, biology, geography, geology, and psychology. The major in actuarial science provides training for careers that involve analyzing and solving business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. The program includes course work for the first three examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries and in some cases for the fourth and fifth examinations. The teaching major and minor satisfy state certification requirements for students preparing to teach mathematics in junior high/middle school or high school. Students preparing to be elementary teachers may add the endorsement for teaching mathematics to their elementary teaching licenses and may also earn certification to teach mathematics in junior high/middle schools. For information on the major in mathematical economics, see Interdepartmental Programs, p. 43. Unless otherwise noted, all students enrolling in courses in the Department of Mathematical Sciences are expected to have completed at least three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school, including two years of algebra and one year of geometry. To begin all programs (except the endorsement for teaching a subject field: mathematics), it is expected that students will have completed high school mathematics courses equivalent to the prerequisite for MATHS 171 (161 for the minor in applied mathematics). In addition, for all programs (except the actuarial science major and the endorsement), it is expected that students will have had some computer programming experience. Each student with a major or minor in the Department of Mathematical Sciences must earn a grade of C or better in each course serving as a prerequisite for other courses applied to meet program requirements. For graduation, a G.P.A. of at least 2.5 is required in a minor or major program. DEPARTMENTAL MAJOR IN ACTUARIAL SCIENCE, 55 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS

title: Intermediate Algebra
description: Review of factoring, quadratic equations and inequalities, relations and functions, rational exponents, systems of linear equations, and exponential and logarithmic functions. Recommended background: two years of college preparatory mathematics in high school.

title: College Algebra
description: Such topics as polynomial functions and equations, exponential and logarithmic functions, determinants, systems of equations and inequalities, mathematical induction, the binomial theorem, permutations and combinations, and progressions. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or appropriate score on mathematics placement test or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS courses numbered 161 or higher.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities, and equations; graphs of the trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions; solution of right and general triangles; polar coordinates; and complex numbers. Scientific calculators will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or 109 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS courses numbered 161 or higher.

title: Pre-Calculus Mathematics
description: Coordinate plane, straight lines and circles, conic sections, elementary transcendental functions, curvesketching, polar coordinates, parametric equations, sequences, and series. Prerequisite: the equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondaryschool level or MATHS 112.

title: Mathematics and Its Applications
description: General Studies course including such topics as mathematical modeling, problem solving, geometrical concepts, growth patterns, and applications to the physical sciences, social sciences, and economics. Recommended background: three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of business majors. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or an appropriate score on the mathematics placement test.

title: Basic Mathematical Analysis 2
description: A continuation of the study of topics in mathematics that are particularly suited to the needs of students with a major in business. Prerequisite: MATHS 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 112 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 171.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 171. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 172.

title: Calculus 1
description: Differential calculus and its applications. Advanced topics from analytic geometry will be introduced as needed. Antidifferentiation and the Reimann integral. Elementary transcendental functions. Prerequisite: elements of analytic geometry from high school or MATHS 117.

title: Calculus 2
description: Standard techniques of integration and applications of the integral. Infinite series. Further development of applications of integral calculus. Vectors. Partial differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 171.

title: Elementary Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, measures of central tendency and dispersion, basic probability concepts, random variables, binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression, and consideration of various applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 109 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 320.

title: Number Concepts in the Elementary School
description: Development of cardinal and unsigned rational number concepts and properties interfaced with selected models and computer software from elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite: appropriate score on mathematics placement test, or credit in MATHS 108, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geometry and Measurement in Grades K-6
description: Development of geometry and measurement concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from mathematics programs for primary and intermediate grades. May be substituted for MATHS 203. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 201. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 203.

title: Geometry and Measurement in the Primary Grades
description: Development of measurement and geometry concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from K-3 mathematics programs. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 201. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 202.

title: Mathematics for the Teacher of the Exceptional Learner
description: Development of number concepts, number operations, measurement, geometric concepts, and problemsolving skills needed by teachers of exceptional learners. Instructional activities use selected models and materials appropriate for teachers of exceptional learners. May not be substituted for MATHS 201 or 202 or 203. Prerequisite: appropriate score on mathematics placement test, credit in MATHS 108, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 201, 202, or 203. Open only to special education majors.

title: Structure of the Number Systems
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and selected number systems. A systematic development is emphasized. Prerequisite: MATHS 162, 171, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Linear Algebra 1
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties and applications, determinants, rank and equivalence of matrices. Introduction to vector spaces and linear transformation. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 171.

title: Linear Algebra 2
description: A continuation of topics from MATHS 212 including transformation of coordinates, diagonalization of matrices, and introduction to canonical forms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 412.

title: Statistical Methods
description: Introduces the application of statistics. Binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, tests of hypotheses, regression, correlation, categorical data analysis, analysis of variance, nonparametrics, sampling, and elementary experimental design. Emphasis is placed on comprehension and interpretation. Statistical computer packages are used. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 171. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 321.

title: Discrete Mathematics
description: Study of contemporary topics in discrete mathematics selected from but not limited to sets, logic, methods of proof, relations, functions, counting, recurrence, graphs, trees, matrix algebra, discrete probability, game theory, Markov chains, and related topics in abstract algebra. Prerequisite: MATHS 132 or 162 or 172, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Geometry
description: Revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Computer applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 211 and one year of high school geometry.

title: Calculus 3
description: Multidimensional calculus and its applications. Topics include vectorvalued functions, partial derivatives, multiple integrals in rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates, and some vector analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems dealing with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite: MATHS 273.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games will be emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 201. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematics for the Junior High/Middle School Teacher
description: Applications of logic, number systems, algebra, geometry, and statistics in the junior high/middle school. Materials, manipulatives, and technology will be used to provide models for the junior high/middle school mathematics curriculum. Prerequisite: MATHS 211, 240. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 201 and 202. Open only to mathematics teaching majors and minors.

title: Algebraic Structures
description: Consideration of the basic algebraic structures: groups, rings, integral domains, and fields. Examples of these structures and elementary proof will be emphasized as will polynomials over rings, integral domains, and the fields of real and complex numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, momentgenerating functions, common distributions, sampling distribution theory, central limit theorem, t, chisquare, and F distributions. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Mathematical Statistics
description: Point and interval estimation, maximum likelihood, Neyman-Pearson Lemma, likelihood ratio tests, classical tests of significance, goodnessoffit, contingency tables, correlation, regression, nonparametric methods, Bayesian methods. Prerequisite: MATHS 320.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, and other distributions. Some problems with momentgenerating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Actuarial review class. Prerequisite: MATHS 321.

title: Computer and Mathematics Enrichment Topics
description: Topics for elementary and junior high/middle school in computer uses and programming, and enrichment topics from such areas as topology, strategy games, and number theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 202.

title: Computer Applications in the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Emphasizes the use of computers in the teaching of mathematics. Students whose area of licensure is mathematics may apply credit in this course toward the undergraduate computer endorsement. Prerequisite: MATHS 240 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models for use with problems in physics, chemistry, biology, and economics. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models. Existing computer software will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in analytic, synthetic, transformational, and vector geometry, closely related to Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 240 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities, equations of value, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, current actuarial topics in finance. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analysis, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, and orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 118 or 120 and MATHS 162 or 172. Not open to students who have credit in CS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 362. Not open to students who have credit in CS 363.

title: Intermediate Calculus
description: Topics include vector functions; displacement; velocity and acceleration of particles in twoand threedimensional space; curvature; torsion and Frenet's formulas; divergence; curl; line integrals; work; surface integrals; theorems of Gauss, Green, and Stokes; orthogonal curvilinear coordinates. Prerequisite: MATHS 273.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nthorder ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equations. Laplace transforms, power series solutions. Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, firstorder partial differential equations. Use of standard computer software for elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood and Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from early childhood through grade three. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. One hour lecture, one hour teaching, and one hour laboratory each week. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 202 or 203. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 391.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood, Primary, and Intermediate Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics from early childhood through intermediate grades. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Two onehour lectures and one onehour laboratory experience each week. May be substituted for MATHS 390. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 202 or 203.

title: Teaching Mathematics to the Exceptional Learner
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics to the exceptional learner. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Three onehour lectures and one onehour laboratory experience each week. May not be substituted for MATHS 390 or 391. Prerequisite: a grade of C or higher in MATHS 207, or a grade of C or higher in both MATHS 201 and 202. Open only to special education majors.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for teaching mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a smallgroup teaching situation. Prerequisite: MATHS 240.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in teaching secondary mathematics. Additional consideration given to methodology and instruction at the junior high/middle school level. Survey of texts, organization of materials, evaluation procedures, instructional aids, and classroom observations. Prerequisite: MATHS 211 and 240.

title: Classroom Use of Methods and Materials
description: Classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics, evaluation of instructional activities, and rationale for including mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever appropriate. Prerequisite: MATHS 313, 340, 395.

title: Abstract Algebra 1
description: Introduction to group theory and ring theory through the isomorphism theorems. Burnside counting and the Sylow theorems. An introduction to polynomial rings, integral domains, and elementary field theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 311.

title: Abstract Algebra 2
description: Continuation of the study of abstract algebra. Topics from series of groups, free groups, group presentations and the word problem, field extensions and geometric constructions, modules, and algebraic coding theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 411.

title: Theory of Numbers
description: Topics include the division algorithm; positional notation; divisibility; primes; congruences; divisibility criteria; the sigma, divisor, and phi functions; diophantine equations; linear, polynomial, and simultaneous congruences; theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson; quadratic reciprocity. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school include Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, magic squares, the calendar problem, polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the fifteen puzzle, Nim, and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 416.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling; ratio estimates; regression estimates; cost and variance functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Topics in Statistics
description: Includes such topics as oneand twoway ANOVA, multiple comparisons, regression analysis, time series analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Analysis of Variance in Experimental Design Models
description: Multivariate normal distribution; quadratic forms; linear models; simple random, randomized block, Latin squares, factorial, splitplot, balanced incomplete block design; analysis of covariance; confounding; multiple comparison tests. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Geometry and Topology 1
description: Introduction to Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometries and the surfaces admitting these geometries. Basic topological notions, such as the boundary operator, continuity, and connectedness, underlying the development of these topics. Elements of linear geometry leading to basic ideas of differential geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 273.

title: Geometry and Topology 2
description: A continuation of MATHS 441 culminating in the treatment of selected advanced topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 441.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 1
description: Survival distributions, life tables; the mathematics of life insurance, life annuities, net premiums, and net premium reserves. Prerequisite: MATHS 321, 351.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 2
description: Mathematics of multiple life functions, multiple decrement models, valuation theory for pension plans, insurance models including expenses, nonforfeiture benefits, and dividends. Prerequisite: MATHS 452.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation math formula. Prerequisite: MATHS 362.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Optimization techniques of linear, dynamic, and integer programming and stochastic simulation. Optimal solutions of PERT-CPM networks. Optimal decision strategies. Elementary queuing theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 320, and working knowledge of scientific computer programming.

title: History of Mathematics
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to the seventeenth century. Topics may include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, and calculus. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 171.

title: Elements of Analysis
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives, and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 172 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Metric spaces, topological concepts in IR and C leading to consideration of connectedness, compactness and completeness, continuous functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrass theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 273.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansions. Prerequisite: MATHS 471.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace's equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATHS 374.

title: Senior Seminar
description: A variety of topics in mathematics presented by three faculty members will be studied and discussed. A short paper on one of the three topics presented to the class is required. Prerequisite: major in one of the mathematical sciences and senior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the mathematical sciences department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 levels. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF MODERN LANGUAGES AND CLASSICS A. King, Chairperson; B. Anderson, L. J. Barnette, W. D. Barnette, R. Fritz, R. Gardiol, D. Gilman, J. Hightower, L. Hodlofski, L. Johnson, E. Kadletz, W. McGrath, W. Moskalew, C. Shea, S. Tomizawa, R. Warner The Department of Modern Languages and Classics offers programs in both ancient and modern foreign languages and works closely with other programs and departments to combine foreign language training with other subjects. Language laboratory practice, computer applications, and opportunities for foreign exchange programs and summer study abroad enhance classroom instruction. The department offers foreign language training for students who want to acquire a broad liberal education; enrich their preparation for their careers; seek certification for teaching at the elementary or secondary level; plan to travel, live, or work abroad; or work as translators. Students may earn credit for previous language study through either advanced placement tests or departmentally administered proficiency tests. These exams also help determine the appropriate classes in which students are placed. Placement credit is not given for the firstlevel (101) course. Students placed in any higherlevel course may receive up to a maximum of 10 credit hours for the courses they test out of by earning grades of C or higher in the course into which they are placed. Native speakers who have completed high school studies in their native countries are not eligible for credit in the first or second year of their native languages. At the end of their last semester, senior majors in French, German, and Spanish are expected to take a proficiency test for assessment of skills in six areas—reading, writing, listening, speaking, grammar, and culture—and, in Latin, in three areas: translation, grammar, and culture. Resulting scores of high, middle, or low are available to faculty members for letters of recommendation. The modern language test is based on content, procedures, and norms published by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages and Educational Testing Services. Students should consult with foreign language faculty advisors about arranging courses to meet their individual needs. The 100- and 200-level courses in foreign languages are sequential and must be taken in order. Only work at the 200 level and above will apply toward any major or minor in foreign languages except those in Chinese, Japanese, and classical culture where firstyear courses may be counted.
