title: Word Origins and Vocabulary Development
description: English vocabulary derived from Latin and Greek, emphasizing wordformation as a means of expanding and enriching students' vocabularies. No knowledge of Greek and Latin is required.

title: Scientific Terminology: Greek
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Greek commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Greek is required.

title: Scientific Terminology: Latin
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Latin commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Latin is required.

title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Main features of the civilization of the Greeks and Romans—their history, political institutions, art, literature, and philosophy. Explores through lectures, readings, and audiovisual materials the nature of the ancients' contribution to Western civilizations.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: A close, interpretive view of Greek cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as individualism, ideals of beauty, social experimentation, competitiveness, and intellectual curiosity, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: A close, interpretive view of Roman cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as respect for tradition, rule of law, social responsibility, and technical expertise, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: The Classical World in Film
description: Aspects of ancient civilization depicted in film (such as Roman history, Greek mythology, etc.). An examination of the accuracy of such portrayals through comparison with ancient sources. The place of such films in the history of cinema. Topics will vary.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: Classical mythology (Greek and Roman) will represent Western tradition in a comparative study with other mythologies of the world. Emphasis on understanding mythologies as symbolic cultural systems expressing societal values.

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selections from the major works of Greek and Roman literature and their continuing influence on Western literature. Emphasis is on prose and poetry in alternate terms. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Women in Antiquity
description: The study of women in ancient Greece and Rome, based on evidence from literary and nonliterary sources. Explores the influence of social, political, and legal institutions on the status of women and on their relationships with men.

title: Greek and Roman Cults
description: Introduces the religions of the ancient Greeks and Romans and examines the nature of their cult activities and theological speculations. Topics include prayer, sacrifice, feasting, ritual, scripture, myth, clergy, etc.

title: The Ancient City
description: Life of the ancient city as mirrored in archaeological and literary sources. The concept of the city, its art and architecture, with special emphasis on Periclean Athens and Augustan Rome.

title: Classical Myth and Theory
description: Major themes of classical myths: creation, the divine and human family, life of the hero, the quest, monsters, etc. Study and employment of modern theories of analysis: mythritual, psychological, structuralist, etc. Prerequisite recommended: CC 205.

title: Readings
description: Individualized course of reading or limited research to allow students to explore special topics in classical antiquity. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Chinese 1
description: The first course in the Chinese language.

title: Beginning Chinese 2
description: The second course in the Chinese language. Prerequisite: CH 101.

title: Intermediate Chinese 1
description: Designed to build n a foundation of firstyear Chinese o to help students achieve greater fluency in oral expression and to emphasize the reading of Chinese character texts containing both old and simplified character forms. Grammar will be taught through the use of sentence P' atterns and character writing will be practiced. Traditional and contemporary aspects of Chinese culture will also be taught. Prerequisite: CH 102.

title: Intermediate Chinese 2
description: Designed to build on the foundation laid thus far in Chinese and to help students achieve greater fluency in the four basic skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will read newspapers, short stories, and essays by modern authors with the help of a dictionary and will write short compositions in Hanzi on their readings. Prerequisite: CH 201.

title: Beginning Readings in Chinese
description: A course designed to develop skills in reading simple Chinese essays, short stories, and newspaper articles, using approximately 2,000 characters and the help of a dictionary. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Chinese Literature in English Translation
description: A brief overview of major Chinese literary trends and works using selections from traditional masterpieces in poetry, myth, legend, short story, and novel and also contemporary essay, short story, and novel. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Beginning Guided Self-Instruction in Common Languages
description: Guided selfinstruction in beginning French, German, Greek, Latin, or Spanish using audiovisual materials, texts, workbooks, tests, and tutors on an arranged basis. Designed to meet the needs of students who cannot otherwise study languages. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Not open to native speakers. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The French-Speaking World
description: Survey of political, cultural, and literary history in areas colonized by France: Quebec, the Caribbean, North Africa, West Africa. Topics include geography, government, and differences in Francophone and Anglophone colonization, using sociopolitical and literary works.

title: Intermediate Guided Self-Instruction in Common Languages
description: Guided selfinstruction in intermediate French, German, Greek, Latin, or Spanish using audiovisual materials, texts, workbooks, tests, and tutors by arrangement. Designed to meet the needs of students who cannot otherwise study these languages. Not open to native speakers. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures in Translation
description: Readings in English translation of selected works of major writers in one of the foreign languages taught in this department. Topics and works may vary. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Foreign Culture through Films
description: Study of cultures of the countries whose languages are taught in this department through the medium of foreign contemporary and classic films. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Indochina: Traditions and Languages of Laos and Vietnam
description: A survey of the high traditions and values of the peoples of Indochina. World view through folklore, literature, arts, and language. Conducted in Lao and Vietnamese. Prerequisite: conversational knowledge of Lao or Vietnamese. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Guided Self-Instruction Studies in Less Common Languages
description: Offers languages such as Japanese, Arabic, modern Hebrew, modern Greek, Chinese, and Portuguese at basic spoken levels by guided selfinstruction. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in one language. Not open to native speakers.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Foreign Language in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and applications of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching foreign language in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite: EDJHM 280 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid, supervised work experience integrating foreign and classical language skills with careerrelated positions in international firms, the travel industry, and local, state, and federal agencies. Work assignments may be partor fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs. Prerequisite: a minimum of two years of universitylevel foreign language study and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Foreign Language
description: Current methods in foreign language teaching in the senior high school. Presentation, texts, teaching materials, CAI, and other supplementary aids. Reviews current professional literature, trends, requirements. Prerequisite: two years of college credit or the equivalent in a modern language and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Foreign Language Trends and CAI
description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of foreign languages, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of foreign languages in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: FL 395.

title: Practical Experience
description: Nonpaid, supervised work experience integrating foreign and classical language skills with careerrelated positions in international firms, the travel industry, and local, state, and federal agencies. Work assignments may be partor fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs. Prerequisite: a minimum of two years of universitylevel foreign language study and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning French 1
description: The first course in the French language.

title: Beginning French 2
description: Prerequisite: FR 101.

title: Intermediate French 1
description: Prerequisite: FR 102.

title: Intermediate French 2
description: Prerequisite: FR 201.

title: Conversation
description: Practice in oral French to increase fluency and authenticity through activities and conversation. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Composition
description: Practice in written French with review of grammatical structures. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Grammar
description: An advanced study of French grammar, stressing creative expression in the language. Prerequisite: FR 302 or its equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Civilization and Culture: Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the French language and the application of phonetics to the understanding and speaking of French. Use of the International Phonetic Alphabet. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business French
description: Designed to make advanced French students familiar with commericial forms and terminology used in business, banking, and industry. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to French Literature 1
description: Selections from various periods of French literature, designed to develop an appreciation of the literary heritage of France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to students who have credit in FR 401 or its equivalent.

title: Introduction to French Literature 2
description: Modern prose and poetry. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent. Not open to students who have credit in FR 402 or its equivalent.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the classical age to 1760. Prerequisite: FR 361 or 362 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: History of French Literature 2
description: From the classical age to the present. The development of eighteenthcentury philosophies, romanticism, realism, naturalism, and symbolism in French literature; literature of modern France. Prerequisite: FR 361 or 362 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar in French Literature
description: Seminar studies by author, genre, period, or theme. Topic to be announced. Prerequisite: six semesters of French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in French Language or Civilization
description: Seminar studies in grammar, style, conversation, or civilization. Topic to be announced. Prerequisite: six semesters of French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings
description: Individualized reading or research to allow students to explore special topics with an individual instructor. Prerequisite: three years of college French or the equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning German 1
description: The first course in the German language.

title: Beginning German 2
description: Prerequisite: GER 101 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate German 1
description: Reading of representative German authors of moderate difficulty. Emphasizes vocabulary, increased knowledge of German idiom, and practice in writing German. Prerequisite: GER 102 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate German 2
description: Prerequisite: GER 201 or its equivalent.

title: Conversation
description: Extensive practice in oral German to increase fluency and authenticity in the language. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Composition
description: Extensive practice of written German with review of the grammatical structure of the language. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Grammar
description: Advanced, indepth study of German grammar and stylistic expression.

title: Contemporary German Culture
description: Lectures, readings, and audiovisual materials introducing students to presentday social mores of Germany. Comparison of American and German cultures. Taught in English.

title: Civilization and Culture
description: Civilization and cultural development of the Germans from ancient times to the present. Taught in German. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the German language and the application of phonetics and phonemics in the understanding and speaking of German. Use of the International Phonetic Alphabet. Prerequisite: two years of German or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business German
description: Designed to make advanced German students familiar with commercial forms and terminology used in business, banking, and industry. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to German Literature 1
description: Selections from prose, short stories, and Novellen of German literature, designed to develop an appreciation of the literary heritage of Germany. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Introduction to German Literature 2
description: Selections from the dramas and radio plays of German literature. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Introduction to German Literature 3
description: Selections from poetry, folksongs, and ballads of contemporary Germany. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: German Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced German language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where German is spoken as a native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of German Literature 1
description: German literature from its beginnings through the age of Goethe. A survey of German literary trends from earliest times to the classical period. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: History of German Literature 2
description: German literature from early to late nineteenth century. The development of nineteenthcentury philosophies, romanticism, and realism. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: History of German Literature 3
description: German literature from the late nineteenth century to the present, from naturalism to the literature of the modern Germanies. Prerequisite: two years of college German or the equivalent.

title: Readings
description: Individual reading or research to allow students to explore special topics with an individual instructor. Prerequisite: three years of college German or the equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Greek 1
description: Introduction to ancient Greek. Emphasis is on the alphabet, pronunciation, elementary grammar, and preparation of students for readings in classical and New Testament Greek.

title: Beginning Greek 2
description: Prerequisite: GRK 101 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate Greek 1
description: Intensive grammar review and readings from classical and New Testament sources. Prerequisite: GRK 102 or equivalent.

title: Intermediate Greek 2
description: Prerequisite: GRK 201 or its equivalent.

title: Advanced Greek 1
description: Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Greek or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Greek 2
description: Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Greek or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Beginning Italian 1
description: The first course in the Italian language.

title: Beginning Italian 2
description: Prerequisite: ITAL 101 or its equivalent.

title: Beginning Japanese 1
description: The first course in beginning Japanese language.

title: Beginning Japanese 2
description: The second course in beginning Japanese language. Prerequisite: JAPAN 101.

title: Intermediate Japanese 1
description: Designed for students with credit in JAPAN 101 and 102. Further develops skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing Japanese, and increases knowledge of Japanese culture. Prerequisite: JAPAN 102 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate Japanese 2
description: Designed for students with credit in JAPAN

title: Advanced Japanese 1
description: Designed for students with credit in JAPAN 202. Further skill development in the idiomatic use of the Japanese language, and increased understanding of Japanese culture. Prerequisite: JAPAN 202 or its equivalent.

title: Advanced Japanese 2
description: Designed for students with credit in JAPAN 301. Enhances skills in fluent idiomatic use of the Japanese language, understanding of Japanese culture. Includes an introduction to some of the masterpieces of Japanese literature in translation. Prerequisite: JAPAN 301 or its equivalent.

title: Beginning Latin 1
description: Introduction to Latin. Emphasis is on pronunciation, elementary grammar, composition, and translation of simple Latin passages.

title: Beginning Latin 2
description: Prerequisite: LAT 101 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate Latin 1
description: Intensive grammar review and readings from Latin prose and poetry. Prerequisite: LAT 102 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate Latin 2
description: Prerequisite: LAT 201 or its equivalent.

title: Introduction to Prose 1
description: Selections from Caesar, Cicero, Livy, and others. Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Poetry 1
description: Selections from Ovid, Vergil, and others. Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Prose 2
description: Selections from Tacitus, Suetonius, Sallust, and others. Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Poetry 2
description: Selections from Roman comedy, Horace, Catullus, and others. Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Prose Composition
description: A detailed grammar review, analysis of Latin prose style, composition of extended passages in Latin. Prerequisite: 9 hours of college Latin or the equivalent. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Literature 1
description: Survey of Latin literature from the beginnings to the fall of the republic. Prerequisite: three years of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the

title: History of Literature 2
description: Survey of Latin literature from Augustus to the end of the empire. Prerequisite: three years of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Latin Prose
description: Cicero. Prerequisite: three years of college Latin or equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Latin Poetry
description: Juvenal, Vergil, and Lucretius. Prerequisite: three years of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Roman Historiography
description: Livy, Suetonius, and others. Prerequisite: three years of college Latin or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Readings
description: Individualized readings or research to allow students to explore special topics with an individual instructor. Prerequisite: three years of college Latin or the equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Spanish 1
description: The first course in the Spanish language.

title: Beginning Spanish 2
description: Prerequisite: SP 101.

title: Intermediate Spanish 1
description: Prerequisite: SP 102 or its equivalent.

title: Intermediate Spanish 2
description: Prerequisite: SP 201 or its equivalent.

title: Conversation
description: Practice in oral Spanish to increase fluency and authenticity through activities and discussion. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Composition
description: Practice in written Spanish with review of grammatical structures. Stress on original composition. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

title: Grammar
description: An advanced study of Spanish grammar, stressing creative expression in the language. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

title: Spanish Civilization and Culture
description: An examination of Spanish history and culture through lectures, readings, and discussions. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Latin-American Civilization and Culture
description: A panoramic view of the culture and customs of the various Latin- American countries. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the Spanish language and the application of phonetics and phonemics to the understanding, speaking, and teaching of Spanish. Use of the International Phonetic Alphabet. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business Spanish
description: Designed to make advanced Spanish students familiar with commercial correspondence forms and terminology used in business, banking, and industry. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Peninsular Spanish Literature
description: Selections by Spanish writers of the twentieth century in all genres. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

title: Introduction to Latin American Literature
description: Selections by Spanish- American writers of the twentieth century in all genres. Prerequisite: two years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

title: Spanish Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced Spanish language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where Spanish is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Spanish Literature
description: Analysis of works and periods in Spanish literature from the beginning to the present. Reading and discussion will include the rudiments of literary criticism. Prerequisite: three years of college Spanish.

title: History of Latin-American Literature
description: Analysis of works and periods in Latin America from the early chronicles to the present. Reading and discussion will include the rudiments of literary criticism. Prerequisite: three years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

title: Seminar in Literature
description: Topics vary according to genre, author, or period and will be studied in depth. Intensive study of authors of a selected period from Spain or Latin America. Research and reports. Prerequisite: SP 361 or 362 or the equivalent or SP 402 or the equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Language
description: Topics vary and will be announced. Topics may be, among others, advanced grammar, linguistics, conversation, composition, translation, or Spanish for the professions. Prerequisite: three years of college Spanish or the equivalent.

Van Meter The Department of Natural Resources prepares students for careers in environmental science and natural resources. The programs offered by the department are designed to give students a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. The department offers a departmental major and minor in natural resources, a teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, and an endorsement for elementary education majors and coordinates an interdepartmental energy minor. Students majoring in natural resources choose one of the following options: natural resource studies, interpretation and public information, outdoor recreation management, environmental protection, and landresource management. All majors must complete a common core requirement. Many courses include laboratory work using analytic equipment. Each year students have opportunities for indepth twoto fourweek field studies in the United States and foreign countries. Students are encouraged to participate in practicums or internships under the supervision of faculty members or professionals working in private consulting firms, governmental agencies, or environmental education centers. title: Natural Resources: Environment, Conservation, and Society
description: Study of natural resources (air, energy, minerals, soil, vegetation, water, wildlife) and the effects of population and technology on environmental systems. Role of resource management, conservation, and outdoor recreation in achieving an environment of high quality. Laboratory and field activities included.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give students knowledge of use of resources in the United States by treating in historical perspective government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis is on the way use of resources has shaped society. Not open to students who have credit in HIST 204.

title: International Natural Resources: Development and Conservation
description: An analysis of problems occurring as a result of development and use of natural resources worldwide. The role of resource management and conservation to enhance the carrying capacity of earth. A casestudy approach to the management of global environmental problems.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to humans. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Includes laboratory and field work.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis on the practical applications of soil science to natural resources planning. Includes laboratory and field work. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be 9-12 earned. 3 hours from

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis is on applying the economist's decisionmaking Natural Resources 247 model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 3 semester hours in NR, preferably NR 101, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in ECON 311.

title: Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Food Production
description: The role of natural resources in producing food for people and the agronomic and animal science practices necessary to provide food for a growing world population. Emphasis is placed on the management talents needed to grow food successfully. Two weekend field trips.

title: Resources for Self-Reliant Living
description: Considers the environmental effects of hard and soft technologies. Focuses on devising a survival strategy based on selfreliant concepts in housing, waste material, water use, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation, and the role of regulatory agencies. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 211; CHEM 111 or the equivalent; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: The basic relationship between soil nutrients and plant growth with emphasis on the conditions affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Includes basic soil testing. Prerequisite: NR 221; CHEM 111 or the equivalent; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Includes soil genesis, morphology, classification, and survey. Stresses the relationship between soils information and the landuse decisionmaking process with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis is placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Stresses principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts. Studies management systems and individual practices with special emphasis on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Energy and Mineral Resources: Issues and Choices
description: Appraisal of the problems, prospects, and societal and technical issues surrounding the use of energy and mineral resources. Emphasis is on environmental problems and ecoenergetics, consideration of the natural resource base, distribution and production problems, conservation, alternative energy systems, resource policy, and research.

title: Air Resources
description: Significance of the atmosphere as a resource; important meteorological parameters in air resources and management; economic, sociological, technical, political, and biological aspects of air pollution; special emphasis on basic principles, practices, and techniques of air resources conservation.

title: Indoor Air Quality Management
description: Indoor air pollution problems of residential and nonresidential environments. Features discussions of pollutants like asbestos, radon, and formaldehyde as well as combustiongenerated pollutants. Topics include energy conservation, building design, modeling, measurement techniques, and mitigation measures. Lab and field experiments.

title: Principles of Industrial Hygiene
description: Designed to introduce the principles of industrial hygiene practice. Topics include toxicological principles, occupational disease, air sampling, ionizing and nonionizing radiation, noise, ergonomics, personal protective equipment, exposure limits, regulatory requirements, engineering controls, and indoor air pollution.

title: Turf-Grass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis is on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. Identification of grass and weed species.

title: Paid Professional Practice
description: Supervised financially supported professional experience in natural resource management, environmental education, or environmental protection. Provides a bridge between academic and professional experiences. Available only on a prospective basis. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. Emphasizes multipleuse concepts of management to meet outdoor recreation demands. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Introductory Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles as applied to the management of natural resources and related environmental problems. Prerequisite: NA 211, 221; GEOL 101; PHYCS 110; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures. Prerequisite: NR 211; one college course in chemistry; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
description: Delineation of solid and hazardous waste management in the United States. Waste reduction, recycling, processing, and disposal methods are discussed. Technical, political, and economic aspects of waste management. Effects of improper disposal on environmental quality. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students; others with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching of Conservation
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating conservation into all areas of the elementary education curriculum. Reviews sources of help in teaching conservation like resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources uniquely appropriate to conservation and outdoor education. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 101; BIO 102; GEOG 111; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Methods and Materials: Environmental Conservation in the Secondary School
description: The opportunities for enriching instruction by integrating environmental conservation into the secondary school curriculum. Reviews sources of help in teaching environmental conservation like resource consultants, teaching techniques, and instructional resources appropriate to environmental conservation. Requires laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a specific area with special emphasis on location of natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence they have on the regional environmental quality. Each time the course is offered a specific geographic area is studied. Includes laboratory and field experience. Prerequisite: NR 101 or its equivalent and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Integrated Resources Planning and Management
description: Introduction to strategies used in environmental planning and resource management in contemporary society. Stresses use of data analysis and its role in the decisionmaking process by conceptually centering on natural and humanmade systems. May require field trips. Prerequisite: all natural resources core courses or concurrent enrollment and senior standing. Students in related disciplines may seek permission from the department chairperson.

title: Seminar
description: Formal reports and discussion of selected natural resource topics, current events, and special articles in natural resourcerelated professional and scientific journals. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered spring semester of evennumbered years. Prerequisite: NR 211; BIO 480; ZOOL 444; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and use of natural resources for outdoor recreation. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Administration and Management of Outdoor Recreation Areas
description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to provide good outdoor recreation experiences. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Wilderness and Society
description: Defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. Includes study of research in user perception and use and a weekend trip to a potential Indiana wilderness area. Prerequisite: junior standing. title: Environmental Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasis is on field work and creative presentation of concepts and on the organization and management of interpretive programs including sites and facilities. Prerequisite: NR 101 or its equivalent; BIO 216.

title: Computer Applications in Natural Resources
description: Experience with a broad array of computer software for the VAX mainframe and microcomputers. Activities are carried out under an instructor's supervision. Assigned work is commensurate with computer experience and interests in natural resources. Taught by arrangement. Prerequisite: CS 116 and permission of the instructor or department chairperson.

title: Professional Practice
description: Supervised professional experience in natural resource management, environmental education, or environmental protection. Provides a bridge between academic and professional experiences. Available only on a prospective basis. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in NR 369. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources
description: An opportunity to pursue special interests in environmental quality. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours in combination with NR 496.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Original research under faculty guidance, including problem definition, literature review, data collection, analysis, and a summary report. May require preparatory or parallel course work in research methodologies, statistics, or computer science. Prerequisite: faculty sponsor and permission of the department chairperson. Foster Learning philosophy is more than simply reading books and memorizing theories and concepts. Learning philosophy involves engaging in philosophy, attempting to answer basic questions about people's values, the meaning of life, the extent of our freedom, and other issues. As the art of discovery, philosophy helps people to develop skills as keen observers, willingness to dig beneath the surface, and the ability to analyze data and think critically. The religious studies program helps people to deepen their understanding of their own religion and to appreciate the wide range of religions in the world. Courses also examine the deepest questions that concern people from a religious point of view: the nature and origin of life, the possibility of life after death, and value issues. The department's programs in philosophy and in religious studies offer excellent preparation for careers in higher education, law, public service, government agencies, writing, and religious vocations. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: An introduction to such important philosophical problems as the existence of God, whether ethical values are subjective, and the extent of our freedom. These topics and others may be approached by examining the ideas of great philosophers or current thinkers.

title: Introduction to Techniques of Critical Reasoning
description: Introduction to basic techniques of critical reasoning in deductive and inductive logic, and strategies for decision making and problem solving.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to the drawing of correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of deduction.

title: Ethics
description: A discussion of some of the central problems in ethics such as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as a discussion of current moral issues.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of such basic social concepts as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of such normative issues as how liberty should be distributed and how justice can be maximized.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Critical analysis of such selected topics as the nature and existence of God, the problem of evil, the justification of religious belief, and the significance of religious experience. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the rise of philosophy in Greece through the medieval period. Emphasis is on the theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Emphasis is on these theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics may include the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading philosophers and movements in the twentieth century. May concentrate on such selected philosophers as Russell, Wittgenstein, and Husserl, or may concentrate on contemporary treatments of selected philosophical problems.

title: Aesthetics
description: Exploration of philosophical views on the nature, interpretation, and criticism of art. Readings and discussion may range from classical to contemporary thinkers and issues.

title: Philosophy of Law
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, and justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of such basic concepts as action, intention, causation, and responsibility.

title: Current Issues in Philosophy
description: Selected current and important issues in philosophy. Topics may include social and ethical problems, recent work on traditional philosophical problems, and other issues of concern.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: An examination of such central philosophical problems in the sciences as the nature of scientific explanation and the testing of hypotheses; a discussion of ethical issues Philosophy 251 arising from science, for example the use of human subjects and prolonging life.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships related to their professional or career goals. Internships may be with educational or religious institutions, public or private agencies, or business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Open only to students in the Honors College or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Allows superior students opportunities for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Introduction to Metaphysics
description: A study of the principal problems of metaphysics including the nature of reality, the relation of mind and body, and the issues of freedom and determinism.

title: Introduction to Theory of Knowledge
description: A critical discussion of leading theories and problems of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge and rational belief, the different kinds of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory and Problems
description: A critical examination of recent ethical theories and their application to contemporary problems.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: Traditional religious groups in the United States with attention to developments, institutions, distinctive practices and beliefs. The groups and the subjects treated will be adjusted to the interests of the students.

title: Religions of the World
description: An introductory survey of the major religions of the world (Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Islam, Christianity, and others), emphasizing how people live out their faiths in their daily lives.

title: Old Testament
description: Our Hebrew- Judaic religious heritage as reflected in various personalities and their religious expressions as found in the literature of the Old Testament.

title: New Testament
description: Our early Christian heritage in relation to its Jewish- Greek background as reflected by various personalities in the literature of the New Testament.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships related to their professional or career goals. Internships may be with educational or religious institutions, public or private agencies, or business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Jesus and the Gospel Traditions
description: The traditions that developed about Jesus among the early Christians as reflected in the four Gospels and the more recent findings of apocryphal Gospels.

title: Methods in the Study of Religion
description: An exploration of the many ways to approach the study of religion, its origins, nature, and functions in human society.

title: Paul and the Developing Church
description: An indepth study of Paul's letters, the traditions as reflected in the Book of Acts, and the development of the early Church through the fourth century.

title: Seminar in Eastern Religions
description: An intensive seminarformat study of the religions of India, China, and Japan, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Shinto, and contemporary Japanese religions.

title: Comparative Religion
description: Investigation, analysis, and comparison of selected major religious traditions with attention to their underlying structures. Particular attention is given to the comparison of Eastern and Western traditions.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: For superior students: an opportunity for guided investigation in aspects of religion not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Special Topics in Religion
description: Indepth focus on a selected issue of central importance. Topics vary each semester and include such subjects as American Indian religions, women and religion, the Pentecostal and charismatic movements. Watson The Department of Physics and Astronomy offers majors in both pure and applied physics for students who want to pursue graduate work in physics, astronomy, or engineering or who are interested in careers in industry. Programs are also available for students who want to teach secondary school physics. Departmental minors are available in astronomy, physics, and applied physics (solar energy and electronics). Students planning to major or minor in physics or astronomy programs are strongly advised to consult with the department to determine the proper course sequence for their needs. Pre-Engineering Major This program is intended for students enrolled at Ball State who hope to transfer to accredited schools of engineering. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program in which students must attend Ball State for three years and then transfer to accredited engineering schools to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of the engineering program students are eligible to receive bachelor's degrees from Ball State in addition to their engineering degrees. Schools of engineering may have requirements not met by the general Ball State preengineering major. Students in this program are responsible for knowing and meeting the requirements of the schools to which they plan to transfer. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not mean automatic admission to any accredited school of engineering. Students must apply for admission to the engineering school and must meet the requirements set by the engineering school. Three options in the preengineering major are available: chemical engineering, metallurgical engineering, and general engineering (such as aeronautical, civil, electrical, industrial, mechanical, and nuclear). title: Introduction to Energy and Space Sciences
description: Nonmathematical study of the basic forms of energy with a special emphasis on nuclear energy generation. Survey of some of the means of transmitting such energy forms as sound, heat, radio, and light. Introduction to astronomy, gravity, and the mechanics of space travel.

title: Physical Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles and concepts of the laws of nature involving mechanical, heat, light, electrical, nuclear, and chemical energy and the conservation laws associated with these forms of energy. Emphasis is on applications appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Preparation of Physical Science Teaching Materials
description: Selected topics in physical science stressing the construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Prerequisite: PHYCS 101 or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students in the teachereducation curriculum.

title: Basic Physics for the Allied Health Sciences
description: A condensed study of basic physics with special emphasis on principles and applications pertinent to the health sciences. Three lectures and one twohour laboratoryrecitation weekly. Prerequisite: one year of high school algebra and one year of high school geometry or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students in the allied health sciences program in respiratory therapy, radiologic technology, nuclear therapy, and ultrasound technology or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: General Physics 1
description: Studies the laws of Newtonian mechanics. Introductory fluid statics and dynamics, heat and thermodynamics, and wave motion and sound. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 (algebra). Recommended prerequisite: MATHS 112 (trigonometry).

title: General Physics 2
description: Static and current electricity, magnetism, light and optics, and an introduction to modern physics including relativity and elements of atomic and nuclear physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 110 or 130.

title: General Physics 1
description: First course in calculusbased physics for students in preengineering, the physical sciences, or mathematics. Topics include Newtonian mechanics, work and energy, motion, impulse and momentum, elasticity and wave motion, sound, and hydrostatics and hydrodynamics. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161 or 171.

title: General Physics 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 120. Topics include heat and laws of thermodynamics, Coulomb's law and the electric field, Ampere's law and the magnetic field, introduction to Maxwell's equation, DC and AC circuits; the nature, propagation, and properties of light; and lens systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120. Parallel: MATHS 162 or 172.

title: Physics for Architects
description: Emphasizes the applications of mechanics and heat. Topics include particle dynamics, resolution of forces, friction, work, energy, static equilibrium, torque, properties of materials, fluids, temperature, thermal expansion, heat energy, heat transfer, phase changes in matter, and thermodynamic engines. Prerequisite: MATHS 112 or an equivalent course in secondary school mathematics. Not open to students who have credit in PHYCS 110 or 120.

title: Sound and Light
description: For music and art students. Sound as a basis of music and light as a basis of art. No regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Topics in Physics
description: Discussion of specific topics in physics, such as lasers, holography, and solidstate electronics. Designed for students not majoring in physics, the course requires no math or science background. Students may consult their curricular advisors or the Department of Physics and Astronomy for the specific topics being studied during a given semester. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Solar Energy Technology and Applications
description: Descriptive study of various techniques and systems using sunlight as a nonpolluting alternative energy source. Principles and design of solar systems for space heating, air conditioning, and heating water for residential and commercial buildings, and systems for the generation of electric power. Includes other related topics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 100 or MATHS 108.

title: Introduction to Modern Physics
description: The underlying principles and theories of modern physics. Topics include introductory relativity, atomic and nuclear structure, quantum theory, and the theory of solids. A regularly scheduled laboratory is included. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Mechanics
description: Basic concepts of particle mechanics. Simple and damped harmonic motion. Particle dynamics in noninertial frames of reference, central forces. Dynamics of a system of particles. Dynamics of a rigid body and the moment of inertia tensor. The wave equation, elasticity, and rigid body vibrations. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120 and MATHS 162.

title: Physical Optics
description: The electromagnetic wave theory of light, spectra, interference, diffraction, polarization, and double refraction. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Acoustics
description: Elements of pure and applied acoustics. Topics include solutions to the wave equation, acoustic impedances, electromechanicalacoustic analogies, directradiator loudspeaker and enclosure theory, and a discussion of room acoustics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Electronics 1
description: Introductory DC and AC circuit theory, semiconductor components, power supplies, transistor amplification; integrated circuit operational amplifiers, active filters, oscillators, and function generators. Basic combinational logic circuits and Boolean algebra. Emphasizes applications of integrated circuits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Electronics 2
description: Sequential logic circuits including scalars, displays, memories, shift registers, analogtodigital and digitaltoanalog conversion techniques. Microprocessor architecture and support electronics for microcomputer design. IC chips and circuits for experimenttomicrocomputer interfacing. Use of a microprocessor development system. Prerequisite: PHYCS 354 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introductory Nuclear Techniques
description: Emphasis is on experimental studies of radioactive disintegrations and decay products and their relation to nuclear structure. Instrumentation in radioisotope measurements. Two lectures and two twohour laboratory periods a week. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid work and learning experience in applied or theoretical physics in an institutional, industrial, or university research or development setting. May occur during one or more semesters. Prerequisite: approval of proposed program by the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics 1
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems, particularly those that occur in classical mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetic theory, and quantum mechanics. Topics include vector methods, generalized coordinates, and methods of applications of differential equations in physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and 260 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introductory Mathematical Physics 2
description: Application of mathematical techniques to the formulation and solution of physical problems. Topics include boundary value problems. Transforms, special functions of mathematical physics, and applications of tensor analysis in physics. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122, 260, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Descriptive Astronomy
description: The celestial sphere, the solar system, formation and decay of stars, instruments and basic laws of astronomy, nebulae, galactic structure, theories of the origin of the universe; constellation and telescope work.

title: Honors Colloquium in Physics
description: Exploration of selected topics in physics, with emphasis on individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students or with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The Teaching of Physics in the Secondary School
description: Aims, nature of the subject matter, calculus concepts, and applications in the teaching of physics, amount and nature of laboratory work, standardized tests, and textbooks used in the teaching of physics. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: 16 hours of credit in physics or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Thermodynamics
description: Laws of thermodynamics and introduction to the kinetic theory of gases. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Celestial Mechanics
description: An application of the laws of classical mechanics to objects under the influence of inversesquare gravitational forces, leading to the theory of orbits and perturbative effects on orbits. Prerequisite: PHYCS 330.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 1
description: Application of vector analysis to electrostatics, dipole and multipole fields, and dielectric theory. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122.

title: Electromagnetic Theory 2
description: Continuation of PHYCS 450 with emphasis on dynamic electrical problems, alternating currents, magnetic fields, and Maxwell's equations. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 450.

title: Elementary Particles
description: The nature and behavior of elementary particles through the study of the symmetries and dynamics responsible for their production, reactions, and decays. Prerequisite: PHYCS 465.

title: Nuclear Physics
description: Nucleus and nuclear interactions. Emphasizes experimental facts about nuclear processes in discussions of particle accelerators, detectors, radioactivity (alpha, beta, and gamma decay), interaction of radiation with matter, nuclear reactions, nuclear structure, nuclear models, and nuclear applications in science and technology. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 1
description: De Broglie's postulate, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the free particle, square well potentials, harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom, and other selected wave mechanics problems. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Quantum Mechanics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 464. Course material includes perturbation theory, oneelectron atoms, magnetic moments, spin, relativistic effects, symmetric and antisymmetric eigenfunctions, the helium atom, the Thomas-Fermi theory, the Hartree theory, and transition rates. Prerequisite: PHYCS 464.

title: Solid State Physics 1
description: An investigation of the structure and physical properties of matter in the solid state. No regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: PHYCS 260.

title: Solid State Physics 2
description: A continuation of PHYCS 466. Topics include the electrical and magnetic properties of solids and the band theory of solids with special emphasis on semiconductors. Examines the optical properties of solids and the effects of lattice defects. Prerequisite: PHYCS 466.

title: Practical Experience
description: Unpaid work and learning experience in applied or theoretical physics or astronomy in an institutional, industrial, or university research or development setting. May occur during one or more semesters. Prerequisite: approval of a proposed program by the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Studies in Physics
description: Pursuit of special lines of scientific investigation in physics on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Radiography 1
description: An overview of radiation physics to include properties of radiation, biological effects, xray production and interaction, and radiation protection. Prerequisite: MATHS 108; PHYCS 106.

title: Introduction to Radioactivity
description: Mechanisms and characteristics of nuclear decay and interaction of radiation with matter. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degr program with electives in nuclear medicieene.

title: Radiopharmaceuticals
description: Preparation, quality control, and the diagnostic and therapeutic application of radiopharmaceuticals in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 247.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation
description: Indepth study of the components and performance characteristics of equipment commonly used in the nuclear medicine clinic. Parallel: APHYS 252.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation Lab
description: A weekly laboratory for nuclear medicine technology students enrolled in APHYS 251.

title: Lasers and Applied Electro-Optic Techniques
description: Principles of laser operation, design, and safety considered within the context of the field of electrooptic techniques. Optical detection devices, photographic techniques, and laser applications stressed in the handson laboratoryoriented portion of the course. Prerequisite: PHYCS 112 or 122 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Fluid Mechanics
description: The forces and motions in fluids. Fluid characteristics and the basic theories of fluid statics and dynamics. Applications of solar energy systems, hydraulics, aerodynamics, meteorology, hydrology, and fluidics, environmental conditioning systems, and other subjects. Prerequisite: MATHS 162; PHYCS 330.

title: Applied Solar Energy 1
description: A study of physics and engineering facets of the solar energy resource, solar collection, concentration, thermal conversion, energy storage, and the design and performance of solar thermal energy systems. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and MATHS 172 or 162.

title: Applied Solar Energy 2
description: Physics and engineering of solar electric power generation with emphasis on properties of solar cells and design, operation, and performance of photovoltaic systems. Prerequisite: APHYS 420.

title: Heat Transfer
description: The basic heat transfer processes in nature. Conduction, convection, and radiation in applied problems using electricalmodelanalogue, graphical, and computerized numerical methods. Prerequisite: MATHS 162; PHYCS 122; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mysteries of the Sky
description: A nontechnical and nonmathematical multimedia excursion into the vast reaches of the sky including information about the sun, the moon, shooting stars, comets, supernovae, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, life on other planets.

title: Astronomy Materials for the Teacher
description: Fundamentals of astronomy including historical aspects and modern astronomy concepts. Emphasis is on construction of models and experimentation appropriate to the classroom. Designed primarily for students in education programs.

title: Observational Astronomy
description: Continuation of ASTRO 100 providing practical experience in observing celestial objects by using telescopes and other astronomical apparatus. Prerequisite: ASTRO 100 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: General Astronomy 1
description: Essential points of modern astronomy, emphasizing the underlying physical principles. Topics include coordinate systems in astronomy, orbital laws, relativity, planetary physics, measurement of stellar distances, and spectral classification of stars. Prerequisite: MATHS 108.

title: General Astronomy 2
description: A continuation of ASTRO 120. Topics include atomic structure and stellar spectra, stellar atmospheres and interiors, multiple star systems and clusters, galactic structure, cosmology, and the origin of the universe. Prerequisite: ASTRO 120.

title: Topics in Astronomy
description: Discussion of specific topics in astronomy, such as comets, eclipses, UFOs, and interstellar travel. Designed for students not majoring in physics, the course requires no math or science background. Students may consult their curricular advisors or the Department of Physics and Astronomy for specific topics being studied during a given semester. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 1
description: A review of mechanics, electromagnetic radiation, and atomic structure in the context of modern observational astrophysics. Solar system astrophysics— including an introduction to celestial mechanics and astronomical coordinate and time systems—are surveyed, and astronomical instruments are discussed. Prerequisite: PHYCS 120, 122.

title: Astronomy and Astrophysics 2
description: An examination of observational stellar astronomy with applications to the study of stellar structure and evolution, and a review of the physics of stellar systems such as star clusters, galaxies, and clusters of galaxies. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330.

title: Seminar in Modern Astronomy
description: Selected topics in contemporary astronomy. Extensive use of library facilities including current journals and periodicals in astronomy. Topics for study may include astronomical research in progress and such esoteric subjects as U.F.O.'s and extraterrestrial life. Prerequisite: PHYCS 122 and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Instruments and Techniques in Planetarium Operations
description: Use of planetarium instruments, console, and chamber. Creation and presentation of planetarium programs including slideduplicating techniques, slide opaquing, and the production of sound tracks. Prerequisite: permission of the planetarium director.

title: Theories and Instruments of the Astronomer
description: Reviews of various atlases, catalogs, ephemerides, and charts. The development of methods used to compute and update stellar positions. Discusses astronomical instruments in the context of their use by research astronomers. Analyzes specific techniques employed in astronomical photometry, spectroscopy, and photography. Prerequisite: ASTRO 332.

title: Advanced Astrophysics
description: A detailed investigation of the frontier areas of modern astrophysics. Possible topics include stellar structure, nucleosynthesis, stellar evolution, stellar atmospheres, and the interstellar material. Prerequisite: ASTRO 330, 332. Program emphases include allied health science (in cooperation with Methodist Hospital of Indiana, Inc., in Indianapolis), anatomy and physiology, community health education, public health, and school health education (leading to 7-12 certification and K-6 endorsements). In addition, the department houses the Public Health Entomology Laboratory. ASSOCIATE DEGREES These associate degree programs prepare students for careers in emergency medical services, nuclear medicine technology, radiography, and respiratory therapy. The first phase of the programs takes place on the Ball State campus, and the second phase is offered in Indianapolis, where medical, technical, and clinical courses are taught at Methodist Hospital of Indiana, Inc., and other affiliated medical centers. Students may apply for admission to the professional/clinical phases of the programs after completing a minimum of 15 required general education hours, including at least 6 hours of the required mathematics and/or sciences courses. Applicants for the clinical phase of any of the programs must have overall gradepoint averages of at least 2.5 on a scale of 4.0 as well as grades of C or higher for each of the science and mathematics courses. Acceptance to the clinical part of the programs is conditional upon satisfactory completion of the remaining courses.
