title: Introduction to Keyboarding/Word Processing
description: Principles of basic keyboarding and word processing skills needed for using computer keyboards and creating simple personal and business documents. Open to students with no prior typewriting/word processing credit. Permission of department chairperson required for those with more than one semester of keyboarding/word processing credit.

title: Keyboarding/Word Processing
description: Refinement of keyboarding and word processing skills with the development of speed and accuracy, using word processing software to prepare business letters, reports, and tables. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or one semester of keyboarding/word processing credit.

title: Computer-Based Document Production
description: Advanced word processing problems including reports, memoranda, letters, statistical tables, rough drafts, legal documents, and other business documents. Continued speed and accuracy development. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business Information Systems
description: Basic concepts of information processing systems with emphasis on computer skills for generating business information, including computing concepts and procedures in business, computer applications, text editing, file processing, and use of commercial software packages on mainframe computers and microprocessors. Prerequisite: MATHS 108. Open only to business majors except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: BASIC Programming for Microcomputers
description: Introductory course in BASIC programming using microcomputer hardware and problemoriented programdevelopment techniques to analyze, design, and code BASIC programs in a structured environment. Prerequisite: Typewriting or keyboarding ability. Not open to students who have credit in CS 116.

title: Shorthand 1
description: Basic symbolic theory fundamentals with emphasis on abbreviated forms. Introduction to skills in writing and transcribing dictation. Student placement is based on departmental advising. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or two semesters of high school or college keyboarding or typewriting.

title: Shorthand 2
description: Continued review of fundamentals; continued emphasis on taking dictation and developing transcription skills. hours EDSEC 205 EDPSY 250 or EDSEC 280 EDJHM 285 Prerequisite: BEOA 222 or student placement based on departmental advising and BEOA 113 or three semesters of high school or college keyboarding or typewriting.

title: Microcomputer Applications for Business
description: Operation of microcomputers in processing business applications using commercial software packages including systems, spreadsheet, database, and word processing. Prerequisite: typewriting or keyboarding ability.

title: Advanced Microcomputer Applications for Business
description: Advanced features of word processing, spreadsheets, and database, and graphics application software; operating system maintenance; and advanced operating system functions. Emphasizes file and document transfer among applications. Prerequisite: BEOA 225 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Applications for Administrative Information Technology
description: Enduser computing applications for administrative support: relationship to operating system/environment, utilities, and connectivity; projects involving graphic user interfaces and networked environments including advanced word processing (multiple packages), presentation graphics, and complex document production. Prerequisite: BEOA 225 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Machine Transcription
description: Computerbased production of documents from voice recordings. Application of English skills necessary to produce errorfree documents as well as the preparation and recording of business documents. Prerequisite or parallel: BEOA 112.

title: Transcription for Specialized Work Environments
description: Document production in specialized work environments such as legal, medical, education, insurance, science and technology, architecture, real estate, government, or engineering. Use of computer technology to complete preferred modules of study. Prerequisite: BEOA 230.

title: Principles of Business Correspondence
description: Principles and basic elements of effective letter writing with emphasis on the psychological approach, reader point of view, positive tone, and appropriate format for personal and business letters and job applications.

title: Personal Word Processing and Graphics
description: Designed to acquaint nonmajors with the word processing and graphics capabilities of microcomputers. Handson instruction in information processing and presentation graphics. Cannot be substituted for BEOA 251. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or high school typing credit. Not open to students who have credit in BEOA 251.

title: Introduction to Word and Information Processing
description: Focuses on understanding word processing concepts and how they fit into a total information processing system. Some handson experience with microcomputers. Prerequisite: BEOA 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Word and Information Processing Applications
description: Emphasizes advanced word and information processing applications, including merging, sorting, file management and transfer, macros, styles, graphics, and some desktop publishing. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or permission of the department chairperson and BEOA 250 or 251. May not be taken concurrently with BEOA 253.

title: Word and Information Processing Hardware and Software
description: Comparison and evaluation of features and capabilities of a variety of word and information processing software and systems. Handson experience included. Emphasizes problem analysis to meet the needs of varying workplace situations. Prerequisite: BEOA 112 or permission of the department chairperson and BEOA 250 or 251. May not be taken concurrently with BEOA 252.

title: Theory of Administrative Information Technology
description: Concepts of office information systems and organizational influences in changing technological environments. Develops competency to assess needs and evaluate, select, and set up hardware and software. Emphasizes contribution of information technology, ergonomics, and other human factors to office productivity. Prerequisite: BEOA 225 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Administrative Support Functions
description: Prepares administrative assistants for electronic offices by focusing on support functions. Integrates problem solving, interpersonal skills, and technology with other knowledge and skills necessary to operate and manage an efficient office. Prerequisite: BEOA 112; 241 or 441, and sophomore standing.

title: Office Technology Cooperative Education
description: Secretarial majors work in an office technology related position to integrate and expand upon theory learned in courses. Paid work and learning experience for students accepted into the cooperative education program. Related class attendance is required. Prerequisite: permission of the cooperative education coordinator or the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one

title: Internship in Marketing Education
description: Fulltime employment in an approved marketing occupation under departmental supervision according to a formal training agreement with the employer. Provides experience in areas in which marketing education teachers instruct. Each hour of credit requires 375 hours of approved employment and submission of various reports by the intern and employer. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to students seeking licenses as marketing education teachers. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teleprocessing and Office Information Systems
description: Integration of electronic office equipment interconnected through telecommunications including concepts of data communications, electronic mail, and networks. Some handson laboratory experience with communicating word processors, microcomputers, and networks. Prerequisite: BEOA 210 or 225 or 251 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Desktop Publishing for Business
description: Preparation of materials for desktop publishing combining word processing and graphics. Elements of desktop publishing including hardware, software, and design. Handson experience. Prerequisite: knowledge of word processing and keyboarding ability or permission of the department chairperson.

title: International Business Communication
description: Explores the communication problems that executives face while working in an international business culture. Emphasis is placed on sensitizing students to important intercultural issues that can facilitate or frustrate international business transactions. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Records Administration
description: Administration and supervision of office records systems; knowledge, techniques, and skills involved in planning, controlling, organizing, selecting, and retaining records in business and industry. Some handson laboratory experience with office automation software for records processing and database management. Prerequisite: sophomore standing and BEOA 210 or 225 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Computerized Multimedia for Business Applications
description: Theories and uses of microcomputerbased multimedia technologies for business presentation and communication problems. Hardware and software for producing multimedia presentations in a handson environment with emphasis on individual student interest and major. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Principles of Office Supervision
description: Principles of effective office supervision with emphasis on the function of the office and the role of the office supervisor. Prerequisite: MGT 200 or 300.

title: Internship in Office Systems Administration
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the business education and office administration department, students majoring in office systems administration will work in an office environment in a public or private organization. Written reports are required. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods of Teaching for the Marketing Education Teacher
description: The role of the marketing education teacher in the teaching of marketing, basic business, and bookkeeping/accounting subjects; courses to be taught and their objectives, teaching strategies, instructional materials, and lesson and unit planning. Prerequisite: ACC 201; ECON 201; EDPSY 251; and at least two courses in marketing. Open only to students majoring in marketing education.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Business Subjects
description: Objectives, planning, methods, techniques, and devices for teaching typewriting, basic business, office machines, and office procedures. Prerequisite: BEOA 112, 225. Open only to students pursuing a teaching curriculum.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Accounting
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, and devices for teaching accounting. Prerequisite: ACC 201 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Parallel: BEOA 490. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Shorthand and Transcription
description: Objectives, planning, methods, materials, and devices for teaching shorthand and transcription. Prerequisite: BEOA 112, 222; EDSEC 280; and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Parallel: BEOA 490.

title: Techniques of Coordinating Cooperative Marketing Education Programs
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and coordinating cooperative marketing education programs. Restricted to persons seeking licenses as teachers or coordinators of vocational marketing education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Organization, Management, and Teaching: Vocational Marketing Education
description: The special techniques and knowledge needed by a person who will be teaching and managing inschool laboratory programs in vocational marketing education. Restricted to students seeking licenses as teachers or coordinators of vocational marketing education. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Philosophy, Organization, and Administration of Vocational Education
description: The principles upon which vocational education is organized, administered, and supervised; federal and state regulations; agencies that provide delivery systems for vocational education, relationship of vocational education to career education, vocational rehabilitation, and programs for persons with special needs. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or 383 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Survey of the Vocational Education Program Areas
description: An overview of the six program areas in vocational education. Includes program administration and supervision, objectives, the occupations for which training is offered, curricula, equipment and facilities, student selection, inschool laboratories, fieldtraining opportunities, and youth organizations. Prerequisite: BEOA 382 or 383 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Microcomputers in Business Education
description: Handson approach to the use of microcomputers in the business education classroom; use of business software; analysis and design of programs for business education courses. Prerequisite: BEOA 112, 225. Open only to students pursuing teaching majors in business or marketing education or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Computerized Business Document Generation
description: An introduction to text editing capabilities of the computer for designing and processing business documents for the modern office. Development of an understanding of the use of the generalpurpose computer for text processing. Prerequisite: BEOA 210 or CS 116.

title: Communications for Business Organizations
description: Techniques used in managementoriented internal and external communications. Emphasis is on theory, planning, oral and written presentations, audience perceptions, data organization, media selection, and preparation techniques for business letters. Overview of reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Business Reports: Written and Oral
description: Techniques used in writing both formal and informal managementoriented reports, including collecting, interpreting, summarizing, and synthesizing data. Principles for selection of tabular and graphic data presentations. Includes written and oral presentations of functional reports with an overview of analytical reports. Prerequisite: sophomore standing.

title: Employment Communications
description: Determining job requirements and writing a letter of application and resume; letters requesting reference permission, expressing appreciation for an interview, acceptance or refusal of a position, and resignation. Includes interview techniques. Open to all students.

title: Office Information Systems Management
description: Implementation and management of integrated office information systems. Study of managerial problems involved with people, procedures, and technology. Prerequisite: MGT 300 or its equivalent; BEOA 210 or 225 or 251; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Office Management and Control
description: The management of the business office as a producing unit and the relation of the office routine to managerial control of the other departments of a business through records, reports, and budgets. Prerequisite recommended: ECON 202 and MGT 300.

title: Principles of Business Education
description: The analysis of a total business education program and the integration of various elements that lead to sound instruction. The effects of past, present, and future legislative and societal developments. Parallel: BEOA 385 or 386. Open only to students approved to pursue a business teaching curriculum.

title: Principles and Philosophy of Marketing Education
description: An investigation of the current status, historical development, philosophy, and principles of marketing education. Components include secondary, postsecondary, and adult marketing education, DECA, and general and specialized curricula. Prerequisite: EDSEC 280. Open only to students pursuing the teaching major in marketing education.

title: Independent Study: Business or Marketing Education; Office Administration
description: For students with excellent academic records who wish to conduct indepth studies in some phase of business education, marketing education, or office administration. The project selected, methods, and credit hours must be approved by the department chairperson and supervising faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. McClure, H. Moehring, N. Palomba, G. Santoni (George and Frances Ball Distinguished Professor of Economics), L. Spector, C. Stone, D. Yoho, A. Zegeye All persons and societies experience conflicts between unlimited desires for higher living standards and limited resources to satisfy these desires. Economics studies how such conflicts are resolved. Because most of our nation's social, political, and economic problems can be traced to these conflicts, a knowledge of economics is important, not only for intelligent citizenship, but also for careers in business, government, and the professions. The Department of Economics offers a major with either a business option or a liberal arts option. The business option is designed primarily for students planning to pursue professional careers in business. The liberal arts option is designed for students who want to pursue careers asprofessional economists. Students interested in attending law school will find that both options provide the necessary undergraduate preparation. The department also offers an interdepartmental major in mathematical economics. For information on this major, see Interdepartmental Programs, p. 49. Students may also select economics as a concentration area in either the teaching major or the teaching minor in social studies. A minor in economics is also available. title: Survey of Economic Ideas
description: The important conclusions of economics are surveyed and applied to topics chosen by the instructor. Especially valuable to students with no high school background in economics. Not applicable to a major or minor in economics. Not open to students who have credit in ECON 201 or 202.

title: Elementary Microeconomics
description: A study of why people specialize as producers and exchange what they produce with others. Includes analysis of how market structure affects prices. Discusses the issue of whether selfinterested economic behavior promotes or hinders society.

title: Elementary Macroeconomics
description: Survey of the major explanations for fluctuations in general business conditions. Focuses on how the private sector's economic behavior is affected by various governmental policies and institutions. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Business Statistics
description: Introduction to various statistical and probabilistic concepts and techniques with application to business problems including random variables and probability distributions, measures of central tendency and ispersion, testing of hypotheses, simple linear regression, and correlation. Prerequisite: MATHS 132 or its equivalent. Prerequisite recommended: BEOA 210. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 181.

title: Economic and Political Problems of Emerging Nations
description: A survey of historical and contemporary problems of the lessdeveloped nations. Conditions contributing to economic, political, and social change. Problems of economic development policies and programs within the institutional structure. Internal and external pressures that influence patterns of development. Not open to students who have credit in POLS 281.

title: Honors Colloquium in Economics
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 in one semester or term. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Intermediate Microeconomics
description: An investigation of the ways in which economic units direct resources into production. Involves analyses of product pricing, output determination, resource pricing, and employment in various market structures. Includes graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
description: Analyzes national income as a measure of economic activity. Emphasizes the determination of national income, employment, and price level and the rate of growth of the economic system. Includes examination of the theories of consumption and investment spending, interaction between money and national income, and implications of alternative models for public policy. Includes graphical and, in some instances, simple algebraic analyses. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Economic History of the United States
description: Survey of our commercial, financial, agricultural, and industrial history. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202, or a combination of ECON 201 and 3 hours of credit in United States history, or 6 hours of credit in United States history.

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmental problems. Emphasis is on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 6 hours of credit in natural resources, NR 101, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in NR 303.

title: Economic History of Europe
description: Origins and development of the European economy. Topics covered may vary, but general emphasis will be on Western European economic development, trade, industrialization, demographic change, and the interaction of these processes with the world. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202.

title: Labor Economics
description: Economic problems of the wage earner; growth, structure, and policies of labor organization; and the employer and governmental policies toward labor. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Labor Relations and Law
description: Study of collective bargaining, the joint determination by employers and employees (through their representatives) of the problems of the employment relationship—encompassing both the negotiation and administration of the labor agreement with primary emphasis upon the rules governing these processes. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: The Economics of Government Budgets
description: Analysis of economic theory behind alternative methods of financing government budgets and debt management. Emphasizes economic consequences of budgets by examining incidence, shifting, and incentives regarding provision of public services and alleviation of economic insecurity. Inflation as tax is considered. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Economic Analysis of Legal Issues
description: Applies microeconomic analysis to legal issues such as property rights, crime, contracts, and liability rules. Strengthens the ability to engage in economic reasoning by demonstrating its applicability to law and economics. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: International Economics
description: International trade, finance, and commercial policy. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Internship in Economics
description: Under a program approved and supervised by the Department of Economics, economics majors work fulltime for one semester as economics interns for private or public organizations. Periodic written reports of job experiences are required. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Credit is not applicable toward meeting the requirements of a major in economics. Open only to secondsemester junior and senior economics majors.

title: Industrial Organization
description: Monopolistic, oligopolistic, and competitive market structures. Unsettled issues concerning structure and conduct of industry; concentration, vertical integration, and problems of economic regulation by government. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Economic Growth
description: An analysis of the causes, mechanisms, and patterns of economic growth. Compares and analyzes growth rates of various countries. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: History of Economic Doctrines
description: The history of how humankind has looked at its economic life, surveys the changing ways economists have rationalized, articulated, and criticized economic organization from biblical times to the present. The successive reformulations place a major emphasis on the economic doctrines of the recent past and the present. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Mathematical Economics
description: Use of mathematics in the development of selected economic theories. Survey of inputoutput analysis and examination of the application of linear programming and Finance 133 the theory of games to selected economic problems. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202; and MATHS 132 or its equivalent.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
description: Quantitative methods in economic research. Emphasis is on constructing economic models and testing their predictive power. Topics include correlation and regression techniques and the specific problems that arise in applying these to economic data. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202, 221; MATHS 132 or its equivalent.

title: The Theory of Monetary Policy
description: A theoretical presentation of how the board of governors of the Federal Reserve System modifies the economic climate within which the institutions of the nation operate and of the problems of government finance as they relate to the board's goal of general economic stability. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Comparative Economic Systems
description: Historical and comparative study of economic theories and systems. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 202.

title: Urban Economics
description: The systematic economic structure of cities and the component parts of that structure. Attention is given to the ways in which the economic structure of cities and regions obstructs or facilitates the attainment of the goals of the community. Prerequisite: ECON 201.

title: Readings and Directed Study in Economics
description: Students will pursue their interests in specialized economics subjects under the direction of a member of the economics staff. Subjects studied will differ from or be studied in greater depth than subjects treated in other economics courses. Prerequisite: 6 hours of credit in economics. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Economics
description: Topics center on economic problems and issues of special interest to students and instructor. Permits indepth studies of topics not formally treated in other courses, thereby exposing interested students to a wider variety of economic problemsolving situations. Prerequisite: ECON 201, 202, and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in one semester or term. DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE K. Mantripragada, Chairperson; H. Banerjee, M. Baur, 0. Benkato, A. Caslan, C. Creviston, M. Engber, J. Fitzgerald, R. Groeber, H. Hammer, J. Hoban, P. Howard, R. Rathinasamy, S. Sundaram, L. Sweeney, G. Wells, T. Zivney (Maxon Distinguished Professor of Finance) Finance is the study of the creation and management of wealth. Finance is especially concerned with the study of raising funds, deploying funds, and managing liquidity in order to achieve a set of objectives for persons or businesses. A finance major will have a clear understanding of the role and the valuation of risky assets. The curriculum for finance majors is designed to give them an understanding of market mechanisms and how these mechanisms may be applied to intraorganizational decisions. The student will gain the analytical and quantitative skills to allocate scarce financial resources to achieve personal and organizational goals. A student of finance is prepared for a career specializing in financial functions and also for generalized management roles in organizations. The basic goals of the finance curriculum are to prepare students to understand the role of financial assets, markets, institutions, and regulation in the framework of U.S. and global financial systems; to have a good working knowledge of the quantitative and analytical techniques of finance as applied to corporate finance, investment management, and management Complete one option Corporate financial management option, 12 hours

title: Principles of Business Law
description: The nature, role, and historical development of the law and the structure and operation of our legal system. The essential elements of tort and contract law and the effect of the law in consumer credit and economic relationships. Prerequisite: sophomore standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: International Business Law
description: Examines legal problems that arise when multinational corporations conduct commercial activity in environments different in history, culture, economy, and politics from domestic markets. Topics include treaties, constitutional law, anti- 36 hours Finance 135 trust, contract negotiation and drafting, civil procedure, and dispute resolution. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: The Law of Business Associations
description: The principles of business law applicable to agencies including employer and employee rights and obligations, partnerships including limited partnership, corporations including fiduciary obligations of directors, security regulations, bankruptcy, and corporate reorganization in bankruptcy. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Uniform Commercial Code Law
description: Principal articles of the code including sales, commercial paper, and security interests, in addition to creditors' rights and property law. Includes state and federal consumer protection laws as they affect commercial law. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Law for Small Business
description: Analysis of the laws affecting small businesses. Emphasis is on the legal aspects and legal implications of formation of a business, employeremployee relationships, consumer protection laws, creditor rights, and closing the business. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Estate Planning and Administration
description: An introduction to problems associated with planning of financial resources during working life, retirement, and after the death of the principal income producer. Included are techniques for fact gathering, tax principles, use of trusts, and will drafting. Prerequisite: BL 260.

title: Current Topics in Business Law
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced business students for study of current topics and problems in business law. Topics may include current activity in property law, commercial law, and government regulation of business. Prerequisite: BL 260 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairperson. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the consumer's point of view. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation. Not open to juniors and seniors majoring in business.

title: Introduction to the U.S. Financial System
description: U.S. financial system and its functions; financial markets, instruments, and intermediaries; growing role of intermediaries in the saving and lending process and implications; regulation, regulatory agencies, and financial safety net; competition, innovation, and integration in financial services industry; globalization and international competition. Prerequisite: ACC 201; ECON 202.

title: Introduction to Financial Investments
description: Topics include financial markets and investment alternatives such as stocks, bonds, convertible securities, mutual funds, options, and futures. Market indexes (Dow Jones, etc.), market practices and timing, sources of financial data, and investing in an international environment will be discussed. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3 -6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Designed to study different areas of financial decision making in a business firm. Specific topics include financial objectives of the firm, sources of funds, working capital management, capital budgeting, investment decisions under uncertainty, valuation, capital structure decisions, and dividend policy. Prerequisite: ACC 202; ECON 201, 221; and junior standing.

title: Intermediate Financial Management
description: Devoted to the study of the current theory of finance. Topics include the nature and methodology of finance, efficient market hypothesis, portfolio theory and market equilibrium, optimal investment and financing decisions under certainty and uncertainty. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Designed to introduce students to areas of investment: securities markets, transaction of stocks and bonds, valuation and timing, fundamental and technical indicators, money markets, and funds. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Financial Markets and the Economy
description: Nature and functions of financial markets; classification and interrelation of domestic and international financial markets; determination of the level and structure of interest rates; effects of monetary policy on financial markets and the economy. Prerequisite: FIN 250, 350.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program with a banking institution, business firm, or government agency for pay under the supervision of the finance department. Requires periodic written reports of job experience. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned in combination with FIN 481.

title: International Finance
description: The financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance, import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some. Prerequisite: FIN 350 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Theory
description: An indepth analysis of valuation theory, capital market theory, and portfolio theory. Prerequisite: FIN 350, 355.

title: Managerial Decision Making in Finance
description: A summary course devoted to the compilation of knowledge and the application of financial analysis to decision making in various subareas of finance. The course is conducted by means of case studies. Prerequisite: FIN 354.

title: Operations of Financial Institutions
description: To integrate the various topics of finance with a view toward applications to the management of financial institutions in the following decision areas: assetliability management, cost control, profitability, capital adequacy, business development. Cases will be integrated in the method of instruction. Prerequisite: FIN 354, 355, 356.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who want to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, researching, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major kinds of insurance such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Internship in Insurance
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program in the insurance industry or government agency for pay under the supervision of the finance department. Requires periodic written reports of job experience. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamentals of Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 270.

title: Fundamentals of Liability Insurance
description: The study of liability insurance and worker's compensation insurance with special emphasis on the insurance needs of the commercial enterprise. Prerequisite: INS 270.

title: Fundamentals of Property Insurance
description: The study of property insurance, including fire and allied lines, inland and ocean marine, and crime insurance with special emphasis on the insurance needs of the commercial enterprise. Prerequisite: INS 270.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 260 and INS 270.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include nofault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, and state versus federal regulations. Prerequisite: INS 270, 371, 375, and 376 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Insurance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who want to study some phase of insurance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various insurance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Real Estate Principles
description: Economic import of real estate, real estate characteristics, landuse and environmental controls, legal aspects of real estate, methods of valuation, mortgage credit sources, secondary mortgage markets and financing techniques, investment analysis, land development, and real estate operations.

title: Real Estate Finance
description: The contractual nature and legal implications of the instruments used in real estate finance; instruments, techniques, and strategies in the financing of real estate investment; and the structure and operation of both primary and secondary mortgage markets. Gives students a background in real estate law and real estate finance. Prerequisite: RE 230.

title: Legal Aspects of Real Estate

title: Independent Study in Real Estate
description: Designed for the academically qualified who wish to study some phase of real estate. Intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analysis of various real estate topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Naffziger, R. Ramnarayanan, R. Ravichandran, B. Smith, E. Tunc, J. Walters In modern organizations, there is a need for competent managers who can address emerging issues in a global economy. Dealing with environmental complexity, technology, employee productivity, international competition, and ethical issues is increasingly important in the managerial decision process. Programs leading to a bachelor of science degree in management are designed to give students the knowledge and skills in the latest concepts, tools, and techniques applicable to entrepreneurship and small business, human resources management, management information systems, production and operations management, and general management. Students can elect to specialize in one of the following five options: The production and operations management option prepares students to assume positions of responsibility in the production of goods and services. Students are introduced to the production functions in detail, are taught the methodology of making productionrelated decisions, and become acquainted with modern techniques used in motivating and leading personnel in a productionoriented occupation. The human resources management option prepares students to improve the effectiveness of employees in organizations. Students study the personnel function and learn the conceptual framework for analyzing and solving problems in the selection, development, compensation, and motivation of human resources. The management information systems option introduces students to the concepts and techniques necessary to use information in the support of operations, control, and planning in organizations. Graduates of this option are familiar with the concepts and techniques of computerized information systems. The entrepreneurship and small business option is designed to give students the knowledge needed to work in a new venture environment. Students learn how to formulate a plan for an entrepreneurial venture and how to implement that plan in small and new businesses. Students also have the opportunity to assist small firms as consultants in team practicums. The general management option acquaints students with the whole gamut of management: production, personnel, management information systems, and other management topics. title: Introductory Operations Management

title: Personnel and Supervision
description: Introduction to the personnel and supervisory functions in organizations. title: Principles of Management
description: Explores management principles, theories, and practices. title: International Management
description: Discussion of management issues related to doing business in an international context, including moving a firm into international competition, and some issues that may be expected. title: Job Search and Transition
description: Prepares students for moving from college to careers. Topics covered include defining career goals, writing resumes, jobsearch correspondence, interviewing, and initial adjustments in the first job position. Open to juniors and seniors in all majors.

title: Information System Concepts and Techniques
description: Introduction to various concepts and techniques of information systems with application to solving managerial problems. Topics covered include information flows, application of computerbased information systems, managerial decision making, and mutual influence of organizations and information systems. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; MGT 300.

title: Quantitative Business Analysis
description: Exploration and application of selected quantitative techniques to business problems. Topics covered include regression and correlation, analysis of variance and contingency tables, decision analysis, linear programming, and networkbased management techniques. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221.

title: Operations Research
description: Basic operations research concepts and techniques for managerial decisions including linear programming, network problems, decision analysis, and computer implementation of these models to solve practical problems. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; MATHS 132.

title: Small Business Venture

title: Entrepreneurship
description: Development and management of an entrepreneurial organization including prestartup, startup, survival, growth, and the transition from entrepreneurial to professional management. Explains the function of entrepreneurship and corporate entrepreneurship. Prerequisite: MGT 341.

title: Introductory Production Management
description: Various functional fields of production and operations management including product analysis, work design and measurement, forecasting, production planning, scheduling and inventory control, facility location and layout, material handling, plant safety and maintenance, and quality control. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; MGT 300.

title: Production Management in Service Sector
description: Various techniques for the design, operation, and control of service operations including service design and process selection, facility location and layout determination, staffing, equipment selection and operations, and scheduling of service operations. Prerequisite: MGT 351.

title: Managing Human Resources
description: Administration of personnel programs in business organizations so as to deal effectively with such problems as selection, training, compensation, promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions; employee services; and industrial relations. Prerequisite: MGT 300.

title: Management Science Internship
description: Job experience (paid) in an organization with an approved innovative management program. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours may be earned including MGT 399.

title: Organizational Behavior
description: Dynamics of human behavior in business organizations with emphasis on problems of motivation and leadership. Examines the behavior of individuals and groups within organizations and the practical interpretation and management of behavioral phenomena. Prerequisite: MGT 300.

title: Business and Society
description: The interrelationships between business and its external environment and the multiple and complex ways business organizations are affected by governmental and societal expectations. Emphasizes contemporary issues through discussions and case analysis. Prerequisite: MGT 300.

title: Honors Colloquium: Readings in Contemporary Business
description: Seminar involving study of contemporary business literature. Interdisciplinary approach, comparing and contrasting ideas, deriving common themes, and drawing links to theory embodied in readings. title: Management Science Practicum
description: Professional practice (unpaid) in an organization with an approved innovative management program. title: Problems in General Management

title: Business Systems Analysis and Design
description: Various systems analysis and design concepts and techniques, including the key steps in the systemsdesign and development cycle. Emphasizes the consideration of practical applications within the business environment. Prerequisite: MGT 311 and proficiency in a programming language.

title: Database: Structures and Management
description: Logical and physical organization of data. Data description, command, and interrogation languages. Examines function of databases in information systems. Prerequisite: MGT 311 and proficiency in a programming language.

title: Information Systems of Small Business
description: Computerbased information systems in small business operations without access to an internal specialist. Includes the identification of information requirements and the use of mainframe and microcomputers and purchased software to satisfy the information needs in small business. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; MGT 341.

title: Information Systems Management
description: Equipment selection, equipment acquisition, computer operations management, project management, computer personnel management, financial control, systems security and control, and the relationship of the information systems function to an organization. title: Business Data Communications
description: Concepts and problem of transmitting, communicating, and managing business data needs through the use of computerbased telecommunication systems. Includes applications of integrated and distributed systems to problems in various functional areas of business. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; MGT 311; and proficiency in COBOL programming.

title: Problems in Information Systems
description: An integration of various information systems principles, theories, and techniques for implementing information systems in organizations, including strategic issues. Includes lectures, tours, readings, cases, and the completion of a major individual project. Prerequisite: MGT 351, 412, 415, 417, and completion of all management core courses.

title: Systems Simulation
description: Concepts and techniques of system modeling and simulation using computers. Includes computer simulation languages, statistical aspects of simulation, and application of computer simulation to various practical business situations in manufacturing and service sectors. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; MGT 351.

title: Small Business Practicum
description: Teams of students consult with local small businesses recommended by the Small Business Development Center. Students work on problems in such areas as accounting, production, marketing, personnel, finance, insurance, law, or information systems. Prerequisite: MGT 346.

title: Operations Planning and Inventory Management
description: Operations planning and inventory management in manufacturing and service industries, including capacity planning, resourcerequirements planning, productionactivity control, and related management models and systems. Prerequisite: MGT 321, 351.

title: Quality Assurance

title: Compensation Administration
description: Reviews basic compensation issues including internal, external, and individual equity, as well as benefits administration. Emphasis on design and implementation of compensation systems. Prerequisite: MGT 361.

title: Personnel Planning and Selection
description: Focuses on organization and humanpower planning, including determination of organization and humanpower needs, analysis and development of job requirements, and necessary qualifications for recruitment and selection procedures, placement and orientation, and evaluation of selection programs. title: Problems in Personnel Administration
description: An integration of various principles, theories, and techniques for solving realistic and complex personnel administration problems in public and private organizations. Includes lectures, tours, readings, cases, and the completion of a major individual project. Prerequisite: MGT 351, 461, 465, and completion of all management core courses.

title: Business Policy and Strategic Management
description: Integration of various functional areas of business. Development and administration of strategy and policy in private and public sector organizations. Case studies focus on strategic decisions that enable an organization to relate effectively to its industrial, national, and international environments. Normally taken during the last semester of a student's program. Prerequisite: senior standing; FIN 350; MGT 300; and MKG 300.

title: Marketing Channel Management
description: Study of marketing channels as economic, political, and social systems. includes retailing, wholesaling, and other channel intermediaries. title: Promotion Management
description: Uses cases and problems to give experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKG 320.

title: Sales Management
description: Policies and practices in organizing, recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and 325 or permission of the department chairperson.

description: Advanced course in retailing management using case studies and special projects to examine current topics and problems in retailing. Prerequisite: MKG 330.

title: International Marketing

description: Advanced examination of such current marketing topics as marketing theory and quantitative, service, nonprofit, bank, comparative, and international marketing. title: Independent Study in Marketing

Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson, marketing major, and MKG 300. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned toward major requirements in combination with MKG 367, 369, and 498, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Practicum in the Consumer Education Council
description: Practical experience in mediating businessconsumer problems. Students use personnel skills in organizing and administering a Consumer Education Council. description: Studio exploration of the integration of twodimensional graphics with spatial environments. Emphasis is on conceptual spatial analysis and human activity. Prerequisite: ADS 242 and admission through successful portfolio review. Open only to art majors.

title: Three-Dimensional Communication Design 2
description: Investigation of structures, materials, and lighting as determinants of threedimensional communication issues. Emphasis is on threedimensional model construction. Prerequisite: ADS 324. Open only to art majors.

title: Photography 2
description: Emphasis is on the further exploration of photographic vision, technical and aesthetic concerns of photography, and further study of photo history; introduction to advertising photography. Prerequisite: ADS 231. Open only to art majors.

title: Advanced Color Photography
description: Focus on ideas and assigned problems expressed through color photography. Basic knowledge of processing color film and color prints is necessary. Prerequisite: ADS 332, 336 or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to art majors.

title: Graphic Design 1
description: Exploration of creative thematic development and its relation to the final stages of the design process. Technical elements of type specification and indication and graphicdesign production are considered. Prerequisite: ADS 242 and admission to the graphicdesign sequence through portfolio review. Open only to art majors.

title: Graphic Design 2
description: Concentrated involvement in problem analysis with emphasis on symbology and image development. Prerequisite: ADS 341. Open only to art majors.

title: Independent Study in Design
description: Designed for professionally oriented students, allowing them to select and explore more intensively a special area. Prerequisite: sponsorship by an art faculty member and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Three-Dimensional Communication Design 3
description: Creative integration of conceptual spatial issues, graphic communication, and threedimensional environments. Topics include environmental graphics, exhibition design, and museum environments. Prerequisite: ADS 330. Open only to art majors.

title: Photography 3
description: Major emphasis on students' personal statements in color and blackandwhite photography through selection of their own projects under the guidance of an instructor. Students furnish their own light meters and cameras with adjustable aperture, time setting, and focusing. Prerequisite: ADS 332 for art majors.

title: Photography 4
description: A further intensification of students' personal statements. Students will be given occasional assignments to introduce new and varied directions in art. Students furnish their own light meters and cameras with adjustable aperture, time setting, and focusing. Prerequisite: ADS 433.

title: Video as Art
description: Through the technology of video, an exploration of the potential of this immediate and temporal medium. Contemporary applications of video and its social and artistic relevance will be addressed. Prerequisite: ADS 332; AHS 264 except for photography majors; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Three-Dimensional Communication Design 4
description: Advanced design problem research stressing the interaction of creative threedimensional communication design within the constraints of the design profession. Professional portfolio preparation is emphasized. Prerequisite: ADS 426. Parallel: ADS 480. Open only to art majors.

title: Graphic Design 3
description: Advanced problem solving in sequential and threedimensional forms. Prerequisite: ADS 342. Open only to art majors.

title: Graphic Design 4
description: Advanced problem solving in graphic design. Refinement of presentation techniques and résumé and portfolio development. Prerequisite: ADS 441. Open only to art majors.

title: Graphic Design Topic Studio
description: Intensive studio exploration of strategies and visual development within specific graphic design areas. Could include computer, letterpress, publications, exhibition and signage, package design, or development of concept and content. Prerequisite: ADS 341 or 324. Open only to art majors. A total of 9 hours of credit maybe earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Graphic Design Practicum
description: Problem solving within and outside the university community. Group and individual projects for nonprofit clients. Requires portfolio review and permission of the instructor. Prerequisite: ADS 341. Open only to art majors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Senior Design Thesis
description: Intensive study with research and resolution of a current problem in twoor threedimensional design. Thesis must be arranged with a design faculty advisor. Prerequisite: ADS 426 or 441. Parallel: ADS 436, 442. Open only to graphic design and environmental/exhibition design majors.

title: Seminar in Design
description: Group or individual investigation and experiences in the fine arts beyond the scope of regular course work. Prerequisite: completion of 30 hours of credit in art or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned. ART: EDUCATION (AED)

title: Understanding Art
description: Introduction to the basic studio processes of drawing, painting, printmaking, and sculpture. Lecture and studio experiences related to the understanding of the elements and principles of art and methods of art criticism. Not open to art majors.

title: Introduction to Art Education
description: Introduction to art education as a teaching profession. Emphasizes investigating artistic growth of normal and special populations and the materials, techniques, tools, art concepts, and strategies appropriate for teaching art to such students. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 202. Open only to art majors.

title: Art in the Elementary School
description: Designed to acquaint students with current teachinglearning strategies in art education. Stresses the developmental stages of artistic growth, curriculum planning, evaluation, aesthetic awareness, and craft media and techniques. Prerequisite: AED 200. Not open to art majors.

title: Art Curriculum and Instruction
description: Designed to develop art students' abilities to make artcurricular judgments by developing artcurriculum plans and designing art experiences. Prerequisite: AED 201 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Art Teaching and Learning Practicum
description: Direct experience in planning, implementing, and evaluating teaching strategies. Includes observation of students participating in an artrelated environment. Laboratory teaching time is arranged. Prerequisite: AED 304 for majors; permission of the department chairperson for minors.

title: Classroom Use of Methods and Materials: Art
description: A study of classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in teaching art, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of art in the secondary public school curriculum. Topics will be developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: AED 305 and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum for majors; permission of the department chairperson for minors. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Independent Study in Art Education
description: Permits professionally oriented art students to select and explore more intensively an area of art education. Prerequisite: sponsorship of an art faculty member and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students with areas in art. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Art Education
description: Group or individual investigation and experience in the various ideas, methods, and research in art education. Prerequisite: completion of 30 hours of credit in art and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to students with areas in art. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned. ART: FINE ARTS (AFA)

title: Drawing 1
description: Introduction to drawing: the application of basic principles and elements of art as they relate to drawing concepts. Emphasis will be on the development of perceptual awareness and familiarity with a broad range of media and techniques. Parallel recommended: ADS 101.

title: Drawing 2
description: Life drawing. Intensive study of the human figure. Descriptive, expressive, and interpretive methods of imaging the figure are explored, and a variety of materials and techniques are introduced. Prerequisite: AFA 101. Parallel: ADS 102. Open only to art majors.

title: Painting 1
description: Introduction to painting: study of basic considerations of image making with oil paint. Focuses on media, techniques, design elements, and concepts. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 202. Open only to art majors.

title: Painting 2
description: Explorations in painting designed to build on initial experiences by studio practice and through slidelectures on contemporary painting. Prerequisite: AFA 211.

title: Watercolor 1
description: Exploration of materials and techniques of transparent watercolor as they apply to the solution of painting problems. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 202. Open only to art majors.

title: Watercolor 2
description: Continued exploration of painting problems in watercolor with emphasis on the unique character of the medium. Prerequisite: AFA 217.

title: Sculpture 1
description: Requires research exploring sculptors or sculptural movements to inspire objects made for formal criticism. The basic skills and materials (plaster, wood, metal, clay, fabric, etc.) associated with additive, subtractive, and substitution techniques will be demonstrated. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 202. Open only to art majors or minors.

title: Sculpture 2
description: Continued exploration of materials used in formal sculpture; welded and forged metal, wood construction and carving, stone carving, clay, wax, and plastic. Prerequisite: AFA 221. Open only to art majors.

title: Introduction to Printmaking
description: Beginning printmaking techniques with an emphasis on intaglio and relief processes. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 202. Open only to art majors.

title: Relief Printmaking
description: Fundamental procedures of relief printing from the woodblock and other surfaces with emphasis on the use of color and new approaches. Students are expected to develop images that have a relationship to this print medium. Prerequisite: AFA 231. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Intaglio Printmaking 1
description: Intermediatelevel printmaking dealing with basic intaglio techniques. Emphasis is on student's ability to deal creatively and conceptually with the technical process. Prerequisite: AFA 231.

title: Drawing 3
description: Analytical and descriptive aspects of drawing are explored. Emphasizes thematic and conceptual development and encourages experimentation with a broad range of techniques and materials. Prerequisite: ADS 102; AFA 202. Open only to art majors.

title: Drawing 4
description: Drawing experiences exploring varied materials and concepts related to drawing as a personal visual statement. Prerequisite: AFA 303.

title: Painting 3
description: Individualized instruction aimed at the continued mastery of technical skills and progress toward the solution of pictorial and conceptual problems. Prerequisite: AFA 212. Open only to art majors.

title: Painting 4
description: Continued interest in the development of technical skills and the solution of pictorial problems with new emphasis on individual creative solutions. Prerequisite: AFA 313.

title: Painting 5
description: Emphasis is on advancing from technical proficiency toward the development of individual conceptual goals relating to painting. Prerequisite: AFA 314.

title: Water Media
description: Advanced study in water media on paper to expand painting skills while narrowing the search for personally significant imagery. Prerequisite: AFA 218. Open only to art majors. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Sculpture 3
description: Introduction to and emphasis on the basic techniques and concepts of mold making and casting aluminum, bronze, and plastics. Prerequisite: AFA 222. Open only to art majors.

title: Sculpture 4
description: Introduction to sculptural alternatives and nontraditional sculptural materials; visual and audio aids, performance, and antiart. Prerequisite: AFA 323. Open only to art majors.

title: Sculpture: Casting and Mold Making
description: Continuation of AFA 323. Advanced casting and mold making procedures. Individual development of the concepts and techniques associated with the casting process. Prerequisite: AFA 323. Open only to art majors.

title: Intaglio Printmaking 2
description: Advanced printmaking dealing with basic intaglio techniques including line etching, drypoint, engraving, softground, and aquatint. Openended problem solving and indepth study with emphasis on students' abilities to deal creatively and conceptually with the technical process. Prerequisite: AFA 243.

title: Lithography 1
description: Fundamental processes of drawing and printing lithographs using stones and aluminum plates. Drawing and painting techniques are used to develop images. Prerequisite: AFA 231.

title: Lithography 2
description: Further development and investigation of the processes of lithography, including color. Exploration of stone and metal plate techniques. Prerequisite: AFA 351.

title: Lithography 3
description: Investigation of additional drawing and painting techniques as they relate to lithography. Further development of printing skills and the lithographic image. Prerequisite: AFA 352. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Serigraphy
description: Introductory printmaking dealing with the processes of serigraphy, including the four basic stencil techniques and their variation. Silkscreen as a fine art form. Prerequisite: AFA 231. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term. Open only to art majors.

title: Sculpture 5
description: Individual instruction and supervision of experimentation in nontraditional materials. Prerequisite: AFA 324. Open only to art majors.

title: Drawing 5
description: Continuation of the drawing experience for advanced students developing further expertise in drawing skills while encouraging research into and experimentation with more personal imagery. Prerequisite: AFA 304.

title: Drawing 6
description: Advanced drawing, stressing individual problem solving with greater expectations of proficiency in each successive course. Prerequisite: AFA 405. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent Study in Fine Arts
description: Designed for professionally oriented students, allowing them to select and explore more intensively a special topic. Prerequisite: sponsorship by an art faculty member and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Painting 6
description: Individualized instruction, continuing the emphasis on student identification and development of personal concepts in painting. Prerequisite: AFA 315.

title: Advanced Problems in Sculpture
description: Designed for students who want to extend their technical understanding and aesthetic development beyond the fundamental level. Prerequisite: AFA 325 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Intaglio Printmaking 3
description: Advanced printmaking emphasizing aesthetic decision making involving the intaglio process through the knowledge of technique and use of personal artistic choices. Prerequisite: AFA 344. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Senior Project in Drawing
description: Synthesis and culmination of undergraduate studio experiences in drawing, with a student exhibition as the concluding effort. Prerequisite: 18 credit hours in drawing, sponsorship by an art faculty member, and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to art majors.

title: Senior Project in Painting
description: Synthesis and culmination of undergraduate studio experiences in painting, with a student exhibition and supporting written composition as the concluding effort. Prerequisite: AFA 416, 18 credit hours in painting, sponsorship by an art faculty member, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Senior Project in Sculpture
description: A synthesis and culmination of undergraduate studio experiences in sculpture, with a student exhibition as the concluding effort. Prerequisite: 21 credit hours in sculpture, sponsorship by a sculpture faculty member, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Senior Project in Printmaking
description: Synthesis and culmination of undergraduate studio experience in printmaking, with a student exhibition as the concluding effort. Prerequisite: 27 credit hours in printmaking, sponsorship by a printmaking faculty member, and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to art majors.

title: Seminar in Fine Arts
description: Individual investigation and experience in the fine arts. Prerequisite: completion of 30 hours of credit in art and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Art
description: A General Studies course that, through a survey of art and artifacts from ancient through modern times and the historical and social elements that helped to shape them, offers an introduction to the understanding and appreciation of painting, sculpture, and architecture. Open only to students not majoring in art.

title: History of Art Survey 1
description: Introduction to art and architecture as social products of a global human history. Both the comparability and diversity of human social organizations and the role of visual culture in them will be discussed. Prehistoric through the end of European Middle Ages.

title: History of Art Survey 2
description: Introduction to art and architecture as social products of a global human history. Both the comparability and diversity of human social organizations and the role of visual culture in them will be discussed. From the fifteenth century to the present.

title: History of Three -Dimensional Design
description: Interdisciplinary study of threedimensional design and function as applied to graphic design, exhibition design, architecture, and industrial design from the eighteenth century to the present with an emphasis on American and European design. Prerequisite: sophomore standing. Open only to art majors.

title: Art in the United States 1
description: Investigation of the role visual culture has played in the United States as Americans attempted to situate themselves geographically, culturally, economically, and politically within their own society and within the world at large from ca. 1600 to ca. 1876. Open to all students.

title: Art in the United States 2
description: Traces the evolution in the United States of American visual arts from ca. 1876 to 1945 within the context of important social, historical, and intellectual events. Open to all students.

title: Art of the Early Civilizations
description: Art and architecture of cultures of the ancient Near East and Egypt. Use of archeological data, visual evidence, and literary records to reconstruct built environments. Special emphasis is given to the cultural significance of monumental architecture, sculpture, painting, and diverse minor arts. Open to all students.

title: Art of the Aegean and the Greeks
description: Bronze Age through the Hellenistic period, covering architecture, pottery, painting, sculpture, minor arts, and the interrelationships of the Aegean Islands and Greek mainland. Archeological data are discussed in terms of revelations about the areas' artistic and cultural development. Open to all students.

title: Art of Rome
description: Art and architecture of early Rome and the Republic to the Late Empire. Architecture and urbanism as vehicles for the political and cultural extension of the empire to the barbarian West and the Hellenized East; missionary role of historic reliefs; Roman concepts of personality and portraiture; and the growth of luxury arts: ornament, interior decoration, and collecting.

title: Early Medieval Art
description: Painting, sculpture, and architecture from the fourth through the tenth centuries in relation to the religious, political, and technological conditions of the period. Rural northwest Europe will be discussed in relation to urban societies in the East. Periods to be covered include early Christian, Merovingian, Carolingian, Ottonian, and Byzantine. Open to all students.

title: Late Medieval Art
description: European art and architecture from the eleventh through the fourteenth centuries. Competing claims of royal and religious sponsors; shifts in the center of production from rural to urban markets, monasteries to bishops' towns, in a period of economic advance, political transformation, and social unrest. Open to all students.

title: Northern European Art 1300-1600
description: Northern European Renaissance art as a specifically northern mode of expression and representation reflecting social, political, religious, and other cultural particularities of specific areas (France, Germany, and southern and northern Netherlands).

title: Art of the Italian Renaissance 1300-1600
description: Art and architecture examined in terms of style, cultural meaning, context, and ideology. Investigation of conditions of art production, change in role of artist, relationship between art theory and practice, and the question or concept of Renaissance.

title: Early Modern Europe 1: Art from 1600 to 1750
description: Exploration of art and architecture of Europe, from the Counter- Reformation shrine of St. Peter to Louis XIV's palace at Versailles; from the Jesuit altarpieces in Antwerp to the Dutch Republic of Vermeer and Rembrandt and more. Italy, Spain, France, Germany, England, Flanders, Netherlands. Open to all students.

title: Early Modern Europe 2: Art from 1750 to 1850
description: Art and architecture in the era of enlightenment and revolution, age of Napoleon, Restoration, reaction, reform, economic advance, and social unrest. From country gardens to urban boulevards, rococo, neoclassicism, romanticism, historicism, realism, and impressionism, England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain. Open to all students.

title: Modern Art
description: Pan-European investigation of the visual arts from French impressionism to the post-World War II abstract expressionists. Special emphasis is on cultural definitions of modernity and modernism and the appearance and ideologies of the avant garde. Open to all students.

title: Contemporary Art
description: Exploration of ideas and issues surrounding the production, reception, marketing, interpretation, and criticism of painting, sculpture, drawing, photography, installations, performance, and video and other mixed media since World War II. International in scope. Open to all students.

title: Film History and Criticism
description: Emphasizes the understanding of cinematic works through the analysis of styles and techniques employed by filmmakers. The historical evolution of these styles and techniques will be addressed, as well as social, cultural, and political influences. Open to all students.

title: History of Photography
description: Introduction to problems in theory, analysis, and history of photography. Study of institutional and discursive orders in which photography functions and produces meaning. Exploration of new forms of critical photographic practice. Open to all students.

title: History of Landscape Painting
description: Indepth survey of the major schools of landscape painting beginning with ancient Rome and continuing up to the present time. Political and economic conditions leading to the rebirth of landscape painting in the Renaissance will be discussed. Open to all students.

title: Special Topics in History of Art
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in art history with emphasis on those not covered in other courses (women in art, history of museums and collecting, problems in methodology, etc.). Exact content will be announced before each offering. Open to all students. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Special Topics in Graphic Design
description: Detailed analysis of graphic design from the late nineteenth century to the present, with emphasis on European and American design. Influential movements, artists, designers, and technology that shape current design thinking will be highlighted. Prerequisite: ADS 242, pass graphic design portfolio review, or the instructor's permission. Open only to art majors.

title: Special Topics in American Art
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American art with focus on subjects not emphasized in other courses. description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in ancient art with focus on subjects not emphasized in other courses. Exact content announced before each offering.
