title: Mass Media in Society
description: Study of mass media in their historical and societal contexts with emphasis on practitioner issues including ethics, state of the art, and future.

title: Communications Graphics
description: Theory of publication and visual communication emphasizing preparation of material for newspapers, magazines, and brochures. Lectures and projects focus on type selection, copy fitting, photo and illustration selection and use, pasteup skills, and printing processes. Includes one hour of lab each week. Open only to students enrolled in a journalism area.

title: Mass Media Writing and Editing 1
description: Theory and practice in writing and editing for journalistic media publications. Includes one hour of lab each week.

title: Mass Media Writing and Editing 2
description: Theory and practice in writing and editing journalistic visual/verbal relationships and analysis needed to train news editors. Introduces the concept of journalistic visual reporting, visual editing, and journalistic graphics technology. 36 hrs for journalistic media publications. Emphasis is on developing editing skills. Prerequisite: JOURN 210.

title: Editorial Presentation
description: Survey of Preparatory for journalism graphics sequence students. Prerequisite: JOURN 125 and enrollment in the journalism graphics prejournalism program. Recommended parallel: JOURN 211.

title: Introduction to Photojournalism
description: Emphasis is on preparing students to take, process, and caption photographs for newspapers, magazines, public relations, and advertising purposes. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies.

title: Photographic Lighting
description: An indepth study of photographic lightin procedures and equipment for studio g and field use by media photographers. Students must provide their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 230 or other basic photography class.

title: Introduction to Advertising
description: A survey of the advertising communication process. Focuses on communication research, creative strategy, campaign planning, function of mass media as carriers of advertising, and evaluation of advertising effectiveness.

title: Principles of Public Relations
description: Survey of the theory, philosophy, and function of public relations practices and programs in American institutions with special attention given to public relations in various fields.

title: Introduction to Newspaper Journalism
description: Analysis of daily and weekly newspapers. Examination of reporting and editing functions and orientations brought to the newswriting profession. Brief look at newspaper management principles and history of newspapers will be included.

title: Magazines in American Life
description: History and significance of magazines in American society. Examination of editorial, production, circulation, and advertising functions, as well as current market conditions and job opportunities. Special study of magazines in a field chosen from students' particular interests. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Journalism
description: History of journalism in the United States from colonial times to the present, presenting the press as an institution against the background of the history of the nation.

title: Feature, Column, and Opinion Writing
description: Researching and writing feature stories, columns, and editorials for newspapers and magazines. Discussion of feature, column, and editorial types and campaigns. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Magazine Article Writing
description: Theory and practice in preparing, writing, and marketing magazine articles. Includes a study of markets for magazine articles and exercises in various facets of writing for general and specialized magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to magazine sequence majors.

title: Sportswriting and Reporting
description: Study and practice in covering and writing about sports events and the people connected with them. Story assignments and research combined with classroom lectures and analysis of best sports stories provide students with skills to cover a wide range of sports activities. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Journalism Prose Styles
description: Writing and editing for students interested in publishing their work in newspapers, magazines, and public relations organizations. Emphasizes works of contemporary prose writers. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students or magazinesequence majors. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Journalism Law
description: Constitutional and statutory law and regulating agencies affecting the operations of the print and broadcast media with special attention given to recent Supreme Court rulings.

title: Magazine Editing and Production
description: Analysis of all facets of magazine publishing: editorial, advertising, circulation, and art. Designed for students interested in working for professional magazines. Prerequisite: JOURN 315. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Photojournalism
description: An extended study of the theory and practice of making photographs and using photography as communicative art. Students must have their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236. Not open to prejournalism students or magazinesequence majors. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Journalistic Visual Reporting
description: Examination of the facets of informational graphics and the job of the modernday graphics reporter. Experience gained in creating and researching explanatory charts, diagrams, maps, and graphics editing. Computers are an integral tool. Prerequisite: JOURN 225, 211. Not open to students in prejournalism. Open only to students with other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Media
description: Strategy and procedures for planning, executing, and controlling the placement of advertising. Examines characteristics of media, techniques of media budgeting and selection, and methods of evaluating media effectiveness. Prerequisite: JOURN 250. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Copy and Layout
description: Instruction in preparing copy for mass media advertising. Major emphasis is on creative thinking and basic writing skills. Students prepare copy strategies, write copy, prepare layouts and storyboards. Discussion of fundamentals of consumer motivation and selecting target audiences. Prerequisite: JOURN 250. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas and minors in campaign communication.

title: Public Relations Writing and Publicity Techniques
description: Theory and practice of producing publicity tools for various media used in campaigns to promote and interpret personal, institutional, and organizational objectives and activities. Emphasis is on writing and publicity problem solving. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 and 261. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Public Relations Publication Design and Production
description: Institutional and industrial publications as an important means of internal and external communications. Design and production techniques. Includes one hour of lab each week. Prerequisite: JOURN 225 or 360. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Journalism Internship
description: Onthejob training in which journalism or public relations students get practical experience in applying what they have learned in the classroom. Involves assigned duties in an offcampus communications organization with appropriate compensation. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson, JOURN 211, and required 300-level sequence courses. Not open to students who have credit in JOURN 375 or 469. May be taken for credit/no credit only.

title: Editorial Practicum
description: Basic practical experience in the production of the campus newspaper, magazine, yearbook, or similar projects on campus or off. Emphasizes sharpened reporting, writing, editing, graphics, photographic, layout, and related activities in preparation for developing a portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 211 and either JOURN 312, 328, 337, or 345. Not open to students who have credit in JOURN 369 or 469.

title: Introduction to Mass Media Research Strategies
description: Practical approaches to research in journalism and media campaigns. Emphasizes survey research, questionnaire construction, interviewing techniques, attitude measurement, copy testing, audience analysis, computer database searches, evaluation of externally supplied research, and data interpretation.

title: Electronic Journalistic Production Techniques
description: Theory, principles, and handson experience in writing for electronic media; camera and videocassette recorder operation; microphones and audio recording; electronic editing; studio production; field production and delivery systems. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Open only to journalism majors and minors.

title: Honors Colloquium in Journalism
description: Readings and indepth exploration and discussion of pertinent issues, movements, and problems in journalism and mass communications research. Open to honors students and to students with areas in journalism by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Journalism
description: The procedures and problems in teaching journalism classes or units and the role of student publications in school journalism programs. Subjects included are curriculum, finance, textbooks, and resources. Discussion of school publicity is included as time permits. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: Advanced Reporting and Newswriting
description: Theory and practice in reporting and writing specialized news stories. Emphasis is on indepth reporting and coverage of specialized areas including public affairs, government, education, and business. Assignments are designed for use in student publications. Prerequisite: JOURN 211. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: World Press Systems
description: Survey of the international news media, with particular attention to the four press theories; ownership, structure, and access to the media; the political, economic, and social environment in which the media operate; governmentmedia relations. Comparison with the American media.

title: Science and Technical Writing
description: Description of methods and techniques of technical and scientific writing and editing. Emphasis on clarity in technical writing and ability to translate terminology into lay language in science writing.

title: Newspaper Design
description: Theory of layout, grid systems, typography, color, and use of photography for newspapers. Emphasizes design problem solving in the editing process and editorial judgment in the newspaper design process. Computerbased production methods employed. Prerequisite: JOURN 125. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Magazine Composition and Layout
description: Study of magazine layout and production from an editor's point of view. Explores journalistic visual literacy, visual/verbal interpretation, and composition unique to magazines and newspaper magazine supplements. Prerequisite: JOURN 225, 211, or JOURN 125, 328. Not open to students in prejournalism. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Magazine Writing
description: A workshop in writing articles. Emphasizes targeting markets for freelance articles and writing for magazines that publish articles of 2,500 words or more. Prerequisite: JOURN 315. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Picture Editing
description: Selecting, editing, and using photographic and other illustrative graphic materials. Includes layout and design of picture pages for newspapers, magazines, books, brochures, and pamphlets.

title: Advertising Photography
description: Advertising, commercial, and concept illustration photography for the print media. Students must have their own 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Color Photojournalism
description: Principles, techniques, and materials of color photography as they apply to color art work and photographs in printed publications. Must have 35mm cameras and photographic supplies. Prerequisite: JOURN 236. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Advertising Media
description: Extended study in developing a comprehensive media plan. Emphasizes consumer research, media habits, creative selection of media vehicles, and use of the computer in planning and buying. Prerequisite: JOURN 352. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Creative Seminar
description: Extended study in the conceptualization and creation of advertising with emphasis on creative direction and visual presentation. Prerequisite: JOURN 352, 354. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advanced Copy Writing
description: Advanced studies in the strategy and creation of advertising for the mass media. Prerequisite: JOURN 354. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising Campaigns
description: Synthesis of skills and concepts acquired in the specialized advertising courses. Research, plan, write, schedule, budget, and evaluate a complete advertising campaign. Prerequisite: either JOURN 452, 453, 454, or 455. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Public Relations Campaigns
description: Allows public relations majors to apply research and problemsolving techniques to actual or simulated public relations case problems using all of the methodologies learned previously. Prerequisite: JOURN 368. Not open to prejournalism students. Open only to students in other journalism areas.

title: Advertising and Public Relations Practicum
description: Practical experience in public relations or advertising projects in preparation of a senior portfolio. Prerequisite: JOURN 352 and 354 or 368 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advising High School Publications
description: Theories of staff organization and content of high school yearbooks, newspapers, and magazines. Emphasizes the role of the advisor, financial management, staff motivation, and trends in scholastic publications.

title: Writing, Editing, and Design Seminar
description: Further develops writing, editing, and design skills for journalistic publications. Specialized writing and design projects within the areas of newspaper, magazine, and information graphics. Topics also include analysis, career planning, and portfolio development. Prerequisite, graphics reporting: JOURN 345, 382, 421; visual editing: JOURN 345, 421, 423, 432.

title: Individual Studies in Journalism
description: Group and individual investigations and experiences injournalistic media and techniques with special attention to social, political, and economic roles of the press in society. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF MATHEMATICAL SCIENCES D. Whitaker, Chairperson; M. Ali, R. Avila, J. Zhang The Department of Mathematical Sciences offers General Studies course work to help all students understand the role that mathematics plays in today's world. The department also offers specialized programs to prepare mathematically oriented students for a variety of careers. The departmental major and minor are designed to prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government as well as for more intense study of mathematics at the graduate level. The major in actuarial science provides training for careers that involve analyzing and solving business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. The program includes course work for the first three examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries and in some cases for the fourth and fifth examinations. The teaching major and minor satisfy state certification requirements for students preparing to teach mathematics in junior high/middle school or high school. Students preparing to be elementary teachers may add the endorsement for teaching mathematics to their elementary teaching licenses and may also earn certification to teach mathematics in junior high/middle schools. For information on the major in mathematical economics, see Interdepartmental Programs, p. 57f. Unless otherwise noted, all students enrolling in courses in the Department of Mathematical Sciences are expected to have completed at least three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school, including two years of algebra and one year of geometry. To begin all programs (except the endorsement for teaching a subject field: mathematics), it is expected that students will have completed high school mathematics courses equivalent to the prerequisite for MATHS 171. In addition, for all programs (except the actuarial science major and the endorsement), it is expected that students will have had some computer programming experience. title: Basic Algebra
description: Emphasis on the concepts of elementary algebra. Intended for those with limited backgrounds in basic algebra skills. Provides appropriate background for MATHS 108. Does not count as directed elective credit in any program of study.

title: Intermediate Algebra
description: Review of factoring, quadratic equations and inequalities, relations and functions, rational exponents, systems of linear equations, and exponential and logarithmic functions. Recommended background: two years of college preparatory mathematics in high school.

title: College Algebra
description: Such topics as polynomial functions and equations, exponential and logarithmic functions, determinants, systems of equations and inequalities, mathematical induction, the binomial theorem, permutations and combinations, and progressions. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or appropriate score on mathematics placement test or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS courses numbered 161 or higher.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities, and equations; graphs of the trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions; solution of right and general triangles;polar coordinates; and complex numbers. Scientific calculators will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or 109 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS courses numbered 161 or higher.

title: Pre-Calculus Mathematics
description: Coordinate plane, straight lines and circles, conic sections, elementary transcendental functions, curvesketching, polar coordinates, parametric equations, sequences, and series. Prerequisite: the equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondaryschool level or MATHS 112.

title: Mathematics and Its Applications
description: General Studies course including such topics as mathematical modeling, problem solving, geometrical concepts, growth patterns, and applications to the physical sciences, social sciences, and economics. Recommended background: three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school.

title: Finite Mathematics for Business
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of business majors, including mathematics of finance, probability, matrix algebra, and linear programming. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or an appropriate score on the mathematics placement test.

title: Brief Calculus for Business 2
description: Brief survey of differential and integral calculus. Emphasis on applications to business. Prerequisite: MATHS 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 112 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 171.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 171. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 172.

title: Calculus 1
description: Differential calculus and its applications. Advanced topics from analytic geometry will be introduced as needed. Antidifferentiation and the Reimann integral. Elementary transcendental functions. Prerequisite: elements of analytic geometry from high school or MATHS 117.

title: Calculus 2
description: Standard techniques of integration and applications of the integral. Infinite series. Further development of applications of integral calculus. Vectors. Partial differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 171.

title: Elementary Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, measures of central tendency and dispersion, basic probability concepts, random variables, binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression, and consideration of various applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 109 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 320.

title: Number Concepts in the Elementary School
description: Development of cardinal and unsigned rational number concepts and properties interfaced with selected models and computer software from elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite: appropriate score on mathematics placement test, or credit in MATHS 108, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geometry and Measurement in Grades K-6
description: Development of geometry and measurement concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from mathematics programs for primary and intermediate grades. May be substituted for MATHS 203. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 201. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 203.

title: Geometry and Measurement in the Primary Grades
description: Development of measurement and geometry concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from K-3 mathematics programs. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 201. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 202.

title: Mathematics for the Teacher of the Exceptional Learner
description: Development of number concepts, number operations, measurement, geometric concepts, and problemsolving skills needed by teachers of exceptional learners. Instructional activities use selected models and materials appropriate for teachers of exceptional learners. May not be substituted for MATHS 201 or 202 or 203. Prerequisite: appropriate score on mathematics placement test, credit in MATHS 108, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 201, 202, or 203. Open only to special education majors.

title: Structure of the Number Systems
description: An introduction to formal logic, set theory, and selected number systems. A systematic development is emphasized. Prerequisite: MATHS 162, 171, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Linear Algebra 1
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties and applications, determinants, rank and equivalence of matrices. Introduction to vector spaces and linear transformation. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 171.

title: Linear Algebra 2
description: A continuation of topics from MATHS 212 including transformation of coordinates, diagonalization of matrices, and introduction to canonical forms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 412.

title: Statistical Methods
description: Introduces the application of statistics. Binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, tests of hypotheses, regression, correlation, categorical data analysis, analysis of variance, nonparametrics, sampling, and elementary experimental design. Emphasis is placed on comprehension and interpretation. Statistical computer packages are used. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 171. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 321.

title: Discrete Mathematics
description: Study of contemporary topics in discrete mathematics selected from but not limited to sets, logic, methods of proof, relations, functions, counting, recurrence, graphs, trees, matrix algebra, discrete probability, game theory, Markov chains, and related topics in abstract algebra. Prerequisite: MATHS 132 or 162 or 172, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Geometry
description: Revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Computer applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 211 and one year of high school geometry.

title: Calculus 3
description: Multidimensional calculus and its applications. Topics include vectorvalued functions, partial derivatives, multiple integrals in rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates, and some vector analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems dealing with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite: MATHS 273.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games will be emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 201.

title: Undergraduate Colloquium
description: A series of brief introductions to the mathematical landscape including glimpses of mathematics in the workplace. Topics are drawn from all areas of the mathematical sciences. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 in any one semester or term. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (1-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematics for the Junior High/Middle School Teacher
description: Applications of logic, number systems, algebra, geometry, and statistics in the junior high/middle school. Materials, manipulatives, and technology will be used to provide models for the junior high/middle school mathematics curriculum. Prerequisite: MATHS 211, 240. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 201 and 202. Open only to mathematics teaching majors and minors.

title: Algebraic Structures
description: Consideration of the basic algebraic structures: groups, rings, integral domains, and fields. Examples of these structures and elementary proof will be emphasized as will polynomials over rings, integral domains, and the fields of real and complex numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Probability
description: Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, momentgenerating functions, common distributions, sampling distribution theory, central limit theorem, t, chisquare, and F distributions. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Mathematical Statistics
description: Point and interval estimation, maximum likelihood, Neyman-Pearson Lemma, likelihood ratio tests, classical tests of significance, goodnessoffit, contingency tables, correlation, regression, nonparametric methods, Bayesian methods. Prerequisite: MATHS 320.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal, and other distributions. Some problems with momentgenerating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Actuarial review class. Prerequisite: MATHS 321.

title: Computer and Mathematics Enrichment Topics
description: Topics for elementary and junior high/middle school in computer uses and programming, and enrichment topics from such areas as topology, strategy games, and number theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 202.

title: Computer Applications in the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Emphasizes the use of computers in the teaching of mathematics. Students whose area of licensure is mathematics may apply credit in this course toward the undergraduate computer endorsement. Prerequisite: MATHS 240 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models for use with problems in physics, chemistry, biology, and economics. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models. Existing computer software will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in analytic, synthetic, transformational, and vector geometry, closely related to Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 240 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities, equations of value, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, current actuarial topics in finance. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analysis, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, and orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 118 or 120 and MATHS 162 or 172. Not open to students who have credit in CS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 362. Not open to students who have credit in CS 363.

title: Intermediate Calculus
description: Topics include vector functions; displacement; velocity and acceleration of particles in twoand threedimensional space; curvature; torsion and Frenet's formulas; divergence; curl; line integrals; work; surface integrals; theorems of Gauss, Green, and Stokes; orthogonal curvilinear coordinates. Prerequisite: MATHS 273.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nthorder ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equations. Laplace transforms, power series solutions. Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, firstorder partial differential equations. Use of standard computer software for elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATHS 172.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood and Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from early childhood through grade three. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. One hour lecture, one hour teaching, and one hour laboratory each week. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 202 or 203. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 391.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood, Primary, and Intermediate Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics from early childhood through intermediate grades. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Two onehour lectures and one onehour laboratory experience each week. May be substituted for MATHS 390. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 202 or 203.

title: Teaching Mathematics to the Exceptional Learner
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics to the exceptional learner. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Three onehour lectures and one onehour laboratory experience each week. May not be substituted for MATHS 390 or 391. Prerequisite: a grade of C or higher in MATHS 207, or a grade of C or higher in both MATHS 201 and 202. Open only to special education majors.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for teaching mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a smallgroup teaching situation. Prerequisite: MATHS 240.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in teaching secondary mathematics. Additional consideration given to methodology and instruction at the junior high/middle school level. Survey of texts, organization of materials, evaluation procedures, instructional aids, and classroom observations. Prerequisite: MATHS 240 and a minimum G.P.A. of 2.5 in all mathematics courses that are to be applied to the major or minor.

title: Classroom Use of Methods and Materials
description: Classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics, evaluation of instructional activities, and rationale for including mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences, whenever appropriate. Prerequisite: MATHS 311, 395, and a minimum G.P.A. of 2.5 in all mathematics courses that are to be applied to the major.

title: Abstract Algebra 1
description: Indepth treatment of group theory. Includes a brief review of basics, followed by topics such as factor groups, isomorphism theorems, series of groups, Burnside counting and the Sylow theorems, free groups, group presentations, and other advanced topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 311.

title: Abstract Algebra 2
description: Indepth treatment of ring and field theory covering ideals, quotient rings, homomorphisms, polynomial rings, unique factorization domains, field extensions and geometric constructions, finite fields and additional topics from field automorphisms, Galois theory and applications to coding theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 411.

title: Theory of Numbers
description: Topics include the division algorithm; positional notation; divisibility; primes; congruences; divisibility criteria; the sigma, divisor, and phi functions; diophantine equations; linear, polynomial, and simultaneous congruences; theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson; quadratic reciprocity. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school include Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, magic squares, the calendar problem, polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the fifteen puzzle, Nim, and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 416.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey designs; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling; ratio estimates; regression estimates; cost and variance functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Topics in Statistics
description: Includes such topics as oneand twoway ANOVA, multiple comparisons, regression analysis, time series analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Analysis of Variance in Experimental Design Models
description: Multivariate normal distribution; quadratic forms; linear models; simple random, randomized block, Latin squares, factorial, splitplot, balanced incomplete block design; analysis of covariance; confounding; multiple comparison tests. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Geometry and Topology 1
description: Introduction to Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometries and the surfaces admitting these geometries. Basic topological notions, such as the boundary operator, continuity, and connectedness, underlying the development of these topics. Elements of linear geometry leading to basic ideas of differential geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 273.

title: Geometry and Topology 2
description: A continuation of MATHS 441 culminating in the treatment of selected advanced topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 441.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 1
description: Survival distributions, life tables; the mathematics of life insurance, life annuities, net premiums, and net premium reserves. Prerequisite: MATHS 321, 351.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 2
description: Mathematics of multiple life functions, multiple decrement models, valuation theory for pension plans, insurance models including expenses, nonforfeiture benefits, and dividends. Prerequisite: MATHS 452.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, math formula. Prerequisite: MATHS 320, 362, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Optimization techniques of linear, dynamic, and integer programming and stochastic simulation. Optimal solutions of PERT-CPM networks. Optimal decision strategies. Elementary queuing theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 320, and working knowledge of scientific computer programming.

title: History of Mathematics
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to the seventeenth century. Topics may include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, and calculus. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 171.

title: Elements of Analysis
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives, and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 172 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Metric spaces, topological concepts in IR and C leading to consideration of connectedness, compactness and completeness, continuous functions, uniform continuity, Stone- Weierstrass theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 273.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansions. Prerequisite: MATHS 471.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace's equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATHS 374.

title: Senior Seminar
description: A variety of topics in mathematics presented by three faculty members will be studied and discussed. A short paper on one of the three topics presented to the class is required. Prerequisite: major in one of the mathematical sciences and senior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the mathematical sciences department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300 and 400 levels. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF MODERN LANGUAGES AND CLASSICS A. Yonamine The Department of Modern Languages and Classics offers programs in both ancient and modern foreign languages and works closely with other programs and departments to combine foreign language training with other subjects. Language laboratory practice, computer applications, interactive multimedia, opportunities for study abroad in the summer and for an academic semester or year, and foreign exchange programs enhance classroom instruction. The department offers foreign language training for students who want to acquire a broad liberal education; enrich their preparation for their careers; seek certification for teaching at the elementary or secondary level; travel, live, or work abroad; or work as translators. Students may earn credit for previous language study through either national advanced placement tests or departmentally administered placement tests. Students are expected to take these department placement tests in any language they studied before entering the university and intend to continue studying. These tests help determine the appropriate student class placement. Students who have completed more than one year of a foreign language in high school may not normally enroll for credit in the 101 level of that language, except in Chinese and Japanese, or with permission of the chairperson. Students placed in any higherlevel course will receive credit for the courses they test out of by earning grades of C or higher in the course into which they are placed. Native speakers who have completed high school studies in their native countries are not eligible for credit in the first or second year of their native languages. At the end of their last semester, senior majors in French, German, Japanese, and Spanish are expected to take a proficiency test for assessment of skills in six areas: reading, writing, listening, speaking, grammar, and culture. Senior majors in classical languages are expected to take a proficiency test for assessment of skills in three areas: translation, grammar, and culture. Resulting scores of high, middle, or low are available to faculty members for letters of recommendation. The modern language test is based on content, procedures, and norms published by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages and by the Educational Testing Services. Students should consult with foreign language faculty advisors about arranging courses to meet their needs. The 100- and 200-level courses in foreign languages are sequential and must be taken in order. Only work at the 200 level and above will apply toward any major or minor in this department, except in Chinese, Japanese, Greek, and classical culture, in which firstyear courses may be counted. Siewert, D. Van Meter The Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Management prepares students for careers in environmental science and management of natural resources. The programs offered by the department are designed to give students a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. The department offers a major in natural resources and environmental management, a minor in natural resources, a minor in environmental management, a teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, and an endorsement for elementary education majors. The department further coordinates interdepartmental minors in energy and environmental policy. Students majoring in natural resources and environmental management choose one of the following options: natural resource studies, environmental interpretation and outdoor recreation management, environmental protection, and land management. All majors must complete a common core requirement. Many courses include laboratory work using sophisticated analytical equipment. Each year, students have opportunities for indepth twotofourweek field studies in the United States and foreign countries. Students are encouraged to participate in practicums or internships under the supervision of faculty members or professionals working in private consulting firms, governmental agencies, or environmental education centers. description: Natural resource use in agricultural systems with emphasis on principles of sustainability. Includes integrated pest management, permaculture, and other production practices that conserve soil, water, and biological resources. Field trips included.

Focuses on devising a survival strategy based on selfreliant concepts in housing, waste material, water use, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation, and the role of regulatory agencies. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NR 211; CHEM 111 or the equivalent; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: Basic relationships between soil nutrients and plant growth with emphasis on the conditions affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Soil chemistry as related to environmental contamination. Prerequisite: NR 221 or its equivalent; CHEM 111 or its equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Includes soil genesis, morpholo gy, classification, and survey. Stresses the relationship between soil information and the landuse decisionmaking process with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis is placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Stresses principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts. Studies management systems and individual practices with special emphasis on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NR 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Energy and Mineral Resources: Issues and Choices
description: Appraisal of the problems, prospects, and societal and technical issues surrounding the use of energy and mineral resources. Emphasis is on environmental problems and ecoenergetics, consideration of the natural resource base, distribution and production problems, conservation, alternative energy systems, resource policy, and research.

title: Air Quality
description: Focuses on the contamination of the atmospheric environment. Topics include major contaminants; measurement techniques; dispersion; effects on the atmosphere, human health, vegetation and materials; regulatory requirements and practices; control measures; noise pollution. Lab and field experiences.

title: Indoor Air Quality Management
description: Indoor air pollution problems of residential and nonresidential environments. Features discussions of asbestos, radon, and formaldehyde as well as combustiongenerated pollutants. Topics include energy conservation, building design, modeling, measurement techniques, and mitigation measures. Lab and field experiments.

title: Occupational and Industrial Hygiene
description: Introduces the principles of assessing and controlling exposures to workplace hazards. Topics include occupational disease; exposure to contaminant gases, dusts, radiation, noise, and biological agents; ergonomic concerns; regulatory requirements; engineering control; and personal protection equipment.

title: Building Asbestos and Lead Management
description: Significance of asbestos and lead hazards in buildings; exposure risks; regulatory requirements; sampling procedures; abatement practices; abatement project design. Field and handson experiences.

title: Ventilation Systems
description: Use of ventilation systems to reduce contaminant exposures in general occupational and industrial environments. Principles of dilution and exhaust ventilation. Prerequisite: NR 347 or permission of the instructor.

title: Turf-Grass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis is on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. Identification of grass and weed species.

title: International Rural Development
description: Analysis of rural development in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Emphasizes the roles of population, agriculture, history, conflict, technology, international debt, multilateral organizations, and political and cultural traditions in development efforts. Interdisciplinary readings and case studies.

title: Paid Professional Practice
description: Supervised financially supported professional experience in natural resource management, environmental education, or environmental protection. Provides a bridge between academic and professional experiences. Available only on a prospective basis. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NR 497.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. Emphasizes multipleuse concepts of management to meet outdoor recreation demands. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures. Prerequisite: NR 211; one college course in chemistry; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
description: Delineation of solid and hazardous waste management in the United States. Waste reduction, recycling, processing, and disposal methods are discussed. Technical, political, and economic aspects of waste management. Effects of improper disposal on environmental quality. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students; others with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Environmental Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasizes field work and creative presentation of concepts, and organization and management of interpretive programs including sites and facilities. Prerequisite: NR 101 or its equivalent; junior standing.

title: Teaching Environmental Education
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction through environmental education in formal and nonformal educational settings. Studies conservation, outdoor and environmental education, including teaching techniques and instructional resources used in each. Prerequisite: NR 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a specific area with special emphasis on location of natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence they have on the regional environmental quality. Each time the course is offered a specific geographic area is studied. Includes laboratory and field experience. Prerequisite: NR 101 or its equivalent and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Integrated Resources Planning and Management
description: Introduction to strategies used in environmental planning and resource management in contemporary society. Stresses use of data analysis and its role in the decisionmaking process by conceptually centering on natural and humanmade systems. May require field trips. Prerequisite: all natural resources core courses or concurrent enrollment and senior standing. Students in related disciplines may seek permission from the department chairperson.

title: Seminar
description: Formal reports and discussion of selected natural resource topics, current events, and special articles in natural resourcerelated professional and scientific journals. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered spring semester of evennumbered years. Prerequisite: NR 211; BIO 480; ZOOL 444; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and use of natural resources for outdoor recreation. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Administration and Management of Outdoor Recreation Areas
description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to provide good outdoor recreation experiences. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NR 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Wilderness and Society
description: Defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. Includes study of research in perception and use. Weekend trip to the Deam Wilderness— Hoosier National Forest or a state forest back country area. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Introduction to Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles applied to specific environmental problems. Design of facilities that Philosophy 273 minimize environmental impact from use of resources; remediation of severely disturbed environments; design of waste management systems. Some environmental chemistry. Prerequisite: NR 211, 221; CHEM 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Computer Applications in Natural Resources
description: Experience with a broad array of computer software for the VAX mainframe and microcomputers. Activities are carried out under an instructor's supervision. Assigned work is commensurate with computer experience and interests in natural resources. Taught by arrangement. Prerequisite: CS 104, permission of the instructor or the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Professional Practice
description: Supervised professional experience in natural resource management, environmental education, or environmental protection. Provides a bridge between academic and professional experiences. Available only on a prospective basis. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in NR 369. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours in combination with NR 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences
description: Opportunities to pursue special interests in natural resources and environmental sciences. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned (9 hours in combination with NR 496).

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Original research under faculty guidance, including problem definition, literature review, data collection, analysis, and a summary report. May require preparatory or parallel course work in research methodologies, statistics, or computer science. Prerequisite: faculty sponsor and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF PHILOSOPHY D. Annis, Chairperson; G. Barker, J. Corbett, J. Eflin, T. Foster, K. Kalumba Learning philosophy is more than simply reading books and memorizing theories and concepts. Learning philosophy involves engaging in philosophy, attempting to answer basic questions about people's values, the meaning of life, the extent of our freedom, and other issues. As the art of discovery, philosophy helps people to develop skills as keen observers, willingness to dig beneath the surface, and the ability to analyze data and think critically. The religious studies program helps people deepen their understanding of their own religion and appreciate the wide range of religions in the world. Courses also examine the deepest questions that concern people from a religious point of view: the nature and origin of life, the possibility of life after death, and value issues. The department's programs in philosophy and in religious studies offer excellent preparation for careers in higher education, law, public service, government agencies, writing, and religious vocations. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: An introduction to such important philosophical problems as the existence of God, whether ethical values are subjective, and the extent of our freedom. These topics and others may be approached by examining the ideas of great philosophers or current thinkers.

title: Introduction to Techniques of Critical Reasoning
description: Introduction to basic techniques of critical reasoning in deductive and inductive logic, and strategies for decision making and problem solving.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to draw correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of deduction.

title: Ethics
description: A discussion of some of the central problems in ethics such as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as a discussion of current moral issues.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of such basic social concepts as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of such normative issues as how liberty should be distributed and how justice can be maximized.

title: Business Ethics
description: Introduction to and analysis of basic concepts, principles, theories, and issues in business ethics.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Critical analysis of such selected topics as the nature and existence of God, the problem of evil, the justification of religious belief, and the significance of religious experience.

title: Environmental Ethics
description: Introduction to and analysis of basic concepts, principles, theories, and issues in environmental ethics. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the rise of philosophy in Greece through the medieval period. Emphasis is on the theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Emphasis is on these theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics may include the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading philosophers and movements in the twentieth century. May concentrate on such selected philosophers as Russell, Wittgenstein, and Husserl, or may concentrate on contemporary treatments of selected philosophical problems.

title: Aesthetics
description: Exploration of philosophical views on the nature, interpretation, and criticism of art. Readings and discussion may range from Philosophy 275 classical to contemporary thinkers and issues.

title: Philosophy of Law
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, and justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of such basic concepts as action, intention, causation, and responsibility.

title: African Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading trends in African philosophy. Ethnophilosophy, philosophic sagacity, liberation philosophy, or modern/critical philosophy are possible topics.

title: Current Issues in Philosophy
description: Selected current and important issues in philosophy. Topics may include social and ethical problems, recent work on traditional philosophical problems, and other issues of concern.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: An examination of such central philosophical problems in the sciences as the nature of scientific explanation and the testing of hypotheses; a discussion of ethical issues arising from science, for example, the use of human subjects and prolonging life.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships related to their professional or career goals. Internships may be with educational or religious institutions, public or private agencies, or business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Open only to students in the Honors College or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Allows superior students opportunities for guided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Introduction to Metaphysics
description: A study of the principal problems of metaphysics including the nature of reality, the relation of mind and body, and the issues of freedom and determinism.

title: Introduction to Theory of Knowledge
description: A critical discussion of leading theories and problems of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge and rational belief, the different kinds of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory and Problems
description: A critical examination of recent ethical theories and their application to contemporary problems.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: Traditional religious groups in the United States with attention to developments, institutions, distinctive practices, and beliefs. The groups and the subjects treated will be adjusted to the interests of the students.

title: Religions of the World
description: An introductory survey of the major religions of the world (Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Islam, Christianity, and others), emphasizing how people live out their faiths in their daily lives.

title: Old Testament
description: Our Hebrew-Judaic religious heritage as reflected in various personalities and their religious expressions as found in the literature of the Old Testament.

title: New Testament
description: Our early Christian heritage in relation to its Jewish- Greek background as reflected by various personalities in the literature of the New Testament.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships related to their professional or career goals. Internships may be with educational or religious institutions, public or private agencies, or business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Jesus and the Gospel Traditions
description: The traditions that developed about Jesus among the early Christians as reflected in the four Gospels and the more recent findings of apocryphal Gospels.

title: Methods in the Study of Religion
description: An exploration of the many ways to approach the study of religion, its origins, nature, and functions in human society.

title: Paul and the Developing Church
description: An indepth study of Paul's letters, the traditions as reflected in the Book of Acts, and the development of the early Church through the fourth century.

title: Seminar in Eastern Religions
description: An intensive seminarformat study of the religions of India, China, and Japan, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Shintoism, and contemporary Japanese religions.

title: Comparative Religion
description: Investigation, analysis, and comparison of selected major religious traditions with attention to their underlying structures. Particular attention is given to the comparison of Eastern and Western traditions.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: For superior students: an opportunity for guided investigation in aspects of religion not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Special Topics in Religion
description: Indepth focus on a selected issue of central importance. Topics vary each semester and include such subjects as American Indian religions, women and religion, and the Pentecostal and charismatic movements. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term. DEPARTMENT OF PHYSICS AND ASTRONOMY D. Ober, Chairperson; R. Cosby, P. Errington, R. Watson The Department of Physics and Astronomy offers majors in both pure and applied physics for students who want to pursue graduate work in physics, astronomy, or engineering or who are interested in careers in industry. Programs are also available for students who want to teach secondary school physics. Departmental minors are available in astronomy, physics, and applied physics. Students planning to major or minor in physics or astronomy programs are strongly advised to consult with the department to determine the proper course sequence for their needs. Pre-Engineering Major This program is intended for students enrolled at Ball State who hope to transfer to accredited schools of engineering. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program in which students must attend Ball State for three years and then transfer to accredited engineering schools to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of the engineering program students are eligible to receive bachelor's degrees from Ball State in addition to their engineering degrees. Schools of engineering may have requirements not met by the general Ball State preengineering major. Students in this program are responsible for knowing and meeting the requirements of the schools to which they plan to transfer. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not mean automatic admission to any accredited school of engineering. Students must apply for admission to the engineering school and must meet the requirements set by the engineering school. Three options in the preengineering major are available: chemical engineering, metallurgical engineering, and general engineering (such as aeronautical, civil, electrical, industrial, mechanical, and nuclear).
