title: General Psychology
description: Introduction to various branches of psychology and the contributions of each to understanding the behavior of people as they interact with their environment.

title: The Psychology of Human Adjustment
description: An introduction to how people can cope more effectively with common emotional, interpersonal, and situational problems. Selfmanagement strategies and positive coping techniques are introduced for the enhancement of personal growth and adjustment. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Not open to students who have credit in PSYSC 317 or 432.

title: Applied Behavior Analysis
description: Introduction to the principles of operant psychology and application of these principles to situations with people outside formal educational settings. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Elementary Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics and statistics of inference. The computation, application, and interpretation of various elementary statistics. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and MATHS 125 or its General Studies equivalent.

title: Introduction to Biopsychology
description: Broadbased survey focusing on the methods and findings relating biological influences to behavior. Emphasis is on the anatomy and functions of the nervous system, as well as other related topics that help to explain behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Not open to students who have credit in PSYSC 468.

title: Psychology of Sexual Behavior
description: An examination of the determinants of human sexual behavior, focusing on the development of sexual identity and attitudes. Uses perspectives from social psychology, personality theory, and physiological psychology to build an understanding of this most complex behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Research Methods in Psychology
description: An introduction to the use of the scientific method in the study of human behavior. Students analyze and evaluate experimental studies to gain experience with research techniques while using essential controls and acceptable procedures. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and a minimum grade of C in PSYSC 241. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Psychology and Health
description: Examines how psychological conditions influence disease prevention, medical treatment, stress and coping, and psychosocial adjustment to illness. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Introduction to Comparative Psychology
description: Surveys the theoretical and empirical foundations of the study of animal behavior. Examination of topics associated with evolutionary principles, behavioral ecology, instinct, neuroethology, behavior genetics, perceptual systems, mate selection, and mating social systems is included. Examples are chosen from a variety of vertebrate and invertebrate species. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 or permission of the instructor.

title: Introduction to Social Psychology
description: Overview of conditions that affect a person in a social context: attitudes, impression formation, interpersonal relations, and group membership. Examines current theories and relevant research. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Introduction to the Study of Personality
description: Presents and compares a wide variety of classical and modern theories of personality and pertinent empirical research. Considers the components of a good theory of personality and the applications of various personality theories. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Experimental Child Psychology
description: A survey of theory and research in child perception, memory, learning, cognition, and language. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, 284.

title: Psychology of Women
description: Psychological study of women with emphasis on achievement motivation and dependency, attitudes toward women, sexrole identity, biological and social influences on women's behavior, selfconcepts and psychological conflicts, and a study of research in sex differences. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Environmental Psychology
description: Presents the current knowledge and research in environmental psychology and studies its relevance to psychological planning for people's special needs. Investigates the psychological effects on persons and groups of selected conditions in various kinds of environments. Prerequisite: PSYSC 316 or permission of the department chairperson. NR 101 is strongly recommended.

title: Intermediate Statistics for Psychological Research
description: Inferential statistics and research design, computation and interpretation of statistics related to psychological research design. Critical analysis of published research literature. Prerequisite: PSYSC 241.

title: Motivation and Emotion
description: Basic theory and research relating to motivation and emotion and applications to various facets of human behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241. Psychological Science 301

title: Psychology of Learning
description: Nature of learning processes, possible influences upon these processes and resultant behavior, and applications of the psychology of learning. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241.

title: Orientation to Cooperative Education Experiences in Psychological Science
description: Seminar designed to orient people interested in cooperative education experiences to ethics, confidentiality, and other concerns of professional citizenship in human services and business settings. Prerequisite: permission of the cooperative education coordinator. Course offered on a credit/no credit basis.

title: Professional Experience
description: Designed to monitor the progress of students working in paid parttime psychologyrelated job settings and to assist them in relating and integrating job experiences with required knowledge of psychology. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Industrial Psychology
description: Application of psychological principles to personnel selection, training, and evaluation, worker motivation and morale, leadership and supervision, job design, and workplace health and safety. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Honors Colloquium in Psychology
description: Explorations of selected issues in psychology with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion of such topics as psychobiology, social psychology, learning, personality, and abnormal psychology.

title: Special Topics in Psychology
description: Surveys theory and research on a selected topic in psychology using a lecture and discussion format. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned provided that no topic is repeated.

title: Sensation and Perception
description: Survey of theories, methods, and knowledge concerning sensory physiology, sensation, and perception. Emphasis is on studies of people. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Prerequisite recommended: PSYSC 241, 284.

title: Psychology of Cognition
description: Survey of theories and research about human thought and memory. Topics include attention, memory, problem solving, and language. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Prerequisite recommended: PSYSC 241 and 284.

title: Abnormal Psychology
description: Systematic study of behavior pathology. Primary emphasis is on the use of theoretical perspectives and empirical data to understand the description, etiology, prognosis, treatment, and prevention of abnormal behavior. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100. Prerequisite recommended: PSYSC 317.

title: Survey of Clinical Psychology
description: Introduction to the roles and functions of personnel in clinical psychology. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
description: Theoretical and practical foundations underlying the construction, use, and interpretation of standardized psychological tests and inventories. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and 284.

title: Physiological Psychology
description: An introduction to the physical basis of behavior, involving primarily the nervous system and its structure and function. Emphasis is on the role of bodily systems in perception, learning, motivation, and conscious function. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100 and 241.

title: Organization Development
description: Presentation of techniques used to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of organizations. Critical examination of these techniques in the light of psychological theory and research. Prerequisite: PSYSC 373 or MGT 371.

title: Psychology of Selection and Placement
description: Introduction to principles of personnel testing as applied to the selection and placement process. Focus is on development of predictors and criteria, selection of an appropriate validation model, and the psychological dynamics of the interview processes. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, or the equivalent.

title: Human Factors Psychology
description: Explores the relation between people and the physical things in their environments. Topics include design of objects based on psychological knowledge about information display, human control, and cognitive capacities. Prerequisite: PSYSC 241 or other statistics course.

title: Practical Experience
description: Monitors the progress of students participating in unpaid psychologyrelated settings and assists them in integrating such experiences with acquired knowledge of psychology. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Systematic Psychology
description: Major concepts of various schools of psychological thought and contemporary theoretical systems as they have evolved historically. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100, 241, and senior standing recommended.

title: Seminar in Psychology
description: Investigations of topics of interest in the current literature of psychology. Prerequisite: psychology major and senior standing.

title: Supervised Empirical Research Experience
description: Experience in the collection of behavioral data in the field or laboratory setting. Students work closely with a supervising faculty member. The credit hours may be accumulated in more than one semester. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent Study in Psychology
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with instructors with special competence in the area involved. The credit hours may be accumulated in more than one semester. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF SOCIAL WORK H. Miller The baccalaureate program prepares students as generalist social work practitioners for entrylevel positions in a broad range of humanservice organizations. Graduates work in public and private settings that offer services to a wide range of clients including children and youth, families, and those who are mentally ill, chemically dependent, and physically ill. An effective social worker knows the community's resources and how to put people in touch with them. When needed services are not available, social workers help to develop them. The bachelor of social work degree program is fully accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of the Council on Social Work Education. MAJOR IN SOCIAL WORK, B.S.W., 69 hours Selective Admission and Retention in the Social Work Major 1. Initial admission to the major. Students must have • submitted a completed social work major application to the department. • earned minimum gradepoint averages of 2.3 in 100- and 200-level required courses completed for the major. • upon completion of SOCWK 220 and 230, completed assessment conferences with faculty instructors of these courses and submitted faculty reference forms to the department. • completed the university Speech and Hearing Clinic Screening administered by the Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology. • completed approved volunteer assignments of a minimum of twentyfive clock hours (course requirement in SOCWK 220) and submitted Performance Evaluations to the department. • completed application interviews with the coordinator of Student Services and received from this coordinator positive recommendations for admission to the major. Upon admission into the social work major, the department will assign a faculty advisor, help students complete a plan of study for completion of the major, monitor academic and professional development progress, and approve application for graduation. 2. Admission to seniorlevel required social work practice courses (SOCWK 424 and 426). Students must have • earned accumulative minimum gradepoint averages of 2.5 in the major in order to register for SOCWK 424 and 426. • successfully completed the university writing competency examination. 3. Admission to social work practicum. Students must have • submitted completed applications for the practicum to the department. • earned grades of C or better in SOCWK 424 and 426. • submitted completed university applications for graduation to North Quad Advising Center. Students denied admission to or continuation in the major may • appeal the decision within fourteen calendar days. • inform the department chairperson in writing that the decision to deny admission Social Work 303 or continuation in the major is being appealed by specifying the basis of the appeal. The department chairperson will convene the social work faculty within fourteen calendar days of notification of the appeal to review all information obtained for the preadmissions interviews and Faculty Advising Conferences and meet with a student within fourteen calendar days. The Faculty Review Committee has the authority to admit or retain students in the major. title: Introduction to Social Work
description: A view of traditional and innovative social work practice. Focuses on the role of the social worker within the various social work service delivery systems and practice settings.

title: Social Welfare and Social Work Practice 1 with Field Experience
description: Focuses on the historical development of social welfare, the social work profession, and the generalist problemsolving methods used by practitioners. Concurrent field experience required. Prerequisite: PSYSC 100; SOC 100; SOCWK 110. Open only to social work majors and minors.

title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment 1
description: Emphasis is on understanding the behavior of the macro social systems and the influence of these systems on human behavior. Prerequisite: SOCWK 110; SOC 100; PSYSC 100. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Work Practice 2 with Laboratory Experience
description: Content focus on core interactional skills in generalist social work practice. Emphasis is on the initial phases of the problemsolving process. Prerequisite: SOCWK 220, 230, or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to social work majors and minors.

title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment 2
description: Presents knowledge and research about major human behavior theories influencing individual and family behavior. Applies content to contemporary client situations affecting social work practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 220, 230, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Development of Knowledge in Social Work
description: Helps students to develop beginninglevel skills for using their practice as a setting for gathering information about the effectiveness of practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 220, 230.

title: Social Welfare Policy and Programs
description: Introduces students to social policy as a focus for social workers engaged in general practice. Prerequisite: SOCWK 220.

title: Social Services Internship
description: Work experience within a social service organization and a careerexploration opportunity. Emphasis is on paid field placements. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in SOCWK 460.

title: Selected Aspects of Social Work Practice
description: Exploration of social work practice with selected client populations and types of practice with emphasis on individualized study, reporting, and group discussion. Study will focus on social work practice and social service delivery within the identified field. Prerequisite: junior standing. Prerequisite recommended: SOCWK 110, 220, 230. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in any one semester or term.

title: Social Work Practice 3
description: Advanced practice course that applies social work methods to individuals, families, and small groups from a generalist social work practice perspective. Integrates content from previous welfare policy, human behavior, practice, and research courses. Prerequisite: SOCWK 322, 332, 340, 350, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Social Work Practice 4
description: Advanced practice course taught in conjunction with SOCWK 424 with an emphasis on general practice in organizations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson; SOCWK 322, 332, 340, 350.

title: Social Work Practicum
description: Fulltime field placement in a social service organization selected and approved by the department. Assignments provide guided instruction, application, and development of general practice competencies. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson; SOCWK 424 and 426.

title: Social Work Practicum Seminar
description: Seminar completed concurrently with agencybased social work practicum; promotes integration and application of knowledge from previous social work curriculum sequences for social work practice, welfare policy, research and human behavior, and the environment. Prerequisite: SOCWK 424, 426, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Social Work
description: Topic to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor with special competence in the subject involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF SOCIOLOGY J. Bode, Chairperson; B. Blakely, R. Bogg, R. Burton, J. Condran, N. Grant, S. Johnson, D. Morris, J. Tamney Sociology is the scientific study of human social relationships, ranging from small groups to whole societies. It deals with the effects of groups upon individuals, interactions among groups and organizations of many kinds, cultural beliefs that direct human behaviors, and comparisons of this society with others around the world. Methods of social research and analysis are part of the study of sociology. Sociology is a major part of the scientific foundation of such applied disciplines as social work, criminal justice, personnel work, counseling, nursing, and law. The Department of Sociology at Ball State prepares students to work in public service, in urban or social planning agencies, or in private organizations where they study, measure, and interpret how people interact in families, communities, and social, religious, political, and business organizations. MAJOR IN SOCIOLOGY, 32 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS

title: Principles of Sociology
description: An introduction to sociology including basic concepts used in sociological analysis. Attention is given to the world as a single society, the nature of society, culture, interpersonal and intergroup relations, and social institutions, world population, and worldwide economic and political arrangements. Intended for students unfamiliar with sociology.

title: Contemporary Social Organization
description: Introduction to sociology for advanced and nontraditional students. Emphasizes American institutions such as the family, political structures, religious groups and movements, the economy, medicine, and the media.

title: Black Americans
description: Social organization of black life in the United States: demography, culture, economy, and politics. Topics include family life, education, black identity, segregation, and discrimination.

title: Sociology of Women
description: Analysis of women's roles, especially in basic institutions of society. Emphasis on recent changes in social expectations for women. Includes experiential investigations of realities of women's lives, personal exploration of one's place in the gender structure, and relevant outside speakers.

title: Deviance
description: Overview of theory and research on deviance. Behavioral topics include drug and alcohol use, sexual nonconformity, mental disorders, and physical disability.

title: Social Problems
description: Discussion and analysis of several current social problems, their sources, and possible solutions. Includes participation in the selection of problems on which to focus.

title: Society and the Individual
description: Analysis of the interaction between people and their social environment. Includes the effects of groups and society on individual psychological makeup and behavior, and the individual's effect on the social setting. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Sociological Research Design
description: Basic principles and techniques for organizing, conducting, and analyzing sociological research. Research strategies and selection of appropriate techniques for a variety of research problems are included. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Social Statistics
description: Calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics used in social and behavioral sciences. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Leisure
description: Focuses on recreation, hobbies, media watching and listening, sports, folk arts, high culture, vacation travel, and the expanding leisure industries. Quality of life issues and effects on the natural environment are also discussed.

title: Social Inequality
description: The effects of education and occupation on access to scarce resources in industrial as well as Third-World societies. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: The Sociology of Modernization
description: The sociology of social and industrial change—modernization in the non-Western world. Study of reasons for change; for example, demographicurban, familysocial, and international pressures. Discussions of Third World social problems and social change models and ideologies. Prerequisite recommended: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Blue Collar Society and Culture
description: Concentrates on the varied lifestyles, socioeconomic realities, and selfconcepts found in workingclass households. Demographic and other data are also presented and discussed. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Global Inequality
description: Social inequalities linked to race, ethnicity, sex, religion, and other conditions occurring worldwide, often creating conflict among groups. Social change and modernization further complicate issues of inequality. Additional topics include occupational stratification, male dominance, women's roles, and individual identity. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Medical Sociology
description: Analysis of relationships between diseases and the social structure and efforts to cope with the phenomenon of sickness. Topics include social conditions in the distribution of disease, social stress, the sick role, conventional and alternative healers, and the medicalcare system.

title: Sociological Internship Experience
description: Paid supervised field experience in a public agency or business setting. Training involves data analysis, evaluation research, and implementation of agency programs under the supervision of the employer and the Department of Sociology. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Honors Colloquium in General Sociology
description: Designed to acquaint honors students with a sociological perspective of life through an openended discussion of a wide variety of fundamental social questions. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College.

title: Sociological Theory
description: Sociological theories of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Includes the intellectual and cultural backgrounds from which theories developed. Modern society, contemporary events, and probable future trends are examined in terms of major sociological theories. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Racial and Cultural Minorities in the United States
description: Examines the causes of prejudice and discrimination toward minorities in America; the consequences for the psychological and group makeup of minorities; proposals for reducing prejudice and discrimination. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Social Trends in Mass Society
description: Major trends in mass society and changes in those trends. Includes guidance in performing analyses of changing trends using existing databases. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Industrial and Post-Industrial Society
description: Considers the social effects of the Industrial Revolution, the continuing importance of technological change, the social structures of industrial organizations, and the expansion of the service and health sectors. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Family
description: How society influences contemporary families and, in turn, each of us. The variety of family arrangements and shifts in relationships through the lifecycle are examined. Roles, occupations, money, status, and sex are among topics covered. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Sociology of World Religions
description: Sociological comparison of Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam. What makes a religion popular? Who is winning the competition between religion and the mass media? What are the relationships between religion and public policy and between religion and the women's movement?

title: Social Gerontology
description: Social aspects of aging in contemporary American society and elsewhere, with emphasis on special needs and emerging community and national programs for meeting them.

title: Sociology of Mental Health
description: Social definitions of mental disorders and their incidence, prevalence, and distribution. Also includes analysis of helpseeking behaviors, the experience of treatment, the psychiatric industry, and the insanity plea. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Sociology of Human Sexuality
description: Gender and sexual issues common in both the developing and current cultures of Western societies. Topics include gender identity and preference, conventional and unconventional behaviors, sociological correlates of sexuality, coercion, and commercialism. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Social Change
description: Why and how groups are formed to change society. Analyzes revolutionary and nationalist struggles and their typical patterns and cycles. Roles of leaders, symbols, slogans, and ideologies. Includes such recent movements as civil rights, feminism, ecology, antinuclear, and New Right. Prerequiste: SOC 100 or 200. Speech Communication 307

title: Sociology of Childhood
description: The place of children in contemporary society, the study of socialization in various cultures and subcultures, and the child's relation to various societal institutions: family, religion, stratification, and education. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Population in the Twenty-First Century
description: Contemporary demographic and social patterns and their implications for the future. Addresses quality, quantity, composition, distribution, and growth of population from several perspectives including social services, marketing, and social polities. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Urban Dynamics and Problems
description: The historical functions and institutional dynamics of the city with special reference to contemporary urban problems, especially the inner city. Issues of community diversity and solidarity. Both industrialized and nonindustrialized urban matrixes of the late twentieth century.

title: Seminar on Middletown
description: Focuses on two works by the Lynds, Middletown and Middletown in Transition, sociological classics about Muncie. Updates have been undertaken by teams of scholars. Includes participation in a continuing sociological project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Urban Survey and Analysis
description: Nature and uses of urban surveys; methods of selecting, evaluating, and using sources of data; and application of survey findings to programs of community action. Includes direct participation in the various phases of a survey research project. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200.

title: Evaluation Research
description: Developing and conducting research to evaluate organizational programs. Topics include the unique nature of evaluation research, operationalizing and assessing variables, goal attainment measures, needs assessments, and developing guidelines for programmatic change.

title: Advanced Sociological Data Analysis
description: Selection and use of advanced statistical techniques for analyzing sociological data. Discusses topics such as nonparametric statistics, factor analysis, sampling statistics, and multiple regression and path analysis in sociological research. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200 and 282 or its equivalent.

title: Internship 1: Computer Learning Laboratory
description: Supervised experience in the computerized Sociology Learning Laboratory. Learning basic computer analysis of social data and departmentspecific software, and assisting students in sociology courses with basic computer work. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Internship 3: Field Experience
description: Unpaid supervised field experience in a business, industrial, governmental, educational, or other setting. Training involves data analysis, research, evaluation, or other applications of sociological theories and methods. Supervision will be provided jointly by the employer and the department. Prerequisite: permission of sociology internship coordinator and department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Internship 4: Analysis of Occupational Experience
description: Primarily for nontraditional students with significant social agency work experience. Initial consultation with department chairperson or advisor and written analysis of sociological conditions observed in work experience. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study of Sociology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor possessing special competence in the subject involved. Prerequisite: SOC 100 or 200 and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Topics in Sociology
description: Capstone study filling any gaps that may exist in a sociological education. Assists in employment preparation. Finally, assessment of the caliber of previous work in sociology. Stamp Speech communication offers programs in rhetorical theory; public, interpersonal, and organizational communication; and communication education. The major and minor are designed to prepare students for careers in business, government, politics, education, public affairs, public relations, and the media as well as for graduate study. title: Fundamentals of Public Communication
description: Principles and practice of effective oral communication; analysis and evaluation of the speakinglistening process; preparation in message construction, emphasizing the selection, organization, and delivery of materials.

title: Introductory Phonetics
description: Complete coverage of the International Phonetic Alphabet, including skill in transcription, knowledge of how speech sounds are made and taught, and study of dialects of the United States and the foreign born. (This course meets requirements of the American Speech and Hearing Association in basic phonetics.)

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: Theory and principles of argumentation and debate, including construction of debate cases, practice in debating, administration of a forensics program, and tournament direction. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Human Speech Communication
description: Focuses on understanding human speech communication as a dynamic and complex system of interactions rather than on the skills of platform speaking. Stresses the importance of understanding and applying communication theory in everyday speech communication situations.

title: Voice and Diction
description: Speech improvement, dealing with voice and articulation.

title: Intercultural Communication
description: Critical survey of major concepts in crosscultural and intercultural interaction. Examines the effects of customs, behaviors, and values on the interpersonal communication process. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Historical and Contemporary Public Address
description: Speechmaking as a force in political and intellectual history; critical analysis of selected speeches in relation to political, social, and economic issues. Analysis of issues dealing with problems of progress, reform, and revolution. Emphasis is on public address in American social and political institutions. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Persuasion
description: Use of persuasion in oral and written discourse. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 240.

title: Contemporary Forms of Persuasion
description: Examines the modes of persuasion reflected in dimensions of American popular culture. Attention focuses on the persuasive appeals used in forms of popular culture and methods of evaluating their persuasive potential and effect. Stresses the importance of applying communication theory in everyday transactions.

title: Interviewing
description: Examines the principles and types of interviews, with application of the principles in informational, persuasive, and employment interviews. Special attention is given to the various communication elements of the employment interview process: résumés, cover letters, selection interviews, and appraisal interviews. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 240.

title: Discussion and Leadership
description: Principles and types of discussion as viewed by the participants as well as the leader. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 240.

title: Topics in Speech Communication
description: Critical examination of selected topics and issues in speech communication. Designed to help students become familiar with current trends and theoretical and methodological issues in the discipline. May be repeated once by permission of the instructor and the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Meeting Management
description: Focuses on the communication elements of effective meetings including the study and practice of parliamentary procedure. Examines how these various communication concepts relate to business, professional, labor, service, and fraternal organizations. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business and Professional Communication
description: Focuses on communication activities in business and the professions: oral reports, persuasive presentations, interpersonal skills, and communication problemsolving strategies. Prerequisite: SPCH 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Communication Theory
description: Introduction to the varied and complex theoretical underpinnings of the human communicationphenomenon. Several theoreticalperspectives and applications will be explored. Topics include message theories, intrapersonal and interpersonal theories, and group and public communication theories. Prerequisite: SPCH 240.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid, supervised work and learning experience related to careers in speech communication with business firms or public agencies. Job description may include, but is not limited to, research, training, organization, and planning informative or persuasive campaigns, problem solving, and conflict management. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 240, and 350, or 451, and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Nonverbal Communication in Human Interaction
description: Examines the nature, forms, and functions of nonverbal codes in human speech communication. Focuses on understanding one's own nonverbal communication and that of others. Speech Communication 311 Prerequisite: SPCH 240 for speech communication majors; recommended for nonmajors.

title: Presentational Communication
description: Preparation and delivery of presentations and longer speeches. Examination and analysis of current theories and research in persuasion as they pertain to managers, executives, and other professionals who submit proposals, ideas, and recommendations to the scrutiny of clients, peers, and superiors. Prerequisite: SPCH 210.

title: Speech for Elementary Teachers
description: Designed for elementary and special education majors. Focuses on the development of the communication skills necessary for the classroom including creative dramatic arts, interpersonal communication, and public speaking. Not open to speech communication majors or minors. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Speech Communication
description: Practical experience in intercollegiate debate, individual events, applied communication research, or alternate speech communication projects. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Human Speech Communication
description: Seminartype class focusing on various aspects and problems of speech communication as they relate to people in their personal and professional relationships. Open to honors students and to students with areas in speech with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Speech
description: Materials and methods to be used in helping students acquire desirable attitudes, habits, and speaking, including discussion forms, debating, dramatics, and radio. Prerequisite: SPCH 210, 216, and THEAT 220 or 232; identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite recommended: EDSEC 280.

title: The Rhetoric of Political Campaigns
description: Examines the nature, forms, and effects of persuasion in organized political campaigns that seek to influence mass publics. Focuses on the skills needed to describe, analyze, and evaluate persuasive uses of language and to understand better the role of campaign persuasion in influencing voter behavior. Prerequisite recommended: POLS 372.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: The description, analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of persuasive uses of language. Theories and methodologies of selected classical and modern critics. Prerequisite: SPCH 320 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Classical Rhetorical Theory
description: Analytical studies of classical rhetoric. Primarily a systematic study of the rhetorical treatises of Aristotle, Cicero, and Quintilian.

title: Interpersonal Communications
description: Examines contemporary theories, concepts, models, and pertinent research related to the communication process in relatively unstructured facetoface settings. Particular emphasis is given to understanding message exchanges between people and how they affect the people involved. Introduces students to the approaches, variables, and topics that influence social interaction. Special attention is given to communication models, perception, symbols, systems, selfconcept, attitudes, meaning, and nonverbal message cues. Prerequisite: SPCH 240 (not required for applied and organizational communication minors, but recommended).

title: Communication and Group Process
description: Survey and analysis of smallgroup literature relevant to speech communication. Major areas included are group formation and structure, group effectiveness and efficiency, group tasks, individual versus group conformity goals, intragroup lines of communication, status and leadership problems, problem solving and conflict resolution, role relationships, and organizational techniques and problems. Prerequisite: SPCH 330 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Communication in Organizations
description: Introduces contemporary understandings of fundamental organizational communication concepts and the basic functions of communication in organizations. Content is approached from a variety of theoretical perspectives. Prerequisite recommended: SPCH 240, 350.

title: Communication Consultation
description: Focuses on the role and obligations of the communication consultant. Emphasis is placed upon interpersonal and team decisionmaking skills as well as developing breadth of knowledge, theoretical coherence, and the capacity to employ practical communication analysis and intervention consistent with organizational goals. Prerequisite: SPCH 451.

title: Human Communication Inquiry
description: Introduces, reviews, and evaluates the various methods of research in the field of human communication from which the discipline's body of knowledge is derived. Open only to juniors and seniors.

title: Practical Experience
description: Unpaid supervised work experience with business firms or public agencies related to careers in speech communication. Job possibilities may include, but are not limited to, working on political campaigns, in business offices, or at summer camps. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to majors or minors in Speech Communication. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Directed Study in Speech
description: Students with areas in the Department of Speech Communication pursue a specific subject in depth in consultation with a member of the faculty. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned. DEPARTMENT OF SPEECH PATHOLOGY AND AUDIOLOGY R. Hoops, Chairperson; M. J. Germani, L. Heady, T. Hemeyer, C. Hubbard, W. Kramer, G. Lindell, C. Saben, C. Updike Speechlanguage pathologists provide diagnostic services and therapy to people with speech or language problems. Audiologists provide testing, hearingaid, and other rehabilitative services to people with hearing problems. Speechlanguage pathologists and audiologists work in medical settings, schools, private practice, community and university clinics, nursing homes, and industrial settings. The Department of Speech Pathology and Audiology's programs are accredited by the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. To become speech pathologists or audiologists, students must complete both bachelor's and master's degrees. As part of their work, students acquire extensive clinical practicum experience working with patients who have speech, language, and hearing problems. The department offers a professional undergraduate major in speechlanguage pathology and audiology. The major, combined with an appropriate graduate program, leads to a state professional license, national certification, and school certification. Admission to the clinical portion of the major is selective. Students should obtain a copy of the department's "Undergraduate Major Admission and Progression Policies" from the departmental office (AC 104). The department operates the Ball State University Speech, Language, and Hearing Clinic as an oncampus facility where students can have their initial practicum experiences under the supervision of the department's faculty. title: Survey of Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to speechlanguage pathology and audiology and a survey of communication disorders. Particularly helpful for persons thinking about careers in communication disorders or in related fields (teaching, nursing, gerontology, etc.).

title: Clinical Phonetics
description: Study of phonetics as applied to communication disorders. Transcription practice of normal and abnormal speech. Relationship of phonological transcription and analysis to communication disorders.

title: Anatomy and Physiology of Speech and Hearing
description: Study of the anatomy and physiology of the speech and hearing mechanisms. Includes respiratory, phonatory, articulatoryresonance, and hearing mechanisms.

title: Disorders of Articulation and Phonology 1
description: Overview of articulatory phonetics and normal/disordered phonological development. Discussion of structural, neurologic, and environmental conditions contributing to phonologic disability in children. Assessment and treatment procedures for children with phonological disorders. Prerequisite: SPAA 101. Speech Pathology and Audiology 313

title: Computer Applications in Speech- Language Pathology and Audiology
description: Introduction to computer applications in speechlanguage pathology and audiology. Overview of computer use in general, then consideration of applications. Word processing, speechlanguage analysis programs, and programs for patient use in therapy will be included. Open only to SPAA majors.

title: Language Development
description: Overview of language and language development. Consideration of phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics. Theories of language acquisition. Cultural diversity as related to language. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Clinical Procedures and Observations
description: Methods course to prepare speechlanguage pathology and audiology students for clinical practicum. Overview of professional, ethical, diagnostic, and therapy topics. Observation of therapy is required. Prerequisite: SPAA 101, 210, and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Diagnosis and Appraisal
description: Techniques in the diagnosis of speech, language, and hearing disorders. Recognizing and understanding the components of differential diagnosis. Practice in the administration and interpretation of selected tests. Prerequisite: SPAA 101, 210, and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to approved clinical SPAA majors.

title: Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology Clinical Practicum
description: Clinical practicum in speechlanguage pathology and audiology. Students perform observations and provide supervised clinical services for persons with various communication disorders. Prerequisite: SPAA 311 and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to approved clinical SPAA majors. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 in any one semester or term.

title: Hearing 1: Anatomy/Physiology, Disorders, and Assessment
description: Overview of the anatomy and physiology of hearing, hearing disorders, and hearing assessment. Hearing screening. Practice in hearing testing.

title: Hearing 2: Aural Habilitation
description: Overview of aural habilitation. Practical implications of various types of hearing losses and appropriate habilitative procedures. Amplification, auditory training, speechreading, education and vocational considerations, and psychosocial implications of hearing loss. Prerequisite: SPAA 343.

title: Clinical Audiology: Orientation and Visitation
description: Orientation to the practice of clinical audiology in various settings and work environments. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to preaudiology preparation majors.

title: Speech Acoustics
description: Introduction to the physical nature of speech and its relationship to speech production and perception.

title: Neuroanatomy and Neurophysiology of Speech, Language, and Hearing
description: Overview of neuroanatomy and neurophysiology with a concentration on neurological mechanisms related to speech, language, and hearing. Prerequisite: SPAA 161.

title: Child Language Disorders 1
description: Introduction to the nature, cause, and treatment of language disorders in children. Prerequisite: SPAA 270.

title: Stuttering 1: Research and Theory
description: An introduction to the disorder of stuttering with attention directed to its symptoms and development. Reviews the research and theoretical formulations regarding stuttering and its treatment. Prerequisite: SPAA 210.

title: Organic Speech and Language Disorders
description: An overview of speech and language disorders resulting from organic pr o bl ems. Areas covered include cerebral palsy, aphasia, cleft palate, dysphagia, vocal abuse, head trauma, and laryngectomy. Prerequisite: SPAA 161.

title: Orientation and Clinical Practicum in School Settings
description: Orientation and clinical practicum in speechlanguage pathology and audiology in school settings. Prerequisite: SPAA 319 and permission of the department chairperson. Open only to approved clinical SPAA majors.

title: Directed Study in Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology
description: Individual directed study in speechlanguage pathology and audiology. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. The department's internships allow selected students to gain an insight into actual work in their chosen careers. These student interns have been placed in markets throughout the United States after course work is complete, but before earning 126 credits. The Letterman Telecommunications Scholarships are offered to majors and minors in telecommunications. One fully funded scholarship (tuition, room and board, personal expenses, and transportation) for one year is awarded each year. The specific amount will be determined by the Office of Scholarships and Financial Aid. A number of partially funded scholarships are also awarded each year. The scholarships are awarded on the basis of creative endeavor. Grades are not a criterion, and only fulltime firstsemester juniors through firstsemester seniors are eligible. Majors must have grades of C or better and a 2.5 G.P.A. for all classes taken in an option including the pretelecommunications courses. They must earn credit for four semesters or the equivalent of study in one modern or classical language. Students may be able to earn some language credit by passing an exam and should consult the Department of Modern Languages and Classics about credit by exam. 2. Telecommunications minors must earn grades of C or better and have a 2.5 G.P.A. for all classes taken in the minor including the pretelecommunications courses. They must also earn credit for two semesters or the equivalent of study in one modern or classical language. 3. Film minors must earn grades of C or better and have a 2.5 G.P.A. for all classes taken in the minor. It is strongly recommended that students completing the film minor also take at least two semesters of either Italian or French. All 300-400 level telecommunications courses required for completion of a required option in the major must be completed at Ball State. title: Developmental History of Telecommunications
description: Historical review of the development of telecommunications as an industry. Emphasis is on growth of radio and television as a communication system in a social setting. Special attention is given to technological advances past and current in the industry.

title: Writing for Telecommunications
description: Designed to provide an understanding of and practice with the styles and techniques used in writing for the media in telecommunications. Includes extensive writing, producing scripts for commercials, news, and programs presented using electronic media. Prerequisite: TCOM 200. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (1-3) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles to be announced before each semester. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors. Does not count toward the telecommunications major or minor. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Media Analysis and Criticism
description: Covers the fundamental critical approaches to narrative study as applied to the telecommunications discipline. Prerequisite: TCOM 200.

title: Regulations of Telecommunications
description: Legal regulations that are foundations of telecommunications. Legal history from 1910 to the present. Actions by Congress, the Supreme Court, federal courts, and the states. Case studies of rulings that most affect daily broadcasting. Prerequisite: TCOM 200.

title: Programs: Evaluation and Analysis
description: Analysis and appreciation of the complexity of programming decisions through examination of concepts, strategies, and techniques practiced by broadcasters. Includes an examination of programmatic content in order to evaluate program quality. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Organizational Video Production
description: Video production that meets the requirements of business, industry, medicine, and special interest organizations. Identifying needs; planning, executing, and evaluating productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses, and TCOM 332. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: News Writing and Performance
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering, writing, and reporting broadcast news. Practical experience in the uses of audio tape recorders and telephone recording, electronic news gathering (ENG) equipment, and other similar equipment used by radio and television news reporters. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Electronic News Gathering
description: Study and practice in the methods of gathering, shooting, editing, and reporting news with electronic news gathering (ENG) video equipment. Students will plan, shoot, edit, and produce a varied series of news reports. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Not open to students who have credit in JOURN 385. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Audio Production
description: Emphasizes techniques and skills needed for audio production. Typical experiences in radio broadcasting. A practical test is part of the final examination, and students are expected to maintain a record of their productions. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Video Production
description: Covers the basic skills of equipment operation in miniproductions that simulate television station programming. A practical test is part of the final examination, and students must maintain a record of their course work. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Single Camera Video Production
description: Orientation and practice in producing, directing, and designing projects in the singlecamera style used in film and television. Preand postproduction processes including planning, writing, editing, and camera operation will be studied as well as film theory and techniques. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. in these four courses, and TCOM 330, 332. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Radio Sales
description: Study and practice of the skills for selling radio time. Both selling strategies and the use of marketing research tools are emphasized. Includes practice in preparing sales presentations for clients. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Broadcast Promotion
description: Promotional concepts, strategies, and methodologies available for carrying out efficient and effective promotional campaigns for broadcast stations. Includes practice designing and executing audience, image, and sales promotions. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses and TCOM 306. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Television Sales
description: Skills needed for selling television time. Emphasizes the use of quantitative audience research tools. Includes practice in preparing sales presentations for clients. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: World Film History 1
description: History of world cinema from its beginning until World War II. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as key movements in other national cinemas before 1941, such as German Expressionism and the Soviet Montage School. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: World Film History 2
description: Continues the study of world cinema from World War II until the present. Study of the continuing influence of American cinema, as well as the post-1945 national cinema movements exemplified by Italian Neo- Realism and the French New Wave films. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Film Genres
description: Study of the general types and forms of film expressions, each identified with a specific tradition. Film genres include westerns, screwball comedies, gangster films, musicals, etc. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Announcing
description: Concentrates on training and practice in the vocal interpretive skills necessary for speech presentation. Studies the structure and use of the human vocal system; analysis of copy; and delivery of verbal messages in radio, television, and recording. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Sports Announcing
description: Research, writing, production, and performance with emphasis on the remote broadcast. Study of rules, organization and planning, promotion and selling, techniques of playbyplay, and color description of major sports. Lab includes onsite practical experience. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Independent Study
description: Special service, directed by a faculty member or an approved representative of an outside agency directly related to the subject. Term project is a written report. A written proposal for a project in telecommunications must be submitted to the department four weeks before the term of study. Prerequisite: junior standing, permission of the department chairperson, and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Internship Study
description: Presents an opportunity to gain practical, applied onthejob experience with an approved agency directly related to the business. Must make written application to the department and meet criteria before enrollment. Prerequisite: junior standing, permission of the department chairperson, and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum
description: Production of an audio or audiovideo project. Requires submission of a detailed outlined proposal of the project to the faculty member who will direct it. A written proposal for a project must be submitted four weeks before the term of study. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Honors Colloquium in Telecommunications
description: Exploration of selected issues in telecommunications with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. Open only to Honors students.

title: Social Responsibility
description: Political, economic, social, and governmental influences on telecommunications. Examines contemporary issues that confront broadcasters today and the ethics surrounding them. Prerequisite: senior standing, and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Organizational Media Management
description: Examination of the special requirements of business, industrial, medical, and other uses of television for instruction, information, public relations, etc. Special emphasis on budgeting and management. Corporate program sources are considered. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Advanced R-TV News Reporting
description: Instruction and practice in reporting, writing, and producing indepth broadcast news stories. Emphasis is on investigative techniques, interviewing, and strategies for finding information from public records and databases. Assignments designed for use in campus electronic media programs. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses, and TCOM 320. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Newscasting
description: Planning, gathering, writing, and presenting a television and radio newscast. Discussion of current events; evaluation of commercial station newscasts; onair production of typical news programs. Productionclass periods are three hours long. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 GPA for these four courses, and TCOM 320, 323, 380. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Advanced Audio Production
description: Application of advanced audio techniques to radio, television, motion pictures, and other electronic media presentation environments. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses and TCOM 330. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Advanced Video Production
description: Advanced television production with more original and longer productions. Format for programs written and produced duplicates typical programming in the commercial broadcast operation. Requires a record of produced projects. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses and TCOM 332. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Directing Drama for Television
description: Introduction to the processes and skills required to design and direct television drama. Emphasizes the effective use of the audiovisual language, camera blocking, and communication between directors and actors. Prerequisite: TCOM 332, 334, and permission of the instructor. Not open to students who have credit in THEAT 299X. Open only to telecommunications production majors.

title: Management of Telecommunications
description: Problems and responsibilities of management in the telecommunications industry. Consists largely of guest lecturers, class discussion, management roleplaying, and computer projects to become familiar with administrative practices in the industry. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses, and TCOM 306, 340, 345. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Film Censorship
description: Emphasizes the moral measurements and restraints that have affected the film industry almost since its inception. A chronology of events influencing both the direction and content of motion pictures. Examines governmental, legal, church, and community pressures and restraints. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Seminar in Film Theory
description: Analysis of the key theorists in the history of world cinema as well as some influential critics of film. A special focus on the documentary film. Examines many dimensions of the documentary film: historical, commercial, informational, educational, and propaganda applications. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Film Production
description: Basic introduction to super-8 film production, as well as the theory behind the technique. Includes planning, writing, and producing minifilms. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses, permission of the instructor, and TCOM 363. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Communications Technologies
description: Explores technologies beyond the conventional broadcast and organizational systems. Topics include computer incorporation into video, fiber optic and laser transmission, teledata, home access, and interactive video. Changes in topics will reflect the newest technologies incorporated into electronic media. Prerequisite: senior standing, and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 G.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Seminar in Television Production
description: Requires planning, writing, and producing a major project in television. Each project, as it moves through development, will serve as a case study for the class to discuss and evaluate. Prerequisite: TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses, permission of the department chairperson, and TCOM 332, 434; THEAT 101.

title: Video Graphics Technology
description: Provides working knowledge of video computer graphic programs using Cubicomp graphics generators. Manipulating DOS files, drawing backgrounds with True Color Paint, creating threedimensional objects with Build, and combining Draw and Build for animation images in Motion program are included. Prerequisite: senior standing and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 C.P.A. for these four courses. Open only to approved telecommunications majors or minors.

title: Senior Telecommunications Seminar
description: Covers the principles of media research. Illustrates applications of research within electronic communication, both for scholarly investigation and for use in support of the functions of broadcasting. Principles and practice in writing about results of research. Prerequisite: senior standing, and TCOM 200, 202, 302, 304 with C or better grades and a 2.5 GPA for these four courses. title: Teachers as Community Leaders
description: Practice in community leadership skills by working in a community agency as a volunteer.

title: Instructional Strategies in Multicultured Schools
description: Theory and application of instructional strategies of teaching and learning in school classrooms with special emphasis on multicultural education situations. Not open to students who have credit in EDSEC 301.

title: Introduction to Computers for Teachers K-12
description: Designed to give prospective teachers a basic understanding of the computer curriculum and of computer applications in grades K-12.

title: Mediation of Instructional Design
description: Theory and application of educational media and technology to improvement of teaching and learning in elementary school and secondary schools. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Cooperative Education Field Experience
description: Paid cooperative education field experiences in schools or other educationrelated settings. Requires periodic reports and completion of a course project. Does not meet professional laboratory experience requirements for teacher certification. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Bilingual Theory and Program Development
description: Survey of linguistic, cognitive, and cultural characteristics of bilingualism emphasizing the effects of these languagerelated features on bilingual/bicultural education in the United States. Emphasizes program design, model programs in operation, and legislative mandates.

title: Bilingual Evaluation and Methods
description: Considers the educational needs of bilingual students with specific regard to the evaluation of existing materials, the development of materials, and appropriate bilingual classroom methodology.

title: Honors Colloquium in Education
description: The critical analysis and evaluation of selected controversial issues in American education. Restricted to honors students.

title: Understanding Cultural Diversity in American Education
description: Designed to prepare prospective teachers to analyze lifestyles of different cultural groups. Emphasizing children's strengths within their cultural contexts will be an important focus. Prerequisite: EDSEC 205. PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES PRE-STUDENT TEACHING PROFESSIONAL LABORATORY EXPERIENCES The purpose of prestudent teaching professional laboratory experiences is to give students pursuing teacher education a systematic, planned sequence of experiences in appropriate educational settings. These experiences are designed to make students familiar with principles of classroom management and the teachinglearning process in practical and real school environments and to help them learn how to teach. The prestudent teaching laboratory experiences culminate in EDEL 360; EDJHM 285; or EDSEC 280 which require assignment to classrooms in appropriate educational settings for the semester to observe, prepare instructional presentations, and undertake other instructional tasks appropriate for students before student teaching. The university provides laboratory settings for EDEL 360; EDJHM 285; and EDSEC 280 in the oncampus Burris Laboratory School as well as in affiliated public school systems in Muncie and others within commuting distance. Seminars with a college supervisor are an integral part of the laboratory experience for these courses. STUDENT TEACHING Student teaching in Indiana gives students an opportunity to develop teaching competence under supervision of professionally licensed teachers cooperating with the university in the studentteaching program. Application for Student Teaching Students should apply for studentteaching assignments in September of the year before that in which they expect to student teach. See the Office of Professional Laboratory Experiences for additional information. Official notification of the studentteaching assignment will be mailed to students after the final eligibility determination, usually during the semester before student teaching. Students needing information about their assignments before this notification may inquire at the studentteaching office. General Consideration Students must be free of outside commitments that might interfere with fulltime studentteaching obligations. Students should not be regularly employed, nor should they carry heavy loads of extracurricular activities. Enrollment for course overload during the semester is permitted only with approval of the coordinator for student teaching. Student teaching requirements also include a set number of days in seminars conducted by the university supervisor at the beginning and end of the semester. Students should be prepared to accept studentteaching assignments wherever the university can place them for the best professional experience. Although requests for particular supervising teachers, schools, or school systems are considered, the placement process requires close cooperation with the public school systems, and there are instances when circumstances within the local school system make it impossible to honor a specific placement request. Student Teaching: Senior High, Junior High/Middle School License, grades 5-12 Student teachers preparing to teach at the senior high, junior high, and middle school levels are required to spend full time for a minimum of ten weeks in student teaching. They must enroll in EDSEC 460 (4 hours) and EDSEC 462 (3 hours). Students may take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching (3-5 hours), to complete an additional part or the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: All-Grade License Student teachers preparing to teach at the allgrade level are required to spend full time for a minimum of ten weeks in student teaching. They must enroll in EDALG 470 (4 hours) and EDALG 472 (3 hours). Students may take EDSEC 465, Elective Student Teaching (3-5 hours), to complete part or the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: Elementary Standard License Students seeking licensure in elementary education must enroll for 9 semester hours in EDEL 463 (3 hours) and EDEL 464 (6 hours) and spend full time for ten weeks in Counseling Psychology and Guidance Services 329 student teaching. Students who want to take elective credits in student teaching may enroll for up to 3 hours in EDEL 465, Elective Student Teaching, for assignment for the rest of the semester. Student Teaching: Early Childhood Standard License Students seeking licensure in early childhood education must enroll in EDEL 461 for 6 hours and EDEL 462 for 3 hours and spend full time for ten weeks in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten-Primary Standard License Students seeking licensure in kindergartenprimary education must enroll for 12 hours in EDEL 467 (6 hours) and EDEL 468 (6 hours) and spend the entire semester in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten- Primary/Early Childhood Students completing the dual major on the standard license for early childhood and kindergartenprimary must enroll for EDEL 467 (6 hours, 8 weeks) and EDEL 465 (3 hours, 6 weeks), spending 14 weeks in student teaching for one semester. In another semester the student will enroll in EDEL 461 for 6 hours, for 8 weeks in student teaching. Student Teaching: Kindergarten Endorsement Students completing the kindergarten endorsement on the standard license for early childhood or elementary education must enroll in EDEL 465 for 3 hours— student teaching in kindergarten fulltime for six weeks. Student Teaching: Special Education Students with allgrade majors in special education will complete 12 hours in either SPCED 489 (Mild Disabilities) or SPCED 491 (Serious Emotional Handicaps) or SPCED 492 (Severe Disabilities). Students with allgrade majors in special education: hearing impairments will complete SPCED 466 (1-12 hours) for a minimum of 12 hours for sixteen weeks of fulltime student teaching. Students pursuing teaching minors or endorsements in special education must complete student teaching requirements in the area of concentration as follows: mildly mentally handicapped, 6 hours (seven to eight weeks); severe disabilities, 12 hours (sixteen weeks); hearing impairments, 6-9 hours (six to nine weeks). title: Career and Life Planning
description: Focuses on helping people make career and life plans. A series of such techniques as role playing, psychodrama, sociodrama, values clarification, and decision making are used to help students examine interrelated value systems associated with education, work, leisure, and selfexpression. Not open to juniors and seniors except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Relationship Development
description: An introduction to the basic psychological principles and techniques of enhancing relationships with self and others. Emphasis is given to understanding selflimiting behavior, selfunderstanding, and skill development and knowledge in the dynamics of interaction with others.

title: Interrelational Aspects of Sexuality
description: Emphasizes the psychological aspects of human sexuality, especially in relation to emotions, attitudes, and values. Stresses the psychological importance of responsibility for self in sexuality. Considers the psychological aspects of human sexual development, adjustment, dysfunction, and remediation. Designed to increase students' understanding and acceptance of their own sexuality and that of others.

title: Fundamentals of Counseling
description: Introduces the principles, purposes, and nature of counseling, including a review of basic counseling theories and the history of counseling, an exposure to research, and a discussion of issues in the practice of counseling.

title: Techniques of Psychological Interventions
description: Basic psychological principles and techniques of counseling. Intended as an exploratory didactic and experimental course for students planning to do graduate work in counseling and related areas or for those in other fields requiring skills in interviewing.

title: Introduction to Cross-Cultural Counseling
description: Opportunity to build expertise in counseling people of African- American, Hispanic, Asian, and American Indian heritage. Emphasizes understanding the social and political bases of counseling and therapy.

title: Issues in Counseling
description: Intensive study in selected areas of student need and interest in counseling. Opportunity for students to choose particular areas for indepth study under faculty supervision.
