title: Introduction to Landscape Architecture
description: An introduction to landscape architecture: lectures, site observations, and environmental experiences that focus on landscape architectural practice, representative projects, philosophy, and areas of specialization within the field.

title: People and the Environment
description: Lectures and seminars from disciplines on and off campus relating to influences of people on the environment and the environment on people as they relate to architecture and landscape architecture. Open to all students.

title: Site Design
description: Application of basic design principles, programming, and analysis to smallscale sitespecific landscape design problems. Visual and functional design principles as they relate to natural and cultural influences in landscape design. Prerequisite: CAP 102. Parallel: LA 214.

title: Park and Open Space Design
description: Design projects emphasizing park design, park and recreational master planning, and openspace design in rural, suburban, or urban settings. Prerequisite: LA 201.

title: Field Studies
description: Onsite studies of landscape architectural projects and practices, natural areas, and historic sites and landscapes. Urban or rural field trips; may include visits to professional offices andpublic planning and design agencies. One threetofiveday field trip is required. This course is offered for credit/no credit only. Parallel: LA 201.

title: Field Studies 2
description: Group field studies of landscape architectural projects and practices, natural areas, and historic sites and landscapes. Urban and rural field trips may include visits to professional offices and public planning and design agencies. A minimum of one threetofiveday field trip is required. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Landscape Architecture History 1
description: The history of landscape architecture from ancient times to 1800. Examples of landscape expressions of the humanenvironment relationship resulting in the conscious shaping of urban and rural landscapes, and the creation of such landscapes as parks, gardens, and urban plazas.

title: Landscape Architecture History 2
description: The history of landscape architecture from 1800 to the present. Emphasis is on the North American humanenvironment relationship, its relationship to European antecedents, and other cultural parallels in landscape design. Prerequisite: LA 220.

title: Landscape Architectural Design Communications
description: Methods of landscape architectural design communications; integrates techniques of handdrawn and computer graphics, photography, and video. Prerequisite: CAP 162.

title: Environmental Systems
description: Qualitative investigations and analysis of landscape systems. Studies include the assessment of vegetation, climate, hydrology, soils, and subsurface geology as determinants of landscape architectural form; natural processes as they relate to the principles of landscape architectural construction.

title: Computer Applications in Landscape Architecture
description: An introduction to the use of microcomputers in landscape architecture. Emphasis is on twoand threedimensional computeraided design and drawing, landscape data inventory and analysis, and landscape engineering. Prerequisite: CAP 162. Parallel: LA 202.

title: Housing and Community Design
description: Design projects focusing on social, political, economic, cultural, and environmental issues as they relate to landplanning and site design for housing developments and residential communities. Prerequisite: LA 202.

title: Planting Design
description: Design problems focusing on the functional, ecological, and aesthetic uses of plants in the landscape. Prerequisite: LA 301, 341; and BIO 112 or 216.

title: Landscape Architectural Engineering 1
description: Principles and practices of landscape engineering. Emphasis is on the techniques and applications of land surveying, earthwork techniques including grading and estimation, and principles of site drainage. Prerequisite: LA 270.

title: Landscape Architectural Engineering 2
description: Principles and practices of landscape architecture engineering and construction with emphasis on landscape materials, structures, planting, and fabrication techniques. Includes design implementation techniques and construction documents. Prerequisite: LA 311.

title: Landscape Plants 1
description: The study of woody landscape plants, including plant identification and plant adaptation to urban and natural environmental conditions.

title: Landscape Plants 2
description: The study of herbaceous landscape plants including plant identification and landscape cultural requirements. Emphasis is on both outdoor and indoor plants.

title: Landscape Architecture Internship
description: A minimum of one semester of supervised, nonpaid employment under the direction of a registered landscape architect. Departmental approval required in advance of qualified employment. Requires employer and selfevaluation reports. This course is offered for credit/no credit only. Prerequisite: LA 302. Not open to students who have credit in LA 369.

title: Landscape Architecture Internship
description: A minimum of ten weeks of supervised, paid employment under the direction of a registered landscape architect or allied design professional. Departmental approval required in advance ofqualified employment. Requires employer and selfevaluation reports. Offered for credit/nocredit only. Not open to students who have credit in LA 368. Landscape Architecture 107

title: Regional Landscape Design
description: The application of principles of landscape architectural design to largescale landscape settings. Topics include land planning, visual quality management, and natural and cultural landscape resource management. Prerequisite: LA 302.

title: Urban Design
description: Design studio emphasizing the physical and sociobehavioral influences on the design of cities. Projects may focus on the design of new urban environments or the redesign and revitalization of existing urban centers. May include interdisciplinary studies. Prerequisite: LA 401 or permission of the instructor.

title: Landscape Architecture Comprehensive Project
description: Analytical, conceptual, and design development processes applied to a comprehensive project in landscape architecture. Emphasis on guided independent design work based on individual initiative. Prerequisite: LA 403 and 451.

title: Special Design Studio
description: Design studio emphasizing special or unique topics in landscape architecture. Studio may be offered at oncampus or offcampus sites, may be part of an approved foreign study program. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor and the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Landscape Architectural Engineering 3
description: Principles and practices of landscape engineering and construction. Emphasis on roadway and parking lot engineering, practices of storm water management, and advanced grading. Prerequisite: LA 312.

title: Historic Landscape Preservation
description: Survey of the history, theory, and methodologies of historic landscape preservation. Includes topics in both vernacular and designed historic landscape preservation, primarily in North America. Prerequisite: LA 221 or permission of the instructor.

title: Philosophy of Landscape Architecture
description: Readings, seminars, and lectures in the background and development of historic and contemporary philosophies of landscape architecture. Includes discussions of design and environmental issues, land use, and professional ethics. Prerequisite: LA 221 or permission of the instructor.

title: Park and Recreation Planning and Design
description: Lectures, case studies, and readings related to the interdisciplinary role of the landscape architect in park and recreation planning, design, administration, and maintenance. Prerequisite: LA 202 or permission of the instructor.

title: Landscape Operations
description: Techniques and practices of landscape grounds development and maintenance. Topics may include plant growth, development, and evaluation; plant and turf installation; pruning, irrigation, and landscape management plans. Prerequisite: LA 341 or permission of the instructor.

title: Interior Landscape Design
description: Techniques and practices of interior planting design, development, and maintenance. Topics may include environmental conditions affecting plant growth, principles of interior planting design, and interior plant management. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Landscape Architecture Research
description: Methods, procedures, and case studies of landscape architectural research. Includes guided development of an individual research program and proposal leading to the landscape architecture comprehensive project (LA 404). Prerequisite: LA 403.

title: Professional Practice
description: Methods and practices of the profession of landscape architecture. Subjects include business and governmental organization, elements of contract law, business management, marketing, professional licensure, and ethics. Prerequisite: LA 302 and 368 or 369.

title: Landscape Architectural Design Communications 2
description: Advanced methods of landscape architectural design communications using a variety of media. Prerequisite: CAP 162.

title: Portfolio Preparation
description: The preparation of resumes, portfolios, and brochures related to securing internship positions and other landscape architectural employment.

title: Environmental Impact Analysis
description: Review of the environmental design arts and their implications relative to proposed actions that affect the environment. Covers procedures and methodologies used in impact analysis and documentation. Prerequisite: LA 302 or permission of the instructor.

title: Computer-Aided Landscape Design
description: Twoand threedimensional computeraided design techniques with emphasis on site design, master planning, and regional landscape design. Incorporates microcomputer or mainframebased CAD systems. Prerequisite: LA 280 or permission of the instructor.

title: Independent Projects
description: An independent study in environmental topics. Prerequisite: approval of the program proposal by a faculty advisor, the professor responsible for study assessment, and the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Special Projects in Landscape Architecture
description: Special and timely landscape architectural projects undertaken by groups of students. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term. Truex The urban planning program prepares students for professional careers as urban planners in the public and private sectors. Graduates work for city, county, and regional planning agencies, planning consultants, nonprofit organizations, and private firms dealing with urban growth and revitalization in large and small communities. Planning at Ball State combines physical and policy approaches. Students are taught to improve the design quality of constructed environments while protecting and managing the resources of our natural environments. Students learn the process of community and economic development, and develop strategies for affordable housing, job creation, and energyefficient development. Whether as private developers or public officials, graduates are expected to have a commitment to improving community life for citizens of all incomes, and a broad competence to make both new and old communities better places to live. The fiveyear Bachelor of Urban Planning Degree, which is fully accredited by the Planning Accreditation Board, prepares students for entry directly into professional planning positions. The fouryear Bachelor of Science in Environmental Design major is for students going directly on to graduate studies or into nonprofessional jobs. Urban Planning 109 MAJOR IN URBAN PLANNING AND DEVELOPMENT (B.U.P.D.), 108 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS

title: Introduction to Urban Planning and Development
description: An introduction to urban planning and development. Open to all students.

title: Community Analysis and Design Studio
description: Analysis and design principles on an urban and metropolitan scale, including location criteria for land use and analysis of environmental suitability for development. Introduces computerassisted models for landsuitability analysis. Prerequisite: CAP firstyear core program.

title: Project Analysis and Design Studio
description: Site analysis and design principles for smallscale urban projects, including building complexes, subdivisions, and neighborhood development. Students present and defend designs for specific site locations. Prerequisite: PLAN 201.

title: History and Theory of Planning 1
description: Growth and evolution of cities. Evolution theories and practice of urban planning, with emphasis on the United States before 1940.

title: History and Theory of Planning 2
description: Evolution of theories and practice of urban planning, with emphasis on the United States since 1940. Interaction of public and private initiatives directed toward urban and environmental problems.

title: Planning and Private Development
description: The process of privatesector land development, including market analysis and site selection, physical design, financing, legal constraints, and assembly of the development package.

title: Communication and Presentation Techniques
description: Development of graphic and visualization skills for planners. Use of a variety of communication techniques and media for public presentation. Open only to planning majors and minors.

title: Information Management for Economic Development Planning
description: Information management and tools and strategies for community economic development, including use of census and other published data sources, generation of community data, community assessment, recommendations, and presentation of findings. Prerequisite: PLAN 202

title: Information Management for Urban and Neighborhood Planning
description: Information management for urbanand neighborhoodscale planning, including design and implementation of data surveys, use and interpretation of census and other published data sources, and analysis and presentation of findings. Use of computers for data storage and manipulation. Prerequisite: PLAN 301.

title: Quantitative Methods for Urban Planning
description: Calculation, application, and interpretation of statistics and quantitative models used in urban planning. Topics include association, variation, probability sampling, regression, and models for population forecasting.

title: Urban Land-Use Planning
description: Principles of urban landuse planning for newly developing areas and for changing older communities. Attention to environmental, efficiency, and aesthetic concerns in urban growth. Preparation of the comprehensive urban landuse plan.

title: Theory of Urban Spatial Planning
description: Seminar in theories of location and development of principal urban activities including transportation, housing, industry, commercial centers, andpublic facilities. Implications for urbanplanning policies.

title: Computer Applications in Planning
description: Microcomputer applications using spreadsheets, databases, and modeling and mapping packages suitable for planning and development office use. Brief overview of Intergraph graphic and mapping applications.

title: Economic Development Planning
description: Strategies and tools for stimulation of local economic growth including government incentives, financing alternatives, and examples of publicprivate partnership in strategic planning.

title: Planning Paid Internship
description: Supervised paid work experience for at least 450 hours in public agency, private firm, or other urban planning and development setting. May not be taken before completing the third year of the program. Normally finished before the fifthyear of the program. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Field Studio
description: Analysis and application of planning skills in a realworld setting, involving an actual community or outside client. Emphasis on smaller town or rural planning issues. Prerequisite: PLAN 302.

title: Field Studio
description: Analysis and application of planning skills in a realworld setting, involving an actual community or outside client. Emphasis on urban planning issues. Prerequisite: PLAN 302.

title: Theory of Urban Design
description: Urban design with emphasis on its vocabulary and scope, especially space, form, scale, time, and function. Aspects of physical planning in relation to social, economic, and political forces, as well as the role of the urban designer in the planning process. Urban Planning 111

title: Planning Research Studio
description: Research techniques for developing and testing planning proposals. Design and submission of a formal research proposal, typically the basis for the student's thesis project. Prerequisite: PLAN 402.

title: Planning Thesis
description: Development of an individual project or urban development design, with emphasis on the evaluation of alternative solutions and presentation of final report. Prerequisite: PLAN 405.

title: Planning Internship
description: Supervised nonpaid work experience for at least 450 hours in a public agency, private firm, or other urban planning and development setting. May not be taken before completing the third year of the program. Normally finished before the fifth year of the program. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Geographic Information Systems for Urban Planning
description: Designed to introduce principles of GIS and GIS applications in an urban,, environment. Topics include GIS components, modeling methodology, and management of environments. Implications for urban and environmental policy development.

title: Advanced Concepts in Geographic Information Systems for Urban Planning
description: Advanced topics in modeling and analysis of urban and regional environments. Techniques for database organization, database development, and analytical processes (algorithm development). Prerequisite: PLAN 412.

title: Theory of Comprehensive Planning
description: Seminar in issues of comprehensive planning, including the planning process, public participation in planning, and the role of political, social, and economic conditions in planning decisions.

title: Urban Impact Analysis
description: Techniques for estimating the environmental, socioeconomic, fiscal, and energy effects of proposed plans and development projects.

title: Housing and Community Development
description: Analysis of public programs, and market conditions affecting housing and community development. Housing supply and demand, finance, the role of government subsidies.

title: Urban Transportation Planning
description: Transportation planning methods and policy, including analysis of travel demand, links between land use and transportation, choice of transportation modes, and design of balanced transportation systems.

title: Environmental Planning
description: Introduction to the fundamental issues and technologies associated with planning for sensitive use of environmental resources. Topics include waste management, air and water quality planning, ecological systems, and methods of environmental analysis and implementation.

title: Energy Planning
description: Energy resource issues in urban planning. Strategies for incorporating energy efficiency in housing, land use, transportation, social services, and community development. Analysis of ener policy, with emphasis on innovative public and private sector initiatives at the community level.

title: Community Facilities Planning
description: Design principles and economic conditions in planning for urban physical facilities, including recreation facilities, streets, sidewalks, drainage, water supply systems, sewerage, waste treatment, and others.

title: Philosophy, History, and Theory of Historic Preservation
description: Survey of the philosophy, history, and theory of historic preservation, primarily in Europe and North America. Not open to students who have credit in ARCH 440.

title: Preservation Techniques and Policies
description: Planning and programming for preservation, restoration, and neighborhood conservation, economic and legal consideration in federal, state, and private programs in preservation and restoration. Not open to students who have credit in ARCH 441.

title: Documentation of Historic Sites and Buildings
description: Methods of documenting historic sites and buildings using various survey and inventory forms. Extensive oral and written descriptive analysis of historic buildings.

title: Neighborhood Planning
description: Planning strategies for revitalization of older residential neighborhoods and neighborhood commercial areas. Includes community organization and the role of public and private neighborhood organizations.

title: Issues of Planning Practice
description: Capstone seminar to explore application of theory to planning practice and management. Issues of planning ethics, citizen participation, styles and strategies for effective implementation of planning. Prerequisite: PLAN 369 or 410, 401 or 402.

title: Urban Planning Law
description: Legal tools for plan implementation, including zoning, subdivision regulations, planned unitdevelopment regulations, and other techniques for guiding urban development while balancing community interests and private property rights.

title: Center City Revitalization
description: Strategies for revitalization of core urban areas, including case studies of successful cities. Examples include employmentbased, recreation and conventionbased, and residentially based revitalization.

title: Alternative and Sustainable Community Planning
description: Seminar course examining nontraditional approaches to community planning and design. Focuses on concepts associated with the design of sustainable communities. Historical precedent, case study, and utopian alternatives are synthesized to project alternative futures for present community planning and design issues.

title: History of Urban Form
description: Analysis of urban centers and city planning, emphasizing spatial organization, order, andphilosophy of planning in architecture.

title: Independent Study in Planning
description: Independent study in urban planning and development topics, undertaken on an individual basis with guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Special Projects in Urban Planning and Development
description: Special projects in urban planning and development undertaken by groups of students under faculty direction. COLLEGE OF BUSINESS N. Palomba, Dean, J. Fitzgerald, Associate Dean All undergraduate programs in the College of Business are accredited by the American Assembly of Collegiate Schools of Business (AACSB). The Department of Accounting has earned separate AACSB Accreditation. AACSB requires that students not take more than 30 hours in the College of Business without formal admission to the college. Therefore, no two minors can be used in combination to fulfill any degree requirements outside the College of Business (except Economics). Requirements for Admission Students interested in pursuing majors in the College of Business will be classified as prebusiness students until they: • Attain junior standing (63 hours) with a minimum gradepoint average of 2.0. • Complete the following courses with a gradepoint average of at least 2.25: ACC 201, 202; BEOA 210; ECON 201, 202, 221; ENG 103, 104; MATHS 132. Students may register for 300- and 400-level business courses only if they have completed the admission courses or if they are currently enrolled in one final course necessary to complete the courses required for admission and if they have met the gradepoint requirement at the time of enrollment. A College of Business major is composed of the business core requirement and major specific requirements. Degree Requirements A bachelor's degree in business is awarded to students who meet these university and College of Business requirements. Students must: • Complete a minimum of 126 credit hours. • Complete all university general studies requirements. • Complete the specific requirements of the major. • Complete at least 63 hours from outside the College of Business (for this purpose, Economics and BEOA 210 are considered outside the college of Business). • Take 30 of the last 40 hours at Ball State University. In addition to this university requirement, students majoring in a program in the College of Business must earn the last 30 credits of their major in residence. • Maintain good academic standing with a minimum gradepoint average of 2.0. Transfer of Credit Transfers from Other Colleges and Universities Acceptance of credit from other institutions will be determined by the Office of Admissions. The applicability of credit toward degree requirements in the College of Business will be determined by the college. Courses in upper division business subjects (300/400-level) may be accepted for specific equivalency if the course work has been taken in the junior or senior year at a fouryear institution that is accredited by the AACSB. If the institution is not so accredited, credit in upper division courses accepted for transfer will be applicable only if prerequisites are similar to those of courses at Ball State University. This decision will be made by each department. • Any student enrolling at Ball State University to complete a second under/graduate degree in business will be required to meet both the residence requirement for the university and the College of Business. Business courses taken at twoyear institutions will not be applied to upper division requirements. Credit by Self-Acquired Competency The College of Business does not award credit in business courses on the basis of selfacquired competency. However, the college will give examinations for credit in specific courses. Consult the appropriate department chairperson for information. The college will not accept the transfer of credit for business courses from other institutions if the credit was awarded on the basis of selfacquired competency. Statute of Limitation If seven or more years have elapsed since last enrollment the student will be required to meet the degree requirements as stated in the current undergraduate catalog. Business Minors AACSB requires that students not take more than 30 hours in the College of Business without formal admission to the college. Therefore, no two minors can be used in combination to fulfill any degree requirements outside the College of Business (except Economics). Business Courses 300/400 Level: Enrollment in business courses numbered 300-499 is limited to • Admitted College of Business students; • Nonbusiness students who are pursuing minors in the College of Business; Business 115 • Nonbusiness students who are pursuing majors that require specific business courses; and • Nonbusiness students who have met all course prerequisites. Prerequisites are vigorously monitored. Students who enroll in classes for which they do not have the prerequisite will be dropped from the class. In addition to the associate and baccalaureate degree programs, the college offers a 3/2 program that allows students to earn both bachelor's degrees in sciences or humanities and master's of business administration (M.B.A.) degrees in five years. This special program is designed to give students an opportunity to combine their undergraduate studies in the sciences and humanities with graduate study in the College of Business. The following departments participate in the 3/2 program: anthropology, biology, chemistry, computer science, economics, English, modern languages and classics, geography, history, journalism, philosophy, political science, psychological science, sociology, social work, and speech communication. For more information, contact the director of undergraduate programs in the College of Business. title: Introduction to Business
description: Emphasizes the vital role of business in our society through a discussion of both the external environment of business and the internal environment of the business enterprise. Assesses the contribution of the social and behavioral sciences in the decisionmaking process. Not open to junior or senior business majors.

title: Internship in Business Administration
description: Under a College of Business approved and supervised program, business administration majors work fulltime as an intern for a business firm, governmental agency, or other type of organization. Effective with the CPA Examination in May of the year 2000, an Indiana candidate must possess 150 semester hours of education containing an equivalent of an accounting major in order to sit for the CPA examination. This means that a candidate can no longer sit for the CPA examination with a 126-hour bachelor's degree in accounting. Freshmen students entering the university in the fall of 1996 will be the first class subject to the 150-hour law. The department believes that if a student must take at least 24 hours beyond the B.S. degree, the student would prefer to have a master's degree rather than just 24 additional hours of undergraduate courses. The 150-hour law does not affect all accounting students equally. Only those entering the public accounting profession with the expectation of obtaining the CPA certificate must comply with the 150-hour law. Those accounting graduates who seek work with private businesses, government agencies, and notforprofit organizations may find the fouryear bachelor of science degree satisfactory. Sundaram, L. Sweeney, G. Wells, T. Zivney (Maxon Corporation Distinguished Professor of Finance) The Department of Finance offers a major and a minor in finance, and a major in insurance. Within the finance major, options are available to specialize in corporate financial management, financial institutions, financial planning, and real estate. A student of finance is prepared for a career specializing in financial functions and also for generalized management roles in organizations. Finance is the study of creation and management of wealth. It is especially concerned with the study of raising funds, deploying funds, and managing liquidity in order to achieve a set of objectives for individuals or businesses. The curriculum for finance majors is designed to provide an understanding of market mechanisms and how these mechanisms may be applied to intraorganizational decisions. The student will gain the analytical and quantitative skills to allocate scarce financial resources to achieve personal and organizational goals. A finance major will have a clear understanding of the role and the valuation of risky assets. The basic goals of the finance curriculum are to prepare students to understand the role of financial assets, markets, institutions, and regulation in the framework of American and global financial systems; to have a good working knowledge of the quantitative and analytical techniques of finance as applied to corporate finance, investment management, and management of financial institutions; to apply finance problem solving techniques to different areas of finance, such as project selection, security analysis and portfolio management, working capital management, financial analysis, sources and costs of capital; and to understand the interactive nature of finance with other functional areas in organizations. The insurance curriculum is designed to prepare students for employment in the insurance industry and organizations employing risk managers. These positions include underwriters, claims adjusters, brokers, agents, and risk managers. The goal of the insurance curriculum is to provide students with an understanding of the insurance industry and markets, risk management, life insurance, personal and commercial insurance, insurance law, and current topics in insurance. title: Current Topics in Business Law
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced business students for study of current topics and problems in business law. Topics may include current activity in property law, commercial law, and government regulation of business. Prerequisite: BL 260 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Business Law
description: An opportunity for students with superior scholastic records to study some special phase of business law. The topic selected, methods of study, and credit hours allowed must be approved by the department chairperson. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Personal Finance
description: The fundamental principles of general business and related economic concepts are considered from the consumer's point of view. Some of the topics studied are consumer buying and the use of credit, banking, insurance, investment, budgeting, and taxation. Not open to juniors and seniors majoring in business.

title: Introduction to the U.S. Financial System
description: U.S. financial system and its functions; financial markets, instruments, and intermediaries; growing role of intermediaries in the saving and lending process and implications; regulation, regulatory agencies, and financial safety net; competition, innovation, and integration in financial services industry; globalization and international competition. Prerequisite: ACC 201. Prerequisite or parallel: ECON 202.

title: Introduction to Financial Investments
description: Topics include financial markets and investment alternatives such as stocks, bonds, convertible securities, mutual funds, options, and futures. Market indexes (Dow Jones, etc.), market practices and timing, sources of financial data, and investing in an international environment will be discussed. Not open to juniors and seniors majoring in business. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Finance
description: Designed to study different areas of financial decision making in a business firm. Specific topics include financial objectives of the firm, sources of funds, working capital management, capital budgeting, investment decisions under uncertainty, valuation, capital structure decisions, and dividend policy. Prerequisite: ACC 202; BEOA 210, ECON 202, 221; junior standing.

title: International Finance
description: Financial problems and opportunities that confront the management of international firms. Sources and instruments of international finance, import and export financing, interrelationship of governmental and international agencies, and the current status of some. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Short-Term Financial Management
description: Designed to study financial tools and analyses relating to shortterm financial decisions. Topics include corporate treasury management, managing accounts receivable and payable, inventory financing, analysis of modeling, and other techniques. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Intermediate Financial Management
description: Designed to provide the foundations for advanced courses in finance. Topics include the nature and methodology of finance, risk and return, portfolio theory, investment decisions, capital structure, dividend policy, and longterm financing decisions. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Principles of Investments
description: Designed to introduce various securities (such as stocks, bonds, and money market instruments), their markets, and their valuation. Emphasizes the fundamental analysis of common stocks. Prerequisite: FIN 350.

title: Financial Markets and the Economy
description: Nature and functions of financial markets; classification and interrelation of domestic and international financial markets; determination of the level and structure of interest rates; effects of monetary policy on financial markets and the economy. Prerequisite: FIN 250, 350.

title: Internship in Finance
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program with a banking institution, business firm, or government agency for pay under the supervision of the finance department. Requires periodic written reports of job experience. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned in combination with FIN 481.

title: Portfolio Analysis and Management
description: Indepth study of portfolio and capital market theories. Topics include index models, portfolio planning, investment analysis and portfolio selection, portfolio evaluation techniques, and portfolio management using futures and options. Prerequisite: FIN 354, 355.

title: Managerial Decision Making in Finance
description: Capstone course emphasizing decision making in corporate financial planning, working capital management, capital budgeting, capital structure, dividend policy, mergers and acquisitions, and business development. Case analysis is commonly used as a method of instruction. Prerequisite: FIN 354, 355.

title: Operations of Financial Institutions
description: To integrate the various topics of finance with a view toward applications to the management of financial institutions in the following decision areas: assetliability management, cost control, profitability, capital adequacy, business development. Cases will be integrated in the method of instruction. Prerequisite: FIN 354, 355, 356.

title: Independent Study in Finance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who want to study some phase of finance. An intensive individualized program of reading, researching, or analyzing various finance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Insurance
description: A survey of the major kinds of insurance such as fire, transportation, casualty, health, life insurance, and fidelity and surety bonds.

title: Internship in Insurance
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program in the insurance industry or government agency for pay under the supervision of the finance department. Requires periodic written reports of job experience. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fundamentals of Life Insurance
description: Important methods of handling personal risks for business and individuals. An analysis of life insurance, annuities, pension plans, and social insurance. Special attention is given to the problems of underwriting, rate computation, and programming. Prerequisite: INS 270.

title: Fundamentals of Liability Insurance
description: The study of liability insurance and worker's compensation insurance with special emphasis on the insurance needs of the commercial enterprise. Prerequisite: INS 270.

title: Fundamentals of Property Insurance
description: The study of property insurance, including fire and allied lines, inland and ocean marine, and crime insurance with special emphasis on the insurance needs of the commercial enterprise. Prerequisite: INS 270.

title: Legal Aspects of Insurance
description: The law as applied to the insurance industry emphasizing the law of torts as the foundation of the insurer's liability, the law of contracts and agency as applied to the insurance policy, and government regulation of insurance. Prerequisite: BL 260 and INS 270.

title: Current Topics in Insurance
description: Designed to meet the needs of advanced insurance students for study of current topics and problems in any insurance or risk management area. Topics may include nofault, competitive rating laws, variable life insurance, and state versus federal regulations. Prerequisite: INS 270, 371, 375, and 376 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Insurance
description: Designed for academically qualified students who want to study some phase of insurance. An intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analyzing various insurance topics under the guidance of a faculty member. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Real Estate Principles
description: Economic import of real estate, real estate characteristics, landuse and environmental controls, legal concerns of real estate, methods of valuation, mortgage credit sources, secondary mortgage markets and financing techniques, investment analysis, land development, and real estate operations. Prerequisite: completion of general studies math requirement or permission of the instructor.

title: Real Estate Finance
description: The contractual nature and legal implications of the instruments used in real estate finance; instruments, techniques, and strategies in the financing of real estate investment; and the structure and operation of both primary and secondary mortgage markets. Gives students a background in real estate law and real estate finance. Prerequisite: RE 230.

title: Legal Aspects of Real Estate
description: Elementary concepts of real estate law and practice, particularly in the state of Indiana. Other topics include estates, property, leaseholds and ownerships, easements, transfers, escrows, contracts, zoning, brokers' regulations, license law, and title insurance.

title: Internship in Real Estate
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program in the real estate industry or government agency for pay under the supervision of the finance department. Requires periodic written reports of job experience. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study in Real Estate
description: Designed for the academically oualified who wish to study some phase f real estate. Intensive individualized program of reading, research, or analysis of various real estate topics under theguidance of a faculty member. Dealing with environmental competition, ethical issues, and diverse work groups is increasingly important in the managerial decision process. Programs leading to a bachelor of science degree in management are designed to give students the knowledge and skills in the latest concepts, tools, and techniques applicable to entrepreneurship and small business, human resource management, information systems, operations and manufacturing management, and general management. Students can elect to specialize in one of the following five options: • Operations and manufacturing management. This option prepares students to assume positions of responsibility in the creation of goods and services. • Human resource management. Students will learn to improve the effectiveness of employees in organizations. • Information systems. This option prepares students to assume positions of responsibility in the management of information systems functions in organizations. • Entrepreneurship and small business management. Students will learn to prepare for the challenges involved in new venture creation and small business management. • General management. This option provides students the skills to coordinate human and physical resources toward accomplishment of organizational goals. The department also offers the following minors: • Organizational communication. This minor is to provide students with exposure to important communication/human relations issues, especially as they relate to improving general communication skills, and applying human relations skills when dealing with supervisors, coworkers and subordinates. • Foundations of management. This program minor offers students the essential fundamental for practicing business management in numerous applied settings. title: Management Principles
description: Introduction to the basic concepts and principles of management. Focuses on structures within companies and processes within firms to bring principles to bear on the practical problems of managing organizations. Not open to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize applications in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: BEOA 210 or CS 116. Not open to students who have credit in CS 210.

title: The Family in Business
description: Focuses on the peculiar elements of familyowned businesses including initiation, development, management, growth, and succession. Special issues concerning the family organization and its dynamic relation to the business are explored from cultural, psychological, organizational, managerial, and legal perspectives. Prerequisite recommended: BUSAD 101. Not open to students who have credit in MGT 341. Open only to students designated as "prebusiness" or to any nonbusiness major.

title: Introductory Operations Management
description: Introduction to the tools and techniques of management with practical applications to the production of goods and services. Prerequisite: MGT 200 or the equivalent or parallel MGT 300. Not open to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major in the College of Business.

title: Personnel and Supervision
description: Introduction to the personnel and PREFIX NO ITMFG 105 9 hours from ITMFG 205 supervisory functions in organizations. Focuses on employee and union relationships; environmental business and social responsibilities; and leadership and supervision techniques, especially for the firstline supervisors. Prerequisite: MGT 200. Not open to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Introductory Organizational Behavior
description: Study of human behavior in organizational settings. Topics covered include individual behavior, group processes including leadership; motivation; and organizational change. Special emphasis is placed on how these concepts can be applied in an organizational setting. Not open to students who are B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Managing Behavior in Organizations
description: Examines the challenges of managing human behavior in organizations. Reviews foundations of modern management thought. Discusses current and emerging management topics with special emphasis on leadership, motivation, communication, human relations, group dynamics, job design, and organizational development. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: International Management
description: Discussion of management issues relating to doing business in an international context, including moving a firm into international competition, and some issues that may be expected. Topics covered include exporting, joint venturing, or licensing as options for global expansion. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 300.

title: Job Search and Transition
description: Prepares students for moving from college to careers. Topics covered include defining career goals, writing résumés, jobsearch correspondence, interviewing, and initial adjustments in the first job position. Open to juniors and seniors in all majors.

title: Information System Concepts and Techniques
description: Introduction to various concepts and techniques of information systems with application to solving managerial problems. Topics covered include information flows, application of computerbased information systems, managerial decision making, and mutual influence of organizations and information systems. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221. Prerequisite or parallel MGT: 300.

title: Business Data Communications
description: Concepts and problems of transmitting, communicating, and managing business data needs through the use of computerbased telecommunication systems. Includes applications of integrated and distributed systems to problems in various functional areas of business. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; MGT 300; proficiency in a programming language. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 311.

title: Quantitative Business Analysis
description: Exploration and application of selected quantitative techniques to business problems. Topics covered include regression and correlation, analysis of variance and contingency tables, decision analysis, linear programming, and networkbased management techniques. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; junior standing.

title: Operations Research
description: Basic operations research concepts and techniques for managerial decisions including linear programming, network problems, decision analysis, and computer implementation of these models to solve practical problems. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; junior standing.

title: Small Business Venture
description: Provides essential knowledge for those interested in small business including search for venture opportunities; economic, technical, and operational feasibility of ventures; financing, marketing, and legal operations; and franchising and partnering. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 300.

title: Entrepreneurship
description: Development and management of an entrepreneurial organization including prestartup, startup, survival, growth, and the transition from entrepreneurial to professional management. Explains the function of entrepreneurship and corporate entrepreneurship. Prerequisite: MGT 300, 341.

title: Operations Management
description: Discusses decision making in the operations function for the creation of goods and services and its relationship with other business functions. Topics include operations strategy, emerging process technologies, planning and scheduling, inventory management, justintime systems, and quality management. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 300.

title: Quality Management
description: Develops an understanding of quality concepts at all levels of business. Topics include operations strategy, emerging process technologies, planning and scheduling, inventory management, justintime systems, and quality management. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 351.

title: Managing Human Resources
description: Identifies the foundations of dealing with human resources in an organizational setting. Elements include selection, training, compensation, promotion, and transfer of workers; working conditions; employee services, and industrial relations. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 300.

title: Employee Development
description: Reviews basic employee appraisal, training and career development issues, special emphasis on program design, implementation and evaluation issues. Experiential activities are utilized to demonstrate the utility of content. Prerequisite: MGT 361.

title: Management Internship
description: Job experience (paid) in an organization with an approved innovative management program. Requires periodic written progress reports that will be evaluated by the assigned faculty member and the intern's supervisor. Topic selected will depend on student's option. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours may be earned including MGT 399.

title: Honors Colloquium: Readings in Contemporary Business
description: Seminar involving study of contemporary business literature. Interdisciplinary approach, comparing and contrasting ideas, deriving common themes, and drawing links to theory embodied in readings. Prerequisite: junior standing in College of Business and completion of "rule of nine." Open only to Honors students; others may enroll by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Management Practicum
description: Professional practice (unpaid) in an organization with an approved innovative management program. Required periodic written progress reports that will be evaluated by the assigned faculty member and the intern's supervisor. Topic selected will depend on student's option. Prerequisite: secondsemester junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned including MGT 369.

title: Contemporary Issues in Management
description: Discusses current and emerging managerial topics including team management, small group management, decision making, problem solving, managerial ethics, and managing diversity. Prerequisite: completion of all management core courses; senior standing.

title: Business Systems Analysis and Design
description: Various systems analysis and design concepts and techniques, including the key steps in the systemsdesign and development cycle. Emphasizes the consideration of practical applications within the business environment. Prerequisite: MGT 311; proficiency in COBOL programming.

title: Database: Structures and Management
description: Logical and physical organization of data. Data description, command, and interrogation languages. Examines function of databases in information systems. Prerequisite: MGT 311 and proficiency in COBOL programming.

title: Information Systems of Small Business
description: Computerbased information systems in small business operations without access to an internal specialist. Includes the identification of information requirements and the use of mainframe and microcomputers and purchased software to satisfy the information needs in small business. Prerequisite: MGT 300; MGT 341.

title: Information Systems Management
description: Equipment selection, equipment acquisition, computer operations management, project management, computer personnel management, financial control, systems security and control, and the relationship of the information systems function to an organization. Prerequisite: MGT 311.

title: Problems in Information Systems
description: An integration of various information systems principles, theories, and techniques for implementing information systems in organizations, including strategic issues. Includes lectures, tours, readings, cases, and the completion of a major individual project. Prerequisite: MGT 351, 412, 415; completion of all management core courses.

title: Systems Simulation
description: Concepts and techniques of system modeling and simulation using computers. Includes computer simulation languages, statistical aspects of simulation, and application of computer simulation to various practical business situations in manufacturing and service sectors. Prerequisite: BEOA 210; ECON 221; MGT 351.

title: Small Business Practicum
description: Teams of students consult with local small businesses recommended by the Small Business Development Center. Students work on problems in such areas as accounting, production, marketing, personnel, finance, insurance, law, or information systems. Prerequisite: MGT 346, 443.

title: Managing the Venture Financing Process
description: Examines the venture financing options available for new business startups. Emphasizes creating and analyzing financial documents, approaching financial sources, selling stock for growing companies, and managing the financial condition of a new venture. Prerequisite: MGT 341; FIN 350.

title: New Venture Creation
description: Advanced small business management entrepreneurship. Requires thorough research project culminating in the development of a finished plan for a small business venture to be approved by an outside board of professional experts. Prerequisite: MGT 346, 351, 443; MKG 300; completion of all management core courses; senior standing.

title: Inventory Management and Control
description: Discusses inventory control activities in manufacturing and service organizations. Topics include independent demand inventory systems, purchasing, and justintime delivery systems. Students are encouraged to take tests for Inventory Management and JIT modules of the certification for Production and Inventory Management. Prerequisite: MGT 351.

title: Operations Planning
description: Discusses all planning activities in manufacturing and service organizations. Topics include master planning, materials requirements planning, and capacity requirements planning. Students are encouraged to take tests for Master Planning and MRP/CRP modules of the certification in Production and Inventory Management. Prerequisite: MGT 351. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 321.

title: Emerging Technologies in Operations Management
description: Discusses technologies used in managing operations. In addition to emerging technologies, topics include JIT, Orr, productionactivity control, international operations management. Students are encouraged to take PAC and SYSTEMS and Technologies modules of the certification for . Production and Inventory Management. Prerequisite: MGT 300, 351.

title: Special Problems in Operations Management
description: Real life problems in operations management. Cases, production simulation games, real life projects are used. Management report writing and oral presentation skills are emphasized. Students are encouraged to enter their term papers in APICS student paper competition. Prerequisite: MGT 452, 454; completion of all management core courses.

title: Compensation Administration
description: Reviews basic compensation issues including internal, external, and individual equity, as well as benefits administration. Emphasis on design and implementation of compensation systems. Prerequisite: MGT 300, 361

title: Human Resource Planning and Selection
description: Focuses on organization and human resource planning, including determination of organization and human resource needs, analysis and development of job requirements, and necessary qualifications for recruitment and selection procedures, placement and orientation, and evaluation of selection programs. Prerequisite: MGT 300, 361. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 321.

title: Contemporary Issues in Human Resource Management
description: Integration of various contemporary principles, theories, and techniques for solving realistic and complex human resource management problems in public and private organizations. Includes lectures, tours, readings, cases, and the completion of a major individual project. Prerequisite: MGT 351, 461, 465, and completion of all management core courses.

title: Business Policy and Strategic Management
description: Integration of various functional areas of business. Development and administration of strategy and policy inprivate and public sector organizations. Case studies focus on strategic decisions that enable an organization to relate effectively to its industrial, national, and international environments. Normally taken during the last semester of a student's program. Prerequisite: FIN 350; MGT 300, 351; MKG 300; senior standing.

title: Colloquium in Business Policy
description: An honors colloquium in business policy studying advanced topics in industry, competitor, and firm analysis; critical thinking; analytic techniques; and strategy formulation culminating in required participation in the College of Business undergraduate case competition. Prerequisite or parallel: MGT 491. Open only to College of Business senior honors students or College of Business seniors with a G.P.A. of 3.0 or higher.

title: Special Topics in Management
description: Exploration of special topics in management of interest to faculty and students. May be repeated for credit with different topics. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent Study
description: Supervised study of some phase of management. May consist of an experiment, library research, or an analysis of current management practices and methods. Prerequisite: senior standing and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in Management
description: Explores current problems, theory, research, and trends in management. Will vary depending upon the current status of managerial research, the instructor, and the needs and interests of the students. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. title: Fundamentals of Marketing
description: Introduction to the basic concepts, strategies, and policies of marketing activity in the business system. Provides a useful mix of theory and practical applications for service, nonprofit, and profitmaking organizations. Not open to students who have credit in MKG 300 or to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Retail Merchandising
description: An introduction to the retail industry with a concentration on the merchandising activities of buying, selling, pricing, and inventory control. Prerequisite: BUSAD 101. Not open to students who have credit in MKG 300 or to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Introduction to Selling
description: Fundamentals of retail, wholesale, outside, and service selling. Emphasizes sales approaches, presentation, closings, and postsale service. Prerequisite: BUSAD 101. Not open to students who have credit in MKG 300 or to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business.

title: Retail Advertising
description: Introduction to advertising with emphasis on the preparation, appeal, and media selection of retail advertising. Prerequisite: BUSAD 101. Not open to students who have credit in MKG 300 or to B.S. or B.A. candidates for a major or minor in the College of Business. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Principles of Marketing
description: Examines marketing as a productive system within our economy. Studies promotional activities, product policies, retail and wholesale activities, pricing policies, international marketing, and the role of marketing in society. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Self Marketing: Tools, Process, Strategies and Experiences
description: Provides experience developing a personal product analysis and personal marketing plan. The student will gain familiarity with the tools, processes, and strategies essential to successful lifelong self marketing. Refinement of portfolio/resume is involved. Guest speakers, onsite visits provide practical and current insight. Prerequisite: junior standing. Cannot be used in any College of Business major or marketing minor requirements.

title: Honors Principles of Marketing
description: Principles of marketing for honors students. Examines marketing as a productive system within our economy. Substitutes for MKG 300. Prerequisite: ECON 201, junior standing; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Consumer Behavior
description: Practical business implications of the various features of consumer motivation and behavior. Students are given information to understand how and why a buyer reacts in a purchasing situation. Prerequisite: ECON 201, junior standing. Prerequisite or parallel: MKG 300.

title: Advertising Management
description: Use of advertising as a communication tool Marketing 145 in marketing management. Analysis of media selection, production and layout, measurement of effectiveness; and social and economic aspects Of advertising. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 310.

title: Professional Selling
description: Detailed introduction to and application of the principles of personal selling as applied to persons pursuing any vocation, as well as those aspiring to careers in marketing. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Retail Management
description: An investigation of store policies, organization, location, layout, buying, stock control, pricing, and sales promotion for retail stores. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Transportation: An International Focus
description: The economics of transportation with an international focus; economic development of various means of transportation and accompanying regulatory problems. Rate, traffic service, and coordination problems, advantages and disadvantages, trends, and peculiarities of the various modes. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Research
description: The basic nature and scope of marketing research; scientific method and research design; specific marketing research procedures; techniques of sampling; and research report, followup, and evaluation of research process. Selected applications in motivation, advertising, and product and sales control research. Prerequisite: MKG 300; admission to the College of Business. Open only to business majors.

title: Nonpaid Internship in Marketing
description: Professional practice during a summer or a semester as an intern in an approved program with a business firm, government agency, or nonprofit organization for nopay under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Requires periodic written reports of job experiences. Prerequisite: permission of the de artment chairperson. en only to secondsemester junior marketing majors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned toward major requirements in combination with MKG 369, 497, and 498.

title: Professional Practice in Marketing
description: Professional practice during a summer or semester as an intern in an approved program with a business firm, government agency, or nonprofit organization for pay under the supervision of the Department of Marketing. Requires periodic written reports of job experiences. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to secondsemester junior and senior marketing majors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned toward major requirements in combination with MKG 367, 497, and 498.

title: Marketing and Consumer Issues
description: Analysis of the consumer issues that relate to marketing practices. Involves study of such topics as consumerism, ecology, fraudulent practices, and disadvantaged consumers. Responsibilities include work experience in the Ball State University Consumer Education Council. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Marketing Channel Management
description: Study of marketing channels as economic, political, and social systems. Includes retailing, wholesaling, and other channel intermediaries. Strong emphasis is given to channel membership, structural and functional relationships, interorganizational management, and channel change and performance. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Promotion Management
description: Uses cases and problems to give experience in making decisions on a firm's promotional mix. Analysis of markets, media scheduling, budget allocation, campaign design, and promotion research. Prerequisite: MKG 320.

title: Seminar in Advanced Professional Selling
description: Examines advanced selling topics such as account management, negotiation, team selling, and selling to buying committees. Introduces interactive video and contact management software. Prerequisite: MKG 325.

title: Sales Management
description: Policies and practices in organizing, recruiting, selecting, training, compensating, and controlling the sales force. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and 325 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Retail Strategy
description: Advanced course in retailing management using case studies and special projects to examine current topics and problems in retailing. Prerequisite: MKG 330.

title: Industrial Procurement Management
description: A basic course in industrial procurement management. Principal topics include make or buy analysis, quality and quantity control, value analysis, price determination, sources of supply, the purchasing system, and legal aspects of purchasing. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Logistics Management
description: Marketing linkage strategy. Focuses on efficient coordination of resources for physical distribution, manufacturing support, and purchasing. Activities include literature searches, professional meetings, guest speakers, and simulation. Prerequisite: MKG 300. Prerequisite recommended: MKG 340.

title: International Marketing
description: Examines legal, economic, and cultural conditions influencing marketing abroad. Commercial policies, practices, and techniques needed to identify and evaluate foreign markets, as well as the problems of pricing, promoting, and distributing products in international markets. Prerequisite: MKG 300.

title: Seminar in European Community Marketing
description: Examines the effect of the single European Market—political and economic integration and removal of trade barriers in Europe—on the marketing strategies of American and European firms. Recommended for honors students. Prerequisite: MKG 300; senior standing or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in EURO 472.

title: Marketing Simulation Game
description: A simulation game in which students are divided into teams or companies. Management in each company makes decisions in marketing, finance, and production. Does not involve writing computer programs or using information from a dataprocessing class. Recommended for honors students. Prerequisite: MKG 300 and junior standing.

title: Marketing Management
description: Marketing by manufacturers as viewed from the marketing manager's position. Principal topics are selecting channels of distribution, determining demand, pricing policies, marketing legislation, advertising policies, and methods of selling. A casestudy approach. Prerequisite: 15 semester hours in marketing, including MKG 310, 325, 350, and senior standing, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Seminar in Marketing
description: Advanced examination of such current marketing topics as marketing theory and quantitative, service, nonprofit, bank, comparative, and international marketing. Specific content is announced when offered. Recommended for honors students. Prerequisite: MKG 300; senior standing; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Independent Study in Marketing
description: Independent study in some phase of marketing that may consist of a marketing research project or the analysis of current marketing practices. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson, marketing major, and MKG 300. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned toward major requirements in combination with MKG 367, 369, and 498, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Practicum in the Consumer Education Council
