Edmonds, Assistant to the Dean The Honors College offers special courses, colloquia, seminars, and independent study designed to challenge talented students. In their first two years, students in the Honors College take honors sections of General Studies courses. Required core courses include three symposia in American contemporary civilization, global studies, and science, as well as a threecourse sequence in the humanities that investigates the great ideas of literature, science, philosophy, politics, and the fine arts. Honors professors often invite guest lecturers to furnish additional perspectives on topics under study. In the sophomore, junior, and senior years, students take at least two colloquia especially developed by honors faculty members to focus on critical issues in their areas of expertise. As seniors, students undertake the capstone of their work in honors—the senior thesis or creative project, prepared under the guidance of a professor selected by the student. Students also have the opportunity to do specialized departmental honors work in their majors and to apply for the Undergraduate Fellows Competition, which awards stipends for independent work with a faculty mentor. Students are often invited to meet with visiting lecturers or dignitaries in small groups and to take advantage of special programs. Admission to the Honors College is based primarily on high school preparation, test scores, and class rank. Students admitted to the Honors College must maintain a gradepoint average of at least 3.0 and must finish with a cumulative gradepoint average of at least 3.25. Transfer students may also enroll. For more information, write or call the dean of the Honors College, (317) 285-1024. The Honors College curriculum is interdepartmental in nature, consisting of courses from a variety of departments.

title: Honors Symposium in Global Studies
description: Focuses on the commonalities and rich diversities in global culture, economy, history, politics, and society. Taught from varied perspectives or disciplines; emphasis is on the non-Western world—Asia, Africa, and Central and South America.

title: Honors Symposium in Contemporary Civilization
description: An examination of some of the critical issues that confront contemporary civilization. Open only to students participating in the Honors College.

title: Honors Humanities 2: Middle Ages, Renaissance, Enlightenment
description: Study of major intellectual and cultural movements of the Middle Ages, Renaissance, and Enlightenment. Open only to Honors College students.

title: Honors Humanities 3: The Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
description: Study of major intellectual and cultural movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Open only to Honors College students.

title: Honors Symposium in Biology: Biology and Human Concerns
description: Basic introduction to biological principles using humans as, the major organism and emphasizing the relationship of contemporary biology to human concerns and society. Included in the course are social and ethical consequences of scientific discoveries and their societal application. Open only to students participating in the honors program except by permission of the Department of Biology chairperson or the dean of the Honors College. Not open to students who have credit in HONRS 299.

title: Honors Symposium in Biology: Human Genetics and Bioethics
description: A General Studies science course. Applying personal knowledge toward the solution of some critical biological issues confronting contemporary society. Open only to students participating in the honors program except by permission of the Department of Biology chairperson or the dean of the Honors College. Not open to students who have credit in HONRS 298.

title: Honors Foreign Study
description: Study in a foreign country as part of honors programs at the university. Coursework undertaken at institutions of higher learning in other countries is granted Ball State University Honors College credit. Offeredlor letter grades or credit/no credit. A total of 32 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to Honors College students accepted in a Ball State exchange or study abroad program.

title: Honors Professional Experience
description: Paid, supervised work and learning experience related to Honors education. Prerequisite: permission of the dean of the Honors College. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to Honors College students.

title: Honors Colloquium
description: Exploration of selected issues linking several disciplines. Emphasis is on discussion, individual projects, and ways of combining information from several sources. Open only to Honors College students by permission. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Candidate
description: May be taken each semester by honors candidates who have already registered in previous semesters for all of their undergraduate course work, including HONRS 499, but have not yet completed their senior honors projects. Students enrolled in this course are entitled to ordinary undergraduate student use of library, health, and other university facilities.

title: Honors Practical Experience
description: Unpaid, supervised work and learning experience related to honors education. Prerequisite: permission of the dean of the Honors College. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. Open only to Honors College students.

title: Senior Honors Project
description: An inquiry culminating in an honors paper prepare in accordance with accepted standards of documentation and presentation under the supervision of a faculty member. Van Meter, Associate Deans The College of Sciences and Humanities possesses two characteristics that also define its mission: diversity and liberal education. The college is the largest academic unit at Ball State University. It is a remarkably diverse unit, housing the humanities; the physical, earth, and life sciences; and the social sciences—subjects central to the General Studies courses required of all students. The College of Sciences and Humanities is committed to liberal education and to the belief that students must be trained in specific skills and be educated to think critically, communicate clearly, solve problems creatively, act responsibly, and live fully. The college is committed to a concept of wholeness, an ideal of coherence that helps faculty and students synthesize knowledge and make connections among the many specialties and subspecialties that compose the universe of knowledge. Academic credit may be earned during this research semester. Students interested in including a research semester at one of the National Laboratories should plan early in their academicprograms for such an experience. title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
description: Introduces the diversity of human social life as shaped by culture, relating the origins and nature of culture to variations in such universal aspects of human experience as the food quest, family organization, social control, the arts, and religion.

title: Archaeology and Culture
description: The nature of archaeological research—its methodology and principles of analysis—and its contributions to our understanding of human behavior and the development of human culture from the Stone Age to the present.

title: Evolution and Human Behavior
description: Modern evolutionary theory, the fossil record for human development from primate ancestors, the relevance of these and studies of other living primates for an understanding of human behavior, and the interrelationships between biology and culture in modem human environmental adaptation.

title: Sophomore Seminar
description: Intended to enculturate students into the discipline, focuses on the personal dimensions of being an anthropologist and thinking like one. Also touches upon major concepts and figures, and practical aspects of fieldwork and writing in anthropology.

title: Fundamentals of Archaeology
description: Introduces the types of data dealt with by archaeology, approaches to data recovery, methods of analysis, and problems of interpretation. Differing problems of traditional research archaeology and modem archaeological resources management are considered. Prerequisite: ANTH 103 or permission of the instructor.

title: Fundamentals of Physical Anthropology
description: Introduces the major concepts, mechanisms, methodology, and types of data dealt with by physical anthropology: primate and human evolution; genetics; primate anatomy, diversity, and behavior; ontogeny and life cycle variations; geographic variation; adaptation; and other interactions between environment, culture, and biology.

title: Ethnicity and Race
description: Explores the concepts of ethnicity and race and how they shape the interaction between individuals and groups in complex society. Devotes particular attention to the Westem world, but also considers similar attitudes in other parts of the world. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to Folklore and Folklife
description: Introduction to the role of tradition in various aspects of American culture, from humor to architecture; the functions of these elements in society, and methodological and theoretical approaches to their study, with comparative examples from Ireland and Great Britain.

title: The African Background of American Black Culture
description: African cultural and historical roots of American blacks—origins of the human species, plant and animal domesticatiOn, metallurgy, art, and state formation. Focus is on West Africa, the source of most of the black population of the United States.

title: History of Method and Theory in Anthropology
description: Surveys the major ideas and issues of anthropology over time. Includes methods and theories from archaeology, physical anthropology, linguistics, and cultural anthropology.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Applies anthropological theory and method to such educational concerns as socialization, peer dynamics, classroom networks, parentteacher interactions, modernization, and multicultural settings.

title: Human Variation and Adaptation
description: Human biological variation in the contemporary world: examination of its distribution, inheritance, development and adaptiveness. Prerequisite: ANTH 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Ontogeny: Human Physical Growth and Development and Its Evolution
description: Studies children's physical growth and development, human adaptive roles and evolutionary history, ranges of variation in presentday populations, effects of stress, changes through time, comparisons with nonhuman primates, and assessment methods. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Applied Anthropology
description: Investigates the problems and work that engage the attention of anthropologists outside the university setting. Examination of new skills needed to supplement those traditionally taught in anthropology.

title: Introduction to Anthropological Linguistics
description: Basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language with particular emphasis on non-European languages and cultural components of language. Knowledge of a foreign language is helpful. Prerequisite: ANTH 101.

title: Topics in Old World Prehistory
description: Prehistory of various Old World regions and time periods. Topics will vary from semester to semester—for example, Europe, the Paleolithic, general survey. May be repeated with different topics. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 101. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Ecological Anthropology
description: Explores the system of relationships between any human.population and its environment focusing on cultural behavior. Uses studies from ancient to modern times and models and theories from ecology and anthropology. Prerequisite: any one of ANTH 101, 103, 105, 201, or permission of the instructor.

title: Human Paleontology
description: Fossil record of the evolution of humans and their primate predecessors. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Topics in New World Archaeology
description: Prehistory of various New World regions or developmental periods. Topics will vary from semester to semester—for example, Meso-America, the Southwest, general survey. May be repeated for different topics. Prerequisite: ANTH 103. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Organization
description: A systematic crosscultural analysis of human organizations from kinshipbased societies to modern bureaucracies. Using an evolutionary approach, develops both theoretical perspectives and practical understanding. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, 201, or permission of the instructor.

title: Art of Prehistoric and Non-Western Cultures
description: Exposes liberal arts students to the artistic accomplishments of prehistoric and non-Western peoples. Art will be interpreted and functionally examined in regard to aesthetic, ceremonial, and informational content.

title: Laboratory Methods in Material Culture
description: Addresses artifacts as reflections of culture. Focuses on ethnoarchaeology and experimental archaeology, as well as the integration of research design, recovery, identification and laboratory analysis of artifacts from archaeological sites. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, 103.

title: Special Topics in Native American Cultures
description: Detailed analysis of selected contemporary issues facing American Indians—for example, religious freedom, property rights—or a focus on the Indian cultures of a particular area, such as the Southwest, Great Lakes, or Northeast. May be repeated for different topics. A total of 6 hours of credit maybe earned.

title: North American Indians
description: Cultures of the North American Indians emphasizing their economic, sociopolitical, and religious institutions. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Native American and American Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Indians of the Great Lakes
description: Indepth study of selected Native American cultures indigenous to the Great Lakes region from the time of European contact to the contemporary period. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Native American Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: Archaeological development of the Midwest traced through the Paleo- Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite: ANTH 103.

title: Anthropology and Women
description: Development of the female phenotype; variation in the roles assigned to women in cultures of differing levels of complexity from gathererhunters to industrial societies—both Western and non-Western—and the contributions of women anthropologists to understanding this variation. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Women's Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Anthropology of American Culture
description: Examines how the values, beliefs, and norms of American culture are integrated into and symbolized in various media. Explores how we experience and resolve cultural tensions between individualism and community, equality and hierarchy, competition and cooperation.

title: Historical Archaeology
description: Covers the major themes and philosophies of the archaeology of post-Columbian America as well as related literature and sources of information on architectural features and items of material culture likely to be encountered in the course of excavation. Prerequisite: ANTH 103, permission of the instructor.

title: Special Topics in Anthropology
description: Detailed analysis of a special problem in cultural anthropology, archaeology, linguistics, or physical anthropology. May be repeated for different topics. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: European Prehistory
description: Prehistory of Europe from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age with an emphasis on the regions north and west of the Classical world. Prerequisite: ANTH 103 or permission of the instructor.

title: Paid Internship in Anthropology
description: Paid, supervised field or laboratory experience in anthropology. Employment should supply an opportunity to use and further knowledge of anthropology. Prerequisite: permission of the internship director. Open only to anthropology majors or minors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Topics in Old World Ethnography
description: Anthropological survey of the cultural patterns of selected continents or regions, such as East Asia, Europe, the island Pacific. Prerequisite: ANTH 101.

title: Topics in Museum Operations
description: Introduces various aspects of museum operations, such as organization, financing, curation, exhibits, public interpretation, and conservation of collections. Emphasizes ethnographic and archaeological collections. May be repeated for different topics.

title: Topics in New World Ethnography
description: Anthropological survey of the cultural patterns of selected continents or regions, such as the Caribbean, Latin America. Prerequisite: ANTH 101. A total of 6 hours of credit may be

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in modern anthropology. Emphasis is on individual study and development of results. Open only to Honors College students by permission of the department chairperson.

title: History of Archaeology
description: Development of archaeological thought over the past two centuries focusing on major figures and their contributions. Prerequisite: ANTH 103.

title: Human Osteology
description: Laboratory dealing with the human skeleton including identification of whole and fragmentary bones and the assessment of the age, stature, sex, and race of a skeleton as applied to paleodemography, paleopathology, and forensicproblems. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Medical Anthropology
description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating non-Western techniques to Western counterparts. Prerequisite: ANTH 101.

title: Contemporary Problems of the American Indians
description: Detailed study of current issues facing Native Americans. Particular issues facing tribes in specific regions and general issues of apan- Indian nature will be covered. Taught in the field with seminars led by Native Americans. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Anthropological Field Studies
description: Methods of field research in ethnography, archaeology, or physical anthropology. Stresses problem formulation, observation, data handling, and interpretation. Taught at various field locations. May be repeated for different topics. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Witchcraft, Magic, and Religion
description: Anthropological study of humankind's ageold concern with life, death, sickness, and the unknown. Discusses human attempts to control life through supernatural beings, prayer, sacrifice, and techniques of magic and witchcraft. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Religious Studies majors), permission of the instructor.

title: Primatology
description: Comparative survey of nonhuman primates, their biology and behavior. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Archaeological Resources Management
description: Special problems of contract, conservation, and public archaeology, including laws and regulations, relations with government agencies, research design and methodology for reconnaissance and test excavations, site interpretation, and predictive modeling. Prerequisite: ANTH 204, permission of the instructor.

title: Quantitative and Qualitative Ethnographic Methods
description: Develops the ability to conduct and comprehend ethnographic research. Includes research design, data collection, analysis, reporting, basic statistics, and computer use. Emphasizes both quantitative and qualitative techniques for basic and applied research. Prerequisite: 15 hours ANTH or permission of the instructor.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland Southeast Asia. Specific emphasis is on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Asian Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Culture Change
description: Surveys the major concepts and processes of culture change, with an emphasis on the causes of change and their effects on individuals and groups. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, permission of the instructor.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory using information on traditional ethnographic groups, particularly in the Americas. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Native American Studies minors), permission of the instructor.

title: Unpaid Internship
description: Unpaid field or laboratory experience that uses knowledge of anthropology in a specific project or work content. Prerequisite: permission of the internship director. Open only to anthropology majors or minors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to formal) view of allocation, conversion, and distribution of resources. Emphasizes economic development in third and fourth world countries. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 or 201 or permission of the instructor.

title: Indians of the American Southwest
description: Surveys prehistoric, historic, and contemporary cultures of selected Southwest Indian groups. Emphasis is on culturespecific solutions to problems perceived in their relationship to their natural and social environments. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Native American Studies minors), permission of the instructor.

title: Independent Study in Anthropology
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor with competence in the area involved. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Senior Seminar in Anthropology
description: Integrates knowledge of current theoretical and methodological issues in the four quadrants of anthropology. Warden The Department of Biology offers programs for students preparing for careers in education, laboratory and field research, biotechnology, ecology, wildlife and fisheries management, and health professions such as medicine, medical technology, and dentistry. The biology major offers a core program intended to develop a common background in biology and additional courses in specialized options designed to prepare students for careers or graduate work in aquatic biology and fisheries, botany, cellular and molecular biology, ecology, genetics, microbiology, wildlife biology, and zoology. Preprofessional majors add selected courses to meet entrance requirements into medical, dental, and medical technology schools. A teaching major in science with biology as a primary or supporting area and a teaching minor in biology are offered for students who plan to teach in the secondary schools. (Additional course requirements for science teaching programs appear in this catalog under the listing, Interdepartmental Programs, College of Sciences and Humanities.) In addition to the major requirements, students who want to become candidates for the National Registry of Microbiologists (ASM) should complete the following recommended electives: BIO 344, 452; CHEM 225, 231; and ZOOL 347. Students interested in pursuing graduate work in a biological science should be aware that graduate schools generally require the following: • proficiency in at least one foreign language, computer science, or statistics; • chemistry through the organic sequence; biochemistry recommended; • one year of college physics; and • mathematics through the calculus sequence. title: People and the Life Sciences
description: Introductory course designed for students not majoring in science. Emphasizes human and social aspects of biology: reproduction, development, genetic counseling, immunology, evolution, biodiversity, ecology, and environmental concerns. Not open to students who have credit in BIO 102,111, or 112.

title: Biological Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles of biology as they relate to energy requirements and reproductive processes of living organisms, including the study of plants and conservation with emphasis on the human role in the environment. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs.

title: Principles of Biology 1
description: Designed for biology, allied health, and other science majors. Emphasis at cellular level: chemical and physical organization of life, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell structure and function, bioenergetics, cell division, genetics, gene expression, protein synthesis, and evolution. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry, one semester of college chemistry, or the equivalent.

title: Principles of Biology 2
description: Emphasis at organism, population, and community levels: major plant and animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification, and phylogenetic relationships; ecology, including human ecology and environmental biology. Lecture and laboratory.

title: Microbiology for the Health Sciences
description: Introductory course for students in applied health curricula. Presents biomolecules of life, enzyme interaction, physiology and structure of representative microorganisms. Emphasis is on bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa of health significance and the hostparasite relationship. Microbiological techniques will be emphasized in laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 101 or its equivalent.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and fungi. Emphasis isplaced on morphology, physiology, genetics, and control. Some consideration of applied microbiology. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 111.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation emphasizing meiosis, Mendelian inheritance and probability considerations, sex and gene transmission and expression, linkage and crossingover, the nature of the hereditary material, gene action, and genetic control of development. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 .

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biology of the cell, including cell differentiation and growth, the nature of the organization of the cell, basic bioenergetics and enzyme function, cell environment, membrane structure and function, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; CHEM 231 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ecology
description: Effects of physical and biotic conditions on the distribution and abundance of plants and animals. Dynamics of ecological systems are examined at the population, community, and ecosystem levels, and from an evolutionary perspective. Practical applications are emphasized. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112.

title: Human Genetics for Special Education
description: Designed for special education majors to foster understanding human inheritance implications in their chosen career. Develops genetic literacy using many instructional techniques. In addition, the social implications of genetic knowledge will be explored. Not open to students who have credit in BIO 453. Open only to special education majors and dual majors in special education and elementary education. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems of Life Systems
description: Examines evolutionary solutions to problems of survival and reproduction faced by all organisms. Problems are investigated from a common basis rather than a taxonomical approach. Physiological processes are emphasized, including the selective pressures involved in the evolution of these mechanisms. Prerequisite: completion of all other core requirements for biology majors.

title: Pathogenic Bacteriology
description: Study of pathogenic bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques for culturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisite: BIO 113 or 213; CHEM 130 or 231.

title: Immunology-Virology
description: Examination of the basic principles of immunology and virology. Topics include the immune system, the variety of immune responses, immunoregulation, and characteristics of viruses. Emphasis will be placed on virushost interactions and serological diagnosis of viral infections. Prerequisite: BIO 213 and one course in organic chemistry.

title: Internship in Biology
description: Paid, supervised field and laboratory experiences in public or private agencies (or in the Department of Biology). Training involves application of biological principles in the work environment. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Biology
description: Exploration of selected issues in biology with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students except by permission of the department A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Biology
description: Practical application of biology in a variety of situations including biology instruction as undergraduate teaching assistants and discussion leaders, and practical experience in government or industrial laboratories and field stations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Biological Communications
description: Introduces biology students to the literature of the life sciences. Focus is on information found in books, journals, indexes /abstracts, and related secondary sources such as handbooks, titles in series, and electronic databases: organization of information and methods of retrieval.

title: Developments in Modern Biology
description: Stresses recent discoveries in biology and integrates and enhances understanding of basic principles of the discipline. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Population Ecology
description: Presents fundamental principles of population growth and regulation, including both withinspecies and betweenspecies interactions. Implications for overpopulation, endangered species, and pest and game management are discussed. Laboratory includes both experimental studies and computer simulation exercises. Prerequisite: BIO 216.

title: Community and Ecosystem Ecology
description: Principles of ecological organization at the community and ecosystems levels. Emphasis on the processes that influence the structure and function of communities and ecosystems. Laboratory includes field and lab studies of plant and animal systems. Prerequisite: BIO 216.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas: ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Biophysics
description: The study of biologic phenomena in terms of contributing physical events. Transport processes. Absorption and emission radiation. Ionizing radiation; its effects on living tissue; use of isotopes in research projects. Prerequisite: BIO 215.

title: Evolution
description: Principles, evidence, and the historical context of modern evolution theory. Some attention will be given to the origin of life and the evolution of plants and animals. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Applied Microbiology
description: The study of microorganisms that are beneficial or detrimental to changes in foods (including milk and milk products) and industrial fermentations. This is a lecture/ lab course. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Biometry
description: Principles and application of statistics to biological problems. The use of parametric and nonparametric tests of significance in the analysis of data and the interpretation of experiments. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or its equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Genetics
description: Bacterial and eukaryotic genetics with emphasis on recent developments in molecular genetics. Topics include alternative structures of DNA, mechanisms of DNA replication, mutagenesis, DNA rearrangements, regulation of gene expression, RNA processing, and molecular and mutagenetic analysis of cell cycle Prerequisite: BIO 214; CHEM 231. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 215.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Humanity
description: Current problems in human heredity. Human chromosome aberrations. DNA, the genetic code, and mutations. Consanguineous marriages and genetic defects. Mendelian principles applied to humans. Pedigrees and probability. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems and advances in genetics.

title: Molecular Biology
description: Structure and function of macromolecules in Living things. Emphasizes threedimensional structures; models for enzyme mechanisms; DNA replication; protein synthesis and membrane function; andapplications of biotechnology. Prerequisite: BIO 215 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Cellular and Molecular Biology
description: Study of recent developments in cell growth and differentiation, DNA and RNA research, membrane biology, cellular and molecular evolution, and cellular control mechanisms. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Bioenergetics
description: The study of flow of energy in biological systems with emphasis on application of laws of thermodynamics to biological processes, energy production metabolism in chemotrophs and phototrophs, and the major uses of energy in biological systems. Prerequisite: BIO 215, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Microtechniques
description: A lecture/lab course in the preparation of biological material for microscopic examination in teaching, research, and clinical applications. Emphasis on preparation of smears, squashes, whole mounts, paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112, 213, and one course of college chemistry.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Recent advances and theories in early embryogenesis and developmental biology. Major emphasis on genetic and molecular mechanisms operating during developmental phenomena. Topics include fertilization, mosaic versus regulative development, regulation of gene expression, patterning, germ line and sex determination, and neoplasia. Prerequisite: BIO 215 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Limnology
description: The physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of inland waters. Laboratory and several field trips will be devoted to exploring techniques for the evaluation of representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Microbiology
description: Microorganisms indigenous to nonpolluted and polluted aquatic ecosystems. Emphasis on nutrient cycling and use of microorganisms as indicators of pollution. Morphology, physiology, and ecology of specific organisms. Lecture/laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Marine Biology
description: Introduction to marine environments. Properties of seawater, 'hydrodynamics. Phytoplankton and benthic plants. Primary production, nutrient cycles. Marine animals, surveys of major taxa. Adaptations for life on the bottom, open water, intertidal zones, estuaries, abyssal regions.

title: Bioethical Decision Making
description: Development of decisionmaking skills through the analysis and personal resolution of bioethical problems created by the application of new biological and biomedical knowledge and technologies. Prerequisite: junior standing and completion of the General Studies science component or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Research Techniques in Laboratory Biology
description: Laboratory principles and applications in cell and molecular biology and microbiology. Includes experimental design, analyses of journal articles, research proposal development and presentation, restriction mapping, cloning, transformation, electrophoretic separations and analyses, bacteria and bacteriophage growth, and DNA fingerprinting. Prerequisite: BIO 215 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Forestry
description: General course in forestry with emphasis on forest policy, ecology, and management. Current issues are discussed with particular reference to their social, political, and environmental implications. Lecture and laboratory.

title: Taxonomy of Vascular Plants
description: Identification, use, and care of native and ornamental trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plant material. The use of botanical keys, manuals, and texts in the identification of the plant taxa. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Economic Botany
description: The cultivation, processing, environmental requirements, and use of planks and plant derivatives for food, drugs, dwellings, clothing, and power.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the different methods of plant propagation, care, and cultivation for use in the home, school, garden, and greenhouse. Also, some emphasis on diseases, pathogens, and pests of the plant.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on pathogenic forms. Discusses methods for identification of fungi along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introductory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photosynthesis, and intermediate metabolism. Prerequisite: BIO 112 and CHEM 231.

title: Plants and Their Allies
description: Evolutionaryphylogenetic survey of plant forms. Includes bacteria, algae, fungi, bryophytes, and vascular plants. Emphasis on comparative morphology and anatomy, reproductive structures, cycles, and adaptations to varying habitats. Prerequisite: BIO 111,112 or permission of the instructor.

title: Dendrology
description: The identification and site characterization of woody plants with an emphasis on midwestern tree species. Use of botanical features and keys in field identification. Correlation of species with site conditions, plant diseases, climatic parameters, associate species, and geographical distribution. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Plant Ecology
description: Factors affecting the distribution and abundance of plants. Patterns, structure, and development of plants at the individual, population, and community level. Laboratory provides experience with ecological experimentation at the physiological, population, and community levels. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of the instructor.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection and identification of nonvascular and vascular plants from fresh water ecosystems. Emphasizes the morphology, physiology, and ecology of these plants to explain their distribution in nature. Class project and field trips may be used to demonstrate ecological relationships. Two Saturday field trips required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Urinalysis
description: A study of basic renal anatomy, physiology, and pathology, as well as training in the preparation of patients and collection of urine samples, conduct of routine and special tests of urine, and identification of the various formed elements in urine sediment. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Serology
description: Principles of immunology. Histology and biochemistry of the immune system. Theory and practice of the detection of antibodies and other serum substances related to disease conditions using various diagnostic procedures. Prerequisite: BIO 344. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Microbiology
description: Study of pathogenic organisms (bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and animal parasites), emphasizing isolation, culture, identification, and antibiotic sensitivity. Experience in media preparation, staining techniques, and various biochemical and serological tests for identification and sensitivity. Prerequisite: BIO 341, 344. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Blood Bank
description: Theory and practice of blood bank organization and procedure. Genetics and immunology of blood group systems; selection of donors; collection, processing, and storage of blood; preparation of blood products; typing, compatibility, and pretransfusion tests. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Radioimmunoassay
description: Theory and practice of the use of radiolabeled substances in the detection of hormones, antigens, antibodies, drugs, and other clinically important molecules in blood and other body fluids. Experience in such related techniques as immunofluorescence and enzyme immunoassay. Prerequisite: BIO 344. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Medical Chemistry
description: Theory and application of physiology, biochemistry, and organic chemistry in the laboratory diagnosis of abnormal metabolism. Experience with a variety of manual and automated test procedures, including preparation of patient samples, instrument calibration and maintenance, and quality control. Prerequisite: CHEM 360. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Hematology
description: Study of blood, other body fluids, and bone marrow: cells, coagulation processes, and pathological conditions. Practice in collection of samples, staining procedures, and various tests concerned with cells and dotting mechanisms, including experience with related instrumentation. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Structure and Development of Vertebrates
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and evolutionary relationships of vertebrates. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth, protozoan, and arthropod parasites of animals and humans. Emphasizes identification, life cycles, hostparasite relationships, and physiology of common species. Some emphasis on medical and clinical aspects of parasites in humans, and tropical forms. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Comparative morphology, physiology, ecology, life histories, and phylogeny of invertebrate animal phyla. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: A comparison of vital activities in the animal groups, particularly the invertebrates. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ornithology
description: The study of birds including identification, systematics, anatomy, physiology, life histories, ecological relationships, and conservation. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ichthyology
description: The study of fish with emphasis on identification, classification, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Emphasizes Indiana species, but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department

title: Herpetology
description: Introduction to the biology of amphibians and reptiles, including their origin, anatomy, physiology, classification, behavior, and ecology. Through extensive field trips, the laboratory will emphasize identification and observation of amphibians and reptiles in their natural habitats. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The economic relationships of mammals. The collection and preservation of specimens. May require additional field work. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identification, population dynamics, and geographic distribution of wildlife species with particular emphasis on those of the United States. The harvest and management of wildlife. May require additional field work. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identification, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasis is on aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress.

title: Physical Science 1
description: Concepts of matter and energy, mechanics, heat, magnetism, electricity, sound, and light, with emphasis on understanding applications through fundamentals. Open only to students with majors in elementary education.

title: Physical Science 2
description: Structure of matter and nature of the universe; atomic structure, chemistry, nuclear physics, and planetary and stellar systems, with emphasis on recent advances in chemistry and the exploration of space. Prerequisite: SCI 290. Open only to students with majors in elementary education.

title: Teaching of Science in the Elementary School
description: Methods of teaching science concepts, process skills, and scientific attitudes are developed through direct experiences. Recent elementary science texts, courses of study, and curricular materials are examined and used as are experiments, field studies, demonstrations, and special methods. Prerequisite: 8 hours of science courses or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching of Science in the Junior High School
description: Recent curriculum developments in junior high school science. Science curriculum instruction related to the physical, mental, and emotional characteristics of the junior high school student. Experiences in public schools may be required. Prerequisite: 24 hours of science courses or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching Science in the Early and Primary Grades
description: Analysis of the cognitive, psychomotor, and affective processes inherent in science investigations for young children. Handson activities with science materials appropriate for early childhood and primary children. Designed primarily for students in early childhood and primary education programs. Prerequisite: 8 hours of science or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching of Science in the Secondary and Junior High/Middle School
description: Philosophy and methodology of science teaching. Emphasis is on laboratory investigations, concepts and conceptual schemes, scienceoriented classroom management, evaluation of instructional activities, supplies, equipment, facilities, and curriculum materials. Experiences inpublic schools will be required. Prerequisite: 13 hours of science courses or permission of the department Chemistry 243 c`"--)CHEMISTRY L. Sousa, Chairperson; M. title: People and Chemistry
description: Introductory treatment of fundamental concepts of chemistry, such as organization and language of chemistry, atomic structure, nature and classification of matter, radioactivity, and the relevancy of these topics to everyday living. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 101, 111.

title: General, Organic, and Biochemistry for the Health Sciences
description: Introduction to and general principles of general chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry. Designed for students in the health sciences and related areas. Four hours of lecture and one twohour recitationlaboratory weekly. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 111.

title: General Chemistry 1
description: Chemistry of the elements and their compounds with emphasis on basic principles. Atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, properties of solutions, and nature of matter. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: one year of secondary school algebra or the equivalent.

title: General Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 111, including chemical kinetics, electrochemistry, chemical equilibrium, chemistry of metals and nonmetals, and radioactivity. Three hours of lecture and one threehour recitationlaboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 111; MATHS 108.

title: Survey of Organic and Biochemistry
description: A broadly based introductory course suitable for life science, natural resources, and general science majors. Three hours of lecture and one twohour laboratory weekly.

title: Chemical Analysis
description: Lecture and intensive laboratory treatment of the theory and practice of representative quantitative chemical measurements, including gravimetry, visual and potentiometric titrations, ion exchange, coulometric and conductometric titrations, and visible spectrophotometry. One and onehalf hours of lecture and four and onehalf hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: Nomenclature, structure, bonding, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 234.

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 231, including the chemistry of natural products and biomolecules. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 235.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
description: A beginning course in organic chemistry for students concentrating in chemistry. Lecture material includes nomenclature, covalent bonding, molecular structure, and functional group chemistry of organic compounds. Laboratory experience includes spectroscopy and syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 112.

title: Organic Chemistry 2
description: A continuation of CHEM 234, including the properties of carbohydrates, proteins, and other natural products. Laboratory experience includes qualitative organic analysis and multistep syntheses. Three hours of lecture and two threehour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 234. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: Practical applications of modern chemical instrumentation: electrometric, chromatographic, and spectroscopic methods. For chemical/medical technologists or departmental minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225.

title: Selected Principles of Physical Chemistry
description: Introduction to the properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions and to the basic concepts of thermodynamics and kinetics. Especially for premedical, biology, and general science majors, chemistry teaching majors, and chemistry minors. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitation/ laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225; MATHS 161. Not open to students who have credit in CHEM 344.

title: Physical Chemistry 1
description: Thermodynamic and structural description of chemical processes and properties of solids, liquids, gases, and solutions. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 235 or 232; MATHS 166; one year of college physics.

title: Physical Chemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM

title: Inorganic Chemistry
description: Chemistry of the elements, including the relationships of chemical properties and atomic and molecular structure, chemical bonding, acidbase theories, chemical periodicity, and modern theories of coordination compounds. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235 or 360; MATHS 161 or 165.

title: Essentials of Biochemistry
description: Organic chemistry of carboxylic acids, amines, and their derivatives; biochemistry of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids; metabolism and the regulation of metabolic processes. For students in life sciences, dietetics, and medical technology. Three hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory session weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 231 or its equivalent. Not open to departmental majors in chemistry.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid work and learning experience as a practicing chemist. Practical problemsolving experience will be gained through such programs as internships, practicums, cooperative education programs, and the Department of Chemistry summer research program. Prerequisite: application, recommendation of the program selection committee, andpermission of the department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. One hour may be counted toward the associate in science in chemical technology degree. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward the departmental major.

title: Specialized Topics in Chemistry
description: Discussion or experimentation, or both, in specialized topics in and related to chemistry. Information concerning specific topics offered during a given semester is available from the departmental office. Lecture, discussion, and laboratory schedules appropriate to the topic offered. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 hour may be counted toward departmental major or minor requirements.

title: Chemical Technology Practicum
description: Practical experience in real or simulated industrial laboratory situations for chemical technologists. Assignments equivalent to four clock hours a week. Prerequisite: CHEM 325 and permission of the department chairperson. Not applicable toward majors or minors in chemistry.

title: Chemical Communications
description: Use of scientific literature; sources and classification systems; current and retrospective searches in the specialized branches of chemistry. Prerequisite: 20 hours of chemistry or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 1
description: Theoretical principles and applications of selected spectroscopic, electrochemical, and chromatographic methods, with illustrative experiments. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 225 and 344 or 340 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Chemical Instrumentation 2
description: Advanced treatment of selected topics in spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and chromatography. Introduction to mass spectroscopy, nuclear methods, thermal and surface analysis. Two hours of lecture and one threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 420 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Organic Laboratory Techniques
description: Laboratory course that includes multistep syntheses of organic compounds, their isolation, purification, and characterization using modem spectroscopic and chromatographic techniques. Six hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or its equivalent.

title: Physical-Organic Chemistry
description: Theoretical aspects of structure, including resonance and molecular orbital descriptions of electron distribution, aromaticity, symmetry, stereochemistry, and effects of structure on reactivity in acidbase reactions. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Theory and Practice of Inorganic and Organometallic Synthesis
description: Practice and principles of both the synthesis and the characterization of inorganic and organometallic compounds. One hour of lecture and three hours of laboratory weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 350. Prerequisite or parallel: CHEM 344.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 1
description: Chemistry and techniques for isolation, purification, and identification of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. For students majoring in chemistry, life sciences, and premedicine. Two hours of lecture and one threehour recitation laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 232 or 235.

title: Principles of Biochemistry 2
description: Continuation and extension of CHEM 463 including biological oxidations and energy transfers; metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids; and regulation of metabolic processes. Three hours of lecture weekly. Prerequisite: CHEM 463.

title: Independent Study and Research
description: Scientific investigation on an individual basis under the supervision of a faculty member. Extensive reading, experimental work, and development of research techniques and skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 5 hours of credit may be earned. No more than 3 hours may be counted as electives toward any departmental major. COMPUTER SCIENCEr C. Fuelling, Chairperson; J. Bagga, P. Buis, K. Keil, J. McGrew, C. Nelson, F. Owens, R. Place, B. Rais, C. Tzeng, W. Zage Computer science is concerned with creating appropriate computational models for problems along with techniques for solving them using computers. Computer science should not be confused with computer programming. Programming is one of the tools of computer science in much the same way that arithmetic and algebra are tools of mathematics. Because computers solve problems from a wide range of disciplines, it is important for computer science majors to be broadly educated and to have good analytical and communication skills. To accommodate student interests, the department offers three distinct options within the major. A fourth option in cooperative education may be added to any of the others. Option 1, Science, provides the student with a disciplineapproved program emphasizing the importance of the scientific method. Option 2, Information Systems, offers a computer science concentration and a management/economies background as the basis for a career in information systems. Option 3, Hardware Systems, gives the student who has an interest in physics and electronics a strong background in the hardware of computing. A cooperative education option is available to all majors in computer science. Students may enter this program after completing two semesters (minimum of 30 credits) in which they have earned minimum cumulative gradepoint averages of 3.0 in the required computer science and mathematics courses and at least 2.5 in all courses. The cooperative education director in the Department of Computer Science advises students in this program and assists in work placement for each student; however, the university cannot guarantee work assignments for all students. The department also offers two minors: one for students majoring in other subjects who want a strong background in traditional computer science, and one for students who want to emphasize personal computer studies. title: Introduction to Microcomputers
description: Introduction to the microcomputer as a word processing, spreadsheet, database, and communications tool. Intended for those in other disciplines. Hardware and software trends, opportunities and responsibilities in computing are discussed. Lecture and laboratory.

title: Introduction to Programming 1
description: Problems of programming in a structured language emphasizing topdown design and modular structure. Designed as a beginning programming course for the nonmajor. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or 125 or 201 or the equivalent. Not open to students who have credit in CS 120 or the equivalent.

title: Introduction to Programming 2
description: An introduction to files and their applications. An introduction to a LOGO environment. Prerequisite: CS 110 or its equivalent. Open only to students not majoring in computer science.

title: Introduction to Computer Information Systems
description: An introductory course in computer science for students in all disciplines other than computer science. Timesharing computer techniques using BASIC with emphasis on nonmathematical applications. Not open to the student who has credit in CS 120, 121, 210, or BEOA 210.

title: Computer Science 1
description: Introduction to programming using a structured, strongly typed language. Topics include: basic control structures, input/output, procedures and functions, arrays, textfiles, sets, records, introduction to software engineering, and ethics of computing. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 161.

title: Computer Science 2
description: Continuation of Computer Science 1. Topics include: pointer variables, linked lists, stacks, queues, binary trees, binary search and its complexity, recursion, sorting algorithms and their complexity, binary files and file organization, and software development tools. Introduction to objectoriented programming. Prerequisite: CS 120; MATHS 161.

title: Discrete Structures
description: Introduction to topics in discrete structures for computer science majors. Topics include propositional and predicate logic, sets, induction, recursion, relations, functions, combinatorial enumeration, Boolean algebra, and finite state machines. Applications of these topics to computer science are discussed. Prerequisite or parallel: CS 120.

title: Business Application Programming
description: Basic COBOL and programming skills using illustrative examples, exercises, and topics that emphasize application in commercial data processing. Prerequisite: CS 110 or 116 or 120. Not open to students who have credit in CS 340 or MGT 213.

title: Assembler Language Programming
description: Introduction to computer architecture, machine and assembly languages. Includes fixedpoint, floatingpoint, and decimal arithmetic, character and bit manipulation, looping, branching, macros, and subroutines. Prerequisite: CS 120.

title: Data Structures
description: Topics include abstract data structures, trees and graphs and their traversal, priority queues, algorithm design techniques, external storage and sorting, hashing, data compression, memory management. Prerequisite: CS 121, 124.

title: Microcomputer System Architecture
description: Elements of microcomputer system architecture and organization. Topics to be discussed include processors, primary and secondary memory systems, and networking principles. Prerequisite: CS 110 or the equivalent. Not open to students who have credit in CS 333.

title: Microcomputer Database
description: Considers how database techniques may be used in personal computer applications, how to design and develop database applications, and how to select a database product for a personal computer. prerequisite: CS 104. Not open to students who have credit in CS 436.

title: Microcomputer Operating Systems
description: Introduction to operating systems for the microcomputer. Topics related to concurrency, process and resource management, input/output control, and design problems are discussed. Comparisons of current microcomputer operating systems will be studied. Prerequisite: CS 233. Not open to students who have credit in CS 476. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Local and Wide Area Networks
description: LAN usage: file servers, print servers, and database servers. LAN design: wiring systems, protocols, interconnection devices, and operating systems. WAN usage: file transfer protocols and remote information systems. WAN design: leased phone lines, protocols, and routers. Prerequisite: any CS class or BEOA 210.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
description: Topics include analysis of algorithms; design techniques for efficient algorithms; induction; recursion; divide and conquer; greedy algorithms; dynamic programming; probabilistic algorithms; examples of geometric, combinatorial, and graph algorithms; pattern matching; fast Fourier transform; introduction to NP-completeness. Prerequisite: CS 121, 124; MATHS 212.

title: Computer Hardware Systems
description: Introduction to computer logic and registertransfer level of systems description. Examines the basic building blocks of a computer system and studies various computer architectures and hardware trends. Develops a general methodology for computer selection and introduces microprogramming. Prerequisite: CS 124, 230; and MATHS 212.

title: Advanced Topics Seminar
description: Indepth study of a topic taught in a seminar format. Topics will be posted in the department before registration. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors.

title: Data Processing Techniques
description: Commercial data processing techniques. Use of COBOL to solveproblems in file maintenance, report writing, and sorting. Emphasizes directaccess processing techniques including development of interactive screens. Prerequisite: CS 121, 230.

title: Computer Simulation Techniques
description: An introduction to the principles of simulation. Use of higher level languages and simulation languages in system studies. Students use examples from different subjects to carry out simulation. Prerequisite: CS 121; MATHS 221 or the equivalent.

title: Graphical User Interfaces
description: An introduction to the principles of design and implementation of user interfaces with emphasis on graphical user interfaces. Topics include design goals, user interface standards, eventdriven programming, application of objectoriented design and programming to GUIs, menus and dialog boxes. Prerequisite: CS 121 or the equivalent. Prerequisite or parallel: CS 232.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analyses, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, and orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 120; MATHS 162 or 166. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and CS 362 or MATHS 362. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 363.

title: Professional Experience
description: Professional computing experience in an approved program with computing facilities in business and industry. Paid positions only. Experience may be through coop, internship, or parttime employment. Requires term activity report. Offered on a credit/no credit basis only. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 16 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 4 in any one semester or term.

title: Systems Programming
description: Considers the computer system from the points of view of its architecture, operating system, and applications. Topics include processor organization, peripheral devices, I/O programming, system programs, monitor services, file organization, and realtime applications. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Programming Languages
description: A comparative study of programming languages. Emphasizes syntactic specification of programming languages and important features, structures, and compile and runtime characteristics of various higher level languages. Prerequisite: CS 230, 232.

title: Database Design
description: An introduction to database design, including physical representation, modeling, database systems, and implementation. Prerequisite: CS 232 and knowledge of C, COBOL, or FORTRAN.

title: Network Programming
description: Clientserver model and software design, program interface to protocols, and algorithms and issues in client and server software design. Remote procedure call concepts and distributed program generation. Prerequisite: CS 430.

title: Computer Graphics
description: Methods of developing, modifying, and rendering graphics displays. Emphasizes the design and writing of graphics software for both twoand threedimensional displays. Knowledge of a structured highlevel language is required. Prerequisite: CS 232; MATHS 212.

title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
description: Introduction to basic programming techniques of artificial intelligence (AI). Primary contents are symbol manipulations and AI problemsolving techniques. Topics include LISP prirnitives, LISP objects and evaluation, recursion and iteration, data abstraction (association lists, properties, and DESTP (UCT), macros, objectcentered programming, symbolic pattern matching, and basic problem solving methods. Prerequisite: CS 324, 435.

title: Principles of Computer Vision and Machine Intelligence
description: Laboratory based, dealing with the basic principles of acquisition and analysis of visual images by means of the computer. Studies the incorporation of vision in machine (robot) operation. Artificial intelligence techniques applied to task planning are used in integrating visual images with manipulator actions. Prerequisite: CS 333 or permission of the instructor.

title: Theory of Computation 1
description: Mathematical logic; alphabets and languages; finite automata, regular and nonregular languages, Kleene's theorem; regular grammars; pushdown automata and contextfree grammars; Turing and Post machines; recursive and recursively enumerable languages, and the Chomsky Hierarchy. Prerequisite: CS 324, 435.

title: Operating Systems
description: The functions and structure of computer operating systems, processors, memory, and device management. Concurrency and process synchronization. Input/output handling, device drivers, and disk scheduling. File systems, operating system design philosophy. Prerequisite: CS 333.

title: Compiler Construction
description: Review of contextfree grammars and basic parsing concept, compiler organization, and construction of components for a compiler. Prerequisite or parallel: CS 470.

title: Software Engineering 1—Systems Analysis
description: Software life cycle, software engineering concepts, systems analysis phase of life cycle. Introduces and applies structured methods to a project. The output of the project is a systems specification from which a software system can be designed and developed. Prerequisite: CS 232. Prerequisite or parallel: CS 436.

title: Software Engineering 2—Design and Development
description: Studies the design and development phases of the software life cycle. Introduces the latest appropriate structured methods and Criminal Justice and Criminology 253 applies them to a software project. This project will take a system specification and develop software from it. Prerequisite: CS 497.

description: Special advanced studies of computer science topics not taught in other courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors. Smith The Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology offers a variety of courses that help students understand the dimensions and causes of crime and delinquency and the theories of crime prevention and control. Students are prepared for entrylevel professional positions in the criminal justice system as well as for graduate study in related subjects. title: Introduction to American Criminal Justice System
description: Overview and analysis of the American criminal justice system.

title: Introduction to Criminology
description: Examines the legal definitions of criminal and delinquent behavior; typologies of crime and criminals; trends in reported distribution of crime and delinquency within the population; and theoretical explanations.

title: Research Methods in Criminal Justice
description: Introduction to research methods pertinent to the study of crime, criminality, and the criminal justice system. Emphasizes the design, development, use, and ethical concerns of both qualitative and quantitative research. Prerequisite: CJC 101, 102 or permission of the instructor.

title: Data Analysis in Criminal Justice
description: Introduction to data analysis in the study of crime, criminality, and the criminal justice system. Emphasizes computer applications in the analysis of data and use of existing records and sources of information. Prerequisite: CJC 220 or permission of the instructor.

title: Introduction to Policing

title: Introduction to Courts/Judiciary
description: Introduction to the American court and judicial systems emphasizing their structure, operation, and objectives. Prerequisite: CJC 101, 102 or permission of the instructor.

title: Juvenile Justice and Delinquency

title: Race, Ethnic, and Gender Issues in Criminal Justice
description: Examination of racial, ethnic, and gender issues regarding criminal offenders, victims of crime, and employees of the criminal justice system. Prerequisite: CJC 220, 221, 230, 240, 250 or permission of the instructor.

title: Victimology
description: Criminological examination of victims including victims' reactions and various responses made by the criminal justice system and other societal agencies. Prerequisite: CJC 220, 221, 230, 240, 250 or permission of the instructor.

description: Examination of the process of decision making in criminal justice agencies and social institutions that influence those agencies in American society. title: Current Topics in Corrections

description: Parttime individual assignment under field supervision in one of a variety of criminal justice settings. Prerequisite: senior standing, 2.5 GPA, permission of the instructor. Open only to criminal justice majors.
