Not open to students who have credit in ENG 104.

title: World Literature
description: Introduction to the study of world literature. Focuses on a generic, historical, or thematic topic. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or 114. Credit does not apply to English majors or minors.

title: World Literature Masterpieces
description: Selected major works of world literature, exclusive of English and American literature, for English majors or minors. Prerequisite: ENG 210.

title: Introduction to English Studies
description: Introduction to the field of English studies. Readinip and written work emphasize the diversity and scope of English studies and provide initial contact with the four areas in the department: Literature, Linguistics, English Education, and Composition and Rhetoric. Required of all English majors and minors. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or 114 or its equivalent.

title: Language and Society
description: Addresses major social issues related to language use in America. Through case studies students learn to identify hidden assumptions, frame questions requiring research, and do the research necessary to make informed decisions about linguistic issues in our society. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Fundamentals of English Grammar and Usage
description: Basic course in English grammar and usage for the underprepared. Cannot be counted as part of major or minor programs in English.

title: Advanced Composition and Creative Writing
description: Instruction in critical writing about literature beyond that provided for the general student, including the study of techniques of literary research, criticism, and documentation. Instruction in creative writing, particularly fiction and poetry. Prerequisite: ENG 210, sophomore standing or permission of the de artment chairperson. en only to English majors and minors except by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Writing in the Workplace
description: Practice in writing effective, professional prose with particular attention to the writing tasks often required in careers. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or its equivalent.

title: American Literature, 1607-1860
description: survey of American literature from its beginning through the middle nineteenth century, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 210, 230 or its equivalent is required for English majors and minors.

title: British Literature 1: The Beginnings to 1780
description: British literature - from about 450 to 1780, with attention to the social, historical, and philosophical backgrounds. Prerequisite: ENG 210, 230 or its equivalent is required for English majors and minors.

title: British Literature 2: 1780 to the Present
description: British literature from 1780 to the present, with attention to the historical, social, and philosophical background. Prerequisite: ENG 210, 230 or its equivalent is required for English majors and minors.

title: Introduction to Creative Writing: Prose
description: Development of the creative process and writing techniques for selfexpression and for exploration of ideas to enhance personal and professional life, such forms as journal, meditation, sketch, vignette, personal and descriptive essay. Prerequisite: ENG 103. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Introduction to Creative Writing: Poetry
description: Introduction to the creative process in the writing of poetry, including the use of traditional and contemporary forms and devices. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Literature and the Narrative Media
description: Consideration of the ways in which the narrative media have been used to develop fictional and nonfictional literature. Special attention to works that have been adapted from one medium to another and to works of lasting significance. Attention will be given to the narrative media and the language arts curriculum in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Prerequisite: ENG 210, 230 or its equivalent is required for English majors and minors.

title: Writing in the Discipline
description: Practice and study of selected rhetorics of inquiry employed in academic disciplines. Portfoliobased, leading to comparative analysis, preparing students for different systems of writing in their professional lives. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Creative Writing: Personal Essay
description: Instruction in the theory and techniques of writing the personal essay. Prerequisite: ENG 104 or its equivalent.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop 1
description: Practice and critique of the art of poetry in a workshop format, with instruction in the use of poetic forms and devices. Prerequisite: ENG 288 and permission of the instructor.

title: The Teaching of Language Arts in the Upper Elementary Grades
description: Modern methods and materials for teaching written and oral expression, language use, spelling, handwriting, and literature. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: Literature for Young Children
description: An introduction to literature for young children. Designed for elementary and early childhood education programs and endorsements and for parents and future parents. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English.

title: English Linguistics
description: Modern English grammar with emphasis on the application of uptodate descriptive linguistics, leading to an understanding of basic grammatical structure, relationship, and terminology, including morphology and phonology.

title: The Development of the English Language
description: Introduction to the historical development of the English language with attention to changes in vocabulary, grammar, and sounds.

title: Discourse Structure and Strategies
description: Application of linguistic and rhetorical methodologies to examine the effects of language on listeners and readers. Relates morphological, syntactic, semantic, and discourse structures to intentions and effects. Requires practice of the structures studied. Prerequisite: ENG 220.

title: Children's Literature
description: An overview of children's literature and an intensive study of various types. Designed for elementary education programs and endorsements. Cannot be counted as an elective in major or minor programs in English. Junior or senior standing recommended.

title: Linguistic Phonetics
description: Speech sounds and the linguistic methods employed in their description, classification, and analysis as elements in language systems.

title: American Literature 2,1860-1945
description: Survey of selected American writers and the various literary movements since 1860, including selections from a broad range of major and minority traditions. Prerequisite: ENG 210, 230 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Nineteenth Century American Fiction
description: Examination of the development of the novel and short story between 1800 and 1900.

title: Twentieth-Century American Fiction
description: Studies in the development and achievement of American fiction in the twentieth century.

title: Twentieth-Century American Drama
description: Themes and techniques of selected American playwrights with pertinent critical and biographical information. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Twentieth-Century American Poetry
description: Examination of the work of selected American poets. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Methods for Teaching Language Arts in Junior High/Middle Schools
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching language arts in junior high/middle schools. Cannot be counted as an elective in other major or minor programs in English. Prerequisite recommended: EDJHM 285.

title: Literature of African-American Traditions
description: Survey of the African- American literary tradition in the United States.

title: American Indian Literature
description: Study of materials from both the oral and written literatures of American Indians.

title: English Drama from Medieval Times to the Restoration
description: English drama from medieval times to 1660, excluding Shakespeare. Special attention is given to The Second Shepherds' Play and Everyman, and to the plays of Marlowe, Jonson, Dekker, Beaumont and Fletcher, and Webster.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid, supervised work experience in which classroomlearned skills are applied in research, critical thinking, and professional writing. Work assignments may be parttime or fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs in organizations, agencies, corporations, banks, or professional offices. Prerequisite: junior standing, permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but only 3 hours may count as credit on an English major or minor program.

title: The English Novel in the Eighteenth Century
description: Introduction to earliest English prose fiction and study of eighteenthcentury novels including the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, and Sterne. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: English Drama from the Restoration to the Present
description: English drama from 1700 to the present. Special attention is given to the plays of Steele, Goldsmith, Sheridan, Wilde, Shaw, Synge, O'Casey, Osborne, Beckett, and Pinter.

title: The English Novel in the Nineteenth Century
description: Nineteenthcentury novels, including works by Austen, Dickens, Thackeray, Eliot, the Brontës, Meredith, and Hardy. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Studies in British Drama
description: Special topics in contemporary British drama. Open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Honors Colloquium in English
description: Exploration of selected issues in English with emphasis upon individualized study and reporting. Open only to honors students. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Writing Competency Examination
description: Open to students who have completed ENG 103 and ENG 104 with have of C or better. Students must have juniorlevel standing, have earned at least 63 semester hours, and must register through the English department three weeks before the examination period. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. This course is offered on a credit/no credit basis.

title: Writing Competency Course
description: Required of all students who have not completed ENG 392 after two attempts. This course is offered on a credit/no credit basis, and credit hours do not count toward graduation requirements.

title: Teaching English in Secondary Schools
description: Materials, methods, and resources used in teaching composition, language, and literature. Required for teaching majors; may be an elective for teaching minors; may not be applied toward any other departmental program.

title: The Contemporary English Novel
description: Twentiethcentury novels, including the works of Conrad, Woolf, Joyce, Lawrence, Forster, Greene, Murdoch, and others. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Literary History
description: Development of the major aesthetic movements in literature from the Middle Ages to the present, emphasis on cultural context of ideas and construction of the literary "tradition." Prerequisite: ENG 210.

title: Special Topics in World and British Literature
description: Special research topics in world or British literature with emphasis on selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in English Education
description: Emphasizes current issues and problems at the elementary, middle, junior high, or senior high school level. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of . the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in American Literature
description: Special research topics in American literature, emphasizing selected writers as they reflect the social, scientific, philosophical, and religious attitudes of the age. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Special Topics in Composition
description: Special research topics in composition and rhetoric. Prerequisite: ENG 230.

title: Independent Study in English
description: Designed for students who want to conduct independent study and research in English. Prerequisite: 24 hours of credit in English at the 200 level or above at Ball State University and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Fiction Writing Workshop 1
description: Practice and critique of fiction writing, in a workshop format, with instruction in the fundamentals of the short story such as plot, character, and setting. Prerequisite: ENG 103.

title: Essay Writing Workshop
description: Advanced instruction in writing the personal and literary essay in a workshop format. Prerequisite: ENG 306 or permission of the instructor.

title: Fiction-Writing Workshop 2
description: Open to students who have had some experience with shortstory or novel writing. Primary emphasis is on instructor evaluation and student discussion of individual manuscripts. Prerequisite: ENG 405 or permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop 2
description: Advanced practice and criticism of the art of poetry in a workshop format, with attention to contemporary poetics and the current state of the art. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Independent Study in English Education
description: Designed for those who wish to conduct independent study and research in English education, preschool through the secondary level. Prerequisite: ENG 210, permission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Special Topics in Creative Writing
description: Emphasizes development of critical awareness of artistry, through knowledge of form or theory in poetry, fiction, or creative nonfiction. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Reading Printed Materials in the English Classroom
description: An overview of the process of reading printed materials with practical suggestions for developing analytic skills for reading and interpreting written communications, including literary and popular materials used in the English classroom.

title: Literature for Adolescents
description: Recent literature suitable for students of varying ability in junior high/middle and secondary schools. Emphasis on reading of selections with some attention given to methodology. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Writing for Young Readers
description: Instruction and practice with attention to the needs and interests of children or adolescents. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Introduction to Linguistic Science
description: The basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language in its descriptive and historical functions.

title: Sociolinguistics
description: A detailed examination of the relationship between language variety and social class, including recent studies in urban social dialectology. Basic issues in the study of bilingualism. Prerequisite: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Theory and Research in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Psychological and linguistic bases of language learning and recent theories concerning the application of linguistic science to methodology and materials in secondlanguage teaching. Prerequisite: knowledge of a foreign language. Prerequisite or parallel: ENG 321 or 420.

title: Methods and Materials in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Study and practice of a variety of methods in teaching English as a second or foreign language. Discussion of pedagogical issues in language teaching. Topics vary each semester; consult the English department for a schedule of offerings. Prerequisite: ENG 420 or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Seminar
description: Investigation in some depth of a problem in English studies, either literature, writing, linguistics, English education, or a combination. Specific topics vary by section and will be announced in advance. Prerequisite: senior standing or permission of the department chairperson. Open only to senior English majors.

title: Contemporary American Literature
description: Examination of literary texts, themes, and techniques from 1945 to the present. Prerequisite: ENG 210 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Practicum in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
description: Practical experience in observation, teaching, and analysis of teaching English as a second or foreign language. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Parallel: ENG 436 or 437. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Chaucer
description: Study of The Canterbury Tales, Troilus and Criseyde, and several minor poems. Emphasizes structure, sources, and significance of the works. Aspects of medieval culture pertinent to the works will be considered.

title: Shakespeare
description: An introductory study of representative plays (comedies, histories, tragedies) and some selections from the sonnets by Shakespeare.

title: Studies in Shakespeare
description: Special topics in a selection of Shakespeare's tragedies, comedies, and histories. Prerequisite: open only to students at the London Centre.

title: Milton
description: Indepth, analytical study of Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, Samson Agonistes, Lycidas, and Areopagitica, as well as a brief study of "The Christian Doctrine" and other selected poems and prose by John Milton.

title: Practical Experience
description: Nonpaid, supervised work experience in which classroomlearned skills are applied in research, critical thinking, and professional writing. Work assignments may be parttime or fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs in organizations, agencies, corporations, banks, or professional offices. Prerequisite: junior standing, permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but only 3 hours may count as credit on an English major or minor program.

title: Independent Creative Writing
description: Directed independent writing of poetry, fiction, or essay. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Women in Literature
description: Investigation of various ways women have beenportrayed in the literature of the Western world. Examination of significant writing by women.

title: The Modern Continental Novel
description: Novels in translation over the last hundred years. Novels will be related to major historical, political, and intellectual currents.

title: Modern British Poetry
description: Important poets of Great Britain from World War Ito the present, focusing on Yeats, Eliot, Auden, and Thomas, with additional attention given to Hopkins, Owen, Lawrence, Graves, Ted Hughes, and others. e----)GEOGRAPHY-) T. title: Earth, Sea, and Sky: A Geographic View
description: Selected aspects of the physical environment and their relationship to human occupancy of the earth. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Not open to students who have credit in GEOG 111.

title: Physical Geography and Earth Science Concepts for Teachers
description: Earthsun relationships, weather and climate, geologic processes (including earth structure and sculpturing of the earth's surface); conservation principles as they pertain directly to the material taught. Designed primarily for students in elementary education programs. Not open to students who have credit in GEOG 101.

title: Economic Geography and Contemporary Issues
description: A systematic approach to economic geography and current economic issues emphasizing local, regional, national, and international economic developments in the geographic setting.

title: Geography of the Cultural Environment
description: A spatial analysis of the interaction of cultural development and the physical environment. Special emphasis upon the processes of cultural change and their effect on the landscape.

title: Global Geography
description: A basic survey course emphasizing geographic facts and interdependencies between the developed and developing world. Particular emphasis is given to physical and social environmental interdependencies.

title: The American Landscape: A Historical Geography of the United States
description: Geography of American landscape in earlier times. Selected regions examined to understand geographical influences on transformation of the wilderness. Emphasis is placed on exploration, discovery, migration routes, settlement, adjustments to the land, and means, of securing a livelihood.

title: Weather 1
description: How and why the weather changes, the characteristics of weather, and an examination of weather instruments.

title: Map Reading and Interpretation
description: Introduction to skills needed to use and appreciate maps as a form of communication and as a research tool. Topics include elements and sources of maps, history of map making, techniques of analysis, and introduction to aerial photography and remote sensing.

title: Introduction to Travel and Tourism
description: A survey of the travel and tourism industry; its various components, dimensions, organization, and structure. Topics include economic, social, cultural, and environmental implications; motivations for travel, and the past and future of the industry.

title: Geography of Tourism
description: Emphasizes spatial interaction arising from the movement of people engaged in travel for leisure and otherpurposes. Models of tourism, measuring spatial variations, patterns of domestic and international flows (regions), and spatial organization are examined. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Urban Geography
description: Distribution, classification, structure, and function of urban centers. Special attention is given to the geographic conditions affecting urban development and growth.

title: Urban Geography: Trends in Theory and Research
description: Survey of the contribution of Weberian, Marxist, and "managerialist" theory to the interpretation of urban spatial organization and change. In the light of these theories, current research trends and techniques are examined. GEOG 230 or GEOL 240 ASTRO 100 or 6 hours from GEOG 331 GEOL 207 ASTRO 382

title: Weather 2
description: Introduction to weather forecasting using applied examples. Students may gain practical experience by working in the university weather station. prerequisite: GEOG 230.

title: Climate
description: Introduction to climate with emphasis on regional distribution. How and why climates differ across the Earth. prerequisite: GEOG 230, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Cartography and Graphics 1
description: The construction and design of maps and graphs. Basic drafting techniques and methods of cartographic presentation. Although the emphasis is on graphic presentation of spatially disposed quantitative and qualitative data, the techniques and methods apply to a wide range of subject areas.

title: Cartography and Graphics 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in the application of mapping and graphics techniques, including an introduction to computer graphics. Projects are selected within students' specializations or topics of interest. Prerequisite: GEOG 340.

title: Remote Sensing 1
description: Principles of photo interpretation, satellite scanners, and radar. Characteristic features of remotely sensed data, classification processes, and algorithms.

title: Remote Sensing 2
description: Additional instruction and practice in remote sensing, including digital data analysis, image enhancement technique as applied to natural resources, urban analysis, soil studies, geology, and other applied branches. Prerequisite: GEOG 342.

title: Geographic Information Systems Analysis
description: Methods of analysis provided by geographic information systems (GIS). Operations on spatial and attribute information including basic functions (e g., map overlay) and special functions (e g., network analysis). Exposure to raster and vector software. Review capabilities of currently available GIS software. Prerequisite: GEOG 240, 340, and 341 or permission of the instructor.

title: Geography of the United States and Canada
description: Comprehensive survey of geographic regions, settlement, land use, natural resources, and potentialities of the United States and Canada.

title: Geography of Latin America and the Caribbean
description: Physical and cultural patterns in a diverse world region. Emphasis is on population and settlement, agriculture, and environmental hazards in the context of development.

title: Geography of Africa
description: A survey and analysis of the physical and cultural environments of Africa.

title: Geography of Indiana
description: A geographic examination of the physical, cultural, and economic diversity of the state. Field experiences supplement classroom activities.

title: Geography of Asia
description: The geography of South, Southwest, Southeast, and East Asia. A survey and analysis of the physical geographic patterns, bases of cultural diversity, and changing spatial aspects of political organization.

title: Geography of Western Europe
description: Treats the spatial elements of the physical and cultural environment of Western Europe. Using a thematic approach, primary emphasis is given to the United Kingdom, Ireland, Scandinavia, France, Benelux countries, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, and the Iberian and Italian peninsulas.

title: Geography of Russia and Its Neighbors
description: Geographic analysis of the locational, environmental, economic, and cultural diversity of the successor countries to the Soviet Union. Regional examination of Russia, Baltic, and other East European countries, Transcaucasia and Central Asia.

title: Geography of Central Europe
description: Addresses the physical and human environments of central and southeastern European nations, from Poland in the north to Albania in the south. Attention given to the physiographic, climatological, cultural, economic, and political geography of the region. Not open to students who have credit in EURO 357.

title: Travel and Tourism Industry
description: Examination of the technical aspects of domestic and international travel, tourism and the hotel industry. Develops research and managerial skills by using professionally prepared materials related to travel, tourism and hotel planning, development, and operations. Prerequisite: GEOG 261, 262, permission of the department chairperson. Open only to geography option 2 majors.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid fullor parttime work experiences with an organization allied to a student's area of specialization. Assignments depend on student interests and the sponsor's convenience. Used for paid work experience only. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Geography of Transportation
description: Geographic considerations of the major modes of transportation of the world and transportation patterns.

title: Population Geography
description: A systematic and regional analysis of areal patterns of population distribution, composition, migration, and growth, as well as their causes and the effects they have on the cultural landscape.

title: Seminar in Geography or Earth Science
description: Advanced study of a selected topic in geography or earth science. Prerequisite: an introductory geography or earth science course or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Advanced Techniques in Remote Sensing
description: Advanced techniques applied to remotely sensed data using stateoftheart software. Review of current methods of computer and manual interpretation techniques. Includes active participation in classroom presentations. Prerequisite: GEOG 342 and 343.

title: Advanced Cartography
description: Application of color theory to thematic mapping. Principles of color separation andproofing. Interfacing graphic and mapping software to obtain quality materials for publications. Survey of current map printing technology. Prerequisite: GEOG 340, 341.

title: Applications of Geographic Information Systems
description: Practical experience applying geographic information system (GIS) tools to analyze spatial data. Workshop format requires studentmotivated projects; diverse disciplines encouraged. Project work involves proposal, work plan, presentation, and final report. Prerequisite: GEOG 344 or permission of the instructor.

title: Automation and the Travel Industry
description: Introduction to the use of automation in the travel industry as it applies to information management and task functions like reservation and ticketing systems. Includes laboratory experience. Prerequisite: GEOG 360. Open to majors only.

title: World Political Geography
description: Analysis of the contribution of physical and cultural characteristics of the nations of the world to domestic and foreign relations problems.

title: Practical Experience
description: Fullor parttime work experience with an organization allied to a student's area of specialization. Assignments depend upon student interests and the sponsor's convenience. Used for nonpaid work experience only. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Distant Areas Field Studies
description: Physical, economic, and cultural geography in areas distant from the campus. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. Open to students in geography, earth science, and allied subjects. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 6 in any one semester or term.

title: Seminar in Travel and Tourism
description: Advanced study exploring problems and issues, theory and research related to travel and tourism. Topics will vary depending upon the instructor and needs and interests of students. Prerequisite: GEOG 360.

title: Geographic Research Methods
description: An introduction to the use of statistics and quantitative techniques in geographic research. Topics include research design, statistical testing, and geographic modeling. Geology 273

title: Readings and Special Studies in Geography and Earth Science
description: Assigned special studies in geography and earth science, including readings, research projects, teaching problems, or assignment to an undergraduate class. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Senior Thesis
description: The formulation and writing of a researchoriented thesis. Working with a faculty advisor, student will write a research paper on a geographic theme or topic of his or her choice. Paper will be evaluated for geographic content and compositional skills. Prerequisite: junior or senior standing and permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geographic Field Methods
description: Introduction to the techniques of field study and analysis of physical and cultural spatial patterns. r"---JGEOLOGYe----) A. Samuelson, Chairperson; R. Fluegeman, J. Grigsby, R. Orr, R. Rice-Snow, H. Roepke Geologists study the earth, paying primary attention to its history, materials, and structure, and to the active processes that continue to change the landscape. Geologists are also concerned with investigating environmental problems such as geologic hazards involving flooding or earthquakes, evaluating groundwater resources, discovering new mineral and petroleum deposits, and studying the oceans, moon, and planets. The department offers two departmental majors in geology. The professional arts major is designed to prepare students for geological careers in industry, environmental consulting, and government agencies and for graduate study that leads to research, teaching, management, and many other positions in industry, government, and universities. The liberal arts major aims to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who have related interests, want to pursue double majors, or do not want to directly enter the geological profession. MAJOR IN GEOLOGY (PROFESSIONAL ARTS), 65-66 hours PREFIX NO SHORT TITLE CR HRS Students are expected to have completed GEOL 101 or GEOG 101 and mathematics through MATHS 117 or high school equivalent as approved by the primary departmental advisor.

title: Planet Earth's Geological Environment
description: Introductory study of the materials, structure, and surface features of the earth; the processes responsible for their development; and the application of geologic knowledge to mankind's environmental and resource problems. Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory.

title: Historical Geology
description: Introduction to the physical history of the earth in relationship to the development of life throughout geologic time. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or GEOG 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Age of the Dinosaurs
description: Discussion of the dinosaurs, their classification, their relationship to the environment, their geographic distribution, and their geologic record. Special emphasis on new theories about dinosaur ecology, behavior, and extinction.

title: Oceans and Nations
description: Worldwide human interactions with the oceans and international conflicts of interest related to the marine environment. Introduction to oceanography, marine law, resource conflicts, pollution, cooperation for research and hazard response, and other topics. Credit does not count toward the geology minor. Open only to sophomores, juniors, seniors.

title: Environmental Geology
description: Examines geologic materials and processes affecting the human environment. Discusses geologic hazards, mineral and energy resources for the future, groundwater, surface water hydrology, and urban geology. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mineralogy
description: Principles of crystallography and mineralogy and the relationships of minerals to the composition and types of rocks of the earth's crust. Laboratory work concerned with crystallographic operations and the identification of minerals by physical and chemical properties. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101; an introductory chemistry course or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geomorphology
description: Study of landforms and their evolution. Local area field trips. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Introduction to Methods in Field Geology
description: Introduces techniques in field geology, including topics in rock and mineral identification and classification, how to read and use geologic maps and air photos, application of GPS, methods in soil and groundwater sampling, and basic mapping techniques. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, permission of the department chairperson.

title: Invertebrate Paleontology
description: Principles of paleontology as revealed by invertebrate fossils. Fossilization, morphology, evolution, and life association of the important invertebrate phyla (Coelenterata, Bryozoa, Brachiopoda, Mollusca, Arthropoda, and Echinodermata). Local area field trip. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Structural Geology
description: An introduction to rockdeformation theory, analysis of deformed systems, and structural interpretation of mapped areas of deformed rocks. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 112 (or the high school equivalent) or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mystery Landforms
description: Landscape features whose origins are unknown, their speculated origins, and the methods/values scientists use to test hypotheses. Major term project in which teams intensively study particular landforms, culminating in group presentations (format, students' choice). Diverse backgrounds welcome.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid professional work and learning experience arranged during one or more semesters or summers. Eligible students will be placed in an approved agency or private business. Assignments, including activity log, selfanalysis, and summary report, are supervised by the department. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson and the coordinator of internships. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Geology Field Camp
description: Application of field techniques to the resolution ofgeologic problems. Assignments include accumulation and interpretation of field observations and preparation of geologic maps, cross sections, and stratigraphic sections. Conducted during a fiveweek summer period in South Dakota and Wyoming. Prerequisite: GEOL 301, permission of the department chairperson.

title: Computer Applications in the Geosciences
description: Survey of the various computer applications in the geosciences. Designed to supplement existing geoscience and computer science courses by providing opportunity to gain experience in working with BASIC and FORTRAN programs in various geoscience datacollection, calculation, and graphic display applications. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 in any one semester or term.

title: Micropaleontology
description: Morphology, classification, preparation techniques, and evolution of paleontologically significant microfossil groups and their biostratigraphic and paleoeeologic significance. Emphasis is on foraminifera, conodonts, and ostracodes. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Petrology
description: Petrography and petrogenesis of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, based on both hand specimens and microscope examination of thin sections. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 220.

title: Sedimentation and Stratigraphy
description: Deals with the description and classification of sedimentary rocks and their formation. Emphasis also on using sedimentary rocks to interpret the geologic history of sedimentary basins. Current research trends in sedimentary geology will be discussed. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or permission of the instructor.

title: Engineering Geology
description: Engineering properties and mechanics of rocks and soil; geologic materials in construction, applied geophysics for subsurface exploration; groundwater engineering problems; dams, tunnels, mines, shoreline structures, and other special construction problems; erosion and mass wasting. Regularly scheduled laboratory. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 and MATHS 112 (or the high school equivalent) or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geological and Physical Oceanography
description: Description of geological and physical characteristics of the oceans, marine processes, and related topics. prerequisite: GEOL 101 or the high school equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geophysics
description: An introduction to refraction and reflection seismology; magnetic, electrical, gravity, radioactivity, and geothermal methods. Emphasis is on geophysical methods applied to such problems as energy resources, mineral and ground water exploration, site evaluation, and pollution detection. Includes laboratory exercises and field investigations. Prerequisite: GEOL 101, 102, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Petroleum Geology
description: Theory and techniques dealing with exploration, drilling, and production of petroleum and natural gas. Prerequisite: GEOL 315 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Geology of Indiana
description: Rocks, structure, fossils, landforms, economic resources, and geologic history of Indiana. Fieldtrip oriented with collection of rock, mineral, and fossil specimens. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Hydrogeology
description: Occurrence and movement of surface water and groundwater, with special reference to the effect of the geologic environment. Prerequisite: GEOL 102 or 207 or 240 or NREM 211; MATHS 108; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Groundwater Geochemistry
description: Introduces the processes controlling the composition of natural waters; streams, lakes, oceans, and nearsurface groundwaters. Focuses on the effects of human activities, biological systems, and inorganic geochemistry processes on water chemistry. Prerequisite: GEOL 101; CHEM 111, 112; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Glacial Geology
description: Indepth study of the physical nature of glaciers, their deposits, and the erosional and depositional landforms they create. Introduction to glacial history of the northcentral United States. Term paper required. Prerequisite: GEOL 240; PHYCS 110 or 120; or permission of the instructor.

title: Special Studies and Field Problems
description: Selected detailed geologic problems under the guidance of a qualified instructor. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term. R. Marek, Chairperson; A. Alves, R. Aquila, J. Barber, L. Birken, A. Edmonds, W. Eidson, M. Fissel, B. Students with degrees in history can pursue graduate degrees or careers in law, teaching, government, business, industry, libraries and archives, museums and art galleries, research, writing, and editing. MAJOR IN HISTORY, 33-45 hours Complete one option Option 1: Major, 33 hours 12 hours from World history (Europe, Africa, Middle East, Asia) 12 hours from American history (United States and Latin America) 9 hours from electives in HIST 33 hrs Option 2: Major with internship, 42-45 hours Admission and retention standards for option 2: • Students must earn grades of at least C in all completed history courses with a combined history gradepoint average of at least 3.0. • Candidates for internships must fill out applications with the program coordinator at least five months in advance of the time of the intended internships. • To qualify for the internship (HIST 300 or 369), students must have taken the required history courses and completed 32 semester hours in HIST. • An overall gradepoint average of 2.75 is required before enrolling in the internship. • A written project approved by the coordinator and related to the internship is required. • Credit received by students serving as assistants in departmental courses is not applicable to internship credit in this option. • Students who do not meet the above requirements may appeal to the program coordinator for a waiver, first by written request and then by making an oral presentation.

title: Introduction to American Studies
description: Survey of American studies as a field and as an interdisciplinary approach to the study of American civilization. Methods and theories of American studies will be discussed, along with major themes and topics of American life and thought. Not open to students who have credit in AMSTU 101.

title: Introduction to the History of Business in the United States
description: Surveys the function of business in United States history from colonial times to the modern day. Focuses on the role of individual business people as decision makers and innovators with primary emphasis on the twentieth century.

title: Western Civilization
description: A survey of the major themes and developments in the evolution of Western civilization from its origins to the present with emphasis on key problems, turning points, recurring issues, and cultural growth and heritage. Special stress on the character and crises confronting the Western world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: World Civilization 1
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the dawn of civilization in Southwestern Asia and North Africa to the early modern world.

title: World Civilization 2
description: A survey of the development of world civilization from the early modern world to the present.

title: Studies in Non-Western Civilizations
description: Examination of a broad range of patterns and problems found in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Latin America with emphasis on recent and contemporary development. Topics vary among political, economic, and social issues of major importance.

title: American History, 1492-1876
description: Survey Of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States to 1876.

title: American History, 1877 to the Present
description: Survey of the political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and sociological forces and adjustments that have affected the history of the United States since 1877.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give students knowledge of resource use in the United States. Government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present are treated in historical perspective. Emphasis is on the way resource use has shaped society. Not open to students who have credit in NREM 204.

title: Introduction to Sport in American Life
description: A thorough examination of the various historical, sociological, and psychological features of sports in our society. Not sportappreciation oriented, but rather an examination of what occurs to both competitors and spectators as they become involved with a sport activity. Open to all undergraduate students except students who have credit in PEP 205.

title: Black History—The United States
description: A survey of blacks in America from the sixteenth century to the present. Emphasis is on the effects of blacks on American culture and vice versa.

title: Women in American History
description: An introduction to the study of women in American history; considers the social and economic status of women at various times, changing conceptions of their roles, attitudes toward women, women's ideas about themselves, and the women's rights movement.

title: The History of American Popular Culture
description: Historical overview of the development of American popular culture. Basic theories, approaches, and topics in popular culture with special attention to amusements, movies, pop music, magazines, pulp novels, and television. Focuses on the relationship o f popular culture to American cultural and social history.

title: Early Latin America
description: The discovery and exploration of America by the Spanish, the conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonization of Spanish America and Brazil, and the civilization of Latin America from 1492 to 1810.

title: Modern Latin America
description: History of major institutions in South America since independence with emphasis on Mexico, Chile, Cuba, and Central America.

title: Introduction to Public History
description: An overview of opportunities for nonteaching historyrelated careers in preservation, archival work, records management, museology, historical editing, living history and public parks programs, corporate history, and others. Students make a concentrated study of at least one field of public history and have contact with working professionals. Open to all students.

title: History of the European Family
description: A survey of the changing social, economic, and political roles of the European family from antiquity to the present. Topics include the distribution of authority, marriage and inheritance, childrearing, domestic labor, and the effects of industrialization. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: The United States and the Vietnam War
description: Historical analysis of American involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1975, with discussions of the military, political, diplomatic, and social effects of the war. Includes background information on Vietnamese history as well as its continuing legacy.

title: Introduction to Peace Studies and Conflict Resolution
description: Interdisciplinary study of methods of achieving peace within communities and among nations; history of peace movements and the causes of conflict; and analysis of principles to resolve conflict using case studies.

title: A Laboratory Course in American History
description: Uses documents and manuscripts to teach the nature of history and historical research. Students learn through their own research how the historian defines topics of research; selects sources, both primary and secondary; evaluates materials; and describes the findings.

title: The Spanish Borderlands
description: The Anglo-American-Spanish-American frontier, 1550 to 1850, from Florida to Texas, New Mexico, and California.

title: United States Urban History
description: Examines the inner dynamics of American cities and theirplace in the history of the United States. Gives students an historical perspective and acquaints them with historical methods of examining cities.

title: Selected Topics in Military History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular period, topic, or issue in military history with emphasis on materials not covered in established courses. Exact content will be announced in advance of each offering. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Paid Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships in careers related to history. Internships may be with historical museums and research institutions; public agencies like the National Park Service, historic preservation offices, and archives; or private institutions like historical galleries and business firms. This course is designed for paid work and learning experience on or off campus. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foundations of Asian Civilization
description: Survey of South, Southeast, and East Asian history from earliest times to roughly 1600 A.D., with special focus on the development of Asian societies and cultures before any significant European presence.

title: Tradition, Conflict, and Change in Modern Asia
description: Survey of South, Southeast, and East Asian history from roughly 1600 A.D. to the present, with concentration on the problems, leaders, and issues that .resulted from Western presence, nationalism, independence, and modernization as well as contemporary issues.

title: Africa Since 1500
description: Stresses the emergence of modern African civilization from roughly 1500 to the present, with particular emphasis on regions south of the Sahara.

title: History of the Middle East
description: Provides indepth knowledge and understanding of the Middle East— today's Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Thrkey, and other states— since Muhammed. Stresses indigenous societies and how they have dealt with Islam, imperialism, nationalism, development, and wars.

title: Honors Colloquium in History
description: Exploration of selected issues, themes, problems, or interpretations with emphasis on individualized study and reporting. Restricted to honors students; others may enroll by permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Colonial America 1492-1756
description: The settlement of North America by the British and the evolution of the distinctive colonial societies that formed the foundation of the United States.

title: The American Revolution, 1756-1789
description: Transformation of American society and politics in the era of the American Revolution with emphasis on the origins of the revolution, the development of a democratic society, and the Constitution of the United States.

title: The Rise of Nationalism in the United States, 1789-1824
description: An analysis of the foundations of the United States as a new nation with emphasis on the major social, political, economic, and diplomatic events of the period.

title: Nationalism Versus Sectionalism in the United States, 1820-1860
description: An analysis of the major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in the United States with emphasis on the major leaders and events involving the sectional conflict leading to the Civil War, 1820-1860.

title: The American Civil War and Reconstruction
description: Survey, analysis, and discussion of events, leaders, and movements, with special emphasis on causes, interpretation, and historiography of the period of national crisis and war followed by national reconstruction.

title: Progressivism and Imperialism: The United States, 1878-1918
description: America's rise to world significance at home and abroad between 1878 and 1918, the political, social, and economic problems entailed therein, and various efforts at reform.

title: The United States from World War I through World War II
description: An examination of the reaction of the American people to a society changing rapidly under the impact of two major wars, the Great Depression, and continuing industrialization and urbanization.

title: Recent United States History: 1945 to the Present
description: A study of the role of the United States in the modern world and an examination of the efforts of . America to preserve a society that is prosperous and humane while adjusting to technological change and continuing social and intellectual ferment.

title: History of Indiana
description: Exploration, colonization, and development of the state from the earliest time to the present.

title: History of the Antebellum South
description: History, institutions, political themes, and problems of the antebellum South.

title: History of the New South
description: Reconstruction, industrial and agricultural progress, social life, and the new leadership after 1865.

title: The Colonial and Trans- Appalachian Frontiers
description: American territorial expansion in the region east of the Mississippi River from the time of the first European penetration to about 1830. Emphasis is on the geographic continuity in the settlement process and on the frontier's effect upon the settlers in particular and American society in general.

title: The Trans-Mississippi Frontier
description: American territorial expansion in the region west of the Mississippi River, with emphasis on the nineteenth century. Focuses on exploration, the movement of settlers, the events that influenced their migration, and the effect of these events and the frontier on national development.

title: Indians in U.S. History
description: Survey of Indian and white relations from 1492 to the present, focusing on the Indian wars, treaty making, various types of Indian and white interaction, and the development of federal and state Indian policy.

title: The Caribbean
description: The Central American republics and Cuba, Haiti, Santo Domingo, Venezuela, and Colombia since 1810, with emphasis on the twentieth century and the Cuban revolution.

title: United States Diplomatic History to 1914
description: History of United States diplomacy from the late colonial period to the eve of World War I.

title: United States Diplomatic History Since 1914
description: Survey of the foreign relations of the United States since the outbreak of World War I.

title: American Life and Thought, 1607-1865
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from the colonial period to the Civil War, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American Life and Thought, 1865 to the Present
description: Survey of American social, intellectual, and cultural history from Reconstruction to the present, including such topics as religion, women, the family, ethnic groups, minorities, the arts, thought, popular culture, and everyday life.

title: American History through Film
description: Introduces techniques to analyze films as primary documents in United States history. Focuses on the most significant feature and documentary films of American society. Compares and contrasts filmic and historic reality.

title: History and Historians
description: Historiography: the major historians and the writing of history from Thucydides to the present.

title: American Culture Field Studies
description: American culture, its art, economic life, educational systems, geography, history, industry, languages, music, and society. Students travel through designated areas in North America. Requires considerable reading before the trip and papers at the conclusion. With departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in United States history may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 3. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Topics for independent study and research to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor possessing special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern Western Culture
description: Development of cultural and intellectual movements in the fine arts, literature, scholarship, political and economic thought, science, and social reform from the eighteenth century to the present. Emphasis on themes and problems of major significance.

title: The Era of World War I, 1870-1918
description: Survey of the background, immediate causes, and the course of the First World War with stress on nationalism, the alliance system, imperialism, militarism, national aspirations, power rivalries, wartime operations, and peace plans.

title: The Era of World War II, 1918-1945
description: The origins, immediate causes, and the course of World War II with emphasis on the peace settlement of 1919, revisionism, appeasement, diplomatic conflicts, military campaigns, and the foundations of the postwar world.

title: The Cold War and Europe since 1945
description: European origin of the Cold War and rebirth of a "new" but divided Europe with stress on East-West conflict, power blocs, international relations, and temporary decline of European influence; ideological, political, economic, and social development, including competition between Western and Sovietized Eastern Europe.

title: Strategy and Diplomacy of the European Great Powers Since 1860
description: Examines, interprets, and evaluates British, German, Russian, French, Italian, and Austrian strategy and diplomacy—and economic, geographic, ideological, and military foundations of national power—focusing upon the "German Question," Eurocentrism, imperialism, two world wars, renewed multipolarity, the European Community, and the Cold War. Not open to students who have credit in EURO 458.

title: The Jews in Europe and the Middle East, 1098 to the Present
description: Survey of the Jewish role in European and Middle Eastern history and society. Focus will be on the commonalities and differences between Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, and changing attitudes toward the Jewish community in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

title: History of Medicine in Western Society
description: A survey of the ideas, attitudes, and institutions of medicine and public health in the Western world from antiquity to modern times. Special attention given to social forces influencing medical knowledge and health care. Not open to students who have credit in HSC 460.

title: Development of Greek Civilization
description: Examination of Greek political institutions, society, religion, and intellectual life in the Hellenic and Hellenistic periods. Emphasis is on the study of Greek forms of democracy and other contributions to Western civilization and culture.

title: Development of Roman Civilization
description: Political, social, and intellectual development of Rome from the beginning of the republic to approximately 500 A.D. Emphasis is on the development of the characteristics of the Romans during the republic and the effect on them of Greek ideas and world domination.

title: Medieval Civilization
description: Political, social, and cultural developments of Europe from the late Roman Empire through the thirteenth century, with special emphasis on the history of medieval thought and art. Material covered in this course is basic for any further work in medieval history.

title: Development of Byzantine Civilization
description: Survey of the political, socioeconomic, and intellectual development of the Byzantine Empire from its beginnings to 1453 with special emphasis on Byzantine religious and cultural contributions and relations with the European and Muslim worlds.

title: The Renaissance and Reformation, 1300-1600
description: Specialized study of the crises, changes, and cultural achievements of Europe in an age of transition. Emphasizes such major topics as the late medieval crises, Italian and northern Renaissance thought and art, the religious crisis of the sixteenth century, and political, social, and economic problems of Renaissance Europe.

title: World Civilizations—Field Studies
description: Studies in world civilizations—their history, art, economic life, educational systems, geography, industry, languages, music, and society—through varied travel programs. Advance reading and a summary paper complement each year's travel program and are required. with departmental approval, secondary social studies teachereducation students with a concentration in world civilization may apply 3 hours of credit to category 1, 2, or 4.

title: France Since 1815
description: Political, social, intellectual, and cultural development of modern France throughout the periods of revolution and reaction, imperial growth, and republican reform and stabilization. Emphasis is on conflicts of state power and individual freedom, capitalism and socialism, and war and peace.

title: France—The Classical Age, 1461-1715
description: Origins and development of French absolutism; classic culture, and society from the Spider King to the Sun King. Focuses on foundations of the ancient regime and its institutions—the monarchy, aristocracy, bourgeoisie, Gallican Catholicism—and France's influence on Europe.

title: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era, 1715-1815
description: Causes of the French Revolution—the great turning point of modern civilization— and revolutions in general. Stresses the development of nationalism, freedom of the individual, concentration of authority in the state, and the goal of national selfdetermination.

title: Britain, 1485-1714
description: A survey of the political, social, and economic history of England in the Tudor and Stuart periods. Emphasis is on the rise of the national state, religious conflicts, the development of the power of Parliament, and overseas exploration and colonization.

title: Britain, 1714 to the Present
description: Survey of the many major changes in British life from the Hanoverian period to thepresent—modernization of political institutions, evolution of the limited monarchy, industrialization and social conflict, effects of imperialism and recent wars, problems of government and society since World War II.

title: Topics in English Constitutional History
description: Selected topics concerning the constitutional history of England, such as the development of the kingship, the common law, Parliament, the Tudor and Stuart theories of government, the cabinet system, and political parties.

title: Modern Germany
description: Experiences of the German people during the critical periods of national unification under Bismarck, the First World War, changing cultural and intellectual life, the Hitler and Nazi era, World War II, and the recent division of West and East.

title: Cultural History of the Celtic Peoples from Prehistory to the Present
description: Surveys the cultural history of the six modern Celtic countries (Brittany, Cornwall, Ireland, Isle of Man, Scotland, and Wales) and their ancient continental forebears, including major political events, literature, social organization, and traditional oral culture.

title: Irish History
description: Covers all of Irish history from pre-Christian Celtic times to the present, including political events, literature (both oral and written), the role of language, music, folklore, and other elements of Irish cultural history.

title: Tzarist Russia
description: Survey of the Russian state and people from about 1500 to the revolution of 1917—stressing political developments and forms, religious and cultural life, economic and social change, geographic expansion, and national goals and issues in foreign affairs.

title: The Soviet Union
description: The development of the Soviet Union from the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 to the present, stressing the evolution of political and economic institutions, social problems, cultural policies, and the ideological aims and changing role of the Soviet Union in world affairs.

title: History of South Asia
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of the subcontinent of South Asia, comprising India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka, from early times to the present.

title: History of Southeast Asia
description: History of the region from earliest times to the present, with special attention to the formation of the earliest civilizations; the influence of Indian, Chinese, and European cultures upon the people of Southeast Asia; and the processes of synthesis that have taken place within these civilizations through the centuries.

title: Economic History of Asia
description: Study of the implications of Asia's economic evolution for the development of Asian civilization, the stimulus of international maritime routes through time, indigenous productive patterns, the effects of imperialism, and Asia's role in the world economy of the twentieth century.

title: Topics in Middle Eastern History
description: Selected issues and problems in the Middle Eastern world since Muhammed. Topics may include the expansion of Islam, slavery in the Middle East, the economic and social history and the Ottoman empire, the Arab/Israeli dispute, and recent national and international crises.

title: History of China to 1600
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of China's history from earliest times to roughly 1600 A.D., with emphasis on the development of the dynastic tradition, Confucianbased society and culture, and China's focal point status in the pre- 1600 world order.

title: History of Premodern Japan
description: Analytical survey of premodern Japanese history to circa 1600, focusing on the ideological, political, social, economic, and cultural developments that build a foundation for the understanding of modern Japan.

title: Selected Topics in Non-Western History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in non-Western history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Topics will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Modern China, 1600 to the Present
description: Descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's changing role as a member of the world community, its response to increased Western contacts, disintegration of traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant elements of contemporary Chinese society and culture.

title: Modern Japan, 1600 to the Present
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on conditions contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Selected Topics in European History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in European history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Topics will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Topics in American History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Topics will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Junior High/Middle School
description: Concentrates on the selection and application of specialized materials and methods appropriate for teaching social studies in junior high/middle schools. Prerequisite or parallel: EDJHM 285; EDSEC 280. Open only to Social Studies teaching majors.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Early Childhood/Kindergarten—Grade 3
description: Materials and procedures for teaching social studies from early childhood through grade three. Emphasis on concepts, behavioral objectives, inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation. Required for early childhood and K-3 teaching programs.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Materials and procedure for teaching social studies from kindergarten through grade six. Emphasis is on behavioral objectives, inquiry techniques, learning resources, individualizing instruction, value clarification, skill development, and program evaluation.

title: Teaching Social Studies in the Elementary School
description: Provides more experience in methods used in teaching elementary social studies and an opportunity to use materials available to teachers. Prerequisite: SS 391 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching Social Studies in Secondary Schools
description: Theory and practice of teaching secondary school social studies. Emphasis is on methodology, materials, and specific application in the secondary classroom. Includes introductory involvement in the teaching of social studies with a focus on rationale, planning, teaching, and evaluation. Prerequisite: SS 350; EDJHM 285; EDSEC 280; and 18 hours of credit in social science. Open only to Social Studies teaching majors.

title: Independent Study
description: Directed study of special problems or research in social science education by individuals or groups of students. Topics to be investigated are chosen after consultation with an instructor with special competence in the area involved. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. The department also offers specialized programs to prepare mathematically oriented students for a variety of careers. The departmental major and minor prepare mathematically trained graduates for positions in business, industry, and government as well as for intense study of mathematics at the graduate level. The major in actuarial science provides training for careers that involve analyzing and solving business and social problems related to insurance and pension plans. The program includes course work that prepares students for most of the Associateshiplevel examinations offered by the Society of Actuaries. The teaching major and minor satisfy state certification requirements for students preparing to teach mathematics in junior high/middle school or high school. Students preparing to be elementary teachers may add the endorsement for teaching mathematics to their elementary teaching licenses and may also earn certification to teach mathematics in junior high/middle schools. For information on the major in mathematical economics, see Interdepartmental Programs, p. 42. Unless otherwise noted, all students enrolling in courses in the Department of Mathematical Sciences are expected to have completed at least three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school, including two years of algebra and one year of geometry. To begin all programs (except the Endorsement for Teaching a Subject Field: Mathematics), it is expected that students will have completed high school mathematics courses equivalent to the prerequisite for MATHS 165 and will have had some computer programming experience. Each student with a major or minor in the Department of Mathematical Sciences must earn a grade of C or better in each course serving as a prerequisite for other courses applied to meet program requirements. For graduation, a GPA of at least 2.5 is required in a minor or major program. Departmental majors who are students in the Honors College and have completed two Honors College colloquia may substitute HONRS 499 for MATHS 498.
