title: Basic Algebra
description: Emphasis on the concepts of elementary algebra. Intended for those with limited backgrounds in basic algebra skills. Provides appropriate background for

title: Intermediate Algebra
description: Review of factoring, quadratic equations and inequalities, relations and functions, rational exponents, systems of linear equations, and exponential and logarithmic functions. Recommended background: two years of college preparatory mathematics in high school.

title: College Algebra
description: Such topics as polynomial functions and equations, exponential and logarithmic functions, determinants, systems of equations and inequalities, mathematical induction, the binomial theorem, permutations and combinations, and progressions. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or appropriate score on mathematics placement test or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS courses numbered 161 or higher.

title: Trigonometry
description: Trigonometric functions, identities, and equations; graphs of the trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions; solution of right and general triangles; polar coordinates; and complex numbers. Scientific calculators will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or 109 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS courses numbered 161 or higher.

title: Pre-Calculus Mathematics
description: Coordinate plane, straight lines and circles, conic sections, elementary transcendental functions, curvesketching, polar coordinates, parametric equations, sequences, and series. Prerequisite: the equivalent of four semesters of algebra and one semester of trigonometry at the secondaryschool level or MATHS 112.

title: Mathematics and Its Applications
description: General Studies course including such topics as mathematical modeling, problem solving, geometrical concepts, growth patterns, and applications to the physical sciences, social sciences, and economics. Recommended background: three years of college preparatory mathematics in high school.

title: Finite Mathematics for Business
description: Topics in mathematics particularly suited to the needs of business majors, including mathematics of finance, probability, matrix algebra, and linear programming. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or an appropriate score on the mathematics Placement test.

title: Brief Calculus for Business 2
description: Brief survey of differential and integral calculus. Emphasis on applications to business. Prerequisite: MATHS 131.

title: Applied Calculus 1
description: Review of algebra, topics in analytic geometry, limits, continuity, derivatives, differentials, and appropriate applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 112 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 165.

title: Applied Calculus 2
description: The definite integral with applications, areas, fundamental theorem of calculus, indefinite integrals, improper integrals, integrals and derivatives of transcendental functions with applications, techniques of integration, calculus in higher dimensions. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 165. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 166.

title: Calculus 1
description: Differential calculus of algebraic and transcendental functions and applications, antidifferentiation and the Riemann integral. Includes the use of graphing calculators and computer software. Prerequisite: high school precalculus or MATHS 117.

title: Calculus 2
description: Standard techniques of integration, applications of the integral, sequences and series, indeterminate forms, and numerical methods. Includes the use of graphing calculators and computer software. Prerequisite: MATHS 165.

title: Elementary Probability and Statistics
description: Descriptive statistics, measures of central tendency and dispersion, basic probability concepts, random variables, binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression, and consideration of various applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 109 or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 320.

title: Number Concepts in the Elementary School
description: Development of cardinal and unsigned rational number concepts and properties interfaced with selected models and computer software from elementary school mathematics programs. Prerequisite: appropriate score on mathematicsplacement test, or credit in MATHS 108, orpermission of the department chairperson.

title: Geometry and Measurement in Grades K-6
description: Development of geometry and measurement concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from mathematics programs for primary and intermediate grades. May be substituted for MATHS 203. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 201. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 203.

title: Geometry and Measurement in the Primary Grades
description: Development of measurement and geometry concepts interfaced with selected models, materials, and computer software from K-3 mathematics programs. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 201. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 202.

title: Mathematics for the Teacher of the Exceptional Learner
description: Development of number concepts, number operations, measurement, geometric concepts, and problemsolving skills needed by teachers of exceptional learners. Instructional activities use selected models and materials appropriate for teachers of exceptional learners. May not be substituted for MATHS 201 or 202 or 203. Prerequisite: appropriate score on mathematicsplacement test, credit in MATHS 108, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 201, 202, or 203. Open only to special education majors.

title: Linear Algebra 1
description: Matrices, matrix operations and their properties and applications, determinants, rank and equivalence of matrices. Introduction to vector spaces and linear transformation. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 165 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Linear Algebra 2
description: A continuation of topics from MATHS 212 including transformation of coordinates, diagonalization of matrices, and introduction to canonical forms. Prerequisite: MATHS 212. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 412.

title: Discrete Systems
description: Topics from discrete mathematics, including formal logic, methods of proof, set theory, relations, recursion, combinatorics, and graph theory. A systematic development of number systems via equivalence classes is included as an application of these topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 165 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Statistical Methods
description: Introduces the application of statistics. Binomial and normal distributions, confidence intervals, tests of hypotheses, regression, correlation, categorical data analysis, analysis of variance, nonparametrics, sampling, and elementary experimental design. Emphasis is placed on comprehension and interpretation. Statistical computer packages are used. Prerequisite: MATHS 162 or 165. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 321.

title: Introduction to Geometry
description: Revisitation of the contents of secondary geometry with emphasis on possible teaching techniques and materials. Introduction to geometric transformations and non-Euclidean geometries. Study of geometric constructions. Computer applications. Prerequisite: MATHS 215 and one year of high school geometry.

title: Calculus 3
description: Multidimensional calculus and its applications. Topics include thmedimensional vector calculus, Gauss's theorem, Green's theorem and Stoke's theorem. Includes the use of graphing calculators and computer software. Prerequisite: MATHS 166.

title: Problems in Calculus
description: Intermediatelevel problems dealing with multiple integration, sequences, series, and theoretical aspects of the calculus. Designed for students preparing to take Part I of the actuarial examinations. Other students may enroll by permission of department chairperson. Prerequisite: MATHS 267.

title: Mathematics Games for Elementary Teachers
description: An introduction to mathematics games and how to use them in teaching mathematics to children. Concrete and pictorial games will be emphasized. The games cover a wide variety of mathematical concepts. Prerequisite or parallel: MATHS 201.

title: Undergraduate Colloquium
description: A series of brief introductions to the mathematical landscape including glimpses of mathematics in the workplace. Topics are drawn from all areas of the mathematical sciences. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 1 in any one semester or term. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (1-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Mathematics for the Junior High/Middle School Teacher
description: Applications of logic, number systems, algebra, geometry, and statistics in the junior high/middle school. Materials, manipulatives, and technology will be used to provide models for the junior high/middle school mathematics curriculum. Prerequisite: MATHS 215, 240. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 201 and 202. Open only to mathematics teaching majors and minors.

title: Algebraic Structures
description: Consideration of the basic algebraic structures: groups, rings, integral domains, and fields. Examples of these structures and elementary proof will be emphasized as will polynomials over rings, integral domains, and the fields of real and complex numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 215. 320 probability. (4) Probability theory for discrete and continuous sample spaces, random variables, density functions, distribution functions, marginal and conditional distributions, mathematical expectation, momentgenerating functions, common distributions, sampling distribution theory, central limit theorem, t, chisquare, and F distributions. Prerequisite: MATHS 166, 215.

title: Mathematical Statistics
description: Point and interval estimation, maximum likelihood, Neyman-Pearson Lemma, likelihood ratio tests, classical tests of significance, goodnessoffit, contingency tables, correlation, regression, nonparametric methods, Bayesian methods. Prerequisite: MATHS 320.

title: Problems in Statistics
description: Deals with the binomial, Poisson, chisquare, normal and other distributions. Some problems with momentgenerating functions, tests of hypotheses and estimation. Actuarial review class. Prerequisite: MATHS 321.

title: Computer and Mathematics Enrichment Topics
description: Topics for elementary and junior high/middle school in computer uses and programming, and enrichment topics from such areas as topology, strategy games, and number theo. Prerequisite: MATHS 202. ry

title: Computer Applications in the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Emphasizes the use of computers in the teaching of mathematics. Students whose area of licensure is mathematics may apply credit in this course toward the undergraduate computer endorsement. Prerequisite: MATHS 240 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mathematical Models
description: Construction of mathematical models for use with problems in phySics, chemistry, biology, and economics. Emphasis is on the construction and interpretation of models. Existing computer software will be used. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: College Geometry
description: Modern developments in analytic, synthetic, transformational, and vector geometry, closely related to Euclidean geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, and 240 or 267 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: Mathematical theory of force of interest, compound interest, annuities, equations of value, amortization, sinking funds, bonds, depreciation, current actuarial topics in finance. Prerequisite: MATHS 166.

title: Numerical Analysis 1
description: Topics include error analysis, approximation and interpolation of functions, solutions of nonlinear equations, approximate differentiation and integration, and orthogonal polynomials. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: CS 120; MATHS 162 or 166. Not open to students who have credit in CS 362.

title: Numerical Analysis 2
description: Topics include approximate solution of linear and nonlinear systems of equations by direct and iterative methods, spline interpolation, numerical solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Includes programming of numerical algorithms. Prerequisite: MATHS 362. Not open to students who have credit in CS 363.

title: Intermediate Calculus
description: Topics include vector functions; displacement; velocity and acceleration of particles in twoand threedimensional space; curvature; torsion and Frenet's formulas; divergence; curl; line integrals; work; surface integrals; theorems of Gauss, Green, and Stokes; orthogonal curvilinear coordinates. Prerequisite: MATHS 267.

title: Differential Equations
description: Introduction to nthorder ordinary linear differential equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equations. Laplace transforms, power series solutions. Method of Kryloff and Bogolinboff, firstorder partial differential equations. Use of standard computer software for elementary differential equations. Prerequisite: MATHS 166.

title: Honors Colloquium in Mathematics
description: Selected topics in mathematics with emphasis upon individualized study. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood and Kindergarten/Primary Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics at various age and grade levels from early childhood through grade three. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. One hour lecture, one hour teaching, and one hour laboratory each week. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 202 or 203. Not open to students who have credit in MATHS 391.

title: Teaching Mathematics in Early Childhood, Primary, and Intermediate Grades
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics from early childhood through intermediate grades. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Two onehour lectures and one onehour laboratory experience each week. May be substituted for MATHS 390. Prerequisite: grade of C or higher in MATHS 202 or 203.

title: Teaching Mathematics to the Exceptional Learner
description: Materials and methods used in teaching mathematics to the exceptional learner. Class ideas applied in teaching situations. Three onehour lectures and one onehour laboratory experience each week. May not be substituted for MATHS 390 or 391. Prerequisite: a grade of C or higher in MATHS 207, or agrade of C or higher in both MATHS 201 and202. Open only to special education majors.

title: The Teaching of Mathematics in the Junior High/Middle School
description: Methods and materials for teaching mathematics in the junior high/middle school. Class ideas will be applied in a smallgroup teaching situation. Prerequisite: MATHS 240.

title: Introduction to the Teaching of Mathematics
description: Materials and methods used in teaching secondary mathematics. Additional consideration given to methodology and instruction at the junior high/middle school level. Survey of texts, organization of materials, evaluation procedures, instructional aids, and classroom observations. Prerequisite: MATHS 240 and a minimum GPA of 2.5 in all mathematics courses that are to be applied to the major or minor. Prerequisite or parallel: MATH 311.

title: Classroom Use of Methods and Materials
description: Classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of mathematics, evaluation of instructional activities, and rationale for including mathematics in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences, whenever appropriate. Prerequisite: MATHS 311, 340, 395, and a minimum GPA of 2.5 in all mathematics courses that are to be applied to the major.

title: Abstract Algebra 1
description: Indepth treatment of group theory. Includes a brief review of basics, followed by topi cs such as factor groups, isomorphism theorems, series of groups, Burnside counting and the Sylow theorems, free groups, group presentations, and other advanced topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 311.

title: Abstract Algebra 2
description: Indepth treatment of ring and field theory covering ideals, quotient rings, homomorphisms, polynomial rings, unique factorization domains, field extensions and geometric constructions, finite fields and additional topics from field automorphisms, Galois theory and applications to coding theory: Prerequisite: MATHS 411.

title: Theory of Numbers
description: Topics include the division algorithm; positional notation; divisibility; primes; congruences; divisibility criteria; the sigma, divisor, and phi functions; diophantine equations; linear, polynomial, and simultaneous congruences; theorems of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Wilson; quadratic reciprocity. Prerequisite: MATHS 212.

title: Enrichment Topics in Number Theory
description: Topics extending number theoretic concepts to enrichment material in junior and senior high school include Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, magic squares, the calendar problem, polygonal numbers, Egyptian fractions, the fifteen puzzle, Nim, and detailed properties of perfect and amicable numbers. Prerequisite: MATHS 416.

title: Theory of Sampling and Surveys
description: Survey desips; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling; ratio estimates; regression estimates; cost and variance functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Topics in Statistics
description: Includes such topics as oneand twoway ANOVA, multiple comparisons, regression analysis, time series analysis. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Analysis of Variance in Experimental Design Models
description: Multivariate normal distribution; quadratic forms; linear models; simple random, randomized block, Latin squares, factorial, splitplot, balanced incomplete block design; analysis of covariance; confounding; multiple comparison tests. Prerequisite: MATHS 321 or its equivalent.

title: Geometry and Topology 1
description: Introduction to Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometries and the surfaces admitting these geometries. Basic topological notions, such as the boundary operator, continuity, and connectedness, underlying the development of these topics. Elements of linear geometry leading to basic ideas of differential geometry. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 267.

title: Geometry and Topology 2
description: A continuation of MATHS 441 culminating in the treatment of selected advanced topics. Prerequisite: MATHS 441.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 1
description: Survival distributions, life tables; the mathematics of life insurance, life annuities, net premiums, and net premium reserves. Prerequisite: MATHS 321, 351, and a minimum GPA of 2.5 in all mathematics courses that are to be applied to the major.

title: Mathematics of Life Contingencies 2
description: Mathematics of multiple life functions, multiple decrement models, valuation theory for pension plans, insurance models including expenses, nonforfeiture benefits, and dividends. Prerequisite: MATHS 452.

title: Graduation of Data
description: Interpolation with equal and unequal intervals, inverse interpolation, summation, and approximate integration. Study of the need for graduation of data and the methods of graduation: graphic, interpolation, adjustedaverage, differenceequation, math formula. Prerequisite: MATHS 320, 362, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Linear Programming and Optimization
description: Optimization techniques of linear, dynamic, and integer programming and stochastic simulation. Optimal solutions of PERT-CPM networks. Optimal decision strategies. Elementary queuing theory. Prerequisite: MATHS 212, 320, and working knowledge of scientific computer programming.

title: History of Mathematics
description: The development of mathematics from prehistoric times to the seventeenth century. Topics may include number concepts and numeration, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, and calculus. Prerequisite: MATHS 161 or 165.

title: Elements of Analysis
description: An introduction to elementary pointset topology; development of the limit concept related to sequences and functions; applications of the limit concept in continuity, derivatives, and integrals of elementary functions. Prerequisite: MATHS 166 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
description: Metric spaces, topological concepts in IR and C leading to consideration of connectedness, compactness and completeness, continuous functions, uniform continuity, Stone-Weierstrass theorem, differentiation. Prerequisite: MATHS 212 and 267.

title: Advanced Calculus 2
description: Topics include the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, series of real and complex numbers and functions, series expansions. Prerequisite: MATHS 471.

title: Boundary Value Problems
description: Fourier Series and integrals, heat and wave equations in one dimension, Laplace's equation in two dimensions, problems in higher dimensions, numerical methods of solving boundary value problems. Prerequisite: MATHS 374.

title: Senior Seminar
description: A variety of topics in mathematics presented by three faculty members will be studied and discussed. A short paper on one of the three topics presented to the class is required. Prerequisite: major in one of the mathematical sciences and senior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the mathematical sciences department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300- and 4 levels. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairperson. Open only to juniors and seniors. A total of 8 hours of credit may b earned. MODERN LANGUAGES AND CLASSICS W. D. Barnette, Chairperson; L. J. Warner The Department of Modern Languages and Classics offers programs in both ancient and modern foreign languages and works closely with other programs and departments to combine foreign language training with other subjects. Language laboratory practice, computer applications, interactive multimedia, opportunities for study abroad in the summer and for an academic semester or year, and foreign exchange programs enhance classroom instruction. The department offers foreign language training for students who want to acquire a broad liberal education; enrich preparation for a career; seek certification for teaching at the elementary or secondary level; travel, live, or work abroad; or work as translators. Students may earn credit for previous language study through either national advanced placement tests or departmentally administered placement tests. Students must take these department placement tests in any language they studied before entering the university and intend to continue studying. These tests help determine the appropriate student class placement. Students who have completed more than one year of a foreign language in high school may not normally enroll for credit in the 101 level of that language, except in Chinese and Japanese, or with permission of the chairperson. Students placed in any higherlevel course will receive credit for the courses they test out of by earning grades of C or higher in the course into which they are placed. In order to receive placement credit for 101, a student must have taken the placement test and have a record of the score on file. Resulting scores of high, middle, or low are available to faculty members for letters of recommendation. The modern language test is based on content, procedures, and norms published by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages and by the Educational Testing Services. Students should consult with foreign language faculty advisors about arranging courses to meet their needs. The 100- and 200-level courses in foreign languages are sequential and must be taken in order. title: Word Origins and Vocabulary Development
description: English vocabulary derived from Latin and Greek, emphasizing wordformation as a means of expanding and enriching students' vocabularies. No knowledge of Latin or Greek is required.

title: Latin and Greek Based Bioscientific Terminology
description: Analysis, formation, and recognition of technical vocabulary derived from Latin and Greek commonly used in the medical and life sciences. No knowledge of Latin or Greek is required.

title: Introduction to the Classical World
description: Main features of the civilization of the Greeks and Romans their history, political institutions, art, literature, and philosophy. Explores through lectures, readings, and audiovisual materials the nature of the ancients' contribution to Western civilizations. or Advan 1 Advan 2 Modern Japan(3) Indpen Study (1-9) 2-3

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Greece
description: A close, interpretive view of Greek cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as individualism, ideals of beauty, social experimentation, competitiveness, and intellectual curiosity, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: Cultural Life of Ancient Rome
description: A close, interpretive view of Roman cultural values, customs, and institutions, such as respect for tradition, rule of law, social responsibility, and technical expertise, as evidenced in primary sources.

title: The Classical World in Film
description: Aspects of ancient civilization depicted in film(such as Roman history, Greek mythology, etc.). An examination of the accuracy of such portrayals through comparison with ancient sources. The place of such films in the history of cinema. Topics will vary.

title: Mythologies of the World
description: Classical mythology (Greek and Roman) will represent Western tradition in a comparative study with other mythologies of the world. Emphasis on understanding mythologies as symbolic cultural systems expressing societal values.

title: Classical Literature in English Translation
description: Selections from the major works of Greek and Roman literature and their continuing influence on Western literature. Emphasis is on prose and poetry in alternate terms. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Women in Antiquity
description: The study of women in ancient Greece and Rome, based on evidence from literary and nonliterary sources. Explores the influence of social,political, and legal institutions on the status of women and on their relationships with men.

title: Greek and Roman Cults
description: Introduces the religions of the ancient Greeks and Romans and examines the nature of their cult activities and theological speculations. Topics include prayer, sacrifice, feasting, ritual, scripture, myth, clergy, etc.

title: The Ancient City
description: Life of the ancient city as mirrored in archaeological and literary sources. The concept of the city, its art and architecture, with special emphasis on Periclean Athens and Augustan Rome.

title: Classical Myth and Theory
description: Major themes of classical myths: creation, the divine and human family, life of the hero, the quest, monsters, etc. Study and employment of modern theories of analysis: mythritual, psychological, structuralist, etc. Prerequisite recommended: CC 205.

title: Ancient Epic
description: Greek and Roman s epicstudied as genres, predecesor of Western epics, and as reflections of their cultures; selections will vary. Prerequisite: CC 105, 301 or permission of the instructor.

title: Ancient Drama
description: Greek and Roman tragedy and comedy studied as genres, as predecessors of Western drama, and as reflections of their cultures; selections will vary. Prerequisite: CC 105, 301 or permission of the instructor.

title: Ancient Historiography
description: Examines the origin and development of the genre of ancient history as well as the nature of ancient testimony and records. Authors include Herodotus, Thucydides, Plutarch, Livy, Tacitus, and Suetonius. Prerequisite: CC 105 and either CC 201, 202, 301, HIST 461 or 462.

title: Special Topics in Antiquity
description: Special research topics in classical culture, including period, author and genre topics, and methods. Prerequisite: either CC 401, 402, 403 or permission of the instructor.

title: Readings
description: Individualized course of reading or limited research to allow students to explore special topics in classical antiquity. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning Chinese 1
description: The first course in the Chinese language.

title: Beginning Chinese 2
description: The second course in the Chinese language. Prerequisite: CH 101.

title: Intermediate Chinese 1
description: Designed to build on a foundation of firstyear Chinese to help students achieve greater fluency in oral expression and to emphasize the reading of Chinese character texts containing both old and simplified character forms. Grammar will be taught through the use of sentence patterns, and character writing will be practiced. Traditional and contemporary aspects of Chinese culture will also be taught. Prerequisite: CH 102.

title: Intermediate Chinese 2
description: Designed to build on the foundation laid thus far in Chinese and to help students achieve greater fluency in the four basic skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will read newspapers, short stories, and essays by modern authors with the help of a dictionary and will write short compositions in Hanzi on their readings. Prerequisite: CH 201.

title: Beginning Readings in Chinese
description: A course designed to develop skills in reading simple Chinese essays, short stories, and newspaper articles, using approximately 2,000 characters and the help of a dictionary. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: Chinese Literature in English Translation
description: A brief overview of major Chinese literary trends and works using selections from traditional masterpieces in poetry, myth, legend, short story, and novel and also contemporary essay, short story, and novel. Prerequisite: two years of college Chinese or the equivalent.

title: The French-Speaking World
description: Survey of political, cultural, and literary history in areas colonized by France: Quebec, the Caribbean, North Africa, West Africa. Topics include geography, government, and differences in Francophone and Anglophone colonization, using sociopolitical and literary works. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course title/s will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Foreign Literatures in Translation
description: Readings in English translation of selected works of major writers in one of the foreign languages taught in this department. Topics and works may vary. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: Foreign Culture through Films
description: Study of cultures of the countries whose languages are taught in this department through the medium of foreign contemporary and classic films. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors.

title: European Women Writers
description: Readings in English translation of selected works of major twentiethcentury women writers in European languages. Topics and works may vary. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors. Not open to students who have credit in EURO 307.

title: European Culture through Films
description: Study of the cultures of European countries through the medium of films. Topics and films may vary. May not be applied to foreign language majors or minors. Not open to students who have credit in EURO 308.

title: Guided Self-Instruction Studies in Less Common Languages
description: Offers languages such as Japanese, Arabic, modern Hebrew, modern Greek, Chinese, and Portuguese at basic spoken levels by guided selfinstruction. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned in one language. Not open to native speakers.

title: Professional Experience
description: Paid, supervised work experience integrating foreign and classical language skills with careerrelated positions in international firms, the travel industry, and local, state, and federal agencies. Work assignments may be partor fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs. Prerequisite: a minimum of two years of universitylevel foreign language study and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Foreign Literature
description: Selected readings and indepth exploration and discussion of literary currents, movements, authors, and themes found in foreign literature. Prerequisite: junior standing in the Honors College or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 4 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Methods awl Materials for Teaching Foreign Language
description: Current methods in foreign language teaching in the senior high school. Presentation, texts, teaching materials, CAI, and other supplementary aids. Reviews current professional literature, trends, and requirements. Prerequisite: two years of college credit or the equivalent in a modern or classical language and identification to pursue a teaching curriculum. Prerequisite or parallel recommended: EDSEC 280; EDJHM 285.

title: Foreign Language Trends and CAI
description: Disciplineoriented classroom management techniques, introductory involvement in the teaching of foreign languages, evaluation of instructional activities, and discussion of rationale for the inclusion of foreign languages in the secondary school curriculum. Topics developed in the context of field experiences whenever possible. Prerequisite: FL 395.

title: Practical Experience
description: Nonpaid, supervised work experience integrating foreign and classical language skills with careerrelated positions in international firms, the travel industry, and local, state, and federal agencies. Work assignments may be partor fulltime for one or more semesters in approved cooperative education (coop) or internship programs. Prerequisite: a minimum of two years of universitylevel foreign language study and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Independent Study
description: Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with the individual instructor. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning French 1
description: The first course in the French language.

title: Beginning French 2
description: Prerequisite: FR 101.

title: Intermediate French 1
description: Prerequisite: FR 102.

title: Intermediate French 2
description: Prerequisite: FR 201.

title: Conversation
description: Practice in oral French to increase fluency and authenticity through activities and conversation. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Composition
description: Practice in written French with review of gramatical structures. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent.

title: Grammar
description: An advanced study of French grammar, stressing creative expression in the language. Prerequisite: FR 302 or its equivalent.

title: Civilization and Culture: The Old Regime
description: Contributions made by France from the beginnings to the French Revolution. Origins of historical and cultural traditions. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Civilization and Culture: Modern France
description: Development of modern France from the French Revolution to the present. Assimilation of traditions into the culture of the industrial age. Supplemental literary selections. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Phonetics
description: Formation of speech sounds in the French language and the application of phonetics to the understanding and speaking of French. Use of the International Phonetic Alphabet. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Business French
description: Designed to make advanced French students familiar with commercial forms and terminology used in business, banking, and industry. Prerequisite: two years of college French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Introduction to French Literary Readings
description: Selected readings from several literary genres (e g., drama, lyric poetry, narrative) drawn from various periods of French literary history; writing on selected literary topics. Prerequisite: two years of college French or permission of the department chairperson.

title: French Study Abroad
description: Study of intermediate or advanced French language, literature, and culture in a foreign country where French is the native language. May include seminars arranged during travel. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of French Literature 1
description: From the beginnings to 1760. Literature of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the classical age to 1760. Prerequisite: two years of college French or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: FR 360 or its equivalent.

title: History of French Literature 2
description: From the classical age to the present. The development of eighteenthcentury philosophies, romanticism, realism, naturalism, and symbolism in French literature; literature of modern France. Prerequisite: two years of college French or permission of the department chairperson. Prerequisite recommended: FR 360 or its equivalent.

title: Seminar in French Literature
description: Seminar studies by author, genre, period, or theme. Topic to be announced. Prerequisite: six semesters of French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Seminar in French Language or Civilization
description: Seminar studies in grammar, style, conversation, or civilization. Topic to be announced. Prerequisite: six semesters of French or the equivalent or permission of the department chairperson. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Readings
description: Individualized reading or research to allow students to explore special topics with an individual instructor. Prerequisite: three years of college French or the equivalent. A total of 9 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Beginning German 1
description: Introduction to vocabulary and structures needed for basic communication in German.

title: Beginning German 2

title: Japanese Culture and Civilization
description: Survey of the origins and development of Japanese culture: art, literature, religion, philosophy, and political and social institutions from earliest to modern times. Provides those with a general interest in Japan an overview of its cultural traditions. Taught primarily in Japanese. Prerequisite: JAPAN 202 or its equivalent or permission of the instructor.

title: Japanese Linguistics
description: Introduction to Japanese linguistics, particularly phonological and syntactical structures and communication patterns. Siewert, D. Van Meter The Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Management prepares students for careers in environmental science and management of natural resources. The programs offered by the department are designed to give students a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of ecosystems. The department offers a major in natural resources and environmental management, a minor in natural resources, a minor in environmental management, a teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies, and an endorsement for elementary education majors. The department also coordinates interdepartmental minors in energy and environmental policy. Students majoring in natural resources and environmental management choose one of the following options: natural resource studies, environmental interpretation and outdoor recreation management, environmental protection, land management, and occupational and industrial hygiene. All majors must complete a common core requirement. Many courses include laboratory work using sophisticated analytical equipment. Each year, students have opportunities for indepth twotofourweek field studies in the United States and other countries. Students are encouraged to participate in practicums or internships under the supervision of faculty members or professionals working in private consulting firms, governmental agencies, or environmental education centers. title: Environment and Society
description: Study of human roles in resource management, environmental quality, and conservation. Effects of population and technology on environmental systems including air, energy, minerals, soil, vegetation, water, and wildlife. Environmental ethics, outdoor recreation, economic development also covered. Laboratory and field activities.

title: American Environmental History
description: Designed to give students knowledge of use of resources in the United States by treating, in historical perspective, government policies and private enterprise practices of exploitation and conservation from settlement to the present. Emphasis is on the way use of resources has shaped society. Not open to students who have credit in HIST 204.

title: International Natural Resources: Development and Conservation
description: An analysis of problems occurring as a result of development and use of natural resources worldwide. The role of resource management and conservation to enhance the carrying capacity of the earth. A casestudy approach to the management of global environmental problems.

title: Water Resources
description: The hydrologic cycle as an integral part of the resource base and the relationship of water to other natural resources; its economic and social importance to humans. Water conservation practices with emphasis on pollution abatement. Government and private participation and responsibilities in water conservation programs. Includes laboratory and field work.

title: Soil Resources
description: Soil as an 9-12 integral part of our resource base and its relationship to other natural resources; its origin, development, and classification. The physical, chemical, and biological properties, with emphasis 9-12 hours from

title: Environmental Economics
description: The application of economic principles to environmentalproblems. Emphasis is on applying the economist's decisionmaking model to environmental issues and the advantages and shortcomings of the economist's analysis. Prerequisite: ECON 201 and 3 semester hours in NREM, preferably NREM 101, or permission of the department chairperson. Not open to students who have credit in ECON 311.

title: Sustainable Agriculture
description: Natural resource use in agricultural systems with emphasis on principles of sustainability. Includes integrated pest management, permaculture, and other production practices that conserve soil, water, and biological resources. Field trips included.

title: Resources for Self-Reliant Living
description: Considers the environmental effects of hard and soft technologies. Focuses on devising a survival strategy based on selfreliant concepts in housing, waste material, water use, agricultural production, and total energy systems.

title: Principles of Water Quality Management
description: Water quality, water . treatment, and planning as related to water quality management, including the Safe Drinking Water Act. Water uses for agriculture, industry, public supply, and recreation, and the role of regulatory agencies. Includes laboratory and field work. Prerequisite: NREM 211; CHEM 111 or the equivalent; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers
description: Basic relationships between soil nutrients and plant growth with emphasis on the conditions affecting the fertility of soils, the role of soil analysis in fertility programs, and fertilizer forms and usage. Soil chemistry as related to environmental contamination. Prerequisite: NREM 221 or its equivalent; CHEM 111 or its equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Classification and Interpretation
description: Includes soil genesis, morphology, classification, and survey. Stresses the relationship between soil information and the landuse decisionmaking process with practical applications provided. Considerable emphasis is placed on field study of soils and their uses. Prerequisite: NREM 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Soil Conservation and Management
description: Stresses principles and methods of control of soil erosion using basic soil concepts. Studies management systems and individual practices with special emphasis on soil resource maintenance. Prerequisite: NREM 221 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Energy and Mineral Resources: Issues and Choices
description: Appraisal of the problems, prospects, and societal and technical issues surrounding the use of energy and mineral resources. Emphasis is on environmental problems and ecoenergetics, consideration of the natural resource base, distribution and production problems, conservation, alternative energy systems, resource policy, and research.

title: Air Quality
description: Focuses on the contamination of the atmospheric environment. Topics include major contaminants; measurement techniques; dispersion; effects on the atmosphere, human health, vegetation and materials; regulatory requirements and practices; control measures; noise pollution. Lab and field experiences.

title: Indoor Air Quality Management
description: Indoor air pollution problems of residential and nonresidential environments. Features discussions of asbestos, radon, and formaldehyde as well as combustiongenerated pollutants. Topics include energy conservation, building design, modeling, measurement techniques, and mitigation measures. Lab and field experiments.

title: Occupational and Industrial Hygiene
description: Introduces the principles of assessing and controlling exposures to workplace hazards. Topics include occupational disease; exposure to contaminant gases, dusts, radiation, noise, and biological agents; ergonomic concerns; regulatory requirements; engineering control; and personal protection equipment.

title: Building Asbestos and Lead Management
description: Significance of asbestos and lead hazards in buildings; exposure risks; regulatory requirements; sampling procedures; abatement practices; abatement project design. Field and handson experiences.

title: Ventilation Systems
description: Use of ventilation systems to reduce contaminant exposures in general occupational and industrial environments. Principles of dilution and exhaust ventilation. Prerequisite: NREM 347 or permission of the instructor.

title: Hazardous Waste Materials Health and Safety
description: Introduction to the health and safety principles and practices of working on hazardous waste sites, handling hazardous materials, emergency responses to chemical spills and confined space entry.

title: Turf-Grass Management
description: Maintenance of turfgrass lawns, golf courses, athletic fields, playgrounds, parks, and roadsides. Emphasis is on practical management recommendations including regional adaptation of grasses, soils, fertilization, general maintenance practices, diseases, and insect control. Identification of grass and weed species.

title: International Rural Development
description: Analysis of rural development in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Emphasizes the roles of population, agriculture, history, conflict, technology, international debt, multilateral organizations, and political and cultural traditions in development efforts. Interdisciplinary readings and case studies.

title: Paid Professional Practice
description: Supervised financially supported professional experience in natural resource management, environmental education, or environmental protection. Provides a bridge between academic and professional experiences. Available only on a prospective basis. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours of credit may be earned in combination with NREM 497.

title: Introduction to Outdoor Recreation
description: A philosophical orientation to the nature and role of outdoor recreation in modern society. Administration, management, research, survey, planning, economics, and interpretation of outdoor recreation. Emphasizes multipleuse concepts of management to meet outdoor recreation demands. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods.

title: Principles of Wastewater Treatment
description: Maintenance of water resources through the application of wastewater treatment with emphasis on needs, treatment methods, and effects on receiving waters and other ecosystems. Basic wastewater analysis and testing procedures. Prerequisite: NREM 211; one college course in chemistry; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
description: Delineation of solid and hazardous waste management in the United States. Waste reduction, recycling, processing, and disposal methods are discussed. Technical, political, and economic aspects of waste management. Effects of improper disposal on environmental quality. Prerequisite: junior standing or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Natural Resources
description: Exploration of selected issues in natural resources, with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students; others with permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Environmental Interpretation
description: Develops skills and techniques necessary to the interpretation of ecological and environmental characteristics of earth systems. Emphasizes field work and creative presentation of concepts, and organization and management of interpretive programs including sites and facilities. Prerequisite: NREM 101 or its equivalent; junior standing.

title: Teaching Environmental Education
description: Opportunities for enriching instruction through environmental education in formal and nonformal educational settings. Studies conservation, outdoor and environmental education, including teaching techniques and instructional resources used in each. Prerequisite: NREM 101 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Natural Resources of a Geographic Area
description: The natural resources of a specific area with special emphasis on location of natural resources, their socioeconomic importance to the area, their management, and the combined influence they have on the regional environmental quality. Each time the course is offered a specific geographic area is studied. Includes laboratory and field experience. Prerequisite: NREM 101 or its equivalent and permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Integrated Resources Planning and Management
description: Introduction to strategies used in environmental planning and resource management in contemporary society. Stresses use of data analysis and its role in the decisionmaking process by conceptually centering on natural and humanmade systems. May require field trips. Prerequisite: all natural resources core courses or concurrent enrollment and senior standing. Students in related disciplines may seek permission from the department chairperson.

title: Fishery Resources Management
description: The relationship of fisheries to other natural resources; a survey of aquatic habitats and the characteristics of fish that affect their management; basic principles, practices, and techniques of management of inland waters for fish production. Offered spring semester in evennumbered years. Prerequisite: NREM 211; BIO 480; ZOOL 444; or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Outdoor Recreation Planning
description: Application of basic principles and procedures in the planning and use of natural resources for outdoor recreation. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NREM 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Administration and Management of Outdoor Recreation Areas
description: Application of basic principles and procedures of managing natural resources and the administration of personnel and financial resources to provide good outdoor recreation experiences. May require one weekend field trip in addition to regular laboratory periods. Prerequisite: NREM 371 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Wilderness and Society
description: Defining wilderness, understanding its unique significance, and analyzing techniques of past and present management. Includes study of research in perception and use. Weekend trip to the Deam Wilderness—Hoosier National Forest or a state forest back country area. Prerequisite: junior standing.

title: Introduction to Environmental Engineering
description: Engineering principles applied to specific environmental problems. Design of facilities that minimize environmental impact from use of resources; remediation of severely disturbed environments; design of waste management systems. Some environmental chemistry. Prerequisite: NREM 211, 221; CHEM 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Computer Applications in Natural Resources and Environmental Management
description: Experience with a broad array of computer software for the VAX mainframe and microcomputers. Activities are carried out under an • instructor's supervision. Assigned work is commensurate with computer experience and interests in natural resources and environmental management. Taught by arrangement. Prerequisite: CS 104, permission of the instructor or the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Professional Practice
description: Supervised professional experience in natural resource management, environmental education, or environmental protection. Provides a bridge between academic and professional experiences. Available only on a prospective basis. Prerequisite: permission of the Philosophy 317 Not open to students who have credit in NREM 369. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned; 9 hours in combination with NREM 497.

title: Special Studies in Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences
description: Opportunities to pursue special interests in natural resources and environmental sciences. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned (9 hours in combination with NREM 496).

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Original research under faculty guidance, including problem definition, literature review, data collection, analysis, and a summary report. May require preparatory or parallel course work in research methodologies, statistics, or computer science. Prerequisite: faculty sponsor and permission of the department chairperson. title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: An introduction to such important philosophical problems as the existence of God, whether ethical values are subjective, and the extent of our freedom. These topics and others may be approached by examining the ideas of great philosophers or current thinkers.

title: Introduction to Techniques of Critical Reasoning
description: Introduction to basic techniques of critical reasoning in deductive and inductive logic, and strategies for decision making and problem solving.

title: Logic
description: The nature of deductive reasoning. Inquiry into the forms and procedures necessary to draw correct conclusions from given premises regardless of the factual content of the premises. Critical introduction to the correct forms of deduction.

title: Ethics
description: A discussion of some of the central problems in ethics such as the justification of ethical beliefs, theories of right and wrong, and the conditions of moral responsibility, as well as a discussion of current moral issues.

title: Social Philosophy
description: Involves a discussion and clarification of such basic social concepts as liberty, justice, and equality, as well as a critical discussion of such normative issues as how liberty should be distributed and how justice can be maximized.

title: Business Ethics
description: Introduction to and analysis of basic concepts, principles, theories, and issues in business ethics.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Critical analysis of such selected topics as the nature and existence of God, the problem of evil, the justification of religious belief, and the significance of religious experience.

title: Environmental Ethics
description: Introduction to and analysis of basic concepts, principles, theories, and issues in environmental ethics. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: History of Ancient Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the rise of philosophy in Greece through the medieval period. Emphasis is on the theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: History of Modern Philosophy
description: The development of philosophical theories and ideas from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Emphasis is on these theories in relation to one another, the times that produced them, and the thinkers who offered them.

title: American Philosophy
description: An introduction to the major American philosophers and their ideas from the time of the Puritans to the present.

title: Introduction to Logical Theory
description: The philosophical problems of logic. Topics may include the application of logic to ethics, logic and ordinary language, deviant logics, truth, metaphysical problems of logic, and other related topics. Prerequisite: PHIL 200 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Contemporary Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading philosophers and movements in the twentieth century. May concentrate on such selected philosophers as Russell, Philosophy 319 wittgenstein, and Husserl, or may concentrate on contemporary treatments of selected philosophical problems.

title: Aesthetics
description: Exploration of philosophical views on the nature, interpretation, and criticism of art. Readings and discussion may range from classical to contemporary thinkers and issues.

title: Philosophy of Law
description: Critical examination of different philosophical theories as to the nature and validity of law, relation of law and morality, and justification and problems of punishment, as well as an analysis of such basic concepts as action, intention, causation, and responsibility.

title: African Philosophy
description: A critical examination of leading trends in African philosophy. Ethrtophilosophy, philosophic sagacity, liberation philosophy, or modern/critical philosophy are possible topics.

title: Current Issues in Philosophy
description: Selected current and important issues in philosophy. Topics may include social and ethicalproblems, recent work on traditional philosophical problems, and other issues of concern.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: An examination of such central philosophical problems in the sciences as the nature of scientific explanation and the testing of hypotheses; a discussion of ethical issues arising from science, for example, the use of human subjects and prolonging life.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships related to their professional or career goals. Internships may be with educational or religious institutions, public or private agencies, or business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson.

title: Honors Colloquium in Philosophy
description: Exploration of selected problems in philosophy with emphasis upon individual study. Open only to students in the Honors College or by permission of the department chairperson.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: Allows superior students opportunities forguided reading and investigation in areas of philosophy not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Introduction to Metaphysics
description: A study of the principal problems of metaphysics including the nature of reality, the relation of mind and body, and the issues of freedom and determinism.

title: Introduction to Theory of Knowledge
description: A critical discussion of leading theories and problems of knowledge. Includes a discussion of the conditions of knowledge and rational belief, the different kinds of knowledge, the nature of truth, and the challenge of skepticism.

title: Contemporary Ethical Theory and Problems
description: A critical examination of recent ethical theories and their application to contemporary problems.

title: Religions in American Culture
description: Traditional religious groups in the United States with attention to developments, institutions, distinctive practices, and beliefs. The groups and the subjects treated will be adjusted to the interests of the students.

title: Religions of the World
description: An introductory survey of the major religions of the world (Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Islam, Christianity, and others), emphasizing how people live out their faiths in their daily lives.

title: Old Testament
description: Our Hebrew- Judaic religious heritage as reflected in various personalities and their religious expressions as found in the literature of the Old Testament.

title: New Testament
description: Our early Christian heritage in relation to its Jewish-Greek background as reflected by various personalities in the literature of the New Testament.

title: Internship
description: Students undertake supervised internships related to their professional or career goals. Internships may be with educational or religious institutions,public or private agencies, or business firms. Prerequisite: permission of the

title: Jesus and the Gospel Traditions
description: The traditions that developed about Jesus among the early Christians as reflected in the four Gospels and the more recent findings of apocryphal Gospels.

title: Research Methods in Religious Studies
description: Research in religious studies covering the basics of computerassisted research and data analysis, integrated with library research and previous class work in thepreparation of an original term project and the presentation of results.

title: Paul and the Developing Church
description: An indepth study of Paul's letters, the traditions as reflected in the Book of Acts, and the development of the early Church through the fourth century.

title: Seminar in Eastern Religions
description: An intensive seminarformat study of the religions of India, China, and Japan, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Shintoism, and contemporary Japanese religions.

title: Comparative Religion
description: Investigation, analysis, and comparison of selected major religious traditions with attention to their underlying structures. Particular attention is given to the comparison of Eastern and Western traditions.

title: Reading and Special Study
description: For superior students: an opportunity for guided investigation in aspects of religion not covered intensively in available courses. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Special Topics in Religion
description: Indepth focus on a selected issue of central importance. Topics vary each semester and include such subjects as American Indian religions, women and religion, and the Pentecostal and charismatic movements. Watson The Department of Physics and Astronomy offers majors in pure and applied physics to students who want to pursue graduate work in physics, astronomy, or engineering or who are interested in careers in industry. Programs are also available for students who want to teach secondary school physics. Departmental minors are available in astronomy, physics, and applied physics. Students planning to major or minor in physics or astronomy programs are strongly advised to consult with the department to determine the proper course sequence for their needs. Pre-Engineering Major This program is intended for students enrolled at Ball State who hope to transfer to accredited schools of engineering. The preengineering major is generally a fiveyear program in which students must attend Ball State for three years and then transfer to accredited engineering schools to finish the engineering degree requirements. Upon successful completion of the engineering program students are eligible to receive bachelor's degrees from Ball State in addition to their engineering degrees. Schools of engineering may have requirements not met by the general Ball State preengineering major. Students in this program are responsible for knowing and meeting the requirements of the schools to which they plan to transfer. Admission to Ball State as a preengineering major does not guarantee automatic admission to any accredited school of engineering. Students must apply for admission to the desired engineering school and must meet the requirements set by that engineering school. Three options in the preengineering major are available: chemical engineering, metallurgical engineering, and general engineering, including aeronautical, civil, electrical, industrial, mechanical, and nuclear specializations.
