description: Introduction to the role of tradition in various aspects of American culture, from humor to architecture; the functions of these elements in society; and methodological and theoretical approaches to their study, with comparative examples from Ireland and Great Britain.

title: The African Background of American Black Culture
description: African cultural and historical roots of American blacksorigins of the human species; plant and animal domestication; metallurgy, art, and state formation. Focus is on West Africa, the source of most of the black population of the United States.

title: History of Method and Theory in Anthropology
description: Surveys the major ideas and issues of anthropology over time. Includes methods and theories · from archaeolo&Y, physical anthro­pology, linguistics, and cultural anthropology.

title: Anthropology and Education
description: Applies anthropological theory and method to such educational concerns as socialization, peer dynamics, classroom networks, parentteacher interactions, modernization, and multicultural settings.

title: Human Variation and Adaptation
description: Human biological variation in the contemporary world: examination of its distribution, inheritance, development, and adaptiveness. Prerequisite: ANTH 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Ontogeny: Human Physical Growth and Development and Its Evolution
description: Studies children's physical growth and development, human adaptive roles and evolutionary history, ranges of variation in present­day populations, effects of stress, changes through time, comparisons with nonhuman primates, and assessment methods. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Applied Anthropology
description: Investigates the problems and work that engage the attention of anthropologists outside the university setting. Examination of new skills needed to supplement those traditionally taught in anthropology.

title: Introduction to Anthropological Linguistics
description: Basic concepts, scope, and methodology of the science of language with particular emphasis on non-European languages and cultural components of language. Knowledge of a foreign language is helpful. Prerequisite: ANTH 101.

title: Topics in Old World Prehistory
description: Prehistory of various Old World regions and time periods. Topics will vary from semester to semesterfor example, Europe, the Paleolithic, general survey. May be repeated with different topics. Prerequisite recommended: ANTH 101. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Ecological Anthropolo~y
description: Explores the system of relationships between any human population and its environment focusing on cultural behavior. Uses studies from ancient to modern times and models and theories from ecology and anthropology. Prerequisite: any one of ANTH 101, 103, 105, 111, or permission of the instructor.

title: Human Paleontology
description: Fossil record of the evolution of humans and their primate predecessors. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Topics in New World Archaeology
description: Prehistory of various New World regions or developmental periods. Topics will vary from semester to semesterfor example, Meso-America, the Southwest, general survey. May be repeated for different topics. Prerequisite: ANTH 103. . A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Social Organization
description: A systematic crosscultural analysis of human organizations from kinship­based societies to modern bureaucracies. Using an evolutionary approach, develops both theoretical perspectives and practical understanding. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, 111, or permission of the instructor.

title: Art of Prehistoric and Non-Western Cultures
description: Exposes liberal arts students to the artistic accomplishments of prehistoric and non-Western peoples. Art will be interpreted and functionally examined with regard to aesthetic, ceremonial, and informational content.

title: Laboratory Methods in Material Culture
description: Addresses artifacts as reflections of culture. Focuses on ethnoarchaeology and experimental archaeology, as well as the integration of research design, recovery, identification and laboratory analysis of artifacts from archaeological sites. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, 103.

title: Special Topics in Native American Cultures
description: Detailed analysis of selected contemporary issues facing American Indiansfor example, religious freedom, property nghtsor a focus on the Indian cultures of a particular area, such as the Southwest, Great Lakes, or Northeast. May be repeated for different topics. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: North American Indians
description: Cultures of the North American Indians emphasizing their economic, socio­political, ana religious institutions.

title: Indians of the Great Lakes
description: In­depth study of selected Native American cultures indigenous to the Great Lakes region from the time of European contact to the contemporary period. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Native American Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Midwestern Archaeology
description: Archaeological development of the Midwest traced through the Paleo­Indian, Archaic, Intermediate, Woodland, and Mississippian stages. Prerequisite: ANTH 103.

title: Anthropology and Women
description: Development of the female phenotype; variation in the roles assigned to women in cultures of differing levels of complexity from gathererhunters to industrial societiesboth Western and non-Westernand the contributions of women anthropologists to understanding this variation · Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Women's Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Anthropology of American Culture
description: Examines how the values, beliefs, and norms of American culture are integrated into and symbolized in various media. Explores how we experience and resolve cultural tensions between individualism and community, equality and hierarchy, competition and cooperation

title: Historical Archaeology
description: Covers the major themes and philosophies of the archaeology of post-Columbian America as well as related literature and sources of information on architectural features and items of material culture likely to be encountered in the course of excavation Prerequisite: ANTH 103, permission of the instructor. Anthropology 231

title: Special Topics in Anthropology
description: Detailed analysis of a special problem in cultural anthropofogy, archaeology, linguistics, or physical anthropology. May be repeated for different topics. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: European Prehistory
description: Prehistory of Europe from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age with an emphasis on the regions north and west of the Classical world. Prerequisite: ANTH 103 or permission of the instructor.

title: Paid Internship in Anthropology
description: Paid, supervised field or laboratory experience in anthropology. Employment should supply an opportunity to use and further knowledge of anthropology. Prer~uisite: permission of the internship director. Open only to anthropology majors or minors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Topics in Old World Ethnography
description: Anthropological survey of the cultural patterns of selected continents or regions, such as East Asia, Europe, or the island Pacific. Prerequisite: ANTH 101. I 377 Topics in Museum Operations. (3) Introduces various aspects of museum operations, such as organization, financing, curation, exhibits, public interpretation, and conservation of collections. Emphasizes ethnographic and archaeolo~ical collections. May be repeated for different topics.

title: Topics in New World Ethnography
description: Anthropological survey of the cultural patterns of selected continents or regions, such as the Caribbean or Latin America. Prerequisite: ANTH 101. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Anthropology
description: Exploration of major issues in moCiern anthropology. Emphasizes individual study and development of results. Open only to Honors College students by J?E!rmission of the department chairperson.

title: History of Archaeology
description: Developme nt of archaeological thought over the past two centuries focusing on major figures and their contributions. Prerequisite: ANTH 103.

title: Human Osteology
description: Laboratory dealin~ with the human skeleton includmg identification of whole and fragmentary bones and the assessment of the age, stature, sex, and race of a skeleton as applied to paleodemography, paleopathology, and forensic problems. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Medical Anthropology
description: Focuses on conceptions of health and illness from a crosscultural perspective relating non-Western techniques to Western counterparts. Prerequisite: ANTH 101.

title: Contemporary Problems of the American Indians
description: Detailed study of current issues facing Native Americans. Particular issues facing tribes in specific regions and general issues of a pan­Indian nature will be covered. Taught in the field with seminars led by Native Americans. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor.

title: Anthropological Field Studies
description: Methods of field research in ethnography, archaeology, or physical anthropology. Stresses problem formufation, observation, data handling, and interpretation. Taught at various field locations. May be repeated for different topics. Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Witchcraft, Magic, and Religion
description: Anthropological study of humankind's ageold concern with life, death, sickness, and the unknown. Discusses human attempts to control life through supernatural beings, prayer, sacrifice, and techniques of magic and witchcraft.

title: Primatology
description: Comparative survey of nonhuman primates, their biology and behavior. Prerequisite: ANTH 105 or 206 or permission of the instructor.

title: Archaeological Resources Management
description: Special problems of contract, conservation, and public archaeology, including laws and regulations, relations with government agencies, research design and methodology for reconnaissance and test excavations, site interpretation, and predictive modeling. · Prerequisite: ANTH 204, permission of the instructor.

title: Quantitative. and Qualitative Ethnographic Methods
description: Develops the ability to conduct and comprehend ethnographic research. Includes research design, data collection, analysis, reporting, basic statistics, and computer use. Emphasizes both quantitative and qualitative techniques for basic and applied research. Prerequisite: 15 hours ANTH or permission of the instructor.

title: Peoples of Southeast Asia
description: A general ethnographic survey of island and mainland Southeast Asia. Specific emphasis is on cultural contrasts between rural and urban communities. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Asian Studies minors) or permission of the instructor.

title: Culture Change
description: Surveys the major concepts and processes of culture change, witn an emphasis on the causes of change and their effects on individuals and groups. Prerequisite: ANTH 101, permission of the instructor.

title: Ethnohistory
description: Methods and techniques of ethnohistory using information on traditional ethnographic groups, particularly in the Americas. Prerequisite: ANTI-I 101 (waived for Native American Studies minors), permission of the instructor.

title: Unpaid Internship
description: Unpaid field or laboratory experience that uses knowledge of anthropology in a specific project or work context. Prer~uisite: permission of the internship director. Open only to anthropology majors or minors. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Economic Anthropolo~
description: Concerned with a substantive (as opposed to formal) view of allocation, conversion, and distribution of resources. Emphasizes economic development m third and fourth world countnes. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 or 111 or permission of the instructor.

title: Indians of the American Southwest
description: Surveys prehistoric, historic, and contemporary cultures of selected Southwest Indian groups. Emphasizes culturespecific solutions to problems perceived in their relationship to their natural and social environments. Prerequisite: ANTH 101 (waived for Native American Studies minors), permission of the instructor. 490IndependentStudyin Anthropology. (1-3) Topics to be chosen and investigated in consultation with an instructor with competence in the area involved. Biology 233 A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term.

title: Senior Seminar in Anthropology
description: Inte~tes knowledge of current theorehcal and methodological issues in the four quadrants of anthropology. A setting for students to explore their own theoretical interests and present them coherently. Open only to seniors. ~BIOLOGY~ C. Preprofessional majors add selected courses to meet entrance requirements into medical, dental, and medical technology schools. A teaching major in science with biology as a primary or supporting area and a teaching minor in biology are offered for students who plan to teach in the secondary schools. (Additional course requirements for science teaching programs appear in this catalog under the listing, Interdepartmental Programs, College of Sciences and Humanities.) In addition to the major requirements, students who want to become candidates for the National Registry of Microbiologists (ASM) should complete the following recommended electives: BIO 344, 452; CHEM 225, 231; and ZOOL 347. title: People and the Life Sciences
description: Introductory course designed for students not majoring in science. Emphasizes human and social aspects of bioiow: reproduction, development, genetic counseling, immunology, evolution, biodiversity, ecology, and environmental concerns. Not open to students who have credit in BIO 10'2,111, or 112.

title: Biological Concepts for Teachers
description: Principles of biology as they relate to energy requirements and reproductive processes of living organisms, including the study of plants and conservation with emphasis on the human role in the environment. Designed primarily for , students in elementary education programs.

title: Principles of Biology 1
description: Designed for biology, allied health, and other science majors. Emphasis at cellular level: chemical and physical organization of life, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell structure and function, bioenergetics, cell division, genetics, gene expression, protein synthesis, and evolution. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: one year of high school chemistry, one semester of college chemistry, or the equivalent.

title: Principles of Biology 2
description: Emphasis at organism, population, and community levels: major plant and animal phyla with emphasis on structure, function, classification, and phylogenetic relationships; ecology, including human ecology and environmental biology. Lecture and laboratory.

title: Microbiology for the Health Sciences
description: Introductory course for students in applied health curricula. Presents biomolecules of life, enzyme interaction, physiology and structure of representative microor~nisms. Emphasizes bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa of health significance and the hostparasite relationship. Microbiolo­gical techniques will be emphasized in laboratory. Prerequisite: CHEM 101 or its equivalent.

title: Microbiology
description: Microorganisms including representative bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and fungi. Emphasizes morphology, physiology, genetics, and control. Some consideration of applied microbiolo$Y.. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 111.

title: Genetics
description: Basic principles of heredity and variation emphasizing meiosis, Mendelian inheritance and probability considerations, sex and gene transmission and expression, linkage and crossingover, the nature of the hereditary material, gene action, and genetic control of development. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 .

title: Cell Biology
description: An introduction to the biolo~ of the cell, including cell differentiation and growth, the nature of the organization of the cell, basic bioenergetics and enzyme function, cell environment, membrane structure and function, cell metabolism, and the work performed by cells. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; CHEM 231 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ecology
description: Effects of physical and biotic conditions on the distribution and abundante of plants and animals. Dynamics of ecological systems are examined at the population, community, and ecosystem levels, and from an evolutionary perspective. Emphasizes practical applications. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112.

title: Human Genetics for Special Education
description: Designed for special education majors to foster understanding human inheritance implications in their chosen career. Develops genetic literacy using many instructional techniques. In addition, the social implications of genetic knowledge will be explored. Open only to special education majors and dual majors m special education and elementary education. Not open to students who have credit in BI0453. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics; (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Problems of Life Systems
description: Examines evolutionary solutions to problems of survival and reproduction faced by all organisms. Problems are investigated from a common basis rather than a taxonomical approach. Physiological processes are emphasized, including the selective pressures involved in the evolution of these mechanisms. Prerequisite: completion of all other core requirements for biology majors.

title: Pathogenic Bacteriology
description: Study of pathogenic bacteria with emphasis on morphology and physiology. Laboratory techniques for cufturing, isolating, and identifying bacteria. Prerequisite: BIO 113 or 213; CHEM 231.

title: Immunology-Virology
description: Examination of the basic principles of immunology and virology. Topics include the immune system, the variety of immune responses, immuno­regulation, and characteristics of viruses. Emphasizes virushost interactions and serological diagnosis of viral infections. Prer9uisite: 1310 213 and one course in organic chemistry. Biology 239

title: Internship in Biology
description: Paid, supervised field and laboratory experiences in public or private agencies (or in the Department of Biology). Training involves application of biolo­gical principles in the work environment. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Honors Colloquium in Biology
description: Exploration of selected issues in biology with emphasis upon individual projects, study, and discussion. Open only to honors students except by eermission of the department chairperson. A total of 2 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Practicum in Biology
description: Practical application of biology in a variety of situations includingbiology instruction as undergraduate teaching assistants and discussion leaders, and practical experience in government or industrial laboratories and field stations. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Developments in Modem Biology
description: Stresses recent discoveries in biology and integrates and enhances understanding of the basic principles of the discipline. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Population Ecology
description: Presents fundamental principles of population growth and regulation, including both withinspecies and betweenspecies interactions. Implications for over­population, endangered species, and pest and game management are discussed. Laboratory includes both experimental studies and computer simulation exercises. Prerequisite: BIO 216.

title: Community and Ecosystem Ecolo~y
description: Principles of ecological organization at the community and ecosystems levels. Emphasizes the processes that influence the structure and function of communities and ecosystems. Laboratory includes field and lab studies of plant and animal systems. Prerequisite: BIO 216.

title: Field Biology of Distant Areas
description: Includes study of the sciences peculiar to selected geographic areas. Ecology, flora, and fauna. Travel may be by air. Seminars may be scheduled regularly throughout the course. Registration fee may include travel charges as well as the general fee. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 12 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Evolution
description: Principles, evidence, and the historical context of modern evolution theory. Some attention will be given to the origin of life and the evolution of plants and animals. Prerequisite: BIO 100, 102, or 111 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Applied Microbiology
description: The study of microor~anisms that are beneficial or detnmental to changes in foods (including milk and milk products) and industrial fermentations. This is a lecture and laboratory course. Prerequisite: BIO 213 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Biometry
description: Principles and application of statistics to biological problems. The use of parametric and nonparametric tests of significance in the anafysis of data and the interpretation of experiments. Prerequisite: MATHS 108 or its equivalent or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Genetics
description: Bacterial and eukaryotic genetics with emphasis on recent developments in molecular genetics. Tofics include alternative structures o DNA, mechanisms of DNA replication, mutagenesis, DNA rearran~ements, regulation of gene expression, RNA processing, and molecular and mutagenetic analysis of cell cycle. Prerequisite: BIO 214; CHEM 231. Prerequisite recommended: BIO 215.

title: Human Genetics and the Problems of Humanity
description: Current problems in human heredity. Human cbromosome aberrations. DNA, the genetic code, and mutations. Consanguineous marriages and genetic defects. Mendelian prin­ciples applied to humans. Pedigrees and probability. Genetic screening and counseling. Social, ethical, and legal problems and advances in genetics.

title: Molecufor Biology
description: Structure and function of macromolecules in living things. Emphasizes three­dimensional structures; models for enzyme mechanisms; DNA replication; protein synthesis and membrane func­tion; and applications of biotechnology. Prerequ1s1te: BIO 215 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Advanced Cellular and Molecular Biology
description: Study of recent develop­ments in cell growth and differentiation, DNA and RNA research, membrane biology, cellular and molecular evolution, and cellular control mechanisms. Prerequisite: BIO 457 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Bioenergetics
description: The study of flow of energy in biolo~ical systems with emphasis on application of Jaws of thermodynamics to biological processes, energy production metabolism in chemotrophs and phototrophs, and the major uses of energy in biological systems. Prerequisite: BIO 215, its equivalent, or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Microtechniques
description: A lecture and laboratory course in the preparation of biolo~ical material for microscopic exarrunation in teaching, research, and clinical applications. Emphasizes preparation of smears, squashes, whole mounts, paraffin and frozen plant and animal sections, and photomicrography. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112, 213, and one course of college chemistry.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Recent advances and theories in early embryogenesis and developmental biology. Major emphasis on genetic and molecular mechanisms operating during developmental phenomena. Topics include fertilization, mosaic versus regulative development, regulation of gene expression, patterning, germ line and sex determination, and neoplasia. Prerequisite: BIO 215 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Limnology
description: The physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of inland waters. Laboratory and several field trips will be devoted to exrloring techniques for the evaluation o representative aquatic ecosystems. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Microbiology
description: Micro­organisms indigenous to nonpolluted aoo polluted aquatic ecosystems. Emphasizes nutrient cycling and use of microorganisms as indicators of pollution. Morphology, physiology, and ecology of specific organisms. Lecture and laboratory. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Marine Biology
description: Introduction to marine environments. Properties of seawater, hydrodynamics. Phyto­plankton and benthic plants. Primary production, nutrient cycles. Marine animals, surveys of major taxa. Adaptations for life on the bottom, open water, intertidal zones, estuaries, abyssal regions.

title: Bioethical Decision Making
description: Development of decisionmaking skills through the analysis and personal resolution of bioethical problems created by the application of new biological and biomedical knowledge and technologies. Prerequisite: junior standing and completion of the University Core Curriculum science component or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Research Techniques in Laboratory Biology
description: Laboratory principles and applications in cell and molecular biology and microbiology. Includes experimental design, analyses of journal articles, research proposal development and presentation, restriction mapping, clonmg, transformation, electrophoretic separations and analyses, bacteria and bacteriophage growth, and DNA fingerpnnting. Prerequisite: BIO 215 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: Designed to give undergraduate biology students with special aptitude an opportunity to participate in scientific investigation. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. · A total of 3 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Forestry
description: General course in forestry with emphasis on forest policy, ecology, and management. Current issues are discussed with particular reference to their social, political, and environmental implications. Lecture and laboratory. Biology 241

title: Taxonomy of Vascular Plants
description: Identification, use, and care of native and ornamental trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plant material. The use of botanical keys, manuals, and texts in the identification of the plant taxa. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Economic Botany
description: The cultivation, processing, environmental requirements, and use of plants and plant derivatives for food, drugs, dwellmgs, clothing, and power.

title: Plant Propagation and Management
description: Practical experience in the different methods of plant propagation, care, and cultivation for use in the home, school, garden, and greenhouse. Also, some emphasis on diseases, pathogens, and pests of the plant.

title: Medical Mycology
description: Study of fungi with emphasis on patho~enic forms. Discusses methods for identifi­cation of fun19 along with morphology and biochemistry of fungi. Prerequisite: BIO 213.

title: Plant Physiology
description: An introduc­tory treatment of the physiological activities of green plants with emphasis on plant growth substances, photo­synthesis, and intermediate metabolism Prerequisite: BIO 112 and CHEM 231.

title: Plants and Their Allies
description: Evolutionaryphylogenetic survey of plant forms. Includes bacteria, algae, fungi, bryophytes, and vascular plants. Emphasizes comparative morphology ancf anatomy, reproductive structures, cycles, and adaptations to varying habitats. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112, or permis­sion of the instructor,

title: Dendrology
description: The identification and site characterization of woody plants with an emphasis on midwestem tree species. Use of botanical features and keys in field identification. Correlation of species with site conditions, plant diseases, climatic parameters, associate species, and geographical distribution. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Plant Ecology
description: Factors affecting the distribution and abundance of plants. Patterns, structure, and development of plants at the individual, population, and community level. Laboratory provides expenence with ecological experimentation at the physiolo~cal, population, and commuruty levels. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of the instructor.

title: Aquatic Botany
description: The collection and identification of nonvascular and vascular plants from fresh water ecosys­tems. Emphasizes the morphology, physiology, and ecology of these plants to explain their distribution in nature. Class project and field trips may be used to demonstrate ecolo&ical relationships. Two Saturday field trips required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Urinalysis
description: A study of basic renal anatomy, physiolo~, and pathology, as well as training in the preparation of patients and collection of urine samples, conduct of routine and special tests of urine, and identification of the various formed elements in urine sediment. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Serology
description: Principles of · · immunology. Histology and biochemistry of the immune system Theory and practice of the detection of antibodies and other serum substances related to disease conditions using various diagnostic procedures. Prerequisite: BIO 344. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Microbiology
description: Study of pathogenic organisms (bacteria, myco­bacteria, fungi, and animal parasites), emphasizing isolation, culture, identification, and antibiotic sensitivity. Experience in media preparation, staming techniques, and various biochemical and serological tests for identification and sensitivity. Prerequisite: BIO 341, 344. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Blood Bank
description: Theory and practice of blood bank or~anization and procedure. Genetics and immunology of blood group systems; selection of donors; collection, processing, and storage of blood; preparation of blood products; typing, compatibility, and pretransfusion tests. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Radioimmunoassay
description: Theory and practice of the use of radiolabeled substances in the detection of hormones, antigens, antibodies, drugs, and other clinically important molecules in blood and other body fluids. Experience in such related techniques as immuno­fluorescence and enzyme immunoassay. Prerequisite: BIO 344. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Medical Chemistry
description: Theory and application of physiology, biochemistry, and organic chemistry in the laboratory diagnosis of abnormal metabolism. Experience with a variety of manual and automated test procedures, including preparation of patient samples, instrument calibration and maintenance, and quality control. Prerequisite: CHEM 360. Open only to medical technology students in the clinical year. A total of 10 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Structure and Development of Vertebrates
description: Comparative study of the anatomy, development, and evolutionary relationships of vertebrates. Lecture and laboratory. · Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Animal Parasitology
description: Helminth, protozoan, and arthropod parasites of animals and humans. Emphasizes identification, life cycles, hostparasite relationships, and physiology of common species. Some emphasis on medical and clinical aspects of parasites in humans, and tropical forms. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112, or permis­sion of the department chairperson.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
description: Compara­tive morphology, physiology, ecology, life histories, and phylogeny of invertebrate animal phyla. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ornithology
description: The study of birds including identification, systematics, anatomy, physiology, life histories, ecological relationships, and conser­vation. Field work in addition to regular laboratory periods may be required. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Entomology
description: Anatomy, physiology, taxonomy, life histories, habits, and adaptations of insects. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Ichthyology
description: The study of fish with emphasis on identification, classi­fication, anatomy and physiology, and ecology. Emphasizes Indiana species, but other important species will be included. Prerequisite: BIO 111 and 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Herpetology
description: Introduction to the biology of amphibians and reptiles, incluaing their origin, anatomy, physiology, classification, behavior, and ecology. Through extensive field trir,s, the laboratory will emphasize identifi­cation and observation of amphibians and reptiles in their natural habitats. Prerequisite: BIO 112.

title: Mammalogy
description: The evolutionary origin, characteristics, and distribution of recent mammals. The economic relationships of mammals. The collection and preservation of specimens. May require additional field work. Prerequisite: BIO 112 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Wildlife Biology
description: The identi­fication, population dynamics, and geograpruc distribution of wildlife Biology 243 species with particular emphasis on those of the United States. The harvest and management of wildlife. May require additional field work. Prerequisite: BIO 216 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Aquatic Entomology
description: Immature and adult stages of aquatic insects, including collecting techniques, identi­fication, ecological requirements, morphology, and evolutionary adaptations to lentic and lotic conditions. Emphasizes aquatic insects as indicators of environmental quality and stress.

title: Teaching of Science in the Secondary and Junior High/Middle School
description: Philosophy and method­ology of science teaching. Emphasizes laboratory investigations, concepts and conceptual schemes, scienceoriented classroom management, evaluation of instructional activities, supplies, equipment, facilities, and curriculum materials. Experiences in public schools will be required. Prerequisite: EDSEC 380; 13 hours of science courses or.permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching Science in the Elementary School
description: Methods for teaching science concepts, skills, and attitudes are developed through classroom and clinical experiences. Special emphasis on makmg connections between science and other areas of the elementary curriculum Prerequisite: 8 hours of science or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Teaching Science in the Early and Primary Grades
description: Analysis of the cognitive, psychomotor, and affective processes inherent in science investigations for young children. Classroom and clinical experience using handson activities with science materials ar.propriate for preschool and primary children. Designed for Early Childhood education programs. Prerequisite: 8 hours of science or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Science as Inquiry
description: An integrated look at the scientific enterprise and the investigative process that drives it. Focuses on the development and use of cognitive and manipulative skills used to think scientifically about matters of personal interest in everyday life. Prerequisite: GEOG 101 or GEOL 101; BIO 102; PHYCS 101; permission of the instructor. Open only to elementary education majors with the science concentration. ~CHEMISTRY~ L. Fuelling, Chairperson Computer science is concerned with creating appropriate computational models for problems along with techniques for solving them using computers. Computer science should not be confused with computer programming. Programming is one of the tools of computer science in much the same way that arithmetic and algebra are tools of mathematics. Because computers solve problems from a wide range of disciplines, it is important for computer science majors to be broadly educated and to have good analytic(ll and communication skills. To accommodate student interests, the department offers three distinct options within the major. A fourth option in cooperative education may be added to any of the others. • The science option offers students a disciplineapproved program emphasizing the importance of the scientific method. • The information systems option offers a computer science concentration and a management/economics background as the basis for a career in information systems. • The hardware systems option gives students interested in physics and electronics a strong background in the hard ware of computing. • A cooperative education option is available to all majors in computer science. Students may enter this program after completing two semesters (minimum of 30 credits) in which they have earned minimum cumulative gradepoint averages of 3.0 in the required computer science and mathematics courses and at least 2.5 in all courses. The cooperative education director in the Department of Computer Science advises students in this program and assists in work placement for each student; however, the university cannot guarantee work assignments for all students. The department also offers two minors: one for students majoring in other subjects who want a strong background in traditional computer science, and one for students who want to emphasize personal computer studies. Venugopal, Chairperson Geography is both a natural and social science of place and space that examines the linkages and interactions between human activities and/ or natural systems. Human geography is concerned with the spatial aspects of human existence, while physical geography examines the spatial processes governing the Earth's environment. Both human and physical geographers Geography 269 develop skills in cartography, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and interpretation of satellite images (Remote Sensing). To meet society's needs for greater geographic understanding in the twentyfirst century, the Department of Geography offers three distinct options within the major. • Option 1. General Geography. The comprehensive general geography option is attractive to liberal arts students seeking careers in education, government, and business at both the national and international level. The theories and methods in physical and human geography and information processing offer opportunities to move beyond entry­level positions in organizations that value knowledge concerning global and environmental issues. • Option 2. Travel and Tourism. The travel and tourism option gives interested students a broad knowledge of the travel and tourism industry. The analytical skills and practical experience gained through this option are beneficial for successful careers in the tourism industry. Students take a sequence of courses addressing spatial aspects of travel and interactions of tourists, businesses, governments, and communities. Majors selecting this option are encouraged to take minors in areas such as business, public relations, and/ or modem languages. • Option 3. Geographic Information Processing and Mapping . In recent years, the dramatic increase in data collection technologies has placed geography at the center of issues related to global change. In addition to field observations, data are collected electronically from space platforms such as aircraft and satellites (Remote Sensing) to provide urgently needed maps for timely decision making. A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a technology used to store, retrieve, and analyze large volumes spatial of data. Cartography as the science of mapped communication is fundamental to presenting the results of a GIS investigation. This option is a technical specialization selected by students interested in solving social and environmental problems through advanced computer technology. Samuelson, Chairperson Geologists study the earth, paying primary attention to its history, materials, and structure, and to the active processes that continue to change the landscape. Geologists are also concerned with investigating environmental problems such as geologic hazards involving flooding or earthquakes, evaluating groundwater resources, discovering new mineral and petroleum deposits, and studying the oceans, moon, and planets. The department offers two departmental majors in geology. The professional arts major is designed to prepare students for geological careers in industry, environmental consulting, and government agencies and for graduate study that leads to research, teaching, management, and many other positions in industry, government, and universities. The liberal arts major aims to broaden the intellectual horizons of students who have related interests, want to pursue double majors, or do not want to directly enter the geological profession. title: Cultural History of the "Celtic Peoples from Prehistory to the Present
description: Surveys the cultural history of the six modern Celtic countries (Brittany, Cornwall, Ireland, Isle of Man, Scotland, and Wales) and their ancient continental forebears, including major political events, literature, social organization, and traditional oral culture.

title: Irish History
description: Covers all of Irish history from pre-Christian Celtic times to the present, including political events, literature (both oral and written), the role of language, music, folklore, and other elements of Irish cultural history.

title: Tzarist Russia

title: The Soviet Union

title: History of South Asia
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of the subcontinent of South Asia, comprising India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka, from early times to the present. 4~9 History of Southeast Asia. title: History of China to 1600
description: Descriptive and analytical survey of China's history from earliest times to roughly A.D. 1600, with emphasis on the development of the dynastic tradition, Confucianbased society and culture, and China's focal point status in the pre- 1600 world order.

title: History of Premodem Japan
description: Analytical survey of premodern Japanese history to circa 1600, focusing on the ideological, political, social, economic, and cultural developments that build a foundation for the understanding of modern Japan.

title: Selected Topics in Non-Western History
description: Survey and investi~ation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in non-Western history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Topics will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

description: Descriptive and analytical survey with emphasis on China's changin& role as a member of the world commuruty, its response to increased Western contacts, disintegration of traditional order, revolutionary changes through the Republic of China and the People's Republic, and significant elements of contemporary Chinese society and culture.

title: Modem Japan, 1600 to the Present
description: Descriptive and analyticalsurvey of political and economic developments, foreign policy, and social and cultural change in modern Japan with emphasis on conditions contributing to its rapid modernization, nationalist and expansionist movements, and dynamic postwar recovery.

title: Selected Topics in European History
description: Survey and investigation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in European history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Topics will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Selected Topics in American History
description: Survey and investi~ation of a particular topic, problem, or issue in American history with emphasis on topics, specialties, and materials not covered in other courses. Topics will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

description: Theory and practice of teaching secondary school social stud_ies. Emphasizes methodology, materials, and specific application in the secondary classroom. description: Materials and methods for teachin~ social studies, grades 1-6. Emphasizes social science concepts, behavioral objectives, teaching strategies, learning resources, attitudes and values, skill aevelopment, and program assessment.

description: Directed study of special problems or research in social science education by individuals or groups of students. title: Reading and Honors
description: Juniors and seniors, with the approval of the mathematical sciences department, may enroll for special advanced work not offered in courses at the 300- and 400- levels. Prerequisite: approval of the department chairperson. . Open only to juniors and seniors. A total of 8 hours of credit may be earned. MODERN LANGUAGES AND CLASSICS W. D. Barnette, Chairperson The Department of Modern Languages and Classics offers programs in both ancient and modern foreign languages and works closely with other programs and departments to combine foreign language training with other subjects. Language laboratory practice, computer applications, interactive multimedia, opportunities for study abroad in the summer and for an academic semester or year, and foreign exchange programs enhance classroom instruction. The department offers foreign language training for students who want to acquire a broad liberal education; enrich preparation for a career; seek certification for teaching at the elementary or secondary level; travel, live or work abroad; or work as translators. Students may earn credit for previous language study through either national advanced placement tests or departmentally administered placement tests. Students must take these department placement tests in any language they studied before entering the university and intend to continue studying. These tests help determine the appropriate student class placement. Students who have completed more than one year of a foreign language in high school may not normally enroll for credit in the 101 level of that language, except in Chinese, German, and Japanese, or with permission of the chairperson. Students placed in any higherlevel course will receive credit for the courses they test out of by earning grades of C or higher in the course into which they are placed. In order to receive placement credit for 101, a student must have taken the placement test and have a record of the score on file. Native speakers who have completed high school studies in their native countries are not eligible for credit in the first or second year of their native languages. At the end of their last semester, senior majors in French, German, Japanese, and Spanish are expected to take a proficiency test for assessment of skills in six areas: reading, writing, listening, speaking, grammar, and culture. Senior majors in classical languages are expected to take a proficiency test to assess skills in three areas: translation, grammar, and culture. Resulting scores of high, middle, or low are available to faculty members for letters of recommendation. The modem language test is based on content, procedures, and norms published by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages and by the Educational Testing Services. Students should consult with foreign language faculty advisors about arranging courses to meet their needs. The 100- and 200-level courses in foreign languages are sequential and must be taken in order. Only work at the 200-level and above will apply toward any major or minor in the department, except in Chinese, Japanese, Greek, and classical culture, in which firstyear courses may be counted. Mortensen, Chairperson The Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Management prepares students for careers in environmental science and management of natural resources. The programs offered by the department are designed to give students a basic scientific and socioeconomic understanding of natural resources and their use. The department offers a major in natural resources and environmental management, a minor in natural resources, a minor in environmental management, and a teaching minor in conservation and environmental studies. The department also coordinates interdepartmental minors in energy and environmental policy. Students majoring in natural resources and environmental management choose one of the following options: natural resource studies, environmental interpretation and outdoor recreation management, environmental protection, land management, and occupational and industrial hygiene. All majors must complete a common core requirement. Many courses include laboratory work using sophisticated analytical equipment. Each year, students have opportunities for indepth twotofour­week field studies in the United States and other countries. Students are encouraged to participate in internships (professional practice) under the supervision of faculty members or professionals working in private con­sulting firms, governmental agencies, or environmental education centers. title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Health and Safety
description: Application of the roles of the health teacher in a school setting. Functions considered include needs assessment, program planning, direct instruction, and evaluation. Prerequisite: EDSEC 380 and identifi­cation to pursue a teaching curriculum

title: Workshop in Health Science
description: Critical contemporary issues in health science. May include consultants, guest lecturers, field trips, and group activities. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Sex Education and School Health
description: Development of an understanding of how to implement and teach a positive program of sex education that will help young people develop constructive attitudes, values, and practices based on sound knowledge in accordance with American Medical Association recommendations and pertinent state guidelines. Prerequisite: HSC 261 or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Patient Education: A Team Approach
description: Theories of client education and application of the education process to individuals and groups in healthcare settings. Emphasizes the multidisciplinary team concept in planning, imJ?lementing, and evaluating client education. Application of knowledge of growth and develop­ment in meeting learning needs of clients.

title: Alcohol Problems
description: A study of alcohol as a mood modifier; its use, nonuse, and abuse in drinking societies. Critical and controversial issues relevant to alcohol ingestion will be explored for medical, economic, legal, educational, historical, physiological, and public health implications.

title: Drug Dependence and Abuse
description: Analyzes the medical, psychological, sociological, and legal dimensions of dru~ use in the United States. Examines the mcidence and prevalence of drug abuse together with the roles played by the school and community in dealing with this health problem.

title: Consumer Health Issues
description: Health services and consumer protection organizations. Analysis of fraudulent health practices and nostrums, available health care systems, and health products.

title: Health and Aging
description: Dynamics of later life and the aging process with specific emphasis on health. The physiolo~ical and behavioral dimensions of the agmg process will be analyzed and discussed.

title: Death and Dying
description: Analyzes the relationship between death and health with emphasis on the fhysiological, medical, psychologica , legal, and consumer aspects of dying in contemporary America. Investigates problems that relate to the meaning of death, care for the dying, death ritual, bereavement, and death education. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or by permis­sion of the department chairperson.

title: Women and Health
description: General overview of issues related to women and health: health needs of working women, special nutritional concerns, the gynecological exam, reproductive anatomy and physiology, fertility and infertility, breast problems, wife abuse, and rape.

title: Practical Experience
description: Intern -assignment to an approved health agency or educational institution for a period of time commensurate with academic credit. Periodic and terminal reports to an academic advisor and to the agency administrator are required for this nonpaid experience. Prerequisite: HSC 386 (waived for nonmajors with a minor in environmental health), permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Environmental Health
description: Physical environment and its relationship to causes of disease. Review of environ­mental health problems and their solutions. Areas of study include air and water pollution, milk and food sanitation, disposal of human excreta and waste, radiological agents in the environment, and occupational health problems.

title: Special Studies in Health Science
description: Designed to give undergraduate health science students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation individually. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned. ANATOMY (ANATI

title: Fundamentals of Mammalian Anatomy
description: Basic study of mammalian anatomy with detailed dissection of an animal or animal tissue and examination of representative microscopic structure. Includes use of animals or animal tissue. Prerequisite: HSC 160 or another biological science course. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Human Embryology
description: Normal development of the human organism including germ cell formation, fertili­zation, implantation, and organ formation. Consideration of embryonic environment, physiology, and abnormal development. Prerequisite: BIO 111, 112; or ANAT 201.

title: Human Neuroanatomy
description: Offers strong background in the basic structural and functional relations of the central nervous system. Emphasizes understanding the location of nerve cell centers and the fiber tracts entering and leaving these centers. Two twohour laboratory periods weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or ZOOL 330. Prerequisite recommended: ANAT 320 and 430.

title: Histology
description: Microscopic structure of organisms with special emphasis on the tissues of vertebrates. Introductory microtechnique. Three lectures and one laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201 or ZOOL 330.

title: Essentials of Human Physiology
description: Basic human physiology emphasizing the major function of each organ system including effects of nutrition, drugs, and drug abuse. Intended primarily for science teaching majors and minors in secondary education. Includes laboratory exercises designed to demonstrate physiological principles to high school students. Includes use of animals or animal tissue. Prerequisite: BIO 102 or 111. Not upen to students who have credit in PHYSL 210. ·

title: Fundamentals of Human Physiology
description: Physiological funda­mentals as applied to human body systems with selected laboratory exercises to establish background for students entering the fields of radiology, nuclear medicine, and respiratory therapy. Includes use of animals or animal tissue. Prerequisite: CHEM 101 or permission of the department chairperson. Not upen to students in nursing or teacher education.

title: Human Physiology 1
description: Vital processes with references to human functional biology. Group experi­mentation with recording apparatus. Includes use of animals or animal tissue. Prerequisite: a course in biological science or permission of the department chairperson.

title: Human Physiology 2
description: Continuation of PHYSL 210. Functions of the human organ systems. Comparisons between vertebrate systems and mechanisms in humans. Includes use of animals or animal tissue. Prerequisite: PHYSL 210. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned.

title: Endocrinology
description: Endocrine functions in humans and mammals with special emphasis on mechanisms. Normal hormone regulation and pathophysiological principles. Laboratory experience with small­mammal surgery and endocrine testing. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerequisite: ANAT 201; PHYSL 210 and 211; one year of general chemistry. Physiology and Health Science 335

title: Renal Physiology
description: A detailed study of the urinary system and excretory functions. Emphasizes human physiology but also includes comparative vertebrate systems. Laboratory study includes gross, microscopic anatomy, and small mammal surgery. One three­hour laboratory a week. Prerl!liuisite: one course each in inorganic chemistry, anatomy, and physiology.

title: Cardiovascular Physiology
description: A study of the dynamics of the human cardiovascular system, stressing applications of basic physical principles and the operation of physical regulatory systems. Includes seminarstyle discussion of recent literature. Prerl!liuisite: one course in physiology and one course in physics.

title: Physiology of Aging
description: Study of how physiological systems change with age and the mechanisms that are thought to cause these changes. Disorders and diseases of aging will also be covered. Prerl!liuisite: one course each in inorganic chemistry and physiology.

title: Human Toxicology
description: A survey of chemical, physical, zoological, and botanical toxicoses in human health. The implications and methodology of dealing with hazardous substances and poisons will be considered in detail. Prerl!liuisite: CHEM 101 or 111 and 112; one year of biology or physiology or combination of both; or permission of the instructor.

title: Neuroscience
description: Introductory study of the organization and function of the nervous system Emphasizes integration of the structure and function of the nervous system .Prerl!liuisite: one year of chemistry; one year of biology or physiology.

title: Pathophysiology
description: The physiologic pathology of selected disease processes and dysfunctions. The pathogenesis of certain derangements with broad applicability. Underlying chemical, biological, and physical mechanisms will be studied. Laboratory experience will include demonstrations, specimen study, and visitations. One threehour laboratory period weekly. Prerl!liuisite: a course in anatomy, physiology, and chemistry.

title: Research Techniques in Physiology
description: Introduction to experimental design, laboratory techniques, and data analysis and interpretation in anatomy and physiology. Laboratory will include methods employing animal prepara­tions, modem cellular I molecular techniques, and general histological procedures. Introduction to computer data acquisition and analysis. Prerequisite: one course in physiology or permission of the instructor. Prerequisite recommended: CHEM 360 or463.

title: Special Studies in Physiology
description: Designed to give undergraduate physiology students who exhibit special aptitude and interest an opportunity to pursue special lines of scientific investigation on an individual basis. Experimental work, wide reading, and development of research techniques or skills. Prerequisite: permission of the department chairperson. A total of 6 hours of credit may be earned, but no more than 3 in any one semester or term. ALLIED HEAL 1H SCIENCE (AHSC)

title: Introduction to Patient Care
description: An introduction to the hospital setting and patient care. Instruction in nursing skills and basic medical technology. Prerequisite: admissiqn to an associate degree program in one of the allied health science options. Open only to allied health science students.

title: Cardiopulmonary Medicine
description: An indepth study of cardiopulmonary diseases. Topics include an extensive study of pharmacology; acute, chronic, and congenital cardiopulmonary diseases; and thoracic trauma. Prerequisite: CHEM 101. Open only to respiratory therapy students.

title: General Pathology
description: Designed to give respiratory therapy students an overview of human pathology. Open only to respiratory therapy students.

title: Pulmonary Function
description: Classroom and laboratory study of the measure­ment and interpretation of lung volumes and mechanics, diffusion and exercise physiology. Labs include basic spirometry, flowvolume loops, and plethysmography. Student must have completed all fall semester respiratory courses. Open only to respiratory therapy students.

title: Basic Clinical Practice
description: Gives students the opportunity to practice clinical skills in oxygen therapy, aerosol and humidity therapy, various . respiratory treatments, and broncho­pulmonary hrgiene. Students must have completed al fall semester respiratory therapy courses and must take all spring semester respiratory therapy courses concurrently. Open only to respiratory therapy students.

title: Pediatric Respiratory Care
description: Designed to provide students with the necessary knowledge for pediatric and neonatal respiratory care. Indepth presentation of oxy~en therapy, mechanical ventilation, resuscitation, and treatment modalities. Prerequisite: students must have completed all fall semester respiratory therapy courses. Open only to respiratory therapy students.

title: Advanced Clinical Practice
description: Gives students the opportunity to practice clinical skills m adult, pediatric, and neonatal critical care. Also includes experience in pulmonary functions, pulmonary rehabilitation, and home care. Skills learned in AHSC 208 will be reinforced. Prerequisite: students must have completed all spring semester respiratory therapy courses. Open only to respiratory therapy students.

title: Radiographic Procedures 1
description: A comprehensive study of skeletal radiographic positioning procedures; introduction to radiography, radio­graphic terminology, procedural orientation, and an indepth description of human structure and function. Prerequisite: ANAT 201; PHYSL 207. Parallel: AHSC 231. Open only to radiography students.

title: Radiographic Procedures 2
description: Continuation of AHSC 224, including skeletal radiographic positioning procedures and the study of special exams of all systems performed with and without contrast materials. Includes contrast materials, reactions, and patient care. Prerequisite: AHSC 224, 231. Parallel: AHSC 232. Open only to radiography students.

title: Radio~raphic Procedures 3
description: Continuation of AHSC 225, including additional special procedures and the equipment used for advanced imaging teclutlques. Introduction to computer literacy, computerized imaging techniques, and crosssectional anatomy. Prerequisite: AHSC 225, 232. Parallel: AHSC 233. Open only to radiography students.

title: Principles of Radiography 2
description: Study of radiographic film and processing, including exposure factors and their effects and special equipment used to perform diagnostic procedures. Prerequisite: APHYS 228. Open only to radiography students.

title: Radiographic Patholo~y
description: Study of clinical diseases and their effects on radiographs including technical adjust­ments, film evaluation, and quality control. Prerequisite: AHSC 229. Open only to radiography students.

title: Clinical Applications 1
description: Directed learning experiences in radiographic clinical procedures through a rotational system including an introduction to routine radiography, file room, office, darkroom, and reading room procedures. Parallel: AHSC 224. Open only to radiograp.hy students.

title: Clinical Applications 2
description: Directed learning experiences in radiographic clinical procedures through a rotational system including routine radiography and rotations through an outside affiliate. Offers the opportunity to master procedures practiced in previous semesters. Prerequisite: AHSC 224, 231. Parallel: AHSC 225. Open only to radiography students.

title: Clinical Applications 3
description: Directed learning experiences in radiographic clinical procedures through a rotational system including routine radiography, tomography, nuclear medicine, radiation therapy;ultrasound, mammography, and rotations through an outside affiliate. Offers the opportunity to master routine procedures. Prerequisite: AHSC 225, 232. Parallel: AHSC 226. Open only to radiography students.

title: Clinical Applications 4
description: Directed learning experiences in radiographic clinical procedures through a rotational system that includes computerized tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, vascular procedures, lithotripsy, and repeat rotations. Offers Physiology and Health Science 337 the opportunity to master procedures prachCed in previous semesters. Prerequisite: AHSC 226, 233. Open only to radiography students.

title: Special Topics in Radiography
description: Designed to give students the opportunity to receive academic credit for the completion of a scientific project. Prerequisite: permission of the program director. Open only to radiography students.

title: Clinical Internship 1
description: An orientation to nuclear medicine tech­nology. Emphasizes elementary patient care procedures and professional ethics. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in nuclear medicine. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Clinical Internship 2
description: Intro­duction to patient processing and nursing care in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: AHSC 240. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Clinical Internship 3
description: Directed learning experiences in special areas of the nuclear medicine clinic. Introduction to scintillation camera and rectilinear imaging, in addition to related instrumentation, hot lab procedures, and dose preparation and administration. Prerequisite: AHSC 241. · Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Clinical Internship 4
description: Directed learning experiences in nuclear medicine clinical procedures that include imaging, quality control of instrumentation, radiopharmaceuticals, and in vitro techniques. Prerequisite: AHSC 242. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Clinical Theory and Administration
description: Indepth study of the clinical theory of nuclear medicine technology as it applies to examinations performed in a nuclear medicine clinic. Introduces administrative and recordkeeping procedures required by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the operation of a nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: admission to a general arts associate degree program with electives in nuclear medicine. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Radiation, Biology, and Safety
description: Somatic and genetic effects of radiation and the procedures for radiological control and safety. Prerequisite: APHYS 247. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation
description: Study of the components and perfonnance characteristics of equip­ment, the mechanisms of detection and measurement of radioactive materials, and descriptive and inductive statistics used in the nuclear medicine clinic. Prerequisite: APHYS 247. Par11llel: AHSC 252. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation Lab
description: A weekly laboratory for nuclear medicine technology students enrolled in AHSC251. Par11llel: AHSC 251 Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: In Vitro Nuclear Medicine Procedures
description: An introduction to the basic principles of radioimmunoassay and in vitro nuclear medicine procedures. Prerequisite: AHSC 248 or APHYS 248. Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Topics in Nuclear Medicine
description: Desi~ned to offer students academic credit for the completion of a scientific project. P11r11llel: AHSC 243 Open only to nuclear medicine technology students.

title: Introduction to Paramedicine
description: Introduction to the role and responsi­bilities of the paramedic, with an emphasis on response management in the prehospital environment. Topics include EMS systems, medicolegal matters, communication and documen­tation, trauma management, psychiatric emergencies, stress management and crisis intervention, hazardous materials, and scene management. Prerequisite: admission to the paramedic program and permission of the department chairperson. P11r11llel: AHSC 261, 262, 263.

title: Pathophysiological Origins of Emergency Therapeutics
description: Comprehensive study of the physiology of human body organ systems as they relate to the provision of emergency medical care. Overview of common pathophysiological conditions encountered by the paramedic. Prerequisite: admission to the paramedic program and permission of the department chairperson. P11rllllel: AHSC 260, 262, 263.

title: Clinical Practice 1
description: Provides the opportunity to review basic lifesupport management and to practice communi­cations and patient rapport in a controlled clinical environment. Prerequisite: admission to the paramedic program and permission of the department chairperson. P11rllllel: AHSC 260, 261, 263.

title: Field Internship 1
description: Provides practice in and evaluation of basic life­support knowledge and skills, and practice in the operational management of prehospital advanced emergency care. Prerequisite: admission to the paramedic program and permission of the department chairperson. P11r11llel: AHSC 260, 261, 262.

title: Pharmacological Therapeutics and Treatment Modalities
description: Compre­hensive survey of drugs used in emergency medical care and overview of common home medications. Topics include pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, drug dosages, calculation, administration, terminology, and legal considerations. Prerequisite: AHSC 260, 261, and permission of the department chairperson. P11r11llel: AHSC 265, 266, 267.

title: Cardiopulmonary Pathophysiology and Therapeutics
description: Diseases, evaluation, and management of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. Management procedures include endotracheal and eso.Phageal intubation, blood gas interpretation, surgical airway mana~ement, EKG interpretation, and electrical and invasive therapeutic techniques. Prerequisite: AHSC 260, 261, and permission of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 264, 266, 267.

title: Clinical Practice 2
description: Provides the opportunity to practice clinical skills in emergency medicine and trauma center, clinical laboratory, surgery, and cardiovascular care. Prerequisite: AHSC 262 and permis­sion of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 264, 265, 267.

title: Field Internship 2
description: Opportunity to practice clinical skills and scene management in the prehospital environment. Prerequisite: AHSC 263 and permis­sion of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 264, 265, 266.

title: Medical and Environmental Emergencies
description: Pathophysiology and treatment of medical and environmental emergencies. Topics include neurological trauma and disease; bums, bites, and stings; substance abuse and toxicological emergencies; OB and gynecological emergencies; pediatrics; gerontology; and communicable diseases. Prerequisite: AHSC 264, 265, and permission of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 269, 271, 272.

title: Advanced Cardiac Life Support
description: Overview of the principles and practices of emergency cardiac care and cardio­pulmonary resuscitation as they relate to the standards of the American Heart Association. Includes case presentation and comprehensive oral, written, and practical examinations. Prerequi~ite: AHSC 264, 265, and permission of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 268, 271, 272.

title: Special Rescue Techniques
description: Introduction to specialized rescue techniques used m various prehospital situations. Labs include water survival, search and rescue, diving emergencies, treatment of hypothermia, cave rescue, rope rescue, and principles of patient extrication. · Prerequisite: AHSC 260 and permis­sion of the department chairperson.

title: Clinical Practice 3
description: Opportunity to practice clinical skills in emergency medicine and trauma center, laoor and delivery, pediatrics, geriatrics, and neurological critical care. Physiology and Health Science 339 Prerequisite: AHSC 266 and permis­sion of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 268, 269, 272.

title: Field Internship 3
description: Opportunity to practice clinical skills and scene management in the prehospital environment. Prerequisite: AHSC 267 and permis­sion of the department chairperson. Parallel: AHSC 268, 269, 271.

title: Orientation to Radiation
description: Introduces the equipment, procedures, and terminology of the radiation therapist. Presents material covering all phases, functions, and roles of the technologist. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Clinical Applications 1
description: Directed learning experiences in basic radiation therapy treatment procedures, equipment, patient care skills, and professional ethics. Parallel: APHYS 247; AHSC 200, 249. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Radiation Oncology Physics
description: Basic theory of radiation therapy physics coverin~ the fundamental concepts, properties, treatment applications, units, and terms relating to the role of the radiation therapist. Prerequisite: APHYS 247 or its equivalent. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Oncologic Pathology 1
description: Didactic experience studying the principles of clinical oncology, anatomy, and malignancies. Leaming experiences on the etiology, treatment, and prognosis of cancer. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Clinical Applications 2
description: Directed learning experiences in basic radiation therapy treatment procedures, equip­ment, planning, and patient interactions. Oneonone skills evaluation through rotation in various technical areas. Prerequisite: AHSC 281. Parallel: AHSC 285. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Technical Radiation Oncolo~ 1
description: Basic concepts in clinical applications of patient setups, treatment conditions, equipment, new procedures, quality assurance, and geometric considerations. Prerequisite: AHSC 281. Parallel: AHSC 284. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Oncologic Pathology 2
description: Didactic experience studying the principles of clinical oncology, anatomy, ano malignancies. Leaming experiences on the etiology, treatment, and prognosis of cancer. Prerequisite: AHSC 283. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Technical Radiation Oncology 2
description: Intermediate concepts in clinical applications of patient setups, treatment conditions, equipment, new procedures, qual!ty ass~rance, and geometric considerations. Prerequisite: AHSC 285. Parallel : AHSC 289. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Treatment Planning and Dosimetry
description: Didactic experience providing the basic concepts of clinical radiation oncology treatment planning and dosimetry. Study of fundamental procedures in dose determination, distribution, measurements, and calibration Prerequisite: AHSC 282. Parallel: AHSC 287. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Clinical Applications 3
description: Directed learning experiences in advanced radiation therapy treatment procedures, equipment, and planning patient interactions. Oneonone skills evaluation through rotation in various technical areas. Prerequisite: AHSC 288. Parallel: AHSC 282. Open only to radiation therapy students.

title: Clinical Applications 4
description: Directed learning experiences in advanced radiation therapy procedures, equipment, planning, patient care assessment by examination; oneonone skills evaluation by rotating through various technical areas. Prerequisite: AHSC 289. Open only to radiation therapy students. 299X Experimental/Developmental Topics. (3-6) Topics relevant to the discipline. Course titles will be announced before each semester.
